3d-printing-service.intro: 3D printing services produce parts and prototypes for hobbyists, engineers, product designers, small manufacturers, architects, and local businesses. Invoices usually cover print time, material used, design or file cleanup work, post-processing, and shipping. Many shops are one or two people running a fleet of FDM, resin, or sometimes SLS machines out of a garage or small studio.
3d-printing-service.pricingModel: Most shops price each part from a mix of material weight, machine time, labor, and a minimum order charge. A common approach is to calculate material cost by grams used (including supports and waste), add machine time at an hourly rate that covers printer depreciation, electricity, and maintenance, then add setup and post-processing labor. Many shops apply a minimum charge per order, often $15 to $40, because slicing, file checks, and bed setup take the same effort for one small part as a larger one. Design work, CAD modeling, and file repair are billed hourly or as a flat fee. Volume discounts for batch runs are common, and rush jobs usually carry a 25 to 100 percent surcharge. Specialty materials such as carbon fiber nylon, flexible TPU, or engineering resins are billed at higher per-gram rates. Prototyping clients often prefer a per-part price, while recurring production clients may agree on a per-unit price at fixed quantities.

rates.service: Resin printing (standard), including wash and cure
rates.unit: per mL of resin used or per part

rates.service: Engineering filament (nylon, ABS, ASA, carbon fiber blends)

items.description: FDM printing, PETG enclosure housings (qty 20), approx. 14 print hours total
PETG filament, black, including supports and purge
File repair and orientation changes for 2 STL files
Support removal and edge cleanup
Packaging and flat-rate shipping

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Parts printed from files supplied by client on 3/4; client approved dimensional sample on 3/6. Reprints for defects in printing are free if reported within 7 days of delivery. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Part name or file name for each line item
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often order several different parts, and matching invoice lines to the file names prevents confusion and disputes about what was printed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material type, color, and layer height or resolution
invoiceChecklist.why: Material and quality settings change both the price and the final result, so this documents what the client agreed to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity and unit price per part, or print hours and grams used
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing how the price was built makes it easier to justify and lets clients compare against future orders.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for design, file repair, and post-processing
invoiceChecklist.why: These are labor, not printing, and clients who only expected a print fee need to see where the extra charges came from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush fee, minimum order charge, or batch discount
invoiceChecklist.why: Surcharges and discounts should appear as their own lines so the client sees the agreed terms were applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping method, tracking number, or pickup date
invoiceChecklist.why: This confirms delivery and helps resolve any claim that a package never arrived or was damaged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, tangible printed parts are taxable, while some buyers such as manufacturers may be exempt with a valid certificate. Check your state's rules.

3d-printing-service.paymentTerms: Many 3D printing shops collect payment up front for small orders and use a deposit of 30 to 50 percent for larger jobs, custom design work, or expensive materials, with the balance due before shipping or on pickup. Established business clients are often given net 15 or net 30 terms, while individuals are usually asked to pay in full before work starts. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Card payments, ACH, and bank transfers are typical, and many shops also accept cash for local pickup. For production runs, some shops bill in installments by batch delivered.

tips.title: Charge for failed prints you did not cause
tips.body: If a client's file has thin walls, bad geometry, or unsupported overhangs and the print fails, state in your terms that failed attempts caused by file issues are billable. Without this, you absorb material and machine time for problems you did not create.

tips.title: Print a sample before a large run
tips.body: For batches of 20 or more parts, offer a billed single-part sample for fit and finish approval. It catches dimensional problems early and gives you a documented approval if the client later complains.

tips.title: Include supports and waste in material weight
tips.body: Slicer estimates often show model weight only. Bill the total including supports, rafts, skirts, and purge, or build a waste percentage into your per-gram rate, so material costs do not eat into your margin.

tips.title: Set a minimum order and enforce it
tips.body: Small one-off prints take about the same setup effort as larger jobs. A minimum charge keeps $4 orders from costing you an hour of your day.

tips.title: Put intellectual property terms in writing
tips.body: State that the client confirms they have the right to have the file printed. This protects you if a client sends a copyrighted or restricted design and a dispute follows.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the price of a 3D print?
faqs.answer: Add material cost (grams used including supports times your per-gram rate), machine time (print hours times your hourly machine rate), and labor for setup and post-processing. Then compare the total to your minimum order charge and use whichever is higher.

faqs.question: Should I charge for failed prints?
faqs.answer: Charge for failures caused by the client's file or requested settings, and absorb failures caused by your equipment or errors. Say this in your terms before work starts so the policy is clear.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on 3D printed parts?
faqs.answer: In many states, custom fabricated physical goods are taxable, but rules differ on custom work, resale, and shipping charges. Check with your state's revenue department, and keep resale or exemption certificates on file for tax-exempt buyers.

faqs.question: Can I charge a design fee separately from printing?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common. Bill CAD modeling, file repair, and design revisions hourly or as a flat fee on separate lines so clients can see the difference between design labor and production cost.

faqs.question: How should I invoice a recurring production client?
faqs.answer: Many shops invoice monthly with a line per part number, showing quantities delivered, unit price, and any purchase order number. Agree on a per-unit price at set quantity tiers so the invoice is simple to verify.

estimate.intro: A 3D printing quote is usually requested after a client sends a file or describes a part, and it needs to be sent before any printing begins. Clients tend to compare your price against online print services, other local shops, and the cost of buying a printer themselves. Your quote should explain what is included so it is not judged on price alone.

scopeChecklist.item: File names, versions, and dimensions of each part
scopeChecklist.why: Files change during a project, and listing the exact version quoted prevents arguments if a revised file affects print time or material.

scopeChecklist.item: Material, color, layer height, and infill
scopeChecklist.why: These settings drive cost and strength, and a client who expected a different material can dispute the result.

scopeChecklist.item: Quantity and what counts as a reprint
scopeChecklist.why: Specifying quantity and who pays for failed or rejected parts sets expectations before problems come up.
Support removal, sanding, priming, or painting can take more time than printing, so list which finishing steps are in the price.
FDM and resin printers have limits on dimensional accuracy. Stating realistic tolerances prevents complaints about parts that do not fit.
Lead time depends on your machine queue, so give a date or range and the cost to move faster.

scopeChecklist.item: Design, file repair, and revision limits
scopeChecklist.why: If the client's file needs work, state the hourly rate and how many revision rounds are included.

pricingTips.title: Price from the slicer, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Slice the file with your actual settings to get print time and material weight, then add 10 to 20 percent for supports, warping risk, and test adjustments. Quotes based on rough guesses tend to run under.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered quantity pricing
pricingTips.body: Show per-part prices at quantities such as 1, 10, and 50. Setup cost is spread across a batch, and clients often order more when they see the discount.

pricingTips.title: Quote file work separately
pricingTips.body: Break out design cleanup or CAD from print cost. Clients can then choose to fix the file themselves, and you are not discounting skilled labor to win the print.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Filament prices, machine availability, and your schedule change. A validity period of 14 to 30 days keeps old quotes from being used at stale prices.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For complex parts that need design review or test prints, many shops charge a quote or feasibility fee and credit it toward the order if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How accurate can my estimate be before printing?
faqs.answer: Slicer estimates are usually close for print time and weight, but supports, failed attempts, and post-processing can change the total. Quote a fixed price when scope is clear and use an estimate range when the file is uncertain.

faqs.question: What if the client changes the file after I send a quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that changes to geometry, material, or quantity require a revised quote. Re-slice the new file and send an updated price before printing.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: For large orders, custom materials, or design work, a 30 to 50 percent deposit is common. It covers material purchases and shows the client is committed before machines are tied up.

accounting.intro: Accounting businesses range from solo bookkeepers and enrolled agents to small CPA firms. They invoice small business owners, self-employed people, and households for bookkeeping, payroll, tax preparation, and advisory work. Billing usually mixes recurring monthly fees with one-time project and seasonal charges.
accounting.pricingModel: Most accounting work is priced either as a flat monthly fee for recurring services or as a flat fee per deliverable. Bookkeeping and payroll are usually monthly retainers based on transaction volume, number of accounts, and employee count. Tax returns are priced per return and per form or schedule, such as a Schedule C, rental schedule, or multi-state filing. Hourly billing is common for advisory, cleanup of past books, IRS notice response, and anything with an unclear scope. Many firms set a minimum engagement fee and charge extra for rush work, late or disorganized records, and added months of catch-up bookkeeping. Value-based or tiered packages are becoming more common for advisory and CFO-style services.

rates.service: Individual tax return (Form 1040 with itemized deductions)
Advisory, planning, or IRS notice response
Business formation and setup (chart of accounts, software setup)

items.description: Monthly bookkeeping, March (bank and credit card reconciliation, up to 150 transactions, monthly financial statements)
Payroll processing, March (2 employees, 2 semi-monthly runs)
Cleanup of prior year uncategorized transactions
Quarterly sales tax return preparation and filing
Advisory call: equipment purchase and depreciation options

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Monthly fees are billed on the first of each month. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days past due. Accepted by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring work like bookkeeping and payroll needs a clear month or quarter so the client can match it to their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables, not just 'accounting services'
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often split costs between business and personal, and a line like 'Form 1120-S and state return' supports a business deduction.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax year and form types
invoiceChecklist.why: Tax prep invoices should say which year and which returns or schedules were prepared, which prevents confusion when you handle amended or prior-year returns.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and hourly rate for time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Cleanup and advisory billing is easier to defend when it shows hours, rate, and a short description of the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line for add-ons and rush fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra schedules, late records, and expedited turnaround should be visible so clients see why the price differs from the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and filing fees
invoiceChecklist.why: E-file fees, state filing fees, and software or third-party payroll charges should be listed separately from your professional fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your credentials and firm details
invoiceChecklist.why: Include your name, firm, and, where relevant, PTIN or CPA license number as required by your state, so clients and their lenders can identify the preparer.

accounting.paymentTerms: Recurring bookkeeping and payroll are usually billed monthly in advance, often with automatic ACH or card payments. Tax returns are commonly billed with a deposit or retainer up front, with the balance due before the return is e-filed or released. Many firms hold the completed return until payment clears, though check your state board rules and engagement letter language. Net 15 is common for project work, and due on receipt is common for individual returns. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical when stated in the engagement letter. Accept ACH, check, and cards, and pass on card fees only where your state permits it.

tips.title: Use an engagement letter
tips.body: Define scope, fees, what the client must provide, and what is excluded. Most billing disputes in accounting trace back to unclear scope, especially around cleanup work and amended returns.

tips.title: Bill recurring work on a schedule
tips.body: Set monthly fees to invoice automatically on the same date each month. Collecting in advance keeps cash flow steady and gives you leverage if a client falls behind.

tips.title: Take a retainer before tax season work
tips.body: Collect a deposit or the full fee for individual returns before you start or before filing. Chasing payment after a return is filed is harder than holding it until payment arrives.

tips.title: Charge for disorganized records
tips.body: If a client delivers shoeboxes of receipts or months of unreconciled accounts, bill the extra time at your hourly rate. State this in your engagement letter so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Review fees annually
tips.body: Raise monthly fees each year, often 3-8%, and give 30 to 60 days notice. Clients whose volume has grown should be moved to a higher tier.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat fee for accounting services?
faqs.answer: Use flat or monthly fees for work with a predictable scope, like bookkeeping, payroll, and standard tax returns. Use hourly for cleanup, advisory work, and IRS notices where the amount of work is unclear. Many firms combine the two.

faqs.question: Can I hold a tax return until the client pays?
faqs.answer: In many cases yes, for work product you prepared, but rules vary by state and professional body. Clients are generally entitled to their own records and source documents. Put your policy in the engagement letter and check your state board of accountancy rules.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on accounting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Most states do not tax accounting or tax preparation services, but a few do tax some professional or bookkeeping services. Check with your state department of revenue.

faqs.question: How do I bill for work that goes over the quote?
faqs.answer: Refer back to your engagement letter. If the extra work is outside the original scope, send a written change notice with the added fee before you do it, then list it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for a tax return?
faqs.answer: Many preparers send it when the return is ready for review and require payment before e-filing. Others collect a deposit at intake and bill the balance at delivery. Either way, state the timing up front.

estimate.intro: Accounting clients usually ask for a quote before hiring, often comparing a few firms for bookkeeping, tax preparation, or a one-time cleanup. They compare fixed monthly fees, what is included, and how extra work is charged. A clear written quote helps you win the work and prevents fee disputes later.

scopeChecklist.why: List exactly what is included, such as monthly reconciliation, financial statements, a 1099 filing, or a specific tax form, so the client knows what they are paying for.
State the number of transactions, bank accounts, employees, or contractors the fee covers, and the extra rate if the client exceeds it.
Define whether you are catching up one year or three, and which tax years are included.
Specify what records, access, and answers the client must provide and by when. Late records can delay filings and justify extra charges.
Say what is not covered, such as audits, IRS notices, amended returns, or sales tax registration, and how those are billed.
Clarify who pays for accounting software, payroll platform fees, and filing fees.
State how long the price holds, the deposit required, and how often you bill.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a sample of the books
pricingTips.body: Ask to see a month of bank statements and the current state of the books before quoting. Messy records are the biggest cause of underpriced bookkeeping engagements.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three tiers, such as basic bookkeeping, bookkeeping with payroll, and full-service with quarterly advisory. Clients tend to choose the middle option, and the tiers show clearly what each includes.

pricingTips.title: Separate cleanup from ongoing fees
pricingTips.body: Price catch-up work as an hourly or one-time project fee, with a cap or estimate. Set the ongoing monthly fee for clean books so the cleanup does not hide inside the recurring price.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for scope growth
pricingTips.body: New entities, new states, and added employees tend to increase work over time. Include a clause that fees will be reviewed if volume or complexity changes.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an estimate range for cleanup work?
faqs.answer: If the condition of the books is unknown, give an estimated range with a not-to-exceed cap and bill hourly against it. Fixed prices work best after you have reviewed the records.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is common. For tax season work, tie the quote to a document deadline, since late records change the workload.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: It is good practice. Many firms combine the quote and engagement letter so the client signs once to accept the scope and fees. Check your state board for any required language.

act-tutor.intro: ACT tutors work with high school students, usually sophomores through seniors, to raise scores on the ACT. Most are independent tutors, former teachers, or small test prep businesses who bill parents for one-on-one sessions, diagnostic tests, group classes, and prep packages. Invoices usually go to a parent or guardian rather than the student.
act-tutor.pricingModel: Most independent ACT tutors charge per hour or per session, with higher rates for tutors who have a high personal score, teaching credentials, or a track record of score gains. Many sell packages of 8, 10, or 12 sessions at a small discount and bill them upfront, which smooths out cancellations and no-shows. Diagnostic practice tests are often billed as a separate flat fee or included with a package. Some tutors add charges for official practice materials, score reports, or extra homework review. Small group classes are typically priced per student per course. Online sessions are often priced the same as or slightly below in-person, and in-person home visits may carry a travel fee. Some tutors offer a flat-fee program that covers a set number of hours through a specific test date.

rates.service: Full-length diagnostic ACT with score review
Study plan and parent progress report

items.description: Diagnostic ACT (full-length, proctored) with score analysis and study plan
One-on-one ACT tutoring, Math and Science focus (sessions held 3/4, 3/11, 3/18, 3/25)
One-on-one ACT tutoring, English and Reading focus (sessions held 4/1, 4/8)
Printed practice test booklets and answer sheets

sampleInvoice.notes: Student: Jordan M. Target test date: June 14. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Accepted: check, Zenelle-style bank transfer, or card. Sessions canceled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at the full hourly rate. Remaining package sessions expire 6 months from purchase.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent/guardian billing name
invoiceChecklist.why: The student is rarely the one paying, and parents often need the student's name for reimbursement, 529 plan, or tax records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and length
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents compare invoices against their calendars. Listing each date prevents disputes over how many hours were delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Focus area per session
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting Math, English, Reading, Science, or Writing shows progress and justifies the hours billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client prepaid a package, show sessions used and sessions remaining so nobody has to ask.

invoiceChecklist.item: Practice test and materials fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Official test prep books, printed tests, and score reports are separate costs that should be itemized and not folded into the hourly rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Target test date
invoiceChecklist.why: It gives context for the work and helps you reference the timeline if the family wants to add or reduce sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and expiration policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Restating the 24-hour cancellation rule and package expiration on the invoice makes late-cancel charges easier to enforce.

act-tutor.paymentTerms: Many ACT tutors collect payment upfront for packages or bill monthly in advance, and others invoice weekly or after each session for pay-as-you-go clients. Net 7 or due on receipt is common, since families are often paying out of a household budget and a long window leads to forgotten invoices. A late fee of 1.5 percent per month or a flat $15-25 is typical when it is stated in advance. Common payment methods are card, bank transfer, check, and peer-to-peer apps. Group courses are normally paid in full before the first class, with a refund policy stated in writing.

tips.title: Sell packages and bill them upfront
tips.body: Prepaid 8- or 10-session packages reduce chasing payments and give families a reason to commit through the test date. Offer a small discount, not a large one, and set an expiration window.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: Students cancel often around sports, exams, and school events. A 24-hour policy stated in your agreement and repeated on each invoice makes late-cancel fees a normal part of the process.

tips.title: Time your billing to the test calendar
tips.body: Demand clusters ahead of national test dates. Invoice for any intensive pre-test block before it starts, since families are most willing to commit when the date is close.

tips.title: Keep invoices addressed to the parent
tips.body: Minors cannot sign contracts, so the parent or guardian should be the named client on your agreement and your invoices.

tips.title: Track materials separately
tips.body: Printing and workbook costs add up across many students. Itemizing them keeps your tutoring rate clean and recovers real costs.

faqs.question: Should I charge per hour or per package?
faqs.answer: Many tutors do both. Hourly works for families who want flexibility, and packages work for families preparing for a specific test date. Packages improve cash flow and reduce no-shows, so most tutors push toward them for committed clients.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a student's no-show?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy says so before the first session. Most tutors charge the full session rate for cancellations under 24 hours. Many allow one courtesy waiver per package for genuine emergencies.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Many states do not tax tutoring services, but some tax certain educational or test prep services, and printed materials may be taxable. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill for diagnostic tests?
faqs.answer: List the diagnostic as its own line item with a flat fee. Some tutors waive or credit it if the family buys a package, which you can show as a discount line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a parent asks for a refund on unused sessions?
faqs.answer: Follow the refund policy you set in advance. A common approach is to refund unused sessions at the package rate minus any discount received, or to let the family use them within an expiration window.

estimate.intro: ACT tutors usually send a quote or proposal when a family asks what a full prep program will cost before a test date. Parents often compare you against other independent tutors, large test prep companies, and online programs, so they look at total cost, hours included, and any score guarantee.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions and session length
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 12 one-hour sessions is very different from 12 ninety-minute sessions. State both so the price is clear.
Defines how many weeks the program covers and avoids confusion if the family reschedules their test.
Specify whether you cover all four sections plus the optional Writing section, or only the ones the student needs help with.
Say how many full-length tests are included, who proctors them, and whether they happen during session time or on the student's own time.
Clarify whether books, printed tests, and online question banks are included or billed separately.
Online, at your space, or at the family's home affects price and travel charges.
Setting these upfront prevents arguments when sessions are missed or unused.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: A short program of 6 sessions, a standard one of 10, and an intensive one of 16 lets parents choose a budget without negotiating your hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Base the price on hours needed, not just the hourly rate
pricingTips.body: Use the diagnostic to estimate how many hours a student needs. A student seeking a 3-point gain needs a different plan than one seeking 8 points.

pricingTips.title: Be careful with score guarantees
pricingTips.body: Score improvement depends heavily on student effort. If you offer a guarantee, define it narrowly, such as additional free sessions if the student completes all homework and tests but does not improve.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Test dates and your calendar both fill up. A quote valid for 14 days encourages a decision and protects your availability.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before a diagnostic test?
faqs.answer: You can give a range, but a firm quote is easier after the diagnostic. Many tutors quote the diagnostic as a standalone fee first, then provide a program quote based on the results.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after sending a quote?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as the family adding sessions or the test date moving. Put in the quote that changes in scope will be priced separately.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short agreement signed by the parent that covers price, session count, cancellation rules, and refunds protects both sides.

acupuncturist.intro: Licensed acupuncturists run solo practices, share treatment rooms in wellness clinics, or work inside chiropractic and physical therapy offices. They bill for initial consultations, follow-up treatments, and add-on services such as cupping, moxibustion, electro-acupuncture, and herbal formulas. Many patients pay out of pocket, while others need a receipt they can submit to their insurance or HSA.
acupuncturist.pricingModel: Most acupuncturists charge per session, with a higher fee for the first visit because it includes intake, health history, and diagnosis. Follow-up sessions are priced at a flat rate, often 45 to 60 minutes. Community acupuncture clinics use a sliding scale, usually $20-60 per treatment. Packages of 5 or 10 sessions are common and are typically discounted 5 to 15 percent and paid upfront. Add-ons like cupping, gua sha, or electro-stim are either folded into the session fee or billed as a small separate line. Herbal formulas and supplements are billed at retail with a markup over wholesale cost. Practices that accept insurance bill the carrier using CPT codes and collect copays or deductibles from the patient, which are separate from cash fees.

items.description: Initial consultation and acupuncture treatment (lower back pain), 90 min
Follow-up acupuncture treatment with electro-stim, 60 min
Cupping add-on
Herbal formula, 2-week supply (Du Huo Ji Sheng Tang)

sampleInvoice.notes: Dates of service: May 2, May 9, and May 16. Payment is due at time of visit or within 14 days of invoice date. This invoice can be submitted to your insurance for out-of-network reimbursement. Please give 24 hours notice to cancel or reschedule; late cancellations are charged 50 percent of the session fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of each treatment
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and HSA/FSA administrators require dates of service on every receipt, and it prevents disputes about how many sessions were used from a package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license number and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network reimbursement claims usually require the provider's state license number and NPI to be listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code (ICD-10) and procedure code (CPT)
invoiceChecklist.why: Patients submitting superbills need codes like 97810, 97811, 97813, or 97814 for acupuncture and the diagnosis that supports medical necessity.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and products
invoiceChecklist.why: Cupping, electro-stim, and herbs are billed differently, and supplements may not be eligible for reimbursement, so they should be on separate lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing sessions purchased, used, and remaining avoids confusion and records when prepaid revenue is being applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Time spent per session
invoiceChecklist.why: Timed codes depend on whether the session involved face-to-face time in 15-minute increments, and patients like to see what they paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing a late-cancel fee as its own line, with the date, keeps it distinct from treatment charges, which are not billable to insurance.

acupuncturist.paymentTerms: Most acupuncture practices collect payment at the end of each visit by card, cash, check, or HSA/FSA card. Packages are paid in full upfront and are often valid for 6 to 12 months. For insurance patients, collect the copay at the visit and bill the carrier for the rest, with the patient responsible for any denied amounts under your signed financial policy. When you do send an invoice or superbill, due on receipt or net 14 is typical. Late cancellation and no-show fees of 50 to 100 percent of the session are common if stated in writing at intake. Some states or insurers restrict what you can charge, so check your rules before setting a no-show fee for insured patients.

tips.title: Collect payment at checkout
tips.body: Because sessions are short and recurring, the simplest approach is to charge the card on file at the end of each visit. This avoids chasing small balances later and keeps your accounts receivable near zero.

tips.title: Sell packages with clear terms
tips.body: Put the number of sessions, price per session, expiration date, and refund policy in writing. Track used sessions on each invoice so patients can see the balance and you know your outstanding obligation.

tips.title: Offer superbills for out-of-network claims
tips.body: Many patients are reimbursed for 50 to 80 percent of the cost by their plan. A clean superbill with codes, license number, and NPI makes you easier to choose and cuts down on follow-up questions.

tips.title: Separate products from services
tips.body: Herbs and supplements may be taxable as retail goods in your state while treatments are not. Keep them on separate lines so your sales tax reporting is accurate.

tips.title: Post your cancellation policy at booking
tips.body: Have patients agree to the policy when they schedule or complete intake forms. A signed policy makes it much easier to enforce a late fee without conflict.

faqs.question: What CPT codes do acupuncturists use on invoices?
faqs.answer: The common codes are 97810 and 97811 for acupuncture without electrical stimulation (first 15 minutes and each additional 15 minutes) and 97813 and 97814 for acupuncture with electrical stimulation. Use only codes that match the services you performed and check each payer's rules.

faqs.question: Should I charge more for the first visit?
faqs.answer: Yes, most acupuncturists do. The initial visit includes intake, health history, diagnosis, and treatment planning, so it runs longer. A premium of $30-70 over a follow-up is typical.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on treatments?
faqs.answer: In most states, health care services such as acupuncture are not taxed, but retail items like herbs, supplements, or cupping sets often are. Rules vary by state, so confirm with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can patients use HSA or FSA funds for acupuncture?
faqs.answer: In general, acupuncture is an eligible expense for HSA and FSA accounts when it treats a medical condition. Provide an itemized receipt with dates, services, and amounts. Some plans may request a letter of medical necessity.

faqs.question: How do I handle patients who stop coming before using their package?
faqs.answer: State an expiration date and your refund policy in writing when selling the package. If there is no policy, many practices refund unused sessions at the regular per-visit rate, minus any discount already received.

estimate.intro: Acupuncturists usually give quotes before a course of treatment, since many conditions need a series of sessions. Patients compare the per-session cost, how many visits to expect, and whether herbs or add-ons are included. A written estimate is also needed for patients paying cash who want to know the total before committing.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated number of sessions and frequency
scopeChecklist.why: Chronic pain or fertility care might need 8 to 12 visits over several months, and patients should know that upfront rather than expecting a single session fix.

scopeChecklist.item: Initial visit fee vs. follow-up fee
scopeChecklist.why: The first visit costs more, and a quote that lists only the follow-up rate will look lower than the real total.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in each session
scopeChecklist.why: State whether cupping, moxibustion, electro-acupuncture, or tui na are included or billed extra, so add-ons do not surprise the patient.
Herbs are often a significant additional cost, billed per bottle or per week, and may be continued for months.
Clarify the discount, how many sessions, and when unused sessions expire.
Make clear whether you bill insurance directly or provide a superbill, and that coverage is not guaranteed.
Explain the late-cancel fee and that the treatment plan may change after a few sessions based on response.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for the course of care
pricingTips.body: Treatment response varies, so give a likely range such as 6 to 10 visits and note that you will reassess after the first 4 to 6 sessions. This keeps the estimate honest without locking you in.

pricingTips.title: Show the package savings
pricingTips.body: Put the pay-per-visit total next to the package price so the patient sees the actual discount. A 10 percent saving on a 10-session package is easy to understand.

pricingTips.title: Keep herbs separate from treatment
pricingTips.body: List herbs as an optional line, with an estimated monthly cost. Patients may decline them, and a separate line keeps the base estimate clear.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a written estimate for acupuncture?
faqs.answer: It is not usually required for cash-pay practices, but it is good practice, especially for a multi-session plan or packages. Some states have rules about disclosing fees, so check your local requirements.

faqs.question: Can I guarantee how many sessions a patient will need?
faqs.answer: No. Say the number is an estimate based on the condition and typical response, and that you will reassess as treatment progresses. Avoid promising specific outcomes.

faqs.question: Should I give free consultations?
faqs.answer: Some acupuncturists offer a short free phone or in-person meeting to explain the approach and pricing, but not a free treatment. Keep it brief, and bill the full initial visit once assessment and treatment begin.

advertising-agency.intro: Advertising agencies, from solo creative directors to small shops of five to twenty people, bill clients for campaign strategy, creative development, media planning and buying, and production. Invoices often combine labor, pass-through media spend, and third-party costs like photographers, printers, or ad platform fees. Getting these lines separated clearly is what keeps clients from questioning the total.
advertising-agency.pricingModel: Agencies price in several ways, often mixed on one account. Monthly retainers are the most common for ongoing clients and cover a set scope of hours or deliverables. Project fees are used for campaigns, brand launches, and video or print production. Hourly billing, usually tied to a rate card by role (strategist, art director, copywriter, account manager), is used for out-of-scope work and for clients who want transparency. Media buying is typically billed either as a percentage of ad spend (commonly 10-20%) or as a flat management fee, with the media cost itself passed through at cost. Third-party production costs such as talent, stock licensing, printing, and studio rental are usually billed at cost plus a markup of about 10-20% for handling and coordination. Many agencies also add a rush fee for work with turnaround under a few days.

rates.service: Creative direction, art direction, or copywriting
Monthly retainer for small business clients

items.description: Monthly retainer, March: strategy, social ad creative, and reporting (up to 40 hours)
Paid social media management fee (15% of $8,000 ad spend)
Meta and Google ad spend, passed through at cost
Additional copywriting for spring promo landing page (out of scope)
Stock photography licenses (4 images), at cost plus 15% handling
Rush fee: 24-hour turnaround on revised banner set

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Ad spend is billed at cost and is non-refundable once served. Out-of-scope work was approved by email on March 12. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or campaign/job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients route invoices through accounts payable, which often rejects invoices without a matching PO or job code.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for fees, media spend, and third-party costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see what is your labor and what is pass-through, and it makes any markup easy to defend.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period or campaign flight dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties charges to specific dates, which helps when a client reconciles against ad platform statements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed scope of work or approved estimate
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets you point to agreed terms if the client questions a line, especially for out-of-scope additions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by role for time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the rate card was applied and backs up any hourly or overage billing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and license terms for creative, stock, and talent
invoiceChecklist.why: Licensed assets often have time, territory, or channel limits. Stating them prevents misuse and later disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax treatment, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states tax certain advertising or creative services and others do not. Check your state rules and show tax as its own line if charged.

advertising-agency.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually billed at the start of the month, due in 7 to 15 days. New clients commonly pay a 25-50% deposit on project work, with the balance split across milestones such as concept approval, production, and delivery. Media spend is often invoiced in advance or paid by the client directly to the platform, because agencies do not want to float tens of thousands of dollars in ad costs. Net 30 is common with larger corporate clients, but it is reasonable to ask for net 15 from small businesses. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are standard if written into the contract. Payment is typically by ACH, wire, or credit card, and some agencies add a surcharge for cards on large invoices.

tips.title: Bill media spend in advance or use client-owned ad accounts
tips.body: If you pay for ads on your own card and invoice later, you carry the risk. Ask for prepayment of media, or have the client set up their own ad accounts and add you as manager.

tips.title: Keep retainer scope in writing and track hours against it
tips.body: State the hours or deliverables included each month and what happens to unused time. Without this, clients assume unlimited revisions and rollover.

tips.title: Get written approval before out-of-scope work
tips.body: A short email approving extra hours or costs is enough. Reference it on the invoice so the charge is never a surprise.

tips.title: Bill production milestones as they are hit
tips.body: Invoice at concept approval, shoot or build completion, and final delivery rather than waiting until the campaign launches. Delays on the client side then do not hold up your cash.

tips.title: Pass through vendor invoices with backup
tips.body: Attach or keep copies of printer, talent, and platform invoices so you can answer any question about pass-through costs quickly.

faqs.question: Should I mark up media spend on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Most agencies either pass media through at cost and charge a separate management fee, or build a commission into the media price. Whichever you choose, state it in your agreement. Hidden markups damage trust and can violate client contracts that require transparency.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a retainer when the client uses fewer hours than agreed?
faqs.answer: That depends on your contract. Many agencies bill the full retainer regardless, since it reserves capacity. Others allow limited rollover for one month. Write the rule into your agreement and note it on the invoice if hours are unused.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on advertising services?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax advertising, design, or certain digital services, while many do not tax professional services at all. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for a campaign?
faqs.answer: For projects, invoice at milestones set in the contract, such as a deposit at signing, then at approval and delivery. For retainers, invoice at the start of the billing month. For media, invoice before the spend occurs where possible.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes the invoice because results were poor?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say you are paid for work performed, not for specific outcomes such as sales or leads, unless you agreed to performance pay. Point to the scope of work and the deliverables completed, and offer to review strategy going forward.

estimate.intro: Agencies send an estimate or proposal before any campaign, rebrand, or production work starts, and often as part of a competitive pitch. Clients compare total cost, what is included, how many revision rounds they get, and whether media and production costs are inside or on top of the fee.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing the number of ad variations, video lengths, and file formats prevents arguments over what was promised.
Two rounds is common. Stating this up front gives you a basis to bill extra rounds.
Make clear whether ad spend is included in your price or billed separately at cost, and who owns the ad accounts.
Talent, stock, printing, and studio costs are often uncertain. Give an estimate range and state they are billed at actual cost plus any markup.
Delays often come from slow feedback. Tie your delivery dates to the client providing assets and approvals on time.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage rights and ownership of final work
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify what the client owns on final payment, and the term and territory for any licensed assets.
Production and media costs change. A 30-day expiry protects you from honoring old prices.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from hours by role, then present a flat fee
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for strategy, creative, production, and account management using your rate card, add a contingency of 10-15%, and present a single project price. Clients prefer certainty, and you keep your internal math.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present good, better, and best packages, for example a basic campaign, a full campaign with video, and one with ongoing media management. Clients often choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Separate fees from pass-through costs
pricingTips.body: Show agency fees in one section and media or production costs in another. It makes the quote easier to compare against other agencies.

pricingTips.title: Charge for discovery and pitch work when it is substantial
pricingTips.body: A paid strategy phase before the full proposal filters out clients who only want free ideas and gives you real information to scope the rest.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: For defined projects, a fixed price with a clear scope works best for most clients. For open-ended or evolving work, use an hourly estimate with a not-to-exceed cap or a monthly retainer.

faqs.question: How do I handle a quote when media costs are uncertain?
faqs.answer: Quote your fee firmly and give media as a budget the client approves, with your management fee as a percentage or flat amount. Note that actual platform costs are billed at what was spent.

faqs.question: Is it normal to charge for a proposal or pitch?
faqs.answer: For small and mid-size work, a free proposal is common. For large pitches involving original creative concepts, many agencies charge a pitch fee or limit the work to strategy and examples.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts the estimate?
faqs.answer: Only for changes outside the agreed scope. Use a short change order that describes the added work and cost, and get the client's written approval before starting it.

air-duct-cleaning.intro: Air duct cleaning businesses, usually owner-operators or small crews with a truck-mounted or portable vacuum system, send invoices to homeowners, landlords, property managers, and light commercial clients. Typical billed work includes whole-house duct cleaning, dryer vent cleaning, and add-ons like sanitizing, coil cleaning, and blower motor cleaning.
air-duct-cleaning.pricingModel: Most residential work is priced as a flat fee for the whole system, often based on the number of supply and return vents or the number of HVAC systems, with a base package that includes a set number of vents and a per-vent charge beyond that. Add-ons such as dryer vent cleaning, furnace or blower cleaning, evaporator coil cleaning, and antimicrobial treatment are priced as separate line items. Commercial and large jobs may be priced per square foot or per hour with a minimum. Many companies set a minimum service charge to cover travel and setup. Difficult access, such as flex duct in tight attics, crawlspaces, or heavy contamination like mold or rodent debris, usually adds a surcharge or is quoted separately after inspection.

rates.service: Whole-house duct cleaning, single HVAC system (up to ~10 vents)
Additional supply or return vent beyond package
Second HVAC system or separate zone

items.description: Whole-house air duct cleaning, 1 HVAC system, up to 10 vents (includes supply and return, main trunk lines, and register cleaning)
Additional vents beyond package (4 supply, 2 return)
Blower compartment and furnace cabinet cleaning
Dryer vent cleaning, exterior termination cleared
Antimicrobial treatment applied to ductwork

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon completion of service. We accept check, card, and bank transfer. Before and after photos are available on request. Return vent filters were not replaced; recommend a new filter now and every 1 to 3 months. Work guaranteed for 30 days; contact us if any vent was missed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of HVAC systems and vents cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing is usually per system and per vent, so a count lets the customer see exactly what they paid for and prevents disputes over missed registers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and location of equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: Notes like attic, basement, or crawlspace air handler document where you worked and justify access surcharges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Methods and equipment used
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating negative-pressure vacuum collection with agitation tools shows the work followed an accepted method such as NADCA standards, if you follow them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Dryer vent, coil cleaning, sanitizer, and blower cleaning are optional services; itemizing them avoids confusion and makes partial refunds or disputes easier to resolve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Findings and conditions noted
invoiceChecklist.why: Recording mold, pest droppings, damaged flex duct, or disconnected runs protects you from blame for pre-existing problems.

invoiceChecklist.item: Products used, including antimicrobial or sealant names
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers with allergies or pets often ask, and some products must be EPA-registered and applied per label; listing them provides a record.

invoiceChecklist.item: License, insurance, and business ID numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states or cities require contractor or HVAC-related licensing for this work, and property managers often need proof of insurance on file.

air-duct-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential duct cleaning is usually paid on completion, often by card, check, or digital payment the same day, with the invoice handed over or emailed before you leave. Deposits are uncommon for standard homes but reasonable for large or commercial jobs, typically 25 to 50 percent. Property managers and commercial clients often pay net 15 or net 30 and may require a PO number. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common on net terms, if stated in advance and allowed locally. Cancellations on the day of service or no-access visits may carry a trip charge.

tips.title: Set a firm minimum and publish what it includes
tips.body: Define how many vents and which components are in the base price. Anything beyond that gets a line item, so the customer is not surprised and you are paid for extra time.

tips.title: Take before and after photos and attach them
tips.body: Photos of inside the trunk lines, coil, and blower are the best proof of work. Attach them to the invoice to head off claims that the job was not done.

tips.title: Be clear about what you do not guarantee
tips.body: Note that cleaning does not fix leaks, poor airflow from bad design, or mold caused by moisture. Put it in writing so results are not blamed on your work.

tips.title: Offer repeat service reminders
tips.body: Most homes need cleaning every 3 to 5 years, and dryer vents yearly. Add a recommended next-service date on the invoice to drive repeat business.

tips.title: Watch out for bait-and-switch pricing
tips.body: Very low advertised prices damage trust in this field. Quote clearly and invoice the quoted amount unless conditions change, and document why with photos.

faqs.question: Should I charge per vent or a flat fee for the whole house?
faqs.answer: Most solo operators use a flat fee for a base package, such as one system and up to 10 vents, then charge per vent beyond that. This is easy for customers to compare and still covers larger homes.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on duct cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning or maintenance services while many tax only goods. Check with your state revenue department, and show tax as its own line if it applies.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for mold or heavy contamination?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you tell the customer before the work. Stop, document with photos, and quote a separate charge. Mold remediation may need special licensing in your state, so check local rules before taking it on.

faqs.question: Should I invoice dryer vent cleaning separately?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a different service with different equipment and often a different customer motivation, such as fire safety. A separate line makes it easy to track and to upsell on later visits.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: For residential jobs, hand over or send the invoice at the end of the visit while you are still on site, and collect payment then. For commercial accounts, send it the same day with any PO number to avoid delays.

estimate.intro: Duct cleaning quotes are usually given by phone or online from a few details about the home, then confirmed on site, or based on a brief inspection for larger or commercial jobs. Customers compare the total price, the number of vents and systems included, what add-ons are bundled, and whether the company follows recognized cleaning standards.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of HVAC systems and vents included
scopeChecklist.why: This is the main pricing driver, and stating the count prevents arguments about whether a vent was part of the quote.

scopeChecklist.item: Components included: ductwork, registers, blower, coil, plenum
scopeChecklist.why: Some customers assume the furnace and coil are cleaned as part of the base price; listing them avoids that misunderstanding.
Dryer vent, sanitizing, and coil cleaning should show their own prices so the customer can accept or decline each one.
Hard-to-reach flex duct, sealed attics, or blocked returns may need extra time or may be excluded, and the quote should say so.
State that if mold, pests, or asbestos-containing material is found, work stops and a revised quote or referral will follow.

scopeChecklist.item: Time on site and customer prep
scopeChecklist.why: Note the expected duration of 2 to 4 hours, that power must be on, and that pets and valuables should be moved.
Labor and chemical costs shift, and a 15 to 30 day validity limit keeps you from honoring old prices.

pricingTips.title: Quote by system, not square footage, for homes
pricingTips.body: Square footage is a poor guide to duct complexity. Counting systems and vents is closer to your real time, and customers can verify the count themselves.

pricingTips.title: Offer good-better-best packages
pricingTips.body: A basic package of ducts only, a standard with blower and dryer vent, and a full service with coil and sanitizer lets customers choose and raises the average ticket without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Verify before finalizing the price
pricingTips.body: If you quote over the phone, say the price is confirmed on arrival after you see the system. Photos from the customer of the air handler and a few vents help quote accurately.

pricingTips.title: Price in your travel and disposal costs
pricingTips.body: Fuel, vacuum filters, bags, and debris disposal are real costs. Build them into your base price or a minimum charge rather than treating them as free.

faqs.question: Should I give a free estimate?
faqs.answer: Most companies do, since customers compare several quotes. For large commercial jobs or those needing a detailed inspection, a paid assessment credited toward the work is reasonable.

faqs.question: Can I give an exact quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a firm price for a standard home if the customer provides the number of systems and vents. State that it is subject to confirmation on site if conditions differ.

faqs.question: What if the job takes longer than I quoted?
faqs.answer: A flat quote should hold unless conditions differ from what was described, such as extra hidden vents or heavy contamination. Put that exception in your quote so a revised price is expected.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 15 to 30 days for residential jobs. Commercial bids may need 30 to 60 days to cover approvals, but note that pricing can change if the scope changes.

airbnb-cleaning.intro: Airbnb cleaning businesses turn over short-term rentals between guest stays for hosts and property managers. Invoices usually cover turnover cleans, laundry, restocking, and extras like deep cleans or damage reports. Most work is recurring, so invoices tend to go out weekly or monthly with many small line items tied to specific properties and checkout dates.
airbnb-cleaning.pricingModel: Most Airbnb cleaners charge a flat fee per turnover, set by the number of bedrooms and bathrooms, with the price held steady for each property. Some bill hourly (often for deep cleans, first-time resets, or unusual properties), and a few use per-square-foot pricing for larger homes. Laundry is billed either as a per-load charge, a per-bed charge, or folded into the turnover fee; linen rental or off-site laundering is usually passed through at cost plus a markup. Supplies restocked for the guest (toilet paper, soap, coffee, trash bags) are typically billed at cost plus 10-20% or covered by a small flat supply fee. Same-day or last-minute bookings, hot tub care, and heavy post-party cleanups carry surcharges. Property managers with many units often negotiate volume rates, and monthly invoicing with itemized turnovers is common.

rates.service: Laundry (sheets and towels, off-site or on-site)

rates.unit: cost plus markup or flat fee per turn

rates.service: Hot tub wipe-down and basic check

items.description: Turnover clean - 2BR/1BA, 14 Lakeview Ct (checkouts Mar 3, 8, 12, 17)
Laundry - extra linen sets for 6-guest bookings
Supply restock (toiletries, coffee, paper goods)
Same-day turnover surcharge (Mar 12)
Deep clean - oven, fridge, baseboards, windows

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Photos of any damage, stains, or missing items are attached by checkout date. Late balances over 15 days incur a 1.5% monthly fee. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address or listing nickname for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosts and managers often own several units, and they need to match charges to the right property for their own books and owner statements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Checkout date for each turnover
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to a specific booking so the host can verify it against their calendar and spot any missed or duplicate cleans.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized extras (laundry, restock, hot tub, rush fee)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating extras from the base turnover fee heads off questions and shows what drove a higher invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies and consumables at cost, with any markup shown
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosts reimbursing or deducting these costs want clear amounts, and receipts back up the charge if challenged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage, stain, or missing-item notes with photo references
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosts may need this for guest claims through the booking platform, and it protects you from blame for pre-existing problems.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, contact info, and tax ID if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and businesses often need a W-9 and a proper invoice for their records, and they may need to issue a 1099 at year end.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms and accepted payment methods
invoiceChecklist.why: With frequent small charges, clear due dates and methods keep recurring accounts from drifting into late payment.

airbnb-cleaning.paymentTerms: Many Airbnb cleaners invoice weekly or monthly in arrears for recurring clients and charge a card on file after each turnover for individual hosts. Net 7 to net 14 is common; larger property managers may ask for net 30, which is worth pushing back on since you pay cleaners and buy supplies up front. A deposit or prepayment is typical for first-time deep cleans or large resets. Late fees of 1.5% per month or a flat fee are commonly stated in service agreements. Most cleaners accept ACH, card, and digital payment apps. Keep a card or ACH authorization on file for recurring accounts so payments do not depend on the host remembering.

tips.title: Invoice by turnover, not by lump sum
tips.body: List each checkout date and property as its own line. Hosts check these against their booking calendar, and itemized lines cut down on disputes and back-and-forth.

tips.title: Document condition at every turn
tips.body: Take timestamped photos on arrival and departure, especially of damage, stains, and missing items. Attach them to the invoice or reference them by date so you are covered if a host disputes a guest claim.

tips.title: Bill extras every time they happen
tips.body: Extra laundry loads, long stays needing mid-stay cleans, bed-count changes, and rush bookings are easy to absorb and forget. Add them as separate line items so you are paid for the real work.

tips.title: Put cancellation and lockout rules in writing
tips.body: Short-term rental schedules change fast. Charge a fee for cancellations under 24 hours, or for trips where you cannot get in, and list it in your agreement before it comes up.

tips.title: Set a card on file for recurring clients
tips.body: Auto-charging after each turnover or each month avoids chasing payments and keeps your cash flow steady when you are paying cleaners weekly.

faqs.question: Should I charge per turnover or per hour?
faqs.answer: Most Airbnb cleaners use a flat fee per turnover based on bedrooms and bathrooms, because hosts want predictable costs and it rewards you for being efficient. Hourly billing works better for deep cleans, first-time resets, and properties in poor condition where the time is hard to predict.

faqs.question: Can I charge guests' extra mess to the host?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you set it up in your agreement. Define what counts as excessive mess (for example, post-party cleanups or pet hair beyond normal) and the surcharge or hourly rate that applies, and document the condition with photos on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for laundry?
faqs.answer: Common methods are a per-load charge, a per-bed or per-set charge, or including standard laundry in the turnover fee and billing extra loads separately. If you use a laundry service or rent linens, pass the cost through with a markup and show it as its own line.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or get a W-9?
faqs.answer: If you pay subcontractor cleaners above the IRS threshold, you may need to collect W-9s and file 1099s. Property management companies that hire you may also ask for a W-9. Rules and thresholds change, so check current IRS guidance or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice a host with several turnovers a month?
faqs.answer: Weekly or monthly invoices that list every turnover work best. Weekly gets you paid faster and keeps the list short enough to check; monthly is less paperwork but ties up more of your money. Pick one and state it in your agreement.

estimate.intro: Airbnb cleaners quote before starting a new account, when a host asks about pricing for a listing, or when a property manager is comparing vendors for several units. Clients usually compare the per-turnover price, what is included (laundry, restocking, photos), and how you handle last-minute bookings. Because the work repeats, a clear quote also sets the baseline for every invoice that follows.

scopeChecklist.item: Bedroom, bathroom, and square footage count, plus sleeping capacity
scopeChecklist.why: These drive time and price, and a listing that sleeps eight takes far longer than a two-person studio even at similar size.
Spell out tasks like bed making, bathroom sanitizing, kitchen wipe-down, floors, trash, and dishes so the host knows what is covered and what counts as an extra.
State whether you wash on-site, take linens off-site, or the host supplies a service, and who pays for linens, detergent, and any lost or stained items.
Clarify whether you buy consumables, who supplies them, and how reimbursement or markup works to avoid surprises on the first invoice.
List lockbox or smart lock codes, earliest start after checkout, and the deadline before check-in, since tight windows affect staffing and rush pricing.
Name the fees for same-day bookings, deep cleans, hot tub care, pet hair, party cleanups, and trips where you cannot access the property.
Bookings get canceled and moved often; stating notice periods and fees avoids unpaid trips.

pricingTips.title: Time the first clean before setting a long-term price
pricingTips.body: Do a first clean or walk-through and time it with your whole team. Set your flat fee from the real time, including drive time, laundry, and restocking, not from an estimate based on bedroom count alone.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers based on what is included
pricingTips.body: A basic tier for cleaning only and a fuller tier with laundry, restocking, and photo reports lets hosts choose and makes your higher price easy to explain.

pricingTips.title: Give volume pricing, not blanket discounts
pricingTips.body: Property managers with many units expect a lower rate, but tie the discount to a minimum number of turnovers or a consistent schedule so your margins stay protected.

pricingTips.title: Revisit pricing after the first month
pricingTips.body: Note in the quote that rates can be adjusted if the listing turns out to need more time than described, such as heavy wear, extra beds, or longer drive distances.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat rate or an hourly rate for a new listing?
faqs.answer: Most hosts want a flat rate per turnover. If you are unsure about the property, quote hourly for the first clean or two, then set a flat fee based on how long it actually takes.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Pricing depends on your schedule and supply costs, and a host may sit on a quote through the off-season, so a short expiry lets you reprice when demand changes.

faqs.question: Do I need to visit the property before quoting?
faqs.answer: It helps. A video walkthrough or photos of the listing often work for small units, but visiting larger homes, or those with unusual features like hot tubs or multiple levels, prevents underpricing.

amazon-seller.intro: Most Amazon sales are paid through Amazon, so invoices come up when a seller does business outside the checkout page. That includes wholesale or bulk orders to retailers and other sellers, FBA prep and fulfillment for other brands, and services such as listing optimization, ad management, and product sourcing. These invoices need unit counts, ASINs or SKUs, and clear separation between your fees and pass-through costs.
amazon-seller.pricingModel: Pricing depends on which side of the business you are billing. Wholesale and bulk sales are priced per unit, usually cost plus a margin, with volume tiers and case or pallet minimums. Prep and fulfillment work is billed per unit or per order, with add-ons for bagging, bundling, or inspection, and storage billed per pallet or cubic foot per month. Service work for other brands is usually a monthly retainer, a flat fee per listing or project, or a percentage of ad spend. Sourcing and inspection can be a flat fee per product or a small percentage of the purchase order. Pass-through costs such as freight, Amazon fees you front, and ad spend should be listed separately from your own fees, with little or no markup unless your agreement says otherwise.

rates.service: FNSKU labeling and basic FBA prep
Listing creation or optimization (copy, keywords, image direction)

rates.unit: percent of ad spend (monthly minimum often $500-1,000)

rates.service: Pallet storage at a prep or 3PL space

items.description: Monthly account management, March (inventory planning, listing upkeep, reimbursement claims)
PPC management, 12% of $4,000 ad spend (ad spend billed to client's card by Amazon)
FNSKU labeling, shipment FBA-2024-0317 (1,200 units)
Poly bagging with suffocation warning label (600 units)
Listing optimization, 4 ASINs (title, bullets, backend keywords)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Ad spend is charged directly to your Amazon Ads account and is not included in this total. Prep counts are based on our receiving log, available on request. Late balances may be charged 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: ASINs, SKUs, and FNSKUs for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Brands often sell dozens of similar products, and tying each charge to an identifier prevents disputes about which items were prepped or listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Unit counts with received, prepped, and rejected quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-unit billing is only defensible if it matches what arrived and what was processed. Damaged or short units explain differences from the client's records.

invoiceChecklist.item: FBA shipment ID or client PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Retail and brand clients usually match invoices to a PO or inbound shipment before approving payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period or service dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers and storage fees cover a time span, and clear dates avoid double billing and confusion over renewals.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately (freight, supplies, fees you fronted)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see what is your fee and what is a reimbursed cost, and it keeps your revenue and expenses clean at tax time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax status or resale certificate on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Direct wholesale sales outside Amazon may be taxable unless the buyer provides an exemption certificate. Rules vary by state, so keep certificates on file and note them on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms, accepted methods, and late fee policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Wholesale buyers commonly assume net 30. Stating your terms up front sets the expectation and supports collection.

amazon-seller.paymentTerms: Service retainers are usually billed at the start of the month, with PPC management fees billed after the month closes once ad spend is known. Sourcing projects often take a 30-50% deposit before supplier outreach or samples, with the balance due on delivery of the report or before the purchase order is placed. Wholesale buyers commonly expect net 30, though new accounts can be asked for prepayment or a deposit until they have a payment history. Prep and fulfillment invoices are often net 15 or billed per inbound shipment. Where allowed, late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common. ACH and wire are typical for larger invoices, and cards work for smaller ones if you pass along processing fees in line with your agreement and local rules.

tips.title: Keep ad spend off your invoice total
tips.body: Have clients run ad spend on their own Amazon Ads account or card. If you front it, bill it as a separate pass-through line with a screenshot or report, and avoid mixing it into your management fee.

tips.title: Bill prep on received counts, not expected counts
tips.body: Inbound quantities rarely match the supplier's paperwork. Count at receiving, record shortages and damages, and invoice from that log so the client has no reason to push back.

tips.title: Set minimums on percentage fees
tips.body: A percentage of ad spend or revenue pays poorly in slow months. Add a monthly minimum so the work stays worth doing when the account is small.

tips.title: Charge for storage and long holds
tips.body: Inventory that sits in your space past an agreed number of days should trigger a storage fee. State the free period in your agreement and show the date inventory arrived on the invoice.

tips.title: Track reimbursements and chargebacks separately
tips.body: If you recover lost inventory or fees for a client and take a percentage, list the claim IDs and amounts recovered so the fee is easy to verify.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice for sales made through Amazon?
faqs.answer: No. Amazon collects payment from the customer and pays you through disbursements. You invoice when you sell directly to a business, sell wholesale outside the marketplace, or provide services to another seller or brand.

faqs.question: How should I bill for FBA prep work?
faqs.answer: Most prep providers bill per unit for each task, such as labeling, bagging, or bundling, plus any supplies used. Add separate lines for receiving, inspection, and storage, and reference the shipment ID.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on wholesale invoices?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and whether the buyer is reselling the goods. In many states, a buyer with a valid resale certificate can purchase tax-exempt. Get the certificate before shipping and check your state's rules or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: What payment terms are normal for wholesale orders?
faqs.answer: Net 30 is common for established retail buyers. For first orders, many sellers require prepayment or a deposit, then offer terms after a few on-time payments.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of a client's Amazon sales?
faqs.answer: Yes, many agencies do, often alongside a base retainer. Define in writing whether the percentage applies to gross sales or net sales, which period it covers, and where the sales figures come from.

estimate.intro: Amazon sellers send quotes for wholesale or bulk orders, prep and fulfillment projects, and service packages like account management or sourcing. Clients usually compare per-unit prices, minimum order sizes, turnaround time, and what is included in a monthly fee. A written quote should make the scope and the cost drivers clear before any inventory moves.

scopeChecklist.item: Units, SKUs, and pack sizes covered
scopeChecklist.why: A quote based on 1,000 units is not valid for 400, and different pack configurations change labor and shipping costs.
Labeling, bagging, bundling, inspection, and relabeling each take different time. Listing them prevents arguments over extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Who pays freight, supplies, and Amazon fees
scopeChecklist.why: Inbound freight, poly bags, and placement fees can exceed your own fee if not assigned clearly.
Missed inbound windows hurt sales, so state how many business days you need after receiving inventory.

scopeChecklist.item: Scope of service work and reporting
scopeChecklist.why: For account management, specify the number of listings, the frequency of reports, and what is billed separately, such as design or A+ Content.

scopeChecklist.item: Price validity period and volume tiers
scopeChecklist.why: Supplier costs and freight rates move, so state how long the quote holds and what happens if quantities change.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment terms, and cancellation rules
scopeChecklist.why: Sourcing and purchase orders involve cash outlay, so the client should know what is refundable if they walk away.

pricingTips.title: Quote per unit with a minimum job charge
pricingTips.body: Small batches take nearly as much setup as large ones. A per-unit price with a minimum, such as $150 per shipment, keeps tiny orders from losing money.

pricingTips.title: Build in rework and inspection time
pricingTips.body: Suppliers ship mislabeled, damaged, or short cartons often enough that you should assume some rework. Add a line for exceptions or set a rate for handling them.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered volume pricing
pricingTips.body: Showing price breaks at 500, 1,000, and 5,000 units lets buyers see the value of ordering more and helps you plan labor.

pricingTips.title: Separate your fee from pass-through costs
pricingTips.body: Present your service price and estimated freight, supplies, and ad spend as different sections. Clients can compare your fee to competitors without hidden extras.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an estimate range for prep work?
faqs.answer: Use a flat per-unit rate when the product and tasks are known. If the condition of the inventory is unclear, give a range and state that final billing follows the received count and actual tasks.

faqs.question: How long should a wholesale quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Often 7 to 30 days, depending on how stable your supplier prices and freight costs are. Put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit on a sourcing project?
faqs.answer: Yes. A 30-50% deposit is common because you spend time and sometimes money on samples before the client commits to a purchase order.

faqs.question: What happens if the client changes quantities after accepting a quote?
faqs.answer: State that pricing is based on the quoted quantity and that changes may adjust the per-unit rate or minimum charge. Send a revised quote for any significant change.
