analytics-consultant.intro: Analytics consultants help companies make sense of their data. They build dashboards, clean and model data, set up tracking, run analyses, and sometimes train internal teams. Most work solo or in small firms and bill for time, fixed-scope projects, or monthly retainers.
analytics-consultant.pricingModel: Most analytics consultants bill hourly for open-ended or exploratory work and fixed fees for defined deliverables such as a dashboard build, a tracking audit, or a customer segmentation analysis. Monthly retainers are common for ongoing reporting, analysis support, and data team advisory work, usually with a set number of hours included. Day rates are used for on-site work and workshops. Rates rise with specialty (data engineering, marketing attribution, machine learning) and with the size of the client. Software licenses and cloud costs are normally paid by the client directly or passed through at cost, and should be listed as separate lines. Many consultants start with a short paid discovery or data audit, then quote the larger build once they know the data quality.

rates.service: Dashboard build (BI tool, such as Tableau or Power BI)
Web analytics and tag setup (GA4, tag manager)
Training or workshop for client team

items.description: Data audit and measurement plan (GA4, CRM, and ad platform sources)
Sales performance dashboard build, including 3 data source connections
SQL data modeling and cleanup of order history tables
Stakeholder review sessions and dashboard walkthrough
Team training session on dashboard use (half day)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Amounts cover work delivered through the dashboard launch on the date shown. Client-owned BI licenses and cloud warehouse costs are billed directly by the vendors. Two weeks of post-launch bug fixes are included; additional changes are billed hourly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and statement of work reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to the agreed scope, which helps when a client's finance team asks what the invoice covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed or milestones reached
invoiceChecklist.why: Fixed-fee invoices are easier to approve when they name the dashboard, audit, or model that was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by task and date for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Data work is hard to see from the outside, so a breakdown such as data cleaning versus modeling versus meetings shows where time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often will not process a payment without a PO or internal code.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs passed through at cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Data connectors, API usage, cloud compute, or purchased datasets should be separate lines so they are not confused with your fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Data sources and platforms covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing systems such as GA4, Snowflake, or Salesforce makes the scope clear if later work touches different sources.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and hours used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the billing month, how many hours were included, and any overage or rollover.

analytics-consultant.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is typical, and larger companies may insist on net 45 or net 60. For fixed-scope projects, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent upfront is common, with the balance at delivery or split across milestones. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common when stated in the contract. Clients usually pay by ACH or wire for larger invoices, with card payments as a convenience that may carry a fee. Put the terms in a signed agreement before you start, including who owns the code, queries, and dashboards once paid.

tips.title: Separate discovery from the build
tips.body: You rarely know how messy the data is until you open it. Bill a short audit first, then quote the build with real information. This avoids absorbing weeks of cleanup in a fixed fee.

tips.title: Define what counts as a revision
tips.body: Dashboards invite endless tweaks. State how many review rounds are included and bill additional changes hourly. Add a window, such as 14 or 30 days, for post-launch fixes.

tips.title: Bill milestones on larger projects
tips.body: Tie invoices to events such as data connections finished, model approved, and dashboard launched. You get paid as work progresses and the client sees steady progress.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed fees
tips.body: Knowing your actual hours per project shows whether your flat fees hold up. If a type of project keeps running over, raise the price next time.

tips.title: Keep client access and credentials clean
tips.body: Delays in getting data access can stall a project. Note in your terms that waiting on access does not pause the billing schedule for retainers or milestone dates.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for analytics projects?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for exploratory analysis, unclear data, or ongoing support. Use a flat fee when the deliverable is clear, such as a specific dashboard or tracking setup. A common approach is a paid audit first, then a fixed fee for the build.

faqs.question: How do I bill for time spent cleaning bad data?
faqs.answer: Include it in the scope as its own line, either hourly or as a defined data preparation fee. If you find problems after quoting, notify the client in writing and ask for a change order rather than absorbing it.

faqs.question: Can I pass software and cloud costs to the client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. The cleanest approach is for the client to hold the accounts and pay vendors directly. If you pay first, list the cost as a separate line and add a markup only if the contract allows it.

faqs.question: How should I invoice a monthly retainer?
faqs.answer: Invoice at the start of the month for the set fee and state the hours included. Say in the agreement whether unused hours roll over or expire, and bill overage hours at a stated rate on the next invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on analytics consulting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax consulting services, but some tax certain digital or data services, and dashboards or software-like deliverables can be treated differently. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant.

estimate.intro: Analytics consultants send estimates after an intro call and a look at the client's data setup, and before any build work begins. Clients usually compare your quote against other freelancers, agencies, or hiring someone in-house, so the scope and deliverables matter as much as the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Business questions the work will answer
scopeChecklist.why: Anchors the project in outcomes, so the dashboard or analysis is judged against agreed goals instead of changing opinions.
Lists which systems are in scope and who provides credentials, since new sources often add cost.
States that the quote assumes reasonably complete, consistent data and that major cleanup is billed separately.
Names the dashboard pages, reports, documentation, or models you will hand over, and the tool they will be built in.
Sets a limit on feedback cycles and defines how extra changes are billed.
Spells out dependencies like data access and feedback turnaround, which are the most common causes of delay.
Says who owns queries, code, and dashboards, and whether training or documentation is included.

pricingTips.title: Price the outcome, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: A dashboard that saves a team ten hours of weekly reporting is worth more than the hours it takes to build. Use hours to check your floor, then price by the value of the deliverable where the client sees it clearly.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic, standard, and extended scope, for example one data source versus three, or static reports versus an interactive dashboard. Clients can choose a level without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Data projects often run over because of undocumented fields, broken tracking, or slow access. Build 15 to 25 percent contingency into fixed quotes or state a clear process for change orders.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Tool costs, your availability, and the client's data can change. A 30-day validity period keeps the pricing from sitting open indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before seeing the data?
faqs.answer: Only a rough range. A firm fixed quote without looking at the data is risky. Offer a paid audit or a short, free scoping call and give a ballpark with clear assumptions until you have reviewed the real systems.

faqs.question: How detailed should an analytics estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list each deliverable, the data sources, the revision limit, and the timeline. It does not need hour-by-hour detail for a fixed fee, but hourly estimates should show an expected range of hours by phase.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of your rate. Drop a data source, cut dashboard pages, or remove training. This keeps your effective rate intact and makes the tradeoff visible.

faqs.question: How do I handle scope changes after the estimate is accepted?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that states the added work, the cost, and any effect on the timeline. Get approval before doing the extra work, and include this process in the original agreement.

animation.intro: Animators are freelancers and small studios who produce motion work for agencies, brands, startups, production companies, and educators. Typical jobs include 2D explainer videos, motion graphics, character animation, logo animations, 3D product renders, and social media loops. Invoices usually cover a mix of design, storyboarding, animation, revisions, and delivery of final files.
animation.pricingModel: Most animators price by the finished second or minute for set-scope projects, by the day for work embedded with an agency or studio, and by the hour for small fixes and add-ons. Flat project fees are common for explainers and logo stings, often broken into milestones such as script and storyboard, style frames, animation, and final delivery. Price per finished second rises with complexity: simple motion graphics sit at the low end, while character animation and 3D sit at the high end. Voiceover, music licensing, stock assets, and render farm costs are usually billed separately or passed through with a small markup. Most contracts include a set number of revision rounds, with extra rounds billed hourly. Rush work often carries a surcharge of 25 to 50 percent. Usage rights, such as broadcast or paid ads, can raise the fee for commercial work.

rates.service: Logo animation or short sting (3-10 sec)
Freelance animator on contract with studio
General animation work and small edits

items.description: Script review and storyboard (12 frames) - 60 sec explainer
Style frames, 3 options, one chosen
2D animation, 60 sec finished runtime
Sound design and music edit (licensed track provided by client)
Revisions beyond two included rounds
Final delivery: MP4 (H.264), ProRes master, and captioned version

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers final milestone balance after 50% deposit paid on 3/1. Payment due within 15 days. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Final project files and source project are licensed to client for web and social use per agreement dated 2/20. Source files available for an additional fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, deliverable specs, and finished runtime
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-second pricing only makes sense if the invoice shows the final length, resolution, frame rate, and aspect ratios delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone reference and deposit received
invoiceChecklist.why: Animation is billed in stages, so the client should see which stage this invoice covers and what has already been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why extra hours are billed and prevents disputes over what counted as a revision versus a change in scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Licensing and usage rights granted
invoiceChecklist.why: Rights for web, broadcast, paid ads, or a time-limited period affect value. Stating them on the invoice ties payment to the license.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs and pass-throughs
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock footage, fonts, plugins, voiceover talent, music licenses, and render farm fees should be listed separately and match your receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or job code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often cannot process an invoice without a PO or job number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date and file formats handed over
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that work was delivered and accepted, which supports your payment due date.

animation.paymentTerms: A common arrangement is 30 to 50 percent upfront, with the balance at final delivery or split across milestones for larger projects. Many freelancers hold final unwatermarked files until the last payment clears. Direct clients typically get net 15 or net 30 terms, while agencies and studios often pay net 30 to net 60, so confirm this before accepting the job. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if written into the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, wire, check, or card, and international clients may use wire transfer or a payment service with currency conversion fees you should account for.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid
tips.body: Deliver watermarked or low-resolution previews for review, and send the master files, project files, and unwatermarked exports only after final payment. Put this in your contract.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Specify how many rounds are included, what counts as a round, and the hourly rate after that. Changing the script or style after animation starts should be treated as a new scope, not a revision.

tips.title: Charge separately for source files
tips.body: Project files contain your rigs, templates, and techniques. If a client wants them, quote a separate fee, since handing them over can reduce your chance of repeat work.

tips.title: Bill rush and weekend work at a premium
tips.body: Compressed schedules push out other clients. Add a rush percentage as its own line item so the client sees what the deadline costs.

tips.title: Track render and software costs
tips.body: Heavy 3D projects can use cloud render time and paid plugins. Estimate these up front and bill them as expenses or fold them into the rate.

faqs.question: Should I bill animation by the hour or by the project?
faqs.answer: Most clients prefer a fixed project fee or per-second price because it gives them a known budget. Hourly billing works better for open-ended work, small fixes, and ongoing support. If you quote a flat fee, track your hours privately so you can check that the pricing works.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for revisions?
faqs.answer: List the number of revision rounds included in the contract, then bill any additional rounds as a separate line at an hourly rate. Reference the date or version that the client approved so it is clear which changes are outside the original scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge for storyboards and style frames if the client does not move forward?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Many animators bill pre-production as its own milestone with a nonrefundable deposit, so the client pays for the design work even if the project is cancelled.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on animation work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax digital goods or certain creative services, while others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client keeps delaying feedback and the project drags on?
faqs.answer: Put a feedback window in your contract, such as five business days per round, and state that the project may be paused or billed on its next milestone if the delay passes a set date. You can then invoice completed work even if the project is not finished.

estimate.intro: Animators send estimates after a discovery call or brief, often when a client is comparing several studios or freelancers. Clients compare the total price, the style shown in your portfolio, the timeline, and how many revisions are included. A clear estimate makes it easier to defend your price against a lower bid that leaves out important work.

scopeChecklist.item: Finished runtime, aspect ratios, and resolution
scopeChecklist.why: A 60-second video in 16:9 differs in cost from the same video with 1:1 and 9:16 cutdowns. Listing formats prevents surprise requests for extra versions.
Specify 2D, 3D, motion graphics, character rigs, or mixed media, and reference examples so you and the client picture the same result.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies script, voiceover, music, and assets
scopeChecklist.why: Missing scripts or unprovided brand assets are a leading cause of delays and extra charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and approval stages
scopeChecklist.why: Defines when changes are free and when they cost more, and sets approval points at script, storyboard, and animatic stages.
Ties your delivery date to timely feedback so client delays do not become your unpaid time.
Spells out where and for how long the animation can be used, and whether source files are included.
List captions, extra cutdowns, translations, and source files as optional items with prices so they can be added without renegotiation.

pricingTips.title: Quote by milestone
pricingTips.body: Break the quote into script and storyboard, design, animation, and delivery with a price for each. Clients can see what they are paying for, and you get paid as work progresses.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for feedback
pricingTips.body: Add 10 to 20 percent to your time estimate for communication, file management, and small changes that do not count as formal revisions.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting tiers, such as a basic motion graphics version, a custom illustrated version, and a full character animation, helps clients choose a budget without pushing you to cut your rate.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Software costs, your schedule, and asset prices change. A 14 to 30 day validity period keeps you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or pitch?
faqs.answer: A basic estimate is usually free. If a client asks for custom concept art, a test animation, or a detailed pitch, charge a design fee, which you can credit toward the project if they hire you.

faqs.question: How do I price when a client has a fixed budget but a big wish list?
faqs.answer: Ask for the budget early, then propose what fits, such as a shorter runtime, simpler style, or fewer versions. Show the full wish list as optional phases with separate prices.

faqs.question: What happens if the project scope changes after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a change order clause in your agreement. When the client asks for something outside the quote, send a short written change order with the added cost and timeline impact, and get approval before doing the work.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for on a quote?
faqs.answer: Many animators ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront for projects under a few thousand dollars, and use milestone payments for larger projects. The deposit secures your schedule slot and covers early pre-production work.

app-developer.intro: App developers build and maintain iOS, Android, and cross-platform mobile apps for startups, small businesses, agencies, and sometimes other developers. Invoices usually cover discovery and design work, development sprints or milestones, QA and app store submission, and ongoing maintenance or retainer hours after launch.
app-developer.pricingModel: Most independent app developers bill hourly for open-ended or ongoing work, and use fixed-price milestones for projects with a clear scope. Hourly billing suits feature work, bug fixes, and projects where requirements will change. Fixed-price bids work when you have written specs and screens, and they are usually split into milestones such as discovery, design approval, beta build, and App Store release, with a deposit up front. After launch, many developers move clients to a monthly retainer that covers OS updates, dependency upgrades, crash monitoring, and a set number of support hours. Third-party costs such as Apple Developer Program fees, Google Play fees, cloud hosting, push notification services, and paid SDK licenses are typically passed through at cost, or billed to the client's own accounts directly. Rates rise with specialization, such as native Swift or Kotlin, health or fintech compliance, or Bluetooth and hardware integration.

rates.service: Senior or specialist developer (native, architecture, security)
App Store / Google Play submission and release setup
Monthly maintenance retainer (updates, monitoring, bug fixes)
Code audit or app rescue review

items.description: Milestone 2: Core features build (user login, profile, push notifications) - iOS
Backend API integration (REST, Stripe subscriptions)
QA testing and bug fixes on TestFlight build 0.9
App Store submission, metadata, and screenshots setup
Third-party: push notification service plan (April, at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Accepted by ACH or card. Source code and App Store Connect transfer occur upon final payment per the signed agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone or sprint reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to the signed scope or statement of work so the client's accounts payable team can approve it without questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by task type (development, QA, meetings, design)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on hourly billing often ask what the time went to, and a breakdown heads off disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Build or version numbers and release dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which deliverable the charge covers, such as TestFlight build 0.9 or version 1.0 release.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party and platform costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Apple and Google fees, hosting, and SDK licenses should be visible as pass-through costs, not buried in your rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change requests with reference to the approval
invoiceChecklist.why: Work outside the original scope should point to the written change order or email that approved it.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size and enterprise clients often will not pay without a purchase order number on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: IP and handover terms
invoiceChecklist.why: A line noting that code ownership or account transfer happens on full payment reinforces the contract and gives you leverage on unpaid balances.

app-developer.paymentTerms: Developers commonly collect 30 to 50 percent upfront on fixed-price projects, then bill remaining milestones on approval, with final payment due before the app is published or the source code is handed over. Hourly clients are usually invoiced biweekly or monthly in arrears, and retainers are billed at the start of the month. Net 14 or net 15 is common for small clients, while larger companies often require net 30. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. ACH and wire transfers are preferred for large amounts, while cards work for smaller invoices if you accept the processing fee.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not dates
tips.body: App projects slip because of client feedback delays, App Store review times, and changing requirements. Billing on approved milestones keeps your cash flow from depending on a launch date you do not fully control.

tips.title: Keep client accounts in the client's name
tips.body: Ask clients to create their own Apple Developer and Google Play accounts and add you as a team member. This avoids messy transfers later and keeps platform fees off your invoices.

tips.title: Price change requests separately and in writing
tips.body: Scope creep is the main cause of unpaid overruns in app work. Use a short change order with an hour estimate, and get written approval before starting.

tips.title: Charge for post-launch support
tips.body: Bug fixes after launch, new iOS and Android versions, and library updates keep arriving. Offer a maintenance retainer or define a short warranty period, such as 30 days, after which support is billed.

tips.title: Hold final deliverables until paid
tips.body: Do not submit to the store or hand over the repository and signing keys until the last invoice is settled, unless your contract says otherwise.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or fixed-price for app development?
faqs.answer: Bill hourly when the scope is unclear or likely to change, and fixed-price when you have detailed specs and designs. Many developers combine both, using a fixed fee for the defined build and hourly rates for changes and support.

faqs.question: Can I invoice for time spent in meetings and project management?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many developers bill calls, planning sessions, and code reviews at their normal rate or a slightly reduced one. List them as a separate line so clients can see them.

faqs.question: Who pays for Apple and Google developer account fees?
faqs.answer: The client should, and ideally on their own accounts. If you pay for something on their behalf, such as a hosting plan, invoice it at cost with a receipt and state in your contract whether you add a markup.

faqs.question: What if a client stops paying after I have delivered a build?
faqs.answer: Pause further work, send a written reminder citing the contract terms and late fee, and withhold store submission, source code, and signing keys if your contract allows it. For larger amounts, consider a demand letter or small claims court, depending on your state's limits.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on app development?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether the deliverable is treated as custom software, a service, or a digital product. Some states tax custom software or SaaS and others do not, so check your state's rules or ask an accountant.

estimate.intro: App developers send quotes after an initial call or discovery session, when the client has an idea, wireframes, or an existing app they want changed. Clients usually compare your quote against agencies, other freelancers, and offshore teams, so they look closely at what is included, what platforms are covered, and what happens after launch.

scopeChecklist.why: iOS only, iOS and Android, tablets, and minimum OS versions all change the cost, so state exactly which are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Feature list with screens or user flows
scopeChecklist.why: A written list of features tied to designs or wireframes gives both sides something to check against if the client later says a feature was assumed.
Clarify whether the client provides finished UI designs or you create them, and how many rounds of revisions are included.
State whether you build the API and database, use a service like Firebase, or integrate with the client's existing systems, and who pays for those services.
Specify the devices you will test on, the number of beta rounds, and whether App Store and Google Play submission and review rejections are included.
List when you need assets, API access, and feedback, and note that delays on the client side move the schedule and may affect pricing.
Define the warranty period for bugs, the rate for later work, and when code ownership transfers.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in ranges tied to phases
pricingTips.body: Early quotes are guesses. Give a range per phase, such as discovery, build, and release, and firm up the build price after discovery when requirements are clear.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for integrations and store review
pricingTips.body: Third-party APIs, payment flows, and App Store rejections regularly take longer than planned. Build 15 to 25 percent contingency into your hours or state that overruns are billed hourly.

pricingTips.title: Offer a smaller first phase
pricingTips.body: Proposing a paid discovery or a minimal first release lowers the client's risk and gets you paid for the work that most improves your later estimate.

pricingTips.title: List exclusions explicitly
pricingTips.body: State what is not included, such as content creation, marketing, ongoing hosting, and features outside the list. Clients compare quotes line by line, and clear exclusions explain a higher price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: For small jobs a free quote is normal. For anything requiring technical research, a prototype, or detailed specs, charge for discovery. Many developers credit the fee toward the build if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Rates, availability, and platform requirements change, so put an expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: For hourly work, say the estimate is not a cap and warn the client when you reach about 80 percent of the hours. For fixed-price work, absorb overruns caused by your own errors and bill approved change orders for new requirements.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Thirty to fifty percent of the first phase or of the total fixed price is typical. Larger projects often use a smaller initial deposit followed by milestone payments.

appliance-repair.intro: Appliance repair technicians diagnose and fix household and light commercial appliances such as washers, dryers, refrigerators, dishwashers, ovens, and ranges. Most are solo operators or small shops that bill for a diagnostic or service call fee, labor, and replacement parts. Invoices are usually issued on the spot at the end of the visit, so they need to be clear about what was found, what was replaced, and what is covered by warranty.
appliance-repair.pricingModel: Most appliance repair businesses charge a service call (diagnostic) fee to cover travel and troubleshooting, then add labor and parts. Many apply the diagnostic fee toward the repair if the customer approves the work the same day. Labor is billed either hourly (often with a one-hour minimum) or as a flat rate per repair based on a standard price book. Parts are marked up from cost, commonly 20-50% on smaller parts and less on expensive ones like compressors, control boards, and motors. Sealed system work on refrigerators, gas appliance work, and commercial equipment usually carries higher rates. Many shops add a trip surcharge for distant addresses, and some charge more for same-day, evening, or weekend calls. Offering a labor warranty (commonly 30 to 90 days) and a longer parts warranty where the manufacturer allows is standard.

rates.service: Common repair labor (belt, igniter, door gasket, drain pump)
Control board or motor replacement labor

items.description: Service call and diagnostic - front-load washer not draining
Drain pump assembly (OEM)
Replace drain pump and clear clogged hose
Replace door boot clamp
Diagnostic fee credit (repair approved same day)

sampleInvoice.notes: Work performed on 6/12. 90-day warranty on labor and 1-year warranty on the replaced part, excluding damage from misuse or foreign objects. Payment due at time of service. Cards, checks, and cash accepted. Model and serial number: see description.

invoiceChecklist.item: Appliance make, model number, and serial number
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly what you serviced, supports parts warranty claims, and protects you if the same unit fails later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reported problem and what you found
invoiceChecklist.why: A short description of the complaint and your diagnosis shows the customer what they paid for and backs you up in a dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with part numbers and whether OEM or aftermarket
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers and warranty providers often ask for part numbers, and it makes returns and warranty replacements easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor warranty and parts warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out the coverage period and exclusions in writing heads off arguments when a problem returns.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnostic fee and whether it was credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often assume the fee applies toward the repair. Showing the credit line, or its absence, avoids confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charges, after-hours surcharges, or disposal fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Add-ons that were not on the quote should be listed separately so they are not mistaken for padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or registration number and EPA 608 certification where it applies
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states or cities require appliance or contractor registration, and refrigerant work requires EPA certification. Check your local rules for what must appear on paperwork.

appliance-repair.paymentTerms: Most residential appliance repair is paid at the time of service, by card, check, or cash, and many technicians collect before leaving the home. Deposits are common when a part must be special ordered, often covering the part cost or 50% of the estimate, with the balance due on completion. For landlords, property managers, and commercial accounts, net 15 or net 30 terms are typical, with a PO number referenced on the invoice. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month on unpaid balances is common for account customers, but state it in writing before the work begins. For warranty work billed to a third party (home warranty companies or manufacturers), expect a longer payment cycle and keep their authorization number on every invoice.

tips.title: Credit the diagnostic fee only on approved repairs
tips.body: Tell the customer before you start that the diagnostic fee applies toward the repair if they approve it that day. It encourages same-day approval and keeps the fee from becoming a complaint if they decline.

tips.title: Get approval before ordering or installing parts
tips.body: Quote the part and labor total after diagnosis and get a signature or written confirmation. Do this especially when the repair cost approaches the price of a replacement unit, which is often when customers push back on the bill.

tips.title: Take deposits on special-order parts
tips.body: If you order a $250 control board and the customer then cancels, you are stuck with the part. A deposit equal to the part cost protects you, and restocking terms should be on the quote.

tips.title: Keep a written price book
tips.body: A flat-rate book for common repairs makes pricing consistent, speeds up quoting at the door, and makes it easier to explain charges. Review it each year as parts costs change.

tips.title: Track home warranty jobs separately
tips.body: Home warranty companies set their own labor rates and often require authorization numbers and photos. Bill them per their rules and keep records, since disputes and denied claims are common.

faqs.question: Can I charge a diagnostic fee if the customer does not approve the repair?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most places, as long as you disclosed the fee before you started. Tell the customer on the phone when booking and confirm it again at the door. Put the fee on the invoice even if they decline the repair.

faqs.question: How long should my repair warranty be?
faqs.answer: Thirty to ninety days on labor is typical for independent technicians, and some offer six months or a year. Parts warranties often follow the manufacturer's terms, commonly 90 days to one year. Write the terms on every invoice.

faqs.question: Should I itemize parts on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. List each part with its part number and price. Customers, landlords, and warranty companies expect it, and it reduces questions about what you replaced.

faqs.question: Do I have to charge sales tax on appliance repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax parts only, some tax labor and parts, and some tax neither for repairs. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant and show tax as its own line if it applies.

faqs.question: What do I do when a customer refuses to pay after the repair?
faqs.answer: Start with a written invoice that shows the approved work and warranty terms, then follow up in writing. Signed approvals and photos of the finished work help. For larger unpaid balances, small claims court is a common next step, and rules vary by state.

estimate.intro: Appliance repair is often quoted after the diagnostic, when you know the failed part and the labor involved. Customers are comparing your price against a competitor's quote and against the cost of buying a new unit. A clear written estimate with a firm repair price helps you win the job and avoids disputes at payment.

scopeChecklist.item: Appliance make, model, and serial number
scopeChecklist.why: The same symptom can need different parts across models, and the quote should be tied to the specific unit you inspected.

scopeChecklist.item: Diagnosed cause and the exact repair proposed
scopeChecklist.why: Naming the failed component keeps the scope clear and prevents the customer from assuming other issues are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts cost, part numbers, and OEM or aftermarket
scopeChecklist.why: Customers want to know what is going into their appliance, and the choice affects price and warranty.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor charge as flat fee or hourly with an estimated time
scopeChecklist.why: A set price avoids surprises, while an hourly quote should state a cap or estimate range.

scopeChecklist.item: Diagnostic fee and how it is applied
scopeChecklist.why: State whether the fee is credited toward the repair or charged separately so the total is not a surprise.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts lead time and deposit terms
scopeChecklist.why: If the part must be ordered, the customer needs to know the wait and what they owe up front.
Stating the labor and parts warranty on the quote sets expectations and is a selling point against competitors who do not offer one.

pricingTips.title: Quote a firm price after diagnosis
pricingTips.body: Do not guess over the phone beyond the service call fee and a general range. Once you have found the failure, give a fixed price for parts and labor so the customer can decide on the spot.

pricingTips.title: Be honest about repair versus replace
pricingTips.body: If the repair cost is more than about half the price of a comparable new appliance, say so. Customers remember honest advice and refer you, even when you lose the repair.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, and best when parts allow
pricingTips.body: Where both OEM and quality aftermarket parts exist, quote both with different prices and warranty terms. It gives the customer a choice and often raises the average ticket.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Parts prices change, and a quote left open for months can leave you underwater. Thirty days is a common window for written estimates.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most appliance technicians charge the diagnostic fee, since the diagnosis is the main cost of the visit. Free estimates are usually only offered for installations or for replacing obviously failed items. Whatever you choose, tell the customer before you come out.

faqs.question: Can the final bill be higher than my estimate?
faqs.answer: Only if you get the customer's approval first. If you find a second failed part, stop, explain it, and give a revised quote in writing or by text before continuing. Many states have rules on how far a final bill can exceed an estimate, so check yours.

faqs.question: How do I quote a repair when I need to order a part?
faqs.answer: Quote the part price and labor based on the supplier's current price, note the lead time, and collect a deposit when the customer approves. Say clearly what happens if the part arrives and does not fix the problem or the customer cancels.

faqs.question: Is a verbal quote enough?
faqs.answer: It is legal in many situations, but a written or texted quote is far better. A written record with the model number, repair, and price settles most disputes in your favor. Some states require written estimates above a certain dollar amount, so check your local rules.

arborist.intro: Arborists are tree care professionals who prune, remove, plant, assess, and treat trees for homeowners, property managers, HOAs, and municipalities. Solo arborists and small crews bill for tree removal, crown work, stump grinding, cabling and bracing, plant health care, and consulting reports. Many jobs involve climbing or aerial lift work, a ground crew, a chipper, and debris hauling, so invoices need to show both labor and equipment.
arborist.pricingModel: Most residential tree work is priced as a flat fee per job based on tree size, species, access, hazards, and cleanup. Crews often estimate internally from crew-hours and equipment time, then quote one price. Hourly crew rates are common for storm work, small pruning jobs, and commercial or utility-type contracts, usually billed per crew or per person with equipment listed separately. Stump grinding is typically priced per inch of stump diameter with a minimum charge. Consulting work such as tree risk assessments, appraisal letters, and arborist reports is billed hourly or as a flat report fee. Plant health care, such as fertilization, soil injections, and pest treatments, is often priced per tree, per inch of trunk diameter, or per visit. Extras like crane rental, bucket truck, wood chip delivery, log hauling, and permit fees are usually listed as separate line items or passed through at cost with a markup.

rates.service: Tree removal, small to medium (under 40 ft)
Tree removal, large or hazardous (over 60 ft, near structures)
Crew labor (climber plus ground crew with chipper)
Tree risk assessment or arborist report

items.description: Removal of 55 ft red oak, rear yard, rigged in sections over garage; includes brush chipping and log cut-up
Crown cleaning and deadwood removal, silver maple (front yard)
Stump grinding, 28 in. oak stump, 8 in. below grade
Bucket truck, rear access
Haul away of logs and debris (dump fee included)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on cards). Stump grinding leaves wood chips in the hole; fill soil not included. Work completed June 12 per signed estimate dated June 3. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and tree location on the property
invoiceChecklist.why: Properties often have several trees, and clients need to match each charge to a specific tree, such as 'rear oak' versus 'front maple'.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tree species, size, and work performed per tree
invoiceChecklist.why: Species and diameter drive the price. Listing them backs up the charge and helps if an insurer or HOA asks for records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment used and hours (bucket truck, crane, chipper, grinder)
invoiceChecklist.why: Equipment is a major cost. Itemizing it explains the price and supports hourly or minimum charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate or work order, plus any change orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden hazards like wires, rot, or extra trees can change the scope. Tying the invoice to the agreement prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cleanup and disposal terms (haul away, wood left on site, chip drop)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume cleanup is included. State what was hauled, what was left, and any dump fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: ISA certification number and license or insurance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients and property managers need proof of credentials. Some states and cities require tree care or pesticide applicator licenses, so check local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit fees or utility coordination charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Some municipalities require permits to remove protected or street trees. Pass-through costs should be shown separately.

arborist.paymentTerms: For residential jobs, many arborists invoice on completion with payment due on receipt or within 7 to 14 days. Larger jobs, especially crane work, often require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover equipment booking. Commercial, HOA, and municipal clients commonly pay net 30, sometimes with a purchase order number required. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance on the estimate. Payment methods typically include check, ACH, and card, and some crews collect payment on site at the end of the job. Storm cleanup is often billed at hourly rates with payment due the same day.

tips.title: Get payment before the crew leaves on one-day jobs
tips.body: Residential removals are physically finished the moment the truck leaves. Collect payment or send the invoice from the driveway while the homeowner can still see the work done.

tips.title: Write the access and hazard conditions into the estimate
tips.body: Power lines, fences, septic tanks, steep slopes, and tight access all affect time and risk. Noting them gives you grounds to adjust the price with a change order if conditions differ.

tips.title: Charge minimums on small jobs
tips.body: Mobilizing a truck, chipper, and crew has a fixed cost. A minimum of 2 hours or a stated minimum job fee keeps a $150 pruning job from losing money.

tips.title: Separate crane, disposal, and permits from labor
tips.body: These costs often come from subcontractors or third parties. Listing them separately makes it easy to pass them through accurately and explain the total.

tips.title: Keep before and after photos with the invoice
tips.body: Photos of the completed work resolve complaints about cleanup or the wrong tree being cut, and they help if a neighbor or insurer disputes the work.

faqs.question: Should I bill tree removal by the hour or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Most residential removals are a flat fee because homeowners want a firm number. Use hourly billing for storm cleanup, unclear scope, or contract work where the amount of work is hard to predict, and state the crew rate and minimum clearly.

faqs.question: How do I charge for stump grinding?
faqs.answer: The usual method is per inch of stump diameter measured at the widest point above ground, with a minimum charge. Add extra for multiple stumps, large surface roots, hard-to-reach locations, or grinding deeper than the standard depth.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on tree work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain landscaping or tree services, while others tax only materials or nothing at all. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client wants more trees done than the estimate covered?
faqs.answer: Stop and get written approval for the added work, even a text or email, then add it as a change order line on the invoice. Doing extra work on a verbal request is the most common source of payment disputes.

faqs.question: Can I bill for wood or chips left on the property?
faqs.answer: You can, but most arborists include chipping and basic cut-up in the price. If you deliver chips elsewhere, haul logs, or sell firewood, list those as separate items or credits. Be clear whether the client keeps the wood.

estimate.intro: Arborists quote before nearly every job, usually after an on-site visit to look at the tree, access, and hazards. Homeowners often collect two or three quotes and compare the total price, but also insurance coverage, cleanup, and what is included. A clear written quote helps you win work without being the cheapest.

scopeChecklist.item: Each tree identified by species, size, and location
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids confusion about which trees are included. Marking trees with a photo or site sketch is even better.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact work for each tree (removal, crown reduction, thinning, deadwooding)
scopeChecklist.why: Pruning terms mean different things to different clients. Specify how much will be removed and to what standard, such as ANSI A300 practices.
Clarify whether you chip, haul, leave logs, or leave wood chips. This is a top source of complaints.

scopeChecklist.item: Stump grinding included or excluded, and depth
scopeChecklist.why: Many clients assume stump removal is included with tree removal. State whether it is, and whether you backfill or remove roots.
If you plan to use a crane, bucket truck, or lawn protection mats, note it. If access changes, the price may change.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, utility clearance, and who handles them
scopeChecklist.why: Protected trees and street trees may need permits. Power lines may require the utility company, which can delay the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Insurance, license, validity period, and scheduling terms
scopeChecklist.why: Show liability and workers' compensation coverage. A quote expiration date, such as 30 days, protects you from price changes.

pricingTips.title: Price from crew-hours, then add equipment and risk
pricingTips.body: Estimate how long the crew will take, multiply by your crew rate, and add equipment, disposal, and a margin for hazards. Trees near structures or lines deserve a higher margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer options on larger jobs
pricingTips.body: Present pricing for removal with and without stump grinding, or full crown reduction versus lighter thinning. Options help clients choose without shopping for a lower bid.

pricingTips.title: Explain what makes your price different
pricingTips.body: If you carry full insurance, use certified climbers, and protect the lawn, say so in the quote. Clients comparing a low bid from an uninsured crew need to see the difference.

pricingTips.title: Visit the site before quoting anything over a small job
pricingTips.body: Photos can hide leaning trees, dead limbs, and tight access. Quoting sight unseen leads to underpricing or arguments about extras.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most arborists give free estimates for removal and pruning. Charge for formal tree risk assessments, written reports, appraisals, and consulting, since these take time and carry professional liability.

faqs.question: How long should a tree work quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Fuel, labor, and equipment costs change, and a tree's condition can worsen after a storm, so avoid open-ended quotes.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A signed estimate or written acceptance by email shows the agreed scope and price, and it protects both sides if there is a dispute over which trees or what cleanup was included.

faqs.question: What if I find something unexpected once the work starts?
faqs.answer: Rot, hidden wires, extra dead limbs, or weak anchor points can change the job. Include a line in the estimate that hidden conditions may require a revised price, and get approval before continuing.

architect.intro: Architects, from solo practitioners to small firms, bill clients for design services delivered in phases: programming, schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, and construction administration. Invoices usually go to homeowners, developers, contractors, or commercial owners, and tie billing to project phases or hours worked, plus reimbursable expenses like printing, permit fees, and consultant costs.
architect.pricingModel: Architects price in a few common ways. A percentage of construction cost is traditional, often 8-15% for residential and 5-12% for commercial, with the percentage shifting by project complexity. A fixed fee per phase is common for well-defined scopes, with the total split across phases such as schematic design (15%), design development (20%), construction documents (40%), bidding (5%), and construction administration (20%). Hourly billing is used for small projects, feasibility studies, as-built drawings, and additional services, with different rates for principal, project architect, designer, and drafter. Reimbursable expenses (plots, printing, courier, travel, permit and filing fees) are billed at cost or cost plus a markup of 10-15%. Subconsultants such as structural, MEP, civil, and landscape engineers are usually billed through at cost plus a markup, or contracted directly by the owner. Most architects start with a signed agreement (often an AIA or similar form) and an initial retainer that is credited against the final phase invoice.

rates.service: Existing conditions survey and as-built drawings
Permit set / construction documents, small addition

items.description: Construction documents phase, kitchen and primary suite addition (60% billed of phase fee $9,000)
Principal time: owner meeting and revisions to floor plan (additional service)
Structural engineer coordination, subconsultant pass-through (Invoice #2218) plus 10% markup
Large-format plots and printing, 6 sets of 24x36 drawings
City permit application filing fee (reimbursable at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Martinez Residence Addition, Contract dated March 4. Phase billing per Section 4 of the agreement. Additional services authorized by email on April 2. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Retainer of $2,500 has been applied to the final invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, address, and contract date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the signed agreement so the client or lender can match it to the scope and fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Phase and percentage complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Phase billing relies on stated completion, so showing the phase fee, percent billed, and amount billed to date prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Additional services listed separately with authorization date
invoiceChecklist.why: Work outside the base agreement is the most common source of fee disagreements, so documenting who approved it protects you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts or backup
invoiceChecklist.why: Permit fees, printing, and courier costs are billed at cost or with a markup, and clients often ask to see the receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subconsultant charges with their invoice reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Engineers' fees can be large, and showing the pass-through and any markup keeps it transparent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Architect license number and firm name, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require licensed firms to show registration details on professional documents; check your state board's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fees billed to date, retainer applied, and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Running totals let owners, lenders, and bookkeepers see where the project stands against the contract fee.

architect.paymentTerms: Architects typically collect an initial retainer of 5-15% of the estimated fee or a fixed amount like $2,500-5,000 at signing, which is often credited against the final invoice. After that, invoices go out monthly or at the end of each phase, usually due in 15 to 30 days. Many agreements include a late charge of 1-1.5% per month and the right to pause work if invoices go unpaid. Commercial and institutional clients may require a purchase order number and pay on net 30 to net 60. Payment is commonly accepted by check, ACH, or wire, and by card for smaller amounts, though card fees are sometimes passed along or discouraged for large invoices.

tips.title: Bill monthly against phase percentage complete
tips.body: Waiting until a phase ends can leave you carrying weeks of unpaid work. Billing monthly on percent complete keeps cash flow steady, especially during construction documents when most hours are spent.

tips.title: Put additional services in writing before doing the work
tips.body: Changes to scope, extra revisions, and new design directions should get a short written authorization with a fee or hourly cap. Then invoice them as a separate line so the base contract stays clean.

tips.title: Tie the final payments to deliverables
tips.body: Hold back the last part of a phase fee until the drawing set, permit submission, or sealed documents are delivered. Release stamped documents only when invoices are current, as your agreement allows.

tips.title: Track hours even on fixed-fee jobs
tips.body: Time records show whether your fee was right and give you a basis for pricing change orders. They also help if a client disputes additional services.

tips.title: Mark up consultants and reimbursables consistently
tips.body: State your markup policy in the agreement, typically 10-15%, and apply it the same way on every invoice. It covers your coordination time and the risk of carrying their costs.

faqs.question: Should I bill as a percentage of construction cost or a fixed fee?
faqs.answer: Percentage works when scope is hard to define up front, but it ties your income to the final construction budget, which can shift. A fixed fee per phase gives the client certainty and suits clear scopes. Many architects use a fixed fee based on an estimated percentage, then adjust through written change orders.

faqs.question: Can I charge for site visits during construction?
faqs.answer: Yes. Construction administration is usually its own phase, billed hourly, per visit, or as a fixed monthly amount. Define the number of included visits in the agreement and bill extra visits, RFIs, and submittal reviews as additional services.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the client delays the project?
faqs.answer: Include a clause stating that if a project is paused beyond a set time, such as 60 or 90 days, you may invoice for work completed and may re-price remaining work. Then bill for the percent complete at the time of the pause.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on architectural services?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional design services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states or localities tax certain services or printed deliverables. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do about a client who won't pay the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder referencing the agreement's late charge and any clause allowing you to withhold sealed documents. If it continues, consider a demand letter or small claims or civil action. In some states, design professionals may also have lien rights on the property, so check local rules quickly because deadlines are strict.

estimate.intro: Architects usually send a fee proposal or estimate after an initial consultation and site visit, and before a contract is signed. Clients typically compare fees across two or three firms, so the proposal needs to make clear exactly which phases, deliverables, and number of meetings are included, not just the total number.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume you cover everything from sketches to final inspection. State which of the phases you are including, such as schematic design through construction administration.
Listing items such as floor plans, elevations, a 3D model, permit drawings, and specifications prevents arguments over what a completed set looks like.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of design revisions and meetings
scopeChecklist.why: Unlimited revisions are the biggest threat to fixed fees. Specify how many rounds of changes and client meetings are included.
Structural, MEP, civil, geotechnical, and surveying work are often separate costs. Say who hires them and whether their fees are in your number.
If your fee depends on a budget or square footage, state those assumptions so you can adjust the fee if the project grows.
Clients should know that printing, travel, and government fees are billed separately, and whether you mark them up.
Interior design, furniture selection, renderings, zoning appeals, and extended construction administration should be listed as extras with hourly rates.

pricingTips.title: Break the fee into phases
pricingTips.body: A phase-by-phase fee table shows clients what they are paying for, lets them stop after schematic design if needed, and gives you natural billing points.

pricingTips.title: Check your fixed fee against hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours by role for each phase, multiply by your rates, and compare with the percentage-of-cost figure. If the two are far apart, revisit your assumptions before sending the proposal.

pricingTips.title: Add contingency for unknowns on renovations
pricingTips.body: Existing buildings often hide problems that need additional measuring or redesign. Include an allowance for existing conditions work or make it hourly until the site is understood.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fees depend on your workload and on how costs are changing. Valid for 30 days is common, and it encourages decisions without pressure.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many architects offer a short free introductory meeting, then charge for site visits, feasibility studies, or zoning research. Credit the paid work against the fee if the client signs a full agreement.

faqs.question: What if the construction bids come in higher than the client's budget?
faqs.answer: Your proposal should say whether redesign to meet budget is included. Many agreements treat redesign after bidding as additional service unless the budget was set and agreed in writing before design began.

faqs.question: Is a fee proposal the same as a contract?
faqs.answer: No. A proposal outlines scope and price, while an agreement adds legal terms such as ownership of drawings, liability, termination, and payment terms. Many architects attach the proposal to a standard agreement form and have the client sign both.

art-director.intro: Freelance and small-studio art directors lead the visual direction of campaigns, brands, photo and video shoots, packaging, editorial projects, and websites. They invoice agencies, in-house marketing teams, and direct clients for concept development, creative direction, shoot supervision, and oversight of designers, photographers, and illustrators.
art-director.pricingModel: Most freelance art directors charge a day rate or hourly rate for ongoing or flexible work, and a flat project fee for defined deliverables like a campaign concept or brand look-and-feel. Day rates are usually based on an 8-hour day, with half-days offered at a slightly higher proportional rate. Shoot days are often billed as full days regardless of length, since prep and wrap-up surround them. Longer engagements are sometimes set up as monthly retainers with a fixed number of days. Third-party costs such as stock imagery, prop and wardrobe purchases, location fees, printing, and contracted freelancers are billed separately as pass-through expenses, often with a 10 to 20 percent handling markup agreed in advance. Usage or licensing fees may apply when you create original artwork that the client will use beyond the agreed scope. Rush work, weekends, and extra revision rounds are commonly billed at 1.5x to 2x.

rates.service: Campaign concept development and mood boards
Photo or video shoot direction on set

items.description: Concept development and mood boards, spring product campaign (2 directions)
Photographer and stylist sourcing, shot list, and pre-production
On-set art direction, studio shoot day
Retouching direction and final image selection
Props and backdrops purchased for shoot (receipts attached)
Handling fee on props and backdrops

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. The 50 percent deposit paid on signing has been applied to the balance. Final images are licensed for web and social use for 24 months per the signed agreement. A 1.5 percent monthly fee applies to overdue balances.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and reference to the signed estimate or agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and price, which settles most questions about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number and client contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often will not process payment without a PO or the name of the approving person.

invoiceChecklist.item: Breakdown by phase (concept, pre-production, shoot, post)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows clients where the time went and makes it easier to bill in stages on long projects.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot and meeting dates with days or hours worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports day-rate billing and prevents disputes over whether a half-day or full day was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized pass-through expenses with receipts and any markup
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see exactly what you bought or contracted for them, and a clear markup line avoids surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when extra rounds fall outside scope and justifies additional charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage and licensing terms for delivered work
invoiceChecklist.why: States how long and where the client can use original creative, and what extended usage would cost.

art-director.paymentTerms: Art directors commonly require a 30 to 50 percent deposit before starting, with the balance due at completion or in milestone payments such as concept approval, shoot wrap, and final delivery. Net 15 or net 30 is standard for direct clients, while agencies and large companies may insist on net 45 or net 60, so confirm this before signing. Retainers are typically invoiced at the start of each month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your agreement. ACH transfer, check, and card payments are all widely used, and ACH is usually cheapest for large invoices. Final files or unwatermarked deliverables are often released only once the last payment clears.

tips.title: Bill shoot days as full days
tips.body: Prep, travel, and wrap-up surround any shoot, and the day is rarely usable for other clients. Set a full-day minimum in your agreement so a short shoot does not turn into a partial payment.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Art direction involves a lot of subjective feedback. Include two or three rounds in the quote and bill additional rounds hourly, and record each round on the invoice when it goes over.

tips.title: Mark up and document pass-through costs
tips.body: When you hire photographers, stylists, or printers on the client's behalf, you carry the cost until they pay. Agree on a handling fee up front, attach receipts, and consider asking the client to pay large vendor costs directly or in advance.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not only at the end
tips.body: Concept approval, shoot completion, and final delivery are natural billing points. Staged invoices keep cash coming in and reduce the risk of a large unpaid balance on a long project.

tips.title: Track overages against the estimate
tips.body: Keep a simple log of hours and days used. If scope grows, send a change note before billing so the higher invoice is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Should I charge a day rate or a project fee?
faqs.answer: Use a day rate when scope is loose, the client controls the schedule, or the work is ongoing. Use a project fee when deliverables are well defined, such as a campaign concept or brand direction. Even with a project fee, estimate your days internally to check that the price is worthwhile.

faqs.question: Can I charge for creative work that was not chosen?
faqs.answer: Yes. Concept development is the work, whether or not the client picks that direction. State in your agreement that the fee covers presenting a set number of concepts, and that unused concepts remain yours unless purchased.

faqs.question: How do I bill when I hire other freelancers for the client?
faqs.answer: List each contractor's cost as a separate line item with their invoice attached, plus your agreed handling fee. Make sure the agreement says who is responsible if the client is late paying, since you may owe the contractor regardless.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on art direction?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax pure services, but some tax certain creative or tangible deliverables like printed materials. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax you collect as a separate line.

faqs.question: What if a client delays a project after I have reserved dates?
faqs.answer: Include a cancellation or rescheduling clause that lets you keep the deposit or charge a fee for dates held, particularly for shoot days. Without it, you have little ground to bill for lost time.

estimate.intro: Art directors send estimates when a client is planning a campaign, shoot, rebrand, or website and wants to compare costs before committing. Clients often compare you against other freelancers, agencies, or an in-house hire, so the quote needs to show clearly what the creative direction covers and what it does not.

scopeChecklist.why: Lists exactly what you will produce, such as mood boards, creative briefs, shot lists, style guides, or final approved layouts, so no one assumes more is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Creative feedback can go on forever without a cap. State how many directions and rounds are included and what extra rounds cost.
Clarifies how many days you will be on set, who books talent and locations, and whether you are managing vendors or only directing.

scopeChecklist.item: Production budget and who pays vendors
scopeChecklist.why: Photographers, retouchers, models, stylists, and printers can cost more than your fee. Say whether these are estimated separately and who pays them.
Defines where and how long the client can use the work, and whether source files, unused concepts, or raw assets transfer.
Ties your schedule to the client providing feedback and assets on time, and protects you when delays push the project out.
Sets out the fees for compressed schedules, moved shoot dates, or scope changes so they are agreed before they happen.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from days, then check it
pricingTips.body: List each phase and estimate the days it needs, including meetings, feedback, and admin time. Multiply by your day rate, then compare against a flat fee that reflects the value of the work to the client.

pricingTips.title: Separate fees from production costs
pricingTips.body: Show your creative fee in one section and estimated third-party costs in another. This makes your price easier to compare and keeps you from absorbing vendor overruns.

pricingTips.title: Offer options when budgets are unclear
pricingTips.body: Present a core package and an expanded one, such as two shoot days versus one or a full brand guide versus a short style sheet. Clients often pick the middle option and see the tradeoffs.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency line for production
pricingTips.body: Shoots and print jobs commonly run over. Including a 10 percent contingency, or stating that costs above the estimate need written approval, protects your margin and the client's budget.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or a range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed fee for your own creative work when the scope is clear. For production costs you do not control, give a range or an estimate with a stated cap, and ask for approval before exceeding it.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Vendor and talent pricing, as well as your own availability, can change, so state an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is it okay to charge for preparing a proposal?
faqs.answer: Short proposals are usually free. If the client wants detailed concepts, mood boards, or a pitch presentation, charge a paid discovery or concept fee, which can be credited toward the project if they hire you.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before I start?
faqs.answer: Yes, whenever possible. A signed estimate or agreement with a deposit confirms the scope, the price, and the usage terms, and gives you something to point to if the project changes.

asbestos-removal.intro: Asbestos removal contractors are licensed abatement companies, often owner-operated or small crews, that remove or encapsulate asbestos-containing materials (ACM) in homes, schools, and commercial buildings. Invoices typically cover containment setup, removal labor, air monitoring, waste disposal, and clearance testing, often tied to a renovation or demolition schedule.
asbestos-removal.pricingModel: Most residential abatement is priced as a flat fee per project based on a site survey and lab results, then broken out by material: per square foot for floor tile, popcorn ceiling, and siding, and per linear foot for pipe insulation. Larger or commercial jobs are often bid as a lump sum or on unit prices with a schedule of values and progress billing. Time-and-materials hourly rates apply to emergency response, change orders, and unexpected discoveries. Containment setup, negative air machine rental, disposal (bagged waste, manifests, landfill fees), and permit or notification fees are commonly itemized or built into the unit price. Many contractors set a minimum job charge of $1,500-$3,000 to cover mobilization, setup, and decontamination regardless of how small the removal is. Third-party air monitoring and clearance testing are usually billed by an independent consultant, so decide whether you pass those through at cost or let the client pay the consultant directly.

rates.service: Vinyl floor tile and mastic removal
Pipe insulation removal (glovebag or small containment)
Containment setup and negative air (small residential)
Waste packaging, transport, and landfill disposal

items.description: Mobilization, containment setup (poly sheeting, decon unit, negative air machines), 1st-floor kitchen
Removal of 9x9 asbestos vinyl floor tile and mastic, kitchen and hallway
Removal of pipe insulation (basement, 3-inch lines), glovebag method
Abatement crew labor, additional hours for discovered tile under subfloor layer (change order #1)
Waste bagging, manifest, transport, and landfill disposal
State notification and permit fee (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $2,000 received at contract signing, applied to this invoice. Balance due within 14 days of passing final clearance air test. Waste manifest copies attached. Clearance sampling billed separately by the independent consultant. Late balances are subject to 1.5% monthly interest.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and certification numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Most states require abatement contractors to be licensed, and clients, insurers, and inspectors want proof on the paperwork.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and scope by material and area
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each ACM type (tile, mastic, pipe wrap, ceiling texture) and location prevents disputes about what was and was not removed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantities in sq ft or linear ft with unit prices
invoiceChecklist.why: Unit pricing makes change orders and measured-quantity adjustments transparent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders with signed approval references
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden ACM found mid-job is common, and referencing the signed change order protects you when the total exceeds the original bid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Waste disposal details and manifest numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Disposal is regulated, and clients often need manifest or chain-of-custody records to close out permits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit, notification, and regulatory fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Many jurisdictions require advance notification for abatement, and these fees should be shown as pass-throughs or included lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Clearance test results reference and payment trigger
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying final payment to a passed clearance test sets a clear, objective due-date milestone.

asbestos-removal.paymentTerms: Residential abatement commonly takes a 25-50% deposit at signing to cover mobilization, permits, and equipment rental, with the balance due on completion or after passing final clearance air testing. Commercial and school jobs usually bill monthly on progress using a schedule of values, with 5-10% retainage held until closeout and net 30 terms. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in the contract. Accepted payment methods include checks, ACH, and cards, though many contractors add a surcharge or limit cards on large balances. Insurance-funded jobs may be paid by the carrier, so confirm who is billed and what documentation they require.

tips.title: Tie final payment to the clearance test
tips.body: Write in your contract that the balance is due upon passing clearance. It gives a clear date, and it avoids arguments about whether the job is done.

tips.title: Price discovery risk with unit rates
tips.body: Include unit prices for additional tile, pipe wrap, or transite found during the work. That way a change order is just quantity times rate, not a new negotiation.

tips.title: Itemize disposal and testing
tips.body: Landfill fees and lab costs vary and can change. Show them as separate lines so you are not absorbing increases on a fixed-price job.

tips.title: Keep paperwork ready for closeout
tips.body: Send manifests, worker certifications, and clearance results with the invoice. Clients who have what they need to close out permits pay faster.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before ordering anything
tips.body: Poly, respirator filters, bags, and equipment rental are real costs, and notification periods mean you commit to a schedule early. Do not mobilize without a deposit.

faqs.question: Should I bill asbestos removal by the square foot or as a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Most contractors quote a flat project price built from per-square-foot or per-linear-foot unit rates after a survey. Invoice with the unit breakdown so adjustments for extra or reduced quantities are easy to explain.

faqs.question: Who pays for air monitoring and clearance testing?
faqs.answer: Often the building owner hires an independent industrial hygienist or consultant directly, which avoids a conflict of interest. If you coordinate it, bill it as a pass-through at cost, plus a handling fee only if your contract says so.

faqs.question: Can I charge a minimum for small jobs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Setup, notification, decontamination, and disposal costs are the same whether you remove 20 or 200 square feet, so a minimum charge of $1,500-3,000 is common. State it in the proposal and show it on the invoice.
