faqs.question: How do I handle ACM found that was not in the original scope?
faqs.answer: Stop work in that area, document it with photos and sample results if needed, and get a signed change order before proceeding. Reference the change order number on the invoice with its own line items.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on asbestos removal?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax certain services or materials and exempt others, and residential versus commercial can matter. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Asbestos contractors send a written estimate or proposal after a site walk and, usually, lab results or a consultant's survey. Clients often collect several bids for the same abatement specification, so the comparison comes down to scope, timeline, insurance, and disposal handling as much as the total price.

scopeChecklist.why: State each ACM type, location, and measured square or linear footage so everyone agrees what is being removed.

scopeChecklist.item: Reference to the survey or lab results
scopeChecklist.why: Tying your bid to a specific survey avoids disputes if other materials turn out to be asbestos-containing.
Say what is not included, such as ACM behind walls, under subfloors, or in areas not surveyed, and how it will be priced if found.

scopeChecklist.item: Containment, air monitoring, and clearance responsibility
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify who pays for the consultant, the setup of negative air, and the final clearance, and what happens if clearance fails.
Note whether waste hauling, landfill charges, permits, and notification fees are included or passed through.
Many jurisdictions require advance notice before abatement starts, which affects start dates and access needs.
Make it clear whether drywall, flooring, insulation, or repainting after removal is the client's or another trade's responsibility.

pricingTips.title: Build from unit rates, then add fixed setup
pricingTips.body: Price each material by square or linear foot, then add containment, mobilization, and disposal as separate lines. This shows how the number was built and helps you defend it against a lower bid.

pricingTips.title: Include a unit price for unknowns
pricingTips.body: List rates for extra tile, pipe wrap, or additional hours so change orders have a pre-agreed price.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Landfill fees, labor, and equipment rental change, so make quotes valid for 30 days or less.

pricingTips.title: Show insurance and licensing up front
pricingTips.body: Attach your license, certifications, and proof of insurance to the estimate. Clients and lenders often require these, and they set you apart from unlicensed bidders.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many residential contractors provide free estimates, but some charge a site visit fee that is credited toward the job if hired. If you sample materials yourself, charge for lab costs.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote without lab results?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range, but a firm bid should be based on confirmed sampling results. Otherwise write in that the price is conditional on testing.

faqs.question: How firm should my bid be?
faqs.answer: A fixed price is fine for well-defined, surveyed areas. Add language that hidden or newly discovered ACM is priced separately under agreed unit rates.

faqs.question: How long should an asbestos estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Disposal costs and schedule availability shift, and permit notification windows can delay projects, so avoid open-ended quotes.

au-pair.intro: Au pairs provide live-in childcare for a host family, usually school pickups, meals, playtime, and light child-related housework. Most billing in this field is a fixed weekly stipend, plus reimbursements, agreed extras, and sometimes private-arrangement hours. Au pairs on a J-1 visa through a State Department-designated sponsor are paid under program rules and usually do not send their own invoices. Invoices mostly come from au pairs working outside that structure (for example, those with their own work authorization or in a private live-in arrangement) and from former au pairs doing similar live-in or part-time work.
au-pair.pricingModel: Au pair work is priced as a weekly amount, not by the hour, because the au pair lives in the home and the family also provides room and board. Under the J-1 program in the US, the minimum weekly stipend is set by federal rules (about $196 for the standard track at the time of writing, with weekly hours capped at 45 and daily hours at 10), and sponsors often set higher amounts. Check current figures with your sponsor. J-1 au pairs generally cannot take on paid work for other families, so extra work usually has to be cleared with the sponsor first. In a private live-in arrangement, pricing is typically a weekly rate for a set number of hours, with an hourly rate for hours beyond that, flat fees for overnights or weekend coverage, and reimbursement at cost for expenses paid on the family's behalf, such as activities, groceries, or mileage when driving your own car. Put the weekly hours, days off, and what counts as extra in writing before the first invoice.

rates.service: Weekly live-in childcare (up to 45 hours, room and board provided)
Part-time live-in or partial au pair (about 30 hours)
Extra evening or date-night babysitting beyond scheduled hours
Extra full day during school breaks (within legal hour limits)
Driving to activities with your own car
Language practice or homework help sessions

items.description: Live-in childcare, 45 hours per week (Mar 3-16)
Extra evening babysitting beyond scheduled hours (Mar 8, Mar 14)
Weekend overnight coverage (Mar 21-22, parents out of town)
Mileage for activity driving in au pair's own car
Reimbursement: craft and art supplies for after-school project (receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date by bank transfer or check. Extra hours were pre-approved by text on the dates listed. Receipts for reimbursed items are attached.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay period dates and weekly hours worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the invoice matches the agreed schedule and makes it easy to check against any weekly hour limits that apply to you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for regular weekly pay, extra hours, and overnights
invoiceChecklist.why: Extras are the most common point of disagreement, so each one should be visible with its date and rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and times of any extra babysitting
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the family a record of when extra care was requested and approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage log with date, destination, and miles driven
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports the reimbursement for driving your own car and shows it was for the children's activities.

invoiceChecklist.item: Receipts for expenses paid on the family's behalf
invoiceChecklist.why: Reimbursements are at cost, so attaching receipts avoids questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your program or arrangement type (sponsor name if applicable, or private arrangement)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies which rules cover pay and extra work, since J-1 sponsor rules differ from private live-in arrangements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment method, due date, and your legal name
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps payment records clear for both sides and for any tax reporting.

au-pair.paymentTerms: Au pair stipends are normally paid weekly, often on a set day, and under the J-1 program the host family pays the stipend directly, so no invoice is involved. In private arrangements, invoice weekly or every two weeks, with payment due in 3 to 7 days. Payment by bank transfer or check leaves a record. Cash is common but should be backed by a signed receipt. Deposits are rare, though some families prepay the first week. Late fees are uncommon and can strain a live-in relationship, so a clear due date and a reminder text usually work better. Check with your sponsor, an immigration adviser, and a tax professional about what payments you may receive and how they are reported, since this varies by visa type and state.

tips.title: Know what your visa allows before billing anyone
tips.body: J-1 au pairs are generally limited to the program's childcare terms and typically cannot invoice other families. Confirm with your sponsor before accepting extra paid work or sending any invoice for services outside your host family arrangement.

tips.title: Agree on the weekly schedule in writing
tips.body: Write down the weekly hours, days off, and what counts as extra. Most invoice disputes come from vague expectations, such as whether a Friday late night counts as regular hours.

tips.title: Get extra hours approved by text or email
tips.body: A short message such as 'OK to stay until 11 on Saturday' gives you a dated record. Quote the message date on your invoice line.

tips.title: Keep personal and family money separate
tips.body: Pay for family purchases with their card when possible. If you use your own money, save the receipt and invoice it as a separate reimbursement line, without markup.

tips.title: Track mileage when you drive your own car
tips.body: Note date, destination, and miles each time. Check whether your car insurance and your sponsor allow driving children, and agree on a per-mile rate in advance.

faqs.question: Can a J-1 au pair invoice the host family?
faqs.answer: Usually not for regular work. The host family pays the program stipend directly under sponsor rules. Any extra payment or work should be cleared with your sponsor, since the program limits hours and outside work.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the week?
faqs.answer: Live-in au pair work is normally a flat weekly rate for a set number of hours because room and board is part of the arrangement. Use an hourly rate only for extra hours that were agreed in advance.

faqs.question: Do I need to pay taxes on au pair income?
faqs.answer: In many cases, yes. Au pairs on J-1 visas generally have US tax obligations on their stipend, and the rules differ for private arrangements. Check with a tax professional or the IRS guidance for your visa type.

faqs.question: Can I charge for room and board or deduct it from my pay?
faqs.answer: In the J-1 program, room and board is provided by the host family as part of the arrangement and should not be deducted from the stipend. In a private arrangement, agree on this in writing and check your state's rules for live-in domestic workers.

faqs.question: What if the family pays late?
faqs.answer: Send a polite reminder with the invoice number and amount, and refer to the due date you agreed on. If it keeps happening, raise it with your sponsor's local coordinator, or in a private arrangement, ask to move to weekly payment by bank transfer.

estimate.intro: Au pairs rarely send estimates, since the stipend and hours are set by the program or an agreement. An estimate or quote comes up in private live-in arrangements, when a family wants to compare a proposed weekly rate, or when you quote extras such as a family vacation or a school-break schedule. Families usually compare the weekly pay, hours expected, days off, and what is covered by them, such as phone, car use, and meals.

scopeChecklist.why: Sets the baseline so the family and the au pair agree on what is regular time and what is extra.
Childcare tasks like school pickups and children's laundry should be listed, and general housework or pet care should be addressed to avoid disputes.
Specifies weekends off, paid vacation, and holidays, which the family should account for in the budget.
Gives a known price when the family needs additional coverage, so they do not have to negotiate it each time.
Spells out the private room, meals, phone plan, and access to a car, which affect the cash rate.
States whether you will drive, which car, who pays for fuel and insurance, and the mileage rate if using your own car.

scopeChecklist.item: Program or visa limits that apply
scopeChecklist.why: Notes any sponsor rules on hours, pay, and outside work so the quote stays within them.

pricingTips.title: Start from the program minimum, not below it
pricingTips.body: If you are on a J-1, the stipend floor and hour limits are set by the program. A quote should never go below the sponsor's required amount, and extras need sponsor approval.

pricingTips.title: Price extras separately from the weekly rate
pricingTips.body: List overnight, weekend, and break coverage as separate lines with their own rates so the base price stays comparable between candidates.

pricingTips.title: Account for what the family provides
pricingTips.body: A private room, meals, and phone can offset a lower cash rate, but state them so the family sees the full package.

pricingTips.title: Put the validity period on the quote
pricingTips.body: Add an expiry date, such as 14 days, and a start date. Childcare needs often depend on school schedules and move-in dates.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding for an au pair?
faqs.answer: A written, accepted quote is a clear record of what was agreed, but it is not a replacement for a program agreement. If a sponsor is involved, follow the sponsor's terms.

faqs.question: How do I quote for a family trip?
faqs.answer: List the dates, daily hours, a daily rate, and who pays for travel, lodging, and meals. Confirm any visa or sponsor limits on hours and travel before accepting.

faqs.question: Should I give a range or a fixed weekly rate?
faqs.answer: A fixed weekly rate for set hours is easier for both sides. If hours may vary, give the base rate for the agreed hours and a separate hourly rate for extra time.

audio-engineer.intro: Audio engineers record, mix, edit, and master sound for musicians, podcasters, filmmakers, businesses, and live events. Most work as freelancers or run a small studio, and they bill for studio time, mixing and mastering by the song or project, editing hours, and live sound or location recording days.
audio-engineer.pricingModel: Pricing depends on the type of work. Tracking sessions in a studio are usually billed hourly or by the block (4-hour half day, 8-10 hour full day), often with a higher rate if you bring your own engineer and gear. Mixing is typically a flat fee per song, sometimes with a set number of revisions, while mastering is priced per track or per album. Podcast editing is often billed per finished hour of audio or as a monthly package. Post-production for video (dialogue editing, sound design, ADR) is usually hourly or a day rate. Live sound and location recording are charged as a day rate or per event, with gear rental, travel, and load-in time listed separately. Many engineers also charge for stems, extra revisions, rush turnaround, drive or storage media, and session file prep. Deposits of 25-50% are common for larger projects.

items.description: Mixing, 10-song EP (includes 2 revisions per song)
Mastering, EP tracks plus streaming and vinyl-ready versions
Instrumental and acapella stems
Additional revision round (song 3)
Rush turnaround, delivered within 3 business days

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $500 received on project start is deducted below. Balance due within 14 days of delivery. Final files are released after payment in full. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by bank transfer, Zelle, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and song or episode titles
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several projects going, and titles make it clear exactly which work is being billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and hours, or number of songs/tracks
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports hourly or per-song charges and helps if a client questions the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revisions included and revisions billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Revision disputes are common, so show how many were included and which were extra.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables list (formats, sample rates, stems, masters)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the client is paying for and ties file delivery to payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gear, studio rental, or travel charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Third-party studio costs, mic or PA rental, mileage, and parking are easier to justify when itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents confusion about what has already been paid, especially on multi-stage projects.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage or credit terms, if relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: If you are charging a buyout or requiring a credit, state it so ownership and licensing are not left vague.

audio-engineer.paymentTerms: Most audio engineers take a 25-50% deposit to book studio time or begin a large mixing or post-production project, with the balance due on delivery or within 7-14 days. For small jobs such as a single mix or mastering, full payment up front is common. Many engineers hold final masters or unwatermarked files until payment clears. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in advance. Payments usually come by bank transfer, Zelle, card, or check, and corporate clients may need a PO number and net-30 terms.

tips.title: Tie file delivery to payment
tips.body: Send low-resolution or watermarked previews for approval and release full-quality masters and stems only after the final payment. This is standard practice and protects you from unpaid work.

tips.title: Define revisions in writing
tips.body: State the number of included revisions per mix and what counts as one round. Charge a flat fee for extra rounds so endless tweaks do not turn into free work.

tips.title: Bill for prep and cleanup
tips.body: Session file prep, comping, tuning, noise removal, and file conversion take real time. Either build them into your rate or list them as separate lines.

tips.title: Charge rush and weekend rates
tips.body: Short deadlines and off-hours work disrupt your other projects. A rush fee of 25-50% is common and easy to explain when listed on the invoice.

tips.title: Keep clear records for taxes
tips.body: Track gear purchases, software subscriptions, studio rent, and mileage. Many audio engineers are self-employed, so ask a tax professional what is deductible in your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or per song for mixing?
faqs.answer: Per song is most common because clients can budget easily. Hourly works better when the material is messy or the scope is unclear. Many engineers quote per song and add an hourly rate for heavy editing or extra revisions.

faqs.question: Can I withhold masters until I am paid?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common. State this on your quote and invoice, and share only watermarked or low-quality previews until payment is received.

faqs.question: How do I bill for studio time I rent from another facility?
faqs.answer: List the rental as a separate line item at cost or with an agreed markup, and show the hours and rate. Be clear on the estimate about whether the studio fee is included in your price.

faqs.question: Do I charge for travel and gear on location or live jobs?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. Add mileage or travel time, parking, and any equipment rental as separate lines. Many engineers also include a minimum call time so short gigs are still worth the trip.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes the number of revisions?
faqs.answer: Point to your written agreement or estimate and your records of delivered versions. Keeping dated versions and email requests makes it easier to show what was included and what was extra.

estimate.intro: Audio engineers send an estimate before booking studio time, starting a mix, or committing to a live or post-production job. Clients usually compare per-song fees, hourly rates, turnaround time, and what deliverables are included. A clear quote helps you stand out from cheaper options that leave out revisions or file formats.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of songs, episodes, or hours of audio
scopeChecklist.why: The total price depends on the amount of material, and clients often add more tracks after you quote.
A 60-track session with poor recordings takes far longer than a clean 12-track session, so note any assumptions.
Setting a number up front keeps feedback manageable and gives you a basis for charging extras.
WAV, MP3, stems, instrumentals, and mastered versions for streaming or vinyl all take time to produce.
Rush work should be priced differently, and delays caused by late file delivery should be addressed.
Specify whether room rental, mic rental, drive time, and parking are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and file release terms
scopeChecklist.why: Establishes when you get paid and when the client receives final files.

pricingTips.title: Quote per song with clear limits
pricingTips.body: Per-song pricing is easy for clients to compare. Include a track count limit, such as up to 48 tracks, and charge extra for larger sessions.

pricingTips.title: Offer packages for albums and series
pricingTips.body: Discounts for EPs, albums, or monthly podcast editing encourage bigger commitments while keeping your per-hour income steady.

pricingTips.title: Ask for reference tracks and a sample of the material first
pricingTips.body: Listening to the raw recordings before quoting prevents underpricing a difficult mix and sets expectations for the final sound.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Add a validity period, such as 30 days, so studio availability and rate changes do not catch you out.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Flat quotes work for mixing, mastering, and defined podcast packages. Hourly estimates suit open-ended tracking or editing, but give a range and agree to check in if hours run over.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a test mix or sample?
faqs.answer: Many engineers offer a short free sample for new clients, such as 30-60 seconds of a mix. Others charge a reduced fee that is credited toward the full project if the client books.

faqs.question: What if the recordings are worse than expected?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that allows you to adjust the price if the material needs heavy editing, tuning, or restoration. Tell the client as soon as you hear the issue and send a revised quote before continuing.

auto-body-repair.intro: Auto body repair shops, from solo painters working out of a rented bay to small collision centers, bill for collision repair, dent removal, refinishing, and panel replacement. Customers are either individual owners paying out of pocket or insurance-backed, where the shop bills the insurer for the approved amount and the customer for the deductible. An invoice has to break out labor by type, parts, paint and materials, and sublet work so it holds up with both customers and adjusters.
auto-body-repair.pricingModel: Most shops price from an itemized estimate built on labor hours, parts, and paint and materials. Labor is billed at different hourly rates by type: body labor, paint (refinish) labor, mechanical, frame, and sometimes aluminum or glass work. Hours usually come from a collision estimating database or from the shop's own experience, not from a stopwatch. Paint and materials are commonly billed per refinish hour, which covers paint, clear coat, sandpaper, masking, and similar supplies. Parts are billed at cost plus a markup, and the type matters: OEM, aftermarket, and used or recycled parts price differently and insurers often dictate which one is used. Paintless dent repair and small cosmetic jobs are often flat-priced per panel or per dent. Sublet work such as alignments, glass, or wheel repair is passed through with a markup. Add separate lines for hazardous waste disposal, storage fees for vehicles left after completion, and towing if you arranged it.

rates.service: Full panel repaint (door, fender, quarter panel)
Mechanical labor (suspension, cooling, A/C after collision)

items.description: Body labor: repair right front fender, replace bumper cover, align hood and headlamp
Refinish labor: fender, bumper cover, blend hood and door
Paint and materials
Parts: aftermarket certified bumper cover
Parts: headlamp assembly (OEM), clips and hardware
Hazardous waste and shop supplies fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Insurance deductible of $500 due at vehicle pickup. Balance billed to the insurance carrier under claim approval. Repairs carry a written lifetime warranty on workmanship and paint for as long as the original owner holds the vehicle. Storage fee of $40 per day applies starting 3 days after notice that the vehicle is ready.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, VIN, color code, and mileage in
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the exact vehicle and paint formula, and protects you if a dispute arises about the condition or mileage when it arrived.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance claim number, carrier, adjuster name, and deductible
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the insurer match your bill to the claim and shows the customer exactly what they owe versus what the carrier covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor broken out by type (body, refinish, mechanical, frame) with hours and rates
invoiceChecklist.why: Each type has a different rate, and insurers and customers expect to see hours tied to specific repairs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts listed by type (OEM, aftermarket, used) with part numbers where possible
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers may only approve certain part types, and customers have a right to know what went into their car.

invoiceChecklist.item: Paint and materials as a separate line
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps refinish supply costs from looking like padded labor and matches how estimating systems report them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sublet work and supplemental approvals
invoiceChecklist.why: Alignments, glass, or hidden damage found after teardown should be itemized with the approval date so the final total ties back to what was authorized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and storage or pickup policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Puts your workmanship warranty and any storage charges in writing before a disagreement over either.

auto-body-repair.paymentTerms: Individual customers paying out of pocket are commonly asked for a deposit, often 25 to 50 percent, before parts are ordered, with the balance due in full at pickup. Many shops hold the keys until payment clears. For insurance jobs, the customer pays the deductible at pickup and the carrier pays the rest, usually within 15 to 30 days of the final invoice and sign-off. Shops typically accept cards, checks, and cash, and some work with repair financing for larger jobs. Large cash payments, card chargebacks, and carrier payments sent to the customer instead of the shop are common friction points, so get a direction to pay or assignment of benefits signed where your state allows it. Storage fees for vehicles left after completion are normal, but state the amount and start date in writing, and check your local rules on lien and storage notice before charging them or selling a vehicle.

tips.title: Document every supplement
tips.body: Hidden damage found after teardown is routine. Photograph it, send the supplement to the adjuster or customer, and get approval in writing before doing the work. Unapproved extra repairs are the most common reason final invoices get disputed or cut.

tips.title: Take photos at intake and at pickup
tips.body: Dated photos of existing damage, dents, and scratches that are not part of the claim protect you from complaints that your shop caused them. Attach or reference them in the file.

tips.title: Hold the vehicle until the deductible clears
tips.body: Collect the deductible or customer-paid balance at delivery. Releasing the car first makes collection much harder, and a mechanic's lien generally depends on you holding the vehicle or following your state's process.

tips.title: Be clear on parts markup and part type
tips.body: If the insurer authorizes aftermarket and you install OEM at the customer's request, bill the difference to the customer on a separate line and get their sign-off first.

tips.title: Keep estimate and invoice lines aligned
tips.body: Use the same line structure on both documents. When the final bill follows the approved estimate plus documented supplements, adjusters and customers have little to question.

faqs.question: Should I bill the insurance company and the customer on the same invoice?
faqs.answer: Many shops use one invoice showing the total repair cost, then show the deductible due from the customer and the balance due from the insurer. Some carriers require their own form or an estimating-system export, so check what each carrier accepts. Either way, the claim number and deductible should be clearly stated.

faqs.question: Can I charge a storage fee if the customer does not pick up the car?
faqs.answer: In many states you can, if you disclosed the fee in writing before or when the work was authorized and gave notice that the vehicle was ready. Rules on amounts, notice, and what you can do about abandoned vehicles vary, so check your state's rules before enforcing them.

faqs.question: How do I bill for paint and materials?
faqs.answer: The standard approach is a flat rate per refinish labor hour. If you refinish a panel for 2.5 hours at a $38 materials rate, the paint and materials line is $95. Some shops use actual material cost plus markup, but the per-hour rate is what insurers and estimating systems expect.

faqs.question: What if the insurer pays less than my invoice?
faqs.answer: Many policies pay a reasonable amount, not your rate, and customers may owe the difference unless the shop agreed to accept the carrier's amount. Tell the customer before starting if there might be a gap. Keep your documentation, such as photos and a supplement request, to support a request for the difference.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on auto body repair?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Parts and materials are commonly taxable, while labor is taxable in only some states. Check with your state's department of revenue or an accountant, and show tax as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Auto body shops write an estimate before any repair starts, either for the customer paying out of pocket or as the first step in an insurance claim. Customers often collect two or three estimates and compare the bottom line, so it helps to show what is included, which parts you plan to use, and where the price could change after teardown.

scopeChecklist.item: Itemized labor hours by type with rates
scopeChecklist.why: Shows how the total was built and makes it easy to compare against other shops or an insurer's estimate.

scopeChecklist.item: Part type for every part (OEM, aftermarket, used, reconditioned)
scopeChecklist.why: Part choice can swing the price by hundreds of dollars and affects fit, warranty, and insurer approval.

scopeChecklist.item: Refinish scope: which panels are painted and which are blended
scopeChecklist.why: Blending adjacent panels for a color match adds labor and materials, and customers often assume only the damaged panel gets paint.

scopeChecklist.item: Statement that hidden damage may require a supplement
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations that the estimate is based on visible damage, so a revised price after teardown is not a surprise.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated repair time and parts lead time
scopeChecklist.why: Backordered parts can add weeks, and a customer without a rental car needs to plan around that.

scopeChecklist.item: Rental, towing, and sublet items and who pays for them
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents arguments over whether alignment, glass, or calibration of driver assistance sensors is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity period and deposit terms
scopeChecklist.why: Parts prices and labor rates change, so the quote should expire, and a deposit protects you on special-order parts.

pricingTips.title: Quote from teardown when you can
pricingTips.body: A visual estimate misses damage behind bumper covers and panels. For anything beyond cosmetic damage, charge a small teardown fee or offer to credit it toward the repair so the quote is based on what is actually damaged.

pricingTips.title: Include sensor and calibration work
pricingTips.body: Many newer vehicles need radar or camera calibration after bumper, windshield, or structural repairs. Add it as a line item, either done in-house or sublet, so you are not absorbing the cost.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, and best options on parts
pricingTips.body: Presenting an aftermarket option, an OEM option, and a used option with different prices lets out-of-pocket customers choose their budget and shows you are not padding the quote.

pricingTips.title: Keep a consistent labor rate
pricingTips.body: Posting your rates by labor type and applying them the same way on every estimate keeps you defensible with insurers who ask for rate surveys.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most shops give free estimates for visible damage. Charging a teardown or diagnostic fee is reasonable for complex jobs, and it is common to credit it toward the repair if the customer books with you.

faqs.question: How long is an estimate good for?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days, since parts prices and paint costs shift. Write the expiration date on the estimate.

faqs.question: What happens if the final cost is higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Contact the customer or adjuster with photos and an updated figure before doing additional work, and get approval. Many states require shops to get authorization when the final cost will exceed the estimate by a set amount or percentage, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: Can I match an insurance company's estimate?
faqs.answer: You can, but you are not required to. If their estimate is missing operations or uses lower labor rates, send a supplement with documentation. Customers generally have the right to choose their repair shop.

auto-detailing.intro: Auto detailers clean, restore, and protect vehicles for private owners, dealerships, fleets, and car enthusiasts. Invoices usually cover interior and exterior detail packages, paint correction, ceramic coating, and add-ons such as pet hair removal or odor treatment. Many work solo from a van or trailer, or out of a small shop, so a clear invoice that lists what was done to which vehicle matters.
auto-detailing.pricingModel: Most detailers price by package and vehicle size rather than by the hour. A full detail is a flat fee that goes up for larger vehicles (sedan, SUV, truck or van) and for heavily soiled condition. Paint correction and ceramic coating are priced by the number of correction stages or the coating tier, and often by vehicle size and paint condition, since the time required varies a lot. Add-ons like pet hair removal, headlight restoration, engine bay cleaning, and odor removal are billed as separate line items. Mobile detailers often add a travel or trip fee, and some charge a water and power fee if they must supply their own. Fleet and dealership work is typically a lower per-vehicle price in exchange for volume, billed monthly or per batch. Some shops sell maintenance plans or memberships for recurring washes, billed in advance.

rates.service: Pet hair removal or heavy soil surcharge

items.description: Full interior and exterior detail - 2021 Toyota Highlander (SUV)
Single-stage paint enhancement polish
Pet hair removal - rear seats and cargo area
Headlight restoration
Mobile service travel fee (14 miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Service completed 6/12 at customer address. Payment due upon completion; we accept card, Zelle, cash, or check. Paint polish removes light swirls and oxidation but cannot remove deep scratches. Please reach out within 48 hours with any concerns about the finish and we will make it right.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, color, and plate or last 6 of VIN
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact vehicle, which helps with repeat customers, fleets, and any later dispute about damage or condition.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile jobs happen at homes and offices, and fleet work is spread across lots. A date and address confirms where and when the work happened.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name plus a list of what it includes
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often forget what a Full Detail covers. Listing items like clay bar, wax, shampoo, and leather conditioning prevents arguments over what was promised.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons and surcharges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Pet hair, heavy stains, odor treatment, and oversized vehicle fees explain why the final price differs from the base package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Coating product, brand, and warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: For ceramic coating, customers need to know what was applied, the rated durability, and any care or maintenance requirements to keep the warranty valid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pre-existing condition notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting scratches, chips, stains, or failing clear coat before work protects you if a customer later says you caused the damage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, water, or power fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile detailers who bring their own water and generator can cover that cost, but only if it is shown and agreed beforehand.

auto-detailing.paymentTerms: Most retail detailing is paid at completion, often by card, Zelle, Venmo, cash, or check handed over at pickup. For high-ticket work such as paint correction or ceramic coating, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is common, with the balance due at pickup, since the vehicle may be in the shop for several days. Fleet and dealership accounts usually pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, billed per batch or monthly. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical for commercial accounts when stated in advance. Many detailers also charge a cancellation or no-show fee for same-day cancellations on mobile appointments.

tips.title: Take before photos at drop-off
tips.body: Photograph every panel, wheel, and interior area before you start, and attach notes to the job. It protects you from damage claims and shows the customer the difference you made.

tips.title: Adjust for condition, not just vehicle size
tips.body: A family SUV with dog hair and spilled drinks takes much longer than the same vehicle kept clean. Define surcharges up front and name them on the invoice so heavy soil does not eat into your margin.

tips.title: Collect deposits on long jobs
tips.body: Coating and correction jobs tie up your bay or schedule for days and use costly product. A deposit covers materials and reduces last-minute cancellations.

tips.title: Bill fleet work on a clear schedule
tips.body: For dealerships and fleets, invoice per batch or on a set day each month and include a list of vehicles with unit numbers or stock numbers. This lets their accounts payable team match and pay faster.

tips.title: Offer maintenance plans in advance
tips.body: Customers with coated vehicles often need regular maintenance washes. Billing a monthly or quarterly plan upfront smooths cash flow and keeps a steady schedule.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the package?
faqs.answer: Most detailers use packages with set prices by vehicle size, because customers want to know the total beforehand. Hourly rates can work for custom or unpredictable jobs, such as restoring a neglected vehicle, but quote an estimated range so the customer is not surprised.

faqs.question: How do I charge for a very dirty vehicle?
faqs.answer: List a condition surcharge or add-on, such as pet hair removal, heavy stain extraction, or mold treatment, as its own line item. Explain it at booking, and ideally send photos before the work begins so the customer approves the extra cost.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on detailing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax car wash and detailing services, some tax only the products sold, and some do not tax either. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant, and show tax as a separate line when it applies.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer disputes the result?
faqs.answer: Refer to your before photos, the package description on the invoice, and any condition notes. Offer to re-inspect within a stated window, such as 48 hours, and correct genuine misses. Having limits in writing, like what polishing can and cannot fix, helps resolve most disputes.

faqs.question: Can I charge a cancellation fee for mobile appointments?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you state it when booking. A common approach is a fee of $25 to $75 or a share of the deposit for cancellations within 24 hours, since you have held the time slot and may have already traveled.

estimate.intro: Detailers usually send an estimate when a customer asks about paint correction, ceramic coating, restoration of a neglected vehicle, or a fleet contract. Customers often compare several shops, so the quote should make clear what each package includes. Many quotes are based on photos or an in-person inspection of the vehicle's condition.

scopeChecklist.why: Year, make, model, color, and existing paint or interior condition determine the work required and prevent price changes later.
List steps such as decontamination wash, clay bar, polish stages, coating layers, and interior steam cleaning so customers can compare quotes accurately.
State that deep scratches, rock chips, stains, or failing clear coat may not be fully removed. This sets realistic expectations.
Coating brand, layers, and rated life affect price. Spell out warranty conditions, such as required maintenance washes or annual inspections.

scopeChecklist.item: Time on site and drop-off or pickup plan
scopeChecklist.why: Multi-day jobs need dates for drop-off and pickup, and a clear plan for where the vehicle is stored overnight.
Say when extra fees apply, such as pet hair, biohazard, or odor issues discovered during work, and that you will get approval before proceeding.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, validity period, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Product prices and your schedule change, so state how long the quote is valid and what the deposit covers.

pricingTips.title: Quote from photos, then confirm in person
pricingTips.body: Ask for photos of each panel and the interior, then confirm the price at drop-off after a quick inspection. Note in the quote that final pricing may adjust if the condition differs from the photos.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present good, better, and best packages, such as a one-step polish with sealant, a two-step correction with a 1-year coating, and a full correction with a 5-year coating. Customers often choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Base correction pricing on hours and paint condition
pricingTips.body: Estimate how many hours the correction will take using a paint depth gauge reading and swirl severity, then price accordingly. Dark paint and soft clear coats take longer than light colors.

pricingTips.title: Price fleet work per vehicle with a volume tier
pricingTips.body: Offer a per-vehicle rate by vehicle class, with a discount at set monthly volumes. State the visit schedule and what is included in a standard cycle, such as interior vacuum and exterior wash.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most detailers give free estimates for standard packages. For major restoration or correction work requiring a long inspection, some charge an inspection fee and credit it toward the job if the customer books.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. Coating product costs and your calendar can change, so include an expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can the final price differ from the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the vehicle's condition differs from what was shown or discussed, such as hidden stains or deteriorated paint. Put this in writing on the estimate and get the customer's approval before doing extra work.

faqs.question: Should the quote include a deposit?
faqs.answer: For high-ticket jobs like ceramic coating or multi-stage correction, request a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date and cover product. For a basic detail, payment at completion is usually fine.

babysitter.intro: Babysitters care for children in the family's home, usually in the evenings, on weekends, or during school breaks. Independent sitters invoice parents for hours worked, extra children, overnight stays, transportation, and any pre-agreed add-ons like meal prep or light housework. Many sitters work for several families on a recurring basis, so a clear invoice helps keep each family's hours and rates straight.
babysitter.pricingModel: Most babysitters charge an hourly rate for one child, then add a flat amount per hour for each additional child. Rates rise for infants, children with special needs, large groups, and sitters with CPR certification or early childhood training. Many sitters set a minimum booking of 3 to 4 hours, charge more on holidays and for late-night hours, and use a flat overnight rate instead of hourly pay. Regular families may get a standing weekly arrangement, and some sitters charge a flat fee for date-night packages or for being on call. Mileage or a travel fee is common when the sitter drives children or lives far from the job. Parents usually cover activity costs, food delivery, and admission fees as separate reimbursements.

rates.service: Holiday or New Year's Eve rate
Driving kids to school or activities

Additional child rate, second child
Babysitting, 2 children, Wed Mar 12, 3:30 pm to 7:00 pm (school pickup and dinner)
Additional child rate, second child
School pickup mileage, Mar 12
Pizza ordered for kids (receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Venmo, Zelle, cash, or check accepted. Thank you for trusting me with your family.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and exact start and end times for each sitting
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents need to verify hours, and times prevent disputes when a night runs late.

invoiceChecklist.item: Names or number of children covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Additional child rates depend on how many kids you watched, so the invoice should match the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly rate and any add-on rates
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing base rate, extra child fee, and holiday or late-night premiums makes the total easy to follow.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage with dates and trip purpose
invoiceChecklist.why: If you drove the children, listing miles shows how the charge was calculated and supports your own records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Food, admission fees, or supplies you paid for should be itemized separately from your pay so they are not mistaken for wages.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimum booking or cancellation fee
invoiceChecklist.why: If a family cancelled late or the job was shorter than your minimum, the invoice should state why the fee applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your name, contact info, and accepted payment methods
invoiceChecklist.why: Families often pay through an app or by check, so they need the exact name or handle to send money to.

babysitter.paymentTerms: Many sitters ask for payment at the end of the night or within a few days, especially for one-off jobs. Regular families are often billed weekly or every two weeks. Cash and peer-to-peer payment apps are common, though some families prefer checks. Deposits are unusual for single evenings but reasonable for holiday dates, overnight stays, or multi-day bookings, since you are turning down other work. A late cancellation policy, such as charging half the minimum if the family cancels with less than 24 hours notice, is worth stating up front. A late fee is less common, but you can note a small fee after 14 days unpaid. Check your local rules on household employment, since some families need to treat a regular sitter as an employee for tax purposes.

tips.title: Put your rates in writing before the first job
tips.body: Send a short message listing your hourly rate, extra child fee, minimum booking, and holiday pricing. When the first invoice arrives, nothing is a surprise.

tips.title: Track the real end time
tips.body: Parents often come home later than planned. Note the actual time you were released, not the time they said they would be back, and bill from that.

tips.title: Separate your pay from reimbursements
tips.body: Keep food, activity costs, and mileage on their own lines. It keeps your income record clean and makes it clear you are not charging extra for your time.

tips.title: Set a late pickup rule
tips.body: For regular families, state that time after the agreed end is billed in 15 or 30 minute increments, possibly at a higher rate after midnight.

tips.title: Keep records for taxes
tips.body: If you are paid directly, you may owe income tax on what you earn, and in some cases self-employment tax. Keep invoices and payment records, and ask a tax professional about your situation.

faqs.question: How much should I charge to babysit two kids?
faqs.answer: A common structure is a base rate for the first child, often $15 to $25 an hour, plus $3 to $7 an hour for each additional child. Rates are higher in large cities and for infants or children with special needs.

faqs.question: Should I charge for time after the parents come home?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you stayed past the agreed end time or waited for a ride or handoff. Bill in 15 or 30 minute increments and state this policy before the first job.

faqs.question: Can I charge a flat rate for overnight babysitting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many sitters charge a flat overnight fee, often $100 to $200, for time when the children are asleep, and an hourly rate for the evening and morning hours when they are awake.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a family an invoice for every sitting?
faqs.answer: Not legally in most cases, but it is a good habit. A simple invoice or receipt shows dates, hours, and amounts, and it helps both you and the family if there is a question later or if the family claims dependent care expenses.

faqs.question: What if a family cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Set a cancellation policy in advance, such as charging half your minimum booking fee if they cancel with less than 24 hours notice. Include it in your messages and on the invoice when it applies.

estimate.intro: Babysitters usually give a quote when a family is booking for the first time, for a long or irregular schedule, or for overnight, holiday, or multi-day care. Families compare hourly rates, extra child fees, experience, certifications, and whether you offer transportation or meal prep. A written estimate ensures both sides agree on hours and pricing before the night begins.

scopeChecklist.item: Dates, start time, and expected end time
scopeChecklist.why: The total depends on hours, and a clear window shows when overtime rates begin.
Rates change with additional children and with infants, so the quote should match who you will actually be watching.
Meal prep, bath and bedtime routines, homework help, and light tidying should be stated so you are not asked to do household chores unexpectedly.
State whether you will drive the children and how you charge for mileage, or whether the family provides the car.
Clarify whether you are charged a flat rate, when the overnight begins, and whether you are expected to be awake.
A family should know up front what they owe for a late cancellation or a late return.

scopeChecklist.item: Who pays for food and activities
scopeChecklist.why: Parents should decide whether you are given cash or reimbursed, so there are no disagreements about expenses.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total, not only an hourly rate
pricingTips.body: Give both the hourly rate and an estimated total, such as $20 an hour for 5 hours with a $5 extra child fee comes to $125. Parents like seeing the number.

pricingTips.title: Use packages for regular care
pricingTips.body: If a family wants you every Tuesday and Thursday, offer a weekly rate or slight discount for a standing commitment. This gives you steady income and gives them predictable cost.

pricingTips.title: Price your qualifications
pricingTips.body: CPR and first aid certification, infant experience, or special needs training justify a higher rate. Mention them in the quote so the price makes sense.

pricingTips.title: Add a holiday premium in advance
pricingTips.body: For New Year's Eve, Valentine's Day, and similar nights, list the higher rate in the estimate, since many families expect it but still want to see it written.

faqs.question: Should I give a written quote for a one-night sitting?
faqs.answer: A short text or email is enough. Confirm the date, hours, number of children, and rate, and ask the parent to reply to agree.

faqs.question: Can I change my rate after giving an estimate?
faqs.answer: If the job grows, such as more children or extra hours, tell the family and update the quote. Avoid raising the rate after the work has been done.

faqs.question: Should I ask for a deposit?
faqs.answer: For single evenings, usually no. For holidays, overnights, or multi-day care, a deposit or a cancellation fee is reasonable because you are holding that time.

faqs.question: How long is a babysitting quote good for?
faqs.answer: Many sitters honor a quote for two to four weeks. For holidays and busy seasons, ask the family to confirm quickly so you can keep the date open.

bail-bondsman.intro: Bail bondsmen and small bail bond agencies post surety bonds so defendants can be released from jail while their case is pending. The bills they send are mostly for the bond premium, plus any payment plan balance, collateral-related charges, and out-of-pocket costs permitted in their state. Invoices often go to a family member or co-signer (the indemnitor) rather than the defendant.
bail-bondsman.pricingModel: Premium is the main charge. It is usually a percentage of the total bond amount, set or capped by the state insurance department. Ten percent is common, some states set a different rate, and a few states restrict or ban commercial bail bonds. Many agencies apply a minimum premium on small bonds. The premium is generally considered fully earned once the defendant is released and is not refundable, but check your state rules. Most clients cannot pay in full upfront, so agencies take a down payment (often 10% to 50% of the premium) and set up a payment plan for the rest, backed by a signed indemnity agreement and sometimes collateral. Other charges, such as travel, notary, transfer, or monitoring fees, are allowed in some states and restricted in others, so list only fees you are permitted to charge. Collateral is held as security, not income, and should be documented separately from the invoice.

rates.service: Payment plan setup or administration fee (where allowed)
Bond transfer to another agency or county (where allowed)
GPS or electronic monitoring coordination (pass-through to vendor)
Notary or mobile signing for indemnitor paperwork
Fugitive recovery or skip tracing costs charged under the indemnity agreement

items.description: Bond premium, $25,000 surety bond at 10% (Defendant: J. Doe, Case No. 24-CR-01482, County Jail booking)
Payment plan administration fee
After-hours jail travel and release processing (out-of-county)
Notary fee, indemnity agreement signing

sampleInvoice.notes: Down payment of $1,000 received at signing. Remaining balance of $1,650 due in 11 weekly payments of $150, first payment due one week from release date. Premium is fully earned upon release and is non-refundable. Defendant must attend all court dates; failure to appear may result in forfeiture and additional costs under the indemnity agreement. Collateral receipt is issued separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Defendant name, booking number, and court case number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to the specific bond and keeps records clear if more than one family member is dealing with you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bond amount, premium percentage, and power of attorney number
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the premium was calculated and links the invoice to the surety paperwork for audits and disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Indemnitor name and contact information
invoiceChecklist.why: The person who signed the indemnity agreement is legally responsible for payment, and it may not be the defendant.

invoiceChecklist.item: Down payment received and remaining balance with a payment schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents disagreements over what has been paid and when the next installment is due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized additional fees, only those allowed in your state
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states regulate extra charges, and unlisted fees can lead to complaints to the insurance department.

invoiceChecklist.item: Agency license number and surety company name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require licensed agents to identify themselves and the underwriting surety on bond-related documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: Next court date and reference to the indemnity agreement terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Reminds the client of their obligations and of the consequences of missed appearances without adding new charges.

bail-bondsman.paymentTerms: Most bail bond businesses collect a down payment at signing, because release does not happen until paperwork is complete and the premium arrangement is set. The balance is usually paid weekly, biweekly, or monthly over several months, often through card, ACH, cash, or money order. Cash is common, so always issue receipts. Late fees are limited or prohibited in some states, so confirm what you can charge and put it in the signed agreement. Collateral such as a vehicle title, property lien, or cash deposit is typically returned when the case is resolved and the bond is exonerated, minus any amounts legitimately owed under the agreement.

tips.title: Know your state's premium rules
tips.body: Premium rates, minimums, and allowed fees are set by state law or the insurance department. Check your current rate filing and do not charge outside it, even if the client agrees.

tips.title: Keep premium and collateral on separate documents
tips.body: Collateral is held security and is not revenue. Use a separate collateral receipt that lists the item, value, and conditions for return, so the invoice only shows what the client owes.

tips.title: Get the indemnitor to sign the payment schedule
tips.body: Having the co-signer sign an agreed schedule gives you a clear record if payments stop, and it makes follow-up calls simpler and more professional.

tips.title: Send payment reminders before the due date
tips.body: A text or call a day or two before each installment due date reduces missed payments, and it matters because a client falling behind may also be at risk of missing court.

tips.title: Record every cash payment immediately
tips.body: Write a receipt with date, amount, and balance remaining at the time of payment, and keep a copy. Cash disputes are common in this business.

faqs.question: Is the bail bond premium refundable?
faqs.answer: In most states the premium is considered earned once the defendant is released and is not refundable, even if charges are dropped or the case ends quickly. Some states have exceptions, such as refunds for bonds posted in error, so check your local rules and state this on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge more than the standard percentage?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Many states set the rate or require agencies to charge only the rate filed with the insurance department. Some allow a minimum premium on small bonds. Confirm with your state regulator before adding extra charges.

faqs.question: Who should I bill, the defendant or the family member?
faqs.answer: Bill the person who signed the indemnity agreement. That person is responsible for the premium and any related costs. List the defendant's name and case number on the invoice for reference, but address it to the indemnitor.

faqs.question: Can I charge for fugitive recovery if the defendant misses court?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, if the indemnity agreement the client signed provides for it and your state allows it. Itemize actual costs such as investigator time, travel, and transport, and keep receipts. Rules on recovery agents vary significantly by state.

faqs.question: How do I handle payment plan interest or late fees?
faqs.answer: Some states restrict or ban interest and late fees on bail bond payment plans. If allowed, state the amount and when it applies in the signed agreement and on every invoice or statement.

estimate.intro: A bail bondsman gives a quote when a family member or defendant calls from the jail and asks what it will cost to get someone out. Most callers are comparing agencies on total premium, down payment, and whether a payment plan is available. The quote needs to be fast, clear, and consistent with your state's rate rules.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients should see the exact dollar premium, based on the bail amount set by the court, before they agree to anything.

scopeChecklist.item: Down payment required to post the bond
scopeChecklist.why: This is the number that decides whether the family can proceed today, so state it plainly along with accepted payment methods.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment plan terms for the remaining balance
scopeChecklist.why: Include weekly or monthly amounts, number of payments, and any setup fee so there are no surprises later.
Large bonds often need a vehicle title, property lien, or cash deposit, and clients need to know this before they commit.

scopeChecklist.item: Who must co-sign and what they are responsible for
scopeChecklist.why: The indemnitor takes on financial liability for the full bond if the defendant skips court, which should be explained up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Additional fees permitted in your state
scopeChecklist.why: Travel, notary, or transfer fees should be quoted if they apply, so the final bill matches the estimate.

scopeChecklist.item: Non-refundable premium and court appearance obligations
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know the premium is not returned after release and that missed court dates can trigger forfeiture and recovery costs.

pricingTips.title: Quote the total in dollars, not just a percentage
pricingTips.body: Saying 10% of a $25,000 bond is $2,500 is clearer than quoting a percentage. Families under stress want the final number and the amount due today.

pricingTips.title: Stay within your filed rates
pricingTips.body: Competing by discounting the premium is often illegal. Compete on speed, availability, payment plan flexibility, and clear communication instead.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three payment structures
pricingTips.body: For example, a higher down payment with a shorter plan or a lower down payment with a longer plan. Giving options helps the family choose without negotiating the premium itself.

pricingTips.title: Put the quote in writing, even by text or email
pricingTips.body: A short written summary of premium, down payment, and plan terms protects both sides and shows the client what they are agreeing to before they come in to sign.

faqs.question: How long is a bail bond quote valid?
faqs.answer: Bail amounts can change after a bail hearing or when charges are added, so a quote is only reliable for the current bail amount. State that the quote applies to the bail as currently set and will be recalculated if it changes.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most agencies do. Give the premium, down payment, and any fees, then follow up in writing before or when the client signs. Final terms are set in the signed indemnity agreement and bond paperwork.

faqs.question: Should the quote include collateral?
faqs.answer: Mention it when it is likely to be required, such as on higher bonds or higher-risk defendants, but present it as security that is returned when the bond is exonerated, not as a cost.

faqs.question: Can I charge for an estimate or consultation?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Quotes are free in this business, and charging for them would hurt you with clients and may conflict with your state's rules on allowable fees.

baker.intro: Bakers who invoice are usually home bakers operating under cottage food rules, custom cake and dessert makers, small bakery owners with wholesale accounts, and caterers who supply baked goods. They bill for custom orders such as wedding cakes and dessert tables, recurring wholesale deliveries to cafes and restaurants, and event or corporate orders with set pickup or delivery dates.
baker.pricingModel: Most bakers price by the product unit: per dozen for cookies and cupcakes, per serving for tiered and custom cakes, per loaf for bread, and per pie or tart. Pricing is built from ingredient cost, labor time, packaging, and overhead, and many bakers aim for ingredient cost to be roughly 25 to 35 percent of the retail price. Custom work such as sculpted cakes, fondant, sugar flowers, and hand piping is priced higher per serving or with a separate design fee. Wholesale accounts get a discounted per-unit price, often 30 to 50 percent below retail, billed weekly or monthly. Delivery, setup, cake stands and rental items, rush orders, and allergen-free or specialty ingredients are usually separate line items. Large orders typically require a non-refundable deposit to hold the date.

rates.service: Wholesale pastries or bread to cafes

items.description: 3-tier vanilla bean and raspberry wedding cake, buttercream finish with fresh florals (serves 120)
Groom's cake, chocolate ganache, 8 inch
Cupcakes, assorted flavors, for dessert table
Cake stand rental (returnable)
Delivery and setup at venue (22 miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: A $500 non-refundable deposit was received on booking. The remaining balance is due 14 days before the event date. Cake stand must be returned within 5 days of the event or a $75 replacement fee applies. Please report any allergy changes at least 7 days before the event.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event or pickup date, time, and delivery address
invoiceChecklist.why: Perishable orders are tied to a specific date and location, and this prevents disputes about when and where the order was due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized product descriptions with flavors, fillings, sizes, and servings
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients compare what they ordered to what they received, and detail makes charges easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most custom orders require a deposit to hold the date, and showing it clearly avoids confusion about what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Allergen and ingredient notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Documenting nuts, dairy, gluten, or egg content, and any client-requested substitutions, protects you if a question arises later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, setup, and rental charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Labor, mileage, and equipment such as stands or pillars are real costs, and separate lines show they are not part of the product price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cottage food or food business license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and counties require home bakers to be registered or labeled, and wholesale customers often ask for proof of permits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax collected, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Taxability of baked goods varies by state and by whether items are sold for takeout, delivered, or for resale, so show tax separately where it applies.

baker.paymentTerms: For custom and event orders, bakers commonly collect a non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking, with the balance due one to two weeks before the event or at pickup. Smaller orders such as a birthday cake or a few dozen cookies are often paid in full at ordering or at pickup. Wholesale accounts are usually on weekly or net 15 or net 30 terms, with a late fee of 1.5 percent per month or a flat fee written into the agreement. Payment methods commonly accepted include card, bank transfer, and digital payment apps. Check your local rules on late fees, and state your cancellation and refund policy on the order form and invoice.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the product leaves your kitchen
tips.body: Cakes and fresh pastries cannot be resold if a client does not pay. Requiring the final payment before delivery or pickup removes most collection problems.

tips.title: Price by serving, not by guess
tips.body: Quote custom cakes per serving with a minimum order, and add design time for fondant, sugar flowers, or sculpted work. This makes it easier to explain price differences between a simple buttercream cake and a detailed one.

tips.title: Charge for the extras that cost you time
tips.body: Delivery, setup, rush orders under a week, special dietary versions, and rental equipment should all appear as their own lines. Clients tend to accept them when they are itemized.

tips.title: Set a firm guest count deadline
tips.body: Agree on a date after which the serving count cannot go down. Lowering the count late leaves you with ingredients already purchased and labor already planned.

tips.title: Invoice wholesale accounts on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Batch weekly deliveries into one invoice with a delivery log that lists dates and quantities. This reduces disagreements about missed or short deliveries.

faqs.question: How much deposit should a baker ask for?
faqs.answer: For wedding cakes and large custom orders, 25 to 50 percent is common, and many bakers make it non-refundable because the date is blocked and ingredients are ordered. For small orders, full payment at ordering is also common.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on baked goods?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and sometimes on how the item is sold. Some states exempt grocery-type baked goods but tax prepared food, delivery, or catering services. Check with your state revenue department and list tax separately on the invoice where it applies.

faqs.question: Can I bill for a cake tasting or consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many bakers charge $25 to $75 for a tasting and credit it toward the order if the client books. This filters out casual inquiries and covers your ingredient and time costs.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client cancels a custom order?
faqs.answer: Follow the cancellation terms you gave them in writing. A common policy keeps the deposit in all cases and may require full payment if the cancellation comes within a week or two of the event, since the product is custom and perishable.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a cafe or restaurant that buys from me weekly?
faqs.answer: Send a weekly or monthly invoice that lists each delivery date, product, quantity, and unit price, with agreed terms such as net 15 or net 30. Include a purchase order number if the buyer uses one.

estimate.intro: Bakers send quotes when a client inquires about a wedding cake, dessert table, corporate order, or wholesale supply. Clients usually compare several bakers on price per serving, design complexity, flavors, and whether delivery and setup are included. A clear written quote also helps you confirm that you can take the date.

scopeChecklist.why: Availability, delivery distance, and venue conditions such as outdoor heat affect both whether you can do the job and the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Serving count and sizes, with the deadline for final numbers
scopeChecklist.why: Price is based on servings, so a firm count and cutoff date prevents late changes that leave you with wasted ingredients.

scopeChecklist.item: Flavors, fillings, finish, and decoration details
scopeChecklist.why: Fondant, hand-painted work, sugar flowers, and fresh flowers change labor time, so the design level should match the price quoted.

scopeChecklist.item: Reference photos and how closely you will match them
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often share inspiration images, and stating that the final design will be your interpretation avoids disputes about exact copies.
Mileage, setup time, and any stands or equipment that must be returned are costs clients often overlook.
Gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free requests can change ingredients, pricing, and whether your kitchen can safely do the work.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Stating these upfront secures the date and sets expectations for what happens if plans change.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from cost plus time
pricingTips.body: Add ingredients, packaging, labor hours at a rate you set for yourself, and a share of overhead such as kitchen costs and insurance. Then compare to local market per-serving prices to make sure you are in range.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum order
pricingTips.body: Small orders take nearly as much setup and cleanup as bigger ones. A minimum, such as a set dollar amount for a custom cake or a minimum of a dozen for decorated cookies, protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: Present a simple version, a mid-level design, and a full custom design with different prices. Clients can choose without negotiating the price of a single package.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Ingredient costs and your calendar change. Valid for 14 to 30 days, or until the date is booked by another client, is a common approach.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Most bakers quote for free by email or form, but charge for in-person tastings. A tasting fee, often credited toward the order, covers the cost of samples and your time.

faqs.question: How do I quote a design I have never made before?
faqs.answer: Estimate the extra hours for testing and building it and add that as a design fee or higher per-serving price. For complex sculpted cakes, it is reasonable to add a buffer for practice and materials.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as more servings, a new design, or a different delivery location. Put this in your terms and send a revised quote in writing when changes are requested.

balloon-artist.intro: Balloon artists design and install balloon decor for birthdays, weddings, corporate events, grand openings, and school functions. Some also twist balloon animals at parties or work as roaming entertainers. Invoices usually cover custom installations like arches and garlands, bouquets and centerpieces, entertainer time, and delivery and setup fees.
balloon-artist.pricingModel: Most balloon artists price decor by the piece or by the linear foot, with the price driven by size, balloon count, and design complexity. Arches, garlands, and columns are quoted as flat fees per installation. Bouquets and centerpieces are priced per unit, often sold in tiers. Entertainment such as balloon twisting is billed per hour, usually with a two-hour minimum. Delivery, setup, and teardown are separate line items based on distance and venue difficulty (stairs, outdoor wind, high ceilings, lift access). Specialty items such as helium-filled foil balloons, LED balloons, custom-printed balloons, and backdrop frames are billed at cost plus markup. Many artists require a deposit to reserve the date and buy materials, with the balance due before or at setup. Rush orders and peak dates (Valentine's Day, prom and graduation season, Mother's Day, December) often carry a surcharge.

items.description: Organic balloon garland, 10 ft, pastel pink/white/gold, installed over dessert table
Spiral balloon arch at entrance, 8 ft tall with hanging flowers
Helium balloon bouquets (5 latex + 1 foil number), table weights included
Delivery and on-site setup (venue 18 miles away, second-floor room)
Teardown and removal after event
Deposit received 03/02 (applied)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due on or before setup day. Accepted: card, Zapp, Venmo, or check. Balloons are non-refundable once inflated. Latex balloons may shrink or pop in heat; please keep installations out of direct sun and away from sharp objects. Teardown must be completed by the agreed time or a $40 per hour fee applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, setup time, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Pins down exactly what was booked and where, which matters if a client disputes timing or delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized design description with size, colors, and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom decor is subjective, so listing 'organic garland, 10 ft, blush/sand/white' prevents arguments about what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for delivery, setup, and teardown
invoiceChecklist.why: These are labor and travel costs, not materials, and clients often try to drop them if they are buried in a lump sum.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what has already been paid and prevents double billing or confusion on the final amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental items and return terms (frames, stands, neon signs)
invoiceChecklist.why: Backdrops and stands are often rented, so note replacement cost and the pickup date to protect your equipment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax tangible goods like balloons and decor, though services may be treated differently, so check your state rules and show tax clearly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Weather and balloon-handling disclaimer
invoiceChecklist.why: Heat, wind, and humidity affect latex balloons, and a written note sets expectations for outdoor jobs.

balloon-artist.paymentTerms: Balloon artists commonly take a non-refundable deposit of 25-50% to hold the date, with the balance due 3-7 days before the event or at setup. For small orders like bouquets, full payment upfront is common. Rush orders are often paid in full at booking. Corporate and school clients may need a PO number and pay net 15 to net 30, so confirm terms before the event. Late fees of 1.5% per month are typical for invoiced clients, and a rebooking or cancellation fee applies if the client changes the date inside a set window. Card, mobile payment apps, and checks are all widely accepted.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before buying materials
tips.body: Helium, specialty foils, and custom prints are purchased in advance and cannot be returned once inflated. A deposit covers those costs and protects you from last-minute cancellations.

tips.title: Charge for the design, not just the balloons
tips.body: A garland uses a few dollars of latex per foot, but the skill, speed, and design planning are what the client pays for. Price by finished look and labor time, not by balloon count alone.

tips.title: Add a surcharge for peak dates and tight turnaround
tips.body: Prom, graduation, Valentine's Day, and holiday weekends fill fast. A rush or peak-date fee compensates for the extra pressure and the supplies you may have to buy at higher prices.

tips.title: Put venue access fees in writing
