tips.body: Stairs, long carries, no elevator, or setup in wind can double your time. List these conditions on the quote and invoice so they are not a surprise.

tips.title: Track rental equipment separately
tips.body: If you lend or rent arches, stands, and frames, add a returnable damage or loss fee and a pickup date. Otherwise equipment can walk away at the end of the party.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the balloon or by the project?
faqs.answer: Most balloon artists charge by the project or by the linear foot. Per-balloon pricing is hard for clients to compare and ignores the labor of building and installing. A per-piece or per-foot rate with a minimum order works better.

faqs.question: Is a deposit refundable if the event is cancelled?
faqs.answer: Most artists make the deposit non-refundable because the date is held and materials may be ordered. State this on your quote and invoice, and consider letting the client apply the deposit to a rebooked date within a set window.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on balloon decor?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Balloons and decor are tangible goods and are taxable in many states, while setup labor may or may not be. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and list tax as its own line.

faqs.question: How should I bill for balloon twisting at a party?
faqs.answer: Bill per hour with a two-hour minimum is common. Include travel time if the venue is far, and note whether tips are expected or included. Some artists offer packages for 1, 2, or 3 hours.

faqs.question: What if the client wants changes after the invoice is sent?
faqs.answer: Issue a revised invoice or a separate add-on invoice that clearly shows the change and the new total. Do not edit a paid invoice, as that creates confusion about what was already collected.

estimate.intro: Balloon artists send estimates when a client asks for a custom installation, a wedding or corporate event package, or a quote for multiple pieces. Clients often compare several vendors, so the estimate needs to show what is included, the size, and the colors. A detailed quote also helps the client see why a custom design costs more than a store balloon bouquet.

scopeChecklist.why: An 8-foot organic arch and a 12-foot spiral arch are very different jobs. Write the size and style so you and the client agree on the final look.

scopeChecklist.item: Balloon type and finish (latex, chrome, foil, helium, air-filled)
scopeChecklist.why: Helium costs more and floats for a short time, while air-filled designs last for days. The client needs to know what they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: Setup and teardown times and access requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Venues often restrict load-in windows. Spell out when you will arrive and whether teardown is included.
Mileage and travel time add up fast for distant venues, and the client should see them before accepting.
Wind, heat, and rain can shorten the life of an installation. State what you cannot guarantee and whether a weather backup is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Rental items, return date, and damage fees
scopeChecklist.why: Frames, stands, and signs belong to you. Listing return terms protects your equipment.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and deposit to book
scopeChecklist.why: Dates fill up and supply prices change. An expiration date lets you release the booking if the client waits.

pricingTips.title: Price from a materials-plus-labor formula
pricingTips.body: Add up balloon and supply cost, estimate build time at your hourly rate, then add delivery and a margin for waste, helium, and design time. Check the result against your per-foot or per-piece standards.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Showing a basic garland, a mid-size arch, and a full backdrop gives the client a choice without negotiating your rate. Most clients pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Attach photos of similar past work
pricingTips.body: A photo of a comparable job anchors the price and avoids confusion about what the finished piece will look like.

pricingTips.title: Include a small buffer for large installs
pricingTips.body: Large installations often need extra balloons, tape, and time on site. Build in a buffer rather than asking for more after the work has started.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or design mockup?
faqs.answer: For simple orders, no. For weddings and large corporate installs, a design fee of $50-150 that is credited toward the booking if the client hires you is common. It filters out clients who are only collecting ideas.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is typical. Balloon artists book by date, so a shorter window is reasonable for busy seasons, and the quote should say the date is not held until the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of the rate, for example a shorter garland, fewer colors, or air-filled balloons instead of helium. This keeps your hourly value intact and gives the client a real choice.

band.intro: Bands are hired for weddings, corporate events, private parties, bars and clubs, festivals, and fundraisers. The band leader or booking manager usually sends the invoice, collects the money, and then pays each musician. Invoices typically cover performance fees, extra sets, sound and lighting, travel, and add-ons like ceremony music or a DJ set between sets.
band.pricingModel: Most bands quote a flat fee per event based on the number of players, the length of the performance, and the date. Saturday nights in peak wedding season cost more than weekdays or off-season dates. Bars and clubs often pay a flat guarantee, sometimes with a door split or tip jar on top. Private and corporate clients usually pay a package price that covers a set length (for example, three 45-minute sets) with add-ons priced separately: extra hours, PA and lighting, ceremony or cocktail-hour sets with a smaller lineup, travel and lodging, and custom song learning like a first dance. Overtime is commonly billed per 30 minutes or per hour. Many bands also add a fee for loading in at difficult venues (stairs, long carries) and require a deposit to hold the date.

rates.service: Bar or club gig (3-4 piece, 3 hours)
Corporate or private event (4-6 piece, 2-3 hours)
Ceremony or cocktail-hour set (duo or trio)

items.description: Wedding reception performance, 5-piece band, 3 x 45-minute sets (Saturday, Oct 12)
Ceremony and cocktail-hour set, acoustic trio
Extra performance time beyond contracted 3 hours
PA system and sound engineer
Travel, venue 85 miles from home base (one way)
Deposit received (Aug 1)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due 7 days before the event date per signed agreement. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or Zelle. Overtime and any additional services requested on the day are billed in 30-minute increments. Cancellations within 60 days of the event forfeit the deposit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, venue name and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and avoids confusion when a client books multiple dates or events.

invoiceChecklist.item: Performance length and set structure
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out what was contracted, such as three 45-minute sets, so overtime and shortened sets are easy to account for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lineup size
invoiceChecklist.why: The fee depends on how many musicians play, so a 5-piece versus 7-piece price should be clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (PA, lighting, ceremony music, extra musicians)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question fees they did not expect, and separate lines show exactly what the extras cover.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit paid and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was already received and the exact amount and date remaining, which prevents disputes at the event.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, lodging and meal charges
invoiceChecklist.why: If the contract says these are billed separately, list mileage or flat travel costs and any hotel rooms so they are not seen as hidden fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or PO number and legal name for payee
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate clients need a PO or reference number to process payment, and the invoice should match the name on the agreement for tax and accounting purposes.

band.paymentTerms: Most bands collect a non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent when the contract is signed to hold the date, with the balance due one to two weeks before the event or in cash or check on the night. Bars and clubs often pay the same night or within a week of the show. Corporate clients may need net 15 to net 30 and a W-9. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common for invoices that go unpaid after the due date, if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, Zelle, and card payments are all used, and card payments sometimes carry a processing fee passed on to the client.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the gig
tips.body: Once the band has played, you lose leverage. Set the final payment due a week before the event, or require cash or check at load-in for smaller private gigs.

tips.title: Put overtime rates in the contract
tips.body: Clients often ask the band to play another set late in the night. A written rate per 30 minutes or hour makes it easy to agree on the spot and to invoice it afterward.

tips.title: Bill travel and lodging separately
tips.body: Set a radius that is included in the base price and charge mileage, hotel rooms, and meals beyond it. This keeps the base fee competitive without losing money on distant gigs.

tips.title: Track what you owe each musician
tips.body: Keep a record of what each player is paid per gig. In the US, you generally need to issue 1099-NEC forms to non-employee musicians paid $600 or more in a year, though thresholds can change, so check current rules.

tips.title: Keep a separate line for gear and sound
tips.body: Sound systems, lighting, and backline wear out. Listing them as their own charges recovers equipment costs and lets clients choose to skip them if the venue provides its own.

faqs.question: How much deposit should a band ask for?
faqs.answer: Most bands ask for 25 to 50 percent of the total fee at signing. For wedding dates in peak season, 50 percent is common. The deposit is usually non-refundable because the band turns away other bookings for that date.

faqs.question: Should the invoice come before or after the performance?
faqs.answer: Send it at booking for the deposit and again 30 to 60 days before the event for the balance. After the event, send a final invoice only if there were extras such as overtime or added services.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax for a band performance?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax live entertainment services, but some tax admission or certain entertainment services, and rules differ for equipment rentals. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to cancel?
faqs.answer: Put a cancellation schedule in the contract, for example the deposit is forfeited at any time, and the full fee is due if canceled within 30 days. Invoice according to that schedule and keep a record of the dates.

faqs.question: How do I invoice when the band leader pays the other musicians?
faqs.answer: Bill the client for the full band fee under the band or leader's name. Then pay each musician from the proceeds according to your own agreement with them, and keep records for tax reporting.

estimate.intro: Bands send quotes when a client is comparing several acts for a wedding, corporate event, or private party, usually after an initial inquiry about date, venue, and budget. Clients compare price, lineup size, set length, music style, and what is included, such as sound and lighting. A clear quote helps them see why one band costs more than another.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, start time, and venue
scopeChecklist.why: Availability and price depend on the date, and load-in times and venue restrictions may affect the setup.
The number of musicians and whether there are horns, vocalists, or a DJ set changes the cost and sound.
Spell out total playing time versus total time on site, such as three 45-minute sets over four hours.
Clients often assume a PA is included. State whether you provide it, who operates it, and whether the venue must supply power.
Learning a first dance song or special requests takes rehearsal time and may cost extra.
Specify what is covered by the client and what is already included in the base fee.
Sets expectations if the event runs long and avoids arguments on the night.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: Present a standard package, such as a 4-piece for three hours, and a larger option with extra musicians or ceremony music. Clients tend to pick a middle option and it helps with comparison.

pricingTips.title: Price peak dates higher
pricingTips.body: Saturdays in May through October and holidays like New Year's Eve command higher fees. Quote a lower rate for weekdays or off-season to fill your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Include what you need to cover
pricingTips.body: Add up each musician's pay, sound crew, gear wear, travel, rehearsal time, and admin time before setting the fee. The fee for an hour on stage covers much more than that hour.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Dates fill quickly. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days, or until another client books the date, encourages a decision.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before the client hears the band?
faqs.answer: Many bands send a quote along with demo videos or a live clip. If the price is a surprise, a short call to understand the budget and event can save time for both sides.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a quote or a rehearsal for a custom song?
faqs.answer: Quotes are normally free. Custom song learning or a special rehearsal can be a separate line item if it requires significant extra time, and should be listed in the quote.

faqs.question: How firm should a band's quote be?
faqs.answer: The fee should hold if the date, set length, and lineup do not change. State that changes to the venue, schedule, or number of musicians can adjust the price, and that the date is only held once the deposit is paid.

bar-catering.intro: Bar catering businesses supply bartenders, mobile bars, drink menus, and often the alcohol and supplies for weddings, corporate events, private parties, and fundraisers. Invoices usually combine staffing, bar setup, beverage packages or per-guest pricing, and add-ons such as glassware, ice, and travel. Most operators are solo owners or small crews who hire bartenders per event.
bar-catering.pricingModel: Bar caterers generally price one of three ways. The first is per-guest packages (for example, beer and wine only, or full bar with signature cocktails) that include staffing, mixers, garnishes, ice, and cups. The second is hourly bartender staffing where the client buys the alcohol, often called dry hire or BYOB service. The third is a flat mobile bar rental fee plus staffing. Most also charge a separate fee for glassware, specialty cocktails, bar backs, travel, and setup or breakdown time. Many bartenders have a 4-hour minimum and charge overtime after the booked window. Where licensing allows the caterer to sell alcohol, the alcohol is itemized or built into the package price. In many states, a caterer who does not hold a liquor license can only serve client-supplied alcohol, so check local rules before choosing a model. Liability insurance and any required permits are usually built into overhead or shown as a flat event fee.

rates.service: Beer and wine package (service only, no alcohol)
Full bar package with mixers and garnishes (service only)
Mobile bar rental (trailer, cart, or portable bar)
Signature cocktail menu design and prep

items.description: Lead bartender, 5 hours (includes 1 hour setup and breakdown)
Full bar service package, mixers, garnishes, ice, cups, and napkins
Signature cocktail menu (2 cocktails), recipe development and batching
Portable bar rental with LED front
Glassware rental and cleanup
Travel fee (35 miles each way)

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: Saturday, June 14, 6:00-11:00 PM. 50% deposit of $1,912.50 received at booking. Balance due within 7 days. Client supplied all alcohol. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Gratuity is not included unless listed above.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Overtime, travel charges, and any dispute over hours are settled against the booked window, so it needs to be on the record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who supplied the alcohol
invoiceChecklist.why: It clarifies whether you sold it or only served it, which matters for licensing, sales tax, and liability.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guest count used for pricing and the final headcount
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-guest packages are based on a number, and a final count that differs from the contract needs to be shown clearly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized staffing with hours per bartender
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question hourly labor, and itemizing setup, service, and breakdown time prevents pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Liquor license or permit number, and any special event permit
invoiceChecklist.why: Where you sell or serve alcohol under your own license, showing it confirms you are operating legally and may be required by the venue.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Most events require a non-refundable deposit to hold the date, and the invoice should show it credited.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity and service charge treatment
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume a service charge is a tip. Spell out whether gratuity is included, optional, or a separate line, and be aware that service charges may be taxable in some states.

bar-catering.paymentTerms: Most bar caterers collect a non-refundable deposit of 25-50% to hold the date, with the balance due 7 to 14 days before the event or on the day of the event for smaller private parties. Corporate clients often pay net 15 or net 30 after the event, and may require a purchase order number. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common and should be written into the contract. Accepted payment methods usually include credit card, ACH, and check; card fees are sometimes passed on as a small surcharge where allowed. Payments for added guests, extra hours, or last-minute changes are typically billed on a final invoice after the event.

tips.title: Require the final headcount in writing
tips.body: Ask for a final guest count 7 to 10 days out and set a floor, such as billing for at least 90% of the contracted number. This protects you from buying supplies and booking staff for guests who never show up.

tips.title: Charge for setup and breakdown time
tips.body: Bartenders arrive early to stock ice, cut garnishes, and set up the bar, then stay to clean. Bill the full window, not just the service hours, or your effective hourly rate drops fast.

tips.title: Separate alcohol from service
tips.body: Whether you sell the alcohol or the client buys it, listing it on its own line keeps pricing clear, makes sales tax and licensing easier to handle, and helps with clients comparing quotes.

tips.title: Add an overtime rate to the contract
tips.body: Events often run long. Set an overtime rate per bartender per hour (often 1.25 to 1.5 times the base rate) and list the extra time on the final invoice.

tips.title: Itemize ice, glassware, and consumables
tips.body: These costs add up on large events. Package them into a per-guest fee or list them separately, but do not absorb them without noticing.

faqs.question: Should I include gratuity on a bar catering invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if the client agreed to it. A common approach is to list an optional tip line or state that gratuity is not included. If you add a mandatory service charge, label it clearly, and be aware that in some states it can be taxable and may not count as a tip for your staff.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on bar catering?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on what you sell. Alcohol sales, prepared drinks, and sometimes service charges can be taxable, while labor billed alone may not be in some places. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change the guest count after I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say that the final guest count is locked a set number of days before the event, and that increases are billed at the per-guest rate. Issue a revised invoice for any change and keep the earlier version for your records.

faqs.question: Is the deposit refundable?
faqs.answer: Most bar caterers make the deposit non-refundable because the date is held and other bookings are turned away. State this clearly in your contract and on the invoice, and note whether it can be transferred to a new date.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the client supplies the alcohol?
faqs.answer: Bill for labor, bar setup, mixers, garnishes, ice, and any rentals. Note on the invoice that all alcohol was supplied by the client, and that you served it under your service agreement. Confirm what your local rules and insurance policy require for this arrangement.

estimate.intro: Bar caterers send a quote after an inquiry about a specific date, headcount, and venue, often before the client has chosen a final caterer. Clients compare per-guest pricing, what is included in each package, and whether alcohol is supplied by the caterer or the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, hours of service, and venue
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on how many hours staff are needed and whether the venue has bar space, power, water, and load-in restrictions.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated guest count and the date it becomes final
scopeChecklist.why: Package pricing scales with headcount, and a locked date prevents last-minute changes from eating your margin.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies the alcohol and what is included
scopeChecklist.why: Spells out whether the quote covers alcohol, mixers, garnishes, ice, cups, napkins, and any specialty items.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of bartenders and bar backs
scopeChecklist.why: A typical rule is one bartender per 50 to 75 guests, and clients may try to reduce staffing to cut costs.
Mobile bar, glassware, coolers, and tubs may be rented or provided by you, and the quote should say which.
Events often run long, and cancellations affect staffing and supply orders. Fees should be known upfront.
Venues often require a certificate of insurance, and a special event permit may be required. State who handles what.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as beer and wine, standard bar, and premium bar. Clients tend to choose the middle tier and it makes comparison easier.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for consumables
pricingTips.body: Ice, garnishes, and mixers are easy to underestimate. Many caterers plan on about 1 to 1.5 pounds of ice per guest and add a small cushion in the per-guest price.

pricingTips.title: Use a minimum event fee
pricingTips.body: Small events cost nearly as much to staff as medium ones. Set a minimum spend or a 4-hour minimum for each bartender so smaller bookings still pay.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Dates and staff fill up fast. A quote valid for 14 days encourages a decision and protects you from price changes in alcohol and labor.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a tasting or cocktail consultation?
faqs.answer: Many bar caterers charge a modest fee, often $50 to $200, and credit it toward the booking if the client signs. This filters out casual inquiries and covers your supplies and time.

faqs.question: How many bartenders should I quote for?
faqs.answer: A common guideline is one bartender for every 50 to 75 guests, with an additional bar back for events over 150. Cocktail-heavy menus and short service windows may call for more staff.

faqs.question: Can I give a flat price instead of per guest?
faqs.answer: Yes, for events with a fixed headcount and hours. Include a clause that adjusts the price if the guest count or time changes by more than a set amount.

faqs.question: When does a quote become a contract?
faqs.answer: When the client signs and pays the deposit. Make sure the signed agreement includes the quote details, the cancellation policy, and payment schedule. Have an attorney review your standard contract if you have not done so.

barber.intro: Barbers cut, fade, and style hair, and shave and groom beards for walk-in and appointment clients. Most barbers are paid at the chair at the end of each service, but invoices come up with booth renters billing a shop, mobile barbers, event and wedding party work, corporate grooming days, and recurring clients on a monthly account. Invoices usually list the services performed, products sold, and any travel or after-hours fees.
barber.pricingModel: Most barbers price per service with a fixed menu: a set price for a haircut, a beard trim, a hot towel shave, and so on, with add-ons priced separately. Prices often depend on the length of the appointment and the barber's experience level, and many shops charge more for senior barbers or master barbers. Mobile and event work is typically priced as a travel fee plus per-person service pricing, or a flat group rate with a minimum number of clients. Booth renters pay the shop weekly or monthly rent and bill their own clients, so their invoices to the shop are rare, but a barber who does contract work (a film set, a corporate event, a team or school) will bill a flat day rate or an hourly rate. Retail products such as pomade, beard oil, and shampoo are sold at a markup of roughly 40 to 100 percent over wholesale. Tips are separate from the service price and should be shown as their own line if paid by card or added to an invoice.

rates.service: Hair color or gray blending add-on

items.description: Groom and groomsmen haircuts and fades (on-site, wedding morning)
Beard trim and shape-up
Hot towel straight razor shave (groom)
Mobile travel fee (22 miles each way)
Early start surcharge (before 7 a.m.)

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: June 14. Deposit of $100 received May 20 and applied to this invoice. Balance due on receipt. Accepted: card, Zelle, cash. Gratuity not included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, start time, and location of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and event work needs a clear record of when and where the work happened, especially if the client disputes hours or an early start surcharge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized services per person or per group
invoiceChecklist.why: Group bookings like weddings, teams, or office days are easier to approve when each haircut, shave, and add-on is listed with a count.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or mileage
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile barbers spend real time and gas getting to the client, and a separate line stops it from looking like a padded service price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retail products sold
invoiceChecklist.why: Pomade, beard oil, and shampoo should be listed by name and price so the client knows what they bought and so sales tax can be applied where required.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the deposit as a credit prevents double payment questions and shows the remaining amount clearly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Barber license number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a barber license, and corporate or venue clients sometimes ask for it on paperwork. Check your state board's rules on what to display.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity line, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: If tips are paid by card or invoice, listing them separately keeps your service revenue and tip income distinct for bookkeeping.

barber.paymentTerms: Most barbers collect payment at the end of each service, via cash, card, or a payment app. For events, weddings, and mobile bookings, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is common, with the balance due on the day or on receipt. Corporate clients and venues often pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, so state the due date plainly on the invoice. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month or a flat fee are used for contract work, but are rarely applied to individual walk-in clients. Many barbers also set a cancellation or no-show fee, often 50 percent of the service price or the full price for same-day cancellations of group bookings, and should state it at booking.

tips.title: Take a deposit on group and event bookings
tips.body: A wedding party or team that cancels the week of the event leaves you with an empty block of time. A non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent holds the date and covers your lost bookings if they back out.

tips.title: Put a minimum on mobile visits
tips.body: Driving to one client for a single haircut rarely covers your time. Set a minimum visit total or a travel fee that applies below a certain number of services.

tips.title: Separate tips from service revenue
tips.body: Tips are taxable income but are not part of your service price. Track them on their own line so your books are accurate and clients see exactly what they paid for the service.

tips.title: Track retail sales and sales tax
tips.body: In many states, retail products are subject to sales tax while haircut services are not, though rules vary. Check your state's rules and list product lines separately so you can report them properly.

tips.title: Send recurring clients a monthly statement
tips.body: If a gym, school, or office uses you on a regular schedule, send one invoice per month listing each visit date. It is easier for their accounts team than separate small bills.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice for a regular haircut?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Walk-in and appointment clients pay at the chair, and a card or app receipt is enough. Invoices make sense for events, mobile visits, corporate accounts, and any client paying after the service.

faqs.question: Should I charge extra for a beard trim on top of a haircut?
faqs.answer: Most barbers do, or offer a combo price. List the beard service as its own line, or show the combo as a single line, so the client sees what is included.

faqs.question: Is a booth renter's rent something I invoice?
faqs.answer: Normally the shop owner bills the renter for chair rent, often weekly or monthly. As the renter, you keep records of your own services and income. If you do contract work for the shop itself, you would invoice for that separately.

faqs.question: How should I handle tips on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Add a separate gratuity line if a client pays a tip by card or after the fact. Keep it separate from service lines, and report tip income on your taxes. Check with a tax professional on how to record it for your setup.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee to a corporate client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state the late fee on the invoice or in a written agreement before the work. Common choices are a percentage per month or a flat fee. Check your local rules on allowable interest or fees.

estimate.intro: Barbers send estimates mostly for events and bookings that are not a standard shop visit: weddings, proms, team photos, corporate grooming days, film or photo shoots, and mobile service for groups or care facilities. Clients usually compare per-person price, travel fees, minimum group sizes, and whether you bring your own equipment and supplies.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of people and services per person
scopeChecklist.why: A quote built on six haircuts changes if ten show up. State the headcount the price covers and what extra people cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, start time, and time window
scopeChecklist.why: Early mornings, evenings, and weekends often carry a surcharge, and the client needs to know how long you will be on site.
A distance from your shop or home base sets the travel charge, and a venue with stairs or no parking can affect setup and time.
Specify that you bring your own chair, clippers, capes, and supplies, or list what the client must provide, such as a chair, mirror, outlet, and a covered floor.
Hair coloring, straight razor shaves, product purchases, and touch-ups after photos are common extras that should be listed as separate priced items.
Spell out the deposit amount, when the balance is due, and what happens if the date moves or the headcount drops.
Your availability on a Saturday in June will not hold forever, so set a date after which the price and date are not guaranteed.

pricingTips.title: Price per person with a minimum
pricingTips.body: Give a per-person rate for group bookings and a minimum total that covers your travel and time. A minimum of three to four people is common for mobile visits.

pricingTips.title: Build in time between clients
pricingTips.body: Fades and shaves take longer than a quick trim. Estimate 30 to 45 minutes per haircut for groups, and price the booking on realistic total chair time, not best-case speed.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package and an a la carte option
pricingTips.body: A wedding package with haircuts, beard trims, and a shave for the groom is simple to compare. Listing the a la carte prices alongside helps the client see the value and add or remove services.

pricingTips.title: Separate travel and surcharges
pricingTips.body: Showing travel and early-start fees as their own lines keeps your service price comparable to shop prices and makes it clear why the total is higher.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Quotes for events and group bookings are free, since they help you win the job. If a client asks for a site visit or a long consultation, you can charge a small fee and credit it toward the booking.

faqs.question: What if the headcount changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that the price is based on a specific number of people and that additions or removals change the total. Ask for a final count a set number of days before the date.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 30 days is typical. Event dates fill quickly, so a shorter window for busy seasons such as prom and wedding months is reasonable.

bartender.intro: Freelance and private-event bartenders get hired for weddings, corporate parties, birthdays, fundraisers, and venue pop-ups. They bill for bar service hours, setup and breakdown, and often supply extras like bar tools, glassware, garnishes, or mobile bar rentals. Some also run small bartending companies and send invoices on behalf of a team.
bartender.pricingModel: Most event bartenders charge hourly per bartender, usually with a minimum of 3 to 5 hours because of travel, setup, and breakdown. Rates go up for holidays, late nights, large crowds, or specialty work like flair or craft cocktail menus. Many add a flat fee for supplies (ice, garnishes, mixers, napkins, straws, bar tools) or charge a per-guest package that covers alcohol-free supplies. If you provide the alcohol, you price it separately at cost plus markup, but many states restrict who can sell alcohol without a license, so most freelancers work on a "bring your own booze" basis where the host buys it. Travel fees, parking, and gratuity policies should be listed as their own lines. Mobile bar rentals and custom cocktail menu development are usually flat fees.

rates.service: Lead bartender / bar manager for large event
Bar supplies package (ice, garnish, mixers, bar tools, cups)
Mobile bar or portable bar rental
Bartending class or private cocktail lesson

items.description: Bartending service for wedding reception (2 bartenders, 5 hours each, 6:00 pm to 11:00 pm)
Setup and breakdown (1 hour before, 1 hour after, 2 bartenders)
Bar supplies package (ice, garnishes, mixers, cups, napkins, straws)
Signature cocktail menu development (2 cocktails)
Travel (42 miles round trip beyond included radius)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $300 received on booking. Balance due within 7 days of the event date. Host supplied all alcohol. Gratuity not included and is at the host's discretion. Late payments subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by check, bank transfer, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the bill to a specific booking and settles disputes about how many hours you actually worked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of bartenders and hours per bartender
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often book several bartenders, and the total only makes sense if the headcount and hours are visible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Setup, breakdown, and minimum-hour charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client that billed time covers more than serving drinks and prevents pushback on short events.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who supplied the alcohol
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that the host provided it, which matters for liability and for licensing rules that vary by state.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies and rentals itemized
invoiceChecklist.why: Ice, garnishes, glassware, and bar equipment are real costs, and listing them supports the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity policy and any service charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents confusion about whether tips are expected, included, or split, and keeps service charges separate from tips for accounting.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what has been paid, what is left, and the due date, which is often tied to the event date.

bartender.paymentTerms: Most bartenders require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date, with the balance due on or just before the event, or within 7 to 14 days after. Corporate clients often pay on net 15 or net 30 terms and may need a PO number. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing up front. Venmo, Zelle, card, check, and bank transfer are all used, and card payments often carry a processing fee you can pass through if you disclose it. Cancellation terms, such as a non-refundable deposit or a fee within 7 days of the event, should appear in the contract and on the invoice.

tips.title: Bill a minimum number of hours
tips.body: Travel, shopping, setup, and breakdown take time whether the party runs two hours or five. A 4-hour minimum keeps short events worth taking.

tips.title: Separate service charges from tips
tips.body: If you add an automatic service charge, label it clearly as a charge. Tips are discretionary and treated differently for tax purposes, and clients get confused when they are mixed together.

tips.title: Charge for extra hours at an overtime rate
tips.body: Events run long. State up front that time past the booked end is billed at 1.25 to 1.5 times the hourly rate, then add it to the final invoice with the actual end time.

tips.title: Collect the deposit before you hold the date
tips.body: Weekend dates in spring and fall fill quickly. A deposit protects you from last-minute cancellations you cannot refill.

tips.title: Keep records of supplies bought for the event
tips.body: Save receipts for ice, garnish, and mixers you purchased. They support your pass-through charges and your business expense deductions.

faqs.question: Should I include tips on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Tips are discretionary and typically paid in cash, through a tip jar, or by digital tip. If you add a mandatory gratuity or service charge, show it as a separate line and describe it clearly. Tips you receive are generally taxable income, so track them.

faqs.question: Can I sell alcohol and put it on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you hold the right license. Rules vary widely by state and county, and many freelance bartenders only provide service while the host buys the alcohol. Check with your state alcohol control agency before billing for alcohol.

faqs.question: How many hours should I charge for a 4-hour party?
faqs.answer: Bill the service hours plus setup and breakdown. A four-hour party often means 5 to 6 billable hours once arrival, prep, and cleanup are included, or you can set a flat minimum that covers it.

faqs.question: What if the event goes over the booked time?
faqs.answer: Bill the extra time at the rate in your agreement, often a higher overtime rate. Note the actual end time on the invoice so the client sees why the total changed.

faqs.question: Do I need liability insurance or a permit to list on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Many venues and clients require proof of liability insurance, and some areas require a temporary event permit or alcohol server certification. Requirements vary, so check locally. Listing your certification or insurance on the invoice can help with corporate clients.

estimate.intro: Bartenders send a quote after an inquiry about a wedding, party, or corporate event, often before the date is confirmed. Clients compare hourly rates, minimum hours, what is included in supplies, and whether you bring the bar equipment or only provide service.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, start and end time, and venue
scopeChecklist.why: Fixes the hours quoted and lets you account for travel and venue access times.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count and number of bartenders
scopeChecklist.why: Drives staffing. A common guideline is one bartender per 50 to 75 guests, depending on the drink menu.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies alcohol, mixers, ice, and glassware
scopeChecklist.why: The biggest source of disputes. Spell out exactly what you bring and what the host provides.
A full bar, beer and wine only, or a limited signature cocktail menu each take different prep and speed.
Prevents the client from assuming you are paid only for the hours guests are drinking.
Lets the client plan for extended events and know whether tips are expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation terms, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Protects the date and makes clear how long the pricing is valid.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A basic package (service only), a standard package (service plus supplies), and a full package (service, supplies, and menu design) makes comparison easier and often leads clients to pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price by headcount, not just hours
pricingTips.body: A 150-guest reception needs more staff and prep than a 40-person dinner. Quote the number of bartenders required, not only the time.

pricingTips.title: Show the supplies as a separate line
pricingTips.body: Clients can drop it if they want to buy their own, and you avoid absorbing ice and garnish costs into a low hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for travel and parking
pricingTips.body: Downtown venues, long drives, and loading fees cut into your pay. Include a travel line or note that parking and venue fees are billed at cost.

faqs.question: How far ahead should I send a quote?
faqs.answer: Send it within a day or two of the inquiry and set an expiration, often 7 to 14 days. Popular dates book quickly, and a deadline encourages the client to confirm with a deposit.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat price or an hourly rate?
faqs.answer: Many bartenders do both: an hourly rate per bartender for service, plus flat fees for supplies and menu design. A flat total is easier for clients to approve, but keep the hourly breakdown so overtime is clear.

faqs.question: What if the guest count changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that pricing is based on the estimated guest count and that a significant change may require more bartenders or supplies. Ask for the final count a week or two before the event and send a revised quote if needed.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the tasting or consultation?
faqs.answer: Many do charge for a menu tasting or planning session, often a flat fee that is credited toward the event if the client books. A free initial phone call is typical, but in-person tastings take time and ingredients.

basement-waterproofing.intro: Basement waterproofing contractors, whether solo operators or small crews, send invoices for interior drainage systems, sump pump installs, crack injection, exterior excavation and membrane work, and window well or grading fixes. Jobs are usually billed per linear foot, per fixture, or as a flat project price, often with a deposit and a progress or final payment.
basement-waterproofing.pricingModel: Most basement waterproofing is priced as a flat project fee built from linear footage of drain tile or perimeter system, the number of sump pits and pumps, and any add-ons such as dehumidifiers, vapor barrier, or wall sealing. Interior drain systems are typically quoted per linear foot, exterior excavation and membrane per linear foot of wall with depth factored in, and crack repair per crack. Small repairs and diagnostic visits may be billed hourly or as a trip-plus-labor charge. Materials such as pumps, basin liners, discharge pipe, gravel, and membrane are either built into the unit price or itemized with a markup of roughly 15-30%. Concrete removal and replacement, difficult access, rock or high water table, and electrical work for pump circuits are the common reasons for change orders. Many contractors also sell warranty tiers and maintenance plans, such as annual sump pump inspections.

rates.service: Interior perimeter drain tile system (French drain with sump discharge)
Sump pump and basin installation (primary pump)
Exterior excavation, membrane, and drain tile
Interior wall sealing or crystalline waterproof coating

items.description: Interior perimeter drain tile system installed along north and east walls, including concrete break-out, gravel bed, and drain tile
Sump basin with 1/3 HP primary pump, check valve, and discharge line to exterior
Battery backup pump system with 12V battery
Epoxy crack injection, south wall
Concrete patch and floor restoration over drain channel
Debris haul-away and disposal

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $3,000 received on contract signing, remaining balance due on completion. Payment due within 7 days by check, ACH, or card (3% card fee applies). Workmanship warranty of 10 years and pump manufacturer warranty of 3 years provided separately in writing. Warranty is conditional on the pump discharge remaining unobstructed and annual pump testing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and the specific walls or areas treated
invoiceChecklist.why: Disputes about where work was done come up when water returns later, and a clear record shows exactly what was covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Linear footage, crack count, and fixture quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-foot and per-unit pricing is easy to verify, so the client can match the invoice to the signed contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pump make, model, horsepower, and serial number
invoiceChecklist.why: Warranty claims depend on identifying the exact equipment, and homeowners will need this for insurance and resale.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require a license for foundation or drainage work, and permits may apply to excavation or electrical work. Showing them proves the work was legal and inspected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders itemized separately with dates and approvals
invoiceChecklist.why: Hitting unexpected rock, additional cracks, or failed concrete changes the price, and signed approvals prevent the client from disputing extra charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and what voids them
invoiceChecklist.why: A written transferable or limited warranty is a major selling point, and stating conditions like pump maintenance prevents claims for unrelated water issues.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Large jobs are paid in stages, and the invoice should show payments already made so the balance due is clear.

basement-waterproofing.paymentTerms: Waterproofing jobs are large enough that a deposit is standard, commonly 10-50% at signing with the rest due on completion or split into progress payments for excavation work. Materials-heavy jobs sometimes require a deposit big enough to cover pumps and membrane. Final payment is typically due on completion or within 7-14 days, with a late fee such as 1.5% per month stated in the contract. Many homeowners pay by check, ACH, or card, and some finance the work through the contractor or a third-party lender, so confirm how and when funds are released. Check your state's rules on deposit limits, right-to-cancel periods for home improvement contracts, and lien rights before setting terms.

tips.title: Take a meaningful deposit
tips.body: Pumps, liners, and membrane are bought upfront and cannot be returned once installed. A deposit covering at least materials protects you if a job is cancelled or delayed by weather.

tips.title: Document before and after with photos
tips.body: Photograph the wet walls, cracks, and open trenches before closing them up, and attach key photos to the invoice or job file. If the client claims work was skipped, you have proof of what is under the concrete.

tips.title: Bill change orders as they happen
tips.body: When excavation uncovers a failed drain, a bigger crack, or extra concrete, get written approval and add it to the invoice immediately rather than adding surprise charges at the end.

tips.title: Separate maintenance and service plans
tips.body: If you sell annual pump checks or backup battery replacement, invoice those as their own line items so recurring revenue is distinct from installation.

tips.title: Be careful with warranty language
tips.body: State what the warranty covers, for how long, and what voids it, such as power failure, clogged discharge, or new foundation movement. Vague promises cause disputes years later.

faqs.question: Should I bill waterproofing by the foot or as a flat price?
faqs.answer: Quote and invoice both ways by showing how the flat price is built from linear feet, fixtures, and add-ons. Unit pricing makes change orders easier because you can add or subtract footage at the same rate.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for on a basement waterproofing job?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25-50% is common on larger jobs, and at least enough to cover materials on smaller ones. Some states cap home improvement deposits, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a diagnostic visit?
faqs.answer: Yes, many contractors charge a flat inspection fee of roughly $150-400 and credit it toward the job if the client signs. State this when scheduling so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who withholds final payment because of a damp spot after rain?
faqs.answer: Refer to the written scope and warranty, inspect the area, and document the cause. If it is a covered item, fix it under warranty. If the work matched the contract, send a reminder citing the due date and late fee terms, and consider a lien notice where allowed.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on waterproofing work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states treat installation as a service or capital improvement and tax the contractor on materials instead, while others tax certain labor. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Waterproofing estimates are usually written after an on-site inspection, because the cause and route of water entry decides the whole scope. Homeowners often collect two or three bids and compare price, system type, and warranty length, so a clear written estimate matters as much as the number.

scopeChecklist.item: Cause of water entry and the system proposed
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare bids for different fixes, such as interior drain tile versus exterior membrane, so explaining what problem each addresses keeps comparisons fair.
A bid covering 40 feet versus 120 feet is not the same product, and precise footage prevents scope disputes.
Horsepower, brand, battery backup, and basin size drive both price and performance, and clients often compare these across bids.
Specify whether new concrete is flush, patched, or left for the homeowner, and whether floor finishes, drywall, or insulation will be removed or replaced.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as mold, finished walls, and landscaping
scopeChecklist.why: Mold remediation, flooring, drywall, and yard restoration are often not included, and listing them avoids surprise expectations.
Where the pump discharges, any required permits, and utility locates can add cost or delay, and clients should know who handles them.

scopeChecklist.item: Warranty, validity period, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: A written warranty is a key selling point, and stating how long the quote is honored and when payments are due sets expectations before signing.

pricingTips.title: Price from measured footage, not guesses
pricingTips.body: Walk the perimeter and measure walls, then add a buffer for obstacles like stairs, furnaces, and water heaters. Underquoting footage is a common source of lost margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic pump install, a pump with battery backup, and a full perimeter system lets the client choose and often raises the average ticket without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Build in contingency for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Exterior excavation can hit utilities, rock, or deteriorated footings. Include a clear unit rate for extra work or a contingency line so you are not absorbing the cost.

pricingTips.title: Explain warranty value in dollars and terms
pricingTips.body: If your warranty is longer or transferable, say so in the estimate. It helps justify a higher price against cheaper bids with limited coverage.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many waterproofing contractors give free estimates for full systems, but some charge a diagnostic fee of $150-400 for complex or inspection-only visits, often credited toward the job. Decide on a policy and state it up front.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical, though material and pump prices can shift. Shorten it if costs are volatile, and note it on the estimate.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after excavation starts?
faqs.answer: Only if your contract allows it and the client approves in writing. Include language about unforeseen conditions and unit rates for extra work so changes are expected.

faqs.question: What if a client wants only part of the work to save money?
faqs.answer: Break the estimate into line items so they can see what each part costs, and note in writing that partial work may not stop all water entry and may limit the warranty.

bjj-coach.intro: Brazilian jiu-jitsu coaches include gym owners, head instructors, traveling seminar instructors, and independent coaches who teach private lessons or run classes in rented mat space. They invoice for private lessons, semi-private sessions, seminars, corporate or school programs, competition coaching, and gym rental or affiliate fees.
bjj-coach.pricingModel: Most BJJ coaches earn through a mix of monthly memberships (billed by the gym), private lessons priced per hour, and one-off events like seminars. Independent coaches who invoice usually charge per session or sell a pack of sessions at a small discount, paid upfront. Semi-private lessons are priced per person or as a flat group rate. Seminars are typically a flat fee, a per-head split, or a guarantee plus a share of attendance, with travel billed separately. Competition coaching is often a day rate or a per-match fee plus travel. Rates depend heavily on belt rank, competition record, lineage, and local market. Black belts in large metro areas charge more than purple or brown belts in smaller towns.

items.description: Private BJJ lessons - gi fundamentals and guard retention (June 3, 10, 17, 24)
Semi-private session (2 students) - competition preparation drilling, June 20
Tournament corner coaching - local IBJJF-style event, June 29
Mat rental fee pass-through (partner gym, June lessons)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Private lessons cancelled with less than 12 hours notice are billed at 50 percent. Unused lessons in a pack expire 90 days after purchase. Accepted: bank transfer, card, Zelle, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, times, and lengths
invoiceChecklist.why: Private lessons are billed by the hour, and a dated list lets the student or parent confirm what they are paying for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and, for minors, the parent or guardian billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents usually pay for kids, and the invoice should match the person who signed the waiver and agreed to rates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson type (private, semi-private, seminar, competition coaching)
invoiceChecklist.why: Each type has a different rate, and listing it avoids disputes over why one hour costs more than another.

invoiceChecklist.item: Location or facility used, and any mat rental passed through
invoiceChecklist.why: If you rent space from a gym, separating that charge shows what part of the price covers the room rather than your time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pack balance and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who prepaid a pack need to see sessions used and remaining, plus the date the pack expires.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, lodging, and mileage for seminars and tournaments
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosts and students expect these itemized, and many seminar contracts reimburse them separately from the instructor fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Last-minute cancellations are common, and stating the policy on the invoice makes late fees easier to enforce.

bjj-coach.paymentTerms: Private lessons are often paid at the time of the session or prepaid in packs, with invoices used for packs, monthly remote coaching, and events. Seminar hosts commonly pay a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date, with the balance due on the day or within 7 to 14 days after. Net 7 is common for individual students, while schools and corporate clients often pay on Net 15 to Net 30. Some coaches add a late fee of 1 to 5 percent per month, but state it in advance. Payment is usually by card, Zelle, Venmo, ACH, or check. Check your local rules on late fees and on sales tax for lessons, since these vary by state.

tips.title: Sell packs and require payment upfront
tips.body: A 10-session pack paid in advance reduces no-shows and chasing. Set an expiration date, such as 90 days, and put it in writing before the first lesson.

tips.title: Get a seminar contract with a deposit
tips.body: Agree on the fee, travel, lodging, number of sessions, and cancellation terms before you book flights. A 25 to 50 percent deposit protects you if the host cancels or attendance is low.

tips.title: Separate coaching income from gym fees
tips.body: If you teach at someone else's gym, keep mat rental, affiliate fees, and your own coaching income on separate lines. It makes taxes and negotiations with the gym much simpler.

tips.title: Confirm insurance and waivers
tips.body: Carry liability insurance that covers instruction, and have each student sign a waiver. Some venues require a certificate of insurance before you can teach there, and you can bill your insurance cost into your rates.

tips.title: Track travel as you go
tips.body: Save receipts and log mileage for seminars and tournaments. Billing expenses to the host is easier when you have the records on hand.

faqs.question: Should I invoice each private lesson or bill monthly?
faqs.answer: Either works. Many coaches take payment per lesson or sell packs. If a student trains several times a month, one monthly invoice listing each date is less work and easier for the student to track.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a no-show?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you told the student the policy beforehand. A common policy is a full or 50 percent charge for cancellations under 12 to 24 hours. Put it on the invoice and in your booking message.

faqs.question: How do I bill a seminar host?
faqs.answer: Invoice the agreed instructor fee, then list travel, lodging, and meals as separate lines with receipts if the contract covers them. Send a deposit invoice when you confirm the date and a final invoice after the event.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax personal instruction, but some tax fitness or recreation services. Check with your state revenue department or a local tax professional.

faqs.question: What if I coach as a contractor for a gym?
faqs.answer: Invoice the gym for your hours or classes at the agreed rate. In the US, contractors typically receive a 1099 if paid over the IRS threshold, and are responsible for their own self-employment taxes.

estimate.intro: BJJ coaches send quotes for seminars, corporate or school programs, multi-week private coaching plans, and competition camps. The client usually compares your fee against other instructors' rates, your rank and credentials, and what is included such as travel, session length, and number of attendees.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: A two-hour seminar and a full-day event with three sessions are very different workloads, and the quote should say which is expected.
Teaching 10 experienced adults is different from 40 mixed-level students or kids, and it affects both your preparation and the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Gi, no-gi, or both, and topics covered
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifying the curriculum prevents a host from expecting something you did not plan to teach.
State whether these are included, reimbursed, or billed separately, and who books them, to avoid surprise costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Venue, mats, and equipment provided by the client
scopeChecklist.why: You need to know the space has enough clean mats, and whether you must bring anything, before you commit.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, balance due date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Events get postponed or cancelled, and a written policy protects you from losing a date you could have booked elsewhere.
Hosts often film seminars or use your name and image in marketing, so clarify what is allowed and whether it affects your price.

pricingTips.title: Price by rank and demand, not hours alone
pricingTips.body: A seminar fee covers preparation, reputation, and the time away from your own classes. Check what comparable instructors in your region charge and set your fee to match your credentials and draw.

pricingTips.title: Offer a flat fee or a guarantee plus split
pricingTips.body: Hosts who are unsure about turnout may prefer a lower guarantee with a share of the door. Spell out how attendance is counted and how you will be paid.

pricingTips.title: Build travel into the quote
pricingTips.body: Itemize flights or mileage, hotel nights, and a per-diem so the host sees the full cost. If you quote travel as a rough number, state that it is an estimate and that actual costs will be billed.

pricingTips.title: Offer packages for ongoing clients
pricingTips.body: For private clients preparing for a tournament, quote a camp of 8 to 12 sessions at a modest discount. Include the end date so the plan has a clear scope.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seminar dates and travel prices change, so 14 to 30 days is typical. State the expiration date on the quote and hold the event date only after the deposit arrives.

faqs.question: Should I give a free trial lesson?
faqs.answer: Some coaches do one, but it is better to offer a short discounted intro session. That way the student commits and you are paid for your time.

faqs.question: How do I handle a host who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope rather than the rate where you can, for example fewer sessions or no travel included. If you do lower the fee, keep the cancellation and deposit terms the same.

faqs.question: Is a quote a binding contract?
faqs.answer: A quote alone is usually not a full contract. Once the client accepts and pays a deposit, you have a stronger agreement. For larger events, use a short written contract that references the quote.

blacksmith.intro: Blacksmiths forge, bend, and fabricate metal by hand and with power hammers, presses, and welders. Clients include homeowners ordering gates, railings, and hardware, designers and builders who need custom architectural ironwork, farmers and ranchers who need repairs and tools, and buyers of knives, fireplace tools, and decorative pieces. Invoices usually cover a mix of labor, raw material, finishing, and sometimes delivery or installation.
blacksmith.pricingModel: Most blacksmiths combine an hourly shop rate with a materials charge, then quote the whole job as a flat price for custom work. Small repairs and on-the-spot jobs are often billed by the hour with a minimum charge. Production items such as hooks, hinges, and fireplace tools are priced per piece, often from a price list built on time, material, and fuel. Architectural work such as gates and railings is often priced per linear foot or as a fixed project price with a deposit up front. Materials are usually passed through at cost plus a markup of 10 to 25 percent to cover waste, handling, and shipping. Finishing (powder coat, paint, wax, clear coat), design or drawing time, on-site installation, and delivery are normally listed as separate lines. Custom commissions often carry a design fee that is credited toward the final price if the client proceeds.

rates.service: Shop labor, general forging and fabrication
Farrier-style or tool repair (sharpening, re-handling, welding)
Powder coat or paint finishing (sublet or in-house)

items.description: Custom forged garden gate, 36 in x 60 in, scrolled top, includes design and fabrication labor
Steel stock (1/2 in square bar, 1/4 x 1 in flat bar, 3/8 in round) plus consumables
Hand-forged gate latch and two strap hinges
Powder coat, satin black (sublet)
On-site installation, including post hardware
Delivery, 35 miles each way

sampleInvoice.notes: 50% deposit of $1,545 was received on the order date. Balance due within 14 days of installation. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or card (3% fee on card payments). Items remain shop property until paid in full. Steel will develop surface rust if the coating is damaged; touch-up instructions provided.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor with hours and rate, split between design, forging, fabrication, and installation
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume handwork is cheap. Showing the hours makes the price understandable and defends it if questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material type, dimensions, and cost (mild steel, stainless, bronze, reclaimed stock)
invoiceChecklist.why: Material prices change with the market, and clients who ask for specialty metals need to see why the price differs from a standard quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finish description and who performed it (powder coat, wax, oil, hot-dip galvanizing, patina)
invoiceChecklist.why: Finish determines durability and maintenance. Naming it avoids disputes about color, sheen, or rust later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed quote or commission agreement and any approved change orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom work drifts from the original design. Tying the invoice to the agreement shows which changes the client approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most commissions require a deposit for materials. Showing it clearly prevents confusion over what is left to pay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery or installation details: date, miles, hours, and site conditions
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel and installation are separate costs from shop work, and unexpected site issues like concrete drilling or uneven grade should be recorded.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line or resale and exemption certificate number, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax tangible goods but treat installation and repair differently. Record what you charged tax on and keep exemption certificates for contractors and resellers.

blacksmith.paymentTerms: Custom commissions typically require a deposit of 30 to 50 percent to cover material and reserve shop time, with the balance due at pickup or on completion of installation. Large architectural jobs may use a three-part schedule, such as a deposit, a progress payment when forging is done, and a final payment after install. Small repairs and retail pieces are usually paid at pickup. For invoices sent after delivery, net 14 or net 30 is common, with a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month if stated in writing beforehand. Checks, ACH, and card are all common, and some smiths add a card fee or offer a small discount for check or cash. For work for contractors and designers, expect net 30 and put the PO number on the invoice.

tips.title: Track your real shop rate
tips.body: Add rent, fuel (coal, propane, or electricity), insurance, tooling, and consumables, then divide by billable hours. Many smiths bill only a fraction of the hours they spend in the shop, so the hourly rate has to cover idle time, sketching, and cleanup.

tips.title: Charge a design fee on custom work
tips.body: Drawings and mockups take real time. A fee of $100 to $500, credited toward the final price if the client proceeds, filters out casual inquiries and pays for the time when they do not.

tips.title: Pass through material price changes
tips.body: Steel prices can move between quote and purchase. Put a validity window on the quote, such as 30 days, and state that large changes in material cost may adjust the price.

tips.title: Take full payment before releasing small pieces
tips.body: A finished knife, hook, or fireplace set is easy to hand over and hard to chase later. For retail and repair work, collect at pickup rather than invoicing afterward.

tips.title: Bill installation and site surprises separately
tips.body: Drilling into concrete, welding on site, or hauling a heavy gate up a hill can take longer than planned. List installation as its own line with an hourly rate so extra time is easy to justify.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat price for custom work?
faqs.answer: Most smiths quote a flat price for defined custom pieces and hourly for repairs or open-ended work. Build the flat price from estimated hours, materials, finishing, and a margin for the unexpected, and get a signed scope so changes can be billed separately.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up materials?
faqs.answer: A markup of 10 to 25 percent over cost is common. It covers waste from cutoffs, shipping, storage, and the time spent sourcing. Some smiths bill material at cost and charge a higher labor rate instead; either approach works if it is consistent and disclosed.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on forged items and repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax finished goods sold to consumers, while treatment of repairs, installation, and custom fabrication varies. Check with your state revenue department, and keep resale or exemption certificates for clients who claim them.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pick up a finished piece?
faqs.answer: State a storage policy on the quote or agreement, such as a storage fee after 30 days and the right to resell after a longer period. Local law on abandoned property varies, so check your rules before acting on it.

faqs.question: Can I charge a minimum for small repairs?
faqs.answer: Yes. A shop minimum of one half hour to one hour covers setup, firing the forge or welder, and handling. Post it in the shop and mention it when you take the job.

estimate.intro: Blacksmiths send estimates for custom commissions, architectural work, and large repairs, and usually before buying any material. Clients often compare a handmade price against factory-made or imported ironwork, or against other local metal shops, so a clear quote has to explain what makes the work different.

scopeChecklist.item: Dimensions, design, and a sketch or drawing attached to the quote
scopeChecklist.why: A gate or railing described only in words leaves room for different expectations about scroll patterns, picket spacing, and overall size.

scopeChecklist.item: Material type, thickness, and any specialty metals
scopeChecklist.why: Mild steel, stainless, and bronze differ widely in cost and workability. Naming them prevents substitution disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Finish and color, with who will apply it
scopeChecklist.why: Powder coat, paint, wax, and patina have different costs, lead times, and maintenance needs. Include the color or sample chosen.
State whether you install, who handles posts, concrete, or drilling, and what the client must prepare, so on-site surprises do not become price disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline with allowance for lead times
scopeChecklist.why: Material delivery, outsourced finishing, and forging schedules affect completion dates. Give a range and note what could delay it.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Metal prices change and shop time is limited. A stated validity window and payment plan protect both sides.

scopeChecklist.item: What is excluded and how changes are priced
scopeChecklist.why: Permits, engineering, hauling, removal of old work, and design revisions should be listed as excluded or priced separately to keep the scope clear.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours task by task
pricingTips.body: Break the job into layout, cutting, forging, welding, grinding, finishing, and installation. Handwork tends to take longer than expected, so add a buffer of 10 to 20 percent on unfamiliar designs.

pricingTips.title: Show a few options
pricingTips.body: Offer a basic version and an upgraded one, such as plain bars versus forged scrolls, or a painted versus powder-coated finish. Clients can then choose within a budget instead of walking away.

pricingTips.title: Explain the handmade difference
pricingTips.body: A short line on forged joints, hand-finished details, and expected lifespan helps a client compare your price to factory ironwork without discounting.

pricingTips.title: Quote materials with a validity date
pricingTips.body: Steel and finishing costs can change within weeks. Give the quote a 14 to 30 day window and note that prices are held only once the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes for repairs and standard items are usually free. For custom designs that need drawings, site visits, or sample pieces, many smiths charge a design fee and credit it to the project if the client goes ahead.

faqs.question: How firm should a quote be?
faqs.answer: A flat-price quote should hold if the scope does not change. Write that changes to design, materials, or site conditions will be priced separately with written approval, so a revised request does not turn into free work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common, shorter if you are using expensive metals or if steel prices are volatile. State the date on the quote and say that the price is secured when the deposit is received.

faqs.question: What if the final cost runs over the estimate?
faqs.answer: If the quote was a flat price, absorb normal overruns and learn for next time. If the overrun comes from client changes or hidden site issues, document them and bill them as agreed in the change-order terms of your quote.

blogger.intro: Bloggers who bill clients are usually freelance writers, niche site owners, or creators who write posts for brands, agencies, and other businesses. They invoice for written posts, sponsored content, content strategy, editing, and sometimes extras like images, SEO research, and social promotion. Bloggers who earn from ads and affiliate links get paid by networks, but the work here is about direct client billing.
blogger.pricingModel: Most bloggers price by the piece, either a flat fee per post or a per-word rate, with the price set by length, research depth, and whether the client wants SEO optimization or original images. Sponsored posts on your own blog are usually priced as a flat fee based on your traffic, audience, and usage terms. Ongoing clients often buy a monthly package of a fixed number of posts, sometimes billed as a retainer. Hourly rates are used for editing, strategy work, and projects where scope is unclear. Add-ons such as keyword research, stock photos, custom graphics, and revisions beyond the included rounds are commonly itemized separately. Rush turnaround and exclusive rights or content buyouts can raise the price by 25 to 50 percent.

rates.service: Long-form or SEO pillar post (1,800-3,000 words)
Sponsored post on your own blog

items.description: Blog post: 'How to Choose a Home Water Filter' (1,500 words, includes keyword placement and meta description)
Keyword research and content briefs
Custom featured images
Additional revision round beyond two included rounds (Post 2)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Final rights transfer to the client on payment in full. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Post titles and word counts
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each deliverable by title and length ties the charge to specific work and prevents disputes about what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery and publish dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates show you met the deadline and help clients match invoices to their editorial calendar.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State whether the client gets full ownership, a license, or exclusivity, and that rights transfer upon payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and extra revisions billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating extra revisions from the base price shows why the total rose when a client asked for rewrites.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or project number
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often cannot pay without a PO or reference code on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons such as images, research, or stock licenses
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing extras makes clear what the client is paying for and lets you recover real costs like paid image licenses.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sponsorship disclosure and link details
invoiceChecklist.why: For sponsored posts, noting the number of links, nofollow or sponsored tags, and disclosure language documents what you agreed to deliver.

blogger.paymentTerms: Common practice is net 14 or net 30 for ongoing clients, with new clients paying 25 to 50 percent upfront or in full before the first post.
