Agencies and larger companies often run on net 30 to net 60 cycles, so confirm their terms before you start. Monthly retainers are typically billed at the start of the month. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if it is stated in your contract or invoice terms, though check your local rules on allowable interest. Most bloggers accept ACH, bank transfer, check, PayPal, or card payments. US clients who pay you $600 or more in a year may send you a 1099, so keep your own income records.

tips.title: Define what a revision is
tips.body: Write down how many rounds of edits are included and what counts as a revision versus a new direction. Bill extra rounds hourly so scope creep does not eat your margin.

tips.title: Charge for research-heavy posts
tips.body: A 1,000-word post that requires interviews, data, or product testing takes much longer than an opinion piece. Price those by effort, not word count alone.

tips.title: Separate writing from usage rights
tips.body: If a client wants exclusive rights, a buyout, or permission to republish elsewhere, add a line item for it instead of folding it into the post price.

tips.title: Invoice at delivery, not at publish
tips.body: Clients can take weeks to publish. Invoice when the final draft is approved or delivered so your payment does not depend on their schedule.

tips.title: Track sponsored posts separately
tips.body: Sponsored content on your own site often involves disclosure requirements, link terms, and promotion. Itemize each element so renewals can be priced from past work.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word or per post?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-word rates are easy to compare and scale for long pieces, while per-post pricing is simpler for clients and works better when research or SEO work varies. Many bloggers quote a flat per-post price and state the expected word count.

faqs.question: Do I need a contract in addition to an invoice?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A short agreement covering scope, revisions, rights, deadlines, and payment terms protects you if there is a dispute. The invoice then reflects what was agreed.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a sponsored post on my own blog?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee based on your traffic, audience, and what is included, such as links, social promotion, and how long the post stays up. List each included element on the invoice so the scope is clear.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit for blog writing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Asking for 25 to 50 percent upfront is common for new clients and larger projects. For small one-off posts, some bloggers require full payment before delivering the final version.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on blog posts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax freelance writing services, but some tax certain digital or advertising services. Check your state's rules or ask a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Bloggers send quotes when a new client asks for a price on a single post, a content package, or an ongoing monthly arrangement. Clients usually compare your per-post price against other freelancers and against agency rates, so the quote needs to show exactly what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of posts and word count for each
scopeChecklist.why: Word count is the main driver of effort, so fixing it prevents a client from asking for 2,000 words on a 1,000-word price.
State whether the client supplies topics or you propose them, and how approval works, to avoid delays and rewrites.
Interviews, original data, or product testing take extra time and should be listed if included or priced separately.
Keyword research, internal links, meta descriptions, and on-page optimization vary widely, so clarify what you will and will not do.
Say whether you provide stock photos, custom graphics, or none, and who pays for image licenses.
Setting the number of edit rounds and the turnaround time limits endless changes and sets expectations on timing.
Clarify who owns the content, whether you may reuse it in a portfolio, and whether you publish it for the client or hand off a document.

pricingTips.title: Quote per post with a stated word count
pricingTips.body: A clear per-post price with a word range is easy for clients to approve and compare. Offer a lower per-post price for a package of several posts.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option with writing only and a fuller option that adds keyword research, images, and promotion. Clients often pick the middle choice.

pricingTips.title: Price rush work higher
pricingTips.body: Add 25 to 50 percent for turnaround under a few days. Put the surcharge on the quote so it does not look like an afterthought.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Rates change as your calendar fills. A 14 to 30 day validity period lets you reprice if the client takes too long to decide.

faqs.question: Should I write a sample post before quoting?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Share published work instead. If a client wants a custom sample, charge for it, and credit that amount toward the project if they hire you.

faqs.question: How do I quote an ongoing content package?
faqs.answer: State the number of posts per month, word count, turnaround, and the monthly fee. Add a minimum term such as three months and explain how either side can cancel.

faqs.question: What if the client's scope is unclear?
faqs.answer: Quote a small paid discovery step, such as a content brief or strategy call, or give a range with assumptions listed. Revise the quote once the scope is firm.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: A written quote the client accepts generally forms the basis of an agreement, but the legal effect varies. Get written acceptance, such as an email approval or signature, before you begin.

boat-repair.intro: Boat repair businesses include marine mechanics, fiberglass and gelcoat specialists, marine electricians, rigging and canvas shops, and mobile techs who work at the slip, the yard, or the owner's driveway. They bill for diagnostic time, repair labor, parts and materials, haul-outs and storage, and shop supplies. Jobs range from a one-hour impeller swap to a multi-month repower or hull restoration.
boat-repair.pricingModel: Most boat repair is billed hourly for labor, plus parts at a markup, plus a small shop supplies or environmental fee. Shop rates are usually lower than mobile rates because mobile work includes travel and a stocked truck. Many shops set a one-hour minimum for diagnostics and a trip charge for dockside calls. Routine jobs such as oil changes, winterization, and commissioning are often sold as flat-fee packages priced by engine type or boat length. Fiberglass and paint work is sometimes quoted per foot of boat length or per square foot of repair. Larger projects such as repowers, engine rebuilds, and refits are typically billed time and materials against a written estimate, with progress billing and a deposit to cover parts. Parts are commonly marked up 15-40%, with special-order and high-cost parts at the lower end. Yard charges like haul-out, launch, blocking, and storage are usually billed per foot of boat length and passed through from the marina or itemized separately.

items.description: Mobile dockside call: diagnose no-start on twin outboard, 24 ft center console
Diagnostic labor, fuel system and starting circuit
Replace fuel/water separator filter elements (2) and clean bowl
Replace starter solenoid, port engine (part, includes markup)
Repair labor, solenoid and battery cable terminal replacement
Shop supplies and disposal fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Parts carry the manufacturer warranty; labor is warrantied for 90 days. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due. Vessel will not be released from the yard until balances on completed work are paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vessel name, hull ID (HIN), make, model, and length
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which boat was worked on, which matters for warranty claims, insurance, and disputes over multiple vessels owned by the same client.

invoiceChecklist.item: Engine make, model, serial number, and engine hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Records the condition of the equipment when you serviced it and supports warranty claims and maintenance history.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with part numbers and quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners and insurers want to see what was replaced, and it makes warranty returns easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor broken out by task with hours and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating diagnostic, repair, and travel time reduces pushback on total hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Yard, haul-out, storage, and launch charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: These are often pass-through costs from a marina or yard and should not be hidden in labor or markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shop supplies, environmental, and disposal fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Covers oil, fuel, bottom paint waste, and solvents. A clear line item avoids looking like padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed work authorization or estimate number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the bill to what the owner approved, including any approved change orders for added work.

boat-repair.paymentTerms: For small repairs, payment is usually due at pickup or on completion, often by card, check, or ACH. Larger jobs typically require a deposit of 25-50% or the full cost of special-order parts before ordering, then progress payments at set milestones and the balance before the boat is launched or leaves the yard. Net 15 is common for commercial clients and marinas. Late fees of 1-2% per month are typical if stated in writing in advance. In many states, a repair shop can file a mechanic's or possessory lien on a vessel for unpaid work, but the rules vary, so check your state's requirements and keep your signed work authorization on file.

tips.title: Get a signed work authorization before touching the boat
tips.body: Include the approved scope, hourly rate, estimate limit, storage terms, and a statement that you may hold the vessel until paid. This supports a lien claim if you need one and prevents arguments about what was approved.

tips.title: Collect deposits for parts
tips.body: Marine parts are often special order and non-returnable. Collect payment for them upfront or require a deposit so you are not carrying the cost of an engine or electronics package if the owner walks away.

tips.title: Bill diagnostic time even if the owner declines the repair
tips.body: Tracing a fault is real work. State the diagnostic minimum on your estimate or authorization and invoice it whether or not the repair goes ahead.

tips.title: Document discoveries with photos and get approval before extra work
tips.body: Soft decking, corroded wiring, and hidden hull damage show up once you open things up. Photograph them, send a written change order, and wait for approval before doing the extra work.

tips.title: Charge storage when jobs stall
tips.body: If an owner delays approval or payment, boats take up yard space. Put a storage rate, such as a per-foot daily or monthly charge, in your authorization and start billing after a stated grace period.

faqs.question: Should I charge a trip fee for mobile boat repair?
faqs.answer: Yes, most mobile techs do. A flat trip charge or a travel-time rate covers drive time and truck costs. Some waive it for customers on a service contract or when multiple boats at the same marina are serviced in one visit.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up marine parts?
faqs.answer: Typical markups run 15-40% over your cost. Smaller, common parts such as filters and impellers carry higher markups, while expensive items like engines and electronics are marked up less. Apply the same policy to all customers and show it consistently.

faqs.question: Can I hold a boat until the invoice is paid?
faqs.answer: In many states, a repair shop has a possessory lien on a vessel in its custody for unpaid repairs, but the rules and notice requirements vary. Keep a signed authorization stating your terms and check your state's law or talk to a maritime attorney before selling or retaining a boat.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on boat repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax parts but not labor, some tax both, and some have exemptions for commercial vessels or work on boats used in certain ways. Check with your state's department of revenue and show tax separately on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I handle warranty work on an invoice?
faqs.answer: List the work with the usual labor and parts detail, then show the warranty credit or manufacturer-billed amount as a separate line so the customer sees a zero or reduced balance. Include the warranty claim number for the manufacturer.

estimate.intro: Boat repair estimates are sent before any work begins, usually after an inspection or sea trial, and for larger jobs such as repowers, refits, and hull repairs. Owners often compare a yard's labor rate, parts pricing, and estimated hours against other shops, and also want to know how long the boat will be out of the water.

scopeChecklist.why: List the repairs by task, such as replace raw water pump and impeller, and note what is not covered, like related hoses or corrosion repair, to avoid assumptions.
Showing estimated hours by task lets the owner see how the total was built and sets expectations for time and materials billing.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts list with new, rebuilt, or OEM designation
scopeChecklist.why: Quality varies widely and affects both price and warranty, so the owner should know what is going into the boat.

scopeChecklist.item: Allowance for hidden damage and the change order process
scopeChecklist.why: Rot, corrosion, and failed fasteners often appear after disassembly. State that extra work requires written approval before proceeding.

scopeChecklist.item: Yard, haul-out, launch, and storage charges
scopeChecklist.why: These costs can be large and vary by boat length and time out of the water, so spell them out and say who pays them.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated timeline and parts lead time
scopeChecklist.why: Special-order parts and weather affect schedules, and owners plan their season around completion dates.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and estimate expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Parts prices and labor rates change, so set a validity window and state when money is due.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range or a not-to-exceed number for open-ended work
pricingTips.body: For jobs where hidden problems are likely, give a range or a cap and promise to call before exceeding it. A fixed price on unknown condition work is risky.

pricingTips.title: Use flat fees for repeatable jobs
pricingTips.body: Winterization, commissioning, oil service, and bottom paint on standard hull sizes can be sold at fixed prices by engine type or boat length. Owners like knowing the total up front.

pricingTips.title: Break big projects into phases
pricingTips.body: Splitting a repower or refit into removal, installation, rigging, and commissioning makes the total easier to review and gives natural points for progress payments.

pricingTips.title: Price in the cost of waiting and rework
pricingTips.body: Allow time for ordering parts, curing fiberglass and paint, and weather delays. If the estimate is too tight, you absorb overruns.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: For simple jobs, free quotes are common. For inspections, surveys-style assessments, or diagnostics that take real time, charge your hourly rate or a flat inspection fee, and credit it toward the repair if the owner proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical, and shorter for work involving expensive parts or volatile material prices. State the expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Hold to the estimate unless the scope changed. If you find additional problems, stop, document them, and get written approval of a change order before continuing. Many states limit how far a repair bill can exceed an estimate without consent, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: Is an estimate the same as a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: No. An estimate is your best projection, and the final bill reflects actual time and parts. A fixed quote is a set price for defined work. Label which one you are giving and say so on the document.

bodyguard.intro: Bodyguards, also called executive protection agents or close protection specialists, are hired by executives, public figures, families, and event hosts to provide personal security. Solo agents and small protection firms bill for hourly or daily coverage, advance work, armed or unarmed posts, driving, and travel costs. Invoices need to show exactly who worked, when, and in what role, because clients often have to justify the expense to a company or insurer.
bodyguard.pricingModel: Most bodyguards bill hourly, with a minimum shift length of 4 to 8 hours, or a day rate for 10 to 12 hour assignments. Armed agents, agents with advanced training or prior federal or military protection experience, and drivers with security training charge more than unarmed or entry-level guards. Overtime past 10 or 12 hours, nights, weekends, and holidays usually carry a premium of 1.25x to 2x. Multi-day or travel details are often quoted as a daily rate plus expenses (airfare, hotel, meals, ground transport) billed at cost or with a small administrative markup. Advance work, such as route surveys, venue walk-throughs, and threat assessments, is billed separately by the hour or as a flat fee. Ongoing clients may move to a monthly retainer with a guaranteed number of hours. Firms that subcontract agents typically bill the client a higher rate than they pay the agent, so solo agents should price from what the client will pay, not what an agency pays its staff.

items.description: Advance work: venue walk-through and route survey (Mar 11)
Armed executive protection, 2-day corporate conference (Mar 14-15), 10 hrs/day
Overtime, Mar 15 (hours 11-12 at 1.5x)
Protective driving, airport transfers and venue shuttles
Mileage in personal vehicle (IRS-rate based, 118 miles)
Parking and tolls, receipts attached

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 15. Payment by ACH or check payable to the business name above. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month after the due date. Expense receipts are attached. Services performed under the signed protection agreement dated March 1.

invoiceChecklist.item: Security license or registration number and issuing state
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require private security and executive protection providers to be licensed, and clients or their insurers often ask for proof.

invoiceChecklist.item: Armed or unarmed designation, with firearm permit details where appropriate
invoiceChecklist.why: Armed posts carry a higher rate, and the invoice should match the role in the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates, start and end times for each shift, and agent names
invoiceChecklist.why: Hours worked are the main charge, and clients need a record of who was on post and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Role breakdown (advance, close protection, driver, residence post)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different roles bill at different rates, and separate lines prevent questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime, night, weekend, and holiday premiums shown separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the premium multiplier ties the charge to the rate in the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized expenses with receipts (travel, lodging, meals, parking, vehicle rental)
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate clients usually require receipts to reimburse or deduct the costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the contract or purchase order number and the client contact name
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable departments often won't process an invoice without a PO or agreement reference.

bodyguard.paymentTerms: Bodyguards commonly require a deposit or retainer before a detail starts, often 25% to 50% of the estimated total or a minimum number of prepaid hours, especially for new clients and travel assignments. Repeat corporate clients are often billed net 15 or net 30, while private individuals and event hosts are usually asked to pay in full before or right after the event. Many agents bill weekly on long assignments. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, wire, check, or card. Cancellation terms, such as a charge for short-notice cancellations under 24 to 48 hours, should be in the agreement, since agents turn down other work to hold the date.

tips.title: Set a minimum shift length
tips.body: A 4 hour minimum is common even for a 2 hour job. Travel to the post, preparation, and the blocked day make short bookings unprofitable without one.

tips.title: Bill advance work and planning
tips.body: Route surveys, venue contact, medical facility mapping, and itinerary planning take real time. List them as their own line items so they are not treated as free.

tips.title: Spell out overtime and call-out rules
tips.body: Details run long. Put the overtime trigger (for example after 10 hours) and the multiplier in the agreement so the extra hours on the invoice are not a surprise.

tips.title: Collect deposits for travel
tips.body: Airfare, hotel, and rental cars come out of your pocket first. Ask for an expense deposit or have the client book and pay directly.

tips.title: Keep records discreet but complete
tips.body: Clients value privacy. Use generic descriptions like 'protective services' and limit detail about locations and principals on invoices, while keeping internal logs of hours and expenses.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a day rate as a bodyguard?
faqs.answer: Hourly works for short events and variable shifts. A day rate fits fixed 10 to 12 hour details and travel. Many agents use a day rate with defined hours and charge overtime by the hour beyond that.

faqs.question: Can I add a markup to travel expenses?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Some agents bill at cost, and others add 5% to 15% for booking and administrative time. Whatever you choose, state it before the job and attach receipts.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to bill as a bodyguard?
faqs.answer: In many states, private security or personal protection work requires a license or registration, and armed work usually requires additional permits. Rules vary widely, so check with your state's licensing agency before taking paid work.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on protection services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax security services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show any tax as its own line if you collect it.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Include a cancellation clause in the agreement, such as charging the minimum shift or 50% of the booked hours if cancelled within 24 to 48 hours. Then bill it as a separate line item referencing that clause.

estimate.intro: Bodyguards give quotes before a detail begins, usually after a call to learn about the principal, the schedule, locations, and threat level. Clients often compare several providers on hourly rate, agent experience, armed versus unarmed coverage, and what is included. A clear written quote also protects you if the scope grows mid-assignment.

scopeChecklist.item: Dates, hours of coverage, and locations
scopeChecklist.why: Defines what you are being paid for and gives a baseline for overtime and extra days.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of agents and their roles
scopeChecklist.why: A one-agent detail and a three-agent team with a driver are very different prices.

scopeChecklist.item: Armed or unarmed, and any licensing or permit limits
scopeChecklist.why: Armed work changes the rate and insurance requirements, and carrying may be restricted in some locations, such as other states.

scopeChecklist.item: Advance work, planning, and assessment included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes over unpaid prep time.
Details that run late are common, and the client should know the rate beforehand.
States who pays for airfare, lodging, meals, vehicles, and whether expenses are billed at cost or with a markup.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation and change terms, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Protects your calendar and lets you re-price if the schedule or threat level changes.

pricingTips.title: Price from the risk and the schedule
pricingTips.body: A low-profile office visit and a high-profile public appearance need different staffing. Ask about threat level, crowd size, and number of venues before giving a number.

pricingTips.title: Include a minimum shift
pricingTips.body: Quote a minimum, such as 4 hours, and apply it to every assignment so short bookings still cover your time.

pricingTips.title: Show a range for uncertain scope
pricingTips.body: If the client's schedule is unsettled, quote a base number of hours and an overtime rate, and say the final invoice will reflect actual hours.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic option with one unarmed agent and a premium option with an armed agent and driver lets clients choose based on budget and risk.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or quote?
faqs.answer: Short calls are usually free. A full risk assessment or detailed protection plan is real work, so many agents charge a flat fee and credit it toward the contract if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical. Availability of agents and travel prices change, so a short validity window is reasonable.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that changes in hours, locations, or staffing will be billed at the quoted rates, and confirm changes in writing or by email before you do the extra work.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, for most protection work. The quote gives the price, and a signed agreement covers liability, use of force and conduct expectations, confidentiality, and payment terms. Have a lawyer review your template.

bookkeeper.intro: Bookkeepers record transactions, reconcile accounts, and keep a small business's books current so the owner and their tax preparer can rely on the numbers. Most work solo or in a small practice and bill for monthly bookkeeping, catch-up or cleanup projects, payroll processing, and sometimes hourly advisory work. Invoices usually go out monthly and need to show which periods and accounts the work covered.
bookkeeper.pricingModel: Most bookkeepers use a mix of monthly flat-fee packages and hourly billing. Ongoing clients are typically on a fixed monthly fee based on transaction volume, number of bank and credit card accounts, and whether payroll or accounts payable is included. Cleanup and catch-up work for months or years of neglected books is usually billed hourly or as a fixed project fee after a look at the files. Add-ons such as payroll, 1099 preparation, sales tax filings, and accounts receivable follow-up are often priced per run or per filing. Hourly rates cover ad hoc work, training, and anything outside the agreed scope. Many bookkeepers also charge a one-time onboarding fee for setting up the chart of accounts, bank feeds, and rules.

rates.service: Monthly bookkeeping (higher volume or multiple accounts)
Hourly bookkeeping and ad hoc support

items.description: Monthly bookkeeping, March 2025 (2 bank accounts, 1 credit card, up to 150 transactions)
Payroll processing, bi-weekly, 4 employees (March 7 and March 21)
Cleanup of prior-year uncategorized transactions (Oct-Dec 2024)
Accounts receivable follow-up, 5 overdue customer invoices
1099-NEC preparation and e-filing

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Monthly fee is billed in advance on the first of each month. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past 30 days. Work outside the agreed scope is billed at $60 per hour. Please send missing receipts and statements by the 5th of each month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered (e.g. March 2025 books)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and their tax preparers need to match your fee to the month of work, and it prevents confusion on recurring invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized scope of each charge: monthly fee, payroll runs, cleanup hours, filings
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating the recurring fee from one-off work shows the client where extra charges come from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and date range for any hourly cleanup or catch-up work
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly charges get questioned most often, so the period and hours worked support the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of accounts or transactions included in a flat fee
invoiceChecklist.why: If volume goes above the package limit, you have a documented basis for adjusting the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payroll run dates and number of employees
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-run fees are easier to verify when each pay date is listed, and it ties to the client's payroll records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Any pass-through costs such as software subscriptions or filing fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing these as separate lines keeps your service fee clear and lets the client see what was reimbursed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, contact details, and any credentials such as QuickBooks ProAdvisor or enrolled status, if relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forward bookkeeper invoices to their accountant, who may need to identify the vendor and expense category.

bookkeeper.paymentTerms: Recurring bookkeeping is commonly billed in advance at the start of the month, with payment due on receipt or within 7 to 15 days. Project work such as cleanup often requires a deposit of 25 to 50 percent, with the balance due at completion or in milestone payments. Net 15 is more common than net 30 because bookkeepers rely on steady monthly cash flow. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your engagement agreement or on the invoice. Many bookkeepers accept ACH transfer, card payments, or checks, and some set up automatic monthly billing so clients are not chasing invoices. Consider pausing work if a client is more than 30 days behind.

tips.title: Bill monthly fees in advance
tips.body: Billing for the coming month means you are never carrying a client's books on credit. State this in your engagement letter so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Define what a transaction cap means
tips.body: If your package covers up to a set number of transactions, write down the cap and the overage rate. Clients whose business grows often outgrow their package without noticing.

tips.title: Quote cleanup work separately from ongoing service
tips.body: Catch-up work is unpredictable. Billing it hourly or as a separate capped project keeps your ongoing monthly fee stable and your cleanup time paid.

tips.title: Charge for late or missing records
tips.body: If you spend hours chasing receipts or statements, include a clause allowing hourly billing for that time. Otherwise the cost comes out of your flat fee.

tips.title: Review your rates every year
tips.body: Client volume, software costs, and your experience all change. A small annual increase with 30 days notice is easier to accept than a large jump every few years.

faqs.question: Should a bookkeeper charge hourly or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Flat monthly fees suit ongoing clients with predictable volume and give you steady income. Hourly billing suits cleanup projects, one-off requests, and clients whose needs are hard to predict. Many bookkeepers use a flat fee for the core service and hourly for anything outside it.

faqs.question: Do bookkeepers charge sales tax on their services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain professional or accounting services, while most do not tax bookkeeping. Check your state department of revenue rules or ask a tax professional before assuming either way.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a bookkeeping invoice?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, if the fee is agreed in advance, usually in your engagement letter or on the invoice terms. Keep the rate reasonable and check any limits on interest or late fees in your state.

faqs.question: How do I bill for catch-up work when I do not know how bad the books are?
faqs.answer: Look at a sample of bank statements and the current state of the software before quoting. Then either bill hourly with a not-to-exceed estimate or quote a fixed fee per month of books cleaned up. Tell the client in writing that missing records may change the price.

faqs.question: Should I invoice the client for software subscriptions I pay for?
faqs.answer: If you buy software on the client's behalf, bill it as a separate pass-through line at cost or with a stated markup. If the tool is part of your own workflow, most bookkeepers include it in their monthly fee rather than billing it separately.

estimate.intro: Bookkeepers send a quote or proposal before taking on a new client or a cleanup project, usually after a short discovery call and a look at the client's accounts. The client is comparing monthly price, what is included, response time, and whether the bookkeeper will handle payroll, sales tax, and tax-year cleanup. A clear scope matters more than the lowest number.

scopeChecklist.item: Accounting software and who owns the subscription
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should own their file and login so they keep access if the engagement ends, and the quote should say who pays for the software.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of bank, credit card, and loan accounts included
scopeChecklist.why: Account count is one of the main drivers of workload, and extra accounts are a common source of disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly transaction limit and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: Sets the boundary for the flat fee and gives you a fair way to adjust if volume grows.

scopeChecklist.item: Period of any cleanup or catch-up work and condition of records
scopeChecklist.why: The price depends on how many months need work and whether statements and receipts are available.

scopeChecklist.item: Included extras: payroll, accounts payable, invoicing, sales tax, 1099s
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume these are covered, so listing what is and is not included avoids surprise charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly deliverables and deadlines, such as reports by the 15th
scopeChecklist.why: Defines what the client receives and when, and ties your deadline to the client sending records on time.

scopeChecklist.item: What you need from the client and what happens if records are late
scopeChecklist.why: Late or missing documents can drive up your hours, so state how you will bill for the extra time.

pricingTips.title: Look at the books before you quote
pricingTips.body: Ask for read-only access or a few months of statements. A quote based on a quick glance at a messy file is how bookkeepers end up working below their hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and full-service tier let clients choose by budget and make your scope easy to compare. Keep the differences concrete, such as account count, payroll, and reporting.

pricingTips.title: Quote cleanup as a capped hourly estimate
pricingTips.body: Give a range or a not-to-exceed number and state what would change it. This protects you if records turn out worse than expected and keeps the client comfortable with the budget.

pricingTips.title: Include a start date and quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Set a date by which the client must accept, usually 14 to 30 days, since your workload and the state of their books can change.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial consultation or quote?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is usually free. If you need to review records in depth to scope a large cleanup, many bookkeepers charge a flat fee for that review and credit it toward the project if the client signs.

faqs.question: What if the cleanup takes longer than quoted?
faqs.answer: If you quoted a capped estimate, tell the client as soon as you see it will be exceeded and get approval before continuing. Your quote should state that missing or inaccurate records may change the price.

faqs.question: Is a bookkeeping quote a binding contract?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. A quote becomes a firm agreement once the client accepts it, ideally by signing an engagement letter that includes scope, fees, payment terms, and how either party can end the arrangement.

bookkeeping.intro: Bookkeepers record and categorize transactions, reconcile accounts, and prepare monthly financial reports for small businesses, freelancers, and nonprofits. Most work solo or in a small practice and bill on a recurring monthly basis, with extra invoices for cleanup projects, catch-up work, payroll processing, and one-off tasks like year-end prep for a tax preparer.
bookkeeping.pricingModel: Most bookkeepers use one of three models: a monthly flat fee tied to a defined scope, hourly billing, or a one-time project fee. Monthly packages are the most common for ongoing clients and are usually priced by transaction volume, number of bank and credit card accounts, and whether payroll, accounts payable, or accounts receivable are included. Hourly billing is typical for cleanup work, messy books, and clients with unpredictable needs. Catch-up or cleanup projects are often quoted as a flat fee based on the number of months behind and the number of accounts, or billed hourly with a cap. Add-ons such as payroll runs, 1099 preparation, sales tax filings, and CFO-style reporting are usually priced separately. Many bookkeepers bill the monthly fee in advance at the start of the month, since the work happens after the month closes.

rates.service: Monthly bookkeeping package (small business, under 100 transactions)
Monthly bookkeeping package (higher volume, multiple accounts)
Accounting software setup and chart of accounts

items.description: Monthly bookkeeping, March 2025 (transaction categorization, bank and credit card reconciliation, monthly P&L and balance sheet)
Payroll processing, bi-weekly, 3 employees
Cleanup of October-December 2024 transactions (uncategorized items, 2 bank accounts)
1099-NEC preparation and e-filing

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Accepted by ACH or check. A late fee of 1.5% per month applies to balances over 30 days past due. Monthly service covers items listed in the engagement letter dated January 6, 2025; work outside that scope is billed hourly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered (for example, March 2025 books)
invoiceChecklist.why: Bookkeeping is recurring, and clients and their accountants need to match each charge to the month of work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope of the monthly package or reference to the engagement letter
invoiceChecklist.why: It makes clear what the flat fee includes and which charges are extra, which prevents disputes over add-on work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for add-ons such as payroll, 1099s, and cleanup
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients can see what is routine and what is one-time, and it supports the fee if they ask for a breakdown.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and hourly rate for any time-based work, with a brief description
invoiceChecklist.why: Cleanup and ad hoc work is often questioned, and a dated description of what was fixed answers most pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of accounts or forms processed
invoiceChecklist.why: If pricing depends on accounts or filings, the count justifies the amount and shows when volume has grown.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as software subscriptions or filing fees
invoiceChecklist.why: If you buy a software seat or pay a filing fee on the client's behalf, list it separately at cost so it is not mistaken for your fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms, accepted methods, and late fee policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Bookkeepers often wait on clients to send documents and pay, so terms in writing support collection.

bookkeeping.paymentTerms: Many bookkeepers bill monthly packages at the start of the month or on a fixed date, with payment due on receipt or within 7 to 15 days. Cleanup projects often require a deposit of 25% to 50% before work begins, with the balance due at delivery. Hourly work is usually billed monthly in arrears, net 15 or net 30. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common but should be in your engagement letter first, and check your state's rules on interest charges. ACH and card payments are the norm, and many bookkeepers set up automatic recurring payments for retainer clients. Some pause work, or stop delivering reports, if an invoice is more than 30 days overdue, which should also be spelled out in writing.

tips.title: Bill monthly fees in advance
tips.body: Since you do the work after the month closes, billing at the start of the month keeps you from financing your clients. Autopay for recurring fees cuts down on chasing late payments.

tips.title: Put scope in an engagement letter and refer to it on invoices
tips.body: List the accounts, transaction limits, reports, and turnaround time. Anything beyond that, such as extra accounts or messy backlogs, is billed hourly, and the invoice can point to the letter.

tips.title: Charge for cleanup separately from ongoing service
tips.body: Fixing prior-period errors takes more time than regular upkeep. Bill it as its own line at a higher rate or as a flat project fee so the monthly price is not dragged down.

tips.title: Review pricing when transaction volume changes
tips.body: If a client doubles their transactions or adds a bank account, raise the monthly fee. Build a volume threshold into your agreement so the change is not a surprise.

tips.title: Set a firm policy on missing records
tips.body: Delays often come from clients who do not send statements or receipts. State that late documents may push back your delivery date, and bill the hours spent chasing them if it becomes a pattern.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat monthly fee for bookkeeping?
faqs.answer: Flat monthly fees work well for stable clients with predictable volume, and they give you steady income. Hourly billing suits cleanup, unclear scope, or clients who ask for frequent extras. Many bookkeepers use a flat fee for the base service and hourly rates for anything outside it.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on bookkeeping services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Most states do not tax bookkeeping services, but a few tax some professional or business services. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional before assuming either way.

faqs.question: Can I stop work if a client doesn't pay?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if your agreement says so. Include a clause allowing you to suspend services, including access to reports, when an invoice is a set number of days overdue. Give written notice before pausing, and be careful about withholding the client's own records, since some states have rules about returning them.

faqs.question: How do I bill for time spent talking to the client's accountant?
faqs.answer: Bill it as time-based work at your hourly rate unless your package includes it. Include a line such as 'Coordination with CPA, year-end questions' with the hours so the client can see what it covers.

faqs.question: What if a client wants a refund because the books had errors?
faqs.answer: Fix the errors at no charge if they were your mistake and note the correction in your records. If the problem came from missing or wrong information from the client, explain that and bill the rework at your hourly rate. A clear scope and a record of what documents you received make this much easier.

estimate.intro: Bookkeepers send estimates before taking on a new client, a cleanup project, or a one-time setup. Prospects usually compare monthly fees and ask what is included, so a clear scope matters as much as the number. Most of the pricing work happens after you have looked at their accounts, software, and backlog.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and type of accounts covered (bank, credit card, loan, payment processor)
scopeChecklist.why: Price scales with accounts, and clients often forget about PayPal, Stripe, or a second card until reconciliation starts.
Setting a ceiling lets you adjust the fee if volume grows well beyond what you quoted.

scopeChecklist.item: Accounting software and who pays for it
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether the client has a subscription, whether you need access, and whether any software cost is passed through.
A monthly P&L and balance sheet are different from full management reporting, and the delivery date affects expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Period of cleanup or catch-up work and condition of the books
scopeChecklist.why: Backlog scope is the biggest source of overruns, so name the months covered and the assumptions about record quality.

scopeChecklist.item: What the client must provide and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Statements, receipts, and payroll reports are usually late, so say that delays move your deadlines.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as tax preparation, tax advice, audits, and financial statements for lenders
scopeChecklist.why: Many clients assume bookkeeping includes tax filing, and spelling out what is excluded avoids misunderstandings.

pricingTips.title: Look at the books before quoting a cleanup
pricingTips.body: Ask for read-only access or sample statements and the last few months of data. A quick review shows uncategorized items, missing reconciliations, and mixed personal spending that change the hours.

pricingTips.title: Quote cleanup as a range or a capped hourly estimate
pricingTips.body: Messy books are hard to predict. A range, such as 20 to 30 hours at your hourly rate, with a promise to check in at 20 hours, is safer than a fixed price based on guesswork.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers for monthly service
pricingTips.body: For example, a basic tier with categorization and reconciliation, a mid tier that adds payroll and bill pay, and a full tier with reporting calls. Tiers help the client choose and make upsells easier later.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date and an adjustment clause
pricingTips.body: A 30-day expiration on the quote and a clause allowing a fee review if volume or accounts change keeps an old quote from locking you into an unprofitable rate.

faqs.question: Should I give a free estimate for bookkeeping?
faqs.answer: A short intro call and a quote for standard monthly service is usually free. For cleanup projects that require reviewing records, some bookkeepers charge a small paid assessment fee, sometimes credited toward the project if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How do I estimate catch-up work when I haven't seen the books?
faqs.answer: Give a range and state your assumptions, such as the number of months, the number of accounts, and that the client will provide statements. Say that significant differences from those assumptions will change the price, and agree to notify the client before going over.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: An estimate is a good-faith approximation, while a quote or fixed-price proposal is a firm offer once accepted. Label the document clearly and have the client sign or approve it so the scope and price are on record.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the estimate?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. An engagement letter that includes the scope, fee, payment terms, and confidentiality protects both sides. Many bookkeepers combine the estimate and engagement terms in one document that the client signs.

boxing-coach.intro: Boxing coaches train beginners, fitness clients, amateur competitors, and sometimes pros, either one-on-one, in small groups, or in classes at a gym. They bill for private sessions, session packages, group classes, corner work at fights, and add-ons like fight camp programming or equipment fitting. Many work as independent contractors inside someone else's gym, so invoices often cover both what the client owes and any gym fees involved.
boxing-coach.pricingModel: Most boxing coaches charge per session for private training, usually 45 to 60 minutes, with a discount when clients buy a package of 5, 10, or 20 sessions up front. Small group training is priced per person, which is lower than the private rate but earns more per hour overall. Group classes are either paid per head by the client or a flat rate per class by the gym. Competitive athletes may pay a monthly fee for fight camp, which covers training, sparring coordination, and programming. Corner work on fight night is usually a flat fee or a percentage of the fighter's purse, which should be agreed in writing in advance. Coaches who rent space from a gym often factor in a mat fee or a percentage split, and should price so that the net rate after the gym's cut still works.

rates.service: Semi-private or small group training (2-4 people)

items.description: Private boxing training, 60 minutes (10-session package, sessions 1-10)
Pad work and mitt rounds add-on for competitive prep (extra 15 min)
Hand wraps, 180 inch (pair)
Gym mat and ring use fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Package sessions expire 90 days from first session. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are charged in full. Payment due within 7 days by Zelle, card, or check. Thank you for training with me.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute package usage less often when each session is listed with a date, and it helps track expiration windows.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session length and type (private, semi-private, group, pad work)
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by format and duration, so the invoice should show exactly what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages create a running balance. Showing sessions used and sessions left prevents confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment or gear sold separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Wraps, gloves, mouthguards, and headgear are retail items and should be listed apart from coaching time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gym or facility fees
invoiceChecklist.why: If you pass through a mat fee, ring rental, or day pass, itemizing it keeps your coaching rate clean and avoids confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellations cost you a booked hour. Listing them separately with the policy date shows the charge is expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance or certification reference, if requested
invoiceChecklist.why: Some gyms, corporate clients, and parents of youth athletes ask for proof of liability coverage or USA Boxing coaching credentials before paying.

boxing-coach.paymentTerms: Private clients often pay at the start of each session or buy a package in advance, which is the most reliable arrangement. For packages, require full payment before the first session and set an expiration window, commonly 60 to 120 days. Fight camp fees are usually billed monthly in advance. For corporate or event work, ask for a 25 to 50 percent deposit and net 14 to 30 days on the balance. Many coaches accept card, Zelle, Venmo, cash, and check. Late fees are less common with individual clients, but a stated cancellation policy, typically 12 to 24 hours notice, is standard. If you are paid a percentage of a fighter's purse, get the split in writing and confirm when the promoter pays out.

tips.title: Sell packages, not single sessions
tips.body: A 10-session package paid up front smooths your income and reduces no-shows because the client has already committed. Offer a modest discount, such as one session off, and put an expiration date on it.

tips.title: Separate coaching from gear
tips.body: Gloves, wraps, and mouthguards are product sales. List them as their own lines so clients see coaching rates clearly and you can track what you spent on gear you resold.

tips.title: Write down the corner and purse arrangement
tips.body: Fighter and coach agreements often get vague. Put the flat fee or percentage, who pays travel and lodging, and the payment date in writing before the bout.

tips.title: Account for the gym's cut
tips.body: If you rent space or split revenue with a gym, calculate your net rate after fees. Many coaches realize a $60 session only nets $40 once costs are included.

tips.title: Keep records of mileage and training costs
tips.body: If you travel to clients, events, or fights, track mileage and expenses such as certifications, insurance, and equipment. These are commonly deductible for self-employed coaches, but check with a tax professional.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the session or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Most boxing coaches charge per session with a set length, usually 30, 45, or 60 minutes. This is easier for clients to understand and avoids arguments about warm-up and cooldown time. Charge extra for sessions that run long.

faqs.question: How do I handle clients who don't use all their package sessions?
faqs.answer: Put an expiration date in writing when they buy. State whether unused sessions are forfeited, extended, or refundable. Many coaches make packages non-refundable but allow a limited extension for illness or injury.

faqs.question: Do I need liability insurance to invoice clients?
faqs.answer: There is no universal rule, but many gyms require independent coaches to carry liability insurance, and it protects you in a contact sport. Some clients and event organizers will ask for a certificate of insurance before paying. Check what your gym and state require.

faqs.question: How should I bill for a fighter's camp?
faqs.answer: A flat monthly fee works well because camp involves training, programming, sparring setup, and availability. Define what is included, such as number of sessions per week, and bill at the start of each month. Corner work on fight night is usually a separate fee.

faqs.question: Can I charge sales tax on sessions?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax fitness services or memberships and others do not, and gear sales are generally taxable. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Boxing coaches send estimates for things that go beyond a standard session rate: fight camps, corporate workshops, youth programs, event appearances, and multi-month training plans. Clients usually compare per-session cost, the experience and credentials of the coach, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether they are paying for private, semi-private, or group sessions and how long each lasts.

scopeChecklist.item: Duration of the program and schedule
scopeChecklist.why: A 12-week camp with three sessions a week is a different commitment than open-ended training, and the quote should state start and end dates.
List things like pad work, strength conditioning, nutrition guidance, sparring coordination, and video review so there are no assumptions.
State who provides gloves, wraps, pads, and bags, and whether mat, ring, or facility fees are on top of the coaching rate.
For competitors, specify whether corner work is included, the fee, travel and lodging responsibility, and any purse percentage.
Setting these up front prevents disputes when sessions are missed or a package runs past its window.
Boxing carries injury risk. Note that a signed waiver and, for competitive clients, a medical clearance may be required before training or sparring.

pricingTips.title: Price from your net hourly target
pricingTips.body: Start with the amount you need to make per hour after gym fees, insurance, gear, and unpaid time such as travel and programming. Then set your per-session rate so that figure holds.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: Showing a 5-session, 10-session, and 20-session option lets clients choose. The larger packages carry a lower per-session rate, which encourages commitment and gives you prepaid income.

pricingTips.title: Quote competitive camps as a flat monthly fee
pricingTips.body: Camp work includes extra hours that do not show up in a session count, like planning, mitt work scheduling, and communicating with the fighter's team. A flat monthly rate covers that without nickel-and-diming.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Gym schedules fill up. A 14 to 30 day validity on your quote protects your time slots and rates.

faqs.question: Should I give free trial sessions?
faqs.answer: Many coaches offer a discounted or free first session to assess fitness and goals. If you do, state it clearly in the quote, limit it to one per client, and tell them what the regular rate is after that.

faqs.question: How do I quote a corporate or event workshop?
faqs.answer: Quote a flat fee based on session length, group size, and equipment you bring. Include setup time, travel, and any gear rental. Ask for a deposit to hold the date.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after a client accepts my quote?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. If the client asks for more sessions, added programming, or different terms, issue a revised quote. Rate increases generally apply to new packages, not ones already paid for.

brand-designer.intro: Brand designers create the visual identity for businesses, including logos, color palettes, typography, and the guidelines that tie them together. Solo designers and small studios invoice for discovery, concept development, revision rounds, final file delivery, and sometimes extras such as collateral or brand guidelines documents.
brand-designer.pricingModel: Most brand designers quote a flat project fee for a defined package, such as a logo and mini identity, a full brand identity, or a brand refresh, and invoice it in milestones. Hourly rates are used for small add-ons, out-of-scope requests, and ongoing support, while monthly retainers cover clients who need steady design help after launch. Packages usually spell out the number of initial concepts, rounds of revisions, and the files delivered. Project fees reflect the client's size and how the identity will be used, not only the hours spent. Extras such as stock photography, custom fonts, trademark research, and printing are billed separately, often at cost or with a small markup. Rush work is commonly priced at a 25 to 50 percent premium.

rates.service: Full brand identity (logo suite, colors, type, patterns)
Brand collateral (business cards, letterhead, social templates)

items.description: Brand discovery workshop and competitor audit
Logo design: 3 initial concepts, 2 revision rounds on selected direction
Color palette, typography selection, and secondary marks
12-page brand guidelines PDF
Additional revision round beyond package scope
Licensed typeface (web and desktop, 1 brand)

sampleInvoice.notes: Final invoice for the Harbor Roast brand identity project. A 50 percent deposit of $3,905 was paid on signing. Balance due within 14 days. Final file package (AI, EPS, SVG, PNG, PDF) was delivered by download link; usage rights transfer upon full payment. Late balances accrue 1.5 percent per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and phase or milestone being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Brand projects are billed in stages, so the client needs to see whether this is the deposit, the concept milestone, or the final balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables list with revision counts
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the concepts and revision rounds included shows what was covered and supports charging for extra rounds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope work itemized separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Added requests such as extra logo variations or social templates should appear on their own lines with hours or flat prices so they aren't disputed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs such as fonts, stock images, or icon licenses
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real expenses, and the invoice should show the license type and who holds the license so the client can reuse it correctly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and ownership terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State when copyright or usage rights transfer, typically on final payment, and note anything excluded such as unused concepts or licensed assets.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the deposit credit prevents confusion over what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or legal entity name
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often need a PO number or exact entity name to process payment through accounts payable.

brand-designer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 40 to 50 percent is standard before work begins, and many designers hold the final files until the balance is paid. Larger identity projects are often split into three payments: deposit, approval of the chosen concept, and final delivery. Net 7 to net 14 is common for milestone invoices, and net 30 is typical when working with larger companies. Late fees of 1 to 2 percent per month are usually written into the contract. Most designers accept bank transfer (ACH), credit card, and check, and some add a card processing fee for large payments.

tips.title: Tie final file delivery to final payment
tips.body: Deliver a watermarked or low-resolution preview for approval, and release the full vector files, source files, and usage rights only after the balance clears. This is the strongest leverage you have, so put it in the contract and on the invoice.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in numbers
tips.body: State how many rounds are included, such as two rounds on the chosen concept, and what counts as a round. Bill additional rounds hourly or at a set price so scope creep gets paid.

tips.title: Bill for strategy, not only drawing time
tips.body: Discovery, research, and positioning work shape the final identity and take real time. Put them on the invoice as their own line item so clients see the value behind the visuals.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: Branding projects can stretch over weeks or months when feedback is slow. Billing at kickoff, concept approval, and delivery keeps cash flowing and gives clients a reason to respond promptly.

tips.title: Add a kill fee for stalled projects
tips.body: If a client goes silent for 30 to 60 days or cancels mid-project, your contract should allow you to invoice for work completed to date and keep the deposit.

faqs.question: Should a brand designer charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Most charge a flat project fee for a defined package because clients want a known cost and the value of a brand is not tied to hours. Use hourly rates for small tasks, revisions beyond the agreed rounds, and work that is hard to scope in advance.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for more revisions?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract or estimate sets the number of included revision rounds. Invoice additional rounds at your hourly rate or at a flat price per round, and list them as a separate line item.

faqs.question: When should I transfer the copyright to the client?
faqs.answer: Most designers transfer rights to the final chosen logo and identity upon receipt of full payment. Unused concepts usually stay with the designer. Put the timing in your contract and repeat it in the notes on your invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for stock photos and fonts?
faqs.answer: List them as separate expense lines at cost or with a modest markup, and say whether the license is in the client's name. Some designers ask clients to purchase fonts directly so the license is correct from the start.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain digital or design services, and others do not tax services at all. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax collected as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Brand designers send a proposal or estimate after a discovery call and before any design work begins. Clients often compare several designers, so the quote has to show what is included, how many concepts and revisions they get, and what the process looks like, not only the total price.

scopeChecklist.why: Spell out what the client receives, such as primary logo, secondary marks, color palette, type system, and guidelines, so there is no assumption of extras like social templates or signage.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Concept and revision counts are the main source of scope creep in branding, so a number agreed up front gives you a basis to bill for more.
State which formats are delivered (vector, PNG, PDF) and whether the identity is for print, web, or both, since it affects both the work and later requests.
Include project phases and how long the client has to give feedback, and state what happens to the schedule if feedback is late.
Mention items not included, such as trademark searches, naming, copywriting, website design, and printing, so clients do not expect them.
Fonts, stock imagery, and printing vary widely, so state who pays and whether the estimate covers them.
A deposit, milestone amounts, and an expiry date, such as 30 days, protect you from price changes and slow decisions.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as logo only, logo with identity system, and full identity with guidelines. Clients tend to pick the middle option, and tiers move the conversation from whether to hire you to which package fits.

pricingTips.title: Price to the client's size and use
pricingTips.body: A local bakery and a funded startup need different levels of research, rollout, and rights, and can pay very different amounts. Adjust scope and price based on audience, number of applications, and business impact.

pricingTips.title: Show the process, not an hourly breakdown
pricingTips.body: Describe phases like discovery, concepts, refinement, and delivery with a price for the whole project. Breaking down hours invites haggling over each line, while a phased scope focuses on outcomes.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for revisions and unclear feedback
pricingTips.body: If the client has several decision makers, build in extra time or specify a single point of contact. Multiple stakeholders are a common reason branding projects run over.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or a range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed price for a clearly defined scope. If the client is still unsure what they need, offer a range with the assumptions behind it and a plan to confirm the final price after discovery.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals or discovery calls?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is usually free. If the proposal requires research, a custom presentation, or spec concepts, charge a paid discovery phase instead. Never create spec logo work for free.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. An expiry date keeps you from being held to old pricing and prompts clients to decide, and you can reissue the quote if your availability or rates change.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change scope after accepting the estimate?
faqs.answer: Issue a short change order with the added work, price, and any timeline effect, and get it approved in writing before starting. Then bill it as a separate line on the next invoice.

branding.intro: Branding designers and small branding studios build visual identities for businesses: logos, color palettes, typography, brand guidelines, and the files that go with them. Invoices usually cover a discovery phase, design rounds, final file delivery, and any add-ons such as stationery, packaging, or a brand strategy workshop.
branding.pricingModel: Most branding work is priced as a flat project fee, often split into phases (discovery and strategy, concept development, refinement, and final delivery). Packages are common, such as a logo-only package, a core identity package, and a full brand system. Hourly rates are used for small tasks, retainers, and out-of-scope changes, typically $75-200 per hour depending on experience and market. Many designers include a set number of concepts and revision rounds in the fee and bill extra rounds separately. Usage rights, trademark-related work, and rush timelines can add to the price. Third-party costs such as stock fonts, stock imagery, printing, and domain or trademark filing fees are usually passed through at cost or with a small handling markup.

rates.service: Core brand identity (logo, palette, type, basic usage rules)
Full brand system with guidelines document
Business card, letterhead, and stationery set
Brand refresh or ongoing design support

items.description: Brand identity project, Phase 1: Discovery, questionnaire, competitor review, and moodboard (50% deposit invoiced separately)
Brand identity project, Phase 2: Logo concepts (3 directions) and one refined direction
Color palette, typography selection, and secondary marks
Brand guidelines PDF (16 pages)
Additional revision round beyond the two included
Font licenses (web and desktop) purchased on client's behalf

sampleInvoice.notes: Final balance due within 14 days of invoice date. Final logo files and guidelines are released upon receipt of payment in full. Font licenses are in the client's name. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and phase being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Branding is billed in stages, and the client needs to see which milestone this invoice covers and how it ties to the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed proposal or contract date
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the invoice to the agreed scope, deliverables, and revision limits if there is any dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed or handed over
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the logo suite, file formats, and guidelines shows what the client is paying for and supports the final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extra revision rounds or out-of-scope work with hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra changes need a clear record so they do not look like a surprise charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as fonts, stock, printing, or filing fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing these separately, with receipts available, keeps them distinct from your design fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and ownership statement
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating that ownership transfers on full payment protects you and tells the client when they can use the final files.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit already paid and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: It shows the running total and avoids confusion about what is still owed.

branding.paymentTerms: A deposit of 30-50% before work begins is standard in branding, and many designers will not start without it. The rest is often split at a midpoint milestone and at final delivery, or billed as one balance at completion. Common terms are due on receipt or net 14 for final invoices, with net 30 more typical for corporate clients. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Most designers hold the final, unwatermarked files and ownership transfer until the last payment clears. Payment is usually accepted by ACH, card, or check, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not dates
tips.body: Billing at kickoff, concept approval, and delivery keeps cash flowing and gives you a natural pause if a client stalls on feedback.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid
tips.body: Share watermarked or low-resolution previews during the project and release vector files and guidelines only after the final payment. State this in the contract and on each invoice.

tips.title: Define revision rounds and bill extras
tips.body: Include a set number of rounds in the fee, such as two. Track extra rounds in hours and bill them at your hourly rate so scope creep gets paid.

tips.title: Pass through third-party costs at cost
tips.body: Fonts, stock photos, printing, and trademark filings should be listed separately. Get client approval before buying anything large.

tips.title: Add a kill fee or stalled-project clause
tips.body: If a client goes quiet for 30 or 60 days, your contract can allow you to close the project and invoice for completed phases. Reference it when you send the invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge per project or by the hour for branding?
faqs.answer: Most branding designers quote a flat project fee because clients want a known cost and value the result, not the hours. Hourly billing works better for small edits, add-on work, and anything outside the original scope.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Between 30% and 50% is typical, and 50% is common for smaller projects. Larger projects are often split into three payments: at kickoff, after concept approval, and at delivery.

faqs.question: When does the client own the logo?
faqs.answer: Usually when the final invoice is paid in full, as stated in your contract. Until then, you keep the rights and the client holds only a license for approved previews. Your contract should say this, and the details can vary by state and agreement.

faqs.question: Can I bill for concepts the client rejected?
faqs.answer: Yes. The fee covers the creative work, not only the chosen option. Your contract should say that concept development is billed at the milestone regardless of whether the client picks a direction.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on branding work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax digital goods or design services, and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant before you decide how to bill it.

estimate.intro: A branding designer sends a proposal or quote after a discovery call and before any design starts. Clients often compare several studios, so the quote needs to show clearly what they get, how many rounds are included, and how the price compares in scope, not just in total.

scopeChecklist.why: List the primary logo, secondary marks, color palette, type system, and file types (AI, SVG, PNG, PDF) so there is no confusion about what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Revision limits are the main protection against endless changes. State, for example, three concepts and two rounds on the chosen direction.
Branding slips when feedback is late. Set review deadlines and say what happens to the schedule if they are missed.
Name items such as website design, packaging, photography, trademark search, and printing so clients do not assume they are covered.
Spell out when ownership transfers and whether you may show the work in your portfolio.
Fonts, stock assets, and print production can add up. Say whether they are estimated, billed at cost, or paid by the client directly.
A deposit amount, milestone dates, and a quote valid for 30 days protect you from pricing changes and delays.

pricingTips.title: Offer three tiers
pricingTips.body: A logo-only, core identity, and full brand system package lets clients choose a level without negotiating the scope from scratch. The middle option often wins.

pricingTips.title: Price the outcome, not your hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours internally, then add for strategy, meetings, and project management. A client with an established business and growth plans can usually afford more than a new freelancer.

pricingTips.title: Include a discovery phase in the price
pricingTips.body: Research and strategy shape the whole project. Charging for it separately or as part of the quote shows the client that it is real work.

pricingTips.title: Add a rush fee when needed
pricingTips.body: If a client needs identity work in half the normal time, add 25-50% and state it on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal?
faqs.answer: Usually not for a short proposal after a call. For large projects that need extensive research or a pitch with custom concepts, a paid discovery phase or pitch fee is reasonable.

faqs.question: How detailed should a branding quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list deliverables, rounds, timeline, and exclusions, but typically one to three pages. Clients should be able to compare it with another studio's quote line by line.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change the scope after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Send a change order with the added work, cost, and timeline impact, and get approval before starting. It keeps the original price intact and the added work billable.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. After that, your availability and prices may change, so ask clients to accept in writing and pay the deposit to confirm their project slot.

brow-artist.intro: Brow artists shape, tint, laminate, and enhance clients' eyebrows, either as independent booth renters, mobile artists, or small studio owners. Invoices typically cover single services like waxing and tinting, lamination, microblading, or powder brow sessions, along with touch-ups, aftercare products, and package purchases.
brow-artist.pricingModel: Most brow artists charge a flat price per service rather than by the hour, since each service has a set time and technique. Basic services like shaping, waxing, threading, and tinting are priced low and booked frequently. Semi-permanent services such as microblading, powder brows, and combo brows are priced higher and usually include a follow-up touch-up session 4 to 8 weeks later, which is either bundled into the price or billed separately at a reduced rate. Many artists offer packages (for example lamination plus tint, or a lamination series) and sell aftercare balms and tint kits as add-ons. Mobile artists add a travel fee, and those who handle events or bridal parties charge a per-person price with a minimum. Pricing varies a lot by city, experience level, and whether you rent a booth or run your own studio. Deposits are standard for longer, high-ticket appointments.
