Additional session outside package (March 28)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Unused sessions in a monthly retainer do not roll over. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Accepted: ACH, credit card, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package or program name and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client exactly which engagement the charge belongs to, such as the 6-month growth program, month 3 of 6.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and durations
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives a record of what was delivered, and settles questions when a client says they were billed for sessions that were missed or rescheduled.

invoiceChecklist.item: Included versus extra services
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating retainer items from add-ons like extra calls, assessments, or workshops prevents surprise charges and shows the value of the package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installment number and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: For clients paying a program in installments, this tracks what has been paid and what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client company name and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: When a business pays for coaching, accounts payable often needs the legal entity name and a purchase order number to process payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and rollover policy reference
invoiceChecklist.why: A short line about missed sessions and unused time backs up charges for no-shows and avoids disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, tax ID details, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for the client to pay you and for their records, and you may need to supply a W-9 for business clients who pay you over the IRS reporting threshold.

business-coach.paymentTerms: Coaches commonly bill monthly retainers in advance, on or just before the first session of the month, with payment due on receipt or within 7 to 14 days. Fixed-length programs are often paid in full upfront, sometimes at a 5 to 15 percent discount, or split into equal monthly installments with a card on file or recurring ACH. One-off sessions and intensives are usually paid before the date, and workshops often require a 25 to 50 percent deposit to hold the date, with the balance due before or on delivery. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the agreement. Credit card, ACH, and check are the usual methods, and corporate clients may need net-30 terms and a W-9.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Coaching is time you reserve for a client whether they use it or not. Invoicing at the start of the period keeps the arrangement predictable and keeps you from chasing payment after the work is done.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in your agreement and repeat it on invoices
tips.body: A common rule is 24 to 48 hours notice to reschedule, with late cancellations counted as used. Say whether sessions roll over. Clients rarely dispute a policy they signed and saw again on every invoice.

tips.title: Define what between-session support means
tips.body: State if email or chat access is included, how fast you respond, and what counts as an extra session. Unlimited access without limits turns into unpaid hours.

tips.title: Offer a discount for paying in full, not for payment plans
tips.body: A paid-in-full discount improves your cash flow. If you allow installments, use a card on file or recurring ACH so you are not sending a reminder each month.

tips.title: Invoice company-paid coaching to the right contact
tips.body: When an employer pays for an executive or manager, find out who approves invoices, whether a PO is needed, and what the payment cycle is before the first session.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the package?
faqs.answer: Most business coaches charge by package or monthly retainer, because the value is in the ongoing relationship and results, not the clock. Hourly rates work for one-off sessions, advisory calls, and work outside an existing package.

faqs.question: Can I require payment upfront for a coaching program?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is common to require full payment or the first installment before the first session. Put this in your coaching agreement so the terms are clear before any invoice is sent.

faqs.question: What happens if a client misses a session?
faqs.answer: Follow the policy in your agreement. Many coaches treat a missed session or one canceled with less than 24 hours notice as delivered, and offer a reschedule only when notice was given in time. Note the policy on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on coaching?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax coaching or consulting services, but some tax certain business services or digital products. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or get a W-9?
faqs.answer: If you are paid as an independent contractor by a US business, the client may ask for a W-9 and may send you a 1099 if payments pass the IRS threshold in a year. You generally do not issue a 1099 to your clients. Ask your accountant about your specific situation.

estimate.intro: Business coaches send a proposal or quote when a prospect asks what an engagement will cost, usually after a discovery call. Clients compare package length, number of sessions, level of access between calls, and total price against other coaches or consultants. A clear quote also helps a company decide whether to fund coaching for a team member.

scopeChecklist.why: A 3-month and a 12-month program are priced very differently, and both sides need to know when it begins and ends.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Specifies how many sessions, how long, and whether they are video, phone, or in person, so expectations match what you deliver.
Spells out whether email, chat, or voice messages are included, and your response time, to prevent unlimited unpaid access.
Lists assessments, workbooks, action plans, or progress reviews that are part of the price, and which cost extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Goals and what you do not guarantee
scopeChecklist.why: Set the objectives you will work toward, and state that results depend on the client's action so you are not held to promised revenue.

scopeChecklist.item: Total price, payment schedule, and deposit
scopeChecklist.why: Shows the full cost, when each payment is due, and any paid-in-full discount.
Covers what happens if the client pauses or ends early, and whether prepaid fees are refundable.

pricingTips.title: Quote a package, not an hourly total
pricingTips.body: Present one price for a defined engagement, such as 6 months with 2 sessions a month. This focuses the client on the outcome rather than on counting hours.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A lighter option with fewer sessions, a standard option, and one with extra access or an intensive lets the client choose and often moves them to the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price to the client's size and the value of the goal
pricingTips.body: A founder trying to double a six-figure business and a company paying for a director's development are different buyers. Adjust your price to the scope and the budget, within a range you can defend.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Hold your price and your calendar space for 7 to 14 days. This keeps you from reserving a client slot indefinitely at an old rate.

faqs.question: Should I give a free discovery session before quoting?
faqs.answer: Many coaches offer a free 20 to 45 minute call to learn the client's goals and fit. Use it to gather what you need to write a specific quote, and keep it limited so it does not become a free coaching session.

faqs.question: Is a proposal the same as a coaching agreement?
faqs.answer: No. A proposal describes the offer and price. The agreement is the signed contract covering confidentiality, payment, cancellation, and scope. Many coaches send the agreement once the client accepts the proposal.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Not for the scope you quoted. If the client asks for more sessions, extra team members, or added deliverables, send a revised quote or a change order for the added work.

business-consultant.intro: Business consultants advise small and mid-sized companies on strategy, operations, finance, sales, and organizational problems. They invoice for hourly advisory work, fixed-scope projects such as a market analysis or process redesign, and monthly retainers for ongoing access and support. Clients are usually owners, executives, or department heads who expect clear deliverables and a paper trail they can show to finance.
business-consultant.pricingModel: Most business consultants use one of four models: hourly billing, a fixed project fee, a monthly retainer, or a day rate. Hourly works for open-ended advisory and short engagements. Fixed fees suit defined deliverables like a business plan, pricing study, or operations audit, and are often split into milestones (for example 50% at kickoff and 50% at delivery). Retainers cover a set number of hours or a set scope each month, such as a fractional COO arrangement, and are billed in advance. Day rates are common for on-site workshops and for larger clients, and usually come out below ten times the hourly rate. Experience, niche, and client size drive pricing more than geography. Value-based pricing, where the fee reflects the expected financial result, is used by senior consultants but needs a tightly written scope. Travel, software subscriptions, research reports, and subcontractor costs are usually billed separately as expenses, sometimes with a small markup stated in the agreement.

rates.service: Fractional COO or fractional executive role

items.description: Operations audit: interviews with department leads and process mapping (Phase 1)
Advisory sessions: pricing strategy review and sales pipeline analysis
On-site leadership workshop, March 12
Written findings report and recommendations deck
Travel: mileage to client site (2 trips, 96 miles each)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Phase 1 of 3 under the consulting agreement dated February 3. Phase 2 invoice will be issued on delivery of the process redesign plan. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Payable by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement or statement of work (date and phase or milestone)
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to the agreed scope so finance teams can approve it quickly and scope disputes are easier to resolve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of deliverables or work performed, with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often ask what they received for a retainer or a lump sum. Dated sessions and named deliverables answer that.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged and rate for time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly clients may audit the invoice. Show the hours, the rate, and the topic of each block of time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center code
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-sized and larger companies often will not process payment without one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized expenses with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel, software, research purchases, and subcontractor fees need to be separate from fees so they can be reimbursed and booked correctly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and what it covers
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the month the retainer applies to and any rollover or overage hours, which prevents confusion when usage varies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, tax ID or W-9 on file note, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need your legal name and details to set you up as a vendor and issue a 1099 where required.

business-consultant.paymentTerms: Consultants commonly collect a deposit of 25-50% of a fixed-fee project before work begins, with the rest tied to milestones or delivery. Retainers are billed in advance on the first of the month. Hourly work is usually invoiced monthly or at the end of each phase. Net 15 and net 30 are the most common terms, and larger companies may push for net 45 or 60, so confirm this in the agreement. Many consultants add a late fee of 1-1.5% per month, and some states cap interest or require it to be stated in writing, so check local rules. ACH and wire transfer are the usual payment methods for larger amounts, with checks and card payments also accepted, sometimes with a card surcharge where permitted.

tips.title: Put the scope and change process in writing
tips.body: Scope creep is the biggest source of unpaid time. State what is included, what counts as an extra, and how change requests are priced. When a client asks for more, send a short written change order before starting.

tips.title: Bill in advance for retainers and early milestones
tips.body: Advance billing protects your cash flow and sets the expectation that work follows payment. Pausing work on an overdue retainer is far easier than chasing payment after the work is done.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed fees
tips.body: Logging hours on a flat-fee project shows you whether the fee was right. It also gives you evidence if the client claims you did not put in the work.

tips.title: Match invoice timing to client approvals
tips.body: If the client needs sign-off on a deliverable before paying, build that review window into the agreement, for example five business days, so the invoice does not stall indefinitely.

tips.title: Ask for the AP contact at kickoff
tips.body: Find out who processes invoices, what format they need, and whether you must register in a vendor portal. Missing that step can add weeks to payment.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or charge a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly when the scope is unclear or the work is mostly advice. Use a flat fee when the deliverable is defined and you can estimate the effort. Many consultants move to flat fees or retainers as they gain experience, because clients prefer predictable costs and you are not penalized for being efficient.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a retainer when the client does not use all the hours?
faqs.answer: State the policy in your agreement. Some consultants let unused hours expire each month, others allow a limited rollover. Invoice the full retainer either way, and include a short summary of hours used so the client sees what they received.

faqs.question: Can I charge clients for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Common approaches are billing travel time at a reduced rate, such as 50%, or including it in a day rate. Bill mileage and other travel costs as separate expenses with receipts where possible.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: You should send a W-9 to US clients who request it, and they may issue you a 1099-NEC if they paid you $600 or more in a year (the threshold may change, so check current IRS rules). As a consultant you generally do not issue 1099s to your clients, though you may need to for subcontractors you pay.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: In most states, consulting services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax certain professional or business services. Rules vary by state and by the type of service, so check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Business consultants send a proposal or estimate after a discovery call and before any paid work starts. Clients often compare it against other consultants, an in-house hire, or a larger firm, so it should show what they get, how long it takes, and what it costs. A clear quote also becomes the basis for the agreement and later invoices.

scopeChecklist.item: Business problem and objectives in the client's words
scopeChecklist.why: Confirms you understood the need and gives both sides a standard for judging whether the engagement succeeded.
A report, a financial model, a workshop, and a set of coaching calls are very different things. Naming them prevents disputes over what was promised.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline with milestones and review periods
scopeChecklist.why: Shows when work starts, when drafts are due, and how long the client has to give feedback. Delays on the client side then have a clear effect on the schedule.
Consulting stalls without data, interviews, and decision makers. List what you need and by when.
Implementation, bookkeeping, legal advice, or software setup are often assumed to be included. State what is not.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee structure, deposit, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Makes clear whether the price is fixed, hourly with a cap, or a retainer, and when each payment is due.

scopeChecklist.item: Expenses and how they are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Travel, research data, and subcontractors can add up. State whether they are included, capped, or billed at cost.

pricingTips.title: Price on value and effort, not just hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours, then check the number against what the result is worth to the client. A pricing review that adds $100,000 in revenue should not be quoted like a few days of spreadsheet work.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and expanded package gives the client a choice and makes it less likely they compare you on price alone. For example, a diagnostic only, a diagnostic with a plan, or a diagnostic, plan, and 90 days of support.

pricingTips.title: Build in a discovery phase
pricingTips.body: If the scope is uncertain, quote a small paid discovery or assessment first, then quote the larger project based on what you find. This avoids guessing and protects you from underpricing.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity date and a cap for hourly quotes
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire, often after 30 days. If you quote hourly, give an estimated range and agree to notify the client before you pass the upper limit.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call is usually free. Detailed proposals that require research, data review, or custom analysis can be paid, or credited toward the project if the client signs. Many consultants offer a paid diagnostic as a first step.

faqs.question: How detailed should a consulting quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that someone who was not on the call could tell what is included, when it happens, and what it costs. Most are two to five pages. Longer documents can wait for the formal agreement.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to negotiate the price down?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of the rate when you can. Remove a deliverable, shorten the timeline, or cut the support period. Lowering the fee for the same work sets a poor precedent and affects future projects.

faqs.question: Can the estimate turn into the contract?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it includes the scope, fees, payment terms, and a signature line, and if you add basic terms such as confidentiality, ownership of work product, and termination. Many consultants attach the quote to a master services agreement. For significant engagements, have a lawyer review your template.

business-development.intro: Business development consultants and contractors help companies find new customers, partners, and revenue channels. They bill for outbound lead generation, partnership sourcing, sales strategy, proposal support, and fractional or outsourced business development roles. Clients are usually small and mid-size companies that need growth work but do not want to hire a full-time person.
business-development.pricingModel: Most business development work is priced as a monthly retainer, an hourly or day rate for project work, or a hybrid of a base fee plus performance pay. Retainers suit ongoing outreach and fractional roles, where the client pays for a set amount of time or activity each month. Hourly and day rates fit strategy sprints, market research, and one-off projects like building a partner program. Commission or success fees, often 5-15% of first-year revenue from deals you source, are common but should be written down in advance, including how deals are attributed and for how long. Pass-through costs such as lead data subscriptions, sales tools, travel, and event fees are usually billed at cost, or with a small markup if agreed in the contract.

rates.service: Outbound lead generation and appointment setting
Market research and target account list build
Day rate for on-site or event work

items.description: Fractional business development services, March (up to 40 hours, includes weekly pipeline review)
Target account research: 75 qualified accounts with decision-maker contacts
Partnership introduction calls and follow-up with 6 prospective channel partners
Proposal support for Harbor Logistics RFP
Lead data subscription, March (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours beyond the 40 included in the retainer are billed at $150 per hour with prior approval. Commission on the Delta Freight contract will be invoiced separately per section 4 of the services agreement. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and retainer scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see which month the retainer covers and what hours or activities it includes so they do not question it against the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Activity summary or deliverables list
invoiceChecklist.why: Business development results are hard to see. Listing accounts researched, calls made, meetings booked, and proposals sent shows the work behind the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for any overage or hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Work outside the retainer needs dates and hours so the extra charge is easy to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Commission basis and deal reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Name the closed deal, contract value, percentage, and the agreement clause that triggers payment to avoid attribution disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Data tools, travel, and event fees billed at cost should be itemized and backed by receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size companies often require a purchase order number or cost center before accounts payable will pay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or statement of work reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying the invoice to the signed agreement makes clear which rates and terms apply.

business-development.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month or billing period, due within 7 to 15 days, while project work often takes 25 to 50% upfront with the rest on milestones or delivery. Commission is typically invoiced after the client receives payment from the customer, so spell out whether you are paid on signing or on cash received. Net 15 or Net 30 is common, and many consultants add a late fee of 1 to 1.5% per month stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, wire, or card, with ACH preferred for larger retainers to avoid card fees.

tips.title: Define commission attribution in writing
tips.body: State which deals count as yours, such as introductions made or accounts you contacted, and how long after your engagement ends you still earn commission. Vague tail terms are the most common source of disputes.

tips.title: Bill for activity, not just outcomes
tips.body: Pipeline results take months. A retainer tied to effort and deliverables keeps you paid while deals mature, and a smaller commission can sit on top for upside.

tips.title: Include a cap on included hours
tips.body: Retainers with no hour limit tend to grow. Set a monthly cap and an overage rate so extra requests are billed instead of absorbed.

tips.title: Send a short monthly report with each invoice
tips.body: A one-page summary of outreach, meetings, and pipeline movement makes the invoice easy to justify and supports renewal.

tips.title: Get expense approval before you spend
tips.body: For travel, conference passes, or paid tools above a set amount, such as $250, get an email approval so the charge is not questioned later.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or on retainer?
faqs.answer: Retainers work better for ongoing outreach and fractional roles because they give predictable income and fit the long sales cycle. Hourly suits short strategy projects or unclear scope. Many consultants use a retainer with a defined hour cap and an hourly overage rate.

faqs.question: When can I invoice for commission?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement. Some consultants invoice when the client signs the deal, others when the client collects payment. Write the trigger into the contract, and invoice promptly once it happens.

faqs.question: Can I mark up software and data costs?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the contract allows it. Many consultants bill tools at cost and cover their management time in the fee. If you add a markup, such as 10 to 15%, state it up front.

faqs.question: What if the client says I did not produce results?
faqs.answer: Point to the scope in your agreement and the activity report. If you were paid for effort and deliverables rather than guaranteed outcomes, results are not a basis for withholding payment. Avoid promising specific revenue numbers in the contract.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: In most states, consulting services are not taxed, but some states tax certain business services. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant. Independent contractors generally also should track income for self-employment tax.

estimate.intro: Business development consultants send proposals or quotes after a discovery call, when a company wants to know what outreach or partnership work will cost. Clients often compare your fee against hiring a full-time salesperson, an agency, or another freelancer. A clear scope and expected activity levels help the client see what they get for the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Target market and ideal customer profile
scopeChecklist.why: Defines who you will pursue. A change in target mid-project changes the workload.
State the number of accounts researched, outreach touches, calls, or meetings so the client knows what the fee covers.

scopeChecklist.item: What counts as a qualified lead or meeting
scopeChecklist.why: Without a definition, clients and consultants can disagree on whether a deliverable was met.
Note who provides messaging approval, CRM access, sales collateral, and follow-up on leads. Slow client response delays results.
Specify which tools the client pays for and which costs you pass through, so there are no surprise charges.
Include rate, deal attribution, payment trigger, and tail period before work starts.
State the minimum engagement length, such as 3 months, and the notice required to end it.

pricingTips.title: Quote a minimum term
pricingTips.body: Pipeline takes 60 to 120 days to show results. A 3-month minimum prevents clients from canceling before the work has time to pay off.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, for example research only, research plus outreach, and full fractional role. Clients tend to choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price against the alternative
pricingTips.body: A full-time business development hire can cost $90,000 or more per year with benefits. Show how your retainer compares for the same coverage without the hiring risk.

pricingTips.title: Separate setup from ongoing fees
pricingTips.body: Charge a one-time fee for list building, messaging, and process setup, then a monthly fee for execution. This covers the heavy front-loaded work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Pricing and your availability change, so put an expiration date on the proposal.

faqs.question: Should I give a free strategy session before quoting?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call is normal. A detailed strategy or account plan is real work, so either charge a paid discovery fee, often $500 to $2,000, or keep it high-level until the client signs.

faqs.question: Can I quote a fixed price for a retainer?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you define the included activity and hours. A fixed monthly fee with a cap on hours and a stated overage rate protects both sides.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower fee in exchange for commission only?
faqs.answer: Be cautious. Commission-only deals shift all the risk to you and can take months to pay. If you agree, ask for a smaller base fee to cover costs, a higher commission rate, and clear attribution terms.

business-services.intro: Business services providers handle the back-office and operational work other companies prefer not to staff in-house: bookkeeping support, virtual administration, document preparation, payroll processing, process consulting, and similar tasks. Most are solo operators or small firms who invoice monthly for retainers, hourly work, or defined projects. A clear invoice matters here because clients often can't see the work being done, so the invoice is the main proof of value delivered.
business-services.pricingModel: Pricing usually falls into three models. Hourly billing is common for ad hoc work, virtual assistance, and consulting, often with a minimum block such as 5 or 10 hours per month. Monthly retainers cover recurring work like bookkeeping, payroll runs, or administrative support, and are priced by scope (number of transactions, employees, or hours included). Flat project fees suit one-time jobs like an SOP manual, a CRM cleanup, or a business license filing package. Pass-through costs such as filing fees, software subscriptions bought on the client's behalf, courier charges, and notary fees are normally billed separately at cost or with a small handling markup. Rush work and work outside the agreed scope are often billed at 1.25x to 1.5x the normal rate.

rates.service: Business license and registration filing assistance

items.description: Monthly bookkeeping retainer, May 2025 (bank reconciliation, categorization, monthly P&L and balance sheet)
Virtual administrative support (email management, calendar scheduling, vendor follow-up)
Payroll processing, 2 semi-monthly runs, 6 employees
State annual report filing preparation
Overnight courier for signed documents (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days past due. Hours beyond the 10 included in the retainer are billed at $45 per hour. Accepted payment: ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and service dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring work blurs together, so naming the month or date range prevents confusion about what the charge covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours by task or category
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who can't observe the work want to see where time went, which cuts down on questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer scope and hours included
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing included hours versus overage makes extra charges easy to explain and defend.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately with receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Filing fees, courier charges, and software purchases should be distinguishable from your fees so the client sees they weren't marked up unexpectedly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients often require a reference number to route the invoice through accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, EIN or tax ID, and remittance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need your tax ID on file for 1099 reporting in the US, and clear payment instructions speed up payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states tax certain business services; rules vary widely, so check with your state's revenue department about what applies to you.

business-services.paymentTerms: Retainer clients are commonly billed at the start of the month or service period, while hourly and project work is billed at month end or on milestones. Net 15 and net 30 are the most common terms, with net 15 or due-on-receipt being easier on cash flow for solo providers. For one-time projects, a deposit of 25% to 50% upfront is typical, with the balance due on delivery. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in your agreement. Most providers accept ACH, check, and card, and often add a small surcharge or build processing fees into rates for card payments where local rules allow it.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoicing at the start of the period protects you from doing a month of work and then chasing payment. Pause service if the retainer is more than a set number of days late, and put that in your agreement.

tips.title: Track time even on flat retainers
tips.body: Logging hours shows whether a retainer is priced correctly and gives you evidence when a client's requests creep past the agreed scope.

tips.title: Define what overage costs
tips.body: State the hourly rate for work beyond the retainer, and note that on each invoice. It makes the extra charge feel expected rather than a surprise.

tips.title: Separate your fees from reimbursable costs
tips.body: Keep filing fees, subscriptions, and courier costs on their own lines. Clients accept pass-through costs more readily when they can see them clearly.

tips.title: Send invoices on a consistent schedule
tips.body: Clients pay faster when invoices arrive on the same day each month. Recurring timing also helps them plan their own cash flow.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat monthly retainer?
faqs.answer: Retainers give you predictable income and suit recurring work with a stable scope. Hourly works better when the workload is unpredictable or you are starting with a new client. Many providers begin hourly, then move to a retainer once they know how much work the client actually generates.

faqs.question: Can I mark up software or filing fees I pay for a client?
faqs.answer: Many providers do add a modest handling fee, often 5% to 15%, but it should be disclosed in your agreement. Government filing fees are usually billed at cost. Whatever you choose, list it as a separate line so it is transparent.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on business services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the type of service. Some states tax services like data processing or administrative support, while many do not tax professional services. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional before assuming either way.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client keeps asking for extra work outside the retainer?
faqs.answer: Point to the scope in your agreement, log the extra hours, and bill them at the stated overage rate. If it happens repeatedly, propose a larger retainer or a separate project quote.

faqs.question: When should I send a 1099 or ask for a W-9?
faqs.answer: Request a W-9 from clients who may need to issue you a 1099-NEC, and be ready to provide yours if you hire subcontractors you pay $600 or more in a year. Thresholds and rules can change, so confirm current requirements with the IRS or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Business services providers send estimates when a prospective client wants a defined project or a monthly package priced before committing. Clients usually compare the total cost, the number of hours or deliverables included, and the contract length. Because the work is often ongoing, a clear estimate sets expectations for scope and response times as much as price.

scopeChecklist.why: Vague terms like 'admin support' invite disputes. List what you will do, such as inbox triage, invoice entry, or monthly reports.

scopeChecklist.item: Hours or volume included per month
scopeChecklist.why: Setting a cap on hours, transactions, or employees tells the client when overage rates apply.
Naming what isn't covered, such as tax return preparation or legal advice, avoids assumptions about your services.
Delays often come from missing logins, documents, or approvals. State what the client must provide and by when.
Clients want to know when work will be done and how quickly you reply to requests.

scopeChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Software, filing fees, and courier costs should be addressed upfront so they are not a surprise on the first invoice.
A 30-day notice clause, or a minimum commitment, protects both sides if the arrangement ends.

pricingTips.title: Price from tracked hours, not guesses
pricingTips.body: Use time logs from similar clients to estimate the true effort, then add 15% to 20% for communication, revisions, and onboarding.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three retainer levels with different hour or volume limits lets clients self-select and makes your pricing easier to compare.

pricingTips.title: Charge separately for onboarding
pricingTips.body: Setting up systems, cleaning up records, or learning a client's processes takes real time. A one-time setup fee covers it without inflating the monthly rate.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from changes in workload, software costs, or your own availability.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or an estimate range?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed quote when the scope is clear, like a license filing or a single manual. Use a range or hourly estimate with a cap when the amount of work depends on the condition of the client's records or systems.

faqs.question: Is it okay to charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many providers offer a free 15 to 30 minute call to scope the work, then charge for any deeper assessment, such as reviewing books or mapping processes. Make clear in advance which one the client is getting.

faqs.question: How do I handle quotes when the client's records are messy?
faqs.answer: Review a sample before quoting, or price the cleanup as a separate line item billed hourly or with a not-to-exceed amount. Quote ongoing monthly work only after the cleanup is done.

cabinet-installer.intro: Cabinet installers hang and set base, wall, and tall cabinets for homeowners, remodelers, general contractors, and kitchen showrooms. Many work solo or with one helper, and bill for installation labor, trim and finish carpentry, countertop prep, and sometimes the hardware and materials they supply. Invoices go to homeowners, builders, or design firms, and often have to match a contract or purchase order.
cabinet-installer.pricingModel: Most installers price by the linear foot of cabinet run or per cabinet box, with a separate line for add-ons like crown molding, filler panels, end panels, and hardware. Production work for builders and showrooms is often quoted as a flat fee per kitchen or per cabinet, while custom or high-end jobs in older homes are more likely to be hourly or day-rate because walls and floors are rarely level. Removal of old cabinets, drywall patching, and electrical or plumbing work are normally billed separately or excluded. Materials you buy, such as shims, screws, blocking, and trim stock, are billed at cost plus a markup or folded into the unit price. Larger jobs usually bill a deposit up front, a progress payment when cabinets are set, and a balance at final punch list.

rates.service: Crown molding, light rail, and toe kick trim
Hourly labor for custom fitting or repairs

items.description: Install base and wall cabinets, kitchen remodel (shimmed, leveled, and scribed to wall)
Install tall pantry cabinet
Install crown molding and light rail
Install cabinet pulls and knobs (customer supplied)
Remove and haul off existing cabinets
Materials: shims, structural screws, blocking, touch-up filler

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received on contract signing. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Cabinet warranty and defects are covered by the manufacturer; installation workmanship is guaranteed for 1 year. Countertop templating cannot be scheduled until final payment for cabinet install is received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and project name or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Builders and showrooms often need to match your invoice to a specific job or purchase order before they release payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cabinet line count and run lengths, or a reference to the quote
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing linear feet or cabinet counts that match your estimate makes it hard to dispute the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for demo, trim, hardware, and add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing extras like filler panels, end panels, and crown molding shows where change-order work was added after the original quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials supplied by you versus the customer
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies who bought the shims, screws, trim, and hardware, and prevents arguments over whether supplies were included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and dates approved
invoiceChecklist.why: Moved walls, out-of-square rooms, and swapped cabinet layouts add time. A written record protects you when the final total exceeds the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and insurance info where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices above a set dollar amount. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and progress payments already received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the remaining balance clearly on multi-stage jobs.

cabinet-installer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common on residential installs, especially when you are buying trim or hardware. Many installers bill a second payment when the cabinets are set and the balance on completion or after a short punch list. Terms of due on receipt to net 7 are typical for homeowners, while builders and showrooms often pay net 15 to net 30, and sometimes only after their own draw from the client. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if it is written into your contract. Checks, ACH transfers, and card payments are all used. Card fees may be passed on if your agreement says so and local rules allow it.

tips.title: Bill on the cabinet delivery date, not just the finish date
tips.body: Cabinet jobs often stall because of damaged boxes, wrong sizes, or backordered pieces. A payment tied to delivery or to the cabinets being set keeps your cash flow from depending on someone else's delay.

tips.title: Document damaged or incorrect cabinets before you install
tips.body: Photograph and note chipped doors, wrong hand hinges, and missing parts on delivery. Write on the invoice that replacement or reorder wait time is not billable installer time, or charge a return-trip fee.

tips.title: Charge for out-of-square walls and uneven floors
tips.body: If a kitchen needs extra scribing, shimming, or custom fillers, add a line item or switch to hourly for that work. Flat per-foot pricing assumes standard conditions.

tips.title: Keep countertop coordination clear
tips.body: If you do not cut sink openings or set tops, say so on the quote and invoice. If you do template support or return visits, bill those as separate trips.

tips.title: Take final payment before leaving the punch list open
tips.body: Agree on a short punch list in writing. Collect the balance once it is finished, and do not let minor items hold up the whole invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge per linear foot or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Per linear foot or per cabinet works well for standard layouts because the client can compare quotes easily. Use hourly or a day rate for older homes, custom or frameless cabinets, heavily scribed work, or repair jobs where the time is unpredictable.

faqs.question: Can I charge for cabinets I did not supply?
faqs.answer: You charge for installation labor. If the client or the showroom supplies the cabinets, state that on the invoice and note that you are not responsible for manufacturing defects, damage in shipping, or missing parts. Handling and inspecting deliveries can be a billable line if it takes time.

faqs.question: How do I bill for demo and haul-off?
faqs.answer: Put it on its own line as a flat fee or hourly charge. Dump fees, dumpster rental, or disposal costs can be added at cost. Make clear whether plumbing disconnects, countertop removal, and drywall repair are included or not.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to install cabinets?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the size of the job. Some states require a contractor or specialty license above a dollar threshold, and others do not license finish carpentry at all. Check your state licensing board and local rules, and include your license number when required.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to pay after the countertops go in?
faqs.answer: Installation is complete once the cabinets are set, level, and secure. Countertops are a separate trade's work and timeline, so your balance should not depend on them. Put this in your contract and the invoice terms.

estimate.intro: Cabinet installers quote before work starts, usually after a site visit to measure the room and review the cabinet layout or order. Homeowners and contractors compare per-foot or flat prices, what is included in demo and trim, and when you can start. A clear quote helps you win jobs from lower bids that leave out the extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Cabinet source and who orders and receives them
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you are installing client-supplied cabinets and who is responsible for inspecting for damage and missing parts.

scopeChecklist.item: Layout reference and cabinet count or linear feet
scopeChecklist.why: Ties your price to a specific plan, so changes in the layout are priced as change orders.

scopeChecklist.item: Demo, haul-off, and wall or floor prep
scopeChecklist.why: Old cabinet removal, drywall patching, and leveling are common surprises that clients assume are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Trim, fillers, end panels, and crown molding
scopeChecklist.why: Finish pieces are often missing from the initial order and add both materials and labor.

scopeChecklist.item: Hardware, appliances, and sink or cooktop cutouts
scopeChecklist.why: Sets limits on what you install and what the plumber, electrician, or countertop fabricator handle.
Prevents disputes over disconnects, outlet relocation, and templating dates.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, start date, and delay conditions
scopeChecklist.why: Backordered cabinets and unfinished prior work can push your start, so state what happens if you have to return.

pricingTips.title: Measure the room, not just the plan
pricingTips.body: Check wall flatness, floor level, ceiling height, and soffits. Add contingency or a clause for conditions that differ from the plans.

pricingTips.title: Price extras as separate lines
pricingTips.body: List crown, valances, panels, and hardware individually. Clients can remove items to lower the total, and you keep your margin on the core install.

pricingTips.title: Include a change-order rate
pricingTips.body: State your hourly rate for work outside scope, such as redoing a layout or adding cabinets. This avoids debates halfway through the job.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Labor and material costs change, and your schedule fills. A 30-day expiration is common.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Many installers quote for free on standard kitchen jobs. If the visit involves a long drive, a complex custom plan, or detailed drawings, a small estimate fee that is credited to the job if you are hired is reasonable.

faqs.question: How firm is a flat-fee quote?
faqs.answer: A flat fee holds as long as the layout, cabinet order, and site conditions match what you quoted. State that changes, hidden damage, or out-of-level framing may add cost, and document those with a signed change order.

faqs.question: Do I include materials in the quote?
faqs.answer: Include small installation materials like shims, screws, and adhesive in your price, or list them as a line. If you are supplying trim, hardware, or the cabinets themselves, itemize them with a markup so the client sees what is covered.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a quote?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common on residential work, especially if you will buy materials before starting. For small jobs, a smaller deposit or payment on completion is fine if you are comfortable with the client.

cad-designer.intro: CAD designers and drafters produce 2D drawings and 3D models for manufacturers, architects, engineers, contractors, and product inventors. Freelancers and small drafting shops typically bill for part modeling, assembly drawings, permit sets, as-built drawings from field measurements, and revisions after client review.
cad-designer.pricingModel: Most CAD work is billed hourly, especially open-ended work like revisions, redlines, and ongoing support for an engineering team. Defined jobs such as a single part drawing, a floor plan set, or a 3D model for printing are often quoted as a flat fee per drawing, per sheet, or per part, based on estimated hours plus a buffer. Architectural work is sometimes priced per square foot of the building. Larger projects may be split into milestones such as concept model, detailed drawings, and final release. Many designers include a set number of revision rounds and bill additional rounds hourly. Rush work usually carries a 25 to 50 percent premium, and on-site measuring is billed separately by the hour or visit plus mileage. Software licensing is usually absorbed into the rate, though some designers pass through the cost of specialized plugins or rendering services.

rates.service: 3D part and assembly modeling (SolidWorks, Fusion 360, Inventor)
Architectural floor plan set from field measurements

items.description: 3D modeling of enclosure assembly (14 parts) in SolidWorks
Manufacturing drawings with tolerances and BOM
Revision round 3 per client markup dated 5/14 (beyond 2 included rounds)
STEP and PDF file export and delivery package
Photorealistic rendering for sales sheet

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Enclosure Rev B, PO 48213. Net 15. Final native files released on payment in full. Revisions beyond the agreed scope are billed at $75 per hour. A 1.5 percent monthly late fee applies after 30 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, drawing numbers, and revision letters
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often track many parts and revisions. Listing which drawings and revisions you billed for prevents confusion about what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or job code
invoiceChecklist.why: Engineering and manufacturing clients usually cannot pay without a PO reference, and accounts payable will reject invoices that lack one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by task and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating modeling, drafting, and revisions shows where time went and supports hourly charges if questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why extra revision time is billed and ties the charge back to the scope you agreed on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable file types and formats
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing DWG, STEP, PDF, or STL files confirms what was handed over and avoids disputes over missing formats.

invoiceChecklist.item: Field visit time and mileage
invoiceChecklist.why: On-site measuring is a separate cost from drafting time and should be itemized with the date and distance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ownership and file release terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating that native files transfer on full payment protects you if the client is late and clarifies who owns the design.

cad-designer.paymentTerms: Many CAD designers take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent on small jobs and bill larger projects at milestones, such as model approval and final drawing release. Hourly work is commonly invoiced every two weeks or monthly. Net 15 or Net 30 is typical, and corporate clients may insist on Net 45 or Net 60, so confirm this before starting. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your agreement in advance. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card. Withholding native editable files until final payment is a common and reasonable way to protect yourself, while delivering PDFs for review.

tips.title: Define revision rounds up front
tips.body: Put a number on included revisions, such as two rounds, and bill further changes hourly. Clients often treat design changes as endless unless the limit is written down.

tips.title: Separate new scope from corrections
tips.body: If the client changes dimensions or requirements after approval, bill it as a change order. Fixing your own mistake is not billable, but a new design direction is.

tips.title: Track time even on flat-fee jobs
tips.body: Logging hours shows you whether your per-sheet or per-model price is working and gives you evidence if a client disputes a change-order charge.

tips.title: Hold native files until payment
tips.body: Send watermarked PDFs or view-only files for review and release editable files such as SLDPRT, DWG, or STEP after payment clears.

tips.title: Charge for setup on messy source material
tips.body: Redrawing from hand sketches, scanned prints, or poor photos takes more time than working from clean data. Add a line for interpretation and cleanup, or quote a higher rate.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or per drawing?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended work, revisions, and ongoing support. Use a per-drawing or flat fee when the scope is clear, such as a fixed set of part drawings. Many designers use a flat fee for the first deliverable and hourly for changes.

faqs.question: Can I charge for revisions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Include a set number of revision rounds in your quote and bill additional changes at your hourly rate. State this in writing before you start so it does not come as a surprise on the invoice.

faqs.question: Who owns the CAD files I create?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement. Many freelancers transfer ownership of the final deliverables on full payment while keeping rights to reusable templates and standard components. Put this in your contract, and check with a lawyer for anything involving patents or complex IP.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on CAD work?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax digital products or certain design services, while others do not tax services at all. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for software costs?
faqs.answer: Most designers fold software licenses into their hourly rate. If a project requires a specialized add-on, simulation module, or rendering service, you can pass the cost through as a line item if you agreed to this beforehand.

estimate.intro: CAD designers send quotes before starting nearly every project, because clients usually compare several freelancers or shops and need a number to budget against. Clients look at price, turnaround time, software compatibility, and how many revisions are included. A clear quote with a defined scope helps you win work and avoid unpaid changes later.

scopeChecklist.item: List of deliverables and file formats
scopeChecklist.why: Naming the exact outputs, such as 3D model, 2D drawings, BOM, STEP, DWG, or PDF, sets expectations and prevents requests for extra formats later.
State whether you are working from sketches, scans, existing models, or field measurements. Poor or incomplete inputs affect the time required and should be noted.
A client on an older version of AutoCAD or a different CAD platform may need exports or conversions that add time.
Limits unpaid rework and gives you a clear point at which to charge for further changes.
ASME, ISO, architectural standards, or GD&T requirements change the effort. Naming them avoids surprises when the client expects a certain level of detail.
Delays in client feedback can stall the project. Set expected review times and note that the schedule shifts if feedback is late.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as engineering stamps or analysis
scopeChecklist.why: Clients sometimes assume drafting includes engineering review, structural calculations, or a licensed professional's seal. State clearly that it does not unless you are licensed and it is quoted.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours by component, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the job into parts, drawings, and review cycles, estimate each, and add 15 to 25 percent for clarification and unexpected changes. Quote the total as a flat fee or a not-to-exceed hourly cap.

pricingTips.title: Offer phases for large projects
pricingTips.body: Quote concept modeling, detailed drawings, and final release as separate phases. This lets the client commit step by step and gives you natural points to bill.

pricingTips.title: Price complexity, not just part count
pricingTips.body: Surfacing, sheet metal, weldments, and tight-tolerance assemblies take longer than simple prismatic parts. Reflect that in your hourly estimate or per-part price.

pricingTips.title: State how long the quote is valid
pricingTips.body: Set a window, such as 30 days, so you are not held to old pricing if the client comes back months later or if your schedule has changed.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed quote when scope and inputs are clear. Use an hourly estimate with a cap when requirements are likely to evolve. Either way, explain what happens if the scope changes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For large jobs that require a site visit, review of complex files, or a detailed feasibility study, some designers charge a fee and credit it toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who keeps adding features after I quote?
faqs.answer: Refer to the written scope and send a change order with the added hours and cost before doing the extra work. Get approval in writing, then add it to the final invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: Many designers ask for 25 to 50 percent upfront, especially for new clients or fixed-fee jobs. It covers your early time and confirms the client is committed. Include the deposit terms in the quote.

cake-designer.intro: Cake designers make custom cakes for weddings, birthdays, showers, corporate events, and other occasions. They are usually home bakers, cottage food operators, or small bakery owners. Invoices typically cover the cake itself, design and sculpting labor, decorations, delivery and setup, and sometimes rentals such as stands.
cake-designer.pricingModel: Most cake designers price by the serving, with the price per serving rising as the design gets more complex. A simple buttercream cake costs less per slice than a fondant-covered, sculpted, or heavily hand-painted cake. Many add separate line items for custom work such as sugar flowers, figurines, or carved shapes, which are billed as a flat fee or at an hourly rate. Delivery is charged by distance or as a flat fee, with setup at the venue often costing extra. Wedding cakes usually require a deposit to hold the date, with the balance due before delivery. Other add-ons include cake stands, boards, boxes, and tasting boxes. Rush orders and peak-season dates (May through October for weddings, and holiday weekends) often carry a surcharge.

items.description: Three-tier wedding cake, vanilla and lemon raspberry, buttercream with fondant accents (serves 100)
Handmade sugar peonies and greenery (cake topper and cascade)
Groom's cake, chocolate stout, 6-inch round (serves 12)
Delivery and on-site setup (venue 35 miles away)
Cake stand rental (refundable deposit billed separately)

sampleInvoice.notes: A 50% deposit of $568.50 was received on booking. Remaining balance due 14 days before the event date. Cake stand must be returned within 7 days or the $75 stand deposit is forfeited. Allergen information was provided at the time of order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, delivery time, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Cakes are made for a fixed date and time. Putting it on the invoice records exactly what was agreed and helps if a venue issue or delay comes up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Servings, tier sizes, and flavors/fillings per tier
invoiceChecklist.why: Disputes often start over cake size or flavor. Listing each tier and filling shows what was ordered and how the price was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design details and reference to the approved sketch or inspiration photo
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom design is subjective. Tying the invoice to an approved design protects you if the client later says it does not match what they wanted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons such as sugar flowers, toppers, and printed edible images
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often see only the cake price. Separate lines show where labor and materials costs went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received, date paid, and balance due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Wedding and large orders usually have a non-refundable deposit. Showing it on the invoice prevents confusion about what has been paid and when the rest is due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental items, return deadline, and refundable deposit terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stands, pillars, and domes are easy to lose. Writing down return terms makes it easier to keep a deposit if they are not returned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Allergen disclosures and cottage food or business license information
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require labeling or allergen disclosure on cottage food products. Including it shows you followed your local rules. Requirements vary, so check with your health department.

cake-designer.paymentTerms: Most cake designers collect a non-refundable deposit of 25% to 50% at booking to hold the date, with the balance due 7 to 14 days before the event for weddings and often at order confirmation or pickup for smaller cakes. Many require full payment before delivery so there is no chasing money at the venue. Late fees of 1.5% per month or a flat fee are common in written terms, and rush orders may require full upfront payment. Accepted methods usually include credit card, debit card, bank transfer, and peer-to-peer payment apps, and some designers still take checks. If you accept cards, consider whether to pass along processing fees, and check your local rules on how to disclose them.

tips.title: Hold the date only with a deposit
tips.body: A cake date cannot be resold on short notice. Do not block the calendar until the deposit clears, and state in writing that it is non-refundable once the date is held.

tips.title: Bill design time separately for complex work
tips.body: If a cake needs hours of sculpting, airbrushing, or sugar flower work, price it as a separate line item. Otherwise a high per-serving price can look unjustified, and you will underprice the next sculpted cake.

tips.title: Set a guest count deadline
tips.body: Lock the final serving count 2 to 4 weeks before the event and bill from that number. Reductions after that point should not lower the price, since ingredients and design time are already committed.

tips.title: Charge for delivery based on risk and time
tips.body: Delivering tiered cakes takes drive time, careful loading, and on-site assembly. Charge by mileage or a flat fee, and add extra for long setups, stairs, or outdoor venues in hot weather.

tips.title: Keep records of approved designs and changes
tips.body: Save emails or messages showing design approval and any changes. If the client changes the design after approval, bill the revision and update the invoice before you start.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the slice or by the cake?
faqs.answer: Most designers charge by the serving for tiered and custom cakes because ingredients and labor scale with size. Small novelty cakes are often priced as a flat fee. Whichever way you quote, show the serving count on the invoice so the client can see how the total was calculated.

faqs.question: Is the deposit refundable if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: That is up to your policy, and it should be written in your terms before the client pays. Most cake designers keep the deposit because the date is blocked and ordering or prep may have started. Some offer a partial refund if the client cancels far in advance and you rebook the date.

faqs.question: Do I have to charge sales tax on cakes?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states exempt certain food items, some tax prepared or decorated baked goods, and some treat delivery and service charges differently. Check with your state's department of revenue, and show tax as a separate line if you collect it.

faqs.question: What if the client adds guests or changes the design after I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: Send a revised invoice that shows the change and the new total, and get written approval before you start. Your terms should say that changes after a certain date may be declined or charged at a higher rate.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a tasting?
faqs.answer: Yes, many cake designers charge a tasting fee, often between $25 and $60, and credit it toward the order if the client books. This discourages casual tastings and covers the cost of ingredients and your time.

estimate.intro: A cake designer sends a quote after the client shares the event date, guest count, and design ideas, and usually before the client commits or pays a deposit. Clients often compare several bakers, so a clear breakdown of servings, design work, and delivery helps them see what they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.why: Availability and delivery cost depend on these. It also confirms you can take the order before the quote is accepted.

scopeChecklist.item: Serving count, tier sizes, and flavors/fillings
scopeChecklist.why: These determine the ingredient cost and size of the cake. Writing them down avoids surprises if the client expects more servings than the cake provides.

scopeChecklist.item: Design description with sketch or reference images
scopeChecklist.why: Custom design is open to interpretation. A written description and sketch sets expectations and notes where your version may differ from an inspiration photo.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: toppers, flowers, stand, boxes, and dowels
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a stand or topper is included. List each item and mark rentals or extras separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery, setup, and venue access requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Long drives, stairs, and outdoor venues change your time and risk. Naming the fee and who handles venue contact prevents disputes on the day.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, payment schedule, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: The client should know before accepting what is due and when, and what is lost if they cancel.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and guest count deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Ingredient costs and your calendar change. An expiry date and a final count date keep the price from being open-ended.

pricingTips.title: Start from a per-serving price tied to design tier
pricingTips.body: Set two or three tiers, such as simple buttercream, fondant, and fully custom, and quote from those. It keeps pricing consistent and makes it easier to explain why one cake costs more than another.

pricingTips.title: Price your hours for complex work
pricingTips.body: For sculpted cakes, sugar flowers, and hand painting, estimate hours and multiply by your hourly rate, then add materials. Many designers underprice these because they forget planning, shopping, and cleanup time.

pricingTips.title: Offer a few options at different price points
pricingTips.body: Show a smaller cake with a dessert table of cupcakes next to a full tiered cake. Clients on a budget can choose without asking you to cut corners on a design you will have to put your name on.

pricingTips.title: Add a peak-season or rush surcharge in writing
pricingTips.body: If your Saturday dates in June or orders under two weeks cost more, say so in the quote. A surcharge listed up front is accepted more easily than one added later.

faqs.question: How long should a cake quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is common, and shorter for popular wedding dates. After the quote expires, you can adjust for ingredient costs or give the date to another client.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or consultation?
faqs.answer: Quotes by email are usually free. For in-person consultations with tastings, many designers charge a fee and credit it toward the order if the client books.

faqs.question: What if the final design costs more than the quote?
faqs.answer: If the client asks for more detail, extra tiers, or added flowers after the quote, send a revised quote and get approval before starting. Your quote should say that changes to the scope will change the price.

faqs.question: Can I give a price range instead of a firm number?
faqs.answer: A range is reasonable early on, before the design is settled, but give a firm number before taking a deposit. Once the design, servings, and delivery are set, the final quote should state a single price.

car-rental.intro: Car rental businesses range from small local fleets and peer-to-peer hosts to operators renting trucks, vans, luxury cars, or event vehicles. They invoice for the rental period, plus add-ons such as insurance products, mileage overages, fuel, tolls, cleaning, and damage or late-return charges. Invoices are common for corporate accounts, insurance replacement rentals, film and event clients, and any rental that closes out with extra charges after the vehicle comes back.
car-rental.pricingModel: Most rental operators price by the day, with lower effective daily rates for weekly (7 days) and monthly (28-30 days) bookings. Each day usually includes a mileage allowance, often 100-200 miles, and extra miles are billed per mile. Add-ons such as collision damage waivers, supplemental liability, child seats, GPS, additional drivers, and one-way drop fees are billed as separate lines, either per day or flat. Fuel is billed at a refuel rate plus a service charge if the car is returned below the pickup level. Many businesses also charge a security deposit hold, a young driver fee for renters under 25, and a cleaning fee for smoking or heavy mess. Insurance replacement rentals are billed to the carrier at an agreed daily rate. Corporate and long-term clients often get a negotiated rate and monthly invoicing. Taxes and fees on rentals vary widely by state and city, so check what applies to you.

Collision damage waiver

Mileage overage (920 miles driven, 750 included)
