sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of return. Security deposit of $250 held at pickup will be released within 5 business days after final payment. Late fees of 1.5% per month apply to unpaid balances. Taxes and airport or local fees, if applicable, are shown on the rental agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental agreement number and renter name
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the signed agreement and the driver who is responsible for the vehicle.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle description, plate, and VIN or unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which vehicle was rented, which matters for tolls, tickets, and damage claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and return date, time, and odometer readings
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports the day count, late-return charges, and mileage overage math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized daily rate, add-ons, and insurance products
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the renter what each charge covers and reduces chargeback disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fuel level at pickup and return, with refuel rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Justifies any fuel charge and the per-gallon rate or service fee used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage, cleaning, or toll and ticket charges with documentation reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Photos, inspection forms, and toll statements back up post-rental charges, which are the most disputed items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Taxes, surcharges, and deposit applied or released
invoiceChecklist.why: Rental taxes and fees differ by location, and clients need to see how the deposit was handled against the final total.

car-rental.paymentTerms: Consumer rentals are normally paid by card at pickup, with a deposit hold on the card that is released after return. Invoices are mainly used for corporate accounts, insurance replacement rentals, and post-return charges such as tolls, damage, or overages. Corporate and insurer invoices commonly run on net 15 or net 30 terms, while post-return charges to a consumer are best collected from the card on file under the terms signed in the rental agreement. State late fees, such as 1.5% monthly, in the agreement before the rental. Accept cards, ACH, and checks for business accounts. Long-term or monthly rentals are often billed in advance.

tips.title: Put post-rental charges in the rental agreement
tips.body: Tolls, tickets, cleaning, fuel, late returns, and damage should be listed in the signed agreement, with the authorization to charge the card on file. This makes later invoices much easier to collect on.

tips.title: Document the vehicle at pickup and return
tips.body: Take dated photos or video of all sides, interior, odometer, and fuel gauge at both ends. Attach or reference them when you bill for damage or cleaning.

tips.title: Show the mileage math
tips.body: List miles driven, miles included, and the overage rate on a separate line. Clients rarely dispute a charge when the calculation is visible.

tips.title: Bill tolls and tickets with an admin fee and proof
tips.body: Many operators add a flat administrative fee for handling tolls and citations. Disclose the fee in the agreement and include the toll statement or citation copy with the invoice.

tips.title: Send corporate and insurer invoices promptly
tips.body: Insurance replacement rentals need the claim number, adjuster name, and authorized daily rate and days. Missing details delay payment, so confirm them before the rental begins.

faqs.question: Should I invoice a rental or just charge the card at pickup?
faqs.answer: For standard consumer rentals, charging at pickup and settling the final total at return is normal. Use an invoice for corporate accounts, insurer-paid rentals, long-term rentals, and any extra charges that come up after the vehicle is returned.

faqs.question: How do I bill for damage found after the car is returned?
faqs.answer: Send an invoice that references the rental agreement, includes before-and-after photos, and attaches a repair estimate or receipt. Apply the security deposit first and bill only the remaining balance. Check your state rules and your insurance terms on how damage claims must be handled.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a rental invoice?
faqs.answer: Generally yes if the fee was disclosed in the rental agreement or invoice terms. Some states limit rates or require specific disclosures, so check your local rules. Late return fees, such as an hourly charge or a full extra day, are separate from late payment fees.

faqs.question: How do I invoice an insurance company for a replacement rental?
faqs.answer: Include the claim number, policyholder name, adjuster contact, authorized daily rate, and the dates the insurer approved. Bill at the agreed rate and attach the rental agreement. Charges beyond what the insurer authorized, such as upgrades, usually go to the renter.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on car rentals?
faqs.answer: In most states, car rentals are subject to some combination of sales tax, rental vehicle tax, and local or airport fees, but the rules and rates vary a lot. Check with your state revenue department and local authorities, and show each tax or fee as its own line.

estimate.intro: Car rental businesses send quotes for event and wedding bookings, corporate accounts, film and production use, long-term rentals, one-way trips, and group bookings that need several vehicles. Clients usually compare the daily rate, mileage allowance, insurance coverage, deposit size, and what happens if they return the car late or damaged.

scopeChecklist.item: Vehicle class and exact dates and times
scopeChecklist.why: Rental periods are often billed in 24-hour blocks, so a late return time can add a full day.
Road trips and deliveries can run far over the allowance, and clients should know the per-mile cost in advance.
Make clear what the renter's own policy or credit card must cover and what your waivers include or exclude.

scopeChecklist.item: Security deposit amount and release timing
scopeChecklist.why: Deposits can be a large part of the up-front cost and are a frequent source of complaints.

scopeChecklist.item: Driver requirements and additional driver fees
scopeChecklist.why: Age limits, license requirements, and who may drive affect eligibility and cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Fuel, cleaning, tolls, and delivery policy
scopeChecklist.why: Listing these up front prevents surprise charges and shows which are optional.

scopeChecklist.item: Taxes, fees, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Availability and pricing change with demand, so state how long the quote is held and which taxes are not yet included.

pricingTips.title: Quote the all-in total
pricingTips.body: Show daily rate, add-ons, estimated taxes and fees, and deposit in one summary. Clients comparing providers often only look at the base daily rate, so a clear total helps you stand out when you are not the cheapest.

pricingTips.title: Price weekly and monthly differently
pricingTips.body: Offer lower effective daily rates for 7-day and 28-day bookings. Long rentals keep a vehicle utilized and reduce turnover costs, so a discount is usually worth it.

pricingTips.title: Adjust for season and demand
pricingTips.body: Holidays, local events, and summer travel support higher rates, while off-season gaps justify discounts. Note that the quote applies to those dates only.

pricingTips.title: Offer vehicle options
pricingTips.body: Give a standard and an upgraded option, such as a mid-size sedan and a full-size SUV. Clients can pick based on budget, and it shows you have thought about their needs.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit to hold a reservation?
faqs.answer: Many operators take a deposit or prepayment for event, long-term, or high-value bookings. State the amount, whether it is refundable, and the cancellation deadline in the quote.

faqs.question: How long should a rental quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven days is common, or until a set date if the booking is close. Fleet availability changes quickly, so make clear the vehicle is not held until the client accepts and pays any deposit.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to extend the rental after I quote?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that extensions are billed at the daily rate or the current rate, depending on availability, and must be approved before the original return time. Send a revised quote or invoice for the extra days.

faqs.question: Can I give a flat price for delivery events or multi-day trips?
faqs.answer: Yes, but define included miles, delivery and pickup locations, and any waiting time. Flat prices work best when the scope is clearly limited, with overage charges for changes.

car-wash.intro: Car wash owners and operators send invoices mostly to business customers: fleet accounts, dealerships, rental agencies, delivery companies, and property managers who have vehicles washed on a schedule. Mobile washers and small detail shops also bill individuals for packages, add-ons, and recurring memberships. Retail drive-up customers pay at the point of sale, so most written invoices cover fleet, monthly, or event work.
car-wash.pricingModel: Retail washes are priced by package tier (basic exterior, wash and vacuum, full interior and exterior) and often adjusted by vehicle size: sedan, SUV or truck, and oversize or van. Mobile and hand wash operators usually charge a flat price per vehicle with add-ons such as wax, pet hair removal, or headlight restoration. Fleet and commercial accounts are billed per vehicle per wash at a discounted volume rate, often itemized by route or location and invoiced weekly or monthly. Memberships are billed as a recurring monthly fee for unlimited or capped washes. Some mobile operators add a travel or service-call fee for short jobs, and water or power hookup surcharges when the site doesn't provide them. Heavy trucks, buses, and RVs are usually priced per vehicle or per foot of length.

sampleInvoice.notes: Service period: June 1-28 at 2200 Industrial Way. Payment due net 15. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Please report any missed vehicles or damage concerns within 48 hours of the service date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service dates and location for each wash
invoiceChecklist.why: Fleet customers reconcile against their schedules, and dated lines settle disputes about whether a wash was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle identifier (unit number, plate, or last digits of VIN)
invoiceChecklist.why: Fleet managers charge costs back to individual vehicles or departments and need to match each line to a unit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package or service tier per vehicle
invoiceChecklist.why: Different vehicle sizes and packages carry different prices, and itemizing shows why totals vary.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Wax, pet hair removal, odor treatment, and engine bay cleaning are extras that should be visible as their own lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Membership billing period and renewal date
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring customers need to see what month the charge covers and when it renews or can be canceled.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or account code
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial and government accounts will not pay an invoice without a purchase order reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Taxability of car washes varies by state and locality, so show tax separately when you charge it and check your local rules.

car-wash.paymentTerms: Retail customers pay at the time of service by card, cash, or app. For invoiced accounts, net 15 or net 30 is common, with monthly billing for fleets and weekly billing for high-volume routes. Mobile operators often take payment on completion and may ask for a deposit on large one-time jobs such as a bus or RV fleet day. Memberships are charged automatically by card on a set monthly date. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical for commercial accounts, and it helps to state this in a signed service agreement. Accept card, ACH, and check, and consider requiring a card on file for new fleet accounts.

tips.title: Price by vehicle size from the start
tips.body: A pickup with a crew cab takes longer than a compact sedan. Set size tiers and apply them on every invoice so customers don't expect one flat price for all vehicles.

tips.title: Put fleet terms in a written agreement
tips.body: Spell out wash frequency, vehicle count, rain policy, and rate per vehicle. When a fleet adds or removes vehicles, the invoice then matches an agreed baseline.

tips.title: Bill weather skips clearly
tips.body: Decide whether rained-out or no-access visits are rescheduled or charged a minimum fee, and state it in your terms. Unvisited vehicles that appear on an invoice cause arguments.

tips.title: Track chemicals and water costs per account
tips.body: Heavy equipment, truck washing, and degreasing use more product and water. If one account costs far more than others, adjust its rate or add a surcharge.

tips.title: Take photos of problem vehicles
tips.body: Document pre-existing damage, heavy soil, or vehicles you couldn't finish. Photos protect you in damage claims and support surcharges for extra-dirty vehicles.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on car washes?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax car wash services, some do not, and some tax only certain services like detailing or membership sales. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant and show tax as its own line on invoices.

faqs.question: How do I bill a fleet that adds and drops vehicles each month?
faqs.answer: List each vehicle by unit number and wash date on the invoice, and bill only for vehicles actually washed. Keep a running list per account so you can match your route sheets to the billing.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for very dirty vehicles?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in your price list or agreement. Define what counts, such as heavy mud, pet hair, or construction residue, and list the extra as a separate line with a photo on file.

faqs.question: How should I invoice memberships?
faqs.answer: Charge the same fee on the same date each month, and send a receipt that shows the period covered. Make the cancellation and pause terms clear when the customer signs up.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice for mobile washes paid on the spot?
faqs.answer: Not always, but a receipt is useful for business customers who need it for expense records. Include date, vehicle, services performed, and amount paid.

estimate.intro: Car wash operators send estimates mainly for fleet contracts, dealership lot work, event washing, and large one-time jobs like buses or RVs. Clients typically compare per-vehicle price, wash frequency, quality, and whether you bring your own water and equipment.

scopeChecklist.why: Price depends on size and category, and a count that changes later should adjust the total.
State whether it covers exterior only, vacuum, windows, tire shine, or interior wipe-down so expectations match.
Weekly, biweekly, or one-time work changes the rate and how you plan your crew.
If the customer must provide a hose bib or you use a water reclaim mat, say so, and note any added fee.
Rain, locked lots, or unavailable vehicles can cost you a trip, so state what happens when a visit can't be done.
Heavy soil, decals, engine bays, and oversized vehicles should be listed as extras to avoid disputes.
Chemical, labor, and water costs change, so give an expiration date and due terms upfront.

pricingTips.title: Offer volume tiers
pricingTips.body: Show a lower per-vehicle rate at higher vehicle counts, such as 1-10, 11-25, and 26 or more. It rewards larger accounts and makes your quote easier to compare.

pricingTips.title: Price from time per vehicle
pricingTips.body: Time a typical wash for each vehicle type, multiply by labor cost, then add chemicals, water, equipment wear, and travel. That keeps low fleet rates from losing money.

pricingTips.title: Quote a trial wash for new accounts
pricingTips.body: A one-time sample of a few vehicles lets the customer judge quality before committing, and lets you check your time estimate on real vehicles.

pricingTips.title: Show add-ons as options
pricingTips.body: List wax, interior detail, and engine bay cleaning as separate priced options. Customers can accept the base quote and add services later without renegotiating.

faqs.question: Should I give a fleet quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: Give a rough range by phone, then send a written quote after you know vehicle types, count, location, and water access. Written quotes reduce disagreements about what was included.

faqs.question: How long should a car wash quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for one-time jobs, and 14 to 30 days for contract bids. Shorter windows make sense if your product or fuel costs are rising.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a large job?
faqs.answer: For one-time events or bus and RV fleets, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is reasonable, especially if you need to rent equipment or schedule extra crew. Recurring accounts are usually billed after service instead.

faqs.question: What if the vehicle count changes after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying pricing is based on the quoted count and that changes will be billed at the stated per-vehicle rate. Large changes may need a revised quote.

career-coach.intro: Career coaches help clients change careers, move up, prepare for job searches, negotiate offers, or figure out what they want to do next. Most work solo or in small practices and bill for one-on-one sessions, multi-month coaching packages, resume and LinkedIn work, interview prep, and sometimes group workshops or corporate engagements.
career-coach.pricingModel: Most career coaches sell packages rather than single hours, because career change takes several sessions and clients get better results with a committed program. A typical package is 3 to 6 months with a set number of sessions (often two a month), plus email or message support between calls. Single sessions are usually priced per hour or per 45 to 60 minute session. Document services such as resume rewrites, cover letters, and LinkedIn profiles are normally flat fees. Add-ons such as assessments (for example, personality or strengths inventories) are billed at cost or with a modest markup. Corporate and outplacement work is billed per participant, per workshop, or at a day rate. Rates depend on niche (executive coaching charges far more than entry-level), credentials, and track record.

rates.service: Career change or job search package (3 months, 6 sessions)

items.description: Career transition coaching package, 3 months (6 sessions, 60 min each, email support between sessions)
Resume rewrite and cover letter template
LinkedIn profile optimization
Strengths assessment and debrief report (assessment cost passed through)
Additional mock interview session

sampleInvoice.notes: Package sessions must be used within 4 months of the start date. Payment is due within 14 days of invoice date. Reschedule requests need 24 hours notice or the session is forfeited. Payment methods accepted: card, ACH, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name, start date, and end date
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often dispute what they bought. Naming the program and its term makes it clear what the fee covers and when it expires.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of sessions included and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the client is paying for and gives you a basis for billing extra sessions later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of individual sessions (for per-session billing)
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the client a record they can match against their calendar, and helps if they submit the bill for reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for deliverables such as resume, LinkedIn, and cover letters
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents billed as flat fees should be itemized so clients see value beyond the calls, and you can track which were delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Assessment or third-party tool costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Assessments often carry a cost to you. Listing them separately keeps them transparent and avoids a client assuming they are included in the coaching rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Employer name, PO number, or participant ID for sponsored clients
invoiceChecklist.why: When a company, university, or workforce program pays, their accounts payable team usually needs a reference number to process the bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and session expiration terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Restating your policy on the invoice reduces disputes over missed or unused sessions.

career-coach.paymentTerms: Most career coaches collect payment up front for packages, either in full (sometimes with a small discount) or in two to three monthly installments. Single sessions are usually paid at booking or immediately after the call. For corporate and outplacement clients, net 15 to net 30 is common, and a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is reasonable for workshops. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in your agreement beforehand. Card, ACH, and check are all common; payment plans should be written down with specific dates and amounts. Many coaches make packages non-refundable once the first session is delivered, with any exceptions spelled out in the coaching agreement.

tips.title: Sell packages, not hours
tips.body: Career change takes months. A package priced at a flat fee gives clients a clear commitment and gives you predictable income. Hourly billing invites clients to stretch out spacing between sessions and stall their own progress.

tips.title: Put an expiration date on sessions
tips.body: Unused sessions create open-ended obligations. Set a window, such as 4 or 6 months, and state it in your agreement and on every invoice.

tips.title: Bill documents separately from coaching
tips.body: Resume and LinkedIn work has a clear scope and finish line. Keep it as its own line item so clients can add or skip it, and you are not doing hours of unpaid rewriting inside a coaching package.

tips.title: Invoice sponsors differently from individuals
tips.body: When an employer, school, or outplacement firm pays, ask for the billing contact, PO number, and payment schedule before you start. Send the invoice to accounts payable, not the participant.

tips.title: Keep outcomes out of your pricing language
tips.body: Do not bill or promise based on getting a job or a raise. Describe the invoice in terms of sessions and deliverables, which you control, to avoid disputes when a search takes longer than expected.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or by package?
faqs.answer: Most career coaches do both. Packages suit clients who want structured support over several months and give you committed revenue. Single sessions suit one-off needs such as interview prep or offer negotiation. Many coaches price single sessions higher than the per-session cost inside a package.

faqs.question: Do I have to charge sales tax on coaching?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax personal coaching services, but some tax certain professional or consulting services, and digital products may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who stops attending sessions?
faqs.answer: Follow the terms in your coaching agreement. If the package is prepaid and non-refundable, the unused sessions generally expire at the end of the term. State this on the invoice and send a reminder before the deadline so it does not come as a surprise.

faqs.question: Can I invoice a client's employer instead of the client?
faqs.answer: Yes. Get the employer's billing contact, any PO number, and approved scope in writing first. Invoice the company by name, include the participant's name as a reference, and follow their payment terms, which are often net 30.

faqs.question: Should I take a deposit for resume services?
faqs.answer: Yes, many coaches ask for 50 percent up front on flat-fee documents and the rest on delivery of the final version. This protects you from doing the work and then being ghosted.

estimate.intro: Career coaches send quotes or proposals when a prospect asks for pricing after a discovery call, when an employer or program requests a bid for multiple participants, or when someone wants a custom mix of coaching and documents. Clients often compare the number of sessions, the length of the engagement, what support is available between calls, and whether resume and LinkedIn work are included.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare coaches by what they get. State exactly how many sessions, how long each lasts, and whether they are by video, phone, or in person.
A 3-month package that runs 8 months because of rescheduling is a common problem. Set the start date, end date, and a deadline for using sessions.
Email or message access is easy to over-promise. Say what is included, such as replies within one business day, and what is not, such as reviewing every job posting.
List resumes, cover letters, LinkedIn profiles, or interview scripts, and the number of revisions for each, so the scope does not expand without a fee.
If you use paid assessments, say whether the cost is included or billed separately so the final total does not surprise the client.
State clearly that you do not guarantee a job offer, interview, or salary outcome. This sets proper expectations and protects you from refund demands.
Putting the deposit, installment dates, and late-cancel rules in the quote means they are agreed to before the first session.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic package of sessions only, a mid-tier adding resume and LinkedIn work, and a premium with extended support gives clients a choice and often moves them toward the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price on the transformation scope, not just time
pricingTips.body: A client changing industries needs more than someone polishing a resume for the same field. Price higher for career pivots, executives, and clients needing negotiation support.

pricingTips.title: Make installment totals match the full price
pricingTips.body: If you offer a payment plan, show both the pay-in-full price and the installment total. Many coaches add a small premium for installments or give a discount for paying in full.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: A 7 to 14 day validity window encourages a decision and lets you adjust pricing if your schedule or rates change.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation before quoting?
faqs.answer: Most career coaches offer a free 15 to 30 minute discovery call. It lets you understand the client's goals and decide if you are a fit before you put a price in writing. Keep it short so it does not turn into free coaching.

faqs.question: Do I need a written agreement as well as a quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. The quote shows scope and price, but a coaching agreement should cover confidentiality, cancellations, refunds, and the fact that outcomes are not guaranteed. Many coaches combine the two into one document the client signs.

faqs.question: How do I quote for a corporate or outplacement client?
faqs.answer: Ask how many participants, what format (individual or group), and how long the engagement lasts. Then quote per participant or per workshop, with a clear total, and confirm who handles scheduling and no-shows.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a discount?
faqs.answer: Instead of reducing your rate, adjust the scope: fewer sessions, a shorter program, or no document work. This keeps your per-session value intact and gives the client a real choice.

career-consultant.intro: Career consultants help clients with job searches, career changes, resumes, interviews, salary negotiation, and long-term planning. Clients include individual job seekers, mid-career professionals, recent graduates, and sometimes employers or outplacement programs that pay for a group of employees. Invoices usually cover coaching sessions, document writing, assessments, and prepaid packages.
career-consultant.pricingModel: Most career consultants mix hourly session fees with flat-fee deliverables and packages. Resume, cover letter, and LinkedIn profile writing are usually quoted as flat fees by career level, since executives need more research and revision than entry-level clients. Coaching is billed per session or sold as a bundle (for example, four or six sessions over two to three months) at a small discount for paying upfront. Some consultants offer monthly retainers for ongoing support during a long search. Corporate and outplacement work is often billed per participant or at a day rate, and may require a purchase order. Paid assessments such as Strong Interest Inventory or MBTI add a separate line item, since the consultant must be certified and pay per-administration fees.

items.description: Mid-career resume rewrite with one round of revisions
Cover letter template tailored to target role
LinkedIn profile optimization (headline, summary, experience)
Career coaching session, 60 min (strategy and target role mapping)
Mock interview with written feedback

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Thank you for your business. Coaching sessions must be used within 90 days of purchase. Additional revisions beyond the included round are billed at $75 per hour. Services are advisory and do not guarantee job offers or specific salary outcomes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables with revision rounds included
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often ask for more edits after delivery. Stating that one or two rounds are included gives you a clear basis to bill extra changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and length
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client match charges to calendar entries and supports disputes over how many sessions were used from a package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client prepaid for six sessions, show how many are used and how many remain, and when the package expires.

invoiceChecklist.item: Assessment fees listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Assessments carry per-test costs and require certification, so a separate line shows what the client paid for and keeps your coaching rate clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or employer reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Outplacement firms and employers paying for an employee's services usually need a PO or case number to process payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client and payer names if different
invoiceChecklist.why: A parent, employer, or severance program may pay for the work. The invoice should name who is billed and who received the service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that results are not guaranteed
invoiceChecklist.why: Sets expectations that you provide guidance and documents, not job placement, which reduces refund requests when a search takes longer than hoped.

career-consultant.paymentTerms: Individual clients commonly pay in full upfront for resume projects and for prepaid coaching packages, or pay a 50 percent deposit with the balance due on delivery. Single sessions are often paid at booking or within 24 hours afterward. Corporate and outplacement clients typically pay net 15 to net 30 and may need a PO. Many consultants state a refund policy, such as no refunds after drafts are delivered or sessions are held, and a cancellation window of 24 to 48 hours. Card, ACH, and bank transfer are the most common payment methods. If you charge late fees, state them on the invoice and in your service agreement, and check your local rules on allowable amounts.

tips.title: Require payment before delivering final documents
tips.body: Share a watermarked or preview version of a resume, then release the final files once paid. Job seekers are often under stress and can delay payment once they have what they need.

tips.title: Sell packages with an expiration date
tips.body: Prepaid bundles are easier to bill and improve cash flow, but unused sessions can drag on for a year. A 90 to 120 day window keeps clients moving and keeps your calendar predictable.

tips.title: Define what a revision is
tips.body: Fixing a typo is not the same as rewriting for a different industry. Spell out that one round of edits is included and that a new target role or major restructuring is billed separately.

tips.title: Bill employers and outplacement firms separately
tips.body: If a company pays for an employee's coaching, invoice the company with its PO and send the client only a session summary. Do not share coaching content with the payer without the client's consent.

tips.title: Invoice follow-up work promptly
tips.body: Quick email reviews of a job offer or a last-minute interview prep call are easy to forget. Log the time and add it to an invoice that week.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for resume work?
faqs.answer: Most career consultants charge a flat fee based on career level and scope. Flat fees protect you from clients who want endless tweaks and give clients a clear price. Include a set number of revisions and bill extra edits hourly.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a prepaid coaching package?
faqs.answer: Invoice the full package price upfront with the number of sessions, the validity period, and your cancellation policy. Then send a short session log or balance update as sessions are used so the client always knows what remains.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit for career services?
faqs.answer: Yes. A 50 percent deposit is common for resume projects and larger packages. It secures the client's commitment and covers the research and drafting you do before the first review.

faqs.question: What if a client says they did not get a job and wants a refund?
faqs.answer: Your invoice and agreement should state that you provide coaching and documents, not job placement. If that is clear, refunds based on search outcomes are not owed. Some consultants still offer a revision or extra session as goodwill.

faqs.question: How should I bill a company that pays for a client's coaching?
faqs.answer: Invoice the company directly, include the PO or case number, name the participant, and list the sessions or deliverables. Confirm with the client and the company what details you may share, since coaching conversations are usually confidential.

estimate.intro: Career consultants send estimates when a prospective client asks about a resume package, a coaching program, or a corporate workshop. Clients usually compare your price with other consultants, resume-writing services, and free options like university career centers. A clear scope and a defined outcome help you stand out on more than price.

scopeChecklist.why: List the resume, cover letter template, LinkedIn update, and any other documents so the client knows exactly what is included.
State how many coaching sessions are included and how long each lasts, so there is no confusion about whether a session runs 45 or 60 minutes.
Say how many edits are included and how many business days each draft takes. This prevents disputes about delays and endless changes.
Draft timelines depend on receiving the current resume, job descriptions, and a completed intake form. Late materials should move your schedule, not your price.
Note that job applications, recruiter outreach, and placement are not included unless quoted separately, so clients do not assume you will apply on their behalf.
Assessment fees, portfolio hosting, or professional headshot referrals should be noted if they are billed separately.
State how long the quote is valid and what triggers the start, such as a signed agreement and deposit.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option (resume only), a mid option (resume, cover letter, LinkedIn), and a full option (those plus coaching sessions and interview prep). Clients tend to choose the middle tier and you avoid one-off custom pricing.

pricingTips.title: Price by career level, not page count
pricingTips.body: An executive resume requires more discovery, positioning, and revisions than an entry-level one, even if the final document is the same length. Quote by level so your time is covered.

pricingTips.title: Quote corporate work per participant and per day
pricingTips.body: For workshops and outplacement, give a per-participant price and a day rate for facilitation, plus prep time and materials. Companies expect a line-by-line breakdown they can approve internally.

pricingTips.title: Do a short intro call before quoting
pricingTips.body: A 15-minute call reveals whether the client needs a resume tune-up or a full career change plan. It prevents underquoting and helps clients self-select into the right package.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation before sending a quote?
faqs.answer: A short, free intro call of 15 to 20 minutes is common and helps you scope the work. Keep it focused on the client's goals and your process, not on free coaching.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Job seekers often delay, so a validity date lets you adjust pricing and manage your schedule if they return months later.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if the client's goals change after I send the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your estimate states the scope and says changes in target role or added deliverables will be quoted separately. Send a revised estimate before doing the extra work.

caregiver.intro: Independent caregivers provide non-medical help to seniors, people with disabilities, and people recovering from illness or surgery, usually in the client's home. They send invoices to the client or a family member, and sometimes to a long-term care insurance carrier, for hourly care, overnight shifts, and related costs such as mileage for errands.
caregiver.pricingModel: Most independent caregivers bill by the hour, with a minimum shift length of 3 to 4 hours so travel time is covered. Overnight care is often a flat rate per shift (awake or asleep), and live-in care is usually a flat daily rate. Holidays, weekends, and short-notice shifts often carry a premium of 1.25 to 1.5 times the normal rate. Clients with heavier needs, such as dementia care or two-person transfers, may pay more. Mileage for errands and doctor visits is billed separately at the IRS rate or a set per-mile rate, and groceries or supplies bought for the client are billed at cost with receipts. Some caregivers offer weekly or monthly packages for a set number of hours. Agencies charge more than independent caregivers because they cover payroll, insurance, and overhead, but independent caregivers must cover their own insurance and taxes.

rates.service: Live-in care (24-hour, with sleep and breaks)

items.description: Personal care, weekday shifts 9am-1pm (Mon, Wed, Fri), week of March 3
Overnight care, Saturday March 8 (10pm-7am, asleep shift)
Holiday/weekend premium, Sunday March 9 companion care
Mileage for pharmacy and doctor visit
Reimbursement: groceries and pharmacy copay (receipts attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Accepted by check, Zelle, or bank transfer. Care log for the week is attached. Late balances after 14 days are subject to a $15 fee. Thank you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and start/end times for every shift
invoiceChecklist.why: Families, and sometimes siblings or insurers reviewing the bill, want to match hours to a care schedule and avoid disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of care per line (companion, personal care, overnight)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different care levels carry different rates, so listing them shows why the amounts differ.

invoiceChecklist.item: Premium and minimum-shift charges labeled separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Holiday, weekend, and short-notice charges are a common source of surprise unless clearly itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage log with date, purpose, and miles driven
invoiceChecklist.why: Client errands and appointments are billable, and a log backs up the charge and supports your own tax records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-pocket purchases with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Groceries and supplies are reimbursed at cost, and receipts keep the client or their power of attorney comfortable with the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and, if different, the name of the person paying (such as an adult child or POA)
invoiceChecklist.why: Care is often paid by someone other than the client, and the invoice needs to reach the right person.

invoiceChecklist.item: Long-term care policy or claim number, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers that reimburse care usually require specific details and may need a provider's name, tax ID, and dates of service.

caregiver.paymentTerms: Most independent caregivers invoice weekly or every two weeks, since caregivers often depend on steady income and clients are used to paying on a cycle. Payment is typically due within 3 to 7 days. Many caregivers ask for a deposit or one week prepaid when starting with a new client, especially for live-in or overnight care. Late fees of a flat amount or 1.5 percent per month are sometimes used, so state them in a written care agreement. Common payment methods include checks, bank transfer, and peer-to-peer payment apps. Long-term care insurance may reimburse the client, so the client may need a clear invoice to submit. Include a cancellation policy in the care agreement, such as 24 hours' notice or payment for a minimum number of hours when a shift is cancelled late.

tips.title: Put the care agreement in writing before the first shift
tips.body: Spell out the hourly rate, minimum shift, overtime or holiday premiums, mileage rate, and payment schedule. A signed agreement makes the invoice a reflection of what was already agreed.

tips.title: Attach a weekly care log
tips.body: A short log of arrival and departure times and tasks completed shows the value of the work and settles questions from family members who are not in the home each day.

tips.title: Separate reimbursements from pay
tips.body: List groceries and supplies as reimbursements at cost, not as part of your hourly charge. Keep receipts, and ask the client to approve larger purchases first.

tips.title: Be clear about overtime and employment status
tips.body: If the client directs your schedule and tasks, some states or the IRS may treat you as a household employee rather than a contractor. Check local rules and consider talking to a tax professional so rates, overtime, and taxes are handled correctly.

tips.title: Bill regularly and promptly
tips.body: Weekly invoices keep balances small and make it easier to raise a problem early. Letting a month go by makes a family more likely to question individual shifts.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat daily rate?
faqs.answer: Hourly billing works best for shifts under about 10 hours. For overnight asleep shifts and live-in care, a flat shift or daily rate is more common because the work is less continuous. Write down what the flat rate covers, such as how many sleep hours and breaks are expected, and what happens if the client needs frequent help overnight.

faqs.question: Can I bill for travel time and mileage?
faqs.answer: You can bill mileage when you drive the client or run errands for them, using a per-mile rate such as the current IRS rate. Commuting from your home to the client's home is usually not billed. If you travel between multiple clients in a day, some caregivers add a travel fee, but state it in the agreement.

faqs.question: Who do I send the invoice to if a family member pays?
faqs.answer: Address it to the client and the person responsible for payment, such as an adult child or someone with power of attorney. Name both on the invoice and confirm who receives it in your care agreement, so there is no confusion about who owes the balance.

faqs.question: Can I accept long-term care insurance payments?
faqs.answer: Some long-term care policies reimburse the client for care by independent caregivers, but rules vary by policy. Ask the client to check what documentation the insurer needs. You may be asked for itemized invoices, your tax ID, and proof of dates and hours worked.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels a shift at the last minute?
faqs.answer: State a cancellation policy in your agreement, such as 24 hours' notice or payment for a minimum number of hours if cancelled later. Exceptions for hospitalizations or emergencies are common, so decide in advance how you will handle those.

estimate.intro: Caregivers usually give a written estimate during the first consultation, when a family is comparing several caregivers or agencies. The estimate covers an expected weekly or monthly cost based on the care schedule, and families often compare hourly rates, minimum shift lengths, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Care schedule: days, hours, and any overnight shifts
scopeChecklist.why: The total cost depends on expected hours, and a clear schedule helps families plan their budget.
Meal prep, bathing, transfers, medication reminders, and laundry take different amounts of time, and some tasks such as heavy lifting or medical care may be outside your scope.

scopeChecklist.item: Hourly rate, minimum shift, and premium rates
scopeChecklist.why: Holiday, weekend, and overnight rates differ from the standard rate, and families should see them before care starts.
Errands and appointments add cost, and clients should know the per-mile rate and how purchases are repaid.
Families want to know what happens when you are sick or on vacation, and whether you can provide a substitute.
Setting expectations about late cancellations avoids disputes over unworked shifts.

scopeChecklist.item: Review period and how rate changes are handled
scopeChecklist.why: Care needs often increase, so note when you will reassess the schedule and rate, such as after 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Quote the weekly total as well as the hourly rate
pricingTips.body: Families think in terms of monthly budgets. Show the hourly rate and the expected weekly cost, for example 20 hours at $28 is $560 per week, so the comparison is easy.

pricingTips.title: Price higher needs honestly
pricingTips.body: Dementia care, heavy transfers, or difficult overnight schedules take more skill and energy. Quote a higher rate up front rather than raising it after you see what the work involves.

pricingTips.title: Know the local agency rate
pricingTips.body: Agencies in your area set the upper end of what families expect to pay. Pricing somewhat below agency rates is common for independent caregivers, but remember you pay your own insurance, taxes, and unpaid gaps between clients.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial period
pricingTips.body: A two-week trial at the quoted rate lets both sides confirm the schedule and tasks before committing to a longer arrangement.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many caregivers offer a free first meeting to assess needs and meet the family. If the assessment is lengthy, such as a home safety review or care plan drafting, some charge a flat fee or one hour at their regular rate. Say so before the visit.

faqs.question: How long is an estimate good for?
faqs.answer: Since availability and care needs change quickly, estimates are often valid for 7 to 14 days. If a client waits longer or the person's condition changes, update the schedule and rate.

faqs.question: What if the client needs more care than the estimate covered?
faqs.answer: Include a line stating the estimate is based on the described needs and schedule. If hours or tasks increase, agree on a revised schedule and rate in writing, rather than adding extra hours without discussion.

carpet-cleaning.intro: Carpet cleaning businesses, from solo operators with a truck-mount or portable extractor to small crews serving homes and offices, send invoices after cleaning rooms, stairs, upholstery, and rugs. Most jobs are billed per room, per square foot, or as a package, with add-ons for stain treatment, pet odor, and protectant.
carpet-cleaning.pricingModel: Residential carpet cleaning is usually priced per room or per square foot, often with a minimum service charge to cover travel and setup. Many companies sell packages such as three rooms plus a hallway at a set price. Commercial work is typically priced per square foot, often at lower rates for large open areas, and may be billed on a recurring schedule. Add-ons are priced separately: pre-spotting of heavy stains, pet urine treatment, deodorizer, stain-resistant protectant, furniture moving, and extra-soiled areas. Upholstery is priced per piece (sofa, loveseat, chair) or per cushion, and area rugs by square foot with fiber type affecting price. Wool and specialty rugs cost more than synthetic. Stairs are usually charged per step. Most operators set a job minimum of $100-175 so short visits stay worthwhile.

rates.service: Standard room cleaning (hot water extraction, up to about 200 sq ft)
Pet urine or heavy stain treatment

items.description: Hot water extraction, living room and hallway (approx. 380 sq ft)
Hot water extraction, bedrooms
Stair cleaning, carpeted staircase
Pet urine spot treatment and enzyme application
Stain protectant, living room and hallway

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon completion of service. Carpets will be damp for 6-12 hours; please allow 24 hours of drying time before heavy use. Pet urine results depend on how deeply the urine has penetrated the pad. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Many customers book multiple visits or properties, and landlords and property managers need the exact unit cleaned for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rooms or square footage cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each room or measured area shows what the price covers and prevents disputes about whether a hallway or closet was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Stain treatment, deodorizer, protectant, and furniture moving are optional extras. Itemizing them makes the total easy to understand.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cleaning method used
invoiceChecklist.why: Hot water extraction, low-moisture, or dry compound methods affect drying time and cost. Naming the method sets expectations and supports your pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Notes on pre-existing damage or stains not fully removed
invoiceChecklist.why: Documenting permanent stains, bleach spots, worn areas, or pet damage protects you if a customer later says the cleaning caused the problem.

invoiceChecklist.item: Care and drying instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Advice on drying time, staying off carpet, and avoiding furniture with wet feet reduces callbacks and damage claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or work order for commercial and property management clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Many businesses will not process a payment without a PO or work order reference.

carpet-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential customers are typically expected to pay on the day of service, often right after the walkthrough, by card, check, or digital payment. Deposits are uncommon for standard jobs but are reasonable for large projects, rug pickup and delivery, or water-damage work. Commercial and property management accounts usually pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, and recurring contracts can be billed monthly. If you charge late fees on unpaid commercial invoices, state the rate (such as 1.5% per month) on the invoice and in your service agreement. Ask for payment before leaving a residential job, since collecting afterward is harder.

tips.title: Set and enforce a minimum charge
tips.body: Travel, setup, and equipment run time cost the same whether you clean one room or five. A minimum of $100-175 keeps small jobs profitable and is easy to explain to customers.

tips.title: Quote add-ons at the walkthrough, not after
tips.body: Point out pet stains, heavy traffic lanes, and areas needing pre-treatment before you start. Get approval for the extra charge so the final invoice does not surprise anyone.

tips.title: Document the carpet before you clean
tips.body: Take photos of existing stains, burns, fraying, and discoloration. Note them on the invoice. This is your best protection against damage complaints.

tips.title: Charge more for furniture moving and difficult access
tips.body: Moving heavy furniture, working in high-rise units with long hose runs, or cleaning heavily soiled carpet takes extra time. Add a line item rather than absorbing it.

tips.title: Offer recurring maintenance pricing
tips.body: Landlords, property managers, offices, and rental turnovers can provide steady work. Quote a lower per-sq-ft rate in exchange for a regular schedule and bill them on terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the room or by the square foot?
faqs.answer: Both work. Per room is simple for homeowners and good for marketing, but room sizes vary widely, so many operators cap room size (such as 200 sq ft) and charge extra beyond that. Square foot pricing is more accurate for large or open layouts and for commercial jobs.

faqs.question: Do I charge for stain removal separately?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, for anything beyond ordinary spotting. Pet urine, rust, ink, and heavy traffic lanes need extra products and time. List them as separate lines and tell customers beforehand that some stains may not come out fully.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on carpet cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning services of real property or all services, while many do not. Check with your state's department of revenue, and show tax as its own line on the invoice if you collect it.

faqs.question: What if the customer is not happy with the results?
faqs.answer: Set a clear policy in writing, such as a free return visit within a few days for areas that still look dirty. Persistent stains and wear usually cannot be fixed with another pass. Having before photos and notes on the invoice helps resolve these disputes.

faqs.question: Can I charge a trip fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many operators include a travel or fuel charge for jobs outside their normal service area, usually a flat amount or a per-mile rate. State the area and the fee on your quote and invoice.

estimate.intro: Most carpet cleaning customers ask for a quote by phone, text, or online form before booking, and many compare two or three companies. Quotes are common for whole-house jobs, commercial accounts, rental move-outs, and anything with pet damage or large rugs. Customers often compare per-room price, what is included, and whether there are hidden fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Rooms, areas, and square footage included
scopeChecklist.why: Closets, hallways, stairs, and bathrooms are common points of confusion. Listing what is included prevents arguments about what was supposed to be cleaned.
Truck-mount hot water extraction, portable extraction, and low-moisture cleaning differ in results and drying time. Naming the method justifies your price.

scopeChecklist.item: Included pre-treatment and what costs extra
scopeChecklist.why: Specify whether routine spotting is included and which items, such as pet urine, rust, or heavy soil, are charged additionally.
Say which items you will move, such as chairs and small tables, and that you will not move heavy items, electronics, or fragile pieces.

scopeChecklist.item: Stain removal limits and carpet condition
scopeChecklist.why: State that some stains, dye damage, and wear may be permanent. This sets expectations before work begins.
You may need water, power, and nearby parking for a truck-mount. Confirm these to avoid delays or extra fees.
Prices change with fuel and chemical costs, so state how long the quote is good for and how much notice is needed to reschedule.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a measured or reviewed space
pricingTips.body: Phone quotes based on room count can miss oversized rooms or heavy soiling. Ask for photos or measure on site, and state that the final price may change if conditions differ from what was described.

pricingTips.title: Offer package pricing
pricingTips.body: A set price for three rooms and a hallway, or a whole-house deal, is easy for customers to compare and encourages larger bookings. Keep the per-room price consistent so packages do not undercut your minimum.

pricingTips.title: Present optional add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: List protectant, deodorizer, and pet treatment as separate optional lines. Customers can accept the base price and add services, which increases average job size without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Account for drive time and job minimums
pricingTips.body: Include travel to distant addresses and apply your minimum charge on small jobs. A low advertised price can lose money once setup and drive time are counted.

faqs.question: Should I give a firm price over the phone?
faqs.answer: Give a price range or a per-room rate, and say it depends on room size and condition. A firm quote is safer after you see photos or visit. Always mention that heavy stains and pet damage may add to the cost.

faqs.question: Are carpet cleaning estimates free?
faqs.answer: Most are free for standard residential jobs, especially when given by phone or photo. Some companies charge for on-site visits for large commercial or restoration jobs and credit the fee toward the work if hired.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. A shorter period makes sense for large commercial or restoration jobs where material and labor costs can change.

faqs.question: What if the job turns out larger than quoted?
faqs.answer: Stop and tell the customer before continuing. Explain the issue, such as extra rooms, heavy soil, or urine damage, and give the added cost. Get approval in writing or by text, and reflect it on the final invoice.

carpet-installer.intro: Carpet installers lay wall-to-wall carpet, carpet tile, and cushion in homes, apartments, offices, and rental units. Many work as independent subcontractors for flooring retailers, property managers, and general contractors, while others run their own shop and sell and install directly to homeowners. Invoices usually cover labor by the square yard or square foot, plus tear-out, prep, and add-on work like stairs and transitions.
carpet-installer.pricingModel: Most carpet installers price labor per square yard or per square foot, with the carpet and pad either supplied by the client or retailer, or sold by the installer with a markup. Stairs are billed per step, and tear-out and disposal of old carpet and pad are billed per square yard or as a flat fee. Extras such as moving furniture, floor leveling, tack strip replacement, seam work in tricky layouts, and metal or wood transition strips are itemized separately. Small jobs often carry a minimum charge to cover travel and setup. Subcontractors working for retailers usually get a set price list per square yard, while direct-to-homeowner installers quote per room or per job. When you supply materials, show them as separate lines from labor so the client can see what is product and what is installation.

rates.service: Carpet installation with new pad (labor only)
Remove and dispose of old carpet and pad
Floor prep and patching, minor leveling
Minimum service or repair call (patching, re-stretching)

items.description: Remove and dispose of existing carpet and pad, three bedrooms and hallway
Install new carpet over 8 lb rebond pad (customer-supplied carpet), labor
Replace tack strip and patch subfloor at closet entry
Move and replace bedroom furniture
Metal transition strip at hallway to tile
Rebond cushion, 8 lb, 6-foot rolls

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on completion. Carpet manufacturer warranty applies to the product; installation is warranted against seam separation and loose stretch for one year. Please keep leftover carpet scraps for future repairs. Late balances over 15 days incur 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square yards or square feet installed, per room if possible
invoiceChecklist.why: Measurements are the most common billing dispute. Room-by-room totals let the client verify the number against their own estimate or the retailer's order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Carpet and pad product name, style, and color (if you supplied it)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what was installed and ties the invoice to the manufacturer warranty.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for tear-out, disposal, and prep
invoiceChecklist.why: These are labor and dump costs that clients often forget about. Itemizing them prevents questions about why the total is higher than the per-yard install price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stair count and style
invoiceChecklist.why: Stairs are priced per step and vary by style, so listing steps and whether they are waterfall or cap-and-band avoids arguments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retailer or general contractor job number or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Subcontractor invoices are often rejected or delayed without the right reference number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance details, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and some property managers require a license number on paperwork. Check your state's rules, since requirements vary.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation date and warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: A dated record helps if a seam opens or the carpet loosens later and sets the start of your workmanship warranty.

carpet-installer.paymentTerms: Direct-to-homeowner jobs often take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent when materials are ordered, with the balance due on completion the same day. Subcontractors working for flooring stores or builders are usually paid net 15 to net 30, sometimes weekly or every two weeks on a batch basis. Many installers charge a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month on overdue balances, stated on the quote or invoice up front. Common payment methods are checks, cash, card, and bank transfer. Commercial and property management clients may need a W-9 and proof of insurance before they pay.

tips.title: Measure and record before you start
tips.body: Write down room dimensions and square yardage on the work order and have the client or site contact initial it. Carpet is cut from 12-foot rolls, so waste is built into the material order, but labor should be billed on installed area unless you agreed otherwise.

tips.title: Bill stairs and odd shapes separately
tips.body: Stairs, curved rooms, patterned carpet that needs matching, and tight closets take far more time per square yard than open bedrooms. Price them on their own lines instead of averaging them into the general rate.

tips.title: Add a minimum charge
tips.body: A single closet or a small patch still needs travel, tool setup, and often a trip to pick up materials. A minimum visit fee keeps small jobs from costing you money.

tips.title: Note subfloor problems before you cover them
tips.body: If you find moisture, uneven concrete, or loose plywood, tell the client in writing and bill prep work separately. Covering a problem without documentation can make you responsible for it later.

tips.title: Invoice the same day on subcontract work
tips.body: Retailers often batch payments by invoice date. Sending the invoice and a photo of the finished job the same day can move you into the next pay cycle.

faqs.question: Should I bill carpet installation by square foot or square yard?
faqs.answer: Either works as long as you are consistent. Carpet is sold by the square yard in the US, so many installers and retailers quote labor that way. Residential clients often understand square feet better. Pick one unit and show the same unit on the estimate and invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for waste or cut-off material?
faqs.answer: If you supply the carpet, the client pays for the full amount of material needed, including waste from the roll width and seam layout. For labor-only jobs, bill installed area, not material ordered. State your approach on the estimate.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a retailer I subcontract for?
faqs.answer: Use the retailer's job or PO number, list each room or the total installed yardage, include any approved extras like stairs or furniture moving, and attach your W-9 if it is your first invoice. Follow their submission deadline if they have one.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on carpet installation?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Materials you sell are taxable in most states, and installation labor is taxable in some and not in others. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant, and show tax on a separate line.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to hold back payment until they are satisfied?
faqs.answer: Set expectations on the estimate: payment is due on completion after a walk-through. Fix any real defects such as visible seams, loose areas, or trimmed edges right away, then collect the balance. Do not agree to open-ended holds.

estimate.intro: Carpet installers give a written estimate before ordering materials or booking a crew. Homeowners often compare two or three quotes from different installers and retailers, so the quote needs to show what is included in each price. Commercial and property manager clients may ask for a per-unit price they can apply across many apartments.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured area per room and total square yards
scopeChecklist.why: Locks in the quantity so the price does not shift after the job begins.

scopeChecklist.item: Carpet, pad type, and weight, and who supplies them
scopeChecklist.why: Pad thickness and density change both cost and feel underfoot. Spelling out who buys the material avoids confusion about what you are quoting.

scopeChecklist.item: Tear-out and disposal of old flooring
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume removal is included. Say whether it is, and what happens with baseboards, tack strip, and staples.

scopeChecklist.item: Stairs, landings, and number of steps
scopeChecklist.why: Stairs are a big labor item and should be quoted per step with the style specified.

scopeChecklist.item: Furniture moving and what you will not move
scopeChecklist.why: Piano, waterbeds, and heavy appliances are usually excluded. State it to avoid damage claims.

scopeChecklist.item: Subfloor condition and what happens if prep is needed
scopeChecklist.why: Hidden damage, moisture, or uneven concrete can add cost. Give an hourly or per-item price for prep so the client knows how extra work is handled.
Clients often care about where seams show. Mark them on a sketch and list the transition strips included.

pricingTips.title: Quote labor and materials as separate lines
pricingTips.body: Clients can compare your labor price against other installers and see the carpet cost separately. It also makes it easier to adjust if they change the carpet choice.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best on pad or carpet
pricingTips.body: Giving three options at different prices helps the client choose without shopping elsewhere. Make sure each option shows the full installed price.

pricingTips.title: Build in travel and setup for small jobs
pricingTips.body: Use a minimum charge for single rooms and repairs. Give the same price whether the job is a closet or a short hallway if the travel and setup are the same.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Carpet and pad prices change, and your schedule fills up. A 14 to 30 day expiration date protects you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most installers give free estimates for standard residential jobs. Some charge a fee for complex commercial bids or long drives and credit it toward the job if it is booked. Say so before you visit.

faqs.question: How accurate does my measurement need to be?
faqs.answer: Measure at the widest and longest points of each room, including closets and door openings. Round up to the next half or whole yard as your pricing practice, and note that the final bill is based on installed area if it differs materially.

faqs.question: What if the client changes the carpet after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Issue a revised quote. Different carpet can change pad requirements, seam layout, and labor, especially with patterned or heavy cut-pile styles. Do not order material until the revised quote is approved.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: A signed or emailed approval is strongly recommended. It records the scope, price, and deposit, and helps if the client later disputes extras or changes.

catering.intro: Caterers are solo operators and small businesses that prepare and deliver food for weddings, corporate lunches, parties, and other events. Invoices usually cover per-person food pricing, staffing, rentals, delivery, and service charges, and are often split into a deposit and a final balance.
catering.pricingModel: Most caterers price per person (per head) for food, with the price depending on menu, service style, and guest count. Drop-off and buffet service cost less per head than plated or family-style service because they need fewer staff. Staff such as servers, bartenders, and chefs are billed hourly, often with a 4 to 5 hour minimum. Rentals (linens, plates, chafing dishes, glassware) are billed at cost plus a markup or as a flat package. Many caterers add a service charge or administrative fee of 15 to 22 percent of the food and beverage total, plus delivery or travel fees. Smaller jobs like office lunches may be priced per tray or per box lunch, and large events often have a minimum spend. Final guest counts are typically locked 7 to 14 days before the event, and billing is based on that guaranteed count even if fewer people attend.

items.description: Buffet dinner: choice of two entrees, two sides, salad, rolls, dessert (final guest count 80)
Servers for 5 hours including setup and cleanup
Bartender, 4 hours (client provided alcohol)
Linen, plate, flatware, and chafing dish rental package
Delivery, setup, and breakdown (22 miles each way)
Service charge (18% of food total)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received on March 4 is applied to this invoice. Balance due within 7 days of the event date, May 18. Guest count was guaranteed at 80 on May 4. Accepted payment: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on cards). Late balances are subject to 1.5% monthly interest.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and confirms what hours staffing was billed for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guaranteed guest count and actual count if different
invoiceChecklist.why: Billing is usually based on the guaranteed count, and showing it prevents disputes when fewer guests show up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Menu items and service style (buffet, plated, drop-off)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often compare the invoice to the proposal, so the menu and service style should match what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Staffing breakdown with number of staff, hours, and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Labor is a major cost and clients question it most often. Showing minimums and overtime up front avoids pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental items, quantities, and whether they are at cost or marked up
invoiceChecklist.why: Rentals are easy to overlook and often come from a third party, so listing them clearly supports the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service charge, gratuity, and delivery fees listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume a service charge is a tip for staff. Labeling these separately avoids confusion and helps with sales tax treatment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax and your food service or business license number if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepared food is taxable in many states, and some jurisdictions require a license or permit number on business paperwork. Check your local rules.

catering.paymentTerms: Most caterers collect a non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date, with a second payment due 7 to 14 days before the event and the final balance due on or shortly after the event. Corporate clients often pay net 15 or net 30 and may need a purchase order number. Small drop-off orders are usually paid in full when ordering or on delivery. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is accepted by check, ACH, or card, and some caterers add a card processing fee. Gratuities are handled separately from the service charge and should be stated clearly in the contract.

tips.title: Bill on the guaranteed count
tips.body: Set a cutoff for final guest count, usually 7 to 14 days before the event, and put it in your contract. Bill for the guaranteed number or the actual number, whichever is higher, so you are not stuck with food you already bought.

tips.title: Separate service charge from gratuity
tips.body: A service charge covers your operating costs and is usually taxable in many states. Gratuity goes to staff. If you list both on the invoice, say what each one covers so clients do not feel double-charged.

tips.title: Set minimums for staff time
tips.body: Servers and bartenders rarely accept short shifts. Use a 4 or 5 hour minimum and include setup, travel, and cleanup in billed hours so your labor costs are covered.

tips.title: Track add-ons during the event
tips.body: Extra guests, an extra hour of bar service, or a last-minute dessert request should be written down with the client's approval and added to the final invoice before you send it.

tips.title: Apply deposits clearly
tips.body: Show each deposit by date and amount on the final invoice, and subtract them from the total so the balance due is easy to understand.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on catering?
faqs.answer: In many states, prepared food and catering services are taxable, and service charges or delivery fees may be as well. Rules vary widely, so check with your state's department of revenue or an accountant before setting up your invoices.

faqs.question: Is a service charge the same as a tip?
faqs.answer: No. A service charge is a fee kept by the business to cover costs like planning, supervision, and overhead. A tip or gratuity is meant for staff. Label them separately on the invoice, and be clear with clients about where each goes.

faqs.question: What if the guest count drops after the final deadline?
faqs.answer: Your contract should state that the guaranteed count is the minimum billed. Food is purchased and prepped based on that number, so the client pays for it even if fewer guests attend.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit that is non-refundable?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is common as long as it is stated in the signed agreement. The deposit holds the date and covers the cost of turning away other bookings. Rules on cancellation terms can vary by state, so keep your wording clear.

faqs.question: How do I bill for rentals I get from another company?
faqs.answer: List them as a line item at your cost plus a markup, or as a flat per-person package. Keep the rental company's invoice on file in case the client questions the charge.

estimate.intro: Caterers send a proposal or quote after an inquiry call or tasting, and usually before the client signs a contract and pays a deposit. Clients compare per-person price, what is included in that price, and how much staffing, rentals, and fees are added on top.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, time, venue, and estimated guest count
scopeChecklist.why: The price depends on the headcount and venue, and the quote should say it is only valid for that date and count.

scopeChecklist.item: Detailed menu with number of entrees, sides, and dessert
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume extras are included, so list exactly what each per-person price covers.
Plated, buffet, and drop-off need very different labor, and the number of servers affects both price and guest experience.

scopeChecklist.item: Rentals, equipment, and who supplies them
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether plates, linens, tables, and glassware are included or come from the venue or a rental company.
State whether you supply alcohol, only provide a bartender, or neither, since licensing and liability rules vary by state.

scopeChecklist.item: Fees, taxes, service charge, and gratuity
scopeChecklist.why: These can add 20 to 30 percent to the food price, so show them in the quote to avoid sticker shock.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count deadline, deposit, cancellation, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Food costs and availability change, so set a date after which the quote is no longer valid and explain when the count is locked.

pricingTips.title: Know your food cost percentage
pricingTips.body: Many caterers target food costs of 25 to 35 percent of the per-person price, with labor and overhead covering the rest. Cost out each menu before quoting rather than copying last year's price.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three menu tiers
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic, standard, and premium package helps clients choose within their budget and gives you room to upsell without negotiating line by line.

pricingTips.title: Show an all-in estimate
pricingTips.body: Give a total that includes staffing, rentals, tax, and service charge alongside the per-person food price. Clients comparing quotes often miss add-ons and feel misled later.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for price changes
pricingTips.body: For events months away, note that menu prices may change if ingredient costs shift significantly, or lock the price at the deposit.

faqs.question: Should I charge for tastings?
faqs.answer: Many caterers charge a tasting fee of $50 to $200 or credit it toward the booking if the client signs. A fee helps cover food and time for clients who are only comparing options.

faqs.question: How long should a catering quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is common. Popular dates book quickly, and ingredient and labor costs change, so an expiration date protects you.

faqs.question: What happens if the guest count changes after the quote?
faqs.answer: State that the quote is based on the estimated count and that the final price will adjust once the guaranteed count is set. Many caterers also set a minimum count or minimum spend.

faqs.question: Can I give a flat price for the whole event?
faqs.answer: You can for simple, small events, but per-person pricing with listed extras is safer for larger events because headcount and hours often change.

chimney-sweep.intro: Chimney sweeps clean and inspect chimneys, flues, fireplaces, wood stoves, and venting for homeowners, landlords, and property managers. Invoices usually cover a cleaning, an inspection at one of the standard levels, and any minor repairs or installed parts such as caps, dampers, or screens. Most work is done solo or with one helper, and the bulk of it falls in late summer through early winter.
