chimney-sweep.pricingModel: Most sweeps charge a flat fee per appliance or flue for a standard cleaning, with an inspection fee added or bundled in. Inspections are priced by level (Level 1, 2, or 3 under the NFPA 211 standard), and a Level 2 camera scan is common when a home is being sold or a fuel type or appliance has changed. Repairs and installs are priced as parts plus labor, with a markup on materials such as caps, dampers, crown sealant, and liner components. Extras are billed on top of the base fee: heavily glazed creosote removal, rooftop access for tall or steep roofs, drop cloths and extra cleanup for gas or pellet units, and travel outside your service area. Many shops set a minimum service charge to cover the truck roll, and some offer annual maintenance plans that lock in a yearly sweep at a slightly lower price.

items.description: Chimney sweep, masonry fireplace, single flue
Level 1 inspection with written findings
Stainless steel chimney cap with mesh, supplied and installed
Smoke chamber and damper cleaning, glaze treatment
Damper replacement hardware

sampleInvoice.notes: Service date 10/14. Findings: light creosote, damper seals poorly, crown has hairline cracks and should be sealed within the year. Payment due on completion. Card, check, or cash accepted. Recommended next sweep: October of next year or after 1 cord of wood burned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and the specific appliance or flue serviced
invoiceChecklist.why: Homes often have several flues, a fireplace, and a stove. Naming each one prevents disputes and creates a record for insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection level performed (Level 1, 2, or 3)
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers, home buyers, and code officials ask which level was done. It also justifies the price difference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Condition findings and creosote stage
invoiceChecklist.why: A short summary of what you found backs up extra charges for glaze removal and supports your repair recommendations.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts and materials itemized with brand or type
invoiceChecklist.why: Caps, dampers, liners, and sealants carry warranties, and customers need to know what was installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification and license numbers (CSIA or similar, state or local license if required)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many insurers and some municipalities want proof that a certified sweep did the work. Check your local rules on licensing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and recommended next service date
invoiceChecklist.why: Annual sweeps are expected. A recorded date helps the customer remember and brings repeat business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Photos or camera scan reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Linking images to the invoice protects you if a customer later disputes the condition of the flue.

chimney-sweep.paymentTerms: Most residential sweeps collect payment on the day of service, by card, check, or cash, and send the invoice by email or print it on site. For repairs or installs over a few hundred dollars, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, mostly to cover parts. Commercial, landlord, and property manager accounts usually get net 15 or net 30 terms. Many shops add a late fee, often 1.5 percent per month, if stated in writing on the estimate or invoice. Real estate inspection jobs are often paid at the time of the inspection or by the agent or buyer before the report is released.

tips.title: Quote the sweep and the inspection as separate lines
tips.body: Even if you bundle them for a discount, list both. If the customer later wants only a sweep, or a buyer needs a Level 2, the pricing is already clear.

tips.title: Document before you sweep
tips.body: Take photos of the firebox, damper, and flue condition before cleaning. Cracked flue tiles or missing mortar are often found during work, and a record protects you if the customer assumes you caused the damage.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge for short or remote jobs
tips.body: Drive time, setup, drop cloths, and vacuum cleanup take the same effort whether the flue is small or large. A stated minimum keeps tiny jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Offer an annual plan with a reminder
tips.body: Booking next year's sweep at the time of service smooths out the seasonal rush. Put the next service date on the invoice so it is easy to follow up.

tips.title: Get written approval before repairs
tips.body: If you find damage mid-job, stop and get approval in writing, even by text, for the added cost. Then invoice repairs as separate line items with parts and labor.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the flue or by the visit?
faqs.answer: Most sweeps charge per flue or per appliance because each one takes separate setup and cleaning. Add a minimum visit charge so that single-flue jobs far from your base still cover your costs.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for heavy creosote?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so up front. List standard cleaning as the base price and note that glazed or Stage 3 creosote requires special tools and time and will be billed as an added line. Show the extra on the invoice with a short explanation.

faqs.question: How do I bill a Level 2 inspection for a home sale?
faqs.answer: Bill it as its own line with the camera scan included, and note that it is for a property transfer. Provide the written report and video or images with the invoice. Real estate buyers and agents often want this for their records.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax services, some tax only parts and materials, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department and list tax separately on the invoice when it applies.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses a recommended repair?
faqs.answer: Note the recommendation and the customer's refusal on the invoice, and have them initial or acknowledge it if possible. This protects you if a problem comes up later.

estimate.intro: Chimney sweeps send estimates for repairs, relines, rebuilds, cap and damper installs, and any job beyond a routine sweep. Routine cleanings are usually quoted by phone at a flat fee. Customers typically compare your price against one or two other sweeps and want to know what is included, what materials you will use, and whether there is a warranty.

scopeChecklist.item: Which flue and appliance the quote covers
scopeChecklist.why: Multi-flue homes and homes with a stove and a fireplace are easy to misquote. Name each one.

scopeChecklist.item: Inspection level included and what the report contains
scopeChecklist.why: A Level 1 look and a Level 2 camera scan are very different amounts of work. Say which is included.
Stainless steel liners, cast-iron dampers, and aluminum caps vary widely in cost and lifespan. Customers should know what they are buying.
Steep roofs, tall chimneys, or tight attic access can raise labor. Note any extra charge for difficult access.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as masonry rebuilds or hidden damage
scopeChecklist.why: Cracked flue tiles or water damage found after starting can change the job. State that hidden conditions will be quoted separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Cleanup and protection of the home
scopeChecklist.why: Customers want to know you will use drop cloths and a HEPA vacuum. Stating it avoids complaints about soot.

scopeChecklist.item: Warranty terms and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Parts and labor warranties vary, and material prices change. A set expiration date protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Use fixed prices for standard work and itemize repairs
pricingTips.body: Customers expect a set price for a sweep or cap install. For repairs, break the quote into labor and parts so they can see where the money goes and approve pieces separately.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best for liners and caps
pricingTips.body: Giving two or three material options, such as a basic cap and a stainless cap with a longer warranty, lets the customer choose and often raises the average ticket.

pricingTips.title: Include a safety note when a finding is a fire risk
pricingTips.body: If a cracked flue or heavy creosote is a hazard, state it plainly in the estimate. This supports the price and shows you are not upselling.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for hidden conditions
pricingTips.body: Rebuilds and crown repairs often reveal worse damage. Quote a clear scope, then add a line that unforeseen conditions are billed after written approval.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Routine sweep quotes are usually free. For repair or reline estimates that require a full inspection or camera scan, many sweeps charge an inspection fee and credit it toward the work if the customer hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Stainless steel and masonry material costs can shift, so a stated expiration protects you from honoring an old price.

faqs.question: Can I quote a relining job without a camera scan?
faqs.answer: It is risky. Without scanning the flue, you may miss cracked tiles or offsets that change the liner size or length. Most sweeps do a scan first, or write the quote subject to a scan.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for repair work?
faqs.answer: For jobs with significant materials, such as a liner, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common. List the amount and due date on the estimate so the customer agrees to it before you order parts.

chiropractor.intro: Chiropractors in solo practices, small clinics, and mobile or cash-based offices bill patients for spinal adjustments, exams, X-rays, soft tissue work, and therapeutic modalities. Many bill insurance, but a growing number run cash or membership models and send itemized statements or invoices directly to patients, attorneys handling personal injury cases, or employers.
chiropractor.pricingModel: Pricing depends on whether you bill insurance or run a cash practice. Insurance-based offices bill by CPT code and collect a copay or deductible portion from the patient, with the rest paid at contracted rates. Cash-based offices usually charge a flat fee per visit, with a higher fee for the new patient exam and X-rays. Many also sell prepaid care plans (for example 12 visits) at a discount, or monthly wellness memberships. Add-on services such as spinal decompression, massage, or cold laser are priced per session or in packages. Personal injury cases are often billed at full usual and customary rates and paid on a lien or at settlement. Supplements, braces, pillows, and orthotics are sold as separate retail line items.

rates.service: Therapeutic massage or soft tissue work
Electrical stimulation, ultrasound, or cold laser

items.description: New patient exam and consultation (DOS 03/04)
Lumbar spine X-rays, 3 views (DOS 03/04)
Chiropractic adjustment, spinal (DOS 03/04, 03/07, 03/11, 03/14)
Electrical muscle stimulation (DOS 03/07, 03/11, 03/14)
Lumbar support brace

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service unless a payment plan is on file. Balance remaining after insurance is due within 30 days of this statement. This itemized statement can be submitted to your insurer for out-of-network reimbursement. Missed appointments without 24 hours notice may be charged $35.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service for every line
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers, attorneys, and HSA/FSA administrators require the date of each visit, and patients often dispute charges when dates are missing.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes and ICD-10 diagnosis codes
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network reimbursement and personal injury claims depend on codes such as 98940-98942 for adjustments and the diagnosis that supports them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurance carriers and HSA/FSA plans typically require these to process a claim or reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Practice tax ID and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Required on most claim submissions and helps patients claim medical expense deductions or reimbursements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for services and retail products
invoiceChecklist.why: Braces, supplements, and pillows may be taxed differently than treatment in some states and are often not covered by insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments, copays, and insurance adjustments applied
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear running balance prevents confusion about what the patient still owes after insurance and prior payments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Case or claim number and attorney name for injury cases
invoiceChecklist.why: Personal injury and auto accident billing is tied to a specific claim, and attorneys need it to match your bill to the case.

chiropractor.paymentTerms: Cash-based practices usually collect at the time of service by card, HSA/FSA card, or digital payment. Insurance-based offices collect the copay or deductible portion at the visit and bill the carrier, with patient balances typically due in 30 days. Prepaid care plans are paid in full upfront or in two or three installments, and the terms should state refund rules for unused visits. Personal injury patients are often treated on a letter of protection, with payment due when the case settles, so keep clear records and send periodic ledgers to the attorney. Late fees are less common in health care; many offices instead send reminder statements and move to a collections process after 60 to 90 days, following state rules.

tips.title: Collect at the visit whenever possible
tips.body: Balances owed by patients are much harder to collect after treatment ends. Take the copay, deductible portion, or cash fee at check-in or checkout and keep a card on file with written consent for future balances.

tips.title: Explain care plans in writing
tips.body: Before a patient buys a package, give them a written plan listing the number of visits, what is included, the total price, and how unused visits are handled. This prevents disputes when a patient stops coming.

tips.title: Give superbills to cash patients
tips.body: Many patients can submit an itemized statement to their insurer or HSA/FSA. Including codes, diagnoses, and your NPI saves them time and makes them more likely to stay with your practice.

tips.title: Keep treatment notes aligned with billing
tips.body: Each billed service should be supported by documentation for that date. Billing for modalities or X-rays that are not clearly noted creates audit and refund risk.

tips.title: Send ledgers to attorneys on a schedule
tips.body: For injury cases, send updated itemized balances after each treatment phase so the attorney has current figures when negotiating a settlement.

faqs.question: Can I send a regular invoice if I accept insurance?
faqs.answer: Yes, for the patient portion such as copays, deductibles, and non-covered services. The insurer is billed separately through a claim. Show the insurance payment and adjustment on the patient statement so the balance is clear.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and when should I give one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with your provider details, CPT and diagnosis codes, dates of service, and charges. Give one to cash or out-of-network patients who want to seek reimbursement from their insurer.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on adjustments or supplements?
faqs.answer: Treatment is generally not taxed in most states, but retail items like braces, pillows, or supplements often are. Rules vary by state, so check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I charge for missed appointments?
faqs.answer: Many practices do, as long as the policy is written, signed by the patient, and applied consistently. Some insurance contracts restrict billing patients for no-shows, so check your payer agreements.

faqs.question: How should I bill a patient who stops paying on a care plan?
faqs.answer: Follow the written plan terms. Send a statement showing visits used and the remaining balance, then follow up by phone or mail. If it remains unpaid, consider a collections agency, but check your state's rules for medical debt first.

estimate.intro: Chiropractors give estimates mostly to cash-pay patients, to people comparing care plans, and to those without coverage for chiropractic. A patient typically wants to know the cost of the first visit, how many visits are expected, and the total for the treatment plan.

scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the exam, X-rays, and first adjustment are bundled or priced separately so there is no surprise on day one.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected number of visits and frequency
scopeChecklist.why: Care plans are estimates based on the exam. Stating a range such as 12 to 16 visits over 8 weeks sets expectations and allows for changes.
List which modalities, massage, or decompression sessions are in the price and which cost extra.
X-rays done in-office may be included, but MRI or outside imaging is billed by another provider and should be called out.
Braces, orthotics, and supplements are optional purchases and should be shown separately from treatment.
Progress exams may be charged separately, and the plan may change if the patient does not respond as expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation and refund policy for packages
scopeChecklist.why: Patients often ask what happens if they stop early. Put refund or credit terms in the quote.

pricingTips.title: Show per-visit cost next to package pricing
pricingTips.body: Listing the single-visit rate beside the package price makes the savings clear and helps patients choose a plan they can finish.

pricingTips.title: Be clear that the plan is an estimate
pricingTips.body: Treatment depends on the patient's response. Present the number of visits as an expected range, not a guarantee of outcome, and avoid language that promises results.

pricingTips.title: Offer a payment schedule for larger plans
pricingTips.body: Splitting a package into monthly payments lowers the barrier to starting care. Put the due dates in the quote.

pricingTips.title: Separate the exam from the treatment plan
pricingTips.body: Quote the new patient exam first, then give a full plan after findings are known. This avoids quoting care you may not recommend.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote before the first exam?
faqs.answer: You can quote the exam and any X-rays, but the treatment plan should wait until you have evaluated the patient. Tell them a full estimate will follow the exam.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include insurance coverage?
faqs.answer: Only if you have verified benefits. Otherwise state the full fee and say the patient's out-of-pocket cost depends on their plan, then follow up once benefits are checked.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: For care plans, 30 days is common. Fees may change, and a patient's condition may be different if they wait longer to begin.

faqs.question: What if the patient needs more visits than quoted?
faqs.answer: Re-evaluate, explain the reason, and give an updated written estimate before continuing. Ask for the patient's agreement to the new plan and price.

civil-engineer.intro: Civil engineers in private practice, usually solo PEs or small firms, bill for site grading and drainage design, stormwater reports, land development plans, structural and geotechnical coordination, construction administration, and inspection. Clients include homeowners, developers, contractors, architects, and municipalities, and each often expects a different billing format.
civil-engineer.pricingModel: Most civil engineering work is priced as a fixed fee per phase or deliverable, such as a grading plan, a stormwater management report, or a site plan set. Hourly billing with a not-to-exceed cap is common for small or undefined scopes, peer review, expert consulting, and construction-phase support. Larger projects are often billed monthly as percent complete against a contract fee schedule. Hourly rates vary by role (principal PE, project engineer, EIT, CAD technician, field inspector). Reimbursable expenses such as plan printing, permit and agency review fees, survey subconsultants, and mileage are billed at cost, often with a markup of 10 percent when the contract allows. Additional services outside the original scope are billed separately under a written change order or amendment.

rates.service: Construction site inspection or field visit
PE stamp and certification letter (e.g., foundation or retaining wall)

items.description: Phase 2: Grading and drainage plan, 1.2-acre commercial lot (60% of $9,500 fee, invoice 2 of 3)
Stormwater calculations and report revisions per county review comments
Project engineer coordination with surveyor and architect
Principal PE review and stamp
Plan set printing (6 full-size sets)
County plan review fee (at cost, receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Project 24-117, Contract dated March 4, 2024. Hourly items are additional services approved by email on May 10. Payment due net 30. Balance of contract fee after Phase 2: $3,800. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, project number, and site address or parcel ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and municipalities run many projects at once, and accounting needs to match the invoice to the right job and budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or proposal date and fee schedule reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to the agreed scope and shows the invoice follows the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Phase or task breakdown with percent complete and fee billed to date
invoiceChecklist.why: Progress billing needs to show contract amount, previous billings, current billing, and remaining balance so the client can verify it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly entries by person, role, and date for time-and-materials work
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often audit hourly billing, and lender or public agency clients may require it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Approved change orders or additional services, with approval date
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents disputes over work outside the original scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts and any markup
invoiceChecklist.why: Permit fees, printing, and subconsultant costs are usually billed at cost and often require backup.

invoiceChecklist.item: PE license number and state, plus firm certificate of authorization where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require this on professional documents, and some clients need it on invoices for compliance.

civil-engineer.paymentTerms: Engineers commonly collect a retainer or initial deposit of 10 to 25 percent at signing, or a minimum retainer for small residential jobs, and then bill monthly or at milestones such as preliminary plans, permit submittal, and final approved plans. Net 30 is standard for commercial and municipal clients, while homeowners usually pay faster at net 14 or on receipt. Many contracts state a late charge of 1 to 1.5 percent per month and allow suspension of work or withholding of stamped drawings until the account is current. Payment is typically by check, ACH, or card, and public clients may require a vendor registration and a purchase order number before any payment is released.

tips.title: Withhold sealed documents until paid
tips.body: Keep stamped final plans and certification letters tied to payment in your contract. Release drafts for review, but deliver the final sealed set only after the milestone invoice is paid, where state rules and your contract allow.

tips.title: Bill permit review rounds as they happen
tips.body: Agency comment cycles can add many hours. Define the number of included review rounds in your proposal, and invoice extra rounds as additional services at the time you do them, not at the end of the project.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed-fee work
tips.body: Log hours against each phase so you can see when a job is running over and justify change orders. It also gives you real data for pricing future proposals.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not completion
tips.body: Tie invoices to deliverables such as survey review, concept plan, permit submittal, and approval. Waiting for final approval can leave you carrying months of unpaid work when a municipality delays.

tips.title: Keep subconsultant billing separate
tips.body: List geotechnical, survey, or environmental subconsultant costs as their own lines with their invoice numbers. This makes markup clear and keeps your fee from looking inflated.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when the scope and deliverables are clear, such as a grading plan for a defined site. Use hourly with a not-to-exceed amount when the scope is uncertain, when you are doing peer review or expert work, or when the client may keep changing requirements.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent responding to municipal review comments?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. State how many review rounds are included in the fixed fee, and bill additional rounds hourly or as an extra service. Without that language, clients often argue that revisions are part of the original fee.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for construction administration?
faqs.answer: Bill it separately from design, either hourly or as a monthly fee against a defined number of site visits, submittal reviews, and RFI responses. List visit dates and hours so the client can see what was done.

faqs.question: Can I mark up subconsultants and reimbursables?
faqs.answer: Many engineers add around 10 percent to subconsultant and reimbursable costs to cover administration and risk, but it must be stated in your proposal or contract. Public agencies sometimes prohibit markup or cap it, so check the contract terms.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pay after the permit is approved?
faqs.answer: Be cautious, because approval timing is outside your control. Bill for work as it is completed, and use a deposit and milestone payments so your payment does not depend on the agency's schedule.

estimate.intro: Civil engineers send a proposal or fee estimate before starting work, often after a site visit and review of the survey, zoning, and any existing plans. Clients, especially developers and contractors, compare fees from several firms, so clear scope and assumptions matter as much as the total price.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables list (plan sheets, reports, calculations, stamped letters)
scopeChecklist.why: Spelling out exactly what the client receives avoids arguments over whether a drainage report or detail sheet was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of review rounds and agency meetings included
scopeChecklist.why: Municipal comments can double the work. A defined number of rounds lets you charge for the rest.

scopeChecklist.item: Information provided by others (survey, geotechnical report, architectural base)
scopeChecklist.why: Your fee assumes this data is accurate and delivered on time. If it is late or wrong, you need grounds to adjust.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as survey, wetlands, traffic study, structural design, and permit fees
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume the engineer covers everything related to the site. Listing exclusions sets limits.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule and key milestones with client response times
scopeChecklist.why: Delays on the client side should extend your timeline and not leave you absorbing costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee type per phase and how additional services are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Shows which tasks are fixed fee and which are hourly, with the rate sheet for extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Proposal validity period and authorization to proceed
scopeChecklist.why: Costs and workload change, and a firm expiry date prevents old quotes from being used months later.

pricingTips.title: Price by phase
pricingTips.body: Break the fee into concept, design, permitting, and construction support. Clients can see where the money goes, and you can bill and get paid as each phase finishes.

pricingTips.title: Build in agency review time
pricingTips.body: Look up the local jurisdiction's typical review process before quoting. Stormwater and site plan reviews often take multiple rounds, so set aside hours for responding to comments.

pricingTips.title: Quote with a range when site conditions are unknown
pricingTips.body: If soils, existing utilities, or boundaries are uncertain, give a base fee with a stated allowance for unknowns, or use hourly with a cap, rather than a low fixed number you will regret.

pricingTips.title: Include a rate sheet for extras
pricingTips.body: Attach hourly rates by role to the proposal so change orders are priced at rates the client already accepted.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or site visit?
faqs.answer: Many engineers do not charge for a proposal on a larger job, but a detailed feasibility review or a site visit for a small client is often billed at an hourly rate or a small flat fee that can be credited against the project if it proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty to sixty days is common. Fees depend on your workload, agency requirements, and the information available, so put an expiration date on the proposal.

faqs.question: What if the scope grows after the client signs?
faqs.answer: Issue a written change order or amendment before doing the extra work, listing the added tasks, the fee, and any schedule effect. Start the work only after the client approves it in writing.

faqs.question: Is a verbal fee estimate enough for a small residential job?
faqs.answer: A written proposal is better even for small work. A one-page letter agreement with scope, fee, deliverables, and payment terms protects you and helps if the client later disputes the charges.

cleaning-service.intro: Cleaning services are run by solo cleaners, couples, and small crews who clean homes, offices, rental properties, and job sites. Invoices usually cover recurring visits such as weekly or biweekly house cleaning, one-time deep cleans, move-out cleans, and add-on tasks like inside-the-oven or interior window cleaning.
cleaning-service.pricingModel: Residential cleaning is most often priced as a flat fee per visit based on home size, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, and condition, with a discount for recurring schedules. Hourly pricing per cleaner is common for deep cleans, heavily soiled homes, and clients who want flexible scope. Commercial and office cleaning is usually billed per square foot, per visit, or as a monthly flat fee for a set number of visits per week. Add-ons such as inside the fridge, inside the oven, interior windows, laundry, or pet hair are priced as separate line items. Post-construction and move-out cleans are quoted higher because of the extra labor and dirt. Many owners charge a supply fee or build supplies into the rate, and bill extra for travel outside the normal service area.

items.description: Biweekly standard house cleaning, 3 bed / 2 bath (service date 5/14)
Inside oven cleaning
Inside refrigerator cleaning
Interior window cleaning
Pet hair surcharge (2 dogs)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of service. Cash, check, Zalle, or card accepted; card payments include a 3% processing fee. Please give 48 hours' notice to reschedule to avoid a $40 late cancellation fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date of each visit
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several properties or recurring visits need to match each charge to a specific clean, and it settles questions about missed or rescheduled dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of clean (standard, deep, move-out, post-construction)
invoiceChecklist.why: The price differs a lot between types, and naming it shows the client why this visit cost more than the usual one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Oven, fridge, windows, laundry, and similar extras are easy for clients to forget they requested, so list each one separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours worked and number of cleaners, if billed hourly
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly clients want to see how the total was reached, for example 2 cleaners at 3 hours each.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supply, travel, or parking fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate fees prevent surprises and make clear that they are standard charges, not arbitrary extras.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or lockout fees, if any
invoiceChecklist.why: If you arrived and could not get in or the visit was canceled late, the fee should be stated and tied to your written policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, license or insurance/bonding status, and tax ID where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers, offices, and some clients need this for their records, and some areas require a business license or sales tax on certain services.

cleaning-service.paymentTerms: Recurring residential clients are often billed after each visit with payment due in 0-7 days, or charged automatically on a card on file. Some owners bill monthly in advance for a set number of visits. New clients and large jobs such as move-out or post-construction cleans commonly pay a 25-50% deposit, with the balance due on completion. Commercial clients usually want net 15 or net 30 terms and may require a certificate of insurance. Late fees of 1.5% per month or a flat fee are common, but state them in your service agreement before the first clean. Accepted methods typically include card, bank transfer, check, and peer-to-peer apps.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing before the first visit
tips.body: Late cancellations and lockouts cost you a booked day. Include a notice period, such as 24 or 48 hours, and the fee in your service agreement, then reference it on the invoice when you charge it.

tips.title: Keep a card on file for recurring clients
tips.body: Charging automatically after each visit removes most chasing for payment. Get written authorization up front and send a receipt or invoice after every charge.

tips.title: Re-price when scope changes
tips.body: If a home gets bigger, a new pet arrives, or the client adds rooms to the routine, adjust the rate and tell them in writing. Quietly doing more work for the same price lowers your hourly earnings.

tips.title: Charge more for the first clean
tips.body: A first visit usually takes longer because the home has not been maintained to your standard. Many cleaners charge an initial deep clean rate, then drop to the recurring rate.

tips.title: Track mileage and supplies for taxes
tips.body: Mileage between jobs, cleaning products, and equipment are usually deductible business expenses for self-employed cleaners. Keep logs and receipts and check with a tax professional about what applies to you.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat rate per visit?
faqs.answer: Flat rates work well for recurring homes you know, because clients like predictable bills. Hourly works better for deep cleans, cluttered or heavily soiled homes, and first visits where the scope is uncertain. Many cleaners quote a flat rate after the first visit shows how long the job really takes.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on cleaning services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning or janitorial services, while many do not tax residential cleaning. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant before you set up your invoices.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee if the client is not home and I cannot get in?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your service agreement says so. A lockout or late cancellation fee, often $25-75 or a share of the visit price, is common. Clients are much more likely to pay it if they agreed to the policy before service began.

faqs.question: How do I bill for supplies?
faqs.answer: Most residential cleaners include supplies in the rate. If you use specialty products, bring in heavy equipment, or the client asks for particular items, list a supply fee as its own line. Commercial contracts often state whether supplies are included.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it the same day as the clean, while the work is fresh. For recurring monthly billing, send it on a set date each month and list every visit with its date.

estimate.intro: Cleaning services send estimates before the first visit for new residential clients, and for move-out, post-construction, and commercial jobs. Clients usually compare two or three quotes, so they look at the price, what is included, how many cleaners will come, and whether you supply products and are insured.

scopeChecklist.item: Home size and layout (square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, floors)
scopeChecklist.why: Size is the main driver of time and price, and a stated size protects you if the home turns out larger than described.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of clean and a room-by-room task list
scopeChecklist.why: Standard and deep cleans mean different things to different people, so list tasks such as baseboards, ceiling fans, and cabinet exteriors as included or excluded.
Oven, fridge, windows, laundry, and wall washing are common disputes, so say which are in the price.
A weekly, biweekly, or monthly schedule changes the price, and the client should know the rate applies only if they keep that schedule.
State that the price assumes normal upkeep, and that heavy buildup, hoarding, pet messes, or construction dust may raise the price after a walkthrough.
Say whether you bring products and a vacuum, whether the client must provide water and power, and how you will get in.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity, deposit, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing and your schedule change, so give an expiration date and note any deposit needed to hold the date.

pricingTips.title: Estimate from time, not just square footage
pricingTips.body: Work out how many labor hours the job takes, multiply by your target hourly rate per cleaner, and add supplies and travel. Compare that to the going flat rate for the home size so you do not underprice dense or cluttered homes.

pricingTips.title: Do a walkthrough for large or unusual jobs
pricingTips.body: For move-outs, post-construction cleans, and commercial accounts, look at the space or review photos first. A quote based on a description alone often leads to underbidding.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a standard clean and a deep clean, or a basic and a premium package, with the add-ons priced. Clients often choose the middle option and it makes the quote easier to compare.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range only when you must
pricingTips.body: If conditions are uncertain, give a price range with a clear point at which you will confirm the final price on site, rather than an open-ended hourly figure.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most cleaners give free estimates for standard homes. For large commercial buildings or post-construction jobs requiring an on-site visit, some charge a fee that is credited if the client books.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after I arrive?
faqs.answer: You can if the condition is much worse than described, but your estimate should say that. Talk to the client before starting, explain what is different, and get agreement in writing or by message.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. A short window protects you from rising costs and schedule changes.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before I clean?
faqs.answer: For recurring homes it is usually not needed. For move-outs, post-construction cleans, and large deep cleans, a deposit of 25-50% helps hold the date and covers lost income if the client cancels.

cloud-consultant.intro: Cloud consultants help companies plan, build, migrate, secure, and cost-optimize workloads on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and similar platforms. Most work solo or in small firms and bill for architecture reviews, migration projects, infrastructure-as-code builds, cost audits, and ongoing advisory or support retainers. Invoices usually combine time-based consulting with fixed-fee deliverables and sometimes pass-through cloud costs.
cloud-consultant.pricingModel: Hourly rates are the most common starting point, with senior independent consultants often charging more for specialized work such as security, compliance, or Kubernetes. Fixed-fee pricing is common for well-scoped deliverables like a well-architected review, a landing zone setup, or a cost audit. Larger migrations are often quoted as a project fee split into milestones, or billed time-and-materials with a not-to-exceed cap. Monthly retainers cover on-call advice, architecture guidance, and light operational support, usually with a set number of hours included and an overage rate. Some consultants offer cost-optimization work with a fee tied to a share of savings, though this needs clear baseline and measurement terms. If you buy cloud services or licenses on the client's behalf, bill them at cost or with a disclosed markup, and separate them from labor. Incident response and after-hours work is commonly billed at 1.5x to 2x the standard rate.

rates.service: Landing zone / multi-account setup with infrastructure as code
Application or server migration (lift and shift)

items.description: AWS landing zone setup: multi-account structure, SSO, guardrails, baseline logging (Terraform), milestone 1 of 2
Migration of production web application and PostgreSQL database to AWS (EC2, RDS, ALB)
Cloud cost review and rightsizing recommendations report
Architecture documentation and runbook handoff
Reserved third-party monitoring license, billed at cost (March)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Cloud provider charges are billed directly to the client's accounts and are not included here. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Remaining milestone is invoiced on completion of the network and security baseline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, SOW or contract reference, and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often route invoices through procurement and will reject or delay anything that does not match an approved SOW or PO.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or deliverable names with completion dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Fixed-fee and milestone billing is easier to approve when each line ties to a deliverable the client has accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by task or workstream, with the period covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Time-and-materials clients want to see what was done, such as migration, IaC development, or security hardening, and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately with provider and account
invoiceChecklist.why: Third-party licenses, marketplace software, or cloud spend you paid on the client's behalf should be clearly marked as reimbursable, at cost or with the agreed markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate type for premium work
invoiceChecklist.why: After-hours, on-call, or incident work at a higher rate should be labeled so the client sees it matches the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer details: hours included, hours used, overage
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on retainer want to see the balance and whether any overage rate applied this month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms, accepted methods, and remittance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Net terms, ACH or wire instructions, and late fee language prevent confusion, especially with business clients who pay by bank transfer.

cloud-consultant.paymentTerms: Business clients typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, and larger enterprises may push for net 45 or net 60 through procurement. For project work, a 25% to 50% deposit before starting is common, with the rest tied to milestones. Time-and-materials work is often invoiced every two weeks or monthly, and retainers are billed in advance at the start of the month. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. ACH and wire transfer are the usual methods for larger invoices, while card payments are used for smaller ones, sometimes with a fee passed on. Include payment terms in your contract, not just on the invoice.

tips.title: Keep cloud spend out of your invoice when you can
tips.body: Have clients pay the cloud provider directly from their own accounts. If you must front costs, you take on credit risk and may complicate your tax and liability position. When you do pass costs through, itemize them and invoice promptly.

tips.title: Tie fixed fees to defined deliverables
tips.body: Cloud projects grow quickly as new services, accounts, and environments appear. List what is included, such as number of accounts, environments, or workloads, and bill extra work as a change order.

tips.title: Bill for discovery separately
tips.body: Assessments and discovery often reveal the real scope. Charging for a paid discovery phase gives you accurate information for the larger quote and protects you from unpaid scoping.

tips.title: Set a minimum for incident and after-hours work
tips.body: Emergency calls interrupt other work. A premium rate and a minimum block, such as two hours, is standard and should be written into the contract.

tips.title: Be careful with savings-based fees
tips.body: If you take a percentage of cloud savings, define the baseline, the measurement period, and what counts as savings in writing. Otherwise invoices become disputes about what was saved.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use hourly or retainer billing for open-ended advisory and support. Use fixed fees for work with clear deliverables, like a cost audit or landing zone. For migrations with unknowns, time and materials with a cap is a common middle ground.

faqs.question: How do I bill for cloud costs I paid on a client's behalf?
faqs.answer: List them as a separate line, with the provider, service, and billing period, at cost or with the markup in your contract. Better still, have the client own the accounts and pay the provider directly.

faqs.question: Can I charge for on-call availability?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many consultants charge a monthly on-call fee for being available, plus an hourly rate for actual work done. Define response times and what hours are covered in the contract.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes hours on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Detailed time entries by task help resolve this quickly. Keep notes or ticket references for the work, and agree in the contract on how and when invoices can be disputed.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on consulting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain IT or software services, while many do not tax consulting. Check your state and the client's state rules or ask a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Cloud consultants send quotes before migrations, infrastructure builds, security reviews, and cost audits, and often after a short discovery call or assessment. Clients compare scope, timeline, who owns the accounts and code, and how much of the cloud bill is separate from your fee.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming the applications, accounts, regions, and environments such as dev, staging, and production keeps scope from quietly expanding.
Terraform modules, diagrams, runbooks, reports, and training sessions should be listed so the client knows what they receive.
State what you expect to find, like documented architecture or access to source code, and that findings that differ may change the price.
Delays often come from waiting on admin access, approvals, or staff time. Spell out what the client must provide and when.
Clarify that provider charges and software licenses are paid by the client and are not part of your fee, or give an estimate if you will pass them through.
Migrations depend on maintenance windows and testing. Dates and acceptance criteria avoid arguments over when work is done.
State who owns the infrastructure code and docs after payment, and whether you retain reusable components.

scopeChecklist.item: Change order process and support after launch
scopeChecklist.why: Define how extra requests are priced and whether post-cutover support is included, and for how many days.

pricingTips.title: Price discovery before the full project
pricingTips.body: If the environment is unknown, quote a short paid assessment first. Credit part of the fee toward the project if you like, but do not guess at a migration price blind.

pricingTips.title: Build in contingency
pricingTips.body: Cloud migrations commonly hit surprises such as legacy dependencies, networking quirks, or undocumented services. Add a buffer of 15% to 25% or quote a range with clear assumptions.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option, such as a review and report, and a fuller option, such as review plus implementation. Clients can choose by budget and you avoid one take-it-or-leave-it number.

pricingTips.title: Show the cost of running it, not just building it
pricingTips.body: Include an estimate of expected monthly cloud spend and optional ongoing support. Clients compare total cost over the year, and this builds trust in your numbers.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an estimate range?
faqs.answer: Fixed price works when scope is well defined. If there are unknowns, give a range with stated assumptions or use time and materials with a not-to-exceed amount.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Cloud pricing and your availability both change, so state an expiration date.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: Many consultants ask for 25% to 50% on acceptance for fixed-fee projects, especially with new clients. It secures your schedule and reduces payment risk.

faqs.question: Should the quote include the client's expected cloud bill?
faqs.answer: Provide an estimate separately, clearly labeled as a projection from the provider's pricing, not a guarantee. Actual usage and pricing can differ.

cnc-machining.intro: CNC machine shops, job shops, and independent machinists send invoices for custom parts, prototypes, and short production runs made on mills, lathes, routers, and multi-axis machines. Most invoices bill for setup, programming, machine time, material, outside processing like anodizing or heat treat, and inspection. Customers are usually engineers, product companies, fabricators, and other shops who expect part numbers, revisions, and PO references on every document.
cnc-machining.pricingModel: Most shops price per part for a quoted quantity, built up from setup time, programming or CAM time, cycle time multiplied by a machine hourly rate, material cost with markup, and any outside services. Setup is usually billed as a one-time charge per job, so unit price drops as quantity rises. Prototype and one-off work is often billed as a flat price per part or by the hour of machine time plus material. Machine rates vary by equipment: a 3-axis mill costs less per hour than a 5-axis machine or a Swiss lathe. Material is normally passed through with a 10-25 percent markup, and outside processing such as plating, anodizing, heat treat, or powder coating is passed through with a handling markup. Add-ons like first article inspection reports, material certifications, and rush fees are listed as separate lines. Repeat customers may get blanket POs with scheduled releases and volume pricing.

rates.service: Job setup (fixturing, tool load, first part proof)
First article inspection report (CMM or manual)

items.description: Bracket, P/N 4410-B Rev C, 6061-T6 aluminum, machined per drawing
Job setup and fixturing, 2 operations
CAM programming
Type II clear anodize (outside processing, includes handling)
First article inspection report with material cert

sampleInvoice.notes: PO 78231. Net 30 from invoice date. Material certs and inspection report attached. Parts shipped UPS Ground, tracking 1Z999AA10123456784; freight billed separately. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer PO number, part number, and drawing revision
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable usually will not pay without a matching PO, and the revision proves which version of the drawing you built to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity shipped versus quantity ordered
invoiceChecklist.why: Over- and under-runs are common. Billing only for what shipped, with the balance noted, avoids short-pay disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material type, grade, and heat or lot number
invoiceChecklist.why: Aerospace, medical, and defense customers need traceability, and cert references let them tie the invoice to the shipment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for setup, programming, and outside processing
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing one-time charges explains why a small run costs more per piece and makes reorders easier to price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection and documentation charges
invoiceChecklist.why: First article reports, CMM time, and certs of conformance are real labor. Listing them keeps them from being treated as free.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping method, tracking number, and freight charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Proof of shipment supports your claim for payment, and a separate freight line avoids confusion about who paid carriers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale/exemption certificate reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Rules vary by state. Noting the customer's resale or exemption certificate on file protects you in an audit.

cnc-machining.paymentTerms: Established commercial customers commonly pay net 30, and larger manufacturers sometimes require net 45 or 60. For new customers, prototype work, and individual buyers, many shops ask for 50 percent down with the balance due before shipment, or full payment up front for small jobs. Material-heavy jobs often require a deposit that covers raw stock and outside processing. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated on the quote and invoice. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, with card payments sometimes carrying a surcharge where allowed. Parts are often held until payment on first orders.

tips.title: Bill setup separately and clearly
tips.body: If setup is buried in the unit price, customers expect the same price on a reorder of 10 pieces. A separate setup line keeps quantity pricing honest.

tips.title: Pass through material and outside processing with a markup
tips.body: You carry the cost and the risk of scrap, rejected plating, and price swings in aluminum or titanium. A 10-25 percent handling markup is standard and should be shown on your quote.

tips.title: Get the PO before you cut
tips.body: A PO number and drawing revision in writing prevent disputes when a customer later says the part was wrong. Do not start without them on production work.

tips.title: Invoice on shipment, not completion
tips.body: Parts sitting on your shelf are not billable on most terms. Invoice the day they ship, and attach certs so the invoice is not held up in receiving.

tips.title: Charge for engineering changes
tips.body: Revisions to the drawing, new fixtures, or reprogramming after approval should be billed as separate lines at your programming rate.

faqs.question: Should I invoice for setup on every reorder?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, unless you kept the fixtures and programs and the setup is truly shorter. Many shops charge a reduced repeat setup fee. State the policy on your quote so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Can I bill for scrap or parts that fail inspection?
faqs.answer: Generally not when the fault is yours. If scrap comes from bad material supplied by the customer or a drawing error, you can bill for the lost machine time and material, ideally with a written note on the quote that covers this.

faqs.question: How do I handle over- and under-shipments?
faqs.answer: Many shops state a tolerance, such as plus or minus 10 percent on production runs, and bill for the quantity actually shipped. Put the tolerance on the quote and the PO acknowledgment.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on machined parts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the customer. Parts sold for resale or for use in manufacturing are often exempt with a valid certificate, but rules differ. Keep certificates on file and check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for a blanket PO?
faqs.answer: Invoice each release when it ships, referencing the blanket PO number and release number. This keeps cash flowing instead of waiting until the whole order is complete.

estimate.intro: CNC shops quote before any chips are made, usually in response to a drawing or a 3D model sent by email. Customers often send the same print to several shops and compare unit price at different quantities, lead time, and whether material and finishing are included. A clear quote with price breaks wins more work than a single number.

scopeChecklist.item: Part number, drawing revision, and file format quoted
scopeChecklist.why: A quote tied to a specific revision protects you if the customer later changes tolerances or features.

scopeChecklist.item: Material specification and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: Grade, temper, and stock form drive cost. State whether you buy it or the customer supplies it, and what happens if supplied material is out of spec.
Quoting 1, 10, 50, and 250 pieces shows how setup spreads out and helps the customer choose the right order size.
Tight tolerances or fine finishes add machining and inspection time. List the tolerance you priced to, such as plus or minus 0.005 in unless noted.
Anodize, plating, heat treat, deburring, and laser marking add cost and lead time. Say whether each is included.
First article reports, material certs, and certificates of conformance take time and should be priced up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Lead time, quote validity, and shipping terms
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change. A 30-day validity period, a stated lead time from PO, and the shipping terms such as FOB your shop prevent disputes.

pricingTips.title: Price from time, not from a feel for the part
pricingTips.body: Estimate setup, programming, and cycle time separately, then apply your machine rate. Check the result against material and outside costs so small parts with expensive finishing are not underpriced.

pricingTips.title: Show price breaks and a setup line
pricingTips.body: Listing setup apart from the per-piece price makes quantity discounts clear and supports a higher price on one-off prototypes.

pricingTips.title: Add risk for unclear prints
pricingTips.body: Missing tolerances, deep pockets in hard alloys, or thin walls raise scrap risk. Build in a margin or note assumptions rather than guess low to win the job.

pricingTips.title: Charge for quoting complex work
pricingTips.body: For large assemblies or reverse engineering, consider a quoting or engineering fee that is credited back if the customer places the order.

faqs.question: How long should a CNC quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. For metals with volatile prices, such as titanium or copper alloys, 14 days is reasonable. Always put the expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I ask for a deposit on a quote?
faqs.answer: For new customers, large material buys, or custom tooling, yes. A deposit of 30 to 50 percent due on PO is common and covers raw stock and outside processing.

faqs.question: What if the customer changes the drawing after I quote?
faqs.answer: Requote against the new revision. State on the quote that pricing applies only to the listed revision and that changes may affect price and lead time.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a quote I send?
faqs.answer: Most simple quotes are free. For work that needs significant engineering, DFM review, or fixture design before pricing, a quoting fee is reasonable if you tell the customer in advance.

coffee-cart.intro: Coffee cart operators run mobile espresso and drip coffee service at weddings, corporate events, office mornings, farmers markets, film sets, and private parties. Most invoices go to event planners, businesses, and hosts who book a set service window and pay for the cart, the staff, and the drinks served.
coffee-cart.pricingModel: Most coffee cart work is priced as a package: a flat fee or hourly rate for a set service window (usually 2 to 4 hours) that includes the cart, a barista, setup, and breakdown. Many operators add a per-guest or per-drink rate when the host wants a guaranteed number of drinks, or a minimum spend that covers the booking if attendance is low. Hosted events are typically billed in advance by guest count or time. Pay-as-you-go events, where guests buy their own drinks, usually have a guaranteed minimum or booking fee that you collect from the host. Extras such as travel, additional baristas, specialty syrups, oat or almond milk, custom cups or sleeves, and late-night or holiday service are billed as separate line items. Recurring office or weekly accounts are often billed monthly with a set per-visit price.

rates.service: Alternative milk or specialty syrup upgrade

items.description: Coffee cart service, corporate team breakfast (1 barista, setup and breakdown included)
Hosted drinks, lattes, cappuccinos, drip, and tea (60 guests)
Additional barista
Oat milk and vanilla/caramel syrup upgrade
Travel (28 miles each way, beyond 20-mile service area)

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: Thursday, May 15, 8:00-11:00 AM. 50% deposit of $474.00 was received on booking; balance due within 14 days of the event date. Guest count was billed at the final number confirmed 3 days before the event. Payment accepted by ACH, check, or card (3% fee on card payments).

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, location, and service window (start and end time)
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to a specific booking and settles disputes about how long you were serving versus setting up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guest count or drink count and how it was billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosted events are often billed per guest or per drink, so the client needs to see the number that drove the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the booking deposit was applied and prevents double payment or confusion over what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (extra barista, alt milks, syrups, custom cups, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: Add-ons are the most common source of pushback; listing them separately makes the total easy to defend.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime or extended service hours
invoiceChecklist.why: If the event ran past the booked window and the host asked you to stay, a clear line item documents it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepared drinks are taxable in many states, and rules differ for catering versus walk-up sales, so check your local rules and show tax on its own line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, health permit or license number if required locally
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate venues, event planners, and some venues ask for proof of permit and insurance details for their records.

coffee-cart.paymentTerms: Most coffee cart operators take a non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date, with the balance due on or shortly before the event for private parties, and net 14 to net 30 for corporate clients. Weddings and large events are often paid in full a week before. Recurring office accounts are usually invoiced monthly or at the start of each month. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Accept ACH, checks, and cards; if you pass on card processing fees, say so in your booking terms.

tips.title: Lock in a final guest count in writing
tips.body: Set a deadline, usually 3 to 7 days before the event, after which the guest count cannot go down. Bill on that number or the actual count, whichever is higher, and put it in your booking terms.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for pay-as-you-go events
tips.body: If guests buy their own drinks, a slow crowd can leave you with a lost day. A booking fee or guaranteed minimum sale, collected from the host, covers your labor and travel regardless of turnout.

tips.title: Price in setup and breakdown time
tips.body: A 2-hour service window usually means 3 to 4 hours of work with loading, drive time, and cleanup. Build that into the package or charge a separate setup fee so short events stay profitable.

tips.title: Bill milk, syrups, and cups as real costs
tips.body: Alternative milks, specialty syrups, and custom-printed sleeves cost more than standard supplies. Offer them as upgrades with a set price instead of absorbing them.

tips.title: Send the invoice the day of the event
tips.body: Send it while the host is still happy with the cart and the guest count is fresh. Include a payment link or clear payment instructions.

faqs.question: Should I charge per drink or per hour?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Hourly or package pricing is simpler and protects your time. Per-drink or per-guest pricing works when the host wants to cap spend or you cannot predict volume. Many operators charge a base package plus a per-guest rate above a certain count.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on coffee cart service?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and how the sale is structured. Prepared drinks are taxable in many states, and catering service fees may be taxable as well. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional, then show tax as its own line.

faqs.question: Can I keep the deposit if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: If your booking terms say the deposit is non-refundable and the client signed or accepted them, you can usually keep it, since you held the date. Terms that spell out cancellation windows and what is refundable avoid most disputes.

faqs.question: How do I bill for tips from a hosted event?
faqs.answer: Tips left directly by guests belong to you and your staff and are not part of the invoice. If the host adds a gratuity, list it as a separate line so it is clear it is not part of the service fee. Tip and payroll reporting rules vary, so check with your accountant.

faqs.question: What if the event runs longer than booked?
faqs.answer: Charge your additional hourly rate and note the actual end time on the invoice. It helps if the host agrees to the extension, even by text, before you keep serving.

estimate.intro: Coffee cart operators send a quote when someone inquires about an event, usually weeks or months ahead. Clients compare you against other carts, coffee caterers, and sometimes a barista-for-hire, so they look closely at what is included, the hours covered, and the drink menu.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, location, and service window
scopeChecklist.why: The price depends on the hours and the venue. Stating them keeps both sides clear on when serving starts and ends.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count or drink cap and what happens if it changes
scopeChecklist.why: Hosted quotes are built on headcount. Spell out the deadline for final numbers and how extra guests are billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Menu included (drinks, sizes, milk options, syrups)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients assume different things about what is on the menu. List what is included and what costs extra.
Number of baristas, cart or espresso machine type, and whether you bring tables, signage, or generators all affect price and expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Venue requirements: power, water, parking, permits
scopeChecklist.why: Some venues require a certificate of insurance or permit, and your cart may need electrical access or a water source. Say who is responsible for what.
These costs are easy to forget and are often the difference between a profitable event and a break-even one.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation terms, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: A quote that holds your date only until a certain day, with a stated deposit, reduces no-shows and last-minute cancellations.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A basic package, a standard package with more hours or drinks, and a premium package with extras like custom sleeves or an extra barista. Clients tend to pick the middle option and compare less on price alone.

pricingTips.title: Work backward from your cost per drink and hourly labor
pricingTips.body: Know your cost per drink (beans, milk, cups, syrups), staff pay, vehicle and fuel, and insurance. Add setup and breakdown time, then add margin. Quoting from gut feel usually underprices short events.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum booking
pricingTips.body: Many carts will not take events under a set number of hours or a minimum total, such as $400 or two hours. State it on your quote so small-ticket requests do not use up a prime weekend date.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for uncertain headcounts
pricingTips.body: If the host is not sure of the guest count, quote at two tiers, such as 50 to 75 guests and 76 to 100 guests, and set a date to lock the final number.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or tasting?
faqs.answer: Quotes are normally free. For larger events like weddings, some operators offer a paid tasting or credit the fee toward the booking. Either way, say so up front.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical for a specific date, since you are holding it for them. After that, availability and pricing can change, especially in busy wedding and holiday seasons.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement or is an emailed quote enough?
faqs.answer: A written quote the client accepts by email or signature can work as a basic agreement. For larger events, a short contract covering deposit, cancellation, and insurance is safer.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Change the scope instead of just cutting the price. Reduce service hours, limit the menu, cap drinks per guest, or remove add-ons so your margin holds.

college-counselor.intro: Independent college counselors help high school students and families choose schools, build a college list, manage deadlines, and complete applications. They bill for one-on-one advising sessions, application packages, essay coaching, and add-ons like interview prep or financial aid planning. Most work solo or in small practices and invoice parents, not students.
college-counselor.pricingModel: Independent college counselors use three main models. Hourly billing, often with a prepaid block of hours, is common for students who need limited help such as essay review or a list-building session. Flat-fee packages are the most common for full guidance and are usually tiered by grade level and scope, for example a junior-year package, a senior-year application package, or a multi-year program starting in 9th or 10th grade. Some counselors also offer per-school pricing for application support, or a monthly retainer during peak season from August to January. Add-ons such as essay editing, scholarship searches, interview practice, and athletic recruiting guidance are often priced separately. Many counselors also give sibling discounts. Fees vary widely by region and by the counselor's background, with former admissions officers often charging at the high end.

items.description: Senior-year application package: college list, application strategy, deadline tracking, Common App review (up to 8 schools)
Personal statement coaching: brainstorming and 3 rounds of feedback
Supplemental essay coaching (school-specific)
Additional school application support (schools 9 and 10)
Mock interview and written feedback

sampleInvoice.notes: Package covers the 2025-26 application cycle. A 50% deposit of $2,800 was received on August 5; the remaining balance is due by October 15. Additional services are billed as used. I do not guarantee admission to any school. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or card; a 3% fee applies to card payments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or guardian billed
invoiceChecklist.why: The parent usually pays, and the invoice should name who is responsible for payment while identifying the student the services are for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and scope of what is included
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists like 'up to 8 schools' or 'three essay drafts' prevent disputes when a family later asks for more work under the same fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Application cycle or graduation year
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which admissions season the fee covers, which matters if a student defers, reapplies, or moves to a transfer plan.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates or number of sessions delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: For hourly work, dated sessions with durations let parents match the invoice to their calendar and support the amount billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons billed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra essays, extra schools, interviews, and financial aid help should appear as their own lines so they are not mistaken for package overages.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most packages are paid in installments, so each invoice should show what has been paid, what remains, and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Outcome disclaimer and refund or cancellation terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Families sometimes assume results are guaranteed. A short reference to your agreement helps if a refund or pause is requested.

college-counselor.paymentTerms: Most counselors collect a deposit of 25% to 50% when the family signs the agreement, with the balance due at a set milestone such as the start of senior year or before the first applications are submitted. Hourly clients often prepay a block of hours or pay after each session, with invoices due in 7 to 14 days. Multi-year programs are sometimes split into annual or monthly installments. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are used by some counselors, though a firm pause on services until payment is received is more common. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or card, and some counselors add a small surcharge for cards where allowed. State your refund policy in writing, since families may leave a program early or change plans after early decision results.

tips.title: Bill ahead of the deadline crunch
tips.body: Schedule balance payments before October and November, when the workload is highest. Collecting after early deadlines have passed gives you less leverage and creates awkward conversations.

tips.title: Define revision limits
tips.body: Essay coaching can expand without limit. Set a number of drafts or review rounds in the package and bill extra rounds at an hourly rate or a flat per-essay rate.

tips.title: Separate package fees from per-school fees
tips.body: Families often add schools late in the process. A clear per-school rate for schools beyond the package limit keeps scope changes from being absorbed at no charge.

tips.title: Bill the paying parent, track the student
tips.body: When parents are divorced or split costs, ask who receives invoices and whether payments are shared. Put it in the agreement so you are not caught in the middle.

tips.title: Keep session notes
tips.body: Short notes on each meeting with date, length, and topics make hourly invoices easy to defend and help if a parent questions the time billed.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat package fee?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Hourly works for limited help like essay review or a single planning session. Flat packages suit full application support because the workload is predictable and families prefer knowing the total cost. Many counselors offer both.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit that is non-refundable?
faqs.answer: Many counselors do, particularly for packages where they reserve limited seats for the season. Refund rules vary by state and by how you word the agreement, so state the terms clearly in your contract and check your local rules.

faqs.question: How do I handle a student who stops responding?
faqs.answer: Include a clause in your agreement stating that the fee covers availability and prepared work, not only completed deliverables. Send a written reminder of what is outstanding and what is due, and bill any remaining installments according to the schedule.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on counseling services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax educational advising services, but some tax certain services or digital products. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Should I bill the family for application fees or test fees?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Families should pay application, testing, and score-report fees directly to the colleges and testing agencies. If you ever pay a fee on their behalf, list it as a separate reimbursement line with a receipt.

estimate.intro: Counselors usually send a quote after an initial consultation, once they know the student's grade, list size, and needs. Families often compare several counselors and look at package scope, the counselor's background, and total cost rather than the hourly rate alone.

scopeChecklist.why: A junior starting early needs different work from a senior with deadlines in eight weeks, and the price should match the timeline.
Stating the cap, such as 8 or 10 schools, sets a clear boundary for extra work and extra fees.
Say whether the personal statement, supplements, and activity descriptions are covered, and how many rounds of feedback are included.
Specify how many sessions, how long they are, and whether they happen in person or by video, so families know what to expect.
List interviews, financial aid planning, scholarship searches, and recruiting guidance as optional so they are not assumed to be part of the base fee.
Families often expect fast responses during deadline season. A stated turnaround time, such as 2 business days for essay drafts, reduces friction.
A plain statement that you do not guarantee admission or scholarships protects both sides and sets honest expectations.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as essentials, full application support, and multi-year planning. Families often choose the middle tier, and the options show what each level covers.

pricingTips.title: Price based on workload, not student prestige
pricingTips.body: A student applying to 12 selective schools with many supplements requires more time than one applying to 5 schools. Set school limits and price extra schools separately.

pricingTips.title: Show a payment schedule with the quote
pricingTips.body: Listing the deposit and installments in the quote makes the total easier to accept and sets the expectation before the agreement is signed.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Limited capacity during application season is real. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days encourages a decision and protects your calendar.

faqs.question: Should I give a free initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many counselors offer a free 20 to 30 minute call to assess fit, then charge for longer strategy sessions. Whether to do so depends on how many inquiries you get and how much time you can spend on unpaid calls.
