faqs.question: How do I quote for a student who is undecided about how many schools to apply to?
faqs.answer: Quote a base package with a set number of schools, then list the per-school rate for additional applications. That way the family can see how the total changes as the list grows.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes and you have said so in the quote. Put the included work in writing, and send a short written change request with the added cost before doing extra work.

faqs.question: Should I include the cost of outside testing or application fees in my quote?
faqs.answer: No. Those are paid by the family to the colleges and testing agencies. Mention in the quote that they are not included so the family budgets for them separately.

colorist.intro: Hair colorists work in salons, rent a booth or suite, or run a private studio, and they bill for chemical color services such as root touch-ups, highlights, balayage, vivid colors, and color corrections. Most clients pay at checkout, but invoices are common for deposits, bridal and event parties, photo shoots, and multi-session corrections. A clear invoice records what was done, how much product was used, and what was agreed beforehand.
colorist.pricingModel: Most colorists price by service with a flat fee, then adjust for hair length, thickness, and the amount of product used. Many menus list a starting price (for example, 'balayage from $200') and add charges for extra length or density. Complex work such as color corrections, going from dark to platinum, or vivid fashion colors is often billed hourly or quoted as a range across several sessions. Add-ons like glosses, toners, and bond-building treatments are separate line items. Some colorists bill extra bowls of color or lightener once a set amount is exceeded. Cuts, blowouts, and retail products are billed separately. Rates depend heavily on the colorist's experience level, the local market, and whether they work in a salon or a private suite.

items.description: Balayage, shoulder to mid-back length
Gloss and toner
Bond-building treatment
Additional lightener and color (thick hair)
Blowout and style

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service. Deposit of $50 paid at booking has been applied to the balance. Gratuity is not included. Please book a toning refresh within 6-8 weeks. Changes to color within 7 days of service may be arranged by appointment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and appointment length
invoiceChecklist.why: Color services can run 3 to 6 hours, and the date and duration support hourly billing and help settle questions about what was done in a given visit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each service listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing color, toner, treatments, and styling as separate lines shows what the client paid for and makes it easy to adjust one item without redoing the whole bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extra product or additional bowls charged
invoiceChecklist.why: If hair length or density needed more color or lightener than planned, naming it as a line item shows why the total differs from the starting price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Deposits for long appointments should be shown as a credit so the client sees how the final amount was reached.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retail products sold
invoiceChecklist.why: Shampoo, purple conditioner, and other retail items are often taxed differently from services in many states, so they should be on their own lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax where it applies
invoiceChecklist.why: Product sales are taxable in most states and some states tax certain services, so check your local rules and show tax as a separate amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session number for multi-visit corrections
invoiceChecklist.why: Labeling a visit as session 2 of 3, for example, ties it to the agreed plan and keeps the client from expecting one price for all of it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license number and business name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a cosmetology license, and some require it to be displayed. Including it on invoices for events or business clients helps with their records.

colorist.paymentTerms: Most colorists collect payment in full at the end of the appointment by card, cash, or a payment app. For long services, such as balayage or corrections, a deposit of $50-100 or 25-50% of the estimated price is common, and it is usually applied to the final bill. Cancellation policies typically require 24 to 48 hours notice, with a late cancellation or no-show fee of 25-50% of the booked service. For bridal parties, photo shoots, or other group bookings, invoices usually go out with a deposit due to hold the date and the balance due on or before the event day. Late fees are rare for individual clients but are more common on commercial invoices with net 15 or net 30 terms.

tips.title: Quote a range, then confirm before you mix
tips.body: Give a price range at the consultation and confirm the final number once you see the hair in person. Changes made after the color is applied cause the most disputes.

tips.title: Charge for time on corrections
tips.body: A correction can take twice as long as a standard service, with extra product and multiple rounds of lightener. Bill hourly or in sessions, and say so before you begin.

tips.title: Track product use
tips.body: If you weigh color and lightener, you can see how much each service really costs you. Use that to set add-on fees for extra length and thick hair, and to catch services that are underpriced.

tips.title: Keep tips separate
tips.body: Record gratuities apart from the service total. Tips are taxable income for you, and listing them separately keeps your books clean at tax time.

tips.title: Collect deposits for anything over three hours
tips.body: Long color appointments block out a large part of your day. A deposit protects that time and cuts down on no-shows.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation?
faqs.answer: Many colorists offer a free 15-minute consultation for standard services and charge $25-50 for correction consultations, applying it to the service if the client books. Whatever you choose, say so when the client books.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra if the client's hair is longer or thicker than expected?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you disclose it. State on your menu or booking page that prices start at a base and increase with length, density, or extra product. Then list the extra charge on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a color correction that takes several appointments?
faqs.answer: Agree on a plan and an estimated range at the start, then bill each session when it happens. Label each invoice with its session number and keep any deposit as a credit toward the first visit or the total.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on hair color services?
faqs.answer: It varies. In many states, services such as hair color are not taxed but retail products are, while some states and localities tax certain services. Check your state revenue department's rules.

faqs.question: What if a client is unhappy with their color?
faqs.answer: Set a clear policy in writing, such as a free adjustment within 7 to 14 days. If you do an adjustment, invoice it at $0 and note it so you have a record of it.

estimate.intro: Colorists give estimates before big or uncertain jobs, such as a first-time balayage, a dramatic lightening, a vivid color, or a correction of someone else's work. Clients often compare starting prices between stylists, so a written range with what is included makes your quote easier to judge. For weddings and group bookings, a quote is usually needed before a date is held.

scopeChecklist.item: Starting price and what changes it
scopeChecklist.why: Naming hair length, density, and previous color as price factors shows clients why their final price may differ from the menu price.
Going from dark to light often takes more than one visit, and clients should know that before they book.
Clients need to plan around a 4-hour appointment, and the time estimate backs up an hourly charge if the work runs longer.
State whether toner, treatment, cut, and styling are included so these are not assumed to be free.

scopeChecklist.item: Realistic result and hair health limits
scopeChecklist.why: If the hair is damaged or has box dye buildup, the final shade may be different from the photo, and it should be written down that you may stop if the hair is at risk.
Deposits and no-show fees are easier to enforce when the client accepted them in the quote.
Toner refreshes, root touch-ups, and home-care products add to the real cost of the color, and clients should know about them up front.

pricingTips.title: Ask for photos and history first
pricingTips.body: Have clients send current photos, inspiration images, and a list of past color, including box dye and henna. This lets you give a more accurate range before they come in.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range with a cap
pricingTips.body: A range such as $250-350, with a note that you will confirm before going over, keeps clients comfortable and protects your time on unpredictable hair.

pricingTips.title: Price in hours for unknowns
pricingTips.body: When you cannot say how many rounds a correction will take, quote an hourly rate and an estimated number of hours, and tell the client you will check in after each hour or each round.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for events
pricingTips.body: For bridal parties and shoots, give a per-person price and a day rate, plus a charge for travel and early start times. Clients can compare options without asking for a custom quote each time.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote without seeing the client's hair?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range from photos and a history of past color. State clearly that it is an estimate and that the final price is confirmed in person before color is mixed.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: For regular clients, 30 days is common. For event bookings, many colorists hold the date only once the deposit is paid and note when the quote expires.

faqs.question: What if the job takes longer than I quoted?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the estimate saying that hourly billing applies past the estimated time or that you will check in before going over. Tell the client mid-appointment, not after, so there are no surprises on the bill.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate on a color correction?
faqs.answer: Many colorists charge a consultation fee of $25-75 for corrections, since it takes time to assess damage and plan. It is often credited toward the first session if the client books.

commercial-cleaning.intro: Commercial cleaning businesses clean offices, medical suites, retail stores, schools, gyms, and other non-residential buildings, usually on a recurring schedule. Most invoices go to property managers, office managers, or business owners who expect a consistent monthly bill that matches the contract. Solo operators and small crews also bill for one-time work such as post-construction cleanup, floor stripping and waxing, and carpet extraction.
commercial-cleaning.pricingModel: Recurring janitorial work is usually priced as a flat monthly fee based on square footage, cleaning frequency, and the scope in the contract, then billed on the same day each month. Under the hood, most owners work backward from an hourly figure: labor hours per visit times a loaded labor cost, plus supplies, equipment, insurance, and a profit margin. Many also quote a per-square-foot rate for comparison, often $0.05-0.15 per sq ft per visit for general office cleaning. Specialty and one-time jobs (strip and wax, carpet extraction, window cleaning, post-construction cleanup) are billed per sq ft, per hour, or as a flat project fee. Extras outside the contract, such as emergency call-outs, event cleanup, or restocking consumables, are billed as separate line items. Medical and other regulated spaces carry higher rates because of disinfection protocols and training requirements.

rates.service: Recurring office janitorial (general cleaning, trash, restrooms, vacuuming)
Hourly cleaning labor (crew member, one-time or extra work)

items.description: Monthly janitorial service, 6,000 sq ft office, 3 visits per week (Nov 1-30)
Carpet hot water extraction, main open office area
Strip and wax, breakroom and reception VCT
Additional labor, post-holiday party cleanup (Nov 22)
Restroom paper and soap supplies, restocked per contract

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Please reference PO #4471 on remittance. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Next scheduled carpet extraction is in May.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location and service period
invoiceChecklist.why: Multi-site clients and property managers need to match each invoice to a building and a billing month for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or contract number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial accounts will not process payment through accounts payable without a PO number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Visit frequency and scope reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing that the monthly fee covers, for example, 3 visits per week under the signed agreement prevents questions about what is included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line items for extras and specialty work
invoiceChecklist.why: Floor care, carpet extraction, and event cleanups fall outside the base contract and should be itemized so they are not disputed as part of the monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies and consumables
invoiceChecklist.why: If you supply paper products, soap, and liners at cost plus markup, listing them separately shows what the client is paying for and supports changes in pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, insurance, and tax ID details
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often require proof of insurance and a W-9 on file, and including your business name and EIN or license number speeds up vendor setup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Whether janitorial services are taxable varies by state, so check your local rules and show any tax as its own line.

commercial-cleaning.paymentTerms: Commercial clients usually pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, and larger property management companies may push for net 45 or net 60. Recurring contracts are best invoiced at the start of the service month, or on the first of the month for the current month, rather than after the fact. Deposits are uncommon for recurring work but common for large one-time jobs such as post-construction cleanup, where 25-50% upfront is typical. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Most accounts pay by ACH or check, and card payments are often accepted at a surcharge or with the fee built into the price.

tips.title: Invoice on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Send the monthly invoice on the same day every month, ideally before the service month begins. Clients with accounts payable departments pay on cycles, and a late invoice can push payment out another 30 days.

tips.title: Put extras in writing before you do them
tips.body: If the client asks for an extra deep clean, event setup cleanup, or a carpet spot treatment, get an email approval with the price. Then you can bill the line item with confidence.

tips.title: Track labor hours against each contract
tips.body: Compare actual crew hours to the hours you priced. If a site regularly takes 20% longer than quoted, raise the monthly fee at renewal or tighten the scope rather than absorbing it.

tips.title: Include a price adjustment clause
tips.body: Wages, supplies, and fuel rise during a contract term. A clause allowing an annual increase, or a rate change with 30 days notice, avoids renegotiating from scratch.

tips.title: Document missed visits and credits
tips.body: If you skip a visit because the building was closed, note the credit on the invoice. If the client cancels late, state your policy so billing stays consistent.

faqs.question: Should I bill commercial cleaning monthly or per visit?
faqs.answer: Monthly is the standard for recurring janitorial work. It gives the client one predictable bill and reduces your paperwork. Per-visit billing makes sense for irregular schedules, trial periods, or one-time jobs.

faqs.question: How do I bill for supplies like toilet paper and soap?
faqs.answer: Either include them in the monthly price and state that in the contract, or bill them as a separate line at cost plus 10-25%. Separate billing is better when usage varies a lot between months.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client pays late every month?
faqs.answer: Confirm your payment terms and late fee are in the signed agreement, send a reminder a few days before the due date, and follow up the day after. If it continues, shorten terms, ask for ACH autopay, or pause service according to the contract.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on cleaning services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax janitorial or building cleaning services and many do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show tax as a separate line if you collect it.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice if the contract already sets the price?
faqs.answer: Yes. A contract sets the terms, but clients still need a dated invoice with an invoice number to process payment and record the expense. It is also your proof of what was billed and when.

estimate.intro: Commercial cleaning estimates usually follow a walkthrough of the building, where you measure square footage, note floor types, count restrooms, and ask about frequency and hours. Clients, often a property manager or office manager, tend to collect two or three bids and compare the monthly price, the scope of work, and your insurance. A clear written quote that lists exactly what is included is often what separates you from a cheaper bid.

scopeChecklist.why: Carpet, VCT, tile, and hardwood each take different time and equipment, and the measured area drives your price.
Three nights per week costs very differently than five days, and after-hours access affects scheduling and staffing.

scopeChecklist.item: Detailed task list per visit and per period
scopeChecklist.why: Spell out daily tasks (trash, restrooms, vacuuming) and periodic ones (dusting high surfaces, floor care) so the client knows what is and is not covered.
Note things like interior windows, appliance cleaning, biohazard cleanup, or moving furniture so these do not become unpaid expectations.
Paper products, soap, and liners can add real cost, and the quote should say whether they are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract term, cancellation notice, and price adjustments
scopeChecklist.why: A 30- or 60-day cancellation clause and an annual increase clause protect you from low-margin sites.
Listing your general liability and workers comp coverage builds trust, and a validity window of 30 days protects you from labor cost changes.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from labor hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate the crew hours per visit from square footage and production rates, multiply by your loaded hourly cost, then add supplies, equipment wear, insurance, and margin. Per-square-foot rates are useful as a check but should not be the only basis.

pricingTips.title: Price for the walkthrough, not the listing
pricingTips.body: Square footage in a listing is often off, and a site with many private offices or heavy restrooms takes longer than an open floor plan. Measure and count fixtures yourself.

pricingTips.title: Quote specialty work separately
pricingTips.body: List strip and wax, carpet extraction, and window cleaning as optional line items with their own prices. It keeps the base monthly number competitive and lets clients add services later.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial period
pricingTips.body: A 30-day trial or a short initial term can win a client who is nervous about switching, while giving you time to see if your hours estimate was right.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a walkthrough and estimate?
faqs.answer: Most commercial cleaners do the walkthrough and quote for free for recurring contracts. For large or complex projects such as post-construction cleanup, some charge a fee that is credited if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a commercial cleaning quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Labor costs and supply prices change, so state an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is a per-square-foot quote enough?
faqs.answer: No. Include the frequency, task list, and exclusions alongside the price. Two buildings of the same size can need very different amounts of labor.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Only if the quote or contract allows it, or the scope changes. If the building turns out larger or the client adds tasks, document the change in writing and issue an updated quote or an amendment.

commercial-printer.intro: Commercial printers produce marketing materials, packaging, signage, forms, books, and other printed goods for businesses, nonprofits, schools, and agencies. Invoices usually cover a specific print job: a quantity of a defined product, plus prepress, finishing, and delivery. Most shops are small operations with a few presses and a bindery, or solo operators who broker work out to larger plants.
commercial-printer.pricingModel: Print jobs are priced per job, then expressed per piece or per thousand (per M) so clients can compare quantities. The price is built from paper cost, press time (setup plus run), ink coverage, prepress or file work, finishing such as cutting, folding, scoring, binding, laminating, and then shipping or delivery. Setup costs are spread over the run, so unit price drops sharply as quantity rises. Paper is usually marked up 15-40% over cost. Digital short runs are often priced per click or per sheet, while offset jobs are priced on a run basis with a make-ready charge. Large-format work is priced per square foot. Design, file correction, and rush work are billed hourly or as flat add-ons. Many shops also quote an overs/unders allowance, since the exact quantity delivered can vary on offset jobs.

rates.service: Finishing: folding, scoring, or die cutting setup

items.description: Trifold brochures, 8.5x11 flat, 100# gloss text, 4/4, scored and folded
Business cards, 3.5x2, 16pt with matte laminate, 4/4
Prepress: file correction, bleed fix, and proof
Die cut setup for custom folder pocket
Local delivery, 4 cartons

sampleInvoice.notes: Job #4821, PO #77310. Quantities delivered within 10% over or under the order are billed as delivered. Payment due within 30 days of delivery. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Reprints due to client file errors are billed at standard rates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job number and client PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable departments match invoices to purchase orders, and missing numbers delay payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Detailed product specs
invoiceChecklist.why: Size, paper stock and weight, ink colors, sides, coatings, and finishing show exactly what was produced, which settles disputes if a reprint is requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity ordered and quantity delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Offset jobs commonly run over or under, and the invoice should show what you billed against the agreed overs/unders policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Price per M or per piece alongside the extended total
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reuse these numbers to reorder and to compare future quotes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for prepress, proofs, and changes
invoiceChecklist.why: Author's alterations and file fixes are billed apart from production, and listing them shows the client what caused extra charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate details
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states printed materials are taxable unless the buyer has a resale or exemption certificate on file, so note the certificate number when applicable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping, freight, and delivery details
invoiceChecklist.why: Carton counts, carrier charges, and delivery dates document that the goods left your shop and when.

commercial-printer.paymentTerms: Many printers require a 50% deposit on new customers, large jobs, or custom-ordered paper, with the balance due on delivery or pickup. Established business accounts are often net 30, and some get net 15 for small jobs. Specialty jobs such as packaging or books can have milestone billing at approval, at press, and at delivery. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Accepted payments typically include checks, ACH, and cards, with some shops adding a card processing surcharge where local rules allow it. Many shops keep finished work until payment clears for first-time customers.

tips.title: Get written proof approval before you run
tips.body: Have the client sign off on the final proof with the date, and note that approved errors such as typos are not grounds for reprint at your cost. This protects you more than any other single step.

tips.title: State your overs/unders policy on every quote and invoice
tips.body: A common industry practice is a variance of up to 10% on offset runs, billed at the per-piece rate. Without it, clients may dispute a count that is slightly off.

tips.title: Charge for paper when prices move
tips.body: Paper costs change between quote and press. Put a validity period on quotes, such as 30 days, and note that paper price changes may adjust the final price on longer-lead jobs.

tips.title: Bill for changes after approval
tips.body: Log extra proof rounds, last-minute copy edits, and rush requests as separate line items at your hourly rate so they do not get absorbed into the job price.

tips.title: Deposit on custom materials
tips.body: Special-order stocks, custom die cuts, and spot-color inks cannot be reused, so collect a deposit that covers those costs before you order them.

faqs.question: Should I invoice at the quoted price or the delivered quantity?
faqs.answer: Invoice what you delivered, within the overs/unders terms in your quote. If you delivered 5% over on an offset job, you can bill the extra pieces at the per-piece rate. If you delivered under by more than the stated tolerance, adjust the bill or reprint.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on print jobs?
faqs.answer: In many states, printed materials are taxable when sold to the end user, while items bought for resale may be exempt with a valid certificate. Rules differ on shipping, design, and mailing services, so check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: When should I bill for a job: at approval, at press, or at delivery?
faqs.answer: Common practice is a deposit at approval and the balance at delivery. For long or expensive jobs, add a billing step when the job hits press or when materials are purchased.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a reprint caused by my error?
faqs.answer: Generally, you absorb the cost and either issue no invoice for the reprint or credit it. Make sure the original proof, specs, and any approval records are on file so you can tell whether the error was yours or the client's.

faqs.question: Can I charge for storing or holding printed work?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in advance. Many shops allow 30 days of free storage and then charge a monthly fee per pallet or carton, and a written note on the quote avoids arguments later.

estimate.intro: Print buyers usually ask for quotes before ordering and often get two or three to compare, sometimes at several quantities. A quote is typically tied to specs, quantity, and turnaround, so even small changes can shift the price. Clients tend to compare the per-unit price at each quantity, the stock, and the delivery date.

scopeChecklist.item: Finished size, flat size, and orientation
scopeChecklist.why: A change from 8.5x11 to 9x12 can alter the sheet layout and paper waste, which changes the price.
Naming stock such as 100# gloss text or 14pt C2S avoids substitutions that lead to disputes.
4/4, 4/1, and spot colors are priced differently, and PMS matching adds cost.
Pricing is tied to the run length, and a stated variance prevents arguments about count.
Folding, scoring, die cutting, coating, drilling, and binding each add setup and run charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Artwork requirements and who is responsible for file fixes
scopeChecklist.why: State file format, bleed, and resolution, and say that file correction or design is billed hourly if files arrive incorrect.
Digital versus hard-copy proofs, production days after approval, and shipping or pickup terms shape both cost and schedule.

pricingTips.title: Quote multiple quantities
pricingTips.body: Show 500, 1,000, and 2,500 on the same quote. Setup costs are fixed, so the higher quantity often costs little more per piece and can lift your average order size.

pricingTips.title: Break out setup from run cost internally
pricingTips.body: Know your make-ready, plate, and cleanup costs so you can price reruns and short quantities accurately, even if the client sees only a total.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Paper, freight, and ink prices change. A 30-day validity period protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer a rush option, not a rush default
pricingTips.body: Quote a standard turnaround and a priced rush option, typically 20-50% more, so the client decides what speed is worth.

faqs.question: How long should a print quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. For jobs that depend on volatile paper pricing or long lead times, 14 days may be safer.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes on complex jobs?
faqs.answer: Simple jobs are quoted free. For packaging, custom dies, or multi-piece projects that take hours of estimating or sample building, some printers charge a fee that is credited if the client orders.

faqs.question: What if the client changes specs after I quote?
faqs.answer: Issue a revised quote. State on the original that the price applies only to the listed specs, quantity, and artwork, and that changes will be re-priced.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before ordering special paper?
faqs.answer: It is a common and reasonable request. Special-order stock and custom tooling are hard to resell, so a deposit covering those costs is standard practice.

composer.intro: Composers write original music for film, TV, games, advertising, theater, podcasts, concert ensembles, and private commissions. They invoice production companies, game studios, agencies, schools, and individual clients, usually for a composition fee, plus separate charges for revisions, stems, mixing, live musicians, and licensing.
composer.pricingModel: Most composers price by project, not by the hour, because the value of the music and the amount of work are not tightly linked. Film, TV, and game scoring is often quoted as a package fee for the full score, or per finished minute of music, with a portion paid up front. Many deals separate the creative fee from a production budget that covers live players, studio time, mixing, and sample libraries; in a package deal, the composer pays those costs out of the fee. Advertising and short-form work is usually a flat fee per spot or per cue, with usage terms (media, territory, length of term) affecting the price. Concert and commission work is a flat commission fee based on ensemble size and length, with parts preparation often billed separately. Hourly rates show up for arranging, orchestration, transcription, music prep, and consulting. Licensing and ownership matter: a work-for-hire buyout costs more than a license where the composer keeps the copyright and publishing share. Rates vary widely with credits, genre, and the client's budget.

rates.service: Indie film or documentary score (original music)
Podcast or YouTube theme and stings

items.description: Original score for short documentary 'River Road' (final payment, 50% of $4,800 fee, 12 minutes of music)
Additional revision round beyond the two included in the agreement (cues 3 and 5)
Stem exports and alternate mixes (dialogue-friendly versions, 6 cues)
Live cello recording session, performer fee (passed through at cost)
Cue sheet preparation and PRO registration support

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 15. A 50% deposit of $2,400 was received on signing. Music is licensed per the signed agreement dated March 3; the composer retains the writer's share of performance royalties. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment by ACH, check, or wire.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project title and cue list or deliverable summary
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to specific music and helps the client's accounting match it to a production budget line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement and its date
invoiceChecklist.why: The agreement sets ownership, license terms, and revision limits, so the invoice should point back to it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and license terms (work-for-hire or license, media, territory, term)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies what the client is paying for and prevents later disputes over use outside the original scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or payment schedule status (deposit paid, balance due)
invoiceChecklist.why: Scoring fees are paid in stages, so the client needs to see what has been paid and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for revisions, extra cues, and out-of-scope work
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows that the extra charges came from changes beyond the agreed rounds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (live players, studio rental, sample libraries, mixing) listed at cost or with markup noted
invoiceChecklist.why: Musician fees and studio costs are often paid by the composer first and reimbursed, and clients want to see the receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Performing rights organization info and cue sheet note
invoiceChecklist.why: Registering the music and splitting royalties depends on correct writer and publisher details; a note keeps both parties aligned.

composer.paymentTerms: Composers typically ask for 25-50% up front on signing, with the rest due at milestones such as delivery of demos, approval of the final cues, or delivery of final stems. Due dates of net 15 to net 30 are common, though production companies and agencies may require net 30 to 60 and a W-9 before payment. Many composers state that rights transfer or the license takes effect only after full payment. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if written into the agreement. Payment is usually by ACH, wire, or check; PayPal and similar methods appear with smaller clients. Clients should receive a W-9, and in the US, composers who are paid $600 or more by a business may receive a 1099 form, so keep records matching what you invoiced.

tips.title: Put the revision limit in the agreement and on the invoice
tips.body: Music revisions can go on indefinitely. State how many rounds are included (two or three is common) and a rate for additional rounds, then bill extras as separate lines.

tips.title: Separate the creative fee from the production budget
tips.body: If live musicians, a studio, or a mixing engineer are needed, list them separately or state clearly that they come out of a package fee. This avoids the client assuming a low price covers a full orchestra.

tips.title: Tie rights transfer to payment
tips.body: Write that the license or copyright assignment becomes effective on receipt of the final payment. Do not deliver final masters and stems until the balance is paid, if the client relationship allows.

tips.title: Bill at milestones, not just at the end
tips.body: Film schedules slip and final picture changes. Link payments to delivery of demos, approved cues, and final mixes so a delay in the production does not delay your income.

tips.title: Keep records of every cue and delivery date
tips.body: A simple log of cue names, versions sent, and approval dates helps resolve disputes about whether work was delivered or revised.

faqs.question: Should I charge per minute or a flat fee for a score?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-minute pricing is easy to explain and scales if the film gets more music, but a flat package fee is more common on indie projects. If you quote a flat fee, state the approximate minutes of music and charge extra if the amount grows significantly.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: 25-50% on signing is typical. For smaller jobs like a podcast theme, 50% or even full payment up front is reasonable. For large scores, a deposit plus milestone payments is more common.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on music?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on what you deliver. Some states tax digital goods or certain creative services, and others do not tax services at all. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant, and invoice tax only if it applies to you.

faqs.question: How do I bill for musicians I hire?
faqs.answer: List performer fees as pass-through costs at actual cost, with receipts available if requested, or include them in a package fee. If you are paying individual musicians $600 or more in a year, you may need to issue them a 1099 form, so collect W-9s from them.

faqs.question: Can I keep my publishing and royalties on a work-for-hire job?
faqs.answer: Often yes for the writer's share of performance royalties through your PRO, while the client owns the copyright and the publisher's share. This is negotiated in the contract, so check the terms and note them on your invoice or agreement.

estimate.intro: Composers send a quote when a producer, game studio, agency, or commissioning group asks what a project will cost, often before the music is written or the picture is locked. Clients compare composers by price, credits, turnaround, and what is included, such as live players, revisions, and stems.

scopeChecklist.item: Total minutes of music, number of cues, or length of the piece
scopeChecklist.why: The amount of music is the biggest cost driver, and a vague count leads to arguments when the project grows.

scopeChecklist.item: Instrumentation and production style (sample-based, hybrid, live ensemble)
scopeChecklist.why: A synthesized score and a recorded string quartet have very different costs and timelines.

scopeChecklist.item: What the fee includes: demos, revisions, stems, mixes, alternate versions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume stems, cutdowns, and edits are free unless the quote says otherwise.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and the rate for extra rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Sets a clear boundary on the most common cause of unpaid time.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery schedule and dependencies (picture lock, feedback turnaround)
scopeChecklist.why: Protects you if the client delays feedback or changes the cut after you've started.

scopeChecklist.item: Rights and license terms (work-for-hire vs. license, media, territory, term, credit)
scopeChecklist.why: Ownership affects price and future earnings, so it needs to be settled before work begins.

scopeChecklist.item: Who pays for musicians, studio, and mixing, and what the budget is
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents a conflict over whether the fee covers production costs or they are billed on top.

pricingTips.title: Ask for the budget range first
pricingTips.body: Many productions have a music budget already. Asking for it lets you propose a scope that fits instead of guessing and underpricing or losing the job.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: For example, a sample-based score, a hybrid score with a few live players, or a full live recording. Clients can see what each level costs and choose, which helps avoid a straight price comparison.

pricingTips.title: Price in the usage
pricingTips.body: For ads, quote different fees for web-only, broadcast, or national use, and for a limited term versus perpetual. The same music is worth more with wider use.

pricingTips.title: Account for revisions and picture changes
pricingTips.body: Build in time for re-cutting music after picture edits. If you quote a flat fee, state that significant changes to the cut may be billed as additional work.

faqs.question: Should I write a demo before I send a quote?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Share your portfolio and, if needed, a short sketch or mockup against a scene, but be careful about unpaid spec work. Some composers charge a small fee for a custom demo that is credited toward the final fee if hired.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is common. Production schedules and budgets change, so a stated expiration date lets you reprice if the project is delayed or the scope shifts.

faqs.question: What if the client's budget is lower than my quote?
faqs.answer: Offer a reduced scope instead of simply cutting your rate: less music, a smaller ensemble, fewer revisions, or a license instead of a full buyout. This keeps your rate steady while giving the client options.

concrete.intro: Concrete contractors pour and finish slabs, driveways, patios, sidewalks, footings, foundations, and retaining walls. Many also do stamped or decorative finishes, demolition and removal of old concrete, and repairs. Invoices usually cover labor, concrete and material costs, equipment, and any extras found once the old surface comes up.
concrete.pricingModel: Most flatwork is priced per square foot, with the price depending on thickness, finish, site access, and prep work. Plain broom-finish slabs sit at the low end, while stamped, stained, or exposed aggregate work costs more. Footings and walls are often priced per linear foot or per cubic yard poured. Demolition and haul-off are usually a separate line, either per square foot or flat. Pump trucks, short-load fees, and extra rebar or wire mesh are commonly itemized or passed through at cost with a markup. Larger jobs are billed in stages, such as a deposit, a draw after forming and prep, and a final payment after finishing. Small repairs and odd jobs may be billed hourly with a minimum charge.

rates.service: Standard broom-finish slab (4 in, driveway or patio)
Demolition and removal of old concrete
Ready-mix concrete (material only, when billed separately)

items.description: Demolish and haul off existing cracked driveway slab
Grade, compact 4 in gravel base, and set forms
Pour 4 in slab, 4000 psi mix, #3 rebar at 18 in grid, broom finish
Control joints saw cut and edging
Concrete sealer, two coats
Additional rebar and chairs for soft spot repair found during excavation (approved change order #1)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $3,000 received at contract signing and applied to this invoice. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Keep vehicles off the slab for 7 days and heavy loads off for 28 days. Cracks from settlement or ground conditions outside our control are not covered by the workmanship warranty.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and business info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a contractor license number on contracts and invoices, and clients need it for permits, insurance claims, and records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and permit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Driveways, foundations, and walls often need permits. Listing the address and permit ties the invoice to the right job and inspection.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage, thickness, and concrete specs
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing slab size, depth, psi strength, and reinforcement proves what was installed and reduces disputes over thin or cheap pours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finish and color details
invoiceChecklist.why: Stamp pattern, color, release agent, and sealer choices are easy to argue about later. Naming them avoids rework claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders with dates and approvals
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra excavation, added rebar, drainage, or a larger pour area should be listed as approved changes so the final total matches what the client agreed to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear running balance prevents confusion on multi-stage jobs where payments were made at forming and at pour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, pump, and short-load charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Ready-mix suppliers charge these separately and they can add up. Itemizing them shows they are real costs, not padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cure time and care instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Putting curing and sealing instructions on the invoice protects you if the client drives on the slab early and it cracks or scales.

concrete.paymentTerms: Most concrete contractors take a deposit of 10 to 50 percent at signing, since materials and crew scheduling are committed upfront. Some states cap deposits on home improvement work, so check local rules. Larger jobs often use a draw schedule tied to milestones such as forming complete, pour day, and final finishing. The final balance is commonly due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Commercial and general contractor work is often net 30 and may involve retainage of 5 to 10 percent held until final inspection. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or card, and some contractors add a card processing fee on large balances. Check your state's mechanic's lien rules, since lien deadlines can be short and often require preliminary notices.

tips.title: Collect before the truck arrives
tips.body: Concrete is perishable and ordered for a specific time. Require the deposit before you schedule the pour, and make sure the next payment is due on pour day or at completion rather than weeks later.

tips.title: Pass supplier costs through clearly
tips.body: Fuel surcharges, short-load fees, and pump rentals can change between the quote and the pour. Include a clause allowing adjustment, and list actual charges on the invoice.

tips.title: Document weather and site delays
tips.body: Rain, frozen ground, or blocked access can cause extra trips or standby time. Note the dates and reasons on the invoice if you bill for them, and back them up with photos.

tips.title: Take photos before and after each stage
tips.body: Photos of the base, rebar, forms, and finished slab show the work done below the surface that the client cannot see later. They resolve most payment disputes fast.

tips.title: Know your lien rights
tips.body: If a client stops paying, a mechanic's lien may be your strongest tool, but deadlines and notice requirements vary by state. Learn them before you start, and keep dated copies of contracts and invoices.

faqs.question: Should I bill concrete work per square foot or itemize everything?
faqs.answer: For standard flatwork, a per-square-foot price on the quote is normal, but the invoice should still show the main components such as demolition, base prep, pour, finish, and sealer. Itemizing helps the client understand the total and makes change orders easier to add.

faqs.question: How do I bill for extra work found after demolition?
faqs.answer: Stop and get written approval before doing it. Document the issue with photos, add it as a change order with its own price, and list it as a separate line on the final invoice with the approval date.

faqs.question: Can I charge for concrete that was ordered but not used?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says the client pays for materials ordered to the agreed plan. Overage is common because suppliers deliver in whole or half yards. Many contractors build a small overage allowance into the price, and charge extra only if the client changes the plan.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to hold payment because of cracks?
faqs.answer: Small hairline cracks are common in concrete and are often outside the warranty. Your contract should say what is and is not covered, such as cracks wider than a stated size or surface scaling from poor workmanship. Point to the control joints and written cure instructions when discussing it.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on concrete work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether the job counts as new construction, a repair, or a capital improvement. Some states tax materials, some tax labor, and some tax neither on improvements. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

estimate.intro: Concrete contractors usually quote after a site visit, since access, grade, drainage, and existing slab condition change the price. Clients often get two or three bids and compare the price per square foot, thickness, reinforcement, and finish. A clear written quote helps you win on detail rather than on the lowest number.

scopeChecklist.item: Dimensions, thickness, and total square footage
scopeChecklist.why: Slab size and depth drive material cost. Written dimensions stop disputes over whether the area or thickness was what the client expected.
Stating psi, fiber or rebar type, and spacing makes bids comparable and shows you are not cutting corners.
Removing old concrete, hauling away debris, and compacting gravel are major costs. State what is included and the base depth.
Broom, stamped, stained, or exposed aggregate finishes differ widely in cost and appearance. Specify control joint layout and sealing.
Clarify who pulls permits and pays fees, and whether inspections can delay the pour.
List what is not covered, such as soft soil, buried tanks, drainage correction, tree roots, or repairs to irrigation lines and landscaping.
Tell the client about cure time, when they can use the surface, weather delays, and that equipment needs clear access to the pour area.

pricingTips.title: Price from the full job, not just the pour
pricingTips.body: Add demolition, haul-off, grading, forms, rebar, pump or wheelbarrow labor, finishing, saw cutting, and cleanup. Many underbids come from pricing only the concrete and forgetting the prep hours.

pricingTips.title: Lock in material prices with an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Ready-mix and fuel costs change. Make the quote valid for 14 to 30 days and add a clause allowing adjustment if supplier prices shift before the job starts.

pricingTips.title: Offer options for finish and thickness
pricingTips.body: Presenting a standard broom finish alongside a stamped or exposed aggregate option, or 4 in versus 5 in for heavy vehicles, lets clients choose and often raises the average job size.

pricingTips.title: Include a contingency or unit price for bad soil
pricingTips.body: If the base may need extra excavation or fill, quote a per-cubic-yard or per-square-foot price for it so extra work has an agreed rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential concrete contractors quote for free, but some charge for complex jobs or credit the fee toward the contract if the client signs. Charging is more common for detailed plans, engineering coordination, or sites far from your normal area.

faqs.question: How long should a concrete quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Material prices and your schedule change, so put an expiration date on the quote and state that pricing after that date may be revised.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only for changes the contract allows, such as unforeseen site conditions or client-requested changes. Get the change in writing with a price before doing the work. Raising the price without that agreement often leads to disputes.

faqs.question: What should I do if my quote is much higher than a competitor's?
faqs.answer: Compare the scope line by line. Differences are often in thickness, base depth, reinforcement, mix strength, or whether demolition and permits are included. Walking the client through those details can justify your price without discounting.

construction.intro: General contractors, remodelers, and small construction companies send invoices for residential and light commercial work such as remodels, additions, decks, framing, concrete, and repairs. Bills usually cover labor, materials, subcontractor work, equipment rental, permits, and change orders, often in stages tied to project progress.
construction.pricingModel: Construction work is priced several ways. Fixed-price (lump sum) contracts are common for defined residential jobs, with payment split into a deposit and progress draws tied to milestones such as foundation complete, rough-in passed, or drywall hung. Cost-plus contracts bill actual labor and materials plus a markup, often 10-20% for overhead and profit, and suit jobs with unclear scope. Time-and-materials billing charges an hourly labor rate plus materials, and is common for repairs and small jobs. Some trades and tasks are quoted per square foot, such as framing, flooring, or concrete flatwork. Subcontractor costs are usually marked up 10-20%. Change orders should be priced and approved in writing before the extra work is done, then added to the next invoice as separate line items.

rates.service: Equipment rental billed to client (mini excavator, lift)

items.description: Progress draw 2 of 3: Framing complete and rough-in inspection passed (Kitchen and mudroom addition, 280 sq ft)
Lumber and sheathing materials (per attached receipts)
Carpentry labor, additional blocking and headers at owner request (Change Order #1)
Mini excavator rental for footing trench repair
Building permit fee reimbursement (city of record)

sampleInvoice.notes: Contract total $46,000; Change Order #1 approved 5/14 for $1,350. Payment due within 10 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Accepted: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on cards). Next draw due at drywall completion. License #CGC-123456.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and business info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require the license number on contracts and sometimes on invoices, and clients and lenders often want it for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address and contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific job and contract, which matters when you have several jobs running or the owner differs from the billing party.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or percent complete for each draw
invoiceChecklist.why: Progress payments hold up better when they match a stated milestone or schedule of values, and lenders often require this before releasing funds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders itemized separately with approval date
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps added work from being disputed later and shows the original contract amount versus the revised total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed with receipts or supplier invoices attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Cost-plus and T&M clients expect proof of cost, and it speeds approval when a bank or owner reviews the bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subcontractor charges and lien waiver status
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and lenders often require lien waivers with each payment, and listing subs clearly shows who has been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit and inspection fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These are often reimbursed at cost and should be shown separately from labor and materials.

construction.paymentTerms: Deposits of 10-30% at signing are common, though some states cap the maximum deposit on residential work, so check your local rules. Progress payments are usually tied to milestones, with the final payment due at substantial completion or after the punch list is done. Net 7 to net 15 is typical for draws, and many contractors hold final payment until the final inspection or certificate of occupancy. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Checks and ACH are standard for larger amounts, and cards are accepted by many contractors with a surcharge where allowed. Keep preliminary notices and lien deadlines in mind, since in many states you must file notices on time to preserve lien rights.

tips.title: Front-load the schedule of values reasonably
tips.body: Tie draws to real progress and keep them close to the cost incurred. Draws that run far ahead of the work can violate state rules and cause disputes or lender pushback.

tips.title: Get change orders signed before you swing a hammer
tips.body: Verbal approvals are hard to collect on. A one-page change order with scope, price, and any schedule impact prevents most end-of-job fights.

tips.title: Track lien deadlines and send required notices
tips.body: Many states require preliminary notices within a set number of days of starting work. Missing them can cost you your lien rights, so calendar them at job start.

tips.title: Exchange lien waivers with payments
tips.body: Provide conditional waivers with the invoice and unconditional waivers when paid. Collect them from your subs too so the owner is protected and your payments are not held up.

tips.title: Bill materials promptly
tips.body: Large material orders can strain cash flow. Bill deliveries on the next draw or ask for a materials deposit on big or special-order items.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice on a construction job?
faqs.answer: Follow the payment schedule in your contract. Fixed-price jobs usually bill at milestones, while T&M and cost-plus jobs are often billed weekly or every two weeks. Short repairs are billed when finished.

faqs.question: Can I charge a markup on materials and subcontractors?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Typical markups run 10-20% on materials and subs. On cost-plus jobs, state the markup or fee percentage in the contract so there are no surprises.

faqs.question: What is retainage and how does it affect my invoices?
faqs.answer: Retainage is a percentage, often 5-10%, held back from each payment until the project is complete. It is more common on commercial work and some public jobs. Show the amount withheld on each invoice and bill it as a separate release invoice at completion.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on construction invoices?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the type of contract. In many states contractors pay tax on materials and do not charge it to the client on lump-sum work, while others require tax on materials or labor in certain cases. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client won't pay the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder referencing the contract and due date, then a formal demand letter. If that fails, consider a mechanics lien, which has strict deadlines in most states, or small claims or civil court. An attorney can help with lien filings.

estimate.intro: Contractors send a written estimate or bid before any work starts, usually after a site visit and measurements. Homeowners often collect two or three bids and compare total price, scope, timeline, and allowances. A clear estimate helps you win the job and gives you something to point to when the project changes.

scopeChecklist.why: List what is included and what is not, such as demolition, haul-away, painting, or permits, so clients do not assume extras are covered.
Specify grade and brand where it matters, and state allowances for items the client picks, like tile or fixtures, with the overage handled as an add-on.
State who pulls permits and who pays for them, since this affects both cost and responsibility for code compliance.
Spell out the deposit and each draw milestone so cash flow is predictable and the client knows when payments come due.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, duration, and delay factors
scopeChecklist.why: Give an estimated timeline and note that weather, inspections, and material lead times can shift it.

scopeChecklist.item: Unknown conditions and change order process
scopeChecklist.why: Hidden rot, outdated wiring, or soil issues are common. Say how these will be priced and that changes require written approval.
Material and labor prices change, so state that the quote is good for 15 to 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency
pricingTips.body: Add a cushion of 5-15% for the risks of the job, higher on remodels of older homes. Show it as part of the price or as a separate allowance, depending on the contract type.

pricingTips.title: Price from takeoffs, not guesses
pricingTips.body: Measure and list quantities for lumber, concrete, and finish materials, then add labor hours and subcontractor quotes. Add overhead and profit on top of direct costs rather than treating them as leftover.

pricingTips.title: Use allowances carefully
pricingTips.body: Underestimated allowances are a common source of disputes. Use realistic figures for fixtures, flooring, and appliances, and note that overages are billed to the client.

pricingTips.title: Offer options instead of discounting
pricingTips.body: If a client says you are high, present a lower-cost alternative such as different materials or a smaller scope, instead of cutting your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors give free estimates on standard jobs. For complex projects that need design or engineering time, a paid estimate or design fee, often credited to the contract if the client signs, is common.

faqs.question: Is an estimate legally binding?
faqs.answer: A quote the client signs can become a contract. A non-binding estimate may allow price changes, but check your state rules, since some states limit how much the final price may exceed the estimate. Label the document clearly.

faqs.question: How long should my estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Shorten it when lumber, steel, or other material prices are volatile, and say so on the estimate.

faqs.question: Fixed price or cost-plus for a remodel?
faqs.answer: Fixed price works when the scope is well defined and the client wants a firm number. Cost-plus fits jobs with unknowns, such as older homes, and gives the client transparency but less certainty on the final total.

consulting-firm.intro: Consulting firms are run by one principal or a small team who sell expertise to other businesses, such as strategy, operations, finance, HR, IT, or process improvement. Invoices usually cover billable hours, fixed-fee project milestones, monthly retainers, and reimbursable expenses like travel. Clients are typically companies with accounts payable departments that expect clear references to a contract, statement of work, or purchase order.
consulting-firm.pricingModel: Most consulting firms use one of four models: hourly billing, fixed-fee projects, monthly retainers, or day rates. Hourly suits open-ended or advisory work, while fixed fees suit defined deliverables like an operations audit or a strategic plan. Retainers cover a set number of hours or ongoing access each month, and day rates are common for on-site workshops and embedded engagements. Rates depend on specialty, seniority, and client size, and firms with several people often set different rates for principals, senior consultants, and analysts. Expenses such as travel, lodging, software licenses, and subcontractors are usually billed at cost or with a modest markup, as the contract allows. Many firms bill fixed-fee work in milestones, for example one-third at signing, one-third at midpoint, and one-third at delivery.

items.description: Operations assessment, milestone 2 of 3: process mapping and interviews (SOW dated 3/4)
Senior consultant time: stakeholder interviews and data review (outside scope hours)
Analyst time: workflow documentation and cost model
On-site leadership workshop
Travel: round-trip mileage to client site (reimbursable at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Reference PO 48213. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date (Net 30). Late balances are subject to 1.5% monthly interest. Expense receipts available on request. Checks payable to the firm name above; ACH details are on the attached remittance sheet.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract, SOW, or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Client accounts payable teams often cannot process an invoice without a matching reference, and missing numbers cause weeks of delay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which engagement and which dates the charges cover, which matters when a client runs several projects at once.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours by person and role
invoiceChecklist.why: When billing hourly, clients want to see who worked, at what rate, and how many hours, especially with a mixed-seniority team.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or deliverable reference
invoiceChecklist.why: For fixed-fee work, tying each charge to a named deliverable or percent complete shows the payment is earned under the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel, lodging, and software costs are usually reviewed line by line, and attached receipts avoid pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining budget or not-to-exceed amount
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing billed to date against a cap prevents surprises and keeps the client informed on capped engagements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your tax ID and remittance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients typically need a W-9 on file and clear payment instructions (ACH, wire, or check address) to pay promptly.

consulting-firm.paymentTerms: Consulting firms commonly invoice fixed-fee projects with a deposit of 25-50% at signing, then milestone payments tied to deliverables. Hourly and retainer work is usually billed monthly, with retainers often billed in advance on the first of the month. Larger corporate clients frequently insist on Net 30 or Net 45 terms, while smaller clients may agree to Net 15 or due on receipt. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if written into the contract, though state limits on interest vary. ACH and wire transfers are the usual methods for business clients, with checks still common and cards accepted by some firms for smaller balances.

tips.title: Put billing terms in the SOW, not just the invoice
tips.body: Rates, payment schedule, expense policy, late fees, and change-order handling should all be agreed in writing before work starts. An invoice can only enforce what the contract already says.

tips.title: Invoice on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Send hourly invoices on the same day each month, such as the last business day, so the client's payables team can plan around them. Delayed invoices usually mean delayed payment.

tips.title: Use change orders for scope growth
tips.body: When a client asks for work outside the SOW, document it and get written approval before doing it. Bill approved changes as separate line items so they are easy to trace.

tips.title: Ask for a deposit or advance retainer
tips.body: Money up front reduces your cash flow risk on long engagements and filters out clients who are not committed. Many firms pause work if a milestone invoice goes unpaid past a stated grace period.

tips.title: Keep time records even on fixed fees
tips.body: Tracking hours on fixed-fee projects tells you whether the price was right and gives you data for future quotes. It also helps if a client disputes scope.

faqs.question: Should a consulting firm bill hourly or flat fee?
faqs.answer: Hourly works when scope is unclear or the client will direct the work. Flat fees work when deliverables are defined and you can estimate the effort with confidence. Many firms use flat fees for assessments and plans, and hourly or retainer billing for ongoing advisory work.

faqs.question: Can I mark up expenses and subcontractor costs?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract allows it. Many firms pass expenses through at cost and apply a markup of 5-15% to subcontractor fees. Whatever you choose, state it in the agreement so the client is not surprised.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional consulting services, but some tax certain services, such as IT or data processing consulting. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: What is a retainer and how should I invoice it?
faqs.answer: A retainer is a recurring monthly fee for a set amount of availability or hours. Invoice it at the start of each month, state what it includes, and specify whether unused hours roll over or expire. Work beyond the included hours is billed at your hourly rate.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client is late paying?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder a few days after the due date, then follow up by phone with the person who approves payment. Refer to the late fee and suspension terms in your contract. If the balance stays unpaid, many firms pause work until it is resolved and consider a demand letter before taking further steps.

estimate.intro: Consulting firms send a proposal or quote before most engagements, often after a discovery call and sometimes a short paid scoping phase. Clients usually compare your price against other firms and against doing the work in-house, so the quote needs to make scope, deliverables, and timeline clear. Once accepted, the proposal often becomes the basis for the SOW.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming the exact outputs, such as a report, model, roadmap, or training session, defines what the client is paying for and when the work is done.
Listing what is excluded, such as implementation or ongoing support, prevents the engagement from growing without extra pay.
Dates tied to deliverables and payments give both sides a way to measure progress.
Access to data, staff, and decision-makers is often the main source of delays, so spell out what the client must provide and by when.
State whether the price is fixed, hourly with a cap, or a retainer, and when each payment is due.
Clarify whether travel and other costs are included, billed at cost, or capped, so the final total is predictable.
Defines how many review rounds are included and how scope changes are priced and approved.

pricingTips.title: Price on value and risk, not only hours
pricingTips.body: A fixed fee based on the outcome and your uncertainty is often better than hours times rate. Add a buffer when the client's data or access is unclear.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three packages, such as assessment only, assessment plus roadmap, and full support, lets the client choose a budget without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Charge for discovery when it is substantial
pricingTips.body: A paid scoping phase produces a better estimate and screens out clients who only want free advice. Credit the fee toward the main project if you want to encourage conversion.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 30 days protect you from changes in your availability and costs. Note that the start date depends on signed acceptance and any deposit.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed price when scope and deliverables are clear. Give an hourly estimate with a not-to-exceed cap when the work depends on information you do not yet have. Either way, explain what happens if scope changes.

faqs.question: How detailed should a consulting proposal be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that the client knows exactly what they get, in about two to six pages for most small engagements. Focus on objectives, approach, deliverables, timeline, and fees rather than long company background.

faqs.question: Can I charge for preparing a proposal?
faqs.answer: Short proposals are normally free. If the proposal requires significant research, data analysis, or custom design, many firms charge a scoping fee and apply it to the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope or deliverables rather than your rate. Removing a workshop or limiting the number of interviews keeps the price-to-work ratio intact and preserves your positioning.

content-writer.intro: Content writers produce blog posts, website copy, white papers, case studies, email sequences, and similar material for businesses, agencies, and publications. Most work solo as freelancers or run small studios, and they invoice for finished pieces, hours of writing and research, or monthly retainers. A clear invoice ties each charge to a specific deliverable, word count, or revision round.
content-writer.pricingModel: Content writers price in a few ways. Per-word rates are common for blog posts and articles, especially with publications and content agencies. Per-project flat fees are standard for website copy, white papers, case studies, and email sequences, where research and interviews take more time than the word count suggests. Hourly rates are used for editing, content strategy, and open-ended work. Monthly retainers cover a fixed number of pieces or hours, which gives the writer steady income and the client predictable output. Many writers charge extra for rush turnaround, subject-matter interviews, SEO research, stock images, and revision rounds beyond the number included in the quote. Rates rise with technical complexity, such as software, finance, or healthcare topics.

rates.service: Blog post, flat fee (1,000 words, researched)

items.description: Blog post: 'How to Choose a Commercial HVAC Contractor' (1,200 words, includes keyword research)
Case study: Riverside Dental implementation (client interview, draft, one revision round)
Additional revision round on case study (requested after approval)
Rush fee: 48-hour turnaround on post #3

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Final copyright transfers to client upon receipt of full payment. Accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Title or description of each deliverable
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often pay several writers. A specific title lets accounts payable match the charge to the right piece of work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Word count or page count delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the charge matches the agreed scope, especially when the rate is per word or per page.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and any extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates included edits from out-of-scope changes, which prevents disputes about extra charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery and approval dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when work was completed and supports the payment due date if the client is slow to respond.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often will not process an invoice without one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States when copyright or licensing transfers, usually on full payment, which gives you leverage if a client publishes without paying.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses (stock images, paid research reports, transcription)
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists pass-through costs separately so they are not mistaken for your fee. Keep receipts on file.

content-writer.paymentTerms: Writers commonly ask for 25-50% upfront on new clients and on projects over $500, with the balance due on delivery or within 15-30 days. Retainers are typically billed at the start of the month. Agencies and larger companies often pay on net-30 or net-45 terms, so confirm this before starting. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is common if stated in your agreement and on the invoice, though rules on interest vary by state. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and some writers use a payment platform for international clients.

tips.title: Quote flat fees for research-heavy work
tips.body: A 1,000-word post on a technical topic can take six hours. A per-word rate undercharges you, so use a flat fee that reflects research, interviews, and outlining.

tips.title: Limit revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Include one or two rounds in your quote and bill extra rounds hourly. Define a revision as changes to existing copy, not a new direction or a rewrite from scratch.

tips.title: Invoice at delivery, not at publication
tips.body: Clients may sit on drafts for weeks. Tie payment to delivery or approval, and add a clause that unapproved drafts are considered accepted after 7-10 days of no response.

tips.title: Bill rush work as a separate line
tips.body: A visible rush fee of 25-50% makes tight deadlines a deliberate choice and keeps your base rate consistent across invoices.

tips.title: Track time even on flat-fee jobs
tips.body: Knowing your effective hourly rate on each project shows which clients and topics are worth repeating and which need higher prices.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word or per project?
faqs.answer: Per word works for simple, predictable articles. Per project is better when the job involves interviews, heavy research, strategy, or multiple formats, because word count does not reflect the effort.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on content writing?
faqs.answer: In most states, writing services are not taxed, but a few states tax certain digital or information services. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, especially if you sell to clients in several states.

faqs.question: What if a client stops responding after I deliver the draft?
faqs.answer: Send the invoice on the delivery date and follow up on a set schedule. If your contract includes an auto-acceptance clause, point to it. Keep rights to the work until you are paid in full.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent on calls and emails?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many writers include a set amount of communication in a flat fee and bill hourly for kickoff meetings, strategy calls, or extended back-and-forth beyond that.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants to cancel mid-project?
faqs.answer: State a kill fee in your agreement, commonly 25-50% of the project fee depending on how much work is done. Invoice for completed work at your hourly or per-word rate, and keep any deposit.

estimate.intro: Content writers send estimates before starting new projects, when a client asks for a quote, or when a retainer is being negotiated. Clients usually compare your price with other freelancers, agencies, and in-house costs, so the estimate needs to show exactly what they receive for the fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables with format and word count
scopeChecklist.why: Saying '4 blog posts of 1,200 words each' avoids arguments over whether a 2,000-word piece was included.
Clarifies whether you will interview experts or customers, and who arranges those conversations, since delays here hold up the project.
Sets the limit on edits and states what counts as a revision versus a new request.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline with draft and final due dates
scopeChecklist.why: Ties your schedule to client turnaround. If feedback is late, your deadlines move too.
Lists brand guidelines, style guides, source material, and login access you need, so you are not blamed for delays.
States whether keyword research, meta descriptions, formatting in the CMS, or image sourcing are included or priced separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Rights, credit, and kill fee terms
