scopeChecklist.why: Covers ownership transfer, whether you can use the work in a portfolio, and what happens if the project is canceled.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in hours, then convert to a flat fee
pricingTips.body: Add up research, outlining, drafting, editing, and revisions. Multiply by your target hourly rate and add a buffer of 10-20% for unexpected feedback.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic, standard, and premium option, such as posts only, posts plus SEO research, or posts plus promotion copy, gives clients a choice without negotiating your base rate.

pricingTips.title: Use retainers for repeat work
pricingTips.body: Offer a modest discount for a three- or six-month retainer in exchange for guaranteed monthly income, and spell out what happens to unused pieces.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: A 14-30 day validity window protects you from rate changes and from taking on work at an old price.

faqs.question: Should I give a free sample with my estimate?
faqs.answer: Point to existing published samples instead of writing new copy for free. If a client insists on a test piece, charge a reduced fee for it and credit it toward the project if they hire you.

faqs.question: How do I price when the client has not defined the scope?
faqs.answer: Quote a paid discovery or strategy session first, or give a price range tied to assumptions such as number of pages and revision rounds. Update the quote once the scope is clear.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: An estimate is a good-faith projection and a quote is a firm price. Label yours clearly, and state that scope changes will be priced separately.

faqs.question: When should I ask for a deposit on a quote?
faqs.answer: Ask for a deposit with the signed estimate on new clients and projects over a few hundred dollars. 25-50% upfront is common, and work starts once it is received.

contractor.intro: General contractors manage residential and light commercial building projects, from kitchen and bathroom remodels to additions, decks, and whole-house renovations. They hire and coordinate subcontractors, buy materials, pull permits, and bill clients for labor, materials, sub work, and their own management fee. Invoices are often tied to project milestones rather than a single bill at the end.
contractor.pricingModel: Most general contractors price in one of three ways. Fixed-price (lump sum) contracts set one total for a defined scope, usually billed in draws tied to milestones such as deposit, rough-in complete, drywall complete, and final completion. Cost-plus contracts bill actual labor, materials, and subcontractor costs plus a markup, commonly 10-25 percent, with receipts or backup attached. Time and materials is used for small repairs, punch lists, and change orders, with an hourly labor rate plus materials at cost plus markup. Many contractors also bill by the square foot as a rough guide for new construction, additions, and flooring or roofing work. Overhead and profit are usually built into the markup or rate, not shown as a separate line, unless the contract is cost-plus and requires a visible fee.

rates.service: General labor or handyman-level carpentry (time and materials)

rates.unit: per sq ft of floor area

rates.service: Materials markup on cost-plus or change orders
Project management fee on cost-plus jobs

items.description: Bathroom remodel - Draw 2 of 3: demolition, rough plumbing and electrical, and tile backer board complete
Labor - framing repair of rotted subfloor (change order #1, approved 3/12)
Materials - 3/4 in. plywood subfloor, joist hangers, fasteners (change order #1)
Materials markup on change order #1 (15%)
Dumpster rental and haul-away (10 yd)

sampleInvoice.notes: Contract total $18,500. Draw 1 ($5,550) paid at signing. This invoice covers Draw 2 plus approved change order #1. Remaining balance after this invoice: $6,475 due at final completion. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Checks payable to the business name above. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Lien waiver for work through this invoice provided on receipt of payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require the license number on contracts and invoices, and clients use it to verify you are in good standing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address and contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific job and signed contract, which matters when you run several projects at once.

invoiceChecklist.item: Draw or milestone description with percent complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and lenders want to see that the work billed has actually been done before releasing payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Approved change orders listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps extra work visible and tied to written approval, which prevents disputes over why the total changed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized materials and subcontractor costs (on cost-plus jobs)
invoiceChecklist.why: Cost-plus contracts require backup. Attach receipts and sub invoices so the client can see what the markup applies to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit numbers and fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows permits were pulled and lets you pass through fees. Inspectors and lenders may ask for the references.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lien waiver or lien rights notice
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, a conditional or unconditional lien waiver is expected with each payment, and preliminary lien notices may be required. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining contract balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows total contract, paid to date, this invoice, and balance left so there are no surprises at final payment.

contractor.paymentTerms: Most residential contractors take a deposit at signing, often 10-33 percent depending on the job and state limits (some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts, so check yours). The rest is billed in draws tied to milestones, typically due within 5-10 days of invoice, with final payment due at substantial completion or after the final walkthrough. Smaller time and materials jobs are often due on receipt or net 15. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Clients pay by check, ACH, or card; if you accept cards, consider whether to pass along processing fees, and check your state's rules on surcharging. Retainage of 5-10 percent is common on commercial jobs and is released after final inspection.

tips.title: Tie every draw to a visible milestone
tips.body: Write the draw schedule into the contract with specific events, such as rough-in inspection passed or cabinets installed. Billing against observable progress is easier to defend than billing by calendar date.

tips.title: Never start change order work without written approval
tips.body: Get a signed or emailed approval with the price before you do extra work. Then list it as its own line on the next invoice with the approval date.

tips.title: Collect lien waivers and give them
tips.body: Exchange waivers with payments so the client knows their property is clear, and so your subs and suppliers are paid before you bill the next draw. Unpaid subs can file liens against the client even if the client paid you.

tips.title: Keep deposits from running ahead of your costs
tips.body: Front-load the schedule enough to cover materials orders and sub deposits, but avoid collecting far more than the work completed. It protects you if a dispute arises and may be required by state law.

tips.title: Invoice the day a milestone is finished
tips.body: Waiting a week to bill after drywall or final paint slows your cash flow. Send the invoice with photos of the completed work attached.

faqs.question: Should I bill a fixed price or time and materials?
faqs.answer: Use fixed price when the scope is clear and drawings or a detailed list exist. Use time and materials or cost-plus when the scope is uncertain, such as repair work that may uncover hidden damage. Many contractors use fixed price for the main contract and time and materials for change orders.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on materials?
faqs.answer: Ten to 25 percent is typical on materials and subcontractor costs, with smaller jobs toward the higher end. The markup needs to cover your overhead, such as insurance, trucks, estimating time, and warranty callbacks, as well as profit.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on my invoices?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax materials in a construction contract, some tax labor on certain work, and some tax neither for real property improvements. Check with your state's department of revenue before setting up your invoice format.

faqs.question: What if a client withholds the final payment over punch list items?
faqs.answer: Keep a signed punch list and set a reasonable holdback in your contract, such as 150 percent of the value of the remaining items. Complete the items promptly and invoice the balance. If it is still unpaid, send a written demand and look into your state's lien deadlines early.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel and dump fees?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. List dumpster rentals, disposal fees, and delivery charges as separate lines or build them into your bid. Mileage and trip charges are more common on small service calls than on large projects.

estimate.intro: General contractors send an estimate or bid before any contract is signed, usually after a site visit and often with plans or photos. Homeowners commonly collect two or three bids and compare total price, scope, timeline, and allowances line by line. A detailed quote helps you win on clarity instead of on being the cheapest.

scopeChecklist.item: Detailed scope of work by area or trade
scopeChecklist.why: Lists what is included, such as demo, framing, electrical, plumbing, drywall, and paint, so a client can compare bids on the same basis.
States what is not included, such as appliances, landscaping, or repair of hidden damage, to prevent assumptions of free extras.
Sets a dollar amount for items the client selects, like tile, fixtures, or cabinets, and explains that overages are billed as a change order.
Says who pulls permits and who pays the fees, since cost and timeline depend on it.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, duration, and completion terms
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations and defines what substantial completion means, which helps if weather or delays come up.
Shows the deposit and draw milestones up front so the client knows the cash flow before signing.

scopeChecklist.item: Change order process and unknown conditions
scopeChecklist.why: Explains how hidden issues like rot, asbestos, or outdated wiring will be priced and approved.
Material and labor prices change, so state how long the price holds, such as 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Price from a takeoff, not just a per-square-foot rule
pricingTips.body: Rules of thumb help for rough budgeting, but build the bid from quantities, sub quotes, and labor hours. Then add overhead and profit, commonly 15-30 percent combined, on top of direct costs.

pricingTips.title: Get written subcontractor quotes before you bid
pricingTips.body: Subs' prices drive much of the total. Having written quotes with an expiration date keeps you from eating a price increase between estimate and contract.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency for remodels
pricingTips.body: Older homes hide problems. Many contractors carry a 5-10 percent contingency internally or include a clear unknown-conditions clause so surprises do not erase profit.

pricingTips.title: Break out options as add-alternates
pricingTips.body: Show upgrades like heated floors or a higher-grade window as separate priced options. Clients can choose without you rewriting the quote, and it frames your base price as complete.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors give free estimates on small and mid-sized jobs but charge a fee for detailed design-build proposals, often $250-1,000 or more, credited to the contract if the client signs. Charging helps screen out clients who are only collecting prices.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: An estimate is generally a rough price that can change, while a quote or bid is a firm offer for stated scope. Label which one you are sending, and put the terms in a signed contract before starting work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is common. In periods of volatile lumber, steel, or copper prices, shorter windows or a clause allowing material price adjustments are reasonable.

faqs.question: What if my bid is much higher than a competitor's?
faqs.answer: Compare the scopes before dropping your price. Often the lower bid leaves out permits, cleanup, or allowances. Offer to walk the client through the differences, and reduce scope instead of cutting your margin if the budget is the issue.

copy-editing.intro: Copy editors are freelancers and small-shop editors who correct and polish text for authors, publishers, agencies, businesses, and academics. Typical invoices cover manuscript copyedits, proofreading passes, style sheet creation, and sometimes light developmental or fact-checking work. Most jobs are billed against a word or page count, so the invoice needs to show exactly what was edited and at what level.
copy-editing.pricingModel: Copy editors price in four common ways: per word, per manuscript page (usually 250 words, or a standard double-spaced page), per hour, or as a flat project fee derived from one of those. Per-word and per-page rates are common for books and long documents because the client can compare quotes easily. Hourly billing is more common for messy, mixed-quality material, corporate content, or ongoing work where the scope shifts. The level of edit matters as much as length: proofreading costs less than a light copyedit, which costs less than a heavy copyedit. Many editors also charge extra for rush turnaround, heavy reference or citation checking, style sheet preparation, tracked-changes cleanup, and fact-checking. Agency and corporate clients may pay monthly retainers or a per-piece rate for blog posts, white papers, and web copy. Many editors set a minimum project fee so very short jobs are still worth taking.

rates.service: Proofreading (final pass on typeset or clean text)

items.description: Copyedit of nonfiction manuscript, 'The Quiet Harvest' (moderate edit, Chicago Manual of Style, tracked changes in Word)
Style sheet (character names, spelling, hyphenation and capitalization decisions)
Reference and endnote consistency check
Rush surcharge (delivery in 8 business days instead of 15), applied to base edit

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers one round of copyediting plus one review of author responses to queries within 30 days of delivery. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Payment accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project title and document names
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, especially publishers and agencies, often handle several projects at once and need to match your invoice to the right file or purchase order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Word count and how it was measured
invoiceChecklist.why: A per-word invoice is only as credible as its count. State whether it came from Word's count, including or excluding notes, references, and front matter.

invoiceChecklist.item: Level of edit performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Proofreading, light copyedit, and heavy copyedit are priced differently, and naming the level prevents arguments about whether you did more or less than agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Style guide followed
invoiceChecklist.why: Chicago, AP, APA, MLA, or a house style affects the workload and shows exactly what standard the edit met.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date and turnaround
invoiceChecklist.why: This documents any rush surcharge and shows you met the deadline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on services listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Style sheets, fact-checking, reference checks, and extra review rounds should appear as their own lines so the base edit stays clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Publishers and corporate accounts payable departments often will not process an invoice without a PO or project code.

copy-editing.paymentTerms: Book-length and large projects commonly require a deposit of 25-50% before work starts, with the balance due on delivery of the edited file. Short jobs are often paid in full on delivery or in advance. Net 14 and net 30 are the usual terms, and publishers and large companies may pay on net 30 to net 60 cycles that are set by their own accounts payable process. Editors often state a late fee in the contract and on the invoice, commonly 1-1.5% per month, and some hold final files until payment clears for new clients. Payment is typically accepted by ACH, check, wire, or credit card. Foreign clients may prefer wire transfer or a payment platform that handles currency conversion.

tips.title: Take a sample edit before quoting
tips.body: Edit 500 to 1,000 words from the middle of the document, then quote based on how much work it needed. Many manuscripts are in worse shape than the first page suggests, and a sample protects you from underpricing.

tips.title: Define what one round includes
tips.body: State in your quote and invoice how many rounds of author review or query follow-up are included. Without this, a single edit can turn into weeks of unpaid back-and-forth.

tips.title: Bill on the final word count, not the estimate
tips.body: If the author adds or cuts text before you start, re-count and adjust. Put a clause in your agreement that allows a revised fee if the final file differs from the sample by more than 10%.

tips.title: Use a minimum fee
tips.body: A 600-word web page takes setup time, style decisions, and file handling. A minimum such as $50-100 keeps tiny jobs from costing you money.

tips.title: Track time even on per-word jobs
tips.body: Log how long each project takes so you can see your real effective hourly rate and adjust your per-word rates for the types of material that run slow.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word or per hour?
faqs.answer: Per word or per page works well when the text is fairly consistent and the client wants a fixed number up front. Hourly works better when the quality is uneven, the scope is unclear, or the work includes research, fact-checking, or many rounds of changes. Many editors quote per word after a sample edit and bill hourly for extras.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the references and footnotes?
faqs.answer: Decide before you start and say so in the quote. Many editors include notes and references in the word count and charge extra when citation work is heavy, such as reformatting a bibliography into a different style or verifying sources.

faqs.question: Can I charge a rush fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. A surcharge of 25-50% is common when the deadline forces you to move other work or work evenings and weekends. State the fee in the quote and show it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to send tax forms to clients or collect them?
faqs.answer: In the US, freelancers are generally independent contractors, and clients who pay you above the IRS threshold in a year commonly request a W-9 and send a 1099 form. Rules and thresholds change, so check current IRS guidance or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the client disputes the edit quality?
faqs.answer: A written scope that names the edit level and style guide is your best protection. Keep tracked-changes files and your style sheet as evidence. Many editors offer to fix specific errors that were within scope, but they do not redo the edit or refund payment for subjective preferences.

estimate.intro: Copy editors send a quote before taking on any project, usually after the client shares a manuscript or sample pages. Clients often compare several editors on price per word, turnaround, and experience in their genre or subject. A clear quote shows what level of edit is included and what is not, which is where most misunderstandings begin.

scopeChecklist.item: Level of edit (proofread, light, moderate, heavy)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often use these terms differently. Describe what you will and will not change, such as whether you rewrite sentences or only fix grammar and consistency.

scopeChecklist.item: Word count basis and fee adjustment
scopeChecklist.why: Spell out how the count was determined and that the fee changes if the final file differs materially from what you were shown.
Naming Chicago, AP, APA, or a house guide, plus the dictionary you follow, avoids disputes over spelling and punctuation choices.
State how many rounds of author or client responses you will handle and what happens when more are requested.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, start date, and delivery date
scopeChecklist.why: Editors usually book weeks in advance. The quote should tie the delivery date to when you receive the final file and any deposit.

scopeChecklist.item: File format and method of editing
scopeChecklist.why: Say whether you will use Word tracked changes, PDF markup, or another tool, and that the client must provide files in a workable format.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as fact-checking, permissions, or formatting
scopeChecklist.why: These tasks are often assumed to be included. List them as optional add-ons with their own price.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a sample, not the first page
pricingTips.body: A sample from the middle of the document shows the real level of work. Quote the full project based on that and note that the quote assumes similar quality throughout.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a proofread, a light copyedit, and a heavier copyedit at different prices when the client is unsure what they need. This helps them choose and keeps you from underquoting.

pricingTips.title: Add a cushion for queries and style decisions
pricingTips.body: Author queries, inconsistent source material, and style sheet work take time that does not show in the word count. Build it into the per-word rate or list a separate line.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Your calendar fills up. State that the quote and the reserved dates are valid for 14 or 30 days, and that a deposit holds the slot.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before seeing the document?
faqs.answer: Only give a rough range. A firm quote needs the actual file or a sample, since the condition of the writing changes the time needed by a large margin.

faqs.question: Is it normal to charge for a sample edit?
faqs.answer: Many editors do a short free sample of up to about 500 to 1,000 words. For longer samples or technical material, a small paid trial is reasonable and is often credited toward the full project.

faqs.question: What if the actual work is more than my quote?
faqs.answer: Include a clause allowing a revised fee if the word count or condition of the text differs significantly from what was quoted. Send the updated figure in writing and get approval before continuing.

copywriter.intro: Copywriters write marketing and sales content for businesses: website pages, email sequences, ads, landing pages, product descriptions, and long-form pieces like case studies and white papers. Most work solo as freelancers or run small studios, and bill per project, per word, per hour, or on monthly retainers. Invoices need to show exactly which deliverables were written, how many revision rounds were included, and what usage rights transfer to the client.
copywriter.pricingModel: Most copywriters price by the project because clients want a known number and because the value of a sales page or email sequence has little to do with word count. Flat project fees are usually built from an estimated hour count multiplied by a target hourly rate, plus research and revision time. Per-word pricing is common for blog posts, articles, and content marketing, typically a few cents to a dollar or more per word depending on topic complexity. Hourly billing shows up for editing, rewrites, strategy calls, and work with unclear scope. Retainers are common for ongoing email, blog, or ad copy, billed monthly for a set number of deliverables or hours. Many writers add a rush fee (often 25-50%) for short turnarounds, charge extra for additional revision rounds beyond what is in the contract, and bill separately for stock images, research tools, or paid interviews if those are passed through. Deposits of 25-50% up front are standard on larger projects.

items.description: Website copy: home page, about page, and 3 service pages (includes brand voice review and 2 rounds of revisions)
Welcome email sequence (4 emails, subject lines and preview text included)
Discovery call and competitor review
Additional revision round requested after final approval

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received on project start has been applied. Balance due within 14 days of invoice date. Copyright and usage rights transfer to the client upon payment in full. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables with word counts or page counts
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget what was in scope. Listing each page, email, or article ties the charge to something they can open and review.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and any extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Scope creep is the most common billing dispute in copywriting. Showing how many rounds were included and which were extra justifies add-on charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and ownership terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Many contracts transfer copyright only after full payment. Stating this on the invoice reinforces that the client owns the work once the balance is paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, brief or contract reference, and PO number if the client uses one
invoiceChecklist.why: Marketing teams and agencies route invoices through accounts payable, and a missing PO or project code can hold payment for weeks.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client exactly what was already paid so the remaining amount is not questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush, research, or pass-through charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Rush fees, paid interviews, stock images, or subscriptions should be visible and not buried in the project fee, so they are not mistaken for padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery or approval dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates of draft delivery and client approval back up the due date and help if the client goes quiet after the work is done.

copywriter.paymentTerms: Copywriters commonly collect 25-50% up front on new projects, with the balance due on final delivery or within 7-30 days of invoice. Net 15 and net 30 are the norm with businesses, and larger companies or agencies may insist on net 45 or net 60 through their payables process, so confirm this before you start. Retainers are typically billed at the start of the month, not the end. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract; check your state's rules on interest. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and some writers add a small surcharge for card payments where permitted. Many writers hold final files or publishing rights until the balance is paid.

tips.title: Define revisions in the contract and invoice
tips.body: State how many rounds are included, what counts as a round, and the hourly rate for extra rounds. Rewriting the brief halfway through is a new project, not a revision.

tips.title: Get a deposit before you start
tips.body: A 50% deposit on projects under a few thousand dollars, or 25-33% milestone payments on larger ones, protects you against clients who disappear after seeing drafts.

tips.title: Bill on delivery, not on approval
tips.body: If payment depends on the client signing off, slow reviewers can stall your income. Set a due date tied to delivery of the first draft or to a fixed number of days after, with a window for feedback.

tips.title: Separate strategy from writing
tips.body: Discovery calls, messaging workshops, and competitor research take real time. Bill them as their own line or include them clearly in the project fee so they are not treated as free.

tips.title: Invoice retainers in advance
tips.body: Bill the retainer at the start of the month, and say what happens to unused deliverables. Most writers do not roll them over unless the contract says so.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word, per hour, or per project?
faqs.answer: Per project works best for web pages, sales pages, and email sequences because it ties the price to the outcome. Per word suits articles and blog content where length is the main variable. Hourly is best for editing, rewrites, and open-ended work. Whichever you choose, estimate your hours privately to make sure the fee meets your target hourly rate.

faqs.question: When does the client own the copy I wrote?
faqs.answer: That is set by your contract. Many freelance writers transfer copyright or grant a license only after payment in full, and in the US, work by an independent contractor is generally not work-made-for-hire unless a written agreement says so. Put the terms in the contract and mention them on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a rush fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in your quote or contract before the work begins. Many copywriters add 25-50% for turnarounds well below their normal schedule. List it as a separate line item on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on copywriting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain digital or advertising services, and many do not tax professional writing services at all. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant, and only add tax to the invoice if it applies to you.

faqs.question: What if a client wants me to keep revising after the final version is approved?
faqs.answer: Point to the revision limit in your contract and offer to do additional rounds at your hourly rate. Invoice the extra time as a separate line so the original project fee stays clean.

estimate.intro: Copywriters send estimates after a discovery call or after reviewing a brief, and before any writing starts. Clients typically compare your number against other freelancers, agencies, and in-house cost, so the quote needs to show what is included and why. A clear scope also sets the foundation for the invoice later.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact deliverables with counts and length
scopeChecklist.why: List the number of pages, emails, or posts and approximate word counts so a 'home page' does not grow into a 3,000-word piece without a price change.
State the number of rounds, how feedback is consolidated, and the rate for extra rounds. This prevents open-ended edits.
Say whether the fee covers customer interviews, subject-matter expert calls, competitor analysis, and who arranges them.

scopeChecklist.item: What the client must provide and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Brand guidelines, product access, brief, and feedback deadlines all affect your timeline. Late input should move the delivery date, not eat your margin.
Give draft and final dates tied to the date you receive the deposit and materials.
Clarify who owns the copy, whether you can show it in a portfolio, and whether a byline is included or excluded.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as SEO, design, or publishing
scopeChecklist.why: Keyword research, uploading to a CMS, A/B test variants, and stock images are often assumed to be included. List what is not covered.

pricingTips.title: Quote a flat fee built from hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate research, drafting, and revision time, multiply by your target rate, and add a buffer for feedback delays. Present only the project fee, not the hours, so the client compares outcomes.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium option, such as copy only, copy plus email follow-up, or copy plus A/B variants, gives clients a choice and tends to land them on the middle tier.

pricingTips.title: Ask about budget and goals early
pricingTips.body: Knowing whether the client is launching a product or refreshing a page tells you how much the work is worth to them and helps you price accordingly.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from rate changes and from clients who return months later expecting the same price.

faqs.question: Should I give a price range or a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: A fixed quote is usually better once the scope is clear. If the brief is vague, give a range tied to defined assumptions and say that the final fee will be confirmed once scope is locked.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or discovery call?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is normally free. If you need to review analytics, audit existing copy, or do competitor research to price the work, many writers charge a small paid discovery fee and credit it toward the project.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope rather than your rate. Cut a page, drop an email, or lower the number of revision rounds. Writers who discount the same work train clients to expect it.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed contract along with the estimate?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. An accepted estimate often serves as a simple agreement, but a written contract that covers payment, revisions, and copyright gives you stronger protection if there is a dispute.

corporate-photographer.intro: Corporate photographers shoot for businesses rather than individual consumers. Typical jobs include employee headshots, executive portraits, office and facility photography, conferences and events, product and marketing imagery, and annual report or website photography. Invoices usually go to a marketing manager, HR department, or accounts payable team, so they need to be clear enough to pass through an approval process.
corporate-photographer.pricingModel: Most corporate photographers charge a creative or day rate (half day or full day) plus separate line items for usage licensing, editing and retouching, assistants, equipment, and expenses. Headshot work is often priced per person for on-site sessions or as a flat fee for a block of time, such as a two-hour mini-session with a set number of finished images per person. Event coverage is typically hourly with a minimum of two to four hours. Licensing is tied to how and where the images will be used and for how long, so a website-only license costs less than a national ad campaign. Many photographers set a minimum booking fee, and charge extra for rush delivery, travel beyond a set radius, and additional retouching beyond what is included.

items.description: On-site employee headshots, 32 staff, includes lighting setup and 2 retouched finals per person
Executive portraits, 4 leadership team members, office location
Additional retouching (skin and background cleanup) beyond included edits
Photo assistant, full day
Usage license: company website, LinkedIn, internal and print materials, 3 years

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date (Net 30). Final images delivered via private download gallery. License covers company marketing and internal use only and does not extend to paid advertising or resale. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. PO number: 48215.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot date(s), location, and project name
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable and marketing teams match invoices to specific projects and budgets, and a clear reference prevents payment delays.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Many companies will not pay an invoice without a PO or internal reference code.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized creative fee, assistant, and equipment charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these shows what the client is paying for and makes it easier to explain changes from the original quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license terms (media, territory, duration)
invoiceChecklist.why: Licensing is a core part of the price. Stating the scope on the invoice protects you if the client later uses images beyond what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of delivered images and retouching included
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents what was delivered and sets up billing for any extra edits requested later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expenses with receipts available (travel, mileage, parking, location fees, models)
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate clients often require expense documentation, and listing them separately keeps your fees clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the booking deposit credited against the total so the client sees the correct amount owed.

corporate-photographer.paymentTerms: Corporate photographers commonly take a 25% to 50% deposit to hold the date, with the balance due on delivery or within 15 to 30 days. Larger companies often pay Net 30 or Net 45 and may need you to register as a vendor and submit a W-9 first. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract or on the invoice. Payment is typically accepted by ACH, check, or credit card, and some photographers add a small card processing fee for large invoices. For first-time clients or large jobs, delivering final images only after payment, or delivering low-resolution proofs first, is common practice.

tips.title: Bill licensing as its own line item
tips.body: Listing usage separately from your shoot fee makes the value of the rights clear and gives you a natural line to adjust if the client later wants broader use, such as paid ads or a longer term.

tips.title: Set a minimum for headshot days
tips.body: On-site headshot sessions have setup and breakdown time that does not change with headcount. Use a minimum booking fee or a minimum number of people so a small group does not cost you money.

tips.title: Get vendor paperwork done before the shoot
tips.body: Ask for the vendor onboarding steps, W-9 requirements, and invoice submission process up front. Large companies can take weeks to set up a new vendor, and this affects when you get paid.

tips.title: Bill change requests and reshoots separately
tips.body: Late schedule changes, added shot lists, rush turnaround, and extra retouching should be added as separate lines on the invoice with a note referencing the client's request.

tips.title: Track mileage and equipment rental
tips.body: Rented lenses, lighting, and travel are real costs. Add them as itemized expenses so they are reimbursed rather than absorbed into your fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge for usage rights on corporate photography?
faqs.answer: Yes, most corporate photographers do. Licensing is separate from the creative fee and depends on where the images will appear, for how long, and in what territory. A simple headshot shoot may include a standard license in the per-person price, while campaign imagery usually has a separate usage line.

faqs.question: Do I charge for editing time?
faqs.answer: Basic editing such as color correction and cropping is usually included in the shoot fee. Charge extra for advanced retouching, compositing, or large batches beyond the agreed number of finished images, and state this on the quote and invoice.

faqs.question: How long should I wait for payment from a corporate client?
faqs.answer: Net 30 is the most common term, and some larger companies use Net 45 or Net 60. Confirm their payment cycle before the shoot. Follow up politely a few days after the due date, and apply any late fee listed in your terms.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on photography services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services or the sale of physical prints, while others do not tax services at all. Check your state's department of revenue rules, and note that digital delivery is treated differently in different places.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit from a large company?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit of 25% to 50% is normal for corporate bookings and helps cover the reserved date. Some large companies prefer to pay after delivery only, so confirm during contract setup and adjust your terms or price if needed.

estimate.intro: Corporate photographers send a quote or proposal before any shoot is booked, often after a call about the number of people, locations, shot list, and intended use of the images. Clients usually compare quotes from two or three photographers and look at total price, number of delivered images, turnaround time, and usage rights.

scopeChecklist.item: Shoot length, number of locations, and number of people or setups
scopeChecklist.why: Time on site is the biggest cost driver, and an unclear scope leads to arguments if the day runs long.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of final edited images and retouching level
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often expect every frame, so state how many finished images they get and what level of editing is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage license: media, territory, and duration
scopeChecklist.why: Defines what the client can do with the images and sets the basis for charging more if their use expands.
Specify file types, resolution, delivery method, and timeline, such as 5 business days, with a rush option and fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Crew, equipment, and expenses included or billed separately
scopeChecklist.why: Assistants, hair and makeup, rentals, travel, and parking can add up quickly, and the client should know what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Client responsibilities (access, permits, schedule, wardrobe, approvals)
scopeChecklist.why: Delays on the client side such as late staff or restricted building access should be covered so they can trigger overtime or rescheduling fees.
Protects you if a date is changed on short notice, especially for outdoor or event shoots.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as basic headshot session, headshots with retouching, and a full brand package. Clients can choose by budget and you avoid a flat yes or no answer.

pricingTips.title: Build in setup, travel, and editing time
pricingTips.body: A four-hour shoot often involves another four to eight hours of travel, setup, culling, and editing. Price the whole project, not just time with the camera.

pricingTips.title: Ask about intended use before pricing
pricingTips.body: The same portrait can be priced very differently for internal use versus a national ad. Asking early lets you set the license fee properly.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Include a date through which the pricing and your availability are held, usually 14 to 30 days, so you are not tied to a quote when schedules and costs change.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Most corporate photographers quote a flat project fee based on a defined scope, because corporate buyers want a fixed number to approve. Use hourly rates for event coverage or as an overtime rate if the shoot runs past the agreed time.

faqs.question: How do I price headshots for a large team?
faqs.answer: Quote per person with a minimum, or a half-day or full-day rate that covers a set number of people. Include the time per person, the number of finished images each, and any volume discount for large groups.

faqs.question: Should I require a signed contract along with the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. Once the client accepts the quote, have them sign an agreement that includes scope, license terms, payment schedule, and cancellation policy. Many photographers collect the deposit at signing to confirm the booking.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to negotiate the price?
faqs.answer: Adjust the scope rather than only dropping the price. You can reduce the number of images, shorten the shoot, narrow the license, or lengthen the turnaround. This keeps your rate intact while meeting their budget.

cosmetic-nurse-injector.intro: Cosmetic nurse injectors are RNs, NPs, and sometimes PAs who administer neuromodulators, dermal fillers, and related aesthetic treatments. They work in medical spas, physician practices, or their own clinics, and bill for treatments by unit, syringe, or session. Invoices usually pair product-based charges with consultation fees and any add-on services.
cosmetic-nurse-injector.pricingModel: Neuromodulators (Botox, Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau, Daxxify) are billed per unit, or sometimes per area, with the per-unit price varying by brand. Dermal fillers (Juvederm, Restylane, RHA, Sculptra, Radiesse) are billed per syringe, and the price depends on the product line and the area treated. Many injectors also sell by vial or in packages, such as a loyalty or membership program with a set number of units each month. Consultations are often free or charged as a fee that is credited toward treatment. Other services include PRP, microneedling, and skin boosters like Skinvive, and these are usually flat fees per session or sold in series. Prices cover the product, your clinical time, and overhead, so they are not set as an hourly rate. Corrective work such as filler dissolving with hyaluronidase is usually billed separately. Injectors who work as independent contractors inside someone else's practice often split revenue or pay a per-treatment fee, so their own invoices may go to the practice rather than the patient.

items.description: Botox Cosmetic: glabella, forehead, and crow's feet (50 units)
Juvederm Voluma XC: cheek augmentation
Juvederm Volbella XC: lip border and perioral lines
Follow-up touch-up visit (units used billed separately if needed)
Numbing cream and post-care kit

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service. Treatment details, product lot numbers, and units used are recorded in the patient chart. Touch-ups requested within 14 days are evaluated at no visit charge; additional product is billed at the standard rate. Deposits for appointments are non-refundable if canceled within 48 hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Product name and brand for each treatment
invoiceChecklist.why: Botox, Dysport, and Xeomin are priced differently and are not interchangeable one-to-one, so the patient and your records need to show exactly what was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Units or syringes used and treatment areas
invoiceChecklist.why: This ties the charge to what was done and answers later questions about why a total was higher or lower than expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and provider name with credentials
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for patient records, receipts for HSA or FSA questions, and any dispute about who performed the treatment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lot numbers or a reference to the chart
invoiceChecklist.why: Lot numbers support traceability if there is a product recall or an adverse event, and many practices record them in the chart and reference them on the receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supervising physician or practice name where required
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, NPs practice independently while RNs and sometimes PAs need physician oversight, so the invoice should reflect the correct practice entity that is billing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits, packages, and membership credits applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing prepaid amounts and credits avoids double charging and makes the remaining balance clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show fee, if any
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellations and missed appointments take up injector and product time, and itemizing the fee shows it follows your stated policy.

cosmetic-nurse-injector.paymentTerms: Most aesthetic treatments are cash-pay and collected at the time of service by card, with some practices accepting financing options such as CareCredit or Cherry. Many injectors require a deposit, commonly $50-100 or a percentage, to book longer appointments or filler sessions, and the deposit is applied to the final bill. Cancellation windows of 24-48 hours are common, with fees or forfeited deposits for late changes. Aesthetic services are usually not covered by insurance, so statements are rarely sent after the fact, but a receipt may be requested for HSA or FSA purposes in the case of certain medical uses. Contract injectors invoicing a med spa typically bill weekly or biweekly with net 7 to net 15 terms. Check your state's rules and your malpractice policy on what you can bill and under whose name.

tips.title: Quote by unit and write down the plan
tips.body: Patients often ask for a price per area, but actual unit use varies. Record the planned units and the price per unit on the treatment plan and invoice so adjustments mid-visit are easy to explain.

tips.title: Charge separately for corrective work and extra product
tips.body: If a patient wants more filler or units after the initial plan, add them as separate lines at the standard rate. Dissolving filler from another provider should have its own fee.

tips.title: Be clear on how packages and memberships work
tips.body: State whether units expire, whether they roll over, and whether they are refundable. Show the prepaid balance on each invoice so the patient sees what remains.

tips.title: Collect payment before the patient leaves
tips.body: Swelling, bruising, and day-after concerns are common, and chasing payment afterward is awkward. Taking payment at checkout, or a card on file, keeps billing simple and professional.

tips.title: Track product cost against your price
tips.body: Neurotoxin and filler costs change with manufacturer promotions and loyalty tiers. Review your per-unit and per-syringe margin every few months so your rates keep covering product, supplies, insurance, and your time.

faqs.question: Should I bill per unit or per area for Botox?
faqs.answer: Per unit is more transparent and is the standard in most practices. Some injectors use per-area pricing for simplicity, but patients may then compare it poorly with per-unit prices elsewhere. If you bill per area, list the typical unit range on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on injectables?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax medical or cosmetic procedures performed by licensed providers, but retail products such as skincare often are taxable. Check with your state's department of revenue or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I send an invoice instead of collecting at the visit?
faqs.answer: You can, and contract injectors billing a practice usually do. For patients, collecting at the visit is far more common because treatments are elective, cash-pay, and the results are immediate.

faqs.question: How do I handle a touch-up after the first visit?
faqs.answer: Set your policy ahead of time and put it on the consent form and invoice. A common approach is no visit fee for a check within about two weeks, with additional units or filler billed at the standard rate.

faqs.question: Do I need to list my license on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Many injectors list the provider name and credentials, such as RN or NP, plus the practice name and address. Some states or employers have specific requirements for how credentials and supervision appear, so check your board and your practice's compliance rules.

estimate.intro: Injectors give estimates at consultations, in treatment plans, and by message when a prospective patient asks what a treatment will cost. Patients compare per-unit and per-syringe prices across practices, along with the injector's experience and the brand of product. A clear written estimate sets expectations before any product is drawn up.

scopeChecklist.item: Treatment areas and expected units or syringes
scopeChecklist.why: Unit needs vary by anatomy and muscle strength, so a range with a clear price per unit prevents surprise totals.
Botox, Dysport, and Xeomin or different filler lines have different pricing and results, and the patient should know which is planned.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether the estimate is a range or a firm total
scopeChecklist.why: Final amounts often depend on what you find at the visit. Say so in writing and explain what could change it.

scopeChecklist.item: Consultation fee and whether it is credited
scopeChecklist.why: Patients should know if the consult is free, charged, or applied to treatment if they proceed.
Clear terms on the time window and cost of adjustments prevent disputes about extra charges later.
A deposit and cancellation window protect your schedule, and stating them in the quote avoids friction at booking.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected results, downtime, and the fact that results vary
scopeChecklist.why: Setting realistic expectations about onset, longevity, bruising, and swelling reduces dissatisfaction that turns into payment disputes.

pricingTips.title: Give a range tied to a per-unit price
pricingTips.body: Quote something like 40-60 units at $13 per unit instead of one number, and explain that the final amount depends on your assessment on the day.

pricingTips.title: Offer a conservative plan and an optional add-on
pricingTips.body: Presenting a baseline treatment with a separate line for optional filler or additional areas lets patients choose without feeling pushed.

pricingTips.title: Account for full product and supply cost
pricingTips.body: Include the cost of product, needles, cannulas, anesthetic, supplies, and malpractice coverage when setting your prices, not just what the vial costs.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Product pricing, promotions, and your availability change, so state that the quote is good for 30 days or until a certain date.

faqs.question: Should I quote a price before seeing the patient in person?
faqs.answer: You can give a general per-unit or per-syringe price, but an exact total requires an in-person assessment. Many injectors state that the quote is an estimate until the consultation.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a consultation?
faqs.answer: Practices differ. Some offer free consultations to win new patients, while others charge $50-100 and credit it toward treatment. Pick one policy and state it in every quote.

faqs.question: What if a patient needs more product than quoted?
faqs.answer: Discuss the change and get agreement before using extra units or syringes. Document the consent in the chart and add the extra product as a separate line item.

costume-designer.intro: Costume designers work on film, television, theater, dance, music videos, commercials, cosplay commissions, and themed events. They bill production companies, theaters, schools, and private clients for design work, shopping and fittings, built or altered garments, rentals, and reimbursable purchases. Invoices often mix creative fees, labor, and pass-through costs, so clear line items matter.
costume-designer.pricingModel: Most costume designers separate the design fee from the costume budget. The design fee is usually a flat fee per production in theater and independent work, or a weekly rate on film, TV, and commercial jobs, often with prep weeks and shoot weeks listed. Union designers (such as those under USA 829 or IATSE agreements) follow contract minimums, while non-union and freelance designers set their own rates. Shopping, fittings, and tailoring are billed hourly or are included in the weekly rate. Garments built from scratch are quoted per piece, based on pattern work, sewing hours, and materials. Materials, rentals, and purchases are billed at cost, sometimes with a handling markup of 10 to 20 percent, or are drawn from a production-supplied budget with receipts submitted. Private commissions such as cosplay, pageant, and dance costumes are usually priced per piece with a deposit up front. Kill fees, rush fees, and extra revision charges are common.

rates.service: Design fee, small theater or school production
Design fee, regional theater or dance production
Custom garment construction (sewing and pattern work)

items.description: Costume design fee: community theater production of 'Into the Woods' (12 principal costumes, concept through opening)
Shopping and thrift sourcing trips
Actor fittings (6 actors, 2 rounds)
Custom construction: Witch's cloak and Baker's Wife dress
Alterations to rented and pulled pieces
Fabric, trims, and notions (receipts attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 14 days. 50% design fee deposit was received on signing and is shown as a credit on the final statement. Receipts for all reimbursable purchases are attached. Garments built or purchased remain property of the theater. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Production title, client, and your role (designer, assistant, costume supervisor)
invoiceChecklist.why: Productions often have several vendors and departments, and accounting needs to match your invoice to the right show and budget code.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design fee separated from labor and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients track the creative fee and the costume budget separately, and reimbursables are often paid from a different account.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized receipts and a purchase log for reimbursables
invoiceChecklist.why: Production accountants usually will not pay for fabric, shoes, or rentals without receipts, and itemizing prevents delays.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fitting, shopping, and build dates with hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Dated hours back up hourly charges and show the client when work happened relative to the schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental charges, pickup and return dates, and any damage or cleaning fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Rental houses bill late returns and damage, so your invoice should show who is responsible for those costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number, cost report code, or union/agreement reference when applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger productions and studios often cannot process payment without a PO or job number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Many designers collect a deposit up front. Showing it as a credit avoids confusion about what remains owed.

costume-designer.paymentTerms: Independent designers commonly ask for 25 to 50 percent of the design fee on signing, with the balance due at opening night, wrap, or within 14 to 30 days of invoicing. Film and television productions often pay on a weekly payroll schedule if you are an employee, or net 30 if you invoice as a contractor. For private commissions, a 50 percent deposit is typical to cover materials, with the balance due before delivery. Reimbursable expenses are best paid promptly or advanced through a production credit card or float, since designers should not carry large fabric and rental costs. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent monthly are common if stated in the agreement. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or card.

tips.title: Ask for a costume budget float
tips.body: Fabric, shoes, and rentals can add up quickly. Request an advance or a production card so you are not financing the show. If you must front costs, bill reimbursables weekly instead of waiting for wrap.

tips.title: Keep receipts organized from day one
tips.body: Photograph every receipt and log it by character or garment. A clean purchase log speeds approval and helps if the production asks why a line went over budget.

tips.title: Track revision and fitting limits
tips.body: State how many fitting rounds and design revisions are included. Bill additional rounds or director-requested changes at your hourly rate and note them on the invoice with dates.

tips.title: Bill for prep and wrap
tips.body: Research, sketches, breakdowns, returns, and cleaning take real time. If you are on a flat fee, make sure it covers these. If you are on a weekly rate, invoice the prep and wrap weeks.

tips.title: Clarify ownership of costumes and designs
tips.body: Say whether finished garments and renderings belong to the client or you, and whether the client may reuse them. Rental or resale of your built pieces may require a separate fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge a markup on fabric and purchases?
faqs.answer: Many designers pass through materials at cost and charge for their time separately. Others add a 10 to 20 percent handling fee for sourcing and carrying costs. Whichever you choose, state it in your agreement before purchasing.

faqs.question: Is the design fee separate from the costume budget?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. The design fee pays for your creative work. The costume budget covers materials, rentals, builds, and purchases. Invoice them separately so the client can see where each dollar goes.

faqs.question: What if the production wraps or cancels early?
faqs.answer: Include a kill fee or cancellation clause in your agreement. A common approach is to bill for work completed to date plus any non-refundable materials, and keep the deposit. Without a written term, it is harder to collect.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on costume work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and what you sell. Some states tax tangible goods such as a finished costume but not design services, and film production may qualify for exemptions. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I invoice rentals I sourced for the client?
faqs.answer: List each rental as a separate line with the rental house, dates, and cost, and attach the rental agreement. If the client is renting directly, make sure the paperwork shows that so you are not responsible for late or damage fees.

estimate.intro: Costume designers send estimates before accepting a show, commission, or build. Clients such as theater producers, directors, and private customers compare your design fee, your proposed costume budget, and how many garments are built versus pulled or rented. A clear estimate shows scope and limits so the budget does not drift.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of characters, costumes, and changes
scopeChecklist.why: A show with 8 actors in 20 looks is a very different job than 8 actors in 8 looks, and the count drives your hours.

scopeChecklist.item: Built, pulled, rented, and purchased breakdown
scopeChecklist.why: Construction costs far more than thrifting or renting. Specifying the mix sets expectations and protects your time.
List whether you provide sketches or renderings, a costume plot, research boards, and shopping lists, since each takes time.
Without limits, fittings and director changes can expand without pay. State what is included and the rate for more.

scopeChecklist.item: Costume budget and who controls it
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the estimate includes materials or if the client supplies a separate budget, and how overages are approved.
Fittings, tech week, photo calls, and shoot days set deadlines. Rush fees may apply if the timeline is compressed.

scopeChecklist.item: Ownership, care, and return of garments
scopeChecklist.why: Decide who keeps the costumes, who handles laundry and repairs during the run, and what happens to rentals after closing.

pricingTips.title: Quote design fee and costume budget separately
pricingTips.body: Give a flat design fee and a separate estimated budget for materials, builds, and rentals. This keeps your fee from being squeezed when materials cost more than expected.

pricingTips.title: Price builds from a muslin and hours estimate
pricingTips.body: For each built piece, estimate pattern drafting, mockup, sewing, and finishing hours. Add a buffer for complex items such as corsets, period tailoring, or heavy beading.

pricingTips.title: Offer a range with assumptions
pricingTips.body: If the script or design is not final, give a range and list assumptions such as the number of looks and built pieces. Update the quote in writing if the scope grows.

pricingTips.title: Get a signed approval and deposit
pricingTips.body: Have the client sign the estimate and pay a deposit before purchasing fabric or starting a build. This protects you if the production changes or cancels.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Fabric prices, rental availability, and your own schedule can change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is normal. Charge for deeper work such as a script breakdown, research, or sketches, or credit that fee toward the project if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client with a very small budget?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of the rate. Propose more pulling and thrifting, fewer built pieces, and fewer fittings, and show what the client gets at each budget level.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: Say in the estimate that changes in scope, script, or cast will adjust the price, and require written approval for overages above a set amount, such as 10 percent. Send a revised estimate before doing the extra work.

counseling-center.intro: Counseling centers are private practices or small group practices where licensed therapists, counselors, and sometimes associates or interns provide individual, couples, family, and group sessions. The invoices go to self-pay clients, to clients who need a receipt to file with their insurer for out-of-network reimbursement, and to organizations such as schools, employers, or courts that contract for services.
counseling-center.pricingModel: Most counseling centers charge a flat fee per session, usually for a 45 or 50 minute hour, with higher fees for intake evaluations, couples or family sessions, and longer sessions of 75 to 90 minutes. Fees often differ by clinician license level, with associates and interns charging less than licensed clinicians or psychologists. Many centers offer a sliding scale for clients with limited income, and some sell prepaid session packages. Group therapy is billed per person per session. Non-clinical or administrative work such as court letters, records copies, forms, and testimony is billed hourly and kept separate from therapy fees. Contracted services for schools, employers, and employee assistance programs are billed per session, per hour on site, or on a monthly retainer. Missed-appointment and late-cancellation fees are common and should be in the written policy the client signed.

rates.service: Sliding scale individual session (associate or intern)

Late cancellation fee, appointment 3/20 cancelled with less than 24 hours notice

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment is due at the time of service unless otherwise arranged. Balance due within 14 days of the invoice date. This statement includes the provider name, license number, diagnosis code, and CPT codes if you wish to submit it to your insurer for out-of-network reimbursement. We cannot guarantee reimbursement. Accepted: card, HSA/FSA card, check, or bank transfer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service for each session
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers need exact dates for out-of-network claims, and clients use them to reconcile payments and HSA or FSA spending.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT code for each service
invoiceChecklist.why: Codes such as 90791 for intake, 90834 or 90837 for individual sessions, and 90847 for family therapy let clients submit a superbill for reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code, when the client has agreed to its use
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers generally require an ICD-10 code to process out-of-network claims. Only include it with the client's knowledge, since it becomes part of a document they may share.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, license type, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and HSA or FSA administrators often require these details to accept a receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Practice name, address, and tax ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for reimbursement claims and for the client's own records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for clinical and non-clinical fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellation fees and report-writing charges are usually not reimbursable by insurance, so keeping them apart avoids rejected claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimal description of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Keep clinical detail out of the invoice. Use the service type and code only, since invoices may be seen by family members, employers, or billing staff.

counseling-center.paymentTerms: Most counseling centers collect payment at the time of service by card on file, with the fee for each session charged after the appointment. Clients who pay by invoice are usually given 7 to 14 days, and sometimes receive a monthly statement instead. Prepaid packages are paid in full before the first session and tracked against sessions used. Late cancellation and no-show fees are typically charged when someone misses an appointment without 24 to 48 hours notice, and the policy should be in the signed informed consent or financial agreement. Courts and employers on contract often pay net 30. Accepted methods commonly include credit and debit cards, HSA and FSA cards, checks, and bank transfer. Late fees on unpaid balances are less common than in other fields, and many practices instead pause scheduling new sessions when a balance gets large.

tips.title: Put your cancellation and fee policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: A signed financial agreement that covers session fees, late cancellation windows, returned payment fees, and what happens with unpaid balances protects you if a client disputes a charge. Remind clients of the policy at intake.

tips.title: Keep a card on file with written consent
tips.body: Having a card on file with signed authorization lets you charge for sessions and agreed fees without chasing payment. It also reduces awkward conversations about money inside the therapy relationship.

tips.title: Offer superbills on a regular schedule
tips.body: Many out-of-network clients need a monthly superbill. Sending them automatically at month end saves repeated requests and shows you are organized about billing.

tips.title: Be careful with collections
tips.body: Sending an account to collections can harm the therapeutic relationship and may raise ethical and licensing board issues in some states. Check your board's rules, give written notice first, and consider payment plans instead.

tips.title: Track sliding scale and package balances clearly
tips.body: Note the agreed reduced rate and how many prepaid sessions remain on each invoice so the client sees exactly what they paid and what is left.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and how is it different from an invoice?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized receipt that includes the details an insurer needs: provider license and NPI, tax ID, diagnosis code, CPT codes, dates of service, fees, and payment received. A basic invoice may not include all of these. Many centers use a single document that serves as both.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a missed session?
faqs.answer: In most private practices, yes, if your written policy says so and the client agreed to it. Insurance generally does not reimburse missed-appointment fees, so list them as a separate line item and be consistent in applying the policy.

faqs.question: Should I include the diagnosis on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if the client needs it for an insurance claim and understands it will appear on the document. For clients paying privately with no reimbursement, you can leave it off and list only the service and code.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on counseling sessions?
faqs.answer: In most states, health and counseling services are not subject to sales tax, but rules vary. Check with your state department of revenue or an accountant, especially for non-clinical services like workshops or sold materials.

faqs.question: How do I bill a school or employer that contracts with my center?
faqs.answer: Invoice the organization, not the individual client, and use a contract or purchase order number. List the date, service type, hours or number of sessions, and the agreed rate, and avoid naming individual clients unless the contract and releases allow it.

estimate.intro: Counseling centers rarely send quotes for standard therapy, but they do provide written fee estimates for self-pay clients, good faith estimates for uninsured or self-pay clients, and proposals for contracted services such as employee workshops, school-based counseling, or group programs. Clients compare per-session cost, how long treatment may last, and whether insurance reimbursement is possible.

scopeChecklist.why: A 45-minute session and a 90-minute session cost different amounts, and clients need to know which one the estimate covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected number and frequency of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Giving a realistic range, such as weekly for 8 to 12 weeks, helps clients plan their costs while making clear that treatment length depends on their needs.
Fees vary by provider, and a client assigned to an associate at a lower rate should know that and who supervises.
Stating the notice window and fee up front prevents disputes later.
Letters, forms, records requests, phone calls longer than a few minutes, and court-related work are usually billed separately.
State whether you are out of network, whether you provide superbills, and that you cannot guarantee reimbursement.

scopeChecklist.item: For contracts: location, headcount, travel, and materials
scopeChecklist.why: Workshops and on-site services should define the number of participants, hours on site, preparation time, and handouts to avoid scope creep.

pricingTips.title: Give a good faith estimate when required
pricingTips.body: In the US, providers are required to give uninsured and self-pay clients a good faith estimate of expected charges for scheduled services. Check the current federal requirements and your state rules for format and timing.

pricingTips.title: Present a range, not a promise
pricingTips.body: Treatment length is uncertain, so quote the per-session fee and a likely range of sessions, and state that the estimate may change if the client's needs change.

pricingTips.title: Price contracted work by the hour plus prep
pricingTips.body: For workshops or on-site services, include preparation and travel time, not just time in the room, and set a minimum fee for short engagements.

pricingTips.title: Show package discounts clearly
pricingTips.body: If you offer a block of sessions at a reduced rate, show the per-session price, the total, your refund policy for unused sessions, and any expiration.

faqs.question: Do I have to give clients an estimate before the first session?
faqs.answer: For uninsured and self-pay clients in the US, a good faith estimate is generally required when services are scheduled at least a few days in advance and on request. Details vary, so check current federal and state guidance.

faqs.question: How do I estimate the number of sessions?
faqs.answer: Use a range based on the presenting concern and your usual approach, such as 6 to 12 sessions, and explain that it is a planning figure. Revisit it during treatment planning and update the client if it changes.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the initial consultation call?
faqs.answer: Many centers offer a free 10 to 15 minute phone consultation to check fit. Longer calls or any clinical work should be billed at your normal rate, and the client should know that before the call.

faqs.question: What should a quote for a workshop or group program include?
faqs.answer: Include the topic, length, number of participants, location or format, preparation time, materials, travel, the total fee, deposit, cancellation terms, and who is responsible for confidentiality and participant consent.

counselor.intro: Counselors in private practice, including licensed professional counselors, marriage and family therapists, school and career counselors, and addiction counselors, bill clients for individual, couple, family, and group sessions. Many also bill for assessments, workshops, clinical supervision, and written reports. Clients may pay out of pocket, use a superbill to seek insurance reimbursement, or pay through an employer or program.
counselor.pricingModel: Most counselors charge a flat fee per session, usually based on a 45 to 55 minute hour. Rates are often higher for couples, family, and intensive sessions that run 75 to 90 minutes. Many offer a sliding scale for a limited number of clients based on income. Extra work such as court-related reports, letters, phone calls beyond a few minutes, records requests, and testimony is typically billed hourly or at a flat administrative fee. Initial intake or assessment sessions are often priced higher than follow-up sessions. Career counselors and coaches sometimes sell packages of sessions at a small discount. Group sessions are billed per person per session. Clinical supervision for associate-level clinicians is billed per hour or per month. Counselors who take insurance bill the contracted rate and collect copays or deductibles, while out-of-network clients receive a superbill.
