sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days. A superbill with diagnosis and procedure codes is available on request for out-of-network reimbursement. Cancellations require 24 hours notice. Card, HSA/FSA card, check, and bank transfer accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service for each session
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and clients reimbursing out of network need exact dates, and it keeps your billing matched to your clinical notes.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT code and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Codes like 90791, 90834, 90837, and 90847 tell an insurer what service was provided and support reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code if issuing a superbill
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers generally require an ICD-10 diagnosis for reimbursement. Include one only when the client has agreed to it, since it goes on a record outside your practice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license type, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network claims typically require provider credentials, and many states expect licensure information on billing documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax ID or SSN used for billing
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers need a billing identifier on a superbill. Many counselors use an EIN to avoid putting a personal SSN on documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimal, neutral service descriptions
invoiceChecklist.why: Invoices can be seen by family members or employers. Use 'counseling session' instead of details about what was discussed to protect confidentiality.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for fees outside sessions
invoiceChecklist.why: Cancellation fees, letters, and report time are not covered by insurance, so listing them separately avoids confusion over what is reimbursable.

counselor.paymentTerms: Most private practice counselors collect payment at the time of the session by card on file, because unpaid balances in therapy can strain the relationship. Clients with a monthly invoice are usually given 7 to 14 days to pay. Cancellation policies of 24 to 48 hours notice are standard and should be signed in the intake paperwork before any fee is charged. Late fees are uncommon, though some practices add a modest fee or pause scheduling after a balance goes unpaid for 30 days. Accepted methods commonly include credit and debit cards, HSA and FSA cards, checks, and electronic transfers. Insurance-billing counselors collect copays at the session and bill the insurer for the rest, with any patient balance invoiced after the claim is processed.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: Have the client sign a fee agreement that states the session rate, cancellation window, no-show fee, and what is not billable to insurance. Charging a late cancellation fee is much easier when it was agreed to in advance.

tips.title: Keep a card on file
tips.body: Storing a card with written consent lets you charge session fees and agreed cancellation fees without awkward conversations. Review your state's rules and your payment processor's terms for recurring or stored charges.

tips.title: Be careful with what the invoice reveals
tips.body: Use general descriptions and send invoices only to the contact method the client approved. Clients may share mailboxes or devices with people who should not know they are in counseling.

tips.title: Offer superbills monthly or on request
tips.body: Out-of-network clients need a clear document to submit to their insurer. Generating one on a set schedule reduces repeated requests and speeds up their reimbursement.

tips.title: Limit and track sliding scale slots
tips.body: Decide how many reduced-fee clients you can carry, set an income-based schedule, and review it each year. Record the agreed rate on the invoice so your income and rates stay consistent.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a missed or late-canceled session?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if the policy was disclosed and signed beforehand. Insurance plans usually do not cover missed appointments, so the fee is billed to the client directly. Many counselors waive it for emergencies or illness at their discretion.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and when do I need to give one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with your credentials, the client's information, dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis codes, and fees paid. Clients who see you out of network use it to ask their insurer for reimbursement.

faqs.question: Should I include a diagnosis on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Only on a superbill or insurance claim, and only after discussing it with the client. A plain invoice for a client paying out of pocket does not need a diagnosis, which helps protect privacy.

faqs.question: Can I bill for phone calls, emails, and letters?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fee agreement says so. Many counselors include brief contact of about 10 minutes at no charge and bill longer calls or documents in prorated time or at a flat fee. Insurance usually does not cover these.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on counseling sessions?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional counseling services are not subject to sales tax. Rules vary and may apply to products or some workshops, so check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Counselors rarely send formal quotes for ongoing therapy, but written fee estimates are common for assessments, evaluations, workshops, group programs, supervision, and employer or school contracts. Clients and organizations compare per-session cost, the number of sessions expected, what insurance may cover, and what extra charges could apply.

scopeChecklist.why: State whether it is a 45, 53, or 90 minute session and what service type it is, so the client knows exactly what each fee covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated number of sessions or duration
scopeChecklist.why: For assessments or short-term programs, a range of sessions helps the client budget. Make clear it is an estimate and treatment length may change.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee per session and any package price
scopeChecklist.why: A clear per-unit price prevents misunderstandings if the client stops early or needs more sessions than planned.

scopeChecklist.item: What insurance may or may not cover
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume coverage. Explain out-of-network status, that you cannot guarantee reimbursement, and that they should check benefits with their plan.

scopeChecklist.item: Costs for extras like reports, letters, and court time
scopeChecklist.why: These are billed outside normal sessions and can be expensive. Listing hourly rates or minimums up front avoids surprise charges.
Including the policy with the estimate sets expectations from the start and makes it enforceable.
State whether sessions are in person or by video, and note any state licensure limits that affect where clients can be located during sessions.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for session count, not a guarantee
pricingTips.body: Treatment needs change and clinical outcomes cannot be promised. Give an estimate such as 6 to 10 sessions and state that the plan can be revised.

pricingTips.title: Price assessments and evaluations separately
pricingTips.body: Intake, psychological or career assessments, and written reports take significant time outside the session itself. Include time for scoring, notes, and report writing in the price.

pricingTips.title: Use package pricing sparingly
pricingTips.body: A modest discount for prepaying a block of sessions works for career counseling or workshops. Define the refund policy if the client stops early, and check your licensing board's rules on prepayment.

pricingTips.title: Give a good faith estimate where required
pricingTips.body: In the US, the No Surprises Act requires a good faith estimate for uninsured and self-pay clients in many situations. Check current federal and state requirements and use a compliant format.

faqs.question: Do I have to give a cost estimate before the first session?
faqs.answer: For self-pay and uninsured clients, federal rules generally require a good faith estimate of expected charges when scheduling services. Check current requirements for your practice type and keep a copy in the client file.

faqs.question: How do I quote a group program or workshop?
faqs.answer: Price per participant per session if enrollment is open, or a flat fee if contracting with an organization. Include the number of sessions, group size cap, materials, and your cancellation terms.

faqs.question: What if the client needs more sessions than I estimated?
faqs.answer: Discuss it with the client and update the plan in writing. An estimate is not a cap, but you should tell them when the expected cost will change and get agreement before continuing.

faqs.question: How should I quote forensic or court-related work?
faqs.answer: Most counselors charge hourly, often with a retainer paid in advance, and a separate higher rate for testimony and travel. Spell out minimums for cancelled court dates and prep time.

countertop-installer.intro: Countertop installers fabricate and set granite, quartz, marble, laminate, butcher block, and solid surface tops in kitchens, baths, and laundry rooms. Clients include homeowners, remodeling contractors, kitchen and bath dealers, and builders. Invoices usually cover templating, fabrication, edge work, cutouts, installation, and removal of old tops.
countertop-installer.pricingModel: Most stone and quartz work is priced per square foot of finished countertop, with the price tied to the material tier and often including templating, fabrication, and basic installation. Extras are billed separately: sink and cooktop cutouts, edge profiles beyond standard, backsplash, waterfall ends, seam fills, and plumbing disconnects. Installers who only set tops, with no fabrication, often charge per square foot or a flat fee per job, and add a minimum trip charge for small jobs like vanities. Tear-out and disposal of old tops is usually a separate line, either per linear foot or flat. Material is either supplied by the installer with a markup or supplied by the client or a dealer, in which case labor-only pricing applies. Deposits of 30 to 50 percent are standard because slabs are ordered and cut to a specific layout and cannot be resold easily.

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $2,000 received at template approval. Balance due on completion of installation. Silicone seams and sealed surfaces need 24 hours before heavy use. Remaining slab offcuts available to client on request. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month after 15 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material type, brand, color name, and slab or lot number
invoiceChecklist.why: Stone and quartz vary between lots, so a record of exactly what was installed settles disputes about color or pattern.

invoiceChecklist.item: Measured square footage and linear footage by section
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often compare the final bill to the quote, and itemized measurements show where the numbers came from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Edge profile, backsplash height, and cutout list
invoiceChecklist.why: These are the most common add-ons, and listing them separately keeps price differences between quote and invoice clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: A deposit is normal on custom-cut material, and the invoice should show it was credited so the client is not billed twice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices for work above a dollar threshold. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and site-condition charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-level walls, extra seams, stairs, or crane and lift fees were not in the original quote and need written support.

invoiceChecklist.item: Care and sealing instructions, and warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Documenting what you told the client about sealing, heat, and cleaning limits protects you from later damage claims.

countertop-installer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 30 to 50 percent is typical at template approval or slab order, with the balance due on completion or within a few days of install. Residential clients commonly pay by check, card, or bank transfer. Card fees are often passed on or built into the price on large jobs. For contractor and dealer accounts, net 15 to net 30 is common, sometimes with progress billing on multi-unit work. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing before work begins. Some states limit what you can charge for deposits or interest, so check local rules.

tips.title: Collect the deposit before you order slabs
tips.body: A cut slab with a specific layout is hard to resell. Get the deposit before you place the order or schedule fabrication, and say in the contract that it is non-refundable once material is cut.

tips.title: Get sign-off on the template and layout
tips.body: Have the client approve seam locations, overhangs, and edge profile in writing after templating. Most complaints come from seams and pattern placement, and a signed layout answers them.

tips.title: Bill the plumbing and tear-out separately
tips.body: Disconnects, reconnects, and demolition take time and carry risk. Listing them as their own lines makes them easy to justify and easy to remove if the client handles them.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for small jobs
tips.body: A bathroom vanity or bar top costs nearly as much in travel, templating, and setup as a kitchen. A minimum job charge keeps small orders from losing money.

tips.title: Invoice remnants and waste honestly
tips.body: If you price by slab rather than square foot, say so. Clients who paid for a full slab may ask for the leftover pieces, so decide in advance whether they are included.

faqs.question: Should I bill by square foot or by the job?
faqs.answer: Most installers quote per square foot for standard kitchens and use a flat fee for small jobs like vanities. Whichever you use, show the measured square footage on the invoice so the total can be checked.

faqs.question: Can I charge sales tax on countertops?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, materials sold and installed as part of a real property improvement are taxed differently than retail sales. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change the layout after templating?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a change order. If the slab is already cut, the client pays for the new material and the additional fabrication. Get the change approved in writing before you proceed.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who withholds final payment over a minor issue?
faqs.answer: Put a punch-list process in the contract. Note any minor items on a completion sheet, collect the balance or an agreed holdback, and schedule the fix. Many states also give contractors lien rights, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: Do I bill for templating if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: You can, if it is in your terms. Many installers include templating in the job price and credit it back only if the job proceeds, or charge a flat templating fee if the order is cancelled.

estimate.intro: Countertop installers send estimates after a site visit and measurement, usually before templating. Clients often collect quotes from several fabricators and compare price per square foot, but they may not notice differences in what is included. A clear written estimate lets them compare fairly and sets the scope before slabs are ordered.

scopeChecklist.item: Material, color, and slab or tier
scopeChecklist.why: Price differences between levels or brands are large, and a vague description leads to disputes about what was promised.
State whether the estimate is based on a rough measurement or a final template, since the price can change after templating.

scopeChecklist.item: Edge profile, backsplash, and cutouts included
scopeChecklist.why: Listing what is in and out of the base price avoids surprise charges later.

scopeChecklist.item: Seam locations and number of seams
scopeChecklist.why: Seams are visible and often a concern. Noting that final seam locations are set at templating avoids arguments.
Clients often assume tear-out and sink hookup are included. State clearly who handles them.
Cabinets must be level, secured, and in place before templating. Say that delays or rework caused by the site may be billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Lead time, validity period, and deposit terms
scopeChecklist.why: Slab prices change, so state how long the quote is valid and when the deposit is due to lock in material.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a template when possible
pricingTips.body: Rough field measurements can be off by several square feet. If the price depends on a final template, say so and give the per-square-foot rate used to adjust.

pricingTips.title: Break out the extras
pricingTips.body: List the base countertop price separately from cutouts, edges, backsplash, and removal. Clients can then remove or add items without you rewriting the whole quote.

pricingTips.title: Account for slab yield and waste
pricingTips.body: Stone is sold by the slab, and layout and pattern matching can leave unusable areas. Price based on the slabs you need, not only the finished square footage.

pricingTips.title: Offer a good-better-best option
pricingTips.body: Showing two or three material tiers at different prices helps clients choose within their budget and often prevents them from shopping the job on price alone.

faqs.question: How long should a countertop quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Slab and material prices can change, so a shorter validity period is reasonable for imported stone or fluctuating markets.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most installers quote free for standard jobs. For complex work like multi-room remodels, curved tops, or out-of-area visits, some charge a fee and credit it to the job if the client signs.

faqs.question: Can I give a price over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range per square foot, but label it as approximate. A firm quote needs a site visit to check cabinets, access, and measurements.

faqs.question: What if the final template is larger than the estimate?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that the price is adjusted per square foot after templating. This keeps the change fair and avoids a dispute when the final invoice is higher.

courier.intro: Couriers are independent drivers, bike messengers, and small delivery businesses who move documents, packages, medical specimens, auto parts, and other time-sensitive items for local businesses. Invoices usually go to law firms, medical labs, print shops, florists, and e-commerce sellers, often on a recurring weekly or monthly basis. A good invoice shows each delivery, the service level, and any extras like waiting time or mileage.
courier.pricingModel: Most couriers price by the delivery, built from a base fee plus mileage, with surcharges for speed and special handling. Common service levels are standard (same-day within a few hours), rush (within 60-90 minutes), and direct or hot-shot (immediate, no other stops). Many add a per-mile charge beyond a set radius, such as the first 5 or 10 miles included. Waiting time is usually billed after a grace period of 5 to 15 minutes. Regular business clients are often put on a monthly account with a negotiated per-stop or zone rate, sometimes with a minimum monthly volume. Add-ons include signature or ID verification, after-hours and weekend fees, fuel surcharges, tolls, parking, and extra pieces or heavy items. Medical couriers often charge a route rate or a flat fee per scheduled stop, and may add a fee for handling specimens or controlled materials.

rates.service: Scheduled route (medical or legal, multiple stops)

items.description: Standard same-day delivery, law office to county courthouse (8 miles)
Rush delivery, signed documents to downtown title company
Additional mileage beyond 10-mile radius
Waiting time at courthouse clerk window (after 10 min grace)
Signature and ID verification
Fuel surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Service period: March 1-15. Individual delivery log with pickup/drop-off times and signatures attached. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Accepted: ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized delivery log with date, pickup and drop-off addresses, and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reconcile against their own records, and a clear log prevents disputes over which deliveries happened and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service level for each delivery (standard, rush, direct)
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by speed, so the client can see why a given stop cost more.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage and any included radius
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how extra distance charges were calculated and that the first miles were already covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Waiting time with start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Wait charges are a common point of pushback, and timestamps back them up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recipient name, signature, or proof of delivery reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Proves the item was delivered, which matters for legal documents, specimens, and high-value goods.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or reference code
invoiceChecklist.why: Many businesses need a PO or matter number to approve payment or bill the cost to their own customer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, parking, and other pass-through costs with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from your fee keeps your rates clear and lets the client recover the costs if needed.

courier.paymentTerms: Couriers serving one-off customers usually collect payment at booking or on delivery by card. Business accounts are normally invoiced weekly, biweekly, or monthly, with terms of net 15 or net 30. Weekly billing helps cash flow because fuel and vehicle costs are paid up front. Many couriers charge a late fee of 1.5% per month on overdue balances and pause service on accounts that are more than 30 days past due. New accounts are sometimes asked for a card on file or a small deposit. Common payment methods are ACH, check, and card, with card fees sometimes passed on or built into rates.

tips.title: Define the included radius and grace period up front
tips.body: State how many miles the base fee covers and how long you wait before billing for time. Putting this in your rate sheet and on each invoice avoids arguments about small charges.

tips.title: Bill recurring clients weekly
tips.body: Fuel, maintenance, and insurance costs hit immediately. Weekly invoicing for regular accounts keeps unpaid balances from piling up, and a short, clean delivery log makes approval quick.

tips.title: Track every stop as it happens
tips.body: Log pickup time, delivery time, and signature at each stop using your phone or a route sheet. Reconstructing a month of deliveries from memory leads to missed charges and disputes.

tips.title: Charge for after-hours and rush work consistently
tips.body: Surcharges only hold if they are in the rate sheet the client agreed to. Apply them every time so a rush job does not become the expected standard price.

tips.title: Keep mileage records for taxes
tips.body: If you use your own vehicle, a mileage log supports your deductions. It also gives you the data to confirm your per-mile rates cover real costs.

faqs.question: Should I charge per delivery or per mile?
faqs.answer: Most couriers use a base fee per delivery with mileage added beyond an included radius. Pure per-mile pricing is more common for direct or long-distance runs. A base fee ensures short trips still cover your time, loading, and parking.

faqs.question: Can I bill for waiting time?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you tell the client in advance. A typical setup is a 5 to 15 minute grace period, then a flat charge per 15 minutes. Record arrival and departure times so the charge is easy to defend.

faqs.question: How do I pass fuel costs on to clients?
faqs.answer: Either build fuel into your per-mile rate or add a separate fuel surcharge line. A surcharge can be a flat amount or a percentage of the delivery fee, and it is easier to adjust when gas prices change. Make sure clients see it in your rate terms first.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on courier services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax delivery or transportation services and others do not, and the rules can differ for local delivery of goods. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional before adding or leaving out tax.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes a delivery?
faqs.answer: Send your proof of delivery: timestamps, recipient name, signature, or a photo if your agreement allows it. Having this ready when you send the invoice usually resolves disputes quickly.

estimate.intro: Couriers quote before work starts when a client has a recurring route, a large one-time job like an event or office move-out, or a multi-stop run that does not fit a standard rate. Business clients often compare a per-stop price, a monthly account rate, and the speed guaranteed against other local couriers or app-based services.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off locations, or the service area and zones
scopeChecklist.why: Distance drives the price, so the quote should state exactly where it applies and what happens outside it.
Standard, rush, and direct deliveries are priced differently, and clients should know what time commitment they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: Package size, weight, and handling needs
scopeChecklist.why: Oversized, heavy, fragile, or temperature-sensitive items may need a larger vehicle, extra time, or a surcharge.
A recurring route can justify a lower per-stop rate, and the quote should say what volume that rate depends on.

scopeChecklist.item: Waiting time, grace period, and failed delivery terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies what is charged if the recipient is not available or the pickup is not ready.

scopeChecklist.item: Extras such as signature, ID check, tolls, parking, and after-hours fees
scopeChecklist.why: Listing these ahead of time stops them from feeling like surprise charges later.
Fuel costs and your schedule change, so the price should hold only for a set period, with clear terms for late cancellations.

pricingTips.title: Price from your real cost per mile
pricingTips.body: Add fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation, and your time to find a cost per mile and per hour. Use that as the floor, then add margin for rush and specialty work.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present standard, rush, and direct choices side by side. Clients often pick the middle option, and you avoid being compared on price alone.

pricingTips.title: Quote routes as a package
pricingTips.body: For scheduled routes, offer a flat rate per stop or per route run rather than a mileage meter. It is easier for the client to budget and for you to invoice.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for traffic and wait time
pricingTips.body: If the route runs through dense traffic, hospitals, or courthouses, include realistic time or state the wait-time rules in the quote.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an estimate for a one-time job?
faqs.answer: Give a flat quote when addresses, timing, and cargo are clear. If wait time, traffic, or number of stops could change, give a quote with a stated base price and the per-mile or per-15-minute rates for anything beyond it.

faqs.question: How long should a courier quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common for recurring accounts. For one-time jobs, a shorter window of a few days keeps the price in line with current fuel costs and your availability.

faqs.question: How do I quote a recurring route?
faqs.answer: Map the stops, estimate the time and mileage per run, and price by stop or by route. Set a minimum monthly volume and state how the rate changes if volume drops or stops are added.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before starting?
faqs.answer: For one-off jobs, written acceptance by email is usually enough. For regular accounts or sensitive cargo like medical specimens, a signed service agreement covering liability, insurance, and handling is a good idea.

court-reporter.intro: Freelance court reporters, small reporting firms, and agency-affiliated reporters invoice law firms, insurance carriers, corporations, and sometimes individual parties for taking down and producing the record of depositions, arbitrations, hearings, and other proceedings. A typical invoice combines an appearance fee, a per-page charge for the transcript, and add-ons such as exhibits, expedited delivery, realtime, and travel.
court-reporter.pricingModel: Most freelance reporting is billed in two parts: an appearance (attendance) fee for showing up and taking the proceeding, and a per-page rate for producing the certified transcript. The original transcript goes to the ordering attorney at a higher per-page rate, and each additional copy for other parties is billed at a lower rate. Turnaround drives price: standard delivery is usually 10 to 20 business days, and expedited, 3-day, next-day, or same-day delivery adds a surcharge per page. Other common line items are exhibit handling, realtime feed, rough drafts, video or remote platform fees, minimum transcript charges, mileage or parking, and late-cancellation fees. Many reporters and firms publish a rate sheet and keep to it, with contract rates for repeat clients. Official court reporters employed by a court often have transcript rates set by statute or court order, so check your jurisdiction's schedule if that applies to you.

rates.service: Appearance fee, half day (up to 4 hours)

rates.unit: per page, added to the base rate

Original certified transcript with e-transcript, standard 15-day delivery
Copy of transcript for opposing counsel (e-transcript)
Exhibit scanning and attachment (Exhibits 1-9)
Realtime feed to counsel
Electronic delivery and secure exhibit folder

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Please reference the invoice number with payment. Checks payable to the reporter named above; ACH and card payments accepted. Federal Tax ID available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Case caption, case number, and jurisdiction
invoiceChecklist.why: Billing departments at law firms match invoices to a specific matter. Without the caption and number, your invoice can sit unpaid while someone tries to figure out which file it belongs to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Proceeding date, location, and witness or hearing name
invoiceChecklist.why: This ties the charges to a specific event and answers questions about whether an appearance fee, a half day, or a full day applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ordering attorney, firm, and party represented
invoiceChecklist.why: The person who ordered the transcript is usually responsible for the original and the appearance fee, and other parties are billed for their copies. A clear record of who ordered what prevents disputes between firms.

invoiceChecklist.item: Page count and per-page rate for each product
invoiceChecklist.why: Original, copy, expedited, and rough draft are priced differently. Showing pages times rate lets the client check your math against your rate sheet or their contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery turnaround and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Expedited surcharges need to match what was ordered. The delivery date also documents that you met the agreed deadline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or certification number, where your state issues one
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states license court reporters, and the number often appears on the certificate. Including it on the invoice helps with client vendor records and shows you are credentialed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons: exhibits, realtime, video or remote platform, travel, parking, cancellation
invoiceChecklist.why: Add-ons are the most common source of pushback. Listing each one separately with quantity and rate keeps the total easy to defend.

court-reporter.paymentTerms: Reporting work is usually billed after the transcript is delivered, on net 30 terms, and many firms and insurance carriers pay on a 30 to 60 day cycle through accounts payable. Deposits are uncommon with established law firms but reasonable for new or self-represented clients, large multi-day jobs, or out-of-town work with significant travel costs. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if they are stated on your rate sheet and on the invoice. Many reporters also hold the final certified transcript, or the expedited portion, until a new client pays or provides a deposit. Payment is typically by check, ACH, or card. Some agencies take payment only through their own system and then pay the reporter on a set schedule.

tips.title: Put cancellation and late-notice terms in writing before the job
tips.body: Last-minute cancellations are a regular loss in this field. Set a clear policy, such as a full or partial appearance fee if the job is cancelled within 24 or 48 hours, and include it on your rate sheet and booking confirmation. Then bill it on its own line so the client sees the policy being applied.

tips.title: Bill each party for their own copy
tips.body: Send the original and appearance fee to the ordering attorney, and invoice other attorneys separately for their copies at the copy rate. Splitting the invoices keeps one firm from paying for another's copy and speeds up payment.

tips.title: Charge a minimum transcript fee for short proceedings
tips.body: A 12-page deposition still takes setup, travel, and certification time. A minimum transcript charge or minimum appearance fee covers that, and it should be listed in your rates so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Track exhibits and delivery separately
tips.body: Exhibit-heavy cases can add hours of scanning and organizing. Count the pages and bill them per page or as a flat fee. The same goes for secure delivery or file hosting you provide.

tips.title: Invoice promptly after delivering the transcript
tips.body: Send the invoice the same day you deliver the transcript, while the case is fresh and the attorney's office is expecting it. Waiting weeks makes it harder to match your bill to a file and delays payment.

faqs.question: Do I charge for pages or for time?
faqs.answer: Most freelance reporters charge an appearance fee for time on site and a per-page rate for the transcript. Some also add an hourly overtime rate after a set number of hours or a certain time in the evening. Check whether your state or the court you work with sets rates, since official reporters often follow a fixed schedule.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a transcript that was ordered but then cancelled?
faqs.answer: If the proceeding went forward, you generally can bill the appearance fee even if the transcript is never ordered, and many reporters set a minimum transcript charge as well. For a cancelled proceeding, you can only charge what your written cancellation policy says, so make sure the client has seen it.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for paying for the original transcript?
faqs.answer: Usually the attorney or party who noticed the deposition or ordered the reporter. Other parties buy copies. Confirm the ordering party when you book and put their name on the invoice so there is no confusion over who owes what.

faqs.question: Is sales tax charged on transcripts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some treat transcripts as taxable, some treat them as a service and exempt them, and exemptions may apply for certain clients. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line if you collect it.

faqs.question: How should I handle an agency that books me?
faqs.answer: The agency usually invoices the end client and pays you according to its own pay schedule and split. Invoice the agency for your agreed appearance fee and per-page rate using their job number, and keep your own record of page counts and delivery dates.

estimate.intro: Court reporters usually give a quote when a firm or agency is booking a large or multi-day matter, comparing vendors, or planning an out-of-town proceeding. Clients compare appearance fees, per-page rates, turnaround options, and add-ons such as realtime, video, and remote platform fees. Since the final page count is unknown at booking, the quote is mostly a set of rates and assumptions rather than a single total.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of proceeding and expected length
scopeChecklist.why: A one-hour hearing, a half-day deposition, and a three-day arbitration are priced differently. State the expected duration and what happens if the proceeding runs long.

scopeChecklist.item: Appearance fee terms: half-day versus full-day, and overtime
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know when the fee moves from half-day to full-day and what rate applies after a set number of hours or after a certain time in the evening.

scopeChecklist.item: Per-page rates for original and copies, with estimated page count
scopeChecklist.why: Page count is the biggest variable. Giving a rate and an estimated range, such as 100 to 150 pages, sets expectations without locking you into a number.
State the standard delivery time and list the expedited choices and their added per-page costs so the client knows the price before choosing.

scopeChecklist.item: Add-ons included or excluded: exhibits, realtime, rough draft, video, remote platform
scopeChecklist.why: These are the items most likely to be disputed. Say which are in the quote and which are billed separately if requested.
Out-of-area jobs can include mileage, tolls, parking, and sometimes lodging. List what applies and at what rate so there is no surprise at invoicing.
Setting the policy up front gives you a basis to bill if the proceeding is cancelled late or a short job triggers a minimum.

pricingTips.title: Quote rates and a page range, not a fixed total
pricingTips.body: Nobody knows how many pages a deposition will produce. Present the per-page rate and an estimated range, and make clear that the invoice will reflect the actual certified page count.

pricingTips.title: Offer clear tiers for turnaround
pricingTips.body: List standard, expedited, and daily delivery with the added per-page cost for each. Clients can then choose a tier and you can plan your workload around the deadline.

pricingTips.title: Price volume and repeat work with a rate sheet
pricingTips.body: Firms and agencies that send you many jobs expect a consistent rate. A written rate sheet with an optional contract discount is easier to maintain than negotiating each quote. Keep the discount modest so it still covers your production time.

pricingTips.title: Build in the work that does not show on the page count
pricingTips.body: Prep, glossary building, scoping, proofreading, and certifying take time that is only partly reflected in per-page pricing. If your rates look too low once those hours are included, adjust the appearance fee or minimum rather than the page rate.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price for a deposition?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Page count varies with the witness, the attorneys, and how long the proceeding runs. A flat total can leave you underpaid on a long transcript. If a client needs a number, give an estimate with a page range and explain it will be adjusted to the actual count.

faqs.question: How long is a quote good for?
faqs.answer: Thirty to ninety days is common for rate quotes. For specific dates, the quote holds only as long as the date is confirmed, since a reporter's calendar can fill. State an expiration date and note that rates are tied to the dates booked.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before a big job?
faqs.answer: It is reasonable to ask for one from new clients, self-represented parties, or for multi-day work with heavy travel. Established law firms and agencies typically pay after delivery on their normal terms, so a deposit is not expected there.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower rate than my rate sheet?
faqs.answer: Consider whether the volume, payment reliability, and ease of work justify it. If you agree to a lower rate, put it in writing for that client, and keep your appearance fee, cancellation policy, and expedited surcharges intact so the discount applies only to the base page rate.

creative-agency.intro: Creative agencies are small studios and teams that produce branding, websites, campaigns, video, and content for business clients. They bill for strategy and design time, production work, third-party costs like stock assets and printing, and often ongoing retainers for continued support.
creative-agency.pricingModel: Most creative agencies mix three models. Project fees cover defined deliverables such as a brand identity or a 10-page website, usually billed in milestones (for example 50% upfront, 25% at design approval, 25% at launch). Monthly retainers cover a set number of hours or deliverables for ongoing work like social content, design support, or ad management. Hourly rates are used for out-of-scope work, small jobs, and change requests, and they often differ by role (strategist, designer, developer, project manager). Pass-through costs such as stock photography, font licenses, printing, media spend, and freelancer fees are billed separately, commonly with a 10-20% handling markup that is stated in the contract. Rates vary a lot by market, agency size, and client budget.

Brand identity package (logo, palette, type, basic guidelines)
Marketing website design and build (5-10 pages)
Social media content retainer (12-16 posts per month)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances are subject to 1.5% monthly interest. Final files are released on receipt of full payment. Third-party license costs are billed at cost plus 10% handling as outlined in the agreement signed March 4.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and contract or SOW reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's finance team can match it to an approved budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or phase being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which stage was completed (discovery, design approval, launch) and justifies why payment is due now.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours for out-of-scope or hourly work, by role
invoiceChecklist.why: Change requests are the most disputed line on agency invoices, so show the date, task, and rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately with markup noted
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock assets, fonts, printing, and freelancer fees need to be visible and match what the contract allows.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number and billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size and corporate clients often reject or delay invoices that lack a purchase order number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and file transfer terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States that licenses and final file ownership transfer on full payment, which protects you if a bill goes unpaid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and hours used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: For retainer clients, shows the month covered, hours consumed, and any overage or rollover.

creative-agency.paymentTerms: Agencies commonly require a deposit of 30-50% before work starts, then bill remaining milestones as they are reached. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month and due on receipt or within 7-15 days. For larger clients, net 30 is common, though many small agencies push for net 15. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in the contract. Accepted methods are usually ACH or bank transfer and credit card, with card fees sometimes passed on to the client. Many agencies pause work or hold final files until overdue invoices are settled, and they should state that in the agreement.

tips.title: Tie final delivery to final payment
tips.body: Hold source files, live site launch, or final artwork until the last milestone is paid. State this in the contract and on each invoice so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Specify how many rounds are included at each stage. Bill extra rounds hourly and list them as separate line items so scope creep is documented.

tips.title: Bill pass-through costs promptly
tips.body: Invoice stock licenses, printing, and freelancer costs in the period they occur. Waiting until the project ends makes them easier to forget and harder to collect.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: Long projects can run for months. Billing at kickoff, approval, and launch keeps cash flow steady and gives the client natural decision points.

tips.title: Track retainer hours monthly
tips.body: Send a short summary of hours used and work completed with each retainer invoice. Clients who see the work are less likely to question the fee.

faqs.question: Should a creative agency charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Project pricing suits defined deliverables like a brand identity or website, since clients want a fixed number. Hourly works for open-ended support and change requests. Many agencies use project fees for the core work and hourly rates for anything outside the scope.

faqs.question: How do I bill for stock images, fonts, and printing?
faqs.answer: List them as separate line items at cost, with a handling markup if your contract allows it, commonly 10-20%. Keep receipts in case the client asks for backup.

faqs.question: What happens if a client stops responding mid-project?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that lets you invoice for work completed to date if the client is inactive for a set period, such as 30 days. Deposits are generally non-refundable for work already done, but check how your contract and local rules handle this.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on creative services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain digital or design services, and many tax physical goods like printed materials. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for creative concepts the client rejects?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says the fee covers time and concepts developed, not only the approved result. Milestone billing makes this easier because you are paid for the discovery and concept phases when they are done.

estimate.intro: Creative agencies send a proposal or quote before any design work begins, usually after a discovery call or brief. Clients often compare several agencies on price, timeline, number of revisions, and what is actually included, so a clear scope matters as much as the total.

scopeChecklist.why: A logo package, website, or campaign can mean very different things. Listing items and formats (AI, SVG, PDF, live site) prevents later disagreement.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Sets limits on the back-and-forth that most often causes overruns. State what a round is and how extra rounds are billed.
Delays often come from slow feedback. Build in review deadlines and note that the schedule shifts if they are missed.
Lists what you need from them, such as copy, photos, logins, and a single point of contact for approvals.
Clarifies whether stock, fonts, printing, hosting, and media spend are included or billed extra, and at what markup.
States what the client owns, when it transfers, and any limits such as licensed fonts or portfolio use.
Shows deposit and milestone amounts and how long the price holds, since costs and availability change.

pricingTips.title: Price on value and scope, not only hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate your hours by role, add a buffer of 15-20% for revisions and coordination, and check the total against what the work is worth to the client. Pure hourly math often underprices branding and strategy.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting three tiers, such as a logo only, a full identity, or identity plus a website, helps clients choose a level instead of just comparing your total to a competitor's.

pricingTips.title: Break the quote into phases
pricingTips.body: Separating discovery, design, and production shows where the money goes and lets a client approve in stages. It also sets up your milestone invoices.

pricingTips.title: Quote retainers with clear inclusions
pricingTips.body: Spell out monthly hours or deliverables, response times, and what happens to unused time. This avoids disputes about whether leftover hours roll over.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals and discovery work?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is normally free. For detailed strategy, research, or custom concepts, many agencies charge a paid discovery phase of a few thousand dollars, which can be credited toward the full project if the client continues.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. A set expiry date protects you from price changes and from a full schedule when the client finally agrees.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that describes the added work, cost, and any timeline change, and get approval before you start. Bill it as a separate line on the next invoice.

faqs.question: Can I give a price range instead of a fixed number?
faqs.answer: Ranges work when the scope is unclear, such as a website with undecided features. Say what drives the price up or down, and convert the range to a fixed fee once the scope is defined.

creative-director.intro: Creative directors set the visual and conceptual direction for brands, campaigns, and products, then lead designers, writers, photographers, and other freelancers to carry it out. Freelance and small-agency creative directors bill for strategy, concept development, art direction, team oversight, and presentations to client stakeholders. Invoices often combine hourly or day-rate leadership time with pass-through costs such as talent, production, and licensing.
creative-director.pricingModel: Most independent creative directors bill by the day, by the hour, or on a monthly retainer, with project fees for defined campaigns or brand launches. Day rates are common because the work is often spent in workshops, shoots, and review meetings rather than in billable chunks of an hour. Project fees usually break into phases such as discovery, concept, development, and production oversight, each with its own price and milestone. Retainers cover a set number of hours or days each month, often with a rollover rule or a use-it-or-lose-it clause. Third-party costs (photographers, illustrators, stock and font licenses, printing, travel) are billed at cost or with a handling markup of 10-20 percent, stated up front. Usage rights and revision limits should be priced explicitly, because rush work, extra concept rounds, and expanded licensing are where scope tends to grow.

Review and feedback on designer deliverables

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Concept and art direction fees cover a license for use in digital and print for 12 months in the US; extended usage is quoted separately. Two revision rounds are included per deliverable. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, phase, and milestone being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Creative work is billed in stages, and clients need to match the invoice to an approved phase such as discovery, concept, or production.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate or statement of work
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the charges to agreed scope and makes it easy for accounts payable to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized pass-through costs with receipts or vendor invoices
invoiceChecklist.why: Photographers, printers, and licenses are often large line items, and clients will want proof of cost and any stated markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and license terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State where, how long, and in what media the work may be used, so extended use later is a clear new charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours or days worked, with dates for time-based billing
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reviewing day-rate or hourly charges expect to see when the work happened and what it covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: It documents when extra rounds trigger additional charges and heads off disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number and billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often will not process payment without a PO or the right contact on the invoice.

creative-director.paymentTerms: Creative directors typically collect 30 to 50 percent upfront on project work, with the balance split across milestones or due on delivery of final files. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month. Standard terms are net 15 or net 30, though agencies and larger companies may push for net 45 or 60, so confirm in the contract. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your agreement. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and final files or usage rights are often released only after the last payment clears.

tips.title: Tie usage rights to payment
tips.body: State in your contract that license for the final work transfers only after full payment. It gives you leverage if an invoice goes overdue and keeps the client from running campaigns unpaid.

tips.title: Bill pass-through costs separately from your fee
tips.body: Keep photographer, illustrator, and production costs on their own lines with a clear markup, if any. It makes your own fee easier to defend and protects you if a client questions the total.

tips.title: Get approval before ordering third-party work
tips.body: Have the client sign off on vendor costs in writing before you commit. If a shoot goes over budget, you are not carrying the expense or arguing about it later.

tips.title: Define revision rounds and bill the extras
tips.body: Include a set number of concept and revision rounds in the estimate, then log extra rounds at your hourly rate. Without that line, endless feedback becomes unpaid work.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: Bill when each phase is approved rather than waiting until launch. Campaigns slip for reasons outside your control, and milestone billing keeps your cash flow from slipping with them.

faqs.question: Should a creative director charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Hourly or day rates suit open-ended or advisory work and ongoing oversight. Project fees suit defined deliverables like a brand launch or campaign concept. Many creative directors use a project fee for the concept phase and a day rate for production oversight.

faqs.question: Can I mark up photographers and other vendors I hire?
faqs.answer: Yes, many creative directors add 10 to 20 percent for coordinating, contracting, and carrying the cost. State the markup in your estimate and contract before work starts, and show the vendor cost clearly on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a pitch that may not win the work?
faqs.answer: Charge a pitch fee when you can, even a reduced one, and say so up front. If a client expects free speculative work, state in writing what is included, who owns the ideas if you are not hired, and whether the fee is credited toward the project if you win.

faqs.question: Do I charge extra for usage rights?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Your fee should cover a defined license, such as 12 months in specific media and territories. Broader use, longer terms, or paid media placement can be priced as add-ons, and the invoice should note the license granted.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on creative services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the type of deliverable. Some states tax certain design or printed goods and not services, and rules vary on pass-through costs. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant to see what applies to you.

estimate.intro: Creative directors send an estimate or proposal before any concept work starts, often after a discovery call or brief. Clients usually compare it against agency quotes and other freelancers, so the document needs to show what leadership, strategy, and oversight are worth, not just a total. A good estimate separates your fee from production costs so the number can be understood line by line.

scopeChecklist.why: List exactly what you are producing, such as a campaign concept deck, brand guidelines, or art direction on set, so there is no argument about what the fee covers.
Breaking the work into discovery, concept, development, and production lets you bill by stage and gives the client clear approval points.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Creative work can expand without limit. Setting the number of concepts and rounds makes extra requests a priced change.

scopeChecklist.item: Who is on the team and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: State whether designers, writers, and photographers are hired by you or by the client, and whether their fees are inside or outside your price.
Defines where and for how long the client can use the work, and what expanded use will cost.
Shoot costs, talent, printing, and licenses can be larger than your fee. Show them as estimates with an allowance for overages.
Delays in feedback or assets can stall the schedule. Spell out turnaround times and what happens to deadlines if the client is late.

pricingTips.title: Quote in phases
pricingTips.body: Price discovery, concept, and execution separately. Clients can approve the first phase with less risk, and you are not locked into a flat price for work that is still undefined.

pricingTips.title: Build in management time
pricingTips.body: Overseeing freelancers, running feedback calls, and handling revisions takes real hours. Include them in your fee or list them as a separate line rather than assuming they are free.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three scopes, such as a core concept, a full campaign, and a campaign with ongoing oversight. Clients compare options on scope instead of only on price.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry and a contingency
pricingTips.body: Make the quote valid for 30 days and include a 10 to 15 percent contingency on production budgets. Costs for talent, venues, and printing change quickly.

faqs.question: Should my estimate include the cost of photographers and other vendors?
faqs.answer: Include them as separate lines so the client sees your fee and production costs apart. Label them as estimates, say whether you will mark them up, and require written approval for any increase.

faqs.question: How detailed should a creative director's estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to define deliverables, phases, revision rounds, and usage rights. One page of clear scope and a pricing table works better than a long document. Larger brand or campaign projects may call for a full statement of work.

faqs.question: Is a creative brief the same as an estimate?
faqs.answer: No. The brief describes the goals and audience for the work. The estimate states what you will do, for how much, and under what terms. Many creative directors request a brief or hold a discovery call before quoting.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to cut the price after seeing the quote?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of the rate. Remove a concept round, a deliverable, or a phase, and let the client see what each change saves. That keeps your rate intact and the agreement balanced.

creative-services.intro: Creative services providers include freelance graphic designers, brand identity designers, illustrators, photographers, videographers, motion designers, and small studios. They invoice for design and production time, deliverables, usage rights, revisions, and out-of-pocket costs such as stock assets, fonts, and printing.
creative-services.pricingModel: Creative work is priced three main ways. Hourly billing is common for ongoing support, small edits, and projects with unclear scope. Flat project fees are standard for defined deliverables like a logo package, a website design, or a product photo shoot. Retainers cover a set number of hours or deliverables each month for steady clients. Photographers and videographers often charge a day rate or half-day rate plus editing time. Many creatives also price usage rights separately, since a logo for a local shop is worth less than the same artwork on national packaging. Rush fees (often 25-50 percent), extra revision rounds beyond the agreed number, stock licenses, and pass-through costs with a modest markup are usually listed as separate lines.

items.description: Brand identity design: primary logo, secondary mark, color palette, type selection
Business card and letterhead design (print-ready files)
Additional revision round beyond the two included
Brand usage guide (PDF, 8 pages)
Licensed typeface (web and print, one business), billed at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Final invoice for brand identity project. 50% deposit of $1,322.50 was received on March 4 and is credited below. Balance due within 14 days. Full copyright transfers to the client on receipt of final payment. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and deliverables list
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to a specific piece of work so the client can match the invoice to the approved scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate or contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms the price was agreed and points to the terms covering revisions, ownership, and cancellation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and license terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States where, how long, and in what media the work may be used, and whether copyright transfers on payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why the total differs from the original quote when the client went past the included revisions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (stock, fonts, printing, props, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing third-party costs separately avoids confusion and lets you document reimbursements or markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear what has already been paid and what the client still owes.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often cannot process payment without it.

creative-services.paymentTerms: Most independent creatives take a deposit of 30-50 percent before starting, then bill the balance on delivery or at agreed milestones. Larger projects such as brand systems or video productions are often split into three payments: start, mid-project approval, and final delivery. Standard terms are due on receipt to net 30, with net 14 common for small clients; agencies and corporations may push for net 45 or 60. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in advance. Common payment methods are ACH transfer, credit card, and check. Many designers hold final files until the last payment clears.

tips.title: Release final files after payment
tips.body: Deliver watermarked or low-resolution previews during the project, and send the layered or high-resolution files only when the balance is paid. State this in your contract and on the invoice.

tips.title: Limit revisions in writing
tips.body: Include a set number of revision rounds, usually two or three, and define a round as one consolidated set of feedback. Bill additional rounds at an hourly or flat rate and list them on the invoice.

tips.title: Charge separately for usage and exclusivity
tips.body: If a client wants broad or buyout rights, perpetual use, or exclusivity in their industry, add a line item for it. Photographers and illustrators in particular often leave money behind by bundling rights into a low fee.

tips.title: Track scope changes as they happen
tips.body: When a client adds pages, extra shots, or new formats, send a short change confirmation by email with the added cost. Then put it on the invoice so nothing is a surprise.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones for long projects
tips.body: A video or branding project that runs for months should not wait until the end to bill. Tie payments to approvals such as concept sign-off or rough cut.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or by flat project fee?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best when the scope is clear and you can estimate your time well, since you keep the benefit of working efficiently. Hourly works better for open-ended work, ongoing edits, and clients who change direction often. Some creatives quote a flat fee and bill hourly for anything outside the defined scope.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on creative work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital goods, design services, or tangible deliverables like prints, while others do not tax services at all. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant, and show any tax collected as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit if the client has not signed anything?
faqs.answer: You can ask for one, but it is safer to get a signed estimate or contract first. A written agreement showing the deposit amount, deliverables, and cancellation terms makes it much easier to enforce if there is a dispute.

faqs.question: How do I bill for stock images, fonts, or printing?
faqs.answer: List them as separate line items. Many creatives bill at cost, while others add a markup of 10-20 percent for handling and purchasing time. Whichever you choose, say so in your estimate so the client expects it.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels mid-project?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say that work completed up to the cancellation date is billable and that the deposit is non-refundable. Invoice for the work done, including any approved concepts, and note whether you retain rights to unused work.

estimate.intro: Creative professionals send an estimate or proposal before starting work, usually after a discovery call or review of a brief. Clients often compare several quotes, so the document needs to show exactly what is included, how many revisions are covered, and who owns the work. Vague quotes tend to produce scope creep and unpaid revisions.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing items like a primary logo, social avatars, and AI, EPS, and PNG files prevents later arguments about what was promised.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Sets a clear limit on how much back-and-forth is included in the price.
Ties delivery dates to the client responding on time, so delays on their side do not become your problem.
Spells out whether the client gets a license or full copyright, and when the transfer takes effect.

scopeChecklist.item: Third-party costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Stock photos, fonts, models, location fees, printing, and travel can add up quickly and should be agreed before they are incurred.
Specifies that the client supplies copy, photos, logos, or approvals, and what happens if they arrive late.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule, deposit, and validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Shows when money is due and how long the quote holds before prices may change.

pricingTips.title: Price the value, not only your hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate your time as a baseline, then adjust for the client's size, how the work will be used, and the expected return. A logo for a regional chain justifies a higher fee than one for a hobby project, even if the hours are similar.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three options, such as a basic logo, a logo with brand guide, and a full identity system, gives clients a way to choose without negotiating the price down. It also anchors the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for revisions and communication
pricingTips.body: Meetings, emails, file prep, and feedback rounds often take 20-30 percent more time than the design itself. Include that overhead in your flat fee rather than treating it as free.

pricingTips.title: Charge a rush fee in the quote
pricingTips.body: If the client needs the work in a shorter time than your normal schedule, add 25-50 percent and state it as a separate line so the reason is clear.

faqs.question: Should I charge for creating an estimate or proposal?
faqs.answer: For a simple project, estimates are usually free. For complex work that needs research, mockups, or a detailed strategy, some creatives charge a paid discovery or scoping phase, often credited toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Include an expiration date so you are not held to old pricing or a schedule slot that has since been filled.

faqs.question: What if the project grows after the client accepts the estimate?
faqs.answer: Refer back to the listed deliverables and revision limits, then send a written change order with the added cost and any timeline changes before doing the extra work. Get approval in writing, even by email.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed contract in addition to the estimate?
faqs.answer: A signed estimate that includes scope, payment terms, and rights can serve as a basic agreement for small jobs. For larger or higher-risk projects, a separate contract is safer and can be reviewed by a lawyer.

credit-note.intro: A credit note is the document a business sends when it needs to reduce or cancel part or all of an invoice it already issued. Freelancers, contractors, shops, and small agencies send them for billing errors, returns, cancelled work, partial refunds, and goodwill adjustments. Each one ties back to an original invoice and shows exactly what is being credited and why.
credit-note.pricingModel: A credit note is not a service you sell, so there is no price for the document itself. What you set is the amount of each adjustment. Most small businesses follow a written policy: overbilled hours or duplicate charges are credited at 100% of the original rate, returned goods are credited at the sale price minus a restocking fee, and cancelled work is credited minus time already spent or a retained portion of the deposit. Goodwill credits for late or unsatisfactory work are usually a percentage of the affected line item, not the whole invoice. Credit the tax in proportion to the amount credited, and decide up front whether the credit is refunded to the original payment method or held as a balance against the next invoice.

rates.service: Credit for overbilled or duplicated hours
Restocking fee kept on returned goods
Retained portion of deposit on cancelled work
Partial credit for incomplete or missed deliverable
Early payment discount applied after payment
Card processing fee withheld from refund

items.description: Credit: duplicated revision hours billed on Invoice #1042
Credit: returned unused 24x36 prints (Invoice #1042, line 4)
Restocking fee, 15% of returned print value ($168.00)
Goodwill credit for delivery 5 days past agreed date

sampleInvoice.notes: Credit note issued against Invoice #1042 dated March 3. Net credit of $477.80 will be applied to your next invoice, or refunded to the original payment method within 10 business days if you reply to request it. Sales tax has been adjusted in proportion to the credited items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Original invoice number and date
invoiceChecklist.why: The credit note has to point to the exact invoice it adjusts so both sides can reconcile their books.

invoiceChecklist.item: Unique credit note number
invoiceChecklist.why: A separate numbering sequence, such as CN-0007, keeps credits from being confused with invoices and gives you an audit trail.

invoiceChecklist.item: Line-by-line description of what is credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and accountants need to see which items, hours, or charges are being reduced, not just a lump sum.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reason for the credit
invoiceChecklist.why: A short reason such as billing error, return, or cancellation prevents questions and supports your records if you are audited.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax adjustment
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charged sales tax, the tax on the credited amount should be reduced too. Check your state rules on how to report it.

invoiceChecklist.item: How the credit will be settled
invoiceChecklist.why: State whether it is a refund, an applied balance, or an offset against an unpaid invoice, and give the timeframe.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining balance on the original invoice
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the new amount owed after the credit avoids the client paying the old total by mistake.

credit-note.paymentTerms: A credit note either reduces what the client still owes or creates money owed back to them. If the original invoice is unpaid, apply the credit and send the client the revised balance with the usual due date. If it was already paid, offer a refund to the original payment method, typically within 5 to 10 business days, or a credit balance applied to the next invoice. Card refunds often do not return the processing fee to you, so mention that in your refund policy. Do not charge late fees on any portion of an invoice that has been credited, and make sure late fees already added are reversed if the underlying charge was an error.

tips.title: Never edit or delete a sent invoice
tips.body: Once an invoice has gone out, issue a credit note instead of changing it. This keeps your numbering clean and leaves a clear record for your accountant and for the client.

tips.title: Write your credit policy before you need it
tips.body: Put restocking fees, cancellation terms, and deposit rules in your contract or quote. A credit note that follows terms the client already agreed to rarely gets disputed.

tips.title: Credit the tax along with the item
tips.body: If the original invoice included sales tax, reduce it in proportion. Leaving the tax in place means the client overpays and you may over-report tax collected.

tips.title: Send the credit note and a revised balance together
tips.body: Clients get confused when they receive a credit and still see the old invoice total. State the new amount due, or the refund amount, in the same message.

tips.title: Keep a log of credits by reason
tips.body: Reviewing credits every quarter shows patterns such as repeated billing errors or scope disputes, which usually point to a problem in your quoting or time tracking.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a credit note and a refund?
faqs.answer: A credit note is the document that records a reduction in what the client owes. A refund is the actual return of money. You can issue a credit note and settle it by refund, by applying it to a future invoice, or by offsetting it against another unpaid invoice.

faqs.question: Should I cancel the original invoice or issue a credit note?
faqs.answer: If the invoice has already been sent, issuing a credit note is the safer practice. Some accounting setups let you void an invoice that was never sent or paid, but check with your accountant before voiding anything the client has seen.

faqs.question: Do I have to adjust sales tax on a credit note?
faqs.answer: In many states, yes. If you credit a taxable item, the tax collected on it is also credited or refunded, and you adjust it on your next sales tax return. Rules differ by state, so confirm with your state's revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I issue a partial credit note?
faqs.answer: Yes. Partial credits are common for a single overbilled line, a damaged item, or a discount. List only the amounts being reduced and show the remaining balance on the original invoice.

faqs.question: How long should I keep credit notes?
faqs.answer: Keep them with your invoices and other financial records. Many small businesses keep records for at least three to seven years, but the right period depends on your tax situation, so check with your accountant.

estimate.intro: A credit note is not quoted like a job, but you often need to give the client a proposed adjustment before issuing one. That happens when a client disputes a charge, asks to cancel part of a project, or wants to return goods. The client compares your proposed credit against what they paid, what they received, and what your contract says.

scopeChecklist.item: Which invoice and line items are affected
scopeChecklist.why: Naming the exact charges under review keeps the discussion focused and stops the client from asking for a credit on the whole invoice.

scopeChecklist.item: Work completed or goods delivered to date
scopeChecklist.why: A credit for cancelled work depends on what has already been done, so list hours spent or items shipped.

scopeChecklist.item: Policy or contract clause that applies
scopeChecklist.why: Pointing to the agreed cancellation, return, or revision terms shows the proposal is based on terms the client already accepted.
Restocking fees, non-refundable deposits, and processing fees should be stated as a number so the client is not surprised.
Showing whether tax is credited too makes the net amount clear and avoids a follow-up question.
Say whether the client gets a refund or an applied balance, and by what date, so expectations are set before the note is issued.

scopeChecklist.item: Deadline to accept the proposed credit
scopeChecklist.why: A response date prevents the dispute from dragging on and holding up payment on the remaining balance.

pricingTips.title: Start from the contract, not from goodwill
pricingTips.body: Calculate the credit from your written terms first. If you want to offer extra goodwill, show it as a separate line so the client sees what is policy and what is a courtesy.

pricingTips.title: Show the math
pricingTips.body: Present original amount, credited amount, retained fees, and net result in a short table. A client who can follow the numbers is less likely to push back.

pricingTips.title: Offer a credit balance as an option
pricingTips.body: Many clients will take a credit toward future work if it is slightly larger than a cash refund. Only offer this if you can honor it and want the repeat business.

pricingTips.title: Price the dispute against your time
pricingTips.body: If a client is asking for a small credit and arguing will cost more hours than it is worth, a quick partial credit can be cheaper than a drawn-out discussion. Record why you made the exception.

faqs.question: Should I send a proposed credit in writing before issuing the credit note?
faqs.answer: Yes, when there is any disagreement. A short written proposal with the amounts and reasons gives the client a chance to accept, and it protects you if the dispute continues.

faqs.question: Can I keep a deposit when a client cancels?
