Homeowners usually collect two or three quotes and compare the total price, decking material, footing and framing details, and how long the work will take.

scopeChecklist.why: Size and height off the ground drive material and labor costs and whether a permit and railings are required.

scopeChecklist.item: Decking, framing, and railing materials by brand and grade
scopeChecklist.why: Quotes that say only composite or treated lumber are hard to compare, and clients may assume a higher grade than you priced.

scopeChecklist.item: Footing type and depth, and ledger attachment
scopeChecklist.why: Footings and ledger flashing are what make a deck safe, and cheaper bids often cut them. Spelling them out justifies your price.
State who pulls the permit, who pays for it, and whether engineered drawings or surveys are needed.
Removing an old deck, grading, and disposal are easy to leave out and expensive to absorb.
Note that rot, buried obstacles, or code upgrades found after opening up the old structure will be priced as change orders.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, duration, and weather policy
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for scheduling, delays from rain, and material lead times for special orders.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a material takeoff, not just a per-foot rule
pricingTips.body: Per-square-foot rates are good for ballpark figures, but a final quote should come from a list of lumber, hardware, decking, and railing with current supplier prices. Add a waste factor of 8 to 15 percent for decking, more for diagonal patterns.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best material options
pricingTips.body: Presenting pressure-treated, cedar, and composite versions of the same deck lets clients choose a budget and keeps the conversation about options rather than haggling over your labor.

pricingTips.title: Set a short quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Lumber and composite prices can move quickly. Valid for 14 to 30 days is common, with a note that prices may change after that.

pricingTips.title: Price add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: Lighting, benches, skirting, pergolas, and built-in planters should be separate lines so clients can remove or add them without a full re-quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many deck builders offer free estimates for standard jobs. For complex designs, drawings, or engineering, a design fee of a few hundred dollars is common, often credited toward the project if the client signs.

faqs.question: How detailed should a deck quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that another builder could price the same job. Include dimensions, materials by name, footing and framing details, railing, stairs, permits, and exclusions. A one-line total invites disputes and makes comparisons unfair to you.

faqs.question: What happens if the quote is lower than the final cost?
faqs.answer: A fixed-price quote means you absorb ordinary overruns, so the scope and exclusions must be clear. Anything outside the written scope, such as rot or a design change, should go through a signed change order before you do the work.

faqs.question: Does the quote turn into the contract?
faqs.answer: It can if the client signs it and it includes the terms a contract needs, but many states require specific language for home improvement contracts, such as cancellation rights and license numbers. Check your local rules and consider using a separate written contract.

delivery.intro: Independent couriers, local delivery businesses, and small fleet owners send these invoices. They bill business clients such as restaurants, florists, law offices, medical labs, furniture stores, and e-commerce shops for same-day runs, scheduled routes, and specialty deliveries. Most invoices cover a mix of per-stop or per-mile charges plus add-ons like wait time, after-hours fees, and fuel surcharges.
delivery.pricingModel: Delivery work is priced by distance, by stop, by time, or by a combination. One-off courier runs usually have a base fee that covers a set number of miles, plus a per-mile charge beyond that. Recurring route clients often get a flat rate per stop or a flat weekly or monthly route fee. Hourly or day rates apply to dedicated driver work, such as a full day moving goods between locations. Add-ons are common and should be itemized separately: rush or same-day premiums, after-hours and weekend surcharges, wait time after a free window (often 10 to 15 minutes), extra stops, heavy or oversized items, stairs or white-glove handling, signature or ID verification, and fuel surcharges when gas prices jump. Tolls and parking are usually passed through at cost. Many solo operators set a minimum charge per run so short trips still cover vehicle costs and time.

rates.service: Local same-day courier run (base, first 5-10 miles)
Cargo van or box truck with driver, full day

items.description: Scheduled route deliveries, Mon-Fri, Oak Street Florist to residential and business addresses (Mar 3-7)
Same-day rush delivery, downtown to airport cargo office (Mar 5)
Mileage beyond 10-mile base, airport run (Mar 5)
Wait time at pickup after 15-minute window (Mar 6)
Weekend delivery surcharge (Sat Mar 8 event order)
Bridge toll reimbursement (receipts attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Accepted: ACH, check, or card. Late balances may be charged 1.5% per month after 30 days. Delivery confirmations and signed proof of delivery available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery dates, pickup and drop-off addresses, and stop count
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reconcile invoices against their own order records, and a missing address or date is the most common reason for a delayed payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or distance for each run
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge per mile or beyond a base distance, the client needs to see how the total was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons: rush fees, wait time, after-hours, extra stops, fuel surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating surcharges from base rates avoids disputes and shows the client these were agreed extras, not padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, parking, and other pass-through costs with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Reimbursable expenses should be listed at cost so they are clearly separate from your service charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Proof of delivery reference (signature, photo, or tracking number)
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client claims a package did not arrive, a reference to your delivery record settles it quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or order reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Many businesses will not process payment without a PO or job number on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, contact details, and any required local or motor carrier registration numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often need these for their vendor records, and some jurisdictions or cargo types require specific registrations. Check your local rules.

delivery.paymentTerms: Occasional customers and one-off runs are often paid at booking or on delivery, by card or digital payment. Recurring business clients are usually invoiced weekly or biweekly with net 15 or net 30 terms, and weekly billing keeps your cash flow steady when you carry fuel and vehicle costs yourself. Large or specialty jobs, such as furniture delivery or multi-day contracts, may call for a deposit of 25 to 50 percent. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing before the work starts. ACH and card payments are the most common methods, and some clients still pay by check.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge per run
tips.body: A 2-mile delivery still costs you a trip to pickup, loading time, parking, and the return. A minimum of $15 to $25 keeps short jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Define free wait time in writing
tips.body: State in your terms how many minutes of waiting are included, such as 10 or 15, and what each block after that costs. Clients are much more willing to accept wait charges when they saw the policy up front.

tips.title: Use a fuel surcharge clause
tips.body: Instead of raising every rate when gas prices spike, add a line that applies a surcharge when fuel passes a set price. Itemize it so clients can see it is tied to costs.

tips.title: Keep delivery proof organized by invoice
tips.body: Save signatures, photos, and timestamps in a folder or log matched to each invoice period. When a client disputes a charge weeks later, you can answer in minutes.

tips.title: Track mileage and expenses separately for taxes
tips.body: What you bill clients for mileage is not the same as what you deduct for vehicle costs. Keep a mileage log and receipts, and ask a tax professional how to handle it for your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge per mile, per stop, or a flat rate?
faqs.answer: It depends on the work. Per-mile pricing fits irregular one-off runs. Per-stop pricing fits dense routes where stops are close together. Flat route rates work for recurring clients with predictable schedules. Many drivers combine them, such as a base fee plus mileage and a per-stop charge for extra drops.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the return trip?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you agree to it. Many couriers price round-trip distance when the vehicle has to come back empty, especially for long or rural runs. State whether your mileage includes the return so the client is not surprised.

faqs.question: How do I bill for tolls and parking?
faqs.answer: List them as separate line items at actual cost and attach receipts when you can. Do not fold them into your base rate unless you quoted an all-inclusive price.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on deliveries?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. In some states delivery charges are taxable, in others they are exempt or only taxable when tied to a taxable sale. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if a client refuses to pay because they say an item was not delivered?
faqs.answer: Provide your proof of delivery, such as the signature, photo, GPS timestamp, or recipient name. A clear record usually resolves it. If the item was truly not delivered, consider adjusting only that stop rather than the full invoice.

estimate.intro: Delivery businesses send quotes for recurring route work, multi-stop jobs, large or fragile items, and long-distance or time-sensitive runs. One-off courier jobs are often priced by phone or text, but business clients usually want a written rate sheet or quote. Clients compare per-stop and per-mile rates, but also fees for waiting, rush service, and insurance coverage.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off locations, or the service area for recurring routes
scopeChecklist.why: Distance drives your cost, and a quote tied to specific addresses or zones prevents arguments when stops change.
A 2-hour window is cheaper to serve than a fixed appointment time. State which one you priced.

scopeChecklist.item: Item type, size, weight, and handling needs
scopeChecklist.why: Heavy, bulky, fragile, or temperature-sensitive items need different vehicles, labor, and care, and your price should reflect that.

scopeChecklist.item: Included wait time and what happens after
scopeChecklist.why: Delays at pickup or drop-off are a major source of lost income, so state the free window and the rate after it.

scopeChecklist.item: Extra stops, returns, and failed delivery policy
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether a no-answer redelivery or a return to sender costs extra so you are paid for repeat trips.

scopeChecklist.item: Surcharges: rush, after-hours, weekend, fuel, tolls
scopeChecklist.why: Listing them in the quote means they are agreed to in advance, not surprises on the invoice.
Clients shipping valuable goods will ask what is covered. Spell out your cargo coverage or declared-value limits so expectations are clear.

pricingTips.title: Price from your real cost per mile and per hour
pricingTips.body: Add fuel, maintenance, insurance, vehicle depreciation, and your own time. Divide by realistic billable miles and hours, including the unpaid drive back. Then add margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer a simple rate sheet for repeat clients
pricingTips.body: A one-page sheet showing base fees, per-mile rates, per-stop rates, and surcharges lets clients self-quote small jobs and reduces back-and-forth.

pricingTips.title: Quote a minimum and a range for uncertain jobs
pricingTips.body: When stop counts or wait times are unknown, quote a minimum charge plus your hourly or per-stop rate beyond it, rather than a fixed number you may regret.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Fuel costs and your schedule change. A 14 to 30 day validity period protects you if a client comes back months later expecting the same price.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or an hourly estimate for a delivery job?
faqs.answer: Use a flat price when distance, stops, and handling are clear. Use an hourly or per-stop rate with an estimated range when the job has unknowns such as long unloading or uncertain wait times.

faqs.question: Do I need a written quote for small jobs?
faqs.answer: A text or email with the price, addresses, and time window is usually enough for a single run. For recurring routes or high-value items, send a formal written quote so terms are on record.

faqs.question: How do I quote a route with changing stop counts?
faqs.answer: Quote a per-stop rate with a minimum per route day, such as a minimum of 8 stops or a flat daily fee. That covers your base cost when volume is low and scales when it is high.

faqs.question: What should I do if the job changes after I quote it?
faqs.answer: Tell the client as soon as scope changes, such as added stops, a longer route, or a heavier load, and send a revised price before you proceed. Keep the change in writing.

delivery-service.intro: Delivery service owners include independent courier drivers, local same-day delivery companies, and small fleets that move packages, food, retail orders, medical specimens, and freight for business clients. Invoices usually go to recurring accounts such as florists, pharmacies, law offices, restaurants, and e-commerce shops, and bill for stops, miles, wait time, and special handling.
delivery-service.pricingModel: Most delivery services price by the delivery, by the mile, or by the hour, then add fees for extras. A common structure is a base fee that includes a set number of miles (often 5 to 10), plus a per-mile charge beyond that. Regular accounts often get a flat rate per route or a discounted per-stop price based on volume. Hourly or dedicated-driver pricing is common for multi-stop days and event runs. Add-ons include wait time after a grace period (often 10 to 15 minutes), after-hours or weekend rush surcharges, oversized or heavy items, signature or ID-verified delivery, returns, and fuel surcharges that move with pump prices. Tolls and parking are usually passed through at cost. Many solo drivers bill weekly or monthly for repeat clients and take card payment up front for one-off customers.

Large or heavy item delivery (cargo van or box truck, with liftgate or help)
Medical or legal document run with chain-of-custody

Mileage beyond 10-mile zone, outlying addresses
Signature-required delivery

Wait time at pickup, Mar 7 (beyond 10-minute grace)
Fuel surcharge, week of Mar 4

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Delivery log with timestamps and signatures available on request. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Please send questions about specific stops within 7 days of receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery dates, pickup and drop-off addresses, and order or tracking numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reconcile invoices against their own orders, and a missing reference number is the top reason a delivery charge gets questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized charges: base fee, mileage, stops, wait time, rush, and fuel surcharge on separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating extras shows what each charge covers and prevents disputes over a single lump total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wait time with start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients rarely remember delays at their dock or counter, so logged times back up the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, parking, and other pass-through costs with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Reimbursable costs should be shown at actual cost and kept apart from your service fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Proof of delivery reference (signature, photo, or timestamp log)
invoiceChecklist.why: If a customer claims a package never arrived, this shows the delivery was completed and supports payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, contact details, and any DOT, MC, or local business license number if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients and their accounting teams often need this to set up a vendor record and verify you are a legitimate carrier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or account code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients often will not process payment without it.

delivery-service.paymentTerms: One-time and residential customers usually pay by card at booking or on delivery. Recurring business accounts are most often billed weekly or monthly on net 15 or net 30 terms, and many small operators prefer weekly billing to keep cash flow steady. Deposits are uncommon for standard deliveries but reasonable for large freight, event logistics, or scheduled dedicated-driver days, often 25% to 50% up front. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in writing ahead of time. Accepted methods are typically card, ACH or bank transfer, and digital payment apps. Many small couriers require a card on file for new accounts until they establish payment history.

tips.title: Set a wait time grace period and enforce it
tips.body: Unpaid waiting is one of the biggest hidden losses for drivers. State a free window of 10 to 15 minutes in your terms, then bill in set increments after that and log the times.

tips.title: Use a fuel surcharge instead of constantly changing your rates
tips.body: Tie the surcharge to a published fuel price or a fixed percentage of the invoice. It lets you cover swings in gas costs without renegotiating with every client.

tips.title: Keep delivery logs that match your invoice
tips.body: Save timestamps, mileage, and proof of delivery for each job. When a client disputes a line, you can answer with records in minutes.

tips.title: Bill repeat clients on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Invoice every Friday or on the first of the month so clients know when to expect it. Predictable billing means more predictable payment.

tips.title: Track vehicle costs against what you charge
tips.body: Fuel, insurance, maintenance, and depreciation add up per mile. Check your per-mile rate against your real cost at least once a year, and keep mileage records for tax purposes.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the mile or by the delivery?
faqs.answer: Many couriers do both: a flat base fee that covers a set distance, then a per-mile rate beyond it. Flat per-delivery pricing works well for repeat routes with consistent distances. Per-mile pricing protects you on long or unpredictable runs.

faqs.question: Can I bill tolls and parking separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most clients expect it. List them as pass-through costs at actual cost and attach receipts or a short log. Mention this in your service agreement so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How do I handle a customer who is not home for a delivery?
faqs.answer: Set a policy up front. Many drivers charge a failed delivery or redelivery fee, or bill for the wait time. Put the policy in your terms and include photos or timestamps of the attempt on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on delivery?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax delivery or transportation charges, some tax them only when bundled with a taxable sale, and many do not tax them at all. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client pays late every month?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder a few days before the due date and again on the day after. If it continues, move them to shorter terms, require a card on file, or ask for payment in advance. Late fees help only if they were in your written terms.

estimate.intro: Delivery services send quotes when a client wants a regular route, a one-time large or specialized job, or an event or multi-stop day. Clients typically compare base rate, mileage rules, extra fees, and reliability, so it helps to explain exactly what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off locations, number of stops, and estimated mileage
scopeChecklist.why: Distance and stop count drive the price, and a changed route is the most common cause of quote disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery window and any rush or after-hours requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Time-sensitive work costs more, and the quote should state what time commitment you are making.

scopeChecklist.item: Item size, weight, and handling needs
scopeChecklist.why: Heavy, fragile, or oversized items may need a larger vehicle, a second person, or a liftgate, all of which change the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Wait time policy and grace period
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know when waiting starts being billed before the day begins.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: signature, photo proof, tracking updates, returns
scopeChecklist.why: Extras like ID checks or returns take time, and listing them clarifies what the quoted price covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Fuel surcharge, tolls, and parking terms
scopeChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should be clearly separate so the final bill does not exceed the quote unexpectedly.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation and failed delivery terms, plus quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: This protects you from wasted trips and from fuel price changes if the client waits too long to accept.

pricingTips.title: Price from your real cost per mile and per hour
pricingTips.body: Add up fuel, insurance, maintenance, vehicle payments, and your own time, then divide by billable miles and hours. Many drivers only count fuel and underprice routes as a result.

pricingTips.title: Offer volume tiers for regular accounts
pricingTips.body: A lower per-stop rate at 20, 50, or 100 deliveries per month encourages steady business. Keep the tiers in writing so the discount does not become permanent when volume drops.

pricingTips.title: Quote routes as a package, with extras listed separately
pricingTips.body: Give one clear price for the standard route, then list rush, wait time, and special handling as add-ons. Clients can compare easily and you are covered when needs change.

pricingTips.title: Build in time for traffic and loading
pricingTips.body: For hourly or multi-stop quotes, estimate based on realistic drive times at the hours the route will actually run, not off-peak map estimates.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an estimate range for a multi-stop route?
faqs.answer: A flat price works when stops and distances are fixed. If addresses may change, quote a base price with a per-stop rate and per-mile rate for changes so you are not locked in.

faqs.question: How long should a delivery quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to thirty days is typical. For fuel-sensitive or peak-season work, a shorter window such as 7 to 14 days is safer.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time spent preparing a quote?
faqs.answer: Most simple delivery quotes are free. For complex logistics planning, route design, or event coordination, some operators charge a planning fee that is credited toward the job if the client books.

demolition.intro: Demolition contractors tear down or strip out structures, interiors, and site features so something else can be built or so a space can be cleared. Solo operators and small crews bill for interior gut-outs, selective demo, full structure teardown, concrete removal, and hauling debris. Invoices usually combine labor, equipment, disposal fees, and permits into one job total or a progress billing schedule.
demolition.pricingModel: Most demolition work is priced as a flat fee per job based on a site walkthrough, with the quote built from labor hours, equipment, haul-off, and dump fees. Residential and small commercial jobs are often quoted per square foot (interior gut) or per job (shed, deck, garage, house). Concrete, asphalt, and masonry are commonly priced per square foot by thickness or per cubic yard. Time and materials with a day rate for a crew and machine is common when scope is unclear, such as in older buildings with unknown conditions. Disposal is usually passed through at cost with a markup of 10 to 20 percent, or built into the price. Hazardous material work (asbestos, lead paint) is typically done by licensed abatement firms, so demo contractors either subcontract it or exclude it in writing. Larger jobs bill in stages: a deposit or mobilization fee, progress billings, and a final invoice after debris is gone and the site is cleaned.

rates.service: Concrete slab or driveway removal and haul-off
Deck, shed, or detached garage demolition
Excavator or skid steer with operator
Dumpster rental and disposal (10-30 yard roll-off)

Removal of concrete porch slab (4 in thick), break up and load out
Skid steer with operator
30-yard roll-off dumpster, delivery, haul, and disposal
Demolition permit fee (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Deposit of $2,500 received on 03/04 has been applied. Scope excludes asbestos or lead abatement and any structural repairs. Dump receipts available on request. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and permit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact property and shows the work was permitted, which owners and lenders often need for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices, and general contractors and property managers often ask for proof of coverage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized scope by area or phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating interior demo, concrete removal, and site cleanup makes it clear what was done and avoids arguments over what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disposal costs with ticket or weight details
invoiceChecklist.why: Dump fees vary by weight and material type. Showing tons or loads justifies the charge and supports any markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment hours and operator time
invoiceChecklist.why: Machine time is a major cost. Listing the machine, hours, and rate keeps the charge defensible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extra work found during demo
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden conditions like extra layers of flooring, buried tanks, or rot are common. Written approvals referenced on the invoice prevent disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments already received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the balance due clearly and prevents double billing on larger jobs.

demolition.paymentTerms: For small residential jobs, many demolition contractors collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking to cover dumpster rental and mobilization, with the balance due on completion. Larger commercial and multi-week jobs usually use progress billing every two weeks or monthly, with net 15 or net 30 terms. Final payment is often tied to site cleanup and, where required, a final inspection. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, and card payments are all accepted, and card fees are sometimes passed on for large balances. Check your state's rules on lien rights and notice deadlines, since preliminary or lien notices can affect how you get paid on commercial work.

tips.title: Collect a deposit that covers your out-of-pocket costs
tips.body: Dumpsters, permits, fuel, and equipment rental come due before you are paid. A deposit sized to cover those costs protects you if the client delays or cancels.

tips.title: Write exclusions into the quote and repeat them on the invoice
tips.body: State that hazardous materials, structural repairs, utility disconnects, and hidden conditions are not included. If you find asbestos or a buried oil tank, the paper trail supports a change order.

tips.title: Keep every dump ticket
tips.body: Landfills charge by weight and may change rates. Tickets let you bill disposal accurately and answer questions from clients or their accountants.

tips.title: Bill extra work as it happens
tips.body: Get written or texted approval for added scope on the day it comes up and list it as a separate line. Rolling it into the final bill later invites pushback.

tips.title: Bill in stages on multi-week jobs
tips.body: Invoice after teardown, after hauling, and after final grading or cleanup. Staged billing keeps cash flowing and limits how much unpaid work you carry.

faqs.question: Should I charge per square foot or per job?
faqs.answer: Per square foot works well for interior gut-outs and slabs where the scope is easy to measure. Flat per-job pricing is better for sheds, decks, and garages. Use time and materials when conditions are unknown, and put a day rate and machine rate in writing.

faqs.question: How do I bill for disposal?
faqs.answer: Either include it in your price or list it as a separate line at cost plus a markup of 10 to 20 percent. Separate lines are clearer when weight is uncertain, and you can attach dump tickets as backup.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the permit on my invoice?
faqs.answer: If you pull the permit, list the fee as a pass-through line and add a small handling charge if your contract allows it. Permit rules vary by city and county, so confirm who is responsible before quoting.

faqs.question: What if I find asbestos or lead paint mid-job?
faqs.answer: Stop work in the affected area and notify the client in writing. Testing and abatement generally must be done by licensed professionals, and rules vary by state. Bill your standby or remobilization time under your change order terms.

faqs.question: Can I put a lien on a property if I am not paid?
faqs.answer: In many states, contractors who improve or prepare property can file a mechanic's lien, but deadlines and notice requirements vary and are strict. Check your state's rules or ask a local attorney, and keep your invoices and contract details organized.

estimate.intro: Demolition contractors send a written quote after a site walkthrough and before ordering dumpsters or equipment. Clients, whether homeowners, builders, or property managers, usually compare the total price, what is included in disposal and cleanup, and how quickly you can start.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact areas and structures to be removed
scopeChecklist.why: Defining what comes out, and what stays, prevents disputes about whether walls, slabs, footings, or landscaping were included.

scopeChecklist.item: Utility disconnects and who handles them
scopeChecklist.why: Gas, electric, water, and sewer must usually be shut off or capped by the utility or a licensed trade before work begins. State who is responsible and who pays.
Asbestos, lead paint, mold, and underground tanks can halt a job. Say they are excluded and describe how they will be handled if found.
Specify the number of dumpsters or loads included and what happens if weight or volume runs over.
Clarify who pulls the demolition permit and pays fees, and whether the quote includes required notices to neighbors or utilities.
State whether you leave rough grade, backfill holes, remove footings, or just clear the structure. Clients often assume more is included than you intend.
Disposal fees and fuel costs change. Set a start window, note access needs for equipment, and limit how long the price is valid.

pricingTips.title: Price from the walkthrough, then add a contingency
pricingTips.body: Add up labor days, machine hours, hauls, and fees, then add 10 to 15 percent for unknowns like extra layers or hidden materials, especially in older buildings.

pricingTips.title: Show disposal separately
pricingTips.body: Listing dump costs as their own line shows clients where the money goes and lets you adjust if weight comes in over or under the estimate.

pricingTips.title: Offer options when scope is flexible
pricingTips.body: For example, price removal of a slab with and without hauling or grading. Options help clients compare quotes on equal terms and sometimes lead to a larger job.

pricingTips.title: Use unit prices for uncertain quantities
pricingTips.body: If the amount of concrete or debris is not clear, quote a price per cubic yard or per square foot with an estimated total so the final bill matches actual work.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most demolition contractors quote simple residential jobs for free. For large or complex projects, a paid site assessment that is credited to the job if accepted is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Dump fees, fuel, and equipment rental rates can change, so set an expiration date and say the price may be adjusted after that.

faqs.question: What if the final cost differs from the estimate?
faqs.answer: A flat-fee quote holds unless conditions change. Include language that hidden conditions or added scope will be billed by approved change order, and for time-and-materials jobs, say the quote is an estimate only.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes. A signed quote or contract with scope, exclusions, price, and payment terms protects you if there is a dispute. Many states have contract requirements for contractors, so check your local rules.

dental-hygienist.intro: Most hygienists are paid as employees, but a growing number bill directly: temp and contract hygienists covering for offices, mobile hygienists serving nursing homes and schools, and hygienists in direct access states who run their own practice. Invoices go to dental offices, facilities, school programs, or patients, and cover chair time, per-patient services, whitening, and travel.
dental-hygienist.pricingModel: Pricing depends on who is paying. Temp and contract hygienists bill by the hour or by a daily rate (often a half day or full day minimum) to the office, and the office bills the patient. Mobile and independent hygienists usually charge per patient or per visit, with prophylaxis, periodontal maintenance, and scaling and root planing priced separately, plus add-ons such as fluoride varnish, sealants, and X-rays if the state and supervision rules allow. Facility and school contracts are often per patient, per student, or per clinic day. Whitening is a flat fee, with take-home trays priced separately. Travel, a portable equipment fee, and disposable supplies are commonly itemized. Scope of practice, supervision rules, and billing to insurance vary by state, so check your state dental board before setting up services.

rates.service: Nursing home or school clinic day

items.description: Temp hygiene coverage, Mon-Wed (8 hrs/day), Lakeview Family Dental
Additional patient care after close, Wednesday (chart completion and recall follow-up)
Travel to office (round trip, beyond 25 miles)
Personal loupes and light sterilization pack (supplies brought by hygienist)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Hours are based on signed time sheets from 3/10-3/12. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment by check or ACH accepted. This invoice is for independent contractor services. I am not an employee of the practice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license number, state, and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: Offices and facilities need proof that you are licensed in the state where you worked, and some require it for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates, start and end times, and breaks for each day worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Contract hygiene is billed by time, and a clear log prevents disputes about lunch, late patients, or no-show gaps.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay basis and any minimums (hourly, half day, full day, or per patient)
invoiceChecklist.why: A short day or a cancellation can still trigger a minimum, and the invoice should show which one applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Procedure types and patient counts for per-patient work, without PHI
invoiceChecklist.why: Facilities and schools pay per patient, but you should use initials or a roster ID rather than full patient names to avoid sharing protected health information unnecessarily.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage, travel time, and equipment or supply fees as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and temp work involves travel and portable equipment costs, and separating them makes them easy to approve and to track for your own taxes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supervising dentist or contact person, and PO or contract number if used
invoiceChecklist.why: Facilities, school districts, and health agencies often won't process payment without a PO, contract number, or approver name.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor status, your business name, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Offices that pay you as an independent contractor need your tax information to report payments, and you are generally responsible for your own taxes.

dental-hygienist.paymentTerms: Temp and contract hygienists commonly invoice weekly or right after an assignment, with net 7 to net 14 terms. Agencies and larger facilities may pay on net 30 or on a fixed schedule. Mobile hygienists serving individuals often collect payment at the visit, and whitening and multi-visit treatment are often paid in full upfront or with a deposit. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common, and you should state it before the first assignment. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or card, and contracts with facilities or school programs may require a W-9 and a certificate of liability insurance before the first payment.

tips.title: Set a minimum for short or canceled days
tips.body: Offices sometimes cancel the morning of a shift or send you home early when the schedule is light. A half-day or four-hour minimum in your written terms protects you from lost income on a day you reserved.

tips.title: Get hours signed daily
tips.body: Ask the office manager to sign or initial your time sheet at the end of each day. It settles questions about late patients, charting time, and lunch breaks before they turn into a disputed invoice.

tips.title: Bill travel and supplies as their own lines
tips.body: If you carry your own loupes, handpieces, or a portable unit, or drive between facilities, charge for that separately. A flat travel fee or per-mile charge looks more reasonable to a client than a higher hourly rate.

tips.title: Keep patient information off the invoice
tips.body: Use patient counts, initials, or roster numbers instead of names and diagnoses. Invoices get forwarded to accounting staff, schools, and agencies who do not need protected health information.

tips.title: Confirm who is billing the patient
tips.body: In a temp placement the office bills the patient or insurance, and you bill the office. For independent or mobile work, decide whether you collect directly or submit claims, since insurance billing rules and credentialing vary by state and payer.

faqs.question: Should a temp hygienist invoice by the hour or by the day?
faqs.answer: Either works, but many temp hygienists quote an hourly rate with a half-day or full-day minimum. That covers cancellations and short schedules while still giving you a fair rate for a full day.

faqs.question: Can I bill a dental office as an independent contractor?
faqs.answer: In many cases yes, but how you are classified depends on how much control the office has over your work, schedule, and tools. Rules differ by state and for tax purposes, so check with your state labor agency or a tax professional if you are unsure.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on hygiene services?
faqs.answer: Professional dental services are generally not subject to sales tax in most states, but take-home whitening kits or products sold to patients may be taxable. Check your state's rules.

faqs.question: How do I bill nursing homes or schools?
faqs.answer: Most use a per-patient or per-student rate or a clinic day rate under a written agreement. Invoice with the dates, number of patients seen, services provided, and any PO number, and list travel and supplies separately.

faqs.question: What should I do about patient names on invoices?
faqs.answer: Avoid them when you can. Use a count or an ID from the facility's roster, and keep detailed records in the chart or your own secure files, since patient health information is protected under HIPAA and state privacy laws.

estimate.intro: Hygienists send quotes before starting contract assignments, facility or school programs, and fee-based services like whitening or a periodontal treatment plan. Clients compare your rate to other temps and agencies, or your per-patient price to what a local office or competing mobile provider charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included and any excluded (cleaning, X-rays, sealants, fluoride, root planing, whitening)
scopeChecklist.why: Scope of practice and what you are allowed to do vary by state and supervision level, and a clear list prevents disagreements about what was agreed.

scopeChecklist.item: Rate basis and minimums (hourly, daily, per patient, or per clinic day)
scopeChecklist.why: The client needs to know whether a canceled or short day still triggers a minimum charge.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment and supplies: who provides them
scopeChecklist.why: Whether you or the client provides handpieces, ultrasonic scalers, disposables, or a portable unit changes your price and your liability.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, and setup or breakdown time
scopeChecklist.why: Mobile work can cost significant unpaid time, so it should be built into the quote or stated as a fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Supervision and legal arrangement (dentist supervision, standing orders, collaborative agreement)
scopeChecklist.why: Some states require a supervising dentist or written agreement, and a quote should make clear who is responsible for what.
A client who cancels the morning of a clinic day should know in advance what they will owe.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and deposit, if any
scopeChecklist.why: Rates and your availability change, and a deposit secures your date for larger programs or whitening appointments.

pricingTips.title: Quote a day rate for temp work and show the hourly equivalent
pricingTips.body: Offices often think in days, while you think in hours. Giving both makes it easy to compare to an agency rate and to explain a minimum.

pricingTips.title: Price per patient for facilities, then check it against your time
pricingTips.body: Work out how many patients you can see per hour including setup, charting, and travel between rooms. A per-patient price that looks fine can lose money if the average patient takes longer than you expected.

pricingTips.title: Offer whitening and treatment as clear packages
pricingTips.body: For whitening, a flat fee with in-chair and take-home options is easier to approve than a list of parts. For multi-visit care, quote by visit or quadrant and state how many visits are expected.

pricingTips.title: Account for insurance versus fee-for-service
pricingTips.body: If the patient or facility will submit to insurance, your price may be limited by what payers allow. Note whether your quote is a fee-for-service price or a contracted amount.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly rate for a temp assignment?
faqs.answer: Quote an hourly or daily rate with a stated minimum, since the number of patients and the length of the day can change. Flat quotes work better for whitening or a defined program.

faqs.question: How do I quote a school sealant or screening program?
faqs.answer: Quote per student or per clinic day, and state how many students you expect to see, supplies included, travel, and who handles consent forms. Programs often need the quote to match a grant or contract amount.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a consult or screening before treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, many independent hygienists charge a consult or assessment fee, or apply it toward the first treatment. State this in the quote so the client knows what is free and what is billed.

dentist.intro: Dentists who own or run a small practice, work as an associate, or provide mobile or contract dentistry bill patients, insurance carriers, and sometimes schools, nursing homes, or other practices. Most billing covers exams, cleanings, X-rays, fillings, crowns, extractions, and cosmetic work, usually coded with CDT procedure codes. Patient-facing invoices (statements) typically show the fee, the insurance portion, and the balance the patient owes.
dentist.pricingModel: Dentists price per procedure using a fee schedule, with each service tied to a CDT code. Most practices set a usual and customary fee for each code, then adjust to the contracted rate when a patient has in-network insurance. Patients without insurance may pay the full fee, a membership plan rate, or a cash discount. Larger treatment like crowns, implants, bridges, and orthodontics is often quoted as a treatment plan with a total fee, sometimes split into phases or monthly payments. Lab fees are usually built into the crown or denture fee rather than billed separately. Contract and mobile dentists may bill per visit or per day instead. Fees vary a lot by region, specialty, and whether you are in-network.

D0274 Bitewing radiographs, four films
D1110 Adult prophylaxis
D2391 Resin composite filling, one surface, posterior (tooth #19)
D2392 Resin composite filling, two surfaces, posterior (tooth #30)

sampleInvoice.notes: Total fees $745. Estimated insurance payment of $420 is pending and will be applied once the claim is processed. Patient portion due today: $325, or the balance after insurance adjustments. Questions about your statement? Call the office within 30 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: CDT procedure code for each service
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and patients match charges to codes, and wrong codes cause denied claims and confusing statements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tooth number and surface or quadrant
invoiceChecklist.why: It shows exactly what was treated and supports the charge if a patient or insurer questions it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurance timely-filing limits and annual maximums depend on the date each procedure was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name and NPI or license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for claims and for patients who submit their own reimbursement, especially with multiple dentists in a practice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance payment, adjustment, and write-off lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Patients need to see the fee, what insurance paid or is expected to pay, and the balance they owe.

invoiceChecklist.item: Patient responsibility and deductible or copay applied
invoiceChecklist.why: It explains why the amount due differs from the fee and reduces billing calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment plan or financing details
invoiceChecklist.why: If the balance is split, the statement should show the schedule, amounts, and any third-party financing used.

dentist.paymentTerms: Most dental offices collect copays, deductibles, and non-covered amounts at the time of service, since chasing small balances is costly. For major work, many practices ask for a deposit or collect the patient portion at the seat or delivery appointment, and some collect half at prep for crowns. Statements for remaining balances are typically due in 30 days, with reminders at 30, 60, and 90 days. Late fees are less common than in other trades and, where used, should be disclosed in writing and follow state rules. Accepted payment methods usually include cards, HSA/FSA cards, checks, and third-party financing such as monthly payment plans. Offer a written payment agreement for large treatment.

tips.title: Collect the estimated patient portion upfront
tips.body: Verify benefits before the visit, then collect the copay and expected deductible at check-in or checkout. Balances left for statements are collected far less reliably.

tips.title: Bill insurance first, then the patient the exact balance
tips.body: If you are in-network, you generally must accept the contracted rate and cannot bill the patient the difference. Wait for the explanation of benefits before billing the remainder.

tips.title: Track timely filing deadlines
tips.body: Many carriers deny claims filed after 90 days to a year. Submit claims the same day as treatment and follow up on anything unpaid after 30 days.

tips.title: Get signed treatment plan acceptance
tips.body: Before starting multi-visit work, have the patient sign the treatment plan and fee estimate so the final bill matches what they agreed to.

tips.title: Handle refunds and credits promptly
tips.body: When insurance pays more than expected, refund overpayments or apply credits clearly. Many states set deadlines for returning patient credit balances.

faqs.question: Can I charge a patient more than the insurance allowed amount?
faqs.answer: If you are in-network, your contract typically limits you to the allowed amount, and you can only bill the patient the copay, deductible, or non-covered portion. Out-of-network dentists can usually bill their full fee, though some states have limits. Check your contracts and state rules.

faqs.question: Should I bill the patient before insurance pays?
faqs.answer: It is best to collect only the estimated patient portion at the visit and wait for the explanation of benefits before billing any remainder. Estimates can be wrong, so note on the statement that the final amount depends on the claim.

faqs.question: Do I charge for missed appointments?
faqs.answer: Many practices charge a missed or short-notice cancellation fee, often $25-100, but only if the policy is written, signed, and disclosed in advance. Some insurance contracts restrict these fees, so check your agreements.

faqs.question: Are dental services taxable?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional dental services are not subject to sales tax. Retail items you sell, such as whitening kits or electric toothbrushes, may be taxable. Rules vary, so check with your state revenue department or accountant.

faqs.question: How long should I keep billing records?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state and payer, and patient records often must be kept for several years or longer for minors. Many practices keep billing and claim records at least 7 years. Check your state dental board and insurer contracts.

estimate.intro: Dentists give estimates, usually called treatment plans, before any treatment beyond routine care such as crowns, implants, bridges, dentures, orthodontics, and cosmetic work. Patients compare total cost, the insurance portion, payment options, and sometimes a second opinion from another practice.

scopeChecklist.item: Procedures with CDT codes, tooth numbers, and fees
scopeChecklist.why: A line-by-line plan shows exactly what is being done and prevents surprise charges later.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated insurance coverage and patient portion
scopeChecklist.why: Patients decide based on what they will pay, so show coverage, deductibles, and annual maximums, and note it is an estimate.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of visits and sequence of treatment
scopeChecklist.why: It clarifies timing, and phasing can spread costs across benefit years.
Porcelain, zirconia, and metal crowns or implant brands differ in price, and the patient should know what the quote includes.
Items such as sedation, bone grafts, build-ups, temporary crowns, or follow-up adjustments may be extra and should be named.

scopeChecklist.item: Alternatives and what happens if untreated
scopeChecklist.why: Offering options such as a filling versus a crown supports informed consent and helps the patient choose a price level.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and fee changes
scopeChecklist.why: Fees and insurance benefits change, so state how long the estimate stands, such as 60 or 90 days.

pricingTips.title: Present options at different price points
pricingTips.body: Show a good, better, and best path when it is clinically reasonable, such as a filling, an onlay, or a crown. Patients are more likely to accept when they can choose.

pricingTips.title: Verify benefits before quoting
pricingTips.body: Check the plan's coverage percentage, deductible used, annual maximum remaining, waiting periods, and frequency limits. A pre-treatment estimate request to the insurer helps for larger work.

pricingTips.title: Offer a cash or membership rate for uninsured patients
pricingTips.body: Many patients without coverage compare your fees to others. A clear in-house plan or prepay discount can win acceptance while keeping pricing consistent.

pricingTips.title: Break big cases into phases
pricingTips.body: For full-mouth work, quote urgent care first, then restorative, then cosmetic. Smaller phased totals are easier to accept and to finance.

faqs.question: Is a dental estimate a guaranteed price?
faqs.answer: No. Fees are usually firm, but the final patient cost can change if clinical findings change the treatment or if insurance pays differently. State this clearly on the treatment plan.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a treatment plan or second opinion?
faqs.answer: Most practices include the treatment plan with the exam fee. A separate consultation fee for complex cases, such as implants or orthodontics, is common if you disclose it first.

faqs.question: How do I handle a patient who wants to shop my quote?
faqs.answer: Give them a printed or emailed itemized plan with CDT codes so they can compare the same procedures. It also shows you are transparent.

faqs.question: What if treatment turns out different from the estimate?
faqs.answer: Stop and explain the change, give an updated fee, and get the patient's agreement before proceeding unless it is an emergency. Document the conversation in the chart.

deposit.intro: This page is for solo operators and small businesses that collect money up front before starting work: contractors, photographers, event vendors, custom makers, consultants, and similar. A deposit invoice asks for a down payment, retainer, or reservation fee that secures the date, covers early costs, or pays for special-order materials. It is billed separately from the final invoice and later credited against it.
deposit.pricingModel: Deposits are almost always set as a percentage of the total job or as a flat reservation fee, not priced like a service. Percentage deposits (10% to 50%) are common for projects with a defined total, such as remodels, custom orders, and event packages. Flat booking fees are common for date-based work like weddings, portraits, and venue or equipment holds. Retainers are used for ongoing or open-ended work and are drawn down against hourly or monthly billing. Special-order materials are often billed as a separate, larger deposit, sometimes 50% to 100% of the item cost, because the supplier will not take returns. Always state whether the deposit is refundable, partly refundable, or non-refundable, and how it will be applied to the final balance.

rates.service: Home remodel or construction down payment
Wedding or event booking retainer (photo, video, DJ, florist)
Portrait or small session reservation fee
Custom or made-to-order product (furniture, signage, apparel)

items.description: Initial deposit, bathroom remodel contract (20% of $14,000 total)
Materials deposit: special-order vanity and tile (50% of $2,400)
Permit fee advance (city building permit)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit is due before the work is scheduled. The $2,800 contract deposit will be credited against the final invoice. The materials deposit is non-refundable once the order is placed with the supplier. Remaining balance of $11,200 is billed in two payments: 40% at rough-in completion and the rest at final walkthrough. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or card (3% card fee applies).

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract, quote, or booking agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the deposit to an agreed scope and total price so there is no dispute over what it covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Total job price and deposit as both a percentage and a dollar amount
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client exactly how the deposit was calculated and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Refund and cancellation terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States whether the deposit is refundable, partly refundable, or non-refundable, and under what conditions, before money changes hands.

invoiceChecklist.item: What the deposit pays for
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates a reservation fee, a materials deposit, and a down payment so each can be treated correctly if the job is canceled.

invoiceChecklist.item: Due date and the date the work or reservation is confirmed
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear that the date or schedule slot is not held until the deposit is received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Schedule for the remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists the milestone or due dates for later payments so the client knows the full payment plan.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require license numbers on contracts and billing documents for home improvement and trade work; check your local rules.

deposit.paymentTerms: Deposits are usually due on signing or within 3 to 7 days of sending the invoice, and the date or schedule slot is held only once payment clears. Many businesses accept ACH, check, or card, and some pass on card fees where allowed. Late fees on the deposit are uncommon; the more common remedy is to release the date if it is not paid by the deadline. Balances are typically due on completion, at milestones, or a set number of days before an event, often 14 to 30 days before. Put the refund policy in writing, because rules on deposits and cancellation vary by state and by industry, and some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts.

tips.title: Never start work or hold a date without the deposit
tips.body: State on the invoice that the schedule slot is confirmed only when payment is received. This keeps you from turning away other clients while waiting on someone who may not commit.

tips.title: Separate deposits by purpose
tips.body: List a reservation fee, a materials deposit, and a contract down payment as separate lines. If the job is canceled, you can point to which part covers costs you already incurred.

tips.title: Show the credit on the final invoice
tips.body: Include a line such as 'Less deposit received, 3/4/2025' so the client sees the deposit applied. It prevents double-payment questions and leaves a clean paper trail.

tips.title: Check your state's limits
tips.body: In many states, home improvement and similar contracts limit how large a deposit can be or require specific wording. Look up your local rules before setting a percentage.

tips.title: Record how you treat deposits for taxes
tips.body: Deposits can be treated differently depending on your accounting method and whether they are refundable. Ask your accountant how to record them, since some are liabilities until earned.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: It depends on your costs and risk. Service and event work often uses 25% to 50%, remodeling often 10% to 33%, and custom products 30% to 50%. Special-order materials can be higher because they cannot be returned. Check whether your state caps deposits for your type of work.

faqs.question: Is a deposit the same as a retainer?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. A deposit is usually a down payment on a specific job and is credited to the final bill. A retainer is typically paid in advance for ongoing availability or future work and is drawn down as you bill. Label which one you are collecting.

faqs.question: Can I keep the deposit if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: Only if your signed agreement says so and the terms are reasonable. Courts and state rules in many places expect non-refundable amounts to reflect real costs or lost business. Put the terms in the contract and on the invoice, and check local law.

faqs.question: Should I send a separate invoice for the deposit?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit invoice gives the client a payment request and a receipt, with its own number and due date. The final invoice then shows the full price and subtracts the deposit already paid.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on a deposit?
faqs.answer: It varies by state and by what you sell. Some states tax goods when the sale is made, others when delivered or paid, and services are taxed differently from goods. Confirm with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: A quote or estimate comes first, and the deposit is usually part of it. Clients compare total price, how much they must pay up front, what is refundable, and when the rest is due. Putting the deposit terms in the estimate means the client agrees to them before signing.

scopeChecklist.why: Shows the full cost and the exact up-front payment, so the client is not surprised by the first invoice.
Clarifies whether it is a reservation fee, a down payment, or a materials purchase, which affects whether it can be refunded.
Sets expectations in writing before the client accepts, which reduces disputes if plans change.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit due date and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents quotes from sitting open indefinitely while material prices or your calendar change.
Lists milestone or date-based payments so the client can plan cash flow.
Allows for supplier price changes between quote and order without eating your margin.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date or hold date tied to receipt of deposit
scopeChecklist.why: Makes clear that scheduling is not guaranteed until payment is received.

pricingTips.title: Match the deposit to your actual up-front costs
pricingTips.body: Add up the permits, materials, subcontractor deposits, and lost bookings you would face if the client walked away. Set the deposit at least to that level so you are not out of pocket.

pricingTips.title: Make the deposit part of the acceptance step
pricingTips.body: Ask clients to sign the quote and pay the deposit together. A signed quote with no payment is a soft commitment that rarely holds your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Offer a short expiration window
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days are common. For materials that change price often, use a shorter window and say so.

pricingTips.title: Show the deposit as a line, not a footnote
pricingTips.body: Put the deposit and remaining balance in a clear summary at the bottom of the quote so comparison shoppers see the payment structure at a glance.

faqs.question: Should the deposit be in the quote or in a separate contract?
faqs.answer: Include it in both if you use both. The quote should state the amount and refund terms, and the contract should repeat them so the signed document controls.

faqs.question: What if the final price changes after the deposit?
faqs.answer: Write change-order terms into the quote. Any approved change should be documented with a new total, and the deposit stays applied against the revised amount.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee just to give an estimate?
faqs.answer: Some businesses do for complex or on-site work, and credit the fee toward the job if the client hires them. Say so up front, and follow any local rules on estimate fees.

faqs.question: How long should I hold a quote after sending it?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Shorten it when prices or availability change quickly, and state the expiration date on the quote.

design-agency.intro: Design agencies are small studios and firms that handle branding, websites, packaging, print, and marketing collateral for business clients. They invoice for discovery, design rounds, production files, project management, and often ongoing retainer work. Many are run by one to ten people, so billing has to cover both creative time and the overhead of managing clients.
design-agency.pricingModel: Most design agencies price projects at a flat fee based on scope, with the fee built from estimated hours multiplied by a blended hourly rate. Hourly billing is common for small changes, out-of-scope requests, and open-ended work. Ongoing clients are often put on monthly retainers for a set number of hours or deliverables. Larger projects are split into milestones, such as discovery, concept, design development, and final files, with a payment tied to each. Pass-through costs like stock photography, font licenses, printing, and freelancer fees are billed separately, often with a markup of 10-20 percent. Revision rounds are usually capped, with extra rounds billed hourly.

rates.service: Website design and build (small business, 5-10 pages)
Packaging design (per product line, concept to print-ready)
Brochure, catalog, or print collateral design

items.description: Brand identity project, milestone 2 of 3: logo concepts and refinement (two rounds)
Brand guidelines document (16 pages)
Business card and letterhead design, print-ready files
Additional revision round requested after approval (out of scope)
Licensed typeface, 1 desktop license (client-owned)
Project management and calls

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Final file transfer and font license assignment occur on receipt of full payment. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Accepted by ACH, check, or card (3% fee applies to card payments).

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone or phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several projects or approvers need to see which stage of work the invoice covers and how it ties to the signed proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract or proposal date
invoiceChecklist.why: It anchors the amount to the agreed scope and reduces pushback on fixed fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and any out-of-scope hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing extra rounds with dates shows why the total exceeds the base fee and supports your change-order policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs with receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock images, fonts, printing, and freelancer charges should be listed separately, with any markup consistent with your contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often reject invoices without a PO number or accounts payable contact.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and file transfer terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State when ownership or licensing of final files transfers, commonly upon full payment, so delivery and payment are linked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states tax digital or creative services or tangible deliverables like printed goods. Check your state's rules.

design-agency.paymentTerms: A common structure is a 30-50 percent deposit before work begins, with the balance split across milestones or due at delivery. Project invoices are usually due in 14-30 days, while retainers are billed at the start of the month. Many agencies hold final files until the last payment clears. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. Payment methods include ACH, check, wire, and card, and some agencies add a card processing fee for larger invoices.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not dates
tips.body: If a client delays feedback, a date-based schedule leaves you working unpaid. Milestone billing keeps cash flowing and gives the client a reason to respond quickly.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Spell out two or three rounds per deliverable in the proposal, then bill extra rounds hourly. Track rounds on the invoice so the charge is not a surprise.

tips.title: Bill pass-through costs promptly
tips.body: Fonts, stock, print runs, and contractor fees can add up and eat margin if they sit unbilled. Add them to the next invoice and keep receipts on file.

tips.title: Use retainers for recurring work
tips.body: A monthly retainer for a fixed number of hours smooths revenue. Define what happens to unused hours, since many agencies let them expire at month end.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid in full
tips.body: Deliver proofs and low-resolution previews during the project, and release editable source files after the final payment. Put this in the contract and on the invoice.

faqs.question: Should a design agency bill hourly or flat fee?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best for defined projects like a logo or website, since clients want a known cost. Hourly billing suits maintenance, small updates, and anything with unclear scope. Many agencies combine both: flat fee for the base scope and hourly for changes.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: 30-50 percent upfront is common, and some agencies take 50 percent on smaller projects. The deposit is usually non-refundable and covers the time reserved for the client and early discovery work.

faqs.question: Can I mark up stock images, printing, and freelancer costs?
faqs.answer: Yes, many agencies add 10-20 percent to cover sourcing, coordination, and the risk of paying vendors before the client pays. Include the markup policy in your contract so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client stops responding mid-project?
faqs.answer: Include a clause in the contract that lets you pause or close the project after a set period of inactivity, such as 30 days, and invoice for work completed. Then send the invoice for the completed milestone and any unbilled hours.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on design work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax digital services or printed deliverables, while others do not tax design services at all. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant.

estimate.intro: A design agency sends a proposal or estimate after an intro call or discovery questionnaire and before any creative work starts. Clients often compare several agencies, looking at total price, number of concepts, timeline, and what is included in the deliverables. A clear estimate sets expectations for revisions, ownership, and the client's responsibilities.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing items like primary logo, secondary marks, and AI, EPS, PNG, and PDF files prevents arguments about what was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Revisions are the biggest source of scope creep. State the count and the hourly rate for additional rounds.
Tie your schedule to timely feedback, and say what happens to the schedule if responses are late.
Specify who supplies copy, photography, and product images. Missing content is a common cause of delays and added costs.
Fonts, stock, printing, plugins, hosting, and developer fees should be listed as separate costs, with who pays and any markup.
State that rights transfer on full payment and whether you keep portfolio rights.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule and estimate expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Prices and availability change, so set a validity window, such as 30 days, and show deposit and milestone amounts.

pricingTips.title: Build the fee from hours, then present a flat price
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours by phase, including meetings, revisions, and project management, and multiply by your blended rate. Present the total as a flat fee so the client compares outcomes, not hours.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three packages, such as a logo only, a logo with brand guidelines, or a full identity with collateral. Tiers help clients choose without pushing you to discount.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for project management
pricingTips.body: Emails, calls, and file organization take real time on every project. Include 10-20 percent for it rather than absorbing it.

pricingTips.title: Separate optional add-ons
pricingTips.body: List extras like social templates, a pitch deck, or additional pages as line items. Clients can add them later at the quoted price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals and discovery?
faqs.answer: A short intro call and a standard proposal are usually free. For complex projects that need audits, research, or detailed scoping, many agencies charge a paid discovery phase that is credited toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope instead of the rate. Remove deliverables, cut the number of concepts, or phase the project. This keeps your hourly value intact and the client sees what the lower price covers.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Design work depends on your schedule, so a validity date protects you from a client accepting months later at an old price.

faqs.question: What happens if the scope changes after the client signs?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that states the added work, cost, and any timeline impact. The client approves it before you start, and the amount is added to the next invoice.

devops-consultant.intro: DevOps consultants are independent engineers and small firms that help companies build and run their delivery and infrastructure systems. Typical billable work includes CI/CD pipeline builds, cloud migrations, Kubernetes setup, infrastructure as code, monitoring and on-call setup, and cloud cost reviews. Invoices usually go to startups, software companies, and IT departments that need senior expertise without a full-time hire.
devops-consultant.pricingModel: Most DevOps consultants bill hourly or on a monthly retainer. Hourly rates suit open-ended work like troubleshooting, ongoing support, and projects with unclear scope. Fixed-fee pricing is common for well-defined projects such as a CI/CD pipeline build, a Terraform rewrite, or a cloud security audit, usually split into milestones. Retainers cover a set number of hours per month, often with a discounted rate and a response-time commitment. Some consultants charge a day rate for on-site work or workshops. Cloud usage that you pay for on the client's behalf (rare, and best avoided) should be billed at cost with receipts. Emergency or after-hours incident response is often billed at 1.5x to 2x the normal rate with a minimum number of hours.

rates.service: Senior or specialist work (Kubernetes, security, SRE)

items.description: Terraform modules for VPC, EKS cluster, and RDS (milestone 2 of 3)
GitHub Actions pipeline: build, test, and deploy to staging and production
Prometheus and Grafana monitoring setup with alert routing
Production cutover support, Saturday 6am-10am
Runbook and handoff documentation

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours are for work between March 1 and March 31 under SOW dated Feb 12. Cloud provider charges are billed directly to the client account. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. ACH preferred.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the SOW or contract and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate accounts payable teams often will not process an invoice without a matching PO or contract reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and dates worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client match your invoice to sprints, change windows, and project timelines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized tasks with hours or milestone names
invoiceChecklist.why: Engineering managers need to justify the spend, and vague lines like 'DevOps work' draw questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line for after-hours or incident work, with the rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Premium rates should be visible and match what the contract allows, so they are not disputed later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs and who pays them
invoiceChecklist.why: Software licenses, cloud usage, or tools you bought for the client should be listed at cost with receipts, or clearly marked as billed to the client directly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone status and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: For fixed-fee projects, it shows what has been delivered and what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal business name, tax ID or W-9 status, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need these to set you up as a vendor and to issue a 1099 if required.

devops-consultant.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is standard, though larger companies often push for net 45 or 60, so negotiate terms before starting. For fixed-fee projects, many consultants take 25% to 50% upfront and bill the rest at milestones. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if written into the contract. ACH and wire transfers are typical for business clients, and credit cards are accepted by some with a processing surcharge. Pausing work on overdue invoices should be allowed in your contract, particularly when you hold access to production systems.

tips.title: Track time by task, not just total
tips.body: Log hours against specific tickets or deliverables. When a client questions a 40-hour invoice, a task-level log settles it quickly.

tips.title: Put on-call and after-hours rules in the contract
tips.body: State the premium rate, minimum billable block (often 2 hours), and response times. Otherwise 2am pages become unpaid goodwill.

tips.title: Keep cloud spend off your invoice
tips.body: Have the client own the cloud accounts and pay the provider directly. This avoids fronting large bills and chasing reimbursement.

tips.title: Bill milestones when delivered, not when convenient
tips.body: Tie fixed-fee payments to concrete outputs like a working pipeline in staging. Clear acceptance criteria prevent payment from stalling on an open-ended review.

tips.title: Invoice monthly at minimum on hourly work
tips.body: Waiting until the project ends builds up a large balance and gives the client time to forget the context. Send invoices on a regular schedule.

faqs.question: Should a DevOps consultant bill hourly or fixed price?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for support, troubleshooting, and unclear scope. Use fixed price for defined deliverables like a pipeline build or Terraform migration, but only after a scoping call and with a change-order clause for extra work.

faqs.question: How do I bill for being on call?
faqs.answer: Many consultants charge a flat monthly on-call fee for availability, plus an hourly rate for time spent actively working incidents. Spell out both in the contract, along with response times and minimum billable blocks.

faqs.question: Do I bill the client for cloud services or software licenses I purchase?
