faqs.answer: It is safer to have the client buy them directly. If you must pay up front, list them at cost with receipts, and consider a small handling fee only if your contract allows it.

faqs.question: What payment terms should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Net 15 is a good ask for small clients, with net 30 as a common compromise. Larger companies may require net 45 or 60. Ask for a deposit on new clients and for milestone payments on larger projects.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: Clients in the US typically ask for a W-9 from contractors and may issue a 1099-NEC if they pay you above the IRS threshold in a year. Check current IRS rules and talk to a tax professional about your situation.

estimate.intro: DevOps consultants send estimates after a discovery call or a short architecture review, before any infrastructure is touched. Clients often compare a fixed quote against another freelancer, an agency, or the cost of hiring a full-time engineer. A clear scope and honest assumptions matter more than the lowest number.

scopeChecklist.why: State the cloud provider, number of services, and existing tooling you based the quote on. If reality differs, the price can change.
List outputs like 'Terraform for staging and production' or 'pipeline for three services' so there is no debate over what is included.
Name things such as application code changes, compliance certification, or ongoing monitoring so they are not assumed.

scopeChecklist.item: Access and dependencies on the client
scopeChecklist.why: Delays often come from missing cloud permissions or slow reviews. Note that timelines depend on timely access and feedback.
Give phases with target dates and acceptance criteria so payment and progress are tied together.
Scope grows in infrastructure work. Define how extra work is quoted and approved, and at what rate.
Say whether bug fixes or questions are covered for 2 or 4 weeks after handoff, and what happens after.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in ranges with a hours basis
pricingTips.body: Infrastructure work hides surprises. Giving a range, such as 60 to 80 hours, with the assumptions behind it sets expectations and protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Legacy systems, undocumented services, and permission issues commonly add time. Many consultants build in 15% to 25% for discovery on messy environments.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers or phases
pricingTips.body: Splitting the work into an assessment phase and an implementation phase lets cautious clients start small, and gives you real data to price the larger job.

pricingTips.title: Price for value, not just hours
pricingTips.body: A pipeline that cuts deploy time from hours to minutes or a cost review that saves thousands per month is worth more than the time it takes. Reflect this in fixed-fee quotes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a scoping or discovery phase?
faqs.answer: Yes for anything beyond a short call. A paid assessment of one to three days produces a better quote and filters out clients who are not serious. Many consultants credit part of it toward the project.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Cloud tooling and your availability change, so an expiry date keeps you from honoring an old price on a different project.

faqs.question: What if the project grows after I send the estimate?
faqs.answer: Refer to the change order clause. Document the new request, give an updated hours or fee estimate, and get written approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include cloud costs?
faqs.answer: Usually no. Exclude provider charges and licenses, or give a separate rough projection labeled as the client's expense, since actual usage depends on their workload.

dietitian.intro: Registered dietitians (RDs and RDNs) in private practice bill individual clients, families, and organizations for nutrition assessments, medical nutrition therapy, and ongoing coaching. Many also invoice gyms, schools, clinics, and companies for group workshops, meal planning, menu analysis, and consulting. Invoices usually go to self-pay clients, but some dietitians also send superbills so clients can seek insurance reimbursement.
dietitian.pricingModel: Most private-practice dietitians charge per session, with a higher fee for the initial assessment (60 to 90 minutes) and a lower fee for 30 to 45 minute follow-ups. Many sell packages, such as a 3-month or 6-session program, billed upfront or in installments, often at a small discount compared with paying per visit. Some offer monthly memberships that include check-ins and messaging. Corporate and consulting work is typically billed hourly or as a flat project fee, and speaking or workshops are charged per event. Meal plans, recipe development, and grocery guides are sometimes priced as separate line items. If you accept insurance, you bill the payer rather than the client, and the client's invoice covers only copays, deductibles, or non-covered services.

rates.service: Consulting (menu analysis, food labeling, content review)

items.description: Initial nutrition assessment and medical nutrition therapy, 60 min (telehealth) - IBS and food sensitivity evaluation
Follow-up counseling session, 45 min (telehealth)
Personalized low-FODMAP reintroduction meal plan, 2 weeks
Food and symptom journal review between sessions

sampleInvoice.notes: Services provided 3/4/25 to 4/15/25. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: credit/debit card, HSA/FSA card, or ACH. A superbill with CPT 97802 and 97803 and diagnosis code is available on request for out-of-network reimbursement. Cancellations under 24 hours' notice are billed at 50% of the session fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your credentials and NPI number
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients submitting a superbill to insurance, HSA, or FSA need your RD credential and NPI to be reimbursed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, length, and format of each session (in person or telehealth)
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and FSA/HSA administrators check dates of service, and session length supports the code billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes for each service (97802 initial, 97803 follow-up, 97804 group)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients seeking reimbursement need the correct codes, and they show exactly what was provided.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code (ICD-10) when provided by the client's referring provider or documented in your assessment
invoiceChecklist.why: Many insurance plans only reimburse nutrition counseling when it is tied to a covered diagnosis, so a superbill without one is often rejected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details, including number of sessions, sessions used, and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents disputes over what a prepaid package covers and when it expires.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for meal plans, assessments, and other non-session services
invoiceChecklist.why: Some of these may not be reimbursable, so itemizing helps clients and payers sort what qualifies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show fees as their own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Late-cancel fees are generally not reimbursable by insurance and should be easy to identify and explain.

dietitian.paymentTerms: Most private-practice dietitians collect payment at the time of service by card on file, or require upfront payment for packages and memberships. For clients billed afterward, due-on-receipt or net 7 to 14 days is common. Corporate and organizational clients often pay net 30, and a 25 to 50 percent deposit is typical for workshops and larger consulting projects. A late cancellation or no-show fee, usually 50 to 100 percent of the session fee with 24 hours' notice, should be written in your intake agreement. Card payments, ACH, and HSA/FSA cards are the usual methods. If you charge late fees on unpaid invoices, state the rate in advance and check your state's rules.

tips.title: Collect a card on file at intake
tips.body: Storing a card with written consent makes it easy to charge late cancellations, no-shows, and package installments without chasing clients for payment.

tips.title: Separate coaching from medical nutrition therapy
tips.body: If you offer both insurance-billable MNT and non-covered services like meal plans or general wellness coaching, bill them on separate lines so clients and payers can tell which is which.

tips.title: Offer superbills only on request and state your policy
tips.body: Providing a superbill is a courtesy, not a guarantee of reimbursement. Tell clients up front that coverage depends on their plan and that payment is due to you regardless.

tips.title: Track package sessions on every invoice
tips.body: Show sessions used and remaining on each invoice or receipt. It reduces questions about expiration and makes renewals easier to bring up.

tips.title: Charge for between-session work clearly
tips.body: Reviewing food logs, labs, or messages takes time. Either build it into your package price or list it as a separate fee, and tell clients which at the start.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and should I include one with my invoice?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with your name, credentials, NPI, dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis codes, and fees paid. Clients submit it to their insurer for possible out-of-network reimbursement. Many dietitians who do not bill insurance directly provide one on request.

faqs.question: Which CPT codes do dietitians use?
faqs.answer: The most common are 97802 (initial MNT assessment and intervention, per 15 minutes), 97803 (reassessment and follow-up, per 15 minutes), and 97804 (group MNT). Some payers also use G0270 and G0271 for Medicare MNT. Check each payer's requirements, as coverage and code rules vary.

faqs.question: Can clients pay with HSA or FSA funds?
faqs.answer: Often yes, particularly when nutrition counseling is recommended for a medical condition. Rules depend on the plan, and some administrators ask for a letter of medical necessity. Itemize your invoice and tell clients to confirm eligibility with their plan.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on nutrition counseling?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional health services like nutrition counseling are not taxed, but sales of physical products such as supplements or printed materials may be. Rules vary, so check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How should I bill for a missed appointment?
faqs.answer: Put your cancellation policy in your intake paperwork, then list the fee on the invoice as a separate line with the date of the missed session. Insurance does not cover these fees, so the client pays them directly.

estimate.intro: Dietitians send estimates or program proposals before a client commits to a multi-session plan, and for workshops, corporate wellness contracts, and consulting projects. Clients usually compare your program length, what's included between sessions, and the total cost against other dietitians or coaches. A written quote helps clients understand the full cost, especially when insurance may not cover it.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know if they are getting 6 sessions of 45 minutes by video or 3 in-person visits, since this drives the price.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included between sessions (messaging, food log review, meal plan updates)
scopeChecklist.why: Unclear access to you between visits leads to unpaid work or client frustration.

scopeChecklist.item: Program start and end dates and expiration of unused sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Sets a clear window to use prepaid sessions and prevents disputes over unused balances.
State whether you are in-network, out-of-network, or self-pay only, and that reimbursement is not guaranteed.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables and revision limits for meal plans or materials
scopeChecklist.why: Specify the number of plans, the time period each covers, and how many adjustments are included.
Clients should see these terms before paying, especially for packages that are partially used.

scopeChecklist.item: For events and consulting: travel, materials, attendee count, and prep time
scopeChecklist.why: A change in headcount, location, or scope can significantly alter your time and costs.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: Present options such as a 3-session starter, a 3-month program, and a 6-month program. Clients can pick without negotiating, and longer plans usually suit conditions that need follow-up.

pricingTips.title: Price packages slightly below per-session rates
pricingTips.body: A modest discount of 5 to 15 percent for prepaying encourages commitment and improves cash flow without undercutting your standard rate.

pricingTips.title: Quote corporate work by the project
pricingTips.body: Include prep, delivery, handouts, and follow-up in a flat fee rather than an hourly rate, since much of the work happens before the event.

pricingTips.title: Be clear on what insurance will not cover
pricingTips.body: If your quote is self-pay, say so plainly and note any superbill policy. It avoids surprise and builds trust before the first session.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation before quoting?
faqs.answer: Many dietitians offer a free 15 minute discovery call to check fit and explain pricing, but not a free assessment. Keep it short, and send a written quote afterward with your package options.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Most dietitians use 14 to 30 days for program quotes. For corporate or event work, tie validity to the event date and your availability.

faqs.question: Can I quote a fixed price for a health goal outcome?
faqs.answer: Price your time and services, not an outcome. Results depend on many factors outside your control, so spell out sessions and support, and avoid guaranteeing weight loss or lab changes.

faqs.question: What if a client's needs change during the program?
faqs.answer: Include a line in your quote stating that major changes, such as a new diagnosis or added family members, may require a revised plan and fee. Send an updated quote for the client to approve in writing.

dj.intro: DJs bill couples, corporate planners, schools, venues, and private party hosts for music and entertainment at weddings, receptions, birthday parties, school dances, corporate events, and club nights. Invoices usually cover the performance block, sound and lighting gear, add-on services like ceremony audio or MC work, and travel. Many DJs run solo or with a small crew, so the invoice also has to show deposits already paid and the balance due on or before the event date.
dj.pricingModel: Most event DJs sell packages priced as a flat fee for a set number of hours, such as a four-hour reception package, with an hourly rate for overtime. Add-ons like ceremony sound, uplighting, a photo booth, or a second speaker setup are priced separately as flat fees. Travel is often free within a set radius and then billed per mile or as a flat fee. Weddings and Saturday evenings in peak season cost more than weekday or off-season events. Club and bar DJs are usually paid per night or per set, and mobile DJs for corporate clients may bill a day rate that includes setup and teardown. A non-refundable retainer to hold the date is standard, with the balance due shortly before or on the day of the event.

rates.service: Wedding reception package (4-5 hours, sound, MC)

items.description: Wedding reception DJ and MC package, 5 hours (Saturday, June 14, Riverside Hall)
Ceremony audio: wireless mic, speaker, processional music
Uplighting, 12 fixtures
Overtime, extended dance floor past 11 PM
Travel beyond 40-mile radius (round trip, 30 extra miles)
Deposit received on contract signing (March 2)

sampleInvoice.notes: Remaining balance of $2,005 is due on receipt. Accepted by card, bank transfer, or check payable to the business name. Late balances over 7 days are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Thank you for including us in your day.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and venue name and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact booking and settles disputes about how many hours were contracted or played.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and what it includes
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget what the package covered, such as MC services, a dance floor light, or a planning meeting, so list it plainly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and equipment (ceremony audio, uplighting, extra speakers, microphones)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was provided beyond the base package and supports the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime hours and who requested them
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra time agreed on the night is the most common billing surprise, so note the time and approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit paid and date received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the balance is correct and keeps the non-refundable retainer visible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel mileage or flat travel fee and any venue fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Covers distance, parking, load-in fees, or venue-required insurance charges that were passed to the client.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract reference and client name as on the booking
invoiceChecklist.why: Connects the invoice to the signed agreement, especially when a planner or parent pays for someone else's event.

dj.paymentTerms: Most DJs collect a non-refundable retainer of 25-50% to hold the date when the contract is signed, with the balance due 7-14 days before the event or on the day of the event before the performance starts. Corporate clients and schools often pay net 15 to net 30 and may need a purchase order or W-9. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Card, bank transfer, and payment apps are all widely used, and cash or checks are often handed over at the event, so write down who received them and give a receipt.

tips.title: Put the balance due date before the event
tips.body: Collecting the balance a week or two before the date avoids chasing a couple who just got married or a host who is busy at their own party. State the due date in both the contract and the invoice.

tips.title: Spell out overtime in advance
tips.body: Include the hourly overtime rate in the contract and ask for approval on the night. Note it on the invoice with the actual end time so the charge is not a surprise.

tips.title: Separate the retainer from the package price
tips.body: Show the retainer as its own line or credit. It makes clear the deposit is not refundable and that the remaining balance is what is still owed.

tips.title: Bill for gear and travel that clients overlook
tips.body: Stairs-only load-ins, long distances, and extra speakers for large rooms all cost time and equipment. Charge for them in the quote and list them clearly so they are not seen as new fees.

tips.title: Keep records of every cancellation and date change
tips.body: Note any rescheduling fees and reference the original contract so refunds and credits are clear if a date shifts.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit as a DJ?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit or retainer of 25-50% is standard because it holds a date you can no longer sell to another client. State in the contract whether it is non-refundable, and show it as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for overtime?
faqs.answer: Use an hourly overtime rate listed in the contract, often the same as or slightly higher than your regular hourly rate. Add a line with the actual extra time played and, if possible, who approved it.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on DJ services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax entertainment or equipment rental, while others tax only physical goods. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and if you charge tax, show it as a separate line.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for a wedding?
faqs.answer: Many DJs send the final invoice 2-4 weeks before the event with the balance due date a week before or on the day. Send a deposit invoice immediately after booking and a reminder before the due date.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a venue or planner instead of the couple?
faqs.answer: Bill whoever signed the contract or agreed to pay, and put the event name and date on the invoice. Include any purchase order number, and ask whether they need a W-9 before payment.

estimate.intro: DJs send a quote when someone inquires about a date, usually after checking availability and learning a few details about the event. Clients commonly compare packages, hours, included equipment, and reviews from several DJs, so the quote should make the value and exclusions easy to see.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, location, and start and end times
scopeChecklist.why: Availability and price depend on the date and hours, and venue details affect setup time and travel.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of hours covered and overtime rate
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know exactly how long you will play and what extra time costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment included (speakers, microphones, lighting, backup gear)
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes over what was promised, especially for large rooms or outdoor events.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included (MC, ceremony audio, planning meeting, music requests, do-not-play list)
scopeChecklist.why: Different DJs bundle different services, and clients assume more is included than it is.
Stairs, long carries, venue insurance certificates, and distance can add cost and should be agreed on before booking.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, balance due date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know what holds the date and what happens if plans change.
A date can be booked by someone else, so state how long the price and availability are held.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and full package let clients compare options without negotiating line by line. Keep the differences clear, such as hours, ceremony audio, and lighting.

pricingTips.title: Price peak dates higher
pricingTips.body: Saturdays in May through October and holiday weekends book first and cost more. Give weekday and off-season dates a lower rate to fill your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Account for unpaid time
pricingTips.body: Include planning calls, music prep, drive time, setup, and teardown in your price. A four-hour reception often takes eight or more hours of your day.

pricingTips.title: List add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: Show uplighting, ceremony audio, and extra hours as individual prices so clients can add them later without restructuring the whole quote.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before knowing the venue?
faqs.answer: Give a ballpark range, but confirm the final price after you know the venue, load-in conditions, and travel distance. Note in the quote that it assumes standard setup.

faqs.question: How long should a DJ quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is common for in-demand dates. Say plainly that the date is not held until the contract is signed and the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: A quote usually becomes binding once the client signs a contract and pays the deposit. Until then it is an offer, so state any terms that would change the price, such as added hours or a venue change.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a consultation before the event?
faqs.answer: Most DJs include one or two planning meetings in the package price. If a client wants extensive extra meetings or custom mixes, set a separate fee and put it in the quote.

doctor.intro: Doctors who bill clients directly include independent physicians in cash-pay or direct primary care practices, concierge doctors, telehealth providers, occupational medicine and independent medical examiners, aesthetic and cosmetic physicians, and locum or consulting doctors. They invoice patients, employers, law firms, and other organizations for visits, exams, procedures, reports, and membership fees. Insurance-billed work follows claim rules and is mostly outside this page, which focuses on direct patient and client billing.
doctor.pricingModel: Pricing depends on the practice model. Direct primary care practices usually charge a monthly membership fee that covers visits and basic services, with labs and procedures billed separately or at cost. Cash-pay and concierge practices often charge a flat fee per visit based on length, such as a 20-minute follow-up or a 60-minute new patient visit. Procedures like joint injections, skin biopsies, or vasectomies are typically flat fees that include supplies. Independent medical examiners, expert witnesses, and consulting doctors bill hourly or per report, often with a retainer and separate rates for record review, exam, report writing, deposition, and testimony. Locum doctors bill hourly or per shift to the staffing agency or facility. Aesthetic practices price per unit (such as neurotoxin) or per treatment. Many practices publish a fee schedule so patients know the price before the visit.

rates.service: Medical record review for legal cases
Procedure, e.g. joint injection or skin biopsy (supplies included)

items.description: New patient comprehensive visit (60 min), 03/12
Point-of-care labs: A1c and lipid panel
Joint injection, right knee (includes supplies)
Follow-up telehealth visit (20 min), 03/26
Completion of employer physical form

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service or within 14 days of invoice date. This itemized statement can be submitted to your insurer for possible out-of-network reimbursement; reimbursement is not guaranteed. Accepted: card, HSA/FSA card, check, or bank transfer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Patient name, date of birth, and account number
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the correct patient and is typically required if the patient submits the statement for reimbursement. Avoid putting diagnoses on invoices that others may see.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Patients, insurers, and HSA/FSA administrators need exact dates to process or verify charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service descriptions with CPT codes where used
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network claims and HSA/FSA reimbursement often require procedure codes. Include diagnosis codes only when the patient needs a superbill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, NPI, practice address, and tax ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Required by most insurers for reimbursement and useful for patient tax records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for supplies, labs, and procedures
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing shows what the visit fee covers and avoids disputes over surprise charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments, deposits, and membership credits applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the true balance due and prevents double billing for prepaid memberships.

invoiceChecklist.item: For legal or IME work: case or claim number, attorney or requesting party, and hours by task
invoiceChecklist.why: Law firms and carriers require this to approve payment and match your invoice to the file.

doctor.paymentTerms: Cash-pay practices commonly collect payment at the time of service by card, HSA/FSA card, or bank transfer, and keep a card on file with the patient's written consent. Membership practices bill monthly or annually in advance. For IMEs, expert work, and record review, doctors usually require a retainer or full payment before the exam or testimony, with remaining balances due in 15 to 30 days. Late fees are less common with patients but are used with law firms and organizations; state them in writing in advance and check state rules on interest and collections. Provide a written good faith estimate for uninsured and self-pay patients, which the No Surprises Act requires in many cases.

tips.title: Collect at the time of service
tips.body: Medical balances are much harder to collect after the patient leaves. Keep a card on file with signed consent and charge the agreed fee at the end of the visit.

tips.title: Publish a fee schedule
tips.body: Listing prices for visits, common procedures, forms, and records requests reduces disputes and phone calls. Include fees for missed appointments and after-hours calls.

tips.title: Get retainers for medical-legal work
tips.body: Attorneys often pay slowly. Require payment before an IME, deposition, or testimony, and bill cancellations and late notices under a written fee agreement.

tips.title: Give patients a superbill
tips.body: Self-pay patients with out-of-network benefits or HSA/FSA accounts will ask for a document with codes and dates. Offering it on request saves staff time later.

tips.title: Keep billing separate from clinical notes
tips.body: Invoices should list services and amounts, not clinical detail. Share only the minimum information needed and follow HIPAA rules for any outside party.

faqs.question: Can I charge a no-show or late cancellation fee?
faqs.answer: In most states you can if the patient was told the policy in writing beforehand. Common fees are $25 to $100 or a percentage of the visit. Many doctors waive the first one.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and should I include one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with CPT and diagnosis codes, your NPI, and tax ID. Self-pay patients use it to seek reimbursement from their insurer. It is not a guarantee of payment, and you can provide it on request.

faqs.question: Can HSA and FSA cards pay for direct primary care memberships?
faqs.answer: HSA rules have limited the use of HSA funds for DPC memberships in some cases, though recent law changes have addressed this. Check current IRS guidance. FSA treatment varies by plan, so tell patients to check with their administrator.

faqs.question: How should I bill for medical records or form completion?
faqs.answer: Charge a flat fee per form or a per-page fee for record copies. Many states cap what you can charge for copies of a patient's own records, so check your state rules before setting fees.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on medical services?
faqs.answer: Medical services are generally exempt in most states, but retail products such as supplements or skincare sold in the office are often taxable. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Doctors give estimates mostly for self-pay and cosmetic patients, procedures not covered by insurance, and expert or IME work. Self-pay patients compare your price with hospitals, urgent care, and other cash-pay clinics. Law firms compare your hourly and flat fees with other expert witnesses.

scopeChecklist.why: List the visit type, length, procedure, and follow-up included so the patient knows what the fee covers.
These are the most common sources of surprise charges. State what is included and what is billed separately.
Anesthesia, pathology, radiology, and surgical center fees are often billed by others. Tell patients so they can plan.
Clarify how many follow-up visits are included and how revisions or complications are billed.
For uninsured and self-pay patients, federal rules in many cases require a written estimate listing expected items and services before scheduling.
Prevents disputes over deposits and fees for reserved procedure or exam time.

scopeChecklist.item: For IME and expert work: scope, hours, and what triggers extra fees
scopeChecklist.why: Records volume, added exams, report revisions, and testimony can change the total. State rates for each.

pricingTips.title: Quote flat fees for defined procedures
pricingTips.body: Patients prefer one price for a procedure with supplies and routine follow-up included. Base it on your time, supply cost, and malpractice exposure.

pricingTips.title: Separate known costs from variable ones
pricingTips.body: Show the fixed fee, then list items that may add cost, such as extra imaging or labs, with their prices.

pricingTips.title: Use retainers for expert and IME work
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for record review and report writing, collect a retainer against it, and bill added time at the stated hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiration date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Supply costs and your schedule change. A 30-day validity period is typical for elective procedures.

faqs.question: Do I have to give a written estimate to self-pay patients?
faqs.answer: Under the No Surprises Act, providers must give uninsured and self-pay patients a good faith estimate when scheduling services in advance or on request. Check current federal rules and your state's requirements.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Federal good faith estimate rules include a dispute process when charges exceed the estimate by a set amount. Even outside that, explain changes before doing extra work and get the patient's agreement.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit for a procedure?
faqs.answer: Deposits are common for elective and cosmetic procedures and for IMEs. A deposit of 20 to 50 percent, or full payment for exams, holds the time slot. State refund terms in writing.

faqs.question: Can I give a price over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a general fee schedule price, but note that the final cost depends on what the visit requires. Follow up in writing for anything beyond a standard visit.

dog-trainer.intro: Dog trainers run private lessons, group classes, board-and-train programs, and behavior consultations for pet owners. Most work solo or in a small business, and invoices cover sessions delivered, program packages, travel, and sometimes equipment. Clear billing matters because clients often pay in advance for packages that run over several weeks.
dog-trainer.pricingModel: Most trainers price by session or by package. Private lessons are billed per session, usually 45 to 60 minutes, with a discount when clients buy a bundle of four to six. Group classes are billed per series, typically six weeks, with payment due at enrollment. Board-and-train programs are priced per week or as a flat program fee, often with a nonrefundable deposit. Behavior consultations for issues like aggression or separation anxiety are usually priced higher, with a longer initial evaluation. Many trainers add a travel fee for in-home sessions beyond a set radius and sell equipment such as leashes, harnesses, or training treats at retail. Expect pricing to vary a lot by region, credentials, and demand.

items.description: Initial behavior evaluation (leash reactivity), 90 minutes, in-home
Private training lesson, loose-leash walking and reactivity work, 60 minutes
Travel fee, client located 22 miles from base
Front-clip harness
Training treat pouch and 2 bags of treats

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Unused sessions in a package expire 90 days after purchase. Late payments are subject to a $15 fee after 14 days. Please keep up the daily practice exercises sent after each lesson.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dog's name and the owner's name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many households have more than one dog, and the record should show which dog was trained and who is responsible for payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, length, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question package use later. Dates and durations show what was delivered and how many sessions remain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service type for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Evaluation, private lesson, group class, and board-and-train carry different rates and cancellation terms, so each should be listed separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: If a package has an expiration or a limit on use, stating it on the invoice prevents disputes about unused sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel charges with distance or zone
invoiceChecklist.why: A line like 22 miles from base explains the fee and avoids pushback on in-home visits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment and supplies sold, itemized
invoiceChecklist.why: Harnesses, leashes, and treats may be taxable in your state even when training services are not. Itemizing makes sales tax easier to handle.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications or business license number, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients, employers, or insurers want proof of credentials, and some cities require a business license for in-home services.

dog-trainer.paymentTerms: Most trainers collect payment before or at the first session for packages and group classes, since no-shows and drop-offs are common. For board-and-train programs, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is typical, with the balance due at drop-off or pick-up. Single private lessons are often paid at the end of each session or invoiced with 7-day terms. Late fees of $10 to $25 or a small percentage are common if stated in advance. Cards, bank transfers, and digital payment apps are the usual methods, and many trainers also keep a written cancellation policy requiring 24 hours notice for private sessions.

tips.title: Bill packages up front
tips.body: Collecting payment for a full package at the start improves client commitment and lowers missed sessions. Spell out what happens if the client stops partway through.

tips.title: Set a written cancellation policy
tips.body: Charge a late-cancel or no-show fee, often 50 to 100 percent of the session, for cancellations inside 24 hours. Put it in your agreement and on every invoice.

tips.title: Separate training from retail
tips.body: List equipment and treats as their own lines. This keeps your service revenue clear and helps with sales tax where it applies.

tips.title: Track mileage and travel time
tips.body: In-home work adds drive time. Either charge a travel fee or build it into your rates, and keep mileage logs for your own tax records.

tips.title: Be careful with outcome promises
tips.body: Avoid invoicing language that guarantees behavior results. Describe sessions delivered and homework provided, and note that results depend on the owner's follow-through.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or sell packages?
faqs.answer: Many trainers offer both. Single sessions suit one-off questions, while packages of four to six lessons fit most behavior goals and give you payment in advance. Packages are usually discounted a little per session.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on dog training?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax training services but do tax physical products like leashes and harnesses. Some states tax certain pet services. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I keep the deposit if a client cancels a board-and-train?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if your written agreement says the deposit is nonrefundable and explains why, since you reserved space and turned away other clients. Make sure the client signs the terms before paying.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a group class if someone misses a week?
faqs.answer: Group classes are normally billed for the full series at enrollment, and missed classes are not refunded. Many trainers offer a make-up class if space allows. State your policy in the registration terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge more for aggression or severe behavior cases?
faqs.answer: Many trainers do, because these cases need longer evaluations, more preparation, higher liability, and follow-up support. A separate consultation rate is common.

estimate.intro: Dog trainers send quotes before board-and-train programs, multi-week behavior plans, and sometimes group or corporate engagements like shelter or daycare staff training. Clients usually compare per-session cost, program length, what is included, and the trainer's methods and credentials. A clear written quote helps owners understand that behavior change takes multiple sessions.

scopeChecklist.why: List what you are working on, such as loose-leash walking, recall, or reactivity, so the client's expectations match the plan.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and location of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether the quote covers four one-hour in-home visits or a two-week stay at your facility.

scopeChecklist.item: What is and is not included
scopeChecklist.why: State whether follow-up emails, phone support, video check-ins, and equipment are included or billed separately.
Owners often care about methods and tools. Naming them up front prevents disagreement over collars, treats, or corrections.
Daily practice, consistent rules, and vaccination records affect results. Listing them shows progress depends on both sides.
Facilities and group classes typically require up-to-date vaccines, and a vet check may be needed for behavior cases.
Packages and deposits cause the most disputes, so state how they work before the client agrees.

pricingTips.title: Quote the program, not just the hour
pricingTips.body: Presenting a four-week plan at a package price shows value and sets expectations for progress, rather than inviting comparison with the cheapest hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers
pricingTips.body: Give two or three options, such as a basic package, a package with video support between sessions, and a board-and-train. Clients choose based on budget and urgency.

pricingTips.title: Price evaluations separately
pricingTips.body: For complex behavior cases, quote the initial evaluation first and a full plan after you meet the dog. You avoid underquoting a case you have not seen.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration on the quote
pricingTips.body: Schedules fill up. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days protects your calendar and prompts a decision.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before meeting the dog?
faqs.answer: For basic obedience or puppy training, a standard package quote is fine. For aggression, bite history, or severe anxiety, quote only the evaluation first, since the right plan depends on what you observe.

faqs.question: Can I guarantee results in a quote?
faqs.answer: It is safer not to. Behavior depends on the dog, the owner's follow-through, and the environment. Promise the sessions and instruction you will provide, and avoid guarantees you cannot control.

faqs.question: Should the quote include a deposit?
faqs.answer: For board-and-train programs and group classes, yes. A deposit holds the spot and shows commitment. Many trainers ask for 25 to 50 percent, due when the client accepts the quote.

faqs.question: What if the dog needs more sessions than quoted?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that the plan is based on typical progress and that extra sessions are billed at a stated rate. Discuss it with the client before adding anything.

dog-walker.intro: Dog walkers are usually solo operators or small businesses who walk dogs on a recurring or one-off basis while owners are at work or away. Invoices typically cover individual walks, weekly or monthly walk packages, add-on services like extra pets or medication, and holiday or last-minute surcharges.
dog-walker.pricingModel: Most dog walkers charge a flat price per walk, set by length (typically 20, 30, or 60 minutes). Many offer discounted packages or a weekly or monthly rate for recurring clients, billed in advance. Additional dogs in the same household usually cost a smaller add-on fee rather than a full second walk. Group walks cost less per dog than solo walks. Common surcharges include holidays, same-day bookings, cancellations with short notice, extra distance outside your service area, and special handling such as reactive dogs, puppies, or medication. Drop-in visits and pet sitting are often billed per visit or per night alongside walks. Prices depend heavily on the local market, with big metro areas at the high end.

rates.service: Puppy potty break or drop-in visit (15-20 min)

items.description: 30-minute solo walk, Biscuit (Mon-Fri, Jun 3-7)
Additional dog, Pepper, same household (Jun 3-7)
60-minute weekend hike, Biscuit (Sat Jun 8)
Holiday surcharge (Juneteenth, Wed Jun 19)
Medication administration, Pepper (Jun 3-7)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Walks are billed weekly. Cancellations with less than 12 hours notice are charged at 50 percent. Thank you for trusting me with Biscuit and Pepper.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dog names and household
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several dogs or multiple addresses need to see which pet each line refers to, especially when add-on dog fees apply.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and times of each walk
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners often want to match charges against their calendar, and a dated list settles questions about missed or extra walks quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Walk length and type (solo, group, drop-in)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different walk types carry different rates, so labeling each one prevents confusion over why charges vary.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons and surcharges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Holiday fees, medication, extra dogs, or late cancellations should be visible line items so they do not look like surprise charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and late-cancel fees
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge for short-notice cancellations, listing the date and policy keeps the charge easy to justify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and package details
invoiceChecklist.why: Weekly, monthly, or prepaid package clients need to see what period is covered and any remaining balance or credits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, insurance or bonding status, and any local license or permit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Some cities require a dog walking permit, and showing insurance details on paperwork reassures clients and supports any claims.

dog-walker.paymentTerms: Many dog walkers bill weekly or monthly in advance for recurring clients and due-on-receipt or net 7 for one-off walks. Pre-billing protects you from missed payments because the walks are already delivered once the invoice goes unpaid. New clients may be asked to pay for the first week or a meet-and-greet upfront. Common payment methods include card payments, bank transfer, and peer-to-peer payment apps, and some walkers keep a card on file for automatic billing. Late fees of around 5 to 10 percent, or a flat amount, are common after 7 to 14 days, and many walkers pause service if a balance goes unpaid. Spell out your cancellation window (often 12 to 24 hours) and holiday pricing in a written service agreement so the invoice matches what was agreed.

tips.title: Bill in advance for regular clients
tips.body: Weekly or monthly prepayment gives you steady cash flow and avoids chasing small amounts. Adjust at the end of the period for any added or canceled walks.

tips.title: Put cancellation and holiday rules in writing
tips.body: Most disputes come from short-notice cancellations and holiday rates. A signed service agreement or a clear policy sent with the first invoice makes these charges easy to enforce.

tips.title: Charge for the dog, not just the time
tips.body: Reactive dogs, puppies, large pulling dogs, and medication add real effort and risk. Price those walks higher or add a handling fee instead of absorbing it.

tips.title: Track mileage and travel time
tips.body: If clients are spread out, consider a travel fee outside a set radius. Also track mileage for your own tax records, since vehicle costs are often a deductible business expense.

tips.title: Offer packages with expiration dates
tips.body: Prepaid packages of 10 or 20 walks usually come with a small discount. Set an expiration period so unused walks do not stay on your books indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I charge per walk or per month?
faqs.answer: Per walk is simple and works for irregular schedules. For clients with a steady weekly schedule, a monthly rate billed in advance is easier to manage and gives you predictable income. Either way, list the number of walks the rate covers.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a second dog?
faqs.answer: Most walkers charge the full rate for the first dog and a reduced add-on, often $5 to $12, for each additional dog from the same household. Show the add-on as its own line so the discount is clear.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a walk the client canceled at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy says so and the client agreed to it in advance. Many walkers charge 50 to 100 percent for cancellations inside 12 to 24 hours. Note the date and policy on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on dog walking?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax pet services like walking, but some tax pet care services or related items. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I need a business license or insurance to bill clients?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by city and state. Some places require a business license or a pet service permit. Liability and bonding insurance are not always legally required but are widely recommended and often requested by clients.

estimate.intro: Dog walkers send a quote after a meet-and-greet or an inquiry about a recurring schedule, a vacation period, or a multi-dog household. Clients usually compare per-walk price, walk length, whether walks are solo or group, and how reliable and insured the walker is.

scopeChecklist.item: Walk length, frequency, and days of the week
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for three 30-minute walks a week is very different from daily 60-minute walks, so be exact about the schedule.
Group walks cost less and carry different risks. Clients should know whether their dog will be with other dogs.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of dogs and their details
scopeChecklist.why: Size, behavior, age, and medical needs affect price and whether you can take the job at all.
State which neighborhoods are included and what you charge if the address falls outside that area.
Spell out what is covered, such as wiping paws, feeding, fresh water, or updates and photos, and what costs extra, like medication or key pickup.
Clients who know these up front are far less likely to dispute them on the first invoice.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, quote expiration, and deposit
scopeChecklist.why: Your availability changes quickly. An expiration date and a deposit or first-week payment hold a spot on your schedule.

pricingTips.title: Quote a weekly or monthly total
pricingTips.body: Show the per-walk rate and the total for the week or month. A single total is easier for a client to compare against other walkers and to approve.

pricingTips.title: Price in the behavior and logistics
pricingTips.body: A dog who needs leash work, a long drive to the client, or a tricky pickup takes more time than the walk itself. Include that in your rate or add a clear surcharge.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: Present choices such as 30 versus 60 minutes, or solo versus small group, with prices for each. Clients often pick the middle option and feel in control of the decision.

pricingTips.title: Do not undercut to win the job
pricingTips.body: Fuel, insurance, gear, and unpaid travel time between clients are real costs. A low rate leaves little room for sick days or cancellations.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the meet-and-greet?
faqs.answer: Many walkers do it free, since it leads to ongoing work. Others charge $20 to $40, often credited toward the first walk, to filter out clients who are not serious. Choose one approach and state it in the quote.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is common. Your schedule fills up and rates may change, so an expiration date protects you from clients accepting weeks later at an old price.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after I start walking the dog?
faqs.answer: Only if the quote allows for it. If you discover behavior issues or extra needs, tell the client right away and send a revised quote. Include a clause that rates may be adjusted if the dog's needs differ from what was described.

door-installer.intro: Door installers hang and replace interior doors, exterior entry doors, patio and sliding doors, storm doors, and garage man doors for homeowners, builders, property managers, and remodeling contractors. Invoices usually cover labor per door, the door and hardware if you supplied them, trim and finish work, and haul-away of the old unit.
door-installer.pricingModel: Most door installers price per door, since a standard job has predictable steps. Interior slab or prehung doors are usually a flat fee per door, with a discount for multiple doors in the same visit. Exterior entry doors, sliding doors, and French doors are priced higher because of framing, flashing, sill work, and weight. Hourly rates ($50-100) are common for repairs, adjustments, and unknown conditions like rot or out-of-square frames. Doors and hardware you supply are billed at cost plus a markup, typically 15-30%. Extras such as new jamb extensions, lockset boring, painting or staining, and old door disposal are listed as separate lines. Builders and contractors often negotiate a per-door rate on volume and pay on net terms.

rates.service: Interior slab door hang (mortise hinges, bore, latch)
Exterior entry door replacement (prehung, existing opening)
French door or double door install
Lockset or deadbolt install, bore new holes

items.description: Remove existing entry door and install new prehung fiberglass entry door, shim, flash sill, and seal
Install customer-supplied deadbolt and handleset, bore new holes
Install interior prehung doors (hall and bedroom), trim and nail set
Additional carpentry: repair rotted jamb section and install sill pan
Shims, foam sealant, exterior caulk, screws, and misc. materials
Haul away and disposal of 4 old doors

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days. Doors supplied by customer; manufacturer warranty applies to the product. Installation labor is warranted for one year against defects in workmanship. Please call if any door sticks during seasonal changes and I will adjust it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Door location, size, and swing for each unit
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing 'master bedroom, 32x80, left-hand inswing' makes clear which door was done and helps with warranty claims or future service calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who supplied the door and hardware
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates your labor from product cost and makes clear who handles manufacturer warranty on defects or damage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials itemized separately from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Shims, flashing tape, sealant, sill pans, and threshold parts add up, and clients and builders often want them shown.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extra work beyond the original quote
invoiceChecklist.why: Rot repair, out-of-square framing, or wall patching found after removal should be listed with the reason to avoid disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices, especially above a certain job value. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or job number for builder and property manager work
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial and contractor clients often will not process payment without a PO, unit number, or job reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the length and scope of your workmanship warranty sets expectations on sticking doors, gaps, and seal failures.

door-installer.paymentTerms: For retail homeowner jobs, many installers collect a deposit of 25-50% when the door is ordered, especially for custom or special-order doors that cannot be returned, with the balance due on completion. Small jobs under a few hundred dollars are often paid in full on the day of install. Builders and property managers typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, so state the terms on the invoice. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is common if it is written in your agreement or on the quote. Accept checks, cards, and bank transfers, and consider requiring payment before leaving for new customers on larger jobs.

tips.title: Get the door money upfront
tips.body: If you order the door, collect the full cost of the product or a large deposit before placing the order. Special-order doors are often non-returnable, and you do not want to be stuck with a custom size if the client backs out.

tips.title: Price by door, then add conditions
tips.body: Quote a base price per door assuming a standard opening, then list rot, out-of-plumb framing, stucco or brick work, and trim changes as extras at an hourly or fixed add-on rate.

tips.title: Charge for haul-away
tips.body: Old exterior doors are heavy and many dump facilities charge by weight. A flat disposal fee per door or per trip covers your time and fees.

tips.title: Bundle multiple interior doors
tips.body: Offer a lower per-door price when a client has four or more doors done in one visit. It wins the job and saves you setup and travel time, while still being profitable.

tips.title: Photograph the finished work
tips.body: Take photos of flashing, sill pans, and the finished install before closing things up. If water problems appear later, photos protect you and support your invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge per door or per hour?
faqs.answer: Use a flat per-door price for standard installs where conditions are known, and hourly for repairs, adjustments, and extra work found after the old door is removed. Many installers combine both on one invoice.

faqs.question: Can I mark up doors and hardware I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: Yes. A markup of 15-30% is common to cover sourcing, pickup, handling, and the risk of returns or damage. Show the product as its own line item so the client can see what is labor and what is material.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a door that arrives damaged or the wrong size?
faqs.answer: Do not install it. Bill any trip or measuring time if it was not your error, and clarify in your quote who is responsible for verifying measurements and handedness. If you ordered it, you typically handle the return or claim with the supplier.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax materials you sell, some tax labor on installations, and others tax neither in certain cases. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax on a separate line when it applies.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses to pay the balance after the install?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder with the invoice and agreed terms, then follow up with a formal demand letter. Depending on your state and license, you may be able to file a mechanic's lien on larger jobs, and small claims court is an option for smaller amounts.

estimate.intro: Door installers usually quote before ordering product or booking a crew, often after a site visit to measure the opening and check the frame, wall, and sill. Clients usually compare your price against other installers and big-box store installation programs, so a clear written scope helps you stand apart.

scopeChecklist.item: Door size, style, swing, and rough opening measurements
scopeChecklist.why: Handedness and size errors are the most common and costly mistakes. Writing them down lets the client confirm before you order.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies the door, hardware, and trim
scopeChecklist.why: Makes clear what your price includes and who deals with defective or damaged product.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the install
scopeChecklist.why: List removal of the old door, shimming, flashing, sealing, weatherstripping, hardware install, and cleanup so the client knows what they are getting.
Painting, staining, caulking, trim, and drywall patching are often assumed to be included. State if they are or are not.

scopeChecklist.item: Unknown conditions and how they will be priced
scopeChecklist.why: Rot, termite damage, out-of-square framing, or a wrong-size opening may only show once the old door is out. Set an hourly rate or approval process for extras.
Special-order doors can take weeks. Giving an estimated delivery and install window prevents complaints about delays that are the supplier's.
Door and material prices change. A 30-day validity and a clear deposit amount protect you from cost increases.

pricingTips.title: Visit before quoting exterior doors
pricingTips.body: Exterior and patio doors vary too much to price from photos alone. Check the sill, framing, and wall type, since stucco, brick, and rotted sills change the labor significantly.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic steel door, a mid-range fiberglass door, and a premium wood or glass option with install prices for each. Clients often choose the middle one and feel in control.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for older homes
pricingTips.body: Houses built before the 1980s often have out-of-square openings and non-standard sizes. Add buffer time or a stated allowance for framing adjustments.

pricingTips.title: Separate product from labor
pricingTips.body: Showing door cost and installation cost on separate lines makes your labor price easier to defend and allows clients to buy the door themselves if they want to.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many door installers give free estimates for standard jobs. For complex projects or long drives, charge a trip or measuring fee, often $50-150, and credit it toward the job if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. If the door is special order or material prices are moving, use a shorter period of 14 days and say so on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than my estimate?
faqs.answer: Only when the client approves a change in writing, ideally before you do the work. Your quote should explain which conditions can raise the price, such as rot or framing repair, and how those will be billed.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed price without seeing the opening?
faqs.answer: For a standard interior prehung swap, you can give a price range from photos and measurements. For anything exterior, confirm on site first, or state that the price is an estimate subject to inspection.

doula.intro: Doulas provide non-medical emotional, physical, and informational support during pregnancy, birth, and the postpartum period. Most are independent contractors or run a small practice, and they bill families directly for birth support packages, postpartum care, and add-on services. Invoices usually cover a package fee split into a retainer and a final balance, or hourly shifts for postpartum work.
doula.pricingModel: Birth doulas usually charge a flat package fee that covers prenatal visits, on-call availability from about 37 to 42 weeks, continuous labor support, and one or two postpartum visits. Prices vary a lot by region and experience, with larger metro areas at the higher end. A non-refundable retainer, often 25 to 50 percent, books the client's due date, and the balance is due by a set date before or shortly after the birth. Postpartum doulas typically bill hourly, often with a minimum shift length of 3 to 4 hours, and may offer discounted blocks of 20, 40, or 80 hours, with overnight shifts priced at a higher hourly rate or a flat rate. Add-ons such as lactation support, placenta encapsulation (if you are trained and your state allows it), childbirth classes, birth photography, or a backup doula fee are listed as separate lines. Some doulas offer sliding scale pricing, payment plans, or work with community-based programs and Medicaid in states where doula services are reimbursable, so check your local rules.

rates.service: Birth doula package (prenatal visits, on-call, labor support, postpartum visit)
Childbirth education or birth preparation class
Doula services for a planned cesarean or induction (extended support)

items.description: Birth doula package: 2 prenatal visits, on-call 37-42 weeks, continuous labor support, 1 postpartum visit
Additional prenatal visit (birth plan and comfort measures)
Extended labor support beyond 24 hours
Postpartum visit (feeding support and birth processing)
Less: retainer paid at contract signing

sampleInvoice.notes: Baby born 3/14, labor support from 9:30 pm on 3/13 to 2:15 am on 3/15. Balance of $1,540 is due within 7 days of the postpartum visit. Payment accepted by check, bank transfer, or card. Retainer is non-refundable per the signed service agreement. Services are non-medical and do not replace care from a physician or midwife.

invoiceChecklist.item: Estimated due date and actual birth date
invoiceChecklist.why: The package is tied to the on-call window, so both dates show the client when services started and ended and support your final balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package contents and number of visits delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients should be able to match each prenatal and postpartum visit on the invoice with what the contract promised.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer paid and date received
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear credit line avoids confusion over how the balance was calculated, especially if the retainer was paid months earlier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours worked and shift times for hourly services
invoiceChecklist.why: Postpartum shifts and extended labor support are billed by time, so start and end times protect you in a dispute about minimums or overnight rates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line items for add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Classes, extra visits, backup doula fees, and encapsulation are optional, and listing them separately keeps the base package price clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or parking charges, if your contract allows
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel outside your usual service area, hospital parking fees, and long drives to a birth center are often billed, but only if the contract says so.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification and business details
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing your certifying organization (such as DONA, CAPPA, or ProDoula, if applicable), business name, and contact info helps clients submit receipts to HSA or FSA accounts or insurance where accepted.

doula.paymentTerms: Most doulas collect a non-refundable retainer of 25 to 50 percent at signing and the balance by around 36 to 37 weeks or within a week after the birth. Postpartum work is often billed weekly or at the end of each block, with larger blocks paid up front. Late fees are uncommon but can be written into the contract, for example 1.5 percent per month after 14 days. Payment methods include bank transfer, card, check, and payment apps. Some doulas offer payment plans so families can pay in installments before the due date. Clients may ask for itemized receipts for HSA or FSA reimbursement, and some states have Medicaid or insurance billing for doula care, which has its own claim rules.

tips.title: Put the retainer and cancellation terms in writing
tips.body: Births are unpredictable, and clients sometimes switch providers or move. A signed agreement that says the retainer is non-refundable and what happens if you cannot attend a birth prevents most disputes.

tips.title: Define on-call and what counts as a missed birth
tips.body: State your on-call window, how fast you arrive, and what refund or partial credit applies if you miss the birth because of a very fast labor or a scheduled cesarean. Backup doula terms belong here too.

tips.title: Set a minimum shift for postpartum work
tips.body: A 3 or 4 hour minimum covers your travel and scheduling. Spell out overnight rates, holiday rates, and charges for last-minute cancellations.

tips.title: Offer payment plans with set dates
tips.body: Many families need to split the fee. Agree on installment dates in advance and make sure the full balance is paid before or soon after the birth, since you cannot easily collect once a newborn is in the house.

tips.title: Keep records for receipts and taxes
tips.body: Save contracts, invoices, and mileage logs. Independent doulas are generally self-employed for tax purposes and should set aside money for self-employment tax and estimated payments. Ask a tax professional about your situation.

faqs.question: Should I bill a birth doula package as a flat fee or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Flat fee is standard because births vary from a few hours to several days. Many doulas add an extended labor fee after a set number of hours, such as 24 or 30, so very long births are covered.

faqs.question: Is the retainer refundable?
faqs.answer: Most doulas make it non-refundable because it reserves your availability around the due date. Put the terms in the contract and show the retainer as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: When should I send the final invoice for a birth package?
faqs.answer: Many doulas invoice the balance at around 36 weeks so it is paid before labor. Others send it after the final postpartum visit. Choose one approach and state it in your contract.

faqs.question: Can clients use HSA or FSA funds for doula services?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Rules vary by plan, and some require a letter of medical necessity. Provide an itemized invoice with your business information and let clients check with their plan administrator.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on doula services?
faqs.answer: In most states, services like doula support are not taxed, but products such as encapsulated placenta or sold items may be. Rules vary, so check with your state's department of revenue.

estimate.intro: Doulas usually give a written quote after an initial consultation, when a family is interviewing several doulas for their due date. Clients compare package prices, what is included, on-call terms, and whether a backup doula is provided. A clear estimate also helps families plan payments before the birth.

scopeChecklist.why: List the number of prenatal visits, the length of each, labor support, and the number of postpartum visits so clients can compare packages fairly.
Clients want to know when you are available, such as 37 to 42 weeks, and how quickly you will join them once they call.
If you are sick, at another birth, or unreachable, the quote should say who steps in and whether the client meets them beforehand.
Showing what is due at signing and when the balance is due prevents surprises, especially for families on a payment plan.
Clarify when additional hourly fees apply, such as after 24 hours, and whether travel beyond a set distance or parking costs are billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation, transfer of care, and missed birth policy
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may switch providers, have a cesarean, or deliver before you arrive. State what happens to the fees in each case.
Make clear that doulas provide non-medical support and do not give medical advice or perform clinical tasks, which sets expectations with clients and hospital staff.

pricingTips.title: Price against local demand and your experience
pricingTips.body: Check what other doulas in your area charge. New doulas often start lower to build reviews and raise prices as they attend more births and add certifications.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic package with labor support and one postpartum visit, plus a fuller option with extra prenatal visits and postpartum hours, lets clients choose without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Account for the unpredictable schedule
pricingTips.body: Remember that on-call time means you cannot travel or take other commitments for several weeks. Your price should cover long labors, missed sleep, and recovery time after a birth.

pricingTips.title: State your sliding scale or community rate clearly
pricingTips.body: If you offer reduced fees, describe the criteria and how many slots you have so families understand how it works and your full price stays clear.

faqs.question: How long should a doula quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Many doulas hold a quote for 7 to 14 days after the consultation, since availability for a due date month can fill quickly. Say clearly that the date is only reserved once the contract is signed and the retainer is paid.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include postpartum support?
faqs.answer: If your package includes any postpartum visits, list them. For extended postpartum care by the hour, provide a separate quote with the hourly rate, minimum shift, and block options.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed package once the contract is signed. You can charge extra only for items the quote described as variable, such as extended labor hours or added visits.

faqs.question: What if the family wants only part of the package?
faqs.answer: Quote each service separately, such as hospital labor support or postpartum hours alone. Many doulas set a minimum fee for partial services because on-call availability is the main commitment.

driving-instructor.intro: Driving instructors teach new and returning drivers through behind-the-wheel lessons, often alongside classroom or online theory. Most work solo or for a small driving school, and bill teens, parents, adults learning to drive for the first time, and sometimes immigrants converting a foreign license or older drivers who want a refresher. Typical invoice items include in-car lessons, road test preparation, use of the school's vehicle for the test, and pickup or travel fees.
driving-instructor.pricingModel: Most driving instructors charge per lesson, usually 60 to 120 minutes, and sell discounted packages such as 6 or 10 lessons paid up front. State-approved teen programs often use a fixed package that covers the required behind-the-wheel hours (commonly 6 to 10 hours, depending on the state) plus classroom instruction. Adult beginners and nervous drivers often pay a higher per-lesson rate because they need more patience and time. Extras include road test car rental (the learner uses your dual-control car at the DMV), pickup and drop-off outside your service area, weekend or evening slots, and specialty lessons such as highway driving, parallel parking, or senior refreshers. Cancellation and no-show fees are common because each missed lesson is an empty slot and wasted fuel. Instructors who own their car should price in fuel, insurance, maintenance, and licensing, not only their own time.

rates.service: Adult beginner or nervous driver lesson
Road test car rental with pre-test warm-up lesson
Pickup and drop-off outside service area

items.description: Behind-the-wheel lesson, 60 min (dates: 3/4, 3/11, 3/18, 3/25)
Highway and merging practice, 90 min (3/29)
Road test car rental with 45-min warm-up (test date 4/3, DMV)
Late cancellation fee (3/21, less than 24 hours notice)

sampleInvoice.notes: Student: Jordan M. Instructor license no. on file. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Cancellations require 24 hours notice or the late fee applies. Unused prepaid lessons expire 6 months after purchase. Thank you for choosing our school.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or guardian name for minors
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents usually pay for teens, and the invoice should name who is responsible for the balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson dates, start times, and durations
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and parents want to match charges to actual sessions, and it protects you in a dispute over hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your instructor license number and driving school license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require licensed instructors and schools, and some insurers or reimbursement programs ask for it. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours completed toward state requirements
invoiceChecklist.why: Teens often need documented behind-the-wheel hours for a permit or license, so a running total helps families and keeps your records consistent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance and remaining lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages create confusion if you do not show how many lessons were used and how many remain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Road test rental line item with test date and location
invoiceChecklist.why: The test car fee is a separate service from lessons and should be easy to see and verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show fees with the date and policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute these charges less often when the invoice shows the date and refers to the policy they agreed to.

driving-instructor.paymentTerms: Many instructors collect payment at or before the lesson, or require a deposit when booking a package. Single lessons are often paid the day of the lesson by card or a payment app, while packages are paid in full before the first session. If you bill after the fact, net 7 days is common and net 14 is generous. Late fees are less common than cancellation fees, but some schools add a small fee after 14 days. Cash, card, and payment apps are all widely used. Refunds for unused package lessons vary by school, so state your policy in writing, including any expiration date and whether a partial refund is available.

tips.title: Sell packages and collect up front
tips.body: Prepaid packages of 6 or 10 lessons improve cash flow and reduce no-shows because the student has already paid. Offer a modest discount compared with the single-lesson price.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: A 24-hour notice rule is standard. Include it on your booking confirmation and print a short reminder on each invoice so a late cancellation fee is not a surprise.

tips.title: Charge separately for the test car
tips.body: Using your insured, dual-control vehicle for a road test carries real risk and takes extra time for the warm-up and waiting at the DMV. List it as its own line item rather than folding it into a lesson rate.

tips.title: Track mileage and vehicle costs
tips.body: Fuel, insurance, extra brake and tire wear, and commercial vehicle registration add up quickly. Review your per-lesson rate once or twice a year against those costs. Ask a tax professional how to deduct vehicle expenses.

tips.title: Bill the payer, not just the student
tips.body: For minors, address the invoice to the parent or guardian. For adult students whose employer or a program is paying, confirm who gets the invoice and whether they need a PO or student ID.

faqs.question: Should I charge per lesson or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Most instructors charge per lesson with a stated length, such as 60 or 90 minutes. This avoids arguments about a few minutes over or under and makes packages easy to price. If a lesson runs long, you can bill the next standard increment.

faqs.question: What should I put on an invoice for a prepaid package?
faqs.answer: List the package name, the number of lessons, the price, and the date paid. On later statements show lessons used with dates and lessons remaining. Include the expiration date if your packages have one.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for no-shows and late cancellations?
