faqs.answer: Yes, in most places, as long as the policy is clear and agreed to before the lesson. Common practice is a fee of half to the full lesson price for cancellations with less than 24 hours notice. Make sure the client has seen the policy in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on driving lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states treat instruction as non-taxable, but some tax certain services or vehicle rentals. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional, especially for the road test car rental.

faqs.question: How do I handle a student who stops mid-package?
faqs.answer: Follow your written refund policy. A common approach is to refund unused lessons at the package per-lesson rate, not the discounted rate, minus any fees stated in your agreement. Show the calculation on a final invoice or credit note.

estimate.intro: Driving instructors send quotes when a family is comparing schools, when a student needs a custom number of lessons, or when someone wants a bundle that includes road test preparation. Clients usually compare per-lesson price, lesson length, what hours count toward state requirements, and whether the test car is included.

scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 6 lessons at 60 minutes is very different from 6 at 90 minutes, and clients often assume more time than you intended.
Teen families need to know if the package satisfies the behind-the-wheel hours required by the state or the insurance discount program.
State where you will meet the student and any extra fee for pickups beyond your normal area.

scopeChecklist.item: Road test car rental and warm-up
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the test car is included, how long the warm-up is, and who pays the DMV test fee, which is usually separate.
Mention that lessons use your dual-control, insured vehicle, and whether a student may use their own car if allowed.
Set expectations on notice, rescheduling, and how long the package remains valid.
Permit fees, DMV test fees, classroom hours, and extra lessons if the student is not ready should be listed as excluded or priced separately.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a basic 6-lesson package, a standard 10-lesson package, and one with test car rental included. Clients tend to choose the middle option, and it helps you plan your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Price in the time you really spend
pricingTips.body: Count drive time between students, fuel, and gaps in your schedule. A 60-minute lesson often takes 75 to 90 minutes of your day, so rates that look fine on paper can fall short.

pricingTips.title: Quote adult beginners with a range
pricingTips.body: Nervous or first-time adult drivers may need more lessons than expected. Quote a starting package and state your per-lesson rate for additional sessions so there is no surprise.

pricingTips.title: Put a validity date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Fuel prices, insurance, and demand change. A 14 or 30 day expiration keeps the price fair for you and encourages a decision.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or a per-lesson price?
faqs.answer: Give both when possible. A flat package price is easy to compare and gets money up front, while a per-lesson price shows what extra sessions cost if the student needs more time.

faqs.question: Can I guarantee a student will pass the road test?
faqs.answer: No. You can promise the preparation you provide, but passing depends on the student and the examiner. Avoid wording that suggests a guarantee, and state that extra lessons are billed at your standard rate.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement for a quote?
faqs.answer: A written acceptance is a good idea, especially for large packages. An email reply or a signed quote that confirms the lessons, price, and cancellation terms is usually enough to prevent misunderstandings.

drone-photographer.intro: Drone photographers and videographers shoot aerial photos and video for real estate agents, construction firms, solar and roofing companies, wedding clients, event organizers, and marketing teams. Invoices typically cover a shoot block (half day, full day, or a set number of properties), editing and delivery, and any extras like licensing, travel, or special permissions.
drone-photographer.pricingModel: Most drone photographers price by the job or by package rather than by the hour. Real estate work is often a flat fee per property with a set number of photos and a short video. Commercial and construction work is commonly a day rate or half-day rate, or a recurring monthly fee for progress documentation. Editing is either bundled into the package or billed hourly for custom work like color-graded video, 3D models, or orthomosaic maps. Add-ons are common: rush delivery, extra locations, travel beyond a set radius, additional insured certificates, airspace authorization, and expanded usage licensing. Many pilots separate the shoot fee from the licensing fee so that commercial or broadcast use costs more than a basic web license. Clients who need a visual inspection, mapping, or survey-grade data pay more than those buying marketing photos.

rates.service: Real estate aerial photo package (10-20 photos)
Real estate aerial photo and video package
Roof or structure inspection with photo report

items.description: Aerial photo and video shoot, 4-acre commercial property (half day, 12 edited photos, 60-second edited video)
Additional location: adjacent parcel, same day
Additional video editing: client-requested revisions and logo overlay
Rush delivery (48 hours)
Travel beyond 30 miles

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Price includes a 12-month web and social media license for the delivered files. Print, broadcast, or paid advertising use requires a separate license. FAA Part 107 certificate and liability insurance on file. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot date, location, and job address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific flight and makes it easy to reconcile if the client has several properties or sites.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables with counts and formats
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the number of photos, video length, and file types (JPEG, RAW, 4K MP4) prevents arguments about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license terms and duration
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out where and for how long the client can use the files, and what triggers an extra licensing fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Part 107 remote pilot certificate number
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients, property managers, and insurers often ask for proof that the flight was legal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance and any airspace authorization noted
invoiceChecklist.why: If you flew in controlled airspace with LAANC or a waiver, noting it shows the flight was compliant and supports your pricing for added prep.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and extra edit rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Video clients often request changes after delivery. A stated limit makes extra edit hours billable without conflict.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, and site fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Remote sites, parking, permits, or park and event access fees are real costs that should be itemized instead of absorbed.

drone-photographer.paymentTerms: Many drone photographers take a 25-50% deposit to book larger commercial jobs and require full payment up front or at delivery for small real estate shoots. Final balances are commonly due net 7 to net 15, and agencies or construction firms may ask for net 30 and a PO number. Many pilots hold final high-resolution files or remove watermarks until payment clears. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Cards, ACH, and online payment links are typical, and weather reschedules or cancellations are often covered by a rebooking policy and a late-cancellation fee.

tips.title: Separate the shoot fee from the license
tips.body: Bill flight and editing time as one line and usage rights as another. This lets you raise the price when a client wants to use footage in paid ads or broadcast without reworking your whole rate.

tips.title: Charge for weather days clearly
tips.body: Decide in advance what happens if wind, rain, or a TFR cancels the flight. Common approaches are a free reschedule for weather, with a fee only if the client cancels on short notice or the crew is already on site.

tips.title: Bill for prep on controlled airspace
tips.body: LAANC approvals, waivers, and coordination with property managers take time. Add a flat airspace and planning fee for jobs near airports or restricted areas.

tips.title: Itemize editing separately from flying
tips.body: Flight time is often short while editing takes several hours. Showing editing as its own line explains your price and gives you a clear basis for billing extra revisions.

tips.title: Keep insurance and gear costs in your base rates
tips.body: Liability insurance, batteries, spare drones, and software subscriptions are ongoing costs. Build them into your day rate so small jobs do not lose money.

faqs.question: Do I need a Part 107 certificate to invoice for drone photography?
faqs.answer: In the US, flying a drone for paid work generally requires an FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate. Clients and insurers often ask for it, so including your certificate number on invoices and contracts is a good habit. Check current FAA rules for your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge per photo, per hour, or per project?
faqs.answer: Per project or package is the most common for real estate and small business work. Day or half-day rates fit commercial shoots. Hourly billing mostly applies to editing, consulting, or extra revisions.

faqs.question: How do I bill for editing time?
faqs.answer: Either include a set amount of editing in your package price and state the number of revision rounds, or list editing as its own line with an hourly rate. Charge extra for revisions beyond what was agreed.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee if weather cancels the shoot?
faqs.answer: Usually not if you can reschedule at no cost, since the work was not done. You can charge a cancellation or trip fee if the client cancels late or if you traveled to a remote site. Put the policy in writing before booking.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on aerial photos?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax photography services or digital products and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line when it applies.

estimate.intro: Drone photographers usually send a quote before booking, especially for commercial, construction, or multi-location jobs. Clients often compare several pilots on price, deliverables, insurance, and turnaround, so the quote needs to make what is included obvious.

scopeChecklist.why: A single site, several parcels, or repeat visits change travel, battery, and time needs and should be priced accordingly.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables with counts, resolution, and formats
scopeChecklist.why: State the number of photos, video length, and file types so the client knows exactly what they are buying.
Clarifies whether the price covers web use only or also print, ads, or broadcast, and avoids disputes after delivery.

scopeChecklist.item: Airspace, permits, and site access responsibilities
scopeChecklist.why: Identify who handles landowner permission, LAANC or waivers, and any park or event fees, and whether those are extra.
Flights get delayed by wind, rain, or low cloud. A clear policy sets expectations and protects your schedule.
Limits unlimited changes and specifies what happens if the client wants a different cut or additional edits.
Lets clients choose standard or rush delivery and gives you a basis to charge for faster work.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present a basic photo package, a photo plus video package, and a full production option. Clients tend to choose a middle tier and can see exactly what extra money buys.

pricingTips.title: Price by value, not just flight time
pricingTips.body: A 20-minute flight over a high-value property or a construction site can be worth more than the time suggests. Account for prep, editing, insurance, and the client's use of the footage.

pricingTips.title: Add travel and setup separately
pricingTips.body: Include a free radius, then charge per mile or a flat trip fee beyond it. Remote sites that need hiking or a second operator should have a higher rate.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Weather, schedules, and gear costs change. A 14 to 30 day validity window keeps you from honoring old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or site survey?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For complex projects such as mapping, inspections, or sites needing airspace planning, many pilots charge a planning or site survey fee and credit it toward the job if the client books.

faqs.question: How detailed should a drone photography quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list locations, deliverables, license terms, revisions, and timelines. One page with line items is typical. The more specific you are, the fewer change requests you get later.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before I schedule the flight?
faqs.answer: For larger or custom projects, a deposit of 25-50% is common. It secures the date and covers prep costs if the client cancels. Small real estate shoots often skip deposits but require payment at delivery.

faqs.question: What if the client wants more than the quote covers?
faqs.answer: Send a revised quote or change order that lists the added work and cost before you do it. Keep the original scope intact so both sides can see what changed.

dropshipping.intro: Dropshipping owners invoice clients when they sell services or wholesale orders, not just retail products. That includes building and launching stores for clients, sourcing and vetting suppliers, listing products, managing day-to-day order fulfillment, and filling bulk or business orders that ship straight from a supplier. Retail customers usually pay at checkout, so the invoices covered here are mostly for B2B and done-for-you work.
dropshipping.pricingModel: Pricing depends on what you sell. Store builds, product imports and branding work are usually flat fees or per-item fees. Ongoing store management and order handling are billed as a monthly retainer, a per-order fee, or both. Sourcing and research work is billed hourly or per product researched. When you resell goods to a business client, you bill supplier cost plus a markup, usually 20-50% depending on volume and category, with shipping listed separately. Pass-through costs such as sample orders, app subscriptions, and ad spend should be itemized at cost, with a handling fee only if your agreement says so. Set minimums on retainers so small order volumes still cover your time.

rates.service: Store setup and theme configuration (platform, payments, policies pages)
Product import, listing and copy cleanup
Store management retainer (catalog upkeep, pricing, customer service routing)
Order processing and supplier order placement
Wholesale or bulk order resale (supplier cost markup)

items.description: Store setup: theme install, payment and shipping configuration, policy pages
Product import and listing cleanup (titles, descriptions, images, variants)
Supplier research and vetting (4 candidate suppliers, shipping time comparison)
Supplier sample orders (pass-through at cost)
Order processing for the month of June

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Sample order costs are billed at actual supplier price with receipts available on request. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month. Monthly order processing is billed on the last day of each month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized services separated from pass-through costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see what you charged for your work versus what you paid suppliers, apps or platforms on their behalf.

invoiceChecklist.item: Order numbers or date range covered by per-order fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-order billing is easy to dispute unless the client can match your count to their store's order list.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplier names and product SKUs for resold goods
invoiceChecklist.why: Wholesale and bulk orders need a clear record of what was bought, from whom, and at what cost for returns and warranty claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping and handling charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Shipping from overseas or multiple warehouses varies a lot, and clients need it broken out to price their own sales.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate details
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, sales to a business with a valid resale certificate are exempt. Record the certificate number or the tax charged. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Currency and any supplier exchange rate used
invoiceChecklist.why: If you pay suppliers in another currency, stating the rate protects you from a dispute over cost differences.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope reference and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers and ongoing work should point to the agreement and the month covered so scope creep and extra requests are clear.

dropshipping.paymentTerms: For store builds, a 50% deposit upfront with the balance due at launch is common. Monthly retainers are typically billed at the start of the month, due in 7-14 days, while per-order fees are billed in arrears at month end. For resold goods, ask for full or at least 50% payment before placing supplier orders, since you often pay the supplier first and refunds can be slow. Late fees of 1-2% per month are usual if stated in writing. Bank transfer, ACH, and card payments are all common. Cards are convenient but carry chargeback risk on large bulk orders, so ACH or wire is often preferred for higher amounts.

tips.title: Never front supplier costs without payment
tips.body: Supplier orders for a client's customers are real money out the door. Collect payment first or require a prepaid balance that you draw from, and invoice any top-ups before the balance runs out.

tips.title: Bill ad spend and app fees separately at cost
tips.body: Ad budgets, theme licenses and app subscriptions should be itemized as pass-through costs or paid directly by the client. Mixing them into your fee hides your actual rate and causes confusion at renewal.

tips.title: Define what counts as an order
tips.body: Decide whether cancelled, refunded, split-shipped, and replacement orders count toward per-order fees. Put it in your agreement so your monthly count is not argued line by line.

tips.title: Keep supplier receipts and screenshots
tips.body: Save supplier invoices, tracking numbers and sample photos. If a client questions a cost or a defective batch, documentation settles it quickly and supports any refund claim you make upstream.

tips.title: Set a minimum monthly fee
tips.body: Order volume can drop in slow months while catalog upkeep and customer support routing continue. A minimum retainer keeps the work worth doing.

faqs.question: Do I invoice my retail customers as a dropshipper?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Retail customers pay at checkout and receive an order confirmation or receipt. Invoices are for business clients, such as stores you manage, resellers, or companies placing bulk orders.

faqs.question: How do I bill for products I buy from a supplier on a client's behalf?
faqs.answer: List them as separate pass-through lines at supplier cost, and add a markup or handling fee only if your agreement allows it. Attach or offer supplier receipts so the client can verify the amount.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on dropshipping services or resold goods?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Goods resold to a business with a valid resale certificate are often exempt, while sales to end consumers are generally taxable where nexus exists. Some states also tax certain digital or setup services. Check your state's rules or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: How should I handle refunds and returns on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Issue a credit note or a corrected invoice that references the original, and note whether the supplier refunded you. Make your return policy part of the agreement so clients know who covers return shipping and restocking fees.

faqs.question: Is a monthly retainer or per-order fee better?
faqs.answer: A retainer gives predictable income and covers non-order work like catalog updates. A per-order fee scales with volume. Many people combine a smaller retainer with a per-order fee.

estimate.intro: Quotes are sent before a store build, a sourcing project, a management engagement, or a bulk order is placed. Clients usually compare your flat fee against freelancers or agencies and want to know exactly what is included, how long it takes, and which costs are theirs.

scopeChecklist.why: State which platform, theme, and apps you will use and who pays for subscriptions, so the client knows what ongoing costs they carry beyond your fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of products and suppliers covered
scopeChecklist.why: A 20-product store and a 200-product store are very different jobs. Cap the count and price extra products individually.

scopeChecklist.item: Supplier selection and sample order costs
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether you choose suppliers, whether the client approves them, and who pays for samples and shipping on them.
Overseas suppliers can take 2-4 weeks. Writing realistic delivery windows into the quote prevents complaints that you promised faster shipping.

scopeChecklist.item: Order volume assumptions for retainers and per-order fees
scopeChecklist.why: State the expected monthly order range and what happens to the price if volume exceeds it or drops below the minimum.
Set how many rounds of changes are included, and list exclusions such as branding, photography, ad management and customer service.
Supplier prices and shipping rates change. A quote valid for 14-30 days and a deposit to start protect you from price shifts.

pricingTips.title: Quote setup as a flat fee and ongoing work separately
pricingTips.body: Flat fees work for builds because the scope is clear. Management and fulfillment are open-ended, so quote them as a retainer or per-order rate with stated limits.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer on supplier-dependent costs
pricingTips.body: Supplier prices, shipping rates and exchange rates move. For resale quotes, add a margin or state that pricing is based on current supplier costs and may be adjusted if they change.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard and full-service tier, such as store build only, build plus sourcing, and build plus ongoing management, lets clients choose and makes your pricing easy to compare.

pricingTips.title: Show your cost lines clearly
pricingTips.body: Separate your labor, pass-through costs and optional add-ons. Clients trust a quote more when they see where the money goes and can remove items they do not need.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For a custom sourcing study or detailed product research, charge a small fee or credit it toward the project if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Supplier costs and shipping rates can change, so state an expiry date and note that prices may be revised afterward.

faqs.question: What if supplier costs change after I quote?
faqs.answer: Include a clause stating that resale pricing is based on current supplier costs and will be adjusted with notice if costs change by more than a set percentage. For fixed-fee services this matters less.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: For services with unknowns, such as sourcing from unfamiliar suppliers, a range with a not-to-exceed amount works. For builds with a defined product count, a fixed price is clearer and easier to approve.

dryer-vent-cleaning.intro: Dryer vent cleaning businesses are usually solo operators or small crews who clean lint from dryer exhaust ducts in homes, apartments, and small commercial laundries. Invoices typically cover a standard vent cleaning, roof or wall termination work, repairs such as replacing a vent hood or flex duct, and inspection or airflow findings.
dryer-vent-cleaning.pricingModel: Most residential work is a flat fee per vent, based on run length, number of elbows, and whether the exit is at ground level, on the second story, or on the roof. Many companies set a base price that covers a run up to about 15 to 20 feet, then add charges for longer runs, roof access, or heavy blockage. Repairs and parts such as new hood caps, rigid duct, clamps, and bird guards are billed as separate line items with a materials markup. Multi-unit properties and laundromats are often priced per unit or per machine, with a volume discount and a service agreement. Annual maintenance plans and add-ons like lint trap deep cleaning or a video inspection are common ways to raise the average ticket.

rates.service: Standard residential dryer vent cleaning (ground-level exit, up to 20 ft)
Long or complex run surcharge (over 25 ft or multiple elbows)
Vent hood or termination cap replacement
Flex duct replacement with rigid or semi-rigid duct
Bird or rodent nest removal and screen install
Video inspection or airflow test report

items.description: Dryer vent cleaning, second-story exit, approx. 22 ft run with 2 elbows
Replace damaged vent hood with louvered cap and install bird guard
Replace crushed 4 in. foil flex duct behind dryer with semi-rigid duct
Remove bird nest from exterior termination
Post-cleaning airflow check and written report

sampleInvoice.notes: Vent was about 70 percent blocked on arrival; airflow at the exterior hood tested normal after cleaning. Payment due on completion by card, check, or cash. Parts carry a 90-day warranty. Recommend cleaning every 12 months.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and location of the dryer and exterior exit
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often own multiple properties, and landlords need to know which unit or vent was serviced.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vent run length, number of elbows, and exit type
invoiceChecklist.why: These details justify the price and explain any surcharge for long runs or roof access.

invoiceChecklist.item: Condition found on arrival and after cleaning
invoiceChecklist.why: A note such as partial blockage or crushed duct documents the need for service and protects you if the dryer has problems later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Hoods, clamps, duct, and screens should be listed separately so clients can see what repairs cost and so you can track materials.

invoiceChecklist.item: Airflow or inspection results
invoiceChecklist.why: Before and after readings or photos give clients proof of the work and support recommended follow-up service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license and insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many property managers and insurers ask for proof of coverage, and some cities require a business license on paperwork.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and recommended next service date
invoiceChecklist.why: It sets expectations for repeat visits and makes it easier to book annual cleanings.

dryer-vent-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential customers usually pay on completion by card, check, cash, or a digital payment link, since the job is short and the ticket is small. Deposits are rare for single-vent jobs but reasonable for large multi-unit or commercial contracts. Property managers and commercial accounts typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, and a late fee of 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in advance. For recurring maintenance plans, bill annually or per visit and keep a written service schedule on file.

tips.title: Quote by run length and exit type
tips.body: Ask for the exit location, approximate duct length, and photos before booking. A roof exit or a 30-foot run takes far longer than a short ground-level vent, and a flat price that ignores it cuts your margin.

tips.title: Take before and after photos for every job
tips.body: Photos of the lint buildup, damaged duct, and the clean exit document your work. Attach them to the invoice so clients understand any repair charges and are less likely to dispute them.

tips.title: List repairs as separate line items
tips.body: Keep the cleaning price clean and put hoods, duct, and nest removal on their own lines. Clients accept add-ons more easily when each cost is visible, and you can track what parts earn.

tips.title: Sell annual service at the time of billing
tips.body: Note the next recommended cleaning date on the invoice and offer a reminder or a discounted yearly rate. Repeat customers cost far less to serve than new ones.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for multi-unit visits
tips.body: Travel and setup time cost the same whether you clean three units or thirty. A minimum trip fee for small batches keeps property jobs profitable.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or by the hour for dryer vent cleaning?
faqs.answer: Most companies charge a flat fee based on run length and exit type because customers want a clear price up front. Hourly rates are more common for repair-heavy jobs or unusual commercial work where the scope is unclear.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a vent that turns out to be damaged or needs repair?
faqs.answer: Finish the cleaning, tell the customer what you found, and get approval before doing repairs. Then add the hood, duct, or other parts as separate line items on the invoice with a short description of the problem.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on dryer vent cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax services, some tax only the parts you sell, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show tax separately on the invoice if you charge it.

faqs.question: What is a fair charge for apartment complexes?
faqs.answer: Per-unit pricing from about $60 to $120 is typical, with lower rates for larger batches. Put the unit numbers on the invoice so the property manager can match them to the work schedule.

faqs.question: Should I include a warranty on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. State what is covered, such as parts for 90 days, and what is not, such as new blockages from damaged ducts you advised replacing. It sets clear limits if the customer calls back.

estimate.intro: Dryer vent cleaning is usually quoted by phone or online form with photos, and a firm price is given before the visit. Clients mainly compare the flat price, whether roof access or repairs are included, and whether you carry insurance and use proper brushes and a vacuum rather than only a leaf blower.

scopeChecklist.item: Vent run length, elbows, and exit location
scopeChecklist.why: These set the base price and justify surcharges for roof or second-story exits.
State whether you clean the full duct, the lint trap housing, and the exterior hood so clients know what they are paying for.
Dryers behind cabinets, tight laundry closets, or ceiling ducts add time and may need extra labor.
Say that damaged hoods, crushed flex duct, or rodent screens are quoted separately if found on site.
Gas dryers and long ducts carry higher fire and carbon monoxide risks, and you may need to recommend a technician if you find issues beyond your scope.
Multi-unit jobs need per-unit pricing, a minimum fee, and a written schedule.
Prices on parts and fuel change, and a stated window limits disputes over missed appointments.

pricingTips.title: Use tiered pricing by exit type
pricingTips.body: Publish a base price for ground-level exits and a higher one for second-story or roof exits. Customers see why prices differ and you avoid undercharging for harder jobs.

pricingTips.title: Quote the cleaning and give repair prices in advance
pricingTips.body: Include a price list for common fixes such as hood replacement and rigid duct per foot. Customers can approve them on site and you avoid return trips.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package for multiple services
pricingTips.body: Pair dryer vent cleaning with a video inspection or an annual plan at a small discount. It raises the ticket and brings the client back each year.

pricingTips.title: Ask for photos before quoting
pricingTips.body: Pictures of the dryer, wall, and exterior vent often reveal roof access, long runs, or damage and prevent price changes when you arrive.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or a range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed price for standard jobs where you have run length and exit type, and a range when you have not seen the vent. State that the price is confirmed on arrival if conditions differ.

faqs.question: Do I charge for an estimate visit?
faqs.answer: For standard residential jobs, most quote free over the phone or by photo. For large commercial or multi-building properties, a site visit fee that is credited toward the work is reasonable.

faqs.question: What if I find extra problems after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Stop, show the customer the issue with photos, and give a written price for the added work. Do not proceed with repairs until they approve.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for residential work. Commercial bids with parts or labor changes may be valid for 14 to 30 days.

drywall-installer.intro: Drywall installers hang, tape, mud, sand, and texture gypsum board for new construction, remodels, additions, and repairs. Clients include homeowners, general contractors, remodelers, and property managers. Invoices usually cover hanging, finishing, texturing, patch repair, and materials, billed by the sheet, by the square foot, or as a flat price per job.
drywall-installer.pricingModel: Most drywall work is priced per square foot of wall and ceiling area or per sheet hung, with finishing priced separately or bundled into a combined rate. New construction and large remodels are usually bid as a flat price based on square footage and finish level. Small repairs, patches, and water damage fixes are billed hourly or as a flat service fee with a minimum trip charge. Ceilings, high walls, stairwells, and 12-foot sheets cost more than standard 8-foot walls. Finish level (Level 3, 4, or 5) changes the labor price significantly. Texture matching, moisture-resistant or fire-rated board, and soundproofing products are priced as add-ons. Materials are either included in the per-square-foot rate or itemized with a markup of about 10 to 20 percent. Subcontractors working for GCs often bill by the sheet and may bill progress payments by phase: hang, tape, finish.

rates.service: Hang and finish, Level 4 (labor and materials)
Hanging by the sheet (4x8 or 4x12, labor only)
Texture application (knockdown, orange peel, skip trowel)
Water damage section replacement and finish

items.description: Hang 1/2" drywall, basement finish (walls and ceiling), 4x8 and 4x12 sheets
Tape, mud, and sand to Level 4 finish, 3 coats
Orange peel texture on ceilings
Drywall materials: 60 sheets, compound, tape, screws, corner bead
Patch and repair of existing wall at stair, texture match

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A deposit of $1,500 was received before work began and is deducted from the total. Price covers Level 4 finish ready for primer and paint. Painting is not included. A late fee of 1.5% per month applies to overdue balances. Accepted: check, ACH, and card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage by area and finish level
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-square-foot pricing is easy to dispute unless the invoice shows what was hung and which finish level (3, 4, or 5) was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Board type and thickness
invoiceChecklist.why: 1/2" standard, 5/8" Type X fire-rated, moisture-resistant, and mold-resistant boards cost different amounts, and building codes may require specific types in garages or between units.

invoiceChecklist.item: Texture type and where applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Knockdown, orange peel, or smooth wall are priced differently and a clear description avoids arguments about what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials itemized or marked as included
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and GCs want to know whether sheets, compound, tape, and corner bead are in your rate or billed on top.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extra work
invoiceChecklist.why: Added closets, repairs after other trades cut into walls, or extra coats of mud should be listed with approval dates so they are not treated as part of the original price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Phase or progress billing for each stage
invoiceChecklist.why: On bigger jobs, billing for hang, tape, and finish separately keeps cash flowing and shows what is complete.

invoiceChecklist.item: License number and insurance (where required)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require contractor license numbers on invoices and contracts, and GCs often ask for proof of insurance before paying subcontractors.

drywall-installer.paymentTerms: For homeowner jobs, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common on projects over a few thousand dollars, with the balance due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Small repairs are often paid at the end of the visit. For GC and commercial work, expect progress billing by phase with net 15 to net 30 terms, and sometimes retainage of 5 to 10 percent held until project completion. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance, though limits on interest vary by state. Most installers accept checks, ACH, and cards, and may add a card fee only where local law allows it.

tips.title: Bill by phase on multi-day jobs
tips.body: Hanging takes a day or two, but finishing takes several days because mud has to dry between coats. Invoice at hang completion and again at finish so you are not waiting a week or more for money after the sheets are up.

tips.title: Separate finish level from hanging
tips.body: Level 5 skim coat for walls with gloss paint or strong lighting takes much more labor than Level 4. State the level on the quote and invoice, and charge more for a higher level.

tips.title: Charge for height and difficulty
tips.body: Vaulted ceilings, stair walls, and rooms that need scaffolding or lifts take more time. Add a line item or higher rate rather than absorbing the extra labor.

tips.title: Track waste and leftover material
tips.body: Typical waste is 10 to 15 percent of sheets on complex layouts. If you bill materials at cost plus markup, base the count on sheets used, and keep supplier receipts to back it up.

tips.title: Document the starting condition
tips.body: Take photos of framing, other trades' work, and damage before you hang. This protects you if a client later blames you for cracks, nail pops, or uneven studs you did not cause.

faqs.question: Should I bill by the sheet or by the square foot?
faqs.answer: Either works if it is clear. Per sheet is common for hanging-only subcontract work with GCs, since it is easy to count. Per square foot is more common for homeowners and for hang and finish combined work because it is easier to compare between bids.

faqs.question: Can I charge for drying time between coats?
faqs.answer: Not as a separate line item in most cases. Drying time is built into your finishing rate and schedule. If a client delays access or you must make extra trips for coats, include the added trips in your price or as a trip charge.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants to pay after paint is done?
faqs.answer: Your invoice should cover your work, not the painter's. Agree on payment due at finish completion, and do not tie your payment to other trades. If a GC does so, note it in the subcontract and consider retainage terms in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on drywall jobs?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax materials on construction contracts, some tax the full job, and some tax neither if you are installing as a contractor. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do about unpaid invoices?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder as soon as the due date passes, then follow up by phone. Many states give contractors lien rights, but strict notice deadlines apply, so check your state's rules early and keep your signed estimate, change orders, and photos.

estimate.intro: Drywall installers send quotes before almost every job beyond a small patch, and clients often compare two or three bids. Homeowners look at total price and finish quality, while GCs compare price per square foot or per sheet. A clear quote prevents disputes over finish level, texture, and what happens when the board does not fit as expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Total square footage and rooms included
scopeChecklist.why: A written list of areas, with measurements, sets the baseline so added closets or rooms are clearly extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Board type, thickness, and sheet size
scopeChecklist.why: Fire-rated or moisture-resistant board, 5/8" versus 1/2", and 12-foot sheets all change cost and may be required by code.
State Level 3, 4, or 5 and the texture style, and note that paint is not included unless it is.
If the client buys board, you need to specify who handles delivery, stocking in rooms, and who pays for shortages or waste.
Note stairs, lift needs, power and heat, and whether framing, insulation, and electrical inspections must be complete before you start.
Finishing takes days. Give a timeline with realistic drying periods so clients do not expect completion in a day or two.
List items like framing repair, insulation, dust barrier setup, paint, and popcorn ceiling removal, and state how extra work is priced.

pricingTips.title: Measure and count sheets before quoting
pricingTips.body: Calculate wall and ceiling area, subtract large openings, and count sheets with 10 to 15 percent waste. Quote from your own count, not a rough guess from the client.

pricingTips.title: Price popcorn removal and skim coating separately
pricingTips.body: Scraping popcorn ceilings, skim coating, and old wall repair vary a lot depending on condition and possible asbestos in older homes. Quote them as options and state that testing may be required.

pricingTips.title: Offer finish level options
pricingTips.body: Presenting Level 4 as the standard and Level 5 as an upgrade lets clients choose, and it explains why your bid may be higher than one that quietly uses a lower finish.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Board and compound prices change, so state that the quote is valid for 14 to 30 days and that prices may adjust after that.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most drywall installers quote for free on standard jobs. For large or complicated projects, or repairs requiring extensive moisture or damage assessment, some charge a fee and credit it toward the job if hired.

faqs.question: How accurate does my quote need to be?
faqs.answer: Measure carefully and quote a fixed price for the defined scope. If conditions are unknown, such as hidden water damage behind walls, add a clause allowing price changes once discovered and approved in writing.

faqs.question: Should I include painting in my quote?
faqs.answer: Only if you actually do it. Most drywall quotes end at primer-ready. Say so clearly, so clients do not assume the walls will be fully finished and painted.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a quote?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common for larger jobs, often to cover materials. Many installers collect it when the quote is accepted and schedule start dates only after it is received.

ebay-seller.intro: eBay sellers who bill clients are usually running a consignment or drop-off selling service, clearing out estates and storage units, or selling bulk lots and wholesale inventory to other businesses. They invoice for listing work, commissions on sold items, pickup and shipping costs, and sometimes for inventory sold outright to resellers.
ebay-seller.pricingModel: Most eBay selling services price in one of three ways. Consignment is a commission, usually a percentage of the final sale price, with a higher percentage for low-value items and a lower one for items over a few hundred dollars. Some sellers add a flat per-item listing or photography fee, charged whether or not the item sells. Estate and cleanout work is often hourly or a flat project fee plus a lower commission. Sellers who sell lots to other resellers invoice by the lot or by the pound, with shipping and any freight charged separately. Make clear whether eBay final value fees, payment processing fees, and shipping labels are deducted from the sale price before your commission is calculated or billed on top. Add a line for passed-through costs such as supplies, storage, and postage at cost or with a small handling markup.

rates.service: High-value or complex listing (research, authentication, multiple photos)
Estate or storage unit sorting and inventory

rates.unit: per month per shelf or bin

items.description: Intake, photography, and eBay listing creation (vintage cameras and accessories)
Pickup of items from client home (22 miles each way)
Storage of client inventory, 2 shelves, 30 days
Relist 6 unsold items for second 30-day period
Consignment commission at 30% on $1,450 in sales (12 items sold, before eBay fees)

sampleInvoice.notes: Amounts above are deducted from sale proceeds held for client. Net payout of $XXX follows within 7 days via check or bank transfer. Unsold items may be picked up or donated after 60 days with written notice. eBay fees and shipping label costs are itemized on the attached sales statement.

invoiceChecklist.item: List of items sold with eBay listing numbers, sale dates, and final sale prices
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to match each charge to a specific item and check your commission math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized eBay fees, payment processing fees, and shipping costs
invoiceChecklist.why: These reduce the proceeds, and clients dispute payouts when they cannot see where the money went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Commission rate and how it was calculated (on gross sale price or net after fees)
invoiceChecklist.why: The same percentage produces a very different number depending on the base, so state it each time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Flat fees for listing, photography, pickup, and storage listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from commission shows what the client paid for whether or not items sold.

invoiceChecklist.item: Returns, refunds, and cancelled sales with the dates and reasons
invoiceChecklist.why: Returned items and refunded sales change the commission owed and should be reflected in the same billing period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax treatment and your seller or resale information if billing business buyers
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states eBay collects tax on marketplace sales, but direct lot sales to businesses may need a resale certificate on file. Check your state rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payout date, method, and any amount held back for pending returns
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients expect to know when they get paid and why a portion might be withheld.

ebay-seller.paymentTerms: For consignment, the client usually does not pay you directly. You deduct your commission and fees from eBay proceeds and send the remainder, typically after the return window closes, often 7 to 30 days after the buyer receives the item. For flat-fee work such as estate sorting, collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent up front and the balance on completion. For bulk lots sold to other businesses, require payment before shipping or net 15 for repeat buyers. Accepted methods are generally bank transfer, check, or card, and card fees can be passed on if disclosed. If you charge late fees or storage fees on unclaimed items, put the rate and time frame in your written agreement.

tips.title: Put the commission base in your agreement
tips.body: Decide whether commission applies to the gross sale price, the price including shipping, or the amount after eBay fees. Write it down and repeat it on every statement.

tips.title: Hold back for returns
tips.body: Keep a short reserve or wait until the return window ends before paying out. Say so in your terms so a held amount does not look like a delay.

tips.title: Charge for work on items that do not sell
tips.body: A per-item listing fee covers photography and research on low performers. Without it, you do the same work for nothing on items nobody buys.

tips.title: Send a statement even when you pay by deposit
tips.body: Clients who see a list of sold items, fees, and net payout rarely ask follow-up questions, and you keep a record for tax time.

tips.title: Track mileage and supplies per client
tips.body: Pickup trips, boxes, tape, and labels add up. Log them per client so they can be billed accurately and deducted correctly on your own taxes.

faqs.question: Should I invoice a consignment client or just send a payout?
faqs.answer: Send a statement showing sales, deductions, and net payout. If you also charge flat fees the client pays directly, such as pickup or storage, issue a separate invoice for those amounts so both sides have a clear record.

faqs.question: Who pays the eBay fees on consigned items?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement. Many sellers deduct the final value fee and shipping from the sale price first and then take commission on the remainder. Others take commission on the gross and pass fees to the client. Choose one and state it in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on eBay sales?
faqs.answer: In most US states eBay collects and remits sales tax on marketplace orders, so you typically do not add it yourself on those. Direct sales outside the platform, such as selling a lot to another business, may be taxable or exempt with a resale certificate. Check your state rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge a client for items that never sold?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement includes a per-item listing or handling fee, or an hourly rate for sorting and photography. Without that agreement, you generally only earn commission on sales.

faqs.question: How long should I wait before paying a consignor?
faqs.answer: Many sellers pay after the buyer's return window closes, often 14 to 30 days after delivery. Whatever you choose, state the timeline up front and stick to it.

estimate.intro: Sellers send quotes before taking on a consignment batch, estate cleanout, or storage unit sale, and before agreeing to sell a large lot to a reseller. Clients usually compare your commission rate against other consignment shops and eBay drop-off stores, and ask what they will net after fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Commission rate, tiered by item value if applicable
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare rates, and tiered rates need to be clear before items are listed.

scopeChecklist.item: Flat fees for intake, photography, listing, pickup, and storage
scopeChecklist.why: These costs apply whether or not an item sells and cause disputes when they appear for the first time on a final statement.

scopeChecklist.item: What counts as the commission base: gross, shipping included, or net of fees
scopeChecklist.why: This changes the client's payout by a noticeable amount.

scopeChecklist.item: Listing period and what happens to unsold items
scopeChecklist.why: Specify the number of days, relisting charges, and whether items are returned, donated, or discounted.

scopeChecklist.item: Items you will and will not accept
scopeChecklist.why: Low-value, damaged, or restricted items take time and may not be worth listing, so set a minimum or exclude categories.

scopeChecklist.item: Payout timing and any holdback for returns
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume immediate payment when an item sells.

scopeChecklist.item: Responsibility for loss, damage, or shipping claims
scopeChecklist.why: Say who is responsible if an item breaks in transit or a buyer files a not-as-described claim.

pricingTips.title: Offer a net estimate range, not just a rate
pricingTips.body: Give a realistic sale range for the batch and show approximate net after fees and commission. Clients understand the deal better, and you avoid overpromising.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum item value
pricingTips.body: Many sellers only accept items likely to sell for $20 or more, or charge a flat fee on lower-value items so the time is covered.

pricingTips.title: Use tiers to attract higher-value items
pricingTips.body: Dropping commission from 40 percent to 25 percent above $200 keeps good items coming in without cutting your margin on small sales.

pricingTips.title: Quote cleanouts by time and volume
pricingTips.body: For estates and storage units, view the space first and quote an hourly or flat sorting fee separately from commission on what sells.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before seeing the items?
faqs.answer: Only a rate range. A firm quote for sorting or pickup should wait until you have seen the items or good photos, since volume and condition drive your time.

faqs.question: Can I promise what items will sell for?
faqs.answer: No. Give a range based on recent sold listings and say that actual sale prices vary. Written estimates that sound like guarantees cause disputes.

faqs.question: How long is a quote good for?
faqs.answer: Many sellers say 14 to 30 days, since market prices and your workload change. Put an expiration date on the quote.

education.intro: Independent educators include private tutors, test prep instructors, homeschool and pod teachers, enrichment class leaders, curriculum writers, and consultants who work with families, schools, or organizations. They bill for instruction time, class enrollment, planning and materials, assessments, and one-off workshops or consulting.
education.pricingModel: Most independent educators charge per hour or per session for one-on-one work, with a lower per-student rate for small groups. Test prep and specialized subjects such as AP Calculus, organic chemistry, or learning-support instruction usually earn more than general homework help. Many educators sell prepaid packages (for example 10 sessions) or monthly rates for a weekly standing slot, which gives them steadier income and makes cancellations easier to manage. Classes and workshops are often priced per student per course or as a flat fee per session when billed to a school, library, or company. Curriculum and consulting projects are usually a flat fee per deliverable or an hourly rate. Materials, practice tests, and printed workbooks are either built into the rate or listed as separate line items. Organizations such as schools and districts often pay on net-30 or net-45 terms and may need a W-9 and a purchase order number.

rates.service: One-on-one tutoring, K-8 or general high school subjects
Advanced subject tutoring (AP, college-level, foreign language)
Guest workshop or classroom visit for a school or organization
Educational assessment and written progress report

items.description: Algebra II tutoring, 60-minute sessions (Oct 2, 9, 16, 23, 30, Nov 6, 13, 20)
SAT math practice test, proctored and scored with written review
Written progress report and 30-minute parent conference
Printed workbook and practice materials

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted by check, bank transfer, or card. Sessions canceled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at the full rate. Unused sessions in a prepaid package expire 90 days after purchase.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and, if different, the name of the parent or organization being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents often pay for a student, and schools or employers may pay for a group. The invoice needs to show who received the service and who owes the money.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, length, and subject covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each date lets a parent or accounting office verify the hours and prevents disputes about how many sessions took place.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for instruction, assessments, and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients may want to see what portion is teaching time versus tests or books, and some can claim certain education expenses.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late cancellation or no-show charges, with the date of the missed session
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the policy and the specific session makes the charge easier to accept, since it refers to a policy the client already agreed to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining balance on any prepaid package
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who bought 10 or 20 sessions up front want to know how many are left and when they expire.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number, course or program name, and your tax ID for school or organization clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Districts, nonprofits, and companies usually need a PO number and a W-9 on file before they can process payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Teaching license, certification, or background check status, if relevant to the contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Some schools and programs require proof of credentials or clearance, and including it can avoid delays in approval.

education.paymentTerms: Private clients usually pay per session, monthly in advance, or when a package is purchased. Billing in advance for the coming month is common and reduces chasing payments. Due dates are typically due on receipt to net-14 for families. Schools, libraries, and companies often use net-30 or longer and may pay only after a PO is approved. Many educators state a 24-hour or 48-hour cancellation policy and a late fee, such as $10-25 or 1.5% per month, in their written terms. Common payment methods are card, bank transfer, check, and peer-to-peer apps. Check your local rules on late fees and on whether any of your services are taxable, since sales tax on educational services varies by state.

tips.title: Bill in advance for standing slots
tips.body: If a student has a regular weekly time, invoice the month ahead. Your time is reserved whether or not the student shows up, so prepayment protects that income.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: State the notice period and charge on your first invoice or intake form. A policy the parent agreed to in writing is much easier to enforce than one explained after a missed session.

tips.title: Charge for prep and reporting time when it is substantial
tips.body: Writing a study plan, scoring practice tests, or preparing a custom unit takes real hours. Either build that time into your hourly rate or list it as a line item.

tips.title: Offer package pricing with an expiration date
tips.body: A discount for 10 or 20 sessions brings in cash upfront. An expiration, such as 90 days, keeps unused balances from carrying on indefinitely.

tips.title: Track mileage and materials for in-home or on-site work
tips.body: If you travel to students or schools, record your mileage and any supplies you buy. Decide whether to include them in your rate or bill them separately, and keep records for taxes.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the session?
faqs.answer: Either works as long as it is clear. Hourly pricing is simpler for variable-length sessions. A per-session rate is easier for clients when sessions are a fixed length, such as 60 or 90 minutes. State the session length on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a parent for a session the student missed?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you told them in writing beforehand that late cancellations and no-shows are billed. Many educators allow one free reschedule per term and charge the full or half rate after that.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax tutoring or instruction, but some tax certain educational services or taxable materials you sell. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What do I do when a school pays late?
faqs.answer: Confirm that the invoice has the right PO number and was sent to the right department, since many delays come from missing paperwork. Then follow up in writing on the due date and again at 7 to 10 days past due. Net-30 or net-45 terms are common with institutions.

faqs.question: Is it okay to invoice monthly instead of per session?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many educators prefer it. List each session date and any extra charges, and invoice at the start of the month for the sessions ahead or at the end for sessions already held. Be consistent so clients know when to expect it.

estimate.intro: Educators send quotes when a school, library, company, or family asks for a defined program, such as a six-week course, a test prep package, a workshop series, or a curriculum project. Clients compare total price, number of hours, group size, and what materials and reporting are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions, length of each, and the date range
scopeChecklist.why: Without a set schedule, clients may assume more sessions or a longer term than you priced.

scopeChecklist.item: Class size and who is covered
scopeChecklist.why: Group pricing depends on the number of students. State the minimum and maximum enrollment and whether siblings or additional students cost extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Location and format (in-person, at the client site, or online)
scopeChecklist.why: Travel, room rental, and online platform costs affect your price, and the client should know where you will be teaching.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials, textbooks, and practice tests, and who pays for them
scopeChecklist.why: Printed materials and test fees can add up. Clarify whether they are included or billed to the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Assessments, progress reports, and parent or administrator meetings
scopeChecklist.why: Reporting takes time. If it is included, say so. If it is extra, list the cost.
Missed sessions and withdrawals are the most common disputes, so settle the terms before the program starts.
You cannot promise a score or grade. Describe what you will deliver, such as hours of instruction and practice, rather than a guaranteed outcome.

pricingTips.title: Price packages by total hours, then give a small discount
pricingTips.body: Work out the hours of teaching, planning, and reporting, then multiply by your rate. A 5-10% discount for a full package is common and encourages prepayment.

pricingTips.title: For organizations, quote a flat fee per session or program
pricingTips.body: Schools and nonprofits usually have budgets set by program, not by hour. A flat fee for a workshop or series is easier for them to approve than an open hourly estimate.

pricingTips.title: Include planning time for custom work
pricingTips.body: Building a new unit, writing a custom study plan, or adapting material to a group takes hours that are not in the classroom. Factor that into the quote or list it as a separate line.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Calendars fill up and costs change. A 14 or 30-day expiration lets you hold a slot without committing indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation or trial session?
faqs.answer: Many educators offer a short, free intake call to discuss goals and fit, and charge their regular rate for any actual teaching. If you offer a discounted trial lesson, state the price and what it includes in the quote.

faqs.question: How do I quote for a student whose needs are unclear?
faqs.answer: Quote an initial assessment or a short block, such as four sessions, and then provide a recommendation for ongoing work. This limits risk for both sides until you know what the student needs.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes. If the client asks for extra sessions, more students, or added materials, send a revised quote or change order. Without a change in scope, the accepted price should stand.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: A written acceptance, by signature or email reply, is a good idea for programs and organizational work. It confirms the scope, price, schedule, and cancellation terms. For large contracts, consider having a lawyer review your standard terms.

electrical-contractor.intro: Electrical contractors wire, repair, and upgrade electrical systems in homes, businesses, and job sites. Invoices usually cover labor, materials, permit fees, and trip charges for service calls, panel upgrades, new circuits, lighting installs, and larger remodel or new-construction work. Solo electricians and small shops bill both homeowners and general contractors, so invoices often need to satisfy a client's accounting department as well as a homeowner.
electrical-contractor.pricingModel: Most residential service work is billed either hourly or by flat rate. Hourly billing is common for troubleshooting and small repairs, often with a minimum charge or trip fee that covers the first half hour to one hour. Flat-rate pricing from a price book is common for repeatable jobs such as installing a ceiling fan, replacing a GFCI outlet, or swapping a 200-amp panel. Remodel and new-construction work is usually bid as a fixed price based on a scope, fixtures, and a number of circuits or devices, sometimes priced per outlet or per fixture. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, typically 15 to 40 percent depending on the item and local market. Permits and inspection fees are passed through or built into the price. Commercial and subcontract work often uses progress billing tied to rough-in, trim-out, and final inspection milestones. Overtime, after-hours, and emergency call rates are usually 1.5x to 2x the standard rate.

rates.service: Journeyman or master electrician service work
Service call / trip charge with diagnostic
Ceiling fan or light fixture installation

items.description: Remove old 100-amp panel and install new 200-amp main breaker panel, including permit coordination
Electrical permit and utility disconnect/reconnect fee
Whole-house surge protector, Type 2
Add dedicated 20-amp circuit for kitchen microwave (labor and materials)
Replace 4 standard outlets with tamper-resistant outlets
Additional labor, relocating service mast bracket

sampleInvoice.notes: Work passed city inspection on the date listed. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to unpaid balances. One-year workmanship warranty on all labor; manufacturer warranties apply to equipment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and state or local registration
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require the license number on contracts and invoices, and clients and insurers often ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and scope of work performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which circuits, panels, or fixtures were touched, which helps with warranty and future service calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and inspection date or result
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the work was permitted and passed inspection, which matters for home sales and insurance claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized materials with quantities and prices
invoiceChecklist.why: Wire, breakers, boxes, and fixtures add up quickly, and clients dispute lump-sum material charges more often than itemized ones.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours, rate, and any overtime or after-hours multiplier
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes the hourly math visible and supports premium rates for emergency or off-hours work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge or service call fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates the fee for showing up and diagnosing from the repair cost so clients understand it applies even if no repair is done.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number, job number, or change order references
invoiceChecklist.why: General contractors and commercial clients usually will not pay without a PO or reference to an approved change order.

electrical-contractor.paymentTerms: Small service calls are typically due on completion, with payment by card, check, or digital payment taken on site. Larger residential jobs commonly require a deposit of 10 to 50 percent, often to cover permits and material purchases, with the balance due at final inspection. Commercial and subcontract work is usually net 15 to net 30, with progress billing at rough-in, trim-out, and final. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if written in the contract or estimate. Retainage of 5 to 10 percent is common on commercial jobs, so track when it comes due. Check your state's rules on deposit limits and lien notice deadlines.

tips.title: Charge a trip fee and say so upfront
tips.body: Driving to a site, diagnosing, and making a safe call can take an hour even if the fix is small. A posted service call fee, applied toward the repair if the client approves, keeps small jobs worth the trip.

tips.title: Mark up materials consistently
tips.body: Supply house runs, small parts, and your time to source them are real costs. Apply a standard markup and itemize larger items so the invoice matches the estimate.

tips.title: Bill change orders in writing before doing the work
tips.body: Hidden conditions like knob-and-tube wiring, undersized conductors, or a damaged service mast are common. Get a signed change order, then reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on longer jobs
tips.body: On remodels and new construction, bill at rough-in, trim-out, and final instead of waiting for the end. This keeps cash flow steady and limits what you carry for materials.

tips.title: Keep records of inspections and photos
tips.body: Photos of work before drywall and a copy of the inspection sign-off help resolve disputes and support your invoice if a client questions the charges.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or flat rate?
faqs.answer: Use flat rate for repeatable jobs where you know the time, such as a panel swap or EV charger, since clients prefer a known price. Use hourly for troubleshooting and open-ended work where the cause is unknown. Many electricians use both.

faqs.question: Can I charge for permits and inspection fees?
faqs.answer: Yes. Permit fees are usually passed through at cost or included in the price, and many electricians add a small charge for the time spent pulling the permit and meeting the inspector. List it as a separate line so the client can see it.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on materials?
faqs.answer: Typical markup is 15 to 40 percent, with lower percentages on expensive items like panels and higher percentages on small parts. Local competition and your overhead will guide where you land.

faqs.question: What if a customer will not pay after the work is done?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice and contract terms, then a written demand. Many states allow mechanics liens on the property for unpaid electrical work, but notice deadlines are strict and vary, so check your state's rules or ask an attorney soon after nonpayment.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on electrical work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, labor on real property improvements is not taxed while materials may be, and some states treat things differently for repairs versus new installs. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Electrical contractors send estimates before any job beyond a simple repair, especially panel upgrades, rewires, remodels, and new circuits. Homeowners usually compare two or three bids, looking at total price, the scope of work, the brand and quality of materials, and whether permits are included. Electrical work is also regulated, so a clear written quote helps separate licensed, permitted work from cheaper alternatives.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact scope: number of circuits, outlets, fixtures, and panel size
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume extras like a few more outlets are included. Counting devices and circuits in writing prevents that.
State whether permit fees and inspections are included. A lower bid that skips permits is not the same job.
If the client picks fixtures, set an allowance. Overages then become a clear, agreed upcharge.
Fishing wire through finished walls often requires holes. Say who repairs them and who paints.
Aluminum wiring, knob-and-tube, code violations, or an overloaded service may need correction. Note that hidden issues are billed through change orders.
Service upgrades require utility disconnects, and scheduling affects timeline and cost. Note who arranges it and expected outages.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, payment terms, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Copper and equipment prices change. An expiration date protects you from material price swings.

pricingTips.title: Walk the job and look at the panel
pricingTips.body: Check panel capacity, available breaker spaces, grounding, and attic or crawlspace access before quoting. A 15-minute look at the panel prevents most underbid surprises.

pricingTips.title: Offer options when it makes sense
pricingTips.body: A good, better, best option for things like surge protection, panel brand, or fixture grade lets clients choose a price point without negotiating you down on the base scope.

pricingTips.title: Price labor by difficulty, not just count
pricingTips.body: An outlet in an open basement and one in a finished plaster wall are not the same job. Adjust per-device pricing for access, ceiling height, and wall type.

pricingTips.title: Charge for large estimates
pricingTips.body: Detailed bids for complex remodels or commercial work can take hours. Many electricians charge a fee for these and credit it to the job if hired.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are common for standard residential jobs. For complex work needing plans, load calculations, or multiple site visits, many electricians charge a fee, often credited toward the job if accepted.

faqs.question: How long should an electrical quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Shorten it to 7 to 14 days if material prices are volatile or the job depends on a specific equipment purchase.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: A written estimate is a rough price that can change as conditions are discovered. A signed quote or contract with a fixed price is binding on both sides. Label the document clearly and state how changes are handled.

faqs.question: What if I find problems after starting the job?
faqs.answer: Stop, document the issue with photos, explain the code or safety concern to the client, and provide a written change order with the added cost. Continue only after the client approves.

electrical-inspection.intro: Electrical inspectors and inspection businesses examine wiring, panels, and service equipment for safety and code compliance. Clients include home buyers, real estate agents, landlords, insurance carriers, property managers, and contractors who need a third-party report. Most invoices cover a flat-fee inspection, an hourly diagnostic or consulting block, report preparation, and travel.
electrical-inspection.pricingModel: Most private electrical inspectors charge a flat fee based on the type and size of the property: a standalone electrical safety inspection for a house is often priced by square footage or number of circuits and panels. Commercial work, expert witness work, and troubleshooting are usually hourly with a minimum. Add-ons such as thermal imaging of panels, a second panel, outbuildings, pool or spa bonding checks, EV charger load review, and rush report turnaround are priced as separate line items. Municipal or third-party code inspectors working for a jurisdiction are typically paid by the jurisdiction or through permit fees, so this page focuses on independent inspectors billing clients directly. Travel is either built into the flat fee within a service radius or billed per mile or as a trip charge beyond it. Re-inspections after a contractor completes repairs are commonly billed at a reduced flat fee or hourly rate.

rates.service: Residential electrical safety inspection (under 2,500 sq ft)
Residential electrical safety inspection (over 2,500 sq ft or multiple panels)
Thermal imaging scan of panels and gear
Written report for insurance or legal use

items.description: Electrical safety inspection, single-family home, 2,200 sq ft, main panel and subpanel
Thermal imaging scan of main panel and subpanel
Detached garage circuit and GFCI check
Written report with photos and deficiency list
Travel beyond 30-mile service area (12 extra miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on delivery of report. Report covers conditions observed on the inspection date only and is not a guarantee of future performance. Re-inspection of corrected items available at $100 within 60 days. Accepted: ACH, card, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and date of inspection
invoiceChecklist.why: Reports and invoices are tied to a specific site and date. This matters if the condition of the system is questioned later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or certification number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and jurisdictions license or certify inspectors. Clients, insurers, and lenders often want it shown.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope of inspection and what was excluded
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing panels, circuits, outbuildings, and items not accessible limits disputes over what you were hired to check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons such as thermal imaging or outbuildings
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show the client what each extra cost and make partial disputes easy to resolve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Report reference or file number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the deliverable and helps agents, lenders, or insurers match paperwork.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who ordered the inspection and who is billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Agents, buyers, sellers, and landlords can differ. A clear bill-to avoids payment confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO or claim number when applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and insurance carriers often will not process payment without one.

electrical-inspection.paymentTerms: Residential inspectors often collect payment at the time of inspection or when the report is delivered, since the report is the product and many real estate deals have tight closing dates. Some release the final report only after payment. For commercial, property manager, or insurance clients, net 15 or net 30 is common, and a PO number may be required. Deposits are less common for small jobs but reasonable for large commercial scopes, multi-day work, or expert witness engagements, often 25 to 50 percent upfront.
