Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common on net terms if stated in advance. Typical payment methods are card, ACH, check, and sometimes payment at closing for real estate transactions.

tips.title: Tie payment to report delivery
tips.body: State that the report is released on payment, or that payment is due at delivery. Collecting before or at release is much easier than chasing a client after they have the report.

tips.title: Price by property size and complexity
tips.body: Panel count, service amperage, age of the home, and outbuildings drive your time. Build these into your fee schedule so a large property with three panels is not billed like a condo.

tips.title: Bill re-inspections separately and clearly
tips.body: Say in the original quote and the notes how many days a reduced-price re-inspection is available. This prevents unpaid return trips.

tips.title: Document access problems
tips.body: If a panel is blocked or the power is off, note it on the invoice and report. Charge a trip fee if you cannot complete the scope, and say so in advance.

tips.title: Separate inspection from expert opinion
tips.body: Court testimony, depositions, and insurance reports take more time and carry more risk. Bill them hourly with a minimum and a retainer.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for electrical inspections?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best for standard residential inspections because clients want a known price. Hourly is better for commercial work, troubleshooting, consulting, and legal or insurance reports where the time is unpredictable.

faqs.question: Can I withhold the report until I am paid?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases, as long as your agreement or terms say so. Put it in your booking confirmation and on the invoice. For real estate deals, many inspectors accept payment at the time of inspection to avoid delays.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on inspection services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional or inspection services, but some do. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a property manager orders inspections for many units?
faqs.answer: Use one invoice per property or per billing period, list each unit or address as its own line, and include their PO number. Many offer volume pricing, so state the per-unit rate clearly.

faqs.question: What if the client disputes findings after paying?
faqs.answer: Your invoice and report should show the scope, date, and limits of the inspection. Offer a re-inspection or follow-up visit if conditions were missed, but do not refund for findings that were accurate on the day. Keep photos and notes.

estimate.intro: Electrical inspectors quote before work when a client asks for a price on a property, a commercial scope, or a series of units. Buyers and agents often compare quotes from several inspectors on price, turnaround time, and report quality. Commercial and insurance clients may want a written proposal with scope and hourly caps.

scopeChecklist.item: Property address, size, and number of panels
scopeChecklist.why: These drive time on site and report length, so the quote should state what price assumes.

scopeChecklist.item: What is and is not included
scopeChecklist.why: List panels, receptacle sampling, GFCI and AFCI checks, smoke and CO devices, outbuildings, and exclusions such as low-voltage or inaccessible areas.
Thermal imaging, pool bonding, EV charger load review, and generator checks should be priced separately so clients can choose.
Power must be on and panels accessible. State that blocked access or power-off conditions may incur a trip fee.
Clients compare delivery time. State if it is same-day, 24 hours, or 3 business days, and the rush fee if any.
State the fee and time window for checking corrected items so follow-up work is not free by default.
Travel costs and schedules change, so specify how long the price holds, such as 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Build a fee table by size and age
pricingTips.body: Publish or keep a simple schedule by square footage, service size, and home age. Older homes with knob-and-tube or aluminum wiring take longer and should cost more.

pricingTips.title: Offer packages
pricingTips.body: Bundling the inspection, thermal scan, and report at one price is easier to compare and often raises your average ticket.

pricingTips.title: Quote commercial work with a cap
pricingTips.body: Give an hourly rate with an estimated number of hours and a not-to-exceed amount, then require written approval to go over.

pricingTips.title: Include travel in the fee within a radius
pricingTips.body: Clients prefer one price. Set a service area and add a clear per-mile charge beyond it.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: For standard residential inspections, quotes are free. For complex commercial scopes, site walks, or expert witness work, many inspectors charge for time spent before an engagement.

faqs.question: How do I price a property I have not seen?
faqs.answer: Ask for square footage, year built, panel count, and service size. Quote a range or a base price with a stated adjustment if what you find on site differs.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after arriving on site?
faqs.answer: Only if your quote says so. Include language that additional panels, outbuildings, or access problems can change the fee, and get the client's approval before continuing.

faqs.question: What should I do when a client says another inspector is cheaper?
faqs.answer: Compare scope, not just price. Point out what your fee includes, such as report detail, photos, thermal imaging, and credentials, rather than discounting immediately.

electrician.intro: Electricians, from solo journeymen to small contracting shops, bill homeowners, landlords, property managers, and general contractors for service calls, repairs, panel work, rewires, and new installations. Invoices usually combine labor, materials, and sometimes permit or inspection fees. Clear itemization matters because customers often compare your bill against a quote or a competitor's price.
electrician.pricingModel: Most residential electricians use one of three approaches: hourly time-and-materials, flat-rate task pricing, or a fixed bid for larger jobs. Service calls typically carry a trip charge or a minimum (often one hour or two) that covers travel and diagnosis. Flat-rate pricing from a price book is common for repeat tasks like replacing an outlet, installing a ceiling fan, or swapping a breaker, because the customer knows the price before work starts. Remodels, rewires, and new construction are usually bid as a fixed price or billed by milestone, with materials marked up 10-30% to cover sourcing, pickup time, warranty, and carrying cost. Commercial work often bills hourly with a separate material line and may use prevailing wage rates on public jobs. After-hours, weekend, and emergency calls are commonly billed at 1.5x to 2x the normal rate. Permits and inspection fees are usually passed through at cost, sometimes with a small handling fee.

rates.service: Service call / trip charge (includes first 30-60 min)
Install ceiling fan (existing wiring and box)
Install EV charger (Level 2, wiring existing in reach)

items.description: Service call and diagnosis, no power to kitchen counter circuit
Replace 3 kitchen countertop receptacles with 20A GFCI outlets (labor)
Replace failed 20A breaker in main panel (labor)
Additional troubleshooting and repair of loose neutral at junction box
Materials: 3 GFCI outlets, 20A breaker, wire nuts, cover plates, wire

sampleInvoice.notes: Work performed to current NEC as adopted locally. 1-year warranty on labor; manufacturer warranty applies to parts. License #EC-123456, insured. Payment due within 14 days. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance status
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require the license number on invoices, contracts, and advertising, and it shows the customer you are legitimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and inspection date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the inspection record and proves the work was permitted, which matters for home sales and insurance claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor broken out by task or hours, with the rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers dispute lump-sum labor charges more often than itemized ones.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately, with major components named
invoiceChecklist.why: Breakers, panels, wire gauge, and fixtures are verifiable items. Listing them supports your markup and helps with future service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge, after-hours, or emergency surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: Surcharges that are not shown clearly are the most common source of billing complaints. Label them and reference what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address, work date, and PO or work order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and general contractors typically will not pay without a PO or work order reference, and the site address matters when you bill an owner at a different address.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and any code issues found
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents what you guarantee and notes problems outside the scope, such as an outdated panel, protecting you if issues arise later.

electrician.paymentTerms: Small service calls are typically due on completion, often by card, check, or digital payment on site. Larger jobs usually require a deposit of 25-50% to cover materials and permits, followed by progress payments at set milestones such as rough-in passed, inspection approved, and final trim. Commercial and contractor accounts commonly run net 15 to net 30. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in writing before the work starts, though some states cap late fees or require specific disclosures. Card payments are widely accepted, and some electricians add a processing fee where local law allows it. Many shops also hold final payment until the inspection passes.

tips.title: Use a minimum charge, not just an hourly rate
tips.body: A 20-minute fix still costs you drive time, fuel, and a slot in your day. A one-hour minimum or a service call fee keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Mark up materials consistently
tips.body: Your supply house trips, return handling, and warranty exposure are real costs. Apply a standard markup, often 15-30%, and keep receipts so you can explain it if a customer asks.

tips.title: Get change orders in writing before doing the work
tips.body: Hidden conditions like knob-and-tube wiring, undersized panels, or aluminum branch circuits are common. Send a short written change order with the added cost and get a reply before you proceed.

tips.title: Collect the deposit before ordering panels or gear
tips.body: Special-order items like panels, subpanels, generators, and EV chargers may not be returnable. Require a deposit that at least covers them.

tips.title: Invoice the same day
tips.body: Customers pay faster when the invoice arrives while the work is fresh. Same-day invoicing also keeps materials and hours accurate while you still remember them.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat rate?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Flat rate works well for repeat tasks where you know the time, such as replacing a fixture or installing a GFCI. Hourly suits troubleshooting and unknown conditions. Many electricians use flat rate for defined tasks and hourly for diagnosis.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, as a trip charge or by billing portal-to-portal time, as long as you state it up front. Most residential electricians use a flat service call fee that covers a set amount of time on site.

faqs.question: Do I need to itemize permit fees?
faqs.answer: It is good practice. List the permit as a separate line at cost, with the permit number. Some jurisdictions require the permit holder to be the licensed contractor, so check local rules.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on electrical work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials only, some tax labor and materials, and some treat repair and new construction differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the customer refuses to pay after the inspection passes?
faqs.answer: Send a written demand referencing your invoice and signed estimate. Many states allow contractors to file a mechanic's lien on the property, with strict deadlines, so check local rules or consult an attorney promptly.

estimate.intro: Electricians send estimates for panel upgrades, rewires, remodels, new circuits, EV chargers, and any job where the scope is clear enough to price before starting. Homeowners usually collect two or three bids, so what is included and excluded matters as much as the total. Small repairs are often quoted by phone from a price book, while larger jobs need a site visit.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact scope: circuits, devices, and fixtures included
scopeChecklist.why: Counts like 'eight recessed lights on one switch' or 'one 50A circuit for a range' prevent disputes about what was covered.
Customer-supplied fixtures can be the wrong size or defective. State that you will install them but do not warrant the product.
Specify who pulls the permit, who pays, and whether utility disconnects for a service upgrade are included.
Fishing wire through finished walls usually means holes. Say whether patching is included or left to the customer or another trade.

scopeChecklist.item: Code upgrades that may be triggered
scopeChecklist.why: Inspectors can require AFCI/GFCI protection, grounding, or bonding corrections. Note that required upgrades found during work are extra.
Old wiring, damaged conduit, or overcrowded panels may only show once walls are open. State how you will price discoveries.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, power shutoffs, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Customers need to plan for outages, and material prices change, so a quote should expire after 15-30 days.

pricingTips.title: Visit the site for anything beyond a simple device swap
pricingTips.body: Panel location, distance to the meter, attic or crawlspace access, and wall construction can swing a job by hundreds or thousands of dollars. A quick visit prevents underbidding.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options when it makes sense
pricingTips.body: For example, a basic panel swap, a swap with surge protection, and a swap with whole-home surge and added circuits. Customers often choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for older homes
pricingTips.body: For remodels and rewires in older houses, include a contingency or clear unit prices for added circuits or boxes, so surprises are priced before they happen.

pricingTips.title: Break out large jobs into milestones
pricingTips.body: List payment stages such as deposit, rough-in, inspection, and final. This helps cash flow and gives the customer a clear picture of the project.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes for common jobs are usually free. For complex work such as load calculations, design, or multi-visit assessments, many electricians charge a fee, often $100-300, and credit it toward the job if the customer hires you.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 15 to 30 days. Copper, panels, and breakers can change in price, so a short expiration protects your margin.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the customer accepts?
faqs.answer: Only for changes in scope or unforeseen conditions, and only with written agreement. If you did not state exclusions or how hidden problems would be handled, it is hard to add cost afterward.

faqs.question: Is a quote the same as a contract?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A signed estimate with scope, price, and payment terms can act as a contract, but larger jobs usually need a written contract. Some states require specific contract language for home improvement work, so check local rules.

email-marketing-specialist.intro: Email marketing specialists build and run email programs for small businesses, ecommerce brands, nonprofits, and agencies. They invoice for things like welcome and abandoned-cart flows, campaign builds and sends, list cleanup, template design, deliverability work, and monthly management retainers.
email-marketing-specialist.pricingModel: Most email marketing specialists use a mix of monthly retainers and fixed project fees, with hourly billing for ad hoc work. Retainers usually cover a set number of campaigns per month plus reporting and list maintenance, and they are the most common model for ecommerce clients. Automation builds (welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase, win-back) are typically quoted as flat fees per flow, often scaled by the number of emails and branching logic. Template design and coding are priced per template. Strategy audits and deliverability fixes are often a flat fee or hourly. Some specialists add a performance bonus tied to revenue attributed to email, but the base fee should cover the work regardless of results. Software subscription costs for the email platform are normally paid by the client directly, or passed through at cost and listed as a separate line.

rates.service: Hourly consulting or ad hoc support
Monthly email management retainer (2-8 campaigns plus reporting)
Single campaign build and send (copy, layout, QA, send)
Automated flow build (welcome, abandoned cart, post-purchase)
Custom responsive email template design and coding
Email program audit with written recommendations
List cleaning, segmentation, and re-engagement setup
Deliverability setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, warm-up plan)

items.description: Monthly email management retainer, March (4 campaigns, 1 monthly report)
Abandoned cart flow build (3 emails, 2 segments, QA and launch)
List cleanup and inactive subscriber suppression
Additional campaign outside retainer scope (spring sale, 3/22)
Strategy call and reporting review beyond retainer hours

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Email platform fees are billed directly to the client and are not included. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Unused retainer campaigns do not roll over.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and campaign or flow names
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forward invoices to finance, who need to match charges to specific sends or builds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of campaigns, emails, or flows delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers are tied to a set volume, and listing the count shows what was included and what went beyond scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope work listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra campaigns, rush sends, or additional segments should be visible so the client understands why the total changed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as stock images, plugins, or platform fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing at cost, with receipts if requested, avoids confusion about who owns the software subscription.

invoiceChecklist.item: Email platform and account referenced (without login details)
invoiceChecklist.why: It clarifies which client account the work was done in, which matters if the client uses multiple brands or sub-accounts.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client reference code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often will not process payment without one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms, accepted methods, and late fee policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring monthly billing works better when due dates and consequences are stated on every invoice.

email-marketing-specialist.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month or billing period, due on receipt or within 7-15 days. Project work such as flow builds or template design commonly takes 50% upfront and 50% on launch or delivery. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for agency and corporate clients, while small businesses are better served by shorter terms. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract or on the invoice. Most specialists accept ACH, card, or online payment links, and some pause scheduled sends if a retainer invoice goes more than 15 to 30 days unpaid, as long as the contract allows it.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoice for the coming month, not the month just finished. You plan, write, and build before sends go out, so the work is already underway when the month begins.

tips.title: Define what a campaign includes
tips.body: Write down the number of revisions, who supplies the copy and images, and how many segments a send includes. Without that, one campaign request can turn into several rounds of changes.

tips.title: Keep platform costs off your invoice when possible
tips.body: Have the client own and pay for the email platform account. If you do pay for it, bill at cost on a separate line and make clear that it is not part of your fee.

tips.title: Separate build fees from ongoing management
tips.body: A flow build is a one-time project, and monitoring and optimizing it is ongoing. Billing them separately makes it clear what the client is paying for and gives you a natural upsell to a retainer.

tips.title: Include a short results summary with the invoice
tips.body: A few lines on open rate, click rate, and attributed revenue help the client see the value and reduce questions at renewal time. Keep it brief and attach the full report separately.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or by retainer for email marketing?
faqs.answer: Retainers are more common for ongoing work because the client gets predictable output and you get predictable income. Hourly works for audits, one-off fixes, and clients whose needs vary a lot. Many specialists use a retainer with a set number of hours or campaigns and bill extra work hourly.

faqs.question: Who should pay for the email service provider subscription?
faqs.answer: Ideally the client, in an account they own, so they keep their list and data if you part ways. If you pay it and bill the client, list it as a pass-through cost at actual price and state this in your agreement.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of email revenue?
faqs.answer: Yes, some specialists do, usually as a bonus on top of a base fee. Attribution can be disputed, so define in writing how revenue is measured, the attribution window, and the reporting source before you agree to it.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client sends late content that delays a campaign?
faqs.answer: Put content deadlines in your agreement and state that delays do not reduce your monthly fee. For retainer clients, a missed send caused by late assets still counts toward that month's volume unless you agree otherwise.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on email marketing services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain digital or marketing services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and add tax to the invoice only if it applies in your situation.

estimate.intro: Email marketing specialists send estimates when a business wants a new program built, an existing one audited, or an agency is comparing monthly management options. Clients usually compare the number of campaigns and flows included, who writes the copy, how reporting works, and whether platform costs are part of the price.

scopeChecklist.why: State the number of campaigns per month, flows, emails per flow, and templates so the client knows exactly what is covered.
The build depends on the platform, and a migration or new account setup adds work that should be priced in.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies copy, images, and offers
scopeChecklist.why: If you write copy and source graphics, that takes more time than editing client-provided material, and the price should reflect it.

scopeChecklist.item: List size, data sources, and segmentation needs
scopeChecklist.why: A list of 2,000 with one segment is a different job than 100,000 with behavioral segments and integrations with a store or CRM.
A set number of revisions, and a named approver, prevents endless edits and delays.
Specify whether you deliver monthly reports, what metrics are included, and whether strategy calls are part of the fee.
List items such as SMS, landing pages, list purchases, or deliverability remediation, and say what extra work costs per hour or per item.

pricingTips.title: Quote flows and retainers as separate lines
pricingTips.body: Show the one-time build for each flow and the monthly management fee separately. Clients can then approve the build now and add the retainer later if needed, and you avoid underpricing setup work.

pricingTips.title: Scale price to list size and complexity
pricingTips.body: Segmentation, product feeds, dynamic content, and multi-brand accounts add real time. Use tiers based on list size or send volume so the quote reflects the actual workload.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: Three retainer levels, for example 2, 4, or 8 campaigns per month, make it easy for the client to compare and choose without negotiating line by line.

pricingTips.title: Add a validity period
pricingTips.body: State that the quote is valid for 14 to 30 days. Platform changes, seasonal demand, and your own availability can affect the price if the client waits.

faqs.question: Should I give a free audit before sending a quote?
faqs.answer: A short review of the client's current account can help you scope accurately, and many specialists offer a brief one for free. A full audit with written recommendations is real work and is better as a paid first step that can be credited toward a retainer.

faqs.question: How do I quote when I don't know the list size or setup yet?
faqs.answer: Ask for list size, platform, send frequency, and a few recent campaigns before quoting. If you still cannot scope it, quote a paid discovery phase first, or give a range with stated assumptions.

faqs.question: How long should a retainer commitment be?
faqs.answer: Three months is a common minimum because email programs take time to show results. After that, month-to-month with 30 days' notice is typical.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: Not by itself in most cases. An estimate becomes a firm commitment once the client accepts it in writing or you sign a contract. State whether the price is fixed or an estimate that may change if scope changes.

energy-auditor.intro: Energy auditors assess how much energy a home or commercial building uses and where it is lost. They are hired by homeowners, landlords, property managers, and small businesses, and sometimes by contractors or utility programs. Invoices usually cover the on-site audit, diagnostic testing such as blower door and duct leakage tests, thermal imaging, and a written report with recommendations.
energy-auditor.pricingModel: Most residential auditors charge a flat fee based on home size and the level of testing, such as a basic walkthrough, a standard audit with blower door, or a comprehensive audit with duct testing, combustion safety checks, and modeling software. Commercial work is usually priced per square foot for ASHRAE Level 1 or Level 2 audits, or hourly on larger scopes. Add-ons like infrared scans, duct blaster tests, follow-up testing after air sealing, and HERS ratings are often priced separately. Work done for utility or rebate programs may follow a fixed program rate, and those jobs often bill through a contractor or program administrator. Travel is typically covered in the flat fee within a service area, with a mileage charge beyond it. Some auditors credit part of the audit fee toward a contractor job if they also do retrofit work, but check your local rules and any conflict-of-interest requirements of the programs you work with.

rates.service: Standard home energy audit with blower door and infrared scan
Comprehensive audit with duct leakage test and combustion safety
HERS rating (new construction, rating and testing)
Consulting, utility bill analysis, and energy modeling

items.description: Standard home energy audit, 2,100 sq ft single-family home (walkthrough, blower door test, infrared scan, combustion safety check)
Duct leakage test (duct blaster), forced-air system
Written report with prioritized recommendations and estimated savings
Utility bill analysis, 24 months of electric and gas data
Travel outside standard service area (18 miles over)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of the report delivery date. Audit performed on 3/12 with the homeowner present. Findings are estimates based on conditions observed on the day of testing. A post-retrofit test-out is available for $200 if completed within 90 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and date of the audit
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific site visit and matters if the report is later used for a rebate, tax credit, or sale disclosure.

invoiceChecklist.item: Level of audit performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates a walkthrough from a standard or comprehensive audit so the client understands what the fee covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: List of tests performed (blower door, duct leakage, infrared, combustion safety)
invoiceChecklist.why: Each test takes time and equipment, and listing them avoids questions about the price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Report delivery date and format
invoiceChecklist.why: Starts the payment clock and documents that the deliverable was provided.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications and ID numbers (BPI, RESNET, state license if required)
invoiceChecklist.why: Utility programs and rebate administrators often require certified auditors, and clients may need this for paperwork.

invoiceChecklist.item: Program name and reference or job number, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Utility and rebate program jobs are often paid only when the invoice matches the program's job ID.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or travel charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how out-of-area charges were calculated so they are not disputed.

energy-auditor.paymentTerms: Residential audits are often paid at the time of service or within 7 to 14 days of report delivery, since the client wants the report quickly. Many solo auditors take payment by card or check on the day of the audit and release the report after payment. For commercial audits, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, with the balance due on delivery of the report, often net 30. Utility or program work may pay on the program's schedule, which can run 30 to 60 days, so check the terms before accepting the job. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common on commercial work if stated in advance. Include a cancellation or no-access fee if clients are not home or the site is not ready for testing.

tips.title: Release the report after payment on small jobs
tips.body: For residential audits, the report is your leverage. State on the estimate that the written report is delivered once the invoice is paid, and collect payment at the visit when you can.

tips.title: Price retest visits separately
tips.body: A post-retrofit blower door test is a second trip with its own equipment setup. Quote it as a separate line item instead of folding it into the original fee, and note the time window in which the price applies.

tips.title: Charge for house size and complexity
tips.body: Large homes, multiple HVAC systems, finished basements, or knob-and-tube wiring take more time. Use tiered flat fees by square footage or add a line for extra systems so the price matches the work.

tips.title: Match invoices to program requirements
tips.body: If you work with utility or state programs, copy the required job ID, auditor certification number, and test results format onto your invoice. Mismatched paperwork is a common reason for payment delays.

tips.title: Keep records of test data
tips.body: Save blower door readings, photos, and infrared images with each job. If a client questions the findings or the bill, you can show what was measured.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for a home energy audit?
faqs.answer: Most residential auditors use a flat fee tied to home size and test level, because clients want a clear price. Hourly billing is more common for consulting, bill analysis, modeling, and commercial work where scope is less predictable.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on an energy audit?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional services, while a few tax certain inspection or consulting services. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can I bill separately for the report?
faqs.answer: Yes, though most auditors include a basic report in the audit fee. A separate line makes sense for extended reports, energy models, or documents prepared for rebate applications, lenders, or real estate transactions.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for utility program audits?
faqs.answer: Use the program's required format and include the customer account or job number, audit date, your certification ID, and the program rate. Confirm the payment schedule up front, since program payments often arrive later than direct client payments.

faqs.question: What if the client cancels on the day of the audit?
faqs.answer: Include a cancellation policy in your estimate or booking confirmation, such as a fee for cancellations within 24 hours or a no-access visit. Invoice that fee as a flat line item with the date and reason.

estimate.intro: Energy auditors send an estimate before the visit, often by email or phone after asking about the home or building. Clients usually compare a few auditors on price, certifications, and what tests are included. A clear quote that lists tests and deliverables separates a full audit from a cheap walkthrough.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume every audit includes blower door, duct testing, and infrared scanning. Listing them avoids disputes over missing tests.

scopeChecklist.item: Home or building size and number of HVAC systems
scopeChecklist.why: Price is based on these details, so the quote should state them and note that changes may affect the fee.
Defines what the client receives, such as recommendations, estimated savings, photos, and a modeling summary, and when.
Testing may require access to the attic, crawlspace, and mechanical rooms, and appliances to be operable. A no-access fee is easier to enforce if it was in the quote.

scopeChecklist.item: Safety-related findings and limits of the audit
scopeChecklist.why: Auditors may find gas leaks, carbon monoxide, or moisture problems. State that the audit is not a code inspection and clarify how safety findings are handled.
Clients who plan retrofits need to know the cost of a test-out and how long that price is held.
Prevents surprise charges for rural or out-of-area sites.

pricingTips.title: Use tiers by test level
pricingTips.body: Offer a basic, standard, and comprehensive option with set prices. Clients can pick the level that fits their budget, and you avoid custom pricing for every inquiry.

pricingTips.title: Ask about the goal before you quote
pricingTips.body: A client seeking a rebate, a lender-required report, or help with high bills needs different deliverables. Confirm the purpose and price the report to match.

pricingTips.title: Quote add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: Thermal imaging, duct testing, combustion testing, and modeling can be listed as optional lines. Clients see the value and you get paid for the extra work.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should be valid for 30 days or so. Equipment, travel costs, and your schedule change, and an expiration protects your pricing.

faqs.question: Should I give a price over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a range or tier price once you know the size, age, and systems in the home, but confirm it in writing. A written estimate listing the tests included protects both sides.

faqs.question: Do I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Residential estimates are usually free. For large commercial buildings that require a pre-visit review of plans or utility data, some auditors charge a small scoping fee or credit it toward the audit.

faqs.question: What if I find more problems than expected on site?
faqs.answer: Include language that the fee covers the stated tests and that extra testing, such as added duct systems or additional combustion appliances, may be billed at an agreed rate. Get the client's approval before doing the extra work.

engraving-service.intro: Engraving services mark metal, glass, wood, leather, acrylic, stone, and other materials with names, logos, serial numbers, and artwork. Customers include trophy and awards buyers, jewelers, corporate gift buyers, schools, sports leagues, manufacturers needing part marking, and individuals ordering personalized gifts. Invoices usually cover setup, artwork, per-piece engraving, and any blank items the shop supplies.
engraving-service.pricingModel: Most engravers combine a one-time setup or artwork fee with a per-piece price. Per-piece pricing depends on the material, the size of the engraved area, the amount of text or detail, and the machine time it takes. Jewelry and hand engraving are often priced per character, per line, or per piece. Production laser or rotary work is often priced per piece with quantity breaks, and some shops bill by machine time (per hour) for large or complex jobs. When you supply the blank item, such as a tumbler, plaque, pen, or knife, you add it at cost plus a markup, commonly 40-100% for retail items. Most shops set a minimum order charge to cover setup on small jobs. Rush work, customer-supplied items that need special fixturing, and artwork cleanup or vectorizing are billed as separate lines.

rates.service: Laser engraving on customer-supplied small items (pens, tags, cards)
Hand engraving or specialty firearm/knife engraving

items.description: Logo artwork cleanup and vectorizing (one-time setup)
Stainless steel 20 oz tumblers, supplied by shop
Laser engraving, logo plus name on tumbler (wraparound, 2 lines)
Individual gift box packaging
Proof approval and test engraving on spare item

sampleInvoice.notes: 50% deposit of $720.00 was received at order approval; balance due on pickup or within 14 days of invoice date. Engraving was done to the approved proof dated 3/12. Please inspect items within 5 days of delivery and report any defects in writing. Custom engraved items cannot be returned except for shop error.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the approved proof or artwork file
invoiceChecklist.why: Engraved items are final. Pointing to the signed-off proof settles disputes over spelling, spacing, and design.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material and item description for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Stainless steel, anodized aluminum, brass, glass, and wood have different prices and results. A clear description shows why prices differ.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity, per-piece price, and setup or artwork fees as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often reorder. Separating one-time setup from per-piece charges makes repeat pricing clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Whether blanks were supplied by you or the customer
invoiceChecklist.why: This affects pricing, sales tax treatment in many states, and who is responsible if a customer-supplied item is damaged or unsuitable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom work usually requires a deposit up front. Showing it prevents confusion about what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Taxability of engraving services and goods varies by state. Record tax charged, or the resale or exemption certificate on file for tax-exempt buyers like schools and nonprofits.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number and job or order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate, school, and league buyers often require a purchase order number before they can pay the invoice.

engraving-service.paymentTerms: Most engravers collect payment in full up front for small retail orders and walk-ins. For custom or large orders, a 50% deposit at proof approval is common, with the balance due at pickup or delivery. Business customers on repeat accounts are often invoiced net 15 or net 30. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical when stated on the invoice or order agreement. Shops commonly accept cards, ACH, checks, and cash, and many hold finished work until the balance is paid.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before you buy blanks or start
tips.body: Custom engraved items usually cannot be resold if the customer walks away. A 50% deposit covers your blank costs and machine time, and it is especially important on orders with name lists or special-order items.

tips.title: Get written proof approval
tips.body: Send a proof showing exact spelling, font, and placement, and keep the customer's written approval by email or signature. Name and date errors are the most common cause of reprint disputes, and an approved proof shows who is responsible.

tips.title: Charge for setup and artwork separately
tips.body: Fixturing, jig building, file cleanup, and test runs take real time. Bill them as their own lines, even if you waive them on larger orders and show the waived amount as a discount.

tips.title: Set a minimum order charge
tips.body: A single pen or one ring can take as long to set up as a dozen. A minimum of $20-40 keeps tiny jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Note risk on customer-supplied items
tips.body: State on the order that you are not responsible for finishes, coatings, or materials that react poorly to engraving. Charge for the test piece if you ask the customer to supply an extra one.

faqs.question: Should I charge per character or per piece?
faqs.answer: Per character pricing is common for jewelry and hand engraving, where each letter takes time. For laser work, per piece is more common, with price tied to size and complexity. Whichever you choose, list the unit on the invoice so the customer can see how the total was calculated.

faqs.question: How do I bill for blanks I supply?
faqs.answer: List the blank as its own line with your cost plus markup, separate from the engraving charge. This keeps the engraving price consistent whether the customer supplies the item or you do, and it makes reorders and tax handling easier.

faqs.question: What should I do if the customer says the spelling is wrong?
faqs.answer: Check the approved proof. If the engraving matches the proof, the customer owes the invoice and any reprint is a new, billable job. If it does not match, the error is yours and you should redo or credit the item. This is why you should keep proofs and approvals with the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on engraving?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax engraving as a service, some tax it as part of the sale of tangible goods, and some exempt it in certain cases. Resellers, schools, and nonprofits may provide exemption certificates. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I price rush orders?
faqs.answer: Many shops add 25-50% to the job for same-day or next-day turnaround, and list it as a separate line. Only offer rush service when you can move the job ahead without delaying other paid work.

estimate.intro: Engravers send quotes before any work starts, especially for custom orders, bulk orders, awards, corporate gifts, and industrial marking. Customers usually compare per-piece price, setup fees, turnaround time, and whether blanks are included. A clear quote helps them see these items side by side.

scopeChecklist.item: Item, material, and who supplies the blank
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for engraving customer-supplied items is very different from one that includes blanks, and the material affects both method and price.

scopeChecklist.item: Engraving size, placement, and number of lines or colors
scopeChecklist.why: Size and detail drive machine time. Specifying them prevents pricing disputes if the design grows after the quote.
Setup costs spread across more pieces. Showing tiers, such as 1-11, 12-49, and 50+, encourages larger orders and sets expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Artwork requirements and who prepares the files
scopeChecklist.why: Low-resolution logos need cleanup or vectorizing. State whether this is included, and what the charge is if the files need work.
Say that production starts only after written approval, and note any limit on proof revisions before extra charges apply.
Lead time starts from proof approval and deposit, not from the quote date. Spelling this out avoids missed event deadlines.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, quote expiration date, and return policy
scopeChecklist.why: Material costs change, and custom pieces cannot be resold. State the deposit, how long the price holds, and that engraved items are non-returnable except for shop error.

pricingTips.title: Price from machine time and setup, not just material
pricingTips.body: Track how long typical jobs run, including loading, focusing, engraving, and cleanup. Use that to set per-piece prices, then add setup for fixtures and artwork so small orders pay for themselves.

pricingTips.title: Offer quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: A tiered price table shows the benefit of ordering more without discounting the first piece. It also helps buyers pick a quantity that fits their budget.

pricingTips.title: Include a test or sample for material you have not engraved
pricingTips.body: Coated, plated, or unusual materials can behave unpredictably. Quote a test piece, or add language reserving the right to adjust the price if the material needs a different process.

pricingTips.title: Keep blank pricing separate
pricingTips.body: Show blank cost and engraving as separate lines. If supplier prices change, you can update the blank line without rewriting the whole quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are normally free. For complex jobs needing custom artwork, fixture design, or material testing, many shops charge a design or sample fee and credit it toward the order if the customer proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. Blank costs, metal prices, and shipping can shift, so put an expiration date on the quote and say that pricing is based on the quantity and artwork described.

faqs.question: What if the customer changes the quantity or text after accepting?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that changes in quantity, size, or design after approval may change the price and the schedule. Send a revised quote for the change before you continue.

faqs.question: Can I give a firm price for hand engraving?
faqs.answer: Often only after seeing the item and design. For hand engraving, quote either an hourly rate with an estimated number of hours or a flat price after reviewing the piece, and state what happens if the work takes longer because of the design.

enrolled-agent.intro: Enrolled agents are federally authorized tax practitioners who prepare returns and represent taxpayers before the IRS. Solo EAs and small firms bill individuals and small businesses for return preparation, bookkeeping cleanup, IRS notice responses, audit representation, and year-round tax planning.
enrolled-agent.pricingModel: Most enrolled agents price return preparation as a flat fee per return or per form, based on complexity. A 1040 with Schedule C, a rental schedule, or multi-state filings costs more than a W-2 only return. Representation work such as audits, collections, penalty abatement, and offers in compromise is usually billed hourly or as a flat fee with a defined scope, often paid in part up front. Tax planning and advisory sessions are billed hourly or as a package. Many EAs also offer monthly or quarterly retainers for small business clients that bundle bookkeeping review, estimated tax calculations, and unlimited short questions. Some states restrict contingent fees on original returns, and IRS Circular 230 limits contingent fees in certain cases, so most EAs avoid them and charge fixed or hourly fees. Fees should be stated in advance and tied to a written scope.

rates.service: Individual 1040 with itemized deductions and Schedule C or rental
Small business return (1120-S or 1065) with K-1s
IRS notice response or penalty abatement request

items.description: 2024 Form 1040 preparation with Schedule C, Schedule SE, and home office (Form 8829)
State resident return (additional state)
Bookkeeping review and categorization of 12 months of business transactions
Response to IRS CP2000 notice, including review of 1099 data and written response
Tax planning call: 2025 estimated payments and SEP-IRA contribution

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A $300 deposit was received at engagement and is not reflected above; it will be applied to the final balance. Returns are e-filed after payment is received in full. Late balances over 30 days are subject to a 1.5% monthly charge. Services are limited to those listed in the engagement letter.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax year and return type for each service (e.g., 2024 Form 1040, 1120-S)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often use you across several years and entities, and each line needs to match a specific filing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Forms and schedules included in flat fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing Schedule C, Schedule E, Form 8829, or state returns shows what the price covers and justifies add-ons.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the engagement letter and its scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the bill to the agreed services and protects you if a client claims something was included that was not.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and task description for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Representation and planning time is scrutinized most, so dated entries like 'Reviewed IRS transcript' prevent disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or retainer received and how it was applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the correct balance due and gives a clear record of funds taken in advance.

invoiceChecklist.item: IRS notice number or case reference where relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which matter you billed for, such as a CP2000, CP14, or audit letter.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your PTIN and firm name and contact details
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients may need these for their records, and paid preparers must have a PTIN on returns they prepare for compensation.

enrolled-agent.paymentTerms: Many EAs collect a deposit or the full fee for simple returns before filing, since it is hard to collect after a client receives a refund. For larger projects, a typical split is 25 to 50 percent at engagement and the balance on delivery or before e-filing. Representation work is often billed with an upfront retainer that is drawn down by hourly time. Due dates are commonly due on receipt to net 15. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the engagement letter. Accepted payment methods usually include ACH, card, and check. Some preparers offer refund-based payment options, though these involve additional rules and should be reviewed carefully.

tips.title: Get an engagement letter signed first
tips.body: Define the tax years, forms, and what is excluded, such as audit representation or amended returns. Then make each invoice line refer back to it.

tips.title: Hold the return until paid
tips.body: Do not e-file until the fee is paid or a deposit covers it. Note that you may not withhold a client's own records, so release original documents even if a balance is owed.

tips.title: Separate preparation from representation
tips.body: If a client later gets a notice or audit, treat it as new work with a new scope and retainer instead of absorbing it into the original return fee.

tips.title: Bill for extra documents and cleanup
tips.body: When clients arrive with shoeboxes of receipts or unreconciled books, add a line for bookkeeping time instead of folding it into a return fee that assumed clean records.

tips.title: Invoice after tax season for off-season work
tips.body: Planning calls and notice responses are easy to forget in busy months. Bill them within a week of completion while the details are fresh.

faqs.question: Should I charge per return or hourly?
faqs.answer: Per return is standard for preparation because clients want a known price. Use hourly rates for representation, planning, and cleanup where the amount of work is uncertain. Many EAs use a flat fee with a clause for extra time if records are incomplete.

faqs.question: Can I charge a contingent fee based on the refund or the amount saved?
faqs.answer: Generally no for original returns. Circular 230 limits contingent fees to a few situations, such as IRS examinations or amended returns claiming a refund, and some states add their own rules. Check the current rules before using one and stick to fixed or hourly fees if unsure.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on tax preparation?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. A few states tax certain professional or tax preparation services, while most do not. Check with your state department of revenue.

faqs.question: Can I keep a client's documents until they pay?
faqs.answer: No. Under Circular 230, practitioners must return client records on request, even if fees are unpaid. You can still hold your own work product, such as an unfiled return, until payment, subject to your state's rules.

faqs.question: How should I handle clients who pay late after filing?
faqs.answer: State late fee terms in your engagement letter, send reminders at 15 and 30 days, and consider requiring payment before filing for clients with a history of late payment.

estimate.intro: Enrolled agents send quotes before taking on a new client, before a representation matter, and when a prospective client needs catch-up filings for several years. Clients usually compare your price with a large chain preparer, a CPA, or a software subscription, so the quote must show what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Tax years and return types covered
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents confusion when a client assumes prior years or amended returns are part of the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Forms and schedules included in the fee
scopeChecklist.why: Schedule C, E, K-1s, and multi-state returns change the workload, so name what is covered and what costs extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Records the client must provide and the deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Late or incomplete documents are the main cause of overruns, so tie your price to receiving organized records.
State whether books are expected to be reconciled and the hourly rate for cleanup if they are not.
Specify whether you are handling a single notice, an audit, or a full collections case, and that Form 2848 is required.

scopeChecklist.item: What happens if the IRS or state follows up after filing
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether post-filing notices and audits are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, payment schedule, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations on when work starts and how long the price holds.

pricingTips.title: Price off the forms, not the hours
pricingTips.body: Build a fee schedule by form and complexity and reuse it. Clients can see why a return with rental properties costs more than a W-2 return.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range with conditions for unknowns
pricingTips.body: For delinquent filings or notice work, give a fee for the known scope and an hourly rate for additional work once you review transcripts.

pricingTips.title: Review prior-year returns before quoting
pricingTips.body: Ask for last year's return or an IRS account transcript. A quick review shows complexity and reveals problems that affect your price.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for ongoing clients
pricingTips.body: Present a return-only option and a year-round option with planning calls and estimated payment calculations so clients can choose a level of service.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: If the client signs your engagement letter with the quoted fee, it becomes the agreed price for that scope. State the expiration date and that changes in scope, such as additional forms, can change the fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many EAs offer a short free call to assess fit, then charge for in-depth review or transcript analysis. A paid consultation that is credited toward the engagement is a common compromise.

faqs.question: How do I quote IRS representation when the outcome is unknown?
faqs.answer: Use an hourly rate with an upfront retainer, or a flat fee for a defined stage such as the initial response. Do not promise a result and avoid quoting a fee tied to the amount of tax reduced.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote before seeing documents?
faqs.answer: You can give a starting range based on the client's description, but mark it as an estimate and confirm the final fee after reviewing the return, prior filings, and records.

entertainment.intro: Entertainment providers are DJs, bands, solo musicians, MCs, magicians, variety performers, and photo booth or party-attraction operators who are booked for weddings, corporate events, private parties, schools, and venues. Invoices usually cover the performance itself, extra equipment such as sound and lighting, travel, and add-ons like overtime or custom song production.
entertainment.pricingModel: Most entertainers price by the event or by the hour with a minimum booking length, often 2 to 4 hours. Bands and variety acts commonly quote a flat fee per performance that covers a set length, such as two 45-minute sets. DJs often sell packages that bundle time, sound, and lighting, then charge for overtime in hourly increments. Equipment, staffing (extra musicians, sound techs, assistants), and travel are priced as separate lines or built into the package. Most bookers collect a non-refundable deposit to hold the date, since a cancelled date is hard to resell, and charge a higher rate for peak dates such as Saturdays in wedding season and New Year's Eve.

rates.service: DJ and MC for a private event or wedding
Solo or duo musician (ceremony, cocktail hour, restaurant)
Sound and lighting package (uplighting, speakers, microphones)

items.description: DJ and MC services, wedding reception (6:00 pm - 10:00 pm)
Ceremony sound system with two wireless microphones
Uplighting package (12 fixtures, setup and teardown)
Overtime, reception extended to 10:30 pm
Travel to venue outside 40-mile radius (30 miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: June 14. The $300 deposit received on March 2 has been applied. Balance is due within 7 days of the event. Payment accepted by check, bank transfer, or card. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and venue name and address
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the invoice to a specific booking and settles any dispute about how long you performed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Performance length and any overtime actually worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Overtime is the most common extra charge, and clients dispute it less when the times are written down.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized equipment and staffing (sound, lighting, extra musicians, techs)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating them from your performance fee shows what the client is paying for and makes add-ons easy to explain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget the deposit they paid months ago. Showing it avoids confusion over the amount owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, lodging, or parking charges
invoiceChecklist.why: These costs are easy to forget and hard to add after the fact, so list them as they were quoted in the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed booking agreement or contract number
invoiceChecklist.why: It links the invoice to the agreed terms, including cancellation, overtime rates, and rider requirements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax, if your state taxes the service or any equipment rental
invoiceChecklist.why: Rules vary by state, and some tax live performance or rentals differently, so check your local rules and show the tax on its own line.

entertainment.paymentTerms: A non-refundable deposit of 25% to 50% is standard to hold a date, with the balance due either a week or two before the event or on the day of the event. Corporate clients and venues often pay on net 15 to net 30 terms and may need a W-9, a certificate of insurance, or a PO number. Weddings and private parties commonly require the full balance before the event or at load-in, since collecting afterward is harder. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Most entertainers accept bank transfer, check, and card, and many add a card processing fee for large balances.

tips.title: Collect the balance before you play
tips.body: For private events, require the final payment a week before or at arrival. Once the party is over, the client has less reason to answer quickly, and chasing a few hundred dollars costs time you can't bill.

tips.title: Put overtime rates in the contract and on the invoice
tips.body: Agree beforehand on the hourly overtime rate and who can authorize it. On the day, ask the planner or client to confirm the extension, and note the time in your records so the invoice matches.

tips.title: Charge for date exclusivity
tips.body: When you turn away other work to hold a Saturday, the deposit should reflect that. State plainly that it is non-refundable and what happens if the client reschedules.

tips.title: Separate talent fees from equipment and travel
tips.body: Listing them on different lines lets you adjust one without discounting the whole booking. It also helps if a client asks to drop lighting or add a second speaker.

tips.title: Send invoices to the right person
tips.body: For corporate gigs, the person who hired you is often not the one who pays. Ask for the accounts payable contact and any vendor onboarding steps before the event.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the event?
faqs.answer: Send the deposit invoice when the client books and the balance invoice about two to four weeks before the event, due before or on the day. For corporate clients on net terms, send the final invoice right after the event.

faqs.question: Is the deposit refundable if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: That is up to your contract, but most entertainers make the deposit non-refundable because the date can't easily be resold. Some refund part of it if the date is rebooked. Put the policy in writing so it is on file before any dispute.

faqs.question: Can I charge a different rate for peak dates?
faqs.answer: Yes. Saturdays in peak wedding season, holidays, and New Year's Eve typically cost more. Show the rate on the quote so the client sees the price before agreeing.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on entertainment services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax admissions or live entertainment, some tax equipment rentals, and many do not tax performances by independent contractors. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for travel?
faqs.answer: Many entertainers include a free travel radius, such as 30 to 50 miles, then charge a per-mile rate or flat fee beyond it. Add lodging and meals for distant bookings. Whatever you do, put it in the quote so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Entertainers send a quote when someone inquires about a date, usually weeks or months before the event. Clients often compare several acts on price, length of performance, and what is included, so a clear quote that lists every item makes yours easy to compare.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, venue, and performance times, including setup and breakdown windows
scopeChecklist.why: Load-in time and performance time affect the hours you are committing and what you charge.

scopeChecklist.item: Length of performance and number of sets or breaks
scopeChecklist.why: A 3-hour continuous DJ set is a different job than two 45-minute band sets, and clients may assume otherwise.

scopeChecklist.item: What equipment and staff are included
scopeChecklist.why: It prevents surprises about whether microphones, lighting, a sound tech, or backup gear are part of the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Overtime rate and how it is approved
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often ask you to play longer, and a stated rate avoids haggling when the event is running late.
Costs for out-of-town or hard-access venues can be significant, and the client should know who pays for them.

scopeChecklist.item: Venue requirements and client responsibilities (power, stage space, insurance, load-in access)
scopeChecklist.why: If the venue cannot meet your needs, you want it on record that the client is responsible.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, cancellation and rescheduling terms, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Dates book up, so the quote should say how long it is held and what the client needs to do to secure it.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A base package, a mid-level one with lighting or an extra hour, and a premium one with extras make it easy for clients to choose without negotiating. Most pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price the date, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: Your cost includes turning down other bookings, so Saturdays, holidays, and peak season should cost more than weeknights. State the reason on the quote if the client asks.

pricingTips.title: Count your unpaid time
pricingTips.body: Add planning calls, song or set list prep, rehearsals, loading, driving, and setup to your fee. A 4-hour performance often takes 8 to 10 hours of your day.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Say that the quote is held for 7 to 14 days, and that the date is only reserved once the contract is signed and the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: Should I give quotes for free?
faqs.answer: Yes, for standard events, since quoting is part of selling. For complex jobs like custom shows, large productions, or multi-day festivals, some entertainers charge a design fee that is credited toward the booking.

faqs.question: Is a quote the same as a contract?
faqs.answer: No. A quote states the price and what is included, but a signed contract and deposit are what secure the date. Many entertainers send the contract together with the quote so the client can accept both at once.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change the event after I quote?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that changes in time, location, or scope can change the price. When the details change, send a revised quote in writing before the event.

faqs.question: How do I respond when a client says another act is cheaper?
faqs.answer: Compare what is included instead of cutting your price right away. Look at performance length, equipment, backup gear, insurance, and experience. If you do offer a discount, reduce the scope to match, such as fewer hours or no lighting.

equipment-operator.intro: Equipment operators run excavators, backhoes, skid steers, bulldozers, loaders, graders, and similar machines, often as owner-operators or small outfits hired by contractors, landscapers, and property owners. They bill for machine time, operator labor, transport of the equipment to and from the site, and fuel or wear items. Many work as subcontractors, so invoices often go to a general contractor and need to match job numbers and daily tickets.
equipment-operator.pricingModel: Most equipment operators bill hourly with the machine and operator bundled into a single "wet rate," which includes fuel, maintenance, and the operator. A "dry rate" covers the machine only, with the customer supplying the operator and fuel. Many jobs have a 2 to 4 hour minimum, and the clock usually starts when the machine is loaded or arrives on site, depending on what you agree to. Transport (lowboy or trailer mobilization) is charged separately, either as a flat fee or per mile each way. Some work is priced by the job, such as a house pad, driveway grading, or a pond dig, or by the unit (per cubic yard, per linear foot of trench, per acre of brush clearing). Add-ons commonly include attachments (hydraulic hammer, auger, grapple, mulching head), fuel surcharges, dump or disposal fees passed through at cost, and traffic control or permits when required. Union and prevailing wage jobs follow set scale rates, which are different from private work.

rates.service: Full-size excavator or backhoe with operator

items.description: Mini excavator with operator, trench for water line at 1420 Ridge Rd (wet rate, fuel included)
Skid steer with operator, backfill and grading
Hydraulic hammer attachment, rock removal
Equipment transport, mini excavator and skid steer, round trip
Disposal fee for spoil hauled to county landfill (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Hours are per signed daily tickets dated 3/11 and 3/12. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly charge applies to balances past due. Utility locates and permits were the responsibility of the customer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Machine type, make, and unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Different machines have different rates, and a unit number lets the client match the charge to the equipment actually on site.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and hours worked per day, with signed daily tickets
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly disputes are the most common billing issue. A ticket signed by the client or site foreman is the strongest proof.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wet or dry rate stated
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear whether fuel and operator are included so nothing is questioned later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mobilization and demobilization charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Hauling a machine takes time and a trailer or lowboy, and clients often forget it is a separate cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Attachments used and their rates
invoiceChecklist.why: Hammers, augers, and grapples add wear and are billed separately from the base machine.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address, PO number, and job or contract number
invoiceChecklist.why: General contractors and municipalities often will not process payment without a PO or job number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as dump fees, permits, or fuel surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing them at cost with receipts keeps them separate from your markup and avoids pushback.

equipment-operator.paymentTerms: Private homeowners and small jobs are often paid at completion or with a deposit of 25 to 50 percent when mobilization costs are high. Commercial and subcontract work commonly runs net 30, and some general contractors pay only after they are paid by the owner, so check for pay-when-paid clauses. Many operators add a late charge of 1 to 2 percent per month, if allowed by local law and written into the agreement. Checks, ACH, and card payments are all common. Card fees are sometimes passed on for large balances. Some states give contractors lien rights, so know your deadlines for filing a preliminary notice or lien if payment stalls, and check your state's rules.

tips.title: Get daily tickets signed
tips.body: Have the client or foreman sign a ticket with start time, stop time, machine, and work done at the end of each day. It settles disputes before they start and makes the invoice easy to support.

tips.title: Set a minimum and say when the clock starts
tips.body: State a 2 to 4 hour minimum and whether billing runs portal to portal or only while the machine is running. Breaks, weather delays, and waiting on other trades are common arguments.

tips.title: Bill transport separately
tips.body: Moving a machine costs fuel, trailer wear, and time. Charge it as its own line, and charge again if you have to move between sites or return for a second phase.

tips.title: Track wear items and breakdowns
tips.body: Hammer work, rock, and demolition wear out teeth, tracks, and hoses faster. Build this into hourly rates or add a wear charge for severe conditions, and note it in the quote.

tips.title: Invoice weekly on long jobs
tips.body: For jobs lasting more than a week, send weekly invoices from your tickets so you are not carrying a large unpaid balance on fuel and payroll.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a wet rate and a dry rate?
faqs.answer: A wet rate includes the machine, operator, and fuel. A dry rate is for the machine alone, and the customer provides the operator and usually the fuel. Dry rates are lower per hour but carry more risk of damage, so many owners require insurance and a signed rental agreement.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time and hauling the machine?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in your quote or agreement. Most operators charge a flat mobilization fee or a per-mile rate each way, and some also bill operator travel time. Put it on its own line item.

faqs.question: Should I charge a minimum number of hours?
faqs.answer: Most operators do, typically 2 to 4 hours or a flat call-out fee. Setting up, hauling, and loading take about the same time whether the job is short or long, so a minimum covers that.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a customer asks for extra work on site?
faqs.answer: Confirm the change in writing, even by text, and note it on that day's ticket. Bill the extra hours at your normal rate or a rate you agree on, and list them as a separate line.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on equipment work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax rentals of equipment but not labor services, and operated equipment may fall in either category. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Equipment operators quote before work starts on excavation, grading, land clearing, demolition, and site prep jobs, usually after a site visit. Clients compare hourly rates, estimated hours, mobilization, and whether the price is fixed or time-and-materials. Ground conditions are the biggest unknown, so a clear quote protects you if the work turns out harder than it looked.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact work to be done and area covered
scopeChecklist.why: Define what is being dug, graded, cleared, or hauled, with dimensions or depth, so extra work is easy to identify.

scopeChecklist.item: Pricing basis: hourly, fixed price, or per unit
scopeChecklist.why: Time-and-materials and fixed bids carry different risks. State which applies and what happens if hours run over.
Prevents disputes if a larger machine, hammer, or auger is needed later.
Clients often assume the machine is already on site. Show the haul cost and any extra moves.
Rock, roots, high water table, buried debris, and old foundations can change the job. State how those will be handled and billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Utility locates, permits, and site access
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify who calls 811, pulls permits, and provides access. Hitting an unmarked line is costly and should not fall on you by default.
Say whether soil is stacked on site, hauled off, or spread, and who pays dump fees and for fill or gravel.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours from production, not guesses
pricingTips.body: Use your typical output, such as cubic yards per hour or feet of trench per hour, then add time for moving, loading, and waiting. Adjust down for tight spaces, rock, or wet ground.

pricingTips.title: Offer a fixed price only when conditions are clear
pricingTips.body: Use time-and-materials or an estimated range with a cap for unknown soil or old structures. Use fixed price for simple, visible work such as a flat pad on open ground.

pricingTips.title: Include a contingency for rock and breakdown risk
pricingTips.body: Add a line or a clause for hammer work or hitting rock, billed at an agreed hourly rate, instead of building a large cushion into the base price.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fuel, trucking, and your own schedule change. A 14 to 30 day expiration keeps you from honoring an old price after costs rise.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site visit to give a quote?
faqs.answer: Many operators give free quotes for nearby jobs and charge a fee for distant or complex ones, sometimes credited toward the work if hired. Say upfront if there is a fee.

faqs.question: Should I quote a fixed price or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Fixed price works for clear, simple jobs. When soil conditions or scope are uncertain, hourly with an estimated number of hours protects you and is common in the industry.

faqs.question: What if the job takes longer than I estimated?
faqs.answer: On an hourly quote, bill the actual hours and tell the client early if the estimate is changing. On a fixed price quote, you absorb overruns unless the extra work comes from conditions or changes excluded in your written scope.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A signed quote or short work agreement confirms the scope, rates, and payment terms, and it helps if you need to pursue payment or file a lien later.

equipment-rental.intro: Equipment rental businesses rent out tools and machinery such as skid steers, scissor lifts, generators, pressure washers, and party or event gear to contractors, homeowners, and event planners. Invoices cover rental time, delivery and pickup, fuel, damage waivers, and cleaning or late fees. Many are solo operators or small yards with a handful of units, so a clear invoice is the main protection against disputes over hours, damage, and return condition.
equipment-rental.pricingModel: Most rental pricing is time-based with tiered rates: a 4-hour rate, a day rate (usually 24 hours), a weekly rate (often about 3 times the day rate), and a four-week or monthly rate (often about 3 times the weekly rate). Heavy equipment may also carry engine-hour limits, such as 8 hours per day or 40 per week, with overage billed per hour. On top of the base rental, most shops add delivery and pickup charges (flat or per mile), a refundable security deposit, a damage waiver (commonly 8-15% of the rental fee), fuel refill charges, cleaning fees, and consumables such as blades, bits, or propane. Small tools are often billed per day with a minimum; party and event gear is often billed per item per event. Sales tax on rentals varies by state, so check your local rules on whether rental charges are taxable.

rates.service: Compact skid steer or mini excavator rental
Hand and power tools (demo hammer, tile saw, plate compactor)
Party tent or table and chair package

items.description: Mini excavator rental, 1 day (8 engine hours included)
Hydraulic breaker attachment
Delivery and pickup, 18 miles each way
Damage waiver (10% of rental charges)
Overage engine hours
Fuel refill at return
