sampleInvoice.notes: Rental period 3/4 to 3/7. Security deposit of $500 was collected at pickup and will be refunded or applied within 3 business days after inspection. Equipment must be returned clean with a full tank. Balance due on receipt. Late returns billed at one additional day rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental start and end date and time
invoiceChecklist.why: Billing is based on time out, so the exact checkout and return times settle disputes about extra days or hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment description, make, model, and unit or serial number
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which machine was rented and ties the invoice to the condition report.

invoiceChecklist.item: Meter reading at checkout and return
invoiceChecklist.why: Engine hours or mileage support overage charges when a rental has a usage limit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate tier applied (4-hour, day, week, month)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the customer which rate they got and why, especially when a rental runs longer than planned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, pickup, fuel, and cleaning charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from the base rental avoids pushback and keeps the rental line clean for tax purposes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage waiver and security deposit amounts
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers need to see what was charged, what was held, and how the deposit was applied or returned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax and customer or PO and job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Taxability of rentals varies by state, and commercial customers often need a PO or job number to process payment.

equipment-rental.paymentTerms: Most rental shops collect payment and a security deposit at pickup, often by card on file, because the equipment is the collateral. Deposits are commonly $100-500 for small tools and a percentage of the rental value for heavy equipment. Established contractors may get net 15 or net 30 terms on a rental account after a credit application. Final charges for fuel, damage, cleaning, or overage hours are usually billed at return and settled against the deposit. Late fees of 1.5% per month or an extra day rate for late returns are common, and both should be written into the rental agreement. Accept cards, ACH, and checks, and keep a card authorization on file for post-return charges.

tips.title: Document condition at both ends
tips.body: Take dated photos and fill out a condition checklist at pickup and return. This is the evidence you need to bill for damage or cleaning without an argument.

tips.title: Put overage rules in writing
tips.body: State the included engine hours or mileage per day, week, and month, and the overage rate. Many customers do not realize a day rate has an hour cap.

tips.title: Bill late returns promptly
tips.body: If a unit comes back late, add the extra day to the final invoice right away and note the original due time. Waiting turns it into a negotiation.

tips.title: Keep a card on file for post-return charges
tips.body: Fuel, damage, and cleaning are often found after the customer leaves. A signed authorization lets you charge them without chasing a check.

tips.title: Track deposits separately from revenue
tips.body: A security deposit is a liability until you keep or return it. Show it as a separate line so your books and the customer's invoice both stay clear.

faqs.question: Should I invoice equipment rentals when the customer picks up or when they return?
faqs.answer: Collect a deposit and a payment method at pickup, then issue the final invoice at return when you know the actual hours, fuel, and condition. For short rentals, many shops charge the estimated rental at pickup and adjust at return.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on equipment rentals?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax rentals of tangible property, and some tax delivery or damage waiver fees too. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can I charge a customer for damage after they return the equipment?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if your rental agreement says so and you have condition records from checkout and return. Send an itemized invoice with photos and repair costs, and apply the security deposit first.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a rental runs longer than planned?
faqs.answer: Bill the extra time at the rate tier in your agreement, usually the daily rate or a prorated weekly rate. Note the original return date and the actual return date on the invoice.

faqs.question: Is a damage waiver the same as insurance?
faqs.answer: Not usually. A damage waiver is a fee that limits the customer's liability for certain damage, and it typically has exclusions such as misuse, theft, or tire damage. Describe it accurately on the invoice and in the agreement, and check rules in your state.

estimate.intro: Rental customers usually ask for a quote when they are planning a project, an event, or a job bid and need a total cost before they commit. They often compare day versus week rates, delivery charges, and what is included across two or three yards. A written quote that shows the full cost keeps the lowest base rate from winning over a more complete price.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment make, model, size, and attachments included
scopeChecklist.why: Customers compare machines by capacity, so be specific about what they get and which attachments cost extra.
State the start, end, and whether the price is a day, week, or month rate so the total is predictable.

scopeChecklist.item: Included hours or mileage and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: This prevents surprise charges when a machine is worked harder than the customer expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery, pickup, and site access requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Tight sites, long distances, or the need for a lowboy trailer change the price, and the customer must confirm the site can accept the unit.
Say whether the unit must be returned full and clean, and which items such as blades or propane are billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, damage waiver, and insurance requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Many customers need to know upfront what is held, what coverage is optional, and whether proof of their own insurance is required.
Rental equipment is time-sensitive, and a quote does not guarantee a unit until it is reserved.

pricingTips.title: Show the best rate tier for the job
pricingTips.body: If a 5-day job costs nearly as much as a weekly rate, point it out. It builds trust and often secures the longer booking.

pricingTips.title: Price the delivered total, not just the base rate
pricingTips.body: List rental, delivery, waiver, fuel policy, and tax together. Customers comparing quotes will see the true cost and your price will look honest.

pricingTips.title: Add a minimum rental
pricingTips.body: Set a minimum charge, such as a half-day or one-day minimum, so delivery and prep time on short rentals is covered.

pricingTips.title: Quote peak seasons carefully
pricingTips.body: Spring construction and holiday event seasons strain inventory. Hold units only with a deposit and set clear cancellation terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or reservation?
faqs.answer: Quotes are normally free. For reservations of large equipment or event gear, a deposit or a cancellation fee protects you if the unit would otherwise sit idle.

faqs.question: How long should a rental quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 7 to 30 days for standard equipment, and shorter in busy seasons. State an expiration date and note that availability is confirmed only when the booking is reserved.

faqs.question: What if the customer's job changes after I quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying that changes in rental length, equipment, or delivery location may change the price. Send an updated quote when the scope changes so the final invoice matches.

faqs.question: Can I quote a flat price for a rental with delivery?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many customers prefer it. Base it on a realistic estimate of delivery distance and time, and note the included hours and the return condition so the flat price holds.

esl-teacher.intro: ESL teachers who work for themselves or run a small tutoring business bill adult learners, parents of school-age students, companies, and language schools for English instruction. Typical invoices cover one-on-one lessons, small group classes, test prep for exams like TOEFL or IELTS, business English training, and conversation practice. Many also bill for materials, assessments, and online platform time.
esl-teacher.pricingModel: Most independent ESL teachers charge per hour or per session, with a lower effective rate when students buy a package of 5, 10, or 20 lessons upfront. Group classes are usually priced per student per class or per course, with a minimum number of enrolled students. Corporate clients are often billed a flat rate per class hour or a monthly retainer for a set number of weekly sessions, sometimes with a separate fee for curriculum design or placement testing. Teachers who hold a TESOL or TEFL certificate, a state teaching license, or specialize in test prep or business English generally charge at the higher end. Online lessons are priced similarly to in-person, but in-person lessons at a student's home or office often add travel time or a mileage charge. Many teachers set a cancellation policy (24 hours notice is common) and bill for late cancellations at the full or half lesson rate.

rates.service: Essay or resume review for English learners

items.description: Business English lessons, 60 min each, Mon/Wed in March (Maria Alvarez)
IELTS Academic writing coaching, 60 min
Initial level assessment (speaking and written)
Printed practice materials and workbook
Late cancellation, March 19 (less than 24 hours notice)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: bank transfer, Zelle, or card. Lessons cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50 percent of the lesson rate. Unused lessons in a package expire 90 days after purchase.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and, if different, the payer's name
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents, employers, or sponsors often pay for the student, and the invoice needs to match whoever is responsible for payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson dates, times, and duration
invoiceChecklist.why: Students and companies want to match charges against their calendar, and it settles disputes about how many sessions took place.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson type and level or focus
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating general conversation, test prep, and business English supports different rates and tells an employer what they are paying for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: If a student prepaid for 10 lessons, show how many were used and how many remain, along with the expiration date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show charges
invoiceChecklist.why: List these as separate line items with the date so the student sees they were covered by your stated policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials and testing fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Textbooks, printed handouts, or practice test fees should be itemized separately from instruction time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number or company contact (for corporate clients)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many companies and language schools will not process payment without a PO number or an approving manager's name.

esl-teacher.paymentTerms: Most independent ESL teachers collect payment before or at the start of a lesson package, or bill monthly in arrears for recurring students. Due dates of 7 to 14 days are common for individuals, while corporate clients and language schools often pay on net 30 terms. Individuals typically pay by card, Zelle, Venmo, PayPal, or bank transfer; international students may need PayPal or a wire, so ask about fees and exchange rates. A written policy covering cancellations, expiration of unused lessons, and late payment fees (often a flat fee or 1 to 1.5 percent per month) should be agreed on before the first lesson. Refunds for unused prepaid lessons are usually handled case by case, so state your policy upfront.

tips.title: Sell packages and bill them upfront
tips.body: Charging for 5 or 10 lessons in advance reduces chasing payments and no-shows. Offer a small discount, such as one lesson at a reduced rate, and put an expiration date in writing.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every invoice
tips.body: A short line about 24-hour notice and what late cancellations cost prevents arguments. Students from different backgrounds may have different expectations about rescheduling, so clear wording helps.

tips.title: Handle time zones and currency clearly
tips.body: If you teach students abroad, state the invoice currency (usually USD), whether the student covers transfer fees, and the time zone used for lesson times.

tips.title: Separate prep time from teaching time
tips.body: If you design a custom curriculum or review writing outside lessons, bill it as its own line at an agreed rate or build it into your hourly rate. Do not leave it as unpaid work.

tips.title: Track income for self-employment taxes
tips.body: Independent teachers are generally treated as self-employed and may owe self-employment tax and estimated quarterly payments. Keep invoices and records of platform fees and materials, and check with a tax professional about deductions.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the lesson?
faqs.answer: Either works as long as it is clear. Hourly billing is simpler for varied lesson lengths, while per-lesson pricing is common when sessions are a standard 45 or 60 minutes. State the length on the invoice either way.

faqs.question: Can I charge for lesson planning time?
faqs.answer: Yes, but most teachers build routine planning into the hourly rate. Charge separately for larger projects like a custom corporate curriculum, placement testing, or exam-specific materials, and agree on the fee before starting.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a company that hires me for employee classes?
faqs.answer: Bill the company, not the employees, and list the class dates, number of attendees if relevant, hours taught, and any PO number. Expect net 30 terms, and confirm the billing contact before the first class.

faqs.question: What if a student's parent pays for lessons but the student is an adult learner abroad?
faqs.answer: Put the student's name as the learner and the payer's name as the bill-to contact. Clarify who is responsible for cancellation fees and send reminders to the payer.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax educational services or tutoring, but some do tax certain services or materials. Check with your state's department of revenue or a local accountant.

estimate.intro: ESL teachers send quotes when a company, school, or family wants to compare instructors before committing, or when the work is a defined program like a 12-week business English course or a TOEFL prep plan. Clients usually compare hourly rate, total cost for the program, teacher credentials, and how flexible the schedule and cancellation terms are.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of lessons, length, and schedule
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 'weekly classes' is vague. State, for example, 12 weekly 60-minute sessions starting on a specific date.

scopeChecklist.item: Student level, goals, and target outcome
scopeChecklist.why: Preparing for an IELTS band score is different work from improving conversation, and the quote should reflect the stated goal without promising a guaranteed result.
Online, in-person at the student's home, or at a company office changes travel time, mileage, and technology requirements.
Say whether textbooks, practice exams, and official test registration fees are included or billed to the student.

scopeChecklist.item: Class size and minimum enrollment for groups
scopeChecklist.why: A group rate depends on the number of students. State what happens if enrollment drops below the minimum.
Spell out notice requirements, make-up lesson rules, and when unused lessons expire so there are no surprises.
State the deposit or upfront payment, due dates, and how long the quoted rate stays available.

pricingTips.title: Quote a program price and show the per-hour math
pricingTips.body: Clients like a total, such as $660 for 12 lessons, but showing the hourly equivalent makes the comparison with other teachers easy and justifies any package discount.

pricingTips.title: Price corporate work above individual rates
pricingTips.body: Companies often need invoices, flexible scheduling, reports, and sometimes curriculum customization. A higher rate, often $50 to $120 per class hour, reflects that added administration.

pricingTips.title: Charge for a placement assessment
pricingTips.body: A short level assessment helps you scope the program accurately. Either charge a small flat fee or credit it toward the first package.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: For example, a single-lesson rate, a 10-lesson package, and a 20-lesson package at a lower per-lesson rate. This lets the client choose and often raises the average order.

faqs.question: Should I give a free trial lesson?
faqs.answer: Some teachers offer a short free consultation of 15 to 20 minutes, while others charge a reduced rate for a full trial lesson. Whichever you choose, state it clearly in the quote and set a limit of one per student.

faqs.question: How firm should my estimate be for a long course?
faqs.answer: For a fixed number of lessons, the quote can be firm. If the student may want additional lessons or goals change, state that extra sessions are billed at the quoted hourly rate.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement or is a quote enough?
faqs.answer: A written quote that the client accepts by email is often enough for individuals. For companies or longer programs, a short signed agreement covering schedule, rates, and cancellation terms is better.

faqs.question: Can I raise my rate for existing students?
faqs.answer: Yes. Give notice, usually 30 days, and apply the new rate to new packages. Honor any prepaid lessons at the old rate.

esthetician.intro: Estheticians provide skin care services such as facials, waxing, peels, lash and brow work, and body treatments. They bill individual clients at the time of service, sell treatment packages and memberships, and sometimes invoice brides, event groups, or spas and salons that hire them as independent contractors or booth renters.
esthetician.pricingModel: Most estheticians price per service, with a set menu price for each facial, wax, or treatment. Add-ons such as extractions, LED light therapy, dermaplaning, or a mask upgrade are priced separately or bundled into a higher tier. Waxing is priced per area. Advanced services like chemical peels, microneedling (where your state allows it), and lash lifts are priced per session and often sold in series of three to six at a discount. Retail skin care products are billed at retail price and taxed as goods in most states. Mobile and event work usually adds a travel fee and a minimum, and bridal or group bookings are quoted as a flat package with a deposit. Memberships (one facial per month at a reduced rate) are billed as a recurring charge. Tips are separate from the service price and should be listed as their own line.

rates.service: Bridal or group event skin prep

items.description: Signature facial with extractions (60 min)
Dermaplaning add-on
Brow wax and tint
Vitamin C serum, 1 oz (retail)
Gratuity

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service. Cancellations within 24 hours of an appointment are charged 50 percent of the service price. Unused treatment series credits expire 12 months from purchase date. Retail products may be returned unopened within 14 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and each treatment performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and card processors can match the charge to a specific visit, and it helps if there is a skin reaction or a billing question later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Dermaplaning, extractions, masks, and peels upgrades are easy to forget or dispute when they are folded into one total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retail products with quantity and price
invoiceChecklist.why: Product sales are taxable in most states while services often are not, so separating them keeps your sales tax records clean.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package or series balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing sessions purchased, used, and remaining (for example, session 3 of 6) prevents disagreements about what is left on a prepaid series.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or prepayment applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Deposits for bridal, group, or advanced treatments should show as a credit so the client sees the correct balance due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license number and business name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require esthetician licenses to be displayed, and including the number on invoices to spas, photographers, or event planners shows you are licensed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or minimum for mobile work
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and on-site appointments carry costs the client may not think about, and a labeled line prevents pushback.

esthetician.paymentTerms: Individual clients usually pay in full at the time of service by card, cash, or a payment app, so invoices are really receipts. For bridal parties, group events, and treatment series, collect a non-refundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking and the balance on or before the day of service. Charge a late-cancel or no-show fee, commonly 50 to 100 percent of the service price inside a 24 to 48 hour window, and put the policy in writing at booking. Series and membership payments are often charged up front or automatically each month. Business clients such as spas or photographers that book you as a contractor typically pay net 7 to net 15, and a late fee should be stated on the invoice.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every booking confirmation and invoice
tips.body: No-shows and last-minute cancels cost you an empty treatment room and product prep. If the policy is in writing and the client has agreed to it, charging the fee is much easier.

tips.title: Take a card on file at booking
tips.body: Holding a card lets you charge no-show fees and balances without chasing anyone. Tell the client at booking exactly when and why the card may be charged.

tips.title: Sell series with an expiration date
tips.body: Discounted packages of three to six peels or microneedling sessions improve results and retention, but unlimited open-ended credits become a liability. State an expiration date and whether the balance is refundable.

tips.title: Bill tips as a separate line
tips.body: Listing gratuity separately keeps your service revenue and tip income clear for taxes, and it matters if you split tips with a spa or assistant.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for group and bridal work
tips.body: Set a minimum total for on-location events so one or two services do not make a long drive and setup unprofitable. Quote travel time and setup as a flat line.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on facials and waxing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax personal services, but some do, and retail products are taxable in most states. Check with your state revenue department and keep products and services on separate lines.

faqs.question: Should I invoice clients or just give a receipt?
faqs.answer: For single appointments paid on the spot, a receipt is fine. Use an invoice when payment comes later, such as for bridal parties, corporate events, spa contract work, or a package with a balance due.

faqs.question: How do I bill a treatment series if the client cancels partway?
faqs.answer: State the policy before purchase. Many estheticians refund unused sessions at the regular single-session price minus the discount already given, or offer credit only. Put whichever you choose on the package invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a no-show fee?
faqs.answer: In most places yes, if the client was told the policy in advance and agreed to it. Keep a record of the agreement, such as a booking confirmation or signed intake form.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a spa or salon that uses me as a contractor?
faqs.answer: Send an invoice with your business name, license number, dates worked, services or hours, and payment terms. In many cases you are responsible for your own taxes as an independent contractor, so keep copies for your records.

estimate.intro: Estheticians send written quotes mostly for bridal and event bookings, on-location group services, multi-session treatment plans, and corporate wellness days. Clients compare per-person pricing, what each service includes, travel fees, and how many sessions are needed to see results.

scopeChecklist.why: A 30-minute express facial and a 75-minute treatment facial are different products, and listing time sets clear expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of people and services per person
scopeChecklist.why: Group quotes change fast when headcount shifts, so state the number of guests the quote covers and the price for each additional person.
On-site work needs a table, power, water access, and space. Say what you bring, what the client supplies, and what travel or setup fee applies.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions in a treatment plan and spacing
scopeChecklist.why: Peels, microneedling, and acne programs are usually done in a series four to six weeks apart, and clients should know the total cost, not just the first visit.
Clarify whether take-home items or samples are included and whether home-care products are an extra purchase.
Quotes for advanced treatments should say that final service depends on a skin assessment, medications, and allergies, and that you may modify or decline a treatment.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Event dates fill up, so state how much holds the date, when the balance is due, and how long the quoted prices are valid.

pricingTips.title: Quote per person, then show the total
pricingTips.body: Bridal and group clients think in per-person cost but approve a total. Give both, plus a clear price for adding a guest.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium option, such as facial only, facial plus brow wax, and facial plus wax and dermaplaning, lets clients pick a budget without negotiating line by line.

pricingTips.title: Price series below single sessions, but not by much
pricingTips.body: A 10 to 15 percent discount on a prepaid series is common. Deeper discounts cut into your margin and can attract clients who never finish the series.

pricingTips.title: Build in travel time and setup
pricingTips.body: For mobile work, count drive time, setup, and breakdown as paid time. Many estheticians charge a flat travel fee or a minimum booking for on-location jobs.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation?
faqs.answer: Basic consults for facials are usually free. For complex treatment plans, bridal trials, or on-site walk-throughs, a fee that is credited toward the booking is common.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. For event dates, state that the date is only held once the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: What if the client's skin needs a different treatment than quoted?
faqs.answer: Write in the quote that services are subject to a skin assessment. If you need to change the treatment, send a revised quote or note the price difference before proceeding.

etsy-seller.intro: Etsy sellers who invoice are usually handling work outside the standard checkout: custom and commissioned pieces, bulk orders for weddings and corporate events, and wholesale orders from boutiques. Most regular Etsy orders are paid through the marketplace, so a separate invoice or quote matters mainly when a buyer wants something that does not fit a listing. These invoices typically bill for the items, design or proof time, personalization, packaging, rush fees, and shipping.
etsy-seller.pricingModel: Most Etsy sellers price by the piece, built up from materials, labor time, packaging, overhead, and a profit margin. A common check is materials plus labor at a set hourly wage, then a markup, with wholesale priced at roughly half of retail. Custom orders often add a one-time design or setup fee, especially for new artwork, engraving files, or custom molds, and then charge a per-unit price that drops at higher quantities. Rush production usually adds 25 to 50 percent. Shipping is billed at actual cost or a flat fee per box, and gift wrapping or branded packaging is often a separate line. Large custom orders normally require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent before materials are bought, with the balance due before shipping.

rates.service: Custom design or proof fee (new artwork, layout, mockup)
Hourly rate for commissioned handmade work
Bulk order discount (events, corporate gifts, 25+ units)
Custom or branded packaging (boxes, inserts, ribbon)
Domestic shipping on bulk or oversized orders

items.description: Personalized leather luggage tags, wedding favor order (names and date stamped)
Custom stamp design and proof (2 revision rounds)
Kraft gift box with ribbon and thank-you card
Rush production (completed in 10 days instead of 21)
Shipping, 2 boxes, tracked ground

sampleInvoice.notes: A 40% deposit was paid at approval of the proof. Balance is due before shipping. Final artwork was approved by email on the date shown. Custom items are made to order and are not returnable except for production errors, which must be reported within 7 days of delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Order or conversation reference and approval date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact design, text, and options the buyer signed off on, which settles disputes over spelling, colors, or sizes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized personalization details
invoiceChecklist.why: Names, dates, fonts, colors, and sizes listed per item show what was custom, justify the pricing, and prove you built what was approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design, proof, and revision charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Setup time is easy to forget and hard to add later, so list it separately along with how many revisions were included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Production time and ship date
invoiceChecklist.why: Buyers for weddings and events work backward from a deadline, and a stated lead time protects you if they approve late.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping method, cost, and tracking number
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating shipping from product price avoids confusion and gives the buyer proof of dispatch and a way to follow the package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number
invoiceChecklist.why: Marketplace sales usually have tax handled by the platform, but direct sales may require you to collect tax unless the buyer is a retailer with a valid resale certificate. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the deposit already paid, the remaining amount, and the date it is due, so there is no argument over what is still owed.

etsy-seller.paymentTerms: For custom and bulk orders, most Etsy sellers collect 25 to 50 percent upfront to cover materials and lock in a production slot, with the balance due before shipping. Small custom orders are often paid in full at approval. Wholesale accounts commonly start as prepaid, then move to net 15 or net 30 once a relationship is established. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common on wholesale terms if stated in writing. Card payments, bank transfer, and check are the usual methods. Orders paid outside Etsy do not carry Etsy's fees or buyer protections, so be clear on refund and remake policies in writing.

tips.title: Get written approval of the proof before you start
tips.body: Send a mockup with all personalized text and have the buyer confirm by message or email. Keep that approval and reference it on the invoice, so a typo is clearly the buyer's responsibility if it was in the approved proof.

tips.title: Ask for a deposit that covers your materials
tips.body: Custom items cannot be resold if an order falls through. A deposit equal to at least your material and packaging cost keeps you from absorbing a canceled event order.

tips.title: Price your time on custom work
tips.body: Messaging back and forth, sourcing, and revisions take real hours. Include a design fee or set a number of included revisions and charge for extras.

tips.title: Add a rush fee that reflects what you give up
tips.body: If a fast turnaround means turning down other orders or working weekends, the surcharge should cover that. State it on the quote before the buyer commits.

tips.title: Keep wholesale and retail pricing consistent
tips.body: Set minimum order amounts and a published wholesale price list so boutiques know your terms and do not undercut your own shop.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice for a regular Etsy order?
faqs.answer: No. Regular orders are paid through checkout and Etsy generates the order record. Invoices are for orders handled outside a listing, such as large custom jobs, wholesale accounts, and corporate or event orders.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on custom orders?
faqs.answer: It depends on where the sale happens and where you and the buyer are. Sales completed on the marketplace typically have tax collected by the platform in many states. Direct sales may require you to collect and remit it yourself. Wholesale buyers with a valid resale certificate are usually exempt. Check your state's department of revenue.

faqs.question: Should shipping be a separate line item?
faqs.answer: Yes. Listing shipping separately shows what is product and what is delivery cost, makes refunds cleaner, and avoids hiding a large freight charge inside item prices.

faqs.question: What if a buyer cancels after I have started a custom order?
faqs.answer: State your cancellation terms on the quote and invoice. A common policy is that the deposit is non-refundable once production begins, with a partial refund only if materials have not been purchased or cut.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for revisions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Include a set number of revisions, usually one to three, in the design fee and charge a flat amount or hourly rate for each additional round.

estimate.intro: Etsy sellers send quotes when a buyer asks for something custom, a large quantity, or a wholesale price list before committing. Buyers often compare your quote to a listing price, other makers, or mass-produced options, so the quote needs to explain what makes the piece custom and how long it will take.

scopeChecklist.item: Item description with size, material, and color
scopeChecklist.why: Specific details prevent the buyer from imagining a different finish, thickness, or shade than what you plan to make.
Shows how the per-unit price changes at higher volumes and helps buyers decide whether to order more.
Defines character limits, number of lines, fonts, and placement so extra changes can be priced fairly.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of proofs or revisions included
scopeChecklist.why: Limits unpaid design time and sets the price for additional rounds.

scopeChecklist.item: Production time and the date the clock starts
scopeChecklist.why: Lead time starts at deposit and proof approval, not when the quote is sent, which matters for event deadlines.
Bulk and fragile orders can have shipping costs that change the total, so state whether it is estimated or fixed.
Spells out what is refundable and what happens if there is a production defect or a late change by the buyer.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from materials, time, and overhead
pricingTips.body: Add materials with a waste allowance, labor at your target hourly wage, packaging, and fees, then add margin. Quoting from a total rather than guesswork keeps custom orders from becoming unprofitable.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Showing prices for 25, 50, and 100 units lets buyers choose and often increases order size, while your setup time is spread across more pieces.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Material costs and your schedule change. A 7 to 14 day validity period keeps you from honoring old prices or holding a production slot indefinitely.

pricingTips.title: Show rush pricing as an option
pricingTips.body: List the standard timeline and price, then a faster option with its surcharge. Buyers can see the cost of speed without feeling surprised later.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a custom quote?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are normally free. For complex custom designs that require sketches, samples, or mockups, many sellers charge a design fee that is credited toward the order if the buyer proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is typical. Shorten it if your materials have volatile prices or your production calendar is nearly full.

faqs.question: What if materials cost more after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Put a clause in the quote that pricing is valid until a stated date and applies only to the described specifications. If the buyer changes the design or quantity, send a revised quote.

faqs.question: Can I give a wholesale quote without a minimum order?
faqs.answer: You can, but most sellers set a minimum order value or unit count, such as $150 to $300, so that packing, shipping, and account setup are worthwhile.

event-decorator.intro: Event decorators design and install the look of weddings, corporate events, birthday parties, baby showers, and galas. They bill for design time, rented and owned decor, floral and balloon work, labor for setup and teardown, and delivery. Most work solo or with a small crew and a mix of owned inventory and rented items.
event-decorator.pricingModel: Most decorators combine a design fee with itemized decor and labor. Design or consultation is often a flat fee or a percentage of the total decor budget (commonly 10-20%). Owned inventory such as chargers, arches, backdrops, and centerpieces is billed as a rental per item or per package. Items bought or rented from third parties (florals, specialty linens, lighting) are usually marked up 20-50% to cover sourcing, handling, and risk. Setup, teardown, and delivery are billed by crew hours or a flat fee, with extra for stairs, long load-ins, late-night strikes, or venues with strict windows. Many decorators sell tiered packages for common events and quote custom work by the project. Deposits are standard because inventory is held and materials are ordered ahead of time.

rates.service: Full event design and styling fee
Setup and teardown labor (per crew member)
Chair sash, cover, or linen styling

items.description: Event design and styling fee - 100-guest wedding reception
Sweetheart table backdrop with draping and floral installation (rental)
Table centerpieces with candles and greenery
Gold charger plates (rental)
Setup and teardown crew labor (2 staff)
Delivery and pickup

sampleInvoice.notes: A 50% deposit of $1,685 was received on booking. Balance due 7 days before the event date. Rental items remain property of the decorator; client is responsible for loss or damage beyond normal wear, charged at replacement cost. Teardown must be completed by the venue's stated end time or additional labor will be billed at $60 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, venue name, and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and records where work took place if there is a dispute or a venue question.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized decor list with rental vs. purchased labels
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to know what they keep and what you take back. It also supports damage and replacement charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Setup and teardown times and labor hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how labor was calculated and backs up overtime or venue delay charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents confusion about what has been paid. Most decorators require the balance before the event.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, load-in, and travel charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Stairs, long carries, and distance to the venue add real cost and should appear as separate lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage and loss terms for rented items
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out replacement cost for broken, stained, or missing inventory so you can bill it later without argument.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on rentals and goods
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax rentals and tangible goods differently than design services. Check your state's rules and show tax as its own line.

event-decorator.paymentTerms: Decorators typically collect a non-refundable retainer or deposit of 25-50% at booking to hold the date and order materials, with the balance due 7-14 days before the event. Some require full payment before delivery for smaller jobs. Corporate clients may pay net 15 or net 30 against a purchase order. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month or a flat fee are common, as are cancellation schedules that keep more of the deposit as the event date nears. Accepted methods usually include card, bank transfer, and check. Collect any damage or overtime charges within a set number of days after the event.

tips.title: Bill the balance before the event
tips.body: Once the decor is installed, you have little leverage. Set the final payment due a week or more before the date so you are not chasing money after the event.

tips.title: Mark up sourced items and say so in your terms
tips.body: Florals, specialty rentals, and custom prints take time to find and carry risk if prices change. Build in a markup and keep receipts in case a client asks.

tips.title: Separate design fees from decor and labor
tips.body: Design time is easy to give away. Listing it as its own line shows its value and protects you when the client cuts items but still used your concept.

tips.title: Charge for changes after the final count
tips.body: Late guest count increases, added tables, or a new color scheme mean new orders and labor. State a cutoff date, often 10-14 days out, and bill changes as add-ons.

tips.title: Document the setup with photos
tips.body: Photos at install and teardown protect you from damage claims and from claims that items were missing, and they help with venue disputes.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit for event decor?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit of 25-50% is standard because you reserve inventory, turn away other bookings for that date, and often order materials in advance. State in your contract whether it is refundable.

faqs.question: How do I bill for rented items I own versus items I buy?
faqs.answer: List owned inventory as rental lines per item or per package, and list purchased consumables like flowers, balloons, or printed signs as materials, usually with a markup. Labeling each one makes clear what returns to you.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on event decorating?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax tangible goods and rentals, and some tax or exempt services differently. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional about what applies to your mix of design, rental, and labor.

faqs.question: What if the venue delays access and my setup runs over?
faqs.answer: Put a clause in your contract that extra labor caused by late access or early strike is billed hourly. Note actual times on the invoice and add the overtime as a separate line.

faqs.question: How do I bill for damaged or missing rental items?
faqs.answer: Your contract should list the replacement cost. After the event, send a follow-up invoice or add a line item with the item, quantity, and replacement price, along with photos if you have them.

estimate.intro: Decorators send an estimate or proposal after an initial consultation or venue walkthrough and before the client signs a contract. Clients usually compare several decorators on total price, what is included, and how clearly the design is presented, so a detailed quote helps you stand out from a lump sum.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, times, venue, and load-in window
scopeChecklist.why: Access times drive labor cost and determine whether your plan is feasible.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count and number of tables
scopeChecklist.why: Per-table items such as centerpieces, linens, and chargers scale with these numbers, so state the counts the price is based on.

scopeChecklist.item: Itemized decor with quantities and colors
scopeChecklist.why: Specific descriptions of arches, florals, signage, and lighting prevent disagreements about what was promised.

scopeChecklist.item: Rented vs. purchased items and who owns them after
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume they keep centerpieces or backdrops. Say which items you take back.
List crew size, hours included, and any extra fees for stairs, long carries, or after-hours strike.

scopeChecklist.item: Change cutoff date and how changes are priced
scopeChecklist.why: Late changes affect orders and labor. A cutoff date gives you a firm basis for charging more.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know what is due when signing and how much is kept if they cancel.

pricingTips.title: Quote in tiers
pricingTips.body: Offer good, better, and best versions of the same event, such as basic tables, added backdrop and lighting, and full styling. Clients can choose a level instead of negotiating line by line.

pricingTips.title: Price from your real labor hours
pricingTips.body: Count design time, shopping, prep and assembly in your shop, transport, setup, and teardown. Many decorators underquote because they count only the hours on site.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for sourced items
pricingTips.body: Prices for florals and rentals can change between quote and event. Add a contingency of 5-10% or state that third-party prices are valid for a limited time.

pricingTips.title: Include mood boards or sketches
pricingTips.body: Visuals with the quote reduce misunderstandings about the look and justify your pricing, which makes it easier for clients to say yes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or quote?
faqs.answer: Many decorators offer a short first call free and charge for in-depth design work or venue visits, often $75-150 per hour or a flat fee that is credited toward the booking.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Most decorators hold pricing for 7-30 days. Your date is not reserved until a deposit is paid, so state that clearly.

faqs.question: What if the client's budget is lower than my quote?
faqs.answer: Offer to reduce scope instead of the rate: fewer centerpieces, a smaller backdrop, or rented pieces in place of custom ones. Show what each change saves.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Only for changes outside the agreed scope, such as a higher guest count, new venue, or added items. Put this in writing and have the client approve revisions before you order materials.

event-photographer.intro: Event photographers cover corporate conferences, galas, fundraisers, product launches, parties, school and community events, and sometimes weddings. Invoices usually bill for time on site, second shooters, editing and delivery of a gallery, and any extras such as prints, rush turnaround, or extended usage rights.
event-photographer.pricingModel: Most event photographers charge by the hour with a minimum booking of two to four hours, then add fees for editing, travel, and extras. Corporate clients often prefer a flat day rate or half-day rate that includes a set number of edited images. Packages are common for private events, for example three hours of coverage plus an online gallery for a fixed price. Add-ons include a second photographer, on-site printing, step-and-repeat or photo booth setups, same-day or next-day edits, and travel beyond a set radius. Licensing matters when a client wants to use images in advertising or on a website, and some photographers charge more for commercial use than for personal use. Deposits and retainers are standard because the date is held exclusively.

items.description: Corporate holiday party coverage, 12/14, 6:00-10:00 PM (4-hour minimum)
Second photographer
Post-event editing and online gallery (approx. 300 edited images, 90-day hosting)
Rush delivery within 48 hours
Travel, venue 38 miles from studio

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $500 received on 11/20 and applied to this invoice. Balance due within 14 days of the invoice date. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month. Images are licensed for internal and promotional use by the client; resale or use by third parties requires written permission. Accepted payment: ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event name, date, venue, and actual start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to a specific booking and settles disputes about overtime or whether coverage ran longer than planned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours of coverage billed, including any overtime
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often add time on the night. Listing overtime separately at the agreed rate avoids surprise questions later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of photographers and their roles
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why the total differs from the base rate and justifies second shooter or assistant charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables: approximate image count, gallery hosting length, and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms what the client received and when, which helps if they later claim files were missing or late.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights granted
invoiceChecklist.why: States whether the client may use images for personal, internal, or commercial purposes, so extra licensing fees are not argued after delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the retainer already paid and the remaining amount, so the client does not pay twice or question the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, parking, and equipment rental charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs such as mileage, parking, or rented lighting are clearer and easier to approve when itemized.

event-photographer.paymentTerms: A non-refundable retainer of 25-50% is standard to book the date, with the balance due on or before the event for private clients or net 14 to net 30 for corporate clients. Corporate accounts often route invoices through accounts payable and may require a PO number or W-9, so ask early. Many photographers hold final gallery delivery until the balance is paid. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually taken by ACH, check, or card, and card fees are sometimes passed on or built into the rate.

tips.title: Set a minimum booking length
tips.body: Travel, setup, and editing take the same effort for a one-hour job as a three-hour one. A two- to four-hour minimum protects your day and keeps short bookings worth taking.

tips.title: Bill overtime in set increments
tips.body: Events often run long. Put an overtime rate in the contract, such as 1.25 to 1.5 times your hourly rate billed in 30-minute increments, and list it as a separate line on the invoice.

tips.title: Hold the gallery until the balance is paid
tips.body: Delivering a watermarked or private preview while the balance is outstanding gives you leverage without damaging the relationship. Release full-resolution files once payment clears.

tips.title: Charge separately for licensing
tips.body: A private party and an ad campaign are different uses. If a corporate client wants images for marketing, add a usage line instead of folding it into the hourly rate.

tips.title: Collect billing details before the event
tips.body: Get the billing contact, PO number, and any vendor onboarding forms in advance. Corporate payment often stalls because an invoice lacks a PO or goes to the wrong person.

faqs.question: How much deposit should an event photographer ask for?
faqs.answer: Most ask for 25-50% at booking, and many make it non-refundable because the date is held and other work is turned away. For large corporate events or those with a second shooter, 50% is common. State the amount and refund terms in your contract and on the first invoice.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the event?
faqs.answer: Send a deposit invoice at booking and a final invoice for the balance. For private events, the balance is often due a week before or on the day. For corporate clients, send the final invoice right after the event with actual hours and any overtime, using net 14 to net 30 terms.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the event runs over the booked time?
faqs.answer: Bill the extra time at the overtime rate in your contract, as its own line with the actual end time. If you did not agree to a rate beforehand, use your standard hourly rate and get the client to confirm the extension in writing or by email on the night.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services or the sale of tangible products such as prints, and others do not tax services at all. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for editing time separately?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many photographers list coverage and post-production separately, either as a flat editing fee or by image count. Itemizing it shows clients that the work continues after the event and makes rush charges easier to explain.

estimate.intro: Event photographers send quotes when a client is comparing several photographers for a date, often after a call or a venue walkthrough. Clients usually compare hourly rates, hours included, image counts, turnaround time, and who shoots, so the quote needs to make those items easy to line up.

scopeChecklist.why: Defines the start and end times being quoted so overtime is clearly anything beyond that window.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of photographers and any assistants
scopeChecklist.why: A second shooter changes both the cost and the coverage, so the client should see exactly what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Shot list or key moments covered
scopeChecklist.why: Lists must-have shots such as keynote speakers, sponsor banners, award presentations, and group photos, so expectations are set before the event.
States approximate edited image count, gallery format, hosting period, and delivery date, which is where most disputes about value begin.
Clarifies whether the quote covers personal, internal, or commercial use, so a client who later wants to run the images in advertising understands extra fees may apply.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel, parking, and venue access costs
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disagreement over mileage, parking, or any permit and venue fees the photographer must pay to work on site.
Explains how the date is held, what happens if the event is moved or canceled, and when the quote expires.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as two hours, four hours, and full-day coverage, each with a clear image count. Clients tend to pick a middle option, and it shows what extra time costs.

pricingTips.title: Price for the full job, not just the hours on site
pricingTips.body: Include travel, culling, editing, and delivery time in your rate. A four-hour event may take six to ten hours of editing, so an hourly rate based only on coverage can leave you underpaid.

pricingTips.title: Quote overtime and extras up front
pricingTips.body: List your overtime rate and add-on prices, such as rush delivery or extra edited images, in the quote. Clients are more willing to approve charges they have already seen.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Hold the quote for 7 to 14 days, as another client may ask for the same date. After that, availability and pricing may change.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: For events with a fixed schedule, a flat package based on set hours is easier for clients to approve. For events with uncertain timing, quote an hourly rate with a minimum and an overtime rate, then bill actual hours.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a venue walkthrough or consultation?
faqs.answer: A short call is usually free. For large or complicated events that need a site visit, many photographers charge a flat fee or hourly rate, often credited toward the booking if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How many edited images should I promise?
faqs.answer: Use a range based on coverage time, such as 40 to 75 images per hour for fast-paced events, rather than an exact number. This sets expectations while leaving room for quality, since the final count depends on what happens at the event.

faqs.question: When does an accepted quote become binding?
faqs.answer: A quote is usually binding once the client signs the agreement and pays the deposit. Until then, the date is not held. Ask for both before blocking the date on your calendar.

event-planner.intro: Event planners run weddings, corporate meetings, fundraisers, milestone parties, and other gatherings, either as full-service planners or as day-of coordinators. They invoice for planning fees, coordination hours, vendor management, design work, and sometimes for vendor costs paid on the client's behalf.
event-planner.pricingModel: Most event planners use one of four models: a flat fee for a defined package (for example, full-service wedding planning or day-of coordination), a percentage of the total event budget (commonly 10-20%), an hourly rate for consulting or smaller jobs, or a monthly retainer for ongoing corporate work. Flat packages are the most common for weddings and private events because clients want a known cost. Percentage fees fit larger budgets where the planner's workload grows with the spend. Planners also decide how to handle vendor costs: either the client pays vendors directly, or the planner pays them and passes the costs through on the invoice, sometimes with a markup of 10-20% for design items, rentals, or sourced decor. Travel, extra site visits, and overtime on event day are usually billed separately. Payment is almost always staged, with a retainer at signing and milestone payments leading up to the event.

items.description: Full-service wedding planning, 150 guests (balance after retainer is applied separately)
Additional venue site visits beyond 3 included
Event-day assistant coordinator, setup through teardown
Welcome table and ceremony decor styling
Rental pass-through: ceremony arch and lounge furniture (vendor invoice attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Retainer of $1,650 paid at signing has been credited on the attached statement. Remaining balance is due 14 days before the event date. Vendor pass-through items are billed at cost. Payments by check, ACH, or card; card payments carry a 3% processing fee. Late balances incur a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event name, date, and venue
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and helps if a client has multiple events or if the date changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package or service tier
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what the fee covers (full planning, partial, day-of) so extras are easy to tell apart from included work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer and prior payments credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients lose track of milestone payments. Showing the original contract total, payments received, and balance due avoids confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized vendor pass-through costs with vendor names
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see what third-party costs are and that you did not add hidden charges. Attach vendor invoices when possible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Markup or service fee on purchased items
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge a percentage on rentals, decor, or sourced items, state it clearly to match your contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime, extra visits, or scope changes
invoiceChecklist.why: Work beyond the contract, such as added guests, a second venue, or extended event hours, should appear on its own line with the date requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: Due date, accepted payment methods, and late fee terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Event deadlines are fixed, so the final balance must be due well before the date. Clear terms support collection.

event-planner.paymentTerms: Event planners typically collect a non-refundable retainer of 25-50% at signing, often with the contract. Further installments are tied to milestones, such as 90 days or 60 days before the event, with the final balance due 7-30 days before the event date so that no money is chased afterward. Corporate clients often pay net 15 or net 30 and may need a purchase order number. Vendor deposits that you pay on the client's behalf should be collected from the client before you pay them, or the client should pay vendors directly. Common payment methods are ACH, check, and credit card, with some planners passing along card fees. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract.

tips.title: Collect the final balance before the event
tips.body: Chasing payment after a wedding or gala is awkward and often fails. Set the final due date one to four weeks ahead, and state in your contract that services depend on receipt of full payment.

tips.title: Keep your fee separate from vendor money
tips.body: Avoid fronting large vendor costs from your own funds. Have clients pay vendors directly, or collect pass-through amounts in advance and list them as a separate section on the invoice.

tips.title: Bill change orders as they happen
tips.body: Guest count increases, added rentals, and extra meetings pile up fast. Confirm each change in writing and add it to the next invoice instead of waiting for a final settlement.

tips.title: Track time even on flat fees
tips.body: Recording hours on each client shows you whether your packages are priced correctly and gives you evidence when a client pushes for extra work that is outside the scope.

tips.title: Use a clear cancellation and postponement schedule
tips.body: Postponed dates are common. Spell out which payments are non-refundable and what a date change costs so that the invoice for a rescheduled event is not disputed.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or a percentage of the event budget?
faqs.answer: Flat fees are easier for clients to understand and work well for weddings and private parties. A percentage suits large or fast-growing budgets, since your work rises with spend. Whichever you pick, set a minimum fee so small budgets still cover your time.

faqs.question: Can I mark up vendor costs?
faqs.answer: Many planners do, commonly 10-20% on items they source and manage, such as decor and rentals. It must be disclosed in your contract. Some planners instead charge a flat design or sourcing fee and pass vendor costs through at cost.

faqs.question: Is the retainer refundable?
faqs.answer: Most planners make the retainer non-refundable because it reserves the date and covers early work. State this clearly in the contract and on the first invoice. Rules on deposits vary by state, so check your local requirements.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on my planning fee?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax pure service fees, but some tax certain event services, rentals, or tangible goods you resell. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a corporate client that uses purchase orders?
faqs.answer: Put the PO number on the invoice, match the amounts to the approved PO, and send it to the accounts payable contact. If scope grows beyond the PO, ask for an updated PO before billing the extra.

estimate.intro: Event planners send a proposal or quote after an initial consultation, before a client signs. Clients usually compare packages, what is included, and the planner's experience, so the quote needs to make scope and costs easy to see.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, location, and expected guest count
scopeChecklist.why: Your price depends on these. State that the quote is based on the guest count given and explain how changes affect cost.
List what you do, such as vendor selection, timeline creation, rehearsal, and event-day management, and what you do not, such as design fabrication or rentals.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meetings and site visits
scopeChecklist.why: Unlimited meetings quickly erode your margin. Set a number and a rate for extras.
Say how many hours you and your team will be on site, and the overtime rate if the event runs long.

scopeChecklist.item: Vendor costs: paid by client or by you
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume your fee covers vendors. State who pays, whether markups apply, and the estimated vendor budget.
Show deposit amounts and due dates up front so clients understand the cash timeline before committing.
Availability and vendor pricing change. An expiration date protects you, and cancellation or postponement terms prevent later disputes.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: Tiered options such as day-of, partial, and full planning let clients choose by budget and make your full-service price look reasonable. Define each tier by deliverables, not just a name.

pricingTips.title: Price from your hours, not just market rates
pricingTips.body: Estimate the total hours for the event, including emails, vendor calls, and travel, then check that your flat fee gives an acceptable hourly return. Full weddings often take 80-200 hours.

pricingTips.title: Show a vendor budget estimate separately
pricingTips.body: Give clients a rough breakdown of expected venue, catering, and other costs, clearly labeled as estimates outside your fee, so they see the full picture without confusing it with your charges.

pricingTips.title: Include a contingency line for large events
pricingTips.body: Corporate and large events often have last-minute needs. A 5-10% contingency in the budget estimate prepares clients for changes without surprise charges.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals and consultations?
faqs.answer: A brief first consultation is usually free. For custom corporate proposals that need research, venue sourcing, or design concepts, many planners charge a planning or design fee, often credited toward the contract if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. Popular dates book quickly and vendor pricing can change, so a short validity window keeps you from holding a date indefinitely.

faqs.question: What if the client's budget is too low for what they want?
faqs.answer: Show what is achievable at their budget, offer a smaller package such as partial planning or day-of coordination, or itemize what can be removed. Avoid discounting your fee to match unrealistic expectations.

faqs.question: Can the final bill exceed the quote?
faqs.answer: Only for changes the client requested or costs outside your control, if your contract says so. Write change orders for additions, and get approval in writing before doing the extra work.

event-rental.intro: Event rental businesses supply tables, chairs, linens, tents, dance floors, lighting, tableware, lounge furniture, and similar gear for weddings, corporate events, parties, and festivals. Most are small teams with a warehouse and a delivery truck. Invoices cover the items rented, delivery and setup, pickup, and any damage or loss fees.
event-rental.pricingModel: Most rental items are priced per item for a single event, usually a one-day or weekend rental period. Common items like chairs, tables, and linens are priced per piece, and larger items like tents, dance floors, and generators are priced per unit or per square foot. Delivery is usually a flat fee or zone-based charge by mileage, and setup and teardown are billed either as a flat labor fee or per hour per crew member. Many companies offer package pricing, such as a wedding package with chairs, tables, and linens, and discount larger quantities. Extra days are often charged at 25 to 50 percent of the base rate. Add-ons include damage waivers (commonly 5 to 10 percent of the rental total), cleaning fees for dirty linens and dishware, after-hours or weekend delivery surcharges, and stair or long-carry fees. Tent installs are quoted by site, since stakes, ballast, utility locates, and permits affect the price.

rates.service: Round or rectangular table (60 in. round, 6-8 ft)
Frame or pole tent (20x20 to 20x40) with install

items.description: White resin folding chairs, Saturday wedding reception
60 in. round tables
Ivory polyester 120 in. round linens
20x40 frame tent with install and removal
Delivery and pickup (within 25 miles)
Setup and teardown crew, 2 people

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due 7 days before the event date. Rental period is Friday 12 PM to Monday 12 PM. Damaged, stained, or missing items are billed at replacement cost per the rental agreement. Please make sure the tent site is clear and accessible at arrival. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, rental period, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Pins down the rental window for billing extra days and shows exactly where gear was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list with quantities and per-unit prices
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients check counts against their guest list, and a clear list prevents disputes over what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, pickup, and setup charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets clients see what is equipment and what is service, and makes it easy to adjust if the venue changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery and pickup time windows
invoiceChecklist.why: Late access or late pickup can trigger extra fees, and the written windows back up those charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage waiver or replacement cost terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out what is covered and what the client owes for broken, lost, or stained items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the booking deposit already applied so the remaining amount is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line and tax-exempt status if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax rental of tangible property, and nonprofits or resellers may provide exemption certificates. Check your state rules.

event-rental.paymentTerms: Most rental companies take a 25 to 50 percent deposit to hold the date and require the balance 7 to 14 days before the event, or at delivery for smaller orders. Large corporate or venue accounts are sometimes invoiced net 15 or net 30 after the event. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the rental agreement. Cards, ACH, and checks are the usual methods, and many companies keep a card on file to cover damage, cleaning, or late return charges. Cancellation and date-change policies, including whether the deposit is refundable, should be written into the agreement before the deposit is taken.

tips.title: Invoice from the final headcount
tips.body: Update the invoice when the guest count changes, and set a cutoff date after which quantities can only go up. This keeps you from holding inventory for events that shrink at the last minute.

tips.title: Document item condition at pickup
tips.body: Take photos or note condition when gear leaves and returns, especially linens, tents, and glassware. Evidence of pre-existing wear or damage makes damage fees much easier to collect.

tips.title: Bill extra days and late returns automatically
tips.body: State the rental period and extra-day rate on the invoice. If gear sits at the venue an extra day, add a line item instead of absorbing it.

tips.title: Charge for access problems
tips.body: Stairs, long carries, rain-soaked ground, and venues without loading access cost extra labor. List a standard fee for these so it doesn't look arbitrary when applied.

tips.title: Collect the balance before delivery
tips.body: Once gear is set up, you have less leverage. Requiring payment in full before the event avoids chasing a client who is busy hosting or heading out on a honeymoon.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on event rentals?
faqs.answer: In many states, rental of tangible property like tables and chairs is taxable, and delivery or setup charges may or may not be, depending on whether they are separately stated. Rules vary, so check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How should I bill a deposit on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Show the full rental total, then list the deposit as a payment received with its date, and show the remaining balance. This keeps the paper trail clear if the client later asks what has been paid.

faqs.question: Can I charge for damaged or missing items?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your rental agreement states the policy. List each item, quantity, and replacement cost on a separate invoice or line, and attach photos if you have them. Normal wear is usually covered by your rental price, and the damage waiver, if purchased, may cover accidental damage.

faqs.question: What is a fair late return fee?
faqs.answer: Many companies charge an additional day at 25 to 50 percent of the base rental rate, or a flat daily fee for large items. Put it in the agreement and on the invoice so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Should delivery be a flat fee or per mile?
faqs.answer: Both are used. Flat fees by zone are simpler for clients to understand, while per-mile pricing is more accurate for long distances. Many companies use zones for local jobs and a custom quote beyond a set radius.

estimate.intro: Event renters send quotes during the planning stage, often months before the event, and clients commonly request quotes from several companies. They compare item prices, delivery and labor charges, product quality, and whether the quote includes everything needed on the day. A quote that lists every line clearly is easier to approve than a single lump sum.

scopeChecklist.item: Itemized equipment list with quantities, sizes, and colors
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids confusion about 60 in. versus 72 in. rounds, linen colors, or chair styles.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, rental period, and venue address
scopeChecklist.why: Availability and pricing depend on the date, and the venue affects delivery distance and access.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery, setup, teardown, and pickup times
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies who is responsible for what and when the venue needs to be accessible.
State whether chairs are set in rows, tables are placed per a floor plan, and linens are put on tables, since these all affect labor.

scopeChecklist.item: Site requirements for tents or large installs
scopeChecklist.why: Cover surface type, stake or ballast needs, utility locates, power for lighting, and permit responsibility so there are no surprises on install day.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and how to reserve
scopeChecklist.why: Inventory is not held until a deposit is received, so state how long the pricing is valid.
Sets expectations on refunds, tent weather contingencies, and last-minute headcount changes.

pricingTips.title: Quote with a headcount buffer
pricingTips.body: Ask for a final headcount range and price the likely number, noting the cutoff date for changes. Clients often add guests, and a policy ahead of time prevents shortages.

pricingTips.title: Offer package pricing alongside itemized lines
pricingTips.body: A bundle such as chairs, tables, and linens for 100 guests is easy to compare against competitors, while the itemized breakdown shows how the package was built.

pricingTips.title: Price delivery from the real route
pricingTips.body: Factor in drive time, truck size, crew size, and venue access, not just mileage. A downtown venue with a loading dock and a hilltop estate with a gravel drive are not the same job.

pricingTips.title: Keep tent quotes site-specific
pricingTips.body: Do a site visit or request photos and measurements before giving a firm price. Slope, trees, pavement versus grass, and utilities can change labor and equipment needs.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or site visit?
faqs.answer: Quotes for standard rentals are normally free. For large tent or multi-day installs, some companies charge a site visit fee and credit it toward the booking if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Many rental companies hold pricing for 14 to 30 days, and state that inventory is only reserved with a signed agreement and deposit, especially in peak wedding season.

faqs.question: What if the final count differs from the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a clause allowing quantities to go up subject to availability and to go down until a set cutoff, often 7 to 14 days before the event. After that, the client pays for the reserved count.

faqs.question: Should I quote taxes and fees in the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Show estimated sales tax, damage waiver, and any fuel or access surcharges so the total is close to the final invoice and clients are not surprised later.

excavation.intro: Excavation contractors dig, grade, and move earth for home builders, property owners, and other trades. Typical invoices cover equipment time with an operator, hauling and dump fees, trenching for utilities, foundation and basement digs, septic installs, and site grading. Most are owner-operators or small crews with a few machines and trucks.
excavation.pricingModel: Excavation is priced either by the hour for machine and operator, or as a flat bid for a defined scope. Hourly rates are common for small jobs, repairs, and work with unknown conditions, and are usually quoted per machine (mini excavator, backhoe, skid steer, dozer) with a minimum, often 3 to 4 hours. Larger jobs such as basement digs, septic systems, and driveways are often bid as a lump sum or by unit, such as per cubic yard, per linear foot of trench, or per load hauled. Trucking is billed per hour or per load, and fill, gravel, and topsoil are billed per ton or per yard with a markup. Add mobilization (lowboy transport) as its own line, plus dump or disposal fees at cost plus a handling charge. Rock, groundwater, and buried debris are normally excluded from fixed bids and billed as extras at your hourly rate.

rates.service: Backhoe or full-size excavator with operator
Skid steer or dozer with operator (grading)
Dump truck with driver (tandem or tri-axle)
Septic system excavation and install labor

items.description: Mobilize mini excavator and trailer to job site (round trip)
Mini excavator with operator, trench for water line and electrical conduit, 4 hr minimum applied
