Dump truck with driver, haul spoil off site
3/4 inch crushed stone for pipe bedding and backfill, delivered
Dump fee for excess spoil (at cost plus 10%)
Extra: removal of buried concrete slab found in trench path, approved by owner on site

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Balance after the 30% deposit received on 6/3. Extra work approved verbally by owner on 6/5 and listed above. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Checks payable to the company name above; ACH and card accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and lot or permit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Excavation is tied to a specific parcel, and the address lets owners, lenders, and inspectors match the invoice to the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment used, operator, and hours per machine
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute machine time more than anything else, so list each machine separately with hours and dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mobilization and trucking lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Moving equipment and hauling are real costs that clients often forget; separate lines prevent them from being questioned as padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials by type, quantity, and unit (tons or yards)
invoiceChecklist.why: Gravel, fill, topsoil, and stone are priced per ton or yard and should match the delivery tickets you can show on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dump or disposal fees and scale tickets
invoiceChecklist.why: These are pass-through costs, and attaching tickets backs up the amount if the client questions it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extras, with date and who approved them
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, buried debris, wet ground, and added trench length are common extras. A written record of approval avoids fights over work outside the original bid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, insurance info, and any permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and counties require a license number on contracts and invoices, and general contractors or lenders often request proof of insurance.

excavation.paymentTerms: Most excavators take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent on larger jobs to cover mobilization and materials, with the balance due on completion or within 7 to 30 days. Small hourly jobs are often paid on the day or within a week. Progress billing is typical for jobs spanning several weeks, such as site prep for a new build, with draws tied to milestones like rough excavation, utilities in, and final grade. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing up front. Checks, ACH, and card are all used; add a card fee only if your state allows it. On commercial and builder work, expect net 30 and possible retainage. Check your state's mechanics lien rules and notice deadlines, since they can protect you if payment stalls.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge for every machine
tips.body: Moving a machine on site costs time and fuel even for a one-hour dig. A 3 or 4 hour minimum, written on the quote and invoice, covers that and stops requests for quick favors at a loss.

tips.title: Bill portal-to-portal when it applies
tips.body: If your quote says hourly rates run from the time the machine leaves your yard until it returns, say so in writing. Otherwise clients assume billing starts when the bucket hits dirt.

tips.title: Get change orders signed before you dig
tips.body: When you hit rock, a buried tank, or soft ground, stop, take a photo, and get a text or signature approving the extra cost. Add it to the invoice with the date.

tips.title: Keep scale tickets and delivery slips
tips.body: Photograph every ticket the day you get it. Matching tickets to invoice quantities settles most disputes about tonnage and loads in minutes.

tips.title: Know your lien deadlines
tips.body: Many states require a preliminary notice within a set number of days of starting work to keep lien rights. Check your local rules and send notices on builder and commercial jobs even when you expect to be paid.

faqs.question: Should I bill excavation by the hour or as a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly when conditions are unknown, such as repair work, old lots, or clearing, and use a flat fee when the scope is clear and you can see the site, such as a standard basement dig or driveway. Many contractors bid flat but list hourly rates for extras like rock or extra hauling.

faqs.question: Can I charge for equipment travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mobilization is normally billed as a separate line for lowboy delivery, or as hourly time from yard to site. State it in your quote so the client agrees to it before the job.

faqs.question: How do I bill for hauling and dump fees?
faqs.answer: List trucking by the hour or load, and list dump fees as a separate line at cost, often with a 10 to 15 percent handling markup. Keep scale tickets so you can show the actual cost.

faqs.question: How do I handle unexpected rock or buried debris?
faqs.answer: Exclude it from fixed bids in writing and bill it at your hourly rate with any needed rock breaker or hammer attachment. When you find it, document with photos and get the client's approval before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on excavation?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials like gravel and fill, some tax certain construction services, and many exempt labor. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax on a separate line when required.

estimate.intro: Excavation contractors give estimates before any digging starts, usually after a site visit. Clients often compare several bids, so the scope, what is excluded, and how unknowns are handled matter as much as the total price.

scopeChecklist.why: State the depth, width, length, or square footage, such as a 24 by 36 foot basement at 8 feet deep. Vague scope leads to disputes over what was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Spoil handling: haul off, stockpile, or spread on site
scopeChecklist.why: Hauling dirt away adds trucking and dump fees. Clients often assume it is included unless you say otherwise.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials included and who supplies them
scopeChecklist.why: Specify gravel, fill, topsoil, pipe bedding, and quantities, and say whether you or the client buys them.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions for rock, groundwater, and buried objects
scopeChecklist.why: These are the biggest sources of cost overruns. State that they are billed as extras at your hourly rate.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, utility locates, and survey stakes
scopeChecklist.why: Say who gets the permit and who calls for utility marking (811 in the US). Digging without locates creates serious liability.

scopeChecklist.item: Site access, restoration, and erosion control
scopeChecklist.why: Note what happens to lawns, driveways, and silt fence, and whether restoration like seeding or regrading is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, weather delays, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Fuel, material, and schedule changes affect cost. A 30-day expiration and weather language protect you.

pricingTips.title: Visit the site before quoting
pricingTips.body: Look at access, soil, slope, nearby utilities, and where spoil can go. A 20-minute walk-through catches problems that change the price by thousands.

pricingTips.title: Build the bid from machine hours plus trucking
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours per machine, add mobilization, trucking, materials, and disposal, then add overhead and profit. Include margin for machine wear and repairs, not just fuel and wages.

pricingTips.title: Use unit prices for uncertain quantities
pricingTips.body: If you cannot know the amount, offer a rate per cubic yard of fill or per foot of trench with an estimated total. The client sees a clear basis for the final bill.

pricingTips.title: Separate options and allowances
pricingTips.body: List add-ons such as finish grading, extra stone, or stump removal as options. For items with unknown cost, such as rock removal, list an allowance and say how overages are billed.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are standard for typical residential jobs. For large site work that needs plan review or engineering input, many contractors charge a fee and credit it toward the job if awarded.

faqs.question: How long should an excavation quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 15 to 30 days. Fuel, trucking, and material costs change, and your schedule fills up, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on an estimate?
faqs.answer: Many excavators ask for 25 to 50 percent on larger jobs to cover mobilization and materials. On small hourly jobs, no deposit is common. State the amount and due date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: For a fixed bid, you absorb normal variation but can bill extras that are excluded in writing, like rock or extra hauling. For an hourly estimate, say it is an estimate and that you will notify the client if hours will go meaningfully over.

executive-coach.intro: Executive coaches work one-on-one with senior leaders, founders, and high-potential managers on leadership, communication, decision-making, and career transitions. Most are independent practitioners or run small firms, and they bill either the executive directly or the employer, often through HR or a learning and development team. Invoices usually cover coaching sessions, assessments, stakeholder interviews, and group or team work.
executive-coach.pricingModel: Most executive coaches sell engagements rather than single hours. A typical package is 6 to 12 months of coaching with two to four sessions per month, billed as a monthly retainer or as a fixed fee split into installments. Hourly or per-session rates are used for short engagements, one-off sessions, and add-on work. Corporate clients, where the employer pays, usually pay higher rates than individuals paying out of pocket, and they often require a statement of work and a purchase order. Assessments such as 360 feedback tools or personality instruments are billed separately, either at cost or with a modest markup for administration and debrief. Stakeholder interviews, kickoff meetings with the sponsor, and three-way progress check-ins with the manager or HR are often built into the package but should be listed so they are visible. Travel for on-site coaching is billed as expenses or a day rate. Rates vary widely by experience, credentials, and client seniority.

rates.service: Individual coaching session (60 min), corporate client
Individual coaching session (60 min), self-paying client
Monthly coaching retainer (2-4 sessions plus email or text support between sessions)
360 feedback assessment with interviews and debrief report
Personality or style assessment and debrief (e.g. DiSC, Hogan, MBTI)
Team offsite or leadership workshop facilitation

items.description: Executive coaching, month 3 of 6: four 60-minute sessions with VP of Operations
Between-session support (email and 15-minute calls), included in monthly retainer
Three-way progress review with CHRO and coachee (45 min)
Hogan assessment and 90-minute debrief
Preparation and written development plan update

sampleInvoice.notes: PO #44871. Engagement period: March 1-31. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed in full. Please remit by ACH or check; wire details available on request. All coaching content is confidential.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name, coachee name, and billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: In corporate work the person coached is often not the person paying. Naming both lets accounts payable match the invoice to the right budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or statement of work reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Many companies will not pay without a PO. Including it avoids the invoice being rejected or sitting in a queue.

invoiceChecklist.item: Engagement period and session dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates tie each charge to delivered work and help the client track how many sessions in the package remain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized services with sessions used and remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing sessions delivered against the package total prevents questions on retainer or prepaid engagements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Assessments and third-party fees listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Licensing costs for 360 or personality tools are often reimbursed or budgeted separately from coaching fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expenses with receipts for travel
invoiceChecklist.why: On-site coaching can involve flights, hotels, and mileage. Clients usually require receipts and a clear split from fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show charges applied
invoiceChecklist.why: If you billed a late cancellation, state the date and refer to the policy in your agreement so the charge is not a surprise.

executive-coach.paymentTerms: Individual clients often pay monthly in advance or by installment, commonly by card or ACH. Corporate clients typically pay net 30, and some large companies run net 45 or net 60, so confirm this before the engagement starts. Many coaches invoice monthly retainers at the start of the month and collect 25 to 50 percent of a fixed-fee engagement upfront. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are sometimes included in the contract, though many coaches prefer to pause sessions after a set number of days past due. Put the cancellation window, usually 24 to 48 hours, and the policy on unused sessions in your coaching agreement.

tips.title: Bill in advance for individuals
tips.body: When the coachee pays personally, invoice at the start of each month or package period. Coaching depends on momentum, and collecting after the fact makes it awkward to raise a late balance while you are still working together.

tips.title: Get the payer's process in writing
tips.body: Before the first session, ask the sponsor who approves invoices, whether a PO is required, and the payment timeline. Some companies need you to register as a vendor, which can take weeks.

tips.title: Keep confidentiality out of the invoice
tips.body: The invoice goes to HR or finance, who may not be entitled to session content. List dates and service types only, and keep topics and notes out of the description.

tips.title: Define what a retainer includes
tips.body: If you offer email or text support between sessions, state the scope and response time in the agreement. Otherwise a flat monthly fee can turn into unlimited availability.

tips.title: Set a policy for unused sessions
tips.body: Decide whether missed sessions are forfeited, rescheduled within a window, or credited, and write it down. Engagements often run past their end date when sessions are postponed.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or a monthly retainer?
faqs.answer: Monthly retainers or package fees are more common for ongoing executive coaching because they give predictable income and signal a committed engagement. Per-session billing works for short engagements, trial sessions, and clients who need flexibility.

faqs.question: Can I bill the company and the executive separately?
faqs.answer: Yes. Some engagements split cost, for example the employer pays for coaching and the executive pays for extras. Use separate invoices with clear references to the agreement, and do not combine them.

faqs.question: How do I handle sales tax on coaching?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax coaching services, but some tax certain consulting or training services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and if tax applies show it as a separate line.

faqs.question: When should I invoice for assessments?
faqs.answer: Invoice when the assessment is administered or at the debrief, depending on your agreement. Because you may pay the tool provider up front, many coaches bill the assessment in the first month.

faqs.question: What if the client ends the engagement early?
faqs.answer: Your agreement should state whether the fee is refundable, prorated, or due in full. A common approach is to bill for sessions delivered plus a notice period, often 30 days, and not refund prepaid periods already started.

estimate.intro: Executive coaches send a proposal or statement of work before a first session, usually after a chemistry call and a conversation with the sponsor. Clients often compare coaches on credentials, approach, number of sessions, and total cost, so the quote needs to be clear about what the engagement includes.

scopeChecklist.why: State the number of months, sessions per month, and session length so the client knows exactly what the fee covers.
Agree on two to four development goals with the coachee and sponsor. This reduces disputes about whether the engagement worked.
360 feedback, interviews, and style assessments take significant time. List which are included and whether they are charged separately.
Clarify whether email, text, or short calls are included, and the expected response time.
State how many progress meetings with the manager or HR are included and what you will and will not share, given confidentiality.
Define notice periods and what happens to missed sessions before the first one is missed.
Say whether sessions are virtual or in person, and how travel is billed, so the client can budget beyond fees.

pricingTips.title: Quote a package, not an hourly rate
pricingTips.body: A total engagement fee with a monthly payment schedule keeps the conversation on outcomes. Hourly rates invite clients to count minutes and cut sessions.

pricingTips.title: Offer two options
pricingTips.body: Present a standard package and a fuller one that adds a 360 assessment and sponsor reviews. Clients often choose the middle option when given a choice.

pricingTips.title: Price corporate work above individual work
pricingTips.body: Employer-funded engagements involve more stakeholders, reporting, and administrative work. Charge higher rates for them rather than discounting to match self-pay clients.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Add a date, often 30 days, after which the price and your availability may change. Coaches have limited client capacity, and open-ended quotes hold a spot you could fill.

faqs.question: Should I offer a free first session?
faqs.answer: A short chemistry call of 20 to 30 minutes is standard, and many coaches do not charge for it. Offering a full free session is less common for executive work, and it is reasonable to begin paid work after the fit is confirmed.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most corporate clients expect a contract or statement of work, and it is wise for individuals too. It should cover fees, confidentiality, cancellations, and termination terms.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the company wants to pay but also wants progress reports?
faqs.answer: Describe the reporting in the quote, such as a mid-point and final check-in with the sponsor, and charge for the time. Agree up front that you share themes and progress, not session content.

faqs.question: What if the scope grows during the engagement?
faqs.answer: Add changes in writing. If the client wants more sessions, a team workshop, or additional assessments, send an updated quote or addendum with the added fee before doing the work.

facebook-ads-manager.intro: Facebook Ads Managers plan, launch, and optimize paid campaigns on Meta platforms (Facebook and Instagram) for small businesses, ecommerce brands, local service companies, and agencies. Invoices usually cover a monthly management fee, one-time setup or audit work, creative production, and sometimes a percentage of ad spend. Many managers also bill for ad spend passed through to the client, which needs to be kept clearly separate from fees.
facebook-ads-manager.pricingModel: Most Facebook ads managers charge a monthly retainer, either a flat fee or a percentage of ad spend (commonly 10-20%, often with a minimum). Flat retainers are typical for accounts spending under $10,000 a month, with percentage fees more common as spend grows. One-time charges cover account audits, pixel and Conversions API setup, and strategy sessions. Creative work such as ad copy, static images, and short video edits is usually billed per asset or as a monthly bundle. Some managers add performance bonuses tied to return on ad spend or cost per lead, but a base fee is still standard because results depend on the offer, site, and budget. Hourly billing ($60-150) is used for consulting, training, and one-off fixes. Ad spend is either paid directly by the client on their own card in Meta Business Manager, which is the cleaner approach, or billed to the client as a pass-through with no markup or a disclosed one.

rates.service: Monthly ad management retainer (small account, under $5k spend)
Pixel, Conversions API, and tracking setup

items.description: Facebook and Instagram ad management, June 2025 (3 active campaigns, weekly optimization, monthly report)
Campaign setup: new retargeting and lookalike audiences for summer promotion
Static ad creative, 1080x1080 and 1080x1920 sizes
Short video ad edit (15-second Reel from client footage)
Strategy call and landing page feedback

sampleInvoice.notes: Ad spend of $3,850 for June was charged directly to the client's card by Meta and is not included in this invoice. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Next month's management fee will be invoiced on July 1.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and service dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers cover a specific month, and clear dates prevent disputes over what period the fee applies to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Management fee basis (flat or percent of spend)
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge a percentage, show the spend figure and the percentage used so the client can verify the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad spend shown separately or noted as paid directly
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often confuse your fee with media cost. State whether spend was billed through Meta or passed through by you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized one-time work such as setup, audits, and tracking
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from the retainer shows what was a one-time cost versus recurring.

invoiceChecklist.item: Creative deliverables with quantity and format
invoiceChecklist.why: Counting assets (images, videos, copy variants) justifies per-asset charges and records what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad account or Business Manager name or ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and multi-brand clients need to know which account the work applies to for bookkeeping.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client reference, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often cannot pay without a PO or cost center code.

facebook-ads-manager.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month, in advance, with payment due in 7 to 15 days. Many managers bill the first month plus any setup fee upfront before launching campaigns. One-time projects such as audits or builds often take a 50% deposit with the balance on delivery. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in your agreement. Payment methods include ACH, card, and bank transfer; card fees are often passed on or absorbed. Pausing campaigns for nonpayment should be written into your contract, since you may be exposed if ad spend is on a card you control.

tips.title: Keep ad spend off your card when possible
tips.body: Have clients add their own payment method in Business Manager. If you front the spend, you carry the risk of unpaid balances and chargebacks, and you may be treated as responsible for it on your books.

tips.title: Set a minimum fee on percentage pricing
tips.body: If you charge 15% of spend and the client cuts budget to $1,000, your fee drops to $150 for the same workload. A monthly minimum protects your time.

tips.title: Define what the retainer includes
tips.body: List the number of campaigns, creative rounds, reports, and calls covered. Bill extra work like new creative batches or additional ad accounts as separate line items.

tips.title: Bill in advance, not in arrears
tips.body: Invoice for the coming month so work does not continue while a previous bill sits unpaid. Pause campaigns if an invoice goes more than a set number of days overdue.

tips.title: Attach a short results summary
tips.body: A one-page report with spend, results, and key changes made makes the invoice easier to approve and reduces cancellations when results are slow.

faqs.question: Should I include ad spend on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you are paying Meta on the client's behalf. In that case, list it as a separate pass-through line, ideally with the Meta billing statement attached. If the client pays Meta directly, note that on your invoice so no one thinks it was missed.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of ad spend?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is common, typically 10-20%. Define whether the percentage applies to actual spend or budgeted spend, and add a monthly minimum so your fee does not fall too low when budgets shrink.

faqs.question: How do I bill for performance-based results?
faqs.answer: Keep a base retainer and add a bonus on top, such as a percentage of revenue above a target return on ad spend. Define how results are measured and which tracking source counts, and invoice the bonus as a separate line after the period closes.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to cancel mid-month?
faqs.answer: Your agreement should state notice requirements, usually 15 to 30 days. Invoice the full month or a prorated amount as agreed, and document the date the client requested cancellation.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on ad management?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax certain marketing or advertising services and many do not. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional, and show any tax as its own line if it applies.

estimate.intro: Facebook ads managers send estimates when a prospect asks for pricing after a discovery call or after an account audit. Clients usually compare monthly fees, what is included, contract length, and whether ad spend is separate. A clear estimate also sets expectations about how long it takes to see results.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly management fee and how it is calculated
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know if the fee is flat or tied to spend, and whether it changes if the budget changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected ad spend and who pays Meta
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents confusion between your fee and the media budget, and sets the budget the plan is built around.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of campaigns, ad sets, and creative variations included
scopeChecklist.why: Defines workload so requests for extra campaigns or new creative are clearly outside the scope.
State whether you produce images and video, edit client footage, or only write copy and run the ads.
Pixel, Conversions API, and event setup affect results. Say who handles them and any costs involved.
Sets expectations for weekly or monthly reports and the number of strategy meetings included.
Ad performance takes time to stabilize, so many managers ask for a minimum of 3 months or a 30-day notice period.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a starter plan with one campaign and a growth plan with creative and retargeting. Tiers help clients choose by scope instead of negotiating price.

pricingTips.title: Price the audit as a paid first step
pricingTips.body: For unclear accounts, quote a paid audit of $300-1,200 and credit part of it toward the first month if the client signs on. It filters out price shoppers and gives you data before committing to a retainer.

pricingTips.title: Do not promise specific results
pricingTips.body: Quote effort and deliverables, not guaranteed returns on ad spend. Results depend on the offer, website, and budget, and guarantees invite disputes.

pricingTips.title: Account for platform changes and learning time
pricingTips.body: Build the first 30 to 60 days into your pricing, since setup, testing, and optimization take more effort up front than in later months.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is typical. Ad costs and your availability change, so state an expiration date on the estimate.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat fee or a percentage of spend?
faqs.answer: Flat fees are simpler for small budgets. Percentages scale with workload at higher spend. Many managers use a flat fee with a minimum and switch to a percentage once spend passes a set level.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, most managers collect the first month's fee and any setup fee before launching. This confirms commitment and covers early work that is hard to recover if the client leaves.

farrier.intro: Farriers trim and shoe horses, usually traveling to barns, boarding stables, and private properties in a truck or van with a portable forge and anvil. Invoices cover trims, shoeing, corrective work, and add-ons like pads, studs, and borium, often billed per horse and per visit across a client's whole string.
farrier.pricingModel: Most farriers price per horse, per visit, based on the service performed: a barefoot trim, a half set (front shoes only), or a full set of four shoes. Shoe type drives the price because steel, aluminum, and specialty shoes cost different amounts and take different time to fit. Corrective and therapeutic work, such as bar shoes, wedge pads, or working with a vet on laminitis or founder, is priced higher, either per horse or per hour. Add-ons like pads, borium, studs, clips, and hoof packing are itemized. Many farriers charge a trip fee or minimum for single-horse stops and for long drives, and offer a small discount for barns where several horses are done in one visit. Regular clients are often booked on a fixed cycle of 4 to 8 weeks, and prices are usually set per cycle rather than negotiated each time. New or difficult horses, emergency resets for lost shoes, and same-day calls often carry a surcharge.

rates.service: Full set of keg shoes, steel
Full set with pads or aluminum/performance shoes
Corrective or therapeutic shoeing (bar shoes, wedges, natural balance)
Trip fee or minimum for single horse / long distance

items.description: Full set of steel keg shoes - Duke (Quarter Horse)
Full set of steel shoes with leather pads - Bella (Warmblood)
Barefoot trim - Scout (pony)
Borium application on shoes - Duke

sampleInvoice.notes: Service date: May 14. Next visit due in 6 weeks. Payment due on receipt; checks payable to the business name. Please have horses caught, clean, and dry on arrival. Cancellations with less than 24 hours notice may be charged the trip fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Horse name and service for each horse
invoiceChecklist.why: Barns with multiple owners need to split the bill, and a per-horse line item settles questions about what was done and for whom.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and next due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the shoeing cycle and helps clients schedule the next visit before shoes grow out or loosen.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of shoe and materials used
invoiceChecklist.why: Steel, aluminum, pads, and specialty shoes cost different amounts, so naming them justifies price differences between horses.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons itemized separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Borium, studs, clips, pads, and hoof packing are easy to forget or dispute when bundled into one number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip fee or mileage
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes travel charges visible so clients understand a single-horse or distant stop costs more.

invoiceChecklist.item: Owner or barn billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: At boarding stables it must be clear whether the owner or the barn manager is responsible for payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vet referral or notes on corrective work
invoiceChecklist.why: When working with a veterinarian on a lameness or hoof condition, a brief note documents the plan and supports the higher price.

farrier.paymentTerms: Most farriers expect payment at the time of service, either handed over at the barn or sent the same day by card, check, cash, or a payment app. For barns billed in a batch, net 7 to 14 days is common. Deposits are rare for routine work but can make sense for new clients with a long drive or large strings. Many farriers state a late fee or a service pause policy, such as no new appointments until the balance is cleared, and a returned check fee. Charging a trip fee for no-shows or last-minute cancellations is common and should be stated in advance.

tips.title: Set a policy for single-horse stops
tips.body: Driving 40 minutes to do one trim can cost more than it earns. A minimum charge or trip fee keeps small stops worthwhile, and clients usually accept it when it is posted up front.

tips.title: Bill the barn manager or each owner, not both
tips.body: At boarding barns, agree early on who pays. If one person collects from the other owners, invoice that person with a per-horse breakdown so they can pass it along.

tips.title: Raise prices on a schedule
tips.body: Steel, fuel, and propane costs move every year. Review prices annually, give clients 30 days notice, and update the price list in writing instead of quietly raising one invoice.

tips.title: Charge for the extra work
tips.body: Difficult horses, extra shoe resets, and corrective work take time and materials. Itemize them rather than absorbing them into a standard price.

tips.title: Keep a record per horse
tips.body: Note shoe sizes, pads, and what worked on each horse. It speeds up the next visit and backs up your invoice if a client questions a charge.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the horse or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Per horse is standard for routine trims and shoeing because clients can predict the cost. Hourly pricing is more common for lengthy corrective work, vet-directed therapeutic shoeing, or special projects where time is hard to estimate.

faqs.question: Can I charge a trip fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. Trip fees and minimums are common for single-horse visits and long drives. State them on your price list and show them as a separate line on the invoice so they are not a surprise.

faqs.question: What should I do about clients who pay late?
faqs.answer: Set terms before the first appointment. Many farriers collect at the time of service and decline to book the next visit until the balance is paid. A written late fee policy gives you something to point to.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax services or the shoes and materials, while others exempt farrier work or agricultural services. Check with your state revenue department or a local tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I invoice when one owner has several horses at a barn?
faqs.answer: List each horse on its own line with the service performed, then total the visit. If a barn manager pays for several owners, you can add the owner name next to each horse so they can split it.

estimate.intro: Farriers quote when taking on a new client, a whole barn, or a horse needing corrective work. Clients usually compare per-horse prices, trip fees, and how reliably you can keep a regular cycle. Written quotes also help when a horse has a hoof problem and the cost depends on what is found.

scopeChecklist.item: Services per horse (trim, half set, full set, reset)
scopeChecklist.why: Each service has a different price, and clients may assume a full set when they only booked a trim.
Steel, aluminum, pads, and specialty shoes change the price, so specify what is included in the base rate.
Borium, studs, clips, and packing are extras that should be priced up front rather than added on the day.
A 6-week cycle versus an 8-week cycle affects price and client expectations about how often you will visit.

scopeChecklist.item: Trip fee, minimum, and travel area
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies when you charge extra for distance, single-horse stops, or locations outside your normal route.
State that horses must be caught, reasonably behaved, and on level, dry ground, and note any surcharge for difficult horses.
For lameness or hoof problems, note that the plan may change after the first visit or after consulting the vet, and that pricing may adjust.

pricingTips.title: Quote a price per horse, with a barn discount in writing
pricingTips.body: If you are taking on a barn, a modest discount per horse for a group visit can win the work. Write it into the quote so it applies only while the group stays the same size.

pricingTips.title: Price the first visit separately
pricingTips.body: New horses often need extra time to correct overgrown or unbalanced hooves. A first-visit rate that is higher than the maintenance rate is reasonable if you explain it.

pricingTips.title: Give ranges for corrective work
pricingTips.body: You cannot know exactly what a foundered or lame horse needs until you see the feet and talk with the vet. Offer a range and a per-visit price, and confirm changes in writing.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Steel and fuel prices change. A 30-day expiry keeps you from being held to old prices.

faqs.question: Should I charge for giving an estimate?
faqs.answer: Usually not for routine work. For farm calls to assess a lameness or a large string far from your route, a trip fee or consult fee is reasonable, and you can credit it toward the first service.

faqs.question: What if the horse needs more work than I quoted?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that the price assumes normal hoof condition and handling. If you find more work needed, tell the owner before proceeding and note the extra charge on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I quote a barn with many horses?
faqs.answer: List each horse and its service, then give a per-visit total. Include any group discount, the shoeing cycle, and whether the barn or each owner pays.

fashion-designer.intro: Fashion designers who work for themselves or run small studios invoice clients for custom garment design, collection development, technical packages, pattern making, sample production, and consulting. Clients include individual customers ordering custom pieces, emerging brands that need a collection developed, boutiques, costume buyers, and manufacturers who need production-ready files. Invoices usually combine design time, material costs, and production or sample work, so clear itemization matters.
fashion-designer.pricingModel: Pricing depends on whether you sell your time or a finished product. Freelance design work is billed hourly, per piece, or as a flat project fee, with a deposit up front. Technical packages (tech packs) and pattern work are usually priced per style. Custom and bespoke garments are priced per piece, built from design time, pattern making, materials, and labor, with fittings often included up to a limit. Sample development is billed per sample, with fabric and trims passed through at cost or with a markup of 10-30 percent. Brands that need ongoing support often pay a monthly retainer. Rush work, extra revisions, and extra fittings are normally charged on top of the base fee. Wholesale and production runs are priced per unit with minimum order quantities.

items.description: Design development and sketches, 6-piece capsule collection
Technical packages with measurements and construction details
First pattern development
Sample garment construction (muslin and final fabric)
Fabric and trims sourced for samples (receipts attached)
Deposit received on 3/4

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 14 days of invoice date. Price includes two rounds of revisions per style; additional revisions billed at $75 per hour. Samples remain property of the designer until paid in full. Design rights transfer to the client on final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Style names or numbers for each piece
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often order many styles at once, and matching line items to style numbers prevents confusion over what was delivered and billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for design, pattern, sample, and production work
invoiceChecklist.why: Each stage has a different cost basis, and itemizing it supports your prices and makes partial billing easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials and trims with supplier receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Fabric can be a large part of the total. Showing it as a pass-through cost helps clients see where the money went and avoids disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and fittings included
invoiceChecklist.why: Revisions and extra fittings are a common source of scope creep. State what is included and the rate for more.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and payment schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Many projects bill in stages, such as design approval, sample delivery, and final production. Show what was paid and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Intellectual property and usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State whether the client receives the patterns, tech packs, and design rights, and when those transfer, usually on full payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Sales tax rules for finished goods and custom clothing vary by state. If a wholesale buyer provides a resale certificate, record it on the invoice.

fashion-designer.paymentTerms: Most fashion designers take a 40-50 percent deposit before starting design or buying materials, since fabric and sample costs are real out-of-pocket expenses. Custom garments often require 50 percent up front and the balance before the final piece is released. Larger projects are billed in milestones, such as design approval, first samples, and production-ready files. Standard terms are net 14 or net 30 for business clients, and due on pickup for individual customers. Many designers charge a late fee of 1-1.5 percent per month, stated on the quote and invoice. Payment is commonly accepted by bank transfer, card, or check. Wholesale accounts may ask for net 30 terms, so check the buyer before shipping a large order.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before buying fabric
tips.body: Fabric, trims, and sample labor are costs you pay before the client sees anything. A deposit of 40-50 percent covers them and shows the client is committed.

tips.title: Cap revisions and fittings
tips.body: Put a number on revisions per style and fittings per garment, then charge an hourly or per-fitting rate beyond that. Without a cap, design projects tend to drift.

tips.title: Hold the finished work until paid
tips.body: Do not release final samples, patterns, or tech pack files until the balance is paid. Say so in your terms so it is expected rather than a surprise.

tips.title: Track time on design work
tips.body: Sketching, sourcing, and fittings are easy to underestimate. Keep a running log so hourly invoices and flat-fee estimates for future projects are based on real numbers.

tips.title: Separate design fees from production
tips.body: Design and pattern work is a service, while production is a product with unit costs and minimums. Billing them separately keeps your margins visible and makes it easier to quote production later.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or per style?
faqs.answer: Hourly works for open-ended design and consulting. Per style is better for defined deliverables such as tech packs, patterns, and samples, because clients can budget and you are paid for the result. Many designers use both, billing design by the hour and technical work per style.

faqs.question: How do I bill for fabric and materials?
faqs.answer: List materials as a separate line, with the actual cost or cost plus a markup of 10-30 percent for sourcing time. Keep receipts and attach them if the client asks. Collect a deposit before purchasing expensive fabric.

faqs.question: Who owns the patterns and designs after I invoice?
faqs.answer: Unless the contract says otherwise, the designer generally keeps the rights to work they create. If the client is buying the designs, patterns, or tech pack, state that on the invoice and transfer the rights on full payment. Consult an attorney for contracts with significant value.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on custom clothing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether you are selling a finished garment or a design service. Some states tax clothing, some exempt it, and services are treated differently from goods. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels after I have made samples?
faqs.answer: Put a cancellation clause in your quote that makes the deposit non-refundable and requires payment for work completed and materials purchased. Invoice the completed stages and any custom materials you cannot reuse.

estimate.intro: Fashion designers send quotes before design work, sample development, or a custom garment begins, often after a consultation or a look at inspiration images and sketches. Clients typically compare designers on total price, number of revisions, timeline, and what files or garments they receive. A clear written quote helps you stand out from low-priced offers that leave out key deliverables.

scopeChecklist.why: List whether the client gets sketches, a tech pack, a pattern, a sample, or a finished garment. Each has a different cost, and clients often assume more is included than you plan to deliver.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revisions and fittings included
scopeChecklist.why: Design changes after approval are the most common source of extra work. Set a limit and state the rate beyond it.
State who sources and pays for materials, whether the quote includes them, and what happens if prices change or a fabric is unavailable.
Delays often come from slow feedback. Tie dates to approvals and note that deadlines shift if the client is late.
Pattern and sample prices assume certain sizes and counts. Note the size range and say that grading or additional sizes are priced separately.
Say whether the client receives patterns, tech packs, and design rights, and whether you may show the work in your portfolio.

scopeChecklist.item: Rush fees, cancellation, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Fabric prices and your calendar change. A validity period of 14-30 days and a stated rush fee protect your schedule.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from stages
pricingTips.body: Price design, pattern, sample, and production as separate stages. The client can approve one stage at a time, and you are paid for each stage rather than guessing the whole project at once.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for first samples
pricingTips.body: First samples often need a second round of corrections, extra muslin, and extra fabric. Allow time and material for this instead of assuming the first attempt is final.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present options such as sketches only, sketches plus tech pack, or full development with samples. Clients can choose by budget and you avoid being compared on a single number.

pricingTips.title: Quote materials at a range until confirmed
pricingTips.body: If the fabric is not yet chosen, give an allowance and say it will be adjusted to actual cost. This avoids losing money on expensive silks or specialty trims.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or consultation?
faqs.answer: Many designers offer a short free call but charge for in-depth consultations, mood boards, or sketches made before a contract. If the fee is credited toward the project when the client hires you, it often filters out casual inquiries.

faqs.question: How do I quote a custom garment when I am unsure how long it will take?
faqs.answer: Estimate hours for design, pattern, and construction based on similar past pieces, add a buffer for fittings, and add materials. Give a flat price with set fittings included, and state the rate for extra work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Fabric prices, your availability, and supplier minimums can change, so a stated expiration date lets you reprice without an argument.

fence-installer.intro: Fence installers build and repair wood, vinyl, chain link, aluminum, and steel fences for homeowners, builders, HOAs, and commercial property owners. Invoices usually cover linear footage of fence, gates, posts and concrete, removal of old fencing, and any permit or survey costs. Most work is done by a small crew or a solo owner who buys materials up front and bills in stages.
fence-installer.pricingModel: Most fence work is priced per linear foot, installed, with the price covering posts, rails, pickets or panels, hardware, concrete, and labor. Gates are priced separately as flat fees per gate because they take more hardware and time. Tear-out and haul-away of old fence is usually a separate per-linear-foot line. Extras such as rock or rough terrain, stepped grades, stain or sealer, permits, and utility locates are listed individually or built into a contingency. Many installers take a deposit of 30 to 50 percent to cover materials, then bill the balance on completion. Larger jobs may be billed in draws: deposit, materials delivery, and final. Material prices (especially lumber) move, so quotes often carry an expiration date of 15 to 30 days.

rates.service: Wood privacy fence (6 ft cedar or pine), installed
Aluminum or steel ornamental fence, installed
Fence repair (post replacement, panel or picket repair)

items.description: 6 ft cedar privacy fence, dog-ear pickets, pressure-treated 4x4 posts set in concrete
Single walk gate, 4 ft, with heavy-duty hinges and latch
Double drive gate, 10 ft, steel frame with cedar pickets
Remove and haul away existing chain link fence
Permit fee (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $4,000 received at signing. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Workmanship warranted for 2 years; wood is not warranted against natural warping or checking. Please confirm property line locations were marked before work began.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and fence location
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often own several properties, and the address ties the invoice to the exact job and any permit on file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Total linear footage by fence type and height
invoiceChecklist.why: Footage is the basis of the price. Listing 6 ft cedar and 4 ft picket separately avoids disputes about what was installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gates listed individually with size and hardware
invoiceChecklist.why: Gates are priced separately and hardware choices (self-closing hinges, drop rods, locks) affect cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Many cities and HOAs require permits. Showing the number and fee proves the work was permitted and justifies the pass-through charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extras
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, roots, grade changes, or added sections should appear as their own lines referencing the signed change order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was already paid so the client sees the correct amount owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a contractor license on contracts and invoices above a dollar threshold. Check your state rules.

fence-installer.paymentTerms: Fence installers commonly collect 30 to 50 percent upfront to buy materials, with the balance due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. For jobs over a few thousand dollars, a three-step schedule works well: deposit at signing, a second payment when materials are delivered or posts are set, and the final payment at walkthrough. Accepted methods are typically checks, ACH, and cards, and some contractors add a card fee for large invoices. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract in advance. Some states cap deposits on home improvement work or require specific contract language, so check local rules. Commercial clients and builders often pay net 30 and may require lien waivers or a W-9.

tips.title: Bill the deposit before ordering materials
tips.body: Lumber, panels, and concrete are your biggest cost. Collect the deposit first so you are not financing the job, and note the amount on the final invoice.

tips.title: Get property lines confirmed in writing
tips.body: Most disputes come from fences set on the wrong line. Have the client sign off that the lines are marked or surveyed, and reference that on the invoice.

tips.title: Price gates and tear-out as separate lines
tips.body: Lumping these into the per-foot price hides cost and makes it harder to adjust when scope changes. Separate lines also make change orders easy to document.

tips.title: Add a material price clause
tips.body: If the quote is valid only for a set number of days, material price swings will not eat your margin on a delayed start.

tips.title: Photograph the finished job before invoicing
tips.body: Photos of the finished line, gate operation, and post depth make it easier to collect the final payment if the client raises a complaint.

faqs.question: Should I charge per linear foot or a flat price?
faqs.answer: Per linear foot is the industry standard and is easy to adjust when the final footage differs. Show the footage and the rate on the invoice, then add gates, removal, and extras as separate lines.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on a fence?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states treat fence installation as a taxable sale of materials, others tax only the materials or do not tax labor. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill for hitting rock or buried obstacles?
faqs.answer: Put a clause in your contract that rock, roots, or buried items are extra, then add a line for the added labor or equipment rental, backed by a signed change order if possible.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the permit and survey?
faqs.answer: Yes. List them as pass-through costs at actual price, or include an admin fee if your contract says so. Attach or reference the receipt if the client asks.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to withhold final payment over a small issue?
faqs.answer: Put a punch list process in your contract. Fix the listed items quickly and invoice the balance. Withholding should be limited to the cost of the specific issue, not the whole balance.

estimate.intro: Fence installers quote before any work starts, usually after a site visit to measure the run, check the grade, and note obstacles. Clients often collect two or three bids and compare price per foot, materials, gate hardware, and warranty. A clear written estimate helps you win the job and sets the scope for the final invoice.

scopeChecklist.item: Fence type, height, and material grade
scopeChecklist.why: Cedar versus pressure-treated pine, or 5 ft versus 6 ft vinyl, changes the price a lot. Naming the grade prevents arguments over what was promised.

scopeChecklist.item: Total linear footage and a sketch of the layout
scopeChecklist.why: A simple drawing with measurements and gate locations makes sure both sides agree on where the fence goes.

scopeChecklist.item: Gates: number, size, swing direction, and hardware
scopeChecklist.why: Gates are easy to misunderstand. Spell out width, latch type, and whether the gate is self-closing or lockable.
State whether the client has a survey or will mark the line. Make clear you install where the client indicates.

scopeChecklist.item: Removal of old fence, haul-away, and site cleanup
scopeChecklist.why: Tear-out is often assumed to be included. List it as in or out to avoid surprise charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions: rock, roots, buried utilities, grade changes, permits
scopeChecklist.why: These are the most common sources of extra cost. State how they will be priced if found.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, duration, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Weather and lumber lead times affect schedules. An expiration date protects you from material price changes.

pricingTips.title: Measure the real run, not just the fence line
pricingTips.body: Account for corners, gate openings, slopes, and tie-ins to existing structures. Slopes require stepping or racking, which adds labor and material.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Show a pine option, a cedar option, and a vinyl or aluminum option. Clients often choose the middle one, and you can make a margin on each.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for the unknown
pricingTips.body: If digging conditions are uncertain, add a small allowance or a per-post rock charge so you are not absorbing problems.

pricingTips.title: Itemize gates and removal, not every screw
pricingTips.body: Separate lines for fence, gates, removal, and permits give clarity without overwhelming the client with a parts list.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential fence installers estimate for free. For complex commercial jobs or when drawings are needed, some charge a fee that is credited if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a fence quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Lumber and steel prices change, so a short expiration protects your margin.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding price?
faqs.answer: It depends on how it is written. A quote marked as a fixed price is generally binding if accepted, while an estimate may allow adjustments. State clearly which one you are giving and how changes are handled.

faqs.question: What do I do if the actual footage differs from the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying the final price is based on actual installed linear footage at the quoted rate. Then the invoice can be adjusted up or down without a dispute.

financial-advisor.intro: Independent financial advisors, fee-only planners, and small RIA owners send invoices when clients pay directly for advice instead of through asset-based fees taken from an account. Typical billables are comprehensive financial plans, hourly planning sessions, monthly or annual planning retainers, one-time portfolio reviews, and specialty analyses such as Roth conversions or retirement income projections.
financial-advisor.pricingModel: Advisors usually combine several models. Assets under management (AUM) fees, often 0.5% to 1.25% a year, are normally billed quarterly by the custodian and deducted from the account, so they rarely appear on a standalone invoice. Invoices are most common for flat-fee financial plans, hourly work, and planning retainers billed monthly or quarterly. Project pricing is usually tied to complexity: number of accounts, business ownership, equity compensation, and estate or tax issues. Commissions on insurance or annuity products are paid by the carrier and are not invoiced. Whatever you charge must match your signed advisory agreement and your Form ADV Part 2 or state-required disclosure, so the invoice should never include fees that are not in those documents.

rates.service: Retirement income projection and Social Security timing analysis
Assets under management fee (for reference, usually deducted by custodian)
Workplace retirement plan consulting for small employers

items.description: Comprehensive financial plan: retirement, cash flow, insurance review, and estate checklist
Plan presentation and implementation meeting
Investment policy statement and portfolio review (3 accounts)
Roth conversion analysis, 2025 and 2026 tax years

sampleInvoice.notes: Fees billed per the advisory agreement dated March 4. Payment due within 14 days by ACH or check. This invoice covers planning services only and does not include securities transactions. Questions about fees: reply to this invoice or call the office.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed advisory agreement and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties every charge to the written fee terms your client already agreed to, which also supports your compliance file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Firm name, registration status, and CRD or SEC/state registration number if your rules call for it
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies you as a registered adviser or adviser representative and lets the client verify you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of service and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the client received, such as a flat-fee plan, a quarterly retainer, or a specific consultation, and which dates it covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fee calculation method
invoiceChecklist.why: For hourly work show hours and rate. For flat fees say so. For any percentage fee show the asset value, the percentage, and the period, so the client can check the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Meeting dates and time spent for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often review planning invoices against their calendar, and a log prevents disputes about how long analysis took.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that no commissions or product sales are included, if you are fee-only
invoiceChecklist.why: Reinforces how you are paid and avoids confusion about conflicts of interest.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment instructions and due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Planning clients often pay from bank accounts, so state whether you accept ACH, check, or card and where to send payment.

financial-advisor.paymentTerms: Flat-fee plans often take half upfront and half at delivery of the plan, while retainers are billed monthly or quarterly, sometimes in advance. Prepaying large fees months ahead can trigger extra disclosure or balance sheet rules for registered advisers, so check your regulator's requirements before collecting more than a quarter or so in advance. Net 14 or net 30 is common. Late fees are less common than in trades, but if you charge one, put it in the advisory agreement. Most advisors accept ACH, checks, and cards, and some allow fee payment from a client's account if the agreement and custodian arrangement permit it.

tips.title: Keep invoices consistent with your disclosures
tips.body: Your Form ADV brochure and advisory agreement describe how you charge. Invoice exactly that way, and update the documents before changing your fee structure for existing clients.

tips.title: Define what a retainer includes
tips.body: State the number of meetings, how fast you respond to questions, and whether tax or estate coordination is included. Without limits, retainer clients tend to expand the scope.

tips.title: Bill the plan in milestones
tips.body: Splitting a flat-fee plan into a deposit at the start and a balance at delivery protects you from clients who gather documents slowly or disappear after the data-gathering stage.

tips.title: Send a fee reminder before each recurring charge
tips.body: A short note before a quarterly or annual billing reduces surprises and chargebacks, and it fits the transparency clients expect from an advisor.

tips.title: Track nonbillable time
tips.body: Compliance work, account paperwork, and client emails add up. Review your effective hourly rate on flat-fee engagements each year and adjust fees for new clients.

faqs.question: Should I invoice AUM fees or let the custodian deduct them?
faqs.answer: Most advisors have the custodian deduct them quarterly because it is simpler and gives clients a clear record on their account statement. Some advisors bill AUM fees by invoice instead. Either way, follow your advisory agreement and any custody rules that apply to you.

faqs.question: Can I charge a flat fee upfront for a financial plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, many planners collect a deposit and the balance on delivery. Large fees collected far ahead of the work may trigger additional disclosure requirements, so check with your regulator or compliance consultant.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on financial planning?
faqs.answer: In many states, advisory services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax some professional or financial services. Check your state's rules before you decide not to charge it.

faqs.question: What happens if a client does not pay for a completed plan?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder, then a written notice referencing the agreement. Many advisors hold the final plan delivery until the balance is paid, which is why a milestone deposit helps. Consider collections only after reviewing your agreement.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent preparing for a meeting?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your hourly terms include preparation and analysis. State this in the agreement and show the preparation line separately on the invoice so clients see what they paid for.

estimate.intro: Advisors send a proposal or fee quote after the discovery meeting and before the client signs the advisory agreement. Prospects compare your fee against other advisors, robo-advisor options, and the cost of staying on their own. The quote should explain what the client gets for the fee and how it is calculated.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included, such as retirement, tax, insurance, and estate review
scopeChecklist.why: Planning scope varies widely, and clients assume a plan covers everything unless you say what it does not.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meetings and delivery format
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for the kickoff meeting, plan presentation, and follow-ups so the work does not become open-ended.

scopeChecklist.item: Information the client must provide and the deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Statements, tax returns, and benefit documents drive the timeline, and delays on the client side should not delay your fee.
Show whether the fee is flat, hourly, retainer, or AUM, and give the first-year total so the client can compare.
Tax return preparation, legal drafting, insurance sales, and investment implementation are often separate, and you should list them to avoid scope disputes.
Clarify whether you place trades, manage accounts, or hand over the plan for the client to carry out.
A set expiration date, such as 30 days, and a note that engagement begins on signing the advisory agreement keeps the proposal clear and compliant.

pricingTips.title: Quote a flat fee after a scoping meeting
pricingTips.body: Ask about accounts, income sources, business ownership, and equity compensation before you give a number. Complex households take far longer than a simple one.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three engagement options
pricingTips.body: A one-time plan, a plan with a year of check-ins, and an ongoing retainer let clients choose without you discounting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Show the value in outcomes, not hours
pricingTips.body: Explain the deliverables, such as a retirement income plan and an action list, rather than just listing hours. Flat-fee clients care about results.

pricingTips.title: Account for the real cost of complexity
pricingTips.body: Add to the base fee for multiple properties, stock options, trusts, or a business sale. State the surcharges in the quote so the price is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Should I give a free initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many advisors do for 30 to 60 minutes to confirm fit and scope the work. Make clear that the free meeting is not a planning session and that paid work starts after the agreement is signed.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding for a financial plan?
faqs.answer: A written quote is normally a proposal until the client signs the advisory agreement. Put the quoted fee and scope in that agreement, and note that substantial scope changes will be priced separately.

faqs.question: Can I quote a range instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: You can for hourly or hard-to-scope work, such as a business owner with multiple entities. For standard plans, a fixed fee is clearer and easier for prospects to accept.

financial-consultant.intro: Financial consultants advise small businesses, families, and individuals on budgeting, cash flow, financial planning, business finances, and investment-related decisions. Independent consultants usually invoice for hourly advisory work, fixed-fee projects such as financial models or plan reviews, and recurring monthly retainers. Invoices need to show the scope of work clearly, since clients often compare them against a signed engagement letter.
financial-consultant.pricingModel: Most independent financial consultants use a mix of hourly billing, fixed project fees, and monthly retainers. Hourly rates suit open-ended advisory calls and ad hoc questions. Fixed fees work for defined deliverables such as a financial plan, a cash flow forecast, a business valuation summary, or a budget build-out. Retainers cover ongoing CFO-style support, monthly reporting review, and a set number of meetings. Some consultants add a one-time onboarding or discovery fee. Fee-only planners often bill flat annual or quarterly fees for planning, while a percentage of assets under management is a separate model that is usually billed by the custodian or advisory platform and is regulated. If you provide investment advice for compensation, registration requirements apply and vary by state and by the size of your practice, so check with your state securities regulator or the SEC. Commissions on products are a different compensation model and are not typically invoiced to clients. Expenses such as software subscriptions, data fees, travel, and filing costs are usually billed at cost or listed separately.

rates.service: Hourly advisory consulting (small business or individual)
Cash flow forecast and budget build
Financial model or business valuation summary

items.description: Monthly advisory retainer, March (includes 2 meetings and monthly financial statement review)
13-week cash flow forecast build and walkthrough
Additional advisory time: lender loan package review
Accounting software subscription for client reporting dashboard (March, at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Retainer covers up to 6 hours of advisory time per month; additional time is billed at $175 per hour as agreed in the engagement letter dated January 10. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. This invoice is for consulting services only and does not constitute tax or legal advice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the engagement letter or agreement date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to the signed scope and fee terms, which prevents disputes over what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of each deliverable or service period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, and their accountants, need to see whether a charge is for a forecast, a plan review, or a retainer month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours worked and hourly rate for any time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemized time on advisory calls, research, and reviews supports the total, especially for work outside the retainer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer hours included and overage hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how much of the retainer was used and why extra time is billed on top.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expenses listed separately (software, data fees, filing costs, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps pass-through costs distinct from your fees and lets the client verify them against receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Licenses or registrations where applicable (for example, state or SEC registered investment adviser, CFP certification status)
invoiceChecklist.why: If you are registered or hold a credential, showing it builds trust and may be expected by regulators or institutional clients.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Business clients with accounts payable departments often cannot process an invoice without it.

financial-consultant.paymentTerms: Financial consultants commonly require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent for fixed-fee projects, with the balance due on delivery. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month or billed in advance, with payment due in 7 to 15 days. Hourly work is typically billed monthly in arrears with net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the engagement letter. Most consultants accept ACH transfer, credit card, and check, and some add a card processing surcharge where state law allows. For ongoing clients, automatic recurring payments reduce chasing. Registered advisers should check how their rules treat fees billed in advance, since limits can apply.

tips.title: Put the scope in the engagement letter, then bill against it
tips.body: Financial advice is easy to stretch. A written scope that lists meetings, deliverables, and included hours lets you point to a document when a client asks for extra work.

tips.title: Set a retainer hour cap
tips.body: State how many hours a retainer covers and what overage costs. Without a cap, a flat monthly fee can quietly turn into unpaid work.

tips.title: Bill expenses at cost with receipts available
tips.body: Data subscriptions, reporting software, and filing fees should be itemized. Clients who see them separated are less likely to question your fee.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones for larger projects
tips.body: For valuations, financial models, or multi-month plans, bill at kickoff, draft delivery, and final delivery so you are not carrying the whole project before getting paid.

tips.title: Separate advice from tax or legal services
tips.body: Add a line stating what you do not provide, such as tax preparation or legal advice, unless you are licensed and engaged for it. This keeps invoices consistent with your engagement scope.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly billing when the scope is unclear or the client asks open-ended questions. Use a flat fee for defined deliverables like a forecast or plan, since clients prefer knowing the cost upfront. Many consultants combine both: a retainer for ongoing work and hourly rates for extra requests.

faqs.question: Can I invoice for time spent on research and preparation?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your engagement letter says preparation and analysis are billable. Most consultants bill for prep, document review, and follow-up emails in addition to meeting time. Describe the work on the invoice so the client understands what the hours covered.

faqs.question: Do I need to be registered to charge for financial advice?
faqs.answer: It depends on what you do. Giving investment advice for compensation generally triggers adviser registration at the state or federal level, with some exemptions. General budgeting, business finance consulting, and education often fall outside it. Check with your state securities regulator or a securities attorney before billing for investment advice.

faqs.question: How do I bill a retainer when the client uses fewer hours than included?
faqs.answer: Follow what your agreement says. Many consultants treat unused retainer hours as expiring each month, since the retainer pays for availability. If you allow rollover, state the limit and expiration clearly on the invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional consulting services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax certain services and rules differ on software or data products you resell. Check your state department of revenue or ask your accountant.

estimate.intro: Financial consultants send a proposal or quote before starting a project, usually after a discovery call. Clients typically compare scope, deliverables, timeline, and whether the fee is fixed or hourly against other consultants or against hiring an in-house bookkeeper or CFO. A clear estimate also sets expectations for what information the client must provide.

scopeChecklist.item: Specific deliverables (for example, 12-month forecast, budget template, written plan, valuation memo)
scopeChecklist.why: Defines exactly what the client receives so they cannot later expect additional reports at the same price.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meetings and revision rounds included
scopeChecklist.why: Advisory projects often expand through extra calls and edits. Setting limits protects your time.

scopeChecklist.item: Client responsibilities and required data (bank statements, P&Ls, tax returns, access to accounting software)
scopeChecklist.why: Delays from missing documents are the most common cause of overruns, and this gives you grounds to adjust timing or fees.
Clients want to know when to expect drafts and final deliverables, and milestones can be tied to payments.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions (tax preparation, legal advice, bookkeeping, investment management, implementation)
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies the boundaries of your service and helps avoid liability for work you were not engaged to perform.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee structure, deposit, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Shows whether the price is fixed or time-based and when payments are due.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and how scope changes are handled
scopeChecklist.why: A 30-day expiration and a change-order process keep pricing fair if the client's situation shifts.

pricingTips.title: Price the project from hours plus a buffer
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours for data gathering, analysis, modeling, and review, then add 15 to 25 percent for client delays and revisions. Quote the total as a flat fee instead of showing the buffer.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and comprehensive package, such as a budget only, budget plus forecast, or full plan with quarterly check-ins, lets clients choose and often leads them to the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Use a paid discovery session
pricingTips.body: Charging for an initial assessment, and crediting it toward the project if the client moves forward, filters out clients who are not ready and compensates you for scoping time.

pricingTips.title: Explain the value in the client's terms
pricingTips.body: Connect the fee to outcomes such as improved cash visibility, loan readiness, or a clearer retirement timeline. Avoid promising specific investment returns or savings amounts.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed quote when deliverables are well defined and you have done similar work. Give an hourly estimate with a not-to-exceed amount when the client's records or goals are uncertain.

faqs.question: How detailed should my proposal be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list deliverables, exclusions, timeline, and fees on one to three pages. Longer documents are fine for large engagements, but the key terms should be easy to find.

faqs.question: Can I charge for preparing a proposal?
faqs.answer: Short proposals are usually free. For complex engagements that require reviewing financial records first, many consultants charge for a paid discovery or assessment phase and then quote the main project.

faqs.question: What if the client's financial records turn out to be worse than expected?
