faqs.answer: Include a clause in your estimate saying the fee assumes reasonably organized records. If cleanup is needed, you can issue a change order or recommend a bookkeeper before the project continues.

financial-planner.intro: Financial planners are independent or small-firm advisors who help individuals, families, and business owners with retirement planning, investments, insurance, tax strategy, and estate coordination. Fee-only and hybrid planners send invoices for planning engagements, hourly consultations, and recurring advisory retainers. Planners who earn commissions or bill assets under management usually have the fee deducted by the custodian, so invoices mostly apply to flat-fee, hourly, and subscription work.
financial-planner.pricingModel: Fee-only planners typically use one of four models: a flat fee for a comprehensive financial plan, an hourly rate for project work or one-off questions, an ongoing retainer (often billed monthly or quarterly) for continuous planning, or a percentage of assets under management (AUM) that is usually deducted from the account by the custodian rather than invoiced. Flat plan fees are often set by the complexity of the household: number of accounts, equity compensation, business ownership, rental properties, and estate issues. Retainers commonly scale with income or net worth. Many planners combine an initial planning fee with a smaller annual or monthly fee for ongoing review. Fees should be disclosed in writing before work begins, and registered advisors must follow the disclosure rules in their Form ADV and state or SEC requirements.

rates.service: Retirement income or Social Security analysis
Equity compensation or stock option planning
Investment policy statement and portfolio review
Financial coaching session for early-career clients

items.description: Comprehensive financial plan: retirement projections, cash flow, insurance review, estate checklist (final deliverable and 90-minute presentation)
Employer stock option and RSU tax timing analysis
Follow-up Social Security claiming strategy meeting
Less: deposit paid at engagement signing

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 15 days of invoice date. Fees are for planning services only and do not include investment management or product commissions. Payment by ACH, check, or card. Deposit was received on the engagement date per the signed advisory agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed advisory or planning agreement and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to the scope and fee schedule the client agreed to, which matters for compliance and disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of each deliverable or service period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients should see whether they are paying for a plan, a quarterly retainer period, or hours of consultation, such as "Q3 planning retainer, July-September."

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and hourly rate for any time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly work needs dates and time spent so the client can verify it against the meetings or analysis they received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or prior payments applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Many planners collect half the plan fee up front. Showing the credit prevents confusion about the remaining balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Firm name, advisor name, and registration status where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Registered investment advisor firms are often expected to identify themselves consistently with their Form ADV and state or SEC registration.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that no commissions or product fees are included (if fee-only)
invoiceChecklist.why: Reinforces the compensation disclosure and distinguishes the invoice from fees charged by custodians or fund companies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment instructions and accepted methods
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often pay large planning fees, so clear ACH or check instructions reduce delays and avoid sending sensitive account details by email.

financial-planner.paymentTerms: Flat-fee plans commonly require 50 percent at signing and the balance on delivery or at the presentation meeting. Retainers are billed monthly or quarterly in advance, often by recurring ACH or card. Hourly work is usually invoiced after the meeting or at month end with net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees are less common in this field than in trades, and many planners instead pause work or deliverables until the balance is paid, as stated in the agreement. Credit card fees can be significant on large plan fees, so many planners prefer ACH or check. Some advisors can bill fees from an account through the custodian, but that requires written client authorization and should follow applicable rules.

tips.title: Put the fee schedule in the engagement agreement
tips.body: State the plan fee, hourly rate, retainer amount, and what is excluded before the first meeting. An invoice should never be the first time a client sees a number.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before starting the data gathering
tips.body: Plan building takes many hours of reviewing statements, tax returns, and benefits documents. A 50 percent deposit protects you if the client disappears after the discovery meeting.

tips.title: Define what a retainer includes
tips.body: Specify the number of meetings, response times, and whether tax return reviews or one-off projects are covered. Without limits, retainer clients tend to expand the scope without paying more.

tips.title: Keep time records even on flat-fee work
tips.body: Tracking hours shows whether your flat fees are profitable and gives you data to reprice complex households or add change-order fees.

tips.title: Send invoices through a secure channel
tips.body: Invoices may reference account or plan details. Avoid putting account numbers or Social Security numbers on them, and use secure delivery when possible.

faqs.question: Should I invoice clients or deduct fees from their accounts?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Invoicing works for flat-fee and hourly planning where you do not manage assets. Deducting AUM fees from an account generally requires written client authorization and compliance with custodian and regulatory rules. Check what applies to your registration.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a planning invoice?
faqs.answer: You can if your signed agreement states the late fee and your state allows it. Many planners avoid late fees and instead specify that deliverables or ongoing services pause until the invoice is paid.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a retainer if the client cancels mid-quarter?
faqs.answer: Spell out the cancellation terms in the agreement. Many planners bill in advance and refund the unused portion on a prorated basis, or require 30 days' notice. Whatever you choose, apply it consistently.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on financial planning services?
faqs.answer: In most states, financial planning services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax certain professional or advisory services. Check your state department of revenue or ask your accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do if my fee is based on a percentage of assets but I still send an invoice?
faqs.answer: Show the calculation: the asset value used, the fee percentage, the billing period, and any proration. Many regulators expect fee calculations to be clear and consistent with your disclosure documents.

estimate.intro: Planners send a proposal or fee quote after an introductory meeting, once they understand the household's complexity and goals. Prospects often compare your fee against other advisors, robo-advice platforms, and the cost of doing nothing, so the quote needs to show what they get and how it is priced.

scopeChecklist.why: List retirement, cash flow, insurance, taxes, education funding, and estate coordination separately so the client knows what is and is not covered.
State whether the client receives a written report, a presentation, a retirement projection model, or an action list, so expectations match.
Planning typically runs three to eight weeks. Specifying meetings and delivery dates keeps the engagement from dragging on.
Tax returns, account statements, pay stubs, and insurance policies are needed to start. Delays on the client's side should affect the timeline, not your fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as investment management, tax preparation, and legal drafting
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a plan includes implementing it. Make clear what is a separate service or requires another professional.
Show the total fee, how much is due at signing, and when the balance is due.

scopeChecklist.item: Ongoing service options and their cost
scopeChecklist.why: Presenting a follow-up retainer or annual review fee at the outset avoids surprises after the plan is delivered.

pricingTips.title: Price by complexity tiers
pricingTips.body: Set a base fee for straightforward households and add fixed increments for rental properties, business ownership, equity compensation, or multiple pensions. This makes quotes consistent and easy to explain.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total, then show the monthly equivalent
pricingTips.body: A $3,000 plan fee can feel large, while a split-payment option or ongoing retainer can make it easier to commit. Offer both only if you are willing to deliver either.

pricingTips.title: Use the hourly rate as a check, not the headline
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours you expect the plan to take and confirm the flat fee yields your target hourly rate. Present the flat fee to the client.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the proposal
pricingTips.body: Fees depend on current workload and the client's financial situation. A 30-day validity period keeps quotes from being used months later.

faqs.question: Should I give a free initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many planners offer a free 30 to 60 minute introductory meeting to determine fit and scope. After that, a paid engagement should be in writing. If the client wants detailed advice during the first meeting, consider charging for it.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of a fixed plan fee?
faqs.answer: A range is acceptable if the complexity is unclear, but a fixed fee is easier for clients to accept. If you quote a range, state what factors would move the final fee and require written approval above the upper end.

faqs.question: What if the client's situation turns out to be more complicated than expected?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that additional work outside the original scope, such as business valuation questions or multiple state tax issues, will be quoted separately or billed hourly with the client's approval.

faqs.question: Does a signed estimate count as an agreement?
faqs.answer: For planners, the proposal usually needs to be accompanied by or converted into a formal advisory agreement and any required disclosures. Check what your registration and state rules require before work begins.

fitness-coach.intro: Fitness coaches include personal trainers, online coaches, small-group instructors, and nutrition-minded strength coaches who work with clients one-on-one or in small groups. They invoice for training sessions, session packages, monthly coaching programs, assessments, and custom programming. Many work independently, rent floor space at a gym, or train clients at home, outdoors, or online.
fitness-coach.pricingModel: Most fitness coaches price by the session or by the package. In-person one-on-one training is usually sold in bundles of 8, 12, or 24 sessions, with a lower per-session rate the larger the bundle. Online coaches tend to charge a flat monthly fee that covers programming, check-ins, and messaging support. Small-group training is priced per person per session or as a monthly membership. Add-ons such as initial assessments, body composition testing, custom meal guidance, and travel to a client's home are billed separately or built into higher rates. Coaches who rent space at a gym often factor in a facility fee or revenue split when setting their rate. Cancellation and expiration rules for packages are part of the pricing and should be stated clearly.

rates.service: Initial fitness assessment and goal setting

items.description: Personal training session package (12 sessions, 60 min each), strength and conditioning
Initial fitness assessment and movement screen
Nutrition guidance add-on, monthly check-ins and meal framework
Home visit travel fee (over 10 miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Package of 12 sessions is valid for 90 days from the first session date. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are forfeited. Payment due within 7 days. Accepted by card, ACH, or Zelle. Thank you for training with me.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and session count
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients should see exactly how many sessions they bought, the length of each, and the per-session rate so the balance is easy to track.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates or start date
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates support expiration terms and help resolve disputes about whether a session took place.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expiration date for the package
invoiceChecklist.why: Unused sessions are a common source of arguments, and a stated expiration keeps things clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the notice window on the invoice reduces pushback when you charge for a missed session.

invoiceChecklist.item: Location or format of training
invoiceChecklist.why: Gym, home, outdoor, and virtual sessions are often priced differently, and some gyms require a facility fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Assessments, nutrition guidance, and travel fees should be itemized so clients understand what is included in the base rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period for recurring coaching
invoiceChecklist.why: Monthly online coaching needs a clear start and end date so renewals and pauses are easy to track.

fitness-coach.paymentTerms: Most fitness coaches bill in advance. Session packages are usually paid in full before the first session, and monthly coaching is charged at the start of each month, often by recurring card or ACH payment. Some coaches offer a small discount for paying a large package upfront or a split-pay option for 24-session bundles. Due dates of due on receipt or within 7 days are common. Late fees are less common than simply pausing sessions until payment clears, but if you charge one, state it in your written agreement. Common payment methods include credit and debit cards, ACH, Zelle, Venmo, and cash or check for in-person clients. Keep a signed client agreement that covers cancellation windows, package expiration, and refund terms.

tips.title: Bill in advance, not after
tips.body: Packages and monthly fees paid upfront protect your income when clients skip sessions. Billing after the fact turns every missed payment into a collections conversation.

tips.title: Write down your cancellation policy and repeat it on invoices
tips.body: A 24-hour notice policy is typical. Putting it in your agreement and on each invoice makes charging for late cancellations easier to defend.

tips.title: Set package expiration dates
tips.body: Without an expiration, clients can hold sessions for a year or more, which makes your schedule and income harder to plan. 60 to 120 days is a common window.

tips.title: Track sessions used against sessions paid
tips.body: Keep a running log of completed sessions. When you invoice a renewal, you can show the balance and avoid disputes about how many sessions remain.

tips.title: Itemize gym and travel costs separately
tips.body: If you pay a floor fee to a gym or travel to clients, build that into your rate or list it as a separate line. Hiding it makes it easy to undercharge for in-home training.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or sell packages?
faqs.answer: Packages are more common and give you upfront cash and more committed clients. Offer a single-session rate that is higher than the per-session package rate so clients have a reason to commit to a bundle.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a session if the client cancels late?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your written policy says so and the client agreed to it. Most coaches require 12 to 24 hours notice. Apply the policy consistently and mention it on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for monthly online coaching?
faqs.answer: Create one recurring invoice or charge per month describing what is included, such as programming updates, weekly check-ins, and messaging access. List the billing period and renewal date.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on training sessions?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax fitness or personal training services and many do not. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant before you set up billing.

faqs.question: What should I do about unused sessions at the end of a package?
faqs.answer: Follow the expiration terms in your agreement. Some coaches allow a short extension for illness or injury, but a clear default of forfeiture after the expiration date keeps things simple.

estimate.intro: Fitness coaches usually send a quote after an initial consultation or assessment, when a prospective client wants to know the cost of reaching a goal such as weight loss, strength gain, or training for an event. Clients compare per-session rates, package sizes, what is included, and whether sessions happen at a gym, at home, or online.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and length of sessions per week
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 2 sessions a week for 12 weeks is very different from 3 sessions, and the client should see the total commitment.
Gym, home, outdoor, and virtual sessions carry different costs, and gym access or facility fees may not be included.
Programming between sessions, messaging support, nutrition guidance, and progress check-ins should be stated so clients know what they are buying.
If the client needs a gym membership, bands, or other equipment, say so and note who pays.
A start date and end date set expectations for how quickly sessions should be used.
Spelling these out in the quote prevents disagreements after the client has already paid.
Many coaches require a health questionnaire, doctor clearance for certain conditions, and a signed liability waiver before starting.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: Show a small, medium, and large package with a decreasing per-session rate. Most clients pick the middle option, and the larger one anchors the price.

pricingTips.title: Price based on goal and commitment, not only time
pricingTips.body: A client training for a marathon or wedding date needs more structure than someone maintaining fitness. Higher-touch programs with check-ins and adjustments justify a higher rate.

pricingTips.title: Account for your real costs
pricingTips.body: Gym floor fees, insurance, certifications, travel time, and software all reduce your hourly take-home. Include them when setting rates, especially for in-home sessions.

pricingTips.title: Make the first step easy to say yes to
pricingTips.body: A paid assessment or a short 4-session starter pack lets a new client try your approach without committing to a large package.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many coaches offer a free 15 to 30 minute consultation to discuss goals, then charge for a full assessment with movement screening and baseline testing. Choose based on your market, and be consistent.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical. Rates and schedule availability change, so a stated expiration date keeps you from honoring old prices indefinitely.

faqs.question: Can I adjust my quote if a client wants fewer sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Recalculate based on your tier pricing, since a smaller package usually has a higher per-session rate. Send a revised quote so the new terms are in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short agreement and liability waiver signed before the first session covers payment, cancellation, and health disclosures. Ask a local attorney or your insurer for template guidance.

flooring.intro: Flooring installers, contractors, and small flooring companies install and refinish hardwood, laminate, luxury vinyl plank, tile, carpet, and other surfaces in homes and commercial spaces. Invoices usually cover installation labor by the square foot, materials, subfloor prep, removal of old flooring, and trim or transition pieces.
flooring.pricingModel: Most flooring work is priced per square foot for installation labor, with the rate depending on the material and the layout. Tile and herringbone patterns cost more than straight-lay laminate or vinyl plank. Prep work is usually billed separately, either per square foot (self-leveling, underlayment) or as a flat line item (furniture moving, demolition, haul-away). Materials are either supplied by the client or bought by the installer and billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10-25%, to cover ordering, hauling, and waste. Include a waste factor of 7-15% in material quantities, higher for diagonal or pattern installs. Stairs are priced per step or per stair, and trim, baseboards, shoe molding, and transitions are priced per linear foot or per piece. Sanding and refinishing hardwood is priced per square foot. Many installers set a minimum job charge for small rooms or repairs.

rates.service: Laminate or luxury vinyl plank installation (labor)
Removal and disposal of old flooring

items.description: Remove and dispose of existing carpet and pad, living room and hallway
Floor prep: scrape, patch low spots, apply self-leveling compound
Install luxury vinyl plank (labor), straight lay
LVP flooring, 7 mm click-lock, 12% waste included (materials at cost plus 15%)
Install new shoe molding and 2 metal transitions
Furniture moving and reset

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received at material order. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Leave 48 hours before moving heavy furniture back onto the floor. Keep leftover planks (3 boxes) for future repairs. Installation is warrantied against workmanship defects for 1 year; the manufacturer's warranty covers the product.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage by room and total
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client check the measured area against the quote and makes any change in billed quantity easy to explain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material brand, product line, color, and quantity ordered
invoiceChecklist.why: Avoids disputes over what was installed and helps with warranty claims or future matching of leftover stock.

invoiceChecklist.item: Waste factor or overage included
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question why they paid for more flooring than their room size. Showing the percentage explains it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for prep, demolition, and haul-away
invoiceChecklist.why: Subfloor work is where surprises appear. Itemizing it shows what was added beyond the original scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders with dates and approval
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden rot, uneven concrete, or added rooms change the price. A reference to the signed or emailed approval prevents arguments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices for flooring work above a set dollar threshold. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the money already paid for materials so the client sees exactly what is owed at completion.

flooring.paymentTerms: Flooring jobs typically take a deposit of 30-50% when the contract is signed or at material order, since special-order flooring is often non-returnable. Larger jobs may add a progress payment when materials arrive or when demolition and prep are done, with the balance due on completion or within 7 days. Residential clients usually pay by check, card, or bank transfer, and commercial clients or builders often use net 15 or net 30 terms. State late fees (commonly 1-1.5% per month) in your contract before work begins. Do not leave a job without clear payment terms in writing, and check your state's rules on deposit limits for home improvement contracts.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before ordering materials
tips.body: Special-order flooring cannot be returned, and restocking fees are steep. A deposit that covers materials means you are never financing the client's floor.

tips.title: Bill prep and subfloor work separately
tips.body: Flatness problems, moisture, and old adhesive are common and time-consuming. Listing prep as its own line item makes it easy to add when you find problems and keeps your installation rate competitive.

tips.title: Document site conditions with photos
tips.body: Take photos of the subfloor, moisture readings, and any pre-existing damage before you start. Attach them to the job record so you can support extra charges or defend against later complaints.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge for small jobs
tips.body: A single room or a repair can take as long to set up and haul as a bigger job. A minimum of $300-600, depending on your market, covers travel, setup, and tools.

tips.title: Invoice at completion, not at your convenience
tips.body: Send the final invoice the day you finish the walkthrough, while the client is happy with the floor. Delays push payment back and invite nitpicking.

faqs.question: Should I charge for materials separately from labor?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Separate lines show the client what they pay for product and what they pay for installation. If you buy materials and mark them up, list the markup as part of the material price or as a handling fee, according to your contract.

faqs.question: How do I bill for waste and extra material?
faqs.answer: Add the waste factor to the quantity you order, typically 7-10% for straight layouts and 10-15% for diagonal or patterned installs, and bill for the total ordered. State the factor in your quote and on the invoice. Leftover material usually belongs to the client, who may want it for future repairs.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra if the subfloor is worse than expected?
faqs.answer: You can, if your contract allows for it. Spell out in the quote that prep is estimated and that unforeseen conditions such as moisture, rot, or severe unevenness will be billed as a change order. Get written approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Do I charge by the square foot or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Square foot is the standard for installation because clients can compare quotes easily. Hourly rates, often $50-100, are used for repairs, small fixes, and tasks where the scope is unclear, such as troubleshooting a squeaky floor.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to withhold payment over a minor flaw?
faqs.answer: Fix legitimate defects promptly, and note any punch-list items at the final walkthrough. If the work is complete aside from small items, your contract can allow a limited holdback tied to those items rather than the whole balance.

estimate.intro: Flooring estimates are sent before any materials are ordered, usually after an in-home measure and a look at the subfloor. Clients typically compare two or three quotes, and they look at the price per square foot, what is included in prep and removal, and who supplies the material.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured square footage and rooms included
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may count only the main room. Listing every room, closet, and hallway prevents a dispute about whether they were included.

scopeChecklist.item: Flooring product, brand, color, and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: Prices differ widely between product tiers. Naming the exact product keeps quotes comparable and confirms what the client chose.

scopeChecklist.item: Subfloor prep included and the limits of it
scopeChecklist.why: State what leveling or patching is covered, and that more extensive repairs, such as replacing damaged plywood or fixing moisture problems, will cost extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Demolition, removal, and disposal of old flooring
scopeChecklist.why: Removing glued-down vinyl, tile, or multiple layers can double the labor. Specify what is being removed and who hauls it away.
These items are often assumed to be included. Listing them, or noting they are excluded, avoids a surprise at the end.
Moving heavy furniture and pulling appliances takes time and creates liability. State whether you do it or the client does.
Hardwood and some LVP need days to acclimate, and finishes need time to cure. Setting expectations explains the timeline and when the room can be used.

pricingTips.title: Price from your own measurements
pricingTips.body: Measure the rooms yourself rather than relying on the client's numbers or a floor plan. Round up for closets, doorways, and angles, and show the waste factor you are using.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, and best options
pricingTips.body: Giving the client a laminate or LVP option, a mid-range engineered wood, and a solid hardwood option with the same scope makes it easier to choose and avoids a flat no.

pricingTips.title: Keep material pricing current
pricingTips.body: Flooring costs can change between the quote and the order. Put a validity period on the estimate, often 14-30 days, and note that material prices are subject to change after that.

pricingTips.title: Break out prep as an allowance
pricingTips.body: If you cannot see the subfloor condition, give a prep allowance and say that the final cost depends on what is found. This keeps your bid competitive without taking on the risk.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential flooring installers give free estimates for standard jobs. For complex projects, commercial bids, or long drives, some charge a fee of $50-150 and credit it back if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Material prices and lead times change, and your schedule fills up, so a fixed validity period protects you.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on how it is written. A fixed-price quote that the client signs usually acts as a contract. An estimate that says it is approximate allows for changes. State clearly which one you are giving and how changes will be handled.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before ordering materials?
faqs.answer: Yes. Get a signed estimate or contract and the deposit first. Special-order flooring is often non-returnable, and you do not want to be stuck with product the client cancels.

florist.intro: Florists design and sell fresh and silk flower arrangements for weddings, funerals, corporate accounts, and everyday occasions. Invoices usually cover custom event florals, delivery and setup, rentals such as arches and vases, and recurring weekly arrangements for restaurants, hotels, and offices.
florist.pricingModel: Most florists price by the piece for retail and event work: a bridal bouquet, a boutonniere, a centerpiece, or a ceremony arch each has its own price. Wedding and event work is often sold as a package or a total budget, with a design fee or minimum order on top. The common approach is to take the wholesale cost of flowers and greens and multiply it by 3 to 4 to cover labor, supplies, overhead, and waste, then add separate lines for delivery, setup and breakdown, and rentals. Sympathy work, such as casket sprays and standing arrangements, is priced per piece. Recurring corporate accounts are usually billed weekly or monthly at a set price per arrangement, with a delivery fee. Rush orders, holiday weeks (Valentine's Day, Mother's Day), and hard-to-source flowers often carry a surcharge or higher pricing.

rates.service: Sympathy standing spray or casket piece

items.description: Bridal bouquet, garden rose and ranunculus, ivory and blush
Bridesmaid bouquets
Boutonnieres
Reception centerpieces, low compote style
Ceremony arch florals (arch rental not included)
Delivery, setup, and breakdown, venue 25 miles away

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,000 received at booking. Balance due 14 days before the event date. Rental vases and stands remain the property of the studio and must be returned within 3 days of the event or a replacement fee applies. Flowers are seasonal and substitutions of similar color and style may be made if a variety is unavailable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, time, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Florals are made for a specific day and place, and this ties the invoice to the signed order and delivery window.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of pieces with quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often add or remove bouquets and centerpieces, so listing each piece shows exactly what was ordered at final count.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for delivery, setup, and breakdown
invoiceChecklist.why: Venue distance and timing affect labor, and separating these fees makes them easy to explain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental items and return terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Arches, stands, and vases are reusable and costly to replace. List each item, the return date, and any replacement fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Flowers are ordered from wholesalers days before an event, so showing the deposit and a firm balance date keeps cash flow predictable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Substitution and seasonal availability note
invoiceChecklist.why: Flower varieties can change due to supply, so a short note sets the expectation that colors and style will be matched but not always exact varieties.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax and tax-exempt details where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax flowers and floral services, while some clients such as nonprofits may be exempt. Record the tax charged or the exemption certificate on file.

florist.paymentTerms: For weddings and large events, most florists collect a non-refundable retainer or deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking, with the balance due 7 to 30 days before the event. Many require the final guest count or order changes by a set date, often 2 to 4 weeks out. Retail and sympathy orders are paid in full at the time of order, since the flowers are perishable. Corporate and restaurant accounts are normally billed weekly or monthly with net 15 or net 30 terms, and a late fee of 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in advance. Cards, bank transfer, and checks are the usual methods, and many florists add a card processing fee only where local rules allow it.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the event
tips.body: Flowers cannot be resold once arranged, and you will be busy on the event day. Require full payment ahead of time, and state it in your contract so you are not chasing a client at a reception.

tips.title: Build in waste and a buffer
tips.body: Wholesale stems arrive with some loss from damage and bloom timing. Price with a margin that covers waste, and add a small buffer of extra stems for repairs and last-minute fixes.

tips.title: Bill rentals and unreturned items clearly
tips.body: Keep a written list of arches, stands, and vases that leave your shop. Add a replacement fee to the terms, and invoice it if items are not returned by the date you set.

tips.title: Update the invoice when the order changes
tips.body: Guest counts and party sizes often shift in the final weeks. Send a revised invoice with a new total each time the order changes so the final balance matches what you actually make.

tips.title: Charge a premium for peak weeks
tips.body: Wholesale prices rise around Valentine's Day and Mother's Day, and labor is tight. Set a holiday pricing policy or minimum order and tell clients before they order.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit for a wedding florist order?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most wedding florists take a non-refundable retainer of 25 to 50 percent to reserve the date, since they turn down other bookings and buy stems specifically for that order. Put the amount and refund terms in your contract and show the deposit as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on flowers and delivery?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states tax flower sales, and some also tax delivery or set-up fees, while some exempt certain services. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant, and list tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for rental items like arches and vases?
faqs.answer: List each rental as its own line with a rental fee, if any, and note the return date. State a replacement fee in your terms, and some florists also hold a refundable deposit on high-value pieces.

faqs.question: What if the client cuts the order after I have bought flowers?
faqs.answer: Your contract should set a cutoff date after which changes cannot reduce the total. Once flowers are ordered from your wholesaler, you are generally owed payment for the order as agreed, so set that date based on your wholesaler's lead time.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice a restaurant or office with weekly flowers?
faqs.answer: Most florists bill monthly for steady accounts, listing each delivery date and arrangement on one statement, with net 15 or net 30 terms. For new accounts, weekly billing or card on file reduces the risk of late payment.

estimate.intro: Florists send estimates when a bride, event planner, or business asks for a price before committing, often after a consultation and often alongside quotes from two or three other florists. Clients compare total cost, the number and size of pieces, and what is included, such as delivery, setup, and rentals.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, venue, and delivery or setup time
scopeChecklist.why: The date and location decide labor, travel, and whether you can take the job at all, and they tie the quote to a specific booking.

scopeChecklist.item: List of pieces with quantities and sizes
scopeChecklist.why: A bouquet or centerpiece can vary widely in size and stem count, so listing each piece prevents disputes about what was expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Color palette and flower types, with substitution policy
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may picture specific flowers that are out of season. State that you will match color and style but may substitute varieties.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: delivery, setup, breakdown, and rentals
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume these are included. Listing them, and their cost, shows what is and is not covered by the price.
Pricing depends on the final number of pieces, so set a date after which counts are locked in.
Wholesale prices and your calendar both change, so state how long the quote holds before it needs to be refreshed.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, balance date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: These show the payment schedule up front and make it clear the date is reserved only once the deposit is paid.

pricingTips.title: Quote from wholesale cost with a markup
pricingTips.body: Price the recipe for each piece by stem count at current wholesale costs, then apply your markup, commonly 3 to 4 times flower cost. Add hard goods such as foam, ribbon, and containers, then labor, delivery, and rentals as separate lines.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Give a good, better, best version, such as fewer large centerpieces versus more small ones, or a full arch versus a smaller installation. Tiers help clients fit their budget without you discounting your standard pricing.

pricingTips.title: Ask for a budget early
pricingTips.body: Many clients have a number in mind but do not share it. Asking about budget at the consultation lets you design toward it and avoids spending time on a proposal that is far out of range.

pricingTips.title: Account for price changes in flower markets
pricingTips.body: Wholesale costs can rise for peonies, garden roses, and holiday-week stems. Note that final pricing may adjust if stems are unusually costly, or lock the price by collecting a deposit and ordering early.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or proposal?
faqs.answer: Some florists offer a short free consultation and charge a design fee, often $50 to $250, for detailed proposals or mockups, and credit it to the order if the client books. This helps filter out clients who only want ideas.

faqs.question: How long should a wedding florist quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. After that, your date may be taken and flower costs may change. Booking is typically confirmed only when the signed contract and deposit are received.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the scope changes, such as more guests, added pieces, or a different venue. Say in the quote that the price applies to the listed items and that changes will be quoted in writing.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the client has only a photo from Pinterest?
faqs.answer: Identify the flowers in the photo and check their availability and cost for your date. Quote the closest version you can make, and note that a photo is used as inspiration and not an exact copy.

food-delivery.intro: Food delivery businesses move prepared meals, catering orders, groceries, and meal-prep boxes from a kitchen or store to a customer. The people sending invoices are usually independent couriers, small local delivery companies, or owner-operators who deliver for restaurants, caterers, offices, and meal-prep brands. They bill for delivery runs, wait time, mileage, and extras like after-hours or bulk orders, and often invoice a business client monthly instead of collecting from each customer.
food-delivery.pricingModel: Most business-to-business food delivery is priced per delivery, with a base fee that covers a set distance (often 3 to 5 miles) and a per-mile charge beyond that. Many operators add surcharges for wait time at pickup, large or multi-stop orders, rush or same-day requests, evenings, weekends, and holidays. Catering delivery is often a flat fee that includes setup, such as placing chafing dishes, labeling, and arranging a buffet. Regular clients such as restaurants or meal-prep companies may get a weekly or monthly rate, a retainer for scheduled routes, or a per-route price with a minimum number of stops. Tips are separate from fees and should be listed that way. If you deliver for a platform, the platform sets your pay, so these rates apply to direct clients you invoice yourself.

rates.service: Wait time at pickup or drop-off (after grace period)

items.description: Standard local deliveries, restaurant to customer addresses (0-5 miles), Oct 1-31
Additional mileage beyond 5 miles
Catering delivery with buffet setup, office lunch for 40 (Oct 12)
Wait time at pickup beyond 10-minute grace period
Weekend and evening surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Delivery log with order numbers, addresses, and timestamps is available on request. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due. Accepted: ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Order numbers or delivery IDs with dates and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients match each delivery to their own records, and a log of pickup and drop-off times settles disputes about late or missed orders.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off addresses (or zones)
invoiceChecklist.why: Mileage and zone charges only make sense if the client can see where each run started and ended.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage per delivery or the zone used
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra distance is a separate line item, and showing it avoids pushback on the per-mile charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wait time with start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Wait charges are the most commonly questioned line, so record when you arrived, when the order was handed over, and the grace period you apply.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surcharges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Rush, after-hours, holiday, and large-order fees should be visible lines so clients can see the base rate has not changed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tips and customer-paid amounts shown separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Tips belong to the driver and are not part of your fee, and food or cash collected on a client's behalf should not be mixed into your revenue.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, commercial insurance, and food handler or permit numbers where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients, especially caterers and corporate accounts, ask for proof of insurance, and local rules may require permits for transporting food.

food-delivery.paymentTerms: Single-customer or one-off catering deliveries are usually paid at booking or on delivery by card. Business clients such as restaurants, caterers, and meal-prep companies are typically invoiced weekly or monthly, with terms of net 7 to net 30. Weekly invoicing keeps cash flow steady for solo drivers who pay for fuel and maintenance up front. For large catering jobs or scheduled routes, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, along with a cancellation fee if the order is cancelled within a few hours. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing before work begins. ACH, card, and checks are widely accepted, and cash is sometimes used for one-time deliveries.

tips.title: Set a clear grace period for waiting
tips.body: Give 5 to 10 minutes free at pickup, then charge in 15-minute blocks. Put the policy in your service agreement and on the invoice so wait time is not a surprise.

tips.title: Invoice weekly for recurring clients
tips.body: Fuel, tolls, and vehicle wear are costs you pay immediately. Weekly billing with a delivery log keeps unpaid balances small and makes errors easier to catch.

tips.title: Track mileage for every run
tips.body: A mileage log supports your per-mile charges and is useful at tax time. In the US, the IRS allows either actual expenses or the standard mileage rate for business driving, so check which fits your situation.

tips.title: Charge for the full trip, not just the drop
tips.body: If the return trip is empty, a long route should be priced to cover it. Build a minimum per-delivery fee so short, low-value runs do not cost you money.

tips.title: Keep tips and reimbursements off your fee lines
tips.body: List parking, tolls, or items bought on the client's behalf as pass-through charges, and show tips on their own. It keeps your invoice clean and your records accurate.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or by mile?
faqs.answer: Many drivers use both: a flat base fee that covers a set radius, plus a per-mile charge beyond it. Flat fees are easy for clients to understand, and the mileage add-on protects you on longer runs.

faqs.question: Can I charge for waiting time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you tell the client in advance. State a grace period and a rate per 15 minutes in your agreement or quote, then list the actual wait on the invoice with times.

faqs.question: How do I handle tips on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Show tips as a separate line or keep them off the invoice if paid directly to the driver. Tips are generally taxable income to the person who receives them, so keep records of them. Check with a tax professional for your situation.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on delivery?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax delivery charges, some only when bundled with taxable goods, and some do not at all. Check your state revenue department's rules or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses an order or is not home?
faqs.answer: Set a policy for failed deliveries in your agreement, such as charging the full delivery fee and any return trip. Record the attempt time and any contact made, and include it on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Food delivery businesses send quotes before taking on catering deliveries, recurring restaurant or meal-prep routes, event runs, and corporate lunch programs. Clients typically compare your price per delivery or per route against other couriers and against the cost of a third-party app, so a clear breakdown helps.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off locations and delivery windows
scopeChecklist.why: Distance and timing drive the price, and a stated window sets expectations for what counts as late.

scopeChecklist.item: Order size, number of items, and handling needs
scopeChecklist.why: Hot, cold, fragile, or oversized orders may need special bags, coolers, or a larger vehicle, which affects your price.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of stops and expected frequency
scopeChecklist.why: A single drop is priced differently than a 15-stop route or a daily recurring run.
State whether you place food, set up chafing dishes, or only hand off at the door so there is no confusion about the catering fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Wait time, grace period, and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: If the kitchen or recipient is slow, the time you wait has a cost that should be agreed before the job.
Food is perishable, so state what happens if the order is cancelled late or no one is available to receive it.

scopeChecklist.item: Who pays for tolls, parking, and packaging
scopeChecklist.why: These small costs can add up on city or event deliveries and are often disputed when not discussed upfront.

pricingTips.title: Price from your cost per mile and per hour
pricingTips.body: Add fuel, insurance, maintenance, and your time to get a floor price. Then add a margin so a short run with a long wait still pays.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered route rate
pricingTips.body: Offer lower per-stop pricing for clients who commit to a minimum number of deliveries a week. It rewards volume and gives you predictable income.

pricingTips.title: Quote surcharges up front
pricingTips.body: List rush, after-hours, holiday, and large-order fees in the quote. Clients accept them more readily when they are part of the original price.

pricingTips.title: Compare against app fees
pricingTips.body: Restaurants often weigh your price against third-party commission, which can run 15 to 30 percent of an order. Showing a flat fee per delivery makes the comparison easy.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate for catering delivery?
faqs.answer: A flat fee is usually easier for clients, as long as the distance, setup, and time on site are defined. Use an hourly rate with a minimum if the event timing is uncertain.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fuel prices and your schedule change, so 14 to 30 days is common. For event dates, note that the date is held only after a deposit or signed approval.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if the order is larger than quoted?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your quote states the order size it is based on and lists a surcharge or rate for additional items or stops. Confirm the change in writing before the delivery.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement for recurring routes?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short agreement covering the route, schedule, rate, payment terms, and how either side can end it prevents most disputes with regular clients.

food-photographer.intro: Food photographers shoot for restaurants, cookbook authors, packaged food brands, beverage companies, grocery and meal-kit businesses, and food bloggers. Invoices usually cover a shoot day or half day, per-image pricing, styling and prop costs, post-production, and licensing for how the images will be used.
food-photographer.pricingModel: Most food photographers price by the day or half day, by the image, or by a flat project fee, then add separate line items for licensing, food styling, groceries, props, and retouching. Restaurants and small brands often buy a package, such as a menu shoot with 15 to 20 finished images. Commercial and advertising clients pay more because licensing covers wider use, longer terms, and exclusivity. Editorial and cookbook work often pays a lower flat fee or a per-image fee. Expenses such as ingredients, rental studio time, assistants, and travel are normally billed at cost or with a modest markup (10 to 20 percent is common). Rush delivery, extra rounds of retouching, and additional usage are billed as add-ons.

rates.service: Half-day shoot (up to 4 hours, small restaurant or blog)
Menu or e-commerce shots (simple white or neutral background)
Licensing for web and social (1 to 2 years)

items.description: Half-day restaurant menu shoot on location (up to 4 hours, 12 dishes)
Additional finished images beyond package (lifestyle plates)
Food stylist
Props and surfaces rental
Groceries and ingredients (receipts attached, billed at cost)
Usage license: website, social media, and print menus, 2 years, non-exclusive

sampleInvoice.notes: 50 percent deposit of $1,163.50 received on booking. Balance due within 14 days of delivery. Images are licensed for the uses listed above; any other use requires a written extension. Final files delivered via online gallery for 90 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot date, location, and number of dishes or setups
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to a specific job and avoids confusion if the client has booked several shoots.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of finished images delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Most agreements promise a set count, and extra images or retouching are billed separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license terms (media, territory, duration, exclusivity)
invoiceChecklist.why: The fee covers specific uses only, and writing them on the invoice makes later extensions easier to negotiate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized expenses with receipts (groceries, props, studio rental, parking, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often need receipts for reimbursement, and itemizing keeps pass-through costs separate from your fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stylist and assistant charges, with names if billed on behalf of a crew
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what portion of the total is subcontracted labor and supports accurate bookkeeping.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents double payment and makes clear what is still owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or job code
invoiceChecklist.why: Brands, agencies, and larger restaurant groups often cannot process payment without one.

food-photographer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is standard and often locks in the shoot date. The balance is commonly due on delivery or within 14 to 30 days, with larger brands and agencies sometimes requesting net 30 or net 60. Many photographers hold final high-resolution files until the invoice is paid, or deliver watermarked proofs first. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in the contract. Payment is typically by ACH, check, credit card, or online payment link. Cancellation or reschedule fees, especially for shoots with perishable food or booked stylists, should be in writing.

tips.title: Separate creative fee from licensing
tips.body: List the shoot fee and the usage license as two lines. If the client later wants a bigger campaign or longer term, you can invoice an extension instead of renegotiating the whole job.

tips.title: Bill groceries and props as expenses, not part of your day rate
tips.body: Food costs vary widely between a burger menu and a seafood campaign. Pass them through at cost or with a stated markup, and keep receipts.

tips.title: Define retouching rounds
tips.body: State how many rounds of revisions are included, such as one round of minor edits. Charge hourly or per image after that.

tips.title: Charge for reshoots caused by client changes
tips.body: If a client changes the menu, delays the food delivery, or cancels dishes on the day, bill the extra time or a rebooking fee as agreed in your contract.

tips.title: Invoice at delivery, not weeks later
tips.body: Food clients often have launches and menu changes tied to your images. Sending the invoice with the gallery link keeps payment tied to the moment they see the value.

faqs.question: Should I charge per image or per day?
faqs.answer: Per image works well for simple e-commerce or menu work where each shot takes about the same time. Day rates fit editorial, brand, and campaign work where setups vary. Many photographers combine both, with a day rate that includes a set number of images and a per-image charge beyond that.

faqs.question: How do I bill for food styling?
faqs.answer: If you hire the stylist, list them as a separate line item at their day or half-day rate, plus a markup if you coordinate and carry the cost. If the client brings their own stylist, the stylist bills the client directly.

faqs.question: Can I charge for usage rights on a restaurant job?
faqs.answer: Yes. Even small clients benefit from a clear license, and many photographers include basic web, social, and menu use in the package price. Wider uses like paid advertising, packaging, or billboards are usually priced separately.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services or digital products and others do not, and rules can differ for licensing versus the shoot itself. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client does not pay and has the images?
faqs.answer: State in your contract that the license takes effect only upon full payment. Then send a reminder, apply the late fee if one was agreed, and consider withholding extra usage or future work until the balance is cleared.

estimate.intro: Food photographers send an estimate before the shoot, usually after a call or brief covering the number of dishes, the style of shots, and where the images will be used. Clients often compare quotes from several photographers, and they look at what is included: images, styling, retouching, and licensing, not just the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of dishes, setups, and final images
scopeChecklist.why: A shoot of 10 plates on a plain background is very different from 10 styled lifestyle scenes, and the count sets expectations.
Studio, restaurant, and client kitchen shoots affect setup time, lighting needs, and travel costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies food, props, and styling
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether groceries, a stylist, and surfaces are in your fee, billed separately, or provided by the client.
Sets the license for web, social, print, packaging, or ads so there are no surprises when the client wants to expand use.
Heavy compositing or color-matching to packaging can take hours, so limits protect your time.
States file types, resolution, and turnaround, such as web-sized JPEGs within 7 business days.
Protects you if the client cancels after you have booked a stylist or purchased perishable ingredients.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present three options, such as 8, 15, or 25 images, with licensing and retouching spelled out. Clients tend to pick a middle package and can see what they gain by choosing more.

pricingTips.title: Build a cushion for food cost swings
pricingTips.body: Ingredient prices and the number of retakes for items like melting ice cream or fresh herbs can vary. Quote expenses as an estimate with a cap and bill actuals.

pricingTips.title: Price licensing by reach
pricingTips.body: A local restaurant using images on its website needs less than a national brand using them in paid ads. Adjust the license fee by media, territory, and term.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity date
pricingTips.body: Include an expiration, such as 30 days, so quotes do not hold your calendar or pricing indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: A flat quote based on a defined shot list works best for most clients. Use an hourly estimate only when the scope is unclear, and note that extra setups or revisions will be billed beyond the quote.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the client has not decided on the menu yet?
faqs.answer: Quote a base price for a set number of dishes and state a per-dish or per-image price for additions. Ask for the final shot list a few days before the shoot.

faqs.question: Do I charge for travel and set-up time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Include travel time or mileage beyond a local radius, and make clear that on-location setup, lighting, and breakdown are part of the booked time.

food-truck.intro: Food truck owners invoice when they are hired instead of selling to walk-up customers. That includes private catering for weddings, corporate lunches, brewery and winery bookings, school and community events, film sets, and festival vendor fees. Most invoices cover a per-person meal price or a flat booking fee, plus extras like travel, staffing, and service fees.
food-truck.pricingModel: Private events are usually priced one of three ways. The first is per person, with a headcount guarantee and a set menu, typically $15-35 a head depending on the food. The second is a flat booking fee or rental for a set service window, often two to three hours, which suits corporate lunches and film crews. The third is a minimum guarantee: the client pays a set amount, and if sales at a public event like a brewery fall short, they cover the difference. Many trucks add a travel charge for distances beyond a set radius, a surcharge for extra staff or long service windows, and a service charge on top of food. Sales tax applies to prepared food in most states, so show it separately. Deposits are standard because the truck blocks out a date and buys food in advance.

rates.service: Minimum sales guarantee (brewery, winery, public event)

items.description: Taco bar catering, 2 proteins, rice, beans, toppings (Saturday 5/17, 5:00-7:30 PM, corporate picnic)
Vegetarian and gluten-free meals, included in headcount upcharge
Travel, 38 miles beyond 20-mile base radius
Additional server for extended service window
Event vendor permit, passed through at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: A 50% deposit of $1,191.00 was received on booking. Balance due within 7 days of the event date. Sales tax is shown separately where applicable. Final headcount was confirmed 7 days before the event. Cancellations less than 14 days out forfeit the deposit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, address, and service window
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and shows the hours you were contracted to serve, which matters if there is a dispute over overtime.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guaranteed headcount and final headcount served
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-person pricing depends on the number. Showing both makes it clear whether the bill reflects the guarantee or actual counts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Menu items and dietary substitutions
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists what was agreed, including vegan, gluten-free, or allergy-specific meals that may be priced differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized fees: travel, staffing, generator, service charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients accept charges they can see and understand. Unitemized lump sums lead to pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax and any service charge or gratuity, listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Tax rules for prepared food vary by state and locality. Separate lines keep the tax portion clear, and a service charge is different from a tip your staff receives.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the money already paid and what remains so the client does not pay twice or underpay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit, health department, or commissary details if requested
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate clients, venues, and event organizers sometimes ask for proof of licensing and insurance along with payment paperwork.

food-truck.paymentTerms: Most food truck bookings require a deposit of 25-50% to hold the date, with the balance due on or before the event for private parties or within 7-14 days for corporate clients. Corporate accounts often need a PO number and may pay net 30, so confirm that before booking. For weddings and large parties, a final payment due a week before the event is common because headcount locks in then. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical but should be stated in your booking agreement. Accept card, ACH, and check; card payments are convenient but carry processing fees, so some trucks add a small surcharge where allowed by their state and card network rules.

tips.title: Get the deposit before you block the date
tips.body: A truck that holds a Saturday for a client who cancels loses a full day of revenue. Take a non-refundable deposit at booking and put the cancellation terms in writing.

tips.title: Lock the headcount a week out
tips.body: Set a deadline for the final guest count and bill for the greater of the final count or a stated minimum. This protects you from buying and prepping food for people who never show.

tips.title: Use a minimum guarantee for public venues
tips.body: At breweries, wineries, and festivals, agree on a minimum sales amount up front. If sales fall short, the venue or organizer pays the difference. Invoice the shortfall separately with the sales report attached.

tips.title: Charge for travel and long service windows
tips.body: Fuel, generator run time, and staff hours add up on long drives and extended events. Build a base radius and a per-mile or per-hour charge into your standard terms.

tips.title: Track event fees you advance
tips.body: If you pay a vendor fee or temporary permit on the client's behalf, list it as a pass-through at cost with a copy of the receipt so it is not mistaken for markup.

faqs.question: Should I charge per person or a flat fee for a private event?
faqs.answer: Per person works best when the client controls the guest count, such as weddings and parties. A flat booking fee or minimum guarantee works better for corporate lunches, film crews, and public events, where your costs are tied to the service window more than the exact headcount.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on catering invoices?
faqs.answer: In most states, prepared food is taxable, and catering is often taxable too, but rules vary on service charges, delivery fees, and tax-exempt clients like schools or nonprofits. Check with your state department of revenue or an accountant and list tax as its own line.

faqs.question: Is a service charge the same as a tip?
faqs.answer: No. A service charge is a fee you set that becomes business revenue, and in many places it is taxable. A tip or gratuity is voluntary and belongs to staff. If your invoice includes a service charge, label it clearly so clients do not assume it covers tips.

faqs.question: What if the client's headcount is lower than guaranteed?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say you bill for the guaranteed minimum or the final headcount, whichever is higher. Put that rule on both the booking agreement and the invoice, along with the date the headcount was locked.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a brewery that pays me a guarantee?
faqs.answer: Invoice the shortfall only: the agreed minimum minus your actual sales for the event. Include the date, the minimum, your total sales, and the difference so the brewery can see how the amount was calculated.

estimate.intro: Food truck owners send quotes when someone asks about a private event, wedding, corporate lunch, or recurring weekly spot. The client usually compares per-person price, menu options, and what the quote includes beyond food, such as staffing, travel, and service time.

scopeChecklist.why: Your truck is booked for a specific block of time. Stating it avoids confusion about setup, service, and breakdown hours.

scopeChecklist.item: Menu and number of options per guest
scopeChecklist.why: Spells out how many entrees, sides, and drinks are included so guests do not expect unlimited extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count, minimum guarantee, and the headcount deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on the numbers. A locked date for the final count prevents last-minute changes after you have bought ingredients.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel radius and any extra mileage charges
scopeChecklist.why: Fuel and drive time can be a significant cost for events outside your usual area.

scopeChecklist.item: Site requirements: parking space, power, water, access
scopeChecklist.why: Tight venues, no level ground, or no power access can prevent service. Note what the client must provide.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, insurance, and who pays event fees
scopeChecklist.why: Some venues require a certificate of insurance or a temporary permit. Say who is responsible for the cost and paperwork.
Outdoor events can be rained out. Define what happens to the deposit before it becomes a dispute.

pricingTips.title: Price from food cost and truck time
pricingTips.body: Work out food cost per plate, labor for the service window, fuel and propane, and a share of truck overhead. A common target is food cost around 28-35% of the menu price, though it varies with the menu.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three menu tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium package gives the client a clear choice. Most people pick the middle option, and it keeps you from custom-pricing every request.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum booking
pricingTips.body: Short events with small headcounts rarely cover the cost of a full day. A minimum fee, such as $800-1,000 for a private booking, filters out jobs that lose money.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Food prices and your calendar both change. A quote valid for 14-30 days lets you reprice or release the date if the client has not confirmed.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote or just a price list?
faqs.answer: For private events, send a written quote. A price list does not cover date, headcount, travel, or site conditions, and those are what drive the final cost.

faqs.question: How do I price a wedding differently from a corporate lunch?
faqs.answer: Weddings usually involve longer service windows, higher per-person prices, more custom menu requests, and more planning time. Corporate lunches are typically shorter, with a fixed menu and a tighter time window, so a flat fee or lower per-person price often works.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a tasting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many trucks charge a tasting fee, often $50-150, and credit it toward the booking if the client confirms. That limits requests from people who are only browsing.

faqs.question: What happens if the headcount changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that the price is based on the stated headcount. Allow reductions only up to the headcount deadline, and add guests at the per-person rate if you can accommodate them.

forklift-operator.intro: Independent forklift operators and small material-handling businesses bill warehouses, contractors, manufacturers, event companies, and retailers for moving, loading, and staging freight. Typical billable work includes loading and unloading trucks, relocating pallets and equipment, jobsite material handling, and short-term operator or equipment rental.
forklift-operator.pricingModel: Most forklift work is billed hourly, with the rate depending on the machine (standard warehouse forklift, rough-terrain, telehandler, or high-capacity), whether you supply the equipment, and the job's risk. Operator-only work, where the client provides the forklift, is priced lower than operator plus machine. Many operators set a two- to four-hour minimum to cover travel and setup. Per-pallet or per-truck flat rates are common for recurring loading and unloading. Equipment delivery, fuel or propane, mileage, after-hours work, and special rigging such as fork extensions or lifting jibs are usually billed as separate lines. Standby or wait time caused by the client is billed at the hourly rate or a reduced standby rate.

rates.service: Operator with warehouse forklift (up to 5,000 lb)
Operator with rough-terrain forklift or telehandler

items.description: Forklift with operator, unloading 3 flatbed trucks of building materials at jobsite (5,000 lb rough-terrain unit)
Equipment delivery and pickup
Fork extensions and pipe attachment use
Fuel surcharge
Client-caused standby time (truck arrived late)

sampleInvoice.notes: Work performed on 3/14 at 4210 Industrial Pkwy, PO #78213. Net 15. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Client responsible for ground conditions and load weights provided. Payment by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address, date, and start and stop times
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing depends on clear time records, and this settles disputes about when you arrived and when work ended.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment type and capacity
invoiceChecklist.why: A 5,000 lb warehouse unit and a 10,000 lb rough-terrain machine carry different rates, and the invoice should show which one was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many warehouses and contractors will not process payment without a PO or job reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for mobilization, fuel, attachments, and standby
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing these shows they were agreed extras and not padding on the hourly rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Operator certification reference
invoiceChecklist.why: OSHA requires powered industrial truck operators to be trained and evaluated, and some clients ask for proof of certification before paying or booking again.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance and certificate of insurance reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often require general liability coverage on file, and referencing it helps their accounts payable team approve the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Signed delivery or work ticket reference
invoiceChecklist.why: A client signature on the day of the job is your best proof of hours worked and conditions on site.

forklift-operator.paymentTerms: Commercial clients typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, while one-time or residential jobs are often paid on completion. New clients may be asked for a deposit or card on file, especially when you deliver equipment to a remote site. Many operators set a minimum charge so short jobs cover travel time. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in advance on the quote and invoice. ACH, check, and card are the usual payment methods, and larger accounts may require a vendor form such as a W-9 before the first payment.

tips.title: Set a minimum callout
tips.body: A two-hour or four-hour minimum protects you from short jobs that cost you a half day in travel, setup, and inspection time. State it on every quote and invoice.

tips.title: Bill standby time separately
tips.body: Waiting on late trucks or unprepared sites is common. Log arrival time, the time work actually began, and charge standby at the full or a reduced hourly rate.

tips.title: Get a signed work ticket
tips.body: Have the site contact sign a ticket with the hours before you leave. It prevents disputes weeks later when the invoice reaches accounts payable.

tips.title: Charge for attachments and wear
tips.body: Fork extensions, side shifters, jibs, and rented attachments cost money to own and maintain. Add them as their own lines instead of absorbing them.

tips.title: Track fuel and mileage
tips.body: Propane, diesel, and trailer hauling add up. Either build a fuel surcharge into your terms or list actual costs so margins do not erode.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the job?
faqs.answer: Hourly works best when the scope is uncertain or the site is unfamiliar. Flat per-truck or per-pallet pricing suits repeat clients where you know the load type and timing. If you quote a flat rate, include a clause for delays and extra loads.

faqs.question: Can I bill for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as it is agreed upfront. Many operators include travel in a minimum charge or a mobilization fee instead of billing drive hours separately, particularly when hauling their own machine on a trailer.

faqs.question: Do I need certification to bill clients for forklift work?
faqs.answer: Under OSHA rules, employers must make sure powered industrial truck operators are trained and evaluated. Independent operators are generally expected to hold current training documentation, and many clients ask to see it. Check federal, state, and client requirements for your situation.

faqs.question: How do I handle damage disputes on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Keep damage claims separate from billing. Document the load condition at pickup and drop-off with photos and the work ticket, carry liability insurance, and do not discount an invoice to settle a claim unless you agree in writing.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on forklift services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether you are providing a service, renting equipment, or both. Equipment rental is taxable in many states, while labor may not be. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Forklift operators send quotes before jobs involving equipment delivery, multi-day work, or large unloading projects, and any time a new client wants a firm number. Clients usually compare hourly rates, minimum charges, whether the equipment is included, and what happens if the job runs long.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment type, capacity, and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for operator only differs greatly from operator plus machine, and mixing them up is a common source of disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated hours, minimum charge, and overtime terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to understand how the final bill can change if the job runs past the estimate.

scopeChecklist.item: Load details: weights, dimensions, and number of pallets or trucks
scopeChecklist.why: Heavy or awkward loads can exceed the machine's rated capacity and change the equipment required.
Soft ground, slopes, tight aisles, and overhead clearances affect safety, speed, and which forklift you can use.
Listing these upfront prevents the client from treating them as surprise extras.
States how you charge when trucks arrive late or the site is not ready.

scopeChecklist.item: Insurance, certification, and who is responsible for the load
scopeChecklist.why: Commercial clients often require proof of coverage, and responsibility for damage should be clear before work starts.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for uncertain jobs
pricingTips.body: If the number of trucks or pallets is unknown, give an hours range with a cap that requires approval to exceed. It keeps the client informed without underpricing the work.

pricingTips.title: Price machine and operator separately
pricingTips.body: Splitting the equipment and labor lines helps clients compare quotes with rental yards and staffing agencies on the same basis.

pricingTips.title: Include a minimum
pricingTips.body: Build a two- to four-hour minimum into the quote so small jobs cover travel, inspection, and setup.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
