pricingTips.body: Fuel, labor, and equipment availability shift, so a quote valid for 15 to 30 days protects your pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most operators quote for free from a phone call, photos, or a brief site description. For large or complex jobs that need a site visit, a fee that is credited toward the work if booked is reasonable.

faqs.question: What if the job runs longer than I quoted?
faqs.answer: Put in writing that the quote is an estimate based on the stated scope and that extra time is billed at the hourly rate. Tell the client on site when you are nearing the cap and get approval before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: For commercial and repeat clients, written acceptance by email or signature is strongly recommended. It records the rate, minimum, and terms you agreed to before any equipment moves.

faqs.question: How do I quote a job where I do not know the site?
faqs.answer: Ask for photos, a load list, and access details, or do a short walkthrough. If you cannot confirm conditions, state your assumptions in the quote and note that changes may affect the price.

foundation-repair.intro: Foundation repair contractors fix settling, cracking, bowing, and water-damaged foundations on homes and light commercial buildings. Invoices usually cover piering or underpinning, wall stabilization, crack injection, slab leveling, and drainage work, often billed in stages because jobs run days or weeks and involve large material costs.
foundation-repair.pricingModel: Most foundation repair is priced per unit of work rather than by the hour: per pier, per linear foot of wall or crack, per square foot of slab, or as a flat job price built from those units. Contractors typically build the price from engineering or inspection fees, number and depth of piers, materials, equipment, labor, permits, and a margin for unknowns like hitting rock, utilities, or groundwater. Larger jobs are billed in stages, such as a deposit, a progress payment when piers are installed, and a final payment after lift, backfill, and cleanup. Change orders are common when soil conditions or hidden damage differ from the original assessment, and should be invoiced as separate line items. Warranties are part of the sale, so many contractors list them on the invoice.

rates.service: Steel push piers or helical piers (installed)
Concrete pressed pilings or drilled piers
Slabjacking or polyurethane foam slab lifting
Wall crack repair with epoxy or polyurethane injection
Carbon fiber strap or wall anchor stabilization for bowing walls
Interior or exterior perimeter drain installation
Crawl space support posts or beam shimming
Foundation inspection or engineer report coordination

items.description: Foundation inspection and written repair plan (credited if work proceeds, shown as billed)
Install steel push piers to refusal, rear and east walls (avg depth 14 ft)
Hydraulic lift and level of east corner, with shimming and pier cap lock-off
Epoxy injection of interior wall crack, north basement wall
Excavation, backfill, compaction, and haul-away of spoils
Permit fee (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $7,000 received at contract signing, credited above. Progress payment of $6,000 due on pier installation completion; balance due within 10 days of final walkthrough. Piers carry a transferable lifetime structural warranty per the signed contract. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and permit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the specific structure and the permit the city or county inspected, which matters for resale and insurance claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pier count, type, and depth per location
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and engineers verify the work against the plan, and this prevents disputes about how many piers were actually installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract, engineer report, and any change orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties extra charges for rock, utilities, or added piers to written approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized materials and equipment charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Steel, concrete, foam, drain pipe, and equipment rental are large costs, and itemizing them supports your pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment schedule with deposits and progress payments credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the remaining balance clearly on multi-stage jobs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and transferability
invoiceChecklist.why: Foundation warranties are a major selling point and are often needed by future buyers and their lenders.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance information
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license number on contracts and invoices, and clients or lenders may ask for proof of insurance.

foundation-repair.paymentTerms: A deposit of 10 to 50 percent at signing is normal, often capped by state law for home improvement work, so check your local rules. Larger jobs usually bill a progress payment when piers or major structural work is complete and the balance after final lift, cleanup, and inspection. Balances are commonly due on receipt or within 7 to 15 days of completion. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, and credit cards are all used, and homeowners paying through a lender or insurance claim may pay on a draw schedule, so confirm requirements before starting.

tips.title: Bill in stages tied to physical milestones
tips.body: Tie each payment to something visible, such as pier installation complete or lift finished. This keeps your cash flow ahead of material and crew costs and gives the client a clear reason for each payment.

tips.title: Write change orders before you dig further
tips.body: Hitting rock, buried utilities, or a second failed section is common. Get written approval for added piers or work and list them as separate invoice lines so the original contract total stays clear.

tips.title: Hold the final payment until the final walkthrough
tips.body: Schedule the walkthrough, confirm any inspection sign-off, then invoice the balance. Clients are far less likely to dispute a payment after they have seen the finished lift and cleaned site.

tips.title: Keep photos and elevation readings
tips.body: Before and after photos, manometer or laser level readings, and pier logs back up your invoice and protect you if a client later claims the work was incomplete.

tips.title: Coordinate with lenders and insurers early
tips.body: If payment is coming from insurance or a mortgage draw, ask what documents they need, such as engineer letters, lien waivers, and invoices, so payment does not stall at the end.

faqs.question: Should I bill the inspection fee separately?
faqs.answer: Either way works. Many contractors offer free inspections, others charge $250 to $800 and credit it toward the job if the client signs. If you charge for it, show it on the invoice, with the credit as a separate line if applicable.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for extra piers added during the job?
faqs.answer: Use a signed change order that states the number of extra piers, the price per pier, and the reason. Then list them as their own line items on the invoice so the client can match them to the approval.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit on a foundation repair job?
faqs.answer: Yes, deposits are normal, but many states limit the amount for residential home improvement contracts. Check your state's rules and state the deposit and its credit clearly on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to put my license number on the invoice?
faqs.answer: In many states contractors must show their license number on contracts and advertising, and some require it on invoices too. Putting it on every document is a safe habit, but check your state licensing board.

faqs.question: What if the client disputes the work after the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Refer to the signed scope, pier logs, photos, and elevation readings. Offer a walkthrough, and put any agreed warranty repairs in writing. Do not release the warranty paperwork until the balance is paid, if your contract allows.

estimate.intro: Foundation repair estimates are sent after an on-site inspection, and sometimes after an engineer's report. Homeowners usually collect two or three quotes and compare repair methods, pier counts, warranty terms, and price, so a clear written scope matters as much as the number.

scopeChecklist.why: Push piers, helical piers, and concrete pilings perform differently and cost differently, so clients need to compare like with like.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, depth, and location of piers or anchors
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a concrete basis for the price and the way to verify the work, and a basis for pricing extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected lift and what it will and will not fix
scopeChecklist.why: Lifting may not close every crack or make doors perfect, so state the realistic result to avoid disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Excluded items such as interior finish repair, landscaping, and plumbing
scopeChecklist.why: Drywall, flooring, sprinklers, and plumbing leaks found during lifting are common sources of disagreements.
Unforeseen conditions can add significant cost, so explain how they will be priced if encountered.
Specifies who pulls permits and pays fees, and whether an engineer's stamped plan is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Warranty terms, estimate expiration, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Steel and material prices change, and clients will compare warranties, so dates and terms prevent confusion.

pricingTips.title: Price from the plan, not a guess
pricingTips.body: Count piers, linear feet, and slab area from your inspection or engineer's plan and multiply by your unit costs. Add a margin for access, equipment, and travel instead of rounding up the total.

pricingTips.title: Include a contingency or unit price for extras
pricingTips.body: State a price per additional pier or per extra foot of depth so surprises are priced before work begins, and the client has agreed to the rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer repair options when appropriate
pricingTips.body: Presenting a minimum fix and a more complete repair, such as piers only versus piers plus drainage, helps clients choose and shows you are not overselling.

pricingTips.title: Explain the warranty beside the price
pricingTips.body: A lower quote with a limited warranty is not the same as a higher quote with a transferable one. Put the warranty in writing on the estimate so clients can compare accurately.

faqs.question: Should I charge for foundation repair estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors offer free estimates to compete, while others charge a fee that is credited to the job. If an engineer's report is needed, it is usually a separate cost. Choose one approach and state it before the visit.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Steel, concrete, and fuel costs can shift, and soil conditions can change after heavy rain or drought, so set an expiration date on the estimate.

faqs.question: Can the final price differ from the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes, if conditions differ from what was visible, such as rock, utilities, or additional damage. Explain this on the estimate and require written change orders before extra work.

freelance.intro: Freelancers are independent contractors who sell their skills to clients on a project or ongoing basis, including writers, designers, developers, editors, video editors, virtual assistants, and consultants. They usually invoice for hours worked, finished deliverables, or a monthly retainer, and they often manage several clients at once with no accounts department to chase payment for them.
freelance.pricingModel: Most freelancers price in one of four ways: hourly, per project (flat fee), per deliverable (per article, per logo, per page), or monthly retainer. Hourly works best when scope is unclear or the client keeps changing direction. Flat project fees reward efficiency and are easier for clients to approve, but they need a written scope and a set number of revision rounds. Retainers suit recurring work such as social media, bookkeeping support, or monthly content, and are billed in advance for a fixed number of hours or deliverables. Your rate has to cover more than your take-home pay: self-employment tax, health insurance, software, equipment, unpaid admin time, and slow weeks. Many freelancers aim for billable time of only 50 to 70 percent of their working hours and set rates accordingly. Rush work is commonly billed at 1.25x to 2x, and expenses such as stock images, fonts, plugins, or paid ads are passed through at cost or with a small handling fee.

rates.service: General freelance consulting or virtual assistance
Freelance writing or copywriting (blog posts, web copy)
Graphic design (logo or brand identity project)
Monthly retainer (social media, content, or support)

items.description: Website copy: home, about, and services pages (first drafts)
Two rounds of revisions, consolidated feedback
Additional revisions beyond agreed scope
Keyword research and competitor review
Licensed stock photography (2 images, at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Website copy refresh, per proposal dated March 4. 50% deposit of $900 was received on March 6 and is deducted below. Balance due within 14 days of invoice date. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Final files are released on full payment. Payment by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and reference to the signed proposal or contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and price so the client's accounts payable team can approve it without questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables or hours broken out by task
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute vague lines like 'design work'. Itemizing shows what they received and makes partial payments or corrections easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or milestone payments already received
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing previous payments and the remaining balance prevents double billing and confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock assets, fonts, plugins, software licenses, and ad spend need to be listed separately, at cost, so clients can verify them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often will not pay without a purchase order number or an invoice addressed to a specific department.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients who pay you $600 or more in a year generally need your W-9 to issue a 1099, and many will hold payment until they have it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and ownership terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating that rights transfer on full payment protects you if the client uses the work before paying.

freelance.paymentTerms: Freelancers commonly collect 30 to 50 percent upfront on new projects and bill the balance on delivery, or split larger projects into milestones. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month. Net 14 or Net 15 is common for small clients, while larger companies often insist on Net 30 or even Net 45 or 60, so it helps to agree on terms in writing before starting. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical where state law allows, and should appear in the contract as well as on the invoice. Payment methods usually include ACH bank transfer, card payments (often with the processing fee built into the price), checks, and sometimes wire transfers for international clients. For new clients with no history, ask for a larger deposit or full payment upfront on small jobs.

tips.title: Put scope and revision limits in writing
tips.body: Most unpaid-work disputes start with scope creep. State the number of revision rounds included, and bill extra rounds at your hourly rate. List out-of-scope requests on the invoice when they happen rather than absorbing them.

tips.title: Take a deposit before starting
tips.body: A 30 to 50 percent deposit filters out clients who are not serious and covers your time if the project stalls. For new clients, hold final files until the last payment clears.

tips.title: Invoice promptly and on a schedule
tips.body: Send invoices the day you deliver or hit a milestone. Waiting a week or two before billing usually delays payment by the same amount. For hourly clients, invoice weekly or biweekly rather than once a month.

tips.title: Track time even on flat-fee jobs
tips.body: Logging hours shows whether your flat rates actually work out to a decent hourly figure. It also gives you evidence when you need to justify a price increase or change order.

tips.title: Set aside money for taxes
tips.body: Clients generally do not withhold taxes from freelancers. Many freelancers move 25 to 30 percent of each payment into a separate account for self-employment and income tax and pay quarterly estimated taxes. Check with a tax professional for your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly when scope is unclear, ongoing, or likely to change. Use a flat fee when the deliverables are well defined and you can estimate your time with confidence. Flat fees reward you for working faster, but only if the scope and revisions are capped in writing.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who pays late?
faqs.answer: Send a polite reminder on the day the invoice becomes overdue, then follow up weekly. Reference the late fee in your contract if it applies. For repeated lateness, pause work until the balance is paid, and for large unpaid amounts consider a demand letter or small claims court, depending on your state's limits.

faqs.question: Do I need a contract if I send an invoice?
faqs.answer: An invoice is a request for payment, not an agreement. A short contract or signed proposal covering scope, price, payment terms, revisions, and ownership of the work gives you something to rely on if there is a dispute. Many freelancers use a simple one-page agreement for small jobs.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on freelance services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and the type of service. Many states do not tax most professional services, but some tax digital products, design, or certain consulting work. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant before you assume either way.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for paying by credit card?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by state and by card network. Some freelancers build the processing cost into their rates, and others add a surcharge with clear disclosure where it is allowed. Check your local rules and your payment processor's terms before adding a surcharge.

estimate.intro: Freelancers send estimates or proposals before a project begins, usually after a discovery call or after the client shares a brief. Clients often collect quotes from two or three freelancers and compare price, timeline, process, and how clearly the scope is defined.

scopeChecklist.why: 'A logo' or 'a blog' is vague. Spell out file types, word counts, page counts, number of concepts, and resolutions so both sides know what done looks like.
Unlimited revisions are the most common source of unpaid hours. State how many rounds are included and what extra rounds cost.

scopeChecklist.item: What you need from the client and when
scopeChecklist.why: Delays in feedback, content, or logins can push a project back. Say that deadlines shift if materials arrive late.
Dates for first draft, feedback, and final delivery set expectations and give you natural points to invoice.
List what is not included, such as hosting, photography, translation, or ongoing maintenance, so the client does not assume it is covered.
Stock assets, fonts, plugins, printing, and ad spend should be listed as client-paid or reimbursable, not folded into your fee unnoticed.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity period and ownership terms
scopeChecklist.why: A 14 to 30 day expiry protects you from price changes, and stating that rights transfer on final payment protects the work.

pricingTips.title: Estimate your hours, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the project into tasks, estimate hours for each, and add 15 to 25 percent for communication, revisions, and surprises. Multiply by your hourly rate to get a flat fee that reflects real effort.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three packages, such as basic, standard, and full, moves the conversation from whether to hire you to which option fits. It also lets budget-conscious clients choose a smaller scope instead of negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Price on value, not just time
pricingTips.body: A sales page that drives revenue or a brand identity used for years is worth more to a client than the hours involved. Ask about goals and budget early so you can price to the outcome.

pricingTips.title: Include the payment schedule in the quote
pricingTips.body: State the deposit amount, milestone payments, and due dates up front. Clients who agree to the schedule in the estimate rarely push back when the invoice arrives.

faqs.question: Should I give a price range or a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed quote when scope is clear. If the scope is uncertain, give a range with the assumptions behind it, or propose a paid discovery phase first. Ranges that are too wide make you look unsure, so keep them to the variables you cannot control.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates and proposals?
faqs.answer: Short quotes are normally free. If a proposal requires significant research, strategy, or custom work, such as a detailed technical plan, consider a paid discovery or scoping fee that is credited toward the project if the client moves ahead.

faqs.question: What do I do when the client asks for more work after I quote?
faqs.answer: Send a change order or revised estimate describing the added work, price, and any change to the deadline, and get approval before starting. Do the new work only after the client agrees in writing.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. A limited window protects you if your availability or costs change, and it encourages the client to make a decision.

freelancer.intro: Freelancers are independent professionals who sell their skills to clients on a project or contract basis, such as writers, designers, developers, editors, consultants, and virtual assistants. They invoice for hours worked, finished deliverables, or monthly retainers, and they usually handle their own contracts, taxes, and collections.
freelancer.pricingModel: Most freelancers use one of four models: hourly, flat project fee, day rate, or monthly retainer. Hourly billing is simple and suits open-ended or uncertain work, but it can penalize you for getting faster. Project fees reward efficiency and are easier for clients to budget, though they need a tightly defined scope and a clear limit on revisions. Day rates are common in consulting and in-house contract work. Retainers give you predictable income in exchange for a set number of hours or deliverables each month. Many freelancers add separate line items for rush work, extra revision rounds, stock assets, software licenses, and pass-through expenses. Rates vary widely by field, experience, and region, so treat any range as a starting point and base your own figure on your target annual income, billable hours, and overhead.

rates.service: General freelance work (writing, editing, design, admin)
Specialized freelance work (development, UX, strategy consulting)
Day rate for on-site or embedded contract work
Small fixed-scope project (logo, landing page, short article series)
Larger project (website build, brand identity, long-form content)
Additional revision round beyond the agreed scope

items.description: Website copywriting: home, about, and services pages (3 pages, includes two revision rounds)
Discovery call and brand voice review
Additional revision round requested after final approval
Stock photo licenses purchased on client's behalf (at cost)
Rush delivery surcharge (5-day turnaround)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. A 50% deposit of $1,400 was received on March 3 and has been applied. Accepted payment methods: ACH transfer, check, or credit card (3% processing fee). Usage rights transfer to the client on receipt of full payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and reference to the signed contract or statement of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and price, which helps if the client questions a line item.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables or hours with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients' accounting teams often need to see what was delivered and when before they approve payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits or prior payments already received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the remaining balance clearly and avoids confusion about what the client has already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client's PO number or internal reference code
invoiceChecklist.why: Many companies will not process an invoice without a purchase order number, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses listed separately with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps your fees distinct from pass-through costs like stock assets, software, or travel, and supports reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients who pay you $600 or more in a year generally need your details to file a 1099, so confirm you have supplied a W-9.

invoiceChecklist.item: Due date, late fee terms, and accepted payment methods
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating terms plainly on the document gives you something to point to when a payment is late.

freelancer.paymentTerms: Freelancers commonly ask for 25-50% upfront on projects, with the balance due on delivery or split across milestones. For retainers, invoicing at the start of the month for that month's work is standard. Net 14 and Net 30 are the most common due dates, though larger companies may insist on Net 45 or Net 60, so confirm this before you sign. A late fee of 1-2% per month is typical where local law allows it, and it should appear in your contract as well as on the invoice. Most freelancers accept ACH, check, and card payments, and some pass card fees on to the client. For new clients or international work, requiring a larger deposit is reasonable protection.

tips.title: Put payment terms in the contract, not just on the invoice
tips.body: A late fee or deposit requirement is much easier to enforce if the client agreed to it before work began. Include due dates, late fees, and kill fees in your agreement.

tips.title: Bill at milestones on longer projects
tips.body: Invoice at signing, at a mid-project checkpoint, and at delivery. This keeps cash flowing and limits how much unpaid work you carry if a client goes quiet.

tips.title: Track scope changes in writing and invoice them separately
tips.body: When a client asks for something outside the original scope, confirm the extra cost by email and add it as its own line item. This prevents disputes over why the total changed.

tips.title: Send invoices promptly and follow up on a schedule
tips.body: Invoice the day work is delivered or the milestone is reached. Send a reminder a few days before the due date, another on the due date, and a firmer one a week later.

tips.title: Set aside money for taxes from every payment
tips.body: In the US, freelancers typically owe self-employment tax and make quarterly estimated payments. Many set aside 25-30% of each payment, but check with a tax professional for your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat project fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly when scope is unclear or likely to change, and a flat fee when the deliverables are well defined. Flat fees reward you for working efficiently, but only if the contract limits revisions and describes what is included.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or receive one?
faqs.answer: In the US, clients who pay an independent contractor $600 or more in a year generally have to report it, often on a 1099-NEC, though thresholds and rules can change. Provide a W-9 when the client requests it, and report all income whether or not you receive a form.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, if you state it in your contract and on the invoice before the payment is late. Rules on maximum rates differ by state, so check your local requirements. A common amount is 1-1.5% per month.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a retainer?
faqs.answer: Invoice at the start of each billing period for the agreed monthly amount, and state what it covers, such as hours or deliverables. Specify whether unused hours roll over and what rate applies to work beyond the retainer.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a polite reminder with the invoice attached, then a firmer written notice that cites the contract terms. If that fails, many freelancers send a demand letter, pause work or withhold final files, and consider small claims court, which is often practical for amounts under your state's limit.

estimate.intro: Freelancers usually send a quote or proposal after an initial call or brief and before signing a contract. Clients often compare several freelancers on price, timeline, and what is included, so a clear scope matters as much as the number.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming exactly what the client receives, such as file types, page counts, or word counts, prevents arguments about whether something was included.
Unlimited revisions are the most common cause of freelancer losses. State how many rounds are included and what extra rounds cost.
Delays often come from late feedback or missing materials. Say when you need input and how deadlines move if it is late.
Listing items like photography, hosting, translation, or ongoing maintenance as out of scope heads off assumptions.
Showing the deposit and milestone amounts up front makes it clear that work starts only after the first payment.
Clarify when rights transfer, usually on full payment, and whether you can show the work in your portfolio.
Your availability and costs change, so a validity window such as 30 days keeps you from being held to an old price.

pricingTips.title: Estimate your hours, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Work out the hours for each phase, including calls, revisions, and project management, and add 15-25% for unknowns. Then divide into a fixed fee or present it as a not-to-exceed amount.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three packages, such as basic, standard, and full, shifts the client's question from whether to hire you to which option fits. It also makes the middle option feel reasonable.

pricingTips.title: Break out the price by phase
pricingTips.body: Showing separate costs for discovery, production, and revisions helps the client understand the value and lets them trim scope instead of negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Charge more for rush and unclear scope
pricingTips.body: Add a surcharge for compressed timelines and price vague projects with a discovery phase first. A small paid scoping project is better than guessing on a large one.

faqs.question: Should I charge for writing a proposal or quote?
faqs.answer: A short quote is normally free. For complex projects that require research, a paid discovery or scoping phase is reasonable, and many freelancers credit that fee toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an estimate and a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: An estimate is an approximate cost that can change as the work develops, while a fixed quote commits you to a set price for a defined scope. Label the document clearly so the client knows which one they are getting.

faqs.question: Can I raise the price after the client accepts a quote?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. You can charge more for changes the client requests, if your quote or contract says that out-of-scope work is billed separately and you confirm the new cost in writing before doing it.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. A shorter window makes sense when your calendar is tight or when the price depends on third-party costs that may change.

freight.intro: Freight invoices are sent by owner-operators, small trucking companies, freight brokers, and dispatch services that move goods for shippers. They typically bill for line haul, fuel surcharges, accessorial charges like detention and lumper fees, and any extra stops on a load.
freight.pricingModel: Freight is priced mostly per mile for truckload (TL) moves or as a flat rate per load on a set lane. Less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments are priced by weight, freight class, and distance, usually through a carrier tariff with a discount. Fuel surcharge is added as a separate line, often tied to the DOE weekly diesel average. Accessorials are billed on top: detention after two hours of free time, layover, TONU (truck ordered not used), lumper fees, liftgate, inside delivery, extra stops, hazmat, and tarps. Brokers price by adding a margin to what they pay the carrier, commonly 10 to 20 percent, or a flat fee per load. Dispatch services often charge 5 to 10 percent of the gross load revenue.

rates.service: Dry van or reefer truckload, line haul
Flatbed or step deck truckload, line haul

Fuel surcharge
Detention at shipper, 3.5 hrs total, 1.5 billable after 2 hrs free
Lumper fee at delivery (receipt attached)
Extra stop, Birmingham AL

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 30 from invoice date. BOL, signed POD, and lumper receipt attached. Please reference load #48213 on payment. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Remit by ACH to the account on file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Load number, PO number, or BOL number
invoiceChecklist.why: Shippers and brokers match invoices to loads by these references, and an invoice without them gets held in accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and delivery dates, origin, and destination
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms the lane and timing, and settles disputes over late or early delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Carrier name, MC number, and DOT number
invoiceChecklist.why: Brokers and shippers verify authority before paying, and it ties the invoice to the vendor setup on file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Signed BOL and proof of delivery attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Most brokers and factoring companies will not pay without a clean signed POD.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized accessorials with timestamps and receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Detention, lumper, and layover charges are the most disputed lines, and gate-in and gate-out times and receipts back them up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate confirmation reference and agreed rate
invoiceChecklist.why: The invoice should match the signed rate confirmation, since any mismatch delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remit-to details or factoring notice of assignment
invoiceChecklist.why: If you factor invoices, the customer must pay the factor, and the invoice must say so to avoid double payment.

freight.paymentTerms: Net 30 is the most common term in trucking, with some shippers at net 45 or net 60 and brokers sometimes offering quick pay at net 7 to 15 for a 2 to 5 percent discount. Many small carriers use factoring to get paid within 24 to 48 hours for a fee of about 2 to 4 percent. Deposits are rare on standard loads but may be used for new customers or oversized loads. Invoices are normally sent as soon as delivery is complete, with the POD attached. Payment is typically by ACH, wire, or check, and some brokers pay by virtual card with a fee. Late fees should be written into your carrier agreement or terms, since they are hard to enforce otherwise.

tips.title: Invoice the day you deliver
tips.body: Most payment clocks start at invoice receipt or POD receipt. Send the invoice and paperwork the same day to avoid losing days on a net 30 term.

tips.title: Document detention in real time
tips.body: Text or email the broker when free time expires, and record arrival, check-in, and departure times. Detention claims without timestamps are often denied.

tips.title: Get accessorials approved in writing
tips.body: Lumper fees, layovers, and extra stops should be added to the rate confirmation or approved by email before you bill them.

tips.title: Check broker credit before hauling
tips.body: Look up the broker's days-to-pay and credit rating, and confirm their bond is active. Slow or unsafe brokers cost more than a lower rate does.

tips.title: Keep fuel surcharge separate
tips.body: Showing fuel as its own line keeps the line haul rate clean and makes it easy to justify when diesel prices move.

faqs.question: When should I send a freight invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it right after delivery, once you have the signed POD. Many brokers will not accept an invoice without the POD, and the payment term usually starts when they receive the complete package.

faqs.question: Can I charge detention if it is not on the rate confirmation?
faqs.answer: You can bill it, but you may have trouble collecting. If the rate confirmation is silent, ask the broker to approve it by email while you are waiting at the dock, and keep your timestamps.

faqs.question: Should I use a factoring company?
faqs.answer: Factoring helps with cash flow if you cannot wait 30 or more days for payment. The cost is usually 2 to 4 percent of the invoice, so compare it to how much your gaps in cash cost you. Recourse and non-recourse terms differ, so read the contract.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a load that was cancelled after I dispatched?
faqs.answer: Bill a TONU charge if it is in your agreement or rate confirmation. Include the load number, the cancellation time, and any proof you were en route or on site.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on freight?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by state, and many states do not tax transportation of goods for hire, but some do under specific conditions. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Carriers and brokers send quotes before a load is booked, usually by email, phone, or a load board reply. Shippers compare the all-in price, transit time, equipment type, and how the quote handles accessorials and fuel.

scopeChecklist.item: Origin, destination, and pickup and delivery windows
scopeChecklist.why: Rate depends on the lane and timing, and a changed appointment can change the price.
Dry van, reefer, flatbed, and step deck are priced differently, and special needs like tarps or temperature settings add cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Commodity, weight, piece count, and dimensions
scopeChecklist.why: Weight and size determine whether the load fits legal limits, needs permits, or moves as LTL with a freight class.
State whether fuel, tolls, and extra stops are in the rate, and list free time and detention rates for accessorials.
Driver assist, live load versus drop and hook, and lumper fees cause frequent disputes if they are not stated.
Fuel and market rates change quickly, so a quote should state how long it is valid and whether fuel floats.
Cargo coverage limits and requirements for high-value freight should be agreed before pickup.

pricingTips.title: Price from the round trip, not just the loaded miles
pricingTips.body: Account for deadhead back out of low-volume areas. A lane at $2.50 per mile may lose money if you return empty for 200 miles.

pricingTips.title: Quote an all-in rate and a line-haul rate
pricingTips.body: Many shippers want a single number, while brokers often want line haul plus fuel. Give both so the comparison is clear.

pricingTips.title: Add a minimum charge for short hauls
pricingTips.body: Loading time, fuel, and wear do not shrink with distance, so set a flat minimum for short-haul work.

pricingTips.title: Put accessorial rates in the quote up front
pricingTips.body: Listing detention, TONU, and stop-off rates before booking makes them far easier to collect later.

faqs.question: Is a freight quote binding?
faqs.answer: A quote usually becomes binding once both parties sign a rate confirmation. Before that, a quote is just an offer and typically expires after a stated period or when market rates change.

faqs.question: How long should a freight quote be valid?
faqs.answer: For spot loads, a day or less is common. For contract or recurring lanes, 30 to 90 days is typical, often with a fuel surcharge that adjusts weekly.

faqs.question: What if the shipment details change after I quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that changes in weight, dimensions, stops, or appointment times may change the price. Send a revised rate confirmation before you move the load.

faqs.question: Should I include fuel in the quote?
faqs.answer: Either way works if it is clear. Many carriers show a separate fuel surcharge tied to the DOE diesel index so the price adjusts when fuel costs move.

furniture-assembly.intro: Furniture assembly professionals build flat-pack and boxed furniture in homes, apartments, offices, and dorms. Customers hire them for IKEA wardrobes, bed frames, desks, patio sets, and fitness equipment, and many jobs come through task marketplaces, property managers, retailers, or direct referrals. Invoices usually cover assembly labor by the item or by the hour, plus add-ons like wall anchoring, haul-away, and travel.
furniture-assembly.pricingModel: Most assemblers price per item for common pieces (a nightstand, a bed, a PAX wardrobe) because customers want to know the total up front, and fall back to hourly pricing for mixed or unusual jobs. Per-item prices are usually set from the time the job takes, so a 30-minute dresser is priced differently than a 4-hour sectional or wardrobe system. Many solo operators set a minimum charge or trip fee of 1 to 2 hours to cover travel, especially for a single small item. Add-ons are billed separately: wall anchoring or mounting, disposal of boxes and packaging, moving the piece to another room, stairs with no elevator, and rush or weekend scheduling. Commercial and property-management work is often billed per unit or per project at a slightly lower rate in exchange for volume. Customers normally supply the furniture and hardware, so there is little materials markup, but replacement hardware or specialty anchors can be added at cost plus a small handling fee.

rates.service: Small items (nightstand, side table, shelf, stool)
Large wardrobe or modular system (e.g., PAX)
Trip fee or minimum service charge

items.description: Bed frame assembly (queen platform bed)
Dresser assembly with wall anchoring (6-drawer)
Nightstand assembly
Home office desk assembly
Cardboard and packaging removal
Trip fee (travel over 20 miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on receipt. Accepted: card, Zvenmo, or check. Anchoring hardware used per manufacturer instructions. Missing or damaged parts from the manufacturer are not covered by this invoice. Please report any assembly concerns within 7 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of each piece assembled with brand and model or description
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have many boxes and want to confirm each one was built, and it helps if a part is missing or a warranty claim comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers, landlords, and corporate clients need to match invoices to specific units or locations.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on charges listed separately (anchoring, haul-away, stairs, trip fee, rush)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating extras from base assembly prices prevents disputes about why the total is higher than a quoted per-item price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Time on site if any work was billed hourly
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly lines need start and end times or total hours so the client can see how the figure was reached.

invoiceChecklist.item: Note on missing, damaged, or substituted parts
invoiceChecklist.why: If the manufacturer shipped a defective or incomplete piece, documenting it protects you from being blamed for the result.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, contact details, and license or insurance number if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients, buildings, and retailers require proof of insurance, and some localities require a business or handyman license for certain work.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO or work order number for retailer, property, or marketplace jobs
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger accounts will not process payment without the reference they issued.

furniture-assembly.paymentTerms: For residential jobs, payment is typically due on completion, collected by card, mobile payment app, or check before you leave or shortly after via an emailed invoice. Many assemblers take a deposit or require card details on file for large projects such as multi-room moves or full apartment setups, often 25 to 50 percent. Property managers and businesses commonly pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, so state the due date on the invoice. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common on commercial accounts if disclosed in advance; check your state's rules on late fees. A cancellation or no-show fee equal to the trip fee or one hour of labor is also common, and works best when stated when booking.

tips.title: Quote per item, but protect yourself on time
tips.body: Fixed per-item prices are easy for customers to compare, but a difficult piece can eat your day. Set a higher price or an hourly option for items with unclear instructions, heavy glass, or custom configurations, and write that on the quote.

tips.title: Charge for anchoring separately
tips.body: Anchoring dressers, bookcases, and TVs to walls takes extra time, tools, and hardware, and it matters for safety. List it as its own line so clients see it as a distinct service instead of something to skip to save money.

tips.title: Document the condition of pieces before you start
tips.body: Photograph damaged panels, missing hardware, or scratches before assembly. Add a line to the invoice noting any issue so you are not blamed for pre-existing defects.

tips.title: Use a minimum charge for small jobs
tips.body: A single stool across town can lose money after fuel and time. A trip fee or one-hour minimum keeps short jobs worthwhile.

tips.title: Bill multi-unit work by the unit
tips.body: For apartment turnovers or office fit-outs, quote and invoice a fixed price per unit or per workstation so the property manager can track costs by unit.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the item?
faqs.answer: Most customers prefer per-item pricing because the total is predictable. Use hourly pricing for mixed lots, unclear scope, or jobs that involve repairs or modifications. Many assemblers use per-item pricing for common pieces and hourly for everything else.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel?
faqs.answer: Yes. A trip fee or a minimum charge is standard for small jobs, and many assemblers add a mileage or zone fee beyond a set distance. Put the policy on your quote and invoice.

faqs.question: What if the furniture has missing or broken parts?
faqs.answer: Note it on the invoice, bill for the time spent, and tell the client to contact the manufacturer or retailer for replacements. If you must return for a second visit once the parts arrive, many assemblers charge a return trip fee or the minimum charge.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on assembly?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax labor or installation services, and others do not, and rules can differ if you also sell hardware. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I need a license or insurance to do furniture assembly?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state and city. Assembly alone often does not require a contractor license, but some places require a business license, and work like wall mounting can fall under handyman rules. General liability insurance is common and often required by property managers and retailers.

estimate.intro: Furniture assemblers send estimates when a client has several pieces, a whole-home setup, or a commercial project, and before accepting jobs from property managers or retailers. Clients usually compare per-item pricing, minimum charges, and what extras like anchoring and haul-away cost. Many jobs are quoted by text from a photo or product list, so the written estimate should confirm exactly what is covered.

scopeChecklist.item: List of every item to be assembled with brand and model
scopeChecklist.why: Similar-looking pieces can take very different amounts of time, and a list prevents arguments about extra items added on the day.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of floors, stairs, and elevator access
scopeChecklist.why: Moving boxes up several flights adds time, and clients rarely think of this unless it is spelled out.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether anchoring, wall mounting, or leveling is included
scopeChecklist.why: Safety anchoring is a separate task with its own hardware and time, and clients often assume it is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies hardware, tools, and replacement parts
scopeChecklist.why: If parts are missing, you need to be clear that replacements come from the manufacturer or are billed at cost.
Boxes from a large order can fill a room, and haul-away may mean a dump run or an extra fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Condition of the space (cleared floor, access, working elevator, parking)
scopeChecklist.why: Cluttered rooms and lack of parking slow work and may trigger extra charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Scheduling, estimated duration, and cancellation or reschedule fees
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know when you will arrive, how long you will be there, and what happens if they are not ready.

pricingTips.title: Build quotes from a standard price list
pricingTips.body: Keep a per-item price sheet for common pieces and use it for every quote. It speeds up estimates and keeps pricing consistent between customers.

pricingTips.title: Add time for complex items
pricingTips.body: Wardrobes with doors, sliding tracks, and drawers with soft-close slides take longer than the box suggests. Check assembly manuals and past jobs for realistic times before quoting.

pricingTips.title: Offer a bundle discount, not a lower rate
pricingTips.body: For five or more pieces, a modest discount or capped total encourages bigger orders without cutting your hourly return. Make the discount a visible line so the standard rate stays intact.

pricingTips.title: State a validity period
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 14 to 30 days protects you if fuel costs, schedules, or your rates change before the client books.

faqs.question: Can I quote from photos or a product list?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common. Ask for model names or links, confirm stairs and access, and state that the quote assumes the list is complete. Say that additional items or complications are billed at your hourly or per-item rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most assemblers quote free for standard jobs, especially remotely. For large or commercial projects that require an in-person walkthrough, some charge a visit fee and credit it toward the job if booked.

faqs.question: What happens if the job takes longer than quoted?
faqs.answer: For fixed per-item quotes, you absorb normal variation. If the client adds items, the space is not ready, or parts are defective, state in the estimate that extra time is billed at your hourly rate and confirm changes with the client before continuing.

garage-door-repair.intro: Garage door repair technicians, usually solo operators or small crews, respond to calls for broken springs, off-track doors, dead openers, and damaged panels. They also install new doors and openers. Invoices typically combine a service call fee, parts, and labor, often collected the same day on site.
garage-door-repair.pricingModel: Most garage door work is priced per job rather than by the hour. Many companies charge a service call or diagnostic fee ($50-100) that is credited toward the repair if the customer approves. Repairs are quoted as flat prices that bundle labor with parts, such as a spring replacement priced per pair of springs. Parts are marked up from wholesale, commonly 30-100 percent depending on the part. Emergency, after-hours, and weekend calls usually carry a surcharge. New door and opener installations are quoted as a package with the unit, hardware, labor, and haul-away of the old door. Annual maintenance tune-ups are sold as a flat-rate visit. Warranty terms on parts and labor are usually stated alongside the price.

rates.service: Opener repair (sensors, logic board, gear kit)

items.description: Service call and diagnostic (credited to repair)
Replace torsion springs, 2 x 0.250 x 2" x 32" (pair), includes labor and winding
Replace lift cables
Replace nylon rollers, 4" stem
Lubricate hinges, rollers, and track; balance and safety reverse test

sampleInvoice.notes: Springs and cables carry a 1-year parts and labor warranty. Rollers carry a 90-day warranty. Payment is due upon completion. We accept card, check, and cash. Door was tested for balance and auto-reverse before leaving.

invoiceChecklist.item: Door and opener details (size, brand, model, approximate age)
invoiceChecklist.why: Spring and part specs depend on door weight and size, and a record helps with warranty claims and future repair calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Spring specifications (wire size, inside diameter, length, cycle rating)
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers can see exactly what was installed, and a cycle rating such as 10,000 vs. 25,000 explains price differences.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with brand or part numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Reduces disputes over markup and makes it easy to match parts for later repairs or warranty replacements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Garage door parts wear out and fail, and customers call back. Stating the warranty period in writing sets clear expectations.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service call fee and whether it was credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often question the trip charge. Showing the credit prevents confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: After-hours or emergency surcharge listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: A separate line shows the extra charge was for timing and not inflated parts or labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Safety checks performed (balance test, auto-reverse, photo-eye alignment)
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that the door was left in safe working order, which matters if there is a later injury or property damage claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or registration number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require a contractor license for garage door work. Check your local rules and print the number if you have one.

garage-door-repair.paymentTerms: Repair work is usually due in full on completion, with payment collected on site by card, check, or cash. For new door or opener installations, a deposit of 25-50 percent is common to cover ordering the door, with the balance due when the install is finished. Custom or special-order doors often require a larger deposit because they cannot be returned. Commercial and property management accounts typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms and may require a PO number. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common on invoiced accounts, and should be written on the invoice or estimate in advance.

tips.title: Credit the service call fee toward the repair
tips.body: Many customers accept a repair more readily when the trip charge is credited to the job. Show it as a line item with a credit so the arrangement is clear on paper.

tips.title: Bundle springs in pairs
tips.body: Springs are best replaced as a pair because the second one is likely near the end of its life. Invoicing them as a pair avoids arguments about why you replaced both.

tips.title: Offer good, better, best options
tips.body: Present standard springs and high-cycle springs, or a basic and a quiet belt-drive opener, as separate priced options. Customers choose and the invoice reflects what they agreed to.

tips.title: Take photos of the failed parts
tips.body: Photos of a snapped spring, frayed cable, or cracked panel back up your invoice if a customer disputes the work or a property manager asks for proof.

tips.title: Collect before leaving on emergency calls
tips.body: Customers with a stuck door are motivated while you are there and less so a week later. Take payment on site, and send a receipt or paid invoice right away.

faqs.question: Should I charge a separate service call fee?
faqs.answer: Most companies do. A fee of $50-100 covers travel and diagnosis time when a customer declines the repair. Many technicians credit it toward the job if the customer approves the work. Tell the customer the fee when they book.

faqs.question: How do I invoice parts and labor?
faqs.answer: You can list a flat price per repair that includes both, or break parts and labor out on separate lines. Flat pricing is common for springs and cables. Itemize on larger jobs like panel or door replacement, where the customer may want to compare parts costs.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on garage door repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax parts only, some tax both parts and labor on repairs, and some treat installations differently from repairs. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant, and show tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer refuses to pay after the repair?
faqs.answer: Keep a signed estimate or work approval, photos of the work, and a dated invoice. Send a written reminder, then a formal demand letter. For larger installations, check whether your state allows a mechanic's lien, and consider small claims court for smaller amounts.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for nights and weekends?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most companies do. Surcharges of $50-150 or a higher flat rate for after-hours calls are common. Disclose the surcharge before you dispatch and list it as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Garage door technicians usually give a quote on site after inspecting the door, and for new doors or openers, after measuring the opening. Customers often compare prices from two or three companies, so they look at spring quality, warranty length, and whether the price includes haul-away and disposal. A written estimate helps you win the job and prevents disagreements about what was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact parts being replaced, with specs
scopeChecklist.why: Spring size, cycle rating, and opener horsepower affect price and quality. Naming them lets customers compare your quote fairly.

scopeChecklist.item: Door and opener make, model, and size
scopeChecklist.why: Records what you inspected and prevents confusion if parts need to be ordered.
Items like drywall repair, electrical work for a new outlet, painting, or insulation upgrades can be disputed if they are not excluded in writing.

scopeChecklist.item: Related parts that may also need replacing
scopeChecklist.why: If a door is off-track, bent tracks or damaged panels might be found once the door is opened up. Note that the price may change and how you will get approval.

scopeChecklist.item: Haul-away and disposal of old door or opener
scopeChecklist.why: Customers assume this is included. State whether it is, or the fee if not.
Warranty length is a major selling point and a frequent source of disputes.
Custom doors can take weeks to arrive. Give an expected install date and what happens if there are delays.
Parts and door prices change, so a 15 to 30 day expiry protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Quote a firm price for standard repairs
pricingTips.body: For springs, cables, rollers, and sensors, give a flat price on the spot. Customers prefer certainty, and you know your typical time and parts cost.

pricingTips.title: Price options side by side
pricingTips.body: Show standard and long-life springs, or chain-drive and belt-drive openers, with a price for each. Most customers choose a middle option when they see the differences.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for hidden problems
pricingTips.body: On older doors, worn bearings, rusted hardware, and cracked struts are common. Mention that additional repairs will be quoted before you do them.

pricingTips.title: Take a deposit on special orders
pricingTips.body: Request 25-50 percent on new doors, custom sizes, and wind-load rated models. This covers the supplier's cost if the customer backs out.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Repair estimates are often covered by the service call fee. For new door installations, many companies measure and quote free. Some charge a fee for complex commercial jobs, credited if the customer hires them.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after starting the job?
faqs.answer: Only with the customer's approval. If you find additional broken parts, stop, explain the problem and the added cost, and get a written or text approval before continuing. Record it on the final invoice.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical for door and opener installations, since supplier prices change. For quick repairs quoted on site, many technicians expect an answer the same day.

faqs.question: Should I give phone quotes?
faqs.answer: Give a price range based on the symptoms and describe it as an estimate. Final pricing should come after you inspect the door, because the real cause is sometimes different from what the customer describes.

gardening.intro: Gardeners and small garden-care businesses maintain residential and light commercial landscapes. They bill for recurring maintenance visits, seasonal cleanups, planting and bed installation, pruning, mulching, and plant and material costs. Most work solo or with a small crew, so clear invoices matter for both repeat clients and one-time projects.
gardening.pricingModel: Most gardeners charge hourly for maintenance and one-off labor, often with a minimum visit charge to cover travel and setup. Recurring clients are commonly billed per visit or as a flat monthly amount based on a set schedule. Larger projects like bed installation, sod, or raised beds are usually quoted as a flat fee or per square foot, with plants, soil, mulch, and stone listed separately. Materials are typically marked up 10-30% to cover sourcing, delivery, and warranty risk. Extras such as debris hauling, dump fees, and equipment rental (stump grinder, sod cutter) are added as separate lines. Many gardeners also add a fuel or trip charge outside their normal service area.

rates.service: Recurring maintenance visit (small to mid-size yard)

items.description: Spring garden cleanup: bed clearing, perennial cutback, edging
Shrub and hedge pruning (boxwood, hydrangea, viburnum)
Hardwood mulch, delivered and spread (labor included)
Perennials, 1-gallon (6 coneflower, 4 salvia, 5 sedum)
Green waste hauling and dump fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Plants are guaranteed for 30 days with proper watering; replacements cover plants only, not labor. Next scheduled maintenance visit: May 14. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and visit dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Gardeners often work at multiple properties and across several visits, so dates and locations prevent disputes over what was done and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours separated by task
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients accept pruning at one rate and weeding at another more easily when the hours are broken out instead of lumped together.

invoiceChecklist.item: Plants and materials itemized with quantity, size, and unit cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing pot size (1-gallon, 5-gallon) and cubic yards of mulch or soil justifies the price and supports any replacement claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disposal, hauling, and dump fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real out-of-pocket costs and clients often forget them if they are not listed as a separate line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Plant guarantee terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating how long plants are covered and what voids the guarantee (overwatering, drought, pets) reduces replacement arguments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license or pesticide applicator license number, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and localities require a license for pesticide or herbicide application, and some clients, HOAs, and property managers ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring service schedule and next visit date
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms the agreed frequency for maintenance clients and prevents confusion about skipped or extra visits.

gardening.paymentTerms: For one-time visits and small jobs, many gardeners bill on completion with payment due in 7 to 14 days. Larger installations typically require a deposit of 30-50% to cover plants and materials, with the balance due at completion. Maintenance clients are often billed monthly, either in advance or at month end, and some use auto-pay by card or bank transfer. Checks, cards, and bank transfer are all common. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is typical if stated in writing beforehand, and some gardeners pause service after one missed payment. Check your state's rules on late fees and interest.

tips.title: Set a minimum visit charge
tips.body: Travel, loading tools, and cleanup take time regardless of job size. A minimum of one hour or a flat $75-100 per stop keeps short visits from losing money.

tips.title: Mark up plants and materials
tips.body: You source, transport, and stand behind the plants. A markup of 10-30% on nursery costs and bulk materials is standard, and listing the items shows the client what they are paying for.

tips.title: Bill seasonally for recurring clients
tips.body: Maintenance visits slow in winter. Consider a flat monthly rate across the year or a seasonal contract so income stays steady and clients know what to expect.

tips.title: Keep photos of before and after
tips.body: Photos attached to an invoice or sent with it settle questions about scope and condition, especially for cleanups and overgrown beds.

tips.title: Charge separately for extras
tips.body: Hauling, stump grinding, extra mulch, and unplanned weeding add up. Add them as separate lines with a short description so they are not seen as part of the base price.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat rate for garden maintenance?
faqs.answer: Hourly works well for first visits and overgrown gardens because the time is hard to predict. Once you know a property, a flat per-visit or monthly rate is easier for the client to budget for and rewards you for working efficiently.

faqs.question: How do I bill for plants that die after planting?
faqs.answer: Decide on a guarantee before the job and write it on the invoice, for example 30 days with replacement of the plant only. Without a stated policy, clients may assume everything is covered indefinitely.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on gardening services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax plants and materials but not labor, others tax certain landscape services, and many do not tax labor at all. Check with your state's department of revenue or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many gardeners include a trip charge or fuel surcharge for jobs outside their regular service area, or bill drive time for distant one-off jobs. Mention it in the quote so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pay in cash?
faqs.answer: You can accept it, but still issue an invoice or receipt and record the income. Written records protect you at tax time and if the client later disputes payment.

estimate.intro: Gardeners send estimates before installations, cleanups, redesigns, and new maintenance contracts. Clients usually compare two or three quotes, looking at the scope, plant quality, and whether materials and disposal are included. A clear written estimate often wins over a lower price that leaves details vague.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact area and boundaries of the work
scopeChecklist.why: Say which beds, borders, or sections are included so there is no argument about whether the back fence line was part of the job.
For maintenance, state what each visit covers (weeding, pruning, edging, blowing) and how often, so clients know what is and is not included.
Specifying 1-gallon versus 5-gallon pots and exact varieties prevents disputes about what was promised, and affects your cost significantly.
State mulch type and depth, soil amendments, edging, and stone, and whether the client may choose or supply their own.
Clarify whether green waste and old plant material are hauled off and whether dump fees are included or extra.
New plantings depend on watering. Stating that the client is responsible for watering after installation protects your guarantee.
Plant and material prices change with season and supply, so an expiration date (often 30 days) keeps your quote from becoming outdated.

pricingTips.title: Visit the site before quoting
pricingTips.body: Overgrown beds, slopes, access limits, and soil condition change labor time dramatically. Photos help, but an in-person look avoids underbidding.

pricingTips.title: Separate labor from materials
pricingTips.body: Showing labor and plants as different line items makes it easier to adjust scope if the client wants to cut cost, and keeps your markup clear.

pricingTips.title: Offer options
pricingTips.body: Give good, better, best choices, such as 1-gallon versus 3-gallon plants, or standard versus premium mulch. Clients feel in control and often choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Roots, buried debris, and poor drainage show up once you start digging. Add a contingency or state that hidden conditions may require a revised price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Simple maintenance quotes are usually free. For design work or large installation plans, many gardeners charge a design fee of $75-300 or more, often credited toward the project if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. For jobs with large plant orders or volatile material prices, 14 days may be safer.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than my estimate?
faqs.answer: Agree in writing before doing extra work. If hidden conditions or client-requested changes increase the scope, send a change note or revised estimate and get approval first.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit when the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: For installations, yes in most cases. A 30-50% deposit covers plants and materials and shows the client is committed. For routine maintenance, a deposit is less common.

general-contractor.intro: General contractors manage residential and light commercial construction projects, from kitchen and bath remodels to additions, decks, and whole-house renovations. They hire and coordinate subcontractors, order materials, pull permits, and bill the client for labor, materials, subcontractor work, and their own management fee. Invoices usually follow a contract schedule, such as a deposit, progress draws, and a final payment at completion.
general-contractor.pricingModel: General contractors price in a few common ways. Fixed-price (lump sum) contracts set one total for a defined scope and are typically billed in draws tied to milestones. Cost-plus contracts bill actual labor, materials, and subcontractor costs plus a markup or fixed fee, often 10-25 percent, with receipts backing each charge. Time and materials is common for small repairs and punch-list work, billed per hour with materials at cost plus markup. Some contractors quote by square foot for new construction, additions, and finish work as a planning number, but still bill against a schedule of values. Change orders are priced separately and added to the contract total. Overhead and profit, usually 15-30 percent combined on top of direct costs, are built into the numbers whichever model you use.

rates.unit: per sq ft of floor area

items.description: Progress draw #2: Demolition complete, framing and rough plumbing/electrical passed inspection (30% of $38,000 contract)
Change order #1: Relocate sink drain and add under-cabinet outlets
Additional carpentry labor, reframe window opening (T&M)
Lumber and headers for window reframing (cost plus 15%)
Dumpster rental, 20-yard, second haul

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Smith kitchen remodel, 214 Maple St. Contract dated 3/4. Draw #2 per payment schedule. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Lien waiver for payment through this draw attached. Checks payable to the company name above; ACH and card accepted, card payments add 3%.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and business information
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require the license number on contracts and sometimes invoices, and it tells the client and any lender you are legitimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address and contract date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific job and agreement, which matters if you have several jobs with the same client or a dispute arises.

invoiceChecklist.item: Draw or milestone description with percent complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and lenders want to see that the amount matches the work finished, not just a number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract total, previous payments, current amount due, and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the running position on the job so the client can reconcile against the contract and the bank can release funds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders listed separately with approval dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps extra work from being disputed later. Reference the signed change order number and its amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subcontractor and material costs with receipts (for cost-plus jobs)
invoiceChecklist.why: Cost-plus clients are paying for actual costs and expect backup. Attach receipts or sub invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lien waiver or reference to one
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, clients and lenders expect a conditional or unconditional lien waiver with each payment. Check your state's rules on required forms.

general-contractor.paymentTerms: Most residential contractors collect a deposit at signing, often 10-30 percent where state law allows, since some states cap deposits. The remainder is billed in progress draws tied to milestones such as demolition, rough-in inspections, drywall, cabinet install, and substantial completion, with a final payment held until the punch list is done. Draws are commonly due within 3-10 days of invoice, and final payments on receipt or within 7 days. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract, though some states limit them. Checks, ACH, and wire are typical for large amounts; card payments are accepted by some contractors with a surcharge where permitted. Some contractors keep the right to pause work if a draw is late, and that right should be written in the contract.

tips.title: Tie every draw to a visible milestone
tips.body: Write the payment schedule so each draw matches finished work, such as framing inspection passed or tile complete. Clients pay faster when they can see the progress, and you avoid being financially ahead of the job.

tips.title: Price change orders in writing before doing the work
tips.body: Get a signed change order with the cost and any schedule impact before starting extra work. Verbal approvals are the most common source of unpaid balances on remodels.

tips.title: Keep draws ahead of your costs
tips.body: Front-load the schedule modestly so deposits and early draws cover materials and sub payments. You should not be financing the client's project from your own credit line.

tips.title: Collect lien waivers both directions
tips.body: Give clients a waiver when you are paid, and get waivers from your subs and suppliers when you pay them. This protects you and the homeowner from duplicate payment claims.

tips.title: Hold final billing until the punch list is signed off
tips.body: Send the final invoice with a completed punch list and any warranty information. A short, clear closeout helps avoid retainage disputes.

faqs.question: How much deposit can a general contractor ask for?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states cap residential deposits at a percentage of the contract or a fixed dollar amount, and some require deposits to be tied to work or materials. Check your state licensing board rules, then state the deposit and schedule clearly in the contract.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on materials and subcontractors?
faqs.answer: Typical markup is 10-25 percent on materials and subcontractor costs, or a management fee of similar size on cost-plus jobs. Overhead and profit combined are often 15-30 percent. Small jobs usually need higher markup to cover minimum time and overhead.

faqs.question: Should I invoice by percent complete or by milestone?
faqs.answer: Either works if it is in the contract. Milestone draws are simpler for homeowners to verify, while percent-complete billing is common on larger jobs and when a lender requires a schedule of values. Pick one method and use it consistently.

faqs.question: What is retainage and do I need to deal with it?
faqs.answer: Retainage is a portion of each payment, often 5-10 percent, held until the project is complete. It is common on commercial work and public jobs, and less so on residential. If your contract includes it, show the amount held on each invoice and invoice for it at closeout.

faqs.question: Can I charge sales tax on a remodel?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. In many states a contractor pays sales tax on materials and does not charge it to the client on a lump-sum contract, while some states require tax on certain materials or on separately stated items. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: General contractors send written estimates or bids before work begins, usually after a site visit and often alongside two or three competing bids. Homeowners compare total price, but also scope, allowances, schedule, and who handles permits. A clear estimate sets up the contract and prevents the "I thought that was included" argument later.

scopeChecklist.item: Detailed scope of work by room or phase
scopeChecklist.why: Specific descriptions such as 'demo existing cabinets, install new base and wall cabinets' make it clear what is and is not included.
If the client picks fixtures, tile, or appliances later, set a dollar allowance for each. Overages become a change order, not a surprise.
