List what you are not doing, such as painting, flooring, appliance purchase, or hazardous material abatement, so the client does not assume it is covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, inspections, and who pulls them
scopeChecklist.why: Permit fees and the time to handle them are real costs. State whether fees are included or passed through at cost.
Spell out the deposit and draws so the client knows when money is due and what milestones trigger each payment.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline with start and estimated completion
scopeChecklist.why: Give a realistic range and note delays that are outside your control, like weather, inspections, and material lead times.
Rot, old wiring, asbestos, and code upgrades are often found after demo. State how hidden conditions will be priced and approved.

pricingTips.title: Build up costs line by line
pricingTips.body: Price labor, materials, subcontractors, permits, dumpsters, and equipment separately, then add overhead and profit. Per-square-foot numbers are good for a first conversation but weak for a final bid.

pricingTips.title: Get written sub quotes and add a contingency
pricingTips.body: Base your bid on current subcontractor and supplier quotes, and include a 5-10 percent contingency on remodels where walls are closed. Material prices move, so state how long the quote is valid.

pricingTips.title: Offer options instead of discounting
pricingTips.body: Present a base scope with priced add-ons or alternates, such as upgraded countertops. Clients can adjust the budget without you cutting margin.

pricingTips.title: Charge for detailed design-phase estimates on big jobs
pricingTips.body: For major projects, a paid preconstruction or design-phase fee, credited toward the contract, protects your time from bid shoppers.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors offer free estimates on small and mid-size jobs. For large remodels or when detailed plans, engineering, or multiple revisions are needed, a paid estimate or preconstruction fee is common and often credited to the contract if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14-30 days. Material costs and sub availability change, so state an expiration date and note that pricing may be adjusted after that.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an estimate and a fixed bid?
faqs.answer: A fixed bid commits to a total price for a defined scope. An estimate is an approximate cost that may change as scope or conditions change. Label the document clearly so the client knows which one they are getting.

faqs.question: What happens if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: If the contract is fixed-price, overruns from your own errors are yours to absorb, while client-requested changes and unforeseen conditions are handled through written change orders. On cost-plus jobs, give a not-to-exceed figure or regular cost updates so the client is not surprised.

generator-installation.intro: Generator installation contractors put in standby (whole-home) and portable-connection generator systems for homeowners and small commercial clients. Invoices typically cover the generator unit, transfer switch, electrical and gas connections, concrete or composite pad, permits, and commissioning. Many are licensed electricians, plumbers or gas fitters, or work as a small crew that subs out part of the job.
generator-installation.pricingModel: Most installs are priced as a flat fee for a defined scope, built from equipment cost plus materials, labor, permits and a margin. Generator and transfer switch costs are usually passed through with a markup of 10 to 25 percent. Labor is estimated in crew-hours or days but quoted as a lump sum. Variable items such as trenching, gas line length and conduit runs are often priced per linear foot so that changes are easy to adjust. Service calls, repairs and annual maintenance are billed hourly or as a flat plan fee. Permit, inspection and utility coordination fees are listed as separate lines. Larger jobs are billed in stages: deposit at signing, equipment order, rough-in, and final after inspection and startup.

rates.service: Standby generator install labor (residential, 10-24 kW), unit not included
Generator unit, 22 kW air-cooled (supplied by contractor)
Automatic transfer switch (100-200 amp) supply and install
Gas line extension (natural gas or propane), black iron or CSST
Electrical conduit and wire run, trenching included
Electrician or gas fitter labor, service and repair
Annual maintenance plan (oil, filters, plugs, load test)

items.description: 22 kW air-cooled standby generator, model and serial no. on file
200 amp automatic transfer switch, supply and install
Composite equipment pad, set and leveled
Natural gas line extension, CSST, including pressure test
Conduit and wire run, trenched
Installation labor, mounting, wiring, commissioning and startup
Electrical permit and inspection coordination

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $6,000 received at signing is credited above. Balance due within 10 days of passed final inspection. Generator warranty registered in the customer's name; manufacturer warranty terms apply. Unit has been tested under load and the owner was walked through operation and exercise settings.

invoiceChecklist.item: Generator make, model, kW rating and serial number
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for warranty registration, insurance records and future service calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Transfer switch type, amp rating and serial number
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents what was installed and which circuits or whole-home loads it covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require license numbers on contracts and invoices, and permit numbers show the work was inspected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fuel type and gas line details
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists natural gas or propane, pipe type and length, pressure test results and any meter or regulator upgrade, which are common dispute points.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized equipment separate from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Helps with sales tax treatment, which varies by state, and shows the client where the money went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection and commissioning dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows when the final inspection passed and when the system was started and load tested, which usually triggers final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and added work
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, extra trenching, panel upgrades or longer gas runs should appear as separate lines tied to a signed change order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the remaining balance clearly on staged jobs.

generator-installation.paymentTerms: A deposit of 30 to 50 percent at signing is common, since equipment is ordered up front and can be costly or non-returnable. Many contractors collect a second payment when the generator and transfer switch are delivered or the rough-in is complete, with the balance due on a passed inspection and startup, typically net 7 to 14 days. Large residential jobs are often paid by check, ACH or card, and some contractors add a card fee or offer a discount for ACH. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Check your state's rules on deposit limits, lien rights and required contract language.

tips.title: Bill equipment and labor separately
tips.body: Generators are expensive, and lumping them in with labor invites arguments over price. Separate lines also protect you if the client cancels after the unit is ordered.

tips.title: Get the deposit to cover the equipment
tips.body: Supply delays and price changes are common. A deposit large enough to cover the unit and switch keeps you from financing a client's generator.

tips.title: Tie the final payment to the inspection
tips.body: State in the contract that final payment is due after the passed inspection and startup, not after the client feels comfortable. It removes ambiguity about when you can send the last invoice.

tips.title: Price site surprises as change orders
tips.body: Rock, tree roots, long gas runs, meter upgrades and panel replacements can swing a job by thousands. Write them up and get a signature before doing the work, then invoice them on their own lines.

tips.title: Sell maintenance at handoff
tips.body: Offer an annual service plan on the final invoice or at startup. Recurring plan invoices smooth out income between install seasons, which spike after storms.

faqs.question: Should I invoice the generator at cost or with a markup?
faqs.answer: Most contractors add a markup of 10 to 25 percent on equipment to cover ordering, delivery, storage, warranty handling and risk. Show it as a single line price for the unit rather than your cost plus a markup, unless the contract is cost-plus.

faqs.question: When can I send the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually after the final inspection passes and the generator has been started and load tested. Put that condition in your contract so the due date is clear.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on generator installations?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether the job is treated as a sale of goods or a real property improvement. Some states tax materials, some tax the whole job, and some do not tax residential installs. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for permits and inspections?
faqs.answer: List the permit fee as its own line, either at cost or with a coordination fee for your time. If the fee is unknown at signing, note that the actual permit cost will be billed.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to pay after the next storm?
faqs.answer: Do not release the unit or energize the system without the agreed payment. A written payment schedule and a lien notice, where allowed in your state, protect you if payment stalls.

estimate.intro: Generator installers send a written estimate after a site visit, and often the client collects two or three to compare. Clients look at brand and kW size, what the transfer switch covers, gas versus propane, and who handles permits and the utility. A clear scope separates a fair bid from a low one that leaves out gas work or the pad.

scopeChecklist.item: Generator brand, model and kW size
scopeChecklist.why: Two bids at different sizes or brands are not comparable, and the load calculation should justify the size you chose.

scopeChecklist.item: Transfer switch type and what it powers
scopeChecklist.why: Whole-home, service-entrance and selected-circuit setups differ greatly in price and clients often assume more is covered.
State fuel type, pipe material, estimated footage, who supplies the propane tank, and whether a meter or regulator upgrade is needed from the utility.
Pad location, setbacks and distances to the panel and gas meter drive trenching and wiring costs. Note the assumed footage so overages are clear.
Say who pulls permits and who pays fees, and note that HOA or utility approval timelines can delay the start.
List items such as panel upgrades, rock excavation, landscaping repair, tree removal, driveway or patio cutting and propane fill, which otherwise get assumed as included.

scopeChecklist.item: Price validity, lead time and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Equipment prices and delivery times change. State how long the quote holds, the expected schedule, and the deposit and progress payments.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a load calculation
pricingTips.body: Size the unit from the panel's actual loads rather than a guess. It supports your price and avoids callbacks for an undersized unit.

pricingTips.title: Price by the linear foot for variable runs
pricingTips.body: Include an assumed footage for gas and electrical runs and a per-foot rate for anything beyond it. The client sees how the number was built and overages are simple to explain.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better and best options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three configurations, such as a smaller unit with a selected-circuit switch versus a larger unit with a whole-home switch, so the client chooses a scope rather than a bidder.

pricingTips.title: Build in lead time and price protection
pricingTips.body: Set a short validity window, often 14 to 30 days, and say that equipment price changes from the manufacturer may adjust the quote after that.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many installers do free site visits for standard residential jobs. Some charge a fee of $100 to $300 for complex or commercial work and credit it toward the job if the client signs.

faqs.question: How firm is a generator quote?
faqs.answer: A flat quote holds for the stated scope and assumptions. Anything outside it, like extra footage or rock, is handled by change order. Write that into the estimate.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Equipment costs and availability can shift, so a short window protects you.

faqs.question: Can the estimate become the contract?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it includes scope, price, payment schedule and signature lines and meets your state's contractor requirements. Many states require specific language, such as cancellation rights or license numbers, so check local rules.

golf-coach.intro: Golf coaches include PGA or LPGA teaching professionals at clubs and ranges, independent instructors, junior program coaches, and swing coaches who use launch monitors or video analysis. They bill for individual lessons, lesson packages, playing lessons on the course, group clinics, junior camps, and on-course or club-fitting sessions.
golf-coach.pricingModel: Most golf coaches charge per lesson, usually 30, 45, or 60 minutes, with a lower per-lesson price when students buy a package of 3, 5, or 10. Rates depend on the coach's credentials, the facility, and the local market. Club pros often split revenue with the facility or pay range and bay fees, so those costs may be built into the price or billed separately. Playing lessons on the course are priced per hour or per 9 or 18 holes, and the student usually pays greens fees and cart fees on their own. Group clinics and junior camps are priced per player. Technology such as launch monitor or video analysis is sometimes included and sometimes billed as an add-on. Some coaches offer monthly memberships or retainers that include a set number of lessons, practice sessions, and video reviews. Packages are typically prepaid and expire after a set period, such as six or twelve months.

rates.service: Group clinic or adult small group

items.description: 60-minute private lesson, swing fundamentals and driver
Lesson package, 5 x 45-minute lessons (prepaid, valid 6 months)
Launch monitor session add-on
Practice range bay fee (coach-paid, passed through)
Video swing review, remote follow-up

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Lesson package expires 6 months from purchase and is non-refundable after the first lesson. Lessons canceled with less than 24 hours' notice are charged in full. Accepted: card, Venmo, Zelle, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson dates, lengths, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often pay in batches or through a parent, and dated entries with the course, range, or bay show exactly what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and remaining lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages create a balance. Showing lessons used, lessons remaining, and the expiration date prevents disputes later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name when the payer is a parent or employer
invoiceChecklist.why: Junior lessons are usually paid by a parent, and corporate or group outings may be paid by a company, so the invoice needs both the payer and the student.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on and technology fees listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Launch monitor sessions, video analysis, and fitting time are extra for many coaches. Separate lines show what is optional.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through facility costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Range bay fees, simulator rental, greens fees, and cart fees should be itemized so the client sees that you are not marking them up, unless you disclose a markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Weather and last-minute cancellations are common, and stating the notice period on the invoice supports charging for missed slots.

invoiceChecklist.item: Credentials or certification (optional)
invoiceChecklist.why: PGA, LPGA, or other teaching certification numbers can help when a club, school, or employer is reimbursing the lesson.

golf-coach.paymentTerms: Many independent golf coaches collect payment at or just before the lesson, by card, Venmo, Zelle, or cash, and invoice only for packages, camps, corporate events, and recurring clients. Packages and camps are usually paid in full upfront, and camps often take a deposit to hold a spot. Terms of due on receipt or net 7 are common for individual clients, while schools, clubs, and companies may pay net 15 to 30. A 24-hour cancellation policy is standard, with late cancellations charged at the full or half lesson rate. Late fees are uncommon with individual students, but they can be written into terms for group programs and corporate clients. If you teach at a club, check whether the facility collects payment and pays you a share, because then you may invoice the club instead of the student.

tips.title: Sell packages to lock in commitment
tips.body: Swing changes take weeks to settle in. A prepaid package of 5 or 10 lessons at a modest discount keeps students coming back and gives you cash upfront. Put the expiration date in writing.

tips.title: Be clear on who pays facility costs
tips.body: Range balls, bay time, simulator fees, and greens fees add up. Decide whether they are included in your rate or billed on top, and list them as separate lines if they are billed.

tips.title: Set a firm cancellation policy
tips.body: Weather, work, and school schedules cause frequent changes. A 24-hour notice rule with a clear charge for late cancellations protects your calendar, and a rain policy that offers a reschedule keeps clients happy.

tips.title: Bill remote video reviews per review or in a bundle
tips.body: Time spent reviewing uploaded swings and writing feedback is real work. Charge per review or sell a monthly bundle so it does not turn into free follow-up.

tips.title: Track mileage and equipment costs
tips.body: If you travel between courses or run a mobile business, keep mileage logs, and track launch monitor, camera, and training aid costs. Many of these are deductible for self-employed coaches, so check with a tax professional.

faqs.question: Should I invoice for every lesson or only for packages?
faqs.answer: Many coaches collect payment on the spot for single lessons and invoice only for packages, camps, clinics, and corporate events. If a student books regularly, a monthly invoice listing each lesson date works well and cuts down on payment handling.

faqs.question: How do I handle unused lessons in a package?
faqs.answer: Put the expiration date and refund terms on the package invoice before the first lesson. Most coaches make packages non-refundable after the first lesson and valid for six to twelve months, with limited extensions for injury or illness.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the time I spend on video analysis or lesson plans?
faqs.answer: If you review swings outside lesson time, charge for it as a separate line item or include it in a package or monthly membership. Otherwise, set a limit on free follow-up so unpaid work does not creep in.

faqs.question: Can I charge sales tax on golf lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax personal instruction, but some tax lessons or related services, and equipment or fitting products may be taxed. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if I teach at a club that takes a cut?
faqs.answer: Find out whether the club bills the student and pays you, or whether you bill the student and pay the club for range or lesson fees. Your invoice or statement should match that arrangement, and you should keep records of what the club retains.

estimate.intro: Golf coaches send quotes before ongoing programs, multi-lesson packages, junior camps, corporate or charity outings, school or team contracts, and travel or destination coaching. Clients usually compare per-lesson rates, package pricing, coach credentials, available technology, and the facility where lessons take place.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Specify how many lessons, whether they are 30, 45, or 60 minutes, and whether they are private, semi-private, or group, so the price lines up with the delivered time.

scopeChecklist.item: Location and who pays facility costs
scopeChecklist.why: State where lessons happen and whether range fees, bay rentals, greens fees, and cart fees are included or extra.
Launch monitor data, video analysis, and written feedback have different value to clients. Say which are included and which are paid add-ons.
Set a start date, how often sessions will happen, and when a package expires so the client knows when they must be used.
Rain, heat, and conflicts are common. Spell out notice requirements, how weather is handled, and whether missed sessions are rescheduled or forfeited.

scopeChecklist.item: Group size and age range for clinics and camps
scopeChecklist.why: The number of players, skill levels, and ages affect staffing and price. Include minimum enrollment and what happens if a camp is canceled.
If you bring training aids, clubs, or travel to a course or event, say who covers mileage, lodging, and rental costs.

pricingTips.title: Anchor on your hourly lesson rate
pricingTips.body: Work out your 60-minute rate first, then discount packages by about 10 to 20 percent for 5 or 10 lessons. Show the per-lesson price next to the package total so the savings are obvious.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for ongoing instruction
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a 5-lesson starter package, a 10-lesson season package, and a monthly membership with video reviews. Clients can pick a level without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Price events per head with a minimum
pricingTips.body: For corporate outings, clinics, and camps, quote per player and set a minimum total. This covers your prep and travel if attendance is lower than expected.

pricingTips.title: Include a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Tee times, range availability, and your own calendar fill up. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days encourages decisions and avoids honoring old prices.

faqs.question: Should I give a free first lesson or evaluation?
faqs.answer: Some coaches offer a short free assessment to win new students, but many charge for it because the first session takes the most preparation. If you offer one, keep it short, such as 15 to 20 minutes, and state clearly what is included.

faqs.question: How should I quote a junior camp or clinic?
faqs.answer: Quote a price per player with a maximum enrollment, a minimum for the camp to run, dates, hours, and what is included such as range balls, snacks, or a shirt. Collect a deposit to hold each spot.

faqs.question: Do I quote lessons in advance for a single student?
faqs.answer: For single lessons, a posted rate is usually enough. A written quote is more useful for multi-lesson packages, season-long programs, and playing lessons where the facility fees and time on course vary.

faqs.question: What if a client wants a swing overhaul with no end date?
faqs.answer: Avoid open-ended promises. Quote a set number of sessions with a review at the end, and offer to extend or renew based on progress. Avoid guaranteeing specific score or handicap improvements.

google-ads-specialist.intro: Google Ads specialists build and manage paid search, Shopping, Performance Max, YouTube, and Display campaigns for small businesses, agencies, and e-commerce brands. Most work solo or in small shops and bill for account management, campaign setup, audits, and conversion tracking work. Invoices usually separate what you charge for your time from what clients spend on ads.
google-ads-specialist.pricingModel: Most specialists bill a monthly management fee, either a flat retainer or a percentage of ad spend, often 10-20% with a minimum. Flat retainers are common for accounts under $10,000 a month in spend because they stay predictable for both sides. One-time work such as account setup, audits, and GA4 or conversion tracking implementation is billed as a flat project fee or hourly. Hourly billing is used for ad hoc requests, training, and overflow work outside the retainer scope. The ad spend itself is usually paid by the client directly to Google through their own billing profile, which keeps it off your invoice and avoids you carrying that cost. If you do pay for ads on a client's behalf, list it as a separate pass-through line and consider requiring prepayment. Landing page work, creative, and reporting dashboards are often quoted separately.

rates.service: Management fee as percentage of ad spend
Shopping feed and Merchant Center optimization

items.description: Google Ads management, March 2025 (search and Performance Max, 3 campaigns)
Conversion tracking setup: GA4 events and Google Ads import for form submissions and calls
Negative keyword cleanup and search term review (outside retainer scope)
New landing page A/B test setup and monitoring

sampleInvoice.notes: Ad spend is billed directly to the client's Google Ads account and is not included on this invoice. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Retainer covers up to 5 hours of requested changes per month; additional work is billed at $110 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and account ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers repeat monthly, so the period and the Google Ads customer ID show exactly which account and month the fee covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad spend for the period, shown for reference
invoiceChecklist.why: If your fee is a percentage of spend, the client needs to see the spend figure and the percentage used so the math can be checked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for management, setup, and hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question charges outside the retainer. Itemizing scope keeps one-time projects from looking like recurring fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs, if any
invoiceChecklist.why: Third-party tools, stock creative, or call tracking numbers you paid for should be listed at cost or with a stated markup, separate from your fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that ad spend is billed by Google directly
invoiceChecklist.why: This prevents confusion about whether your invoice includes media costs and clarifies who owns the billing relationship.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and dates for any time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Ad hoc requests need a short description and hours so the client can match them to what they asked for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late fee and payment terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers are easy to let slip. Stating terms on each invoice gives you something to point to if payment is late.

google-ads-specialist.paymentTerms: Management retainers are commonly invoiced at the start of the month, in advance, with payment due in 7 to 15 days. Setup and audit projects often take 50% upfront and 50% on delivery. Percentage-of-spend fees are billed in arrears once the month's spend is final. Many specialists charge a late fee of 1 to 1.5% per month where allowed and pause management on accounts that are more than 30 days overdue. Clients usually pay by ACH, credit card, or check. Card fees are sometimes passed on or built into rates. Month-to-month agreements with 30 days' notice to cancel are standard.

tips.title: Keep ad spend off your invoice
tips.body: Have clients add their own payment method in Google Ads. You avoid fronting thousands of dollars, you are not responsible for overspend disputes, and your invoice stays a clean record of your fees.

tips.title: Set a minimum fee on percentage pricing
tips.body: A 15% fee on a $1,000 monthly budget is $150, which will not cover the work. Set a floor such as $750 so low-spend months do not undercut you.

tips.title: Define what the retainer includes
tips.body: List number of campaigns, reporting frequency, and a cap on change requests. Anything beyond that, such as new landing pages or creative, is billed hourly or quoted.

tips.title: Bill setup separately from management
tips.body: Building a account from scratch takes much more time than maintaining it. A distinct setup fee also makes it easier to keep your monthly rate sensible.

tips.title: Get access through a manager account link
tips.body: Request access from the client's account to your manager account so you never hold their login. If the client leaves unpaid, you can request removal cleanly, and the account stays theirs.

faqs.question: Should I charge a percentage of ad spend or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Percentage pricing scales with the workload as spend grows, but it can reward higher spend rather than better results. Flat retainers are easier for small clients to budget. Many specialists use a percentage with a minimum monthly fee.

faqs.question: Should ad spend appear on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Clients typically pay Google directly through their own billing profile. Only include ad spend if you are paying Google on their behalf, and in that case list it as a separate pass-through line, ideally collected in advance.

faqs.question: Can I charge for reporting and calls?
faqs.answer: Yes. Either include a set amount of reporting and one monthly call in the retainer, or bill them hourly. State what is included in your agreement so extra meetings do not eat into the retainer.

faqs.question: What if a client's performance drops and they refuse to pay?
faqs.answer: Management fees are for work done, not guaranteed results. Your agreement should say that you do not guarantee specific conversions or return on ad spend. Keep monthly reports to show the work you completed.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on management fees?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital advertising or marketing services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and add tax to the invoice only where it applies.

estimate.intro: Specialists send quotes when a prospect asks for a proposal after a discovery call or account review. Clients usually compare monthly fees, what is included, contract length, and whether setup is charged separately. A clear scope matters because the effort depends on account size, number of campaigns, and how clean the tracking is.

scopeChecklist.why: Search, Shopping, Performance Max, YouTube, and Display each take different effort. Naming them avoids assumptions that everything is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly ad budget the quote is based on
scopeChecklist.why: Your fee, especially a percentage, depends on spend. If the budget grows significantly, the fee or workload changes.
Specify whether you are building conversion tracking, GA4 events, and audiences, since broken tracking is the most common hidden cost.
Weekly dashboards and calls take real time. Stating frequency keeps expectations in line with the fee.
Ad copy may be included, but images, video, and landing pages are often separate. Say who supplies them.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revisions or change requests per month
scopeChecklist.why: Without a cap, retainers turn into unlimited on-call support.
Clarify minimum term, notice period, and who owns the account and data after the engagement ends.

pricingTips.title: Audit before you quote a large account
pricingTips.body: Ask for view access or a short paid audit first. Existing structure, tracking errors, and wasted spend change the time needed, and quoting blind often means underpricing.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: Package options such as search-only, search plus Shopping, and full-funnel management let clients choose by budget and make it easier to close without discounting.

pricingTips.title: Separate setup from monthly management
pricingTips.body: Quote the one-time build and the ongoing fee as distinct lines. The client sees the real cost of launching and you are covered if they stop after a few months.

pricingTips.title: Tie the fee to a minimum
pricingTips.body: If you use percentage pricing, show the percentage and the minimum together so low-budget months do not shrink your fee below what the work takes.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before looking at the account?
faqs.answer: Give a range at most. Account quality varies a lot, so a firm number is safer after you have seen the account, tracking, and past performance, or after a paid audit.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Ad costs, seasons, and your availability change, so an expiry date keeps you from honoring an old price after the scope grows.

faqs.question: Should I include projected results in a quote?
faqs.answer: Avoid guaranteeing numbers. You can share ranges based on past accounts or industry benchmarks, labeled as estimates, but results depend on budget, offer, website, and competition.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement or is the quote enough?
faqs.answer: A signed quote or short services agreement is better. It should cover scope, fees, account ownership, payment terms, and cancellation so both sides have a written record.

grant-writer.intro: Grant writers are freelancers and small consultancies who research funding opportunities and write proposals for nonprofits, schools, municipalities, tribes, and small businesses. Invoices usually cover discovery calls, prospect research, narrative drafting, budget development, letters of inquiry, and reporting or other post-award work.
grant-writer.pricingModel: Most grant writers charge a flat project fee per proposal, an hourly rate for research, editing, and strategy work, or a monthly retainer for ongoing development support. Fees are based on the work required, not the grant outcome. Many professional codes, including the Association of Fundraising Professionals' ethics standards, prohibit commission or percentage-of-award compensation, and many government funders do not allow grant-writing costs to be paid as a percentage of an award. Flat project fees typically scale with the complexity of the application: a short letter of inquiry costs far less than a federal application with a 30-page narrative and attachments. Retainers often cover a set number of hours or deliverables per month. Rush work, extra revision rounds beyond the agreed number, and work on funder portals are often billed separately.

rates.service: Hourly grant writing, research, and editing
Letter of inquiry or short foundation application
Full foundation proposal (5-15 pages with budget)
Federal or state grant application (e.g., SAMHSA, HUD, NEA)
Grant report or final evaluation narrative
Grant strategy session or calendar planning

items.description: Discovery call and funder guideline review - Community Health Foundation request
Prospect research: 12 regional foundations, summary with deadlines and fit notes
Full foundation proposal: narrative, logic model, and budget narrative (Youth Literacy Program)
Additional revision round requested after staff review (beyond 2 included)
Online portal entry and attachment upload

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Fee covers writing services only and is not contingent on award. Final submission confirmation will be forwarded upon submission. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Funder name, program, and application deadline
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to a specific submission so the client's finance team can code it to the right project or budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable description with stage completed
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows whether you are billing for research, a draft, final submission, or reporting, which matters for milestone-based fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that fees are not contingent on award
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear you are not paid on commission, which many funders and ethics codes prohibit, and helps if the client wants to charge the cost to a grant.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of included revision rounds and any extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents disputes when staff or board members request additional rewrites.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for hourly line items
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, especially public agencies and foundations, may require time detail to approve payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client's PO number, grant code, or cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Nonprofits and government agencies often will not process payment without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your W-9 status and EIN or business name
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients paying you over the IRS reporting threshold typically need a W-9 on file to issue a 1099.

grant-writer.paymentTerms: Most grant writers collect a deposit of 30-50% before starting a proposal, with the balance due on delivery of the final draft or on submission. Retainers are normally billed at the start of each month. Net 15 or net 30 is common, though nonprofits and municipalities can be slow, so confirm their approval process and board meeting schedule up front. Some writers add a late fee of 1-1.5% per month, stated in the contract. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or card. Larger federal applications are often split into milestones such as research, first draft, and submission.

tips.title: Never bill as a percentage of the award
tips.body: Contingent or percentage fees violate widely followed fundraising ethics standards and are disallowed by many funders. Quote a fixed fee or hourly rate and state in your agreement that payment does not depend on funding.

tips.title: Bill by milestone on large applications
tips.body: For a federal application that takes six weeks, invoice at kickoff, first draft, and submission. This keeps cash flowing and gives the client natural checkpoints before you do more work.

tips.title: Put revision limits in writing
tips.body: Specify two rounds of consolidated edits. Extra rounds are billed hourly. Without this, a committee with five reviewers can double your time on a flat-fee project.

tips.title: Bill for waiting on the client
tips.body: If the client misses an agreed date for data, financials, or letters of support, note that the deadline risk is theirs and charge for rework or rush time if you have to compress the schedule.

tips.title: Separate award-period work from pre-award work
tips.body: Post-award reporting, budget revisions, and grant management are different scopes. Invoice them separately so clients can charge them to the grant if the funder allows it.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of the grant I help win?
faqs.answer: You should not. Professional fundraising ethics codes prohibit percentage-based compensation, and many funders, including federal agencies, do not allow it. Use a flat fee, hourly rate, or retainer instead.

faqs.question: Should I still get paid if the grant is not funded?
faqs.answer: Yes. You are paid for the work of researching, writing, and submitting, not for the result. Put this in your contract and on each invoice so expectations are clear.

faqs.question: Can my client pay my fee out of the grant?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Some funders allow proposal writing costs in the budget, but many do not allow pre-award costs. The client should check the guidelines. Your invoice should show the dates and work performed clearly in case it is allowed.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: As an independent contractor, you usually give your client a W-9 and they issue you a 1099-NEC if they pay you above the IRS threshold in a year. Check current thresholds and your state rules.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a retainer when the work varies by month?
faqs.answer: State what the retainer covers, such as a set number of hours or deliverables. Invoice the same amount monthly and track hours. Note any overage billed at your hourly rate, and say whether unused hours roll over.

estimate.intro: Grant writers send a quote or proposal before any work begins, usually after a discovery call where you review the funder's guidelines, the nonprofit's readiness, and the deadline. Clients often compare your fee against other freelancers, agencies, or the cost of using staff time, so the quote needs to show what is included and what is not.

scopeChecklist.why: The scope depends on the funder's requirements, and a fixed deadline determines whether rush charges apply.
List narrative, budget narrative, logic model, letters of support drafts, and attachment prep so the client knows what they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: Information and materials the client must supply
scopeChecklist.why: Financial statements, board lists, outcomes data, and letters of support are the most common causes of delay. Set due dates for each.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of draft and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Limits unlimited edits and gives the client a clear review process, such as one draft and two consolidated rounds.

scopeChecklist.item: Who submits the application and handles the portal
scopeChecklist.why: Some clients expect you to submit through Grants.gov or a foundation portal, which adds time and requires registration access.

scopeChecklist.item: Statement that the fee is not contingent on award
scopeChecklist.why: Sets ethical and legal expectations before work starts and avoids clients assuming you work on success.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as post-award reporting or grant management
scopeChecklist.why: Keeps follow-on work from being assumed to be part of the original fee.

pricingTips.title: Price by application complexity, not page count
pricingTips.body: A 10-page foundation proposal for a returning grantee can take 8 hours, while a federal application with a data plan and evaluation section can take 60. Estimate hours per section and add time for research, calls, and revisions.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a research-and-outline package, a full draft, and a full draft plus submission. Clients with in-house staff may only want a draft to edit, and tiers let them choose without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for client delays
pricingTips.body: Build in time for slow responses and new information. If the project depends on data you have not seen, state your assumptions and say the quote may change if they are wrong.

pricingTips.title: Require a deposit to hold the deadline
pricingTips.body: Accept the quote with a signed agreement and a 30-50% deposit. Deadlines are fixed, so your calendar is committed once you accept the work.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when the scope is clear, such as a specific foundation proposal. Use an hourly estimate with a cap when the scope is uncertain, such as a program still being developed or a funder's guidelines not yet released.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days, or until a date tied to the deadline. If the application is due in three weeks, a quote that stays open for a month does not make sense because you may no longer have time.

faqs.question: What if the client asks me to guarantee funding?
faqs.answer: Do not guarantee outcomes. Funding decisions are made by the funder. You can describe your experience and past success, but your quote should be for the work and make clear that results are not promised.

faqs.question: Do I charge for preparing a quote?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call and a simple quote are normally free. For a complex federal application, a paid grant readiness assessment or prospect research phase can be quoted first and credited toward the full project if the client continues.

graphic-designer.intro: Graphic designers send invoices to small businesses, agencies, nonprofits, and individuals for visual work such as logos, brand identities, print collateral, packaging, social media graphics, and layouts. Most work is billed by project, by the hour, or on a monthly retainer, and invoices often have to account for revisions, usage rights, and out-of-pocket costs like stock images and fonts.
graphic-designer.pricingModel: Most graphic designers quote a flat project fee for defined deliverables such as a logo package or a brochure, because clients want a fixed number and designers want to be paid for the value of the result rather than the hours. Hourly billing is common for ongoing edits, small tasks, and work with an unclear scope, and it is also how many designers calculate the internal math behind a flat fee. Retainers (a set number of hours or deliverables per month) suit clients who need steady social, email, or marketing assets. Brand identity work is often sold in tiered packages. Many designers charge a deposit of 30 to 50 percent upfront, include a set number of revision rounds, and bill extra for additional rounds, rush turnaround, and licensing beyond standard use. Stock photos, font licenses, printing, and shipping are usually billed as pass-through costs, sometimes with a small handling markup that is disclosed in the agreement.

rates.service: Full brand identity (logo, palette, type, guidelines)

items.description: Brand identity design: logo concepts, one selected direction, two revision rounds (50% deposit already paid, see notes)
Brand guidelines document (PDF, 12 pages)
Business card and letterhead layouts, print-ready files
Additional revision round requested after approval
Stock photography licenses (2 images) and font license, at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Total shown before deposit credit. 50% deposit of $2,260.50 received on 3/4; balance due within 14 days of invoice date. Final files released upon full payment. Usage rights transfer to the client on payment as outlined in the signed agreement. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and deliverables list
invoiceChecklist.why: Naming each deliverable (logo files, guidelines, print-ready PDFs) ties the charge to something the client received and prevents disputes about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing which revisions were part of the fee and which were additional explains charges beyond the original quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights or license terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Exclusive vs. non-exclusive use, term, and media (print, web, packaging) affect price, so the invoice should reference what the client is licensed to do.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock images, font licenses, printing, and shipping should appear as their own lines, with receipts available, so clients see they are not part of your design fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Crediting the deposit with its date shows exactly what remains and avoids double billing questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush fee or deadline note, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client asked for a compressed timeline, a line item records the agreement and explains the higher price.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often cannot process payment without a purchase order or job number.

graphic-designer.paymentTerms: Designers commonly ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront on projects, with the balance due on delivery of final files or within 14 to 30 days of the invoice. Larger projects may use milestone billing, for example one third at kickoff, one third after concept approval, and one third at delivery. Retainers are usually billed at the start of the month. Many designers hold final source files or release of usage rights until payment is complete. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract in advance, and check your state's rules on late fees. Payment is usually accepted by ACH, card, check, or online transfer; card fees may be passed on to the client if disclosed.

tips.title: Tie rights transfer to payment
tips.body: State in your contract and on the invoice that final files and usage rights transfer only once the invoice is paid in full. This gives you leverage on slow payers without needing to argue about it later.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Specify how many rounds are included and what counts as a round, such as one consolidated set of feedback. Bill extra rounds hourly. Without this, projects drift and the effective hourly rate drops.

tips.title: Bill milestones on longer projects
tips.body: For brand identities and multi-piece campaigns, invoice at kickoff, concept approval, and delivery so you are never more than a stage of work ahead of payment.

tips.title: Charge for scope changes when they happen
tips.body: When a client adds a deliverable, such as a new format or extra application, send a short change note and add it to the next invoice rather than absorbing it.

tips.title: Keep receipts for pass-through costs
tips.body: Save stock license and printing receipts. If a client questions a line, you can show the exact cost, and the records help at tax time.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Project pricing suits well-defined work like logos, brochures, and packaging, and tends to reward efficiency. Hourly suits open-ended work, small edits, and clients whose scope keeps changing. Many designers quote a flat fee and bill hourly for anything outside it.

faqs.question: Do I charge for unused concepts or abandoned projects?
faqs.answer: Yes, you should. Include a kill fee or a clause that work completed to date is billable if the client cancels. Deposits are often non-refundable once work begins, and your contract should say so.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on design work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital goods or certain design services, and others do not. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant before assuming either way.

faqs.question: How do I bill for stock images and fonts?
faqs.answer: List them as separate lines at your actual cost, or include a clearly stated handling markup. Some clients prefer to buy licenses in their own name, which avoids the line altogether.

faqs.question: What if a client pays late or stops responding?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder on the due date, then a follow-up with the late fee terms, and pause any further work or file release until the balance is paid. If it continues, a formal demand letter or small claims court is an option for unpaid balances, depending on the amount and your state's limits.

estimate.intro: Graphic designers send estimates before starting a logo, brand identity, packaging, or print job, and often after a discovery call or a short brief. Clients usually compare your price against other designers, agencies, and template-based tools, so the estimate needs to show exactly what they are getting for the fee.

scopeChecklist.why: List each piece (logo, business card, social templates) and the formats provided, such as AI, EPS, PDF, PNG, and SVG, so there is no argument about missing files.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of concepts and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: This is the biggest source of scope creep in design work. Stating how many concepts and rounds are included protects your time.
Give dates for first concepts and final delivery, and note that delays in client feedback move the schedule.
Say what the client can do with the work, whether they receive source files, and when rights transfer, usually on final payment.
Copywriting, photography, illustration, printing, web development, and trademark searches are often assumed to be included. Naming exclusions avoids surprise requests.
Stock images, fonts, and printing can vary widely, so state whether they are included or billed at cost on top.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and quote expiry
scopeChecklist.why: Stating the deposit amount and how long the price is valid locks in terms and encourages a prompt decision.

pricingTips.title: Price the outcome, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate your hours to check the number, but present a flat fee tied to deliverables. Clients tend to compare packages more easily than hourly estimates, and you are not penalized for working efficiently.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and expanded option, for example logo only, logo with brand guidelines, and full identity with collateral, lets clients choose a budget without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unclear scope
pricingTips.body: If the client is vague about the number of pieces or approvals involved, build in time for extra communication and revisions or quote a discovery phase first.

pricingTips.title: Separate rush and licensing premiums
pricingTips.body: Show rush fees and extended usage rights as their own lines, so clients can see the cost of tight deadlines or broad licenses and decide whether they need them.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates or proposals?
faqs.answer: Short estimates for standard projects are usually free. For complex work that requires research, strategy, or a detailed proposal, a paid discovery phase is reasonable and filters out clients who are not serious.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Software costs, your availability, and project scope can change, so an expiry date lets you reprice if the client takes longer to decide.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. But you can bill for work outside the written scope. Send a short change request describing the added work and its cost before doing it, and get written approval.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope instead of the rate, for example fewer concepts, fewer applications, or fewer revision rounds. This keeps your hourly value intact and gives the client a clear choice.

grout-cleaning.intro: Grout cleaning businesses are usually solo operators or small crews who restore tile and grout in kitchens, bathrooms, showers, entryways, and commercial floors. Invoices typically cover deep cleaning by square foot, color sealing or sealing, and add-ons like caulk replacement or stain removal. Customers are mostly homeowners, property managers, realtors preparing a listing, and small businesses such as restaurants and gyms.
grout-cleaning.pricingModel: Most grout cleaners price by the square foot of tile, with a job minimum to cover travel and setup, typically $150 to $250. Floors are quoted per square foot, while showers and backsplashes are often priced as flat fees because vertical surfaces take longer and require more care. Sealing, color sealing (grout recoloring), and grout repair are separate line items. Heavily soiled or neglected grout, epoxy grout, natural stone, and large-format tile with narrow joints change the price, so many operators use tiered pricing for light, moderate, and heavy soil. Commercial work is often quoted per sq ft with a recurring schedule discount, and some contractors offer packages such as clean plus seal for a bundled price. Charge hourly only for odd repair work, such as regrouting small sections or caulk replacement, and mark up any materials beyond the basics.

rates.service: Shower or tub surround grout cleaning
Spot regrouting of cracked or missing grout
Commercial tile and grout cleaning (restaurant, restroom)

items.description: Kitchen and entry floor grout deep clean (porcelain tile, moderate soil)
Master shower grout cleaning (walls and floor)
Penetrating grout sealer, kitchen and entry floor
Shower caulk removal and replacement (corners and base)
Spot regrout of cracked joints near tub

sampleInvoice.notes: Do not mop or get floors wet for 24 hours after sealing; avoid showering for 24 hours after caulk replacement. Payment due within 7 days of service. Accepted: card, check, or bank transfer. Late balances after 14 days incur a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and exact areas cleaned (kitchen floor, hall bath shower, etc.)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several tiled areas, and listing each one prevents disputes over what was and wasn't included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage per area and the rate applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-sq-ft pricing needs to match the measurement on your estimate so the total is easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tile and grout type (porcelain, natural stone, epoxy, sanded or unsanded)
invoiceChecklist.why: Material affects price and cleaning method, and documents that you used appropriate products on sensitive surfaces like marble or travertine.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sealer or colorant product used, and cure or dry time
invoiceChecklist.why: Records what was applied and gives the client the aftercare window, which helps if a floor is walked on early and a problem arises.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for sealing, color sealing, caulk, and repairs
invoiceChecklist.why: Add-ons are optional and priced differently, so itemizing them clarifies the total and makes future repeat work easier to quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pre-existing damage noted (cracked tile, hollow spots, stained or etched grout that will not come clean)
invoiceChecklist.why: Protects you if a client later says the damage or remaining discoloration was your fault.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license and insurance details, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and commercial clients often require proof of liability insurance, and some local jurisdictions require a business license, so check your local rules.

grout-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential jobs are most often paid on completion by card, check, or digital payment, with terms of due on receipt or within 7 days. Many cleaners collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent only on larger jobs, such as whole-house tile or color sealing projects that need materials and scheduling. Commercial customers usually pay net 15 or net 30 and may need a purchase order or vendor form on file. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common and should be stated on the estimate and invoice before work starts. For recurring commercial accounts, monthly invoicing with a service log keeps things tidy.

tips.title: Set a job minimum and stick to it
tips.body: Small jobs like a single backsplash or powder room floor cost nearly as much in travel, setup, and equipment as larger ones. A $150 to $250 minimum keeps those visits profitable.

tips.title: Price showers separately from floors
tips.body: Vertical surfaces, tight corners, and glass doors take more time and protective prep than a flat floor. A flat shower fee based on size and soil level is simpler than counting square feet on walls.

tips.title: Photograph before and after, and attach to the invoice record
tips.body: Photos of stained grout before cleaning justify the heavy-soil rate and show results. They also protect you if a client later claims damage or says the work was not done.

tips.title: Offer clean plus seal as a bundle
tips.body: Sealing right after cleaning is the natural upsell, and a small bundle discount increases acceptance while still earning more per visit than cleaning alone.

tips.title: Bill for conditions you cannot fix
tips.body: Some grout is cracked, permanently stained, or failing from moisture. Note on the invoice that cleaning does not repair damaged grout, and offer regrouting or color sealing at a separate price.

faqs.question: Should I charge per square foot or a flat fee for grout cleaning?
faqs.answer: Use per square foot for floors, where the area is easy to measure and the work scales evenly. Use flat fees for showers, tub surrounds, and backsplashes, where size varies less and the difficulty comes from the layout. Always apply a job minimum.

faqs.question: Do I charge extra for heavily stained or neglected grout?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many cleaners use two or three soil tiers, such as light, moderate, and heavy, with heavy grout costing 30 to 60 percent more due to extra dwell time, scrubbing, and repeat passes. Explain this on the estimate so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Can I charge for sealing separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. Sealing is a distinct product and step, and some clients decline it. Listing it as its own line item with the sealer type and square footage makes the invoice clear and supports your pricing.

faqs.question: What if the grout does not come clean?
faqs.answer: State on your estimate that results depend on grout condition and that deep stains or old, porous grout may not fully lift. If it does not, offer color sealing or regrouting as an alternative, and bill the cleaning you performed.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on grout cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax cleaning or maintenance services, while others tax only materials or nothing at all. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant about how to treat services versus sealer and product sales.

estimate.intro: Grout cleaners usually quote before the visit, often after a phone call with photos or a quick walkthrough. Clients compare square-foot price, what is included in the cleaning, whether sealing is part of the price, and whether the company is insured. A clear written quote helps you stand apart from low-ball competitors who skip sealing or use weak chemicals.

scopeChecklist.item: Areas and measured square footage for each space
scopeChecklist.why: Per-sq-ft pricing depends on measurement, so agreeing on areas up front prevents disagreements when the final invoice arrives.

scopeChecklist.item: Tile and grout type and current condition
scopeChecklist.why: Natural stone, epoxy, and sanded versus unsanded grout need different products and care, and condition determines how much labor is needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Cleaning method (steam, alkaline cleaner, rotary scrub, hand scrub)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients want to know what is being used on their surfaces, and it justifies price differences against cheaper competitors.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether sealing, color sealing, or caulk work is included or optional
scopeChecklist.why: Sealing is the most common point of confusion. State whether it is in the price or an add-on.

scopeChecklist.item: Furniture moving, appliance access, and prep responsibilities
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know whether you will move items or whether the floor must be cleared before you arrive.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected results and limits, including stains that may remain
scopeChecklist.why: Sets realistic expectations and reduces complaints when old or damaged grout does not return to its original color.

scopeChecklist.item: Dry and cure times, and the quote validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Tells the client when the area can be used again, and protects you from material or labor cost changes if they wait to book.

pricingTips.title: Ask for photos and measurements before quoting
pricingTips.body: Photos of the worst areas and approximate room dimensions let you give a realistic range without a site visit, and help you spot epoxy grout, stone, or heavy buildup that raises the price.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present clean only, clean plus seal, and clean plus color seal. Clients tend to choose the middle option, and it shows the value of each step.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for uncertain conditions
pricingTips.body: If grout is heavily soiled or you suspect mold or damage underneath, give a range and confirm the final price after testing a small area on site.

pricingTips.title: Include a travel or minimum charge
pricingTips.body: Put your minimum visit fee on the quote so small jobs are not a surprise and rural trips cover your drive time.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most grout cleaners quote for free by phone or photo. For large commercial jobs or on-site assessments far from your base, a trip fee credited toward the work is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a grout cleaning quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Chemical, equipment, and labor costs do not change much month to month, but a validity period gives you room to reprice and to manage your schedule.

faqs.question: What if I find damage or mold after starting?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the estimate stating that hidden damage, failing grout, or mold remediation is outside the quoted scope. If you find it, stop, document it with photos, and give the client a revised price or a recommendation to call a tile contractor.

faqs.question: Can I quote by phone without seeing the job?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range from photos and square footage, but state that the final price is confirmed on site. Surprises with soil level, grout type, or tile size are the main reason phone quotes miss.

guitar-teacher.intro: Guitar teachers give private lessons, small group classes, and workshops in acoustic, electric, classical, and bass styles. They work from a home studio, a music store, the student's house, or online. Invoices usually cover monthly tuition, single lessons, missed-lesson policies, and extras like books, strings, or recital fees.
guitar-teacher.pricingModel: Most guitar teachers charge per lesson, set by length (30, 45, or 60 minutes). Many bill monthly tuition in advance, based on the number of lessons in the month or a flat monthly rate that averages out over the year, so the amount stays the same whether a month has four or five weeks. Lesson packages (such as 4 or 10 lessons) are common for new students and for adults with irregular schedules. Rates go up with experience, teaching credentials, genre specialization, and local cost of living. Travel to a student's home normally adds a fee or a higher rate. Other billable items include a one-time registration or trial lesson fee, printed method books and sheet music, picks, strings, and tuners, recital or performance fees, and recording or transcription work. Group classes are priced per student per session or per term. Online lessons are typically priced the same or slightly lower than in-person.

items.description: Monthly tuition, 30-minute private lessons (October, 4 lessons)
Make-up lesson for teacher cancellation, credited
Method book: Hal Leonard Guitar Method Book 2
Acoustic guitar strings, light gauge, and string change
Fall recital participation fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due by the 1st of the month. Lessons canceled with less than 24 hours' notice are billed at the full rate. Accepted payment: Zelle, check, or card. Late payments after the 7th are subject to a $10 fee. Thank you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and, for minors, the parent or guardian billed
invoiceChecklist.why: The person paying is often not the person taking lessons, and parents need clear records for their own budgeting or reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and lesson dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the dates shows exactly which lessons are covered and settles questions about how many weeks were in the month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson length and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Students may switch between 30 and 60 minute lessons, so each line should show the length and the per-lesson price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellations, make-ups, and credits
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing a credited lesson or a billed no-show keeps your cancellation policy visible and avoids arguments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials and supplies as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Books, strings, picks, and capos should be itemized so tuition is not confused with one-time costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recital, workshop, or event fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These are irregular charges and families should see them labeled with the event name and date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment methods, due date, and late fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out how to pay and when keeps payments from drifting, especially with monthly tuition.

guitar-teacher.paymentTerms: Most guitar teachers bill monthly in advance, with payment due on or before the first lesson of the month. Some collect weekly or per lesson, mainly with new or drop-in students. A common setup is a trial lesson paid at the time, followed by monthly tuition. Late fees of $5-25 after a grace period of a few days are typical, and some teachers pause lessons until the balance is paid. A written cancellation policy is standard, often requiring 24 hours' notice, with late cancellations billed in full and teacher cancellations made up or credited. Payment is usually by Zelle, Venmo, check, cash, or card. Teachers who work through a music school or store are often paid by the school instead and do not invoice families directly.

tips.title: Bill monthly in advance
tips.body: Charging for a set number of lessons per month, paid before the month starts, protects your income from last-minute cancellations and cuts down on chasing payments after the fact.

tips.title: Put your cancellation and make-up policy in writing
tips.body: State the notice period, what counts as a make-up, and whether make-ups expire. Include a one-line summary on each invoice so students are reminded without a conversation.

tips.title: Use a flat monthly rate for steady students
tips.body: Dividing the yearly lesson count by twelve gives a consistent monthly amount. It avoids awkward five-week months and makes budgeting easier for families.

tips.title: Offer a discounted multi-lesson package for new students
tips.body: A four-lesson starter package gives students a reason to commit and gives you payment up front. Set an expiration, such as 60 days, to keep scheduling manageable.

tips.title: Track income for taxes
tips.body: Independent teachers usually report lesson income as self-employment income. Keep invoice records and note expenses like books, teaching software, and studio supplies, and ask a tax professional what applies to you.

faqs.question: Should I charge per lesson or monthly?
faqs.answer: Either works. Monthly billing in advance is more common for regular students because it gives predictable income and fewer payment reminders. Per-lesson billing suits drop-in, adult, or irregular-schedule students.

faqs.question: Do I charge for lessons a student misses?
faqs.answer: Most teachers do, since the time was reserved for that student. A typical policy is full charge for cancellations with less than 24 hours' notice and a make-up or credit when you cancel.

faqs.question: How do I bill a parent for a child's lessons?
faqs.answer: Address the invoice to the parent or guardian and list the child's name as the student. Include lesson dates and any recital or book charges so the parent has a clear record.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on guitar lessons?
faqs.answer: In many states private music instruction is not taxed, but rules vary and sales of physical items like books and strings may be taxable. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I charge for lesson prep or transcription?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so up front. Many teachers include normal prep in the lesson rate and charge separately for custom transcriptions, arrangements, or recordings made at the student's request.

estimate.intro: Guitar teachers rarely send formal quotes for standard weekly lessons, but written estimates matter for lesson packages, group classes, school or event contracts, and home-visit arrangements. Clients typically compare lesson length, per-lesson price, travel fees, and cancellation terms across teachers.

scopeChecklist.item: Lesson length, frequency, and start date
scopeChecklist.why: Clearly stating 30 or 60 minutes, weekly or biweekly, and when lessons begin sets the basis for the total cost.
Say whether lessons are at your studio, the student's home, or online, and what any travel fee covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of lessons and how long the package is valid
scopeChecklist.why: A package without an expiration can leave you with unused lessons months later.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials the student must buy or you will supply
scopeChecklist.why: Books, a tuner, and a guitar rental or loan can add cost, and students should know whether they are included.
Agreeing to these terms before the first lesson prevents disputes about missed sessions.
Optional costs like recitals or exam entry fees should be flagged so families are not surprised later.

scopeChecklist.item: Group class size and minimum enrollment
scopeChecklist.why: If a class runs only with a minimum number of students, state what happens if enrollment falls short.

pricingTips.title: Quote the monthly total, not just the lesson rate
pricingTips.body: Many families think in monthly cost. Showing both the per-lesson price and the monthly amount makes comparison easier and avoids confusion about month length.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial lesson at a set price
pricingTips.body: A single paid trial lesson, quoted separately from ongoing tuition, lets the student check the fit and gives you a clear basis for the next step.

pricingTips.title: Price in travel for home visits
pricingTips.body: Include drive time and mileage in the per-visit price or as a flat add-on. A 60-minute lesson that takes 90 minutes with travel should not be billed at your studio rate.

pricingTips.title: Set rate review dates
pricingTips.body: Note in the quote that rates are reviewed each year, with notice given in advance, so an increase is expected rather than a surprise.

faqs.question: Do I need a written quote for private lessons?
faqs.answer: Not always, but a short written summary of rate, schedule, and policies is useful. It works as an agreement and can be a simple email or form.

faqs.question: How long should a lesson quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for a quoted rate or package price. After that, your rates or schedule availability may change.

faqs.question: Can I quote a school or music store for teaching hours?
faqs.answer: Yes. Quote an hourly or per-session rate, the number of hours, travel or prep time if any, and who supplies equipment. Institutions often have their own contract forms, so compare terms.

faqs.question: What if a student wants to change from 30 to 60 minute lessons?
faqs.answer: Provide an updated quote showing the new rate and effective date. Confirm it in writing before the change takes effect.

gutter-cleaning.intro: Gutter cleaning businesses are usually solo operators or small crews who clear leaves, debris, and clogs from gutters and downspouts for homeowners, landlords, and small commercial properties. Invoices typically cover a cleaning priced by home size or linear feet, plus add-ons such as downspout flushing, minor repairs, and gutter guard cleaning. Most jobs are one visit, so invoices are often sent the same day.
gutter-cleaning.pricingModel: Most gutter cleaners charge a flat price per job based on the home's size, number of stories, and linear feet of gutter, rather than hourly. A single-story home is often priced lowest, and two- and three-story homes cost more because of ladder time and safety setup. Many operators set a minimum charge to cover travel and setup. Add-ons are priced separately: downspout flushing or unclogging, roof debris blow-off, gutter guard cleaning, small repairs like resealing seams or re-securing hangers, and pressure washing fascia. Some charge per linear foot for larger or commercial properties. Recurring customers may get a discount for seasonal plans, such as two cleanings a year, billed per visit or prepaid.

rates.service: Gutter cleaning, single-story home (up to 2,000 sq ft)
Gutter cleaning, two-story home (up to 3,000 sq ft)
Gutter cleaning, three-story or steep-roof home
Gutter cleaning, per linear foot (larger or commercial)
Minor repairs (reseal seams, reattach hangers, replace screws)

items.description: Gutter cleaning, two-story home, approx. 180 linear feet, debris bagged and removed
Downspout flushing (4 downspouts, 1 clogged and cleared)
Reseal two gutter corner seams, rear of house
Replace gutter hangers (materials)
Roof debris blow-off, front slope

sampleInvoice.notes: Service completed 10/14. Before and after photos available on request. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Repairs carry a 30-day warranty. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Many customers are landlords or property managers with several addresses, and a clear address and date prevents mix-ups and supports repeat billing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Home size, stories, and linear feet cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: This justifies the price and shows why a three-story home costs more than a ranch, which heads off pricing questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons such as downspouts, guards, and repairs
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often only expect a base cleaning, so separating extras shows exactly what was done beyond the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials used with quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Sealant, hangers, screws, downspout elbows, and splash blocks should be listed so the charge is clear and reimbursable for landlords.

invoiceChecklist.item: Debris disposal or haul-away note
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating that debris was bagged and removed or left on site for composting avoids disputes about cleanup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or registration number, if required locally
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require a license or home improvement registration, especially when repairs are involved. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty or recheck terms on repairs
invoiceChecklist.why: A short warranty statement, such as 30 days on sealant work, sets expectations if a leak appears after a rain.

gutter-cleaning.paymentTerms: Most residential gutter cleaners ask for payment on completion, either by card, check, cash, or an electronic payment link sent right after the job. Net 7 or Net 14 is common for landlords, property managers, and commercial accounts. Deposits are rare for single-visit cleanings but more common for larger repair or gutter guard installs, often 25 to 50 percent. Prepaid seasonal plans are sometimes billed up front at a small discount. Late fees, if used, are commonly 1.5 percent per month and should be written on the estimate and the invoice. Check your state's rules on late fees and on written contracts for home service work.
