tips.title: Send the invoice before you leave the driveway
tips.body: Gutter jobs are quick and the customer is often not home. Send the invoice with photos from your phone as soon as the job is done, while the result is obvious and the payment request feels fair.

tips.title: Take before and after photos of every job
tips.body: Photos of clogged gutters, flushed downspouts, and any damage you found protect you from disputes and justify add-on charges. Attach them or keep them tied to the invoice.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: Travel, ladder setup, and cleanup take the same time on a small house as a medium one. A minimum visit fee keeps tiny jobs from costing you money.

tips.title: Bill repairs separately from cleaning
tips.body: If you find loose hangers, bad seams, or sagging runs, list the repair as its own line with materials and time. This also helps customers decide on future work.

tips.title: Offer seasonal plans with automatic reminders
tips.body: Twice-a-year cleanings in spring and fall are easy to schedule and bill. A recurring invoice or reminder cuts down on re-quoting and smooths out your slow months.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the job for gutter cleaning?
faqs.answer: Most gutter cleaners charge a flat price per job based on home size, stories, and linear feet. Hourly rates are more common for repairs and unusual situations like severely neglected gutters with years of buildup.

faqs.question: How do I bill for heavily clogged gutters or standing water?
faqs.answer: State a surcharge in your estimate for excess debris, plant growth, or clogged downspouts, or bill the extra time at your hourly rate. List it as its own line on the invoice and include photos.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on gutter cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax certain home services or the materials you supply, and many do not tax labor for cleaning. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer says the gutters still leak after cleaning?
faqs.answer: Cleaning removes debris but does not fix leaks, bad pitch, or failed seams. Note any existing problems you saw on the invoice, include photos, and offer a repair quote as a separate item.

faqs.question: Can I require payment before starting the job?
faqs.answer: You can, but most residential cleaners collect after completion. For new customers, large properties, or jobs with materials costs, asking for a deposit or card on file is reasonable.

estimate.intro: Gutter cleaners usually send an estimate after a phone call, a photo review, or a satellite view of the property, and sometimes after a short walk-around. Customers compare price per job, what is included such as downspouts and bagging, and whether the company carries insurance. Quotes should be fast, since many homeowners call several companies the same day.

scopeChecklist.item: Linear feet, stories, and roof pitch
scopeChecklist.why: These drive your price and safety needs. Writing them down avoids arguments if the home turns out larger or steeper than described.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: gutters, downspouts, roof debris, bagging
scopeChecklist.why: Customers assume different things. Spell out whether downspouts are flushed and whether debris is hauled away.
Note that repairs, gutter guard removal, and severe clogs or plant growth may cost extra so the final invoice does not surprise anyone.
If the quote assumes normal leaf buildup, say so. Heavy moss, shingle grit, or standing water changes the work involved.
Locked gates, dogs, steep yards, or low-hanging trees can slow the job. Ask the customer to clear access before you arrive.
Homeowners worry about falls and property damage. Listing liability insurance and any required license builds trust and separates you from uninsured operators.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and scheduling window
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing and weather change. A 14 to 30 day validity period and a rain-delay policy keep schedules realistic.

pricingTips.title: Price from measurements, not guesses
pricingTips.body: Use satellite imagery or the customer's photos to estimate linear feet and stories. A quick quote is fine, but confirm on arrival and note that final price may change if the measurements differ.

pricingTips.title: Quote add-ons as options
pricingTips.body: List the base cleaning, then downspout flushing and gutter guard cleaning as optional lines. Customers can pick what they want, and your average ticket goes up without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Build in a dirty-gutter allowance
pricingTips.body: If the gutters look neglected, quote a higher price or state a clear per-hour overage. Do not rely on a normal-condition price for a job full of compacted muck.

pricingTips.title: Offer a discount for recurring service
pricingTips.body: A lower price for twice-yearly cleanings gives customers a reason to book you again and gives you predictable work.

faqs.question: Can I give an accurate gutter cleaning quote without visiting?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Many cleaners use satellite maps and photos to estimate linear feet and stories. State that the price is subject to confirmation on site, especially for steep roofs, heavy debris, or complex rooflines.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most gutter cleaners do not charge for standard cleaning quotes. For repair or gutter replacement work that requires a detailed inspection, some charge a fee that is credited toward the job.

faqs.question: What if the actual job is bigger than quoted?
faqs.answer: Include language in the estimate that the price may change if the gutter length, condition, or access differs from what was described. Contact the customer before doing extra work and get approval in writing, even by text or email.

gutter-installer.intro: Gutter installers fit new rain gutters, downspouts, and gutter guards on homes and small commercial buildings, and many also repair, replace, and clean existing systems. Most are solo operators or small crews who bill homeowners, property managers, roofers, and general contractors for linear footage of gutter, accessories, and labor.
gutter-installer.pricingModel: Most gutter work is priced per linear foot installed, with the price depending on material (aluminum, steel, copper, vinyl), size (5-inch or 6-inch), and gauge. Downspouts are usually priced per foot or per piece, and corners, end caps, and outlets are either built into the per-foot price or itemized. Gutter guards, cleaning, and repairs are priced separately, with repairs often charged as a minimum service fee or hourly. Many installers form seamless gutters on site from coil stock, so the per-foot rate covers material, machine time, hangers, sealant, and labor. Add-ons like fascia repair, difficult access (three stories, steep roofs), and haul-away of old gutters are billed as separate lines. Most jobs are quoted as a flat total based on measured footage, then invoiced to match the accepted quote plus any approved changes.

rates.service: Copper or heavy-gauge steel gutters, installed
Gutter guards or leaf screens, installed
Removal and haul-away of old gutters

items.description: Seamless 5-inch white aluminum gutters, formed on site and installed with hidden hangers
2x3 aluminum downspouts with elbows and brackets
Inside/outside corners and end caps with sealant
Remove and haul away existing gutters
Splash blocks
Replace rotted fascia board section, 12 ft

sampleInvoice.notes: Total matches accepted quote dated May 2 plus approved fascia repair. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Workmanship warranty: 2 years on installation, against leaks at seams and loose hangers. Material warranty per manufacturer. Checks payable to the business name above; card payments accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Total linear footage by gutter size and material
invoiceChecklist.why: Footage is the main pricing driver, so showing it lets the client match the invoice to the quote and settles later disputes about how much was installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gutter profile, color, and gauge
invoiceChecklist.why: K-style versus half-round, white versus bronze, and .027 versus .032 gauge all change cost. Listing them proves the client got what they chose.

invoiceChecklist.item: Downspout count, size, and placement notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Downspouts are easy to dispute. Note the number and size, and any extras added during the job.

invoiceChecklist.item: Accessories and add-ons itemized
invoiceChecklist.why: Guards, splash blocks, hidden hangers, and fascia repair are often agreed verbally on site. Listing them separately shows what was approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the original quote and any change orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and explains any difference in total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and completion date
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients are landlords, property managers, or buyers paying for a different address than their billing address. The date starts the warranty period and payment clock.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or registration number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require contractor or home improvement registration to appear on contracts and invoices. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating what is covered and for how long reduces callbacks about issues outside your workmanship, like clogging or ice damage.

gutter-installer.paymentTerms: Gutter jobs are short, often one day, so terms are tight. Many installers take a deposit of 20-50 percent when the client accepts the quote, mainly to cover material coil and color orders, with the balance due on completion or within 7 days. Jobs for roofers and contractors are more often net 15 or net 30. Common payment methods are check, card, and bank transfer. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common on commercial accounts, but state them on the quote and invoice up front, and check your state's rules on late fees and deposit limits for home improvement work.

tips.title: Measure and record footage before you quote
tips.body: Walk the house and write down each run. A 10-foot error on a 160-foot job is real money at $9 a foot. Keep those measurements with the job so the invoice footage can be verified.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for small repairs
tips.body: A reseal or a single downspout swap takes a truck trip, ladder setup, and cleanup. Use a minimum service fee so a 20-minute fix does not cost you the afternoon.

tips.title: Bill access and height as separate lines
tips.body: Three-story homes, steep roofs, and jobs needing a lift or extra ladders take longer and carry more risk. A line for high-access work is easier for clients to accept than a higher base rate.

tips.title: Pass on material price swings with a quote expiry
tips.body: Aluminum coil and guard prices move. Put a validity period of 15 to 30 days on quotes so you are not locked into old pricing.

tips.title: Photograph the finished work before you leave
tips.body: Photos of seams, hangers, downspout outlets, and discharge points help if a client later claims a leak or damage and support your invoice if a payment is questioned.

faqs.question: Should I charge per foot or per hour for gutter installation?
faqs.answer: Per linear foot is standard for installation because clients can compare quotes easily and it rewards an efficient crew. Hourly billing is more common for repairs, cleaning add-ons, and unusual jobs where scope is unclear.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on gutter installation?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. In many states, installation labor on a real property improvement is not taxed, while the contractor pays sales tax on materials, but some states tax the whole job or only certain parts. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a roofer or general contractor who hired me as a subcontractor?
faqs.answer: Reference their job number or purchase order, list footage and materials, and follow the payment terms in your subcontract. Many contractors pay net 15 to net 30 and may request lien waivers, so keep your paperwork current.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit on a gutter job?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common, especially when you order custom-colored coil or specialty materials. Many states limit deposit amounts for home improvement contracts, so check your local rules and state the deposit on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to add downspouts or guards mid-job?
faqs.answer: Write the change down, give a price, and get the client to approve it by text or signature before you do the work. Then list it as a separate line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Gutter installers quote before nearly every job, usually after a site visit to measure the roofline and check the fascia. Homeowners often collect two or three bids and compare price per foot, material and gauge, guard options, and warranty.

scopeChecklist.item: Total linear footage and the number of downspouts
scopeChecklist.why: This is the basis of the price. If measurements change on site, the quote gives a clear reference for adjusting.

scopeChecklist.item: Gutter material, size, gauge, and color
scopeChecklist.why: Clients comparing bids need to know whether they are looking at 5-inch or 6-inch, and .027 or .032 aluminum.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether old gutters are removed and hauled away
scopeChecklist.why: Removal is often assumed to be included. Stating it avoids disputes over disposal charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Fascia, soffit, and roof edge repair exclusions
scopeChecklist.why: Rotted fascia is often found only when old gutters come off. Say what happens, and at what price, if hidden damage turns up.
Specify whether downspouts end in splash blocks, extensions, or underground drain tie-ins, since underground connections are usually extra.
Clients often assume guards come with new gutters. Say whether they are included or optional.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, duration, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for scheduling and protects you from material price changes.
Shows what is covered and what is due to book the job, which helps clients decide and reduces later arguments.

pricingTips.title: Quote a flat total built from per-foot pricing
pricingTips.body: Work out footage, downspouts, accessories, and labor, then present a single total with a short breakdown. Clients like a clear number, and you keep the detail for your invoice.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Show 5-inch aluminum, 6-inch aluminum, and 6-inch with guards as separate prices. Many clients pick the middle option, and you avoid a lost bid because of one fixed spec.

pricingTips.title: Include a fascia repair allowance
pricingTips.body: Add a per-foot or per-board price for replacing rotted fascia that you find after tear-off. This prevents a surprise and lets you bill fairly without renegotiating.

pricingTips.title: Account for height and access
pricingTips.body: Price steep roofs, third stories, and tight side yards with a surcharge or a higher per-foot rate. Looking only at a street photo often leads to underquoting.

faqs.question: Should I charge for gutter estimates?
faqs.answer: Most installers give free estimates for standard installs because competition expects it. Some charge a fee for complex commercial jobs or drawings, and credit it toward the work if the client accepts.

faqs.question: How long should a gutter quote be valid?
faqs.answer: 15 to 30 days is common. Aluminum coil, guards, and fuel costs change, so an expiry date keeps you from honoring an outdated price.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote from satellite images or measurements the client sends?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough estimate that way, but state that the final price is subject to on-site measurement. Complex rooflines, hidden damage, and access problems are hard to see remotely.

faqs.question: What happens if the actual footage differs from my quote?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote whether the price is fixed or adjusted per foot after installation. Many installers use a fixed price within a small tolerance and bill the per-foot rate for significant differences, with the client's approval.

hair-stylist.intro: Hair stylists send invoices when they bill outside the usual salon checkout: booth renters and independent stylists billing clients directly, mobile stylists, bridal and event hair artists, and stylists working on photo shoots or film sets. Typical charges include cuts, color services, treatments, extensions, travel fees, and retail products.
hair-stylist.pricingModel: Most stylists price by service, not by the hour, with a set price for each cut, color or style. Color work is often priced by stage (root touch-up, all-over color, highlights, balayage) and many stylists add a charge for extra product when the hair is long or thick. Extensions are priced per bundle, per track or per install, plus the hair itself. Bridal and event work is usually sold as a package: bride's hair, a trial, and a per-person rate for the bridal party, with a travel fee and a minimum for on-location work. Editorial and set work is typically billed as a day rate or half-day rate. Many stylists require a deposit to hold large bookings, and retail products are listed as separate line items at retail price. Booth renters set their own prices; commission stylists usually do not invoice clients at all, so the page applies mostly to independents.

items.description: Bridal hair trial (March 8)
Bridal updo, wedding day (June 14)
Bridesmaid styling
Mother of the bride styling
On-location travel fee (35 miles each way)
Early start fee (before 7:00 a.m.)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $300 received on booking is shown as a credit when you send the final invoice. Balance is due 7 days before the event date. Accepted payment: card, Zelle, or cash. Deposits are non-refundable within 30 days of the event.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date and time of each service
invoiceChecklist.why: Trials, event days and appointments often happen on different dates, and listing them prevents confusion about what was billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized service per person
invoiceChecklist.why: Group bookings like bridal parties need a clear count of who received what service so the total can be checked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee and distance
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile work costs time and gas. Showing the miles or flat fee keeps the charge from looking like an add-on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients forget what they have already paid. A credit line shows exactly what is left.

invoiceChecklist.item: Product and extension charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Hair extensions, color additions and retail products are priced differently from labor and may be taxed differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cosmetology license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients, venues and event planners ask for it, and many states require licensed practitioners to display it. Check your state board's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and late policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Putting the policy on the invoice and booking agreement gives you something to point to if a client disputes a no-show or deposit.

hair-stylist.paymentTerms: For regular appointments, payment is normally taken at the end of the service by card, cash or a payment app, so invoices are rare. For weddings and events, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is common, with the balance due one to two weeks before the date. Editorial or set clients such as photographers and production companies often pay net 15 to net 30, so invoice promptly after the job. Late fees are uncommon with individual clients, but a stated policy (for example, 1.5 percent a month after 30 days) is reasonable for business clients. Whether a deposit is refundable should be in writing before you accept it.

tips.title: Require a deposit for anything that blocks your calendar
tips.body: A wedding morning or a full day of color work can't be rebooked easily. A non-refundable deposit protects that time and filters out unsure clients.

tips.title: Price by the stage of the service, not just the name
tips.body: Two balayage clients can take very different time depending on hair length, starting color and density. Use starting prices with an adjustment for length and extra product, and tell the client before you begin.

tips.title: Add a travel and early-start fee for location work
tips.body: Driving, setup time and early mornings aren't covered by the per-person rate. Charging for them separately is standard for bridal and event stylists.

tips.title: Keep tips separate from the invoice total
tips.body: Gratuity belongs on its own line or is handled at payment. This keeps your service revenue and tip income clearly separated, which helps at tax time.

tips.title: Track product costs per job
tips.body: Color, developer and extension hair add up quickly. If you record what each client used, you can adjust your pricing when supplier costs rise.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice a regular salon client?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most clients pay at the end of the appointment and you give them a receipt if they want one. Invoices make sense for weddings, events, group bookings, mobile visits, and business clients who pay after the work is done.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on hair services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states don't tax personal services like haircuts, but retail products usually are taxable. Check with your state's revenue department about what applies to services, products and extensions.

faqs.question: How do I bill for extensions?
faqs.answer: List the hair and the labor as separate lines. The hair is billed at its cost plus your markup, per bundle or pack, and the install is billed as a flat fee or per track. This makes it clear what the client paid for if they need a move-up or removal later.

faqs.question: Can I charge a cancellation fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you disclose it before the booking. Many stylists charge 50 percent of the service price for same-day cancellations and keep the deposit on events. Put it in writing and repeat it on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do booth renters handle billing?
faqs.answer: A booth renter is typically self-employed. You collect payment from your clients directly, pay the salon rent separately, and keep your own records for income and expenses. Check the tax rules for self-employed people in your state.

estimate.intro: Stylists send estimates before bridal and event bookings, extension installs, major color corrections, and on-location work, where the price depends on the number of people, travel and time. Clients usually compare your package against other stylists, and sometimes against a salon's wedding package.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of people and services for each
scopeChecklist.why: The count drives the whole price, and a late addition of two bridesmaids changes your schedule as well as the total.
Early starts, long drives and venues without good lighting or outlets affect pricing and set-up.

scopeChecklist.item: Hair length, texture and starting condition
scopeChecklist.why: Very long, thick or damaged hair takes longer and needs more product, which is why many stylists quote a range after seeing photos.
A trial is billed separately by many stylists. Saying whether it is included avoids a disagreement later.
Clients often assume these are included. State who supplies them and what they cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel, parking and early start fees
scopeChecklist.why: Spelling out these charges ahead of time prevents the final total from surprising the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, cancellation terms and how long the quote is valid
scopeChecklist.why: Your date is not held until the deposit is paid, and the terms say what happens if plans change.

pricingTips.title: Quote bridal parties as a package
pricingTips.body: List the bride's rate, a per-person rate for the party, and the minimum you will travel for. A clear package is easier to compare and easier to approve.

pricingTips.title: Quote color corrections as a range
pricingTips.body: You can't know the true time until you see the hair. Give a range with an hourly rate or a per-session price, and say you will re-quote if the work goes beyond it.

pricingTips.title: Build in time between clients
pricingTips.body: On event days, allow time for setup, touch-ups and the occasional late arrival. If you underestimate, you lose money or run behind for the bride.

pricingTips.title: Include a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Calendar dates and supply costs change. A 14 to 30 day expiration encourages a decision and protects your availability.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation?
faqs.answer: Many stylists offer a free short consult for standard services and charge for long consultations on corrections or extensions, often applying the fee to the service if the client books. Decide on a policy and state it up front.

faqs.question: How firm is a quote for color work?
faqs.answer: A quote based on photos is an estimate. Say so in writing, and note that the final price depends on the hair's condition and the amount of product used. Tell the client before you go beyond the range.

faqs.question: What if the wedding party size changes after the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying that final headcount must be confirmed by a set date, such as two weeks out, and that additions are accepted only if your schedule allows. Price changes follow the per-person rate in the quote.

handyman.intro: Handymen are solo operators and small crews who take on the small repairs and odd jobs around a home or rental property: patching drywall, hanging doors, fixing leaky faucets, assembling furniture, mounting TVs, and similar work. Clients include homeowners, landlords, property managers, and realtors preparing a house for sale. Invoices usually combine labor, materials, and sometimes a trip charge or disposal fee.
handyman.pricingModel: Most handymen charge either an hourly rate or a flat price per job. Hourly rates are common for repair work with unknown scope, often with a 1 to 2 hour minimum or a service call fee to cover travel and setup. Flat pricing is common for well-defined tasks such as mounting a TV, installing a ceiling fan, or hanging a door. Materials are billed at cost or with a markup, typically 10 to 25 percent, to cover shopping time and returns. Some handymen offer a half-day or full-day rate for punch lists, where a client has a long list of small tasks. Larger or specialty work such as electrical panels, gas lines, or structural changes often requires a licensed contractor, and the limit on what a handyman can do without a license varies by state, so check your local rules.

rates.service: Drywall patch and paint (small hole to medium)

items.description: Labor: repair drywall holes in hallway and prime/paint patched areas
Replace kitchen faucet (customer-supplied fixture)
Mount 55" TV on customer-supplied bracket, conceal cables in wall
Replace 2 interior door hinges and adjust latch on bedroom door
Materials: joint compound, mesh patch, primer, paint sample, supply lines, anchors
Trip charge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: check, Zelle, card. Materials receipts available on request. Workmanship warranted for 30 days from completion. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances over 30 days past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor or handyman license number, if your state or city requires one
invoiceChecklist.why: Many places require a license or registration above a dollar threshold, and showing it protects you and reassures clients and property managers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and date(s) of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with rentals or multiple properties need to know which address the work was on, and dates help resolve warranty questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of tasks with hours or flat prices
invoiceChecklist.why: A line for each task makes it easy for a client to see what they paid for and reduces pushback on total hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately from labor, with receipts for larger purchases
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question material costs. Separate lines, and a markup that matches your quote, avoid disputes and help landlords with their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge, minimum fee, or disposal and haul-away fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These small charges are easy to forget and easy to dispute if they were not mentioned up front.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or work order number for property managers
invoiceChecklist.why: Property management companies and realtors often will not process an invoice without a PO or ticket number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty or workmanship guarantee terms
invoiceChecklist.why: A stated period, such as 30 or 90 days, sets expectations for callbacks and what is not covered.

handyman.paymentTerms: Handymen usually collect payment on completion for small jobs, often the same day by card, check, Zelle, or Venmo. For jobs that need larger material purchases, ask for a deposit or have the client pay for materials up front, commonly 30 to 50 percent of the estimate. Property managers and landlords typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, so state the due date on the invoice. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common but should be written in your quote or terms before work begins. Some states limit deposits or require specific contract language for home improvement work, so check your local rules.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for every visit
tips.body: A 30-minute fix still costs you drive time, parking, and setup. A 1 or 2 hour minimum or a flat trip fee keeps small jobs worth taking.

tips.title: Bill for material runs
tips.body: Time spent at the hardware store is real labor. Either bill it at your hourly rate, add a flat pickup fee, or build it into a materials markup, and say which on the quote.

tips.title: Photograph work and keep receipts
tips.body: Before and after photos and itemized receipts settle most disputes quickly and support your invoice if a client or property manager asks questions.

tips.title: Invoice the same day
tips.body: Send the invoice before you leave the driveway or that evening. Payment comes faster while the finished work is fresh.

tips.title: Separate emergency and after-hours work
tips.body: Weekend, evening, and same-day calls often carry a premium of 1.5 times your rate. List it as its own line so it is clear.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat rate?
faqs.answer: Use flat rates for tasks you can predict, like mounting a TV or replacing a faucet. Use hourly for repairs where the scope is unclear, such as tracing water damage or fixing something that has failed before. Many handymen quote a flat price for the known part and bill hourly for anything beyond it.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on handyman work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax labor on repairs, some tax only materials, and some tax neither. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant, and show tax as its own line if you collect it.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on materials?
faqs.answer: A markup of 10 to 25 percent is common. It covers your time buying materials, returns, and the cost of carrying the purchase until the client pays. Tell the client about the markup in your quote so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice attached a few days after the due date, then call. Apply any late fee you agreed to in writing. For larger unpaid balances, a demand letter or small claims court is an option, and in some states you may have lien rights on the property, which vary by location.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to be a handyman?
faqs.answer: Rules vary widely. Many states let you do small jobs below a dollar limit, often between $500 and $5,000, without a contractor license, but electrical, plumbing, and gas work often require a licensed trade. Check with your state licensing board and city before taking larger jobs.

estimate.intro: Handymen send an estimate when a job is bigger than a quick fix, when the client is comparing several bids, or when a landlord or property manager needs approval before work begins. Clients compare the total price, what is included, how soon you can start, and whether materials are part of the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Specific list of tasks and locations
scopeChecklist.why: Write down each repair and where it is, such as 'patch two holes in hallway wall and paint to match.' This prevents a client from adding more work under the same price.
Clients often assume you will buy the faucet, light, or paint. State what you supply, what they supply, and the markup if any.
Matching existing paint or texture is difficult. Say what level of match you will provide and whether a full wall repaint is extra.
Rot, mold, old wiring, or non-code plumbing can appear after opening a wall. State that these are outside the quote and will be priced separately.
Give a start date and expected duration, and note if the work depends on materials arriving or on the client being home.
Say whether haul-away of old fixtures, doors, or debris is included or billed as a separate fee.
State the deposit, when the balance is due, and how long the price holds. Material prices change, so 14 to 30 days is typical.

pricingTips.title: Visit before pricing anything uncertain
pricingTips.body: Photos are fine for simple tasks, but for repairs involving water damage, structural issues, or older homes, look at the site first. Charge a small assessment fee that you credit if they hire you.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Build in 10 to 15 percent on jobs where you cannot see behind walls or floors. Handymen who quote tight on every job lose money on the unexpected ones.

pricingTips.title: Offer a list-based quote for punch lists
pricingTips.body: Price each item separately on a multi-task list. Clients can drop items to meet a budget, and you can bundle the remaining ones to save travel time.

pricingTips.title: Quote labor and materials separately
pricingTips.body: Splitting labor and materials makes it easier to explain price differences when material costs change or a client wants cheaper fixtures.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are common for straightforward jobs. For jobs that need a long site visit or measuring, a $50 to $100 fee credited toward the work is reasonable. Always say so before you go.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes or hidden conditions turn up. Put the change in writing, with the added cost, and get approval before continuing. If your quote says it excludes hidden damage, this is much easier to explain.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Material prices and your schedule shift, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I get a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, for anything more than a small job. A signature or emailed approval confirms the scope and price, and it gives you a record if a disagreement comes up later. Some states require a written contract for home improvement work above a certain amount, so check your local rules.

hardscaping.intro: Hardscaping contractors build the non-plant parts of outdoor spaces: paver patios, walkways, driveways, retaining walls, fire pits, outdoor kitchens, and steps. Invoices usually cover excavation, base prep, materials, labor, and sometimes drainage or lighting work. Most jobs run from a few thousand dollars to tens of thousands, so clear billing matters.
hardscaping.pricingModel: Most hardscaping work is priced per square foot for patios, walkways, and driveways, and per face foot or per square foot of wall face for retaining walls. Those unit prices bundle excavation, base, bedding sand, pavers, edge restraint, and labor. Many contractors instead itemize labor and materials separately, with a markup of 10-30% on materials to cover sourcing, delivery, waste, and warranty risk. Extras such as demolition of an old slab, rock excavation, hauling spoil, drainage, polymeric sand, sealing, and permits are usually line items or change orders. Larger jobs are billed in stages: a deposit, a payment at material delivery or base completion, and a final payment at completion. Small repair or hourly jobs may be billed by the hour with a crew rate.

rates.service: Paver patio or walkway installation (labor and materials)

rates.unit: per sq ft of wall face

items.description: Excavation, haul-off of spoil, and compacted 6" crushed stone base for patio
Concrete pavers (supplied and installed) with bedding sand and edge restraint
Segmental seat wall, 18" high, with capstones
Demolition and disposal of existing concrete slab
Polymeric sand and sealing
Drain pipe and gravel backfill behind wall

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $5,000 received on contract signing. Balance due within 10 days of completion. Paver installation carries a 2-year workmanship warranty. Keep foot traffic off the surface for 24 hours and avoid vehicles for 7 days after sealing. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and project description
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have multiple properties or phases, and a clear location and scope ties the invoice to the signed contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage or linear footage installed
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-square-foot pricing is easy to dispute if measurements are not shown. List the actual installed quantity next to the rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed by type and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Pavers, base stone, sand, block, and capstones are major costs. Naming brand, color, or product line prevents disagreements about what was installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extras with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, unexpected utilities, extra demolition, or added steps are common. Reference the signed change order so these charges are not challenged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the remaining balance clearly on multi-stage jobs and avoids confusion about what was already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and insurance info where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a contractor license number on contracts and invoices for work above a dollar threshold. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit numbers and inspection sign-off
invoiceChecklist.why: Retaining walls over a certain height and some driveway work need permits. Listing them documents compliance and who pulled them.

hardscaping.paymentTerms: Hardscaping contractors commonly collect a deposit of 20-50% at signing, since materials like pavers and block are bought up front. Larger jobs are split into stages tied to milestones such as material delivery, base completion, and final walkthrough. Final balances are typically due on completion or within 7-14 days. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, and card payments are all used, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client on large balances where allowed. Check your state's rules on maximum deposits and on lien notices, which in many states must be sent within set deadlines to preserve your rights.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not dates
tips.body: Weather delays are routine. Schedule payments at material delivery, base completion, and final cleanup so cash flow does not depend on the calendar.

tips.title: Bill materials separately when prices are volatile
tips.body: Pavers, natural stone, and fuel for hauling can change quickly. Itemizing materials or including a price-validity period protects your margin on longer jobs.

tips.title: Document the base before it is covered
tips.body: Take dated photos of excavation depth, geotextile, and compacted base. If a client disputes quality later, those photos back up the work and the price.

tips.title: Get change orders signed before doing the work
tips.body: Hitting rock, finding a buried line, or expanding the patio are common. A short signed change order prevents arguments at final payment.

tips.title: Know your lien deadlines
tips.body: In many states, contractors must file or send preliminary notices within a set time to keep lien rights. Learn the rules where you work and note them on large jobs.

faqs.question: Should I invoice by the square foot or itemize labor and materials?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-square-foot pricing is simpler for the client and common for patios and walkways. Itemizing is better when material costs vary, when jobs include many extras, or when the client wants to see where the money goes. Whichever you choose, match the invoice to what the contract and estimate said.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Many hardscapers ask for 25-50% up front, especially when materials must be ordered. Some states limit deposits on home improvement contracts, so check your local rules before setting a percentage.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on hardscaping jobs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials you buy and treat the job as a service, while others require tax on the full contract or only on materials. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for extra excavation or rock?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that states the additional price or an hourly or per-yard rate, and have the client sign it before work continues. List it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client withholds the final payment over a minor issue?
faqs.answer: Complete a punch list at the final walkthrough and get it signed. Fix the listed items promptly, then invoice the balance. If payment still does not arrive, follow your contract's late terms and consider lien rights where available.

estimate.intro: Hardscaping estimates are sent after a site visit, often before the client has chosen materials. Homeowners usually compare two or three bids, so differences in base depth, materials, and exclusions matter as much as the total price. A detailed quote also becomes the basis for the contract and later invoices.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured area and dimensions with a sketch
scopeChecklist.why: Square footage drives the price. A simple drawing with measurements shows both sides what is included.
State the excavation depth, base stone type and thickness, and compaction method. Thin base is the main way cheaper bids cut cost, and clients should see the difference.

scopeChecklist.item: Paver, block, or stone product and color
scopeChecklist.why: Prices vary widely across product lines. Naming the product avoids disputes over substitutions.
Removing old concrete, soil, and sod is costly. State whether it is included and where spoil goes.
Water runoff is the most common cause of failed patios and walls. Say what is included and what is excluded.
List rock, buried utilities, tree roots, and soil issues as outside the base price, with a rate for handling them.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, utility locates, and HOA approvals
scopeChecklist.why: Specify who obtains them and who pays, since delays can affect schedule and cost.

pricingTips.title: Price from actual site conditions
pricingTips.body: Access for equipment, slope, soil type, and haul distance change labor hours. A flat square-foot number from a phone call often leaves money on the table.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic paver, a premium paver, and an upgraded layout with a seat wall or lighting. Clients choose based on budget and you avoid bidding only on price.

pricingTips.title: Include a price-validity period
pricingTips.body: Material prices and availability change. State that the quote is good for 14-30 days and that pricing may adjust after that.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency line for unknowns
pricingTips.body: On older properties, include an allowance or per-yard rate for extra excavation or unsuitable soil so surprises do not come out of your profit.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most hardscapers provide free estimates for standard residential jobs. For complex designs or drawings, many charge a design fee and credit it toward the project if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. Shorter periods make sense when material prices are changing quickly or products are special order.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding price?
faqs.answer: It depends on how you word it and on state law. A quote labeled fixed price is usually binding for the defined scope, while an estimate may allow for adjustments. State clearly which one you are giving and how changes are handled.

faqs.question: What should I do when a client wants to cut cost by reducing the base?
faqs.answer: Explain the risk of settling and heaving, and offer other savings such as smaller area, simpler pattern, or a less expensive paver. If you must reduce the spec, note it in writing and consider limiting the warranty.

hauling.intro: Hauling businesses pick up and dispose of junk, debris, and unwanted items for homeowners, landlords, contractors, and property managers. Typical jobs include furniture and appliance removal, garage and basement cleanouts, yard waste, construction debris, and estate or eviction cleanouts. Most operators are solo or run a few trucks, and invoices need to cover labor, volume, disposal fees, and any special-handling items.
hauling.pricingModel: Most haulers price by volume, based on how much space the load takes up in the truck or trailer, usually quoted as a fraction of a truck (quarter, half, three-quarter, full) or in cubic yards. Minimum charges are common for single items like a couch or a refrigerator. Heavy materials such as concrete, dirt, roofing shingles, and brick are often priced by weight or by the dump truck load because disposal is billed by the ton. Dump or transfer station fees are either built into the price or listed as a separate line. Add-ons include stairs or long carries, same-day service, hazardous or restricted items (tires, mattresses, appliances with refrigerant, electronics), and labor-heavy sorting or demolition. Contractors and property managers on repeat work may get a per-job flat rate or a per-load rate.

rates.service: Extra labor for cleanouts or stairs
Tire, mattress, or e-waste disposal surcharge

items.description: Garage cleanout: half truck load of household junk and boxes
Old refrigerator removal (refrigerant recovery fee included)
Mattress and box spring disposal
Additional labor: moving items from second-floor storage
Dump fee, county transfer station (receipt available)

sampleInvoice.notes: Job completed 6/14 at 1420 Maple Ave. Payment due on completion. We accept card, cash, Venmo, and check. Disposal receipts available on request. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Hauling is often done at a property the payer doesn't live at, such as a rental, estate, or job site, so the location ties the charge to the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Load size or volume (quarter, half, full truck or cubic yards)
invoiceChecklist.why: Volume is the main price driver, and showing it lets the client see how the total was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of special items with surcharges
invoiceChecklist.why: Tires, appliances, mattresses, paint, and electronics often have separate disposal fees, and listing them avoids surprise disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dump or transfer station fees, with weights or ticket numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Weight-based disposal costs vary by job, and a ticket number backs up the pass-through charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours and crew size for extra work
invoiceChecklist.why: Stairs, long carries, sorting, and light demolition take extra time beyond the load price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license or registration number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many cities and counties require a business license or hauler permit, and property managers and commercial clients often ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO or work order number for commercial clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers, contractors, and realtors often cannot pay without a reference number matching their records.

hauling.paymentTerms: Residential hauling is usually paid on the day of service, after the truck is loaded and the final volume is known, by card, cash, or a payment app. Deposits are uncommon for standard pickups but are reasonable for large cleanouts, estate jobs, or scheduled demolition debris removal, often 25 to 50 percent. Commercial clients, contractors, and property managers typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms. A late fee of 1.5 percent per month is common on those accounts, but state the term on the invoice and in your quote and check your local rules on maximum rates. Some haulers add a card processing fee or offer a small discount for cash, which should be stated up front.

tips.title: Quote by volume, then confirm at the truck
tips.body: Give a range from photos or a walk-through, then finalize the price after loading when the real volume is clear. Write the pricing method on the quote so the final number is not a surprise.

tips.title: List disposal fees separately
tips.body: Dump fees rise and fall, and heavy loads can cost far more than light ones. Separate lines protect your margin and let you pass through actual costs on loads of concrete, dirt, or roofing.

tips.title: Keep dump receipts for every job
tips.body: Receipts show the weight and fee for the load, settle any client questions, and support your expense records at tax time.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: Fuel, drive time, truck wear, and dump runs cost the same for one chair as for a full load. A minimum keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Set up repeat accounts with clear terms
tips.body: Property managers, realtors, and contractors can provide steady work. Agree on rates, payment timing, and required reference numbers before the first job.

faqs.question: Should I include the dump fee in my price or list it separately?
faqs.answer: Either works. Listing it separately is clearer on heavy or variable loads such as concrete, dirt, or construction debris. For ordinary household junk, many haulers fold the fee into a per-load price to keep the quote simple.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for stairs or long carries?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so before the job. Many haulers add a flat fee or an hourly labor line for multiple flights of stairs, carries over a set distance, or items that need two people.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on hauling?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes the city. Some states tax junk removal as a service, others do not, and rules can differ for disposal fees. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the load is bigger than the quote?
faqs.answer: Your quote should state that the final price is based on actual volume or weight. If the job grows, tell the client before you continue, and list the added volume or labor on the invoice.

faqs.question: Should I bill hazardous items?
faqs.answer: Many haulers refuse hazardous materials like paint, chemicals, and asbestos, because disposal rules are strict and vary by area. If you do accept some, such as appliances or electronics, list a disposal surcharge for them and follow local rules.

estimate.intro: Hauling quotes are usually given before the job from photos, a phone description, or an on-site walk-through. Clients often get two or three quotes and compare the price, what is included, and whether the final number can change. A clear quote that explains how volume and disposal fees affect the total makes it easier to win the job and get paid without arguments.

scopeChecklist.item: Items or areas included and excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Specifying what is going (the garage, the shed, only the items marked) avoids disagreements about what you were supposed to take.

scopeChecklist.item: Pricing method and estimated load size
scopeChecklist.why: State whether you price by truck fraction, cubic yard, item, or weight, and give the estimated volume so the client knows how the final price is set.
Disposal costs vary, especially for heavy debris. Saying whether they are built in or billed at cost avoids surprise charges.
Tires, mattresses, refrigerators, electronics, and paint often carry extra fees or are refused, so list them in the quote.
Hard access adds labor time, so note what you assumed, such as ground-floor pickup or curbside loading.
Hazardous waste, asbestos, chemicals, and biohazards are typically excluded and should be named clearly.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, time window, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Fuel and disposal prices change, and a valid-through date keeps the quote from being used months later.

pricingTips.title: Give a range, then commit to a final price on site
pricingTips.body: A range based on photos is honest about the uncertainty. Once you see the pile, confirm a firm price before loading so the client can approve it.

pricingTips.title: Price the hard jobs by the hour plus disposal
pricingTips.body: Estate cleanouts, hoarding situations, and demolition debris are difficult to price by volume. Quote labor hours and disposal separately so you are covered if the job takes longer.

pricingTips.title: Factor in the full cost of a dump run
pricingTips.body: Include drive time to the transfer station, wait time, fuel, and tipping fees. Rural jobs or far dump sites should be priced higher.

pricingTips.title: Offer a discounted rate for multiple jobs
pricingTips.body: For contractors and property managers, a flat per-load rate for repeat work can win the account while keeping your pricing predictable.

faqs.question: Can I quote from photos?
faqs.answer: Yes, many haulers do. State that the quote is an estimate based on the photos and that the final price will be confirmed on site once the actual volume and access are known.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an on-site estimate?
faqs.answer: Most haulers do free estimates for typical residential jobs. For large estate cleanouts or distant jobs, some charge a trip fee that is credited if the client books.

faqs.question: What if the client has more items on the day of the job?
faqs.answer: Your quote should say that extra items change the price. Tell the client the new price before loading, and write it on the invoice.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to thirty days is common. Shorter periods make sense if disposal fees or fuel prices are changing quickly, or if your schedule fills fast.

healthcare.intro: This page is for independent clinicians and small practices that bill patients directly: cash-pay and direct primary care practices, mobile nurses, private-duty nurses, independent therapists and physical therapists, and clinics that collect copays, deductibles, or self-pay fees. Invoices usually cover visits, procedures, point-of-care tests, supplies, and memberships or care packages. If you also bill insurance, the patient-facing invoice or statement covers only what the patient owes.
healthcare.pricingModel: Pricing in private-pay healthcare is mostly per visit, with the fee set by visit length and complexity (new patient vs. follow-up, 20, 40, or 60 minutes). Private-duty and home nursing is usually billed hourly, often with a 2 to 4 hour minimum and higher rates for nights, weekends, and holidays. Direct primary care and concierge practices charge a monthly or annual membership that covers a defined set of services. Procedures, in-office tests, injections, and supplies are listed as separate line items. Telehealth visits are often priced a little below in-person visits. Many solo providers publish a fee schedule and list the same fee for each service every time. Where insurance is involved, the patient's portion is set by the plan, and you bill the allowed amount, copay, or deductible rather than your cash rate.

rates.service: Mobile nurse home visit (blood draw, injection, wound care)
Point-of-care tests and supplies (A1c, strep, urinalysis)
Injection administration (vaccine or medication cost billed separately)

items.description: New patient visit, 60 minutes, comprehensive history and exam (DOS 03/04)
Point-of-care hemoglobin A1c test
Vaccine administration, influenza (vaccine billed at cost: $28)
Influenza vaccine, supply cost
Follow-up telehealth visit, 20 minutes, lab review (DOS 03/18)

sampleInvoice.notes: Self-pay patient. Amount due within 30 days of statement date. A superbill with CPT and ICD-10 codes is available on request for out-of-network reimbursement. Payment accepted by card, HSA/FSA card, or check. Questions about this statement: call the office during business hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service for every line item
invoiceChecklist.why: Patients, HSA/FSA administrators, and insurers all need exact dates. A single total with no dates is often rejected for reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, credentials, license or NPI number, and practice address
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network claims and HSA/FSA reimbursements usually require the rendering provider's identity and NPI.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service descriptions with CPT or HCPCS codes where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Codes make the charges clear and let patients submit a superbill to their plan. Use the code that matches the service you actually performed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis codes only when needed for reimbursement
invoiceChecklist.why: Include ICD-10 codes on a superbill the patient will submit, but keep detailed clinical information off a routine invoice to limit exposure of protected health information.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for supplies, vaccines, and lab fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should be visible and match what you quoted, and some are billed at cost rather than at your service rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments, insurance adjustments, and remaining patient balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Patients need to see what was paid, what was written off, and what they still owe, or they will call to dispute the balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment instructions and a secure way to pay
invoiceChecklist.why: Healthcare invoices carry sensitive data, so give clear payment options and avoid asking patients to send card numbers by email or text.

healthcare.paymentTerms: Most cash-pay practices collect payment at the time of service by card, HSA/FSA card, or ACH, and send an invoice only for balances or services billed afterward. Membership practices bill monthly or annually in advance, often by automatic card charge. Home nursing and private-duty care are commonly billed weekly or biweekly with net 7 to 14 day terms. For insurance copays and deductibles, statements are typically due in 30 days. Late fees and collections are allowed in many places but are regulated, so put your policy in writing at intake, keep fees modest, and check your state rules before sending an account to collections. Many practices also charge a fee for no-shows or late cancellations (often $25 to $100, or the visit fee for longer appointments) if the patient agreed to it in advance.

tips.title: Collect at the time of service
tips.body: Unpaid balances are the biggest cash flow problem for small practices. Keep a card on file with written consent, or collect the visit fee at check-in or check-out, so you aren't chasing small amounts later.

tips.title: Provide a superbill with every self-pay visit
tips.body: Many patients with out-of-network benefits or HSA/FSA accounts need codes and your NPI to be reimbursed. Giving it automatically cuts follow-up requests and makes patients more likely to return.

tips.title: Put your no-show and cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: Have patients sign the policy at intake, state the notice period (commonly 24 hours), and list the fee. A signed policy is much easier to enforce than a verbal one.

tips.title: Keep billing separate from clinical notes
tips.body: Invoices should show services, codes, and amounts, not clinical details. Store billing records in a system that meets your privacy obligations, and send them only through secure channels.

tips.title: Track what each patient has been told to expect
tips.body: Keep a copy of the estimate or fee schedule you gave the patient. If the invoice differs, note why, such as a longer visit or an added test the patient agreed to.

faqs.question: Do I need to put diagnosis codes on a patient invoice?
faqs.answer: Not for a routine self-pay invoice. Diagnosis codes are needed on a superbill the patient will submit to their insurer. If you include them, share the document only with the patient or their authorized representative, through a secure method.

faqs.question: Is healthcare subject to sales tax?
faqs.answer: Professional medical services are exempt from sales tax in most states, but rules vary, and some taxable items, such as certain retail products or supplements, may be charged tax. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for missed appointments?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, if the patient was told about the fee in writing beforehand. Some payers and states restrict no-show fees for insured patients, so check your contracts and local rules.

faqs.question: How do I bill a patient who has insurance but I am out of network?
faqs.answer: Collect your fee from the patient, then give them a superbill with dates of service, CPT and ICD-10 codes, your NPI, and the amount paid. The patient submits it to their insurer for any out-of-network reimbursement. Reimbursement is not guaranteed.

faqs.question: How long should I keep billing records?
faqs.answer: Retention periods vary by state and by payer, and are often several years or longer. Check your state medical board and any insurance contracts, and keep records longer for minors.

estimate.intro: Healthcare providers give estimates before care starts, mainly for self-pay and uninsured patients, planned procedures, home care arrangements, and membership plans. In the US, providers are generally required to give uninsured and self-pay patients a good faith estimate of expected charges when care is scheduled in advance, so check the current rules for your practice. Patients typically compare your total fee against the cost of an in-network visit, urgent care, or another cash-pay provider.

scopeChecklist.why: List each expected visit, test, or procedure so the patient knows what the estimate covers and what it doesn't.

scopeChecklist.item: Expected number and length of visits
scopeChecklist.why: Cost depends on visit time and frequency, so state your assumptions, such as four 30-minute visits over eight weeks.
Third-party labs and specialists bill separately. Say which charges come from you and which will come from others.
Pass-through costs change with supplier pricing, so state whether they are included, billed at cost, or marked up.
A complication, extra testing, a longer visit, or a change in diagnosis can raise the cost. Give a range and say you will discuss any significant change before proceeding.

scopeChecklist.item: Insurance status and who is responsible for what
scopeChecklist.why: Say whether you are billing insurance, or whether the patient is paying a cash rate. This prevents confusion about reimbursement.
Fees and schedules change. Give an expiration date, such as 90 days, and state your cancellation and no-show policy.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a published fee schedule
pricingTips.body: Using one fee schedule for every patient keeps pricing consistent, speeds up quoting, and avoids accusations of unfair treatment. Update it once a year.

pricingTips.title: Offer a range for open-ended care
pricingTips.body: For ongoing care, quote a likely range rather than a single number. Tell patients the estimate covers what is expected now and that new needs will be quoted separately.

pricingTips.title: Bundle predictable care into a package
pricingTips.body: A package for a physical, labs, and a follow-up visit, or a monthly membership, is easier for patients to compare and budget for, and it reduces billing steps for you.

pricingTips.title: Explain the price difference clearly
pricingTips.body: If your cash price is higher than an in-network copay, explain what the patient gets for it, such as longer visits, same-week access, or direct messaging, without disparaging other providers.

faqs.question: Do I have to give a good faith estimate?
faqs.answer: In the US, providers and facilities are generally required to give uninsured and self-pay patients a good faith estimate for scheduled care, usually when the service is booked at least a few business days ahead or on request. Details and deadlines are set by federal rules, so check the current requirements for your type of practice.

faqs.question: Can the final bill be higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: It can, if the care changes, but you should tell the patient as soon as you know. Federal rules give some patients a way to dispute bills that exceed a good faith estimate by a set threshold, so keep your estimates accurate and documented.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or a consultation to discuss costs?
faqs.answer: Most providers don't charge for a price estimate or a brief call about fees. A full visit to evaluate the patient's needs is billed as a regular visit, and you should say so before scheduling.

faqs.question: Should I ask for a deposit before treatment?
faqs.answer: For ongoing programs, procedures, or private-duty care, many providers collect a deposit or the first month in advance, and for single office visits they collect payment at the time of service. State the deposit and refund terms in writing on the estimate.

herbalist.intro: Herbalists include clinical and community herbalists, custom tincture and tea makers, and herbal educators who work with clients one-on-one or sell products directly. They typically bill for consultations, follow-up visits, custom herbal formulas, ready-made products, and classes or workshops.
herbalist.pricingModel: Most herbalists charge a flat fee for an initial consultation, which is longer and includes intake review and a written plan, then a lower flat fee for follow-up visits. Custom formulas are billed separately from the visit, usually by ounce or by the batch, with the price based on herb cost, labor, and packaging. Some herbalists offer packages, such as an initial visit plus two follow-ups, at a small discount paid up front. Ready-made products like salves, teas, and tinctures are priced per unit, and many herbalists use a markup of two to three times materials cost to cover labor and overhead. Classes and workshops are priced per seat, or as a flat fee when taught for a store or organization. Sliding scale pricing is common in community practice. Herbalists in the US are generally not licensed as such, so keep services within education and wellness, and avoid language that diagnoses or treats disease.

rates.service: Custom tincture or liquid extract formula
Herbal product development or formulation for a brand

items.description: Initial herbal consultation, 90 minutes, with intake review and written plan
Custom digestive tincture formula (2 oz bottle)
Custom evening tea blend (4 oz bag)
Calendula and plantain salve (2 oz tin)
Follow-up consultation, 30 minutes, scheduled within 6 weeks

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon receipt. Herbal consultations and products are for educational and wellness purposes and are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease. Please tell your healthcare provider about all herbs you take. Formulas are custom-made and non-refundable once prepared. Follow-up must be booked within 6 weeks of the first visit to keep the listed rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized services and products on separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Consultations and products are often taxed differently, and separate lines make it clear what the client paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Formula name or batch/lot number with the date made
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client reports a reaction or asks for a refill, you can trace exactly what they received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Size and quantity of each product (oz, bag, tin)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reorder by size, and the unit makes the price per ounce clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date, length, and type (initial or follow-up)
invoiceChecklist.why: This supports package tracking and avoids disputes about how many visits were used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Educational-use disclaimer
invoiceChecklist.why: It reinforces that you are not diagnosing or treating disease, which matters because rules on health claims vary by state.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where it applies
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax physical goods such as teas and salves, and some treat services differently. Check your state rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client prepaid for visits, showing remaining sessions and the use-by date prevents confusion.

herbalist.paymentTerms: Most solo herbalists collect payment at the time of the visit or require payment when the appointment is booked, since a no-show costs an hour or more of prep time. For custom formulas, many take full payment before making the batch, or a deposit of 50 percent when the herbs are costly or the order is large. Packages and classes are usually paid in full up front. Wholesale or brand formulation work is more often billed net 15 or net 30, sometimes with a deposit. Late fees are uncommon for individual clients, but a cancellation policy of 24 to 48 hours notice is common. Card, digital wallet, and bank transfer are typical, and some practices accept HSA or FSA cards, though eligibility depends on the plan and is not guaranteed.

tips.title: Bill the consultation and the formula separately
tips.body: Your time and your products have different costs and may be taxed differently. Separating them also lets a client buy a refill without paying for another visit.

tips.title: Price formulas from real herb cost plus labor
tips.body: Track the per-ounce cost of each herb, alcohol or glycerin, and bottles, then add time for weighing, macerating, pressing, and labeling. Costly herbs can change in price by season, so review your formula prices a couple of times a year.

tips.title: Sell packages with an expiration window
tips.body: A bundle of follow-ups improves client results and gives you steady income. Set a use-by date, such as 90 days, so unused sessions do not stay open indefinitely.

tips.title: Keep your health-claim language careful
tips.body: Describe services as education and support for wellness, not as treatment for a condition. Use the same wording on invoices, product labels, and your website, and check your state rules.

tips.title: Offer sliding scale openly and in limited slots
tips.body: If you reduce fees for some clients, set a fixed number of slots per month and state the range on your booking page. This keeps your income predictable.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on herbal consultations?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax physical goods such as teas, tinctures, and salves, while services are often not taxed, though some states differ. If you sell products, you generally need a seller's permit. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Should I charge separately for the herbs in a custom formula?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. List the consultation and each formula as separate lines so clients can see what they paid for and can reorder formulas without booking a new visit.

faqs.question: Can clients use HSA or FSA funds to pay me?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but not always. Eligibility depends on the plan and on whether the service is considered medical care. Some clients are asked for a letter of medical necessity. Do not promise reimbursement, and provide an itemized invoice they can submit themselves.

faqs.question: How do I handle refunds on custom formulas?
faqs.answer: Most herbalists state that custom-made formulas are non-refundable once prepared, but will replace a product that arrives damaged or is made incorrectly. Put this policy on the invoice and in your intake paperwork, and apply it consistently.

faqs.question: What should I do about clients who cancel or no-show?
faqs.answer: Set a cancellation window, often 24 to 48 hours, and state it when booking. Charge a partial or full fee for late cancellations, or hold a card on file. Applying the policy consistently matters more than the exact amount.

estimate.intro: Herbalists send estimates before large custom formula orders, product development for a brand, event or workshop bookings, and multi-visit care plans. Clients usually compare the total cost of a plan against other practitioners or store-bought products, so a clear breakdown helps.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and length of consultations included
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume follow-ups are included in the first fee unless you say otherwise.

scopeChecklist.item: Formula quantities and how long they should last
scopeChecklist.why: A 2 oz tincture may last two to four weeks depending on dose, which tells the client how many refills to budget for.

scopeChecklist.item: Ingredient cost assumptions and price-change clause
scopeChecklist.why: Herb prices can change with harvest and supply, so note how long the quote is valid.
Sourcing choices can raise costs sharply, and clients should agree to them before you buy.
The recommendation depends on accurate health history and medication use, and the client should know that changes may alter the plan and the price.

scopeChecklist.item: For workshops: group size, materials, location, and setup time
scopeChecklist.why: Costs of herbs, jars, handouts, and travel vary by headcount and venue.

scopeChecklist.item: For brand formulation: number of revisions, sample batches, and ownership of the formula
scopeChecklist.why: Revisions and rights to the final recipe are common sources of disputes.

pricingTips.title: Quote a care plan as a package
pricingTips.body: Present the initial visit, follow-ups, and first round of formulas as one price, with each part listed. Clients can see the total up front, and you can offer a modest package discount.

pricingTips.title: Build in a materials buffer for rare herbs
pricingTips.body: If a formula includes costly or hard-to-source herbs, add a small cushion or state that the price may change if the supplier price shifts before you place the order.

pricingTips.title: Price workshops per head with a minimum
pricingTips.body: Set a per-attendee price and a minimum total, so a small turnout still covers your prep time, materials, and travel.

pricingTips.title: Give a validity date
pricingTips.body: Say how long the quote holds, commonly 14 to 30 days, because herb costs and your schedule can change.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or discovery call?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call of 10 to 15 minutes is usually free and helps both sides decide on fit. For product development or detailed formulation proposals, many herbalists charge a paid scoping session, often credited toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: Can I quote a flat price for a custom formula before the consultation?
faqs.answer: It is better to quote the consultation fee first and give the formula price afterward, since the formula depends on the client's needs. You can share typical formula price ranges in advance so there are no surprises.

faqs.question: What if herb costs change after I give a quote?
faqs.answer: State a validity period on the quote and include a line saying prices may change if ingredient costs shift significantly. For large orders, take a deposit when the client accepts so you can lock in supplies.

faqs.question: How detailed should a quote for a workshop be?
faqs.answer: List the topic, length, maximum attendees, what materials are included, what the host provides, and your travel or setup fees. Include the cancellation terms and the per-person price so both sides can plan.

holiday-lighting-installer.intro: Holiday lighting installers hang, maintain, take down, and store seasonal lights for homeowners and commercial properties such as storefronts, HOAs, restaurants, and office parks. Most are solo operators or small crews who run a compressed season from October through early January. Invoices usually cover design and installation, lighting materials, maintenance visits, takedown, and off-season storage.
holiday-lighting-installer.pricingModel: Most installers quote a flat price for the full-service package: design, custom-measured lights, installation, mid-season repairs, takedown, and storage. Price is usually built from linear feet of roofline, number of trees or shrubs wrapped, wreaths and garland, and the time and equipment needed for height or difficult access. Many shops also offer a customer-owned option, where they charge hourly labor or per-foot installation only. Commercial work is often priced per project or per square foot of facade with a deposit, and large jobs may include lift rental. Add-ons such as timers, smart controllers, extra service calls, and rush installs are itemized separately. Many companies require a signed multi-year agreement and charge a renewal fee in the following season, with a discount for early booking.

rates.service: Roofline LED light installation (commercial-grade, includes lights)
Tree wrapping (trunk and large limbs, includes lights)
Pre-lit wreath or garland installation (includes product)
Mid-season service call (bulb or strand repair)

items.description: Warm white C9 LED roofline installation, front and garage (design, lights, clips, labor)
Mature tree wrap, 2 front yard maples (trunk and lower limbs)
Shrub net lighting, front beds
Outdoor timer and power stake installation
Takedown and off-season storage
Mid-season service call (not used, covered in package)

sampleInvoice.notes: Package includes one complimentary repair visit during the season. Additional visits are $95 each. Installed lights remain the property of the installer until the season ends and are stored by us. 50% deposit paid at booking; balance due on completion of installation. Payment due within 7 days. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.
