invoiceChecklist.item: Install date, takedown date, and storage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget what the fee covers, and clear dates prevent arguments about early or late takedown.

invoiceChecklist.item: Linear feet, trees, and pieces installed
invoiceChecklist.why: Measured quantities show how the total was calculated and match the estimate if the client questions it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Whether lights are installer-owned or client-owned
invoiceChecklist.why: It determines who is responsible for replacing, storing, and repairing the lights after the season.

invoiceChecklist.item: Included service visits and the rate for extras
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out what a mid-season repair costs so a burnt-out strand does not become a billing dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lift or equipment rental charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Tall rooflines and commercial jobs may need a bucket lift or scaffolding, which you will want to pass through at cost or a stated markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license and insurance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients and property managers often ask for proof of liability coverage, and some local jurisdictions require a contractor license or permit for electrical work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or work order number for commercial clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and HOAs often cannot pay without a PO reference.

holiday-lighting-installer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25-50% at booking is common, especially for custom-ordered materials and early-season slots. The balance is usually due on completion of installation or within 7 to 14 days. Commercial clients often pay net 15 or net 30, so send the invoice the day the lights go on. Many installers charge a late fee of 1.5% per month or a flat fee, and some hold takedown until the balance is paid. Common payment methods are credit card, ACH, check, and digital payment apps. Storage and renewal fees for next season may be billed separately in the fall or spring.

tips.title: Bill the deposit before ordering materials
tips.body: Custom-length strands, commercial LEDs, and specialty clips are bought up front. A non-refundable deposit protects you from cancellations that leave you holding unused stock.

tips.title: Take photos at completion
tips.body: Photograph the finished job and attach them to the invoice or send them with it. It confirms work was done and quickens payment, which matters when you are juggling dozens of installs in November.

tips.title: Invoice takedown and storage up front or at installation
tips.body: Collecting for the full season at the start avoids chasing payment in January when you are tired and clients have moved on to other expenses.

tips.title: Charge for access problems
tips.body: Steep roofs, locked gates, dogs, ice, and the need for a lift add real time. Note surcharges on the estimate and show them as separate lines on the invoice.

tips.title: Offer a renewal discount
tips.body: Offering returning clients a rate lock if they pay a renewal deposit by spring fills your calendar early and spreads out your cash flow.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the foot or a flat package price?
faqs.answer: Many installers measure by the foot to build the price, then present a flat package price to the client. Showing the per-foot quantities on the invoice helps explain the total, but the client pays the agreed flat price.

faqs.question: Can I charge for takedown separately?
faqs.answer: Yes. Takedown and storage are often listed as their own line, either a flat fee or a percentage of the installation cost. Some installers bundle them into a full-service price, which should be stated on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for repairs during the season?
faqs.answer: Include one or two service visits in the package and state the rate for extra visits, commonly $75-150. Bill extra calls on a separate invoice with the date and what was repaired.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and whether you are selling materials or providing a service. Rules differ on installation labor, tangible goods, and rentals, so check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to cancel after I have ordered materials?
faqs.answer: State in your agreement that the deposit is non-refundable once custom materials are ordered. Reference the deposit terms on the invoice so there is no confusion.

estimate.intro: Holiday lighting installers usually quote after a site visit, often in late summer or early fall, since the best dates book first. Clients typically compare price per foot, the lighting quality, what is included such as repairs and storage, and the calendar date of installation. Quote quickly, because homeowners often get two or three bids.

scopeChecklist.item: Areas to be lit with measurements
scopeChecklist.why: List roofline sections, trees, shrubs, railings, and wreaths with linear feet or counts so both sides agree on the scope.
Specify C9, mini, or net lights, warm white versus multicolor, and commercial-grade LEDs so the result matches what the client expects.
Give target dates, such as installed by Thanksgiving and removed by mid-January, and note weather delays.
State how many repair visits are covered and what a call costs after that to avoid disputes over burnt-out strands.

scopeChecklist.item: Ownership and storage of the lights
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether lights are rented or purchased and who stores them, which affects renewal pricing.
Note the need for working outdoor outlets, timers, GFCI protection, and clear access to the roof, trees, and gates.
Material costs and booking slots change, so say how long the quote is good and when payment is due.

pricingTips.title: Measure on site
pricingTips.body: Walk the property and measure roof edges, peaks, and trees. Estimating from satellite images often misses height, dormers, and obstructions that raise labor time.

pricingTips.title: Build in setup, repairs, and takedown
pricingTips.body: A full season costs more than the day of installation. Include the cost of one or two service calls, takedown, and storage in your per-foot price so you are not losing money in January.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic roofline, a roofline with trees, and a full-property design lets clients pick a budget and often raises the average ticket.

pricingTips.title: Reward early booking
pricingTips.body: A small discount for deposits paid before a set date, such as September 1, secures work early and helps you order materials before supplier prices rise.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most installers offer free residential estimates. For large commercial or custom design work, some charge a design fee and credit it toward the job if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days, and it should end before your installation slots fill. Late-season quotes may be good for only a week because of limited availability and material costs.

faqs.question: What if the final footage differs from the quote?
faqs.answer: Quote a flat price based on measured scope, and state that changes such as extra trees or added rooflines will be billed at the quoted unit rates. Get written approval before adding work.

faqs.question: Should I include lift rental in the quote?
faqs.answer: If the job requires a lift or scaffolding, include it as its own line or fold it into the price and say so. Do not leave it out and bill it later without notice.

home-appraiser.intro: Home appraisers are licensed or certified professionals who give an opinion of value on residential property. Most work as independent contractors or run small firms, taking orders from mortgage lenders, appraisal management companies (AMCs), attorneys, homeowners, and estate representatives. Invoices usually cover a single report fee per property, plus add-ons such as rush turnaround, extra units, or travel to rural locations.
home-appraiser.pricingModel: Most appraisers charge a flat fee per assignment, set by the type of report and the property. A standard single-family report on a conventional or FHA loan has a base fee, with adjustments for size, complexity, acreage, outbuildings, and distance. Lender work often goes through AMCs that set a fee schedule, and federal rules for mortgage appraisals call for customary and reasonable fees, so many appraisers keep a fee grid by loan type and region. Private-client work such as divorce, estate, date-of-death, pre-listing, and litigation support is more often billed hourly or as a higher flat fee, since it involves more research and sometimes testimony. Extras like rush orders, second units, manufactured homes, and long drives are usually billed as separate line items. Retainers are common for litigation and expert-witness work.

rates.service: Complex or high-value home (large acreage, custom, luxury)
Appraisal update or recertification of value
Expert witness, consultation, or testimony prep

items.description: Full interior/exterior appraisal, single-family, 1004 form (FHA case, 123 Maple St)
Additional acreage adjustment (6.5 acres, rural comparable search)
Rush turnaround (report delivered within 3 business days)
Travel beyond 30-mile service area (22 extra miles each way)

sampleInvoice.notes: Order/loan number: 2024-08817. Payment due at delivery of report unless billed through the lender or AMC. Accepted: check, ACH, or card. A $35 fee applies to returned payments. Fee is for the appraisal only and does not depend on the value concluded.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and client file or loan number
invoiceChecklist.why: Lenders and AMCs match payments to a specific order, and a missing reference number is the most common reason payment is delayed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or certification number, state, and expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients and AMCs require it on every document, and it shows you were credentialed when the work was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Report type and form (for example 1004, 1073, 1025, or 2055)
invoiceChecklist.why: Fees depend on the form used, so naming it shows what was delivered and supports the price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized base fee and add-ons (rush, extra unit, acreage, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating extras prevents disputes and helps an AMC approve fees above its standard schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection date and report delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: These set the timeline for rush fees, payment terms, and any later dispute about turnaround.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who is responsible for payment (borrower, lender, AMC, or private client)
invoiceChecklist.why: Payment at closing, upfront through the borrower, or through an AMC are handled differently, and the invoice should say which applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: A statement that the fee is not contingent on the value reached
invoiceChecklist.why: Appraisal standards require independence, and a clear statement helps show the fee was not tied to a loan outcome.

home-appraiser.paymentTerms: Practice varies by client type. For lender and AMC work, appraisers often get paid upon completion, with AMCs paying on net 30 to 45 day cycles, so many appraisers ask for the borrower's payment up front when possible. For private clients, a common arrangement is full payment at the time of inspection or before the report is released, since many appraisers do not release the report until paid. For litigation or large assignments, a retainer of 50 percent or a deposit against estimated hours is typical. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month on overdue balances are common if stated in your engagement letter or terms. Most accept checks, ACH, and cards, and some pass card fees on to the client. Check your state's rules and your engagement terms about withholding a report until payment is received, since rules differ for lender-ordered reports.

tips.title: Collect before delivery on private jobs
tips.body: For homeowners, estates, and attorneys, request payment at inspection or before releasing the final report. Once the report is delivered, you lose leverage and collecting can take months.

tips.title: Keep a written fee schedule by loan and property type
tips.body: A fee grid with base fees and standard add-ons makes quoting consistent and gives you a clear answer when an AMC asks for a fee reduction or when you bill above their usual amount.

tips.title: Bill add-ons as separate lines
tips.body: Rush fees, extra acreage, a guest house, or long drives take real time. List them separately so the base fee is not questioned, and so you can show the reason if you need a complexity fee approved.

tips.title: Track AMC payment cycles
tips.body: Note the order date, delivery date, and expected pay date for each AMC. Follow up on anything unpaid after its stated terms rather than waiting, as small balances tend to be forgotten.

tips.title: Keep a copy of every invoice with the workfile
tips.body: Appraisal standards require you to keep workfiles for a set number of years, commonly five. Storing the invoice with the file helps if a fee or payment question comes up later.

faqs.question: Can I charge the borrower directly for an appraisal ordered by a lender?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Many lenders collect the appraisal fee from the borrower at application, then pay the appraiser or AMC. If you bill the borrower directly, make clear on the invoice who is responsible. Check with your lender client on how they handle it.

faqs.question: Should I invoice at delivery or at inspection?
faqs.answer: For private clients, at or before inspection is common, with the report released after payment. For lender and AMC work, you generally invoice at delivery, and the client pays per its agreement.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on an appraisal?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax professional services such as appraisals, but a few do. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if an AMC pays less than my normal fee?
faqs.answer: Federal rules call for customary and reasonable fees for mortgage appraisals, and many appraisers keep records of local fees. You can accept, counter, or decline the order. If you accept, bill any approved add-ons separately.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a re-inspection or a value dispute?
faqs.answer: You can charge for extra work that is outside the original scope, such as a new inspection after repairs or a new effective date. State this in your terms. A reconsideration of value on lender request, based on corrections to your own errors, is usually not billable.

estimate.intro: Appraisers quote before accepting an order, either by email to a homeowner, attorney, or estate, or as a fee and turnaround reply to an AMC or lender. Clients compare price, turnaround, and your familiarity with the area. A clear quote with the report type, fee, and delivery date prevents disagreements over what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Property address, type, and approximate size
scopeChecklist.why: A condo, a 3,000 sq ft home, and a 10-acre property each take different time, so the quote has to match the actual property.

scopeChecklist.item: Purpose and intended use of the appraisal
scopeChecklist.why: Lending, divorce, estate, and pre-listing each call for a different report and assumptions, and the intended use affects what you can legally and ethically deliver.

scopeChecklist.item: Report form and scope of work
scopeChecklist.why: State whether it is a full interior inspection, an exterior-only report, or a desktop appraisal so the client knows what they are paying for.
Date-of-death or retrospective appraisals take more research and cost more than a current-value report.

scopeChecklist.item: Turnaround time and rush fee terms
scopeChecklist.why: Standard delivery might be 5 to 10 business days, and a faster date should have a stated surcharge.

scopeChecklist.item: Access requirements and what you need from the owner
scopeChecklist.why: Missing access, no utilities, or missing documents can delay the inspection, and you may need to charge for a return trip.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment timing and cancellation or trip fee
scopeChecklist.why: If the client cancels after inspection, you have already done much of the work, so state how much is owed at each stage.

pricingTips.title: Price by complexity, not just square footage
pricingTips.body: Acreage, outbuildings, unique features, poor comparable data, and rural locations all add research time. Add a stated complexity fee in the quote rather than absorbing it.

pricingTips.title: Quote hourly for litigation and expert work
pricingTips.body: Testimony, depositions, and research are open-ended. Quote an hourly rate with a retainer instead of a flat fee, and say how court time and travel are billed.

pricingTips.title: Put the quote in writing with an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Market conditions and workload change, so a quote valid for 30 days lets you reprice without an argument.

pricingTips.title: Show the fee does not depend on the value
pricingTips.body: A quote that states the fee is fixed and independent of the conclusion supports your independence and protects you if a client later pressures you.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a ballpark, but confirm the actual fee in writing once you know the address, purpose, and any special features. A written quote gives you something to point to if the scope turns out larger.

faqs.question: Can I quote a price before knowing what the value will be?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. The fee should not change with the value you reach. Quoting before you have any view of value keeps the assignment independent.

faqs.question: What if I get to the property and it is more complex than described?
faqs.answer: Include a line in your quote that the fee may be adjusted if the property differs from what the client described, such as extra units or more acreage. Tell the client before you proceed and confirm the new fee in writing.

home-health-aide.intro: Independent home health aides and small home care businesses bill clients or their families for in-home personal care, companionship, and basic health support. Typical invoices cover hourly care shifts, overnight stays, live-in days, and extras such as mileage for errands or transportation to appointments. Clients are usually private-pay individuals, family members who arrange care for a parent, or occasionally a long-term care insurance carrier that reimburses the family.
home-health-aide.pricingModel: Most home health aides bill by the hour, with a minimum shift length of 3 to 4 hours so that travel time is covered. Rates rise for overnight care, weekends, holidays, and clients who need heavier physical help such as transfers, incontinence care, or dementia supervision. Live-in arrangements are often billed as a flat daily rate (typically 24-hour or 12-hour with sleep allowed), though rules on sleep time and overtime vary by state, so check your local labor rules. Many aides charge 1.5 times the regular rate for holidays. Mileage is usually billed separately when you drive the client or run errands in your own car, either at the IRS standard rate or a flat per-mile amount. Agencies bill higher hourly rates than independents because they cover insurance, payroll taxes, and supervision. Independents should set rates that account for self-employment tax and unpaid gaps between clients.

rates.service: Standard hourly care (personal care, meals, light housekeeping)
Dementia or high-needs care (transfers, incontinence, wandering supervision)

items.description: Personal care shifts, weekdays 9am-1pm (bathing, dressing, meal prep, medication reminders)
Weekend care shift, Sat 10am-4pm
Holiday shift, Memorial Day 9am-3pm
Transportation to cardiology appointment and pharmacy
Reimbursable groceries (receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Accepted by check, Zelle, or bank transfer. Care dates and shift times are listed above. Receipts for reimbursed purchases are attached. Cancellations with less than 24 hours notice are billed for a 3-hour minimum.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and start/end times of every shift
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing is the core of the invoice, and families and insurers want to match it against their own notes or a care log.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and name of the person paying
invoiceChecklist.why: The client receiving care and the adult child or trustee paying are often different people, and long-term care insurers need the client's name.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of shift and rate applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Standard, overnight, weekend, and holiday shifts carry different rates, and listing them prevents questions about why hours cost different amounts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage with dates and destinations
invoiceChecklist.why: Driving the client in your own vehicle is billable, and a log makes the charge easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized reimbursable purchases with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Groceries, supplies, or pharmacy pickups paid out of pocket should be listed separately from care fees so they are not mistaken for income or markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification or registration details, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many long-term care insurers and some families want to see your HHA or CNA certificate number or state registry listing, where your state requires one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your tax ID or business name and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who claim medical expense deductions or submit claims need documentation of who was paid.

home-health-aide.paymentTerms: Private-pay home care is commonly billed weekly or every two weeks, with payment due in 3 to 7 days, since aides depend on steady cash flow. Many independents ask for the first week in advance or a small deposit when starting with a new client. Late fees of 1.5% per month are sometimes written into a care agreement, but they work best when agreed to in writing before care begins. Payment is usually by check, Zelle, Venmo, or bank transfer, and some clients pay through a family member or a care manager. Where a long-term care insurance policy reimburses the family, the family typically pays you first and submits your invoices for reimbursement.

tips.title: Put a care agreement in place before the first shift
tips.body: A one-page agreement that lists duties, hourly rates, overtime or holiday premiums, minimum shift length, cancellation policy, and billing schedule prevents most payment disputes. It also helps separate what you will do from tasks outside your scope, such as medication administration or nursing care.

tips.title: Set a minimum shift length
tips.body: Short visits cost you travel time and may block other work. A 3 or 4 hour minimum, written into your rates, keeps one-hour visits from costing you money.

tips.title: Bill weekly rather than monthly
tips.body: Weekly invoices keep balances small, make it easier for families to review shifts while they are fresh, and reduce the chance that you carry thousands of dollars in unpaid hours.

tips.title: Keep reimbursed expenses separate
tips.body: List groceries, supplies, and other out-of-pocket purchases as their own lines with receipts. Do not add markup unless you agreed to it. This keeps trust high when family members are scrutinizing every charge.

tips.title: Track employment status and tax rules
tips.body: If clients pay you directly, you may be treated as a household employee rather than an independent contractor in some states or under IRS rules. Check with a tax professional or your state labor department so your invoices and tax filings match how you are actually working.

faqs.question: How often should a home health aide send invoices?
faqs.answer: Weekly or every two weeks is most common for private-pay clients. Weekly billing keeps balances small and matches how most families budget for care.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time or mileage?
faqs.answer: You can charge mileage when you drive the client or run errands in your own vehicle, usually at the IRS rate or a flat per-mile rate. Commuting to the client's home is generally not billed, though some aides add a travel fee for distant clients or short shifts.

faqs.question: How do I bill for overnight or live-in care?
faqs.answer: Overnight awake care is usually an hourly rate, sometimes slightly higher than daytime. Live-in care is often a flat daily rate, but sleep time, breaks, and overtime rules vary by state, so check your local labor laws before setting a flat rate.

faqs.question: Do I need to be licensed to invoice for home health aide services?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state. Some states require a certification or registry listing for aides working through agencies, while private-duty companionship and personal care rules differ. Check your state health or labor department, and include any certificate number on your invoice if it is relevant.

faqs.question: What if the client's family disputes the hours?
faqs.answer: Keep a daily care log with arrival and departure times and have the client or family sign weekly. Attach it to the invoice if there is a question. Clear records settle most disagreements quickly.

estimate.intro: Home health aides give estimates when a family is first arranging care, usually after an initial consultation or home visit. Families compare hourly rates, minimum shift lengths, and how much weekly care they will need, often alongside agency quotes. A clear estimate shows the expected weekly and monthly cost so the family can plan.

scopeChecklist.why: Bathing, dressing, meal prep, toileting, transfers, and light housekeeping all take different effort, and a written list prevents arguments about what is covered.
The total depends on days, start times, and shift length, so state the expected schedule and what happens if hours change.
Overnight, weekend, and holiday hours cost more, and the family should see those rates before they need them.

scopeChecklist.item: Minimum shift length and cancellation policy
scopeChecklist.why: This protects you from short visits and last-minute cancellations that leave you without income.
Say whether driving the client and running errands are billed, at what rate, and whether you will be reimbursed for purchases.
Medication administration, wound care, and skilled nursing may require a licensed nurse depending on state rules. Stating limits protects you and the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, review period, and how either side can end care
scopeChecklist.why: Care needs change, and a notice period such as 7 or 14 days gives both sides time to adjust.

pricingTips.title: Quote a weekly estimate as well as hourly rates
pricingTips.body: Families think in weekly budgets. Showing that 25 hours at $28 is $700 per week makes the cost easier to understand than an hourly figure alone.

pricingTips.title: Build in a shift minimum
pricingTips.body: Quote 3 or 4 hours as the minimum so travel and lost availability are covered, particularly for clients who only want short morning visits.

pricingTips.title: Price higher-needs care accordingly
pricingTips.body: Heavy transfers, dementia care, and incontinence care are more demanding. Quote a higher rate when the initial assessment shows these needs rather than raising rates after you start.

pricingTips.title: Explain what you charge versus an agency
pricingTips.body: Families often compare to agency rates of $30 to $40 per hour. If you charge less, point out that you are a direct hire without agency overhead, and be clear about what that means for backup coverage if you are sick.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation or home visit?
faqs.answer: Many aides do the first meeting free to assess needs and meet the family. If the visit is long or involves significant travel, a small assessment fee that is credited toward the first week is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long is an estimate valid?
faqs.answer: Care estimates are usually valid for 14 to 30 days. Needs and availability change quickly, so note an expiration date and say that rates may change if the care needs differ from the assessment.

faqs.question: What if the client's needs increase after I give a quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying the estimate is based on the initial assessment and that rates or hours may be revised if needs change. Discuss any change with the family in writing before applying a new rate.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include a deposit?
faqs.answer: A deposit or prepayment of the first week is common for new private-pay clients. State the amount in the estimate and say it will be applied to the first invoice.

home-inspector.intro: Home inspectors perform visual, non-invasive inspections of residential properties, most often for buyers during a purchase contingency period. Invoices cover the base inspection fee plus add-on services such as radon testing, sewer scope, wood-destroying insect inspections, and re-inspections. Most inspectors are solo operators or run small firms with a few inspectors, and most are paid on the day of the inspection.
home-inspector.pricingModel: Most home inspectors charge a flat fee for the base inspection, set by the home's square footage, with tiers such as under 1,500 sq ft, 1,500 to 2,500, 2,500 to 3,500, and so on. Many add surcharges for older homes (often 40 to 50+ years), homes with outbuildings, crawl spaces, multiple HVAC systems, or long drive distances. Ancillary tests like radon, mold sampling, water quality, sewer line camera scopes, thermal imaging, pool and spa inspections, and wood-destroying organism (WDO/termite) reports are priced as separate line items, and many inspectors offer a bundle discount. Re-inspections after repairs are usually billed as a flat fee or a short hourly charge. Commercial and multi-unit work is typically quoted per job. Lab fees for radon, mold, or water samples are either passed through at cost or built into the add-on price.

items.description: Full home inspection, 2,200 sq ft single-family, built 1994
Radon short-term test (48 hr), incl. lab report
Sewer line camera scope with recorded video
Wood-destroying insect inspection
Detached garage and shed surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of inspection or at delivery of the report. Accepted: card, check, or ACH. Report delivered by email within 24 hours of inspection. Invoices unpaid after 10 days are subject to a $35 late fee. Inspection performed per the signed pre-inspection agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and inspection date
invoiceChecklist.why: The invoice must tie to one specific inspection, which matters for disputes, agent records, and your own files.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and, if different, the person paying
invoiceChecklist.why: Buyers, agents, or relatives sometimes pay on the client's behalf, and the payer needs a correct receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage or fee tier used
invoiceChecklist.why: It shows how the base fee was calculated and heads off questions about why the price differs from a friend's quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each ancillary service as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Radon, sewer scope, WDI, and pool inspections often have separate reports and sometimes separate lab or licensing requirements, so itemizing keeps everything traceable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your state license or certification number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require the inspector's license number on contracts and reports, and putting it on the invoice is a simple way to stay consistent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed inspection agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: The agreement sets the scope and limits of liability. Linking the invoice to it reinforces what was and was not covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Discounts, bundle pricing, or agent referral credits
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the discount as a line keeps your books accurate and makes your standard rate visible.

home-inspector.paymentTerms: Most home inspectors collect payment on the day of the inspection or when the report is released, since the buyer is on a tight contingency clock and the relationship is usually one-time. Some firms hold the report until payment clears, which is allowed in many places but should be stated in your agreement. Deposits are uncommon for standard residential inspections but are used for large, distant, or commercial jobs. Cards, ACH, and checks are standard, and many inspectors accept payment at closing through the title company for buyers who ask. When invoices go out after the fact, net 7 to 10 days is typical, with a modest flat late fee. Cancellation or lockout fees for no-shows, or for properties with utilities off, are common and should be in the agreement.

tips.title: Release the report on payment
tips.body: Spell out in your agreement that the report is delivered upon payment. Once the buyer has the report and the contingency period ends, collecting becomes much harder.

tips.title: Separate lab and third-party costs
tips.body: Radon labs, mold labs, and subcontracted sewer or pool specialists have real costs. Price each add-on so it covers those costs and your time instead of absorbing them into the base fee.

tips.title: Charge for the conditions, not just the size
tips.body: Add surcharges for crawl spaces, old homes, multiple units, well and septic, or long travel. Put them on the invoice as lines so clients see the reason.

tips.title: Handle agent-paid or closing-paid invoices clearly
tips.body: If payment comes from the title company or an agent, confirm the payer name and billing address before the inspection. Include the property address and file number so the payment matches the invoice.

tips.title: Bill re-inspections as separate invoices
tips.body: A re-inspection weeks later is a new visit. Create a new invoice referencing the original inspection date so each job stands alone.

faqs.question: Should I charge by square footage or a flat rate?
faqs.answer: Most inspectors use square footage tiers because larger homes take longer. Add age, foundation type, and extra structures as separate surcharges so your pricing stays consistent.

faqs.question: Can I withhold the report until the client pays?
faqs.answer: In many places yes, provided your pre-inspection agreement says so. Check your state's rules and your inspector association's guidance, and apply the policy the same way every time.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on inspections?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax inspection services and others do not, and the answer can differ for lab tests or reports. Check with your state's revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who disputes the invoice after the report?
faqs.answer: Point to the signed agreement and the itemized services performed. A finding that was less dramatic than the client hoped for is not grounds to reduce the fee, but a documented missed service or scheduling error might be.

faqs.question: What should I do if the buyer backs out of the sale after the inspection?
faqs.answer: You still performed the work, so the full fee is owed. State in your agreement that payment is due regardless of whether the transaction closes.

estimate.intro: Home inspectors usually quote by phone, text, or online booking form when an agent or buyer is comparing several inspectors during a short due diligence window. Clients compare the total price, which tests are included, how fast the report arrives, and how soon you can be on site. A clear written quote keeps you from being compared on the base fee alone.

scopeChecklist.item: Property address, square footage, and year built
scopeChecklist.why: These set the fee tier and surcharges, and if the real house differs from the listing, you have a basis to adjust.

scopeChecklist.item: Included services and standards of practice
scopeChecklist.why: State the standard you follow, such as your state's rules or a national association standard, so the client knows what a general inspection covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Each add-on test with its price
scopeChecklist.why: Radon, sewer scope, WDI, mold, and pool inspections are optional, and listing them separately lets the client choose.
Note that inspections are visual and non-invasive, and that areas like roofs, crawl spaces, or attics may be skipped if unsafe or inaccessible.
Utilities must be on, and appliances, panels, and attics must be reachable. Say there may be an extra fee if you have to return.
Clients want to know when they will receive the report, since it affects their negotiation window.
Pricing is tied to the property details and your calendar, so say how long the quote holds.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a published fee schedule
pricingTips.body: Keep a fee table by square footage, age, and add-ons. Quoting from it keeps your prices consistent and makes surcharges easy to explain.

pricingTips.title: Offer bundles without cutting the base fee
pricingTips.body: Discount the add-on package, such as radon plus sewer scope plus WDI, instead of the core inspection. It raises the average ticket while giving the buyer a clear saving.

pricingTips.title: Confirm property details before locking a price
pricingTips.body: Ask about outbuildings, finished basements, in-law units, well and septic, and pools. Missing details are the usual cause of day-of price changes.

pricingTips.title: Price distance and difficulty honestly
pricingTips.body: A property an hour away or a large multi-unit building takes much more of your day. A travel fee or higher tier is reasonable if stated upfront.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a price, but follow it with a written quote or confirmation listing the services and the fee. Send the inspection agreement before the appointment so the scope is clear.

faqs.question: Do I charge for quotes on commercial or multi-unit properties?
faqs.answer: Usually no for a straightforward quote. For large or complex properties that require a site visit or detailed scoping, some inspectors charge a fee that is credited to the job if hired.

faqs.question: What if the home turns out larger than the listing said?
faqs.answer: State in your quote that the fee is based on the information provided and may be adjusted if the actual size, age, or features differ. Tell the client before starting.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Many inspectors hold a quote for 30 days or until the inspection is scheduled. Schedule-based pricing, such as rush or weekend fees, should be confirmed when the appointment is booked.

home-organizer.intro: Home organizers help clients sort, declutter, and set up storage systems in rooms like closets, pantries, garages, kitchens, and home offices. Solo organizers and small teams bill for hands-on session time, planning and design work, product shopping and installation, and sometimes moves such as unpacking or staging. Invoices usually combine labor with purchased supplies and trip charges.
home-organizer.pricingModel: Most home organizers charge hourly, with a 2 to 4 hour minimum per session because setup, sorting, and cleanup take time regardless of room size. Rates are often lower for each additional team member. Some organizers sell flat-fee project packages for a defined space, such as a single reach-in closet or a pantry, once they know how fast they typically work. Virtual or coaching sessions are billed per hour or per session. Shopping for containers, labels, and shelving is billed either as an hourly errand charge or built into a project fee, and products are passed through at cost or with a modest markup of 10 to 25 percent. Donation and haul-away runs are often billed as a flat trip fee or per load. Larger projects such as whole-home organizing, downsizing, or move-in unpacking may be quoted as a day rate or a retainer with a set number of hours per month.

items.description: Master bedroom closet organizing: sort, purge, categorize, and reset (lead organizer)
Assistant organizer, same session
Shopping trip for bins, shelf dividers, and matching hangers
Organizing products purchased (receipt attached, at cost)
Donation drop-off to local charity, with receipt provided

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Product receipts are attached. Donation receipt is provided for your tax records. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, start and end times, and the spaces worked on
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget how long a session ran, and hourly billing is easier to approve when each day and room is listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of organizers and each person's hourly rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Lead and assistant rates differ, so showing them separately prevents questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized product purchases with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see exactly what you bought for them, and receipts support reimbursement or any markup you disclosed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shopping and errand time listed separately from hands-on time
invoiceChecklist.why: Shopping is a different kind of work and sometimes billed at a different rate, so separating it keeps the invoice clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Donation or haul-away details, including the charity name
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients may want to claim a donation deduction, and a note on what was taken away avoids disputes about discarded items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or trip charge, if you bill for travel
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel between the client's home, stores, and donation sites is a real cost and should be stated as a line item rather than hidden in the rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or prepaid hours applied, with remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Many organizers collect a deposit up front, and showing the credit makes the amount due obvious.

home-organizer.paymentTerms: Many home organizers collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent, or prepay for the first session, when the project is booked, especially for multi-day jobs. Balances for hourly work are commonly due at the end of each session or within 7 to 14 days of invoicing. For multi-day projects, billing weekly keeps cash flow steady. Product purchases above a set amount, such as $150, are often paid by the client in advance or reimbursed immediately. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Cards, ACH transfers, and digital payment apps are the usual payment methods, and many organizers also take checks. A cancellation policy of 24 to 48 hours' notice, with a late-cancel fee, should be written into the booking agreement.

tips.title: Set a minimum session length
tips.body: Travel, setup, and wrap-up take about the same time whether you work 2 hours or 6. A 3 or 4 hour minimum makes short sessions worth booking and lets you plan your day.

tips.title: Decide how you handle product markup before the first purchase
tips.body: Choose whether you pass products through at cost, add a markup, or charge a shopping fee, and say so in your agreement. Surprises about product pricing are among the most common disputes.

tips.title: Keep receipts and photograph them
tips.body: Attach a receipt to every invoice that includes purchases. It protects you if a client questions a total and gives you records for your own bookkeeping.

tips.title: Take before and after photos with permission
tips.body: Photos show the value of the work, support your portfolio, and help if the client later questions the results. Get written permission before using them publicly.

tips.title: Bill weekly on long projects
tips.body: Whole-home or downsizing jobs can run for weeks. Invoicing at the end of each week or milestone avoids a large unpaid balance at the end.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the project?
faqs.answer: Hourly billing is safer when you are new or when the amount of stuff is unknown. Once you can predict how long a pantry, closet, or garage takes, flat project fees are easier for clients to approve and reward you for working efficiently.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Practices vary. Some organizers offer a free 15 to 30 minute phone call and charge for an in-home walkthrough, often $50 to $200, which can be credited toward the project if the client books.

faqs.question: Can I mark up organizing products I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as the client agrees in advance. Common approaches are passing items through at cost and charging shopping time, or adding 10 to 25 percent. Put your policy in the agreement and itemize products on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax tangible products you sell, such as bins or shelving, and some tax certain services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant about how to handle products and labor.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Include a cancellation policy in your agreement, such as 48 hours' notice or a fee of one to two hours of your rate. Invoice the fee as a separate line item referencing the cancelled session date.

estimate.intro: Home organizers usually send an estimate after a walkthrough, photos, or a discovery call, before booking a project. Clients often compare your estimate against other organizers, and against their own sense of how long it should take. Because the amount of belongings is hard to judge, a clear estimate sets expectations on time, products, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a closet job includes the adjoining shelves or the hallway linen closet. Naming each space prevents scope creep.
A range such as 8 to 10 hours with two organizers shows how the total was built and gives room if the job runs longer.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether the estimate is hourly, capped, or fixed
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know if the figure is a ceiling, a guess, or a locked price, and what happens if more time is needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Product budget and who purchases it
scopeChecklist.why: State a product allowance and whether you shop, the client shops, or you order online, to avoid disputes about costs.
Decisions about what to keep depend on the client being present. If they are not, say how decisions will be made and the risk of discarding items.
Disposal of bulky items, hazardous materials, or large loads may cost extra or be excluded entirely.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation and rescheduling terms, plus validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Estimates should expire, such as after 30 days, and clients should know the rules for changing the schedule.

pricingTips.title: Estimate from the amount of stuff, not the size of the room
pricingTips.body: A small closet that is packed with items can take longer than a large, lightly used one. Look at photos or do a walkthrough and consider how many categories need sorting and how decisive the client is.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range and note what changes it
pricingTips.body: An estimate of 10 to 14 hours with a stated reason for variation, such as the client's decision speed or extra items found, protects you and is more honest than a single number.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for the same space
pricingTips.body: Present a basic sort and reset, a full organizing project with new products, and an optional maintenance visit. Clients can choose based on budget and see what each level includes.

pricingTips.title: Keep products separate from labor
pricingTips.body: Showing labor and product allowance as separate lines makes the estimate easier to compare and lets the client adjust the product budget without changing your fee.

faqs.question: Is it okay to charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many organizers charge for an in-home walkthrough that includes a plan, since it takes real time. Some credit the fee toward the project once the client books.

faqs.question: What if the project takes longer than the estimate?
faqs.answer: If the estimate was a range or hourly, bill the actual time and tell the client as soon as you see the job running over. If it was a fixed price, include a clause allowing change orders when the scope grows.

faqs.question: Should I give an estimate without seeing the space?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range from photos and a call, but label it as preliminary. Confirm the final estimate after a walkthrough or at the start of the first session.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Rates, schedules, and product prices change, and an expiration date lets you update the quote if the client waits.

home-repair.intro: Home repair contractors, handymen, and small repair businesses fix and maintain residential properties: drywall patches, leaky faucets, door and trim work, deck repairs, minor electrical and plumbing swaps, caulking, and punch-list items. Most work is short, often one visit to a few days, so invoices need to cover labor, materials, trip charges, and any extras added on site.
home-repair.pricingModel: Most solo repair pros bill hourly, often with a one-hour or two-hour minimum to cover travel and setup. Many also quote flat fees for common, well-defined tasks such as mounting a TV, replacing a toilet, or patching a hole in drywall. Larger repairs, like rotted deck boards or a bathroom subfloor, are usually quoted as a fixed price or time-and-materials with a cap. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10-25%, to cover pickup time, returns, and warranty risk. Many contractors add a trip or service-call fee and charge a higher rate for emergency or after-hours calls. Some handymen sell half-day and full-day rates, which clients like because the cost is predictable. Specialty work such as electrical, plumbing, or gas often requires a license in many states, which limits what a handyman can bill for, so check your local rules.

items.description: Labor: repair water-damaged drywall in hallway, tape, mud, sand, prime, and paint
Labor: replace kitchen faucet and supply lines
Materials: drywall sheet, joint compound, primer, paint (at cost plus 15%)
Materials: kitchen faucet and braided supply lines (customer-approved, cost plus 15%)
Trip charge and debris haul-away

sampleInvoice.notes: Work completed 6/12 at 214 Maple Ave. Receipts for materials available on request. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Repairs are warranted for 90 days on workmanship; manufacturer warranty applies to fixtures.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and date(s) of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Repair pros often work at several properties for the same client, such as landlords, and this prevents mix-ups and supports disputes or insurance claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor with hours and hourly rate or flat-fee description
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients question vague lines like 'repairs'; naming each task makes the total easy to defend.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately with markup shown or built into the price
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was bought for the job and avoids disagreements about hardware store receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge, minimum fee, or disposal fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Fees that were agreed on verbally still need to appear in writing so they are not seen as surprises.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and added work, with date approved
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden damage found behind walls is common; documenting approved extras protects you when the total exceeds the estimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: License number and insurance info, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a contractor or home improvement license above a dollar threshold, and landlords or property managers often ask for proof of insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: A stated workmanship warranty reduces callback arguments, and clear payment methods and due date speed up payment.

home-repair.paymentTerms: For small jobs under a few hundred dollars, most repair pros collect on completion by card, check, or digital payment, or invoice with net 7 to net 14 terms. For larger repairs, a deposit of 25-50% is common, often to cover materials, with the balance due at completion. Multi-day jobs may use a progress payment after materials are bought or at the halfway point. Property managers and landlords often pay net 30, so confirm terms before starting. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in writing in advance. Check your state's rules, as some limit deposit sizes on home improvement contracts and require specific written contract language.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: Short jobs lose money once drive time, parts runs, and setup are counted. A one-hour or two-hour minimum or a flat trip fee keeps a 20-minute fix from costing you half a day.

tips.title: Get approval before extra work
tips.body: When you open a wall and find rot, mold, or bad wiring, stop and get a written or texted approval for the added cost. Then list it as a change order on the invoice.

tips.title: Charge for materials pickup time
tips.body: Store runs eat hours. Either bill that time at your labor rate or build it into a markup on materials so it is not unpaid.

tips.title: Keep receipts and photos
tips.body: Take before and after photos and keep receipts for every job. They settle disputes quickly and support your records at tax time.

tips.title: Invoice the same day
tips.body: Clients pay fastest while the work is fresh. Send the invoice from the driveway or the same evening, with payment links or instructions included.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat rate for repairs?
faqs.answer: Use flat rates for defined, repeatable tasks like mounting a TV or replacing a toilet, and hourly for open-ended repairs where the scope is unclear. If you quote hourly, give a rough range so the client is not surprised.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up materials?
faqs.answer: Many repair pros add 10-25% to cost. The markup covers shopping time, transport, returns, and the risk of a part failing. Show it as a line item or fold it into the price, but be consistent.

faqs.question: Can I do plumbing or electrical work as a handyman?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and the job. Many states limit handyman work to small jobs under a dollar threshold and require licenses for electrical, plumbing, and gas work. Check with your state licensing board before billing for these.

faqs.question: What if the client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder, then a written demand citing your invoice terms. Depending on your state, you may be able to file a mechanic's lien on the property for unpaid work, usually with strict deadlines, or go to small claims court. Check local rules early, since lien deadlines can be short.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on repairs?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax labor on repairs, some tax only materials, and some tax neither. Check with your state's department of revenue and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Home repair contractors send estimates before starting any job beyond a quick fix, and especially when the client is comparing two or three quotes. Clients mostly compare the total, the start date, and whether materials are included. Repairs often involve unknowns behind walls and floors, so the estimate needs to say what is and is not covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Specific tasks and locations in the home
scopeChecklist.why: Writing 'patch two holes in the hallway drywall and paint the wall' avoids arguments over whether the whole room was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies materials and what grade
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may assume a basic faucet and receive a premium one, or vice versa. State brand, model, or allowance amounts.
Matching paint, texture, and stain are common disputes. Say whether you prime, paint, or leave the surface ready for the client's painter.
Rot, mold, asbestos, old wiring, or code issues may be found after work starts. State that they are not included and will be quoted separately.
Some repairs, such as electrical, structural, or water heater changes, need permits in many areas. Say who pulls the permit and who pays.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, duration, and access needs
scopeChecklist.why: Clients plan around your visit. Note any need for power, water shutoff, or an empty room, and the weather dependency for exterior work.
Material costs change. A 14 to 30 day expiration and a clear deposit amount protect you from price swings.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Older homes hide surprises. Add a buffer of 10-20% for repairs behind finished surfaces, or quote the visible work and state that discovered damage is extra.

pricingTips.title: Offer fixed price for defined work and time-and-materials for unknowns
pricingTips.body: A fixed price gives clients certainty for simple tasks. For diagnosing leaks or structural repairs, use time and materials with a not-to-exceed amount.

pricingTips.title: Itemize tasks so clients can trim scope
pricingTips.body: A list with a price per task lets the client drop the lower-priority items instead of walking away from the whole job, and it makes your pricing look transparent.

pricingTips.title: Price the travel and parts runs
pricingTips.body: Include a trip charge or account for supply runs in your labor estimate. Estimates that ignore these steps tend to run over.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: For simple jobs, free estimates are standard. For jobs that need a long diagnostic visit or drawings, such as tracking a leak, many contractors charge a fee, often $50-150, and credit it toward the work if hired.

faqs.question: Is an estimate legally binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on the wording and your state. A fixed-price quote that the client signs can act as a contract, while an estimate is usually a good-faith approximation. Label which one you are giving and state the conditions for changes.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Most repair pros use 14 to 30 days. Lumber, fixtures, and other materials can change in price quickly, so an expiration date lets you update the number if the client waits.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over the estimate?
faqs.answer: If the scope changes, send a written change order and get approval before continuing. Some states cap how much a final bill can exceed a written estimate without approval, so check your local home improvement rules.

home-staging.intro: Home stagers prepare occupied and vacant homes for sale or photography, working with listing agents, sellers, builders, and investors. Invoices typically cover a consultation, the design and setup work, furniture and accessory rental for a set period, and removal at the end of the term. Many stagers are solo operators or small teams who own their own inventory or rent from a warehouse.
home-staging.pricingModel: Most stagers use a mix of flat fees and recurring rental charges. A paid consultation (often a walk-through with a written action list) is billed as a flat fee or hourly, and is sometimes credited toward a full staging if the client books. Vacant staging is usually quoted as a one-time design and installation fee plus a monthly rental fee for furniture and accessories, with a minimum term of 30 to 90 days and extension billed monthly. Occupied staging (re-arranging and adding accessories from the seller's own belongings) is more often billed hourly or as a flat fee. Stagers also bill separately for items such as extra months, storage, delivery and pickup fees, handyman-type tasks, rush scheduling, and any items purchased or rented specifically for the job. Pricing generally scales with square footage, number of rooms, and the home's price point, and many stagers set a minimum project fee to cover the cost of moving inventory.

rates.service: Initial staging consultation with written report
Vacant home staging, design and installation (key rooms)

items.description: Vacant staging design and installation: living room, dining room, primary bedroom, and entry (2,400 sq ft home)
Furniture and accessory rental, initial 60-day term (billed monthly)
Delivery, setup, and styling labor (2 movers, 4 hours)
Purchased accessories: bedding and throw pillows (retained by client)
Photo-day touch-up visit

sampleInvoice.notes: Staging property: 412 Maple Ct. Initial term runs 60 days from install date; extensions billed at $1,400 per month, prorated by week after day 60. Deposit of 50% of the design fee is due to book the install date. Removal is scheduled once the listing is under contract or the term ends. Balance due within 7 days of installation. Late fees of 1.5% per month apply after 15 days. Client is responsible for replacement cost of damaged or missing rental items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and listing agent name
invoiceChecklist.why: Staging contracts are tied to a specific property, and agents often pay or reimburse on behalf of the seller, so the right party and location must be clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation date and rental term start and end dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Monthly rental fees and extension charges depend on exact dates, which prevents disputes about when the clock started.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized rooms staged
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and agents compare quotes by room count, so listing each room confirms what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental versus purchased items
invoiceChecklist.why: Rental inventory returns to you, while purchased accessories stay with the client. Separating them avoids confusion about ownership and pickup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extension and removal terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Homes often sit longer than planned, and stating the monthly extension rate and pickup fee up front makes later charges expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage and loss policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Rental furniture can be stained, scratched, or kept by buyers. A line on the invoice referencing replacement cost supports collecting for damage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most stagers collect a deposit to hold dates and inventory, so showing what was paid keeps the balance accurate.

home-staging.paymentTerms: Stagers commonly collect a 50% deposit on the design fee to reserve the install date, with the balance and first month of rental due on or before installation. Occupied-home consultations and hourly work are usually due on completion or within 7 days. Ongoing rental months are billed in advance, often on the same date each month, and extension invoices are typically due on receipt. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common, and some stagers hold removal or charge a restocking fee if the account is past due, as long as the contract allows it. Payment is typically accepted by card, ACH, check, or through the closing agent. Some stagers arrange payment from sale proceeds at closing, but this should be written down and not relied on without a signed agreement.

tips.title: Set a minimum term and a clear extension rate
tips.body: A 60 or 90 day minimum covers the cost of moving and storing inventory. State the monthly extension rate in your contract so a slow listing does not turn into free rental.

tips.title: Bill the deposit before you hold the date
tips.body: Installation days are limited by your crew and truck. A non-refundable deposit protects you if the seller cancels or the listing is delayed.

tips.title: Confirm who is paying before you stage
tips.body: Agents sometimes promise to cover staging, while the seller signs the contract. Put the responsible party on the agreement and invoice, and ask for a card on file for extensions.

tips.title: Schedule removal and bill promptly
tips.body: Contact the agent when the listing goes under contract and set a removal date. Billing extra months only for the time inventory was still in the home keeps the invoice defensible.

tips.title: Track inventory costs per job
tips.body: Record delivery labor, truck time, and any damage so you can see whether a flat install fee still covers your actual costs.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a staging consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes, most stagers do. A paid consultation with a written action list is a billable service. Many offer to credit the fee toward a full staging if the client books within a set time.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the house sells before the term ends?
faqs.answer: Your contract should state that the minimum term applies regardless of when the home sells. If you choose to prorate or refund, do it as a courtesy and not as a default, because most of your cost is in the install and removal.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on staging rental?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if it is stated in your signed agreement and permitted by your state. Many stagers use 1 to 1.5 percent per month after a grace period. Check local rules on maximum interest or late fee amounts.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on staging?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether you are selling a service, renting tangible property, or selling goods. Some states tax furniture rental, and others tax services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Who do I invoice, the agent or the seller?
faqs.answer: Invoice whoever signed your agreement. If the agent pays on behalf of the seller, put that in the contract and list the agent as the billing contact, but make clear who is legally responsible for payment.

estimate.intro: Stagers send an estimate after walking the property, or after reviewing photos and a floor plan for vacant homes. The estimate is usually part of a listing pitch, so agents and sellers often compare two or three stagers on room count, rental term, and total cost. A clear written quote also sets up the contract and deposit.

scopeChecklist.item: Rooms and areas to be staged
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume the whole house is included. Listing each room prevents disputes about the kitchen, patio, or bonus room.

scopeChecklist.item: Rental term, extension rate, and minimum
scopeChecklist.why: The length of the initial term and monthly extension cost are the biggest sources of surprise bills.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the install
scopeChecklist.why: State whether art, rugs, lamps, bedding, towels, and greenery are included, and what labor and delivery are covered.
Walk-ups, narrow stairs, or HOA move-in rules add labor time and may require a certificate of insurance or reserved elevator time.

scopeChecklist.item: Decluttering, packing, or storage of client belongings
scopeChecklist.why: Occupied staging often involves moving the seller's items. Say whether that is included and where items will be stored.
Define the client's responsibility for damaged rental items and whether the buyer or seller can purchase pieces.
Inventory availability changes. A quote that expires in 7 to 14 days protects your calendar and pricing.

pricingTips.title: Price by room and by home size
pricingTips.body: Most clients compare quotes by room count and square footage. Show a per-room price for key rooms such as living, dining, and primary bedroom, and add secondary rooms as options.

pricingTips.title: Separate the install fee from monthly rental
pricingTips.body: A one-time design and installation fee covers your labor, truck, and styling time, and the monthly rental covers inventory use. Splitting them makes your quote easier to compare and defend.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: A basic package (living room, primary bedroom, entry), a standard package (adding dining and kitchen), and a full package give the client a choice without discounting your rates.

pricingTips.title: Build in a minimum project fee
pricingTips.body: Small condos and single-room jobs cost nearly as much to deliver as larger ones. A floor price, such as $1,000 for vacant staging, keeps small jobs worthwhile.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: A free quote based on photos or a quick walk-through is common when pitching an agent. For a detailed in-person consultation with a written plan, many stagers charge a fee and credit it toward the staging.

faqs.question: How long should a staging quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is common. Inventory and truck availability change quickly, especially in spring and early summer, so state an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the install if the scope grows?
faqs.answer: Only if your quote or contract allows it. Define what is included and state that added rooms, extra pieces, or changes after install are billed as change orders at your listed rates.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before staging?
faqs.answer: Yes. A signed quote or staging agreement with the deposit, term, extension rate, damage policy, and removal terms is the document you will rely on if the seller disputes a charge.

horse-trainer.intro: Horse trainers start young horses under saddle, correct behavior problems, and train horse and rider for disciplines such as western, English, reining, jumping, and trail. They bill horse owners for monthly training board, individual lessons, tune-up rides, trailering, and show fees. Most are self-employed and run out of a leased or owned barn, or travel to client properties.
horse-trainer.pricingModel: Most trainers bill a flat monthly training fee that covers a set number of rides per week, with board, feed, and farrier billed separately or bundled into a full-care rate. Starting a colt is often priced as a 30, 60, or 90-day package. Lessons and clinics are priced per session, and travel work is priced per day or per trip plus mileage. Show weekends are billed as a day fee plus pass-through costs such as entries, stalls, shavings, and hauling. Reimbursable expenses like vet, farrier, and supplements are usually billed at cost, sometimes with a small handling fee if you agreed to that up front.

rates.service: Monthly training with board (full care, 4-5 rides/week)
Colt starting (30-90 day package, board included)

items.description: Monthly training, 5 rides/week, Quarter Horse gelding 'Dusty' (June 2025)
Board, stall with daily turnout, hay and grain (June 2025)
Private lesson for owner, 1 hour
Hauling to regional show, round trip (120 miles)
Show day coaching and handling
Farrier, front shoes reset (paid at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on the 1st of each month. A 5% late fee applies after 10 days. Vet, farrier, and show fees are billed at cost with receipts available on request. Please make checks payable to the business name above.

invoiceChecklist.item: Horse name, breed, and age
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with multiple horses need to know which horse each charge belongs to, and it protects you in a dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and number of rides or sessions
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the training fee covered and makes it easy to adjust when rides are missed due to weather, lameness, or travel.

invoiceChecklist.item: Board and care line items separate from training
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners often compare board costs to other barns, and separate lines make partial-month changes simple to calculate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized pass-through costs with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Vet, farrier, dewormer, supplements, and entry fees are reimbursed expenses and clients expect to see the actual cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Show details: event name, dates, class entries, stall and hauling charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Show weekends add many small costs, and clear detail prevents questions weeks later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage and trailer charges with start and end points
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel is a real cost and listing distance backs up the amount charged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed training agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to the terms the client agreed to, including notice periods and what happens if a horse is injured.

horse-trainer.paymentTerms: Training and board are normally billed monthly in advance, due on the first of the month. Many trainers require a deposit or first month up front when taking in a new horse, especially for colt starting. Pass-through expenses and show costs are often billed with the next monthly invoice, or collected as a deposit before a show. Late fees of 1.5% per month or a flat 5% are common if stated in the agreement. Accepted methods are typically check, ACH, card, or digital payment apps. Many trainers state that a horse may be held until the account is paid, but lien rules for animals vary by state, so check local rules.

tips.title: Bill training and board in advance
tips.body: Horses eat and need care every day whether or not the owner pays. Billing the month ahead keeps your cash flow steady and gives you leverage if payment lags.

tips.title: Write down your missed-ride policy
tips.body: Decide in the agreement whether rides lost to weather, a lame horse, or your own travel are credited, made up, or not refunded. Then apply it the same way to every client.

tips.title: Collect show money before you leave
tips.body: Entry fees, stalls, and hauling add up quickly. Ask for a deposit before the event, and invoice the balance right after so you are not carrying the costs.

tips.title: Keep receipts for every reimbursable item
tips.body: Photograph farrier, vet, and feed receipts and attach them to the invoice. It avoids pushback and also supports your own tax records.

tips.title: Charge for extra care
tips.body: Medicating, bandaging, blanketing, and special feeding take time. Set a per-task or monthly fee and list it so it is not given away.

faqs.question: Should I bill training and board as one line or two?
faqs.answer: Two lines is usually better. It lets clients see what they pay for riding versus care, and it makes it easy to prorate if a horse goes home mid-month or if board changes.

faqs.question: What do I do when a horse goes lame and cannot be ridden?
faqs.answer: Follow your written agreement. Many trainers keep charging board and a reduced training or care fee, and credit or reschedule rides once the horse is sound. Whatever you choose, state it before work starts.

faqs.question: Can I add a markup to vet and farrier bills I front for clients?
faqs.answer: You can if you disclosed it in your agreement, often as a small handling fee or percentage. Without prior agreement, bill at cost to avoid disputes.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on training?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Services are taxed in some states and not in others, and boarding or feed sales may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who is behind on payments?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder referencing the agreement and late fee terms. If it continues, follow your contract and your state's rules on notice and any lien on the animal before restricting access or releasing the horse.

estimate.intro: Horse trainers send quotes before taking on a new horse, starting a colt, or planning a show season. Owners usually compare monthly rates, what is included in board, and how many rides per week they get. A clear written quote helps you stand out from barns that look cheaper but leave out costs.

scopeChecklist.why: Specifies whether you are starting a colt, building a reining horse, or fixing a problem, so expectations match the work.

scopeChecklist.item: Rides per week and session length
scopeChecklist.why: Clients pay for riding time, and a stated number of rides prevents disagreement about what a month includes.
List stall type, turnout, hay, grain, bedding, and blanketing so owners know what costs extra.
Farrier, vet, dewormer, supplements, shows, and hauling should be named as extra costs, not surprises.
Training takes time, so a 30 or 60 day minimum and notice to end the contract protect your stall and schedule.
Current vaccinations, Coggins test, and dental or farrier up to date reduce risk to other horses in your barn.
Horses can be injured during training. A liability release and notes on mortality or medical decisions should be set before the horse arrives.

pricingTips.title: Price by the package for colt starting
pricingTips.body: A 30, 60, or 90-day package gives the owner a clear total and gives you a committed income, instead of open-ended monthly billing.

pricingTips.title: Account for slower horses
pricingTips.body: Some horses need more time than planned. State that extensions are billed at the monthly rate, so a difficult horse does not cost you unpaid weeks.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers
pricingTips.body: A training-only, partial-care, and full-care option lets owners choose based on budget and keeps your quote competitive without cutting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Stall space is limited. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days makes it clear that the opening is not held indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an evaluation ride?
faqs.answer: Many trainers do, often $50 to $100, and may credit it toward the first month if the owner signs on. It covers your time and screens out people who are only shopping.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit to hold a stall?
faqs.answer: A deposit of one month or a portion of the first month is common. It confirms commitment and covers the stall if the owner backs out.

faqs.question: Can I guarantee results from training?
faqs.answer: Avoid guarantees. Horses vary in temperament, ability, and soundness. Describe the work you will do and the typical progress, not a fixed outcome.

hospitality.intro: This page is for small hospitality operators who bill clients directly: boutique inns and B&Bs, private event venues, caterers and private dining rooms, and independent hospitality consultants or staffing providers. Invoices usually cover group room blocks, event and venue fees, food and beverage minimums, service staff, and add-ons such as rentals or AV.
hospitality.pricingModel: Hospitality pricing is mostly per unit of something the guest uses: per room night, per guest for food and beverage, per hour for staff, and flat fees for space rental. Events are often quoted as a package with a food and beverage minimum, and a service charge (commonly 18-22%) is added on top. Group bookings usually use a room block with a negotiated nightly rate and an attrition clause. Consultants and staffing providers bill hourly, per shift, or on a monthly retainer.
