Most event work requires a signed contract and a deposit, and the final invoice settles the balance after the guest count is confirmed.

rates.service: Group room block (boutique inn or B&B)
Plated dinner or buffet for private events

items.description: Private event space rental, Saturday 4pm-11pm (garden room and patio)
Plated three-course dinner, rehearsal dinner (guest count confirmed at 40)
Beer and wine bar package, 3 hours
Bartender, 5 hours including setup and breakdown
Guest room block, Friday and Saturday nights, standard queen rooms
Service charge on food and beverage (20%)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $2,000 received on signing is credited against this invoice. Balance due within 7 days of the event date. Taxes and lodging fees are applied per local rules and shown on the final statement. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. We accept ACH, check, and card; card payments carry a 3% fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and space used
invoiceChecklist.why: Overtime and double-booked space disputes are easier to settle when the invoice matches the contract times.

invoiceChecklist.item: Final guest count versus contracted guarantee
invoiceChecklist.why: Most contracts bill the guaranteed minimum or the actual count, whichever is higher. Showing both prevents arguments over plates and bar packages.

invoiceChecklist.item: Food and beverage minimum and how it was met
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client fell short, the shortfall is usually billed. Showing the math keeps it from looking like a surprise fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service charge versus gratuity, listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: A service charge is generally part of the house revenue and may be taxable in many states, while gratuities for staff are treated differently. Labeling each one correctly matters for tax and payroll.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax, lodging tax, and any local occupancy fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Tax rules for rooms, food, and space rental vary by state and city. Itemizing them makes the invoice auditable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Room names, check-in and check-out dates, and room block pickup
invoiceChecklist.why: For group stays, the invoice should match the rooming list and any attrition clause in the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits received and the dates they were paid
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see every payment credited so the balance due is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as rentals, florals, or outside vendors
invoiceChecklist.why: Third-party costs should be listed separately from your own fees, with any markup disclosed in your contract, so the client understands what they paid for.

hospitality.paymentTerms: Event and group bookings in hospitality usually require a non-refundable or partially refundable deposit at signing, often 25-50% of the estimated total, with a second payment 30 to 14 days before the event. The final balance is typically due on the event date or within 7 to 14 days after, once the final guest count and add-ons are settled. Corporate clients often ask for net 30 and a purchase order number. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Most operators accept ACH, check, and credit card, and many pass on card fees for large balances. Keep a card authorization on file for incidentals and damage charges, and state the cancellation schedule in writing.

tips.title: Bill from the contract, not from memory
tips.body: Build the final invoice from the signed banquet event order or contract, then add changes. Any extra hours, bar time, or guests added at the event should be noted on a signed change sheet that day.

tips.title: Keep service charge and tax logic consistent
tips.body: Decide how you treat the service charge, gratuity, and tax on each line, and apply it the same way every time. Ask your accountant or state revenue department how they treat service charges and lodging in your area.

tips.title: Invoice final counts quickly
tips.body: Send the final invoice within a day or two of the event while the client is still happy. Delays make clients more likely to question line items or dispute charges.

tips.title: Separate staff costs from venue costs
tips.body: Clients accept staff charges more readily when they see hours and headcount. It also helps you track labor against what you billed.

tips.title: Collect an incidentals authorization
tips.body: For group stays and events, get a card authorization for damages, extra bar tabs, and late room charges. Chasing these after the guests leave is slow and often unsuccessful.

faqs.question: Should I list a service charge or a gratuity on the invoice?
faqs.answer: List what it is. A service charge is a fixed percentage that the business sets and keeps, though you may choose to share it with staff. A gratuity is a tip that belongs to the staff. Rules on tax and payroll treatment differ by state, so label them correctly and check local rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the guaranteed guest count if fewer people show up?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says guests are billed at the guaranteed number or the actual count, whichever is higher. Put the guarantee deadline in the contract, and show the guaranteed and actual counts on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice when a client cancels an event?
faqs.answer: Follow the cancellation schedule in the contract. Invoice for the deposit retained or the percentage due at that stage, and note the cancellation date and the clause used. If you resell the date, many contracts credit part of the deposit.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on venue rental and food?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and city. Food and beverage is taxable in most places, and venue rental or room charges may carry sales or lodging tax. Check with your state revenue department or accountant, then itemize each tax on the invoice.

faqs.question: How should I invoice a corporate client that needs a PO number?
faqs.answer: Ask for the PO number before the event and put it at the top of the invoice, along with the billing contact and payment terms. Without it, many accounts payable departments will reject the invoice and delay payment.

estimate.intro: Hospitality businesses send a proposal or quote when a client is shopping for a venue, a group room block, a private dinner, or ongoing consulting. Clients usually compare per-person prices, room rates, minimums, and what is and is not included, so a clear quote that shows total cost wins more bookings than a low headline number.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, time window, and spaces included
scopeChecklist.why: Setup, breakdown, and rehearsal time are often assumed to be included. State exactly how many hours the price covers and what overtime costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count range and guarantee deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on headcount. Give the estimated count, the date the final number is due, and what happens if it changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Food and beverage menu, minimum spend, and substitutions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare menus line by line. Listing courses, bar hours, and dietary accommodations avoids mid-planning surprises.

scopeChecklist.item: Service charge, gratuity, and tax shown as separate lines
scopeChecklist.why: Per-person prices that leave out a 20% service charge and tax can look 25-30% cheaper than they are. Showing them upfront builds trust.

scopeChecklist.item: Staffing, rentals, and vendor items included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Bartenders, coordinators, linens, AV, and security are common add-ons that clients assume are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Room block terms, attrition, and release date
scopeChecklist.why: Group stays need clear pickup targets, cutoff dates, and what happens to unsold rooms.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and cancellation policy
scopeChecklist.why: Putting these in the quote means they are not new terms when the contract arrives.
Dates and rates can book up. An expiration date lets you re-price or release the date if the client delays.

pricingTips.title: Quote an all-in estimate
pricingTips.body: Show the subtotal, service charge, estimated tax, and total. Clients who see the real number upfront are less likely to push back on the final invoice.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A standard, mid-level, and premium package with different bar hours, menus, or staffing lets clients choose without asking you to discount line by line.

pricingTips.title: Price off your minimums
pricingTips.body: Set a food and beverage minimum or space fee for each day of the week and season. Saturday nights in peak season should cost more than a weekday in winter.

pricingTips.title: Build in a labor and waste buffer
pricingTips.body: Staff hours for setup, breakdown, and last-minute changes usually run over. Price in a margin so a small guest count change does not erase your profit.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Most hospitality quotes are valid for 7 to 30 days, depending on how soon the date is. Peak dates may only be held for a few days. State the expiration and that the date is not reserved until the deposit and contract are received.

faqs.question: Should I include the service charge in my per-person price?
faqs.answer: It is clearer to list it separately. If you quote an all-inclusive per-person rate, say that it includes the service charge and what tax is still to be added, so clients can compare properly.

faqs.question: What if the final guest count is lower than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Set a guarantee date in the quote, often 7 to 14 days before the event, and bill at the guaranteed count or the actual count, whichever is higher. Explain this up front, since minimums are one of the most common disputes.

faqs.question: Can a quote change after the client accepts it?
faqs.answer: Once the client signs and pays the deposit, the price should hold for the scope listed. Changes to guest count, menu, hours, or add-ons should be priced in writing as a change order, and any sales tax or fee changes imposed by the government can be passed through if your contract says so.

house-cleaning.intro: House cleaners are solo operators and small crews who clean private homes on a recurring or one-time basis. Invoices usually cover routine cleanings, deep cleans, move-in or move-out cleans, and add-ons such as inside the oven, refrigerator, or windows.
house-cleaning.pricingModel: House cleaners price in three main ways: hourly per cleaner, flat rate per visit based on home size and condition, or per square foot for deep and move-out cleans. Recurring clients (weekly, biweekly, monthly) often get a lower per-visit price than first-time clients, and the first visit is usually priced higher because the home needs a reset. Many cleaners set a minimum visit charge to cover travel and supplies. Add-ons are billed as separate line items, either at a flat price or by time. Some cleaners include supplies in the price, while others add a small supply fee or charge extra if the client wants specialty products. Pricing shifts with home size, number of bathrooms, pets, and how long since the last clean.

items.description: Deep clean, 3 bed / 2 bath home (approx. 1,800 sq ft), 2 cleaners
Inside oven
Inside refrigerator
Interior windows
Supplies fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Service date: March 14. Payment due within 7 days of the invoice date. Accepted: card, bank transfer, or check. Recurring biweekly service begins March 28 at the standard rate of $150 per visit. Please notify us 48 hours ahead to reschedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date and address cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several properties or rentals need to match each charge to a visit, and it settles disputes about which day you came.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of clean (standard, deep, move-out)
invoiceChecklist.why: The scope drives the price, so naming it shows why the amount differs from a regular visit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of cleaners and hours worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly and team billing is easier to accept when the person-hours are visible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Oven, fridge, windows, and laundry are easy to forget and easy to question if bundled into one total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies or equipment fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the charge is intentional and separate from labor, especially if you bring a vacuum or specialty products.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring schedule and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: A reminder of the agreed frequency and per-visit price prevents confusion about changes or skipped visits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or lockout fee, if applied
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charged for a late cancel or a visit where you could not get in, naming the fee and date ties it to your policy.

house-cleaning.paymentTerms: Many house cleaners collect payment on the day of service or within a few days, since the work is repeated and cash flow is tight. Recurring clients are often billed after each visit, or monthly for weekly service, with card-on-file autopay as a common option. Deep cleans and move-out cleans for new clients often require a deposit of 20-50% when booking, with the balance due at completion. Late fees of a flat amount or 1.5% per month are common but should be written in your service agreement before you apply them. Cards, bank transfer, and checks are the usual methods; cash is still seen, so keep a record of it either way. Many cleaners also charge a fee for cancellations under 24 to 48 hours.

tips.title: Charge more for the first visit
tips.body: A home that has not been professionally cleaned takes much longer. Price the first visit as an initial or deep clean, then drop to the recurring rate once the home is at baseline.

tips.title: Put your cancellation and lockout policy in writing
tips.body: Cleaners lose real income when a client cancels at the door or no one is home. State the notice window and fee in your agreement and reference it on the invoice when applied.

tips.title: Review rates once a year
tips.body: Supply costs, fuel, and labor rise. Give recurring clients 30 days of notice before a rate change, and note the new rate on the next invoice.

tips.title: Itemize extras instead of absorbing them
tips.body: Inside the oven, pet hair, heavy buildup, and extra rooms add time. If you do them without charging, clients come to expect them as part of the base price.

tips.title: Keep records of cash and tips
tips.body: Income paid in cash or tips is generally still taxable. Log each payment so your bookkeeping matches what you earned.

faqs.question: Should I bill by the hour or a flat rate per visit?
faqs.answer: Flat rates are easier for recurring clients and reward you for being efficient. Hourly billing is safer for deep cleans, cluttered homes, or first visits where you cannot predict the time. Many cleaners quote a flat rate after seeing the home and bill hourly for extras beyond the agreed scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge for supplies separately?
faqs.answer: Yes. Some cleaners build supplies into the rate, while others add a flat fee per visit or bill for specialty products. Whichever you choose, list it as its own line or state in your agreement that supplies are included.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a recurring client?
faqs.answer: Many cleaners send an invoice after each visit or one monthly invoice listing every date of service. Monthly invoices work well for weekly clients. Include each visit date and any add-ons so the total is easy to verify.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on house cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning services and many do not. Check with your state revenue department, and if tax applies, show it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee when a client cancels late?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you told the client about the fee beforehand. Put the notice window and amount in your service agreement or booking confirmation, then list the fee on the invoice with the date of the missed visit.

estimate.intro: House cleaners send estimates for first-time clients, deep cleans, move-in or move-out cleans, and recurring service proposals. Clients often compare several quotes, so they are looking at price, what is included, whether you bring supplies, and whether you are insured. Many estimates are based on a walkthrough or on photos and answers about home size, bathrooms, pets, and condition.

scopeChecklist.why: These are the main price drivers, and a quote based on the wrong size leads to a dispute on the day.
Spell out what a standard clean covers, such as dusting, vacuuming, mopping, kitchen, and bathrooms, so the client knows what to expect.
Items like interior windows, inside appliances, wall washing, and laundry are often extra. Listing them avoids surprise requests.
Heavy buildup, hoarding, or long gaps between cleanings can raise the price. State that the quote assumes normal condition.
Pet hair takes time, and natural stone, hardwood, and delicate finishes may need specific products.
Clients may expect you to bring everything, or they may ask you to use their products. Make clear which applies.

scopeChecklist.item: Frequency, start date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: The recurring rate depends on the schedule, and the quote should state the notice needed to skip or cancel.

pricingTips.title: Quote the first visit separately from recurring visits
pricingTips.body: Give one price for the initial clean and a lower per-visit price for the ongoing schedule. This explains why the first visit costs more and makes the recurring rate look like the benefit of staying on.

pricingTips.title: Do a walkthrough or request photos for larger jobs
pricingTips.body: Square footage alone misses clutter, heavy buildup, and layout. A short visit or photos of the kitchen and bathrooms gives you a much better time estimate.

pricingTips.title: Build in travel and supply costs
pricingTips.body: Fuel, supplies, and equipment wear are real costs. Set a minimum visit price so a small apartment does not come in below what it costs you to show up.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and deep clean option lets the client choose their budget while you control the scope of each.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or a price range?
faqs.answer: For standard cleanings of a home you have seen, a flat quote works. For deep cleans or homes in unknown condition, a range with a stated cap is safer, and you can confirm the final price after you see the work.

faqs.question: Do I charge for an in-person estimate?
faqs.answer: Most house cleaners do not charge for a walkthrough for regular cleaning. Some charge for large post-construction or hoarding jobs and credit the fee to the final bill if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Prices for labor and supplies change, and the home may change as well, so put an expiration date on the estimate.

faqs.question: What if the home is dirtier than expected on the day?
faqs.answer: Include a line in your estimate that the price assumes normal condition and that extra time will be billed or the scope adjusted. If you find the problem, talk to the client before continuing and note any agreed change in writing.

hr-consultant.intro: HR consultants are independent practitioners and small firms who help small and mid-sized businesses with work they don't have a full-time HR department for. Typical invoices cover employee handbook writing, compliance audits, hiring support, investigations, manager coaching, and ongoing advisory time.
hr-consultant.pricingModel: HR consultants most often bill hourly for advisory work, investigations, and ad hoc questions, and use flat project fees for defined deliverables like a handbook, a compensation study, or an I-9 audit. Many also sell monthly retainers that include a set number of hours, which gives the client predictable cost and gives you steady income. Recruiting support is sometimes priced as a percentage of first-year salary or a flat fee per hire. Training and workshops are usually priced per session or per attendee. Out-of-pocket costs such as background check fees, job board postings, survey software, and travel are typically passed through at cost or with a small markup that is stated up front. Rates depend heavily on certifications (PHR, SPHR, SHRM-CP, SHRM-SCP), legal background, and whether you work in a high-cost metro.

items.description: Employee handbook development (state-specific policies, 42 pages), per proposal dated March 3
HR advisory: termination review and documentation guidance
Supervisor training: documentation and performance conversations (90 min, 12 attendees)
Job descriptions for 5 positions
Background check fees (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Handbook is delivered for client and legal counsel review; this invoice does not constitute legal advice. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Accepted by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project or retainer reference and scope
invoiceChecklist.why: HR work often overlaps with legal questions; tying each line to a signed proposal or agreement keeps the scope clear and avoids disputes about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service and hours per task
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reviewing advisory or investigation time want to see what was done and when, especially if the bill goes to an owner or board that wasn't involved day to day.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer hours used and remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows whether the client is under or over their included hours and sets up a conversation about overages or upgrading the plan.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Background checks, job postings, survey tools, and travel should be itemized at cost or at your stated markup so clients can trace them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Confidentiality-safe descriptions
invoiceChecklist.why: Invoices get forwarded to accountants and bookkeepers. Describe an investigation as 'workplace investigation, matter 2024-03' rather than naming employees or details.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or percentage complete for project work
invoiceChecklist.why: Large deliverables like handbooks and compensation studies are often billed in stages, so each invoice should show which milestone it covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disclaimer that services are not legal advice
invoiceChecklist.why: If you are not an attorney, a short statement clarifies the limits of your role and encourages clients to consult counsel on legal questions.

hr-consultant.paymentTerms: Many HR consultants take a deposit of 25-50% on fixed-fee projects before starting and bill the balance on delivery or at milestones. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of each month and are due on receipt or within 7 to 15 days. Hourly work is commonly billed monthly in arrears with net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the agreement. ACH and card payments are typical, and check is still used by some small employers. For investigations, some consultants require an upfront retainer that is drawn down as hours are billed.

tips.title: Use a retainer for ongoing clients
tips.body: Small businesses ask quick questions all month. A retainer with a set number of hours covers those calls and emails, and a defined overage rate prevents free work from creeping in.

tips.title: Put scope limits in writing
tips.body: State what the project includes, how many revision rounds are covered, and what happens if the client wants additional policies or states added. Handbooks in particular grow when the client has employees in more than one state.

tips.title: Bill investigations with an upfront deposit
tips.body: Investigations can run long and clients may be stressed or in dispute with an employee. Collecting a retainer first and invoicing against it keeps payment from becoming a problem partway through.

tips.title: Track time in small increments
tips.body: Short calls and email reviews add up. Billing in 15-minute increments with a minimum, such as 30 minutes for any call, protects your time without feeling excessive.

tips.title: Review rates yearly
tips.body: Employment rules change, and your experience grows. Raise rates for new clients first, then give existing clients notice of 30 to 60 days before applying an increase.

faqs.question: Should an HR consultant charge hourly or flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended work like advisory calls and investigations, and a flat fee for defined deliverables like a handbook or audit. If you use a flat fee, specify what is included and set an hourly rate for anything beyond scope.

faqs.question: Can I mark up background checks and other pass-through costs?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many consultants pass costs through at cost and list them as a separate line. If you add a markup, disclose it in the proposal so there are no surprises on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for confidential work like an investigation?
faqs.answer: Use a matter number and a general description rather than employee names or allegations. Detailed notes should stay in your own files, not on an invoice that others at the client company may see.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on HR consulting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional services, but a few tax some consulting or digital deliverables. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client stops paying mid-project?
faqs.answer: Pause work as your agreement allows, send a written reminder with the overdue invoice, and offer a short payment plan if appropriate. Having a deposit and milestone billing reduces how much you are exposed at any point.

estimate.intro: HR consultants send estimates when a new client asks for a defined project such as a handbook, an audit, a compensation review, or a training day, and for retainer proposals. Clients often compare several consultants, so they look at deliverables, timeline, and whether the price is fixed or open-ended.

scopeChecklist.why: List each document, policy, training session, or report by name and approximate length so the client knows exactly what they receive.
Headcount and states of operation affect how many policies are needed and which laws apply, and changes to either can change your price.
State how many rounds of edits are included and who gives final approval, so a handbook doesn't go through endless rewrites.
Delays often come from the client not sending existing policies, payroll data, or feedback. Set deadlines for their inputs and note that your schedule moves if they are late.
Clarify that you do not provide legal advice, that attorney review is separate, and that implementation or ongoing updates are not included unless listed.
Name which costs are billed in addition, such as travel, background checks, and survey tools, and whether they are at cost.
State the deposit, milestone amounts, and how long the quote is good for, since client needs and compliance rules can shift.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours, then convert to a fixed fee
pricingTips.body: Work out research, drafting, review calls, and revisions in hours, add a buffer of 15-25%, and multiply by your rate. Present the total as a flat fee so clients can budget.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and comprehensive option, such as handbook only, handbook plus manager training, or handbook plus a full compliance audit, helps clients choose and often leads to the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Quote investigations as an hourly estimate with a cap or deposit
pricingTips.body: The scope of an investigation is hard to predict. Give an estimated hour range, require a retainer, and agree to check in with the client before exceeding the range.

pricingTips.title: Show the retainer value
pricingTips.body: When proposing a retainer, compare it to what the same hours would cost at your hourly rate and list what is included, such as response times and a monthly check-in call.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial consultation or estimate?
faqs.answer: Many HR consultants offer a free 20 to 30 minute call to understand the need. For larger audits or compensation studies that require reviewing documents beforehand, a paid discovery session that is credited toward the project is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should an HR estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is common. Employment laws and client headcount change, so an expiration date lets you reprice if the situation is different when they accept.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to add policies after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a change order. Give a short written add-on with the extra fee and timeline, and get approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed price for an investigation?
faqs.answer: It is possible for narrow, well-defined matters, but most consultants use an hourly estimate because the number of witnesses and documents is unknown at the start. Explain the range and agree on an update point.

hr-services.intro: HR services providers are independent consultants and small firms that handle people-related work for businesses that don't have a full in-house HR department. They bill for things like employee handbook writing, compliance reviews, recruiting support, investigations, and ongoing HR advisory. Clients are usually small and mid-sized employers with 5 to 250 employees.
hr-services.pricingModel: Most HR consultants mix three models. Hourly billing is common for advisory calls, employee relations issues, and work where scope is unclear. Flat project fees are standard for defined deliverables such as a handbook, job descriptions, an HR audit, or a policy rollout. Monthly retainers, often with a set number of included hours, cover ongoing outsourced HR support, and extra hours are billed at a stated overage rate. Recruiting work is usually priced either as a percentage of first-year salary (commonly 15 to 25 percent) or as a flat fee per hire. Out-of-pocket costs such as background check fees, job board postings, and software subscriptions are typically passed through at cost or with a small handling fee. Investigations and expert-witness-style work usually carry a higher hourly rate and are billed against an advance deposit.

items.description: Monthly HR advisory retainer, March (includes up to 10 hours)
Additional advisory hours beyond retainer (termination review and PIP coaching for two managers)
Employee handbook update: PTO, remote work, and anti-harassment policies
Job descriptions: Operations Supervisor, Customer Service Rep
Background check fees (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Retainer hours do not roll over. Additional hours are billed at $150 per hour. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Services are advisory and do not constitute legal advice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and engagement reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainer clients need to see which month the charge covers and which agreement it falls under.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours used versus hours included in retainer
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what they got and justifies any overage charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of each deliverable or matter by name
invoiceChecklist.why: Handbook sections, audits, and training sessions should be listed so the client can match them to the proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client matter or employee-case code instead of names
invoiceChecklist.why: Invoices get forwarded to accountants and owners; keep sensitive employee names and details off the document.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Background checks, job posting fees, and software costs should be itemized so they are not confused with your fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recruiting placement details
invoiceChecklist.why: For placements, include the candidate start date, accepted salary, and fee percentage so the calculation can be verified, and note any guarantee period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope disclaimer and confidentiality note
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies that you provide HR guidance and not legal advice, and reminds the client that the work is confidential.

hr-services.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month, due on receipt or within 15 days. Project work commonly splits into a 30 to 50 percent deposit at signing with the balance on delivery, or into milestone payments for longer projects like a full audit. Investigations are often funded with an advance deposit that is drawn down against hourly billing. Recruiting fees are typically due within 15 to 30 days of the candidate's start date. Many consultants charge a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month if terms say so in the agreement. ACH and credit card are the most common payment methods, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client.

tips.title: Define what a retainer includes
tips.body: State the included hours, what counts as billable time (calls, emails, document review), the response time, and the overage rate. Vague retainers are the main source of billing disputes in HR consulting.

tips.title: Track time in small increments
tips.body: Short questions from owners and managers add up. Logging in 6 or 15 minute increments keeps retainer usage accurate and supports overage charges.

tips.title: Keep employee details out of the invoice
tips.body: Use a matter name or code for terminations, complaints, and investigations. This protects privacy if the invoice reaches people who should not see the details.

tips.title: Tie placement fees to the guarantee period
tips.body: If you offer a replacement or partial refund when a hire leaves in the first 60 to 90 days, put that in writing and reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Review rates when scope grows
tips.body: A client that grew from 15 to 60 employees needs different support than at signing. Revisit the retainer annually rather than absorbing extra work.

faqs.question: Should I bill HR consulting hourly or by flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended advice and employee issues where you cannot predict the scope. Use flat fees for defined deliverables like a handbook or audit. Many consultants combine both through a retainer with an overage rate.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for confidential work like investigations?
faqs.answer: Use a case code or general description such as 'Workplace investigation, Matter 2024-03' instead of names. Break down time by task (interviews, document review, report writing) without revealing sensitive details, and keep detailed notes in your own files.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on HR services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional or consulting services, but some tax certain business services or software. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: When is a recruiting fee earned?
faqs.answer: Usually when the candidate accepts the offer or starts work, depending on your agreement. Put the trigger and the due date in your contract, and invoice on that event.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time and mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many consultants bill travel time at a reduced rate or a flat trip fee and add mileage at the IRS standard rate or a stated per-mile rate.

estimate.intro: HR consultants send proposals or quotes before starting project work such as a handbook, an HR audit, a recruiting search, or an ongoing retainer. Clients usually compare total price, the number of deliverables, turnaround time, and whether state-specific compliance is included. A clear scope is the main difference between quotes that win and quotes that lead to disputes.

scopeChecklist.why: List exactly what the client receives, such as a handbook of about 40 pages in editable format, so they know what is and is not included.
Employment law varies by state and many rules depend on employee count, so pricing should be based on named locations and the current number of employees.
Limit revisions, for example two rounds of edits, and state the rate for additional rounds.
Delays often come from the client not supplying existing policies, org charts, or approvals. Set deadlines for these.

scopeChecklist.item: Included hours and overage rate for retainers
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents unlimited access expectations and gives a clear rate for extra work.
State that you are not an attorney and that employment counsel review of policies is separate and not included unless specified.
Identify who pays for job postings, background checks, assessments, and travel, and how they are billed.

pricingTips.title: Price audits and handbooks by size and complexity
pricingTips.body: A 12-person single-state company and a 120-person multi-state company need very different work. Use headcount and number of states as pricing tiers.

pricingTips.title: Offer a phased option
pricingTips.body: Start with a paid audit, then quote remediation separately. This lowers the client's risk and gives you real information before pricing larger work.

pricingTips.title: Show retainer tiers
pricingTips.body: Present two or three levels, such as 5, 10, and 20 hours per month, with the effective hourly rate falling at higher tiers. Clients tend to pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Thirty days is common. Headcount, laws, and your availability change, and an expiry date lets you reprice.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals?
faqs.answer: Usually not for standard proposals. For a custom audit or a detailed scoping session that takes several hours, many consultants charge a discovery fee and credit it toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How do I quote an investigation when I don't know how long it will take?
faqs.answer: Quote an hourly rate with an estimated range and a deposit, and agree to check in with the client if hours are likely to exceed the range. A flat fee is rarely safe because the number of witnesses and documents is unknown.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price for a smaller scope?
faqs.answer: Remove deliverables instead of cutting your rate. For example, offer a handbook with core policies only, or reduce included retainer hours, and write the change into the scope.

hubspot-consultant.intro: HubSpot consultants help companies set up, migrate to, customize, and get more out of HubSpot's CRM and its Marketing, Sales, Service, Operations, and CMS hubs. Most work solo or in small agencies and bill for portal audits, implementations, data migrations, workflow and automation builds, reporting, training, and ongoing admin support. Invoices usually tie to a defined project, a block of hours, or a monthly retainer.
hubspot-consultant.pricingModel: Most HubSpot consultants mix three models. Hourly billing is common for support, troubleshooting, and work with unclear scope. Fixed-fee projects are standard for implementations, migrations, and audits, often split into milestones such as discovery, build, and training. Monthly retainers cover ongoing admin, reporting, list and workflow maintenance, and a set number of hours, with unused hours either expiring or rolling over for a short time. Training is often billed per session or as a half-day or full-day workshop. Pass-through costs such as the client's HubSpot subscription, onboarding fees paid to HubSpot, third-party connectors, or contractor help should be listed separately from your labor. Clients usually buy their own HubSpot licenses directly, so most consultants do not resell software.

rates.service: Sales Hub or Marketing Hub implementation (small business)
Data migration from another CRM (contacts, companies, deals)
Team training session (live, remote or on-site)

items.description: Sales Hub implementation: pipeline and deal stage setup, properties, user permissions (milestone 2 of 3)
CRM data migration: 8,200 contacts and 1,100 companies from legacy CRM, field mapping and deduplication
Lead routing and follow-up task workflows
Sales team training session (2 hours, recorded)
Additional configuration work outside original scope (email integration troubleshooting)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Milestone 2 of 3 per the signed statement of work dated March 4. HubSpot subscription fees are billed to the client directly by HubSpot and are not included here. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the statement of work and milestone
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to an agreed scope and deliverable so the client can match it to the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hub and portal name or ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients have multiple portals or sandboxes, and this shows exactly where the work was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed with counts
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing workflows built, records migrated, and properties created proves what was delivered and avoids disputes over scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for time-and-materials work, with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Support and troubleshooting are easy to question without a dated breakdown of what was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope work labeled separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows change requests as distinct from the fixed fee, so extra charges are not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs and pass-throughs
invoiceChecklist.why: Connector subscriptions, contractor fees, or paid onboarding services should be itemized apart from your labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and hours used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies what the monthly fee covers and whether any hours expired or rolled over.

hubspot-consultant.paymentTerms: Fixed-fee projects commonly require a 30-50% deposit at kickoff, with the rest tied to milestones such as end of build and go-live. Retainers are usually billed in advance on the first of the month. Net 15 is typical for project invoices, and net 30 is common when working with larger companies that have an accounts payable process. Many consultants add a late fee of 1-1.5% per month, stated in the contract before work starts. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check, and some consultants pause admin access or new work on accounts that are more than 30 days past due.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not just dates
tips.body: Billing at discovery, build, and go-live keeps cash flowing on long implementations and gives the client clear checkpoints. It also protects you if the client delays feedback and the project drags on.

tips.title: Write change-request language into every SOW
tips.body: HubSpot projects grow easily: another pipeline, another integration, one more import. Define what is included and bill additions at your hourly rate with written approval.

tips.title: Be clear about who owns the HubSpot subscription
tips.body: Have clients buy and hold their own licenses. Keep your invoice limited to your services and any pass-through costs you actually paid, so you are not on the hook for software renewals.

tips.title: Set retainer rules for unused hours
tips.body: State whether unused hours expire at month end or roll over for a set period. Without that, clients may expect banked hours indefinitely.

tips.title: Get admin access in writing
tips.body: Document your access level and when it ends. Billing for work in a portal is easier to defend when the client has acknowledged what you were authorized to change.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a HubSpot implementation?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work well when the scope is clear, such as a defined number of pipelines, properties, and workflows. Use hourly for audits that lead to unknown work, troubleshooting, and projects where the client keeps changing requirements. Many consultants quote a flat fee with hourly rates for anything outside the scope.

faqs.question: Can I resell HubSpot licenses on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you are an authorized partner with a reseller arrangement and your agreement with HubSpot allows it. Most solo consultants have clients buy directly from HubSpot, which keeps the license in the client's name and keeps your invoice to labor only.

faqs.question: How do I bill for time spent in meetings and discovery?
faqs.answer: Include discovery in a fixed fee as its own line, or bill it hourly if the scope is not yet defined. For ongoing projects, state in your SOW how many status meetings are included, and bill extra calls at your hourly rate.

faqs.question: What if a client stops responding mid-project?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that work pauses if feedback or access is delayed beyond a set period, such as 14 days, and that remaining milestones may still be invoiced on schedule or the project re-quoted to resume. Bill completed milestones promptly rather than waiting for the project to finish.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax software-related services or digital services, while many do not tax professional consulting. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax you collect as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: HubSpot consultants send estimates after a discovery call or portal review, before signing an SOW. Clients often compare several consultants or agencies, and they focus on total price, timeline, the hubs involved, and how much of the work they will need to do themselves.

scopeChecklist.why: Features differ between Starter, Professional, and Enterprise, so the work you can quote depends on the client's plan.

scopeChecklist.item: Record counts and data sources for migration
scopeChecklist.why: Cost depends on the number of contacts, companies, deals, and custom objects, and on how clean the source data is.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of pipelines, workflows, forms, and templates
scopeChecklist.why: Counting the deliverables gives a clear boundary for what the fixed fee covers.
Native connectors, third-party tools, and custom API work vary widely in effort, so name each one you are covering.
Delays in data exports, approvals, and portal access are a top cause of overruns, so state what you need and by when.
Clarify the number of sessions, recordings, and written guides so clients know what to expect at handoff.

scopeChecklist.item: Revision rounds and post-launch support window
scopeChecklist.why: Setting a defined number of revisions and a support period, such as 30 days, limits unpaid follow-up work.

pricingTips.title: Quote a paid discovery or audit first for unclear scopes
pricingTips.body: If the client cannot describe their processes or data, sell a short paid audit and quote the build afterward. It prevents you from underpricing a project you do not yet understand.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a core setup, a standard package with automation and reporting, and a full package with training and a support window. Clients can compare options and many choose the middle one.

pricingTips.title: Price migration by data complexity
pricingTips.body: Include the number of objects, custom fields, and associations, and add a contingency for messy data or missing exports. State that unusually dirty data may change the price.

pricingTips.title: Show a milestone schedule
pricingTips.body: List deposit, build, and go-live payments with expected dates. It makes a large number easier to approve and sets the payment rhythm from the start.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or a range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed price once scope is defined. If there are unknowns like data quality or integrations you have not seen, give a range or quote discovery separately, and say what would move the price within the range.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Pricing and your availability change, and clients' HubSpot plans or requirements may change too, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I charge for writing the estimate?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call is usually free. A detailed review of a client's portal or a written proposal with recommendations is often billed as an audit, and many consultants credit that fee against the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: What happens if the client adds work after accepting the estimate?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a change request. Describe the added work, give the hours or fixed price, and get written approval before starting. Then bill it as a separate line on the next invoice.

hvac.intro: HVAC technicians and small HVAC contractors install, repair, and maintain heating, cooling, and ventilation systems for homes and light commercial buildings. Invoices typically cover service calls, diagnostic time, repair labor, parts and refrigerant, maintenance plan visits, and full system installations.
hvac.pricingModel: Residential service work is usually priced either by flat-rate book (a fixed price per task, regardless of how long it takes) or by time and materials (hourly labor plus parts with a markup). Most shops charge a trip or diagnostic fee up front, which is often credited toward the repair if the customer approves it. Parts are marked up, commonly 30 to 100 percent depending on the part, to cover sourcing, warranty, and return trips. Refrigerant is billed by the pound and priced separately because costs vary widely by type, and R-410A and newer refrigerants cost more than older ones. Installations are quoted as a flat price per system, often in good, better, and best tiers, with equipment, labor, permits, and materials bundled or itemized. Maintenance agreements are sold as annual or semiannual plans with a fixed fee. After-hours and emergency calls usually carry a premium of 1.5 to 2 times the normal rate.

items.description: Diagnostic service call, no cooling (credited toward repair)
Labor: replace dual run capacitor and condenser fan motor
Part: 45/5 MFD dual run capacitor
Part: 1/4 HP condenser fan motor
Refrigerant R-410A top-off after leak check
Less: diagnostic fee credit

sampleInvoice.notes: Work performed at 412 Maple St on 6/14. Parts carry a 1-year warranty and labor a 90-day warranty. Payment due upon completion; we accept check, card, and ACH. Balances unpaid after 30 days are subject to a 1.5% monthly late fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and EPA 608 certification
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require the license number on invoices and contracts, and it shows the customer the work was done by a qualified, certified person.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment make, model, serial number, and install date
invoiceChecklist.why: Warranty claims depend on these details, and they give you a record if you service the same unit again.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with part numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers and insurers question lump-sum parts charges, and part numbers back up warranty claims with manufacturers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Refrigerant type and pounds added
invoiceChecklist.why: Federal rules require record keeping for refrigerant use, and customers need to know if a system is leaking when it keeps needing a recharge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date, arrival and departure times, and tech name
invoiceChecklist.why: This supports time-based labor charges and resolves disputes about when work was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit and inspection numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Installations and major replacements often require a permit. Listing it shows the job was legally completed and passed inspection.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the coverage period on the invoice avoids arguments if a part fails later.

hvac.paymentTerms: Repair and service calls are most often due at completion, and many shops collect by card on site before leaving. For installations, a common structure is a deposit of 30 to 50 percent at signing to order equipment, with the balance due on completion or after final inspection. Larger jobs sometimes use three payments: deposit, equipment delivery, and completion. Commercial clients and property managers typically pay on net 15 or net 30 terms. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common where state law permits it, and it should be stated in writing before the work. Accepted methods usually include credit card, check, and ACH, and many homeowners also use financing offered through the contractor for system replacements.

tips.title: Collect payment before you leave on repairs
tips.body: Homeowners are easiest to collect from while you are standing in the house with the system running again. Send the invoice and take payment on the spot instead of billing later, which adds weeks and sometimes goes unpaid.

tips.title: Credit the diagnostic fee clearly
tips.body: If you apply the trip charge toward a repair, show it as a separate line and a credit. Customers see the value, and the original fee stays on record if they decline the work.

tips.title: Get approval in writing before extra work
tips.body: When you find a bad blower motor behind a bad capacitor, stop and get approval for the added cost. A signed or texted approval makes the final invoice easy to defend.

tips.title: Bill refrigerant by the pound as its own line
tips.body: Refrigerant costs fluctuate, and bundling it into labor hides what the customer paid for. A separate line with type and weight keeps pricing honest and your records compliant.

tips.title: Invoice equipment orders as deposits
tips.body: Special-order equipment is hard to return. Collect a deposit that covers at least your cost of the equipment before ordering, and state that it is nonrefundable once the unit is ordered.

faqs.question: Should I charge flat rate or hourly?
faqs.answer: Both work. Flat-rate pricing gives customers a firm price before work starts and rewards efficient technicians. Hourly time and materials is simpler for small shops and for unpredictable diagnostic work. Many small businesses use flat rate for common repairs and tune-ups and hourly for troubleshooting and custom jobs.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on HVAC work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax parts and materials but not labor, some tax both, and some treat installation as a capital improvement with different rules. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant before setting up your invoices.

faqs.question: Can I put a lien on a property if a customer doesn't pay?
faqs.answer: In many states, licensed contractors can file a mechanic's lien for unpaid work, but deadlines and notice requirements are strict and vary by state. Keep your signed contract and invoices, and check your state's rules early, since filing windows can be short.

faqs.question: How do I handle warranty work on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Create an invoice that lists the work performed, the part and serial numbers, and the warranty claim number, and mark the customer balance as zero if the manufacturer covers it. Keep a copy so you can bill the manufacturer for any labor allowance they offer.

faqs.question: What should I charge for maintenance agreements?
faqs.answer: Plans commonly run $150 to $400 per year for one system with two visits, often including priority scheduling and a discount on repairs. Bill them annually in advance or monthly, and list the visits included on the invoice.

estimate.intro: HVAC contractors send estimates before replacing a system, installing new equipment, running ductwork, or making a repair that costs more than a typical service call. Homeowners often collect two or three quotes and compare equipment brand, efficiency rating, warranty, and total price, so a clear written quote matters.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment brand, model numbers, tonnage, and SEER2 or AFUE rating
scopeChecklist.why: Two quotes with different efficiency ratings or sizes are not comparable, and listing the exact equipment prevents a customer claiming they were promised something different.
Showing that the system was sized by a Manual J calculation rather than guesswork backs up your price and prevents callbacks over comfort problems.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: pad, line set, disconnect, thermostat, drain, and duct modifications
scopeChecklist.why: Customers assume everything needed is included. Listing each item shows where your price ends and what would be a change order.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, inspections, and who pulls them
scopeChecklist.why: Permit costs and timing are often missed, and unpermitted work can cause trouble for the homeowner when selling.

scopeChecklist.item: Haul-away and disposal of the old equipment and refrigerant recovery
scopeChecklist.why: Disposal is real labor and cost. Stating it avoids surprises and shows you will follow refrigerant handling rules.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions and conditions that could change the price
scopeChecklist.why: Hidden problems such as rotted platforms, undersized electrical circuits, asbestos-wrapped ducts, or poor access can raise the cost. Naming them up front makes later change orders easier to accept.

scopeChecklist.item: Warranty terms, estimate expiration date, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Equipment prices change and manufacturer rebates end. An expiration date, usually 15 to 30 days, protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, and best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting three tiers, such as a single-stage, two-stage, and variable-speed system, lets the customer choose based on budget instead of just comparing you to the cheapest bidder. Show the price difference and what each tier adds in comfort and efficiency.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from cost, not from competitors
pricingTips.body: Add equipment cost, materials, labor hours at a loaded rate, permit fees, overhead, and a target margin. Many shops aim for gross margins of 35 to 50 percent on installs. Adjust after checking the local market, but do not start with the lowest bid.

pricingTips.title: Account for current equipment pricing
pricingTips.body: Equipment and refrigerant costs can change between quote and install. Include a price validity period and note that the price may be adjusted if the order is delayed by the customer.

pricingTips.title: Show available rebates and financing separately
pricingTips.body: Utility rebates, manufacturer incentives, and tax credits can lower the net cost, but eligibility varies. List them as possible savings apart from your price so you are not promising what you do not control.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors provide free estimates for replacements and installs, since the sale covers the cost of the visit. Charging a fee is common for repair diagnostics and for detailed work such as duct design or load calculations, and it can be credited if the customer hires you.

faqs.question: How long should an HVAC estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Equipment costs, rebate programs, and your schedule can all change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What happens if I find more problems after starting the job?
faqs.answer: Stop and write a change order with the added work, cost, and any schedule impact, and get the customer to approve it before continuing. Without that approval, it is hard to bill for the extra work.

faqs.question: Can I turn an estimate into an invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. Once the customer accepts, use the quote as the basis for your deposit invoice and final invoice, adjusting for any approved change orders. Keeping the same line items makes the final bill easy to reconcile with the original quote.

illustration.intro: Illustrators create original artwork for books, editorial pieces, packaging, advertising, apparel, games, and web or app interfaces. Most work as freelancers or run small studios, and they invoice art directors, publishers, agencies, and small businesses. Invoices usually cover concept sketches, final art, revisions, and the usage rights granted to the client.
illustration.pricingModel: Illustration is priced by project, not by the hour, because the value depends on how the art will be used. A flat fee per piece is common, with the price set by complexity, number of finished pieces, size or detail, and usage rights (where, how long, and whether exclusive). Children's book work is often priced per spread or per page, or as an advance against royalties. Editorial work usually follows a set fee per spot or full-page piece. Many illustrators charge 50% upfront, then the balance on delivery. Hourly rates, typically $50-125, are used for revisions beyond the agreed rounds, client-requested changes, and open-ended work such as storyboards or concept exploration. Rush fees of 25-50% and buyout fees for full copyright transfer or exclusive rights are added on top of the base fee.

items.description: Final illustrations for children's book 'The Night Garden' (full-color spreads, digital, 300 dpi files)
Front cover illustration
Character sheet and style exploration (approved sketches)
Additional revisions beyond two included rounds (spreads 4 and 9)
Less: 50% deposit received 03/04

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 14 days of invoice date. License: non-exclusive print and ebook rights in North America for the first edition, per signed agreement dated 02/20. Copyright remains with the illustrator. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Final files released on payment in full.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project title and client's PO or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Art directors and publishers route invoices through accounts payable, which often will not process without a reference number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables with quantity and dimensions or format
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists exactly what was delivered, such as 12 spreads at 300 dpi, so there is no dispute over scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights granted
invoiceChecklist.why: Fees depend on where and how long the art is used. Stating media, territory, term, and exclusivity ties the price to the license.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract or estimate and its date
invoiceChecklist.why: Links the invoice to agreed terms on revisions, kill fees, and copyright.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what has been paid so the amount owed is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear which changes were included and which went beyond the agreed rounds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients who pay you $600 or more in a year generally need a W-9 to issue a 1099, so make it easy to supply.

illustration.paymentTerms: Most illustrators take a 30-50% deposit before starting, since sketches are real work whether or not the client proceeds. Larger book projects are often split into milestones: deposit, approved sketches, and final delivery. Standard terms are net 14 or net 30, though publishers and agencies may pay on net 45-60 cycles, so confirm before accepting a job. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is common and should be written into the contract. Payment is accepted by ACH, check, card, or PayPal-style transfers. Many illustrators hold final high-resolution files or license activation until payment is complete.

tips.title: Bill usage rights, not just time
tips.body: Two clients may pay very different amounts for the same drawing depending on print run, territory, and duration. Put the license in the invoice so any extended use triggers a new fee.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in advance
tips.body: Two rounds of changes at the sketch stage and one at final is a common structure. Charge hourly for anything past that, and list those hours as their own invoice line.

tips.title: Use a kill fee
tips.body: If a client cancels after sketches, you still need to be paid for work done. A kill fee of 25-50% of the project fee, plus full payment for completed stages, is standard in contracts.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on big projects
tips.body: For a 32-page picture book, invoice at deposit, sketches approved, and final delivery. This keeps cash flowing during months of work.

tips.title: Send W-9 and ask about payment cycles early
tips.body: Publishers and agencies often need a W-9 and vendor setup before the first payment. Submitting it at signing avoids delays.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or per project?
faqs.answer: Per project is the norm for illustration, because clients are buying finished art and rights, not time. Track your hours privately to check your effective rate, and use hourly billing only for revisions beyond scope or open-ended work.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for licensing or usage rights?
faqs.answer: Include the license terms in the contract and repeat a short summary on the invoice: media, territory, duration, and exclusivity. If the client wants broader rights later, issue a new invoice for the additional license.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on illustration?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital goods, creative services, or tangible products such as original physical art, while others do not. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay after I deliver the art?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder citing the due date and late fee, then a firm written notice. If you only released a watermarked or low-resolution file, the license generally does not begin until payment. For larger amounts, small claims court or a demand letter are common next steps.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit from a publisher or agency?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many illustrators do. Some large publishers pay a set advance or split payments by contract, and the terms are usually in the agreement. For small businesses and individuals, 50% upfront is typical.

estimate.intro: Illustrators send estimates when a client asks for a project quote, often after an inquiry that includes a brief, a usage description, and a deadline. Clients usually compare your price against other illustrators and against their own budget, so the quote should show what is included and what the usage rights cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and size of final pieces
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for one cover differs from one for a cover and ten interior pieces, so state count, dimensions, and orientation.

scopeChecklist.item: Style reference and level of detail
scopeChecklist.why: Defines whether the work is simple spot art or fully rendered scenes with backgrounds, which affects the hours behind it.
Specify media, territory, duration, and exclusivity. Pricing depends on this, and changes later require a new fee.
List thumbnails or sketches, color, and final, and how many changes are included at each stage.
Layered PSD, flat PNG, vector AI, or print-ready CMYK can mean extra work, so state what is included.
Gives realistic dates for sketches and finals, and notes what happens if feedback is late or a rush is needed.
Shows the deposit, milestones, and what is owed if the project is cancelled partway.

pricingTips.title: Price from the usage first
pricingTips.body: Start with a base fee for the art, then adjust for use. A small web-only job costs less than a national ad campaign or packaging that will sit on shelves for years.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Show a basic option, such as one illustration with limited rights, and a larger one with extra pieces or broader rights. Clients often choose the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Account for unpaid sketching time
pricingTips.body: Concept work and back-and-forth communication take hours that do not show up in the final art. Build them into the flat fee instead of absorbing them.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire in 30 days or so, since your schedule and rates may change.

faqs.question: Should I provide free sketches to win the job?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Spec work undervalues your time and often leads to disputes. Share your portfolio, and if a test is needed, charge for it and credit the fee against the final project.

faqs.question: How detailed should an illustration estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list the pieces, stages, revision rounds, rights, and schedule, usually one page. A clear scope reduces later disagreements about extra changes.

faqs.question: What if the client's budget is lower than my quote?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope instead of price: fewer pieces, simpler backgrounds, limited usage rights, or a longer timeline. This keeps your rate consistent and gives the client a real choice.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the estimate is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, and the change should be put in writing. Refer to your estimate and contract, and send a revised quote for added pieces, extra revisions, or expanded rights.

immigration-consultant.intro: Immigration consultants help individuals, families, and employers with the paperwork side of US immigration: preparing forms, organizing supporting evidence, tracking deadlines, and explaining the process. Many work solo or in small offices serving a specific community. They bill for form preparation, consultations, document work, and sometimes translation or courier costs. Consultants who are not attorneys or DOJ-accredited representatives generally cannot give legal advice or represent clients before USCIS or immigration court, so invoices should describe the work as what it is.
immigration-consultant.pricingModel: Most consultants charge a flat fee per form or case type, because clients want to know the total before they commit. Common flat-fee units are per form (N-400, I-90, I-765), per package (a family-based petition with I-130 and I-485 together), or per renewal. Hourly billing is used for consultations, document reviews, and work that is hard to scope, such as responding to a Request for Evidence. Government filing fees are billed separately at cost and are not part of your service fee. Translations, certified mail, and courier charges are typically passed through, sometimes with a small handling charge. Some consultants offer payment plans for larger packages, with the work released in stages. Fees vary by city, language services offered, and how complex the case is.

rates.service: Green card renewal or replacement (I-90) preparation
Family petition package (I-130 with supporting forms)
Adjustment of status package (I-485, I-765, I-131)
Work permit (I-765) or DACA renewal preparation
Document review and Request for Evidence support

items.description: Initial consultation, eligibility screening for naturalization
Form N-400 preparation (flat fee)
Supporting document review and organization
Certified translation of marriage certificate and divorce decree
USCIS filing fee for Form N-400 (paid-through at cost, verify current fee)
Certified mail with tracking

sampleInvoice.notes: Service fees cover form preparation and document organization only. This office does not provide legal advice or legal representation. The USCIS filing fee is a government fee, listed at cost, and is not refundable by this office. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Deposit of $200 previously received will be applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Clear description of services as preparation or assistance, not legal advice
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states regulate how non-attorney consultants describe their work, and a vague description can look like unauthorized practice of law.

invoiceChecklist.item: Government filing fees listed on a separate line at cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see that USCIS fees are not your income, and it prevents disputes if a fee changes or an application is rejected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Form numbers and case type (for example I-130, N-400)
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties each charge to a specific filing and makes it easy to match the invoice to your contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Applicant name and, if different, the person paying
invoiceChecklist.why: Family members and sponsors often pay for the applicant, and your records should show who is responsible for the bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Translation, courier, and copying charges itemized
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real pass-through costs. Itemizing them avoids questions about your service fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract date and deposit received
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require a written contract for immigration services, so referencing it and the deposit shows the invoice follows the agreed terms.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business registration, bond, or registration number where your state requires it
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states, such as California, require immigration consultants to register or post a bond and to display certain notices on documents. Check your local rules.

immigration-consultant.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent at signing is common, with the balance due on delivery of the completed forms or before you submit anything. Many consultants refuse to release prepared forms until paid in full, since clients can file on their own once they have them. Payment plans are common for larger packages and should be written down, with each installment tied to a stage of work. Due dates of 7 days or due on receipt are typical for small flat-fee jobs. Accepted payments include checks, money orders, cards, and bank transfer. Government fees paid to USCIS usually come from the client directly by check, money order, or online card payment, so be clear about who pays them. Late fees are uncommon, but if you charge one, state it in the contract and check whether your state limits it.

tips.title: Keep government fees out of your revenue
tips.body: List USCIS and other agency fees as separate pass-through lines. If you collect them on the client's behalf, record them separately from your service fees so your income, and your books at tax time, are accurate.

tips.title: Get a written contract before you start
tips.body: Many states require one for immigration services, and it protects you either way. Spell out the services, the fee, what is not included (such as RFE responses or interview preparation), and what happens if the application is denied.

tips.title: Quote RFE and appeal work separately
tips.body: A flat fee for the original filing should not cover a Request for Evidence, a Notice of Intent to Deny, or a re-file. Bill these hourly or as a stated add-on, and say so in the contract.

tips.title: Stage payments to the work
tips.body: Take a deposit at intake, a second payment when forms are drafted, and the balance before the client signs the final packet. This reduces the risk of unpaid work, since the client can take the forms elsewhere.

tips.title: Give a receipt for every payment
tips.body: Clients often pay in cash or money orders. A dated receipt that names the service protects both sides if the client or a regulator later asks what was paid and for what.

faqs.question: Should I include USCIS filing fees on my invoice?
faqs.answer: If you collect them from the client, yes, as a separate line at cost, labeled as a government fee. If the client pays USCIS directly, leave them off the invoice but note in the contract that the fee is their responsibility. Check current fees on the USCIS website, since they change.

faqs.question: Can I charge a flat fee instead of hourly?
faqs.answer: Yes, and flat fees are the norm for standard forms like the N-400 or I-90. Define exactly what is included, and bill extra work such as RFE responses or interview prep separately.

faqs.question: What if USCIS rejects or denies the application?
faqs.answer: Say in your contract what happens to your fee. Many consultants keep the service fee for work already done but fix and re-file rejected paperwork at no or reduced cost when the error was theirs. The government fee refund depends on USCIS, not you.

faqs.question: Can I call my charges legal fees?
faqs.answer: Not unless you are an attorney. Non-attorney consultants should describe charges as preparation, translation, or administrative services. Rules differ by state, so check your state's requirements for immigration consultants or document preparers.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and on whether services are taxable there. Most states do not tax professional services, but some tax certain services or resold items like translations. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Prospective clients usually ask for a price before booking, and they often compare two or three consultants or a low-cost attorney. A written quote sent after the first consultation helps clients see exactly what is covered and what the government will charge on top. It also sets limits on the work before any forms are started.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact forms and case type covered
scopeChecklist.why: List each form by number (for example I-130, I-485, I-765) so the client knows what the fee covers and what would be extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Government filing fees and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often confuse your fee with USCIS fees. State the current fee amounts, that they are separate, and that they can change.

scopeChecklist.item: What you do and do not do
scopeChecklist.why: State that you prepare forms and organize documents but do not give legal advice or represent the client before USCIS or a court, unless you are authorized to.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of family members or applicants included
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing often depends on the number of people. Adding a spouse or child later changes the fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as RFE responses, interviews, appeals, and re-filing
scopeChecklist.why: These are the most common sources of unplanned work, and a quote that leaves them out avoids disputes.
State whether they are included or billed at cost, and whether the client can supply their own certified translations.
Forms and fees change. Give an expiration date for the quote and state the deposit and installments.

pricingTips.title: Price by case complexity, not just form count
pricingTips.body: A straightforward N-400 for a client with a clean history takes far less time than one with travel gaps, prior arrests, or name changes. Set a base fee and state what raises it, such as extra documents or a complicated history.
