pricingTips.title: Offer a package price for related filings
pricingTips.body: Adjustment of status commonly involves several forms filed together. A single package price for the set is easier for clients to compare and gives you a clear scope.

pricingTips.title: Show your fee and government fees side by side
pricingTips.body: Present a total with two sections: your service fee and the government fees. Clients can then compare you fairly with others and see that you are not marking up USCIS charges.

pricingTips.title: Be cautious about promising outcomes
pricingTips.body: Never quote a price that implies approval or a timeline you cannot control. Describe the work you will do, not the result, and note that processing times are set by the agency.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many consultants charge a modest fee, often credited toward the service fee if the client hires them. Free consultations are common too, but limit them to 15 or 20 minutes so screening does not turn into unpaid work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Government fees and forms can change, so state that the quote is based on current requirements and may be adjusted if they change before filing.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed price if I have not seen the client's documents?
faqs.answer: Give a conditional quote instead. State the price for a standard case and the conditions, such as the number of applicants and a clean record, then confirm or adjust it after you review the documents.

faqs.question: Does the quote need to be signed?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea to get a signature or written acceptance, and in some states a written contract is required for immigration services. Many consultants turn the accepted quote into the service contract, with the required notices added.

industrial-cleaning.intro: Industrial cleaning businesses clean factories, warehouses, processing plants, and commercial facilities. They bill for pressure washing, degreasing, equipment and tank cleaning, floor scrubbing, and scheduled or one-time deep cleans. Customers are usually plant managers, facility directors, or property managers who need a clear invoice that matches a purchase order and a defined scope.
industrial-cleaning.pricingModel: Most industrial cleaning is priced by the hour per crew member, by square foot for floors and large surfaces, or as a flat fee for a defined job such as a tank cleanout or a shutdown clean. Recurring contracts are usually a fixed monthly or per-visit price based on facility size and cleaning frequency. Specialty work such as confined space entry, hazardous waste handling, or high-pressure hydro blasting is billed at higher rates because of training, permits, and insurance. Equipment (pressure washers, industrial vacuums, scrubbers, vac trucks), chemicals, disposal fees, and waste hauling are often itemized separately or marked up 10-25%. Night, weekend, and emergency work typically carries a 1.5x to 2x premium.

rates.service: General industrial cleaning labor (per crew member)
Pressure washing and degreasing, floors and exteriors
Industrial floor scrubbing and auto-scrubber service
Industrial vacuum truck service with operator

items.description: Pressure wash and degrease production floor, Building B (hot water, 3,500 PSI)
Crew labor for equipment pit and conveyor line cleaning (3 workers)
Vacuum truck with operator for sludge and wastewater removal
Degreaser and cleaning chemicals
Wastewater and sludge disposal (manifested)
After-hours premium (Saturday shift)

sampleInvoice.notes: PO #44721. Work completed 03/08 per Scope of Work dated 02/26. Net 30. Disposal manifests attached. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or work order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable at most plants will not process an invoice without a matching PO, so a missing number delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Site name, building, and areas cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Large facilities have multiple buildings and cost centers, and the invoice needs to match the work to the right one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and shift times, including after-hours work
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports labor hours and any premium rates, and lets the customer verify the work against their schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor, equipment, chemicals, and disposal
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often reimburse or allocate these separately, and itemizing makes markup and pass-through costs easy to see.

invoiceChecklist.item: Waste manifests and disposal receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Proves proper handling of waste and wastewater, which protects both you and the customer in an audit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance and license references (COI on file, contractor license if required locally)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many facilities require current certificates of insurance and vendor compliance before they will pay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed scope of work or contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to what was agreed and helps resolve disputes over extras or change orders.

industrial-cleaning.paymentTerms: Industrial customers typically pay on Net 30 terms, and some large companies push to Net 45 or Net 60 through their vendor agreements. For new customers or jobs with significant material or disposal costs, ask for a 25-50% deposit, or bill disposal and rental costs upfront. Recurring contracts are normally invoiced monthly in advance or at month end. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract or on the estimate. Most payment comes by ACH or check, with credit cards accepted for smaller jobs, and customers often need a W-9 and vendor setup forms before the first payment.

tips.title: Get the PO before you start work
tips.body: Ask for the PO number when you book the job. Without it, an invoice can sit in accounts payable for weeks while someone tracks down the approver.

tips.title: Bill disposal and rentals as pass-through lines
tips.body: Dumpsters, vac truck dump fees, and chemical disposal can be large costs. Show them as separate lines with receipts so you recover them and the customer sees they are not padded labor.

tips.title: Document change orders in writing
tips.body: Industrial jobs often expand once you open up equipment and find more buildup than expected. Get a signed or emailed approval for extra hours or scope before doing the work, then list it as its own line.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on large jobs
tips.body: For shutdown cleans or multi-week projects, bill weekly or at milestones instead of waiting until the end. It keeps cash moving when you are paying crews and equipment costs.

tips.title: Take before and after photos
tips.body: Attach dated photos to the invoice package. They settle disputes about quality quickly and support the work you billed for.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the square foot?
faqs.answer: Square foot pricing works well for open floors, exteriors, and recurring cleaning where the area is measurable. Hourly pricing is better when conditions are unknown, such as equipment cleaning, heavy buildup, or confined areas. Many companies use square foot pricing for the base job and hourly rates for extras.

faqs.question: Can I mark up chemicals, equipment, and disposal?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is common to add 10-25% on materials, chemicals, equipment rental, and disposal to cover handling and procurement. Check your contract, since some customers specify cost-plus terms or require receipts for pass-through items.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on industrial cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning services, others tax only materials or none of the work, and some exempt manufacturers. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional, and ask customers for exemption certificates when applicable.

faqs.question: What if the customer disputes part of the invoice?
faqs.answer: Point back to the signed scope, change orders, photos, and manifests. Ask them to pay the undisputed portion on time and work out the rest separately. Clear documentation upfront prevents most disputes.

faqs.question: Can I charge a premium for after-hours or emergency work?
faqs.answer: Yes. A premium of 1.5x to 2x the normal rate is standard for nights, weekends, holidays, and emergency callouts. State it on the estimate so it does not come as a surprise on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Industrial cleaning estimates are usually sent after a site walkthrough, and often as part of a bid process where the customer collects quotes from several vendors. Plant managers compare total price, schedule and downtime, safety record, insurance, and how clearly the scope is defined. A thorough written quote helps you avoid underbidding jobs with hidden conditions.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact areas, equipment, and square footage included
scopeChecklist.why: Defines the boundaries of the job so the customer cannot expect extra areas at the same price.

scopeChecklist.item: Cleaning methods and chemicals to be used
scopeChecklist.why: Pressure, temperature, and chemical choices affect surfaces, wastewater, and safety, and plants often have approval requirements.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, shift hours, and expected downtime
scopeChecklist.why: Work during shutdowns or off hours changes labor costs and customer expectations on completion.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies water, power, lifts, and access
scopeChecklist.why: If you have to bring your own water tanks or generators, it should be priced in, and if the customer supplies them, it should be stated.
Disposal of sludge, wastewater, and hazardous material can be a major cost and a liability, so state who is responsible.
Confined space entry, lockout/tagout, and site safety training add time and cost and should be acknowledged upfront.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions, exclusions, and how extras are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Gives you a basis for charging additional time if conditions are worse than seen in the walkthrough.

pricingTips.title: Walk the site before quoting
pricingTips.body: Never price a plant job from photos alone. Look at buildup, access, ceiling heights, drains, and waste volume, since these drive labor hours more than square footage.

pricingTips.title: Build in safety and setup time
pricingTips.body: Site orientation, permits, lockout coordination, and staging equipment take real hours. Include them in the price rather than treating them as free.

pricingTips.title: Quote a fixed price with an hourly rate for extras
pricingTips.body: A flat price gives the customer certainty, while a stated hourly rate for unforeseen work protects your margin when conditions change.

pricingTips.title: Offer options for recurring work
pricingTips.body: Present weekly, biweekly, and monthly schedules at different per-visit prices. It helps the customer budget and often wins you a longer contract.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site walkthrough and estimate?
faqs.answer: Most industrial cleaners provide free estimates for standard jobs. For complex projects that require significant engineering, sampling, or planning time, a paid assessment that is credited toward the job is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should my quote be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is typical. Chemical, fuel, and disposal costs can change, so state an expiration date and say that pricing may be adjusted afterward.

faqs.question: What if the actual job is bigger than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that allows additional charges for conditions not visible at the walkthrough. When you find them, stop and get written approval from the customer before continuing at your stated extra rates.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: For commercial and industrial work, yes. Get a signed quote, contract, or PO that references your scope. It protects your payment and is often required for the customer's own vendor process.

influencer.intro: Influencers create sponsored content for brands on platforms like Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and podcasts, and invoice the brand or its agency once deliverables are posted or approved. Typical line items include sponsored posts, short-form videos, stories, long-form integrations, usage rights, and affiliate or event appearances.
influencer.pricingModel: Most influencers charge a flat fee per deliverable, set by audience size, engagement rate, platform, and content format. Video costs more than a static photo, and a YouTube integration costs more than a story frame. Many creators bundle deliverables into campaign packages, such as one Reel, three stories, and a link in bio for a set price. Add-ons are billed separately: usage rights or whitelisting (the brand running your content as paid ads), exclusivity windows that bar you from working with competitors, rush turnaround, extra revision rounds, and raw footage. A rough starting point for per-post pricing is $10-$25 per 1,000 followers for smaller accounts, though engagement and niche matter more than follower count. Some deals include product gifting, commissions, or affiliate payouts, which should be listed on the invoice or contract alongside any cash fee. Agency-brokered deals often net payment 30 to 60 days after posting, so price with that delay in mind.

rates.service: Instagram or TikTok sponsored video (micro-influencer, 10k-50k followers)
Usage rights / whitelisting for paid ads
Brand event appearance or in-person content day

items.description: Sponsored Instagram Reel (up to 45 seconds), posted 3/12, 1 round of revisions included
Instagram Stories set (4 frames with link sticker), posted 3/13
Whitelisting / paid ad usage rights for Reel, 60 days
30-day category exclusivity (skincare)
Additional revision round requested after approval

sampleInvoice.notes: Campaign: Spring Skincare Launch, PO #SK-2291. Net 30 from invoice date. Payment by ACH or check. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Usage rights run 3/12 through 5/11 and require a new license after that date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Campaign name and PO or contract number
invoiceChecklist.why: Brand accounts payable teams and agencies match invoices to campaigns, and a missing reference number is a common cause of delayed payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each deliverable with platform, format, and post date
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what was delivered and when, and lets the brand confirm it matches the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Post links or handles used
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the client proof of completion and speeds approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights, whitelisting, and exclusivity as separate line items with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: These carry their own fees and expiration dates, and listing them prevents the brand from assuming they are unlimited.

invoiceChecklist.item: Value of gifted product or affiliate terms
invoiceChecklist.why: If part of the deal is non-cash, noting it keeps the record clear and helps you track income for tax reporting.

invoiceChecklist.item: Agency name and the end brand
invoiceChecklist.why: When an agency pays you, the invoice should go to the correct billing entity while still identifying the brand.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 status
invoiceChecklist.why: US brands usually need a W-9 on file and may issue a 1099 if you are paid $600 or more in a year (check current IRS thresholds).

influencer.paymentTerms: Brands and agencies commonly pay net 30, and some large companies use net 45 or net 60. Many creators ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront on larger campaigns, with the rest due after posting, and sometimes the full fee upfront for new clients. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common when written into the contract. Payment usually arrives by ACH, wire, PayPal, or check. Confirm in the contract whether payment is triggered by posting or by brand approval, since approval delays can hold up the money.

tips.title: Charge separately for usage rights
tips.body: A post that only appears on your feed is worth less than the same post used in the brand's paid ads. Price whitelisting and usage by duration, and bill it as its own line so the term is clear.

tips.title: Put the revision limit in writing
tips.body: Include one or two revision rounds in the fee and state a per-round charge after that. Brands that request reshoots after approval should be billed for the extra work.

tips.title: Ask for a deposit on larger campaigns
tips.body: Content creation takes unpaid time before anything posts. A 50 percent deposit protects you if the brand cancels or delays approval.

tips.title: Track gifted products and affiliate income
tips.body: Gifted items and commissions can be taxable income in the US. Keep a record of the retail value and payouts next to your invoices.

tips.title: Invoice when the post goes live
tips.body: Send the invoice on the posting date, or on the date specified in the contract, so the net 30 clock starts as early as possible.

faqs.question: When should an influencer send an invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually on the day the sponsored content goes live or is approved, depending on the contract. If you took a deposit, send the final invoice for the remaining balance at that point.

faqs.question: Do I need a contract as well as an invoice?
faqs.answer: A written agreement is strongly recommended. The contract sets deliverables, usage rights, exclusivity, and payment terms, and the invoice bills for what was delivered under it.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for free products?
faqs.answer: If the deal includes product in place of or in addition to cash, list it as a line item with its retail value and mark it as already received. This keeps the record accurate for both sides and for your taxes.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on sponsored content?
faqs.answer: Usually not, since most states do not tax advertising or influencer services, but rules vary. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a brand pays late?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder the day after the due date, then follow up with a written notice citing the late fee in your contract. For agency deals, also contact the agency's accounts payable team directly.

estimate.intro: Influencers send a quote or rate proposal when a brand or agency asks for pricing on a campaign, often alongside a media kit. Brands compare your fee against other creators on cost per deliverable, audience fit, and what rights are included.

scopeChecklist.why: State the number of Reels, TikToks, stories, or YouTube integrations, with length, so the brand knows what the fee covers.
Delays in brand approval are common, and dates keep both sides on schedule.
Setting a limit prevents unlimited rework and gives you a basis for charging extra.
Define where the content may appear, for how long, and whether it can be run as paid ads.
Blocking competitor work costs you income, so specify how long and which brands are excluded.
Clarify that you keep ownership unless transferred, and price any buyout or raw file delivery.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Lock in deposit, due dates, and how long the rate is valid in case follow-up drags on.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as one Reel, a Reel plus stories, and a full campaign with usage rights. Brands tend to pick the middle option and it keeps the conversation about scope rather than haggling over one price.

pricingTips.title: Base your rate on engagement, not just followers
pricingTips.body: Use your average views and engagement rate from recent posts, and include screenshots of audience demographics. Brands pay more for proven results in their target market.

pricingTips.title: Quote high enough to leave room to negotiate
pricingTips.body: Brands often counter lower. Build in room so a reduced rate still covers your time, and trade fee cuts for narrower rights rather than lowering the price alone.

pricingTips.title: Price rush work at a premium
pricingTips.body: If the brand wants posting within a few days, add 25 to 50 percent to cover bumping other work.

faqs.question: Should I share my rates publicly?
faqs.answer: Many creators share a starting rate in a media kit and send custom quotes for campaigns. Custom quotes let you account for usage rights, exclusivity, and timeline.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. Audience size and engagement change, and brand budgets shift, so an expiration date keeps you from being held to an old rate.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the pitch or concept work?
faqs.answer: If the brand asks for a detailed creative concept or mockups before signing, many creators charge a small development fee or credit it toward the campaign if the deal goes ahead.

insulation-contractor.intro: Insulation contractors install batt, blown-in, spray foam, and rigid board insulation in attics, walls, crawl spaces, basements, and new construction. Most are solo operators or small crews who bill homeowners, builders, and general contractors. Invoices usually combine material, labor, and sometimes prep work such as air sealing, old insulation removal, and baffle installation.
insulation-contractor.pricingModel: Most insulation work is priced per square foot of area covered, with the price tied to the material and the R-value or thickness installed. Blown-in attic work is often quoted per sq ft at a given R-value, while spray foam is priced per board foot (1 sq ft at 1 inch thick) or per sq ft at a stated depth. Batt installation in new construction is often a per sq ft rate for the whole house. Add-ons such as air sealing, removal of old insulation, rodent cleanup, baffles, and vapor barriers are usually separate line items, priced per sq ft, per hour, or flat. Many contractors set a minimum job charge to cover travel, setup, and equipment (especially for spray foam rigs). Builders and general contractors often negotiate lower per sq ft rates for volume work, and progress billing is common on larger jobs. Rebates and utility incentives may affect what the customer pays, so spell out who handles them.

rates.service: Blown-in attic insulation (fiberglass or cellulose, to R-38 to R-49)

items.description: Attic air sealing: top plates, wire and plumbing penetrations, sealed with foam and caulk
Install attic ventilation baffles (rafter vents)
Blown-in cellulose insulation to R-49 (approx. 16 inches), labor and material
Attic hatch cover with weatherstripping and rigid foam dam
Insulation depth markers installed (6)

sampleInvoice.notes: Total includes all materials and labor. Work completed 6/12. R-value installed: R-49, with bag count and coverage chart attached. 50% deposit received at scheduling; balance due on receipt. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or card (3% fee on card). Keep this invoice and the coverage chart for any utility rebate or tax credit claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: Area insulated and location (attic, exterior walls, crawl space, rim joists)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different areas have different prices and R-value targets, and the customer needs a record of what was done where.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material type, R-value, and installed thickness
invoiceChecklist.why: This is the main thing the customer is paying for and is needed to prove code compliance or support rebate claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage or board feet and the rate used
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the total was calculated and prevents disputes over measurements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bags installed and coverage chart (for blown-in)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many inspectors and rebate programs require it, and it shows the specified R-value was met.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for prep, air sealing, and removal
invoiceChecklist.why: These are labor-heavy extras that customers often forget were included in the scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and insurance numbers where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and localities require a license number on contracts and invoices, and builders often need proof of insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job address, PO number, or permit number for builder or GC work
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial and builder accounts usually will not process payment without a PO or job reference.

insulation-contractor.paymentTerms: For residential jobs, many insulation contractors take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials, with the balance due on completion. Small jobs are often paid in full on the day of the work. Builders and general contractors usually pay on net 15 to net 30 terms, sometimes with progress billing tied to stages like rough-in or drywall-ready inspection. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in the contract; check your state's rules on late fees and lien notice deadlines. Customers pay by check, ACH, and card, and some jobs are paid through utility rebate programs or financing that can delay the final payment.

tips.title: Bill by measured area, not estimated area
tips.body: Measure the attic or wall area at the start and note it on the invoice. If the actual area differs from the quote, you have a record to support the adjustment.

tips.title: Keep prep and extras on their own lines
tips.body: Air sealing, old insulation removal, rodent cleanup, and baffles take real time. Listing them separately makes it easier to charge for them and to explain changes when the scope grows.

tips.title: Collect a deposit for materials
tips.body: Spray foam chemicals and large bulk orders are expensive up front. A deposit protects your cash flow if a job is canceled or delayed.

tips.title: Attach the coverage chart or spray foam depth record
tips.body: Give the customer proof of the R-value you installed. It cuts down on callbacks and helps them claim rebates or tax credits.

tips.title: Know your lien deadlines on builder jobs
tips.body: If you work for a GC or builder, find out your state's preliminary notice and lien filing deadlines. Missing them can cost you your right to file if payment stalls.

faqs.question: Should I charge by square foot or by R-value?
faqs.answer: Most contractors charge by square foot but set the price based on the R-value or thickness required. Write both on the invoice, for example 1,400 sq ft at R-49, so the rate and the result are clear.

faqs.question: How do I bill spray foam?
faqs.answer: Spray foam is usually billed per board foot (1 sq ft at 1 inch thick) or per sq ft at a stated depth. Record the thickness sprayed in each area, and add a minimum charge for small jobs to cover rig setup and travel.

faqs.question: Do I charge for removing old insulation?
faqs.answer: Yes, as a separate line. Removal is labor and disposal heavy and is often priced per sq ft or per hour. Add extra for contaminated insulation such as rodent damage or vermiculite, and check local rules if asbestos is possible.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common, often 25 to 50 percent. Put the deposit amount and the balance due date in your contract and show the deposit as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do if the customer is using a utility rebate?
faqs.answer: Say in writing who applies for the rebate and whether the customer owes you the full price up front. Include R-values, material details, and your license number on the invoice, since programs often ask for them.

estimate.intro: Insulation contractors send estimates before almost every job, after measuring the attic, walls, or crawl space and checking existing conditions. Homeowners often collect two or three quotes and compare the price per sq ft, the R-value, the material type, and what prep is included. A clear, itemized quote helps you stand out from a bid that looks cheaper but leaves out air sealing or removal.

scopeChecklist.item: Areas to be insulated with measured square footage
scopeChecklist.why: Defines exactly what is covered and gives you a basis for adjusting the price if the area differs.

scopeChecklist.item: Material type, target R-value, and installed thickness
scopeChecklist.why: Customers compare bids on these, and a lower price may be for a thinner or lower-grade installation.

scopeChecklist.item: Air sealing, baffles, and ventilation work included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Prep work is a common source of disputes and a major difference between bids.

scopeChecklist.item: Removal and disposal of existing insulation
scopeChecklist.why: If it is not listed, customers assume it is included, and the cost can be significant.

scopeChecklist.item: Access and hidden conditions (knob-and-tube wiring, vermiculite, mold, moisture, pest damage)
scopeChecklist.why: Conditions found after you start can change the scope, so state how you will handle and price them.

scopeChecklist.item: Customer responsibilities such as clearing the attic and providing power and parking
scopeChecklist.why: Delays from blocked access cost you time and should be tied to a trip or standby charge.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, payment terms, deposit, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change, and a clear expiration date protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Price from measured area and a labor and material breakdown
pricingTips.body: Calculate material cost per sq ft at the R-value, add labor time, equipment, travel, and overhead, then add your margin. Use measured dimensions, not guesses based on house size.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Show a couple of R-value or material choices, such as cellulose versus fiberglass or open-cell versus closed-cell foam, so the customer can choose based on budget and performance.

pricingTips.title: Itemize prep and extras
pricingTips.body: List air sealing, baffles, and removal as separate lines. It shows the value of your work and lets a customer drop an item without confusing the comparison.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum charge and quote expiration
pricingTips.body: A minimum job fee covers small jobs that are not worth the trip, and a 15 to 30 day expiration protects you from material price swings.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential insulation contractors quote for free. Some charge for a full energy audit or blower door test, and some credit the fee toward the job if the customer signs.

faqs.question: How do I handle unknown conditions in the attic or walls?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that hidden issues such as wiring problems, moisture, mold, or vermiculite are not included and will be priced separately after discovery. Get written approval before doing extra work.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 15 to 30 days. Material costs, especially for spray foam, can change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I give a price range instead of a fixed number?
faqs.answer: You can for jobs with unknowns, like wall work in older homes. For standard attic jobs, a fixed price based on measured area is easier for the customer to accept and compare.

insurance-agent.intro: Most insurance agents are paid by carriers through commission, but many also invoice clients directly. Common cases are fee-based coverage reviews, commercial risk assessments, broker or policy fees where state law allows them, employee benefits consulting, claims advocacy, and agency-billed premium. This page covers the fees agents bill clients for, not carrier commissions.
insurance-agent.pricingModel: Pricing depends on whether you are paid by commission, by fee, or both. Commission-only agents usually invoice for premium only when they run agency billing. Fee-based work is typically a flat fee per project, such as a policy review, a risk assessment, or a renewal marketing package. Hourly billing is common for consulting, claims advocacy, and contract review. Benefits consultants often charge per employee per month (PEPM) or an annual retainer. Where state law permits a broker or policy fee, it is usually a flat amount per policy and must be disclosed in writing before the client agrees. Some states require a separate license or written consent for fees, or limit fees on certain lines such as personal auto or Medicare products. If you earn commission on a policy, check whether charging a fee for the same work is allowed in your state. Premium collected on behalf of a carrier is not your revenue and should be kept separate from your fees.

rates.service: Personal policy and coverage review (home, auto, umbrella, life)
Commercial risk assessment and coverage gap analysis
Broker or policy fee, where permitted
Contract and certificate of insurance review (vendor or lease requirements)

items.description: Commercial risk assessment and coverage gap report - general contractor, 8 employees
Renewal marketing: quotes requested from 5 carriers, comparison summary prepared
Broker fee - commercial general liability policy (disclosed and signed 03/04)
Review of 3 subcontract insurance requirement clauses
Additional consulting - workers' compensation class code review

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Fees are for professional services and are separate from insurance premium, which is billed by the carrier. Broker fee is fully earned at policy binding and is non-refundable per the fee agreement signed 03/04. Late balances may be charged 1.5% per month where permitted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your agency name, license number, and state of licensure
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states expect licensed producers to be identifiable on documents, and clients and auditors use the license number to verify you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed fee agreement or disclosure and its date
invoiceChecklist.why: Fees are regulated in many states. Tying the invoice to a written disclosure protects you if a client or the department of insurance questions the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Policy number, carrier, line of coverage, and effective dates for any broker or policy fee
invoiceChecklist.why: The client and their accountant need to match the fee to the right policy and term, and it ties the fee to the service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fees listed separately from premium
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeping fees apart from premium avoids confusion about what goes to the carrier and what you keep, and keeps your fiduciary funds clean.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of each service with date or scope (review, marketing, consulting hours)
invoiceChecklist.why: Fee-based clients often expect a deliverable. A clear description shows what was done and reduces disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and hourly rate for any time-based work, including claims advocacy
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see how consulting time was calculated, especially if the work was open-ended.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name, business name, and PO or project number if provided
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often require a PO or reference number before accounts payable will pay.

insurance-agent.paymentTerms: For flat-fee projects such as risk assessments or renewal marketing, many agents take 50% upfront and the balance on delivery. Broker or policy fees are often due at binding, sometimes added to the premium invoice if the carrier or state rules allow it. Consulting and claims advocacy are usually billed monthly with net 14 or net 30 terms. Retainers for benefits consulting are commonly billed monthly or quarterly in advance. Late fees of 1 to 1.5% per month are used where permitted and should be stated in the fee agreement. Clients commonly pay by ACH, check, or card. If you collect premium under agency billing, deposit it into a separate fiduciary or premium trust account as your state requires, never into your operating account.

tips.title: Get the fee disclosed in writing before you bind
tips.body: Many states require written disclosure or client consent for broker fees. Have the client sign a fee agreement that states the amount, what it covers, and whether it is refundable. Check your state's rules and your carrier and agency agreements first.

tips.title: Keep premium and fees on separate documents
tips.body: If you bill premium under agency billing, issue a premium invoice or statement separately from your fee invoice. This helps with trust account reconciliation and makes it clear what portion is yours.

tips.title: Decide where you charge a fee and where commission covers the work
tips.body: Clients push back when they feel they pay twice. Set a clear policy, for example fees only for risk assessments, complex marketing, and consulting beyond normal service, and keep routine service changes included.

tips.title: Price commercial work by complexity, not just premium size
tips.body: A small contractor with several subcontractors and multi-state exposure can take more work than a larger, simpler account. Base project fees on exposures, locations, and number of carriers approached.

tips.title: Document claims advocacy time as you go
tips.body: Log calls, emails, and adjuster follow-up by date. Clients often question hourly claims work months later, and a time record settles it.

faqs.question: Can an insurance agent charge a fee on top of commission?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the line of business. Many states allow broker or policy fees with written disclosure, and some restrict or prohibit them on certain products. Check with your state department of insurance and your carrier agreements before charging both.

faqs.question: Should I include premium on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you run agency billing and collect premium on behalf of the carrier. In that case, show premium separately from your fees and handle the money as fiduciary funds. If the carrier bills the client directly, leave premium off your invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a Medicare or health plan enrollment?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Federal rules prohibit charging Medicare beneficiaries for help enrolling in Medicare Advantage or Part D plans, since the carrier pays you commission. Fee-based work is more common for employers, such as benefits consulting. Confirm the rules for your product.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a certificate of insurance?
faqs.answer: Many agents include routine certificates as part of service. For high-volume requests or complex contract reviews, a per-document or monthly fee is reasonable if you disclose it. Some carriers or states limit what can be charged, so check first.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on insurance fees?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by state. Insurance premiums are generally taxed differently from services, and some states tax certain consulting or service fees. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Agents send quotes for fee-based work such as commercial risk assessments, renewal marketing projects, benefits consulting, and claims advocacy. Insurance premium quotes come from carriers and are separate from your fee proposal. Clients compare your fee against what other agents or brokers charge, or against doing nothing and renewing as is.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact services included (review, carrier marketing, report, meetings)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a review includes placing the coverage or ongoing service. Spell out what ends at delivery.
A property and liability review is not the same as including workers' compensation, cyber, or employee benefits. Name each line.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of carriers or markets you will approach
scopeChecklist.why: Marketing to 3 carriers costs far less time than 8. Setting a count prevents scope creep.

scopeChecklist.item: Information the client must provide and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Loss runs, payroll, schedules of values, and prior policies drive your timeline. Delays should not be your cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee, whether it is refundable, and how it relates to commission
scopeChecklist.why: Clients want to know if they pay a fee, commission, or both. State it plainly and note any state disclosure requirements.
A written report, comparison summary, or renewal presentation by a specific date sets clear expectations.
State that coverage terms, pricing, and carrier acceptance are not guaranteed and depend on underwriting.

pricingTips.title: Quote a flat fee for defined projects
pricingTips.body: Clients prefer a known number for reviews and renewal marketing. Estimate your hours from past accounts and add a buffer for slow client responses.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for commercial clients
pricingTips.body: A basic review, a review with carrier marketing, and a full program with annual service meetings give clients a choice and make it easier to close.

pricingTips.title: Credit the fee against placement where allowed
pricingTips.body: Some agents waive or reduce the fee if the client places the coverage through them and commission is earned. Only offer this if your state and carrier agreements permit it, and put it in writing.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 30 days protects you from workload changes and from changing market conditions, such as hardening rates in a line.

faqs.question: Is a fee proposal the same as an insurance quote?
faqs.answer: No. An insurance quote comes from a carrier and shows premium and terms. Your estimate covers your professional fee. Keep them as separate documents so the client does not confuse them.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or proposal?
faqs.answer: For simple personal lines, quoting is usually free because commission covers it. For complex commercial accounts or consulting, a fee for the analysis is common, especially if the client may take the work elsewhere.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes mid-project?
faqs.answer: Include a change clause in the estimate that says additional lines, locations, or carrier requests are billed at your hourly rate or a revised flat fee. Confirm changes in writing.

faqs.question: How long should my estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 30 days. For commercial work tied to a renewal date, you can also state that the fee applies only if the engagement starts at least 60 to 90 days before expiration.

interior-decorator.intro: Interior decorators style and furnish residential and small commercial spaces. They select paint colors, furniture, window treatments, lighting, rugs, and accessories, and they manage ordering and delivery. Invoices usually cover design time, product purchases, and project management fees, often split across several billing events.
interior-decorator.pricingModel: Decorators commonly use one or more of four models: hourly rates, flat room or project fees, a percentage of the total project budget, or cost-plus on products. Hourly billing suits consultations and small tasks. Flat fees per room are common for full-service design and give clients a fixed number. Many decorators also earn a markup on furnishings, typically 20 to 35 percent over their trade price, or they charge a design fee and pass through trade discounts. Some offer e-design packages at a set price per room. Product purchases are usually billed separately from design fees and paid up front, since the decorator is often placing orders in their own name or on the client's behalf. Charges for installation, delivery, and storage are listed as separate lines.

rates.service: E-design package (concept board, layout, shopping list)

items.description: Living room design: concept board, floor plan, and furniture selections (50% of flat fee)
Sofa, two accent chairs, and coffee table purchased per approved proposal
Custom drapery panels and hardware, including measuring
Sourcing trip with client to showrooms
Procurement and project management fee on product purchases
Delivery and white-glove setup

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $2,500 received on contract signing and applied to this invoice. Balance due within 14 days. Custom and special-order items are final sale and non-refundable. Remaining 50% of design fee will be billed at installation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and room or area
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with multiple rooms or properties need to see which charges belong to which space.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design fees separated from product costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps the creative work and merchandise clearly distinct, which also helps with sales tax treatment and client budgeting.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized products with vendor, SKU, quantity, and finish
invoiceChecklist.why: Avoids disputes about what was ordered and makes returns or replacements easier to track.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line and resale details
invoiceChecklist.why: Product sales are taxable in many states, and rules for design services vary, so show the tax separately and check local requirements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and prior payments applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Decorators often collect retainers and product deposits, and the client needs to see the balance owed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, freight, and storage charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Furniture freight and warehouse holding fees can be significant and are a common source of surprise charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lead times and special-order terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States that custom items are non-returnable and gives expected delivery windows, which reduces later disputes.

interior-decorator.paymentTerms: Most decorators collect a design retainer or 30 to 50 percent of the design fee at contract signing, with the balance at set milestones such as concept approval and installation. Product purchases are commonly paid in full before ordering, or 50 percent at order and the rest before delivery, since special-order items cannot be returned. Standard terms on invoices for services are due on receipt to net 14. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by check, ACH, or credit card, and many decorators pass along card processing fees on large product orders or have clients pay vendors directly.

tips.title: Collect product money before you order
tips.body: Never place a large special-order purchase on your own credit without payment in hand. Many custom pieces cannot be cancelled once ordered, so get full or at least 50 percent payment first.

tips.title: Bill design fees in milestones
tips.body: Splitting the fee into deposit, concept approval, and installation keeps cash flowing and gives the client natural decision points. Tie each payment to a specific deliverable.

tips.title: Track every hour even on flat fees
tips.body: Keep a simple log of time per project. It shows whether your flat fee covers the real work and gives you data to price scope changes.

tips.title: Put revisions and extra rounds in writing
tips.body: Limit the number of design revisions in your contract, and bill extra rounds hourly. Clients who keep changing selections are the most common cause of unpaid overtime.

tips.title: Invoice storage and receiving separately
tips.body: If you receive deliveries at a warehouse, charge a receiving and inspection fee and storage after a free window. Damage claims are easier when the receiving record is documented.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Hourly works for consultations and open-ended projects. Flat fees per room work better for defined full-service jobs because clients like knowing the cost. Whichever you choose, define the scope and cap the revision rounds.

faqs.question: How do I bill for furniture and products?
faqs.answer: Either mark up items from your trade price and show clients the retail price, or charge a design fee plus a procurement percentage on cost. Be clear in your contract which model you use so clients are not surprised.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax tangible goods you sell but treat design services differently, and some tax both. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and use a resale certificate when buying items you resell.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent shopping?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sourcing and shopping time is real work. Either build it into your flat fee or bill it hourly, and note the hours on the invoice if billing by time.

faqs.question: What if a client refuses to pay for a special-order item?
faqs.answer: Your signed contract should say custom orders are non-refundable once placed and that deposits are applied to those items. Keep signed approvals for each selection, since they are your best evidence.

estimate.intro: Decorators send a proposal or estimate after an initial consultation and before any contract is signed. Clients usually compare the design fee, the product budget, and how much of the work you handle versus what they handle themselves. A clear quote separates what you charge for design from what the furnishings will cost.

scopeChecklist.why: A living room and adjoining dining nook can easily be treated as one or two rooms. Naming the spaces avoids disagreement about what the fee covers.
List concept boards, floor plans, shopping lists, paint schedules, and any renderings so the client knows what they get at each stage.
Unlimited revisions erode your margin. State how many rounds are included and the hourly rate for more.

scopeChecklist.item: Product budget range and who purchases
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether you place orders, the client does, or both, and whether your fee is separate from product costs.
Clients should know whether they pay retail, trade, or trade plus a fee, to avoid trust issues later.
State who coordinates delivery, assembly, hanging art, and styling, and whether those are billed separately.
Lead times for furniture can run 8 to 16 weeks. Spell out that delays in approvals push back installation dates.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as e-design, design plus shopping list, and full-service with procurement. Clients can choose their level of involvement and you avoid a simple yes or no.

pricingTips.title: Estimate a product budget range, not a fixed number
pricingTips.body: Product prices change by the time you order. Give a range with a reasonable allowance and say the final figure depends on selections.

pricingTips.title: Price from your hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for planning, sourcing, meetings, and installation, then add a buffer of 15 to 20 percent. Convert to a flat fee only if the number still pays your target rate.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Furniture prices and your own schedule change. A 14 to 30 day validity period keeps the quote from sitting open indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Many decorators charge a consultation fee of $100 to $350 and credit it toward the project if the client signs. This filters out casual inquiries and pays for the site visit.

faqs.question: How detailed should a decorating estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to show rooms, deliverables, fee structure, and product budget range. You do not need to list every furnishing item before design starts, but you should explain how products will be priced.

faqs.question: What happens if the project grows after the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a change clause stating that added rooms, major design changes, or new scope are billed at your hourly rate or a revised fee, and get the change approved in writing.

interior-designer.intro: Interior designers plan and furnish residential and commercial spaces, from a single room refresh to a full renovation. They bill for design time, concept and drawing packages, product sourcing and purchasing, and project management through install day. Most are solo or run small studios, and their invoices often mix professional fees with client-owned furniture and materials purchases.
interior-designer.pricingModel: Interior designers use several models, and many combine them. Hourly billing is common for consultations, small projects, and add-on work. Flat fees are used for defined deliverables such as a room design package, a space plan, or an e-design service, often priced per room. Full-service projects are sometimes billed as a percentage of the total project cost (often 10-30%) or as a flat fee split into phases such as concept, design development, and procurement. Product is handled either by charging clients retail with a trade discount kept as markup, by charging cost plus a procurement fee (often 15-35%), or by billing a separate purchasing fee. Whatever the mix, keep design fees and product purchases on separate lines. Many designers collect a retainer up front and require full payment for furnishings before placing orders.

items.description: Living room design: concept board, space plan, and furniture selections (Phase 1, 50% of $4,800 flat fee)
Sourcing visits to showrooms and trade vendors
Custom drapery and window treatment specification and measurements
Procurement fee on furnishings ordered (25% of $9,200 product total)
Fabric and finish samples, shipping and courier

sampleInvoice.notes: Furniture and materials are invoiced separately on purchase orders and require 100% payment before ordering. Payment due within 14 days. Custom and special-order items are non-cancellable and non-refundable once ordered. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to overdue balances.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, room or area, and phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Design projects run for months in phases, and clients need to match each invoice to the stage of work and the original proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design fees listed separately from product and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating professional services from furniture purchases avoids confusion and may matter for sales tax, since many states tax goods but treat design services differently. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or item list with vendor, SKU, finish, and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Clear item details prevent disputes when a fabric, finish, or size arrives and the client says it is not what they approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax and resale certificate information
invoiceChecklist.why: If you buy product wholesale for resale to clients, you generally need a resale certificate, and you may need to collect sales tax on the items. Rules vary by state.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping, freight, white-glove delivery, and storage charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Freight and warehouse fees can be large on furniture orders and should be itemized so they are not mistaken for markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit applied and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how prior payments reduce the current amount, which matters on long projects with several invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and return terms for custom orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom upholstery, rugs, and window treatments are usually non-returnable, and restating this on the invoice protects you if a client changes their mind.

interior-designer.paymentTerms: Most designers collect a retainer or first-phase payment before starting, commonly 25-50% of the design fee or a flat amount such as $1,000-5,000 for larger projects. Design fees are then billed at phase milestones or monthly. Furniture and materials are typically paid in full, or at least 50% for large orders, before the designer places purchase orders, since many vendors require payment up front for custom goods. Invoices for design time are commonly due in 7-14 days. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract. Clients usually pay by check, ACH, or credit card; if you accept cards, decide whether to pass processing fees on to the client on large product purchases, and confirm that is allowed in your state.

tips.title: Require payment before ordering product
tips.body: Never place a custom order on your own credit. Get full payment, or at minimum a large deposit, before the purchase order goes out. A client who walks away from a custom sofa leaves you holding the cost.

tips.title: Keep fees and product on separate invoices
tips.body: Send a design fee invoice and a separate product invoice or purchase order. It keeps your income clear, simplifies sales tax handling, and prevents a large furniture total from hiding what your time is worth.

tips.title: Track time even on flat-fee projects
tips.body: Log hours against each project. Revisions, extra meetings, and added rooms creep in. Records let you bill additional work at your hourly rate and help you price future flat fees realistically.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: State how many rounds of changes are included in each phase, such as two revisions to the concept board. Bill extra rounds hourly so the scope does not expand without payment.

tips.title: Be open about markup
tips.body: Decide whether you charge retail, cost plus, or a separate fee, and state it in the agreement. Clients who understand the structure at the start rarely question it at invoice time.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for consultations, small or uncertain projects, and add-on work. Use flat fees when the scope is clear, such as a room design package. Many designers use a flat fee for design and bill procurement and project management separately.

faqs.question: How do I bill for furniture and materials I purchase for a client?
faqs.answer: Either invoice the client for the items at retail price, which includes your markup, or bill at cost and add a procurement fee. Itemize each product with vendor and item details, and collect payment before ordering.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax the sale of furniture and goods, and some also tax design services or the design portion of a bundled sale. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant, and itemize fees and product separately.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay for custom items after they arrive?
faqs.answer: Your contract and invoice should state that custom items are non-refundable and that you may hold delivery until paid. Getting paid before ordering avoids most of this problem. If it happens, follow your contract terms and consider demand letters or small claims court.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent shopping and driving?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many designers bill sourcing, showroom visits, and site visits at their hourly rate, and some charge a reduced rate or mileage for travel. Spell this out before the project starts.

estimate.intro: Interior designers send a proposal or estimate after an initial consultation and before any design work begins. Clients usually compare the fee structure, the deliverables, and how product costs are handled, not just the bottom line. A clear proposal also doubles as the basis for your agreement.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming each space prevents a client from assuming the hallway or adjoining room is part of a single-room price.
Concept boards, floor plans, elevations, 3D renderings, and shopping lists take different amounts of time, and clients should know which they receive.
Limits open-ended changes and gives you a basis to bill extra rounds.

scopeChecklist.item: Product budget and who approves purchases
scopeChecklist.why: A stated budget range sets expectations, and written approval before each order protects you from disputes over spending.
State whether you charge retail, cost plus, or a procurement fee so markup is never a surprise.
Lead times for custom furniture can run 12-20 weeks, and delays in client decisions should not become your liability.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as contractors, permits, and architectural drawings
scopeChecklist.why: Makes clear that construction, trades, and engineering are separate from design fees unless you are coordinating them.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours before choosing a flat fee
pricingTips.body: List every phase, estimate the hours for each, then multiply by your rate and add a buffer. This gives a flat fee that reflects the real work, including meetings, sourcing, and revisions.

pricingTips.title: Present packages for different budgets
pricingTips.body: Offer tiers such as e-design, design plus shopping list, and full-service with procurement and installation. Clients can choose their level of involvement, and you avoid being compared on price alone.

pricingTips.title: Give product budgets as ranges
pricingTips.body: Furniture prices change and clients revise their taste. Quote product as an allowance or range and finalize costs through approved purchase orders.

pricingTips.title: Set a short validity window
pricingTips.body: Pricing from vendors and your own availability change. Stating that the proposal is valid for 14-30 days encourages a decision and keeps you from honoring outdated terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many designers do, often $100-250 per hour or a flat fee that is credited toward the project if the client signs. A paid consultation filters out people who are not ready to hire and values your time.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed quote for a full-service project?
faqs.answer: You can, but only if the scope and number of rooms are well defined. Many designers quote the design fee as fixed and keep product and project management as separate, estimated or hourly items.

faqs.question: What happens if the project grows after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Your proposal should say that work outside the stated scope is billed hourly or through a written change order. Raise it as soon as you notice, and get approval in writing before doing the additional work.

faqs.question: Is an estimate legally binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on how it is written and your state. A signed proposal that includes terms and acceptance generally works as a contract, while a rough estimate may not. Use language that says whether the figures are fixed or estimated, and have a lawyer review your template.

interior-stylist.intro: Interior stylists arrange furniture, decor, art, textiles, and accessories to make a space look finished and photograph well. Clients include homeowners, real estate agents, short-term rental hosts, builders, furniture retailers, and photographers. Invoices usually cover styling time, shopping or sourcing, purchased or rented items, delivery, and installation.
interior-stylist.pricingModel: Most interior stylists bill hourly for consultations and on-site styling, or a flat fee per room or project once the scope is clear. Home staging for listings is often priced as a flat fee for a set rental period (commonly 30 to 90 days) plus a monthly extension fee. Shopping and sourcing is billed by the hour or as a percentage of the purchase, and many stylists pass through retail items at cost plus a markup of 10 to 30 percent, or at trade discount with the markup disclosed. Editorial and commercial shoot styling is usually a day rate with a separate prop budget. Set a minimum project fee so small jobs still cover travel and prep. Bill prop rentals, delivery, storage, and pickup as their own lines so they are not lost in the styling fee.

rates.service: Single room styling (using client's existing items)
Home staging for a listing (furniture and decor rental)
Photo shoot styling (editorial, retail, or listing)
Prop and decor delivery and pickup

items.description: Initial on-site consultation and measurements, living room and dining room
Shopping and sourcing: pillows, throw, art, and accessories (2 store trips plus online)
On-site styling and installation, living room and dining room
Purchased decor at cost (receipts attached)
Markup on purchased decor (20%)
Delivery and pickup of rented accessories

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Purchased items are the client's property once paid for. Returns accepted within 14 days if tags are attached; a 15% restocking charge applies to returned items. Rented accessories are due back by the date listed on the rental agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address and rooms styled
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several properties or agents with multiple listings need to match each invoice to a specific space.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for time, purchased items, rentals, and delivery
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients will question a single lump sum, and separate lines make it clear what is a service and what is a product.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized product list with cost and markup
invoiceChecklist.why: If you buy on the client's behalf, they expect to see what was bought, and your markup should match what you agreed to in writing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental period start and end dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Staging and prop rentals are billed by period, and extension fees need a clear start date to be enforceable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on products
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax tangible goods you sell, while services may or may not be taxed. Show the tax separately and check your state's rules and resale certificate requirements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return, damage, and restocking terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Staged furniture and decor can be damaged or kept, so state who is responsible and what happens if items are not returned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit already paid and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most styling jobs take a deposit up front, and the invoice should show it credited against the total.

interior-stylist.paymentTerms: Most interior stylists take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent before starting, and require full payment of product purchases up front or on a client-approved shopping list, so they are not floating retail costs. Consultations are usually paid at booking. Staging is often billed monthly in advance, with the first month due before installation. Final balances on one-time styling projects are commonly due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your agreement. Clients typically pay by card, ACH transfer, or check. Card payments are convenient for large product purchases but carry processing fees you may want to build into your pricing.

tips.title: Charge clients directly for purchases
tips.body: Have clients pay retailers directly, give you a deposit for purchases, or pay before you order. Putting thousands of dollars of decor on your own card until the client pays creates risk, especially for custom or non-returnable items.

tips.title: Track and bill prep time
tips.body: Shopping, loading the car, steaming linens, and returning items take real hours that clients do not see. Log them and bill them, or build them into a flat fee that assumes them.

tips.title: Put a minimum on short jobs
tips.body: A two-hour shelf styling job can turn into five hours with travel and parking. A minimum visit fee or a half-day minimum protects your time.

tips.title: Document the before and after
tips.body: Take dated photos at install and again at pickup for staging jobs. They help with damage disputes and also serve as portfolio material, if the client agrees to it in writing.

tips.title: Charge for revisions and extra trips
tips.body: State how many rounds of changes are included, and bill additional shopping rounds or reinstalls at your hourly rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for styling?
faqs.answer: Hourly works well when scope is unclear, such as shopping or open-ended consulting. Flat fees work better for defined jobs like styling one room or staging a listing, as long as you account for prep, shopping, and travel. If you quote a flat fee, state the number of rooms, visits, and revisions it covers.

faqs.question: How do I bill for items I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: List each purchase or a clear category total on the invoice, attach receipts, and show your markup as a separate line or built into the price as agreed. Whichever method you use, tell the client before you purchase. If you use a trade discount, say whether you pass the savings on or keep them.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on styling services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax the sale of physical goods, and a few tax certain design services, while others do not tax services at all. Products you sell to a client are generally taxable, so check with your state tax agency or an accountant about both products and services.

faqs.question: How do I price staging when a house does not sell in the first term?
faqs.answer: Include a monthly extension rate in your staging agreement, often the same as or slightly lower than the initial monthly fee. Invoice it automatically at the end of the term unless the client gives notice, and state the minimum notice needed to end the rental.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to keep staged pieces?
faqs.answer: Put a buyout option in your agreement. Invoice the item at an agreed retail or depreciated price, subtract any rental already paid if you offer that, and add sales tax where required. Get the change confirmed in writing before you invoice.

estimate.intro: Interior stylists send estimates before a consultation turns into a project, and again before a staging or shoot is booked. Clients often compare you to other stylists, stagers, or the design service of a furniture store, so the estimate needs to show clearly what is included. Product budgets and styling fees should be quoted separately.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume an entryway or hallway is part of a living room job. Naming each space prevents scope creep.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of site visits and shopping trips
scopeChecklist.why: Shopping and installation are where time overruns happen, so state how many trips are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Product budget and who pays for purchases
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the client pays retailers directly or reimburses you, and whether the budget is a cap or an estimate.
Clients get upset if they discover a markup they did not agree to, so state it up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Rental items, period, and extension fees
scopeChecklist.why: For staging, name the rental term, what happens at renewal, and the fee for damaged or missing pieces.
A clear number of included revisions and a target install date keeps projects from dragging on.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as painting, hanging, assembly, or hauling
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may assume you handle hands-on labor. List what is not included, or price it as an add-on.

pricingTips.title: Quote styling fees and product budget separately
pricingTips.body: Show your professional fee on one line and the decor budget on another. This keeps your fee from looking inflated by purchases and makes it easy to adjust one without the other.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for staging
pricingTips.body: Offer a partial option that uses the client's furniture with accent pieces, and a full option with rented furniture. Clients can choose based on budget, and the options anchor the price of the full service.

pricingTips.title: Build in prep and return time
pricingTips.body: When pricing flat fees, count the hours spent loading, steaming, shopping, returning, and traveling, not just time on site. Underquoting those is the most common cause of low margins.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Retail prices, rental inventory, and your calendar change. A 14 to 30 day quote validity protects you from honoring old prices.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Many stylists charge a consultation fee of $100 to $300 that covers the walkthrough and a written proposal, and credit it toward the project if the client books. Free quotes are common for simple staging jobs but cost you travel and time.

faqs.question: How detailed should a product budget be in an estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a budget by room or category, such as textiles, art, lighting, and accessories, rather than listing every item. Note that final selections may vary within the budget and that the client approves purchases above a set amount.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client approves the estimate?
faqs.answer: Only for changes outside the agreed scope, such as added rooms, extra revisions, or a price increase on items a client chose. Write a short change order and get approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for with an estimate?
faqs.answer: A 25 to 50 percent deposit on the styling fee is typical, and purchases are usually funded before ordering. Staging first-month fees are often due before installation, so state this in the estimate.

interpreter.intro: Freelance and small-agency interpreters bill for spoken-language work in settings like medical appointments, courtrooms, depositions, conferences, business meetings, and remote video or phone sessions. Invoices usually go to a language services agency, a law firm, a hospital or clinic, a court, a school district, or a corporate client, and they cover time on assignment plus related charges such as travel and cancellations.
interpreter.pricingModel: Most interpreters charge by the hour with a minimum booking, commonly two hours for in-person work and often one hour for remote work. Conference and simultaneous interpreting is usually priced by the half day or full day, because it requires preparation and a team of two. Rates rise for rare language pairs, certified or credentialed work (court, medical, ASL with certification), after-hours or rush bookings, and specialized subject matter. Many interpreters add portal time, travel time at a reduced hourly rate or flat fee, mileage, and parking. Late cancellation fees are standard, typically charging the minimum or a percentage of the booked time if the client cancels within 24 to 48 hours. Agency work often pays less than direct client work but brings steadier volume, and agencies set their own rate sheets and payment cycles. Translation of documents is a separate service priced per word or per page.

rates.service: Medical or community interpreting (in person, Spanish)
Legal or court interpreting (certified, deposition or hearing)
Travel time beyond a set radius

items.description: Spanish/English deposition interpreting, Smith v. Delgado Logistics, 3/12, 9:00 AM-1:30 PM (2-hour minimum met; 4.5 hours billed)
Preparation time, case glossary and witness document review
Travel time, round trip (beyond 30-mile radius)
Mileage, 74 miles round trip
Parking, downtown garage (receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month. Cancellations with less than 48 hours' notice are billed at the 2-hour minimum. Please reference the case number on your payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, start time, end time, and total billed hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and agencies check billed time against their own records, and disputes usually come down to a 15-minute difference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Assignment location or platform, and client reference or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and courts often cannot process payment without a job ID, case number, or purchase order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Language pair and type of interpreting (consecutive, simultaneous, sight translation)
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by mode and language, so stating it justifies the rate on the line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Credentials relevant to the job (court certification, CMI or CHI, RID number)
invoiceChecklist.why: Certified work carries a higher rate and some clients need the credential on file for compliance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimums, travel, mileage, and parking as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating them shows what is time and what is reimbursement, and makes receipts easy to match.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show charge, with the date notice was received
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellation fees are often questioned, so the booking terms and notice time should be clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your tax ID or W-9 status, and remit-to information
invoiceChecklist.why: Many agencies and government clients require a W-9 before paying, and a clear payee name avoids misdirected checks.

interpreter.paymentTerms: Direct clients such as law firms and businesses usually pay net 15 to net 30, and some interpreters require a deposit or prepayment for large conference bookings, often 25 to 50 percent. Agencies commonly pay net 30 to net 60 and may pay on a fixed monthly cycle, so check their terms before accepting work. Courts and government bodies often follow their own voucher or claim process and can take longer. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Typical payment methods are ACH, check, and card, and some interpreters add a small surcharge for card payments where allowed.

tips.title: State your minimum and cancellation policy before the job
tips.body: Put the two-hour minimum, travel rules, and cancellation window in your booking confirmation or contract. It is much easier to collect a cancellation fee that the client agreed to in writing.

tips.title: Bill preparation separately for complex assignments
tips.body: Depositions, technical conferences, and medical specialties often require hours of glossary building and document review. List prep time as its own line so it is not treated as free.

tips.title: Track actual start and end times
tips.body: Assignments often run over or start late. Note arrival time, start, and end in your calendar the same day so you can bill overage accurately and answer questions later.

tips.title: Know each agency's invoicing rules
tips.body: Some agencies require you to submit through a portal, within a set number of days, or on their own form. Missing their window can delay payment by a full cycle.

tips.title: Set aside money for taxes
tips.body: Independent interpreters are typically self-employed and owe self-employment tax in addition to income tax. Many put aside 25 to 30 percent of each payment and make quarterly estimated payments, but check with a tax professional for your situation.

faqs.question: Should I charge a minimum for short assignments?
faqs.answer: Yes. A one-hour appointment still takes travel, waiting, and a blocked-out window of your day. Two hours is a common in-person minimum, and one hour is common for remote work. State it on your rate sheet and invoice.

faqs.question: Can I bill for travel time and mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you agree to it ahead of time. Many interpreters bill travel time at a reduced hourly rate or a flat fee, plus mileage at or near the IRS standard rate. Some agencies do not pay travel, so confirm before accepting.

faqs.question: How do I charge when a client cancels at the last minute?
