faqs.answer: Follow the cancellation policy you gave the client in advance. A common policy bills the full minimum, or a percentage of the booked time, if notice is under 24 to 48 hours. List it as its own line with the cancellation date.

faqs.question: Do I charge per hour or per day for conferences?
faqs.answer: Conference interpreters usually charge a half-day or full-day rate, since the work involves preparation and a team of two alternating. Quote the rate per interpreter and say what hours a day covers and what overtime costs.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice to an agency or just report hours?
faqs.answer: It depends on the agency. Some pay from hours you submit in a portal, while others need a formal invoice with your name, address, and tax information. Ask for their process when you onboard.

estimate.intro: Interpreters send quotes when a client books a multi-hour or multi-day assignment, such as a deposition, a conference, a hospital series of appointments, or an event. Clients compare hourly rates, minimums, and extra charges like travel, prep, and equipment, so the quote should show all of them.

scopeChecklist.item: Language pair, dialect, and mode of interpreting
scopeChecklist.why: Consecutive, simultaneous, and sight translation are priced differently, and a dialect mismatch can lead to a dispute about whether you were the right fit.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, start time, expected duration, and location or platform
scopeChecklist.why: The quote depends on the length of the booking, and a change in the schedule or format should trigger a revised price.

scopeChecklist.item: Billable minimum and what happens past the booked time
scopeChecklist.why: Assignments often run long, so stating the overtime rate and increments prevents arguments afterward.

scopeChecklist.item: Preparation materials the client must provide and by when
scopeChecklist.why: You cannot prepare without agendas, slides, or case documents, and late materials can affect quality and pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, parking, and lodging terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether these are included, estimated, or billed at cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Team size and equipment for simultaneous work
scopeChecklist.why: Simultaneous interpreting normally needs two interpreters per language and booth or headset equipment, which affects the total cost.
Written terms agreed at the quote stage make a late-cancellation charge much easier to enforce.

pricingTips.title: Quote by the hour for short work and by the day for long events
pricingTips.body: Hourly with a minimum suits appointments and depositions. For conferences, a half-day or full-day rate is cleaner and reflects the prep and fatigue involved.

pricingTips.title: Build in preparation time
pricingTips.body: Technical or legal assignments need research. Either add a prep line or build it into the rate, and tell the client which approach you used.

pricingTips.title: Charge more for rush and unusual languages
pricingTips.body: Short-notice bookings, evenings, weekends, and rare language pairs justify a higher rate because fewer people can do the work and your schedule is disrupted.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date
pricingTips.body: Rates and availability change, so state how long the quote holds, for example 14 days, and that the booking is confirmed only when the client accepts in writing.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: For single appointments and depositions, an hourly rate with a minimum and an estimated duration works well. For conferences and multi-day events, a flat day rate is more common.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a booking?
faqs.answer: It is common for large or multi-day jobs, often 25 to 50 percent, especially with new direct clients. For repeat clients and agencies, deposits are less common.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Adjust the scope rather than only the rate. Options include a shorter booking, remote instead of in person, or sending prep materials earlier. Avoid dropping your rate while keeping the same workload.

irrigation-installer.intro: Irrigation installers put in, repair, and winterize underground sprinkler and drip systems for homeowners, HOAs, builders, and commercial properties. Invoices usually cover a new system install, add-on zones, backflow devices, controller or smart timer upgrades, seasonal service calls, and repairs billed by the hour plus parts.
irrigation-installer.pricingModel: New installs are most often priced per zone or as a flat fee for the whole system, built up from a count of zones, heads, valves, pipe footage, trenching, controller, and backflow preventer. Residential lawns commonly come out to a total per zone, while larger or commercial jobs are bid per head or per square foot of coverage. Repairs and service calls are usually billed as a trip charge or minimum (often covering the first half hour to hour) plus labor by the hour and parts at cost plus markup, typically 15 to 40 percent. Seasonal work such as spring start-ups and fall blowouts is a flat fee per visit, sometimes scaled by zone count. Drip conversions and landscape bed irrigation are priced per zone or per linear foot of tubing. Permits, utility locates, rock or heavy clay surcharges, and sod or landscape restoration are listed as separate lines so they do not get buried in the base price.

rates.service: Add a zone to an existing system

items.description: Install 6-zone residential system: trenching, 1" poly mainline and lateral pipe, 28 rotor and spray heads, 6 valves in manifold box
Reduced pressure backflow preventer, supplied and installed with test
Wi-Fi smart controller, supplied and mounted in garage
Drip line for front shrub bed, tie-in to new valve
Rock excavation surcharge, back lawn trench section
Permit fee, passed through at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: 50% deposit of $3,060 received at contract signing. Balance due on completion and walkthrough. Net 10. Late balances charged 1.5% per month. One-year warranty on parts and labor for installed components. Controller schedule programmed and reviewed with owner.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require a license number on contracts and invoices, and the permit number shows the work was inspected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Zone-by-zone description of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the number of zones, heads, valves, and pipe type lets the client verify what was installed and helps with future service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Backflow device make, model, serial number, and test date
invoiceChecklist.why: Many water utilities require backflow preventers to be tested and registered, and the serial number links your work to that record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute lump sums less when parts like valves, controllers, and pipe are itemized and markup is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and surcharges
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, roots, buried utilities, or added zones discovered mid-job should be listed with dates so they match approved changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing payments already made against the contract total avoids confusion on the remaining balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and start-up or winterization notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating what is covered and for how long, plus any required annual blowout, protects you from freeze damage claims.

irrigation-installer.paymentTerms: For installs, a deposit of 30 to 50 percent at signing is common, covering materials and scheduling, with the balance due at completion or after a final walkthrough. Larger jobs may use progress payments tied to milestones such as trenching and pipe complete, then heads and controller. Repairs and seasonal visits are usually due on completion or net 7 to 15 days. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. Most installers accept checks, ACH, and cards, and some pass along card fees on large invoices where state rules allow. Commercial and HOA clients often pay net 30 and may require a PO number and lien waiver paperwork.

tips.title: Bill rock and root work separately
tips.body: Soil conditions are the biggest source of overruns. Put a per-hour or per-foot rate for rock, caliche, or heavy roots in your contract, then bill the actual time as its own line.

tips.title: Mark up parts and say so
tips.body: Valves, solenoids, heads, and controllers take time to source and you warrant them. A consistent markup on parts, shown on the invoice, is normal and easier to defend than a hidden padded labor rate.

tips.title: Set a trip charge minimum
tips.body: Short repairs like a broken head can eat an hour once you count driving. A minimum call-out fee that includes the first portion of labor keeps small jobs profitable.

tips.title: Offer seasonal service plans
tips.body: Bundling spring start-up, mid-season check, and fall blowout at a set annual price gives steady revenue in slow months and is simple to invoice every year.

tips.title: Get final payment at the walkthrough
tips.body: Program the controller and show the client the zones working before you leave. Collecting the balance while they see the finished system reduces later disputes over coverage.

faqs.question: Should I charge per zone or per hour for a new install?
faqs.answer: Per zone or a flat bid is most common for new systems because clients want a fixed number. Hourly billing works better for repairs, troubleshooting, and jobs with unknown conditions like older systems or heavy rock.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit before ordering materials?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is standard. Many states cap deposits on home improvement contracts or require specific contract language, so check your state's contractor rules before setting the percentage.

faqs.question: Do I bill sales tax on irrigation work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials only, some tax labor on certain work, and some treat installs as real property improvements with different rules. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a freeze-damaged repair if I did the original install?
faqs.answer: Review your warranty terms. Freeze damage from a system that was not winterized is usually excluded, so bill labor and parts at normal rates and note the cause on the invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do about a client who will not pay the final balance?
faqs.answer: Send the invoice with the contract and walkthrough sign-off attached, then follow up in writing. In many states contractors can file a mechanic's lien within a set window, so know your deadlines and notice requirements early.

estimate.intro: Irrigation installers quote before almost every install, zone addition, and major repair. Homeowners often collect two or three bids and compare the zone count, brand of components, backflow and controller choices, and warranty, so a clear written scope matters more than the lowest number.

scopeChecklist.item: Zone count, head types, and coverage areas
scopeChecklist.why: Rotors, sprays, and drip serve different areas. Writing down what is included prevents arguments about a missed corner or flower bed.

scopeChecklist.item: Pipe type, size, and mainline route
scopeChecklist.why: PVC versus poly pipe and 1 inch versus 1.25 inch mainline change cost and performance, and clients should know what goes in the ground.
Naming valves, heads, controller, and backflow device lets clients compare bids fairly and avoids substitution disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Water source, meter, and pressure assumptions
scopeChecklist.why: If the design depends on a certain flow or pressure, state it. Low pressure or an undersized meter can change the number of zones per valve.
State who pulls the permit and who pays for it, and note the time needed for a 811 locate before digging.
Say whether trenches will be raked and seeded, sod replaced, or left for the client. Lawn repair is a common complaint.
Rock, buried debris, existing unmarked lines, and private utilities not located by 811 should be listed with how added work will be priced.

pricingTips.title: Measure and design before you price
pricingTips.body: Walk the property, note pressure at the hose bib, and sketch zones. A quote based on a real layout is more accurate than a rule-of-thumb per-zone number, and it shows the client you did the work.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present a base system, a version with a smart controller and rain sensor, and one with drip beds added. Clients often choose the middle tier when it is laid out side by side.

pricingTips.title: Build in a materials price buffer
pricingTips.body: Pipe, fittings, and valve prices move. Put a validity period of 15 to 30 days on the quote and state that pricing may change after that.

pricingTips.title: State the unit price for extras
pricingTips.body: List what an added zone, extra head, or hour of rock work costs. Clients accept change orders more easily when they saw the rate up front.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are common for standard residential installs. For complex designs, commercial plans, or large properties, many installers charge a design fee and credit it toward the job if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is typical. Material costs and your schedule can change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is an estimate the same as a fixed bid?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Say clearly whether your number is a fixed price or an estimate that can change with conditions. A fixed bid with listed exclusions and unit prices for extras is the cleanest approach.

faqs.question: What should I include if the client wants to keep part of an old system?
faqs.answer: Inspect what you can and write down which parts you are reusing. State that you are not warranting existing pipe, valves, or heads, and quote repair of hidden problems as extra work.

it-consultant.intro: IT consultants advise and support small businesses, nonprofits, and sometimes larger organizations on networks, cloud services, security, hardware, and software. They invoice for hourly support, project work like office moves or Microsoft 365 migrations, monthly managed service agreements, and pass-through costs like licenses and equipment.
it-consultant.pricingModel: Most solo and small-shop IT consultants use a mix of models. Hourly billing is common for break-fix work, troubleshooting, and advisory time, often with a minimum block such as one hour or a half-day onsite. Projects like server replacements, network buildouts, or cloud migrations are usually quoted as a flat fee based on estimated hours plus a buffer. Ongoing support is often sold as a monthly retainer or managed services agreement, priced per user, per device, or as a block of included hours. Hardware, software licenses, and subscriptions are billed separately, either at cost or with a markup (commonly 10-30%) and listed as their own line items. After-hours, emergency, and travel time often carry a premium or a separate trip charge.

rates.service: Project work (migrations, network setup, security hardening)
Monthly retainer for a block of support hours

items.description: Microsoft 365 tenant migration: 12 mailboxes, SharePoint setup, MFA enrollment
Onsite workstation setup and Outlook profile configuration (6 workstations)
Microsoft 365 Business Premium licenses, first month (resold)
Firewall replacement: hardware (Fortinet 60F with 1-year support bundle)
Firewall configuration, VPN setup, and cutover (after hours)
Travel / trip charge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hardware remains covered by manufacturer warranty; license renewals are billed annually on the anniversary date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Please reference invoice number on ACH or check payments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service and tech name
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several people calling for help, and dated entries make it easy to match the bill to tickets and resolve questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ticket or work order numbers with a short description of each task
invoiceChecklist.why: Vague lines like 'IT support' invite disputes. Tying time to a ticket shows what was fixed and why it took the time it did.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by rate type (remote, onsite, after-hours, project)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different rates apply to different work, and clients need to see the correct rate was used for each block.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hardware and software itemized with make, model, quantity, and serial numbers where useful
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need the records for warranty claims, asset tracking, and depreciation. It also separates product costs from labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subscription and license details: product, seat count, term, and renewal date
invoiceChecklist.why: Resold licenses recur. Listing the term avoids confusion when a renewal charge shows up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Managed services agreement reference and included versus out-of-scope hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the monthly fee covered and why additional time is billed separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number and sales tax status
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients and nonprofits often require a PO to pay. Tax treatment of hardware, software, and services varies by state, so show tax or exemption clearly.

it-consultant.paymentTerms: IT consultants commonly bill managed services and retainers monthly in advance, and hourly work monthly in arrears or on completion of a ticket batch. Net 15 or Net 30 is standard; net 15 is easier for small clients. For projects, a deposit of 25-50% is typical, and hardware is often paid in full upfront or by deposit since the consultant is fronting the cost. Many consultants charge a late fee of 1-1.5% per month and reserve the right to pause support or remote access on seriously overdue accounts, if the contract allows it. ACH and credit card are the most common payment methods, with card fees sometimes passed through on large invoices.

tips.title: Put a minimum on small calls
tips.body: A 15-minute fix still costs you the context switch and travel. Set a minimum such as 30 or 60 minutes for remote and a two-hour minimum for onsite, and state it in your agreement.

tips.title: Bill hardware separately and take payment upfront
tips.body: Do not carry thousands of dollars in equipment on your own credit. Collect a deposit or full payment before ordering, and list each item as its own line so the markup is clear.

tips.title: Track recurring renewals
tips.body: Domain names, SSL certificates, backup subscriptions, and licenses renew on different dates. Keep a renewal calendar and bill on a schedule so you are not covering costs out of pocket.

tips.title: Define scope in your service agreement
tips.body: Spell out what a monthly fee covers, response times, and what counts as a project. Anything outside scope gets billed at your hourly rate with prior approval.

tips.title: Document every change
tips.body: Admin credentials, config changes, and who approved what protect you if something breaks later. Attach a short work summary to invoices for larger projects.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat fee for IT projects?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended troubleshooting and ongoing support. Use a flat fee for projects with a clear scope, like a migration for a set number of users, and build in a buffer for surprises. If the scope is unclear, bill hourly with a not-to-exceed estimate.

faqs.question: Can I mark up hardware and software I buy for clients?
faqs.answer: Yes, most consultants do, typically 10-30% on hardware and licenses, since they handle sourcing, configuration, warranty, and the risk. Be upfront about it in your agreement, and show products as separate lines from labor.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on IT services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Hardware is generally taxable, but treatment of software, SaaS, and consulting labor varies widely. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional, and show tax as its own line if you collect it.

faqs.question: How do I bill for time spent on travel?
faqs.answer: Most consultants either charge a flat trip fee or bill travel time at a reduced hourly rate. Mileage can be added at a set per-mile rate. Whatever you choose, put it in your agreement and itemize it on the invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do when a client does not pay a monthly support invoice?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder at the due date, then follow up again at 15 days. If your agreement allows it, give written notice and suspend non-emergency support until the balance is paid. Make sure you keep a copy of the agreement and the invoice history.

estimate.intro: IT consultants send estimates before projects such as network buildouts, server or cloud migrations, security assessments, and new managed service agreements. Clients usually compare total cost, scope, timeline, and who is responsible for hardware and licensing, and they often get multiple quotes.

scopeChecklist.why: State the number of users, devices, locations, and servers. Cost changes quickly if the count grows from 10 to 15 users mid-project.
Define the end state, such as all mailboxes migrated and tested, so the client cannot keep adding requests under the same price.

scopeChecklist.item: Hardware and software costs, and who owns them
scopeChecklist.why: List equipment and licenses separately from labor, with model numbers and whether prices are quoted or estimated, since vendor pricing changes.
Admin credentials, vendor contacts, building access, and approvals can delay work. Spell out what the client must provide and by when.
Cutovers often happen on nights or weekends at a higher rate. Clients need to know when systems will be offline.
Issues with an ISP, line-of-business software vendor, or old equipment can derail a project. List what is not included, such as data cleanup or application vendor support.

scopeChecklist.item: Change order process and quote validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Explain how extra work is approved and billed, and how long the quote is valid, since hardware prices and your availability can change.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours by task, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the project into discovery, setup, migration, testing, and training. Add 15-25% for unknowns, especially in environments you have not seen before.

pricingTips.title: Charge for discovery or assessment first
pricingTips.body: For unclear environments, quote a paid assessment before a full project price. It protects you from underpricing and gives the client a documented plan.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three tiers of hardware, backup, or support level helps clients choose on features rather than just the lowest number.

pricingTips.title: Show recurring costs next to one-time costs
pricingTips.body: Clients often forget that licenses, backup, and monitoring recur. Separating one-time and monthly totals avoids sticker shock later.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Quick quotes for simple work are usually free. For complex projects that need a site survey or environment review, many consultants charge a fixed assessment fee and credit it toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: Should my quote be fixed-price or an estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed price only when the scope is well understood. Otherwise give an estimate range or a not-to-exceed figure, and state that changes in scope will be handled through written change orders.

faqs.question: How long should an IT quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for labor. Hardware pricing can change faster, so some consultants make equipment quotes valid for 7 to 14 days or note that prices are subject to vendor changes.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, get written acceptance of the quote or a signed statement of work before ordering equipment or touching client systems. It confirms scope, pricing, and access permissions, and many consultants collect a deposit at the same time.

it-services.intro: IT services providers are solo consultants, managed service providers (MSPs), and small shops that support businesses with networks, computers, cloud accounts, security, and help desk needs. Invoices typically cover hourly support, monthly managed service agreements, project work such as migrations or office setups, and hardware or software resold to the client.
it-services.pricingModel: IT work is priced in a few common ways. Break/fix support is billed hourly, often with a minimum such as one hour or a half-day onsite, and a higher rate for after-hours or emergency calls. Managed services are billed monthly, either per user, per device, or as a flat fee for a defined scope, and usually renew automatically. Projects like email migrations, server replacements, or network buildouts are quoted as flat fees or time-and-materials with a cap. Hardware, licenses, and subscriptions are resold with a markup (commonly 10-30% on hardware, less on licenses) or passed through at cost with a separate service fee. Block-of-hours packages sold at a discount are also common. Travel time, mileage, and after-hours multipliers should be priced in rather than negotiated afterward.

rates.service: Network or Wi-Fi installation and configuration

items.description: Managed IT services, March 2025 (12 users, monitoring, patching, help desk)
Onsite support: printer and switch troubleshooting, 3/14
New workstation setup and data transfer (Dell Latitude)
Dell Latitude 5440 laptop (resale)
Microsoft 365 Business Premium licenses, annual prepay
Travel and mileage, onsite visit

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Managed services are billed monthly in advance under the signed service agreement dated 1/1/2025. Hardware carries the manufacturer warranty. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service agreement or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties monthly charges to the signed scope, term, and rates so clients cannot dispute what is covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ticket numbers and dates for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client match each billed hour to a request, which cuts down on questions about time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hardware and software with model, quantity, and serial or license details
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the client an asset record for warranty claims and renewals, and justifies resale pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and user or device count
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-user and per-device agreements change as staff come and go, so show the count you are billing for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate type: standard, after-hours, or project
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why one hour costs more than another and prevents surprises on emergency calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel time and mileage as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps trip charges transparent and consistent with what you agreed to in writing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax treatment and client PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Taxability of services, software, and hardware varies by state, and larger clients often require a PO to pay.

it-services.paymentTerms: Managed service fees are usually billed monthly in advance, due on receipt or net 15. Project work often takes 25-50% down, with the balance at milestones or completion. Hardware is commonly paid in full or at least 50% up front before ordering, since you are carrying the cost. Hourly work is typically net 15 to net 30. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the agreement. Most providers accept ACH, card, and check, and many use ACH autopay for recurring agreements to avoid chasing monthly payments. Some contracts allow suspending non-critical support on seriously overdue accounts.

tips.title: Put recurring work on autopay
tips.body: Monthly agreements are the steadiest income in IT. Get ACH or card authorization at signing so invoices pay themselves and you are not collecting from the same client every month.

tips.title: Collect hardware money first
tips.body: Laptops, firewalls, and servers can cost thousands. Require full or majority payment before ordering so you are not financing a client's equipment, especially for special orders that cannot be returned.

tips.title: Define what is out of scope
tips.body: Managed agreements should state what counts as a project, such as office moves, new server builds, or major migrations, and bill those separately. Otherwise they get absorbed into the flat fee.

tips.title: Track time in small increments
tips.body: Use ticketing or time tracking that logs 15-minute increments. Quick remote fixes add up, and a log of each ticket is your best defense when a client questions a bill.

tips.title: Review pricing annually
tips.body: Vendor licensing costs rise each year. Build a yearly increase clause into agreements and pass through license price changes with notice.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Hourly suits occasional clients with no regular needs. A monthly fee suits clients who want predictable cost and you want predictable revenue. Many providers do both: a flat fee for defined services and discounted hourly rates for projects outside that scope.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on hardware and software?
faqs.answer: Hardware is commonly marked up 10-30%, with lower margins on large orders and higher on small ones. Licenses such as Microsoft 365 often have thin margins, so some providers charge a separate management fee instead. Whatever you choose, apply it consistently and list it on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on IT services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax hardware and software but not labor, some tax certain services, and others tax most digital products. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and keep taxable and non-taxable items on separate lines.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in your agreement or quote. Common approaches are billing travel at a reduced hourly rate, charging a flat trip fee, or including travel within a defined local radius and billing mileage beyond it.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client does not pay a managed services invoice?
faqs.answer: Follow the terms in your agreement. Send a reminder, then a formal notice, and if the contract allows, pause non-critical support until the account is current. Avoid locking a client out of systems in a way that could cause data loss or legal exposure. Get legal advice before taking any step that restricts access.

estimate.intro: IT providers send estimates for projects such as office setups, server or cloud migrations, network upgrades, and new managed service agreements. Clients usually compare your price against other providers, an in-house hire, or a vendor's own services, so clarity about what is included matters as much as the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of users, devices, locations, and systems covered
scopeChecklist.why: Scope and price scale with headcount and equipment, and a wrong count is the most common cause of a quote going over.

scopeChecklist.item: Hardware and software list with model numbers and who owns them
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes about substitutions, price changes, and whether licenses stay with the client or with you.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor estimate by phase, with assumptions
scopeChecklist.why: Splitting out planning, setup, migration, and testing shows where the time goes and makes changes easier to price.
Admin credentials, vendor contacts, and downtime windows are often late. State that delays may affect the schedule and cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Downtime, cutover timing, and after-hours work
scopeChecklist.why: Evening or weekend migrations cost more, and clients should agree to the schedule and the rate before work starts.
Examples are fixing unknown legacy problems, third-party vendor fees, data cleanup, and training. Listing them avoids unpaid extras.
Hardware and license prices change quickly, so say how many days the quote is good for and what happens if a vendor raises prices.

pricingTips.title: Separate labor from hardware and licenses
pricingTips.body: Show them on distinct lines. Clients can compare equipment prices easily, and this keeps your labor value from being judged against retail pricing.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Older networks and undocumented systems cause surprises. Build in 10-20% contingency or quote a discovery phase first, then price the full project after assessing the environment.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three tiers, such as basic firewall, firewall with managed security, and full monitoring, lets the client choose by budget and often raises the average sale.

pricingTips.title: Use time and materials with a cap when scope is unclear
pricingTips.body: If you cannot define the work up front, quote an hourly estimate with a not-to-exceed figure and require approval before going past it.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site assessment or quote?
faqs.answer: Many providers do for larger projects, usually a flat fee of a few hundred dollars up to a couple thousand, often credited toward the project if the client signs. Simple quotes are generally free.

faqs.question: How long should an IT quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is typical. For hardware-heavy quotes, shorter validity or a clause allowing price adjustment protects you from supplier price changes.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change scope after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that describes the added work, its cost, and any schedule impact. Get approval before doing the work, and bill it as a separate line or addendum.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on how you word it. A fixed-price quote is generally a firm commitment for the stated scope, while an estimate can be marked as approximate with a clear process for overages. Label which one you are sending.

janitorial-service.intro: Janitorial businesses clean commercial spaces such as offices, medical suites, schools, gyms, retail stores, and churches, usually on a recurring schedule. Most are solo operators or small crews who bill monthly for routine nightly or weekly cleaning, plus extra charges for floor work, window cleaning, carpet extraction, and supplies.
janitorial-service.pricingModel: Most janitorial work is sold as a flat monthly fee for a defined scope and schedule, for example five nights a week for a 5,000 sq ft office. That fee is built from an hourly labor cost, square footage, how many visits happen per week, and the type of space (medical and restrooms take longer than open offices). Per-square-foot pricing is common for bids and for one-time work like post-construction cleaning. Periodic work such as strip and wax, carpet extraction, pressure washing, and window cleaning is billed separately as a flat fee or per square foot. Supplies like paper goods, liners, and soap are either included in the monthly fee or billed at cost plus a markup of about 10 to 25 percent. Many contracts add annual or fuel-related increases. Hourly billing is used for day porters, special events, and small accounts.

rates.service: Strip and wax vinyl tile floors

items.description: Monthly janitorial service - 4,500 sq ft office, Mon/Wed/Fri evenings (13 visits)
Carpet hot water extraction - main office and conference room
Strip and wax - break room and entry VCT
Restroom supplies (paper towels, toilet tissue, hand soap)
Interior glass - lobby doors and partitions

sampleInvoice.notes: Service period: March 1-31. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month. Extra services were approved by the office manager on March 12. Please report missed areas within 48 hours so we can correct them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location and service period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with multiple sites or monthly billing need to match each invoice to a building and date range.

invoiceChecklist.item: Schedule and number of visits
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the agreed days and the actual visits completed prevents disputes when holidays or closures change the month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized extras separate from the base contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Floor refinishing, carpet extraction, and windows are outside the monthly scope, and listing them separately shows what was added and why.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies and consumables
invoiceChecklist.why: If paper goods and liners are billed, list them so the client can see they are not part of the flat fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or PO number and approver name
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and larger companies often cannot pay without a PO, and a named approver speeds up accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, insurance, and bonding details
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial clients require proof of general liability coverage and bonding, and some local rules require a business license number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states tax janitorial services or supplies while others do not, so check your state rules and show tax separately when it applies.

janitorial-service.paymentTerms: Recurring accounts are usually billed at the start or end of the month with net 15 or net 30 terms, and commercial clients often push for net 30. Ask for the first month in advance or a deposit on new accounts, and require a deposit or half up front for one-time jobs like post-construction cleaning. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if written into the service agreement. ACH or auto-pay is the best fit for monthly accounts, with checks and card payments also common. Put cancellation terms in the contract, typically 30 days written notice.

tips.title: Bill the monthly fee on a fixed amount
tips.body: Charge the same amount each month based on the average number of visits, instead of recalculating for weeks with five or four visits. Clients budget easier and you avoid monthly arguments.

tips.title: Get written approval for extras
tips.body: Strip and wax, carpet cleaning, and window jobs often come up mid-month through a text or a hallway request. Get an email or signed work order before doing them and reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Track supplies by account
tips.body: Paper goods and chemicals add up. Keep a simple log of what you restock at each site and either bill at cost plus markup or build a realistic amount into the base price.

tips.title: Review pricing every year
tips.body: Wages, chemicals, and fuel rise. Include an annual increase clause in your contract and send notice 30 to 60 days before it takes effect.

tips.title: Invoice on a set day
tips.body: Send invoices on the same day each month so the client's accounts payable team knows when to expect them, and follow up the day after the due date.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat monthly rate?
faqs.answer: Flat monthly rates work best for recurring commercial accounts because clients prefer a predictable cost. Use hourly rates for day porters, events, and small or uncertain jobs. Even with a flat rate, calculate your price from the hours the job takes.

faqs.question: How do I bill for supplies like toilet paper and soap?
faqs.answer: Either include them in the monthly fee or list them as a separate line at cost plus 10 to 25 percent. Make it clear in the contract which approach you use so there are no surprises.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client skips a service day?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say whether you bill for visits missed because the building was closed or inaccessible. Many cleaners still charge for scheduled visits with a short notice window, such as 24 hours, to cancel.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on janitorial services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax cleaning services, some tax only supplies or certain types of work, and many do not tax services at all. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel between sites?
faqs.answer: For small jobs or sites far from your base, a trip charge or minimum service fee is reasonable. For regular accounts, most cleaners include travel in the monthly price, so list it only if the contract says to.

estimate.intro: Janitorial quotes are usually requested by office managers, property managers, and business owners comparing several bids for a recurring contract. They compare the monthly price, the tasks included, the days and hours of service, and whether supplies are covered. A walkthrough of the space is normally done before the quote is given.

scopeChecklist.why: Restrooms, kitchens, and hard floors take more time than open office areas, so the quote should say what was measured and counted.
Three nights a week costs very different from five, and the quote should state days and time windows.
List tasks such as trash removal, vacuuming, restroom sanitizing, dusting, and mopping so the client knows what is and is not included.
State what is not covered, like interior windows, moving furniture, biohazards, or cleaning inside refrigerators, to avoid disagreements later.
Clarify whether you provide chemicals, vacuums, liners, and paper goods, and who pays for restroom consumables.
Quote carpet extraction, floor stripping, and window cleaning with their frequency and price so they are not a surprise add-on.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract term, start date, and cancellation notice
scopeChecklist.why: A 30-day cancellation clause and defined start date protect both sides and set expectations for the first month.

pricingTips.title: Start from labor hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours per visit from the walkthrough, multiply by your fully loaded hourly cost including payroll taxes, insurance, and supplies, then add overhead and profit. Check the result against a per-square-foot figure to see if it is in line with the market.

pricingTips.title: Price the first deep clean separately
pricingTips.body: New accounts often need a one-time initial clean because the previous service was poor. Quote this as a separate line instead of absorbing it into the monthly rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer two scope options
pricingTips.body: Giving a basic and a more complete package, such as three nights versus five, lets the client choose based on budget without you cutting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Labor and supply costs change, so state that the quote is valid for 30 days.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a walkthrough or estimate visit?
faqs.answer: Most janitorial companies offer free walkthroughs for recurring commercial accounts. For large or distant sites, or one-time jobs like post-construction cleaning, a small fee that is credited if the client hires you is reasonable.

faqs.question: How firm should my quote be?
faqs.answer: A quote for a defined scope and schedule should be fixed. State that changes in square footage, frequency, or tasks will change the price, and put any adjustment in writing.

faqs.question: How do I compete against lower bids?
faqs.answer: Do not match a price you cannot sustain. Point to your insurance, bonding, reliable staffing, and supervision. Many clients leave low bidders after missed visits and turnover.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: For recurring work, yes. A signed service agreement that includes scope, price, term, payment terms, and cancellation notice is the document you rely on if there is a dispute.

junk-removal.intro: Junk removal businesses haul away unwanted household items, construction debris, yard waste, appliances, and furniture from homes, offices, and job sites. Most are owner-operators or small crews with one or two trucks who bill by the volume of truck space used, plus fees for heavy or special items and disposal.
junk-removal.pricingModel: Most junk removal is priced by volume, measured as a fraction of a truck or in cubic yards. A typical operator quotes a minimum charge, then prices by quarter, half, three-quarter, or full truck load. Special items such as mattresses, TVs, refrigerators, tires, and paint often carry flat per-item surcharges because of recycling or disposal fees. Labor-heavy jobs like stairs, long carries, basement cleanouts, or hoarding situations may add a labor charge or an hourly rate. Dump fees and recycling costs are usually built into the price, but some operators list them separately on larger jobs, especially when billing by weight at the transfer station. Commercial and property-management clients may be billed hourly, per unit turnover, or on a monthly account.

rates.service: Refrigerator, freezer, or AC unit (refrigerant handling)
Hourly labor for cleanouts, stairs, or long carries

items.description: Garage cleanout: half truck load of general household junk
Mattress disposal (queen)
Refrigerator removal (refrigerant recovery required)
Old CRT television recycling fee
Extra labor: second-floor carry-down

sampleInvoice.notes: Service completed 03/14 at 412 Maple Street. Prices include loading, hauling, and disposal fees. Payment due upon completion or within 7 days of invoice date. Cash, check, card, and mobile payment accepted. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to unpaid balances after 30 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date of pickup
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific job and helps resolve disputes about when and where the work happened.

invoiceChecklist.item: Load size used (quarter, half, full, or cubic yards)
invoiceChecklist.why: Volume is the main pricing driver, so the client can see how the total was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized special-disposal charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Mattresses, appliances, TVs, tires, and similar items carry surcharges that clients forget they agreed to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extra labor, stairs, or long-carry charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Explains why a job cost more than the base load price and supports the difference from the original quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dump, recycling, or transfer station fees if billed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing disposal costs as pass-through lines is transparent, and you can attach receipts for large jobs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license number and insurance statement where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers, HOAs, and commercial clients often require proof of licensing and liability coverage before paying.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or work order number for commercial clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and contractors often cannot process payment without a reference number.

junk-removal.paymentTerms: Residential junk removal is usually paid on the day of service, often by card or mobile payment as the crew finishes loading, since the work is a one-time job. Deposits are uncommon for standard pickups but are reasonable for large cleanouts, estate cleanouts, or hoarding jobs that need scheduled crews and multiple trucks, often 25 to 50 percent. Commercial clients, contractors, realtors, and property managers are often billed net 15 or net 30. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common on account customers if stated in writing. Keep a card on file for repeat commercial accounts to reduce collection time.

tips.title: Quote on-site volume, then confirm in writing
tips.body: Photos or a walkthrough before loading set a price range. Send the confirmed price in a text or estimate so the final invoice matches what the client expects.

tips.title: List surcharge items separately
tips.body: Appliances with refrigerant, tires, mattresses, and electronics cost you extra to dispose of. Listing them as separate lines avoids arguments and keeps your base load price easy to compare.

tips.title: Take payment before the truck leaves
tips.body: Once the junk is gone, leverage is gone. Collect payment on site or send an invoice with a payment link while the crew is still there.

tips.title: Track dump fees per job
tips.body: Scale tickets and recycling receipts show your real cost per load. Review them monthly so your rates keep up with rising disposal fees.

tips.title: Offer a recurring account rate to property managers
tips.body: Contractors, realtors, and landlords send repeat work. A set rate sheet and monthly invoicing keeps these clients and reduces one-off quoting.

faqs.question: Should I charge by volume or by weight?
faqs.answer: Most residential junk removal is priced by truck volume because it is easy for customers to understand. Weight-based pricing is more common for heavy materials like concrete, dirt, roofing, or shingles, where the dump charges by the ton.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fuel or disposal fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as it is disclosed before the job and shown on the invoice. Many operators build these costs into their load price, but separate lines are fine if they are agreed to in advance.

faqs.question: What if the job is bigger than the quote?
faqs.answer: Stop and tell the client before loading more. Give the updated price and get approval in writing or by text. If you do not, you will have a hard time defending a higher invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on junk removal?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax hauling or waste removal services and some do not. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant before deciding how to bill.

faqs.question: How do I handle items I resell or donate?
faqs.answer: Some operators discount the job if items have resale value, while others keep the price and keep the proceeds. Whichever approach you use, state it in the estimate so the client knows whether a credit is included.

estimate.intro: Junk removal quotes are usually given before the crew arrives, by phone, from photos, or during a short on-site walkthrough. Clients typically compare your price against other haulers and against national franchises, so a clear price range and a statement of what is included matter. Quotes are often given as a range based on truck volume.

scopeChecklist.item: What is being removed and where it is located
scopeChecklist.why: A garage pile costs less to load than items in an attic or basement, and the quote should reflect the actual location.
Gives the client a basis for the price and a reference point if the final load is larger or smaller.
Appliances, mattresses, tires, paint, and electronics should be named with their surcharges so they are not a surprise.

scopeChecklist.item: Access conditions such as stairs, elevators, or long carries
scopeChecklist.why: Labor time rises quickly with difficult access, and the quote should say whether that is included.
Hazardous waste, chemicals, asbestos, and medical waste are generally not accepted, and listing them prevents a dispute on the day.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether pricing is a flat quote or a not-to-exceed range
scopeChecklist.why: The client needs to know whether the final price can change based on the actual volume loaded.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and scheduling window
scopeChecklist.why: Disposal costs and your schedule change, so a stated expiration date protects your pricing.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range, then lock it on arrival
pricingTips.body: Photos are rarely accurate. Quote a range, then confirm a firm price after a quick walkthrough and before loading.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum charge
pricingTips.body: Short trips still cost you fuel, drive time, and dump fees. A minimum covers those costs on small jobs.

pricingTips.title: Price for the dump, not just the truck
pricingTips.body: Heavy debris like wood, tile, or concrete costs more to dispose of. Increase the price or switch to weight-based billing when loads will be dense.

pricingTips.title: Offer a discount for flexible scheduling
pricingTips.body: If the client allows a pickup window rather than a specific time, you can route jobs more efficiently and pass on some savings.

faqs.question: Do I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most junk removal estimates are free, especially over the phone or by photo. For large cleanouts that require a long site visit, some operators charge a fee that is credited toward the job if booked.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote from photos alone?
faqs.answer: You can give a range, but state that the final price depends on the actual volume and items. Photos often miss items in closets, attics, and back rooms.

faqs.question: What if the customer changes what they want removed?
faqs.answer: Update the quote before you load anything new. A short written confirmation of the change protects both sides.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to thirty days is common. Shorter windows make sense for jobs that depend on landfill fees or seasonal demand.

land-surveyor.intro: Land surveyors are licensed professionals who measure and map property boundaries, topography, and site features. They bill homeowners, builders, engineers, title companies, and developers for work such as boundary surveys, ALTA/NSPS surveys, topographic surveys, and construction staking. Many work solo or in small firms, and invoices often tie to field days, office drafting time, and recorded deliverables.
land-surveyor.pricingModel: Most residential and small commercial work is quoted as a flat fee per survey type, based on parcel size, terrain, age and quality of existing records, and how much research is needed. Larger or less defined projects, such as construction staking, expert witness work, and ongoing site support, are usually billed hourly or by crew day, with separate rates for a licensed surveyor, a party chief, an instrument operator, and a drafter or CAD technician. Many firms bill a crew rate that includes the equipment (GPS/GNSS rover, robotic total station). Common add-ons are title research, monument setting, recording fees, travel or mileage, rush fees, and extra copies or certifications. Deposits or retainers are standard, with the balance due when the signed and sealed survey is delivered. Staking is often billed per visit with a minimum, since re-staking after damaged stakes is a common extra.

rates.service: Boundary survey (rural, per acre over base)
Licensed surveyor office or consulting time

items.description: Boundary survey, 0.75 acre residential lot, includes records research and field work
Set 4 new iron rod monuments with caps at lot corners
Topographic features and utility locations along rear easement
Additional field time, locating fence lines and encroachment
Signed and sealed survey plat, 3 paper copies plus PDF
Less deposit received 3/4

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 15 days of delivery. Survey remains the property of the surveyor until paid in full. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Survey reflects conditions found on the date of field work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address, parcel number, and legal description
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact parcel surveyed, which matters if the client, lender, or title company asks later about the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Survey type and scope
invoiceChecklist.why: A boundary survey, a topographic survey, and an ALTA survey carry very different standards and prices, so the invoice should match the signed proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surveyor license number and firm registration number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require the licensee's name and number on work products, and including them on the invoice supports documentation of who performed the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Field dates and crew hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing field days and hours backs up hourly charges and any extra visits caused by weather, access problems, or changed scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Monuments set and deliverables
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing monuments, plats, CAD files, and certifications shows what the client received and what is covered by the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Additional-service and change-order lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Added research, re-staking, extra copies, or revised plats should appear separately and reference the approval, so clients do not dispute them as part of the original fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable costs (recording fees, record retrieval, mileage)
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should be listed with receipts or clear amounts so they are not mistaken for markup.

land-surveyor.paymentTerms: Surveyors commonly collect a deposit of 30 to 50 percent at signing, or full payment up front for small residential jobs such as mortgage surveys. Larger projects may bill in stages, such as after field work, then on delivery of the final signed and sealed plat. Balances are usually due on delivery or within 15 to 30 days. Many firms hold final sealed documents until payment is received, and some charge late fees around 1.5 percent per month if the contract states it. Checks, ACH, and card payments are all common, and title companies may pay at closing.

tips.title: Hold the sealed plat until paid
tips.body: Your contract can say that the signed and sealed survey is released once the balance is paid. Sending a draft or unsealed copy for review lets the client check it without giving them a finished product they could use for closing or permits.

tips.title: Bill for field changes the same week
tips.body: Buried monuments, blocked access, heavy brush, and conflicting records add time. Document these on the day, send a change-order note, and invoice the extra hours promptly so they do not get lost.

tips.title: Separate field and office time on hourly work
tips.body: Crew rates and drafting rates differ. Showing them as separate lines makes the invoice easier to understand and easier to defend.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for staking visits
tips.body: Mobilizing a crew for a small stake-out costs nearly as much as a bigger one. A minimum per visit and a clear re-stake fee for damaged or removed stakes protects your margins.

tips.title: Keep pass-through costs visible
tips.body: Recording fees, record copies, and title report charges should be listed separately so clients see them as reimbursements, not part of your professional fee.

faqs.question: Should I bill a surveying job flat fee or hourly?
faqs.answer: Flat fee works for well-defined jobs like residential boundary and mortgage surveys, where you can predict the work. Hourly or crew-day billing fits staking, uncertain research, litigation support, and anything where scope may change. Many firms quote a flat fee with an hourly rate for extras.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit before starting a survey?
faqs.answer: Yes, deposits are common, often 30 to 50 percent, and many surveyors require full payment up front for small residential surveys. State the deposit amount and when the balance is due in your proposal and show the deposit as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: What if the client refuses to pay after I have done the field work?
faqs.answer: Check your contract first. If it says the sealed plat is released on payment, you can withhold it. Send a written demand referencing the agreement and the work done. Rules on liens and collections for professional services differ by state, so check local rules or ask an attorney before filing.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on surveys?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional services, while some tax surveying or tangible deliverables such as printed copies. Check your state's department of revenue guidance before assuming either way.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a survey takes longer than expected because of bad records?
faqs.answer: If your agreement covers only normal research, additional time resolving conflicting deeds or missing monuments can be billed as an extra. Notify the client when you find the issue, explain the added time, and get approval in writing before continuing.

estimate.intro: Surveyors send a proposal or quote before any field work, usually after a site visit or a review of the deed, plat, and county records. Clients, especially builders and buyers, compare fees from several firms, so they often check whether the quotes cover the same survey type, deliverables, and timeline.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of survey and standards followed
scopeChecklist.why: A boundary survey, topographic survey, ALTA/NSPS survey, and flood elevation certificate differ in effort and cost, and clients sometimes assume a cheaper type covers what they need.
The fee depends on the acreage and boundaries included, so state exactly what area is being surveyed.
Specify whether title research, deed retrieval, and adjoining parcel records are included or provided by the client, since these can vary significantly.
State whether you will set new corner monuments, flag them, or only recover existing ones, as materials and time differ.
List signed and sealed paper plats, PDFs, CAD files, and certifications so there is no dispute over extra requests later.
Dense brush, locked gates, and utilities can slow field work. Say who clears access and what happens if the crew must return.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline and what could delay it
scopeChecklist.why: Weather, records requests, and backlog all affect delivery. Give a realistic turnaround and note what the client must provide, such as a title commitment.

pricingTips.title: Price from records and site, not just acreage
pricingTips.body: Acreage alone misleads. Old metes-and-bounds descriptions, missing monuments, steep or wooded terrain, and urban lots with conflicting neighbors can double the work. Review the records and, when possible, visit before quoting.

pricingTips.title: Offer a base fee with listed extras
pricingTips.body: A flat base survey fee plus stated rates for added work, such as re-staking, extra copies, rush delivery, or additional corners, keeps the quote competitive and covers likely changes.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fuel, labor, and workload shift, and a quote left open for months can be a problem. Thirty days is common.

pricingTips.title: Explain why your quote differs
pricingTips.body: If you price above a competitor, note things like title research, monument setting, or sealed deliverables. Many clients do not know what is included in a cheaper offer.

faqs.question: Should I quote before visiting the property?
faqs.answer: For a typical residential lot, many surveyors quote from parcel records and aerial imagery. For rural, wooded, or complex parcels, a site visit or a request for more information avoids underquoting.

faqs.question: Is a survey estimate binding?
faqs.answer: A flat-fee quote that the client signs is a contract for the scope listed. If you give a rough estimate, label it as an estimate and state that fees may change if conditions or scope differ.

faqs.question: How long should a survey quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 30 days. Real estate deals move quickly, so you may want to align the quote with the client's closing or permit timeline, and update it if either changes.

faqs.question: Should I include a deposit request in the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stating the deposit amount, when the balance is due, and that sealed documents are released on payment sets expectations before work begins.

landscape-design.intro: Landscape designers plan residential and small commercial outdoor spaces, including planting plans, hardscape layouts, grading and drainage concepts, lighting, and irrigation coordination. Most are solo practitioners or small studios who bill for site visits, design phases, drawings, and sometimes plant sourcing or project oversight. Invoices usually follow project phases rather than a single end-of-job bill.
landscape-design.pricingModel: Landscape designers most often charge a flat fee per project phase, such as site analysis, concept design, and final construction drawings, with hourly billing for revisions, meetings, and extra site visits. Small residential jobs may be priced per square foot of design area or as a percentage of the estimated installation cost, commonly 8 to 15 percent for full-service design and project management. Some designers offer packages, such as a front yard planting plan or a full backyard master plan. Design-build firms may fold design fees into the installation contract, while independent designers usually bill design separately and charge hourly for construction administration and site visits. Plant and material purchases, if the designer handles them, are typically billed at cost plus a markup of 10 to 25 percent, and reimbursable costs like printing, permit fees, and mileage are listed separately.

rates.service: Hourly design work, revisions, and meetings
Site survey and measured base plan
Full master plan with construction drawings
Design by area (small to mid-size residential)
Project oversight and plant selection trips

items.description: Site visit, measurements, and photo documentation
Base plan preparation (scaled drawing of existing conditions)
Concept design: patio, raised beds, and foundation planting
Revisions after client review (round 2)
Planting plan and plant schedule
Large-format plan prints (24x36)

sampleInvoice.notes: Phase 1 and 2 invoice. Remaining balance due within 14 days of receipt. Deposit of $1,000 received on signing has been applied. Drawings remain the property of the designer until paid in full. Additional revisions beyond two rounds are billed hourly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project phase and deliverables
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each phase (site analysis, concept, planting plan, construction drawings) shows exactly what the client is paying for and matches your contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Site address and project name
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often own multiple properties, and contractors or HOAs may need the address for reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and hours billed beyond scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows that overages were agreed on and tracked, which prevents disputes about why the final bill exceeds the base fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Printing, survey fees, permit application costs, and mileage should be separate lines so the client sees they are not part of your design fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Plant and material purchases with markup shown or disclosed
invoiceChecklist.why: If you buy plants or materials for the client, itemizing quantities and costs avoids confusion and supports sales tax handling where it applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Design deposits are standard, and showing the credit applied keeps the balance accurate.

invoiceChecklist.item: License number and copyright or usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: If your state requires a landscape architect or contractor license for the work, display it as required. A usage note clarifies that drawings are for this project only.

landscape-design.paymentTerms: Most landscape designers collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at signing, often a flat retainer that is credited to the final invoice, then bill by phase as each deliverable is handed over. Net 14 is common for design phases, and some designers require payment before releasing final drawings or construction documents. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH transfers, and card payments are all common, and many designers add a card processing fee only if the contract allows it. For hourly consulting, billing at the end of each month or after each site visit keeps balances small.

tips.title: Tie payments to deliverables
tips.body: Bill at the end of each phase and hold the next phase until it is paid. A client who has paid for the concept plan is more committed than one who has only seen it.

tips.title: Cap revisions in writing
tips.body: Include two rounds of revisions in the flat fee and bill additional changes hourly. Landscape clients often keep tweaking plant choices and patio shapes, and uncapped revisions can quietly erase your margin.

tips.title: Control release of drawings
tips.body: Release final plans only after the final payment clears. Drawings are what contractors use to bid and build, so they give you leverage.

tips.title: Separate design fees from installation costs
tips.body: If you also source plants or manage installers, list those on their own lines or invoice them separately. Mixing them makes it unclear what the design fee covers and complicates sales tax.

tips.title: Track site visit time and travel
tips.body: Walkthroughs with contractors and nursery trips add up. Log them and bill hourly or by visit, with mileage listed, so they do not get absorbed into the flat fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for landscape design?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work well for defined deliverables like a planting plan or master plan, because clients prefer knowing the cost upfront. Use hourly rates for revisions, meetings, and construction-phase support where the scope is hard to predict.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of the installation cost?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many designers charge 8 to 15 percent of the estimated construction budget for full-service design and oversight. Put the budget assumption in your contract and state how the fee changes if the actual budget differs.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Design services are often not taxed, but plants and materials you sell may be. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant about how to treat each line item.

faqs.question: What if a client stops after the concept plan?
faqs.answer: Bill the concept phase in full and keep any deposit applied to it. Your contract should say that fees are due for each completed phase whether or not the client moves ahead with the next one.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to bill for landscape design?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the scope. Some states reserve certain work, such as grading, drainage, or stamped drawings, for licensed landscape architects or engineers. Check your state board's rules before advertising or invoicing those services.

estimate.intro: Landscape designers send a proposal or fee estimate after an initial consultation and site visit, before any design work begins. Clients usually compare your fee structure against other designers and against design-build firms that offer free design with an installation contract. A clear scope helps clients see what they are actually getting for the fee.

scopeChecklist.why: Spell out whether the fee covers a concept sketch, a scaled plan, a planting plan, or construction drawings, so the client does not expect more than they are buying.
Define which parts of the property are included, such as front yard only or backyard with side access, to prevent scope creep.
Two rounds is typical. Stating the limit and the hourly rate for extra rounds keeps changes from becoming free work.

scopeChecklist.item: Site survey and base map responsibility
scopeChecklist.why: Say whether you will measure the site or the client must provide a survey. A professional survey can cost extra and affects plan accuracy.
If your fee is a percentage or the design depends on a budget range, write the number down. Clients often underestimate what hardscape and installation cost.
List what is not included, such as engineering, stamped drawings, permit applications, irrigation design, lighting design, or on-site supervision.
Note how long each phase takes and what you need from the client, such as feedback within a set number of days, HOA guidelines, or utility locates.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present options such as a consultation-only package, a concept and planting plan, and a full master plan with construction drawings. Clients can choose their level and you avoid a single take-it-or-leave-it number.

pricingTips.title: Price by complexity, not only size
pricingTips.body: A small sloped yard with drainage problems and retaining walls takes more time than a large flat lawn. Adjust the fee for grading, existing structures, and permit requirements.

pricingTips.title: Be clear that installation is a separate cost
pricingTips.body: Many homeowners confuse design fees with the cost to build. Include a rough installation budget range so clients know the full picture before committing.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 30 days protect you from changes in workload and rates. Plant and material prices also shift seasonally if you are sourcing them.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many designers charge $100 to $350 for the first site visit and credit it toward the design fee if the client signs. This filters out casual inquiries and compensates you for travel and prep time.

faqs.question: How detailed should a landscape design quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that the client knows the phases, deliverables, revision limits, and exclusions. One page is usually enough for a residential project, with a separate agreement covering copyright and usage.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed price before I know the installation budget?
faqs.answer: You can quote a fixed fee for the design itself, but note the budget assumption. If the client's budget turns out to be much higher or lower, state that the fee may be adjusted.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on an estimate?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent of the first phase or of the total design fee is common. Work begins when the signed quote and deposit are received.

landscaper.intro: Landscapers bill homeowners, property managers, HOAs, and small commercial clients for recurring maintenance and one-time projects. Typical invoices cover lawn mowing and edging, mulch and rock installs, planting, sod or seed, cleanups, irrigation repairs, and light hardscape work, plus materials, disposal, and equipment charges.
landscaper.pricingModel: Most landscapers mix pricing methods. Recurring maintenance is usually a flat price per visit or a monthly rate based on lot size and service frequency, with extras like edging, blowing, or hedge trimming included or listed separately. One-time jobs such as cleanups, mulching, and planting are priced either hourly per crew member or by unit, such as per cubic yard of mulch installed, per square foot of sod, or per plant. Materials are typically billed at cost plus a markup of 15 to 30 percent to cover sourcing, delivery, and waste. Larger design-build projects are quoted as a flat fee with a deposit and progress payments. Dump fees, equipment rental, and fuel surcharges are often itemized rather than buried in the labor rate.

rates.service: Lawn mowing and maintenance (average residential lot)
Crew labor (landscaper plus helper, with basic equipment)
Tree, shrub, or perennial planting (labor only)
Irrigation repair or sprinkler head replacement

items.description: Spring cleanup: leaf removal, bed cleanout, debris hauling
Hardwood mulch, delivered and installed in front and side beds
Bed edging, re-cut existing borders
Shrub trimming: 8 boxwoods, 3 hydrangeas
Dump fee for yard waste

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on card payments). Balances over 30 days past due are subject to a 1.5% monthly late fee. Next scheduled mow: Tuesday, weekly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and dates of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with multiple properties, and property managers handling many sites, need to match each charge to a location and visit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed by type and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Cubic yards of mulch, number of plants, tons of gravel, and square feet of sod show where the money went and head off questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor broken out from materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating the two makes it easier to apply sales tax where required, since many states tax materials or certain landscaping services differently. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disposal, delivery, and equipment charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Dump fees, trucking, and rentals like a sod cutter or skid steer are real costs. Itemizing them keeps them from looking like padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license and insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require a contractor or pesticide applicator license for certain work. Showing license numbers builds trust with commercial and HOA clients.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring service schedule and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: For monthly maintenance accounts, stating the visits covered avoids disputes about skipped weeks due to weather or holidays.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or work order reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients, schools, and HOAs often will not pay without one.

landscaper.paymentTerms: Maintenance clients are commonly billed monthly in advance or at the end of each month, often with a card or ACH on file. One-time jobs under a few hundred dollars are usually due on completion, while larger projects typically require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials, with progress payments tied to milestones and the balance due at finish. Net 14 or net 30 is common for commercial accounts. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in writing in advance. Many landscapers also pause service after a missed payment or two, and say so in their service agreement.

tips.title: Collect a deposit for materials
tips.body: Plants, pavers, and stone are paid for before the job ends. A deposit that covers materials keeps you from carrying the cost of a job on your own credit card, and protects you if a client cancels.

tips.title: Bill monthly for recurring accounts
tips.body: A flat monthly rate, charged on a card or ACH on file, smooths out your cash flow through slow winter weeks and rainouts. Put the number of visits and the season in your service agreement.

tips.title: Charge for extra work as it comes up
tips.body: Clients often ask for one more thing while you are on site, like pulling a stump or hauling old pavers. Write it on the invoice as a separate line, and confirm it by text or email before doing it.

tips.title: Document before and after
