tips.body: Photos of the site before work starts and after you finish help resolve complaints about plant losses, damaged lawns, or work you did not do. Attach them or keep them tied to the invoice record.

tips.title: Include a plant warranty policy
tips.body: If you guarantee plants for a period, put the terms on the invoice. Many landscapers exclude losses from lack of watering, and stating that up front avoids free replacements.

faqs.question: Should I bill landscaping by the hour or by the job?
faqs.answer: Use flat per-visit pricing for routine mowing and maintenance, and hourly or per-unit pricing for cleanups and small installs. Larger projects are usually a flat price with milestones, so clients know the total. Hourly works best when the scope is unclear, as long as you track time.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on plants and mulch?
faqs.answer: A markup of 15 to 30 percent over your cost is common. It covers sourcing, delivery, handling, and replacing the occasional dead plant. Some landscapers instead build the margin into per-unit installed prices, such as dollars per cubic yard of mulch installed.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on landscaping?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some tax materials only, some tax certain services like lawn maintenance, and some tax both. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax as its own line on invoices.

faqs.question: How do I handle weather delays for maintenance clients?
faqs.answer: State in your service agreement that rain delays push visits to the next available day rather than cancelling them. With monthly flat billing, include a line that the rate covers a typical season's number of visits, not a fixed number each month.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for dump runs and debris removal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dump fees, fuel, and your time to haul are real costs. List them as a separate line, either a flat charge per load or a charge based on the dump receipt.

estimate.intro: Landscapers send estimates before almost every new job, and often for new maintenance accounts. Clients usually collect two or three bids and compare the bottom line, so the written scope matters as much as the price. Most estimates follow an on-site walkthrough where you measure beds, lawn area, and access.

scopeChecklist.why: State square footage of lawn or beds, linear feet of edging, and the number of plants, so everyone agrees on what is included.
Name the mulch type and color, plant species and size (for example, 3-gallon), paver brand, or sod variety. Cheaper substitutes are a common source of disputes between bids.
Say whether you are removing existing sod, plants, stumps, or rock, and who pays for disposal. Surprises here are expensive.
Note that buried utilities, rock, roots, or poor drainage could change the price. Mention that the client should have utilities marked, or that you will call 811 before digging, where applicable.
Give a target start window and say that rain, frozen ground, or supplier delays can shift dates.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule and change order process
scopeChecklist.why: List the deposit, progress payments, and how added work will be priced and approved in writing.
Plant and stone prices change, so quotes should be valid for a set time, often 14 to 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Measure before you quote
pricingTips.body: Use a measuring wheel or satellite measurement tool to get real lawn and bed sizes. Guessing at square footage is the most common reason landscapers lose money on maintenance contracts and sod jobs.

pricingTips.title: Price in your drive time and equipment
pricingTips.body: Include travel, fuel, trailer, and equipment wear, not just labor and materials. A small job across town can cost more than it looks.

pricingTips.title: Offer options
pricingTips.body: Give a base option and an upgrade, such as standard mulch versus premium, or basic planting versus a fuller design. Clients feel in control and often choose the middle or higher option.

pricingTips.title: Separate design from installation
pricingTips.body: For larger projects, charge a design fee that can be credited toward the install. This covers your time if the client takes the plan to someone else.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are standard for maintenance and small installs. For complex design work or large projects, many landscapers charge a design or consultation fee, often credited toward the job if the client signs.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Shorten it if you are quoting during a period when plant or material prices are changing quickly.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Stick to the quoted price unless the scope changes. If you find extra work, such as hidden roots or extra drainage work, stop and give the client a written change order before continuing. Make sure your estimate states how these cases are handled.

faqs.question: Can I give a price range instead of a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: A range works when the scope is uncertain, such as cleanups on overgrown properties. For defined work like a mulch install or sod job, a fixed price based on measurements is clearer and tends to win more bids.

large-format-printing.intro: Large format print shops and solo wide-format operators produce banners, posters, vehicle wraps, trade show graphics, window clings, yard signs, and architectural plots. Clients include small businesses, contractors, event planners, schools, real estate agents, and marketing agencies. Invoices usually cover printing, substrate and material, finishing, design or file prep, and installation or delivery.
large-format-printing.pricingModel: Most large format work is priced per square foot, with the rate set by the material (adhesive vinyl, banner scrim, photo paper, rigid board, fabric) and the ink and printer used. Finishing such as grommets, hemming, lamination, contour cutting, and mounting is added as a per-piece, per-linear-foot, or per-square-foot line. Setup or file prep is typically billed hourly or as a flat fee, and design work is separate. Volume discounts apply when the same artwork runs in quantity, since setup is spread across more pieces. Installation is billed hourly or as a flat fee, plus travel, lift rental, or a second installer when needed. Rush jobs usually carry a 25 to 100 percent surcharge. Many shops set a minimum order charge to cover setup on very small jobs.

Indoor poster print on photo or matte paper
Adhesive vinyl decal or window graphic, printed and laminated
Rigid signs on coroplast or foam board
Fabric display or trade show backdrop (dye-sublimation)
Full vehicle wrap, printed, laminated, and installed
Artwork setup, file prep, and proofing

Window cling, 24x36 in, printed on clear static cling vinyl
Coroplast yard signs, 18x24 in, double-sided, with H-stakes
Artwork setup and proof revisions
Local delivery

sampleInvoice.notes: Estimate #1048 approved 3/4. 50% deposit of $689.25 received. Balance due within 15 days of delivery. Colors may vary slightly from on-screen proofs. Reprints for production errors must be reported within 7 days of delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Final size of each piece, in inches or feet
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing is per square foot, so dimensions let the client verify the math and prevent disputes over what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material and finish for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: A 13 oz banner, a 18 oz banner, and mesh are priced differently. Listing laminate, matte or gloss, and adhesive type documents what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finishing details
invoiceChecklist.why: Grommets, hems, pole pockets, contour cutting, and mounting are separate costs and a frequent source of questions if not itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity and approved proof or estimate number
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying the invoice to a signed proof shows the client approved the artwork, spelling, and colors before printing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design and revision charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Setup hours and extra proof rounds beyond what was quoted should be visible so they are not seen as hidden fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation, travel, and equipment costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Lifts, scaffolding, second installers, and travel time are real costs on wraps and large wall graphics and should be separate lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number and job or site name
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies, schools, and businesses often cannot pay without a PO, and multi-location jobs need the site identified.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate reference
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states printed goods are taxable unless the buyer provides a valid resale certificate. Check your state rules and keep the certificate on file.

large-format-printing.paymentTerms: Many print shops require a 50 percent deposit before production on custom work, and 100 percent upfront for new clients or small jobs under a few hundred dollars. Vehicle wraps and large installation jobs often use a deposit of 50 percent with the balance due at completion or on pickup. Established business clients are commonly given net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in writing in advance. Most shops accept cards, ACH, and checks. Because custom printed work cannot be resold if the client walks away, a deposit that covers materials and setup is standard.

tips.title: Get written proof approval before printing
tips.body: Send a proof showing size, text, colors, and bleed, and have the client approve it by email or signature. Most disputes are about typos, wrong sizes, or color expectations, and an approved proof protects you.

tips.title: Charge for waste on rolls and sheets
tips.body: Rolled media and rigid sheets leave leftover material that cannot always be reused. Price on nested or billable area, not just finished size, or use a minimum per-piece price to cover it.

tips.title: Bill file fixes separately
tips.body: Low-resolution art, missing fonts, and wrong color modes take real time to correct. Quote a base setup fee and bill additional prep hourly, and tell the client before you start.

tips.title: Collect deposits on custom and oversized work
tips.body: Wraps, wall murals, and trade show graphics have no resale value. Requiring a deposit to buy materials and schedule the printer protects you if a client cancels.

tips.title: Add rush fees as a line item
tips.body: If you move a job ahead of other work or run overnight, show the surcharge on its own line so it is clearly an agreed cost and not a price change.

faqs.question: Should I charge by square foot or by the piece?
faqs.answer: Use square foot for materials and printing so pricing scales with size, then add per-piece charges for finishing such as grommets or cutting. For standard items like yard signs, a flat per-piece price based on quantity is easier for clients to understand.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on printed banners and signs?
faqs.answer: In many states, printed tangible goods are taxable, and installation labor may or may not be, depending on the state. Clients with a resale certificate may be exempt. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client says the color does not match what they expected?
faqs.answer: State on estimates and invoices that colors may vary from screens, and ask for approval on a proof. If you printed what was approved, the client owns the cost of a reprint. If the print differs from the proof, reprint it at your cost.

faqs.question: How do I bill for design work?
faqs.answer: Quote design as its own line, either hourly or as a flat fee for a defined scope, and state how many proof revisions are included. Additional rounds are billed hourly.

faqs.question: Can I charge a minimum order?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many shops set a minimum of $25 to $75 to cover machine setup, file handling, and finishing time. Put it on your price list and estimates so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Large format printing is almost always quoted before production because size, material, and finishing change the price significantly. Clients commonly compare quotes from several shops and look at per-square-foot pricing, material quality, turnaround, and whether installation is included. A clear written estimate also doubles as a record of what the client agreed to.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact dimensions and quantity for each item
scopeChecklist.why: Even a few inches of difference changes the square footage, material waste, and price.
Banner weight, vinyl type, and gloss or matte options affect durability and cost, and the client should know what they are buying.

scopeChecklist.item: Indoor or outdoor use and expected lifespan
scopeChecklist.why: Outdoor materials and laminates cost more. Stating expected use prevents claims when a cheaper indoor material fades outdoors.

scopeChecklist.item: Artwork responsibility and design hours included
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the client supplies print-ready files, what format is required, and how many proof revisions are included.
Grommets, hems, pole pockets, stands, frames, stakes, and mounting hardware are often assumed to be included when they are not.

scopeChecklist.item: Installation scope, site access, and surface conditions
scopeChecklist.why: Wall texture, vehicle condition, height, and lift requirements can change the labor. State what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.item: Turnaround time and proof approval requirement
scopeChecklist.why: Production time starts after proof approval and deposit. Writing this down avoids disputes over missed deadlines.

pricingTips.title: Build quotes from material cost plus labor and machine time
pricingTips.body: Know your cost per square foot for media, ink, and laminate, then add setup, finishing labor, and a margin. Printing at a loss on small jobs is common when setup time is ignored.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered quantity pricing
pricingTips.body: Show price breaks at quantities such as 10, 25, and 50 pieces. Clients often order more when they see the per-unit savings, and it helps you use setup time efficiently.

pricingTips.title: Separate print, finishing, and installation
pricingTips.body: Itemized quotes make it easy to compare with competitors and let clients remove optional items like installation to meet a budget.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Vinyl, ink, and substrate prices change. A 14 to 30 day validity period protects you from honoring outdated pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most shops quote standard print jobs for free. For vehicle wraps, complex installs, or jobs requiring a site visit or mockup, a quote fee or design deposit that is credited to the final order is common.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Material costs shift, so put an expiration date on the estimate and state that prices are subject to change after that.

faqs.question: What if the client changes the size or quantity after approving the quote?
faqs.answer: State that the quote is based on the listed specifications and that changes require a revised estimate. Recalculate the price before printing, not afterward.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A signature or written email approval on the estimate and proof, plus the deposit, gives you a clear record if there is a disagreement about size, wording, or price.

lash-technician.intro: Lash technicians apply eyelash extensions, lifts, and tints for clients in salons, suites, or home studios. Invoices usually cover full sets, fills, removals, and add-on services, plus retail items like cleanser and lash serum. Many techs also bill for deposits, late cancellations, and no-shows.
lash-technician.pricingModel: Most lash techs price by service, not by the hour. A full set is a flat price by style (classic, hybrid, volume, mega volume), and fills are priced by the time window since the last appointment, usually 2, 3, or 4 weeks. Fills that come in after the cutoff, often 4 to 6 weeks, are typically billed as a new set or at a higher fill tier because too many lashes have shed. Lash lifts and tints are flat fees. Removals are a separate flat fee, and many techs discount or waive them when the client books a new set. Add-ons like lower lashes, colored lashes, or bottom lash sets are priced per service. Retail sales, tips, deposits, and package prepayments should be listed separately. Booth renters and independent techs set their own prices, while salon employees may follow house pricing. Prices rise with experience, training, and demand, so many techs adjust them once a year.

items.description: Hybrid full set lash extensions (0.07 mm, C curl, 12 mm mapped)
Lower lash add-on
Lash cleanser and foam brush kit
Deposit paid at booking (credit)

sampleInvoice.notes: Thank you for your visit. Balance is due at the end of your appointment. Your next fill is recommended in 2 to 3 weeks. Fills after 3 weeks are charged at the 3-week rate or higher. Please give at least 24 hours' notice to reschedule to avoid a $50 late cancellation fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service name and lash style
invoiceChecklist.why: Classic, hybrid, and volume are priced differently, and listing the style avoids confusion on the next visit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fill interval or time since last appointment
invoiceChecklist.why: Fill price depends on how many weeks have passed, so noting this explains the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons and removals as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Lower lashes, colored lashes, and removals are extra and clients can easily forget them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and prepaid package credits
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was already paid so the balance due is accurate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late cancellation or no-show fee with date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the fee to the missed appointment and your written policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retail products sold
invoiceChecklist.why: Aftercare items like cleanser, sealant, or serum may be taxable, so list them apart from services.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tip line and sales tax where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps tips separate from income for your records. Sales tax rules on services and retail vary by state, so check locally.

lash-technician.paymentTerms: Most lash techs collect payment at the end of the appointment, since the work is done in one sitting. A deposit of $25 to $50, or 20 to 50 percent of the service, is common when booking, often credited toward the final bill. Full sets with long appointments may require larger deposits. Late cancellation and no-show fees are usually charged when a client cancels with less than 24 to 48 hours' notice, and should be stated in your booking policy before the first appointment. Typical payment methods include cards, contactless payments, and cash. Packages and gift cards are paid up front, and you should note expiration terms if allowed in your state. For event or group bookings, such as bridal parties, invoice with a deposit due at booking and the balance due on the day.

tips.title: Set a clear fill cutoff
tips.body: Decide in advance when a fill becomes a new set, such as after 4 weeks or when less than 40 percent of lashes remain. Put it in writing and on the invoice so clients understand the price change.

tips.title: Charge a deposit at booking
tips.body: Lash appointments take 1.5 to 3 hours, so an empty slot costs real income. A non-refundable deposit applied to the final bill reduces no-shows.

tips.title: Bill removals separately
tips.body: Removing another tech's lashes takes time and can damage your schedule. List it as its own line, and discount it only when you choose to.

tips.title: Track product costs
tips.body: Lashes, adhesive, tape, and pads are consumables. Review your costs every few months and adjust prices when supplies go up.

tips.title: Keep tips separate
tips.body: Record tips apart from service revenue so your income reporting is accurate. Tip income is generally reportable, so keep good records.

faqs.question: Should I charge more for volume than classic lashes?
faqs.answer: Yes, most techs do. Volume takes longer, needs more skill, and uses more product, so it is typically $25 to $75 more than classic.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a late fill?
faqs.answer: List it as a fill at the higher tier, or as a new set if you require that after your cutoff. Add a line note such as 'Fill at 4 weeks' so the price is clear.

faqs.question: Can I charge a no-show fee on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy was agreed before the appointment. Add a line with the missed date and the fee, and keep a copy of the booking confirmation showing the policy.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on lash services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax personal services and some do not, while retail products are commonly taxable. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How should I handle a prepaid package?
faqs.answer: Invoice the package as one payment, then record each visit as a credit used. Show the remaining balance on each receipt and note any expiration terms.

estimate.intro: Lash techs send quotes mostly for bridal parties, group events, photo shoots, mobile appointments, and clients who need a corrective removal and new set. Clients compare price per set, the time involved, and whether a fill schedule is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Lash style and curl, length, and thickness range
scopeChecklist.why: Style affects both price and time, and clients may expect a look from a photo that does not match their natural lashes.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of people and appointment times
scopeChecklist.why: Group quotes depend on how many sets fit in the day and how much time each takes.
Prior lashes may add time and cost, and clients often forget to mention them.
Mobile appointments need travel charges and a bed, lighting, and space.
Spells out what is non-refundable if the event date or time changes.
Clarifies whether any touch-up or aftercare product is part of the price.
Some techs require a patch test or health form before work, which can affect scheduling.

pricingTips.title: Price by chair time
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours for each set and make sure your group price covers your hourly target, plus supplies and travel.

pricingTips.title: Offer set-based packages
pricingTips.body: A set plus two fills at a bundled price gives clients a clear total and secures repeat visits.

pricingTips.title: Add a travel minimum
pricingTips.body: For mobile work, set a minimum charge or per-mile fee so short appointments still cover drive time.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiry date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Supply costs and your schedule change, so state that the quote holds for 7 to 14 days.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a quote for a regular full set?
faqs.answer: Usually not. A posted price list is enough. Quotes are more useful for groups, events, mobile work, and complicated removals.

faqs.question: How do I quote a bridal party?
faqs.answer: Count the number of sets, estimate time per person, add any travel and early-hour fees, and require a deposit to hold the date. Confirm headcount a week before.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the appointment starts?
faqs.answer: Only if you explain it before the work. If you find extra removal needed or heavy retention issues, tell the client and get approval first.

faqs.question: Should the quote include tips?
faqs.answer: No. Keep tips separate from the service price and leave them to the client at payment.

law-firm.intro: Solo attorneys and small law firms send invoices for legal work such as contract drafting, litigation, estate planning, real estate closings, and business formation. Bills usually combine attorney and paralegal time, flat-fee services, and out-of-pocket costs advanced for the client, such as filing fees and court reporters.
law-firm.pricingModel: Most firms bill by the hour in six-minute (0.1 hour) or fifteen-minute increments, with different rates for partners, associates, and paralegals. Routine matters such as simple wills, uncontested divorces, LLC formation, trademark filings, and residential closings are often sold as flat fees. Litigation and large matters commonly use an advance deposit placed in a trust account (a retainer) that is drawn down as work is billed. Personal injury and some collections work is done on contingency, where the fee is a percentage of the recovery and the client is billed for costs only. Hybrid arrangements, such as a reduced hourly rate plus a success fee, exist in some practice areas. Costs are billed separately from fees, usually at actual cost. Fee agreement rules, trust accounting rules, and limits on contingency and flat fees vary by state, so check your state bar's rules.

rates.service: Attorney time (solo or small firm, general practice)
Simple will or basic estate plan

items.description: Attorney time: review of commercial lease, markup, and negotiation call with landlord's counsel (J. Rivera)
Attorney time: drafting lease addendum and personal guaranty review
Paralegal time: corporate good standing certificate request and document organization
Cost advanced: certificate of good standing (state filing fee)
Cost advanced: overnight courier for signed originals

sampleInvoice.notes: Matter: Lease Review, 410 Main St. Billing period: March 1-31. Time is billed in 0.1-hour increments. $2,500 retainer held in trust was applied to this invoice; remaining balance is due within 30 days of the invoice date. Please reference the matter number with your payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and matter name or number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients have more than one matter with a firm, and separate matter numbers keep billing, conflicts, and trust balances clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized time entries with date, timekeeper, task description, and time
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and courts reviewing fees expect to see who did what and for how long, and vague entries like 'work on file' invite disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly rate for each timekeeper
invoiceChecklist.why: Partner, associate, and paralegal rates differ, and the client should be able to match each rate to the fee agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Costs listed separately from fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Filing fees, service of process, court reporters, and copying are reimbursements, not fees, and many fee agreements treat them differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or trust account activity
invoiceChecklist.why: Show the starting trust balance, amounts applied to the invoice, and the remaining balance. Many state bars require clear accounting for client funds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Balance due, due date, and accepted payment methods
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear total and deadline reduce follow-up and give you a basis for late charges if your fee agreement allows them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed fee agreement or flat-fee scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying the bill to the written agreement shows the charges match what the client agreed to and heads off billing complaints.

law-firm.paymentTerms: Most firms require a signed fee agreement and an upfront retainer or flat-fee deposit before starting, often 50 to 100 percent of a flat fee and a replenishing deposit for hourly matters. Retainers for future work generally belong to the client until earned and must be held in a trust account in most states, so do not deposit them in your operating account. Invoices are commonly issued monthly with payment due in 15 to 30 days. Late interest, often 1 to 1.5 percent per month, is only appropriate if it is stated in the fee agreement and permitted in your state. Firms typically accept checks, ACH, and credit cards, but card payments for trust funds need to be handled so they go to the correct account and comply with your bar's rules. Contingency matters are settled through a closing statement rather than a standard invoice.

tips.title: Record time as you work
tips.body: Entries rebuilt from memory at month end are usually shorter than the real time and less detailed. Log time in 0.1-hour increments throughout the day, and write entries that describe the task and the result.

tips.title: Replenish retainers before they run out
tips.body: For hourly matters, set a minimum trust balance in the fee agreement and bill when it drops below that level. This keeps you from carrying unpaid work on a long case.

tips.title: Send invoices on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Monthly invoices let clients see charges while the work is fresh. Large bills that arrive after months of silence are the ones most often disputed.

tips.title: Keep earned fees and trust funds separate
tips.body: Move money from trust to operating only after the fee is earned and billed, and keep records that match your invoices. Commingling is a leading cause of bar discipline.

tips.title: Explain flat fees and what they exclude
tips.body: State what the flat fee covers and what is billed extra, such as appeals, hearings, or extra revisions. Some states require specific wording about whether flat fees are refundable.

faqs.question: Should I bill in six-minute or fifteen-minute increments?
faqs.answer: Six-minute (0.1 hour) increments are the most common and are generally seen as more precise and fair to clients. Quarter-hour billing is also used, but whichever you choose should be stated in your fee agreement and applied consistently.

faqs.question: Can I charge clients for administrative work like copying and scheduling?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement and your state's ethics rules. Many firms bill paralegal time for substantive tasks but treat general overhead and clerical work as part of their rates. Charges for costs generally should reflect actual cost unless the agreement says otherwise.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice for a flat-fee matter?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is good practice to send a receipt or invoice showing the fee, any deposit paid, costs, and the balance. If any part of the fee was paid in advance, the record should show when it was earned and moved out of trust, where your state requires that.

faqs.question: Can I charge interest on late legal bills?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but only if the client agreed to it in writing and the rate is lawful in your state. Check your bar's rules and state usury limits, and state the rate and start date in the fee agreement.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a client's retainer is not enough to cover the invoice?
faqs.answer: Apply the available trust balance to the invoice, show that credit, and bill the remaining amount as the balance due. Your fee agreement should say whether you will require a new deposit before continuing work.

estimate.intro: Law firms give fee quotes or engagement proposals when a prospective client is deciding whether to hire them, especially for flat-fee services, business matters, and litigation where the client wants a budget. Clients usually compare hourly rates, flat-fee scope, and expected total cost across several firms. A written quote becomes the basis for the fee agreement, so it should be specific about what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.why: Say whether you are drafting an LLC operating agreement, handling a closing, or defending through trial. Broad language leads to disagreements about whether extra work is covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee structure: hourly, flat, retainer, or contingency
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know how they will be charged. State any hourly rates for each timekeeper, flat-fee amounts, or contingency percentage and how costs are treated.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions and what triggers additional fees
scopeChecklist.why: Appeals, added parties, hearings, discovery disputes, and out-of-scope requests can all grow a matter. Naming them avoids surprise bills.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Filing fees, expert fees, depositions, title charges, and service of process are often separate from your fee. List known costs and note that others may arise.

scopeChecklist.item: Retainer amount and how it will be held and applied
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know how much is due upfront, that it is held in trust in most states, and when it is applied or refilled.
A quote for an uncontested divorce assumes cooperation, and a lease review assumes a normal form. State assumptions so you can revise the fee if they prove wrong.

scopeChecklist.item: Conflict check, engagement terms, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: A quote is not an engagement until conflicts are cleared and the agreement is signed. An expiration date prevents old quotes being used after your rates change.

pricingTips.title: Offer flat fees only for predictable work
pricingTips.body: Wills, entity formation, trademark applications, and routine closings follow set steps and suit flat pricing. For disputes where the other side controls the pace, use hourly billing or a phased fee.

pricingTips.title: Give a range and a budget for hourly matters
pricingTips.body: Provide an estimated range for each phase, such as pleadings, discovery, and trial preparation. Make clear it is an estimate, not a cap, and tell the client when you will update it.

pricingTips.title: Phase large engagements
pricingTips.body: Breaking a matter into stages lets the client approve each one and lets you reassess scope and fees at natural points, which reduces billing conflict.

pricingTips.title: Price to your actual time
pricingTips.body: Include time for client calls, emails, document review, and court travel. Many small firms underquote because they count only drafting or appearance time.

faqs.question: Is a fee estimate binding on the firm?
faqs.answer: A flat-fee quote that the client accepts in a signed agreement is binding for the defined scope. An hourly estimate is usually a good-faith projection, but you should say so in writing and update the client if the work will exceed it.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Practices vary. Many firms charge a set consultation fee, often $100 to $500, while personal injury and some other practices offer free consultations. Whatever you choose, state it clearly before the meeting and say whether the fee is credited toward future work.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before giving advice based on a quote?
faqs.answer: A signed engagement or fee agreement should come before substantial work. Most states require written fee agreements for contingency matters, and many encourage them for all matters.

faqs.question: What if the case turns out bigger than quoted?
faqs.answer: Tell the client as soon as you see the scope change and send a revised estimate or written amendment. Billing beyond the agreed scope without notice often leads to fee disputes.

lawn-care.intro: Lawn care businesses, from solo operators with a single mower and trailer to small crews running several routes, bill homeowners, property managers, and HOAs for recurring mowing and seasonal work. Invoices usually cover weekly or biweekly mowing, edging, and trimming, plus one-time jobs like aeration, overseeding, fertilizer applications, and spring or fall cleanups.
lawn-care.pricingModel: Most lawn care is priced as a flat fee per visit based on lot size, terrain, and the work included, not by the hour. Recurring mowing is often billed monthly in arrears or per visit, with a set price for the season. Add-on services such as aeration, overseeding, mulch, and leaf removal are priced per job, per 1,000 square feet, or per cubic yard of material. Fertilizer and weed control programs are usually sold as multi-application packages (4 to 6 rounds per year). Many operators set a minimum service charge to cover drive time and fuel, and charge extra for overgrown lawns, steep slopes, or heavy debris. Hourly rates are used mainly for odd jobs, small crews, and work that is hard to scope in advance.

rates.service: Lawn mowing (average residential lot, up to 1/4 acre)
Mowing, edging, trimming, and blowing (1/2 acre lot)

items.description: Weekly mowing, edging, trimming, and blowing - May (4 visits)
Core aeration - front and back lawn (6,000 sq ft)
Overseeding with tall fescue blend (6,000 sq ft)
Starter fertilizer application
Hedge trimming - front foundation hedges

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Please keep dogs off the seeded areas and water lightly twice daily for 2 to 3 weeks. Mowing will resume on the regular schedule once new grass reaches 3 inches. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service dates for each visit
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring clients often forget how many visits happened in a month. Listing dates settles questions about skipped or extra cuts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and service area
invoiceChecklist.why: If you work for landlords, property managers, or clients with several properties, the address shows which lot the charges belong to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons separate from base mowing
invoiceChecklist.why: Aeration, mulch, cleanup, or shrub trimming should appear as their own lines so the client sees what is outside the regular price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Product names and application dates for fertilizer, herbicide, or pesticide
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license for applying certain products and records of what was used. A record also helps with callbacks about results or pets and kids on the lawn.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials with quantity and unit price
invoiceChecklist.why: Seed, mulch, sod, or topsoil should show bags, yards, or square footage so the cost is clear and a markup is not mistaken for labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or insurance number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and municipalities require a pesticide applicator license or business license number, and commercial clients and HOAs often ask for proof of insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surcharges such as overgrowth, debris haul-off, or dump fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra charges need a plain label so they do not look like a billing error, especially when the lawn was cut after a long gap.

lawn-care.paymentTerms: For recurring mowing, many operators bill monthly in arrears, due in 7 to 15 days, or charge per visit with payment due on receipt. Seasonal contracts are sometimes paid in equal monthly installments, which smooths out slower months. One-time jobs like cleanups, sod, or large mulch jobs often require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials, with the balance due on completion. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance; check your state's rules on maximum fees. Most clients pay by card, ACH, check, or digital payment apps. Card on file with autopay reduces chasing, particularly for residential clients on weekly routes.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge per stop
tips.body: Small lots still cost you drive time, fuel, and setup. A minimum of $35 to $45 per visit keeps tiny yards from losing you money.

tips.title: Put your skip and weather policy in writing
tips.body: State what happens during rain delays, drought dormancy, and when a gate is locked or the client is not ready. Charge a trip fee for locked gates or lawns that are not accessible.

tips.title: Price extra growth separately
tips.body: If a lawn goes two or three weeks without a cut, the first visit takes longer and may need bagging or multiple passes. Add a clearly labeled overgrowth fee.

tips.title: Bill mowing and applications on separate lines
tips.body: Fertilizer programs and mowing run on different schedules. Separating them makes it easy for clients to cancel one service without confusion about the other.

tips.title: Adjust prices once a year
tips.body: Fuel, equipment, and labor costs rise. Send a price notice in winter or early spring with 30 days of lead time instead of changing rates mid-season.

faqs.question: Should I charge per visit or a flat monthly rate for mowing?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-visit billing is easier to understand and handles uneven months, since grass grows faster in spring than in midsummer. A flat monthly rate gives steady income and predictable bills for the client, but make sure it is based on the average number of cuts across the season and spell out what happens in winter.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to apply fertilizer or weed killer?
faqs.answer: In many states, applying herbicides or pesticides for hire requires a commercial applicator license, and some states regulate fertilizer too. Mowing alone usually does not. Check with your state department of agriculture and your local city or county.

faqs.question: Should I collect sales tax on lawn care?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax lawn care or landscaping services, others tax only materials, and many do not tax labor at all. Check with your state revenue department and show any tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder as soon as the due date passes, then pause service if the balance goes past your stated limit, such as 30 days. Your terms should say that service may be suspended for unpaid invoices. For larger balances, a demand letter or small claims court is an option.

faqs.question: Do I invoice for materials separately from labor?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. List seed, mulch, sod, fertilizer, and disposal fees as their own lines with quantity and price. It keeps the invoice transparent and makes it easier to explain a markup on materials.

estimate.intro: Lawn care estimates are sent before the first mow of a new account, before seasonal programs, and for one-time projects like sod installation, aeration, cleanups, and mulch. Clients usually collect two or three quotes and compare per-visit price, what is included in each visit, and how the company handles extras.

scopeChecklist.why: State square footage or acreage and whether the quote covers front, back, side yards, and any hillsides or hard-to-reach areas.
Clients assume different things. Spell out mowing, edging, string trimming, blowing hard surfaces, and whether clippings are bagged or left.
A weekly versus biweekly schedule changes price. State when service starts and ends, and how you handle slow growth periods.

scopeChecklist.item: Price for extras and conditions that change it
scopeChecklist.why: List the rate for overgrowth, debris removal, extra-tall grass, or gate and pet issues, so the price is not a surprise later.
For seed, sod, mulch, or fertilizer, name the product type and amount so the client can compare quotes accurately.
Note items like clearing toys and hoses, unlocking gates, keeping pets inside, and marking sprinkler heads or invisible fence lines.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and acceptance method
scopeChecklist.why: Prices shift with fuel and labor costs. A 14 to 30 day expiration keeps you from honoring an outdated number.

pricingTips.title: Measure before quoting
pricingTips.body: Use satellite maps or a measuring app to get turf square footage, then confirm with a site visit when possible. Subtract house, driveway, and beds from total lot size, since mowable area drives your time.

pricingTips.title: Price by time on site
pricingTips.body: Estimate cut time based on your mower width and obstacles, add trim and blow time, then add drive time. Divide by a target hourly rate to find a fair per-visit price.

pricingTips.title: Offer a seasonal package
pricingTips.body: Bundle mowing with a few fertilizer applications, one aeration, and overseeding. A package price with a small discount increases the job size and helps you keep the account.

pricingTips.title: Show good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: A basic mow-and-go plan, a full-service plan with trimming and edging, and a lawn health program give clients a choice without you cutting your price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most lawn care companies give free estimates for routine mowing. For large projects like grading, sod installation, or detailed landscape plans, a design or site visit fee, often credited toward the work if accepted, is reasonable.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote without seeing the property?
faqs.answer: For basic mowing, many operators quote from satellite imagery and a client's address, then confirm after the first visit. Say in the quote that the price is subject to change if the actual conditions differ from what was measured.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. For seasonal contracts, tie the price to the contract dates, and for material-heavy jobs, shorten the window since mulch, seed, and fertilizer prices can change.

faqs.question: What if the lawn turns out bigger or harder than quoted?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the estimate allowing a price adjustment if lot size, slope, or condition differs from the description. Tell the client before you adjust the price, and get approval in writing, even by text or email.

legal-consultant.intro: Legal consultants are attorneys, former attorneys, and legal professionals who advise businesses and individuals without acting as counsel of record in litigation. They bill for contract review and drafting, compliance reviews, policy writing, regulatory guidance, expert input on legal operations, and project-based advisory work. Invoices usually go to small businesses, startups, in-house legal departments, and other law firms that need outside help.
legal-consultant.pricingModel: Most legal consultants bill hourly, often in six- or tenth-of-an-hour increments, with a stated minimum such as 0.25 hours per task. Flat fees are common for defined deliverables like a standard contract template, a privacy policy, or an entity formation package. Monthly retainers work well for ongoing advisory access, usually with a set number of included hours and a discounted or standard rate for overage. Some consultants use a blended approach: a flat fee for scoped work and hourly billing for anything outside scope. Out-of-pocket costs such as filing fees, court record pulls, and registered agent fees are passed through at cost. Attorneys must follow their state bar rules on fees, trust accounting for advance deposits, and written fee agreements. Non-attorney consultants should not present work as legal advice or representation and should check unauthorized practice of law rules in their state.

rates.service: Privacy policy and terms of service package

items.description: Review and redline of master services agreement (42 pages), including summary memo of key risks
Drafting of mutual non-disclosure agreement, two revision rounds included
Call with client and vendor counsel to negotiate indemnification and limitation of liability terms
Employee handbook compliance review (state wage and leave sections)
Secretary of State certified copy of articles of incorporation (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours are billed in 0.25-hour increments per the engagement letter dated March 4. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month. This invoice reflects consulting services only and does not create an attorney-client relationship beyond the scope stated in the engagement letter.

invoiceChecklist.item: Engagement letter date and matter or project name
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and fee terms, which protects both sides if the bill is questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized time entries with dates, task descriptions, and time increments
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients expect to see what was done and when; vague entries like 'legal work' lead to disputes and write-downs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly rate or flat fee basis for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Mixed billing is common, so the client should see which items are hourly and which are fixed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately at actual cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Filing fees, certified copies, and courier costs should be distinguishable from your fees and backed by receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit applied and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how advance payments were used. Attorneys holding client funds in trust should keep records that match the invoice under their state bar rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bar number or jurisdiction of licensure, if you are an attorney
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies where you are licensed and avoids confusion about whether you are giving legal advice or consulting in a non-attorney capacity.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or matter code
invoiceChecklist.why: In-house legal departments and larger companies often cannot process payment without one.

legal-consultant.paymentTerms: Legal consultants commonly require an advance deposit or retainer before starting, often 25-50% of a flat fee or one to two months of a retainer. Attorneys holding unearned funds should follow trust account rules in their state. Hourly work is usually invoiced monthly or on milestone completion, with payment due in 14 to 30 days; corporate clients may ask for net 30 or net 45. Late fees or interest, often 1-1.5% per month, should be written into the engagement letter, and check your state rules on what is allowed. Payment is typically accepted by ACH, check, wire, or card, and attorneys should be careful about how card payments of unearned funds are handled and recorded.

tips.title: Put the fee structure in a signed engagement letter
tips.body: Define scope, rate, billing increments, expenses, and what is excluded. Many state bars require written fee agreements for attorneys, and even where they do not, it prevents most fee disputes.

tips.title: Bill in small increments and record time as you go
tips.body: Short calls, emails, and document reviews add up. Tracking in 0.1 or 0.25 hour increments avoids under-billing and gives you proof if the client questions an entry.

tips.title: Write time entries clients can understand
tips.body: Use specific descriptions such as 'Reviewed lease amendment and drafted summary of tenant obligations' instead of 'review documents.' Clear entries reduce pushback and requests for discounts.

tips.title: Send a scope-change notice before billing extra
tips.body: If a contract review turns into a negotiation or a new matter, tell the client in writing before you do the extra work. This keeps the final invoice from being a surprise.

tips.title: Keep retainer funds and earned fees separate
tips.body: If you are an attorney, deposit unearned retainers in the proper trust account and move funds out only when earned. Check your state bar rules, since commingling is a common reason for discipline.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or flat fee as a legal consultant?
faqs.answer: Use flat fees for clearly defined deliverables like an NDA, a policy package, or an entity setup. Use hourly billing for open-ended work such as negotiations, ongoing advice, or compliance questions where scope is hard to predict. Many consultants combine both.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent on invoicing or administrative tasks?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Routine billing, scheduling, and file setup are treated as overhead. Time on substantive work, such as research, drafting, and client communication, is billable. Check your engagement letter and any applicable bar guidance.

faqs.question: What increments should I use for billing time?
faqs.answer: Tenths of an hour (6 minutes) and quarter hours (15 minutes) are the most common. Pick one, state it in your engagement letter, and apply it consistently. A minimum charge per task, such as 0.25 hours, is also common.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on legal consulting?
faqs.answer: In most states, legal services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax certain professional or consulting services. Rules vary, so check with your state's department of revenue or a tax adviser.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice and engagement letter terms, then a formal demand letter. Attorneys should check state rules on fee disputes, since some jurisdictions require or offer fee arbitration before a lawsuit. Small claims court is an option for smaller balances.

estimate.intro: Legal consultants usually send a quote or fee proposal before work begins, often after an intake call or a review of the documents involved. Clients typically compare your fee against other consultants, small law firms, and online legal services, so the proposal needs to show exactly what is included and what is not.

scopeChecklist.why: State whether you will provide a redlined contract, a clean draft, a memo, or a call only. Unclear deliverables are a common source of disagreement.
Contract drafting can go through many rounds. Defining how many are included keeps a flat fee from turning into unlimited work.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions about document length and complexity
scopeChecklist.why: A quote based on a 10-page agreement does not hold if the client sends a 60-page one. State page counts or limits so you can reprice if needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as negotiation, court appearances, or filings
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume these are covered. Listing them as out of scope or separately priced avoids confusion.
Your advice may apply only to certain states or to federal law. This also clarifies where you are licensed, if you are an attorney.
Filing fees, registered agent fees, notary costs, and expert fees should be identified as extra or included.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline and what you need from the client
scopeChecklist.why: Turnaround depends on the client delivering documents and answers promptly. Set expected dates and note that delays can move the schedule.

pricingTips.title: Offer a range for hourly estimates
pricingTips.body: For open-ended work, give an estimated range such as 6 to 10 hours and state that it is an estimate, not a cap. Commit to notifying the client if you expect to exceed it.

pricingTips.title: Price flat fees from your own time records
pricingTips.body: Use past matters to see how long a standard NDA, policy, or review actually took, then add a buffer for revisions. Flat fees set by guess tend to lose money on complex clients.

pricingTips.title: Present tiered packages
pricingTips.body: For recurring needs like startup legal setup, offer basic, standard, and full packages with clear differences. Clients can compare options without negotiating line by line.

pricingTips.title: Require acceptance and a deposit
pricingTips.body: Include a signature line or written acceptance and a deposit before you start. This turns the quote into a documented engagement and screens out clients who are only shopping.

faqs.question: Can I charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many consultants charge a flat fee or their hourly rate for a first call, often credited toward later work. Others offer a free 15 to 30 minute intake to assess fit. Whichever you choose, state it before the call.

faqs.question: Is a legal quote binding?
faqs.answer: A quote that the client accepts in writing generally becomes the fee agreement. State how long the quote is valid, commonly 14 to 30 days, and the conditions under which you can reprice, such as a change in scope.

faqs.question: How do I quote work when I have not seen the documents?
faqs.answer: Give a conditional quote or an estimate range, and say it is subject to review of the actual documents. Another option is to charge a small flat fee for a review and scoping memo, then quote the main work.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include a disclaimer about legal advice?
faqs.answer: If you are not a licensed attorney, state clearly that you provide consulting and not legal representation. If you are an attorney, state the scope of the engagement and that no outcome is guaranteed. Check your state's rules on required disclosures.

legal-services.intro: Solo attorneys, small law firms, and independent paralegals send these invoices. They bill for attorney and paralegal time, flat-fee matters such as wills or entity formation, and costs paid on the client's behalf, such as filing fees, service of process, and records requests.
legal-services.pricingModel: Most legal work is billed hourly in tenth-of-an-hour (6-minute) increments, with different rates for attorneys, associates, paralegals, and clerks. Many practices also offer flat fees for routine, well-defined matters like uncontested divorces, simple wills, trademark filings, and LLC formation. Hourly matters usually start with an advance fee or retainer, and in many states that money must go into a client trust account until it is earned. Costs advanced for the client, such as court filing fees and court reporters, are listed separately from fees. Contingency fees, common in personal injury, are a percentage of the recovery and are governed by state rules, so they are billed through a settlement statement and not a regular invoice. Some firms also offer limited-scope or unbundled services, such as document review or a single court appearance. Rules on fee agreements, flat fees, and trust accounting differ by state, so check your bar's rules.

rates.service: Attorney time, general practice (solo or small firm)
Simple will or basic estate planning package
LLC or corporation formation (excluding state fees)
Advance fee retainer for hourly matters

items.description: Attorney: draft operating agreement and member consent for Harbor Street Provisions LLC
Attorney: client conference and revisions to operating agreement
Paralegal: prepare and file Articles of Organization, obtain EIN, assemble minute book
Cost advanced: State Secretary of State filing fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Matter: Formation of Harbor Street Provisions LLC. Time billed in 0.1-hour increments. Retainer of $2,500 held in trust has been applied to this invoice per the engagement agreement; balance of $112.50 is due within 30 days. Please contact the office with any questions about an entry within 14 days of receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and matter name or number
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with more than one matter need each invoice tied to the right file, and it keeps your records clear if a bill is questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, timekeeper, and time for each entry in 0.1-hour increments
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and fee arbitrators expect to see who did what and when. Itemized entries are the best defense against fee disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Specific task descriptions
invoiceChecklist.why: An entry like 'Draft motion to compel; review discovery responses' justifies the charge. 'Work on file' invites questions and may not satisfy your bar's expectations.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each timekeeper's hourly rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Attorney and paralegal rates differ, and the client should be able to check the math and see it matches the fee agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Costs and expenses listed separately from fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Filing fees, service of process, copies, and court reporter charges are reimbursements and should be itemized so the client can see what was paid to third parties.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or trust account activity
invoiceChecklist.why: Show the starting trust balance, the amount applied to the invoice, and the remaining balance. In many states, you must be able to account for client funds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the engagement or fee agreement, and for flat fees the milestone being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the charge to terms the client already signed. For flat-fee work, it shows which stage of the matter the payment covers.

legal-services.paymentTerms: Hourly matters usually begin with an advance fee retainer, held in trust where required and replenished when it falls below an agreed level. Flat-fee matters are often paid in full upfront or split into installments tied to milestones, and some states have specific rules on whether flat fees go into trust. Invoices are commonly sent monthly with payment due in 15 to 30 days. Late interest is allowed in many places if it is written in the engagement agreement, but check your bar's rules and local law first. Accepted methods typically include checks, ACH or bank transfer, and credit cards, and many bar associations require that trust funds be processed in a way that keeps client money separate from operating funds. Do not mix earned and unearned funds.

tips.title: Get the fee agreement signed before any work
tips.body: Many states require a written fee agreement for hourly matters above a certain fee level and for contingency fees. Spell out rates, billing increments, retainer terms, costs, and what happens on termination. An invoice is far easier to collect on when it matches a signed agreement.

tips.title: Record time as you go
tips.body: Reconstructing time at month-end leads to missed hours and vague descriptions. Log time right after each call, email, or drafting session, and round only according to the increment in your agreement.

tips.title: Keep trust and operating money separate
tips.body: Only move funds from trust to operating after the work is billed and the client has been notified, in line with your state's rules. Reconcile your trust account every month, since commingling is a common cause of bar discipline.

tips.title: Bill on a regular schedule
tips.body: Monthly invoices keep the work fresh in the client's mind and prevent a large surprise bill. If a matter is quiet, a brief status line helps explain why there are no charges.

tips.title: Send a final bill and closing letter
tips.body: At the end of a matter, send a final invoice that shows any remaining trust balance and refund the unearned portion promptly. This avoids confusion about whether you are still representing the client.

faqs.question: Should I bill in 6-minute or 15-minute increments?
faqs.answer: Tenth-of-an-hour (6-minute) increments are the most common and are usually seen as more precise to clients. Quarter-hour billing is also used. Whichever you choose, put it in your fee agreement and apply it consistently.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time and administrative tasks?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if your agreement says so. Many attorneys bill travel time at a reduced rate or full rate and charge paralegal rates for clerical-type filing work. Overhead like rent and general office supplies typically cannot be passed on as separate charges, and clerical work billed at attorney rates tends to draw objections.

faqs.question: Can I charge interest on unpaid legal bills?
faqs.answer: In many states you can, but only if the client agreed to it in writing and the rate is reasonable and within usury limits. Check your state bar's guidance and put the rate and start date in your engagement agreement.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a flat-fee matter?
faqs.answer: Reference the fee agreement, name the service or milestone being billed, and show the flat amount and any payments already received. Costs that are not included in the flat fee, such as filing fees, should be listed separately.

faqs.question: What happens if a client disputes my invoice?
faqs.answer: Ask which entries concern them and walk through the time records. Many state bars offer fee dispute programs, and some require you to inform clients about them. Keep detailed time entries and correspondence, since they are your main evidence.

estimate.intro: Legal clients often ask for a fee quote or estimate at the first consultation, especially for defined matters like wills, business formation, or a contract review. They compare flat fees against hourly estimates from other practitioners, and they want to know what could cause the total to change. For ongoing litigation, you can usually give a range for a specific phase but rarely a total.

scopeChecklist.why: Say whether the fee covers drafting only or also negotiation, filing, court appearances, and follow-up. Unclear scope is the biggest source of fee disagreements.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee structure: flat, hourly with an estimate, or a capped fee
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether the figure is a fixed price or a projection, and whether you will tell them before exceeding it.

scopeChecklist.item: Costs and third-party fees not included
scopeChecklist.why: Court filing fees, state registration fees, service of process, recording fees, and expert costs are usually extra. List them or give estimates so the final bill does not surprise the client.
A flat fee for an uncontested divorce depends on both spouses agreeing. State the assumption and what happens if it turns out to be wrong, such as converting to hourly billing.

scopeChecklist.item: Retainer amount and how it is applied
scopeChecklist.why: The client should know the upfront amount, whether it is held in trust, when it must be replenished, and how any unused portion is refunded.
Delays often depend on the client supplying documents or signing. Setting expectations protects you if the matter stalls.

scopeChecklist.item: Statement that no outcome is guaranteed, and that no attorney-client relationship exists until the agreement is signed
scopeChecklist.why: This is a standard clarification. Many bar rules limit statements about outcomes, and a quote alone usually does not form a representation.

pricingTips.title: Use flat fees only for predictable work
pricingTips.body: Wills, entity formation, trademark applications, and basic contract reviews fit flat pricing because the steps are known. For matters where the other side controls the pace, such as litigation or contested family law, an hourly rate with a phase estimate is safer.

pricingTips.title: Give a range, and explain what moves it
pricingTips.body: A range like $2,500 to $4,000 for a contract negotiation, with notes on what pushes it higher, such as multiple rounds of redlines, is more honest than a single number and easier to defend later.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages when it fits
pricingTips.body: For estate planning, a basic package, a package with trust documents, and one with full funding assistance let clients choose by need. Each tier should list its documents and meetings.

pricingTips.title: Quote phases for litigation
pricingTips.body: Estimate pleadings, discovery, and pretrial separately, and say that trial costs are not covered. Update the estimate in writing when the case changes direction.

faqs.question: Is a fee estimate binding?
faqs.answer: An estimate is a projection, while a flat or capped fee is a commitment. Label your quote clearly, and say if you will notify the client before exceeding an estimate. Check your state's rules on fee communications.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Practices vary. Many offer a free or low-cost first meeting for common matters, while others charge a set consultation fee, often credited toward the fee if the client hires them. Either way, tell the client upfront.

faqs.question: How long should a fee quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Legal needs and deadlines can change quickly, and statutes of limitation or new facts may alter the scope, so put an expiration date on it.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement after the client accepts a quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. Turn the accepted quote into an engagement or fee agreement that the client signs before you start work. Many states require written fee agreements in certain situations, so check your local rules.

life-coach.intro: Life coaches work one-on-one or with small groups to help clients set goals, make career or personal changes, and build habits. They invoice for individual sessions, multi-month coaching packages, intake or discovery calls, group programs, and sometimes workshops or corporate engagements.
life-coach.pricingModel: Most life coaches sell packages rather than single sessions. A common format is a three- or six-month program with a set number of sessions (often two to four per month), billed as one upfront payment or as monthly installments. Single sessions are usually priced per 45 to 60 minutes, with a higher rate than the per-session cost inside a package. Many coaches add between-session support such as email or messaging access, which is either included in the package or billed as a separate line. Group coaching is priced per seat, and workshops or corporate work is priced per event or per day. Rates depend heavily on niche, certification, and experience. Executive and career transition coaches tend to charge more than general life coaches. Some coaches offer sliding-scale pricing or a small number of reduced-fee spots, which should be stated clearly on the invoice.

items.description: 3-month coaching package: 8 one-on-one video sessions (50 min each), Jan 8 - Apr 7
Between-session messaging support (weekday replies within 24 hours)
Values and strengths assessment with written summary
Additional 60-minute session outside package (Feb 20)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Package sessions must be used within the 3-month term and are non-transferable. Sessions can be rescheduled with 24 hours' notice; late cancellations are counted as used. Coaching is not therapy and is not a substitute for medical or mental health care. Payment accepted by card or bank transfer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Program or package name and term dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often pay for a defined period. Stating the start and end dates avoids disagreements about when unused sessions expire.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of sessions included and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what was purchased, such as eight 50-minute sessions, and makes it easy to track what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of sessions delivered (for per-session billing)
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the client a record of each charge and supports your records if they question a bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and no-show charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellations are common. Listing them separately, with the date, keeps the charge clear and shows you applied your policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons such as assessments, workbooks, or messaging support
invoiceChecklist.why: These are easy to forget and are often priced separately from sessions. Itemizing them avoids confusion about what the package covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payer name if an employer or third party is paying
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients are reimbursed through an employer development budget, which may require the company name, a PO number, or a W-9 from you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installment schedule and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: If a package is split into monthly payments, showing each due date and the balance helps both sides track payments.

life-coach.paymentTerms: Many life coaches collect payment in full before a package begins or require the first installment to start. Single sessions are often paid at booking or by the time the session starts. Monthly installment plans are common for larger packages, with automatic card charges on a set date. Net 7 or due-on-receipt terms are typical for one-off invoices, and corporate clients may ask for net 15 to net 30. Late fees are less common in coaching than in other fields, but some coaches pause sessions until an overdue balance is paid. Most accept cards and bank transfers, and some take digital wallets. State your refund and cancellation policy in your coaching agreement and repeat the key points on the invoice.

tips.title: Sell packages and bill them upfront
tips.body: Single-session billing leads to more cancellations and lapsed clients. A defined package paid upfront or in scheduled installments commits the client to the process and gives you predictable income.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: A 24-hour notice policy is common. Put it in your coaching agreement and reference it on the invoice so a charge for a missed session is not a surprise.

tips.title: Define what between-session support includes
tips.body: Unlimited messaging can turn into unpaid work. Say how many messages or what response time is covered, and bill extra calls or reviews as separate lines.

tips.title: Be clear about refunds
tips.body: Decide whether payments are refundable, partially refundable, or not at all once sessions begin, and state it. Disputes in coaching usually come from unclear expectations, not the amount.

tips.title: Keep separate records for corporate and personal clients
tips.body: Employer-paid work may need a PO number, W-9, and different terms. Tracking these per client keeps payment from stalling in an accounts payable queue.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or per package?
faqs.answer: Most coaches do better with packages because change takes several sessions and upfront payment improves commitment and cash flow. Keep a single-session rate for people who want to try one session, and price it higher than the per-session cost inside a package.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the discovery call?
faqs.answer: Many coaches offer a free 20 to 30 minute discovery call to see if there is a fit. Some charge a small fee that is credited toward a package if the client signs up. Either approach works; just make it clear before the call.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on coaching?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax coaching or personal services, but some tax certain services or digital products. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client stops showing up but has paid for a package?
faqs.answer: Follow your written policy. Many coaches state that package sessions expire at the end of the term and that missed sessions are forfeited. Send a polite reminder of the remaining sessions and the expiry date before the term ends.

faqs.question: Can I offer payment plans?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many coaches do. Set equal monthly payments that finish before or by the end of the program, put the schedule on the invoice, and use automatic card payments if possible so you are not chasing each installment.

estimate.intro: Life coaches usually send a proposal or quote after a discovery call, when the client wants to know what a program will cost and what it includes. Clients compare the total cost, number of sessions, length of the program, and how much support they get between sessions. Corporate or group clients often ask for a written quote for their budget approval.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know whether they are getting eight 50-minute video calls or twelve 30-minute phone calls. This is the main thing they are buying.

scopeChecklist.item: Program start date, end date, and session expiry
scopeChecklist.why: Sets the time frame in which sessions must be used and prevents open-ended claims on your calendar.
Naming the client's goals, such as a career change or building a routine, keeps the engagement on track and gives you something to refer back to.
Specify whether messaging, worksheets, or session recaps are included and what response time to expect, so support does not grow beyond what is priced.
Putting these in the quote means the client agrees before paying, which reduces disputes later.

scopeChecklist.item: Fees, payment schedule, and accepted payment methods
scopeChecklist.why: Shows the total price, any installment plan, and due dates so the client knows what to expect.
A short statement that coaching is not therapy, medical advice, or a guarantee of results sets honest expectations and protects both sides.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: Present a shorter, standard, and extended option, such as three months, six months, and a six-month plan with added support. Clients tend to choose a middle option, and it frames the value of longer engagements.

pricingTips.title: Price by the program, not by the hour
pricingTips.body: Quoting a program fee focuses the conversation on the outcome instead of an hourly rate. Show the per-session equivalent only if the client asks.

pricingTips.title: Give a pay-in-full discount
pricingTips.body: A modest discount of 5 to 10 percent for paying upfront can improve cash flow while still giving installment plans as a choice.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: A 7 to 14 day validity period encourages a decision and keeps you from holding calendar space indefinitely.

faqs.question: Is a quote different from a coaching agreement?
faqs.answer: Yes. A quote states the price and scope for the client to review. A coaching agreement covers the terms of the relationship, such as confidentiality, cancellation, and refunds. Many coaches combine them or send the agreement once the quote is accepted.

faqs.question: How do I quote a corporate workshop or group program?
faqs.answer: Estimate preparation time, delivery time, materials, and any travel. Quote a flat fee for the event, or a per-participant price for a group program, and state the minimum number of participants.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a custom proposal?
faqs.answer: For individual clients, no. For larger corporate engagements that need extensive customization or research, some coaches charge a design fee that is credited to the project if it goes ahead.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. If the client asks for more sessions or added services, send a revised quote or an add-on price before doing the extra work.

lighting-rental.intro: Lighting rental companies supply fixtures, stands, truss, dimmers, controllers, and cabling for weddings, corporate events, concerts, theater, trade shows, and film shoots. Many are solo operators or small crews who also deliver, set up, program, and strike the gear. Invoices usually combine equipment rental, labor, delivery, and fees for damage or lost items.
lighting-rental.pricingModel: Most lighting rental businesses price equipment per item per day or per event, with a lower rate for additional days (often 50 percent for a second day and a weekly rate of about 3 times the daily rate). Common add-ons are delivery by distance or flat zone, setup and strike labor billed hourly per technician, and a lighting designer or operator billed per hour or per day. Many shops sell packages, such as a wedding uplighting package with a set number of fixtures, and then charge extra for add-ons like gobos, truss, or haze. Consumables like gels, gaffer tape, and batteries are billed at cost plus a markup or built into a small fee.
