A security deposit or damage waiver (commonly 5 to 10 percent of rental value) is typical, and minimum order charges keep small jobs worthwhile.

rates.service: LED uplight (battery or wired), wedding package
LED par can or wash fixture
Truss, stands, or totem with clamps

items.description: Wedding reception lighting package: 16 LED uplights (RGBWA), cabling and power distribution
Moving head wash fixtures for dance floor
Truss totems with par cans, pair (1 day)
Technician: setup and strike
Delivery and pickup (within 30 miles)
Damage waiver (7 percent of equipment rental)

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: Saturday, June 14. Equipment returned in good condition and counted at pickup. Balance due within 7 days of the event; a 50 percent deposit was received at booking. Lost or damaged items are billed at replacement cost. Late payments are subject to a 1.5 percent monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, venue name, and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the job and the load-in location, and helps resolve disputes about when and where the gear was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized equipment list with quantities and rental days
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and corporate accounts compare line items to the quote, and you need the list to prove what went out.

invoiceChecklist.item: Setup, show, and strike labor with hours and tech count
invoiceChecklist.why: Labor is a common point of dispute, so show hours separately from equipment and note any overtime or after-midnight rates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, pickup, and mileage or zone charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows travel costs were part of the agreement, especially for out-of-area venues or multiple trips.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage waiver, deposit received, and replacement cost terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear what was collected up front and what the client owes for lost or damaged gear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overage and extension charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Late load-out, extra days, or added fixtures on site should appear as separate lines so they do not look like surprise charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number and sales tax or resale details
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate and venue clients often require a PO. Rental of equipment is taxable in many states, so show tax or the exemption certificate on file; check your state's rules.

lighting-rental.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking holds the date and gear, with the balance due before the event for small private jobs or within 7 to 30 days for corporate and production clients. Many rental shops require full payment before delivery for new clients or last-minute orders. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the rental agreement. Card, ACH, and check are typical, and a card on file can cover damage or late return charges. Keep the signed rental agreement and the deposit terms with the invoice.

tips.title: Use a check-in and check-out count
tips.body: Count fixtures, cables, clamps, and safety cables at pickup and return and put the counts on the paperwork. This protects you when a client disputes missing or damaged items.

tips.title: Bill additional days and overtime separately
tips.body: Late strikes, delayed returns, and extended hours cost you in labor and equipment availability. Show them as separate lines so clients see why the total changed.

tips.title: Put a minimum order on small jobs
tips.body: A delivery, setup, and strike for two fixtures can cost as much in time as a full package. A minimum order or minimum labor call (such as 4 hours) keeps small jobs profitable.

tips.title: Take the deposit before holding gear
tips.body: Gear held for one client is gear you cannot rent to another. A non-refundable or partly refundable deposit at booking reduces cancellations.

tips.title: Charge replacement cost, not rental rate, for lost items
tips.body: State in the agreement that lost or destroyed gear is billed at replacement cost. Include power cables and clamps, which get lost often.

faqs.question: Should I charge per day or per event for lighting rentals?
faqs.answer: Per event works well for packages like wedding uplighting where the rental period is one night. Per day is better for production, film, and multi-day events, with a reduced rate for additional days.

faqs.question: Is lighting equipment rental taxable?
faqs.answer: In many states, rental of tangible personal property is subject to sales tax, and some states also tax delivery or labor when bundled with the rental. Rules vary by state and locality, so check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for damaged or lost equipment?
faqs.answer: State in your rental agreement that the client is responsible for loss or damage beyond normal wear and is billed at repair or replacement cost. List the item, the issue, and the cost on the invoice, and attach photos if possible.

faqs.question: What is a typical deposit for a lighting rental?
faqs.answer: Many companies take 25 to 50 percent at booking to hold the date. Large productions may require more, and some require full payment before delivery for first-time clients.

faqs.question: Should labor be bundled into the equipment price?
faqs.answer: Either works, but listing labor separately makes it easier to adjust when the schedule changes. Bundled packages are common for weddings and small events, as long as the package states what is included.

estimate.intro: A lighting rental quote is sent after a client describes the event, venue, date, and look they want, and often before a site visit. Clients compare total price, the equipment list, what labor is included, and whether setup and strike are covered. A clear quote helps them judge you against competitors with different package contents.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, load-in time, show time, and load-out time
scopeChecklist.why: Labor and equipment hold times drive the price, and late load-outs or early load-ins change the cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Venue name, address, and access details
scopeChecklist.why: Stairs, long carries, no elevator, and loading dock limits add labor time and affect delivery pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact equipment list with quantities and model or type
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes about what was promised, such as the number of uplights or whether truss is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Power requirements and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you provide distribution and cable runs, or the venue provides outlets, and avoids last-minute generator or power add-ons.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor included: setup, operator, strike, and hours covered
scopeChecklist.why: States how many technicians and hours are in the price and what the overtime rate is if the event runs long.
Defines the delivery window and when gear must be accessible for pickup, which affects extra-day charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Damage waiver, deposit, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for upfront payment and refund rules before the client commits.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: Three tiers, such as basic uplighting, uplighting with dance floor fixtures, and a full design with truss and haze, help clients choose without negotiating each fixture.

pricingTips.title: Price for the total job time
pricingTips.body: Include drive time, loading, setup, show, strike, and return to the shop. A four-hour event can take ten hours of your day.

pricingTips.title: Separate optional add-ons
pricingTips.body: List gobos, monogram projection, haze, and extra fixtures as add-ons so the base quote stays competitive and clients see where they can adjust.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Gear availability changes, especially in wedding season. A 7 to 14 day expiration and a note that dates are held only with a deposit keeps the schedule accurate.

faqs.question: Should I visit the venue before quoting?
faqs.answer: For larger events or unusual venues, yes. A site visit reveals ceiling height, rigging limits, power, and access issues that change the price. For standard weddings, photos or a venue contact call may be enough.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or design?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For custom lighting designs, renderings, or multiple site visits, many companies charge a design fee that is credited toward the rental if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a lighting rental quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 7 to 30 days depending on how far out the event is. State that the date is not held until a deposit and signed agreement are received.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as added fixtures, a longer schedule, or a different venue. Put a clause in the quote that changes in scope or schedule will be billed at your stated rates.

limo-service.intro: Limo services are owner-operators and small fleets that provide chauffeured transportation for weddings, proms, airport transfers, corporate travel, concerts, and nights out. Invoices usually cover hourly vehicle charges, flat airport transfers, gratuity, fuel and other surcharges, and extras like wait time or tolls.
limo-service.pricingModel: Most limo work is priced per hour with a minimum booking, often 2 to 4 hours for sedans and SUVs and 3 to 6 hours for stretch limos, party buses, and weekend evenings. Airport transfers and point-to-point trips are usually a flat rate based on distance and vehicle type. Many companies add a standard gratuity of 15 to 20 percent, a fuel surcharge, and fees for tolls, parking, and airport fees. Peak dates such as prom, New Year's Eve, and Saturdays in wedding season often carry higher rates or longer minimums. Extras like child seats, red carpet, decorations, and champagne setups are billed as add-ons. Time is typically calculated garage to garage or from pickup to drop-off, so state which method you use. Deposits are standard, and corporate accounts are often billed monthly.

rates.service: Extra wait time beyond included window

items.description: Stretch limousine (10 passenger) - prom night charter, 5/17, 6:00 PM to 11:00 PM
Fuel surcharge
Extra wait time at venue (30 minutes past scheduled departure)
Photo stop at park, red carpet and bottled water setup
Driver gratuity (18% of charter)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $200 received 4/20 and applied to this balance. Balance due upon completion of service. We accept card, Zelle, and check. Cancellations within 72 hours forfeit the deposit. A $150 cleaning fee applies for spills or damage to the vehicle interior.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off addresses with date and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing depends on exact start and end times, and clients dispute charges when the timeline is unclear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle type and number of passengers
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by vehicle, and capacity limits matter if the group size changed after booking.

invoiceChecklist.item: How time is calculated and the booked minimum
invoiceChecklist.why: Garage-to-garage versus pickup-to-drop-off can change the bill by an hour or more, and minimums explain a charge for a shorter trip.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized surcharges, tolls, parking, and airport fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients accept pass-through costs more readily when they are listed separately from the base rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity line, labeled as included or optional
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume tip is already covered, and unclear gratuity leads to double tipping or complaints.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was already paid, so the final amount is clear and the deposit is not charged twice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Operating authority, license, or permit number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require charter or limousine operating authority, and corporate clients often ask for it for their records. Check your local rules.

limo-service.paymentTerms: Limo companies usually take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent when the reservation is made, sometimes full prepayment for peak dates like prom or New Year's Eve, with the balance due on the day of service or before. Corporate and event planner accounts are often invoiced net 15 or net 30. Cards are the most common payment method, along with ACH, Zelle, and checks for corporate clients. Many companies keep a card on file to cover overtime, damage, or cleaning fees. Cancellation policies commonly make deposits nonrefundable inside 48 to 72 hours of the booking, and late fees of 1.5 percent per month are typical on overdue business accounts.

tips.title: Put the minimum and overtime rule in the booking
tips.body: State the minimum hours and how overtime is billed before the trip. Most disputes come from a ride that ran 45 minutes over and a client who did not expect to pay for a full extra hour.

tips.title: Track actual times with a trip log
tips.body: Have drivers record arrival, pickup, and drop-off times. A simple log lets you back up wait time and overtime charges when a client questions the bill.

tips.title: Be clear about gratuity
tips.body: If you add gratuity automatically, say so on the quote and the invoice and show it as a separate line. If it is optional, tell the client the driver is not paid from the base fare so tipping is expected.

tips.title: Keep a card on file for incidentals
tips.body: Get written authorization to charge the card for overtime, tolls, cleaning fees, and damage. It is much easier than chasing a group organizer days after an event.

tips.title: Invoice corporate accounts per trip with reference numbers
tips.body: Include the passenger name, PO number, or cost center on each trip. Accounts payable departments often reject invoices that lack these details.

faqs.question: Should gratuity be included in my limo invoice?
faqs.answer: It is common to include an automatic gratuity of 15 to 20 percent, especially for groups and events. If you do, list it as its own line so the client sees it, and tell them in advance. If you leave it optional, say so clearly on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for wait time at airports?
faqs.answer: Most companies include a free window, often 30 to 60 minutes for domestic flights and up to an hour for international ones, tracked from flight landing time. After that, charge per 15 minutes or per hour at your standard rate. State the policy on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fuel surcharge?
faqs.answer: Yes, many companies add a flat or percentage fuel surcharge. It should be disclosed in the quote or booking terms and appear as a separate line on the invoice so it does not look like a hidden fee.

faqs.question: What if the client cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Use a written cancellation policy accepted at booking. A common approach is a nonrefundable deposit, with the full minimum charged if the cancellation happens within 24 to 48 hours of the trip. Invoice the amount owed and reference the policy.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on limo service?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes the city. Some places tax passenger transportation or charter service, and others do not, and gratuity may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Limo companies send quotes when someone is planning an event or trip, such as a wedding, prom, bachelor party, corporate roadshow, or airport run. Clients often request quotes from several companies and compare the hourly rate, minimum hours, vehicle, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, pickup time, and full itinerary with all stops
scopeChecklist.why: The route and stops determine hours and mileage, and added stops are the usual reason a trip runs over.

scopeChecklist.item: Vehicle type, capacity, and passenger count
scopeChecklist.why: Locks in the vehicle class and prevents a last-minute headcount increase from forcing a larger vehicle at the same price.

scopeChecklist.item: Hourly rate, minimum hours, and how time is measured
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare quotes by hourly rate, so the minimum and the start and end of the clock matter as much as the rate.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: gratuity, fuel, tolls, parking, water, decorations
scopeChecklist.why: A low rate can hide add-ons, and clients need to see what the total will actually be.
Sets expectations if the event runs long or a flight is delayed.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, balance due date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Protects you from holding a vehicle and driver on a busy date with no commitment.

scopeChecklist.item: Alcohol, smoking, and damage and cleaning policies
scopeChecklist.why: Passengers often bring alcohol, and clear rules and fees cover the cost of cleaning or damage.

pricingTips.title: Quote an all-in total
pricingTips.body: Show the base fare, fuel, gratuity, and expected tolls together as a single estimated total. Clients compare totals, and a clearly all-in quote can win against a lower hourly rate with fees added later.

pricingTips.title: Price peak dates higher or require longer minimums
pricingTips.body: Prom, New Year's Eve, Saturdays in wedding season, and holiday weekends fill fast. Set higher rates or a 4 to 6 hour minimum so you are not locking up a vehicle for a short, low-revenue trip.

pricingTips.title: Offer vehicle options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three choices, such as an SUV, a stretch limo, and a party bus, with clear per-person cost. Groups often pick based on cost split among passengers.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fuel prices, driver availability, and vehicle bookings change. Make the quote valid for 7 to 14 days and say the date is not held until the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Quotes are a normal part of winning bookings. Reserve your time for those who pay a deposit to hold the date.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: A quote for a defined itinerary can be treated as firm if the trip stays as described. State that changes to the time, stops, or passenger count may change the price, and that the booking is confirmed only after a deposit.

faqs.question: How do I quote a trip with an uncertain end time?
faqs.answer: Quote the booked hours and list the overtime rate in 15 or 30 minute increments. If the schedule is truly open, quote a minimum and bill actual time beyond it.

faqs.question: How far in advance should I send quotes?
faqs.answer: Respond within a few hours when you can, since clients often book the first company that replies with a clear price. For weddings and proms, quotes may go out months ahead, so include an expiration date and the current peak-date pricing.

locksmith.intro: Locksmiths handle lockouts, rekeying, lock installation, key cutting, safe work, and security upgrades for homes, businesses, and vehicles. Most are solo operators or small shops with a service van, and they bill per call-out plus labor and hardware. Invoices usually cover a service call fee, labor, parts, and sometimes after-hours or emergency surcharges.
locksmith.pricingModel: Most locksmiths charge a service call (trip) fee that covers travel and the first few minutes on site, then add labor and parts. Labor is billed either hourly or as a flat price per task, such as a flat rate per lock for rekeying or a flat price for a residential lockout. Hardware is sold at a markup over wholesale cost, commonly 30 to 100 percent depending on the item. After-hours, holiday, and emergency calls carry a surcharge or a higher call fee. Automotive work is often priced per key or per programming job, and commercial work such as master key systems, access control, and door hardware is quoted per door or per project. Many locksmiths quote a firm price by phone for standard jobs and confirm it on site before starting.

rates.service: Install a deadbolt or knob set (labor only)
Car key replacement with transponder programming

items.description: Service call, weekday evening
Rekey front door deadbolt and back door knob (new pins and keys, 2 keys per lock)
Install new grade 2 deadbolt, customer-selected (labor)
Grade 2 deadbolt, satin nickel (hardware)
Additional key copies

sampleInvoice.notes: Due upon completion. Rekeyed locks and new hardware are warrantied for 90 days against defects in workmanship. Please keep old keys for rekeyed locks out of circulation. Cash, card, and Zelle accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date/time of arrival
invoiceChecklist.why: Locksmith work is location-specific and often urgent, so a record of when and where you worked helps resolve disputes and supports after-hours charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized call fee, labor, and parts
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often object to lump sums, and unclear bills are a common source of complaints about locksmiths. Separate lines show exactly what was charged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lock brand, model, and grade for installed hardware
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the customer a record for warranty claims, insurance, or future rekeying, and shows what they paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of cylinders rekeyed and keys cut
invoiceChecklist.why: Rekeying and key copies are priced per unit, so counts justify the total and let the customer verify the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: After-hours or emergency surcharge shown as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows that the higher price was a known surcharge and not an inflated rate, which heads off chargebacks.

invoiceChecklist.item: Proof of authorization or ID verification note
invoiceChecklist.why: For lockouts and vehicle or safe work, noting that you verified the customer's ID or ownership protects you if someone later disputes the entry.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license number and your business name and phone
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities license locksmiths, and showing your license number and a real business name builds trust and meets local rules where they apply.

locksmith.paymentTerms: Residential and emergency jobs are normally paid on completion, before you leave, by card, cash, or a mobile payment app. Take a card on file or payment before cutting or programming a key for a vehicle, since the work cannot be undone. For larger commercial jobs such as master key systems, access control, or multi-door hardware installs, ask for a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover parts, with the balance due on completion or net 15 to 30 days for established business accounts. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common on net terms, but state them on the quote and invoice up front. Property managers and facilities departments often pay by check or ACH after receiving a PO number.

tips.title: Quote a total price before you start
tips.body: Tell the customer the call fee, the labor price, and any expected parts cost before you touch the lock. Customers who feel surprised by the final bill are the ones who dispute card charges or leave bad reviews.

tips.title: Collect payment before you leave
tips.body: A locksmith has no leverage after the door is open and the customer is inside. Take payment on site and send a receipt or invoice by text or email immediately.

tips.title: Charge for the call even if you cannot finish
tips.body: If you arrive and the job is not what was described, such as a high-security lock that needs special tools, the call fee still covers your time and travel. State this when booking.

tips.title: Mark up hardware and show it as a separate line
tips.body: Keeping parts separate from labor makes your markup less of a point of argument and lets you adjust labor without changing hardware pricing. Track your supplier cost on each item.

tips.title: Keep records for commercial accounts
tips.body: Property managers and businesses want PO numbers, job site names, and door or unit numbers on each invoice so their accounting can code the cost. Add them as you go and you will get paid faster.

faqs.question: Should I charge a separate service call fee and labor?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. The call fee covers vehicle costs and your time getting there, while labor covers the actual work. Splitting them makes your pricing clear and ensures you are paid for travel even on short jobs.

faqs.question: How do I invoice an after-hours lockout?
faqs.answer: List the standard call fee and lockout labor, then add a separate line for the after-hours surcharge. Some locksmiths use a higher call fee instead, but a separate line is clearer to the customer.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on locksmith work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax parts and hardware you sell, and some also tax labor or repair services, while others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant and show tax on its own line if you collect it.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to bill as a locksmith?
faqs.answer: Some states and cities require a locksmith license, and others do not. Where one is required, many jurisdictions expect the license number on your invoices, ads, or vehicle. Check your state and local rules.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer disputes the charge after I left?
faqs.answer: Keep a signed work order or a text confirmation of the quote, plus photos of the work and the final itemized invoice. This documentation is what you will need to respond to a chargeback or a complaint.

estimate.intro: Locksmiths send written quotes for jobs that go beyond a simple lockout or key copy, such as rekeying a whole property, installing new hardware, high-security locks, safes, access control, and commercial door work. Phone quotes are common for routine calls, but a written estimate matters when parts are involved or several doors are included. Customers compare the total price, hardware quality, and whether the price includes the trip fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of doors, locks, and cylinders included
scopeChecklist.why: Rekeying and installation are priced per unit, so the count sets the price and prevents arguments if the customer adds locks later.
A Grade 1 commercial deadbolt and a Grade 3 hardware store lock differ widely in price. Naming the product avoids disputes about what was promised.
State whether locks will be keyed alike, keyed differently, or on a master key system, and how many keys each lock includes.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether the call fee is included in the total
scopeChecklist.why: Customers often assume the quoted price is all-in. Say clearly if the trip fee is separate or credited toward the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Door or frame repair not included
scopeChecklist.why: Doors with damaged bores, misaligned strikes, or warped frames often need extra work. State that carpentry or repairs are quoted separately.
If the customer wants work outside normal hours, the higher price should be spelled out in the quote.
Manufacturer warranties differ from your workmanship warranty. Stating both prevents confusion if a lock fails.

pricingTips.title: Price per door for multi-lock jobs
pricingTips.body: Give a per-door or per-lock price with a total. Property managers and homeowners can compare it easily, and you can add or remove doors without redoing the quote.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best hardware
pricingTips.body: Present two or three hardware options at different grades and prices. Customers pick the middle option often, and it avoids a yes or no decision on a single price.

pricingTips.title: Build in travel and parking for commercial sites
pricingTips.body: Downtown buildings, hospitals, and multi-tenant properties can add time for parking, check-in, and escorts. Factor that in or add a line for it.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Hardware prices and your schedule change. A 14 to 30 day validity period keeps you from honoring an old price on new parts costs.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: For standard jobs like a house lockout or single rekey, a phone quote is fine if you state the call fee and total range. Confirm the final price on site before you start and note it on the work order.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a written estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For complex commercial projects like master key design or access control layout, some locksmiths charge a site survey fee that is credited if the customer hires them.

faqs.question: What if the job costs more than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Stop and get the customer's approval for the new price before continuing, ideally in writing by text or email. State in the quote that hidden damage or unexpected conditions may change the price.

faqs.question: How long should a locksmith quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days for installation and commercial work. Hardware costs and availability change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

logistics.intro: Logistics providers include independent freight brokers, owner-operator carriers, last-mile delivery businesses, freight forwarders, and small third-party logistics (3PL) companies. They invoice shippers, retailers, and manufacturers for moving, storing, and coordinating freight. A typical invoice covers line haul or delivery charges, fuel surcharges, accessorials like liftgate or detention, and warehousing or handling fees.
logistics.pricingModel: Pricing depends on the mode and the service. Truckload freight is usually priced per mile or as a flat lane rate between two points, with a fuel surcharge added. Less-than-truckload (LTL) shipments are priced by weight, freight class, and distance, often with a minimum charge. Local and last-mile delivery is priced per stop, per package, or per hour for a driver and vehicle. Warehousing is billed per pallet per month, plus handling charges for receiving, picking, and shipping. Brokers earn a margin over the carrier cost, commonly 10 to 20 percent of the load. Accessorial charges such as detention, layover, lumper fees, liftgate service, inside delivery, and redelivery are billed separately and should be agreed on before the shipment moves.

rates.service: Local or regional box truck delivery

items.description: Truckload, 53' dry van, Dallas TX to Atlanta GA (781 mi), BOL #48213
Fuel surcharge
Detention at delivery, 3.5 hrs total less 2 hrs free time
Lumper fee at receiver (receipt attached)
Pallet storage, 12 pallets, June

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due Net 30 from invoice date. Invoice references PO #77104 and BOL #48213; signed proof of delivery and lumper receipt attached. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. ACH preferred.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bill of lading (BOL) number and signed proof of delivery
invoiceChecklist.why: The signed POD proves the freight was delivered in good condition. Many shippers and brokers will not pay without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and delivery dates, origins, and destinations
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the customer match the charge to a specific shipment and lane, and settles questions about timing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer PO or load reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable departments often match invoices to POs and reject ones that do not carry the number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Line haul, fuel surcharge, and accessorials listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines make it clear what was agreed in the rate confirmation and what was added, which reduces disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supporting receipts for pass-through costs (lumper, tolls, scale tickets)
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers rarely pay third-party fees without a receipt, and attaching it avoids a back-and-forth.

invoiceChecklist.item: Detention and layover times with timestamps
invoiceChecklist.why: Detention is a common dispute. Gate-in, gate-out, and free time details back up the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: MC number, DOT number, and remit-to information
invoiceChecklist.why: Shippers use these to verify you as an authorized carrier or broker and to set up payment correctly.

logistics.paymentTerms: Net 30 is standard in freight, and larger shippers often push for Net 45 or Net 60. Small carriers commonly ask for faster terms such as Net 15 or use factoring, where a factoring company advances most of the invoice for a fee of roughly 1 to 5 percent. Quick-pay programs offered by brokers trade a small discount for payment in a few days. For warehousing and recurring delivery work, bill monthly and require a deposit or first month in advance for new accounts. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your contract. ACH and wire are typical for larger invoices, and checks are still used by some shippers.

tips.title: Get the rate confirmation in writing before the truck moves
tips.body: A signed rate confirmation or service agreement should list the rate, fuel surcharge, free time, and accessorial prices. It is the document you point to if the customer disputes the invoice.

tips.title: Invoice the day of delivery
tips.body: Send the invoice as soon as you have the signed POD. Payment terms usually start from the invoice date or receipt of documents, so delays push your cash back.

tips.title: Document detention as it happens
tips.body: Record arrival time, check-in time, and departure time, and notify the broker or shipper while the truck is still waiting. Detention claimed after the fact is often denied.

tips.title: Know your deadlines for freight claims and billing
tips.body: Many contracts set short windows for submitting invoices and for disputing charges. Check your agreements so you do not lose payment on a technicality.

tips.title: Watch customer credit
tips.body: Check credit on new shippers and brokers, and set a limit on open balances. A single unpaid load can wipe out the margin on many others.

faqs.question: Should I charge a fuel surcharge separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. A separate line, often tied to the national average diesel price, keeps your base rate stable and shows the customer how the charge is calculated. Make sure the method is in your agreement.

faqs.question: How do I bill for detention?
faqs.answer: Set free time in your rate confirmation, commonly two hours. Bill hours beyond that at the agreed hourly rate, and include arrival and departure times as proof.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a freight invoice?
faqs.answer: You can if the fee is stated in your contract or terms before the work is done. Common rates are 1 to 1.5 percent per month. Check your state's rules on maximum interest.

faqs.question: Do I need to attach the bill of lading?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. Most shippers and brokers require a signed BOL or POD with the invoice, and it is the best proof that the delivery was completed.

faqs.question: What if a customer short-pays because of a damage claim?
faqs.answer: Ask for the claim in writing with photos and the notation on the delivery receipt. Pay attention to the claim deadline in your contract, and invoice any undisputed portion separately so it gets paid.

estimate.intro: Logistics providers send quotes before moving freight or starting a storage or delivery arrangement. Shippers often compare several carriers or brokers on the same lane, so the quote has to be clear about what is included. Quotes are commonly a per-load rate, a lane rate valid for a period, or a per-pallet and per-order schedule for warehousing.

scopeChecklist.item: Origin, destination, and pickup and delivery windows
scopeChecklist.why: Distance and timing drive the price, and a changed address or window can change the cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Freight details: weight, dimensions, pallet count, commodity, and freight class
scopeChecklist.why: Rates depend on these, and a wrong weight or class leads to reweigh or reclass charges.
Dry van, reefer, flatbed, or box truck have different costs, and temperature control or hazmat adds requirements and fees.
Liftgate, inside delivery, residential delivery, and appointment scheduling are common sources of surprise charges.
Sets how long the driver will wait at no cost and what the hourly charge is after that.
Shows how the surcharge is calculated so the customer is not surprised when fuel prices change.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and insurance or liability limits
scopeChecklist.why: Market rates change quickly, and the customer should know the cargo liability limit and whether added coverage is available.

pricingTips.title: Price from your cost, not just the market
pricingTips.body: Know your cost per mile, driver pay, insurance, and deadhead before quoting. For brokers, check carrier cost first and add a margin that covers payment terms and claims risk.

pricingTips.title: Quote a lane rate with a volume range
pricingTips.body: For repeat shippers, offer a lane rate for a set number of loads per month. It gives the customer predictability and gives you steady work.

pricingTips.title: List accessorials as a rate sheet
pricingTips.body: Attach a short schedule showing detention, liftgate, redelivery, and storage prices. Customers can accept these up front instead of arguing about them later.

pricingTips.title: Set a short expiration date
pricingTips.body: Spot rates move daily. A quote good for 24 to 72 hours, or 30 days for contract lanes, protects you from a market change.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: A written quote that the customer accepts, usually through a signed rate confirmation, is generally treated as the agreed price. State the expiration date and conditions so changes in freight details can adjust the price.

faqs.question: What if the freight weighs more than quoted?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that the rate is based on the stated weight and dimensions and that changes will be re-rated. Ask for a scale ticket or BOL weight to support any adjustment.

faqs.question: Should I quote all-in or break out the fuel surcharge?
faqs.answer: Both are used. All-in rates are simpler for customers to compare, while a separate fuel line protects you if diesel prices move. Pick one and state it clearly.

faqs.question: How long should a warehousing quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Include the minimum monthly charge, the storage and handling rates, and any setup fees so the customer can compare it with other providers.

machinist.intro: Machinists run manual mills, lathes, CNC machining centers, and grinders to make or repair metal and plastic parts. Independent machinists and small job shops invoice manufacturers, contractors, repair customers, and hobbyists for prototype runs, production batches, one-off repairs, and reverse-engineered replacement parts. A typical invoice covers setup, machine time, material, outside processing, and shipping.
machinist.pricingModel: Most shops price by machine time at a shop rate that depends on the equipment: manual machines cost less per hour than 3-axis, 5-axis, or multi-axis turning centers. Setup and programming are usually billed separately as a one-time charge, then run time is billed per hour or folded into a per-piece price. Production work is quoted per piece with quantity breaks, since setup cost spreads across the run. Material is billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 15 to 30 percent, and outside services such as heat treating, plating, anodizing, or grinding are passed through with a handling markup. One-off repairs and prototypes are often a flat fee or hourly with a minimum charge. Many shops add fees for rush work, first article inspection reports, and material certifications.

rates.service: First article inspection or CMM report
Reverse engineering and CAD drawing from a sample part

Machine setup and fixturing, 3-axis VMC (two operations)

6061-T6 plate 0.75 in x 6 in x 12 in with mill cert (material cost plus 20%)

sampleInvoice.notes: PO #44718. Net 30. Parts shipped UPS Ground, tracking sent by email. Material certification and inspection report attached. Please report any discrepancies within 10 days of receipt. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer PO number, part number, and drawing revision
invoiceChecklist.why: Purchasing departments match invoices to POs and print revisions. A missing PO number is the most common reason a manufacturing customer delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized setup, programming, and run time or per-piece price
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often question setup charges on small runs. Showing them separately explains why a batch of 5 costs more per piece than a batch of 100.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material description, grade, size, and cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Metal prices swing, and customers want to see what alloy and stock you used. Include heat or lot numbers if you supplied mill certs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Outside processing line items with vendor names
invoiceChecklist.why: Heat treat, plating, anodize, and grinding are real costs you front. Listing them avoids disputes and documents your pass-through markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity shipped versus quantity ordered
invoiceChecklist.why: Partial shipments, overruns, and underruns are common. Clear counts keep billing and customer receiving records in agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection, certification, and documentation charges
invoiceChecklist.why: First article reports, material certs, and certificates of conformance take real time. Listing them keeps them from being treated as free.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale exemption certificate reference
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, parts for resale or manufacturing may be exempt with a certificate on file. Note the certificate or the tax charged so your records hold up in an audit.

machinist.paymentTerms: Commercial customers usually pay net 30, and larger manufacturers sometimes stretch to net 45 or 60, so confirm terms before quoting. New customers, one-off jobs, and individuals are commonly asked for 50 percent upfront, with the balance due before parts ship. Jobs with expensive material or custom tooling often require a deposit that covers material cost. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated on the quote and invoice. Most shops accept checks, ACH, and credit cards, and some add a surcharge for cards on large invoices where the law in their state allows it.

tips.title: Charge setup separately from run time
tips.body: Setup, programming, and first-piece proving take the same time whether you make 1 part or 500. Billing it as its own line makes repeat orders easier to price and stops customers from expecting a low piece price on a tiny run.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge per job
tips.body: Small repair jobs eat time in quoting, material pickup, setup, and deburring. A minimum of one hour of shop rate or a flat $75 to $150 keeps tiny jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Bill scrap and rework honestly
tips.body: If you scrap a part from your own error, absorb it. If scrap comes from bad customer-supplied material or a drawing change, document it and bill it. Keep notes and emails so the charge is not a surprise.

tips.title: Add a material surcharge clause
tips.body: Steel, aluminum, titanium, and tool steel prices can change between quote and purchase. A line stating that quotes are valid for 30 days and material is subject to price changes protects you on longer jobs.

tips.title: Hold customer-owned property in writing
tips.body: When customers send material, fixtures, or finished parts for rework, record what you received and its condition. Storage fees for unclaimed work can be stated on the invoice and in your terms.

faqs.question: Should I bill by the hour or by the piece?
faqs.answer: Bill by the hour for repairs, prototypes, and jobs with unknown scope. Bill per piece for repeat or production work where you know the cycle time. Either way, show setup as its own charge so the customer sees what drives the price.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up material?
faqs.answer: Many shops add 15 to 30 percent to material cost to cover purchasing time, cutting, waste, freight, and the risk of price changes. Exotic alloys or very small orders may justify the higher end. State the markup policy in your terms.

faqs.question: Can I invoice before the parts ship?
faqs.answer: Yes, for deposits or when you are doing progress billing on a long job. For standard jobs, most shops invoice on shipment so the invoice matches the packing slip. Get agreement on this in the quote.

faqs.question: What do I do if a customer rejects parts?
faqs.answer: Compare the parts to the print and PO. If they are out of tolerance, rework or remake them at your cost. If they meet the print, send your inspection data and keep the invoice active. Clear drawings and a signed quote make these disputes easier to settle.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on machined parts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on how the customer uses the parts. Many states exempt parts that become part of a product for resale when you have a resale or exemption certificate on file. Repair work and sales to end users are often taxable. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Machinists send quotes before every job that involves new parts, a new customer, or a changed print. Customers often send the same drawing to several shops and compare unit price, lead time, and what is included. A clear quote with stated assumptions lets you compete on more than price.

scopeChecklist.item: Part number, drawing revision, and quantity
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing is tied to the exact print and quantity. If the revision or quantity changes, the quote should be revisited.

scopeChecklist.item: Material grade, form, and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: 6061 versus 7075 or 304 versus 316 changes cost and cycle time. State whether you buy the material or the customer provides it.

scopeChecklist.item: Tolerances and surface finish you are quoting to
scopeChecklist.why: Tight tolerances and fine finishes add time and inspection. If the print has tolerances you did not price for, you need a basis for a change order.
Custom fixtures, special cutters, and soft jaws are real costs. State whether they are included, one-time, or owned by the customer.
Deburring, heat treat, plating, anodize, and passivation add cost and lead time. List which are included and who is responsible for vendor delays.
First article reports, CMM inspection, material certs, and CoCs are extra work. Quote them as line items if the customer needs them.

scopeChecklist.item: Lead time, quote validity, and delivery terms
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices and shop schedules change. State how long the quote is good, when work will ship, and whether freight is included.

pricingTips.title: Quote quantity breaks
pricingTips.body: Offer prices at 1, 10, 50, and 100 pieces when the customer is unsure. Spreading setup over larger runs shows value and often leads to bigger orders.

pricingTips.title: Build price from cycle time, not guesswork
pricingTips.body: Estimate setup, run time per piece, tool changes, and deburring, then multiply by your machine rate. Add material, outside services, and a margin. Track actual times afterward so the next quote is more accurate.

pricingTips.title: Add contingency for first-time parts
pricingTips.body: A new part with thin walls, hard materials, or tight tolerances may need extra proving time. Build in a modest buffer or note that prototype pricing may change if the print requires it.

pricingTips.title: List your assumptions on the quote
pricingTips.body: Note that pricing assumes the supplied print, standard tolerances where not called out, and no more than the stated number of operations. This gives you a clear basis if the customer changes the print later.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Most shops quote simple jobs for free. For complex parts that need reverse engineering, model building, or detailed process planning, a quoting or engineering fee is reasonable, and many shops credit it toward the order.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. For jobs with volatile material such as stainless, titanium, or nickel alloys, 7 to 14 days is safer, or the quote can say material is priced at time of order.

faqs.question: What if the customer changes the drawing after I quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line in your quote that pricing applies to the stated print revision. When a new revision arrives, review it and send a revised quote or change order before cutting any more parts.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit on a quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit of 30 to 50 percent is common for new customers, custom tooling, or jobs where you must buy expensive material upfront. State the deposit terms on the quote so the customer accepts them when approving it.

maintenance.intro: Maintenance technicians and small maintenance businesses handle repairs and upkeep for landlords, property managers, HOAs, small commercial buildings, and homeowners. Invoices usually cover a mix of labor, parts, and trip charges across several small jobs, often tied to a work order or unit number.
maintenance.pricingModel: Most maintenance work is billed hourly, with a minimum charge (often one hour) or a flat trip fee to cover travel and setup. Common repairs such as replacing a faucet, patching drywall, or swapping a door lock are sometimes priced as flat fees once you know how long they take. Parts and materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10 to 25 percent, to cover sourcing time, store runs, and warranty risk. Property managers and commercial clients often negotiate a lower hourly rate in return for steady volume, and some pay monthly retainers for scheduled inspections, filter changes, and routine rounds. After-hours and emergency calls usually carry a 1.5x to 2x rate. Larger jobs, like a bathroom refresh or deck repair, are better quoted as a project than billed by the hour.

rates.service: Apartment unit turnover (touch-up paint, cleaning checks, minor repairs)
Drywall patch and paint (small hole or water stain)
Faucet, toilet, or garbage disposal replacement (labor only)
Door lock or deadbolt replacement (labor only)
Scheduled property inspection and routine rounds

Replace kitchen faucet - labor
Kitchen faucet, single-handle pull-down (cost plus 15%)
Supply lines and plumber's putty
Reset and re-hang bedroom door, replace strike plate - labor
Smoke detector battery replacement, 3 units

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Parts receipts available on request. Work warrantied for 30 days on labor. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Maintenance clients often manage many buildings, and their accounting needs each charge tied to the right property or tenant.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work order or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and commercial clients usually will not process payment without the reference number they issued.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and time on site
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing and any after-hours multiplier are easier to defend with clear dates and start and end times.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor with a description of each task
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines for each repair show the client what they paid for and make it easier to bill owners or tenants individually.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts and materials listed separately with quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients expect to see what was installed, and itemized parts help if they ask about markup or need to track a repair for warranty.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge or minimum fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing this as its own line avoids arguments about short visits where labor alone would be small.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or insurance information, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license for plumbing, electrical, or work over a certain dollar amount, and commercial clients often ask for proof of insurance.

maintenance.paymentTerms: Homeowners and one-time clients are commonly asked to pay at completion by card, check, or electronic transfer. Property managers and commercial accounts usually pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, sometimes after a monthly statement, so set expectations before the first job. For larger projects or jobs requiring special-order parts, a deposit covering materials, often 30 to 50 percent, is standard. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance on your estimate or agreement. Check your state's rules on late fees and lien rights, which vary.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge and stick to it
tips.body: A 20-minute fix still costs you drive time, fuel, and the gap in your schedule. A one-hour minimum or a flat trip fee keeps small calls worth taking.

tips.title: Bill parts at cost plus markup
tips.body: Store runs, returns, and wrong-part trips take unpaid time. A consistent markup of 10 to 25 percent covers this. Keep receipts in case a client asks.

tips.title: Invoice per work order for property managers
tips.body: Separate invoices for each work order or unit make approval and payment faster than one lump sum covering several buildings.

tips.title: Take photos before and after
tips.body: Photos of the problem, the repair, and any extra damage you found support your invoice if a tenant or owner disputes the work or the charge.

tips.title: Send the invoice the same day
tips.body: Maintenance jobs are small and easy to forget. Billing the day you finish keeps the work fresh in the client's mind and keeps cash coming in steadily.

faqs.question: How much should a maintenance technician charge per hour?
faqs.answer: Many independent maintenance technicians charge $50 to $95 per hour depending on region, experience, and whether the client is a homeowner or a property manager. Emergency and after-hours work often runs 1.5x to 2x that.

faqs.question: Should I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Most do, either through a flat trip charge or by billing portal-to-portal time. Whatever you choose, state it on your estimate or service agreement before the first visit.

faqs.question: Can I mark up parts I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is standard practice. A markup of 10 to 25 percent is common. If a client or contract requires receipts at cost, agree on that up front and charge a higher labor rate or a handling fee instead.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to do maintenance work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and the work. Many states let you do minor repairs without a license, but require licensed trades for plumbing, electrical, and HVAC work, or set a dollar limit on unlicensed jobs. Check with your state licensing board.

faqs.question: What if a property manager pays late?
faqs.answer: Put payment terms in writing before you start, send invoices with the work order number, and follow up a few days before the due date. If you have a late fee clause in your agreement, apply it consistently.

estimate.intro: Maintenance technicians send estimates for repairs beyond a simple service call, such as water damage repair, deck or fence work, appliance replacement, or turnover work on multiple units. Clients, especially landlords and property managers, often compare several quotes and look at total price, timeline, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact scope of work by location
scopeChecklist.why: Naming the room, fixture, or unit prevents arguments about whether something like the second bathroom or the fence gate was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies materials and which grade
scopeChecklist.why: A builder-grade faucet and a premium one can differ by hundreds of dollars, so name brand, model, or allowance.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor as flat price or hourly estimate
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether the number is fixed or a not-to-exceed figure that could change.
Rotted subfloor behind a toilet or old wiring behind a wall can add cost, so state that unforeseen conditions will be quoted separately.
If the job needs a permit or a licensed plumber or electrician, say who arranges and pays for it.
Start date, expected duration, tenant access needs, and debris removal all affect cost and client expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate expiration date and deposit terms
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change, so limit how long the quote holds, typically 14 to 30 days, and state any deposit required to order parts.

pricingTips.title: Price the job, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: Add drive time, material pickup, cleanup, and a cushion for surprises. Underestimating small repairs is the most common way solo technicians lose money.

pricingTips.title: Offer a not-to-exceed number for uncertain repairs
pricingTips.body: When you cannot see the full problem, quote a cap and bill actual time up to it. Clients appreciate the ceiling and you are protected if the job is simple.

pricingTips.title: Separate labor and materials on the quote
pricingTips.body: Showing both lines builds trust and makes it easy to adjust if the client wants a cheaper fixture or supplies their own.

pricingTips.title: Give volume pricing for multi-unit work
pricingTips.body: Landlords with several units may accept a lower per-unit price if you can batch similar tasks, which also saves you setup and travel time.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many maintenance technicians offer free estimates for straightforward jobs but charge a fee, often $50 to $100, for time-consuming diagnostics or large projects. Credit the fee toward the work if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Shorter windows make sense when material prices are changing quickly or your schedule is tight.

faqs.question: What if the job costs more than my estimate?
faqs.answer: Do not exceed the quote without written approval. Stop, explain the cause, such as hidden damage, and send a change order with the added cost before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A signature or written email approval confirms the scope and price, and it gives you something to point to if a dispute comes up later.

maintenance-services.intro: Maintenance services businesses handle the ongoing upkeep of homes, rental properties, and small commercial buildings. That includes small repairs, seasonal tasks, punch-list work, and recurring service contracts. Clients are usually homeowners, landlords, property managers, and HOAs, and the invoices cover labor, materials, trip charges, and sometimes monthly retainers.
maintenance-services.pricingModel: Most maintenance work is billed hourly, often with a one-hour or two-hour minimum to cover travel and setup. Small jobs are often quoted as a flat fee per task, such as replacing a faucet or patching a section of drywall. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10 to 25 percent, to cover sourcing, pickup time, and returns. Property managers and landlords often get a contracted hourly rate or a monthly retainer for routine visits, with after-hours and emergency calls billed at 1.5 to 2 times the normal rate. Many solo operators add a trip charge or service call fee that is waived or applied toward the job. Specialty work that needs a license, such as electrical or plumbing beyond minor fixes, is often subcontracted and billed through with a markup.

Monthly maintenance contract (small rental or office)
