sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Work order #2291 from property manager. Receipts for materials available on request. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Landlords and property managers track costs per unit, and they can't pay or allocate an invoice that doesn't say where the work happened.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work order or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property management companies and commercial clients often won't process payment without the reference number they issued.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service and hours per visit
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing by visit lets clients match your bill to tenant requests and prevents disputes over time on site.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, and tax rules in many states, treat parts and labor differently, and separate lines make your markup transparent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge or minimum fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing it as its own line explains why a 20-minute fix cost more than 20 minutes of labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or registration number, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a contractor or handyman license above a dollar threshold, and some clients require proof before paying.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on materials or services where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Rules vary by state on whether labor, materials, or both are taxable, so check yours and show the tax as its own line.

maintenance-services.paymentTerms: Small residential jobs are usually due on completion, by card, check, or electronic transfer. For larger repair projects, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials is common. Property managers and commercial accounts typically pay net 15 or net 30, and some pay only after a monthly statement is reconciled. Recurring contracts are best billed in advance at the start of each month. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated on the invoice or contract up front. Emergency calls should be paid at the time of service whenever possible.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: A 30-minute repair still takes drive time, parts pickup, and setup. A one-hour minimum or a trip charge keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Mark up materials consistently
tips.body: Your time buying and returning parts is real work. Apply the same markup to every client, put it in your contract, and keep receipts to show actual cost if asked.

tips.title: Bill property managers on a schedule
tips.body: Send invoices per work order right after completion, with photos of finished work attached. Quick, documented invoices get approved faster in a manager's queue.

tips.title: Write up scope creep as you find it
tips.body: When you open a wall and find water damage, stop and get written approval, even by text, before continuing. Then bill the added work as its own line.

tips.title: Separate recurring and one-off work
tips.body: On contract clients, show the monthly fee and any out-of-scope work separately so the client sees that extra jobs aren't covered by the retainer.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat rate for maintenance work?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended repairs and troubleshooting where the scope is unknown. Use flat rates for repeatable tasks you can time reliably, like gutter cleaning or hanging a door. Flat rates reward efficiency but need a cushion for surprises.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up materials?
faqs.answer: Ten to 25 percent over your cost is typical. Smaller jobs with many small trips can justify the higher end. Whatever you choose, state it in your estimate or contract so it doesn't come as a surprise.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to invoice for maintenance work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and city. Many states exempt small jobs under a dollar limit from contractor licensing, but limits vary widely and electrical and plumbing work usually requires a licensed trade. Check with your state licensing board before taking larger or specialty work.

faqs.question: How do I bill a tenant emergency that a landlord approved by phone?
faqs.answer: Invoice the landlord or management company, not the tenant, unless they agreed otherwise. Note the date and time of the call, who authorized the work, and the emergency rate. Send it the same day with photos.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most maintenance businesses charge either a flat trip fee or bill drive time at a reduced hourly rate. Put the policy in your estimate and show it as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Maintenance providers quote before work starts on repairs, turnovers, and anything with parts involved. Clients often get two or three quotes and compare the total price, the hourly rate, and whether materials are included. Landlords and property managers may require a written estimate approved before you begin.

scopeChecklist.why: List each repair and where it is, such as 'replace toilet fill valve, upstairs bath', so nobody assumes extra work is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies materials and what grade
scopeChecklist.why: Builder-grade and premium fixtures differ a lot in price. Naming the brand or tier prevents arguments when the receipt arrives.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor basis: hourly estimate or fixed price
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know if the number is a cap, a guess, or a firm price, and what happens if the job runs long.
State that rot, mold, outdated wiring, or code issues found during work are not included and will be quoted separately.
Note tenant coordination, key pickup, or utility shutoffs. Delays caused by access problems can be billed.
If part of the job needs a permit or a licensed trade, say who handles it and whether the cost is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate expiration date and payment terms
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices move, so a 14 to 30 day window protects you, and listing deposit and due dates up front avoids later disputes.

pricingTips.title: Price the whole visit, not just the repair
pricingTips.body: Include drive time, parts runs, cleanup, and disposal. Many small jobs lose money because only the hands-on time was counted.

pricingTips.title: Give a range for unknowns
pricingTips.body: When a problem could be a loose fitting or a failed line, quote a range with the conditions that put it at each end instead of guessing one number.

pricingTips.title: Bundle small tasks
pricingTips.body: Offering a discount for a punch list of several items in one visit helps clients say yes and saves you repeat trip charges.

pricingTips.title: Break out options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic fix and a longer-lasting replacement as separate line items so the client chooses and the approval is clear.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes for small jobs are normally free. For complex jobs requiring a long site visit or diagnostic work, a fee of $50 to $150 is common, often credited back if the client hires you.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: Say in the estimate how overages are handled. A common approach is to contact the client for written approval before exceeding the quote by more than 10 percent, and to bill approved additions as change orders.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding contract?
faqs.answer: Not by itself in most cases, but once the client accepts it in writing it can serve as the agreement. Add scope, price, and terms so it holds up if there is a dispute, and check your state's rules for larger jobs.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to 30 days is typical. Use a shorter window when the job depends on materials with volatile prices, such as lumber or copper.

makeup-artist.intro: Makeup artists bill brides, wedding parties, photographers, production companies, and individual clients for applications, trials, and on-location work. Invoices usually combine a service fee, a travel or early-start charge, and sometimes products or kit fees. Many freelancers also work with salons, studios, or agencies, so some jobs are invoiced to a business rather than a person.
makeup-artist.pricingModel: Most makeup artists charge a flat fee per application, with different prices for bridal, bridal party, special occasion, and editorial or commercial work. Bridal work is often sold as a package that covers a trial, the wedding-day application, and sometimes touch-up time or a second artist. Travel is billed separately, either as a flat fee, a per-mile rate, or a day rate for destination work. Early start times (before 6 or 7 a.m.) usually carry a surcharge. Film, TV, and commercial jobs are more often priced by day rate or half-day rate, with a kit fee added on top of the artist's rate. Lash strips, airbrush, and hair styling are sold as add-ons. Deposits and non-refundable booking fees are standard, since a single wedding date takes up an entire day that can't be rebooked.

rates.service: Special occasion or event makeup (prom, photoshoot, party)
Lash strip or individual lash application
Commercial, editorial, or film set work

items.description: Bridal makeup, wedding day (includes lashes)
Bridesmaid makeup
Mother of the bride makeup
Early start surcharge (before 7:00 a.m.)
Travel to venue, 35 miles each way
Bridal trial (paid previously, 3/12)

sampleInvoice.notes: Wedding date: June 14. Deposit of $300 received on booking is applied to this invoice. Remaining balance is due 7 days before the wedding date. Payments accepted by card, Zelle, or check. Late touch-up time beyond 2 hours after application is billed at $60 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, address, and start time
invoiceChecklist.why: Makeup jobs are tied to a specific date and call time, so listing them confirms exactly what was booked and supports early start or location charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Names and count of everyone receiving services
invoiceChecklist.why: Group bookings change often. Listing each person or a headcount avoids disputes when someone is added or dropped.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service type for each person
invoiceChecklist.why: Bridal, bridesmaid, airbrush, and lash add-ons are priced differently, so each line should say what was applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trial date and whether it is included or billed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget they already paid for a trial as part of a package, or that it was extra.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and the date
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how much has been credited toward the total and makes clear that the booking fee is non-refundable if that is your policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, parking, and early start charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Breaking these out keeps the base service price consistent and shows the client what drove the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cosmetology or esthetics license number, where your state requires it
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license for makeup application for pay, and some clients, venues, and productions ask to see it. Check your state board's rules.

makeup-artist.paymentTerms: Most makeup artists take a non-refundable deposit of 25-50% to hold the date, often paid when the contract is signed. The balance is typically due 1-2 weeks before a wedding, or at the time of service for smaller appointments. Commercial and production clients usually pay on net 15 to net 30 terms, and may require a W-9 and a purchase order or call sheet reference. Late fees of 1.5% per month or a flat amount are common for business clients, but for private clients it is more effective to collect the full balance before the event. Cards, Zelle, Venmo, and checks are all common, and day-of payment is often handled by sending a payment link in advance.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the event
tips.body: On wedding mornings, nobody wants to handle money. Set a due date a week or two ahead so the invoice is settled before you arrive and you are not chasing a bridal party member afterward.

tips.title: Put the deposit policy in writing
tips.body: Spell out that the deposit is non-refundable and what happens if the date changes. A short contract signed at booking prevents most cancellation disputes.

tips.title: Charge for headcount changes
tips.body: Set a deadline, such as 30 days out, after which the final count is locked. Adds after that date are billed at the standard rate if you can fit them, and drops are still charged.

tips.title: Bill travel and wait time separately
tips.body: Long gaps between clients, parking fees, and venue distance eat into your day. Add travel, parking, and an hourly rate for extended standby time as their own lines.

tips.title: Track kit and product costs on commercial jobs
tips.body: For set work, a kit fee on top of your day rate covers consumables like sponges, disposables, and sanitizing supplies. State it as a line item rather than raising your day rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a bridal trial?
faqs.answer: Yes, most makeup artists do. A trial takes one to two hours and uses products and your time. Some include a trial in a bridal package at a bundled price, while others charge separately and credit it toward the wedding booking. Either way, list it on the invoice so the client sees what they paid for.

faqs.question: Is the deposit refundable if the client cancels?
faqs.answer: Standard practice is that the deposit is non-refundable because you turned away other bookings for that date. Make sure your contract says so and that the client agreed to it before paying.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on makeup services?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Services are often not taxed, but products you sell to the client, such as lipstick they take home, usually are. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional about how your services and retail items are treated.

faqs.question: Can I charge for products used on a client?
faqs.answer: You can, but most artists include product use in the service price. If you add a separate product fee, state it up front in your quote. Retail items the client keeps are normally listed as separate lines.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a production company or photographer?
faqs.answer: Include your day or half-day rate, the shoot date, the production name, your kit fee, and any overtime. Many businesses ask for a W-9 first, and some require a PO number or call sheet reference on the invoice. Use net 15 to net 30 terms and state them clearly.

estimate.intro: Makeup artists send quotes when a client inquires about a wedding, event, photoshoot, or production, usually before a date is held. Clients compare the per-person price, what is included, travel charges, and how much of the day you stay. A clear quote also tells them what they need to do to secure the booking.

scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on the day, the hour, and the distance. Holding the quote to a specific date and address avoids surprises if the venue changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact headcount and who is receiving which service
scopeChecklist.why: The number of people is the biggest factor in total price and in how many hours or assistants you need.
State whether lashes, airbrush, skin prep, and a touch-up kit are included or extra so clients do not assume they are covered.
Specify whether a trial is included, how long it lasts, and where it takes place, so the client understands what the package covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel, parking, and early start fees
scopeChecklist.why: These charges often change the total by $50-200. Listing them upfront prevents sticker shock on the final invoice.
Clients often assume you will remain through photos or the ceremony. Define whether that is included and how it is billed if extended.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, balance due date, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: The quote should show how to hold the date and what happens if plans change, which protects you from losing an entire day of income.

pricingTips.title: Offer packages with clear tiers
pricingTips.body: Bundle the trial, wedding-day application, and a bridal party rate into two or three packages. Clients find it easier to choose between options, and you avoid pricing every service individually.

pricingTips.title: Price for the full time block, not just the application
pricingTips.body: A bridal party of six can take four hours or more, plus setup and travel. Calculate what the day would earn you and set the total accordingly, rather than only multiplying per-person prices.

pricingTips.title: Add an assistant fee for large groups
pricingTips.body: When the party is too big for one artist to finish on time, quote a second artist and show the cost. It keeps the schedule realistic and explains why the total is higher.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Wedding dates fill quickly and your rates may change. A quote that is valid for 7 to 14 days encourages a decision and keeps your calendar from being held indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or a per-person price?
faqs.answer: Give both. Show the per-person rate for each service and a total for the headcount at that time. If the number of people changes, the client can see how the price adjusts.

faqs.question: Do I charge for quotes or consultations?
faqs.answer: Quotes are generally free. A brief consultation call is often free too. A full trial is a paid service because it takes real time and product, though some artists credit it toward the booking.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to negotiate the price?
faqs.answer: Rather than lowering your rate, adjust the scope. Remove airbrush, shorten the touch-up time, or reduce the number of services. This keeps your pricing consistent with past clients.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is typical for event work, and it should state that the date is not held until the deposit is paid. For busy seasons like spring and fall wedding months, a shorter window is reasonable.

management-consultant.intro: Management consultants advise small and mid-sized companies, nonprofits, and sometimes government agencies on strategy, operations, organizational design, and performance. Solo and boutique consultants invoice for diagnostic work, project phases, ongoing advisory retainers, workshops, and expenses incurred on the client's behalf. Invoices usually need to tie back to a signed statement of work and often pass through a client's accounts payable department.
management-consultant.pricingModel: Most independent management consultants use one of four models: hourly or daily rates for open-ended advisory work, fixed fees for defined projects such as an operations assessment or strategic plan, monthly retainers for ongoing access and a set amount of hours, and value-based fees tied to an agreed outcome. Fixed-fee projects are often split into phases (diagnostic, recommendations, implementation support) and billed at milestones. Day rates are common for on-site work and workshops. Expenses such as travel, lodging, and third-party survey tools are typically billed at cost, sometimes with a small administrative markup if the contract allows it. Rates rise with specialization, industry credentials, and prior experience at larger firms, and they usually run higher for larger clients.

rates.service: Interim management or fractional executive role

items.description: Operations assessment, Phase 1: stakeholder interviews, process mapping, and findings report (50% milestone)
Leadership team workshop facilitation, on-site (Mar 12)
Additional advisory hours outside SOW scope: vendor contract review
Travel: round-trip airfare and ground transportation (receipts attached)
Lodging, 1 night (receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Reference SOW dated February 5 and PO #48213. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Remaining 50% of the assessment fee will be invoiced on delivery of the final recommendations. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement of work or contract reference and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to agreed scope so accounts payable and the sponsor can approve quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client purchase order number and cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Many mid-sized and large clients will not process payment without a PO, and missing it delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or phase name and percentage complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why the fixed-fee installment is due and prevents questions about what has been delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and dates of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Required for retainers and hourly work and helps the client match the invoice to their project timeline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours or days worked with a brief task description
invoiceChecklist.why: Time-based clients often audit these entries, and detail reduces pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized expenses with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients typically reimburse expenses at cost only with documentation, and many have travel policies you should follow.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need this to set you up as a vendor and to issue a 1099 at year end in the US.

management-consultant.paymentTerms: Net 30 is the norm for corporate clients, though small businesses and nonprofits may accept net 15. Many consultants collect a deposit of 25% to 50% on signing for fixed-fee projects, with the balance tied to milestones, and bill retainers monthly in advance. Larger clients may push for net 45 or net 60 through their vendor policies, so agree on terms in the contract before work starts. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if written into the agreement. Payment is usually by ACH or wire for larger amounts, with checks and card payments used less often because of processing costs.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoice the retainer at the start of the month, not the end. State how many hours or what deliverables it covers and what happens to unused time, whether it expires or rolls over.

tips.title: Tie fixed fees to milestones, not dates
tips.body: Link installments to deliverables such as the findings report or the final presentation. If the client delays feedback, the payment schedule does not stall with it.

tips.title: Track out-of-scope work as it happens
tips.body: Scope creep is the main margin killer in consulting. Keep a running log of extra requests and flag them in writing, then bill them as a separate line or change order.

tips.title: Find out the client's payment process early
tips.body: Ask who approves invoices, whether a PO is needed, how often payment runs occur, and what vendor forms are required. Many late payments come from missing paperwork rather than unwillingness to pay.

tips.title: Send the invoice when the deliverable lands
tips.body: Invoice the same day you present the report or complete the workshop, while the value is fresh. Waiting until month end adds weeks to your collection cycle.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or charge a fixed fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly or daily rates when scope is unclear or the client will direct the work. Use a fixed fee when the deliverables are well defined. Fixed fees reward efficiency, but they need a clear scope and a change process to protect you.

faqs.question: Can I bill clients for travel time?
faqs.answer: Only if your contract says so. Many consultants bill travel time at 50% of their rate or not at all, and bill actual travel costs as expenses. Put the policy in the agreement before the first trip.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Most states do not tax professional consulting services, but some tax certain services or business services. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who disputes part of an invoice?
faqs.answer: Ask which line items they question and refer to the signed scope and your time log. Offer to resolve the disputed items quickly and request payment of the undisputed amount in the meantime.

faqs.question: Can I add a markup to expenses?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the contract permits it. Some consultants add 5% to 15% to cover administrative costs, while others pass expenses through at cost. If your agreement is silent, bill at cost.

estimate.intro: Management consultants send a proposal or quote after an initial discovery conversation and before signing a statement of work. Clients usually compare scope, timeline, team, and total fee across two or three firms, and they pay close attention to what is excluded. A good estimate frames the problem, the approach, and the price in a document that can double as the contract.

scopeChecklist.why: Confirms you and the client agree on what success looks like, which prevents disputes over whether the work met its goal.
A written report, a slide deck, a financial model, and a workshop are priced differently, so name each one.
Sets expectations for when work starts, when you need client input, and when each milestone is due.
Delays often come from slow data, unavailable stakeholders, or missing approvals, so list what the client must provide and by when.
State the number of interviews, workshops, review rounds, and any implementation support not included, so extra work is clearly out of scope.
Spell out whether the price is fixed, capped, or time and materials, and when each installment is due.
Clarifies whether travel and other costs are included, billed at cost, or capped, avoiding surprises on the final invoice.

pricingTips.title: Price against the value of the problem
pricingTips.body: A project that saves a client $200,000 a year can support a larger fee than hours alone suggest. Ask about the cost of the problem during discovery and anchor your price to it.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic diagnostic, a diagnostic with a plan, and a full engagement with implementation support. Options shift the discussion from whether to hire you to which scope fits.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Add a buffer of 10% to 20% for projects where data quality or stakeholder availability is uncertain, or use a phased quote with the second phase priced after the first.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity period
pricingTips.body: State that the quote holds for 30 days. This protects you if your availability or the client's scope changes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal?
faqs.answer: Short proposals after an introductory call are usually free. If the client wants a detailed diagnostic, a custom scoping study, or significant upfront analysis, charge a paid discovery phase and credit it against the full project if they proceed.

faqs.question: How detailed should my estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to define deliverables, timeline, assumptions, and price, usually two to five pages. Avoid listing every task, since that invites line-by-line negotiation of your fee.

faqs.question: Should I show my hourly rate in a fixed-fee quote?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Showing hours invites the client to haggle over the rate instead of the value. You may reference an hourly rate for work outside the agreed scope or for change requests.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that describes the added work, the cost, and the effect on the timeline. Get approval before doing the work, and bill it as a separate line item.

manufacturing.intro: Small manufacturers, job shops, and contract fabricators invoice customers for parts, assemblies, and production runs made to their specifications or from the shop's own designs. Typical billing covers per-piece production, setup and tooling charges, materials, finishing, and freight. Many work from a customer purchase order, so the invoice has to match the PO closely to get paid.
manufacturing.pricingModel: Most manufacturing work is priced per piece or per lot, built up from materials, machine time, labor, setup, and overhead, plus margin. One-time costs such as setup, programming, fixtures, and tooling are usually billed separately (non-recurring engineering, or NRE) or amortized into the piece price at stated volumes. Prototype and short runs carry a higher unit price because setup is spread across fewer parts, and price breaks apply at higher quantities. Shops that bill by time use machine-hour rates that differ by equipment (a CNC mill versus a manual lathe), plus a separate rate for hand labor, assembly, or inspection. Materials are either passed through at cost plus a markup or built into the piece price, and surcharges for volatile metals or resin are common. Outside services like plating, heat treat, or powder coating are billed at cost plus a handling markup. Freight and packaging are typically separate lines unless quoted as delivered.

rates.service: CNC machining (mill or lathe) shop rate

items.description: Aluminum 6061 bracket, P/N BR-2210 Rev C, machined and deburred (PO 48217)
Setup and CNC programming (one-time NRE)
Clear anodize, outside service (cost plus 15% handling)
First article inspection report with dimensional data
Packaging and palletizing
Freight, LTL to customer dock

sampleInvoice.notes: PO 48217. Shipped complete, 500 of 500 pieces, on 3/14. Net 30 from invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Any quality claims must be reported within 15 days of receipt. Certificate of conformance and material certs attached.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer PO number and line item
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable departments often match invoices to POs and reject or hold anything that does not line up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Part number and revision level
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms exactly which drawing version was built, which settles disputes if the design changed mid-order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity ordered, shipped, and remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Partial shipments and overruns or underruns are common, and the invoice should show what is being billed now versus later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Setup, tooling, and NRE as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers need to see one-time charges apart from piece price so they can compare reorder pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials, material surcharges, and outside services
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows pass-through costs clearly, especially when metal or resin prices moved after the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Packing slip, ship date, and tracking or BOL number
invoiceChecklist.why: Proves delivery and starts the payment clock for customers who pay from receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications and sales tax or resale exemption status
invoiceChecklist.why: Material certs and certificates of conformance may be required to pay, and tax treatment depends on the state and whether the buyer provides a resale certificate.

manufacturing.paymentTerms: Net 30 is the standard for commercial manufacturing, with larger customers sometimes pushing for net 45 or net 60. New customers and custom work usually warrant a deposit of 30-50% up front to cover material and tooling, with the balance due on shipment or net terms. Tooling and NRE are often billed in full at order or at first article approval. Progress billing is common on long production runs or large assemblies. Early-pay discounts such as 2% 10 net 30 are used occasionally. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated on the quote and invoice in advance. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or wire, and card payments are accepted by some shops with a surcharge.

tips.title: Bill setup separately from piece price
tips.body: If setup is buried in the unit price, a customer who reorders 50 pieces will expect the same price as the original 500. Listing NRE and setup on their own lines keeps reorders priced fairly.

tips.title: Invoice at shipment, not at completion
tips.body: Many customers treat the ship date as the start of payment terms. Invoice the day the parts leave, and send the packing slip and certs with it so nothing delays approval.

tips.title: Put material surcharges in writing
tips.body: State on the quote that pricing is good for a set number of days and that material cost changes may be passed through. Without that language, you absorb price swings on steel, aluminum, or resin.

tips.title: Handle overruns and shortages up front
tips.body: Agree on an acceptable quantity tolerance, such as plus or minus 5-10%, so you can bill what you actually shipped without a dispute.

tips.title: Track customer-supplied material and tooling
tips.body: If a customer sends material or owns the tooling, note it on the invoice and your records. It affects billing, storage charges, and who is responsible for scrap.

faqs.question: Should I charge for setup on every order?
faqs.answer: Yes, unless the setup is already built into a quoted price at a specific quantity. Repeat orders still require setup time, tooling changes, and first piece checks, so many shops charge a reduced reorder setup fee.

faqs.question: How do I bill a partial shipment?
faqs.answer: Invoice only what shipped, with the PO line showing quantity ordered, quantity shipped, and balance remaining. Do not bill one-time charges like NRE twice, so mark them as billed on the first invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on manufactured parts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the buyer. Many states exempt items bought for resale or for use as components in other products if the buyer gives you a valid resale or exemption certificate. Keep that certificate on file, and check your state's rules or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the customer rejects some parts?
faqs.answer: Review the drawing and inspection data first. If the parts are out of tolerance, rework or remake them and credit or reissue the invoice as agreed. If they meet the print, document it with inspection records and hold to your terms.

faqs.question: Can I charge for storage if the customer delays pickup?
faqs.answer: You can if the quote or terms state it. Include a clause that finished goods held more than 15 or 30 days after notice are billed at a storage rate or invoiced in full.

estimate.intro: Manufacturers quote before cutting any material, usually in response to a drawing, sample, or request for quote (RFQ). Customers often send the same RFQ to several shops and compare unit price, lead time, tooling cost, and quality documentation side by side.

scopeChecklist.item: Part number, revision, and drawing or model reference
scopeChecklist.why: Ties the price to a specific design so later revisions can be requoted rather than argued about.

scopeChecklist.item: Quantity breaks and annual volume assumptions
scopeChecklist.why: Unit price depends on lot size, so listing prices at several quantities shows the customer where the savings are.

scopeChecklist.item: Material specification and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: Alloy, grade, or resin type drives cost, and a substitution or customer-supplied material changes both price and liability.
Separates one-time costs from piece price and states who owns fixtures, molds, or dies after payment.
Tight tolerances, coatings, and required reports add cost, and the quote should say exactly what was priced.
Customers compare shipping dates, and the quote should state whether it is ex-works or delivered, and who pays freight.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and material price clause
scopeChecklist.why: Limits your exposure when raw material costs shift between the quote and the order.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from real costs
pricingTips.body: Add material with scrap allowance, machine time at the correct shop rate, labor, outside services, setup divided by quantity, and overhead, then apply margin. Quoting from a guess is how shops lose money on repeat jobs.

pricingTips.title: Quote multiple quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Show prices at, for example, 100, 500, and 1,000 pieces. Customers see the benefit of larger runs, and you get a chance to win a bigger order.

pricingTips.title: Price prototypes higher than production
pricingTips.body: Short runs absorb full setup and programming time. Say so on the quote so the customer understands why a 5-piece prototype costs far more per part than a later production run.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for outside services
pricingTips.body: Plating, heat treat, and coating vendors can raise prices or add lead time. Quote them at current cost with a handling markup and note that they are subject to vendor pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quoting?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free, but complex jobs that need engineering, design for manufacturability review, or sample parts often justify a quoting or engineering fee. It is common to credit that fee back if the customer places the order.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 30 days, and shorter, such as 7 to 14 days, when the job depends on volatile metals or resin prices. State the expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if the customer changes the drawing?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your quote references the drawing revision and says changes may affect price and lead time. Issue a revised quote for any new revision before work continues.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit to start production?
faqs.answer: For custom parts, new customers, or orders with expensive material or tooling, requesting 30-50% upfront is common. Put the deposit requirement on the quote so it is agreed before the order starts.

marketing-agency.intro: Marketing agencies, from solo consultants to teams of five or ten, invoice small and mid-size businesses for ongoing and project-based work. Typical line items include monthly retainers for social media, SEO, or paid ads management, one-time projects like a website or brand launch, and pass-through costs such as ad spend, stock assets, and software subscriptions.
marketing-agency.pricingModel: Most agencies use a mix of models. Monthly retainers are the backbone for ongoing work like SEO, content, social media management, email marketing, and paid media, and are usually priced as a flat fee tied to a defined scope or hours. Projects such as a brand identity, a website build, or a campaign launch are priced as flat fees, often billed in milestones. Hourly rates are used for consulting, strategy sessions, and out-of-scope requests. Paid media management is often priced as a flat fee or a percentage of ad spend (commonly 10-20%, with a minimum). Third-party costs like ad spend, stock photography, paid tools, and freelancers are either passed through at cost or with a modest markup, and should always appear as separate lines from your own fees.

rates.service: Agency hourly rate (strategy, consulting, ad hoc work)

items.description: Social media management retainer, June (12 posts, community management, monthly report)
SEO retainer, June (on-page updates, 2 blog posts, keyword tracking)
Google Ads management, June (fee on $3,000 ad spend at 15%)
Google Ads spend, June (billed at cost, no markup)
Landing page copy revisions outside retainer scope
Stock photo licenses for June campaign

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Ad spend is billed at cost per the platform statement, available on request. Retainer covers the scope in the service agreement dated 1/15; additional requests are billed at $110 per hour. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered (e.g., June 1-30)
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers are billed for a period of time, and clients need to match the invoice to the month's deliverables and reports.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer scope or reference to the service agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what is included, which supports billing separately for out-of-scope work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad spend listed separately from your management fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often confuse the two. Separate lines prevent disputes and make your fee percentage easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs with description and any markup
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock assets, software, printing, and freelancer costs should be itemized so the client sees what is yours and what is third-party.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope hours with dates and a short task description
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra work is the most commonly disputed line on an agency invoice. Specific entries make it easy to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size clients often require a PO number or a specific accounts payable contact before they will process payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone name and percentage for project work
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which stage was reached (for example, 50% on design approval) and ties payment to the agreed schedule.

marketing-agency.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the service month, or on the first of the month, and due on receipt or within 7-15 days. Project work commonly requires a 30-50% deposit before starting, with the balance split across milestones or due at launch. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for larger clients, though shorter terms protect cash flow. Many agencies charge a late fee of 1-1.5% per month and pause work or campaigns if an account is more than 15-30 days overdue, which should be stated in the contract. Ad spend is often collected in advance or charged directly to the client's own card on the ad platform so the agency does not front the money. ACH and credit card are the most common payment methods; card fees are sometimes passed on to the client.

tips.title: Never front ad spend
tips.body: Have clients put their own card on the Google or Meta account, or collect ad budget before the month begins. Floating thousands of dollars in ad spend while waiting on a net 30 invoice is a common way agencies get hurt.

tips.title: Define retainer scope in numbers
tips.body: State the number of posts, blog articles, reports, revision rounds, and meetings included each month. Vague retainers lead to scope creep, and a numbers-based scope gives you a clear basis for billing extra.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoice at the start of the month, not the end. Work such as campaign setup and content planning happens before results appear, and advance billing keeps you from carrying costs.

tips.title: Decide what happens to unused hours or deliverables
tips.body: If the retainer includes a set number of hours or posts, say whether they roll over or expire. Putting it in the contract avoids arguments when a client has a slow month.

tips.title: Review pricing yearly
tips.body: Retainers tend to stay frozen while workload grows. Build an annual increase clause of 3-8% into the agreement, and send notice 30-60 days ahead.

faqs.question: Should I mark up ad spend?
faqs.answer: Most agencies bill ad spend at cost and charge a separate management fee, either flat or as a percentage of spend. Hidden markup on ad spend can damage trust if the client sees the platform statement. If you do add a markup on other pass-through costs like software or freelancers, disclose it in your agreement.

faqs.question: Should I bill retainers at the start or end of the month?
faqs.answer: The start of the month is more common and better for cash flow, since much of the work is ongoing. Invoicing at the end makes sense only if you bill for variable usage, such as hours or ad spend that is not known until the month closes.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client disputes a retainer invoice because results were low?
faqs.answer: Point to the agreement. Retainers pay for work performed and deliverables, not guaranteed outcomes, unless you agreed to performance terms. Share your monthly report showing what was done and offer a strategy call to adjust the plan, but avoid discounting the invoice as a first response.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on marketing services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax services, but some tax advertising, digital products, or certain marketing deliverables like printed materials. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and add tax to the invoice only where it applies.

faqs.question: How should I bill for work done by subcontractors?
faqs.answer: Either include it in your fee as part of the deliverable or list it as a separate pass-through line, with or without markup. Whichever you choose, say so in your contract so the client knows how third-party work is billed.

estimate.intro: Marketing agencies send estimates or proposals before starting a new engagement, usually after a discovery call or audit. Clients often compare several agencies on price, scope, and expected deliverables, so the quote needs to show clearly what is included. A retainer proposal and a one-time project quote are structured differently, and both should be explicit about what is not covered.

scopeChecklist.why: State how many posts, articles, ad variations, landing pages, or reports are included so both sides agree on what the fee buys.
Unlimited revisions are the main source of lost margin on creative and copy work. Cap them, and give a rate for extra rounds.

scopeChecklist.item: Ad spend and who pays it
scopeChecklist.why: Make clear that the management fee does not include the ad budget, and say whether the client pays the platform directly.
List stock images, paid plugins, email platform fees, and freelancer costs, and whether they are billed to the client.
Delays in feedback, logins, and assets are a common cause of missed deadlines. State what the client provides and by when.
Retainers need a minimum term (often 3-6 months) and a notice period, usually 30 days, so you can plan capacity.
Say what reports you provide and how often, and state that results such as rankings or leads are not guaranteed unless you have agreed to specific terms.

pricingTips.title: Offer three tiers
pricingTips.body: Presenting good, better, and best retainer packages helps clients choose a level instead of deciding whether to hire at all. Define each tier by deliverables, not vague labels.

pricingTips.title: Price a paid discovery phase for larger projects
pricingTips.body: For complex work like a rebrand or a site build, charge for an audit or strategy phase before quoting the full project. It covers your time and produces a better scope.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours internally, quote a flat fee
pricingTips.body: Work out the hours for each task, multiply by your target rate, and add a buffer of 10-20% for revisions and meetings. Present the total as a flat fee so the client is not comparing hourly numbers.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should be valid for 14-30 days. Platform costs, your capacity, and market conditions change, and an expiry date encourages a decision.

faqs.question: Should I charge for proposals?
faqs.answer: Short proposals for standard services are normally free. For custom strategy work, such as a detailed audit or a competitive analysis, many agencies charge a fee and credit it toward the project if the client signs.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: A written quote that the client accepts, especially when paired with a signed agreement, generally forms the basis of the contract. State that changes in scope will be quoted separately and that the price holds only for the described work.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the client has no budget in mind?
faqs.answer: Ask about goals and the value of a new customer, then propose two or three options at different price levels. Seeing the options helps the client reveal what is realistic for them.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for on a project?
faqs.answer: 30-50% upfront is common for projects, with the remainder tied to milestones. For retainers, collecting the first month in advance before work starts is standard.

marketing-automation-consultant.intro: Marketing automation consultants set up and manage the systems that send emails, score leads, and move contacts through a funnel without manual work. Clients are usually small businesses, agencies, and in-house marketing teams that use platforms like HubSpot, Klaviyo, Marketo, ActiveCampaign, or Salesforce Marketing Cloud. Invoices typically cover audits, workflow builds, CRM integrations, migrations, training, and ongoing optimization retainers.
marketing-automation-consultant.pricingModel: Most consultants mix project fees and monthly retainers. Discovery and audits are often a flat fee, builds like a lead nurture program or platform migration are priced per project based on the number of workflows, emails, and integrations, and ongoing work is billed as a monthly retainer with a set number of hours. Hourly billing is common for ad hoc support, troubleshooting, and scope changes. Consultants with platform certifications or deep technical skills (API work, data hygiene, lead scoring models) usually charge at the higher end. Client-paid software licenses, ad spend, and third-party tools such as connectors or email verification services are generally passed through at cost, sometimes with a small handling markup that should be agreed in writing. Many consultants also charge a rush fee for work needed in under a week.

rates.service: Email workflow or nurture sequence build (3-5 emails)
Lead scoring and lifecycle stage setup

items.description: Lead nurture program build: 3 workflows, 12 emails, enrollment and exit logic
Website form and CRM field mapping, including duplicate rules
Lead scoring model setup and testing
Email deliverability setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and domain warm-up plan
Team training session on reporting and workflow edits (recorded)

sampleInvoice.notes: Milestone 2 of 3 for the nurture program project (SOW dated March 4). Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Client-held platform license is not included. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Additional requests outside the SOW are billed at $125 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed statement of work or proposal and milestone number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to an agreed scope, which settles most disputes about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Platform and account name worked in
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have multiple accounts or sandboxes, and accounting teams need to know which one the work covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables by name, such as workflows, emails, integrations, and reports
invoiceChecklist.why: Specific line items show what was built and make approvals easier for clients who did not watch the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for hourly work, with dates and short task notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Time-based charges are questioned more often than flat fees, so detail prevents pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs passed through at cost or with the agreed markup
invoiceChecklist.why: Connector subscriptions, data enrichment credits, and verification services should be itemized separately from your labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often reject invoices without a PO, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and hours used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what they received for the month and clarifies whether overage or rollover applies.

marketing-automation-consultant.paymentTerms: Project work is commonly billed with 30 to 50 percent upfront, then milestone payments tied to delivery such as workflow build complete or go-live. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month, due on receipt or within 15 days. Net 15 and Net 30 are both common, with Net 30 more typical for mid-size and enterprise clients. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are often written into the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check, and card payments sometimes include a processing surcharge where permitted by local rules. Some consultants pause active automations or stop new work on accounts that are more than 30 days past due, but this should be stated in the contract first.

tips.title: Bill milestones tied to go-live, not just calendar dates
tips.body: Break larger builds into stages such as audit, build, testing, and launch. Each stage gets its own invoice, which keeps cash flowing and avoids a large unpaid balance if the client delays approvals.

tips.title: Keep retainer hours and scope in writing
tips.body: State what the monthly fee covers, such as campaign builds, reporting, and list maintenance, and what it does not. Say whether unused hours roll over or expire. Without this, retainers drift into unpaid extra work.

tips.title: Separate software costs from your fees
tips.body: Have clients hold their own platform licenses and billing when possible. If you buy tools on their behalf, itemize them at cost and get written approval before purchasing.

tips.title: Charge for revisions beyond the agreed rounds
tips.body: Email copy and workflow logic tend to go through many rounds of change. Include two rounds in the fixed fee and bill additional rounds hourly.

tips.title: Document access and approvals
tips.body: Record when the client approved a workflow, supplied access, or delivered assets. If delays push the schedule, this supports change fees or rescheduling charges.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use flat project fees when scope is clear, such as a defined number of workflows or a migration with a known contact count. Use hourly billing for support, troubleshooting, and open-ended work. Many consultants combine them: a fixed fee for the build and an hourly rate for changes.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a retainer when the client doesn't use all the hours?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say whether unused hours expire or roll over. Many consultants let hours expire at month end or roll over for one month only. Show hours used and remaining on each invoice so there are no surprises.

faqs.question: Can I mark up software and tools I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you agree to it in writing beforehand. Many consultants pass costs through at cost and charge a small handling fee. Be clear on whether the license is in your name or the client's, since the client should own their data and account.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pay after the campaign proves results?
faqs.answer: Avoid tying payment to performance unless you have a written agreement on how results are measured. Marketing outcomes depend on offers, lists, and sales follow-up that you do not control. Bill for the work delivered and treat performance bonuses as a separate, clearly defined add-on.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax consulting services, but some tax digital services, software setup, or configuration work. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Clients usually ask for a quote after an intro call or when comparing a few consultants and agencies for a build, migration, or ongoing support. They compare total price, the number of deliverables, timeline, and whether platform costs are included. A clear scope matters more than a low number, because automation projects often grow once data and integrations are examined.

scopeChecklist.item: Platform, plan tier, and who owns the account
scopeChecklist.why: Features and limits differ by plan, and the work assumes access to certain tools.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact deliverables with counts, such as number of workflows, emails, forms, and segments
scopeChecklist.why: Counts set the boundary for the fixed fee and make additions easy to price.

scopeChecklist.item: Integrations and data sources in scope, such as CRM, ecommerce, webinar, or billing tools
scopeChecklist.why: Integrations are the most common source of hidden work and delays.

scopeChecklist.item: Data migration details: contact count, cleanup, field mapping, and what is left behind
scopeChecklist.why: Messy data can take longer than the build itself, so set the assumptions on its condition.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies copy, design, and brand assets
scopeChecklist.why: Writing emails and building templates are separate tasks, and unclear ownership leads to delays and extra cost.
Limits the back-and-forth and ties the schedule to client response times.

scopeChecklist.item: Testing, launch support, and post-launch support window
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether bug fixes after go-live are included and for how long.

pricingTips.title: Charge for discovery first
pricingTips.body: A paid audit or scoping session lets you see the actual platform setup and data before committing to a fixed price. Many consultants credit part of the fee toward the build if the client proceeds.

pricingTips.title: Price by deliverable, then add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for each workflow, integration, and migration step, then add 15 to 25 percent for data problems and approval delays. Present the total as a fixed fee with defined assumptions.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and full-build option, such as a single welcome series, a full lifecycle program, or lifecycle plus reporting, helps clients choose based on budget and shows what each level includes.

pricingTips.title: List exclusions and change rates
pricingTips.body: State that new integrations, extra workflows, and added revisions are billed at your hourly rate. This makes scope changes a normal, priced event.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote before seeing the client's account?
faqs.answer: It is risky. Without seeing the account, you cannot judge the data quality or existing automations. Offer a paid audit first, or give a range with stated assumptions and confirm the final fixed price after access is granted.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Client platform setups and priorities change, and your own schedule fills up, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should the quote include software license costs?
faqs.answer: Usually no. List them as separate client-paid costs or estimate them as pass-through items. Including them in your fee makes your price look higher than competitors and complicates account ownership.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a project quote?
faqs.answer: Thirty to fifty percent upfront is common for projects, with the rest tied to milestones or go-live. For small projects under a couple thousand dollars, some consultants ask for full payment at the start.

marketing-consultant.intro: Marketing consultants are independent advisors who help small and mid-size businesses plan and improve their marketing. They send invoices for strategy work, audits, ongoing advisory retainers, campaign oversight, and sometimes hands-on execution such as email setup or ad management. Clients are usually business owners or marketing managers who expect clear deliverables and a record of what was done each month.
marketing-consultant.pricingModel: Most marketing consultants use one of four models. Hourly billing is common for new clients, short advisory calls, and work with unclear scope. Project fees cover defined deliverables such as a marketing audit, a go-to-market plan, or a brand positioning workshop. Monthly retainers cover a set number of hours or a set list of tasks, such as weekly strategy calls, reporting, and campaign review. Some consultants also offer day rates for workshops and on-site training. Ad spend and software subscriptions are normally billed to the client separately, either paid directly by the client or passed through at cost with a clearly labeled line. Value-based pricing and performance bonuses exist but should be written into the agreement, with a stated way to measure results, before they appear on an invoice.

rates.service: Email marketing setup and automation build

items.description: Marketing strategy retainer - May (4 weekly strategy calls, priorities and campaign review)
Email welcome sequence: strategy, outline, and review of 5 emails
Google Ads account review and keyword restructuring
Monthly performance report and recommendations
Reimbursable: landing page testing software, May subscription (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Ad spend is billed directly to the client's ad accounts and is not included here. Hours beyond the retainer scope are billed at $140 per hour with prior approval. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and retainer scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on retainers need to see which month and which services the charge covers, so it matches the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables or hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Strategy work is hard to see. Listing audits, calls, reports, and campaign work shows what the client received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad spend and media costs shown separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps your fee distinct from pass-through costs and avoids confusion over where the client's budget went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Software and tool reimbursements with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Subscriptions or stock assets bought on the client's behalf should be labeled at cost, with a receipt available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement or project name
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the scope of work and helps resolve disputes about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center, if they use one
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often will not pay an invoice without it, and missing numbers cause delays.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope work flagged as approved change
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra revisions or added channels should note the approval date or email so the added fee is not questioned.

marketing-consultant.paymentTerms: Many marketing consultants invoice retainers at the start of the month, due in 7 to 15 days, and bill projects with a deposit of 30 to 50 percent upfront and the balance at delivery or in milestones. Hourly work is usually invoiced monthly or biweekly. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for business clients, and larger companies may require net 45 or 60 through accounts payable. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually accepted by ACH, card, or check. Check your local rules on late fees and interest before you apply them.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoice at the start of the period rather than the end. Advance billing keeps cash flow steady and makes it easier to pause work if payment stalls.

tips.title: Define what a retainer includes
tips.body: State the number of calls, hours, or deliverables and whether unused hours roll over. Most disputes come from clients assuming unlimited access.

tips.title: Keep ad spend out of your fees
tips.body: Have clients pay ad platforms directly where possible. If you front the cost, bill it at cost or with a disclosed fee, and never mix it into your consulting line.

tips.title: Tie milestone invoices to deliverables
tips.body: For strategy projects, name the milestone, such as research complete, draft plan delivered, and final presentation, so payment triggers are clear.

tips.title: Report with every invoice
tips.body: Attach a short summary of work completed and results. Clients who see progress pay more promptly and are more likely to renew.

faqs.question: Should a marketing consultant charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended advice and early engagements where scope is unclear. Use project or retainer pricing once you understand the work. Fixed fees reward efficiency and are easier for clients to budget.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for ad spend?
faqs.answer: The cleanest approach is for the client to pay the ad platform directly. If you pay it and get reimbursed, list it as a separate line at cost and include platform statements. Do not mark it up unless your agreement says so.

faqs.question: Can I charge for discovery calls and proposals?
faqs.answer: Short intro calls are usually free. Paid discovery sessions, audits, or research done before a proposal can be charged as a separate flat fee, and many consultants credit it toward the full project if the client continues.

faqs.question: What if a client wants results guaranteed?
faqs.answer: Most consultants avoid guaranteeing outcomes because many factors are outside their control. If you offer performance fees, define the metric, tracking method, and time period in the contract and bill the bonus as a separate line.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax consulting or marketing services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax as its own line when it applies.

estimate.intro: Marketing consultants send estimates or proposals before a retainer or project begins, often after a discovery call. Clients usually compare several consultants on price, deliverables, timeline, and how results will be measured. A clear quote helps show the value of your approach and avoids disagreements later.

scopeChecklist.why: Name what the client receives, such as an audit document, a 12-month plan, or 8 email templates, so they know what the fee covers.
State which channels you will work on, such as search ads, email, and social, so the client does not assume everything is included.
Specify the number of calls, response times, and reporting schedule to set expectations on availability.
Limits on revisions and who signs off protect you from endless rework and delays.
List what you need, such as analytics access, brand assets, and timely feedback, since delays on their side affect your timeline.
Make clear that media budgets and software fees are separate from your fee and who pays them.

scopeChecklist.item: Success metrics and what is not guaranteed
scopeChecklist.why: Define how progress will be measured and state that results depend on factors outside your control.

pricingTips.title: Offer three tiers
pricingTips.body: Present a basic, standard, and full option, such as audit only, audit plus plan, and audit plus plan plus 3 months of advisory. Clients tend to choose the middle option and feel in control of the decision.

pricingTips.title: Price on outcomes and effort
pricingTips.body: Estimate your hours, then adjust for the business impact. A plan that guides a $500,000 ad budget is worth more than the same hours for a small local shop.

pricingTips.title: Break out one-time and recurring fees
pricingTips.body: Show setup or strategy costs separately from monthly retainer fees so the client understands the ongoing commitment.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire in 14 to 30 days, since your availability and the client's situation change.

faqs.question: How detailed should a marketing proposal be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to cover scope, deliverables, timeline, and price on a few pages. Small clients prefer a short one to three page quote, while larger companies may expect background research and a longer document.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal?
faqs.answer: Quick quotes are normally free. If the proposal requires substantial research, such as a competitive analysis or audit, consider a paid discovery phase that can be credited against the full project.

faqs.question: What if the scope grows after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Include a change clause in the quote. When requests go beyond the agreed deliverables, send a written change estimate and get approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: Yes, when scope is uncertain. State what drives the range, such as number of channels or rounds of revision, and agree on a cap or checkpoint so the client does not face an open-ended bill.

marketo-consultant.intro: Marketo consultants are independent specialists or small agency owners who help companies build, fix, and run Adobe Marketo Engage. They bill for instance setup and audits, email and landing page builds, lead scoring and nurture programs, CRM integrations, and ongoing admin support. Clients are usually B2B marketing teams that lack a full-time marketing operations person.
marketo-consultant.pricingModel: Most Marketo consultants charge hourly for open-ended admin work and support, and flat project fees for defined work such as an instance audit, a Salesforce sync setup, or a lead lifecycle build. Monthly retainers with a set block of hours are common for ongoing campaign execution and database hygiene, often with a discount on the hourly rate in exchange for a commitment. Per-asset pricing is used for repeatable builds like email templates, landing pages, or program templates. Certified experts and those with deep CRM integration experience charge at the higher end. Rush work, weekend launches, and migrations from another platform are often priced at a premium. Training sessions are billed per session or per day. Third-party tools, such as data enrichment or email deliverability software, should be passed through at cost or listed separately if you purchase them for the client.

Lead scoring and lifecycle model design and build
Nurture program build (4-6 emails with logic)
CRM integration setup (Salesforce or Dynamics sync)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours beyond the agreed scope are billed at $135/hour with prior written approval. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. ACH and card payments accepted; card payments carry a 3% processing fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project or statement of work reference and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate accounts payable teams often reject invoices that lack a PO or SOW number, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables with dates or billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Marketing leaders need to match your charges to launches and milestones when they review budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged per task for time-based work
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what each block of time covered, which prevents disputes over open-ended admin hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Marketo instance or Munchkin ID or workspace name
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies which instance or workspace the work applies to when clients have multiple business units or a sandbox.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party tools or pass-through costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Data enrichment, deliverability tools, or stock assets are not your labor, and clients want to see them at cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change requests billed against the original scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Marks which items were added after the SOW was signed so extra charges are not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal business name, tax ID or W-9 on file, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients need this to set you up as a vendor and issue a 1099 where applicable.

marketo-consultant.paymentTerms: For project work, a 30 to 50 percent deposit at signing is common, with the balance due at delivery or split across milestones such as audit complete, build complete, and launch. Retainers are typically invoiced at the start of the month and due within 15 days. Enterprise clients often require net 30 or net 45 terms, so build that into your cash flow or ask for a larger deposit. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in your agreement. Most consultants accept ACH or wire transfer, and some accept cards with a surcharge. Check your state rules on late fees and on surcharging cards.

tips.title: Define what counts as a revision
tips.body: Email and landing page builds drift into endless copy changes. State how many rounds of revisions are included, and bill extra rounds at your hourly rate.

tips.title: Separate build work from ongoing admin
tips.body: Bill projects as flat fees and day-to-day support by the hour or on a retainer. Mixing them makes it hard to show the value of either and invites scope creep.

tips.title: Log time for troubleshooting
tips.body: Sync errors, deliverability issues, and broken tokens can take hours to track down. Keep notes on what you found so a time-based charge is easy to defend.

tips.title: Bill access and approval delays
tips.body: Projects often stall waiting for Salesforce admin access or brand approvals. Put a clause in your agreement that pauses the timeline and lets you bill completed milestones when the client causes the delay.

tips.title: Rollover rules for retainer hours
tips.body: Decide whether unused retainer hours expire or roll over and state it on every invoice. Most consultants let hours expire at month end or after one additional month.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat fee for Marketo work?
faqs.answer: Use flat fees when the scope is clear, such as an audit, scoring model, or integration. Use hourly or a retainer for support, troubleshooting, and campaign work where requests change week to week.

faqs.question: How do I bill for work done in a client's Marketo instance?
faqs.answer: List each deliverable or task with the hours or fee, and name the workspace or instance. Attach or link a short summary of what changed so the client has a record of the work.

faqs.question: Can I mark up third-party tools I buy for a client?
faqs.answer: Many consultants pass tools through at cost and some add a small handling fee. Whatever you choose, state it in your agreement and show tool costs as separate lines on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pay after a campaign launches?
faqs.answer: Tie payment to delivery of the build, not to campaign results. Results depend on list quality, offers, and sales follow-up, which you may not control. Ask for a deposit and milestone payments if the client wants to defer the balance.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: In the US, clients typically collect a W-9 from independent contractors and may issue a 1099-NEC if they pay you above the IRS threshold in a year. Check current rules with your accountant.

estimate.intro: Marketo consultants send estimates after a discovery call, an audit, or a review of the client's current instance. The client usually compares your quote to other freelancers, agencies, and the cost of hiring a marketing operations hire. A clear scope and a fixed price or capped hours help them decide quickly.

scopeChecklist.item: Systems in scope: Marketo, CRM, and any connected tools
scopeChecklist.why: A sync with Salesforce, a webinar platform, or an enrichment tool adds work. List what you will touch and what is excluded.
Say how many emails, landing pages, programs, or smart campaigns are included so the client cannot assume unlimited builds.
Copy, design files, list data, and admin access are common causes of delay. State what you need and by when.
Specifies how many rounds of feedback are included and who gives final sign-off.
Clarify whether QA, test sends, and launch-day monitoring are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Out-of-scope items and change request rate
scopeChecklist.why: Lists exclusions such as data cleanup, reporting dashboards, or migration, and states the hourly rate for additions.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline, validity period, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a start date, estimated duration, how long the quote holds, and when deposits and milestones are due.

pricingTips.title: Audit first for unclear instances
pricingTips.body: If you have not seen the instance, quote a paid audit before a build. Inherited Marketo setups often contain broken sync rules, duplicate programs, and undocumented logic that change the price.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: Present a basic build, a standard build with nurture and scoring, and a full build with integration and training. Clients tend to pick the middle option and see what each level adds.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for integrations
pricingTips.body: CRM sync and field mapping work run over more often than email builds. Add a contingency or quote a range with a cap so you are not absorbing unexpected hours.

pricingTips.title: Show the hours behind flat fees
pricingTips.body: Even with a flat price, give a short breakdown by phase. It helps the client compare quotes and gives you a basis for pricing changes.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed quote when deliverables are defined and you have seen the instance. Use an hourly estimate with a cap when the work depends on unknowns such as data quality or integration complexity.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Marketo projects depend on your calendar and on the client's access, so an expiration date protects you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time spent building an estimate?
faqs.answer: A short discovery call is usually free. A detailed audit or technical assessment needed to scope a large project is often paid, and many consultants credit the fee toward the project if the client moves forward.

martial-arts-instructor.intro: Martial arts instructors run dojos, dojangs, and gyms, teach private lessons, lead seminars, and coach students for belt tests and competitions. Invoices usually cover monthly tuition, private instruction, testing fees, uniforms and gear, and special events. Many instructors also bill schools, community centers, and organizations for classes or self-defense workshops.
martial-arts-instructor.pricingModel: Most schools charge monthly tuition for a set number of classes per week, often with a discount for families or for paying quarterly or annually. Private lessons are billed per session, usually 30 or 60 minutes, with prepaid packages at a lower per-session rate. Belt testing, promotion, and competition fees are billed separately as flat amounts, and uniforms, sparring gear, and belts are sold at a markup over cost. Off-site work such as school programs, corporate classes, and self-defense seminars is typically a flat fee per session or a per-head rate for groups. Instructors who rent mat space or teach at other gyms often split revenue or charge a per-class rate.

items.description: Monthly tuition, Youth Karate (2 classes/week), March
Sibling tuition, Youth Karate (2 classes/week), March
