Registration fee, new student
Uniform (gi) with school patch, size youth 3
Belt test fee, yellow to orange belt
Private lesson, kata and test preparation

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due by the 1st of the month. A $15 late fee applies after the 7th. Private lessons require 24 hours notice to cancel or reschedule. Uniform and registration fees are non-refundable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and the name of the billing parent or guardian
invoiceChecklist.why: Many students are minors, and the person paying is often a different person from the student. Clear names prevent confusion in families with several students.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and class plan
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the month covered and the plan (for example, 2 classes/week or unlimited) makes it easy to see what the tuition buys.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized fees separate from tuition
invoiceChecklist.why: Registration, testing, and event fees are not recurring. Listing them separately avoids disputes over why a bill changed from one month to the next.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gear and uniform line items with size
invoiceChecklist.why: Uniforms, belts, and pads are sold at a markup and often returned or exchanged. Size and item names help with exchanges and with your own inventory records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Private lesson dates and durations
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-session charges are easier to verify when each date and length is listed, especially when lessons are drawn from a prepaid package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance or remaining sessions
invoiceChecklist.why: If a student has prepaid for a block of lessons, showing how many remain reduces questions and encourages renewal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late fee, cancellation, and refund terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Tuition disputes usually involve missed classes, injuries, or quitting mid-contract. Stating terms on the invoice supports what is in your enrollment agreement.

martial-arts-instructor.paymentTerms: Most schools bill tuition on the 1st of the month and collect through automatic card or bank draft, since recurring payments reduce late balances. Enrollment usually requires the first month plus a registration fee up front. Late fees are commonly $10-25 after a grace period of 5 to 10 days, and many schools suspend class access after a second missed payment. Annual or quarterly prepayment discounts are common. Private lessons and seminars are often paid in advance or at the time of service by card, cash, or digital payment. Check your state's rules on automatic renewals and long-term membership contracts, as some limit contract length and cancellation terms.

tips.title: Put cancellation terms in the enrollment agreement
tips.body: Decide how much notice you need to stop tuition, whether the last month is refundable, and what happens during injury or travel. Write it down before the student starts and refer to it on the invoice.

tips.title: Offer family and prepay discounts as line items
tips.body: Showing a sibling discount or annual prepay discount as a separate line makes the savings visible. It also tells you at a glance what each family is on.

tips.title: Bill testing and event fees ahead of the date
tips.body: Send belt test, tournament, and seminar invoices two to four weeks early, with a firm deadline. This lets you plan testing slots, order belts, and register students without chasing money at the door.

tips.title: Track gear sales separately from instruction
tips.body: Gear carries a cost and often sales tax, while tuition may not be taxed in your state. Keeping them on separate lines makes bookkeeping and tax filing simpler. Check your state's rules on taxing classes and retail items.

tips.title: Use packages for private lessons
tips.body: Selling 5 or 10 lessons at a small discount brings in money upfront and reduces last-minute cancellations. Set an expiration date on the package so unused sessions do not carry forever.

faqs.question: Should I charge tuition monthly or per class?
faqs.answer: Most schools charge monthly because it gives steady income and encourages regular attendance. Per-class pricing is more common for drop-ins, seminars, and private lessons.

faqs.question: Do I charge for classes a student misses?
faqs.answer: Usually yes for monthly tuition, since the fee covers access to the schedule, not each class. Many schools allow makeup classes within the same month. Spell out your policy in the enrollment agreement.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on tuition?
faqs.answer: In most places you can, as long as the fee is stated in advance and is reasonable. Common amounts are $10-25. Put the fee and the grace period in writing and on each invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tuition or gear?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Many states do not tax instruction but do tax retail items such as uniforms and equipment. Some states do tax fitness or recreation memberships. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill a family with multiple students?
faqs.answer: You can send one invoice to the parent with each student listed as a separate line, including any sibling discount. This keeps one payment and one record per family while still showing who each charge is for.

estimate.intro: Instructors send quotes mostly for work outside regular tuition: school and corporate programs, self-defense workshops, birthday parties, seminars, and private group training. Clients compare the price per participant, the length of the session, and whether equipment and insurance are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Class length, number of sessions, and schedule
scopeChecklist.why: A one-hour workshop and a six-week program are very different jobs. Dates and times prevent misunderstandings about how much instruction is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Maximum number of participants and age range
scopeChecklist.why: Group size affects the number of instructors needed and the safety of the class. Age range affects curriculum and pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Location and who provides the space
scopeChecklist.why: If you teach at the client's site, confirm floor type, size, and whether you need to bring mats. Rental fees for a venue should be stated if you are passing them on.
Pads, mats, and loaner gear may be included or billed separately. Spell out what you bring and what participants must provide.
Schools and companies often require proof of liability insurance. State whether you will supply a certificate and whether participants must sign your waiver.
Off-site work takes time beyond the class itself. Include a travel fee or mileage charge so it does not come out of your rate.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation, and rain or illness policy
scopeChecklist.why: Events get rescheduled. A deposit and a clear policy protect your calendar when a client cancels late.

pricingTips.title: Price per session first, then show per participant
pricingTips.body: Work out the flat fee that covers your time, travel, and prep, then divide by expected headcount. Clients like to see the per-person number, and you stay covered if attendance is low by setting a minimum fee.

pricingTips.title: Quote assistants separately
pricingTips.body: Larger groups or children's classes may need a second instructor. List the assistant as its own line so the client can see why the price rises with the headcount.

pricingTips.title: Offer a short series at a lower per-class rate
pricingTips.body: A four-week self-defense course often books easier than a single class. Offering a discount for the series gives you repeat income and gives clients a reason to commit.

pricingTips.title: Give a quote an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Holding a date on your calendar has a cost. State that the quote is good for 14 or 30 days and that the date is confirmed only after the deposit.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly rate for group classes?
faqs.answer: A flat fee per session is more common and easier for clients to approve. Base it on your hourly rate plus prep and travel time, and note the class length it covers.

faqs.question: Do I need a written quote for birthday parties and one-time events?
faqs.answer: A short written quote is a good idea. It should list the date, length, number of kids, what you provide, the price, and the deposit. This prevents disputes over headcount changes and extra time.

faqs.question: What if the client wants more participants than quoted?
faqs.answer: State a maximum headcount and a per-person charge above it. If the group grows, you can add an assistant or adjust the price without renegotiating the whole job.

masonry.intro: Masonry contractors, bricklayers, stonemasons, and block layers send invoices for building and repairing structures from brick, concrete block, natural stone, and manufactured stone. Typical jobs include chimneys, retaining walls, patios, veneer, fireplaces, foundations, and tuckpointing. Most are solo operators or small crews who bill for labor, materials, equipment, and sometimes a helper or mason tender.
masonry.pricingModel: Masonry is priced by the job, by the unit of work, or by time. New walls, veneer, and patios are usually priced per square foot of finished surface, or per brick or block for production work. Repairs such as tuckpointing, chimney rebuilds, and crack repair are often priced per linear foot, per square foot, or as a flat fee after an inspection. Small or uncertain jobs are billed hourly or by the day, with a minimum charge. Materials (brick, block, stone, mortar, rebar, flashing, sand, cement) are either passed through at cost with a markup of roughly 10-25 percent or built into the square-foot price. Add separate lines for scaffolding, mixer or saw rental, demolition, debris haul-off, and permits. Stone work costs more than brick, and complex patterns, arches, and curves cost more than straight runs. Larger jobs are commonly billed in stages: deposit, materials delivery, progress draws, and final payment.

rates.service: Brick or block wall, labor only
Natural or manufactured stone veneer, installed

items.description: Tuckpointing, rear brick wall: grind out old mortar and repoint with Type N mortar
Replace spalled face bricks, matched to existing
Mortar, sand, and brick materials
Mason tender labor
Scaffold rental, 3 days
Debris removal and site cleanup

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received on 03/04 is credited on this invoice. Balance due within 14 days of completion. Mortar color and joint profile matched to existing wall as approved by the owner. Workmanship warranted for 2 years; masonry will naturally develop hairline cracks in mortar over time, which are not covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and scope of work completed
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several areas or structures worked on, and the invoice should match the signed estimate item by item.

invoiceChecklist.item: Measured quantities (sq ft, linear feet, brick count)
invoiceChecklist.why: Unit-based pricing is easier to defend when the measurements are written next to the rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed by type and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Brick style, stone type, mortar type (N, S, or M), rebar, and flashing affect cost and long-term performance, and they document what was installed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extra work
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden damage, extra demolition, or added courses are common. Listing them separately with the approved amount avoids disputes at the final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment and access charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Scaffolding, mixer, saw, and lift rentals are real costs that clients often forget about unless they are shown.

invoiceChecklist.item: License and insurance information and permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require contractor license numbers on invoices or contracts, and permit numbers tie the work to the inspection record. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits, progress payments, and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing payments already received prevents double billing and gives a clear remaining balance on staged jobs.

masonry.paymentTerms: Masonry contractors typically take a deposit of 25-50 percent on larger jobs, often enough to cover material orders, with the balance split into progress draws or paid at completion. Small repairs are commonly due on completion or within 7-14 days. Net 15 or net 30 is more common with general contractors, who may hold back retainage of around 5-10 percent until final inspection. A late fee of 1-1.5 percent per month is common if it is written in the contract and on the invoice, though state limits vary. Accept checks, ACH transfers, and card payments, and consider passing on card fees where local law permits. Many states allow contractors to file a mechanic's lien for unpaid work, and strict notice deadlines usually apply, so keep dated records of what was agreed and delivered.

tips.title: Bill materials as they are bought
tips.body: Brick, stone, and block are heavy and expensive, and special orders cannot be returned. Collect a materials deposit before ordering, and bill delivery as a milestone on larger jobs.

tips.title: Take photos before, during, and after
tips.body: Photos of existing damage, hidden conditions behind walls, and finished work protect you if a client claims you caused a crack or stain. Attach them to the final invoice if the job was disputed.

tips.title: Put weather delays in writing
tips.body: Mortar cannot be laid in freezing or heavy rain conditions without precautions. Agree on how delays affect the schedule and whether standby time or remobilization is billed.

tips.title: Price minimums for small repairs
tips.body: A small repair still requires a trip, setup, mixing, and cleanup. Set a minimum charge of 2-4 hours so a few bricks do not cost you money.

tips.title: Get a signed change order before extra work
tips.body: Mason work often uncovers rot, failed flashing, or crumbling footings. Get written approval for the added cost before continuing.

faqs.question: Should I bill masonry by the square foot or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Square-foot pricing works best for walls, veneer, patios, and tuckpointing where the area is easy to measure. Hourly or day rates suit small repairs, unclear conditions, and work with a lot of demolition or access problems. Many contractors use unit pricing for the main work and hourly rates for extras.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up materials?
faqs.answer: A markup of 10-25 percent on materials is common, covering ordering time, delivery, waste, and the risk of mistakes. If you build materials into a square-foot price, allow for 5-10 percent waste on brick and block and more for irregular stone.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is standard for masonry. Many states limit how large a deposit on home improvement work can be, so check your local rules. State the amount on the contract and show it as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client refuses to pay for completed work?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder with the invoice, contract, change orders, and photos. If that fails, many states allow a mechanic's lien on the property, but notice deadlines are short and vary by state, so act promptly and consider legal advice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on masonry work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the type of job. Some states tax materials on repair work, others tax labor or treat new construction differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Masonry contractors send estimates before nearly every job, usually after a site visit to measure and inspect the existing work. Homeowners and general contractors typically compare several bids, looking at price, brick or stone match, schedule, insurance, and how much of the cost is labor versus materials.

scopeChecklist.why: State the wall length, height, or area, and the number of courses or repairs, so the price is tied to something measurable.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials, brand, color, and mortar type
scopeChecklist.why: Brick and stone colors vary between lots, and mortar mix and joint style change the look and durability. Spelling these out avoids disagreements over a mismatch.
Tearing out old masonry and hauling debris is heavy work. Say whether it is included or priced separately.
Many failures start below grade. Clarify whether you are building on an existing footing, pouring a new one, or relying on someone else's work.
Retaining walls, chimneys, and structural work often need permits or engineer sign-off. State who pays and who arranges them.
List what is not covered, such as hidden water damage, failed lintels, or rotten framing behind veneer, and how those will be priced if found.
Set an expected start and duration, say how weather delays are handled, and list deposit and draw amounts so clients know the cash flow.

pricingTips.title: Inspect before you quote repairs
pricingTips.body: Chimney and old-wall repairs hide problems. Look at flashing, caps, mortar depth, and foundation settlement before pricing, and give a range or allowance for areas you cannot see.

pricingTips.title: Show labor and materials separately
pricingTips.body: Splitting them helps clients compare bids fairly and makes it easier to adjust if they change brick or stone. It also supports a clear change order if material prices move.

pricingTips.title: Add waste and cutting allowances
pricingTips.body: Stone and patterned brickwork waste more material than straight running bond. Include 5-15 percent depending on the layout, and more for complicated cuts.

pricingTips.title: Limit how long the quote is valid
pricingTips.body: Brick, cement, and fuel prices change. A validity period of 15-30 days protects you from being held to old numbers.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most masonry contractors quote simple jobs for free. For complex work that needs drawings, engineering, or a lot of time on site, some charge a fee and credit it toward the job if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How do I price a job when I cannot see the condition behind the wall?
faqs.answer: Quote the visible work as a fixed price and add an allowance or unit prices for hidden repairs, such as a price per replaced lintel or per square foot of extra rebuild. Put this in writing before starting.

faqs.question: How detailed should a masonry estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that another mason could read it and understand the scope: measurements, materials, prep, cleanup, and exclusions. A one-line total invites disagreements about what was included.

faqs.question: Can I raise the price after the estimate is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only for changes in scope or unforeseen conditions, and only with written client approval. If the scope matches the estimate, changing the price is likely to hurt trust and may violate your contract.

massage-therapist.intro: Massage therapists bill for hands-on sessions in a clinic, spa, client's home, or workplace. Invoices typically cover session time, add-ons like hot stones or cupping, packages and memberships, travel for mobile work, and corporate or event chair massage. Some therapists also bill auto insurance, workers' comp, or a client's HSA/FSA account, which means paperwork needs to be more detailed.
massage-therapist.pricingModel: Most massage therapists charge per session by length: 30, 60, 75, 90, or 120 minutes. Rates rise with specialty (deep tissue, prenatal, sports, lymphatic drainage, myofascial release) and with the setting, since a solo practice in a major city usually charges more than a spa-employed therapist or a rural clinic. Add-ons such as aromatherapy, hot stones, or cupping are often a flat $10-30 on top of the session. Mobile or in-home massage adds a travel fee or a higher base rate. Packages and monthly memberships (for example, one 60-minute session per month at a reduced rate) are common and give predictable income. Corporate chair massage is billed per hour or per event with a minimum, often with a two-hour floor. Insurance-billed work (auto accident or injury claims where available) uses set fee schedules and requires documentation like CPT codes, a diagnosis from a referring provider, and treatment notes.

rates.service: Mobile or in-home massage travel fee

items.description: Deep tissue massage, 90 minutes (focus: neck, shoulders, lower back)
Hot stone add-on
Mobile visit travel fee (12 miles each way)
Follow-up 60-minute therapeutic massage
Gratuity (added at client's request)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at time of service. Accepted: card, cash, HSA/FSA card. A receipt with session details is available on request for reimbursement. Cancellations within 24 hours of the appointment are charged 50% of the session fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, HSA/FSA administrators, and insurers all want to see exactly when treatment happened and for how long.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of massage or modality
invoiceChecklist.why: Therapeutic, prenatal, and lymphatic work are priced differently and some plans only reimburse therapeutic or medically directed work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or certification number and state
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states license massage therapists, and reimbursement requests often require a license number on the receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing hot stones, cupping, or aromatherapy keeps the base session price clear and avoids questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or mileage for mobile sessions
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the extra charge is for drive time and equipment, not part of the session price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating tips from fees keeps your income records clean for taxes and avoids confusion for the client's reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Referring provider, claim number, and billing codes (insurance work)
invoiceChecklist.why: Auto and workers' comp payers generally reject claims without a referral, claim number, and treatment documentation.

massage-therapist.paymentTerms: Most massage therapists collect payment at the end of the session by card, cash, or mobile payment, so invoices are often sent as receipts. Packages and memberships are usually paid in full upfront or billed monthly on a set date. Many practices have a 24-hour cancellation policy with a late-cancel or no-show fee of 50% to 100% of the session. Corporate and event clients are usually invoiced with net 15 or net 30 terms, and a deposit is common for events. Insurance and injury claims can take 30 to 60 days or longer to pay, so state that clearly and decide whether the client is responsible for any unpaid balance.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every invoice
tips.body: No-show fees are easier to collect when the client has seen the policy in writing at booking and again on the receipt. Keep the wording short: window, fee, and how it is charged.

tips.title: Offer packages and memberships
tips.body: A prepaid package of three or five sessions or a monthly membership smooths out income and cuts down on no-shows. Note the expiration date and refund terms on the invoice.

tips.title: Price mobile work to cover travel time
tips.body: Drive time and setting up a table are unpaid hours if you only charge the session rate. Use a flat travel fee or a mileage-based fee beyond a set radius.

tips.title: Track tips separately
tips.body: Tips are generally taxable income. Recording them as their own line makes your bookkeeping and year-end taxes simpler.

tips.title: Send a corporate invoice quickly
tips.body: Event and workplace clients usually pay through accounts payable. Include the PO number, event date, hours worked, and number of therapists so it can be approved without back and forth.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on massage?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and sometimes your city. Many states do not tax therapeutic massage, but some tax it or tax retail items such as oils and products you sell. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can clients use HSA or FSA funds for massage?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if the massage is for a medical condition and the plan administrator requires a letter of medical necessity. Provide an itemized receipt with your name, license number, date, service, and amount so the client can submit it.

faqs.question: Should I include tips on the invoice?
faqs.answer: List gratuity as a separate line if it is paid with the same transaction. That keeps it distinct from your service fees, which helps with bookkeeping and reimbursement requests.

faqs.question: How should I bill a no-show?
faqs.answer: Send an invoice that references the missed appointment date and your written cancellation policy, and charge the stated fee. Many therapists charge 50% to 100% of the session. Charging cards on file is easier if the client agreed to it at booking.

faqs.question: What do I do if I get paid by auto insurance or workers' comp?
faqs.answer: You typically need a referral or prescription, a claim number, treatment notes, and the right billing codes. Payment is slower than with private clients, so confirm the payer's requirements and filing deadlines before the first session.

estimate.intro: Most massage sessions are priced from a menu, so formal estimates come up mainly for corporate chair massage, events, mobile or in-home visits, wedding or retreat packages, and treatment plans for injury recovery. Clients typically compare your per-hour or per-session price, travel charges, minimum booking length, and what is included, such as table, linens, and supplies.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of therapists and total hours on site
scopeChecklist.why: Event pricing scales with headcount and time, and clients often assume more coverage than they paid for.
Specify 10, 15, or 20 minute chair sessions versus full table massage, because the number of guests served changes sharply.
A quiet private room versus an open corridor changes the experience, and parking or load-in time affects your cost.
State whether you bring tables, chairs, linens, oils, and sanitizing supplies, so the client does not expect to provide them.
Mobile and event work includes drive time that should be separate from the hourly or session rate.
Event dates are hard to refill, so state the deposit, when the balance is due, and what happens if the date changes.
Note that you may decline or modify treatment based on intake forms or contraindications, and that you do not diagnose conditions.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum booking for events
pricingTips.body: A two-hour minimum for chair massage covers setup, travel, and the income you give up by blocking the day. Spell it out in the quote.

pricingTips.title: Quote treatment plans as bundles
pricingTips.body: For clients recovering from an injury, offer a package of four or six sessions at a modest discount and state the validity period. It helps them commit and gives you scheduled work.

pricingTips.title: Show the per-guest cost for corporate clients
pricingTips.body: Companies often budget per employee. Giving both a total and a per-person cost makes it easier for them to compare and approve your quote.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Add a validity window, such as 30 days, so you are not held to old pricing or a date that has already filled.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or intake?
faqs.answer: For standard sessions, the intake is usually part of the first appointment's time. For longer treatment plan consultations or on-site assessments, some therapists charge a flat fee or credit it toward the first session.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for on events?
faqs.answer: Many therapists ask for 25% to 50% to hold the date, with the balance due on or before the event. Larger or out-of-town events may justify a higher deposit.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as more hours, more guests, or a different location. Put that in the quote, and send a written update before the event when something changes.

math-tutor.intro: Math tutors work one-on-one or with small groups to help students from elementary school through college. They bill for regular weekly sessions, test prep blocks, homework help, and sometimes lesson planning or materials. Clients are usually parents, but can also be adult learners, schools, or tutoring companies that contract tutors directly.
math-tutor.pricingModel: Most math tutors charge per hour or per session, with the rate set by subject level and experience. Elementary and middle school math sits at the low end, while calculus, statistics, linear algebra, and standardized test prep (SAT, ACT, AP exams) cost more. Many tutors sell packages of 4, 8, or 10 sessions at a small discount and require payment up front or monthly. Online sessions are usually priced the same as in-person, though in-person tutors may add a travel fee for home visits beyond a set distance. Small group sessions are often billed per student at a lower rate than a private session. Some tutors charge a flat fee for an intensive exam prep program or a summer catch-up plan. Short-notice cancellations are commonly billed at the full or half session rate.

rates.service: Elementary and middle school math tutoring
High school math (Algebra, Geometry, Algebra II)
SAT, ACT, or AP exam math prep

items.description: Algebra II tutoring, 60-minute sessions (Oct 2, 9, 16, 23)
Extra 30-minute session before unit test (Oct 26)
Printed practice problem sets and answer keys
Late cancellation fee (Oct 18, less than 24 hours notice)

sampleInvoice.notes: Student: Maya R. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Accepted by check, Zvenmo-style transfer, or card. Sessions cancelled with at least 24 hours notice are not charged. Thank you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or payer name
invoiceChecklist.why: The person paying is often a parent, so the invoice should name both to avoid confusion and to help with records for dependent care or tutoring reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, length, and format
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each date and whether it was in person or online lets parents check the charges against their calendar and cuts down on billing questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subject and course level
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing Algebra II or AP Calculus supports the rate you charged and helps if the family submits receipts to a school program or employer benefit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate per hour or per package
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients should see how the total was calculated, especially when a session ran shorter or longer than the usual hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show charges, labeled separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeping missed-session fees on their own line shows they follow your stated policy and are not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials or workbook costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Printed worksheets, prep books, or graphing calculator rentals should be itemized so they are not confused with tutoring time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining sessions on a prepaid package
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the balance of prepaid sessions prevents disputes about how many are left and prompts renewal at the right time.

math-tutor.paymentTerms: Many tutors bill monthly in arrears for ongoing weekly sessions, or require full payment up front for a package or exam prep program. Due dates of 5 to 14 days are common, and some tutors ask for payment before each session. A written cancellation policy, often 24 hours notice, is standard, with late cancellations billed at the full or half rate. Late fees are less common than with other trades, but a flat fee or a pause on scheduling after a missed payment is typical. Payment is usually by check, bank transfer, payment apps, or card. Tutors who work through a school or agency may be paid on that organization's schedule, so confirm terms in writing.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: Send the policy with your first invoice or intake form. A clear 24-hour rule, with a stated charge for late cancellations, makes it easy to bill a missed session without an argument.

tips.title: Bill packages up front
tips.body: Collecting for 8 or 10 sessions in advance keeps cash flow steady and reduces chasing payments each week. Track used and remaining sessions so clients can see the balance.

tips.title: Raise rates at natural points
tips.body: Increase your rate at the start of a school year or semester, and give existing families at least 30 days notice. Students preparing for exams like the SAT or AP tests will often accept higher prep rates.

tips.title: Separate tutoring from extras
tips.body: Charge for materials, diagnostic tests, and travel on their own lines. It keeps your hourly rate clean and makes each charge easy to explain.

tips.title: Keep session notes
tips.body: A short log of the topics covered each session backs up your invoice if a parent asks what they paid for, and it helps you report progress.

faqs.question: Should I bill per session or per month?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-month billing is simpler for weekly students because the parent gets one invoice and one payment. Per-session billing suits irregular schedules or new clients. Whichever you pick, list every session date on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax tutoring services, but a few tax some educational services. Materials you sell, like printed workbooks, may be taxable in some places. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle a student who misses a session?
faqs.answer: Follow the policy you gave the family in advance. Most tutors charge the full or half rate for cancellations with less than 24 hours notice and list the charge as a separate line item. Some allow one free reschedule per term.

faqs.question: Can I invoice a school or tutoring company instead of parents?
faqs.answer: Yes. If you are paid by a school, district, or agency, include their name, any purchase order or contract number, student identifiers they require, and your tax ID or W-9 if requested. These payers often pay on net 30 or longer terms.

faqs.question: Do I need to send tax forms to clients?
faqs.answer: Usually not for individual families. As an independent tutor you report your income yourself, and you may receive a 1099 from a company or school that pays you above the IRS reporting threshold. Keep your own records of all invoices.

estimate.intro: Math tutors send estimates when a family wants a defined program, such as SAT prep, a summer catch-up plan, or a semester of weekly support. Parents often compare hourly rates, number of sessions, and whether materials and practice tests are included. A clear quote helps them see the total cost and what results to expect from the time commitment.

scopeChecklist.item: Subject, course, and student grade level
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on level, so naming the course (for example, Geometry or AP Calculus AB) sets the rate and avoids a mismatch in expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions, length, and weekly schedule
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 12 sessions of 60 minutes is easy to compare and gives a firm total, while open-ended help is not.
Travel fees, platform needs, and tools like a shared whiteboard may differ between formats.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: materials, practice tests, progress reports
scopeChecklist.why: Parents should know if practice exams, workbooks, or written updates are in the price or extra.
Stating the rule in the quote means the family agrees to it before the first session.
If a prepaid package must be used within a set period, say so, so unused sessions do not lead to disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Goals and what you can and cannot promise
scopeChecklist.why: State the learning goal, but do not guarantee a grade or score. This protects you and sets honest expectations.

pricingTips.title: Start with a diagnostic
pricingTips.body: For test prep or a student who is far behind, offer a paid diagnostic first. It lets you quote the right number of sessions instead of guessing.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package sizes
pricingTips.body: Presenting 4, 8, and 12 session options with a small discount for larger ones lets families choose a budget and makes the commitment clearer.

pricingTips.title: Price by level, not by your time alone
pricingTips.body: Set different rates for middle school math, high school math, and college or test prep. Advanced subjects take more preparation and justify higher rates.

pricingTips.title: Include prep time in your rate
pricingTips.body: If you build custom problem sets or review school materials, factor that time into the hourly rate instead of billing it separately, unless you state otherwise in the quote.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote or just an hourly rate?
faqs.answer: For ongoing weekly tutoring, an hourly rate is enough. For a defined program like SAT prep or a summer plan, a written quote with the number of sessions and total cost is clearer and easier for parents to approve.

faqs.question: How long should a tutoring quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Your availability is the main limit, since evening and weekend slots fill quickly, so some tutors hold a time slot for only 7 to 14 days.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the first trial session?
faqs.answer: Yes, many tutors do, and some offer a discounted rate for the first meeting. If you offer a free consultation, keep it short and make clear it is for discussing goals, not for teaching.

faqs.question: What if the student needs more sessions than I quoted?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that additional sessions are billed at the same hourly rate. When you see the student needs more time, tell the parent before adding sessions and send a revised quote.

meal-prep-service.intro: Meal prep services are run by personal chefs, home cooks with commercial kitchen access, and small food businesses that cook and portion meals for clients to eat during the week. Invoices usually cover weekly or per-meal food, grocery costs, in-home cooking sessions, delivery, and add-ons like containers or custom diets.
meal-prep-service.pricingModel: Pricing depends on whether you cook in your own licensed kitchen and deliver, or cook in the client's home. Kitchen-based services mostly charge per meal or per weekly package (for example 10 or 14 meals), with a price that already includes groceries and labor. In-home personal chefs usually charge a flat session fee or hourly rate for cooking time, with groceries billed separately at cost or at cost plus a small handling fee. Subscriptions and recurring weekly plans are common and often billed in advance. Premium diets (keto, allergen-free, high-protein macros), organic or specialty ingredients, and large portions raise the per-meal price. Delivery is either a flat fee, a zone-based fee, or waived above a minimum order. Many cooks target a food cost of about 28-35 percent of the meal price, so quotes should be built from ingredient cost, labor, packaging, and overhead rather than guessed.

rates.service: Prepared meals, specialty diet or macro-counted

rates.unit: percent of grocery cost or flat fee

items.description: Weekly meal plan, 12 meals (6 high-protein lunches, 6 dinners), week of March 10
Dietary customization: dairy-free, no tree nuts
Breakfast egg bites add-on
Local delivery, Sunday 4-6 pm window
Reusable glass container deposit (refundable on return)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due by Friday before the delivery week. Please return glass containers at your next delivery for a deposit credit. Changes or cancellations must be made by Wednesday 5 pm. Allergen details are listed on each meal label; tell us right away if anything changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Meal plan dates and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Weekly clients often pay in advance, and clear dates show exactly which week and delivery the charge covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized meals with counts and portion sizes
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients compare what they ordered with what they received, and counts settle disputes about missing or extra meals.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dietary restrictions and allergens noted
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents what the client asked for and protects you if there is a question about a recipe or substitution.

invoiceChecklist.item: Grocery costs listed separately (in-home chefs)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows food cost apart from your labor, and receipts attached or available build trust when you bill at cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery fee and delivery window
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients see what they paid for and it supports charging a redelivery fee if nobody is home.

invoiceChecklist.item: Container deposits or return policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Reusable containers are a real cost, and listing deposits stops them from disappearing without credit or charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license or food permit number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many areas require a cottage food permit, commercial kitchen license, or health department registration, and showing it reassures clients and some corporate buyers.

meal-prep-service.paymentTerms: Most meal prep businesses collect payment before cooking because ingredients are purchased in advance and food cannot be resold. Weekly plans are commonly billed 2-4 days before the cook day, and subscriptions are charged automatically on a set weekday. In-home chefs often take a deposit or require a payment method on file, and bill groceries on the day of service or reimburse from a prepaid amount. Corporate or gym clients may pay net 15 or net 30. A cancellation cutoff, often 48-72 hours before the cook day, is standard, with late cancellations billed at full or partial price. Accepted methods usually include card, ACH, and payment apps. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are used for business accounts but are rarely applied to individual weekly clients, who are more often paused until the balance is paid.

tips.title: Bill before you buy groceries
tips.body: Food is perishable and custom, so you cannot return it. Collect payment or a deposit before shopping, and set a firm cutoff for order changes so you are not stuck with ingredients.

tips.title: Build price from true food cost
tips.body: Include ingredients, packaging, labels, delivery, kitchen time, and waste. Specialty proteins and organic produce can shift cost week to week, so review your per-meal price every few months and tell clients about increases ahead of time.

tips.title: Separate groceries from labor for in-home sessions
tips.body: Clients often assume groceries are included. Show them as a separate line with receipts and a stated handling fee, or quote a flat all-in price, so there is no surprise at the end of the day.

tips.title: Write down your cancellation and skip policy
tips.body: Put the cutoff time on every invoice. Skipped weeks are the biggest source of lost revenue for subscription meal prep.

tips.title: Keep records for taxes
tips.body: Track grocery receipts, mileage for shopping and delivery, packaging, and kitchen rental. Sales tax rules for prepared food vary by state and sometimes by city, so check with your state revenue department about whether to collect it.

faqs.question: Should I charge per meal or per week?
faqs.answer: Per meal is easier to compare and works well for custom orders. Weekly packages are simpler to sell and invoice, and they encourage a set number of meals. Many services list a per-meal price on the invoice inside a weekly package so clients can see the math.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on prepared meals?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax prepared or ready-to-eat food even when groceries are exempt, while some treat personal chef services differently. Check with your state department of revenue before you set up invoices.

faqs.question: How do I bill groceries for an in-home cooking session?
faqs.answer: List groceries as a separate line at actual cost, attach or offer the receipt, and add a handling fee if you included one in your quote. Some chefs collect an estimated grocery amount in advance and settle the difference afterward.

faqs.question: Can I charge for food that a client cancels last minute?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy states a cutoff and it is on your quote or invoice. Most services charge the full price or at least ingredient cost for cancellations after groceries are bought or cooking has started.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to sell meal prep?
faqs.answer: In most places, yes. Requirements range from a cottage food permit for limited items to a commercial kitchen license and a food handler certification. Rules vary widely, so check with your local health department.

estimate.intro: Meal prep services send quotes when a new client asks about a weekly plan, a one-time cooking day, an event or office order, or a custom diet. Clients usually compare price per meal, portion size, ingredient quality, and whether groceries and delivery are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meals, portions, and servings per meal
scopeChecklist.why: A 10-meal plan for one person is very different from 10 family-size trays, and portion size drives food cost.
State whether the client picks from a set menu or gets custom recipes, since custom menus take more planning time.
Allergen-free cooking can require separate prep and special ingredients, and clear notes protect you from later disputes.
This is the most common source of price confusion for in-home chefs.

scopeChecklist.item: Where cooking happens and who supplies equipment
scopeChecklist.why: In-home cooking depends on the client's kitchen, cookware, and cleanup, which affects how long the session takes.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery or pickup details and fee
scopeChecklist.why: Distance and time windows add cost, and clients should know what happens if nobody is home.

scopeChecklist.item: Containers, labels, reheating instructions, and shelf life
scopeChecklist.why: Packaging is a real cost and setting expectations for how long meals stay fresh prevents complaints.

pricingTips.title: Work backward from food cost
pricingTips.body: Total your ingredient, packaging, and labor costs per meal, then price so food cost lands around 28-35 percent. Quoting from a number you saw elsewhere can leave you underpaid on expensive menus.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present options such as 8, 12, and 16 meals per week, with a slightly lower per-meal price at higher counts. Clients tend to pick a tier rather than negotiate.

pricingTips.title: Quote ingredient-sensitive menus with a price range or review date
pricingTips.body: Meat, seafood, and produce prices shift. Say how long the quote is valid and that you may adjust for major ingredient changes with notice.

pricingTips.title: Add a trial week
pricingTips.body: A one-week trial at standard pricing lets the client test portions and taste before committing to a longer plan, and it gives you real data on their appetite and preferences.

faqs.question: How long should a meal prep quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is typical. Food costs change quickly, so a short validity window protects your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or tasting?
faqs.answer: Many cooks offer a free 15-30 minute call to discuss goals and diet, and charge $50-150 for a full tasting or menu planning session, sometimes credited toward the first order.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before starting?
faqs.answer: For one-time events or large orders, a 25-50 percent deposit is common. For weekly plans, collecting the first week in advance works as the deposit.

faqs.question: What if the client's dietary needs change after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that changes to restrictions, meal count, or menu may change the price. Send a revised quote before the cook day if costs go up.

measuring-service.intro: Measuring services take field measurements of buildings, rooms, windows, countertops, and land features, then deliver sketches, floor plans, or measurement reports. Clients include contractors, architects, real estate agents, appraisers, property managers, interior designers, and homeowners. Invoices usually cover on-site time, square footage or opening counts, drafting, travel, and any rush or revision work.
measuring-service.pricingModel: Most measuring work is priced either as a flat fee tied to the size of the property or as a per-square-foot or per-opening rate. Small residential jobs, such as a square footage report or a floor plan, usually get a flat fee with a size cap and an overage rate above it. Larger commercial as-built jobs are often priced per square foot, with a minimum fee to cover travel and setup. Templating and window measuring are commonly priced per visit or per opening. Drafting from field notes is billed separately by the hour or as a set deliverable fee. Many solo operators add a travel charge beyond a set radius, a surcharge for rush turnaround, and a fee for extra revisions or return visits caused by blocked access.

rates.service: Residential square footage measurement and basic floor plan (up to 2,500 sq ft)
Commercial as-built measuring and floor plan
Window and door measuring for treatments or replacements

items.description: Field measurement of 6,200 sq ft office suite, interior walls, columns, and perimeter
CAD floor plan drafting (PDF and DWG delivered)
Ceiling height notation and door and window schedule
Mileage to job site (round trip)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Measurements are accurate to within 1 inch under normal field conditions and reflect areas that were accessible on the date of the visit. One round of revisions is included; additional revisions are billed at $75 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit or suite number
invoiceChecklist.why: Measurement work is tied to a specific location, and the client may need to match the invoice to the right project or file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of site visit and the measuring method used
invoiceChecklist.why: Property conditions change, and stating whether you used a laser measure, tape, or scanner documents what the numbers are based on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Measured area or opening count with the unit rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-square-foot and per-opening billing needs visible quantities so the client can check the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables list and file formats
invoiceChecklist.why: Naming the PDF, DWG, or sketch files shows what was delivered and avoids disputes over what the fee covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Accuracy statement and access limitations
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting tolerance and any areas you could not reach protects you if someone later disputes a figure.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, and rush charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from measuring fees makes the invoice easier to approve, especially for property managers and contractors who pass costs on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or job reference, plus your license or insurance info if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often cannot pay without a PO number, and some jurisdictions or clients require proof of license or insurance.

measuring-service.paymentTerms: Residential clients and individual homeowners usually pay at completion or on delivery of the files, and many solo operators ask for payment before sending final drawings. For larger commercial jobs, a 25-50% deposit is common, with the balance due net 15 or net 30 after delivery. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in advance. Most measuring services accept checks, ACH transfer, and card payments, and card fees are sometimes passed to the client or built into the rate. Contractors and property managers on net 30 terms often need an invoice with a PO number before they will release payment.

tips.title: Set a size cap on flat fees
tips.body: A flat fee for a home up to 2,500 sq ft works until you arrive at a 4,000 sq ft house with a finished basement. State the cap and an overage rate per square foot so you are paid for the extra work.

tips.title: Charge for return visits caused by access problems
tips.body: Locked rooms, furniture blocking walls, or tenants who are not home cost you a trip. Put a return-visit fee in your terms and list it as its own line when it applies.

tips.title: Bill drafting separately from field time
tips.body: Field work and drafting have different costs and different skill levels. Showing them separately makes it easy to quote future jobs and to bill revisions fairly.

tips.title: Define what a revision is
tips.body: Fixing your own error is free. Changing the layout after delivery, adding rooms, or re-drawing to a new standard is billable. Say this in writing before you start.

tips.title: Deliver files after payment on small jobs
tips.body: For residential and one-time clients, send a watermarked preview and release final files once paid. This avoids chasing small invoices.

faqs.question: Should I bill measuring by the square foot or a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee with a size cap for typical homes, since clients like knowing the price up front. Use per-square-foot pricing for commercial and large jobs, where the cost scales with the area, and add a minimum fee to cover travel and setup.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most measuring services include a service radius in the base price and charge mileage or a trip fee beyond it. List it as a separate line so the client sees it is not part of the measuring rate.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to bill for measuring?
faqs.answer: It depends on the work and the state. Basic square footage measuring and floor plans often do not require a license, but boundary or topographic work generally requires a licensed surveyor. Check your state and local rules, and do not present measurements in a way that implies a survey if you are not licensed.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who disputes my measurements?
faqs.answer: Refer to your accuracy statement, the date of the visit, and the method listed on the invoice. Offer a paid re-measure for disputes that involve changed conditions, and a free re-check if the error was yours.

faqs.question: Should I take a deposit?
faqs.answer: For commercial and large jobs, yes, usually 25-50% before you schedule the visit. For small residential jobs, many people collect payment at the visit or before releasing final files instead.

estimate.intro: A measuring service sends an estimate before the site visit, usually after a call or a look at the property size and purpose. Clients compare price, turnaround time, deliverable formats, and accuracy. Contractors and agents often request quotes from several providers and choose on speed and price, so clarity about what is included matters.

scopeChecklist.item: Property type, address, and approximate square footage
scopeChecklist.why: This is the basis for the price, and a wrong size estimate is the most common cause of a changed quote.
Attics, crawl spaces, garages, basements, and exterior areas take extra time. Listing them avoids arguments about whether they were covered.
Measurements for an appraisal, a remodel, a window order, or a lease may need different detail and tolerance.
State whether the client gets a sketch, a PDF floor plan, a DWG file, or a written report, since each takes different drafting time.
If the client needs a specific standard, such as BOMA or ANSI for square footage, say so. Otherwise state your normal tolerance.
Furniture moved, rooms unlocked, and someone on site to let you in all affect time. State that return visits for access problems are billable.

scopeChecklist.item: Turnaround time, validity period, and what triggers a revised quote
scopeChecklist.why: Setting a delivery date and a quote expiration protects your schedule and your pricing if the scope changes.

pricingTips.title: Price the minimum, not just the rate
pricingTips.body: A per-square-foot rate on a 900 sq ft space may not cover your drive and setup. Set a minimum job fee so small jobs are still worth taking.

pricingTips.title: Quote field work and drafting as separate lines
pricingTips.body: This lets clients who only need field notes skip the drafting, and lets you add drafting later without repricing the whole job.

pricingTips.title: Offer two tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic sketch with key dimensions and a full scaled CAD plan at a higher price lets the client choose based on budget and keeps you from being compared on price alone.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for hard-to-measure sites
pricingTips.body: Cluttered, occupied, or irregular buildings take longer. Add a modest complexity factor to the quote and explain it, rather than absorbing the extra hours.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most measuring services quote for free from a phone call or basic details. Charge for a site visit just to scope a large or complex job, and credit that fee toward the work if the client hires you.

faqs.question: Is a measuring estimate binding?
faqs.answer: If you call it a quote with a fixed price, treat it as binding unless the scope changes. If you give an estimate based on approximate size, state that the final price depends on the actual measured area.

faqs.question: What if the property turns out larger than the client said?
faqs.answer: Include a clause that the price is based on the stated size and will be adjusted at your per-square-foot overage rate if the measured area exceeds it by more than a set percentage, such as 10%.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is common. Shorten it if your schedule fills quickly or if travel and fuel costs are changing.

media-buyer.intro: Media buyers plan, purchase, and manage paid advertising for clients across channels like Meta, Google, TikTok, programmatic display, connected TV, podcasts, and local radio or print. Freelancers and small agencies bill for strategy, campaign setup, ongoing optimization, reporting, and sometimes the ad spend itself. Invoices have to separate the buyer's fee from media costs so the client can see exactly what went to the platform and what went to the buyer.
media-buyer.pricingModel: Most media buyers use one of four models: a percentage of ad spend (commonly 10-20%, with lower percentages at higher spend), a flat monthly retainer for management, an hourly rate for audits and one-off projects, or a hybrid of a base retainer plus a performance bonus tied to agreed metrics like ROAS or cost per lead. Setup work such as account structure, pixel and conversion tracking, and audience builds is usually billed as a separate one-time fee. Media spend is either paid by the client directly to the platform on their own card, which keeps it off your invoice, or passed through on your invoice at cost (or with an agreed markup) when you front the money. Be explicit about which applies, because it changes your cash flow and your liability if a platform charges late or a client disputes a charge. Many buyers set a minimum monthly fee so small budgets are still worth managing.

rates.service: Monthly management retainer (single platform, small budget)
Ad account audit with written recommendations
Monthly performance report and client call
Traditional media planning and negotiation (radio, print, OOH)
rates.unit: % of media cost or flat fee

items.description: Paid social and search management, March 2025 (Meta and Google Ads)
Creative testing setup: 3 new ad sets, audience builds, and UTM tagging
Monthly performance report and strategy call
Additional landing page conversion tracking troubleshooting
Pass-through media spend: Google Ads (billed through agency account), March 1-31

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Media spend is billed at cost with no markup and is based on platform invoices, copies attached. Management fee is a flat monthly retainer and does not change with spend. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and campaign names
invoiceChecklist.why: Ad work is ongoing, so the client needs to see which month and which campaigns the fee and spend apply to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Management fee shown separately from media spend
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to know what the platforms charged versus what you earned, and it keeps your fee from being confused with ad costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Platform and ad account IDs
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies which accounts the spend ran through and helps match your invoice to platform billing statements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Basis for the fee (flat retainer or percentage and the spend it was calculated on)
invoiceChecklist.why: If the fee is a percentage, showing total spend and the percentage lets the client verify the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs with supporting platform invoices
invoiceChecklist.why: Attaching the platform invoice or statement proves the amount and prevents disputes over spend discrepancies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Any markup on media or third-party tools
invoiceChecklist.why: Disclosing markup avoids trust problems and may be required by your contract or the client's procurement rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or insertion order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many mid-size and corporate clients will not pay without a PO or IO reference on the invoice.

media-buyer.paymentTerms: Retainers are typically invoiced at the start of the month or billing period, with net 7 to net 15 terms. Percentage-of-spend fees are usually invoiced after the month closes, when final spend is known. If you front media costs on your own card or account, many buyers require payment in advance or a deposit equal to expected spend, because platform charges hit before the client pays. A late fee of 1 to 2 percent per month is common and should be written into your contract. Payment is usually taken by ACH or card, and larger clients may pay by check or through an accounts payable portal on net 30 terms. Set a clear rule that campaigns can be paused if an invoice goes unpaid past a stated number of days.

tips.title: Keep client spend off your card when you can
tips.body: Have clients add their own payment method to the ad platforms and give you partner or manager access. You avoid floating thousands of dollars, chasing reimbursement, and carrying chargeback risk.

tips.title: Collect a deposit if you do front spend
tips.body: If you do pay for media, bill an advance equal to the first month's expected spend or hold a prepaid balance. Platform charges can come before your invoice is due.

tips.title: Use a minimum fee with percentage pricing
tips.body: A 15% fee on a $1,500 budget is $225, which may not cover your time. Set a monthly minimum so low-spend months and ramp-up periods are still worth doing.

tips.title: Bill setup separately from management
tips.body: Pixel installation, account structure, and conversion tracking take real hours before any ad runs. Charge them as a one-time fee so they are not hidden in the first retainer.

tips.title: Define what a performance bonus is measured on
tips.body: If part of your pay depends on ROAS or cost per acquisition, write down the data source, the attribution window, and the calculation date. Platform numbers and the client's own numbers often differ.

faqs.question: Should I include ad spend on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you are paying the platform on the client's behalf. If the client pays the platform directly, your invoice should cover only your fees. If you do pass spend through, list it on its own line at cost or with a stated markup and attach the platform billing statement.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a percentage-of-spend fee?
faqs.answer: Wait until the billing period closes so you know final spend, then show total spend, your percentage, and the resulting fee on the invoice. Some buyers invoice an estimated fee up front and true it up the following month.

faqs.question: Can I charge a markup on media?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is agreed in writing and disclosed. Some agencies earn a margin on media instead of, or on top of, a management fee. Many clients prefer transparent at-cost billing plus a clear fee, so be ready to explain the difference.

faqs.question: What if the platform bills the client more than the budget I quoted?
faqs.answer: Put daily and monthly caps in your campaigns and a clause in your contract that says you are not liable for spend within approved budgets. Platforms can overdeliver slightly on daily budgets, so note that in your terms.

faqs.question: Do I charge for reporting separately?
faqs.answer: Basic monthly reporting is often included in the retainer. Custom dashboards, deep-dive analyses, and extra client calls beyond an agreed number are usually billed separately or by the hour.

estimate.intro: Media buyers send a proposal or estimate before taking on a new client or a new campaign, often after a short audit or discovery call. Clients compare your fee structure, the channels you plan to use, and how much of their money goes to ads versus management. The quote also sets expectations for budget, reporting, and who controls the ad accounts.

scopeChecklist.why: Managing Meta and Google is a very different workload than adding TikTok, LinkedIn, or programmatic, so name each one covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly media budget and who pays the platforms
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether spend runs through your account or the client's and prevents confusion over what the fee covers.
State whether you charge a flat retainer, percentage of spend, or hybrid, and what happens if spend rises or falls.
Say whether the client supplies ad creative, copy, and landing pages or whether you do, and how many variations are included.
Specify weekly, biweekly, or monthly reports and the number of calls so reporting does not expand without pay.

scopeChecklist.item: Performance expectations and what is not guaranteed
scopeChecklist.why: Nobody can guarantee ROAS or lead cost, so state targets as goals and list factors outside your control such as offer, site, and sales follow-up.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract length, notice period, and account ownership
scopeChecklist.why: Commit to a minimum term, set a cancellation notice, and confirm the client owns the ad accounts and data after you leave.

pricingTips.title: Audit first, then quote
pricingTips.body: Look at the existing ad accounts or a test of the offer before pricing. A short paid audit exposes tracking problems and wasted spend and gives you a fair basis for a retainer.

pricingTips.title: Scale your fee to budget and complexity
pricingTips.body: A flat percentage can be unfair at very low or very high spend. Use tiers, such as 20% up to $5,000 and 10% above, or a retainer based on the number of campaigns and channels.

pricingTips.title: Offer a ramp-up period
pricingTips.body: The first 30 to 60 days involve more setup and testing. Quote a setup fee or a higher first month so heavy early work is paid for.

pricingTips.title: Show the budget split plainly
pricingTips.body: Present a simple table with media budget, management fee, and setup. Clients trust quotes that show how every dollar is divided.

faqs.question: Should I promise results in an estimate?
faqs.answer: No. Share target ranges based on benchmarks or past work, but state they are not guarantees. Results depend on the product, price, website, and sales process as much as the media buying.

faqs.question: How long should a media buying quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Platform costs, seasonality, and your own availability change, so an expiration date protects you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I quote a fixed fee or a percentage?
faqs.answer: A flat retainer is easier for clients to budget and for you to forecast. A percentage ties your pay to spend and works well for growing accounts, but add a minimum fee so you are covered if the budget is small.

faqs.question: What should I include if the client wants a trial?
faqs.answer: Offer a defined test, such as 30 to 60 days with a set budget and agreed success metrics, and bill the setup and first month as normal. Free trials of management time tend to turn into unpaid work.

mediator.intro: Mediators are neutral third parties who help people settle disputes without going to court. Solo and small-practice mediators handle divorce and custody, workplace conflicts, business and contract disputes, landlord-tenant matters, and civil cases. They bill for session time, preparation, document review, and drafting settlement agreements, usually split between the parties.
mediator.pricingModel: Most private mediators charge by the hour or by a half-day or full-day session rate. Fees are usually split equally between the parties, though some agreements allocate by income or by who requested mediation. Many mediators also bill preparation and follow-up time (reading position statements, intake calls, drafting the memorandum of understanding) at the same hourly rate or a reduced one. Commercial and employment mediators often use flat day rates with a case-filing or administrative fee. Family mediators sometimes offer flat packages that include a set number of sessions and a drafted agreement. Court-roster and community mediation programs often pay or charge on a sliding scale or a low fixed rate per case. Cancellation and late-cancel fees are common because a blocked session is hard to refill. Because the mediator must stay neutral, invoices are addressed to each party separately or to both with a clear split, never to just one side without an agreement in writing.

rates.service: Drafting memorandum of understanding or settlement agreement

items.description: Intake call and case setup (Party A and Party B)
Review of position statements and financial disclosures
Joint mediation session, March 12 (parenting plan and property division)
Second joint mediation session, March 26
Drafting memorandum of understanding

sampleInvoice.notes: Total shown is the full fee for the matter; each party is billed 50% ($1,387.50 each) under the signed mediation agreement. Payment due within 14 days. Mediation sessions canceled with less than 48 hours notice are billed at 50% of the scheduled time. I do not provide legal advice; please have your attorney review the memorandum before signing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Names of all parties and the matter or case reference
invoiceChecklist.why: A neutral must bill clearly for a dispute between several people. Naming each party and the matter avoids confusion about who owes what.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fee split and each party's share
invoiceChecklist.why: The signed mediation agreement usually sets the split. Showing each share prevents one party from paying the whole bill or disputing the amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and durations of each session
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing needs a record of when sessions occurred and how long they lasted, including joint sessions, caucuses, and phone calls.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for preparation, session time, and drafting
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question time spent outside the room. Itemizing shows the work behind the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the mediation agreement and fee terms
invoiceChecklist.why: The agreement is the basis for the rates, cancellation policy, and payment terms, so citing it supports the charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit applied and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Many mediators collect an advance. Showing credits keeps the accounting clear for each party.

invoiceChecklist.item: Court case number or referral source, if any
invoiceChecklist.why: Court-annexed and agency referrals often require the case number on the invoice for payment or reporting.

mediator.paymentTerms: Many mediators collect a retainer or deposit before the first session, often one to three hours of fees from each party, and bill the balance at the end of each session or monthly. Invoices are commonly due in 7 to 30 days, with 14 days typical for private clients. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the mediation agreement. Some mediators require payment in full before releasing a signed settlement document, though that practice should be disclosed up front and checked against local ethics rules. Payment is usually by check, bank transfer, or card, and each party generally pays their own share directly.

tips.title: Get fee terms signed before the first session
tips.body: A mediation agreement should state your rate, how fees are split, the retainer, and the cancellation policy. Having both parties sign avoids later disputes about who owes what.

tips.title: Collect a retainer from each party
tips.body: Taking funds from both sides in equal amounts protects against one party refusing to pay after an agreement is reached. Hold unused amounts and refund them in the final invoice.

tips.title: Bill each party separately when possible
tips.body: Sending separate invoices for each share is cleaner than one invoice that one side has to chase the other to cover. It also reinforces your neutrality.

tips.title: Charge for preparation and drafting
tips.body: Reading documents and writing the agreement take real time. State up front that these hours are billable, or quote a flat drafting fee.

tips.title: Enforce your late-cancel policy consistently
tips.body: A session blocked for several hours is hard to fill. Apply the same policy to both parties and note it on the invoice when it applies.

faqs.question: Who gets the invoice in a mediation, one party or both?
faqs.answer: It depends on the mediation agreement. Most mediators split fees equally and send each party an invoice for their share, or send a single invoice that clearly lists each share. Avoid billing only one party unless both agreed in writing.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent preparing and writing the agreement?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your fee agreement says so. List preparation, session time, and drafting as separate lines, or use a flat drafting fee, so clients can see what they are paying for.

faqs.question: What if one party doesn't pay their share?
faqs.answer: Check your agreement. Many mediators require retainers up front so this rarely comes up. If it does, you can ask the other party whether they will cover it, or pursue the unpaid party directly. Avoid releasing a final agreement until the issue is addressed, if your agreement allows that.

faqs.question: Should I charge for no-shows and late cancellations?
faqs.answer: Many mediators do, typically 50 to 100 percent of the scheduled time when notice is under 24 to 72 hours. It must be stated in the agreement beforehand, and applied evenly to both parties.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on mediation?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by state, and many states do not tax professional services, but some do. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional about whether your fees are taxable.

estimate.intro: Mediators usually give a fee quote after an intake call, when they know the number of parties, the type of dispute, and whether the case is already in court. Clients compare hourly rates, flat package prices, and what is included, such as preparation and the written agreement.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of parties and issues covered
scopeChecklist.why: A two-party custody dispute and a multi-party business conflict take very different amounts of time. Naming the parties and issues sets the scope.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated number and length of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients want a sense of total cost. A range of sessions and hours gives a realistic budget without promising a result.
Preparation, document review, calls, and emails add up. State whether they are billed hourly or included in a flat fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Whether a written agreement is included
scopeChecklist.why: Drafting a memorandum of understanding is often an extra charge. Clarify if it is included and how many revisions.

scopeChecklist.item: How fees are split between parties
scopeChecklist.why: Equal splits are common but not universal. Settle this before the first session.

scopeChecklist.item: Retainer, cancellation, and late payment terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should see deposit amounts and cancellation charges before they commit.
State that you are neutral, do not give legal advice, and cannot guarantee a settlement, so clients understand what they are buying.

pricingTips.title: Offer an hourly rate with an estimated range
pricingTips.body: Because the number of sessions depends on how the parties engage, quote the rate and a likely range of total hours rather than a fixed total for the whole case.

pricingTips.title: Use flat day rates for commercial cases
pricingTips.body: Business and employment disputes are often scheduled as a half or full day. A flat rate is easier for companies and their insurers to approve.

pricingTips.title: Package family mediation
pricingTips.body: A set number of sessions with a drafted agreement gives couples a predictable cost. Note what happens if more sessions are needed.

pricingTips.title: Price in preparation time
pricingTips.body: If you review long documents or hold pre-mediation calls, include that time in your estimate so you are not unpaid for the work that makes the session productive.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Either works. Hourly with an estimated range suits cases where the length is uncertain. Flat fees suit defined scopes, such as a one-day commercial mediation or a standard package of family sessions.

faqs.question: What happens if the case needs more sessions than quoted?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote that additional time is billed at the stated rate and that you will tell clients when the estimate is likely to be exceeded.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before sending a quote?
faqs.answer: A quote can be informal, but a signed mediation agreement with fee terms should be in place before the first session. Many mediators send both together.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many mediators offer a short free intake call and charge for longer consultations or screening sessions. State which applies in your quote so there is no surprise.
