medical-billing-service.intro: Medical billing services handle claim submission, payment posting, denial follow-up, and patient statements for physician practices, therapists, chiropractors, dental offices, and other providers. Most are solo billers or small firms that bill each client monthly, usually as a percentage of what the practice collects or as a flat monthly fee. Invoices need to tie the fee back to collections, claim volume, or specific projects so the practice can see what it paid for.
medical-billing-service.pricingModel: The most common model is a percentage of net collections, typically 4% to 9% depending on practice size, specialty, and how much of the revenue cycle you handle. Larger practices with high volume pay toward the low end, while small solo practices often pay more. Some billers charge a flat monthly fee based on provider count, or a per-claim fee, commonly $3 to $8 per claim submitted. Hourly rates apply to project work such as credentialing, AR cleanup, and coding review. Many billers add a monthly minimum so that a slow collection month does not leave them underpaid. One-time setup fees cover clearinghouse enrollment, EDI and ERA setup, and loading the fee schedule into the practice management system. Credentialing is usually a separate flat fee per payer or per provider. Make clear whether your percentage applies to payments received or to charges billed, and whether patient payments collected at the front desk are included.

rates.service: Flat monthly billing fee, small practice
Accounts receivable cleanup (aged claims over 90 days)
Patient statement mailing and phone follow-up

items.description: Billing services, March 2025 - 6% of net collections ($38,400 collected)
Patient statements mailed (print and postage)
AR cleanup, claims over 120 days (Aetna and UnitedHealthcare)
Credentialing application, Blue Cross Blue Shield (Dr. Patel)

sampleInvoice.notes: Collections figure is based on ERA and patient payments posted March 1-31 and is attached in the monthly report. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Payments by ACH preferred. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances over 30 days past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and collections basis
invoiceChecklist.why: A percentage fee needs a clear dollar figure and date range so the practice can check it against its own deposits and your reports.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name or NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Multi-provider practices often allocate costs by provider, and credentialing or per-provider fees need to be traceable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Claim counts or statement counts
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-claim and per-statement charges are easy to dispute without volume numbers that match your system reports.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payer names for project work
invoiceChecklist.why: AR cleanup, appeals, and credentialing are tied to specific payers, and listing them shows what was done and for whom.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Clearinghouse fees, postage, printing, and paper claim costs should be shown apart from your service fee so they are not mistaken for markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the business associate agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting the BAA on file reminds the client that you handle protected health information under HIPAA, and keeps the paperwork connected to the billing relationship.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed service agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: The fee percentage, minimums, and what counts as collections are defined in the contract, so referencing it settles most questions.

medical-billing-service.paymentTerms: Most medical billing services invoice monthly after the month's payments have been posted, so the invoice reflects actual collections. Net 15 is common, and net 30 is also seen, especially with larger groups. Some billers pull their fee directly by ACH from the practice account under a signed authorization, which cuts down on late payments. Setup and credentialing fees are often collected upfront or at 50% deposit, since they require work before any revenue arrives. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are typical when written into the contract. Avoid taking payment out of the practice's deposits without written authorization, and keep your fee accounting separate from patient funds. Do not accept payment by sending patient information over unsecured email.

tips.title: Define collections in the contract
tips.body: Specify whether your percentage applies to insurance payments only or also to patient payments, copays collected at the desk, and recoupments. Also state how refunds and payer takebacks are handled, because a payer clawback months later can change what the base amount should have been.

tips.title: Set a monthly minimum
tips.body: A percentage fee falls when a provider takes vacation, a payer delays payment, or a practice has a slow month. A minimum monthly fee based on provider count covers your fixed workload.

tips.title: Attach your reports to the invoice
tips.body: Send the collections summary, aging report, and denial report with each invoice. Clients who can see the work are less likely to question the fee or ask for discounts.

tips.title: Charge separately for cleanup of inherited problems
tips.body: New clients often arrive with months of unbilled charges or unworked denials. Bill that work hourly or as a flat project, or negotiate a higher percentage on recovered old AR, rather than burying it in the standard rate.

tips.title: Bill after collections, but not too late
tips.body: Waiting to invoice until all payments are posted keeps the amount accurate, but delay past the first week or two of the following month stretches your own cash flow. Pick a fixed invoicing date and stick to it.

faqs.question: Should I bill on charges or on collections?
faqs.answer: Collections is the standard for percentage billing because it aligns your pay with the practice getting paid. Billing on charges would mean you earn the same when claims are denied, and most practices will not agree to that.

faqs.question: Do I charge a percentage on payments that come in after a client terminates?
faqs.answer: Many contracts include a tail period, often 60 to 90 days, in which you are paid a percentage on claims you submitted before termination. This must be written in the service agreement, since it is difficult to enforce otherwise.

faqs.question: Can I charge for clearinghouse and postage fees?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. List them as a separate pass-through line at cost, or include them in the base fee and say so. Hidden charges cause more disputes than higher honest rates.

faqs.question: Do I need a business associate agreement before invoicing?
faqs.answer: If you handle protected health information for a covered entity, HIPAA generally requires a business associate agreement before you start. It is separate from your invoice, but you should have it signed before accessing any patient data.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes my percentage because of payer delays?
faqs.answer: Point to the collections report and the contract definition. If the dispute is about timing, the invoice should be based on posted payments in the billing period, so payments received later fall into the next invoice.

estimate.intro: Medical billing services send proposals when a practice is looking to outsource billing, switch vendors, or fix a backlog of unpaid claims. Practices compare percentage rates, but also what is included, such as denial work, patient statements, and reporting. A clear proposal explains what the percentage covers so it can be compared fairly.

scopeChecklist.item: Practice size, specialty, and provider count
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on claim volume and specialty complexity, and a change in provider count later should trigger a defined fee adjustment.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included in the base fee
scopeChecklist.why: List claim submission, payment posting, denial follow-up, patient statements, and eligibility checks so nothing is assumed to be free.
Credentialing, coding review, AR cleanup, and appeals often cost extra, and stating that upfront avoids surprise add-ons.
State whether the percentage applies to net collections, whether patient payments count, and what the monthly minimum is.
Working in the practice's existing software or in yours affects setup time and who pays for licenses and per-claim fees.
Existing aged claims should be reviewed in the quote, with a stated approach for working or writing them off.
A 30 to 90 day notice period and any tail fee on pending claims protect your revenue after a client leaves.

pricingTips.title: Ask for an aging report and recent collections before quoting
pricingTips.body: Request the last three to six months of charges, payments, and an AR aging summary. Your percentage should reflect actual volume and payer mix, not the practice's estimate.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered percentage
pricingTips.body: A rate like 7% on the first $30,000 collected per month and 5% above that rewards growth and is easy to explain. Practices often prefer it to a single flat percentage that feels expensive as they grow.

pricingTips.title: Price the setup separately
pricingTips.body: Enrollment, EDI and ERA setup, and fee schedule loading take real time before you earn anything. A one-time setup fee keeps the monthly rate competitive.

pricingTips.title: Quote cleanup as a project
pricingTips.body: Old AR is often a different job from ongoing billing. Offer an hourly rate with a cap, or a contingency percentage on recovered claims, so the practice sees it as separate from the monthly fee.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed percentage quote before seeing the practice's data?
faqs.answer: Give a range only. Final pricing should wait until you review claim volume, specialty, payer mix, and denial rates, since these drive your workload.

faqs.question: How long should a billing proposal be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Collections patterns and your own capacity change, and a valid-through date gives you a clear point to revisit the rate.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the proposal or practice audit?
faqs.answer: Some billers charge a flat fee of $300 to $1,000 for a billing audit and credit it toward setup if the practice signs. A free quote is more common for standard practices, but a paid audit makes sense for complex or troubled accounts.

faqs.question: What happens if the practice's actual volume differs from the estimate?
faqs.answer: If you quote a flat monthly fee, include a provision to adjust it if claim volume or provider count changes by a set amount, such as 20%. Percentage-based fees adjust on their own.

mep-engineer.intro: MEP engineers design and document the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems in buildings. Solo consultants and small firms bill architects, developers, general contractors, and building owners for design phases, site surveys, load calculations, permit drawings, and construction-phase support. Invoices usually tie to project phases, hourly time, or a percentage of work completed.
mep-engineer.pricingModel: MEP work is priced three main ways. Hourly time-and-materials is common for small tenant improvements, field surveys, code reviews, and open-ended coordination, with different rates for principal, project engineer, and CAD/BIM technician. Lump-sum fees by phase (schematic design, design development, construction documents, bidding, construction administration) are typical for new construction and larger renovations, and are billed as a percentage of each phase complete. Some firms quote a percentage of construction cost, often in the range of 8 to 15 percent of the MEP construction cost on commercial work, but small projects are more often fixed per drawing set or per square foot. Reimbursable expenses such as plan printing, permit filing fees, travel, and sub-consultants (for example a fire protection or commissioning specialist) are usually billed at cost plus a 10 to 15 percent markup, as stated in your agreement. Additional services such as revisions after design approval, owner-driven scope changes, and extra site visits are billed separately from the base fee.

rates.service: Existing conditions site survey and report
Tenant improvement MEP design (small office or retail)
Heating and cooling load calculations (Manual J/N style or ASHRAE)
Construction administration (RFIs, submittal review, site visits)

items.description: Tenant improvement MEP design, 4,200 sq ft office - Construction Documents phase (60% of $9,450 phase fee)
Existing conditions site survey and mechanical equipment report
Principal engineer time - coordination with architect and utility provider
CAD technician time - revisions per architect's revised floor plan (Additional Service)
Plan set printing and permit submittal fee advance (reimbursable, at cost + 10%)

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Suite 300 TI, 1200 Commerce St. Contract dated March 3. Invoice 2 of 4 for design fees. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Additional services are billed at contract hourly rates. Please reference project number on payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, address, and your project number
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and accounts payable departments handle many projects at once. A consistent project number gets your invoice coded and paid faster.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or proposal date and fee basis
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying each line to the signed agreement makes it clear what is base scope and what is billed under the contract's hourly or additional services terms.

invoiceChecklist.item: Phase name and percent complete
invoiceChecklist.why: For lump-sum work, owners and lenders expect to see the phase, total phase fee, percent billed to date, and the amount billed this period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Additional services listed separately with the reason
invoiceChecklist.why: Revisions caused by architect changes, owner changes, or new code comments should be itemized and dated so they are not mistaken for base scope errors.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by person or role for time-and-materials lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients may audit hourly billing. Showing role, hours, and rate supports the charge without needing a follow-up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursables with markup and receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Printing, permit fees, courier, mileage, and sub-consultant costs need to match what your agreement allows. Separate lines avoid disputes over markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: PE license number and state, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many firms include license information on proposals and invoices, and some clients or public agencies require it. Check your state board rules for what applies to you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or owner/lender requisition reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate and institutional clients often reject invoices without a PO number, and lender-funded projects may require a matching draw reference.

mep-engineer.paymentTerms: Most MEP consultants require a retainer or initial payment of 10 to 25 percent of the fee, or a flat amount for small jobs, before starting work. Progress invoices are then sent monthly or at phase completion, with net 30 the most common term, though some general contractors and developers push for net 45 or 60. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract, and check your state's rules on allowable interest. Some firms stop issuing stamped drawings until overdue balances are cleared, but that should be stated in the agreement. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or wire for large invoices, with credit cards used mostly for small residential or one-off work.

tips.title: Bill monthly even when phases are long
tips.body: A construction documents phase can last two or three months. Invoice the percent complete each month so you are not carrying the work until the end of the phase.

tips.title: Keep base scope and additional services apart
tips.body: Track revisions, owner-requested changes, and extra site visits with dates and a short note on who requested them. Send a written change notice before doing the work when the cost is significant.

tips.title: Hold sealed drawings until the retainer or phase payment clears
tips.body: Releasing stamped permit sets before payment removes your leverage. Put a clause in your agreement that sealed documents are released on payment, and apply it consistently.

tips.title: Pass through sub-consultant costs clearly
tips.body: If you bring in a fire protection, controls, or commissioning sub-consultant, show their invoice amount and your markup as a separate line. Pay terms from the client may be slower than what you owe the sub, so check the agreement for pay-when-paid language.

tips.title: Bill construction administration by time
tips.body: Construction-phase work is unpredictable. Hourly billing with a not-to-exceed budget keeps you covered when RFIs and submittals run beyond what you expected.

faqs.question: Should I bill MEP design hourly or as a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Flat fees by phase work well when the scope is clear, such as a defined tenant improvement or new building with fixed drawings. Hourly is safer for surveys, code studies, existing building work with unknowns, and construction administration. Many firms use both on one project.

faqs.question: Can I charge for revisions after the design is approved?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement defines the approved design as the baseline and lists revisions as additional services. Document the change request, the date, and the hours, and bill at your contract hourly rates.

faqs.question: Do I need to include my PE license number on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state and client. It is common to include it on proposals and drawings, and some public or institutional clients ask for it on invoices. Check with your state engineering board and your client's contract.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a contractor or owner is slow to pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder at the due date, then a written notice referencing the late fee and any clause on withholding sealed documents. For unpaid design work, many states allow lien rights for design professionals on certain projects, but the rules and deadlines vary, so check with a local attorney.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on engineering services?
faqs.answer: Professional engineering services are not taxed in many states, but some states tax certain services or tangible items such as printed plan sets. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: MEP engineers send a fee proposal before any design starts, usually after a request from an architect, developer, contractor, or building owner who is comparing several firms. Clients look at total fee, what drawings and calculations are included, the schedule, and how changes are handled. A clear proposal also doubles as the scope of the contract.

scopeChecklist.item: Disciplines included (mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire protection, controls)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume fire sprinkler design, fire alarm, lighting controls, or low-voltage are included. State which ones are in and which are by others.
List each phase and what is delivered, such as stamped permit drawings, specifications, load calculations, energy compliance forms, and one round of review comments.
State the building area, existing system conditions, utility capacity, and code edition you assumed. If these prove wrong, the fee can be adjusted.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of site visits and meetings
scopeChecklist.why: Site visits, design meetings, and construction-phase visits cost time and travel. Set a number included and a rate for additional ones.
Define how many rounds of review are included and that owner or architect changes after approval are additional services.
Specify whether responding to plan check comments is included, and for how long after submittal.
Name items not included, such as commissioning, energy modeling, utility applications, and field-testing. List how printing, permit fees, and travel are billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule and information needed from client
scopeChecklist.why: Link your timeline to receiving architectural backgrounds, surveys, and decisions on time, so delays on the client side do not become your cost.

pricingTips.title: Price from hours, then cross-check against cost and area
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours by role for each phase, then compare the total to a per-square-foot figure or a percentage of MEP construction cost. If the two are far apart, review your assumptions before sending the quote.

pricingTips.title: Add contingency for existing buildings
pricingTips.body: Renovations often have missing or wrong as-built drawings. Include a site survey line and a time allowance for field verification, or price the design after the survey is finished.

pricingTips.title: Break the fee down by phase and discipline
pricingTips.body: A table with fees per phase makes it easier for the client to approve work in stages and for you to invoice progress. It also shows exactly what is cut if the client asks for a lower price.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity period
pricingTips.body: Fees depend on current workload and labor costs. State that the proposal is valid for 30 to 60 days and that the schedule begins on receipt of a signed agreement and retainer.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed fee or an estimate range?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed fee when the scope and drawings are clear. Use an hourly estimate with a not-to-exceed amount when conditions are uncertain, such as existing building work or early-stage projects with unsettled layouts.

faqs.question: How do I respond when a client says another firm is cheaper?
faqs.answer: Compare scope line by line first. Lower bids often leave out site visits, construction administration, or revisions. Offer to remove services or reduce deliverables rather than discounting the same scope.

faqs.question: What if the project scope grows after the proposal is accepted?
faqs.answer: Refer to the additional services clause in the agreement. Send a short written change request with the added scope, hours, and fee, and get approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Should I charge for preparing a proposal?
faqs.answer: Most MEP firms provide simple proposals free. For large projects that need detailed pre-design studies, feasibility analysis, or a significant site visit, a paid pre-design phase is reasonable.

metal-fabricator.intro: Metal fabricators cut, bend, weld, and assemble steel, stainless, and aluminum into finished parts and structures. Customers include contractors, homeowners, restaurants, farms, and manufacturers who need railings, gates, brackets, frames, trailers, custom enclosures, and one-off or short-run parts. Invoices typically cover shop labor, materials, outside services like powder coating, and delivery or installation.
metal-fabricator.pricingModel: Most fabricators combine shop labor billed by the hour with materials billed at cost plus a markup, often 15 to 40 percent depending on material and volume. Production or repeat parts are often priced per piece after the first job sets up the process, with a one-time setup or programming charge for CNC, laser, or press brake work. Larger custom jobs such as stair rails, gates, and structural steel are usually a flat price based on a quote, split into deposit, progress, and final payments. Outside services (galvanizing, powder coat, waterjet or laser cutting sent out, engineering stamps) are passed through with a handling markup. Field work and installation are billed at a higher hourly rate than shop work, plus travel time, mileage, and equipment such as lifts or welders. Many shops set a minimum charge to cover small repairs and quick jobs.

rates.service: CNC plasma, laser, or press brake setup
Small repair or minimum shop charge

items.description: Fabricate steel handrail, 2" square tube frame with 1/2" pickets, welded and ground smooth (shop labor)
Materials: A500 square tube, flat bar, pickets, base plates, anchor hardware
Powder coat, satin black (outside vendor, includes 10% handling)
On-site installation, 2-person crew, includes core drilling and epoxy anchors
Truck and delivery, round trip

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $2,000 received on 3/4. Balance due within 15 days of installation. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Work warranted against weld defects for 12 months; powder coat warranty per vendor terms. Checks payable to the shop or pay by ACH or card (3% card fee).

invoiceChecklist.item: Job number, PO number, and quote reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Contractors and manufacturers usually cannot pay without a PO number, and tying the invoice to the original quote settles scope questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials list with type, grade, and thickness
invoiceChecklist.why: Steel prices swing, and customers may question the bill. Listing A36, 304 stainless, or 6061 aluminum and gauge shows what was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for shop labor, installation labor, and travel
invoiceChecklist.why: Shop and field rates differ, and itemizing them prevents disputes over blended hourly rates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Outside services and pass-through costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Galvanizing, powder coating, laser cutting, and engineering stamps come from third parties. Show them separately with any handling fee so they are not mistaken for shop labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finish, tolerance, and spec or drawing revision
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting the drawing revision and finish called out protects you if the customer later claims the part was made to a different version.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications and documentation provided
invoiceChecklist.why: Mill certs, weld procedure references, or inspection reports may be required on structural or code work. Noting what was delivered supports payment and warranty claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax status or resale or exemption certificate on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Rules vary by state on taxing fabricated goods, installation, and materials. Record whether tax was charged or an exemption certificate applies, and check your state rules.

metal-fabricator.paymentTerms: For custom work, a deposit of 30 to 50 percent is common, especially because you buy material up front. Larger jobs often use progress billing at milestones such as material purchase, completion of shop fabrication, and installation. Commercial and contractor accounts commonly pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, while individuals are usually asked to pay the balance at pickup or installation. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated on the quote and invoice. Accepted payment methods usually include checks, ACH, and cards, with some shops adding a card fee. Do not release finished parts until paid on small jobs, and on larger commercial jobs, ask about lien rights and notice deadlines in your state.

tips.title: Price steel at today's cost and put an expiry on the quote
tips.body: Material prices can change quickly. Limit quote validity to 15 or 30 days, and add a clause that lets you adjust the price if material costs change significantly before purchase.

tips.title: Bill the deposit to cover materials
tips.body: Set the deposit at least equal to the cost of material and outside services so you are not financing the customer's job from your own pocket.

tips.title: Charge for setup and programming separately
tips.body: Time spent on CAD drawings, nesting, CNC programming, and fixturing is real work. List it as its own line so repeat orders can be priced without it.

tips.title: Track change orders in writing
tips.body: Customers often alter dimensions or add features mid-job. Get written approval for each change and add it as a separate line on the invoice.

tips.title: Add a minimum charge for small jobs
tips.body: Quick repairs still take time for pickup, setup, cleanup, and consumables. A $75 to $150 minimum keeps small jobs from losing money.

faqs.question: Should I charge a markup on materials?
faqs.answer: Yes, most fabricators do. A markup of 15 to 40 percent is common because it covers purchasing, handling, cutoff waste, storage, and the risk of price changes. Smaller or specialty orders often carry a higher markup than large steel purchases.

faqs.question: How do I bill for scrap and waste?
faqs.answer: Either build waste into the material price, usually 5 to 15 percent for sheet and plate, or bill the full stock lengths and sheets purchased. State which method you use on the quote so the invoice does not surprise the customer.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on fabricated work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether the work is a product sale, a repair, or real property improvement. Many states treat these differently, and exemptions for resale or manufacturing may apply. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I hold finished parts until I am paid?
faqs.answer: Generally you can keep goods in your possession until payment, especially if your terms say so. For installed work on real property, mechanics' lien rights may apply, and deadlines vary by state, so check local rules early.

faqs.question: How should I invoice for a job in phases?
faqs.answer: Use a deposit invoice, then milestone invoices for material purchase, shop completion, and installation, with a final invoice for the balance. Each invoice should reference the original quote total and show what has already been paid.

estimate.intro: Fabricators quote before any steel is cut, usually after reviewing drawings, sketches, or a site visit. Customers often collect several quotes and compare total price, lead time, finish, and whether installation is included. A clear itemized quote helps you win jobs on more than the lowest number.

scopeChecklist.why: Attach or reference the drawing and revision so the quote matches what you will build, and so changes can be priced as extras.
A36 versus stainless, or 11-gauge versus 14-gauge, changes cost significantly. Naming it prevents substitution complaints.
Mill finish, primer, paint, powder coat, galvanizing, or brushed stainless have different costs and lead times. State exactly what is included.
Say whether installation is included, who supplies power, access, lifts, and concrete work, and what happens if site conditions differ from what you saw.
Structural, railing, and code-related work may need stamped drawings or permits. State who pays and who arranges them.
Material lead time, outside finishing, and shop backlog affect delivery. Give an estimated timeline and note it depends on deposit and drawing approval.
List what is not covered, such as demolition, removing old railings, or patching concrete, and state that changes in scope will be priced separately.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours by operation
pricingTips.body: Break the job into cutting, fitting, welding, grinding, finishing, and installation, and estimate hours for each. This is more reliable than guessing a total and shows where time actually goes.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for rework and waste
pricingTips.body: Include waste on stock material and a few percent for rework or fit-up issues. One-off jobs without a proven process usually run over.

pricingTips.title: Quote outside services at their current price
pricingTips.body: Get written pricing from the coater, galvanizer, or laser shop before quoting, and pass it through with a handling fee.

pricingTips.title: Offer options, not discounts
pricingTips.body: Present choices such as paint versus powder coat, or galvanized versus raw, so customers can adjust cost without you cutting your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For jobs that need site measurement, detailed drawings, or engineering, many shops charge a design or quoting fee, often credited toward the job if it goes ahead.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical because steel and aluminum prices can change. Shorten the window during volatile markets.

faqs.question: What if the final cost runs over the quote?
faqs.answer: On a fixed-price quote, you absorb normal overruns, but changes requested by the customer or unforeseen site conditions should be handled through written change orders. State this on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I require a signed quote before ordering material?
faqs.answer: Yes. A signed quote and deposit confirm the scope and price, and protect you from buying custom material that the customer later cancels.

midwife.intro: Independent midwives, including certified professional midwives (CPMs), certified nurse-midwives (CNMs) in private practice, and licensed direct-entry midwives, bill families for prenatal, birth, and postpartum care. Most clients pay a global fee that covers the whole course of care, and some also bill insurance or provide a superbill so the family can seek reimbursement.
midwife.pricingModel: Most home birth and birth center midwives charge a global fee that bundles prenatal visits, attendance at labor and birth, and postpartum visits through about six weeks. The fee is usually paid in installments that finish before the due date, often starting with a deposit at intake or after the first visit. Services outside the package are billed separately, such as lab work, ultrasounds, birth supplies kits, newborn screening and metabolic card fees, transfer-of-care mileage, doula-style extended labor support, lactation visits, and well-woman care. Some midwives accept Medicaid or private insurance and bill by CPT code, while others work self-pay and give clients a superbill. Sliding-scale fees and payment plans are common. Rates vary widely by state, licensure, and whether the practice includes an assistant or a birth center facility fee.

rates.service: Global maternity care package (home birth, prenatal through 6 weeks postpartum)
Birth center global package (includes professional fee)
Additional prenatal or postpartum visit outside the package

items.description: Global midwifery care: prenatal visits, labor and birth attendance, postpartum visits through 6 weeks (EDD 10/14)
Birth supplies kit
Newborn screening card and processing fee
Additional lactation visit (day 10)
Deposit received 04/02
Installment payments received (May-July)

sampleInvoice.notes: Remaining balance of $1,590 due within 30 days of birth. Payment accepted by check, card, HSA/FSA card, or bank transfer. A superbill with CPT and ICD-10 codes is available on request for insurance reimbursement. The global fee is non-refundable after 36 weeks except as described in your care agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Estimated due date and actual date of birth
invoiceChecklist.why: The global fee is tied to the pregnancy, and clients and insurers need dates to match services to the right episode of care.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of what the global fee includes
invoiceChecklist.why: Families want to see the number of prenatal and postpartum visits and birth attendance so they know what was covered and what is extra.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for supplies, labs, and screening fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These are often pass-through costs or billed separately, and itemizing avoids confusion about the global fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or certification type and number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and reimbursement requests usually require provider credentials, and many states require licensure to be identifiable.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT and ICD-10 codes (superbill)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients seeking out-of-network reimbursement will need codes such as global obstetric care codes and diagnosis codes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments received and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Installment plans mean most invoices show several credits, and a clear balance prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Transfer of care or partial-care adjustments
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client transfers to a hospital or care ends early, the invoice should show the services actually provided, per your written agreement.

midwife.paymentTerms: A deposit of $500-1,500 at intake or booking is typical to reserve a due-date spot, with the remaining fee split into monthly installments due by 36-37 weeks. Many practices require the full fee before birth, while others allow a small balance after. Insurance and Medicaid claims follow the payer's timeline, and the client is billed for any portion not covered. Policies for transfers, miscarriage, and early termination of care should be written in the care agreement, including what is refunded. Accepted methods commonly include checks, bank transfer, debit and credit cards, and HSA or FSA cards. Late fees are less common in this field than payment plans, so many midwives address late payments by agreement rather than penalty.

tips.title: Put the refund policy in writing before the first payment
tips.body: Pregnancy can end early, clients can transfer care, and births can happen before the final installment. A signed agreement stating what is refunded at each stage prevents the hardest billing conversations.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the birth when you can
tips.body: Collecting after birth is harder because families are focused on the baby and may have new expenses. Finishing installments by 36-37 weeks keeps your income predictable.

tips.title: Offer a superbill with every paid-out-of-pocket client
tips.body: Many families can recover part of the fee from their insurer or use HSA or FSA funds. A clear superbill with codes and your credentials makes that easier and sets you apart.

tips.title: Bill pass-through costs at actual cost
tips.body: Labs, ultrasounds, medications, and newborn screening fees are better listed on separate lines so clients can see the global fee is for your professional care.

tips.title: Keep records of every payment and visit
tips.body: Track visit dates alongside payment dates. If a client transfers care or an insurer asks questions, you can show exactly what was provided and paid.

faqs.question: Should I bill a global fee or per visit?
faqs.answer: Most independent midwives use a global fee because it matches how families budget for pregnancy. Bill per visit only for care outside the package, such as extra visits, well-woman exams, or clients who join late.

faqs.question: Can I give clients a superbill if I'm not in-network?
faqs.answer: Yes. A superbill lists your credentials, NPI, dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis codes, and fees charged. Reimbursement depends on the client's plan, so say you cannot guarantee it.

faqs.question: What if a client transfers to a hospital during labor?
faqs.answer: Your care agreement should state this in advance. Many midwives keep the full fee if labor care began, while others prorate. Invoice according to the written policy and itemize what was provided.

faqs.question: When should the final payment be due?
faqs.answer: Many midwives set it at 36-37 weeks, before the birth window opens. Check your state rules and your agreement, and adjust for clients on sliding-scale or insurance payment arrangements.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on midwifery care?
faqs.answer: Health care services are generally not subject to sales tax, but supplies you sell may be taxed in some states. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Prospective clients often request a fee quote at the first consultation, and many interview several midwives before choosing. They compare the global fee, what it includes, payment schedules, and whether the practice works with insurance. A written estimate lets families plan and shows exactly what is and isn't covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of prenatal visits and postpartum visits included
scopeChecklist.why: Families compare packages by what care is included, and visit counts prevent misunderstandings later.

scopeChecklist.item: Birth setting covered (home or birth center) and facility fees
scopeChecklist.why: Birth center fees and home birth fees differ, and clients need to know if the facility cost is separate.

scopeChecklist.item: Items billed separately: labs, ultrasounds, supplies, newborn screening
scopeChecklist.why: These costs can add hundreds of dollars, and clients should know about them before committing.
Clear due dates let families budget and show when the full fee must be paid.
The estimate should say what happens if care ends early, the client transfers, or the pregnancy ends.
Clients need to know if you bill insurance directly, provide a superbill only, or accept Medicaid.
Long drives to a home birth affect cost, and a stated radius avoids surprise mileage fees.

pricingTips.title: Quote one global number with a clear list of inclusions
pricingTips.body: A single figure with itemized inclusions is easier for families to compare than a long menu of fees.

pricingTips.title: Offer a sliding scale or payment plan in writing
pricingTips.body: If you adjust fees by income, state the criteria and schedule on the estimate so the arrangement is consistent and fair to every client.

pricingTips.title: Account for time, call coverage, and backup
pricingTips.body: Your fee should cover on-call time, a second attendant or assistant, supplies, insurance, and continuing education, not just hours spent at births.

pricingTips.title: Review your rates yearly
pricingTips.body: Costs for liability insurance, supplies, and assistants rise, so update your quote and apply new rates only to clients who sign after the change.

faqs.question: Is a midwife's quote binding?
faqs.answer: Only if your care agreement says so. State how long the quote is valid, such as 30 days, and note that medical needs can change which services are required.

faqs.question: What if a client develops complications and needs a hospital?
faqs.answer: Explain in the estimate that risk-out or transfer can change care and fees. Describe how you will bill for services provided up to that point.

faqs.question: Should I give an estimate for insurance-based care?
faqs.answer: Yes, give a good-faith estimate of the client's expected cost based on their plan, while noting that final amounts depend on what the insurer pays. Under the No Surprises Act, uninsured and self-pay clients in many cases are entitled to a good-faith estimate.

ml-engineer.intro: Freelance and independent ML engineers build, deploy, and maintain machine learning systems for startups, agencies, and internal teams at larger companies. Invoices usually cover model development, data pipeline work, MLOps setup, and ongoing advisory or support hours. Many work through their own LLC or as 1099 contractors on monthly or milestone-based engagements.
ml-engineer.pricingModel: Most independent ML engineers bill hourly for open-ended or exploratory work and a flat fee per milestone for well-scoped projects such as a prototype, a deployed inference service, or a model evaluation. Monthly retainers are common for ongoing model monitoring, retraining, and on-call support. Day rates are used for short consulting engagements and workshops. Discovery or feasibility studies are often priced separately from the build, because the outcome of the research is uncertain. Cloud compute, GPU time, labeling costs, and third-party API usage are either billed through at cost (sometimes with a small handling markup) or paid directly by the client from their own accounts, which is the cleaner option. Rates rise for specialized work such as LLM fine-tuning, computer vision in production, or regulated domains like healthcare and finance.

rates.service: General ML engineering (model development, training pipelines)
Senior or specialized work (LLM fine-tuning, RAG systems, computer vision)

items.description: Data pipeline development: feature extraction and cleaning for churn dataset
Model training and hyperparameter tuning (gradient boosted trees, 3 iterations)
Model evaluation report and stakeholder review call
Inference API deployment on client AWS account with logging
Cloud GPU training costs (pass-through, receipts attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers work performed March 1-31 under SOW dated February 20. Payment due within 30 days by ACH or wire. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. All code and trained model artifacts transfer to client upon payment in full, per the services agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement of work or contract reference and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate accounts payable teams often will not process an invoice without a PO or matching contract reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work period and milestone name
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties charges to specific deliverables such as 'v1 model trained' or 'API deployed' so the client can approve them quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by task
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating data prep, training, evaluation, and deployment shows where time went and heads off questions about why a model took longer than expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Compute and infrastructure pass-through costs with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: GPU hours, API credits, and labeling fees can be large; itemizing them separately keeps them distinct from your labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party licenses or datasets purchased on the client's behalf
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents who owns the purchase and avoids disputes over reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: IP and delivery terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States when code, weights, and datasets transfer to the client, usually upon full payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal business name, EIN or tax ID, and remittance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for the client to issue a 1099 where required and to pay by ACH or wire correctly.

ml-engineer.paymentTerms: Net 15 to Net 30 is standard, and larger companies often push for Net 45 or Net 60, so confirm this before signing. For new clients, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent on fixed-fee projects is common, with the balance tied to milestones. Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month. Many engineers add a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month and the right to pause work on unpaid invoices. ACH and wire transfers are the most common payment methods for larger amounts; cards are occasionally accepted with the processing fee passed on, where allowed.

tips.title: Separate discovery from the build
tips.body: Model performance depends on data you have not seen yet. Bill an initial data audit or feasibility phase on its own so you are paid even if the data turns out to be too thin for the project.

tips.title: Tie milestones to measurable outputs
tips.body: Define payment triggers like 'baseline model delivered with evaluation report' rather than 'model is accurate enough.' Avoid linking payment to a specific accuracy target unless the target is agreed in writing and the data is verified.

tips.title: Have the client own the cloud accounts
tips.body: Setting up compute under the client's account keeps large GPU bills off your books and removes the risk of fronting thousands of dollars in costs you must then chase.

tips.title: Track experiment time honestly
tips.body: Failed experiments and dead ends are real work. Log time by task so you can show the client the iteration behind the result if questions come up.

tips.title: Invoice retainers for support in advance
tips.body: Monitoring and retraining work is unpredictable. A monthly fee with a stated hours cap, and an overage rate beyond it, keeps billing simple and income steady.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or per project as an ML engineer?
faqs.answer: Hourly suits exploratory work where scope is unclear, such as research or debugging an existing model. Fixed fees work once the data and deliverables are understood, for example a deployed API with a defined interface. A common approach is hourly or a fixed fee for discovery, then a fixed fee or capped hourly estimate for the build.

faqs.question: How do I bill for GPU and cloud costs?
faqs.answer: The cleanest option is to have the client pay the cloud provider directly from their own account. If you pay upfront, list the costs as a separate line item with receipts and invoice them at cost, or with a small handling fee if your contract allows it.

faqs.question: What if the model does not hit the target performance?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say you are paid for the work performed, not for a guaranteed metric. If a target exists, define the dataset, metric, and test method in the SOW, and note that results depend on data quality the client provides.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on ML work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on what you deliver. Some states tax custom software or SaaS-like services while many do not tax professional services. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, especially if you sell access to a hosted model.

faqs.question: When does the client own the model and code?
faqs.answer: Whatever your contract says. Many engineers state that ownership transfers on full payment, and that they retain rights to pre-existing tools and general know-how. Put this in the agreement and repeat it briefly on the invoice.

estimate.intro: ML engineers send a quote or proposal before any significant work starts, usually after a scoping call and a look at the client's data. Clients compare price, timeline, how much risk you take on, and whether you can deploy the model rather than just train it.

scopeChecklist.why: Writing down what the model should predict and how it will be measured prevents arguments later about whether it worked.
State the volume, format, labeling quality, and access you expect. If the data is worse than described, the estimate should be allowed to change.
List what is handed over: notebooks, training code, model weights, an API, documentation, a dashboard. Unlisted items become scope creep.
Specify where the model runs (client cloud, your account, on-device) and what serving setup is included.
Say who pays for GPUs, API usage, labeling, and licensed data, and give an expected range if you will front them.
Model work is experimental. State how many training rounds or review cycles are included before extra time is billed.
Delays in data access are common. List what you need from the client and how long bug fixes or monitoring are covered after launch.

pricingTips.title: Quote in phases
pricingTips.body: Split the proposal into discovery, prototype, and production. The client can approve one phase at a time, and you can reprice later phases once the data is understood.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for data problems
pricingTips.body: Cleaning and labeling take longer than expected on most projects. Build 20 to 30 percent contingency into the data phase, or write it as a separate hourly line.

pricingTips.title: Offer a range with assumptions
pricingTips.body: When uncertainty is high, give a low and high figure and name what moves the price, such as dataset size or number of model iterations.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity window
pricingTips.body: GPU prices, your availability, and the client's data change over time. A 14 to 30 day expiry on the quote protects you from stale pricing.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed quote before seeing the data?
faqs.answer: It is risky. Offer a paid discovery phase or an hourly estimate first, then a fixed quote for the build once you have reviewed the data and tried a baseline.

faqs.question: Should the quote include compute costs?
faqs.answer: List them separately, either as an estimated range billed at cost or as costs the client pays directly. Folding them into your rate hides a variable expense that can swing widely.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a guaranteed accuracy?
faqs.answer: Explain that results depend on data and cannot be promised in advance. Offer a baseline and an evaluation process, and agree on what happens if the target is not met, such as extra phases at an agreed rate.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit when the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, for most projects. A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, and it signals commitment and covers early data and setup work.

mobile-car-wash.intro: Mobile car wash operators wash and detail vehicles at the customer's home, office, or fleet yard, usually working solo or with one or two helpers out of a van, truck, or trailer. Invoices cover wash and detail packages, add-on services, vehicle size surcharges, and recurring fleet or membership plans. Clients range from individual car owners to dealerships, apartment communities, and businesses with company vehicles.
mobile-car-wash.pricingModel: Most mobile car wash work is priced per vehicle by package: exterior wash, interior clean, or a full wash and detail, with a size multiplier for SUVs, trucks, and vans. Add-ons such as wax, pet hair removal, headlight restoration, and engine bay cleaning are priced as flat fees on top. Heavily soiled vehicles often carry a surcharge or are billed hourly. Detailing work like clay bar, polish, and ceramic coating is usually a flat fee per vehicle, quoted by condition. Fleet and commercial accounts get volume discounts, typically billed weekly or monthly per vehicle. Many operators sell monthly memberships or prepaid wash plans for steady income. A travel or trip fee is common for jobs outside the core service area, and some operators add a water or power fee when the customer cannot supply either and the truck has to carry its own.

rates.service: SUV, truck, or van size surcharge
Pet hair removal or heavy soil surcharge

items.description: Full wash and interior detail - 2021 Toyota Highlander (SUV)
Full wash and interior clean - 2019 Honda Civic
Pet hair removal - Highlander rear seats and cargo area
Paint sealant application - Civic
Travel fee - outside 15 mile service area

sampleInvoice.notes: Service performed at customer's residence on 6/14. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Accepted: card, Zapp-style mobile payment apps, check, or cash. Please book your next appointment within 4 weeks to keep your member discount. Report any concerns within 48 hours so we can make it right.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, and color or license plate
invoiceChecklist.why: Tells the customer exactly which vehicle each line refers to, which matters with multiple cars or a fleet, and helps resolve damage or quality disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Proves where and when the work happened, which is useful for recurring visits, fleet routes, and disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and every add-on listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers can see what they paid for and it prevents arguments over whether wax, pet hair removal, or engine bay cleaning was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Size or condition surcharges
invoiceChecklist.why: Lines like SUV size or heavy soil explain why the price is above the base package and avoid pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, water, or power fees
invoiceChecklist.why: These are separate costs of mobile work. Listing them shows they are standard and not arbitrary.

invoiceChecklist.item: Membership or prepaid plan balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring customers need to see which visit this is, how many remain, and what discount was applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or fleet unit number for commercial accounts
invoiceChecklist.why: Businesses and dealerships often cannot pay without a PO or unit number to match the invoice.

mobile-car-wash.paymentTerms: Individual customers are usually charged at the time of service by card or mobile payment, or sent an invoice due on receipt or within 7 days. For large detailing jobs, coatings, or multi-vehicle bookings, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, along with a cancellation or no-show fee for late cancellations. Fleet and commercial accounts are typically billed weekly or monthly on net 15 or net 30 terms. Many operators keep a card on file for memberships and bill automatically each month. A late fee of 1.5 percent per month is common on commercial accounts if stated in advance. Check your state rules on late fees and sales tax, since some states tax car wash services and others do not.

tips.title: Take payment at the vehicle
tips.body: The easiest time to collect is when the customer sees the clean car. Carry a card reader and send a receipt on the spot so you are not chasing small balances later.

tips.title: Photograph before and after
tips.body: Take photos of existing scratches, stains, and damage before you start, and of the finished result. Attach them to the job record so you can answer damage claims or support a surcharge for a heavily soiled interior.

tips.title: Charge for condition, not just size
tips.body: Mud, pet hair, smoke odor, and sticky spills take far more time than a light clean. Set clear surcharges and tell the customer before you start so the final invoice holds no surprises.

tips.title: Sell memberships and fleet contracts
tips.body: Monthly plans with a card on file smooth out income in rainy weeks and cut the time spent collecting. Offer a modest discount for committing to a regular schedule.

tips.title: Track water, fuel, and supply costs per job
tips.body: Your truck, water, chemicals, and drive time are real costs. Review them each quarter and adjust your travel fee and package prices before margins slip.

faqs.question: Should I charge a travel fee for a mobile car wash?
faqs.answer: Many operators include a set service radius in the base price and add a flat travel fee beyond it, often $10 to $40. Put the radius and fee on your booking page and show the fee as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill a customer who is not home during the wash?
faqs.answer: Collect payment ahead of time or keep a card on file with written permission. Send the invoice and before-and-after photos right after the job, and note where the vehicle was parked and any access arrangements.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on a car wash?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax car wash and detailing services, some tax only the products sold, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax as a separate line if you collect it.

faqs.question: How should I invoice a fleet or dealership account?
faqs.answer: List each vehicle by unit number or plate with the service performed and date, include the PO number if one was issued, and bill on the agreed cycle, usually weekly or monthly. State net terms and any late fee on every invoice.

faqs.question: What if a customer disputes the quality of the wash?
faqs.answer: Use your before-and-after photos and your stated policy. Many operators offer a free touch-up if the customer reports the issue within 24 to 48 hours. Keep that policy in the notes on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Mobile car wash operators usually quote before the visit by phone, text, or online booking form, and give a firm price for standard packages. For detailing, heavily soiled vehicles, ceramic coating, and fleet contracts, a written estimate based on photos or an on-site look is more common. Clients usually compare package contents, vehicle size pricing, and whether you bring your own water and power.

scopeChecklist.why: A sedan, three-row SUV, and lifted truck take different amounts of time. Pricing by vehicle class avoids a surprise upcharge on arrival.
State what is included, such as hand wash, wheels and tires, window cleaning, vacuum, and dash wipe-down, so the customer knows what is and is not covered.
List wax, shampooing, odor treatment, or engine bay cleaning as optional extras, and say which are not included so they do not become disputes.
Say the price assumes normal soil. Heavy mud, pet hair, mold, or biohazard messes should be flagged as extra or quoted after photos.
State whether you bring your own water and power or need access to the customer's spigot or outlet, and any fee if you supply it.
Note service area, parking needs, shade or covered space for coatings, and your rescheduling policy for rain or extreme heat.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation terms, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Protects your time slot on larger jobs and sets how long the price is held.

pricingTips.title: Quote from photos for detail jobs
pricingTips.body: Ask for photos of the interior, seats, and paint before giving a detailing price. It shows you the true condition and lets you give a range or a firm number with less risk.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: Three tiers, such as exterior only, wash plus interior, and full detail, make it easy to compare and often lift the average ticket over a single flat price.

pricingTips.title: Price in drive time
pricingTips.body: Back-to-back stops in one neighborhood are efficient. Spread out stops are not. Use a travel fee or minimum job charge so a single far-off car wash still pays.

pricingTips.title: Give fleet pricing per vehicle with a minimum
pricingTips.body: Quote a per-vehicle rate with a minimum visit charge and a count range, such as 10 to 20 vehicles. State what happens when the count is lower or higher.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or a range for a detail?
faqs.answer: A flat price works for standard packages on normal vehicles. For heavily soiled interiors, pet hair, or paint correction, give a range or quote after photos, and say the final price will not go above the top of the range without approval.

faqs.question: Do I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Quotes by text, phone, or photos are normally free. If you drive out to inspect a vehicle for a large job like ceramic coating, some operators charge a small fee and credit it to the work if the customer books.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 30 days is typical. Fuel, chemical, and labor costs shift, and your calendar fills, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the vehicle is dirtier than expected on arrival?
faqs.answer: Stop and tell the customer before starting. Offer the extra charge or a reduced scope, and get a text or verbal approval. Note the approval on the invoice.

mobile-mechanic.intro: Mobile mechanics travel to a customer's home, workplace, or roadside and repair vehicles on site. Invoices usually cover diagnostic time, labor, parts, a trip or service call charge, and shop supplies or fluid disposal. Many work solo from a van or truck, so the invoice also has to show how travel and parts sourcing were handled.
mobile-mechanic.pricingModel: Most mobile mechanics bill labor either hourly or by flat rate per job, often based on a labor guide's book time for the repair. Hourly rates tend to be lower than a brick-and-mortar shop's posted rate in some markets and higher in others, because the customer is paying for convenience. A trip or service call fee covers drive time and fuel, and is often waived or reduced when the customer approves the repair. Parts are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 20 to 50 percent, with higher percentages on cheaper parts. Diagnostic fees are charged separately and sometimes credited toward the repair. Small charges for shop supplies, fluid disposal, and core or battery disposal are common. Many mechanics quote flat prices for routine jobs like brake pads, batteries, and oil changes, and bill hourly for diagnostics and open-ended problems.

rates.service: Brake pad and rotor replacement (labor only, one axle)
Oil and filter change (synthetic, labor and disposal)

items.description: Trip fee (applied to customer's driveway, 2018 Honda Accord)
Diagnostic: brake squeal and grinding, front and rear inspection
Front brake pads and rotors, parts (ceramic pads, 2 rotors)
Front brake pad and rotor replacement, labor
Brake fluid flush
Shop supplies and brake cleaner

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on completion. Cards, Zelle, and cash accepted. Parts carry a 12-month / 12,000-mile warranty and labor is warranted for 90 days. Please retain this invoice for warranty claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, and VIN
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the exact vehicle serviced, supports parts fitment, and protects you if a warranty or dispute comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Odometer reading at time of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for warranty terms based on mileage and gives the customer a maintenance record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Because you work at the customer's location, this documents where the work was done and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with brand, part number, and whether new, remanufactured, or used
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers and insurers often want to know what went into the car, and part numbers make warranty claims easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor description with hours or flat rate used
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how labor was calculated and heads off questions about time on the job.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip fee, shop supplies, and disposal or core charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Small fees look arbitrary when lumped into labor. Listing them clearly reduces pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Sets expectations in writing and limits disputes if a part fails or the same issue returns.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your contractor or repair license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require automotive repair registration and may require it on invoices. Check your state's rules.

mobile-mechanic.paymentTerms: Most mobile mechanics collect payment the same day, at the end of the job, since they are working on a driveway or parking lot and may never see the customer again. Card readers, tap-to-pay, and digital transfers are standard, and cash and checks are still accepted. For larger repairs or special-order parts, a deposit covering the parts cost is common, often 50 percent or the full parts price. Fleet and commercial accounts are usually billed net 15 or net 30, with a late fee such as 1.5 percent per month stated on the invoice and in the service agreement. Some mechanics hold the vehicle's paperwork or keys only in the sense that they do not start work until a deposit clears; check your state's rules on repair liens before relying on one.

tips.title: Get written approval before exceeding the estimate
tips.body: Many states require a customer's authorization before you go over the quoted amount by a set percentage. Text or email the new total and get a written reply before continuing, and attach it to the invoice.

tips.title: Collect parts money upfront on special orders
tips.body: If you order a part for a specific car, the customer can cancel and leave you holding it. Take a deposit for at least the parts cost before you buy.

tips.title: Charge the trip fee consistently
tips.body: Decide a rule, such as waiving the fee when the repair is approved, and apply it to everyone. Show it as a line item with a discount line if waived, so the customer sees the value.

tips.title: Bill diagnostic time even when the customer declines the repair
tips.body: Diagnosing a fault takes real time and equipment. State the diagnostic fee in the quote so it is not a surprise, and consider crediting it toward the repair if approved.

tips.title: Photograph the work and the old parts
tips.body: Photos of the failed part, VIN plate, and odometer attach to the invoice and settle most disputes about whether a part was actually bad or replaced.

faqs.question: Should I charge a trip fee or build travel into my hourly rate?
faqs.answer: Either works, but a separate trip fee is more transparent and lets you adjust by distance. Many mechanics charge a flat fee within a set radius and add a per-mile charge beyond it. Whatever you choose, list it on the invoice.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up parts?
faqs.answer: A markup of 20 to 50 percent over your cost is common, with smaller percentages on expensive parts and larger ones on cheap items. The markup covers sourcing time, returns, and warranty risk. If the customer supplies the part, many mechanics charge higher labor or offer no warranty on the part.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on repairs?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax parts but not labor, some tax both, and some tax neither. Check with your state's department of revenue, and show tax on a separate line if you collect it.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses to pay after the repair is done?
faqs.answer: Start with the signed estimate or approval message and your invoice with photos. Send a written demand, then consider small claims court. Some states give repair shops a possessory lien, but this usually applies to vehicles in your custody, so check local rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a diagnosis if I could not find the problem?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you told the customer upfront that diagnostic time is billed. Record what you tested and the results on the invoice so the charge is clearly tied to work performed.

estimate.intro: Mobile mechanics send an estimate before starting any repair beyond a basic service, especially when parts must be ordered or the problem is not yet diagnosed. Customers often compare your quote to a shop's, so it should show labor, parts, and the convenience of coming to them. A clear written quote also serves as the customer's authorization to start work.

scopeChecklist.why: Parts pricing and book time depend on the exact engine and trim, so a wrong vehicle can make the quote wrong.

scopeChecklist.item: The specific repair and symptoms being addressed
scopeChecklist.why: Ties the quote to the customer's complaint, so you are not blamed for other problems that appear later.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts list with brand and quality tier (OEM, aftermarket, remanufactured)
scopeChecklist.why: Part quality changes the price and warranty. Customers should know what they are approving.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor as flat price or estimated hours with the rate
scopeChecklist.why: Shows how the total was built and sets expectations if the job runs longer.

scopeChecklist.item: Trip fee, diagnostic fee, and disposal charges
scopeChecklist.why: Extra fees are the most common reason a customer says the final bill was higher than quoted.

scopeChecklist.item: Conditions that could change the price
scopeChecklist.why: Seized bolts, broken clips, or related failed parts can add work. Say that you will contact the customer for approval before going over.
You need a level, safe surface and enough room to work. State that jobs may be rescheduled for rain or unsafe locations.
Parts prices change, so a quote that is valid for 7 to 14 days protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for undiagnosed problems
pricingTips.body: If you have not yet found the cause, give a diagnostic fee and a likely repair range, then send a firm quote once you know. Avoid committing to a fixed price on a guess.

pricingTips.title: Price flat rate from book time, not your speed
pricingTips.body: Use a labor guide's time for the job, then adjust for working outdoors without a lift. Charging for how fast you are punishes you for experience.

pricingTips.title: Present convenience as part of the value
pricingTips.body: Note that the customer saves a tow, a ride, and a day without their car. Put the trip fee and the repair on the same quote so the total can be compared to a shop's.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best parts options
pricingTips.body: Giving two or three part tiers lets the customer pick by budget and makes the quote easier to accept. Show the price and warranty difference for each.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding for a mobile mechanic?
faqs.answer: Rules differ by state. Many states require a written estimate for repairs above a set amount and limit how far the final bill can exceed it without the customer's approval. Check your state's automotive repair rules.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes for known repairs are usually free. If an estimate requires diagnostic work, charge a diagnostic fee and tell the customer before you start.

faqs.question: What do I do if I find more problems during the repair?
faqs.answer: Stop and contact the customer with the issue, price, and photos. Get their approval in writing, such as a text reply, before doing the extra work, and add it to the final invoice.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical. Parts prices and availability shift quickly, so put an expiration date on the quote and re-quote if the customer waits longer.

mold-remediation.intro: Mold remediation contractors are solo operators and small crews who contain, remove, and clean up mold growth in homes and commercial buildings, often after water damage, leaks, or flooding. Invoices go to homeowners, landlords, property managers, and sometimes insurance carriers or restoration companies. Typical billing covers containment setup, removal of affected materials, HEPA cleaning, equipment rental days, and disposal.
mold-remediation.pricingModel: Most residential jobs are priced as a flat fee per project based on a written scope, which is usually built from square footage of affected area, number of containment zones, and the materials that must be removed (drywall, insulation, subfloor, carpet). Small spot jobs may be priced per square foot, while larger or uncertain jobs are sometimes billed time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap. Equipment such as air scrubbers, negative air machines, and dehumidifiers is commonly billed per unit per day. Add separate lines for disposal, permits where required, and any post-remediation verification (PRV) coordination. Insurance work is often priced to an itemized estimate or a price list such as Xactimate, so line items need to match what the adjuster reviews. Many contractors also charge a minimum job fee to cover mobilization, PPE, and setup.

rates.service: Mold removal and cleaning, small area (surface cleaning, HEPA vacuum, antimicrobial)
Drywall or porous material removal and disposal
Containment setup (poly barriers, zipper door, negative pressure)
Air scrubber / HEPA air filtration device
Crawl space or attic mold remediation

items.description: Containment setup, basement bathroom wall and ceiling area (poly sheeting, zipper door, negative air)
Removal and bagged disposal of mold-affected drywall and insulation
HEPA vacuuming, wire brushing, and antimicrobial treatment of exposed framing
HEPA air scrubber rental
Dehumidifier rental
Debris disposal and dumpster fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Total due within 14 days of completion. Post-remediation verification testing by an independent assessor is not included and is billed separately by the testing company. Work performed per the signed scope dated on the estimate. Moisture source repair is the owner's responsibility and is not covered by this invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and date range of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Remediation often spans several days, and insurers and property managers need to match the invoice to the loss and the work period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and certification numbers (state license where required, IICRC S520 or similar credential)
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states license mold contractors, and carriers or commercial clients often ask for proof of qualifications.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized scope by area or room, with square footage treated
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and adjusters compare the invoice to the original protocol, so each area and measurement should be traceable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment days by unit type (air scrubbers, negative air, dehumidifiers)
invoiceChecklist.why: Equipment is billed per day, and disputes are common if the days are not itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disposal and materials removed, with dumpster or haul fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Disposal is a real cost and clients are more likely to accept it when it is listed as its own line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the written remediation protocol, change orders, and insurance claim or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra removal discovered mid-job needs a paper trail, and claim or PO numbers are needed for payment processing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement on clearance testing and moisture source
invoiceChecklist.why: It makes clear what is and is not included, such as third-party post-remediation verification and leak repair, and limits liability for regrowth.

mold-remediation.paymentTerms: Deposits of 25-50% are common on residential jobs, especially when materials, disposal, or equipment rentals must be paid up front. Larger jobs are often billed in stages, such as at containment setup, at completion of removal, and at final clearance. Final balances are typically due on completion or within 7-14 days, with net 30 common for commercial and property management accounts. Insurance jobs usually split payment between the carrier and the homeowner's deductible, so state clearly who owes what. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract and on the invoice. Most contractors accept checks, ACH, and cards, and some charge a card surcharge where permitted.

tips.title: Tie final payment to clearance, but define clearance clearly
tips.body: If you want to hold the last payment until post-remediation verification passes, put that in the contract and say who hires the tester. Independent testing avoids the appearance of a conflict of interest, and many states or clients require it.

tips.title: Use written change orders for hidden mold
tips.body: Opening a wall often reveals more growth than expected. Get a signed or emailed approval with the added square footage and price before continuing, then list it as its own line on the invoice.

tips.title: Bill equipment by the day and log it
tips.body: Record when each air scrubber and dehumidifier goes in and comes out, with photos or a daily log. Clients rarely dispute a rental day when you can show the dates.

tips.title: Separate the moisture fix from the mold work
tips.body: Make clear that stopping the water source is not part of remediation unless you quote it. This prevents arguments if mold returns because of an unrepaired leak.

tips.title: Document with photos before, during, and after
tips.body: Dated photos of the affected areas, containment, and cleaned surfaces support your invoice with insurers and protect you if a client later disputes the work.

faqs.question: Should I charge per square foot or a flat fee for mold remediation?
