faqs.answer: Most contractors quote a flat fee for the project based on a measured scope, then show per-square-foot lines for transparency. Pure per-square-foot pricing works for small, well-defined areas, but hidden damage makes flat or time-and-materials pricing with a cap safer on larger jobs.

faqs.question: Can I bill for testing and inspection on my own invoice?
faqs.answer: Many states restrict or discourage the same company doing both the assessment and the remediation, and some prohibit it. If testing is needed, it is usually billed by an independent assessor. Check your state's mold licensing rules before adding testing to your invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice an insurance-covered job?
faqs.answer: Use itemized lines that match the approved scope or estimate, include the claim number, and bill the carrier for the covered amount and the homeowner for the deductible and any non-covered items. Many carriers also require photos, drying or equipment logs, and a signed work authorization.

faqs.question: Can I charge for equipment that sat unused?
faqs.answer: You can bill for equipment days that were part of the agreed protocol, such as running a scrubber until clearance. Avoid billing for idle days caused by your own scheduling, and state your rental terms in the contract.

faqs.question: What if the client refuses to pay because mold came back?
faqs.answer: Your contract and invoice notes should say that regrowth caused by unresolved moisture is not covered. Keep moisture readings, photos, and clearance results so you can show the work met the protocol at completion.

estimate.intro: Mold remediation estimates are usually sent after an on-site inspection, often at the same time the client is dealing with a leak, flood, or a failed home inspection. Clients compare scope, containment methods, and whether clearance testing is included, so a vague quote that looks cheaper often hides missing work. A clear written protocol helps you win jobs on more than price.

scopeChecklist.item: Areas and square footage to be remediated, with a simple sketch or room list
scopeChecklist.why: Square footage and location define the price, and a written boundary prevents arguments about what was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Containment and air control methods (poly barriers, negative air, air scrubbers) and number of days
scopeChecklist.why: These are major cost drivers and clients should see why they are needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials to be removed versus cleaned and treated
scopeChecklist.why: Porous materials like drywall and insulation are typically removed, while framing is cleaned. Listing both keeps expectations clear.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions: moisture source repair, rebuild, drywall replacement, painting, and content cleaning
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume remediation includes putting the room back together, which it usually does not.

scopeChecklist.item: Post-remediation verification plan and who pays for it
scopeChecklist.why: Clearance testing affects timeline and final payment, and independent testing is typically hired separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Hidden damage clause and change order process
scopeChecklist.why: Mold behind walls is often larger than it appears, and you need agreed terms for added scope.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity period, schedule, and access requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Material and disposal costs shift, and you need power, water, and clear access to start.

pricingTips.title: Price to the protocol, not to a guess
pricingTips.body: Write the scope from measured areas and moisture readings. A documented protocol lets you defend your price against a lower, thinner competing quote.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency or unit-price add-ons
pricingTips.body: State a per-square-foot price for additional drywall or insulation removal if more damage is found. The client sees the cost in advance and you avoid renegotiating mid-job.

pricingTips.title: Show equipment and disposal as separate lines
pricingTips.body: Listing air scrubbers, dehumidifiers, and disposal separately makes the total easier to understand and makes it easier for adjusters to review.

pricingTips.title: Offer options when it makes sense
pricingTips.body: A base scope and an optional add-on, such as treating an adjoining crawl space or extending drying days, lets clients choose without you rewriting the quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the inspection and estimate?
faqs.answer: Many contractors provide free estimates on remediation jobs, but charge a fee for detailed assessments, moisture mapping, or protocol writing. If you charge, say so when booking and consider crediting it toward the job.

faqs.question: How long should a mold remediation quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Mold can spread and conditions can change, so many contractors state that the price is subject to revision if the area grows or the site conditions change before work begins.

faqs.question: Can I give a firm price before opening the walls?
faqs.answer: You can give a firm price for the visible, measured scope and a unit price for hidden damage. Promising a fixed total without seeing behind walls is risky.

faqs.question: What should I do when a client wants a lower price than my quote?
faqs.answer: Offer to reduce scope rather than cut corners on containment or safety, such as handling cleaning of non-affected areas separately. Do not drop containment or clearance steps to match a lower bid.

mortgage-broker.intro: Mortgage brokers connect borrowers with wholesale lenders and are paid for originating, packaging, and closing loans. Most residential compensation is collected at closing through the settlement statement, but brokers still send invoices or fee statements for commercial and investor loan engagements, borrower-paid fees, pass-through costs, consulting work, and freelance processing for other brokerages.
mortgage-broker.pricingModel: Residential brokers are paid either by the borrower or by the lender, not both on the same loan. Borrower-paid compensation is usually a percentage of the loan amount, often 0.5% to 2%, sometimes with a flat processing or underwriting fee. Lender-paid compensation is built into the interest rate and paid by the lender at closing, so there is nothing to invoice the borrower. Commercial and investor loan brokers typically charge 1% to 2% of the loan amount, often with a refundable or creditable engagement fee up front to cover packaging and third-party costs. Pre-approval consulting, loan scenario reviews, and freelance file processing are billed hourly or per file. Third-party costs such as credit reports and appraisals are passed through at actual cost.

rates.service: Underwriting or application fee charged by broker
Commercial or investor loan brokerage fee
Freelance loan processing for another brokerage

items.description: Origination fee, 1.0% of $450,000 purchase loan (borrower-paid), 123 Maple St
Processing fee
Credit report, two borrowers (at cost)
Appraisal fee paid to appraisal management company (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Fees match the Loan Estimate dated March 4 and are due at closing from settlement proceeds through the title company. Broker compensation is borrower-paid; no lender-paid compensation applies to this loan. Broker NMLS #123456, individual MLO NMLS #654321.

invoiceChecklist.item: Company and individual NMLS IDs and state license numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Federal and state rules require loan originators to be identified, and many states expect license numbers on documents tied to a loan.

invoiceChecklist.item: Borrower names, property address, and loan number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to a specific transaction so the title company, borrower, and your records match.

invoiceChecklist.item: Loan amount and the percentage used for compensation
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how a percentage fee was calculated so the borrower or lender can check the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Whether compensation is borrower-paid or lender-paid
invoiceChecklist.why: A broker generally cannot be paid by both the borrower and the lender on the same loan, and the invoice should not suggest otherwise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure date
invoiceChecklist.why: Fees should agree with what was disclosed, and a mismatch can cause tolerance problems or delay closing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately at actual cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Credit reports, appraisals, and flood certifications are third-party charges and should not carry a markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payee and payment instructions, including title or settlement agent
invoiceChecklist.why: Most fees are paid at closing, so the settlement agent needs to know who gets paid and how much.

mortgage-broker.paymentTerms: Residential broker fees are almost always collected at closing and paid out of the settlement statement, so the due date is the closing date. Some borrower-paid fees, such as a credit report, may be collected at application, but check the rules on when fees can be charged. Commercial and investor brokers usually collect an engagement fee when the agreement is signed, with the success fee due at funding. Freelance processors and consultants commonly bill net 15 or net 30 by check, ACH, or wire. Late fees are uncommon on closing-based compensation, but they can be written into engagement letters and processor agreements.

tips.title: Match every fee to your disclosures
tips.body: For most residential loans, the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure control what you can charge. Do not bill anything that was not disclosed or that exceeds allowed tolerances. Check the final numbers against the latest disclosure before sending a fee statement.

tips.title: Keep pass-through costs at cost
tips.body: List credit, appraisal, and flood certification charges separately and attach the vendor invoice when you can. Marking up third-party fees can create compliance problems, and in many states it is restricted.

tips.title: Use engagement letters for commercial work
tips.body: Commercial deals can take months and fall through for reasons outside your control. A written agreement should state the retainer, whether it is refundable or credited at closing, the success fee percentage, and any tail period after the agreement ends.

tips.title: Avoid referral fee mistakes
tips.body: RESPA prohibits paying or accepting fees for referrals on federally related mortgage loans. If you split work with another party, invoice for services actually performed, and ask a compliance professional before setting up any referral arrangement.

tips.title: Bill freelance processing per file, with stages
tips.body: If you process files for other brokerages, set a price per file and define what counts as complete, such as submission to underwriting or clear to close. State what happens when a loan is canceled partway through.

faqs.question: Do mortgage brokers send invoices to borrowers?
faqs.answer: Usually not for residential loans. Compensation and fees are shown on the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure and paid at closing. Invoices or fee statements are more common for commercial loans, consulting, and pass-through costs.

faqs.question: Can I charge the borrower and also get paid by the lender?
faqs.answer: For residential loans covered by the federal loan originator compensation rules, a broker generally cannot receive compensation from both the borrower and the lender on the same transaction. Decide which one applies before you quote the loan.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee if the loan does not close?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement, the loan type, and state rules. For most residential loans, you generally cannot charge fees other than a credit report before the borrower receives the Loan Estimate and says they want to proceed. Commercial engagement fees can be non-refundable if the agreement says so, but check your state's rules.

faqs.question: Should I include my NMLS number on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes. Include your company and individual NMLS IDs and your state license number where required. It identifies you as a licensed originator and many states expect it on loan-related documents.

faqs.question: How do I bill for loan processing done for another broker?
faqs.answer: Invoice the brokerage per file, not the borrower. List the loan number or file name, the stage completed, and the agreed flat fee. Many processors also add a reduced fee for files that are canceled before submission.

estimate.intro: Residential brokers give a Loan Estimate within three business days of receiving a complete application, which is the main way a borrower compares fees. Commercial and investor brokers send a fee proposal or engagement letter before starting. Clients compare the broker fee, the interest rate and lender credits, third-party costs, and how likely the loan is to close.

scopeChecklist.why: Fees depend on whether it is a purchase, refinance, cash-out, bridge, or investor loan, and a change in loan size changes a percentage fee.
State whether you are borrower-paid or lender-paid and show the percentage or flat fee, so the client can compare offers.

scopeChecklist.item: Third-party costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Appraisal, credit, title, and flood certification charges are separate from your fee, and clients often assume otherwise.

scopeChecklist.item: Rate lock terms and extension costs
scopeChecklist.why: A delayed closing can lead to extension fees, and the client should know the cost before it happens.
Rates and fees assume a credit score, loan-to-value ratio, and documentation. If those change, the pricing changes.
Clarifies what is charged up front, what is credited at closing, and what happens if the deal fails.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration and estimated closing timeline
scopeChecklist.why: Market pricing moves daily, so the quote needs an end date, and clients need a realistic closing date.

pricingTips.title: Show the full cost, not just your fee
pricingTips.body: Borrowers compare the total cost of the loan. Show your compensation, the rate, any lender credits or points, and estimated third-party costs together so the quote can be compared with other lenders.

pricingTips.title: Price commercial deals by complexity
pricingTips.body: A stabilized rental property with clean financials takes far less packaging than a construction loan or a borrower with messy tax returns. Set the engagement fee to the work needed before a lender commits.

pricingTips.title: Keep percentages within your own rules
pricingTips.body: Choose a consistent compensation schedule and a minimum fee for small loans. Many states and lenders cap or review broker compensation, so check your local rules before setting it.

pricingTips.title: Re-quote when the file changes
pricingTips.body: If the loan amount, property, credit profile, or lock date changes, send an updated quote. Residential changes may require a revised Loan Estimate, so follow the disclosure rules.

faqs.question: Is a Loan Estimate the same as a quote?
faqs.answer: For most residential mortgages, the Loan Estimate is a required federal disclosure and works as the formal quote. You can give informal pricing earlier, but it should be consistent with the Loan Estimate you later issue.

faqs.question: Can I charge for giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Generally not for residential loans. Before the borrower receives the Loan Estimate and indicates intent to proceed, you usually can only charge for a credit report. For consulting or commercial scenarios, you can charge an agreed fee in a written agreement.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Residential pricing is tied to the rate lock and market conditions, so quotes are valid for a short time unless the rate is locked. Commercial fee proposals often stay open 14 to 30 days.

faqs.question: What should I put in a commercial engagement letter?
faqs.answer: State the loan request, the fee and any retainer, whether the retainer is refundable or credited, who pays third-party reports, the term of the agreement, and any tail period that protects your fee if the client closes with a lender you introduced.

motion-designer.intro: Motion designers create animated graphics, explainer videos, title sequences, social media animations, UI animation, and broadcast packages for agencies, brands, startups, and production companies. Most work as freelancers or run small studios, and they bill for design, animation, revisions, and sometimes music, voiceover, or stock assets. Invoices usually follow a project milestone, a day rate, or a per-second-of-finished-animation price.
motion-designer.pricingModel: Motion designers price in four main ways. Day rates are common for work inside an agency or production team, where the client controls the schedule. Flat project fees are the norm for explainer videos, logo stings, and social packages, usually built from a per-second or per-deliverable estimate and a set number of revision rounds. Hourly rates are used for small fixes, retainers, and open-ended work. Retainers with a monthly block of hours suit brands that need steady social or product animation. Storyboards, style frames, and design work are often billed as a separate phase from animation, since a client may stop after approving the look. Licensed assets, stock footage, music, voiceover, plugins bought for a job, and render farm time are passed through at cost or with a modest markup. Rush work, extra aspect ratios, and revisions beyond the agreed rounds are billed as add-ons. Usage rights matter for broadcast and paid advertising, and some designers charge more when a piece will run as a national ad.

rates.service: Social media animation package (6-10 short clips)

items.description: Storyboard and 5 style frames, 60-second explainer video (approved 3/4)
2D animation in After Effects, 60-second explainer, 1920x1080
Sound design and licensed music track (1 license, web use)
Additional revision round (round 3, client-requested scene changes)
Square 1:1 and vertical 9:16 social cutdowns (30 seconds each)

sampleInvoice.notes: Final files delivered via shared link as H.264 MP4 and ProRes 422. Project files are not included unless agreed in writing. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Deposit of $1,500 received 2/20 has been applied to this invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and deliverable list with specs
invoiceChecklist.why: Resolution, frame rate, length, and file format tell the client exactly what was delivered and prevent later claims that the wrong version was supplied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or phase breakdown
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating storyboard, style frames, animation, and revisions shows how the total was built and supports partial billing if a project stops midway.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and included
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing how many rounds were in the contract and how many were used justifies charges for extra rounds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs for music, stock footage, fonts, and plugins
invoiceChecklist.why: Licensed assets are real costs and clients often forget them. Itemizing them avoids disputes and documents the license terms.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and license terms
invoiceChecklist.why: State where and how long the work may run, such as web only, paid social, or broadcast, so the client knows what they paid for and what would need a new fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and prior payments applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Most motion work requires an upfront deposit, and showing it as a credit keeps the balance due clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Source file and project file policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Say whether After Effects, Cinema 4D, or other project files are included or sold separately, since clients often ask for them after delivery.

motion-designer.paymentTerms: Most motion designers ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront to start, with the balance due on delivery of final files or split across milestones on larger jobs. Net 14 or net 30 is typical, and agencies and production companies often pay on net 30 to 60 terms, so confirm that before starting. Holding final files, or delivering watermarked previews until payment clears, is a common way to protect against non-payment. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check, and larger studios may require a W-9 and vendor setup before they can pay you.

tips.title: Bill the design phase separately
tips.body: Storyboards and style frames are real work even if the animation never happens. Invoice them when approved so a client who drops the project still pays for the creative development.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Specify that a round is one consolidated set of feedback, not a stream of emails. Bill extra rounds at an hourly rate and track them as you go so the invoice matches what happened.

tips.title: Hold final files until the balance is paid
tips.body: Deliver watermarked or low-resolution previews for review, and release full-resolution files and project files after payment. This is standard practice and reduces chasing money.

tips.title: Charge for rush and format add-ons
tips.body: Tight turnarounds, weekend work, and extra aspect ratios or localized versions take real time. List them as separate line items instead of absorbing them.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on longer projects
tips.body: For anything over a few weeks, bill at storyboard approval, animation approval, and delivery. Cash flow stays steady and the client has less leverage to delay approvals.

faqs.question: Should I bill per second or per hour?
faqs.answer: Per second works well for explainer and promo videos because clients can compare it to other quotes and scope is easy to understand. Hourly or day rates are better when the scope is unclear, the work is edits and fixes, or you are embedded in a client's team.

faqs.question: Do I charge for revisions?
faqs.answer: Include a set number of rounds, usually two or three, in the base price. Anything beyond that is billed hourly. Put this in your contract or estimate so the extra charge is expected.

faqs.question: Can I mark up stock footage and music?
faqs.answer: Yes, many designers add 10 to 20 percent to cover time spent finding and licensing assets, as long as it is disclosed in the estimate. Otherwise pass the cost through at what you paid and keep the receipt.

faqs.question: Should I give clients the project files?
faqs.answer: Not by default. Project files contain your templates, rigs, and plugins, and many designers sell them separately or only on request. Decide this before the job and state it in the contract and on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if an agency pays me months late?
faqs.answer: Confirm payment terms before starting and send invoices as soon as milestones are met. Send reminders on the due date and follow up regularly. If your contract includes a late fee, apply it consistently, and consider requiring a deposit from slow-paying clients.

estimate.intro: Motion designers send estimates before any design work begins, often after a brief call or a creative brief from an agency or marketing team. Clients usually compare total price, number of revisions, turnaround time, and what is included in the final deliverables. A clear estimate also helps the client understand how a longer video or extra versions will change the cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Final running time and number of deliverables
scopeChecklist.why: A 30-second video and a 90-second video are very different workloads, and extra cutdowns or aspect ratios add time.
Simple kinetic typography, flat 2D character animation, and 3D renders vary widely in cost, so name the style and reference examples.

scopeChecklist.item: Who provides scripts, voiceover, music, and brand assets
scopeChecklist.why: Missing scripts or poorly prepared brand files cause delays and extra work, so say what the client must supply and by when.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and approval stages
scopeChecklist.why: Defining rounds at storyboard, style frame, and animation stages keeps feedback organized and limits scope creep.
Resolution, frame rate, codecs, and platforms such as broadcast, web, or social affect both the work and the render time.
Set dates for each milestone and state that delays in feedback can shift the delivery date or trigger a rush fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Licensing, usage rights, and project file ownership
scopeChecklist.why: Spell out where the piece may run and whether source files are included so rights questions do not appear after delivery.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from shots or seconds
pricingTips.body: Break the video into scenes, estimate hours per scene, and compare to a per-second figure. If the two numbers are far apart, check your assumptions before sending.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic, standard, and premium version, such as different levels of animation detail or numbers of cutdowns. Clients often choose the middle option and it makes comparison with other bids easier.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for feedback and technical issues
pricingTips.body: Renders fail, files arrive late, and feedback often changes direction. Build in 10 to 20 percent for the unexpected, or state that changes beyond scope will be quoted separately.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Software costs, your schedule, and demand change. A 14 to 30 day expiration keeps you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best when scope is well defined, such as a 60-second explainer with a script. Use hourly or day rates for exploratory work, ongoing edits, or when the client keeps changing direction.

faqs.question: Should I charge for pitch work or spec work?
faqs.answer: Unpaid spec work is risky because the client may use your ideas without paying. Many designers charge for style frames or a short test, and credit that fee toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How detailed should my estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that the client sees phases, deliverables, and revision limits, but not an hour-by-hour log. Listing storyboard, design, animation, sound, and delivery as separate lines is usually enough.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes, get written approval of the estimate or a contract and collect the deposit before starting. That protects both sides if scope or payment becomes an issue.

motorcycle-repair.intro: Motorcycle repair invoices come from independent mechanics, mobile techs, and small shops that service street bikes, cruisers, dirt bikes, scooters, and ATVs. A typical bill covers shop labor, parts, fluids, tires, shop supplies, and sometimes disposal fees, pickup and delivery, or storage.
motorcycle-repair.pricingModel: Most shops charge an hourly labor rate and bill parts separately at a markup. Many also use flat-rate pricing for common jobs such as oil changes, tire mounting, chain and sprocket replacement, and valve adjustments, where the labor time comes from a flat-rate manual or from the shop's own history. Diagnostic time is usually billed as a set fee or one hour of labor, and many shops credit it toward the repair if the customer approves the work. Parts are typically marked up 20 to 50 percent over cost, with a lower markup on expensive items like engines or complete tire sets. Small charges for shop supplies (rags, cleaners, grease, fasteners) and for environmental disposal of oil, coolant, and tires are common, either as flat amounts or as a small percentage of labor. Seasonal packages such as spring tune-ups and winter storage prep help smooth out demand.

rates.service: Tire mount and balance (per wheel, off the bike)

items.description: Spring service labor: oil and filter change, chain clean and adjust, brake and fluid inspection
Synthetic 10W-40 motorcycle oil
Oil filter
Front brake pads (set)
Brake pad installation labor
Shop supplies and oil disposal

sampleInvoice.notes: 2019 Honda CB500F, VIN ending 4821, odometer in 11,240 mi. Parts warranted per manufacturer; labor warranted 90 days. Payment due on pickup. Bikes left more than 7 days after completion notice may incur a $15 per day storage fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bike year, make, model, VIN, and odometer reading
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the exact machine, ties the work to a service history, and protects you if a warranty or ownership question comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date in and date completed
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports storage fee charges and gives a clear record if the customer disputes how long the work took.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor with hours or flat-rate job names
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers question lump-sum labor charges. Listing each job makes the total easy to defend.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts list with part numbers and OEM or aftermarket noted
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was installed and matters for warranty claims, recalls, and later repeat repairs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shop supplies and environmental or disposal fees as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines keep these charges from looking like padding and make them consistent from invoice to invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate or work authorization
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the customer approved the work and the price, and flags any added work that was approved by phone or text.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Sets clear expectations on what is covered, for how long, and what voids coverage such as racing or misuse.

motorcycle-repair.paymentTerms: Most motorcycle shops require payment in full at pickup, since the bike is the leverage and many repairs are small. For larger jobs such as engine rebuilds, custom work, or special-order parts, a deposit of 30 to 50 percent is common, or at least payment up front for parts. Accepted methods usually include cards, cash, and debit, with some shops adding a card fee where local rules allow it. Storage fees for bikes left after completion are typically stated on the work order and invoice, often starting after 5 to 10 days. For fleet, dealer, or rental customers, net 15 or net 30 terms are common, with a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month if your local rules permit. Check your state's rules on mechanic's liens and storage of unclaimed vehicles before relying on them.

tips.title: Get written approval before added work
tips.body: When you find a worn steering head bearing or a leaking fork seal during a tire change, stop and contact the owner. Record the approval with a text, email, or signature, including the added cost. Many states have rules about authorizing repairs beyond the original estimate.

tips.title: Collect payment for special-order parts up front
tips.body: Tires in unusual sizes, OEM fairings, and engine components are often non-returnable. Take a deposit at least equal to the parts cost so you are not stuck with a part when the customer changes their mind.

tips.title: Keep parts and labor separate on every invoice
tips.body: Splitting them lets you explain markup, apply tax correctly where parts are taxable and labor is not, and handle partial returns or warranty replacements without reissuing the whole bill.

tips.title: Put storage terms in writing at drop-off
tips.body: A line on the work order about daily storage fees after completion notice makes it much easier to collect and to deal with abandoned bikes. Check local rules on required notice before charging.

tips.title: Note pre-existing damage and condition
tips.body: Record scratches, cracked fairings, leaks, or missing parts at intake. It prevents disputes when the owner picks up the bike and thinks the damage happened in your shop.

faqs.question: Should I charge a diagnostic fee on motorcycle repairs?
faqs.answer: Most shops do, because diagnosing electrical faults, fuel issues, or intermittent problems takes real time. A flat fee or one hour of labor is common. Many shops credit the fee toward the repair if the customer goes ahead. State the fee when the bike is dropped off.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on parts and labor?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Parts are taxable in nearly all states that have a sales tax, while labor is taxable in only some. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show parts, labor, and tax as separate lines.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up parts?
faqs.answer: A markup of 20 to 50 percent over your cost is typical, with higher percentages on small items like gaskets and fasteners and lower on big-ticket parts such as tires or engines. If the customer supplies their own parts, many shops charge higher labor or decline warranty on the work.

faqs.question: Can I keep a bike if the customer does not pay?
faqs.answer: In many states a mechanic has a possessory or storage lien on work you performed, which allows you to hold the vehicle until you are paid. The rules on notice, fees, and selling an unclaimed bike vary, so check your state's statutes before acting.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a job that takes longer than quoted?
faqs.answer: Contact the customer as soon as it becomes clear the job will exceed the estimate, explain why, and get approval for the new amount. Bill the approved amount and note the approval on the invoice. Billing a large overage without telling the owner leads to disputes.

estimate.intro: Motorcycle shops give estimates before any repair beyond a basic service, and always before engine, transmission, or electrical work. Customers often compare your number against a dealer or another independent shop, so the estimate should show what is included, what is not, and what could change once the bike is opened up.

scopeChecklist.item: Bike details, VIN, and odometer reading
scopeChecklist.why: Ensures the quote is for the right machine and records its condition at intake.

scopeChecklist.item: The reported problem and the work you propose
scopeChecklist.why: Describes the scope in plain terms so the customer knows exactly what they are approving.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor estimate in hours or flat-rate amount
scopeChecklist.why: Lets customers compare apples to apples and shows how you arrived at the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts with OEM, aftermarket, or used noted
scopeChecklist.why: Parts choice affects price, quality, and warranty, and customers often want to pick.

scopeChecklist.item: What could add cost once disassembled
scopeChecklist.why: Worn bearings, seized bolts, or hidden damage often appear mid-job. Naming them in advance sets expectations for a revised quote.

scopeChecklist.item: Diagnostic fee and whether it is credited
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids arguments when a customer declines the repair after paying for diagnosis.
Parts prices change and your schedule fills. A date limits your exposure and tells the customer when to expect the bike back.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for open-ended diagnostics
pricingTips.body: For electrical gremlins or a bike that will not start, give a range or approve diagnosis first, then quote the repair. A fixed price on an unknown problem usually costs you money.

pricingTips.title: Price from flat-rate times, not just your stopwatch
pricingTips.body: Use published flat-rate times or your own records of how long similar jobs took. It keeps quotes consistent and rewards faster work instead of penalizing it.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best parts options
pricingTips.body: Present choices such as budget tires, mid-range, and premium sport-touring tires with each total. Customers feel in control and you can sell the higher-margin option without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Include shop supplies and disposal in the quote
pricingTips.body: If you charge for them on the final invoice, show them on the estimate so the final bill does not surprise anyone.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Simple estimates on known jobs like tires or brake pads are usually free. If the estimate requires teardown or troubleshooting, charge a diagnostic fee and say so before starting.

faqs.question: How accurate does an estimate need to be?
faqs.answer: Many states have rules limiting how far the final bill can exceed a written estimate without customer approval, often by 10 percent or a set dollar amount. Check your state's rules, and get approval for anything beyond the quote.

faqs.question: Do I need a signature on an estimate?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A signed estimate or work order is proof of authorization, and some states require written or recorded consent for repairs. An email or text reply approving the quote also works for many shops.

move-out-cleaning.intro: Move out cleaning businesses clean vacant or nearly vacant homes and apartments after a tenant or owner has moved out. Clients include tenants trying to get a security deposit back, landlords and property managers turning a unit, homeowners getting ready to sell, and real estate agents prepping a listing. Invoices usually cover a base clean priced by home size plus add-ons like inside appliances, cabinets, windows, and carpet cleaning.
move-out-cleaning.pricingModel: Most move out cleaners quote a flat price based on square footage, bedroom and bathroom count, and the condition of the place. Hourly pricing per cleaner is also common, especially for solo operators and for jobs with heavy buildup, and it is often used as the fallback when a unit turns out dirtier than described. Add-ons are priced separately: inside oven, inside refrigerator, inside cabinets, interior windows, blinds, wall washing, garage sweeping, and carpet steam cleaning. Heavy-soil surcharges, trash or junk removal, and pet hair or odor treatment are usually billed as extras. Property managers and agents who send repeat work often get a per-unit rate by unit type (studio, 1BR, 2BR) in exchange for volume and quick payment. Supplies are normally built into the price, though some companies list a supply fee on very large or very dirty jobs. A typical move out clean costs 30 to 50 percent more than a standard recurring clean of the same size because it covers every surface, inside fixtures, and empty cabinets.
