2-bedroom apartment or small home move out clean
Heavy soil or pet odor surcharge

items.description: Move out clean, 2 bed / 2 bath apartment (approx. 1,000 sq ft), all rooms, baseboards, doors, light fixtures, closets, floors
Inside oven cleaning
Inside refrigerator and freezer cleaning
Inside kitchen cabinets and drawers wipe-down
Interior windows and tracks
Removal of left-behind trash (3 bags)

sampleInvoice.notes: Service date: May 30. Unit 4B, 218 Maple Street. Payment due within 7 days of the invoice date. Please report any missed areas within 48 hours so we can return and correct them at no charge. Accepted: card, ACH, Zelle, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and landlords handle many units, and they need to match each invoice to the right one for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date and time of the clean
invoiceChecklist.why: Cleaning is often tied to a lease end date, inspection, or closing, and a clear date helps if a deposit dispute comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized scope: rooms and add-ons included
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing inside oven, inside fridge, cabinets, and windows separately shows what was done and supports the price if the client questions it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Home size and condition notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Square footage, bedroom and bathroom count, and notes like heavy grease or pet stains explain the price and any surcharge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extras billed beyond the quote
invoiceChecklist.why: Trash removal, extra hours, or a return visit should be listed as their own lines so they don't look like padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference number or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property management companies and real estate offices often need a work order or PO number before they can pay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Re-clean or satisfaction policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Landlords and tenants may ask for a re-clean after an inspection, so stating the window and terms up front avoids disagreements.

move-out-cleaning.paymentTerms: Because the work is a one-time job and the client is often leaving town, many cleaners take payment on the day of service or right after the client or agent signs off at a walkthrough. Deposits are not always used on small jobs, but a 25 to 50 percent deposit is common on large houses or when booking weeks ahead, and it helps limit last-minute cancellations. Property managers and agencies usually pay on net 7 to net 30 terms, and it helps to confirm this before the first job. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common on commercial accounts, but state the fee on the quote and invoice. Cards, ACH transfer, Zelle, and checks are all widely accepted; cash is used less often for documentation reasons.

tips.title: Collect payment before the keys change hands
tips.body: Tenants return keys and leave quickly. If possible, get payment at completion or ask for a deposit when booking so you are not chasing someone who has moved across the country.

tips.title: Take dated before and after photos
tips.body: Photos protect you if a landlord or tenant claims the unit was not clean, and they support extra charges when a place was far dirtier than described. Attach or reference them when you send the invoice.

tips.title: Set a hourly fallback for unknown condition
tips.body: If you quote a flat price from photos or a description, write that it assumes normal condition and that extra time is billed at an hourly rate. That way a neglected unit does not wipe out your margin.

tips.title: Build relationships with property managers
tips.body: Agents and property managers send repeat work. Offer a fixed per-unit price, invoice each unit separately with the unit number, and agree on payment terms in writing.

tips.title: Charge separately for carpet cleaning and hauling
tips.body: If you subcontract carpet steam cleaning or junk removal, bill them as their own lines with a handling markup so your base price stays comparable to competitors.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat rate or hourly for move out cleaning?
faqs.answer: Flat rates are easier for clients to compare and approve, and they work well when you have seen the unit or photos. Hourly pricing fits unclear conditions. Many cleaners quote a flat rate and state that heavy soil or extra work is billed hourly, which covers both cases.

faqs.question: Who do I bill: the tenant or the landlord?
faqs.answer: Bill whoever hired you and agreed to pay. If a landlord books and pays for the clean, invoice the landlord. If a tenant hires you to protect a deposit, invoice the tenant. When a property manager or agent books on behalf of an owner, confirm in writing who the bill-to party is.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra if the place is dirtier than expected?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your quote says so. Put a clause in your estimate that the price assumes normal move-out condition and that heavy grease, mold, pet waste, or trash removal are billed extra. Show the extra work on the invoice as a separate line and send photos.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on move out cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning or janitorial services and many do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and if tax applies, show it as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if the landlord says the clean failed the inspection?
faqs.answer: Ask for specifics and photos of the problem areas. Most cleaners offer a return visit within 24 to 72 hours for legitimate missed items at no charge. State this policy on your quote and invoice so the process is clear before a dispute starts.

estimate.intro: Move out cleaners send estimates before booking, often after a client sends photos, a video walkthrough, or an address and room count. Clients usually compare a few companies on price, what is included, and whether a re-clean is offered. Because condition varies widely, the estimate needs to be clear about what the price assumes.

scopeChecklist.why: These drive the base price, and writing them down prevents arguments if the home turns out to be bigger than described.
Spell out baseboards, door frames, closets, light fixtures, floors, and bathroom fixtures so the client knows what a standard clean covers.
Inside oven, fridge, cabinets, windows, blinds, and wall washing are often assumed by clients but priced separately.
State that the price assumes the home is empty and in normal move-out condition, with no heavy grease, mold, or pet damage.
List exclusions such as carpet shampooing, trash and furniture removal, biohazard cleanup, and exterior work.
You need power, water, and keys or lockbox access, and the unit must be empty of belongings on the service date.
A set window for reporting missed spots and a valid-through date keeps the price from being held open for months.

pricingTips.title: Quote from photos, then verify on site
pricingTips.body: Ask for photos of kitchen, bathrooms, and floors before giving a firm number. If the unit looks different on arrival, you have a basis to adjust the price.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A basic clean, a standard move out clean, and a deep package with oven, fridge, cabinets, and windows lets clients choose and often leads them to pick the middle or top tier.

pricingTips.title: Price in your travel and supplies
pricingTips.body: Include fuel, parking, and supplies in the base price, especially for large homes or long drives, instead of itemizing small costs.

pricingTips.title: Use a minimum charge
pricingTips.body: Small studios still take travel time and setup, so set a minimum job price that covers your cost of showing up.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote without seeing the place?
faqs.answer: You can give a range based on size and photos, but label it as an estimate and confirm on arrival. A firm flat price from a text description alone often leads to losing money on dirty units.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common, but move out dates are fixed, so many cleaners tie the quote to a specific date. Prices can change if the move date shifts or the condition changes.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit to hold a date?
faqs.answer: For large homes or peak move-out times such as the end of the month or summer, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is reasonable. State the deposit and cancellation terms on the estimate.

faqs.question: What should I do when an estimate is much higher than a competitor's?
faqs.answer: Compare scope before dropping the price. Cheaper quotes often exclude ovens, cabinets, or windows, and a clear list of what is included shows the client what the difference is.

moving-company.intro: Moving companies, from a two-person truck operation to a regional crew business, send invoices for local and long-distance household and commercial moves. A typical bill covers crew labor and truck time, travel, packing materials and packing labor, and extra charges such as stairs, long carries, heavy items, and storage.
moving-company.pricingModel: Local moves are usually billed by the hour for a crew and truck, with a 2 to 4 hour minimum and a trip or travel charge for getting the crew and truck to and from the job. Rates rise with crew size and truck size. Long-distance and interstate moves are usually priced by shipment weight and mileage, or by a binding quote based on an inventory of the home. Add-ons are itemized separately: packing labor and materials, stairs, long carries, shuttle service when the truck cannot reach the door, piano and safe handling, appliance disconnects, storage, and valuation (liability coverage) beyond the basic minimum. Some companies offer flat-rate local moves for small apartments. Fuel surcharges are common, but they should be disclosed before the move, not added afterward.

rates.service: Storage in a container or vault

items.description: Local move, 3 bedroom home: 3 movers and 26 ft truck (4 hour minimum met)
Trip charge (truck and crew travel to and from origin)
Medium moving boxes
Wardrobe boxes
Long carry at destination (over 150 ft from truck to door)
Mattress bags and stretch wrap

sampleInvoice.notes: Move date: as scheduled on the booking confirmation. Deposit paid at booking is credited to this invoice. Balance is due on completion of unloading by card, check, or cash. Basic released-value liability of $0.60 per pound per article applies unless full-value protection was purchased in writing. Gratuities for the crew are not included. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly charge after 15 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Origin and destination addresses and move date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific job and supports the travel time and mileage charges. It also helps resolve questions about which day charges apply.

invoiceChecklist.item: Crew start time, end time, and any breaks
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly moves are the most disputed bills. Showing when the clock started and stopped, and how travel time was counted, prevents arguments over hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: USDOT number, MC number, and state license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Interstate movers must be registered with the FMCSA, and many states license intrastate movers. Putting the numbers on the invoice shows clients you are authorized to operate. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized accessorial charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Stairs, long carries, shuttles, heavy items, and packing materials each get their own line, so the client sees what drove the total above the base estimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Valuation or insurance coverage chosen
invoiceChecklist.why: Records whether the client accepted basic released-value protection or bought higher coverage. This matters if a damage claim comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the estimate, bill of lading, or inventory
invoiceChecklist.why: For binding or weight-based moves, the invoice must match what was agreed. Reference the document number so charges can be checked against it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was paid at booking and what remains, so the final payment on moving day is clear.

moving-company.paymentTerms: Most local movers take a deposit at booking, often a flat $100-300 or 10-25% of the estimate, with the balance due when the job is finished, before the crew leaves or right after unloading. Long-distance and interstate movers often require payment in full, or in certified funds, cash, or card, before the shipment is unloaded at the destination. Card payments are standard, and many companies add a card fee only where local law allows it and it is disclosed in advance. Cancellation and rescheduling fees should be spelled out in the booking terms. Commercial clients, such as offices or property managers, may be billed net 15 or net 30 with a PO number.

tips.title: Collect payment before unloading on long-distance jobs
tips.body: Once furniture is on the truck, you hold the leverage, but only if your contract says payment is due before delivery. State the payment terms at booking and repeat them on the bill of lading. Check the federal and state rules for your type of move.

tips.title: Put the clock rules in writing
tips.body: Say whether billing starts when the crew leaves the shop or arrives at the origin, and whether it ends at the destination or back at the yard. List the minimum hours, how partial hours are rounded, and any charge for breaks. This avoids most hourly disputes.

tips.title: Bill extras on moving day, not weeks later
tips.body: If a client adds items, a second stop, or a piano, write it on the work order and have them sign it. Later charges are harder to collect when the client did not see them at the time.

tips.title: Keep a photo and inventory record
tips.body: Photos of the furniture before loading, and a signed inventory list, protect you in damage claims. They also support charges for items that were not in the original quote.

tips.title: Separate tips from the invoice
tips.body: Do not add gratuity to the bill. If a client tips the crew, it goes to the crew. Put a gratuity note in your communications if clients ask.

faqs.question: Should I invoice a mover by the hour or by weight?
faqs.answer: Local moves are usually billed by the hour with a crew and truck. Long-distance moves are typically billed by weight and distance, or by a flat binding quote. Use whichever your state allows for the type of move and make sure the estimate and invoice use the same method.

faqs.question: Can I charge more than the estimate?
faqs.answer: It depends on the type of estimate and the rules in your state. For interstate moves, federal rules limit how much extra you can require at delivery on a non-binding estimate, and a binding estimate locks the price unless services change. For local hourly moves, a quote is an estimate, and the final total follows the actual hours. Document any additions in writing.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on moving services?
faqs.answer: This varies by state. In many states moving labor is not taxed, but materials such as boxes may be. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill a customer who disputes damage on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Keep the payment and damage claim separate. Collect the undisputed balance, give the client the claim form and your process, and follow the valuation terms in the contract. For interstate moves, there are federal claim handling time limits to follow.

faqs.question: What should I do about a client who cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Have a cancellation policy in your booking terms, such as the deposit being non-refundable within 48 to 72 hours of the move. Invoice the fee and refer to the agreed policy if the client pushes back.

estimate.intro: A moving company sends an estimate before the job, often after a phone call, video walkthrough, or in-home survey. Clients usually get two or three quotes and compare hourly rate, crew size, minimum hours, extra fees, and liability coverage rather than just the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of estimate: binding, non-binding, or not-to-exceed
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether the price can change on moving day. For interstate moves, federal rules cover these estimate types, so name which one you are giving.

scopeChecklist.item: Crew size, truck size, and hourly rate or total price
scopeChecklist.why: Shows exactly what the client is buying and lets them compare quotes on equal terms.

scopeChecklist.item: Minimum hours, travel charge, and how time is counted
scopeChecklist.why: These items cause many surprise bills. Say when billing starts and ends and how partial hours are rounded.
The estimate depends on what is being moved. List major items, number of rooms, and anything unusual, such as a piano, safe, or outdoor equipment.

Stairs, elevators, long carries, narrow doors, and parking restrictions add time and fees. Note them in the quote, and note what happens if the conditions turn out to differ from what the client described.

scopeChecklist.item: Packing, materials, and disassembly services included
scopeChecklist.why: Make clear whether boxes, wrap, mattress bags, and furniture disassembly are in the price or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Valuation coverage and the validity period
scopeChecklist.why: State the basic liability amount and the options to upgrade. Add an expiry date for the quote, since fuel costs and schedules change.

pricingTips.title: Give a range for hourly moves
pricingTips.body: A local move can run an hour or two over or under, depending on the crew, stairs, and how well the client packed. Give an estimated hour range and the hourly rate, so the final bill is not a surprise.

pricingTips.title: Price by inventory, not by bedroom count
pricingTips.body: A three-bedroom home with a garage full of tools is a different job from one with minimal furniture. Ask for photos or do a video survey and price against what will go on the truck.

pricingTips.title: Build in a heavy-item and access charge
pricingTips.body: Pianos, safes, gun safes, and treadmills take extra labor and sometimes extra equipment. Quote them as separate lines so you are paid for the added risk.

pricingTips.title: Show the quote with options
pricingTips.body: Offer a basic move, a move with packing, and a full-service option. Clients often choose the middle option, and the list helps them see where costs come from.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most movers do not charge for a standard estimate, including video or in-home surveys for local moves. Some charge for complicated commercial walkthroughs, or credit the fee toward the move if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common, but peak season, such as May through September, often calls for a shorter period. State the expiry date on the quote and note that it is subject to availability on the move date.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding contract?
faqs.answer: A quote is generally not a contract until the client accepts it and you confirm the date, usually with a deposit and signed agreement. For interstate moves, federal rules require specific paperwork. Check your state and federal requirements.

faqs.question: What if the actual move is bigger than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Revise the estimate in writing before loading continues if possible. Explain what changed, such as extra items or a different access situation, and get the client's approval, then record it on the work order.

music-instructor.intro: Music instructors teach private lessons, small group classes, and ensemble coaching in instruments, voice, and theory, either from a home studio, a rented room, the student's home, or online. Invoices usually cover monthly tuition, single lessons, registration fees, and extras like recital costs or sheet music. Most instructors are self-employed and bill families or adult students on a recurring schedule.
music-instructor.pricingModel: Most music instructors charge per lesson, set by length (30, 45, or 60 minutes), and then bill monthly or by term so that families pay a predictable amount. Monthly tuition is often calculated as a flat rate for a set number of lessons, which smooths out months with five weeks versus four. Rates rise with the instructor's experience, credentials, and local market, and advanced or audition-prep students pay more. Many studios add a yearly registration fee, charge for recitals and materials separately, and offer a small discount for prepaid terms or siblings. Travel to a student's home is usually priced with a higher rate or a travel fee. Online lessons are typically priced the same as or slightly lower than in-person lessons.

rates.service: Group class or small ensemble (3-6 students)

items.description: Piano lessons, 30 minutes, weekly (October, 4 lessons)
Annual registration fee, 2024-25 school year
Fall recital participation fee (hall rental share and programs)
Lesson book: Faber Piano Adventures Level 2A
Late cancellation, Oct 17 (less than 24 hours notice)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment is due by the 1st of the month. Lessons canceled with at least 24 hours notice may be rescheduled; shorter notice is billed at the full lesson rate. A $15 late fee applies to balances unpaid after the 10th. Payment accepted by card, check, or bank transfer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or guardian billing name
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents usually pay for minors, and the person paying may differ from the person taking lessons, which matters for records and tax reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson dates and lesson length
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each date and whether it was 30, 45, or 60 minutes lets families check the charges and avoids disputes about how many lessons occurred.

invoiceChecklist.item: Instrument or subject
invoiceChecklist.why: Students who take more than one instrument or add theory or voice need each billed correctly at its own rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and makeup lessons applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing credits for makeups or charges for late cancellations ties the invoice to your written studio policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for fees and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Registration, recital fees, books, and strings or reeds should be itemized apart from tuition so families see what is recurring and what is one-time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Monthly or term billing needs a clear period covered and a firm date, or payment drifts into the following month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment methods and where to send payment
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents pay by card, check, or transfer and a missing instruction delays payment.

music-instructor.paymentTerms: Most independent instructors bill monthly in advance, due on or before the first lesson of the month, or by term (semester or 10-12 weeks) with a small discount for paying up front. A registration fee is usually collected when a student enrolls and is typically non-refundable. Late fees of $10-25 after a grace period of about 5-10 days are common, and some instructors pause lessons until the balance is paid. A written studio policy covering cancellations, makeups, and holidays should be given to families at enrollment. Card payments, checks, and bank transfers are widely used, and recurring autopay reduces chasing.

tips.title: Bill in advance, not after the lesson
tips.body: Charging for the month or term before lessons happen protects your income when students cancel, because the slot is already paid for. It also removes the awkwardness of asking for money after each lesson.

tips.title: Use a flat monthly amount
tips.body: Divide the yearly lesson count by the number of months so tuition is the same each month, whether it has four or five Tuesdays. Parents prefer a predictable amount and you avoid recalculating every invoice.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing and refer to it on the invoice
tips.body: A standard rule is 24 hours notice for a makeup, with shorter notice billed in full. Printing the rule in the invoice notes makes late-cancellation charges easier to explain and collect.

tips.title: Separate pass-through costs from tuition
tips.body: Hall rentals, accompanist fees, exam board fees, and books should be listed at cost on their own lines. This keeps your lesson rate clean and makes it clear you are not marking up what you pay others.

tips.title: Track income for taxes
tips.body: As a self-employed instructor you generally owe self-employment tax and income tax on net earnings, and may need to make quarterly estimated payments. Keep invoices organized by month, and ask an accountant about deductions such as instrument upkeep, studio space, and professional memberships.

faqs.question: Should I charge per lesson or per month?
faqs.answer: Many instructors set a per-lesson rate but invoice monthly or by term as a flat amount. This gives families predictable payments and gives you steady income, while the per-lesson rate still guides pricing for single or makeup lessons.

faqs.question: How do I handle missed lessons on an invoice?
faqs.answer: State your policy up front. A common approach is to offer a makeup if the student gave at least 24 hours notice and to bill the full lesson if they did not. If you are the one who cancels, credit or reschedule the lesson and show that on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on music lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax private instruction services, but some do, and the rules can differ for physical goods like books or accessories. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on tuition?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is in your written policy and the family agreed to it. Keep the fee modest, state the grace period, and include the policy on the invoice. Some states limit late fees, so check local rules.

faqs.question: What should I do about a student who quits mid-month?
faqs.answer: Your enrollment policy should say whether tuition is refundable. Many instructors require a notice period, such as 30 days or the end of the current month, and bill the lessons that were scheduled during that period.

estimate.intro: Music instructors send estimates or written fee quotes when a new family asks about lessons, or when the job is something beyond regular tuition, such as a school program, a workshop, or a series of group classes. A prospective student typically compares the lesson length, the rate, the cancellation rules, and the instructor's credentials. A clear quote prevents misunderstandings about the extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Lesson length, frequency, and start date
scopeChecklist.why: A 30-minute weekly lesson and a 45-minute lesson cost different amounts, and the family should know exactly what they are buying.
Studio, in-home, and online lessons may have different rates, and travel fees apply only to in-home visits.
State whether tuition is billed monthly or per term and when it is due, so families can plan their budget.

scopeChecklist.item: Registration fee and other one-time costs
scopeChecklist.why: Registration, books, and recital fees should be stated before enrollment to avoid surprise charges later.
This is the most common source of disagreements, so the quote should say how missed and canceled lessons are handled.
Clarify who supplies the instrument, music books, metronome, or tuner, and what the student must have at home to practice.
A notice requirement of 2-4 weeks protects your income if a student decides to stop.

pricingTips.title: Price by lesson length and level
pricingTips.body: Charge more for longer lessons and for advanced students who need audition or exam preparation. Keep a simple rate card so you can quote the same price to every family at the same level.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial lesson at a set price
pricingTips.body: A single paid trial lesson, often at your normal rate or a small discount, lets the student try your teaching before committing to a term. Say in the quote that continuing is optional.

pricingTips.title: Show the term total and the monthly amount
pricingTips.body: Parents often want to know the full cost of a semester. Giving both the total and the monthly figure makes the commitment clear and helps them compare you with other teachers.

pricingTips.title: Quote group and school work by the session
pricingTips.body: For workshops, school programs, or group classes, use a flat per-session or per-student price and list the minimum and maximum class size so you are covered if enrollment is low.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a written quote for private lessons?
faqs.answer: It is not required, but a short written rate sheet or enrollment agreement is good practice. It sets the price, schedule, and policies in one place and gives you something to point to if there is a disagreement.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the first lesson or evaluation?
faqs.answer: Many instructors charge for a trial lesson, often at the regular rate or slightly less, because it uses a real lesson slot. Some offer a free 15-minute meet-and-greet instead. Pick one approach and state it in your quote.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: For lessons, 2-4 weeks is typical, since your open time slots change. State an expiry date and note that the lesson time is held only once the registration fee or first payment is received.

faqs.question: Can I raise my rates after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Rates are usually fixed for the term or school year stated in the agreement. If you plan an annual increase, say so in the quote and give current students notice, commonly 30-60 days, before the new rate takes effect.

music-producer.intro: Music producers work with artists, bands, labels, podcasters, and brands to take a song from demo to finished master. They bill for beat creation, full song production, recording and engineering time, mixing, mastering, session musician coordination, and sometimes points on the finished record. Most work solo or out of a small studio, and invoices often need to cover both fees and the rights that come with the work.
music-producer.pricingModel: Producers mix several pricing models. Studio and engineering time is usually billed per hour or per day, often with a block discount for booking 8 or 10 hours. Full song production is commonly a flat fee per song or per track, sometimes with an advance against royalty points (often 2-5% of the record, or a share of the master). Mixing and mastering are almost always priced per song, with extra charges per stem or per revision beyond the included rounds. Beats are leased or sold: a non-exclusive lease is cheap and limited in streams and units, while exclusive rights cost much more. EP and album projects are often quoted as a package with a deposit and milestone payments. Session players, studio rental, and hard drive or plugin costs are passed through at cost or with a small markup. Rush turnarounds, extra revisions, and stem delivery are usually add-ons.

rates.service: Additional revision round or stem export

items.description: Production of single 'Night Drive' (arrangement, programming, instrument tracking)
Vocal recording session, lead and backing vocals
Vocal tuning and comping
Mixing, includes 2 revision rounds
Mastering, stereo master plus streaming-optimized version
Stem export and delivery (extra)

sampleInvoice.notes: 50% deposit of $1,087.50 received on signing. Balance of $1,087.50 due within 14 days of final delivery. Final masters and stems are released on payment in full. Producer retains a 3% royalty on the master as outlined in the signed production agreement. Late balances incur 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Song or project title and session dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Producers often work on several tracks for one client, so naming each song and the dates worked prevents disputes over what was billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized split of production, recording, editing, mixing, and mastering
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients may only want some of these services later, and a split shows what each stage cost and makes revision billing clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revisions included and extra revision charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Mix revisions are the most common source of unpaid extra work, so state how many rounds were included and bill additional rounds as line items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights, royalty points, or split terms and reference to the signed agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: If you are owed points, a producer fee advance, or a master share, the invoice should point to the agreement so the fee is not mistaken for a full buyout.

invoiceChecklist.item: License type for beats (non-exclusive or exclusive)
invoiceChecklist.why: The price depends on usage rights, so naming the license, stream or unit limits, and credit requirements avoids later disagreements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as session musicians, studio rental, and sample clearances
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real expenses that should appear separately and at cost, with receipts available if the client asks.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and delivery conditions
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the deposit and stating that final files are released on full payment protects your masters, stems, and project files.

music-producer.paymentTerms: Most producers take a deposit of 25-50% before starting, especially on full song or album production, and bill the balance on delivery of the final mix or master. For longer projects, milestone payments tied to tracking, rough mix, and final master are common. Hourly studio time is often paid at the end of each session or weekly. Due dates of 7 to 14 days are typical for independent artists, while labels, publishers, and agencies often pay on net 30 to net 60 terms. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated up front. Payments usually come by bank transfer, ACH, card, or payment apps. For beat leases sold online, payment is collected before the files are delivered. Keep final files and project sessions locked until the balance clears.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid
tips.body: Send watermarked or low-quality mixes for approval and release the full-quality masters, stems, and session files only after payment. This is the main leverage a producer has.

tips.title: Cap revisions in writing
tips.body: Include two or three mix revision rounds in the price and charge a set fee for each additional round. Without a cap, a mix can turn into unpaid hours.

tips.title: Put royalty terms in a signed agreement
tips.body: If you take points or a master share, a producer agreement should state the percentage, how it is paid, and whether a fee is an advance against royalties. The invoice should reference it.

tips.title: Bill block time up front
tips.body: Selling 10-hour blocks or day rates and collecting before the first session reduces no-shows and short-notice cancellations. State a cancellation window, such as 48 hours.

tips.title: Track extra time separately
tips.body: Editing, tuning, and file prep often run past what was quoted. Log those hours as they happen and bill them as separate lines so the client sees what the extra time was.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or per song?
faqs.answer: Per song works best for production, mixing, and mastering because clients can budget and you get paid for skill rather than speed. Hourly makes sense for open-ended recording sessions, vocal editing, and work where scope is unclear.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for royalty points?
faqs.answer: Points are not paid up front, so they usually do not appear as a charge. List your upfront fee on the invoice and reference the producer agreement that sets out your points and how royalty statements and payments will be handled. If part of your fee is an advance, say so.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on production services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether you are selling a service or a tangible or digital product. Some states tax digital goods or certain services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to cancel mid-project?
faqs.answer: Your agreement should say that the deposit is non-refundable and that work completed to date is billable. Invoice for the finished stages at your normal rates, apply the deposit, and hold files until the balance is paid.

faqs.question: Can I charge for sample clearance or session players?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pass-through costs like hired musicians, studio rental, and sample or loop licensing are normally billed to the client as separate lines, at cost or with a modest markup agreed in advance.

estimate.intro: Producers send a quote before a project starts, usually after hearing a demo or discussing the sound the artist wants. Clients compare per-song production fees, hourly studio rates, what is included in a mix, and whether you ask for points on the record.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of songs and what each involves
scopeChecklist.why: A song with live instruments and full production is a different job than one that only needs a mix, so each track should be described.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included from production to mastering
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume mixing and mastering are in the fee. Say exactly which stages the quote covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Revision rounds and the price of extras
scopeChecklist.why: A set number of rounds keeps feedback from dragging on, and a stated price for more makes extra work billable.
State whether the client gets a stereo master, stems, instrumentals, or session files, since stems and sessions are often extra.
Spell out whether you are paid a flat fee, hold points, or retain any ownership, and how you will be credited.
List delivery dates and what you need from the client, such as vocals, reference tracks, or lyrics, because delays on their side should move the schedule.

scopeChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and expiry of the quote
scopeChecklist.why: Session players, outside studio time, and clearances can change the total, and a quote expiration date protects you if rates change.

pricingTips.title: Quote by song, with tiers
pricingTips.body: Offer options such as a demo-level production, a full production, and a full production with mix and master. Tiers let clients choose based on budget instead of negotiating the price down.

pricingTips.title: Use package pricing for EPs and albums
pricingTips.body: A discount for 4 to 6 songs or a day-rate block rewards bigger commitments and gives you steady work, but only when the deposit is paid before booking dates.

pricingTips.title: Adjust for the artist's budget with points
pricingTips.body: If you lower your upfront fee in exchange for royalty points, put both numbers in the quote and make clear that points depend on sales and are not guaranteed income.

pricingTips.title: Price in prep time
pricingTips.body: File cleanup, tuning, comping, and reference matching take hours that clients do not see. Build them into the per-song fee or list them as hourly lines.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a flat per-song fee when the scope is clear, such as a defined production or a mix. Use an hourly estimate with a cap for recording sessions or editing where the amount of work is hard to predict.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. Studio time, your own schedule, and session musician availability can change, so an expiry date lets you reprice or rebook.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before I start?
faqs.answer: Most producers do, typically 25-50% for production projects. The deposit holds the dates you reserve and covers early work if the client disappears.

faqs.question: Can I charge for demos or test mixes?
faqs.answer: Many producers charge a small fee for a test mix or a custom demo, sometimes credited toward the project if the client books. If you offer free samples, limit them to a short clip or a single section.

music-teacher.intro: Music teachers are usually independent instructors who teach piano, guitar, voice, violin, drums, or other instruments from a home studio, a rented room, or the student's house. They bill for weekly lessons, monthly tuition, group classes, recital fees, and sometimes sheet music or method books. Many also teach online, coach for auditions, or accompany students at performances.
music-teacher.pricingModel: Most private teachers charge per lesson at a set length, usually 30, 45, or 60 minutes, and then bill monthly or by term so income stays predictable. Monthly tuition is often calculated as a flat amount covering a fixed number of lessons (for example, four lessons at $50 each is $200 per month), regardless of whether a month has four or five weeks. Rates rise with the teacher's experience, degrees, and the student's level, and advanced or audition-prep students pay more. Common add-ons include annual registration fees, recital fees, book and materials costs, travel fees for in-home lessons, and fees for group classes or theory workshops. Many teachers offer a small discount for prepaying a semester, and some charge for missed lessons under a written cancellation policy.

rates.service: Private lesson, intermediate or advanced (60 minutes)

items.description: Private piano lessons, 30 minutes, weekly (October: 4 lessons)
Annual studio registration fee (2024-25 school year)
Fall recital participation fee (Nov 16)
Alfred's Basic Piano Library, Lesson Book Level 2
Make-up lesson, 30 minutes (Oct 28, for teacher cancellation Oct 21)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due by the 1st of the month. Late payments after the 7th incur a $15 fee. 24 hours' notice is required to cancel or reschedule a lesson; lessons missed without notice are billed in full. Accepted: Zelle, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and, if different, the parent or guardian billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents often pay for minors, and separate names prevent confusion when siblings take lessons or when the payer claims a tax benefit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Instrument, lesson length, and lesson dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each date lets families check the invoice against their calendar and settles disputes over how many lessons took place.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period or term (month, semester, or school year)
invoiceChecklist.why: Tuition is often a flat monthly or term amount, so the invoice should say what period it covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Make-up, cancelled, and no-show lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing which lessons were rescheduled, credited, or charged under your policy makes the total easy to explain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for fees and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Registration, recital, and book charges are not tuition, and itemizing them avoids questions about what each fee covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and late-payment policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Repeating the policy on the invoice gives you a clear basis for charging missed-lesson or late fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, payment methods, and tax ID if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Families need to know where and how to pay, and some may ask for a receipt for reimbursement or a dependent care or education account. Check whether your state taxes lessons.

music-teacher.paymentTerms: Most private teachers bill monthly in advance, due on or before the first lesson of the month, or bill by semester with a prepay discount. Many require a registration fee at enrollment, which also acts as a commitment from the family. A late fee of $10-25 after a grace period of a week is common and works best when written into a studio policy that families agree to at sign-up. Payment is usually by check, Zelle, Venmo, ACH, or card; card processing fees are sometimes passed on or built into the rate. Lessons missed by the student with short notice are typically not refunded, while lessons the teacher cancels are made up or credited.

tips.title: Bill in advance, not after the lesson
tips.body: Collecting tuition at the start of the month or term reduces chasing payments and protects you when students drop out mid-month. Flat monthly tuition also smooths out months with five weeks versus four.

tips.title: Write a studio policy and get it acknowledged
tips.body: Put cancellation rules, make-up limits, holidays, and late fees in one page that parents sign or accept by email. An invoice is much easier to enforce when it matches a policy the family already agreed to.

tips.title: Keep fees separate from tuition
tips.body: List registration, recital, and book charges as their own lines. Families accept them more readily when they can see the tuition rate has not changed.

tips.title: Charge for travel time
tips.body: If you teach in students' homes, add a travel fee or a higher rate. A 30-minute lesson can take 75 minutes once driving is counted, and the rate should reflect that.

tips.title: Raise rates on a schedule
tips.body: Review your rates once a year and give families at least 30 to 60 days' notice. Small annual increases of 3-5% are easier for families to accept than a large jump every few years.

faqs.question: Should I charge per lesson or a flat monthly rate?
faqs.answer: Both work. A flat monthly rate based on a set number of lessons per year, divided evenly, gives you steady income and fewer invoice changes. Per-lesson billing is simpler for drop-in or irregular students. Whichever you choose, state it in your policy.

faqs.question: Do I have to make up lessons the student misses?
faqs.answer: No. Many teachers do not offer make-ups for student absences, or allow only a limited number with enough notice. You should usually make up or credit lessons you cancel yourself. Put your rule in writing before the term starts.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on tuition?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, as long as the fee was disclosed in advance and is reasonable. Typical amounts are $10-25 after a one-week grace period. Check your local rules if you are unsure.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on music lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax private instruction, but some do tax certain lessons or related sales such as books. Check with your state's revenue department. Also, report lesson income as self-employment income even if you do not issue 1099s to yourself.

faqs.question: How do I bill for sibling or group discounts?
faqs.answer: Show the full rate and the discount as a separate negative line, or list the discounted rate on each student's lines. Either way, the family can see what they are saving, and your records stay clear.

estimate.intro: Most music teachers do not send formal quotes for weekly lessons, but written estimates are common for trial lesson packages, group classes, exam or audition prep, accompanist work, and custom projects like recording or composing. Families usually compare your rate with other teachers, music schools, and online platforms. A clear written estimate helps them see what is included and how long the commitment runs.

scopeChecklist.item: Lesson length, frequency, and number of lessons
scopeChecklist.why: A quote of $200 per month means little unless it says four 30-minute lessons a week or month, so there is no confusion about what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, term length, and holiday schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Families need to know when lessons begin and end and which weeks are skipped so they can compare the cost accurately.
State whether lessons are at your studio, online, or at the student's home, and include any mileage or travel charges.
Method books, sheet music, and instrument rentals can add significant cost, so list whether they are included or purchased separately.
These extras often surprise new families. Naming them upfront prevents disagreement later.
Clear terms on notice, credits, and ending lessons protect your schedule and set expectations before the first payment.

scopeChecklist.item: Expiry date of the quote and deposit required
scopeChecklist.why: Rates and open slots change, so say how long the offer holds and whether a registration fee reserves the student's time slot.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial lesson at a set price
pricingTips.body: A single trial lesson, or a short package of three to four lessons, lets families try you before committing to a term. Price it at your normal rate or slightly lower, and state how it converts into regular tuition.

pricingTips.title: Quote by the month or term, not just per lesson
pricingTips.body: Presenting a monthly total, such as $200 for four 30-minute lessons, is easier for families to budget than a per-lesson rate, and it makes the commitment clear.

pricingTips.title: Price special projects by the hour with a cap
pricingTips.body: For audition prep, accompanying, or arranging music, estimate hours and set a cap or a clear scope. Note that extra rehearsal time is billed at the hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Show a prepay discount
pricingTips.body: If you offer 5-10% off for paying a semester upfront, list both prices side by side. It gives families a choice and gets you cash earlier.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a first lesson or trial?
faqs.answer: Many teachers do, often at the standard rate or a small discount. A free first lesson can attract no-shows. A paid trial shows commitment and covers your time, and you can apply it toward the first month if the family enrolls.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: For ongoing lessons, 14 to 30 days is typical, since your open time slots can fill. For group classes or recitals, tie the quote to the registration deadline.

faqs.question: What if a family asks me to match another teacher's lower rate?
faqs.answer: You can decline, or explain what is included in your rate, such as your training, studio materials, recitals, and flexibility. If you choose to offer a discount, limit it in time or in scope rather than lowering your standard rate.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short studio agreement or an emailed acceptance of the quote and policy gives you written proof of the rate, schedule, and cancellation terms if a dispute comes up.

nail-technician.intro: Nail technicians bill clients for manicures, pedicures, enhancements like acrylic and gel extensions, nail art, and add-on treatments. Invoices come from booth renters, salon owners, mobile techs, and event or bridal nail services. Most work is paid at the end of the appointment, but invoices matter for deposits, group bookings, mobile visits, and corporate or party jobs.
nail-technician.pricingModel: Nail techs usually price per service rather than per hour, using a menu with a base price and add-ons. A set of acrylics or gel extensions is priced by length and shape, with fills priced separately on a two to three week cycle. Nail art is commonly charged per nail or per design level (simple, detailed, hand-painted, 3D charms). Removals, repairs, and extra length are separate line items. Mobile and event services add a travel fee or a per-person minimum. Booth renters set their own prices, while employees often follow salon pricing. Many techs also collect a deposit to hold the appointment, which is applied to the final total, and tips are tracked separately from service revenue.

rates.service: Acrylic or hard gel full set
Mobile or event service travel fee

items.description: Bridal party gel manicure (bride and 4 bridesmaids)
Bride: French tip design with hand-painted accent nails
Gel removal (2 guests)
Mobile service travel fee (on-site at venue)
Deposit received (applied to balance)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance of $295 due on the day of service. Tips are not included. Cancellations within 48 hours forfeit the deposit. Please let me know of any nail allergies or conditions before the appointment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Appointment date, time, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and event jobs need a clear record of where and when the service happened, which helps with disputes and your own bookkeeping.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each service listed separately, including add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing the set, art, repairs, and removals shows how the total was reached and prevents questions about extra charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and number of guests for group bookings
invoiceChecklist.why: Parties and bridal groups often split the bill or pay one person, so each service should be traceable to a guest.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit paid and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the deposit as a credit keeps the total accurate and proves the client already paid part of it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or mileage for mobile services
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel is a real cost and should be a visible line item rather than folded into service prices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tip line, kept separate
invoiceChecklist.why: Tips are generally reported differently from service income, so recording them separately makes tax time cleaner.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license number or business name where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a cosmetology or nail technician license, and some salons or clients ask to see it. Check your local rules on what must appear.

nail-technician.paymentTerms: Most nail appointments are paid at checkout by card, cash, or a payment app. Invoices are mainly used for deposits, bridal and event bookings, corporate wellness days, and mobile visits. A deposit of $25-50 per client, or 25-50% for group bookings, is common and is usually non-refundable if the client cancels late. Balances for events are typically due on the day of service, or a few days before for large groups. Late cancellation and no-show fees of 25-50% of the service price are common, and any such policy should be stated at booking. If you invoice a business, net 15 or net 30 terms are typical.

tips.title: Take deposits for long or high-value services
tips.body: Full sets, nail art sessions, and group bookings take a large block of time. A deposit protects that slot and reduces no-shows.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every invoice
tips.body: Write the notice window and fee on the invoice or booking confirmation so a late-cancel charge is not a surprise.

tips.title: Charge separately for removals and repairs
tips.body: Removing another salon's work or fixing broken nails takes extra time. List them as their own lines so clients see what the extra cost covers.

tips.title: Price nail art by level
tips.body: Define a few tiers, such as simple accent, detailed, and fully custom, and apply a per-nail price to each. This avoids haggling over each design.

tips.title: Track supplies against high-cost services
tips.body: Gel products, rhinestones, and charms add up. Review your material costs now and then so your add-on prices still leave a margin.

faqs.question: Should I include tips on a nail invoice?
faqs.answer: Keep tips on a separate line or record them apart from the service total. Tips are generally reported as income, but how they are handled depends on whether you are an employee or a booth renter, so check with a tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for no-shows and late cancellations?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you tell clients the policy in advance. State the notice window and fee at booking and repeat it on the invoice or confirmation.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a bridal party or group event?
faqs.answer: List each service by guest or by type, add any travel or setup fee, and show the deposit as a credit. Agree up front whether one person pays or each guest pays their own share.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on nail services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax personal services, but retail products you sell, such as polish or nail care kits, are often taxable. Check with your state revenue department.

faqs.question: How should I invoice as a booth renter versus a salon employee?
faqs.answer: A booth renter is generally self-employed and bills clients directly under their own business name. An employee is usually paid by the salon, which handles the client's payment. Your arrangement affects who issues receipts and who reports the income.

estimate.intro: Nail technicians send estimates mostly for events, bridal parties, corporate bookings, mobile visits, and complex custom art sets. Clients usually compare per-person prices, travel fees, and how much time is blocked. A written quote sets expectations before the appointment day.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing manicure, pedicure, or enhancement type per person avoids confusion about what the price covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of guests and a headcount deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Group totals change when people drop out or add on, so set a date after which the count is locked.

scopeChecklist.item: Nail art level and design limits
scopeChecklist.why: A reference photo does not always match the price tier. State how many nails, what techniques, and what is extra.
Clients often arrive with existing gel or acrylic. State whether removal is included or priced separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Location, setup needs, and travel fee
scopeChecklist.why: Mobile jobs need table space, power, and lighting. Spell out what you need and what the travel fee covers.
A clear start time and estimated time per guest prevent delays and overtime disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation terms, and quote expiry
scopeChecklist.why: Stating how to confirm the booking and when the quote expires protects your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Quote per person with a group minimum
pricingTips.body: Per-guest pricing is easy to compare, and a minimum total covers your travel and setup time for small groups.

pricingTips.title: Add time for transitions
pricingTips.body: Set up, cleaning between guests, and breakdown take time. Build that into your timeline and price, especially for on-site work.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium option, such as polish only, gel, or gel with art, helps clients choose without negotiating each line.

pricingTips.title: Show the deposit in the quote
pricingTips.body: List the deposit amount and what the remaining balance will be so the client sees the full total before confirming.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or consultation?
faqs.answer: Most nail techs quote for free, but for complex custom art or large events some charge a consultation fee and credit it toward the booking.

faqs.question: How do I quote nail art from a photo?
faqs.answer: Review the photo, count the nails with detail, and note the techniques involved. Give a set price or per-nail price and say that major changes to the design may change the total.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is common for events, since your calendar and product costs can change. State the expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the guest count changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Set a headcount deadline in the quote. Before the deadline, update the total. After it, you can charge for the original count or add a fee for late changes, as long as you stated this in advance.

nanny.intro: Nannies provide in-home childcare for families, either full-time, part-time, or on a set schedule. Some work as household employees on a payroll, while others work as independent contractors or run a small nanny business with several families. Invoices cover hours worked, overtime, extra children, transportation, and out-of-pocket expenses paid on behalf of the family.
nanny.pricingModel: Most nannies charge by the hour, with the rate set by region, experience, number of children, and duties. Full-time nannies are often paid a weekly or biweekly amount based on a guaranteed number of hours, with overtime at 1.5 times the hourly rate for hours over 40 in a week, as required in many places for household employees. Rates usually go up for each additional child, for infants or multiples, and for extra duties like driving, meal prep, or light housekeeping for the children. Many nannies also charge a guaranteed-hours fee, so they are paid for scheduled hours even if the family cancels. Occasional or short-notice work, holidays, and overnight care are billed at higher rates. Reimbursable costs such as mileage, activity fees, and groceries are listed separately at cost. Whether you are an employee or an independent contractor depends on the facts of the arrangement, and many nannies working in a family's home are treated as household employees, so check the rules with a payroll or tax professional.

rates.service: Driving children in your own car

Overtime, Thursday late evening shift (parents' work event)
Additional child rate, ages 2 and 5 (included in base rate above)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due Friday by end of day via direct deposit or Zelle. Hours are based on the weekly schedule plus the approved Thursday extension. Receipts for reimbursed expenses are attached. Late payments may delay the next week's scheduled care.

invoiceChecklist.item: Exact dates and hours worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Childcare is billed by time, and a daily log with start and end times settles disputes about pickups, late returns, and overtime.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number and names or ages of children
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates often depend on how many children you are caring for, so the invoice should show what the rate was based on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime hours listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Hours over 40 in a week are commonly paid at 1.5 times the base rate, and a separate line makes the calculation clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guaranteed hours or cancellation charges
invoiceChecklist.why: If your agreement pays for scheduled hours the family cancels, showing it as its own line ties the charge to the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage log with dates and destinations
invoiceChecklist.why: Driving the children for school, activities, or errands is billed per mile, and a log supports the amount and your own records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Admission fees, supplies, and food you paid for are repayments, not income for your work, so keep them separate and documented.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay period and payment method
invoiceChecklist.why: Families paying weekly or biweekly need to know exactly which days the invoice covers and how to send payment.

nanny.paymentTerms: Most nannies are paid weekly or biweekly, often on the last day of the work week or the Friday of a pay period, with payment due on receipt. Families who hire a nanny for the first time often sign a work agreement that states the hourly rate, guaranteed hours, overtime, paid time off, sick days, and notice for schedule changes. Some nannies who work as independent contractors or through their own business ask for a deposit or retainer, equal to a week of pay, before they begin. Late fees are less common than with other trades, but a written policy of a flat fee or a percentage after a set number of days is reasonable. Common payment methods are direct deposit, bank transfer, and payment apps, while checks are still used by some families. Household employees are usually paid through payroll with taxes withheld, so confirm with the family and a tax professional how your arrangement is set up.

tips.title: Put guaranteed hours in writing
tips.body: Agree on a set number of paid hours each week, whether or not the family uses them. This protects your income when parents travel, work from home, or cancel at the last minute.

tips.title: Track time every day
tips.body: Keep a simple log with start and end times, signed or texted to the parents at the end of the week. It prevents arguments about late pickups and shows why overtime was owed.

tips.title: Keep expense reimbursements separate
tips.body: List spending for outings and supplies as its own section with receipts, apart from your wages. This keeps your pay record clean and makes it easy for the family to see what they are repaying.

tips.title: Charge for extra duties
tips.body: Cooking for the family, laundry beyond the children's, pet care, or extra siblings can all raise your rate. Name these in your agreement so the invoice matches the job.

tips.title: Review your rate every year
tips.body: Raise your rate by a modest amount each year, often 3 to 5 percent, and tell the family in advance. Annual raises are common and easier to ask for when written into the agreement from the start.

faqs.question: Should I invoice or get paid through payroll?
faqs.answer: Many nannies who work in a family's home are treated as household employees, which means the family may need to withhold and pay taxes through payroll. Nannies who run their own business with several clients may be independent contractors. The rules depend on the details and your state, so check with a payroll service or tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for overtime?
faqs.answer: In many places, household employees working over 40 hours in a week must be paid at least 1.5 times their regular rate for those hours. List overtime hours on a separate line with the higher rate. Live-in nannies and some states have different rules, so check your local requirements.

faqs.question: Do I get paid when the family goes on vacation?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement. Many full-time nannies negotiate guaranteed pay for the family's vacations and a set number of paid days off for themselves. Write these terms into the work agreement so the invoice follows them.

faqs.question: Can I charge for gas and mileage?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you drive the children or run errands in your own car and have agreed to be reimbursed. Many nannies charge at or near the IRS standard mileage rate, and keep a log of dates, destinations, and miles.

faqs.question: What if a family pays late?
faqs.answer: Remind them promptly in writing and refer to the due date in your agreement. If late payment is a pattern, add a late fee or a rule that care pauses after a certain number of days unpaid, and put that policy in writing before you begin.

estimate.intro: Nannies give a quote or rate proposal before starting with a new family, usually after an interview or trial day. Families compare your hourly rate, guaranteed hours, overtime terms, and what duties are included against other nannies and agencies.

scopeChecklist.why: Setting the days, start and end times, and minimum paid hours prevents confusion about what a normal week looks like.
Your rate depends on how many children you care for and whether any are infants or have special needs, so the quote should state what it assumes.
List what you will do, such as meals, laundry for the children, school pickups, and playdates, and what is outside the job, like general housekeeping.
Say how extra hours, late returns, and short-notice requests are billed so the family knows the cost before it happens.

scopeChecklist.item: Paid time off, sick days, and holidays
scopeChecklist.why: These are a major part of the total pay package, and unclear terms cause disputes later.
State whether you will drive your own car, the mileage rate, and how activity costs and groceries are repaid.
A defined trial of one to four weeks with an agreed rate gives both sides a way to confirm the fit before a longer commitment.

pricingTips.title: Quote an hourly rate and a weekly total
pricingTips.body: Give the hourly rate and the expected weekly amount at guaranteed hours. Families budget by week, so the total makes the offer easier to compare.

pricingTips.title: Price by region and experience
pricingTips.body: Check what local nannies and agencies charge, then set your rate based on certifications such as CPR and first aid, years of experience, and special skills like newborn care or multiple languages.

pricingTips.title: Show add-ons as separate lines
pricingTips.body: List extra children, overnight care, and driving as their own prices instead of folding them in. Families can then choose what they need.

pricingTips.title: Offer a short trial before a full commitment
pricingTips.body: A paid trial week at your standard rate lets the family see your work and gives you a chance to see if the household suits you.

faqs.question: Should I give my rate before or after meeting the family?
faqs.answer: After a first conversation is best. You can then base the quote on the number of children, the schedule, and the duties, instead of giving a single number that may not fit the job.

faqs.question: Can I change my rate after the trial period?
faqs.answer: Only if you said so in the original quote. State clearly that the trial rate is for a limited time, or that the rate will be reviewed after a set period, so a change is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two weeks is common. Nannies are scheduled in advance, so a quote with an end date helps you hold the spot without turning down other families indefinitely.

faqs.question: Do I need a written agreement as well as a quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. A quote covers price, but a work agreement covers schedule, pay, time off, and duties. Many nannies and families sign one before the first day of work, and it can be updated as the job changes.

naturopath.intro: Naturopaths, including licensed naturopathic doctors (NDs) and non-licensed naturopathic practitioners, bill clients for consultations, follow-up visits, lab review, supplement protocols, and sometimes in-office treatments. Most work solo or in small integrative clinics, and many collect payment at the time of the visit. Invoices matter for self-pay clients, for clients who want to submit a receipt to insurance or an HSA/FSA, and for package or program billing.
naturopath.pricingModel: Most naturopaths charge a flat fee per visit, with a higher price for the initial visit because it includes intake review, history, and a written plan. Follow-ups are shorter and cheaper. Many offer prepaid packages (for example, an initial visit plus three follow-ups) at a small discount, or monthly care programs with a set number of visits and messaging access. Lab work is either billed at the lab's cost through the client's own account, passed through at a set price, or sold as a panel. Supplements dispensed from the office are billed as retail items at a markup, though some practitioners use a online dispensary and bill nothing for them. Short phone or email check-ins are either bundled into the visit fee or billed per 15 minutes. Licensed NDs in states that regulate the profession may bill insurance in limited cases, but most visits are self-pay. Scope of practice varies a lot by state, so only bill for services you are legally allowed to provide where you practice.
