sampleInvoice.notes: Payment is due at time of service. Accepted: card, HSA/FSA card, check. A itemized receipt is provided for self-submission to your insurer; payment does not guarantee reimbursement. Appointments cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are charged 50% of the visit fee. Supplements are non-returnable once opened.

invoiceChecklist.item: Practitioner name, credentials, and license number (where licensed)
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers, HSA/FSA administrators, and clients need to see who provided the care and under what authority.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service for each line item
invoiceChecklist.why: Reimbursement claims and HSA/FSA reviews require the date each service was provided.

invoiceChecklist.item: Visit type and length (initial, follow-up, telehealth, 30 or 60 minutes)
invoiceChecklist.why: It explains the price difference between visits and supports a client's reimbursement request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized supplements and products with quantity and price
invoiceChecklist.why: Dispensed products are often taxed or reimbursed differently from visits, and clients need to see them separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lab fees listed separately from your interpretation fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Labs are often billed by the lab directly, and mixing the two causes confusion about what the client already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis codes or a diagnosis statement only if the client requests it and you are authorized to provide one
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients need this for out-of-network claims, but scope rules vary and you should not add a diagnosis you are not qualified to make.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and refund policy, and package expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages and late cancellations are the most common source of billing disputes.

naturopath.paymentTerms: Most naturopaths collect payment at the time of service, often by card on file, and send a receipt afterward. Initial visits for new clients are often paid when booking to cut down on no-shows. Packages and monthly programs are paid in full upfront or billed on a recurring date, with a stated refund policy for unused visits. A 24 to 48 hour cancellation window with a fee of 50 to 100 percent of the visit is common. Lab fees paid through a third-party lab are usually billed by that lab directly. Accept cards, HSA/FSA cards, and bank transfers, and state your policy on payment plans in writing. If you send invoices after the visit, net 7 to 14 days is typical for a service business of this size.

tips.title: Separate visits, labs, and products
tips.body: Put consultations, lab fees, and supplements on different lines. It makes HSA/FSA claims easier, helps with sales tax on retail items where it applies, and shows clients exactly what they paid for.

tips.title: Write package terms down
tips.body: State how many visits are included, how long the package is valid, and whether unused visits are refundable. Without this, clients often come back months later expecting visits that have expired.

tips.title: Charge for time spent outside the room
tips.body: Lab interpretation, protocol writing, and long email threads take real time. Either price them as a flat fee, include them in a monthly program, or define what is included in a visit fee.

tips.title: Collect a card on file
tips.body: Keeping a card on file with written consent makes it simple to charge late cancellation fees and recurring program payments without awkward follow-up.

tips.title: Check scope-of-practice before adding services
tips.body: What a naturopath can legally offer, such as injections, IV therapy, or ordering certain labs, varies by state and license type. Confirm your rules before listing a service on an invoice.

faqs.question: Can I give clients a receipt for insurance reimbursement?
faqs.answer: Yes. An itemized receipt with your name, credentials, license number if you have one, the date of service, the service provided, and the amount paid is what most clients need. Whether the insurer reimburses is up to the plan, so tell clients that payment does not guarantee reimbursement.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on supplements?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states tax retail sales of supplements, some exempt them, and services are usually not taxed. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and list products on separate lines so tax can be applied correctly.

faqs.question: Should lab fees go on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Only if you are collecting the lab fee yourself. If the lab bills the client directly, list only your interpretation fee. If you pass through lab costs, show the lab fee as its own line so it is not confused with your professional fee.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who stops coming partway through a package?
faqs.answer: Follow the terms you gave at purchase. Many practitioners make packages non-refundable after the first visit or refund unused visits at the standard rate minus the discount. Whatever you choose, put it in writing before the client pays.

faqs.question: Can I charge for phone calls and emails between visits?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you tell clients up front. You can include brief messaging in the visit fee, offer it as part of a monthly program, or bill time beyond a set limit in 15-minute increments.

estimate.intro: Naturopaths rarely send formal quotes for a single visit, since fees are posted. Written estimates are useful for multi-visit care plans, prepaid packages, IV or injection series, and protocols that include labs and supplements. Clients usually compare the total cost of a plan against other practitioners or against what they would pay in copays and out-of-pocket supplement costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and type of visits included
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know how many follow-ups are covered and how long each one is.
A plan that runs 3 months and one that runs 12 months are priced very differently, and an end date prevents open-ended expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Lab tests recommended and who bills for them
scopeChecklist.why: Lab costs can exceed the visit fees. Say whether they are included, paid directly to the lab, or extra.
Protocols can cost $50 to $300 a month, and clients often feel surprised if this is not mentioned early.
List items like extra messaging, repeat labs, specialty tests, or in-office treatments so they are not assumed to be free.
Prepaid plans produce the most disputes when terms are verbal.

scopeChecklist.item: Statement that outcomes are not guaranteed
scopeChecklist.why: Health results vary, and a plain statement avoids implied promises about results.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package price with the per-visit price shown
pricingTips.body: Showing the regular price next to the package price makes the savings clear without heavy discounting. A 5 to 10 percent discount is usually enough.

pricingTips.title: Quote supplements as a range
pricingTips.body: Protocols change after lab results and follow-ups. Give a monthly range and say it will be updated as the plan changes.

pricingTips.title: Separate fixed costs from variable ones
pricingTips.body: Show your professional fees as fixed and lab and supplement costs as estimates. That keeps your quote accurate even if testing changes.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the estimate
pricingTips.body: Lab and supplement prices change, and your schedule fills. A 14 to 30 day validity period is common.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a written estimate for every new client?
faqs.answer: No, a posted fee schedule is enough for most single visits. Give a written estimate when the plan involves multiple visits, a package, testing, or a series of treatments.

faqs.question: How do I estimate the cost of labs?
faqs.answer: Use the price list from the lab you work with, and give the client the expected total for the panels you plan to order. State that additional tests may be recommended after results come back.

faqs.question: Can I change the estimate after the first visit?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the plan changes. Send an updated estimate and get the client's agreement before adding visits, tests, or treatments that raise the cost.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include what insurance might cover?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Coverage varies by plan and by state, and you cannot predict it. State your self-pay fees, and let the client check with their insurer if they plan to submit a claim.

network-engineer.intro: Independent network engineers and small network consulting firms design, install, and support the wired, wireless, and WAN infrastructure that small and mid-size businesses rely on. Invoices typically cover site surveys, switch and firewall configuration, Wi-Fi deployments, VPN setup, troubleshooting, and ongoing managed support. Work is billed by the hour, by the project, or as a monthly retainer, often with hardware resold at a markup.
network-engineer.pricingModel: Most independent network engineers bill hourly for troubleshooting, small changes, and support, and use fixed project fees for defined work such as an office network build, a firewall replacement, or a Wi-Fi redesign. Fixed fees are usually built from estimated hours plus a contingency, with a clear scope and a change-order rate for anything extra. Emergency and after-hours work commonly carries a 1.5x to 2x multiplier, and many engineers set a minimum charge of one or two hours for on-site visits. Ongoing monitoring and support is often sold as a monthly retainer, either a block of prepaid hours or a flat per-site or per-device fee. Hardware, licenses, and cabling are billed separately, typically at cost plus 10 to 25 percent, and subscription items like firewall security licenses are often passed through at renewal. Travel time and mileage are billed when the client is outside your normal service area.

rates.service: Wireless site survey and Wi-Fi design
Small office network build (firewall, switch, APs)

items.description: Network assessment and Wi-Fi coverage survey, 4,500 sq ft office
Firewall replacement and configuration (VLANs, site-to-site VPN, content filtering)
48-port PoE managed switch installation and configuration
Wireless access point mounting and configuration (4 units)
Network documentation and IP address plan
Hardware: firewall, switch, 4 access points (equipment cost plus 15%)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hardware remains subject to manufacturer warranty; license renewals are billed separately at renewal. Support after cutover is billed at the standard hourly rate. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized labor with dates, hours, and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often review time entries against a ticket or change window, and clear dates prevent disputes over what was done and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hardware list with make, model, and serial numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Serials let the client register warranties, process RMAs, and track assets, and they prove what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: License and subscription terms and renewal dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Firewall security bundles, wireless controller licenses, and support contracts expire, and the client needs to know what they bought and when it renews.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope reference (proposal, SOW, or ticket number)
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying each line to an agreed scope or PO number makes approval easier, especially for clients with accounts payable departments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel time and mileage, shown separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel is often billed at a different rate, and listing it on its own avoids questions about the hourly total.

invoiceChecklist.item: After-hours or emergency premium noted on the line
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charged 1.5x or 2x for a maintenance window or outage call, stating it explicitly shows the rate was agreed to and not an add-on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or prepaid hour balance
invoiceChecklist.why: For managed clients, showing hours used, hours remaining, and any overage keeps the monthly billing transparent.

network-engineer.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is standard for business clients, with net 15 common for small projects and time-and-materials work. For project work, many engineers take 30 to 50 percent upfront, and require full prepayment or a deposit for hardware orders so they are not financing equipment. Larger builds are sometimes split into milestones such as design approval, hardware delivery, and cutover. Monthly retainers are usually invoiced in advance on the first of the month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the agreement. Payment is typically by ACH, check, or credit card, and card fees are sometimes passed on for large hardware invoices.

tips.title: Collect hardware money before you order
tips.body: Get a deposit that covers equipment cost before placing orders. Network gear is expensive and often non-returnable once opened or licensed, so you do not want to carry that cost while waiting on payment.

tips.title: Bill time spent documenting
tips.body: Diagrams, IP plans, configuration backups, and password handoff documents take real time. List them as their own line so they are treated as part of the deliverable and not free extras.

tips.title: Set a minimum for on-site visits
tips.body: A one- or two-hour minimum covers drive time, setup, and the disruption to your schedule. State it in your agreement and show it on the invoice when it applies.

tips.title: Separate project work from support
tips.body: Once a build is finished, further changes and troubleshooting should move to hourly or a retainer. Note the cutover date on the final invoice so the line between warranty-type fixes and billable support is clear.

tips.title: Track license renewals and bill them early
tips.body: Renewals for firewall subscriptions and support contracts can be invoiced 30 to 45 days before they are due. This avoids lapses in coverage and gives the client time to approve the cost.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for network projects?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for open-ended troubleshooting and unclear problems. Use a flat fee when the scope is well defined, such as a firewall swap or an office build with a known device count. If you quote a flat fee, write down exactly what is included and set an hourly rate for changes.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on hardware?
faqs.answer: Resellers commonly add 10 to 25 percent over their cost. The markup covers sourcing, configuration, shipping handling, warranty management, and the risk of returns. Be upfront about it, and some clients will prefer to buy equipment themselves while you bill labor only.

faqs.question: Can I bill for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common to do so. Many engineers bill travel time at a reduced hourly rate or include a trip charge beyond a set radius, plus mileage. Put the policy in your service agreement so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on network services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Hardware sales are generally taxable, but labor and IT services are taxed in some states and not in others. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and itemize hardware and labor separately on invoices so each can be treated correctly.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a managed support retainer?
faqs.answer: Invoice in advance, usually monthly, with a description of what the fee covers such as monitoring, patching, and a set number of support hours. If the client goes over the included hours, bill the overage at your hourly rate on the next invoice and show the hours used.

estimate.intro: Network engineers send estimates before building a new network, replacing a firewall, deploying Wi-Fi, or migrating to new equipment. Clients often compare your quote against a managed service provider, a hardware reseller bundling installation, or another independent. They are usually comparing total cost, equipment choices, and how much downtime to expect.

scopeChecklist.why: State the number of users, access points, switches, drops, and locations you priced for, since a change in any of them changes the labor.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment list and who supplies it
scopeChecklist.why: Specify the make and model, whether you are buying it or the client is, and what happens if prices change or items are back-ordered.
Clarify whether structured cabling is included or handled by a separate cabling contractor, since it is a common source of delay and finger-pointing.
Say whether the work is during business hours or a maintenance window, and whether after-hours rates apply.
List subscription costs for security, cloud management, or support, and the term, so clients see the ongoing cost and not just the build.
Note that you assume working internet service, adequate power, a usable ISP handoff, and accessible equipment rooms. If those turn out to be wrong, it justifies a change order.
Name what is not included, such as server work, ISP troubleshooting, or end-user device setup, and the hourly rate for extra work.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Undocumented networks, unlabeled cabling, and missing credentials slow jobs down. Add 10 to 20 percent to the labor estimate for fixed-fee work, or do a paid assessment first and quote the build afterward.

pricingTips.title: Show hardware and labor as separate lines
pricingTips.body: This makes comparison with reseller bids easier and lets clients see what they are paying for. It also helps with sales tax handling, which may differ between hardware and services.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers when there is a real choice
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic option and a more redundant option, such as a single firewall versus a high-availability pair, lets the client choose based on budget and downtime tolerance without you guessing.

pricingTips.title: Put a validity date on hardware pricing
pricingTips.body: Equipment pricing and availability change quickly. A 14 to 30 day expiration protects you from honoring a price that no longer works.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site survey or assessment before quoting?
faqs.answer: For anything beyond a simple office, yes. A paid assessment covers your time and produces a more accurate quote. Many engineers credit the fee toward the project if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: How detailed should a network quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that the client knows what is included and what is not. List phases, equipment, licenses, and assumptions. A single lump sum with no breakdown tends to cause disputes when the scope shifts.

faqs.question: Can I give a not-to-exceed estimate instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: Yes. This works well when the environment is unclear. You bill actual hours up to a cap, and the client gets a ceiling on cost. Say clearly that going beyond the cap requires written approval.

faqs.question: How do I handle a quote when the client wants to buy their own equipment?
faqs.answer: Quote labor only and state that you are not responsible for the hardware selection, delivery timing, or warranty. Ask for the model list in advance so you can confirm compatibility and price the configuration time accurately.

newborn-photographer.intro: Newborn photographers shoot babies in roughly their first two weeks to one month of life, usually in a home studio, rented studio, or the family's home. Invoices typically cover a session fee, a digital or print collection, add-ons like props or extra family poses, and sometimes a maternity or milestone bundle.
newborn-photographer.pricingModel: Most newborn photographers charge a session fee up front that covers time, studio use, props, and editing of a set number of images, then sell digital files or print products separately. Others sell all-inclusive packages that bundle a session with a set number of edited digital images. Session fees are usually flat, not hourly, because newborn sessions run long (2 to 4 hours) with feeding and soothing breaks. Add-ons are common: extra edited images, sibling or family poses, custom outfits or backdrops, rush editing, and prints or albums at a markup over lab cost. Many photographers offer a bundle covering maternity, newborn, and a few milestone sessions at a discount, billed in installments. Travel fees apply for on-location sessions. Pricing depends heavily on market, experience, and portfolio.

rates.service: Printed wall art or framed print

items.description: Newborn studio session (approx. 3 hours, includes props and backdrops)
Digital collection, 25 edited images with print release
Additional edited images beyond collection
Sibling and parent poses add-on
11x14 matted print, lab-printed
Retainer paid at booking (credited toward session fee)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 7 days of receipt. Digital files are delivered by online gallery after payment in full. Gallery link stays active for 60 days. Print orders are final once sent to the lab. Thank you for letting us photograph your new baby.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date, location, and baby's age or due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Newborn sessions often get rescheduled around the birth date, so the invoice should match the session that actually happened.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized session fee, collection, and add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often don't remember what package they chose months after booking, and separate lines make the total easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the nonrefundable booking fee as a credit prevents confusion about the remaining balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of edited images and file format delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: States exactly what the client is paying for and sets the limit before they ask for more edits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage or print release terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies that the client can print and share images personally, and that you keep copyright and portfolio rights.

invoiceChecklist.item: Print and product orders with sizes, quantities, and shipping
invoiceChecklist.why: Lab costs and shipping are separate from session fees, and clients need to see what will arrive.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on physical products, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states tax printed products and sometimes digital files or photography services, so check your state's rules and show tax as its own line.

newborn-photographer.paymentTerms: Most newborn photographers collect a nonrefundable retainer at booking, commonly $100 to $250 or 25 to 50 percent of the session fee, because the date is held around an unpredictable due date. The balance is often due at or before the session, or within 7 days of the session, with digital files released only after payment in full. Package bundles such as maternity plus newborn plus milestones are often split into two or three installments. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month or a flat fee are common if written in a signed contract. Clients usually pay by card, bank transfer, or digital wallet. Print orders are typically paid in full before they go to the lab.

tips.title: Hold the date with a retainer
tips.body: Newborn dates are limited and tied to a due date window. A nonrefundable retainer protects you if a client cancels and covers the time you blocked off. State how it is handled if the baby arrives early or late.

tips.title: Deliver files after payment
tips.body: Release the gallery or download links only after the balance is paid. Online galleries with locked downloads make this simple and avoid chasing payment after the files are gone.

tips.title: Charge for extras that cost time
tips.body: Extra outfits, additional family members, custom props, and rush editing take real time. List them as add-ons on your price sheet and invoice them as separate lines instead of absorbing them.

tips.title: Separate session fee from product sales
tips.body: Keeping the session fee, digital rights, and prints on different lines lets you adjust pricing for each and makes sales tax easier to track on physical goods.

tips.title: Put rescheduling terms in writing
tips.body: Babies and parents run late, and sessions get moved. A contract that explains how many reschedules are included and when a new retainer applies keeps invoices from becoming disputes.

faqs.question: Should I charge a session fee and sell images separately, or use all-inclusive packages?
faqs.answer: Both work. A session fee plus separate collections lets clients choose a budget level and gives you room to sell more. All-inclusive packages are simpler to quote and invoice. Pick one model and use it consistently so clients know what the total will be.

faqs.question: How much retainer should I take for a newborn session?
faqs.answer: Commonly $100 to $250 or 25 to 50 percent of the session fee. Make it nonrefundable and credit it toward the final balance. Spell out in your contract what happens if the date changes because of the birth.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: Send the retainer invoice when the client books. Send the final invoice at the session or right after, before delivering the final images. For print orders, invoice when the client selects products.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services, some tax only physical prints, and some tax digital files as well. Check your state revenue department's rules and consider asking a tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra if a session runs long?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Newborn sessions often run long because of feeding and settling breaks, so many photographers quote a session length that includes breaks and only add fees for requests beyond the agreed scope, like extra setups or additional family members.

estimate.intro: Newborn photographers send a quote or price guide when a parent inquires, often during pregnancy, and the client usually compares session fees, how many edited images are included, and whether digital files cost extra. A clear estimate shows the total before the baby arrives so there are no surprises after the session.

scopeChecklist.why: Says whether the quote covers a studio session or an in-home visit and how long you will stay, including feeding breaks.
Clients often assume they get every photo taken. State how many final edited images are in the price.
Makes clear whether the quote includes digital downloads, print release, or physical products.
Lists what you provide and whether client-supplied items or custom requests cost extra.
Prevents disputes when a larger group shows up than expected.
Explains how you handle sessions scheduled around a due date and what happens if the baby is early or late.
Sets expectations for when money is due and when images will be ready, commonly 1 to 3 weeks after the session.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic session with a small collection, a mid-tier with a full gallery, and a premium with prints or an album lets clients choose without negotiating. Most pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Show what is included, not just the price
pricingTips.body: List session length, image count, props, and delivery time next to the price. A higher fee looks reasonable when the client can see the value.

pricingTips.title: Bundle maternity and milestones
pricingTips.body: Parents who book early often want more than one session. A bundle with a modest discount raises the booking value and secures the newborn date sooner.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Quotes tied to an availability window should expire, commonly 14 to 30 days, since your calendar and pricing may change.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before the baby is born?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most parents book during pregnancy. Send a quote with a retainer to hold a date window, and note that the final session date will be set once the baby arrives.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: Only if you say so. Include an expiration date and state that the price is confirmed when the client signs and pays the retainer.

faqs.question: How do I handle clients who ask for a discount?
faqs.answer: Rather than lower the price, offer a smaller package, fewer images, or a different session type. This keeps your rates consistent and gives the client a choice within their budget.

faqs.question: What should I do if the client wants more than the quote covers?
faqs.answer: Refer back to the written scope and offer the extra as an add-on with a price. Updating the estimate in writing before doing the extra work avoids billing disputes.

notary.intro: Notaries public, including mobile notaries and loan signing agents, bill for witnessing signatures, administering oaths, and verifying identity on documents. Clients include individuals, title and escrow companies, signing services, law offices, and small businesses. Most invoices combine a state-regulated notarial fee with a separate travel or service fee.
notary.pricingModel: Notary pricing has two parts. The first is the per-act notarial fee, which most states cap by statute (often between $2 and $25 per signature or act; some states have no cap, so check your state's rules). The second is everything the state does not regulate: travel, after-hours service, waiting time, printing, and the convenience of a mobile visit. Mobile notaries usually charge a flat trip fee, often based on distance, plus the per-act fee. Loan signing agents are typically paid a flat fee per signing by a title company or signing service, with extra charges for printing, double sets, or last-minute scheduling. Many notaries also offer packages for businesses that need regular notarizations, and flat fees for remote online notarization where the state allows it.

rates.service: Notarial act (signature or acknowledgment) within state fee cap
Mileage beyond the included service area

items.description: Mobile notary travel fee, 12 miles each way (included service area 10 miles)
Notarial acts: acknowledgment on power of attorney (2 signers)
Notarial act: jurat on affidavit
Evening appointment surcharge (after 6 p.m.)
Mileage beyond included service area (4 miles round trip)

sampleInvoice.notes: Appointment completed on the date shown at the client's home. Payment due upon completion of services or within 7 days of invoice date. Notarial fees are set by state law. Travel and service fees are separate. Accepted payment: card, Zelle, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, time, and location of the notarization
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to a specific appointment and matches your notary journal entry if a dispute comes up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line for each notarial act with the per-act fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states cap notarial fees, so showing them separately proves you stayed within the limit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel or service fee listed apart from notarial fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel is not a notarial act and is generally not capped, but it needs to be clearly labeled as a separate charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Document type and number of signers (not the document contents)
invoiceChecklist.why: Explains the quantity of acts billed without exposing private information in the document.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage, wait time, and surcharges with how they were calculated
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra charges are the most common point of pushback, so show distance, minutes, or the after-hours reason.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your notary commission number and expiration date, if required or customary in your state
invoiceChecklist.why: Some clients and signing companies expect it for their records, and it confirms you are commissioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Signing service name, order or file number, and borrower name for loan signings
invoiceChecklist.why: Title and signing companies match payments to files using this reference, and missing it delays payment.

notary.paymentTerms: Individual clients are usually asked to pay at the time of the appointment by card, mobile payment, or cash, since the work is a single short visit. Many mobile notaries take a deposit or a cancellation fee for long-distance trips or after-hours calls. Signing services and title companies typically pay by ACH or check on net-15 to net-45 terms, and some pay per file after the documents are returned or the loan funds. Consider stating a late fee or a return-trip fee for no-shows in your terms, and confirm any fee is allowed under your state's rules.

tips.title: Know your state's fee cap before quoting
tips.body: Look up the maximum fee per act in your state and never bill the notarial portion above it. Keep your travel and service fee as its own line so it is clear you are charging for the trip, not inflating the notarial fee.

tips.title: Define your included service area and wait time
tips.body: State in your quote that the trip fee covers a set radius and 15 to 30 minutes of waiting. Clients who run late or need extra signers then understand why the extra charges appear.

tips.title: Charge for no-shows and cancellations
tips.body: If you drive 30 minutes and the signer is not there, you still lost the time. A modest no-show or late-cancel fee, stated when booking, is common and easier to collect when agreed in advance.

tips.title: Track mileage and print costs for signing jobs
tips.body: Loan signing fees are often flat and have to cover printing, fuel, and your time. Record miles, pages printed, and time per file so you can see which signing services pay well and which ones do not.

tips.title: Keep invoices free of confidential details
tips.body: Your journal holds signer details, but an invoice does not need them. Use the client name, date, and a general document type so a forwarded invoice does not reveal private information.

faqs.question: Can I charge more than my state's notary fee?
faqs.answer: Not for the notarial act itself if your state sets a maximum. You can usually charge a separate, clearly labeled travel or service fee for coming to the client, since that is not a notarial act. Rules differ by state, so check with your commissioning office.

faqs.question: Should I bill a loan signing as a flat fee or per signature?
faqs.answer: Loan signings are almost always billed as a flat fee, because the package contains many signature pages and the document count varies. Per-act pricing is more typical for general mobile notary work such as powers of attorney, affidavits, and vehicle documents.

faqs.question: Can I charge if the notarization does not happen?
faqs.answer: Generally yes for your time and travel, but not for a notarial act you did not perform. If a signer lacks valid ID or refuses to sign, bill a trip or no-show fee that you disclosed beforehand, and note the reason on the invoice.

faqs.question: How long should I wait for payment from a signing service?
faqs.answer: Terms vary a lot, from a few days to 45 days or more. Ask for the payment schedule when you accept the first order, keep the order number on every invoice, and follow up the day after the due date.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on notary services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax notary fees, but some tax certain services or travel charges. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Notaries give quotes when someone calls to ask how much a mobile visit costs, or when a business needs recurring notarizations at an office, facility, or event. Clients compare the total cost including travel, not only the state-set per-signature fee. A clear upfront total prevents surprises at the signing table.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of notarial acts and signers expected
scopeChecklist.why: The per-act fee multiplies by every signature or act, so a miscount at the table changes the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Appointment location and distance from your base
scopeChecklist.why: Travel is the largest variable and should match the address that is actually used.

scopeChecklist.item: Included wait time and what happens beyond it
scopeChecklist.why: Signers who are late or still gathering documents can cost you an hour, so set the limit and the overage rate up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Document type and who provides it
scopeChecklist.why: Make clear whether the client brings documents, you print them, or the signer must have them complete beforehand. Notaries cannot give legal advice or fill in blanks.
Without acceptable ID, you may be unable to notarize, and the client should know the trip fee still applies.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, time window, and any after-hours surcharge
scopeChecklist.why: Evenings, weekends, and same-day requests are priced higher and should be stated in the quote.
Sets the expectation that a missed appointment still carries a fee for your travel time.

pricingTips.title: Quote one all-in total
pricingTips.body: Clients ask for a price, not a formula. Add up trip fee, per-act fees, and surcharges and give a single number, with a breakdown available if they ask.

pricingTips.title: Build a simple distance tier
pricingTips.body: Set a base fee for a radius, such as 10 miles, then a flat step or per-mile charge beyond it. This lets you quote quickly over the phone and keeps pricing consistent.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package for repeat business clients
pricingTips.body: Law offices, property managers, and small businesses may need several notarizations a month. A discounted trip fee for scheduled visits or a monthly minimum helps you keep steady work.

pricingTips.title: Price loan signings by the full job
pricingTips.body: For signing services, account for printing, drive time, the signing itself, and return shipping. If the fee offered does not cover those, decline or counter with a higher rate.

faqs.question: Is a notary quote binding?
faqs.answer: Treat it as binding for the scope you listed. If the number of signers, documents, or the location changes, say so in writing and reissue the quote before you arrive.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote over the phone or in writing?
faqs.answer: Phone quotes work for simple jobs, but a text or email with the total, date, and address gives both sides something to refer to. For business clients or longer trips, send it in writing.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a quote or consultation?
faqs.answer: Most notaries do not charge for a price quote. If a client wants extended help, such as figuring out which notarization they need, remember you cannot give legal advice and should refer them to an attorney.

nutritionist.intro: Nutritionists work with individuals, families, athletes, and sometimes businesses to improve eating habits, manage health conditions through food, and reach wellness goals. Invoices usually cover initial assessments, follow-up sessions, meal plans, and package programs. Some also bill for group workshops, corporate wellness talks, and food journal reviews between sessions.
nutritionist.pricingModel: Most nutritionists charge per session, with a longer and higher-priced initial consultation followed by shorter follow-ups. Many also sell packages (for example, a 3-month program with an assessment and six follow-ups) at a modest discount, usually paid up front or in installments. Custom meal plans, grocery guides, and recipe collections are often billed as flat fees or bundled into a program. Group classes and workshops are priced per attendee or as a flat speaking fee. Some add monthly check-in or messaging subscriptions for ongoing support. Rates depend on credentials (a registered dietitian with medical nutrition therapy experience typically charges more than a certified health coach or nutrition consultant), location, and whether you work in person or by video. Titles and scope of practice are regulated differently from state to state, so check your local rules before describing your services.

rates.service: Initial consultation and nutrition assessment (60-90 min)
Food journal or lab review between sessions
Grocery store tour or pantry cleanout

items.description: Initial nutrition assessment and goal setting (75 min, video)
Follow-up session (45 min, video) - dates 3/12, 3/26, 4/9
Custom 4-week meal plan with grocery lists
Food journal review between sessions

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Accepted: card, ACH, HSA/FSA card. A superbill is available on request for out-of-network reimbursement. Sessions canceled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50%.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of each session and service type
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need dates to match their calendar, and insurers or HSA/FSA administrators often require them for reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your credentials and license or certification number where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows your qualifications and is often required on superbills submitted to insurance. Many states license dietitians or nutritionists, so check what applies to you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session length and format (in person or video)
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates often differ by length, and some insurers handle telehealth differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized meal plans, reviews, and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating deliverables from sessions avoids confusion about what was included in a package.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis and procedure codes when billing insurance or providing a superbill
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients seeking reimbursement may need ICD-10 and CPT codes (such as MNT codes) from a qualified provider. Only include them if you are credentialed to use them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance and remaining sessions
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on prepaid programs want to see how many sessions they have used and what is left.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or late fees applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing them as a separate line makes it clear they come from your policy, not an error.

nutritionist.paymentTerms: Most nutritionists collect payment at the time of service or require packages to be paid in full before starting, with some offering two or three installments. Initial consultations are often charged at booking to reduce no-shows. For invoiced clients, net 7 to 14 days is common. A written cancellation policy with 24 to 48 hours notice is standard, and late-cancel or no-show fees typically range from 50 to 100 percent of the session. Common payment methods include credit cards, ACH transfers, and HSA/FSA cards, which many clients use for nutrition counseling tied to a medical condition. Corporate and workshop clients usually pay net 15 to 30 and may need a PO number.

tips.title: Charge for the first session at booking
tips.body: Collecting payment when the appointment is scheduled cuts no-shows and makes the long intake session worth reserving time for.

tips.title: Bundle your prep and follow-up work into the price
tips.body: Meal plan building, chart notes, and message replies take real time. Either price them into sessions and packages or list them as separate line items so unpaid work does not pile up.

tips.title: Offer packages with clear end dates
tips.body: A 12-week package that expires after 16 weeks avoids clients holding unused sessions indefinitely and gives you predictable income.

tips.title: Provide a superbill for out-of-network clients
tips.body: Many clients can claim reimbursement or use HSA/FSA funds. A clear receipt with dates, services, and credentials helps them get paid back and makes your rates easier to accept.

tips.title: Separate coaching from messaging support
tips.body: If you offer text or email check-ins, state the response window and whether they are included or billed monthly so scope does not creep.

faqs.question: Should I bill per session or per package?
faqs.answer: Both work. Per-session billing is flexible for new clients, while packages bring in money up front and keep clients committed through the weeks it takes to see change. Many nutritionists offer both and give a small discount on packages.

faqs.question: Can clients use HSA or FSA funds to pay me?
faqs.answer: Often yes, especially when nutrition counseling is tied to a medical condition and you provide documentation. Rules vary by plan, so tell clients to check with their administrator and give them an itemized receipt or superbill.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on nutrition services?
faqs.answer: In most states, professional counseling services are not taxed, but products such as supplements or printed materials sold separately may be. Rules vary, so check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I handle missed appointments?
faqs.answer: State your cancellation policy in your intake paperwork and repeat it on the invoice. A fee of 50 to 100 percent for sessions canceled inside 24 hours is typical. Waiving it once for a good reason is a courtesy you can offer without changing the policy.

faqs.question: Can I bill insurance directly?
faqs.answer: Only if you are credentialed with the payer, which usually requires being a registered dietitian or holding specific state credentials. Otherwise, you bill the client and provide a superbill they can submit themselves, if their plan allows it.

estimate.intro: Nutritionists send estimates or program proposals when a client wants a multi-week plan, a corporate wellness series, or a group workshop. Clients typically compare the number of sessions, the length of support, and what is included, such as meal plans, messaging, and lab review, rather than just the hourly rate.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know whether they are getting six 45-minute video sessions or four in-person ones, since this drives the price.
A clear start and end date prevents sessions from being carried indefinitely.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables such as meal plans, recipes, and grocery lists
scopeChecklist.why: Spelling out what is included avoids requests for extra plans after the program starts.
State whether email or app messaging is included, how often you respond, and what counts as extra.
Make it clear you do not diagnose or treat medical conditions unless licensed to, and that clients should keep their doctor informed. This varies by state and credential.

scopeChecklist.item: Cost of labs, supplements, or tools
scopeChecklist.why: If the plan involves third-party lab tests, food sensitivity panels, or supplements, clarify that these are billed separately by the provider.
Clients prepaying for a program want to know what happens if they pause or stop early.

pricingTips.title: Price the outcome window, not just sessions
pricingTips.body: A 12-week program with defined check-ins and a meal plan feels more concrete than a list of hourly sessions and lets you price above the sum of the parts.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: For example, a basic package with sessions only, a standard with a meal plan, and a premium with messaging support. Clients tend to choose the middle and see exactly what extra costs.

pricingTips.title: Include prep time in the fee
pricingTips.body: Plan building, chart review, and research can take as long as the session itself. Factor that into your rate so a $100 session is not really a $60 hour.

pricingTips.title: Quote corporate work by audience and format
pricingTips.body: For workshops, base the quote on the length, group size, customization needed, and any handouts, and add travel if on-site.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation before quoting?
faqs.answer: A short 15-minute discovery call is common and helps you understand goals before proposing a package. A full free assessment usually is not necessary and cuts into paid time.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical for program quotes. Schedule availability and pricing can change, so put an expiration date on the document.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if the client's needs turn out to be more complex?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your quote says so. Note that the estimate is based on the information given at intake, and that added conditions or extra sessions will be quoted separately before you proceed.

occupational-therapist.intro: Occupational therapists who bill clients directly are usually in private practice, run a small pediatric or adult clinic, or contract with families, schools, and employers. They invoice for evaluations, individual treatment sessions, home visits, and written reports. Many also send self-pay clients a superbill so the client can seek reimbursement from their own insurance.
occupational-therapist.pricingModel: Most private-pay OTs charge per session, with a higher fee for the initial evaluation and a standard fee for 45 or 60 minute treatment sessions. Some bill per 15-minute unit to match CPT coding, especially when also billing insurance. Home visits, school observations, and workplace or home ergonomic assessments are often priced separately and may include travel time or mileage. Report writing, IEP or team meetings, and phone consultations are commonly billed hourly or as a flat fee. Some practices sell packages of sessions at a small discount, and sensory gym or group programs are priced per child per class. Contract OTs working for agencies or schools may bill hourly or per diem. Cancellation and no-show fees are usually part of the fee schedule.

rates.service: Home safety or ergonomic assessment with report
Written report, letter of medical necessity, or progress report
IEP, team meeting, or caregiver consultation
Small group session (social skills, handwriting, feeding)
Contract OT services for a school or agency

items.description: Individual OT treatment session, fine motor and sensory regulation (CPT 97530), 60 min
Home visit and environment observation, 60 min
Travel mileage to home visit
Progress report for school team
Caregiver consultation by phone

sampleInvoice.notes: Dates of service: March 4, 11, 18, 25 and March 20 (home visit). Payment due within 14 days. A superbill with diagnosis and CPT codes is attached for out-of-network reimbursement. Cancellations with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50% of the session fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service for each session
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and insurers need exact dates to reconcile reimbursement, and it supports your treatment records.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Self-pay clients submitting to insurance need codes such as 97165, 97166, 97530, or 97535 and the time spent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code (ICD-10) if the client requests a superbill
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers generally require it for out-of-network reimbursement, and it must match the referral or evaluation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your name, credentials, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Reimbursement claims usually require the provider identifiers, and it shows you are a licensed OT.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and date of birth, with the parent or guardian listed for minors
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the correct patient and the responsible party for payment without exposing more health detail than needed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for non-treatment time (reports, meetings, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: These are often not reimbursable by insurance, so listing them separately avoids confusion and denials.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late cancellation or no-show fees with the policy date
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the charge is based on a policy the client agreed to in writing.

occupational-therapist.paymentTerms: Many private-pay OT practices collect payment at the time of service by card, HSA or FSA card, or bank transfer, and send an invoice or superbill after each session or monthly. For evaluations or large packages, a deposit or prepayment is common. Invoices for reports, school contracts, or agency work are often net 15 to 30. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are used by some practices if stated in the signed service agreement. Cancellation policies of 24 to 48 hours notice are standard. Keep invoices free of unnecessary clinical detail, and check HIPAA and state rules on how you send billing documents.

tips.title: Keep treatment billing separate from admin time
tips.body: Put sessions, reports, meetings, and travel on separate lines. Clients submitting superbills avoid denials when only treatment time appears with codes, and non-clinical time is clearly yours to collect.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in the intake paperwork
tips.body: Have clients sign a policy covering late cancels, no-shows, and missed home visits before the first session. Refer to it on the invoice when you apply a fee.

tips.title: Offer superbills to out-of-network clients
tips.body: Many families reimburse part of your fee through their own plan. A clear superbill with codes, NPI, and diagnosis saves you repeated requests for documents.

tips.title: Charge for reports and letters up front
tips.body: Letters of medical necessity, school reports, and forms take real time. State your hourly or flat fee in your fee schedule and invoice before releasing the document where your rules allow.

tips.title: Track mileage on home and school visits
tips.body: Record start and end addresses and miles driven. You can bill travel as a line item at a stated rate, and the records help at tax time.

faqs.question: Should I bill by session or by 15-minute unit?
faqs.answer: For private-pay clients, a flat fee per session is simpler and easier to explain. Use 15-minute units if you also bill insurance or the client needs a superbill that matches CPT time-based codes.

faqs.question: Can I charge for writing reports and attending IEP meetings?
faqs.answer: Yes, for private-pay work. Put your rates in the service agreement and invoice the time as separate lines. Insurance usually does not cover these, so families should know before you start.

faqs.question: What should be on a superbill?
faqs.answer: Provider name, credentials, license number, NPI, tax ID, client name and date of birth, dates of service, CPT codes, ICD-10 diagnosis codes, fees charged, and amounts paid. Requirements vary by plan, so ask the client to check with their insurer.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on unpaid invoices?
faqs.answer: In most places yes, if you disclosed the fee in writing before providing services. Check your state rules on interest caps, and be careful about applying fees to families in hardship.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on OT services?
faqs.answer: Healthcare services are generally not subject to sales tax in most states, but rules vary. If you sell products such as adaptive equipment or sensory tools, those may be taxable, so check with your state department of revenue.

estimate.intro: Private-practice OTs send estimates when a family or organization needs to know the cost of an evaluation plus a course of therapy, or when pricing a home modification assessment, school contract, or workplace ergonomic review. Clients compare your fee against insurance copays, other clinics, and agency rates, so the estimate should show the total expected cost and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Evaluation fee and what it includes
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether the written report and treatment plan are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Session length, frequency, and expected number of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a realistic total and makes clear that the plan can change after reassessment.

scopeChecklist.item: Location of service (clinic, home, school, telehealth)
scopeChecklist.why: Travel, facility, and visit fees differ by setting.

scopeChecklist.item: Reports, letters, and meetings not included in session fees
scopeChecklist.why: These are common sources of surprise charges, so list their rates.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment, materials, or supplies the client must buy
scopeChecklist.why: Splints, adaptive tools, and sensory items can be added costs if you supply or recommend them.
Sets expectations before the first appointment and limits disputes later.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity period and reassessment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Fees may change and goals may be revised after a set number of sessions or months.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range tied to the treatment plan
pricingTips.body: Therapy needs depend on progress, so give a range such as 8 to 12 sessions and note it will be reviewed at reassessment. Avoid promising an outcome or fixed duration.

pricingTips.title: Show evaluation and treatment as separate lines
pricingTips.body: Families can then see the one-time cost of the evaluation versus the ongoing cost of sessions.

pricingTips.title: Offer a session package if it fits your practice
pricingTips.body: A prepaid block of sessions at a modest discount helps cash flow. State the refund and expiration terms in writing.

pricingTips.title: Include travel in the quote for home and school visits
pricingTips.body: Either build it into the hourly rate or add a clear mileage or travel time line so the estimate matches the final bill.

faqs.question: Can I guarantee the total cost of therapy?
faqs.answer: Not reliably. Provide an estimate based on your recommended frequency and an expected range of sessions, and note that the plan will be updated after reassessment.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote for an evaluation before the client books?
faqs.answer: Yes. Evaluation fees are usually fixed, so state the price and what it includes, such as testing, observation, and a written report, before scheduling.

faqs.question: How is an OT estimate different from a good faith estimate?
faqs.answer: In the US, the federal No Surprises Act requires good faith estimates for uninsured or self-pay patients for many healthcare providers when scheduling care in advance. Check current federal rules and your state requirements to see what applies to your practice.

office-cleaning.intro: Office cleaning businesses, from solo operators to small crews, clean workplaces such as small offices, medical suites, coworking spaces, and retail back offices, usually after hours. Invoices typically cover recurring janitorial visits billed monthly, plus add-on work like carpet extraction, window cleaning, floor stripping and waxing, and supplies.
office-cleaning.pricingModel: Most office cleaning is priced as a flat monthly fee for a set schedule, such as three nights a week, which is worked out from square footage, cleaning frequency, and the time the job takes. Many cleaners build the quote from an hourly labor target (often $25-50 per labor hour billed) and then express it as a per-visit or per-month price. Per-square-foot pricing is common for larger spaces and for one-time or specialty work. Add-ons like carpet cleaning, strip and wax, window washing, and deep cleans are billed separately as flat fees or per square foot. Restroom supplies (paper, soap, liners) are either included in the monthly price or billed at cost plus a markup. Initial deep cleans for new accounts are often charged as a one-time fee, and many cleaners require a contract term of 6-12 months with 30-day cancellation notice.

rates.service: Initial deep clean for new account

items.description: Monthly janitorial service, 4,000 sq ft office, 3 visits per week (13 visits)
Restroom and break room supplies (paper towels, toilet paper, soap, liners)
Carpet extraction, main work area and hallways
Interior window cleaning, conference room and lobby
Trash removal to dumpster, extra bags from office event

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Recurring service continues under the agreement dated January 5, with 30 days written notice to cancel. Please report any missed areas within 48 hours so they can be corrected at no charge. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location and square footage
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients have multiple suites or buildings, and the square footage ties the charge back to the quoted scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service dates or visit count for the billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who pay monthly want to confirm the number of visits matched the agreed schedule, especially after holidays or skipped nights.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring service separated from add-ons
invoiceChecklist.why: Carpet cleaning, floor work, and window cleaning are outside the base contract, so listing them separately avoids questions about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Supplies line with cost or flat charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Consumables are a common source of disputes. Show whether they are included or billed so the client sees what they paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or work order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and larger companies often cannot pay without a PO or cost center reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract reference and term
invoiceChecklist.why: Points to the signed agreement for schedule, cancellation notice, and rate increases if a client questions the amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, insurance, and tax details where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often request proof of insurance and a W-9. Sales tax on cleaning services varies by state, so show tax separately if it applies where you work.

office-cleaning.paymentTerms: Commercial clients usually pay recurring accounts monthly, with invoices sent at the start or end of the month and due in 15 to 30 days. Net 30 is common with larger companies and property managers, while smaller offices may agree to net 15 or autopay. One-time jobs such as strip and wax, post-construction cleanup, or initial deep cleans often require a 25-50% deposit, with the balance due at completion. Many cleaners add a late fee of 1.5% per month, stated in the contract. Common payment methods are ACH transfer, check, and card, and card fees are sometimes passed on or built into the price.

tips.title: Bill recurring service in advance
tips.body: Invoicing at the start of the month rather than the end keeps cash flow steadier and gives you leverage if an account falls behind, since you can pause service after a stated grace period.

tips.title: Put the schedule and scope in writing
tips.body: List which rooms, tasks, and days are included, and what counts as extra. Vague scope leads to requests for free window wiping or trash from events that then show up as complaints about the bill.

tips.title: Track supply costs per client
tips.body: Paper goods and soap can eat into thin margins. Record what each site uses and adjust the supply line or monthly rate at renewal if costs rise.

tips.title: Add a rate review clause
tips.body: Wages, supplies, and fuel costs rise. A clause allowing an annual increase with 30 days notice lets you raise rates without renegotiating the whole contract.

tips.title: Handle holidays and skipped visits consistently
tips.body: Decide whether closed days are credited, made up, or still billed, and write it into the agreement. Clients notice when the invoice does not match the calendar.

faqs.question: Should I charge per square foot or per hour for office cleaning?
faqs.answer: Either works. Many cleaners estimate the hours a job takes and multiply by a labor rate, then present it as a flat monthly price. Per square foot is easier to quote for large or simple spaces. Check that the result covers labor, supplies, insurance, travel, and some profit.

faqs.question: Do I charge for supplies separately?
faqs.answer: It depends on the contract. Many cleaners include basic supplies in the monthly price, while others bill restroom paper and soap at cost plus a markup. Whichever you choose, state it on the quote and show it on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on cleaning services?
faqs.answer: It varies by state and sometimes by city. Some states tax janitorial services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant before adding or omitting tax.

faqs.question: What should I do when a client pays late?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder a few days after the due date, then follow up by phone. If your contract includes a late fee and a service pause clause, apply them consistently. For repeated late payment, consider requiring autopay or payment in advance.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a one-time deep clean?
faqs.answer: List it as its own line item with the square footage, the tasks covered, and the flat fee or per-square-foot rate. Collect a deposit before starting if the job is large, and show the deposit as a credit on the final invoice.

estimate.intro: Office cleaners send quotes after walking the space and before agreeing to a recurring contract or a one-time job like floor refinishing. Clients usually compare bids from two or three companies, looking at the monthly price, visit frequency, what is included, and whether the company is insured.

scopeChecklist.why: Spell out offices, restrooms, kitchens, hallways, and any areas excluded so the price matches the space you actually walked.
Three nights a week costs very different money than once a week, and clients should know your arrival and finish times.

scopeChecklist.item: Task list per visit and per period
scopeChecklist.why: Separate nightly tasks like emptying trash and vacuuming from weekly or monthly ones like dusting vents or detailing glass.
State who provides paper goods, soap, liners, and cleaning chemicals so there is no argument about restocking.
Listing carpet extraction, floor waxing, and window cleaning rates upfront prevents surprise charges later.
Clients give you building access after hours, so confirm liability coverage, any bonding, and how keys or alarm codes are handled.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract term, cancellation, and rate changes
scopeChecklist.why: Shows the length of commitment, notice needed to cancel, and when prices can be adjusted.

pricingTips.title: Walk the site before quoting
pricingTips.body: Floor types, number of restrooms, clutter, and foot traffic affect the time needed more than square footage alone. A quick visit prevents underbidding.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from time and costs
pricingTips.body: Estimate labor hours per visit, multiply by your loaded labor cost, add supplies, travel, equipment, and insurance, then add margin before turning it into a monthly price.

pricingTips.title: Offer a first-clean charge
pricingTips.body: New accounts are often dirtier than the maintenance level you are pricing. Quote a separate initial deep clean rather than absorbing the extra hours into the monthly rate.

pricingTips.title: Present tiers when it helps
pricingTips.body: Giving options such as two or three visits a week lets the client choose by budget while each option stays profitable for you.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most office cleaners provide walk-throughs and quotes free for recurring accounts. For large or complex jobs like post-construction cleanup, some charge a fee that is credited if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Labor and supply costs change, and the client's space or needs may too, so put an expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the first month?
faqs.answer: Only if the quote or contract allows it or the scope turns out to differ from what you walked. If the space is dirtier or larger than described, document the difference and discuss an adjustment promptly.

faqs.question: What if a client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope or frequency instead of cutting the rate on the same work, for example dropping a night per week or moving detail tasks to monthly. That keeps your margin intact.

office-maintenance.intro: Office maintenance providers keep commercial spaces running: small offices, medical suites, retail units, and shared workspaces. They are usually solo operators, small crews, or handymen with commercial accounts who bill property managers and office managers for recurring service and one-off repairs. Invoices typically cover monthly maintenance contracts, hourly repair work, materials, and after-hours or emergency calls.
office-maintenance.pricingModel: Most office maintenance work is priced one of three ways. Recurring accounts are usually a flat monthly fee for a defined scope, such as a weekly walkthrough, light bulb and ceiling tile replacement, door and hardware adjustments, and filter changes. On-demand repairs are billed hourly, often with a one- or two-hour minimum and a trip charge for short calls. Larger projects like repainting a suite, replacing flooring, or building out a partition are quoted as a flat price. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10-30%, and the markup should be stated in your agreement. After-hours, weekend, and emergency calls are commonly billed at 1.5x to 2x the regular rate. Subcontracted work such as HVAC, electrical, or plumbing is passed through with a handling markup, or billed by the licensed sub directly.

rates.service: Monthly maintenance contract (small office, weekly walkthrough)
Light fixture, bulb, and ballast/LED driver replacement
Interior painting touch-up or suite repaint
Ceiling tile and drywall patch repair
HVAC filter replacement and basic inspection

Replace 6 failed LED troffer drivers and 4 ceiling tiles, labor
Materials: LED drivers, ceiling tiles, fasteners (cost plus 20%)
Adjust and re-hang conference room door, replace closer
Door closer hardware
After-hours call, water leak at break room sink (Sat. 7 PM)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Work orders #1042 and #1047 referenced. Materials billed at cost plus 20% per service agreement. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and suite or unit number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers often handle many locations and tenants, and unclear locations delay approval and payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work order or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial clients cannot pay without a reference number that ties the invoice to an approved request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of each visit and who performed the work
invoiceChecklist.why: Recurring contracts need proof that scheduled visits happened, and it settles questions about who was on site.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours separated from materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients audit these lines separately, and the markup on materials should be visible and match your agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: After-hours or emergency rate labeled clearly
invoiceChecklist.why: A higher rate with no explanation is the most common reason a line item gets disputed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subcontractor work and license numbers where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC work often requires a licensed contractor, and the client may need the license on file for insurance or the landlord.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, tax ID or W-9 on file, and certificate of insurance reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial accounts payable departments typically need vendor paperwork before they release payment.

office-maintenance.paymentTerms: Commercial clients usually pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, and larger property management companies may push to net 45 or 60 through their accounts payable process. Recurring contracts are best billed at the start of the month or service period rather than after. Ask for a deposit or prepayment on materials for larger projects, commonly 25-50%, and on special-order items. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if they are written into your agreement before work begins. Most clients pay by ACH, check, or card, and card payments often involve a processing fee you can choose to absorb or pass on where permitted.

tips.title: Put the contract scope in writing
tips.body: List exactly which tasks are included in the monthly fee and which are billed extra. Disputes usually come from assumptions about what a walkthrough covers.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge per call
tips.body: A 20-minute fix still costs you drive time and setup. A one-hour minimum or trip charge keeps small calls from losing money.

tips.title: Track materials with receipts
tips.body: Keep receipts and attach or reference them on the invoice. Clients who see actual costs rarely push back on a stated markup.

tips.title: Invoice per work order for on-demand work
tips.body: Property managers match invoices to tickets. One invoice per work order, or one monthly invoice listing each order separately, gets approved faster than a lump sum.

tips.title: Bill promptly after the visit
tips.body: Send invoices the same day or at least weekly. Commercial payment cycles start from the invoice date, so delays push your cash back.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat monthly fee or hourly for office maintenance?
faqs.answer: Use a flat monthly fee for predictable recurring tasks like scheduled walkthroughs and filter changes, and bill repairs hourly or by quote. A flat fee gives the client a steady budget and gives you steady income, but set a cap on included hours.

faqs.question: How much markup should I put on materials?
faqs.answer: Ten to thirty percent over your cost is common. Smaller parts often carry a higher percentage than large purchases. State the markup in your service agreement so it does not surprise anyone.

faqs.question: Can I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, many providers do, either as a trip charge per visit or by billing drive time at a reduced hourly rate. For clients with multiple sites, you can waive it on days when you service several locations.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and on what you are billing. Some states tax materials, some tax certain repair or maintenance services, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show tax as its own line if it applies.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client pays late?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder a few days before the due date and a follow-up the day after. If your agreement includes a late fee, apply it consistently. For repeat late payers, consider requiring prepayment or pausing non-urgent work.

estimate.intro: Office maintenance providers send quotes for recurring contracts, suite refreshes, flooring or paint projects, and larger repairs. Property managers often collect two or three bids, so clients compare scope, response time, and insurance as much as price.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming the suite, floor, or rooms prevents arguments over whether the break room or common area was part of the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Task list for recurring contracts, with visit frequency
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether a visit means a quick look or actual repairs, and how often you will be there.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor and materials split, with markup stated
scopeChecklist.why: It shows where the money goes and makes later change orders easier to explain.
Noisy or disruptive work may need to happen after hours, which can change the price and the schedule.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions and work that needs a licensed trade
scopeChecklist.why: Electrical, plumbing, and HVAC repairs beyond basic tasks may need a licensed contractor and a separate price.

scopeChecklist.item: Change order and extra work rate
scopeChecklist.why: Hidden damage behind walls or ceilings is common, and an agreed rate avoids stalled projects.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change, and a deadline protects you from honoring an old price months later.

pricingTips.title: Walk the space before quoting a contract
pricingTips.body: Look at the age of fixtures, HVAC units, flooring, and doors. Older buildings generate more calls, and a quote built on a quick guess often underprices the first year.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered monthly plans
pricingTips.body: Present a basic plan with monthly inspections and a fuller plan with included labor hours. Clients tend to pick the middle option, and you set the limits.

pricingTips.title: Price projects with a contingency
pricingTips.body: Add a small buffer, often 5-10%, for hidden conditions on repairs and refreshes, or clearly state that unforeseen conditions will be billed separately.

pricingTips.title: Include your insurance and license details
pricingTips.body: Property managers usually require general liability insurance. Listing coverage on the quote helps you stand out from lower bidders who lack it.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: For simple jobs, most providers quote free. For large projects that need detailed measuring or drawings, a paid estimate that is credited toward the job if accepted is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Shorten it to 7-14 days when the quote depends on volatile material prices like lumber or flooring.

faqs.question: What if the actual work costs more than my quote?
faqs.answer: For a flat quote, you generally absorb ordinary overruns. For true surprises, such as water damage found behind a wall, stop and send a written change order for approval before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: It is strongly advised. A signed or emailed written approval, ideally with a PO number, protects you and gives the client's accounting team what it needs to pay.

painter.intro: Painters, both solo contractors and small crews, bill homeowners, landlords, property managers, and general contractors for interior and exterior painting, staining, and surface prep. Invoices typically cover labor, paint and materials, prep work like patching and priming, and any extras such as ceiling work, trim, or cabinet refinishing.
painter.pricingModel: Most residential painters quote a flat price per job based on square footage, number of rooms, or surfaces, then invoice against that quote. Interior walls are often priced per square foot of floor or wall area, while trim, doors, and cabinets are priced per piece or per linear foot. Hourly rates are used for small repairs, touch-ups, and change orders, and for commercial work billed on time and materials. Paint is either included in the flat price or listed separately with a markup, commonly 10 to 20 percent over cost. Prep work (scraping, sanding, caulking, drywall patching, pressure washing) is a major labor driver and should be itemized or clearly included. Larger jobs are usually billed in stages, such as a deposit, a midpoint payment, and a final payment on completion.

rates.service: Interior wall painting (walls only, two coats)
rates.unit: per sq ft of wall area
