items.description: Interior painting: living room, hallway, and two bedrooms, walls, two coats (customer-approved color, Sherwin-Williams Eggshell)
Ceiling paint, flat white, two rooms
Baseboard and door trim, semi-gloss, two coats
Drywall patching and sanding (nail pops, two small holes)
Paint and supplies (5 gallons wall paint, 2 gallons trim paint, tape, drop cloths, caulk)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $1,500 received on 3/4 and applied to this invoice. Balance due within 7 days of completion. Accepted: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on card payments). Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Touch-up visit within 30 days of completion is included at no charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job address and work areas
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists exactly which rooms or surfaces were painted so the client and any property manager can match the invoice to the completed work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Paint brand, product line, color name or code, and sheen
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the client a record for future touch-ups and settles disputes about whether the agreed paint was used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of coats and prep work performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the labor behind the price, including priming, sanding, caulking, and patching, which clients often overlook.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately or noted as included
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear whether paint, primer, and supplies were billed apart from labor, which matters for markup transparency and for clients who reimburse materials.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extras
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents added work such as extra rooms, a color change after painting started, or unexpected repairs so the final total matches what was approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents double billing and shows the remaining balance clearly on multi-stage jobs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance info, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a contractor license number on contracts and invoices above a certain job size. Check your local rules. Property managers and GCs often also ask for proof of insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO or work order number for commercial clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers, builders, and businesses often will not process payment without it.

painter.paymentTerms: For residential jobs, painters commonly collect a deposit of 10 to 50 percent before starting, often enough to cover paint and materials, with the balance due on completion or within 7 days. Larger jobs may use a schedule such as one third at signing, one third at the midpoint, and one third at final walkthrough. Commercial and GC work is more often net 15 to net 30, sometimes with retainage held until final sign-off. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract or on the invoice. Checks, ACH transfers, and cards are all accepted; many painters add a small surcharge for cards or encourage bank payment on large balances. Many states also allow contractors to file a mechanics lien for unpaid work, with strict notice deadlines, so check your local rules.

tips.title: Collect a deposit that covers materials
tips.body: Paint, primer, and supplies can run hundreds of dollars on a mid-size job. Ask for a deposit at least equal to your material cost so you are never financing the client's project.

tips.title: Do a final walkthrough before you send the last invoice
tips.body: Walk the job with the client, note any touch-ups, and fix them on the spot. Clients are far more likely to pay promptly once they have signed off on the finished work.

tips.title: Put extras in writing before you do them
tips.body: Color changes, extra coats over dark colors, and additional repairs found after prep all add cost. Get written or text approval and list each as a separate line item on the invoice.

tips.title: Keep the paint receipt and color info
tips.body: If a client disputes the materials charge or wants to match a color later, receipts and the paint code settle it quickly. Photos of the label on the can are enough.

tips.title: Invoice the day the job finishes
tips.body: Painters often finish on a Friday and send the bill a week later. Send the invoice the same day while the result is fresh and the client is happiest.

faqs.question: Should I bill painting by the hour or by the job?
faqs.answer: Most residential painters bill by the job using a flat quote, because clients want a fixed price and it rewards efficiency. Use hourly billing for small repairs, touch-ups, and change orders, or on commercial work where the scope is uncertain.

faqs.question: Do I charge for paint separately?
faqs.answer: Either approach works if it is clear. Many painters include paint in a flat price. Others list materials as a separate line, often with a 10 to 20 percent markup to cover pickup time and waste. Whatever you choose, state it on both the estimate and the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for prep work?
faqs.answer: Include it in the flat price if it is normal prep like light sanding and caulking. For heavy prep such as scraping peeling paint, extensive drywall repair, or lead-safe work on older homes, list it as its own line item so the client can see why the price is higher.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for a repaint because of a color change?
faqs.answer: Yes. If the client changes color after work has started, you can bill the extra labor and paint as a change order. Document the approval before you proceed and list it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: What can I do if a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Start with a written reminder that references the invoice date and agreed terms, then send a formal demand letter. In many states, painters can also file a mechanics lien on the property, but deadlines are strict and vary by state, so check your local rules or consult an attorney.

estimate.intro: Painters send a written estimate before almost every job, and homeowners often collect two or three to compare. Clients compare the total price, but also what is included: number of coats, prep work, paint quality, and cleanup. A clear estimate helps you win the job without underbidding.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact areas and surfaces to be painted
scopeChecklist.why: Specify rooms, walls, ceilings, trim, doors, closets, and exterior sides so there is no argument about whether a closet or garage ceiling was included.
State what you will do, such as washing, scraping, sanding, caulking, patching, and priming, and note what is excluded, such as major drywall repair or rotted wood replacement.

scopeChecklist.item: Paint brand, product line, sheen, and number of coats
scopeChecklist.why: Paint quality affects both cost and durability. Naming the product prevents a lower-quality substitution claim and lets clients compare bids fairly.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies paint and who moves furniture
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether the client chooses and buys the paint or you do, and whether furniture moving, wall hanging removal, and outlet cover removal are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, expected duration, and weather contingency
scopeChecklist.why: Exterior work depends on weather. Stating a timeline and a rain delay policy sets expectations and avoids complaints about schedule slips.
Spell out the deposit amount, progress payments, and final payment so clients know what is due and when.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate expiration date and change order policy
scopeChecklist.why: Paint and labor costs change. A 30-day expiration protects you, and a change order clause covers extra work found after you begin.
A one to two year workmanship warranty is common and gives clients a reason to choose you over a cheaper bidder.

pricingTips.title: Measure and count before you quote
pricingTips.body: Calculate wall and ceiling square footage, count doors, windows, and cabinet fronts, and note the ceiling height. A quick measurement beats guessing from the size of the house and keeps your margins consistent.

pricingTips.title: Price prep honestly
pricingTips.body: Prep often takes as long as painting. Look closely at wall condition, caulk lines, peeling areas, and dark colors that need extra coats, and price that time in. Underestimating prep is the most common way painters lose money on a job.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best paint options
pricingTips.body: Present one or two paint grades with the price difference listed. Clients often choose the middle option, and you avoid the argument later about why the cheap paint did not cover in two coats.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for older homes
pricingTips.body: Houses built before 1978 may contain lead paint, which triggers federal lead-safe work practice rules for renovation work in many cases. Build certification, containment, and cleanup into your price or decline the job if you are not certified.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential painters give free estimates for standard jobs. For large or complex projects, such as full exterior repaints or historic homes, some charge a fee of $50 to $200 and credit it toward the job if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Paint prices and your schedule change, so put an expiration date on the estimate and state that prices may change after that.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding price?
faqs.answer: It depends on how you word it. A quote labeled as a fixed price for a defined scope is generally treated as binding for that scope. If conditions might change, label it as an estimate and include a clause that hidden damage or added work will be billed as a change order.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to supply their own paint?
faqs.answer: You can agree, but note on the estimate that you are not responsible for coverage, color match, or finish problems caused by the client's paint. Some painters charge a slightly higher labor rate or require the client to buy enough paint for two full coats.

paralegal.intro: Freelance and contract paralegals send invoices to law firms, solo attorneys, corporate legal departments, and in some states to the public as legal document preparers. They typically bill for document review, drafting, legal research, discovery work, trial preparation, and filing costs advanced on the client's behalf.
paralegal.pricingModel: Most freelance paralegals bill hourly, usually in six-minute (0.1 hour) or fifteen-minute increments, with the rate set by specialty, experience, and certifications. Litigation support, e-discovery, and intellectual property work tend to pay more than general document work. Repeatable tasks such as discovery responses, deposition summaries, trust document assembly, or uncontested divorce paperwork (where non-lawyers may legally do this) are often quoted as flat fees. Some firms pay a monthly retainer for a set number of hours. Court fees, records fees, courier charges, and similar costs are usually passed through at cost and listed separately. Rules on who a paralegal may work for and what they may charge the public vary by state. A paralegal generally must work under an attorney's supervision and cannot give legal advice or set fees for legal services on their own, so check your state's rules.

rates.service: General paralegal work for attorneys (drafting, file management, calendaring)
Litigation support (discovery responses, trial binders, exhibit prep)
Uncontested family law or simple document preparation (where permitted for non-lawyers)
Monthly retainer for ongoing attorney support

items.description: First-level document review, Smith v. Alder Logistics (production set 2)
Draft responses to first set of interrogatories and requests for production
Deposition summary, R. Alder (112 pages)
Prepare and e-file motion to compel, with proof of service
Court e-filing fee (advanced at cost, receipt attached)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Time is billed in 0.1-hour increments. Court fees are billed at cost. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. All work performed under the supervision of the engaging attorney and subject to confidentiality terms in our agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and matter or case number
invoiceChecklist.why: Law firms track billing by matter, and a missing case number often delays payment or forces a reissue.

invoiceChecklist.item: Name of the supervising attorney
invoiceChecklist.why: It shows the work was done under attorney supervision, which matters for ethics rules and for any later fee recovery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, task description, and time for each entry
invoiceChecklist.why: Detailed time entries let the attorney pass your time through to their client or support a fee petition.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing increment and hourly rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating that you bill in 0.1-hour increments at a set rate avoids questions about how the totals were calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Costs advanced, itemized with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Filing fees, records fees, and courier charges should be separate from fees so they can be reimbursed and billed through at cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or client reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate legal departments often require it before accounts payable will release payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your certification, bar-registered status, or document preparer registration where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require non-lawyer document preparers to display registration details, and it helps firms confirm your credentials.

paralegal.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is common when billing law firms, and some firms pay only after they collect from their own client, so confirm in writing that your payment is not contingent on that. New clients often pay a retainer or deposit of one to two weeks of expected work, or half of a flat fee up front. Invoice monthly for ongoing work and on completion for flat-fee projects. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in your agreement. Most paralegals accept ACH, check, and card payments. If you hold client funds, follow your state's rules and consult the supervising attorney, since trust account requirements generally apply to lawyers rather than freelancers.

tips.title: Keep contemporaneous time records
tips.body: Log time as you work instead of rebuilding it at month end. Firms often review paralegal time closely, and detailed entries are hard to dispute.

tips.title: Separate fees from advanced costs
tips.body: List court fees, certified copies, and courier charges on their own lines with receipts. It keeps your fee total clean and makes reimbursement easy to verify.

tips.title: Get the engagement terms in writing
tips.body: A short agreement covering rate, increments, payment timing, confidentiality, and who supervises you prevents most billing disputes with attorneys.

tips.title: Quote flat fees only for defined tasks
tips.body: Flat fees work for discovery responses or a standard document package. If the scope can grow, such as trial prep, bill hourly or set a cap with a change-order clause.

tips.title: Invoice on a regular schedule
tips.body: Send invoices at the same point each month or at matter milestones. Firms batch their payments, and a late invoice can push payment back a full cycle.

faqs.question: Can a paralegal bill clients directly?
faqs.answer: In most states, paralegals must work under a licensed attorney and bill the attorney or firm, not the public, for legal services. A few states allow registered or licensed legal document preparers or similar roles to serve the public directly for limited tasks. Check your state bar and court rules before taking direct clients.

faqs.question: Should I bill in six-minute or fifteen-minute increments?
faqs.answer: Six-minute (0.1 hour) increments are the most common in law firms and are seen as more precise. Fifteen-minute increments are simpler and used by some small firms. Whichever you choose, state it on your agreement and invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for travel to court or a client's office?
faqs.answer: Many paralegals bill travel time at a reduced rate, often half, and list mileage separately at a stated per-mile rate. Agree on this in advance, since some firms do not allow travel time to be passed through to their clients.

faqs.question: Can I charge a contingency fee or percentage of a case?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Fee-sharing with non-lawyers and contingency arrangements are restricted by legal ethics rules in most states. Paralegals typically charge hourly or flat fees for their own work. Ask the supervising attorney or your state bar if you are unsure.

faqs.question: What if a firm says it will pay me when the client pays them?
faqs.answer: Avoid that arrangement unless you agree to it knowingly. Your agreement should say payment is due on a fixed date regardless of the firm's collections, otherwise you carry the risk of their client's slow payment.

estimate.intro: Paralegals send estimates when an attorney or a client needs to budget a project, such as a discovery response, a document review, a trial prep push, or a set of formation documents. Firms usually compare your hourly rate, your estimated hours, and whether you will cap the total.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming what you will produce, such as responses to one set of interrogatories or a summary of one deposition, keeps a project from expanding without pay.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated hours and hourly rate, or the flat fee
scopeChecklist.why: It shows how the total was built and lets the attorney check it against their client's budget.
State page counts, number of documents, or number of exhibits. Review time can double if the volume does, and this gives you grounds to reprice.

scopeChecklist.item: What the attorney must supply and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Delays in receiving files, client answers, or approvals affect your schedule and can justify rush charges.
Filing fees, certified copies, records requests, e-discovery platform fees, and courier costs are usually extra and should be listed as pass-through.
Stating that you work under attorney direction and do not provide legal advice protects both you and the client.
Define how many edits are included and how scope changes will be priced and approved in writing.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in a range with a cap
pricingTips.body: Give a low and high hour estimate, for example 10 to 14 hours, and a not-to-exceed figure. Attorneys prefer predictable costs and the cap builds trust.

pricingTips.title: Price flat fees from your own time data
pricingTips.body: Use records of how long similar tasks took you and add a margin for revisions. Flat fees fit repeatable work, not uncertain litigation tasks.

pricingTips.title: Add rush and weekend rates
pricingTips.body: If a deadline requires evenings or weekends, quote a premium, often 25 to 50 percent above your normal rate, and put it in the estimate.

pricingTips.title: Break large projects into phases
pricingTips.body: Splitting work into stages such as intake, review, and drafting lets the attorney approve each part and gives you natural billing points.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when the task and volume are well defined and you have done it many times. Use an hourly estimate with a cap when volume or complexity is unknown, such as document review before you have seen the files.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time it takes to prepare an estimate?
faqs.answer: Brief estimates are normally free. For a large project that needs you to review files first, you can charge a small scoping fee or credit it toward the project if the client hires you.

faqs.question: What if the project goes beyond my estimate?
faqs.answer: Tell the attorney as soon as you see it happening and send a written revised estimate before doing additional work. A change-order clause in your original quote makes this routine.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. For work tied to court deadlines, state that your availability and price are held only until a certain date.

parking-lot-striping.intro: Parking lot striping contractors paint and maintain pavement markings for retail centers, apartment complexes, churches, schools, warehouses, and municipal lots. Invoices usually cover restriping existing layouts, new layouts from scratch, ADA stalls and signage, curb painting, and traffic arrows or stencils. Many are solo operators or small crews who bill per stall, per linear foot, or as a flat lot price.
parking-lot-striping.pricingModel: Most striping is priced either per stall for standard restriping or as a flat lot price built from stall count, linear feet of line, and number of stencils. New layouts cost more than restriping because they require layout time, measuring, and chalk or string lines. Stencils such as ADA symbols, arrows, and 'No Parking' or 'Fire Lane' text are priced per piece. Curb painting is charged per linear foot. Add-ons like wheel stops, signs, and bollards are charged at cost plus markup, with installation labor listed separately. Surface prep such as sweeping, pressure washing, or grinding off old paint or oil spots is billed hourly or as a line item. Most contractors set a minimum job charge to cover mobilization, since small lots can cost nearly as much to reach and set up as larger ones. Night or weekend work for businesses that cannot close the lot during the day often carries a surcharge of 15 to 30 percent.

rates.service: New layout and striping (layout time included)
Single or double line striping (lane lines, crosswalks)
ADA handicap stencil and blue background
Pressure washing or heavy sweeping prep

items.description: Restripe existing 4-inch white stalls, 90-degree, retail center lot
ADA stalls restriped with blue background and new stencil
Directional arrows and stop bars repainted
Fire lane curb painted red with stenciled text
Surface prep: sweeping and blowing debris from lines
Mobilization and traffic cones/barricades

sampleInvoice.notes: Work completed per signed estimate dated 3/4. Paint is traffic-grade, fast-dry; lot may be reopened after 30 minutes. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Balance past 30 days subject to 1.5% monthly late fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property name, lot address, and site contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and owners often have multiple sites, and accounts payable needs to match the invoice to the correct location.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date(s) of work and any after-hours or phased schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when the lot was closed or partially blocked and supports any night or weekend surcharge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stall count, linear feet, and stencil count
invoiceChecklist.why: Quantities are what the price is built on, so listing them prevents disputes about how much was painted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Paint type and color (traffic paint, water-based, epoxy, or thermoplastic) and number of coats
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients compare bids on materials, and it shows the product meets any spec or municipal requirement.

invoiceChecklist.item: ADA and fire lane work listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: These items often have code or local-authority requirements, and clients may need a record of compliance for inspections or insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate, PO number, or work order
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients often require a PO number to pay, and it ties the invoice to the agreed scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance info, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states or cities require license numbers on contracts and invoices, and property managers often need proof of insurance on file.

parking-lot-striping.paymentTerms: Small private lots such as churches and small businesses are often paid on completion, sometimes by check on site. Larger commercial and property management accounts usually pay net 30, and some pay net 45 or 60 through accounts payable, so confirm terms before you start. For large jobs or those needing special materials such as thermoplastic or custom signage, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, with the balance due on completion. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is typical if stated in the estimate and on the invoice. Accepted methods generally include check, ACH, and card. Government and school district work may require registration as a vendor, certified payroll, or prevailing wage documentation, and payment can take 30 to 60 days or longer.

tips.title: Get the stall count and layout in writing before you quote
tips.body: Count stalls and note which are ADA, compact, or angled. Attach a simple sketch or mark-up to the estimate and invoice so any added or removed stalls are easy to adjust.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge and stick to it
tips.body: A 20-stall lot still requires loading the truck, driving, setup, cones, and cleanup. A minimum job charge keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: List weather and reschedule terms
tips.body: Paint needs dry pavement and suitable temperatures, typically above about 40 to 50 degrees depending on the product. State that weather delays reschedule the work and do not void the estimate, and consider a fee for last-minute cancellations after you have mobilized.

tips.title: Bill extras as change orders
tips.body: If the client adds stencils, extra curb, or removal of old lines mid-job, get a quick written or emailed approval and list those items separately on the invoice.

tips.title: Invoice the same day the lot is done
tips.body: Property managers process invoices in batches. Sending an invoice with before and after photos right away shortens the wait and heads off complaints.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the stall or by the linear foot?
faqs.answer: Per stall is the easiest for standard restriping because clients can compare bids quickly. Linear foot pricing fits long lane lines, crosswalks, and curbs. Many contractors use per stall for the main lot and linear foot or per piece for everything else.

faqs.question: How do I bill for removing old lines?
faqs.answer: Line removal by grinding, water blasting, or blacking out is usually a separate line item priced per linear foot or per hour, since it takes much more labor and equipment than painting. Do not bundle it into the stall price unless you have measured the amount first.

faqs.question: Can I charge a surcharge for night or weekend work?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in the estimate. Many contractors add 15 to 30 percent when the client needs the work done outside business hours to avoid blocking customers or tenants.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on striping?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some treat striping as taxable repair or maintenance, others as a nontaxable real property service, and materials may be taxed differently. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the client disputes the paint job because of rain or fading?
faqs.answer: Include your paint type and cure time in the estimate and invoice, and take dated before and after photos. If your terms say that weather or heavy traffic before curing is not covered, you will have documentation to point to.

estimate.intro: Striping contractors usually quote after a site visit or from an aerial or photo review, and commercial clients often collect two or three bids. Property managers compare total price, paint type, schedule, insurance coverage, and what is included for ADA and fire lane markings.

scopeChecklist.item: Stall count, linear feet, and number of stencils
scopeChecklist.why: These quantities are the basis of the price, so a clear count prevents arguments about what was included.
A new layout requires measuring and design, and the cost is higher. State which one the quote covers and who supplies the layout plan.

scopeChecklist.item: Paint type, color, and number of coats
scopeChecklist.why: Traffic paint, water-based paint, and epoxy have different costs and lifespans, and clients need to know which they are getting.
Sweeping, pressure washing, or grinding off old lines adds time. Spell out what is included and what is extra.
Make clear whether you are matching existing layouts or following current code. Say that the owner is responsible for confirming local requirements unless you have agreed to handle it.

scopeChecklist.item: Traffic control and lot closure plan
scopeChecklist.why: Cones, barricades, phased sections, and customer access affect scheduling and pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Weather delays, cure time, and validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Painting depends on weather. State that dates may move and how long the quote stays valid since material costs change.

pricingTips.title: Measure before you price
pricingTips.body: Walk the lot or use satellite measurements and count stalls, arrows, and curb footage. Underestimating a large lot by even 10 percent can wipe out your margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer options
pricingTips.body: Give a base price for restriping and optional add-ons such as curb painting, new stencils, signs, or wheel stops. Clients can choose and you can raise the average job size.

pricingTips.title: Account for travel and paint costs
pricingTips.body: Include mobilization, fuel, and the cost of paint and glass beads, since paint prices can change. Build a margin into stall pricing rather than discounting to match a competitor.

pricingTips.title: Bundle multiple sites
pricingTips.body: Property managers with several lots will often give you all of them for a lower per-stall price. Offer a modest discount in exchange for a multi-site or annual contract.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most striping contractors give free estimates for standard restriping. For large new layouts requiring a drawn plan, some charge a design fee and credit it toward the job if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is typical. Paint, fuel, and labor costs change, and a limited validity period lets you reprice if the client takes too long.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit on an estimate?
faqs.answer: Not usually for small lots. For larger jobs, custom materials, or new clients, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is reasonable and should be stated on the estimate.

faqs.question: What if the actual stall count differs from the quote?
faqs.answer: Write on the quote that the price is based on the stated counts and will be adjusted at the quoted unit rates if the final count differs. That way both you and the client have a clear way to adjust the price.

pastry-chef.intro: Independent pastry chefs and small bakery owners bill clients for custom cakes, dessert tables, wedding cakes, wholesale pastries, and baking for restaurants, cafes, and events. Invoices usually cover a mix of product, design time, delivery and setup, and rentals such as stands or cake pillars.
pastry-chef.pricingModel: Pastry work is priced mostly by the unit of product: per slice or serving for wedding and tiered cakes, per dozen for cookies, cupcakes, and macarons, per piece for entremets and tarts, and per item for wholesale. Custom design work such as sugar flowers, fondant sculpting, or hand-painting is often added as a separate line, billed as a flat fee or an hourly charge. Many pastry chefs set a minimum order, charge delivery by distance, and add setup fees for large installations. Cake stands, boxes, and cake boards are either included, sold, or rented with a refundable deposit. Wholesale accounts are usually priced per unit at a discount of 30 to 50 percent off retail, with standing weekly orders. Consulting, recipe development, and private classes are billed hourly or per session. Most price from ingredient cost, labor hours, and overhead, since butter, chocolate, and nut prices shift through the year.

items.description: Three-tier wedding cake, vanilla bean sponge with raspberry filling, buttercream finish (100 servings)
Hand-piped sugar flower cascade design
Cupcakes, assorted flavors, 3 dozen
Cake stand rental (refundable deposit billed separately)
Delivery and on-site setup, 28 miles

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $500 received on booking is shown as a credit. Balance due 14 days before the event date. Cake stand deposit of $75 will be refunded when the stand is returned within 3 days of the event. Please confirm allergen requirements in writing; products are made in a kitchen that handles wheat, eggs, dairy, and tree nuts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, delivery time, and venue address
invoiceChecklist.why: Pastry is perishable and time-sensitive, so the invoice should match the agreed delivery window and location.

invoiceChecklist.item: Flavors, fillings, servings, and tier sizes
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out each cake and the number of servings prevents disputes about size or what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Design work as a separate line
invoiceChecklist.why: Sugar flowers, hand-painting, and custom toppers take real labor, and showing them separately explains the price difference between a simple and an elaborate cake.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most custom orders require a nonrefundable deposit, so the invoice should show what was paid, when, and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental items and refundable deposits
invoiceChecklist.why: Stands, pillars, and display pieces need to be tracked with return dates and amounts, so the deposit refund is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Allergen and ingredient notice
invoiceChecklist.why: A short statement about common allergens helps protect you and shows the client what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, food permit, or cottage food registration number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many wholesale buyers, venues, and event planners ask for proof of a licensed kitchen. Requirements vary by state and county, so check local rules.

pastry-chef.paymentTerms: Custom orders usually require a nonrefundable deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking, which holds the date on the calendar. The balance is commonly due 7 to 14 days before the event, since ingredients are bought and work begins ahead of time. Smaller orders such as a birthday cake are often paid in full when ordered. Wholesale accounts are commonly billed weekly or net 15 to 30, with some charging a late fee of 1.5 percent per month after that. Accepted payment methods usually include card, bank transfer, and digital payment apps, with cash for small local orders. Cancellation and date-change policies should be stated in your contract.

tips.title: Collect the balance before delivery
tips.body: A cake cannot be taken back and resold, so avoid delivering with an unpaid balance. Set the final payment date before the event and tell clients that final guest counts lock at that time.

tips.title: Bill design time separately
tips.body: Intricate decoration can take more hours than baking. Listing it as its own line, such as 6 hours of sugar work, makes the price easier to defend and lets clients choose a simpler design.

tips.title: Set a minimum order
tips.body: Small orders cost nearly as much in setup, cleanup, and packaging as larger ones. A minimum such as $150 for delivery orders or $60 for pickup keeps tiny jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Update prices for ingredient swings
tips.body: Butter, chocolate, vanilla, and nut prices can change quickly. Review your price list every few months, and for large wholesale accounts include a clause allowing adjustment when costs rise.

tips.title: Track delivery costs by distance
tips.body: Fragile tiered cakes may need a second person or a refrigerated vehicle. Charge by mileage or zone, plus a setup fee when you assemble on-site.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit for a custom cake?
faqs.answer: Yes, most pastry chefs do. A deposit of 25 to 50 percent secures the date and covers early ingredient and supply purchases. State clearly that it is nonrefundable and show it as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a cake stand or display rentals?
faqs.answer: Add a rental fee line for use of the item, and list a refundable deposit separately with the return date and the amount. Keeping them separate avoids confusion when the deposit is returned.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on cakes and pastries?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes on the product. Many states tax prepared food or bakery items, some exempt certain groceries, and delivery or service charges may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How should I bill wholesale accounts?
faqs.answer: List items by unit with the delivery date, and include a standing order or PO number if the buyer uses one. Weekly or monthly invoices with net 15 to 30 terms are common. Keep the wholesale price list in writing.

faqs.question: What if the guest count drops after I've started?
faqs.answer: Include a final-count deadline in your contract, often 10 to 14 days before the event. After that date, the invoice stays at the agreed servings because ingredients are already purchased and production is scheduled.

estimate.intro: Pastry chefs send estimates after a consultation or tasting, when a client is comparing bakers for a wedding, party, or corporate event. Clients compare per-serving price, design complexity, flavors, and what is included in delivery and setup. A clear quote also helps hold the date once the client accepts.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, venue, and delivery window
scopeChecklist.why: Timing and location affect how early you must start, whether you need a helper, and what you charge for delivery.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of servings and cake dimensions
scopeChecklist.why: The serving count drives price. Stating tier sizes and whether servings are wedding-size or party-size slices avoids disagreements.
Some fillings, such as fresh fruit or specialty chocolate, cost more. Listing them locks in the agreed design.
Attach or reference the inspiration photo and note what is included, such as sugar flowers, gold leaf, or a custom topper. Changes after approval can then be billed as extras.
State the delivery fee, whether you assemble on-site, and which stands or displays are included or rented.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know when the deposit is due, when the balance is due, and what happens if the date changes or the event is canceled.
Gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free orders may require separate ingredients and prep. Note what you can and cannot guarantee in a shared kitchen.

pricingTips.title: Price from cost, labor, and overhead
pricingTips.body: Add ingredient cost, hours of labor at your hourly rate, packaging, kitchen overhead, and delivery. Many bakers then convert the total to a per-serving price for the client.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a simple buttercream cake, a version with fresh flowers, and a fully sugar-decorated one. Clients can pick a budget without asking you to cut corners on one design.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 14 to 30 days is common. Your calendar and ingredient costs change, and an expiry date encourages clients to book the date.

pricingTips.title: Charge for tastings
pricingTips.body: Tasting boxes cost time and ingredients. Many pastry chefs charge $30 to $75 and credit it toward the order if the client books.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or tasting?
faqs.answer: Estimates are usually free, but tastings often carry a fee because of ingredient and prep costs. Many bakers credit the tasting fee toward the final order when the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a pastry quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical. Peak wedding dates can fill quickly, so some bakers state that the date is not held until a deposit is received.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client approves the design?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes. If the client adds tiers, increases the guest count, or requests a more detailed design, send a revised quote. Your contract should say that changes after approval may change the price.

payroll-service.intro: Payroll services run payroll for small businesses: calculating wages, withholding taxes, issuing paychecks or direct deposits, and filing payroll tax returns. Owners of these businesses, including solo payroll specialists and small firms, invoice clients each pay cycle or each month for processing, tax filing, and add-on work such as new hire setup or year-end forms.
payroll-service.pricingModel: Most payroll services charge a recurring base fee per payroll run or per month, plus a per-employee fee. A typical structure is a base of $25-75 per pay run and $4-12 per employee per run. Independent bookkeepers and payroll specialists often charge a flat monthly fee instead, tiered by employee count and pay frequency. Quarterly and annual filings (Form 941, state unemployment returns, W-2s, 1099-NECs) are either bundled into the monthly fee or billed separately as flat fees. One-time work such as setup, migrating from another provider, or fixing prior-period errors is billed as a setup fee or hourly. Extras like off-cycle checks, manual check printing, garnishment administration, and multi-state registration are usually itemized. Pass-through costs, such as software subscriptions or state filing fees, should be listed separately from your service fees. Many firms bill in advance for the coming month so the invoice is paid before payroll funds are debited.

rates.service: Payroll processing base fee (weekly, biweekly, or semi-monthly run)
Flat monthly payroll package (up to 10 employees, biweekly)
New client setup and employee data entry
Quarterly payroll tax filing (Form 941 and state returns)
Year-end W-2 and 1099-NEC preparation and filing

items.description: Biweekly payroll processing, base fee (pay dates 3/7 and 3/21)
Per-employee processing, 12 employees
Off-cycle bonus check run (3/14)
New hire setup and onboarding entry
Q1 Form 941 and state unemployment return preparation and filing

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due 5 business days before the next pay date so funds clear before payroll is submitted. Payroll tax deposits are debited separately and are not included on this invoice. Late payments may delay payroll processing and are subject to a $25 late fee. ACH preferred.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay period and pay date for each run
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several runs in a month, and tying each charge to a specific pay date prevents confusion and duplicate-charge disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Employee count per run
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-employee fees depend on headcount, which changes with hires and terminations. Showing the count lets the client verify the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line items for service fees, pass-through costs, and tax deposits
invoiceChecklist.why: Your fees are different from the client's payroll liabilities. Keeping them apart avoids the client thinking tax money is part of your bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (off-cycle runs, new hires, terminations, garnishments)
invoiceChecklist.why: These are out-of-scope extras for most flat packages, and listing them shows why the total changed from the usual amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Filing type and period (Form 941 Q1, state UI, W-2 tax year)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to match charges to compliance deliverables, and it gives a record of what you filed and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business info and the client's legal name and EIN reference (last four digits only)
invoiceChecklist.why: Payroll accounts are tied to the legal entity. Using the correct name avoids mix-ups when a client owns several businesses.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment due date relative to the payroll deadline
invoiceChecklist.why: If payroll depends on the invoice being paid first, the due date should state that and be earlier than the submission deadline.

payroll-service.paymentTerms: Payroll services commonly bill monthly in advance or per run, with due dates set before the payroll submission deadline, often 3 to 5 business days before the pay date. Many firms collect fees by ACH debit authorized in the service agreement, which reduces late payments. Setup fees are usually due upfront or at signing. Late fees of $25-50 or 1.5% per month are common, and many agreements allow the firm to pause processing if fees are unpaid. Keep the fee invoice separate from any funding or tax liability debits, and check your state's rules and your contract on how client funds are held and how you may handle them.

tips.title: Tie your due date to the payroll deadline
tips.body: An invoice due in 30 days does nothing for you if payroll runs in 5. Set terms so payment lands before you submit the run, and state in your agreement that unpaid fees can delay processing.

tips.title: Use ACH authorization for recurring fees
tips.body: Getting a signed ACH authorization at onboarding removes most chasing. Make sure the agreement spells out the amount, timing, and how clients can update bank details.

tips.title: Define what the base fee covers
tips.body: Spell out the number of runs, employees, and filings included. Charge extra for off-cycle runs, retroactive corrections, multi-state filings, and notices from tax agencies, which are common sources of unpaid work.

tips.title: Bill for agency notice and cleanup work hourly
tips.body: Responding to IRS or state notices, fixing prior provider errors, and reconciling quarterly filings can take hours. Quote an hourly rate or minimum in advance and log time by task.

tips.title: Review pricing when headcount changes
tips.body: Clients grow and add employees. Check headcount quarterly and adjust the monthly tier or per-employee charges so your fee keeps pace with the work.

faqs.question: Should I include payroll tax deposits on my service invoice?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Tax deposits and net pay funding are the client's liabilities and are usually handled through separate debits or transfers. Your invoice should cover only your fees and any approved pass-through costs, so the two amounts are not confused.

faqs.question: Do I charge per employee or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Per-employee pricing scales with headcount and suits larger or changing teams. Flat monthly packages are easier for small clients with stable staff. Whichever you use, define the headcount limit and what happens when the client exceeds it.

faqs.question: How do I bill for year-end W-2 and 1099 work?
faqs.answer: Many firms charge a per-form fee, such as $10-30 per form, or include year-end filing in an annual package. Show the form type, tax year, and number of forms on the invoice, and add any e-filing or mailing costs as a separate line.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a payroll invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, if it is in your signed service agreement and allowed in your state. Put the late fee on the invoice terms, and consider also stating that processing may be paused until fees are paid.

faqs.question: How should I bill for fixing a client's previous payroll mistakes?
faqs.answer: Treat it as separate project work. Quote an hourly rate or a flat fee after reviewing the records, and list it as its own line item with the periods corrected, so it is not mistaken for regular processing.

estimate.intro: Payroll services send a quote when a business is choosing a provider, switching from another one, or adding services such as multi-state payroll or HR support. Clients usually compare the per-run and per-employee prices, what filings are included, and whether there are hidden fees for year-end forms or off-cycle runs.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of employees and contractors, and pay frequency
scopeChecklist.why: Price depends on headcount and how often payroll runs. State the assumptions so you can reprice if they change.
List whether Form 941, state withholding, state unemployment, local taxes, W-2s, and 1099s are covered, and which are extra.
Multi-state payroll adds registration, filing, and compliance work that single-state quotes do not include.
Specify whether you enter year-to-date data, import from the old provider, and how many prior quarters you will reconcile.
Off-cycle runs, terminations, garnishments, agency notices, and corrections should have listed rates so clients are not surprised later.
State when hours and changes must be submitted before each run. Late data is a common cause of errors and rush fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract term, price review, and cancellation
scopeChecklist.why: Clients want to know the minimum commitment and when your fees can increase.

pricingTips.title: Quote a monthly all-in figure alongside the unit prices
pricingTips.body: Owners think in monthly cost. Show the per-run and per-employee math, then give the expected monthly total, noting the employee count it assumes.

pricingTips.title: Charge setup separately
pricingTips.body: Onboarding takes real time, especially when moving mid-year with year-to-date balances. A separate setup fee covers that work and keeps your recurring rate competitive.

pricingTips.title: Price in tiers by headcount
pricingTips.body: Tiers such as 1-5, 6-15, and 16-30 employees are simple to explain and give you a natural point to adjust fees as the client grows.

pricingTips.title: List software costs honestly
pricingTips.body: If you use payroll software, decide whether its cost is built into your rate or passed through. Either way, tell the client in the quote so the total is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How long should a payroll quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is typical. Quotes depend on headcount and the client's start date, so a limited validity period lets you update pricing if the scope or your costs change.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat monthly fee or per-run pricing?
faqs.answer: Flat monthly fees suit clients with steady headcount and a predictable pay schedule. Per-run pricing is better when pay frequency varies or when you are unsure about volume. Many firms offer both and let the client choose.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a quote before sharing employee details?
faqs.answer: Ask for headcount, pay frequency, and states at minimum. If they cannot provide it, give a price range and state that the final quote depends on those details.

faqs.question: Do I need to quote for cleaning up a prior provider's errors?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only after seeing the records. Quote the review first, then a separate estimate for corrections. Prior-period problems often turn out larger than they first appear.

penetration-tester.intro: Penetration testers are independent consultants and small security firms hired to find and demonstrate weaknesses in web applications, networks, cloud environments, and people before real attackers do. Invoices usually cover scoped testing engagements, retesting after fixes, and the written report. Clients are often software companies, healthcare and fintech firms, or businesses that need a test for SOC 2, PCI DSS, or HIPAA-related security work.
penetration-tester.pricingModel: Most pen testers price by scoped engagement, not by the hour, because clients want a fixed number they can get approved. The fee is built from estimated testing days times a day rate, plus reporting time, project management, and a retest. Scope drivers include the number of web app roles and endpoints, API count, IP addresses or hosts in range, wireless sites, cloud accounts, and whether social engineering is included. Hourly or daily billing is common for ad hoc work, advisory, remediation support, and out-of-scope requests. Some testers sell retainers for ongoing testing or quarterly retests. Travel for on-site internal or physical tests is billed separately at cost, and expenses such as cloud testing infrastructure or commercial scanner licenses are usually absorbed in the rate unless they are unusual.

rates.service: Web application penetration test (small to mid-size app)

items.description: Web application penetration test, customer portal and REST API (3 user roles), testing performed May 6-17
Written report with executive summary, findings, evidence, and remediation guidance
Findings walkthrough call with development team
Retest of remediated high and critical findings (completed June 3)
Additional testing of staging API endpoints added after kickoff (change order #1)

sampleInvoice.notes: Engagement performed under the Statement of Work and Rules of Engagement signed April 22, PO 48213. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Report and retest letter are confidential and provided to the named client contact only. ACH preferred.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed SOW, rules of engagement, and any authorization letter
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charges to written authorization and the agreed scope, which protects both sides if a dispute or an audit question comes up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Testing dates and target description (apps, IP ranges, or cloud accounts)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what was tested and when, and helps the client match the work to their compliance evidence window.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line items for testing, reporting, readouts, and retest
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often need to allocate cost or show a retest was completed, and separate lines make partial payments and approvals easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders or out-of-scope work with approval reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra endpoints, added hosts, or extended test windows are the most common source of invoice disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number and billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients often reject invoices without a PO or the correct accounts payable contact.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses such as travel, lodging, or hardware shipped for on-site tests
invoiceChecklist.why: Expense items should be itemized at cost with receipts available, as stated in the SOW.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, EIN or tax ID details as needed, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for the client to set you up as a vendor and file any required 1099 reporting.

penetration-tester.paymentTerms: Net 30 is the norm for companies, with Net 15 common for small clients. Many testers require 25-50% upfront at signing or before the test window starts, with the balance due on report delivery. Large or multi-phase engagements are sometimes split into milestones. Some testers hold the final report until payment clears, though this should be written into the contract and not used as a surprise. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the agreement. Payment is typically by ACH or wire, with cards used for smaller jobs and the processing fee sometimes passed on.

tips.title: Get written authorization before billing starts
tips.body: Never test without a signed SOW and authorization that confirms the client owns or controls the targets. This also covers third-party hosting or cloud providers. The same document is your basis for billing.

tips.title: Define what counts as a retest
tips.body: State how many days the client has for a free or discounted retest, how many rounds are included, and that new findings or changed code are billed separately. Without limits, retests tend to stretch indefinitely.

tips.title: Bill for report revisions with a cap
tips.body: Clients often ask for edits, rewording, or a second version for auditors. Include one round of revisions in the fee and bill additional rounds hourly.

tips.title: Invoice on delivery milestones
tips.body: Tie the final invoice to report delivery, not to the client's remediation. Clients can take months to fix issues, and you should not wait on their schedule to be paid.

tips.title: Document scope changes the day they happen
tips.body: If the client adds hosts, asks for an extra role, or extends the window, send a short written change order and bill it as its own line so it does not look like a surprise at the end.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or by the hour for a penetration test?
faqs.answer: Flat fees are standard for defined engagements because clients need a fixed budget and the scope is clear. Use hourly or daily rates for open-ended work, advisory, and anything out of scope.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for a pen test?
faqs.answer: Many testers invoice a deposit at signing and the balance when the report is delivered. For shorter jobs, a single invoice on report delivery is common. Put the schedule in the SOW.

faqs.question: Can I withhold the report until the client pays?
faqs.answer: You can if your contract says so. Many testers deliver a draft or summary and release the final signed report on payment. Make sure the client agrees to this before the work begins.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a retest?
faqs.answer: Either include a retest window in the original fee or list it as a separate line. A separate retest line, usually 10-25% of the original test price, keeps the first invoice clean and sets clear limits.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on penetration testing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain IT or security services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant before adding tax to invoices.

estimate.intro: Penetration testers send a proposal or quote after a scoping call and before any testing starts. Clients typically get quotes from two or three providers and compare price, methodology, timeline, report quality, and credentials. A clear scope is the main thing that separates a good quote from a vague one.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact targets: URLs, IP ranges, cloud accounts, apps, and user roles
scopeChecklist.why: The price depends on the size of the attack surface, and unclear targets lead to arguments about what was in scope.

scopeChecklist.item: Testing type and depth (black box, gray box, authenticated, credentialed)
scopeChecklist.why: Different levels of access change how much time is needed and what findings are likely.
Denial-of-service testing, social engineering, production data access, or third-party systems should be called out as included or excluded.

scopeChecklist.item: Testing window, hours, and client contacts for emergencies
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may limit testing to off-hours or specific dates, and you need a contact in case something breaks.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables: report format, readout, and compliance mapping
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know whether the report will satisfy an auditor, and whether a presentation or call is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Retest terms: number of rounds and time limit
scopeChecklist.why: Without a defined window, a retest request six months later can cause friction.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions about client readiness (test accounts, VPN access, allowlisting)
scopeChecklist.why: Delays caused by the client should extend the timeline or trigger additional charges.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in testing days, then convert to a fixed price
pricingTips.body: Break the job into scoping, testing, reporting, and readout days. Add a buffer of 10-20% for surprises. Present the total as a flat fee but keep the day count for pricing change orders.

pricingTips.title: Price by scope tiers
pricingTips.body: Offer a basic, standard, and extended option, such as unauthenticated only, authenticated with two roles, or full coverage with API testing. Clients can then choose based on budget and compliance needs.

pricingTips.title: State what changes the price
pricingTips.body: List the factors that will trigger a change order: additional hosts, more roles, major application changes during testing, or rescheduled test windows.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiry date
pricingTips.body: A 30-day validity period keeps you from honoring old pricing when your calendar is full or when the target environment has changed.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before a scoping call?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Rough ranges are fine, but a firm number needs details such as app size, number of roles, and IP count. A short scoping call or questionnaire gives you what you need.

faqs.question: How long should a pen test quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Testing calendars fill up and client environments change, so an expiry date protects your pricing and schedule.

faqs.question: Can I charge for scoping and proposal work?
faqs.answer: Short scoping calls are usually free. For complex environments that need architecture review or document analysis, some testers charge a paid scoping fee that is credited toward the test if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the actual work takes longer than I quoted?
faqs.answer: For a fixed fee, you absorb normal overruns. If the client changes scope or causes delays, send a change order. Your quote should list the assumptions that would justify extra charges.

personal-chef.intro: Personal chefs cook for private clients in their homes or prepare meals in their own licensed space and deliver them. Typical work includes weekly meal prep, in-home dinner parties, special diet cooking, and short-term help after a birth or surgery. Invoices usually combine a service fee with groceries and other costs passed through to the client.
personal-chef.pricingModel: Most personal chefs charge a service fee plus the actual cost of groceries, listed separately. The service fee is set per cook session (a weekly meal prep day of 4 to 6 hours), per meal or per portion, or per person for dinner parties and events. Some chefs use an hourly rate that covers shopping, cooking, packing, and cleanup, while others use a flat weekly package such as five dinners for a family of four. Groceries are billed at receipt cost, sometimes with a small handling markup of 0 to 15 percent that should be stated up front. Travel, specialty equipment rental, hired help such as a server or assistant, and containers are commonly itemized. Recurring clients often get a weekly or monthly rate, while one-off events usually carry a minimum fee and a deposit.

rates.service: Weekly meal prep session (4-6 hours, cooking at client's home)
Meal prep priced by portion (delivered or in-home)
In-home dinner party or multi-course tasting dinner
Grocery shopping when billed as a separate task
Server or kitchen assistant for events
Cooking class or private lesson in the client's home
Travel outside the normal service area

items.description: Weekly meal prep, 5 dinners for family of 4 (shopping, cooking, packing, kitchen cleanup)
Groceries per attached receipts (Whole Foods, farmers market)
Glass storage containers and labels
Additional gluten-free dessert, 8 portions
Mileage to second grocery stop

sampleInvoice.notes: Service week of March 10. Receipts attached for all grocery charges. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date by bank transfer, card, or check. Menus and reheating instructions were left in the refrigerator. Please give 48 hours notice to change or cancel a cook day.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cook date and menu summary
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which meals were delivered for which week, which settles questions about what was included in the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service fee listed separately from groceries
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see what they pay for your labor versus food cost, and separation makes disputes about price easier to resolve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized grocery receipts or total with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Passing through actual cost is only credible with proof, and clients often ask to see it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dietary and allergy notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Records that you prepared meals per agreed restrictions, which is useful if a question about an ingredient comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Handling markup, if any
invoiceChecklist.why: A grocery markup should be a visible line or a stated percentage so it is not mistaken for padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Extra charges: staff, rentals, travel, containers
invoiceChecklist.why: Costs outside the base fee are the most common source of surprise on a bill and should be itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license, food handler or ServSafe certification, and liability insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Local rules differ, and some clients or venues ask for proof. Listing your license number can help establish credibility.

personal-chef.paymentTerms: Recurring clients are usually invoiced weekly or biweekly with payment due in 3 to 7 days, or billed monthly in advance for a set number of cook days. For dinner parties and events, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is common, with the balance due before or on the event day. Many chefs require groceries to be reimbursed quickly or collect a grocery float up front so they are not financing the client's food. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are used by some, though a simple clear policy and a pause on service for unpaid invoices is often more effective. Payment is typically accepted by card, bank transfer, or check, and a short cancellation policy (24 to 72 hours notice) is standard.

tips.title: Collect a grocery float for new clients
tips.body: Ask for a prepaid amount, such as $200 to $400, to cover the first shops. This keeps you from carrying large grocery costs on your own card, and you can reconcile against receipts on each invoice.

tips.title: Bill shopping and planning time
tips.body: Menu planning, shopping, and travel are real labor. Build them into your session fee or list them as separate lines so clients understand why a 4-hour cook day costs more than 4 hours of cooking.

tips.title: Put cancellation terms on every invoice
tips.body: Since you buy ingredients ahead, a late cancellation costs you money. State the notice period and what you will charge if food has already been purchased.

tips.title: Charge more for complex diets
tips.body: Allergy-safe, keto, renal, or multi-diet households take extra care in sourcing, cross-contact prevention, and recipe development. A small surcharge or higher base fee is reasonable.

tips.title: Track mileage and receipts for taxes
tips.body: Business mileage and food purchases are items to track carefully. Ask your tax preparer how to treat client-reimbursed groceries so they are not counted twice.

faqs.question: Should I charge groceries separately or build them into my rate?
faqs.answer: Most personal chefs list groceries separately at actual cost, because food prices vary by menu and week. A flat all-inclusive price works for fixed packages, but you take on the risk of price increases. Whichever you pick, state it in your agreement.

faqs.question: Can I add a markup on groceries?
faqs.answer: Yes, many chefs add a modest handling fee, often 0 to 15 percent, to cover shopping logistics. Tell the client before the first job and show it as its own line, so it is clear and agreed in advance.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on my services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax prepared food or meal services, and some tax only the food, not labor. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant to see how your services are treated.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice a weekly client?
faqs.answer: Invoice at the end of each cook week, or at the start of the week for prepaid arrangements. Regular weekly billing keeps the amounts small, and it makes it easier to notice a late payment right away.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to cancel after I've bought the groceries?
faqs.answer: Your cancellation policy should cover this. Typically, you charge the service fee per policy and bill for any non-returnable ingredients. Offer to deliver the food to the client or to freeze it where that makes sense.

estimate.intro: Personal chefs send a quote before the first cook day for a new weekly client, and for any dinner party, holiday meal, or event. Clients usually compare per-meal cost, what is included in the fee, and how groceries are handled. A clear quote also helps them tell the difference between you and a meal delivery service.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meals, servings, and cook days
scopeChecklist.why: Defines the core deliverable, such as five dinners for four people, so a request for extra portions can be priced as an add-on.

scopeChecklist.item: Menu approach and how many revisions are included
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether the client picks from a set menu, shares preferences, or gets custom menus each week.
Special diets affect ingredients, cost, and time, and should be documented from the start.
State whether groceries are billed at cost, with a markup, or included in the fee, and whether there is a prepaid float.
Cooking in the client's kitchen may require you to bring knives, pans, or small appliances, and a poorly equipped kitchen can add time.
Say whether the kitchen will be left clean, and who pays for storage containers, which can be a recurring cost.
For parties, state the service window, guest count cutoff, whether servers are included, and who provides plates, glassware, and tables.

pricingTips.title: Start from your target hourly income
pricingTips.body: Add shopping, prep, cooking, packing, cleanup, and travel to estimate total hours for a session. Divide your desired earnings by those hours to confirm that your per-session or per-portion price works.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present options such as three, four, or five dinners a week, with a lower per-meal price as volume increases. Clients can compare the choices easily, and many pick the middle one.

pricingTips.title: Quote events per person with a minimum
pricingTips.body: A per-person price with a minimum total protects you when the guest list is small, since shopping and setup take the same effort for 4 guests as for 8.

pricingTips.title: Give a grocery estimate range
pricingTips.body: Estimate food cost as a range, for example $150 to $220 per week, and state that the final amount follows receipts. That sets expectations without locking you into a price that rising costs could undercut.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a consultation or tasting?
faqs.answer: Many chefs offer a free 20 to 30 minute call, then charge for a tasting menu or in-person consultation, typically $75 to $200, and credit it toward the first booking if the client signs on.

faqs.question: How long is a quote valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical for events, because ingredient costs and your calendar can shift. For ongoing meal prep, state a start date and hold the price for a stated period, such as 3 months.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: A written agreement is a good idea, especially for recurring work and events. It can include the quote, menu, grocery policy, cancellation terms, and allergy disclosures. Check local rules and consider having a lawyer review a template.

faqs.question: What if the final grocery cost is higher than my estimate?
faqs.answer: If you gave a range and the total falls outside it, tell the client before you buy. Written approval by text or email for a large overage helps avoid disagreement later.

personal-trainer.intro: Personal trainers bill clients for one-on-one and small-group fitness sessions, usually in gyms, private studios, client homes, or online. Invoices typically cover session packages, monthly training memberships, assessments, and program design. Many trainers are independent contractors or run their own small business, so clear billing records matter for both cash flow and taxes.
personal-trainer.pricingModel: Most trainers charge per session, with a discount when clients prepay for a package of 5, 10, or 20 sessions. Others bill a flat monthly rate for a set number of sessions per week, which smooths income and reduces no-show disputes. Small-group training is priced per person at a lower rate than one-on-one, while online coaching is often a monthly fee covering a custom program, check-ins, and app access. Initial assessments and program-only writing are commonly billed separately as flat fees. Trainers who rent gym floor space or pay a facility fee may build that cost into their session rate. Rates depend heavily on region, certification level, specialty (such as post-rehab or sports performance), and session length (30, 45, or 60 minutes).

rates.service: Initial fitness assessment and goal setting

items.description: Initial fitness assessment and goal setting (Mar 3)
One-on-one training session, 60 min, 10-session package (Mar 3 - Apr 10)
Custom 8-week strength program with written plan and updates
In-home session travel surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Package sessions expire 90 days from purchase date. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are charged in full. Accepted: card, Zelle, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget which sessions occurred, and dated entries settle questions about no-shows and package usage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and sessions remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing how many sessions were purchased, used, and left prevents disputes over balances and expiration.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session length and format
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ for 30 vs. 60 minutes and for one-on-one vs. small group, so each line should state which applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Location or facility fee
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge extra for in-home visits, travel, or gym floor rental, listing it separately keeps your base rate clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and late-cancel charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing a late-cancel or no-show fee with the date it happened ties it to your stated policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package expiration date
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the expiry on the invoice makes the term part of the agreement the client paid under.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, certification, and contact info
invoiceChecklist.why: Certification (such as NASM, ACE, or NSCA) and a business name make the invoice look professional and help with insurance or reimbursement paperwork.

personal-trainer.paymentTerms: Most trainers collect payment before training, since the service cannot be taken back once delivered. Packages and monthly memberships are usually paid in full upfront or on the first session of the month, with automatic card billing common for recurring clients. For one-off invoices such as assessments or program design, due on receipt or net 7 is typical. A 24-hour cancellation policy is standard, with the late-cancel session charged at the full or half rate. Late fees, if used, are often a flat $10-25 or 1.5% per month, and should be written in your client agreement before they apply. Common payment methods include credit and debit cards, ACH transfer, Zelle, Venmo or similar apps, and checks.

tips.title: Sell packages, not single sessions
tips.body: Prepaid packages of 10 or 20 sessions improve commitment and cash flow. Offer a modest discount, such as 5-10% off the single-session price, and set an expiration date so unused sessions do not carry forever.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: Have clients sign or acknowledge a 24-hour cancellation policy before the first session. When a late cancel occurs, list it on the invoice with the date so the charge is easy to explain.

tips.title: Track sessions as you go
tips.body: Keep a simple log of dates, session type, and package balance after every workout. Invoices built from a running log are accurate and rarely questioned.

tips.title: Separate taxable and non-taxable items where required
tips.body: Some states charge sales tax on certain fitness services or on products like supplements or equipment. Check your state and local rules, and list product sales on their own line.

tips.title: Bill monthly for recurring clients
tips.body: A flat monthly fee for a set number of weekly sessions reduces invoicing work and makes your income predictable. State what happens to missed sessions, whether they roll over or are forfeited.

faqs.question: Should I charge per session or per month?
faqs.answer: Both work. Per-session pricing is flexible for clients with unpredictable schedules, while monthly pricing gives you steady income and fewer billing conversations. Many trainers offer monthly plans to regular clients and per-session or package rates to everyone else.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on training sessions?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax fitness or gym services, while many do not tax personal training. Product sales such as supplements or equipment are more commonly taxable. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What should I do about clients who skip sessions without notice?
faqs.answer: Follow the cancellation policy you gave them in advance. Most trainers charge the full session for no-shows and late cancels, and some allow one courtesy waiver. Document the date on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I invoice if I work out of someone else's gym?
faqs.answer: Yes, but check your agreement with the gym. Some gyms require trainers to pay a rental or revenue split and may restrict how you collect from clients. Your invoice should reflect your own agreed rates with the client, not the gym's internal arrangement.

faqs.question: Should I refund unused sessions?
faqs.answer: Set this in your terms before the sale. Common policies are no refunds on opened packages, a prorated refund minus the package discount, or a credit toward future sessions. A written policy prevents arguments later.

estimate.intro: Trainers send quotes or proposals when a prospect asks about pricing, wants a custom package, or is comparing you against other trainers or gym membership add-ons. Small-group programs, corporate wellness sessions, and event-based training such as wedding prep or race training also call for a written quote. Clients usually compare session price, number of sessions, what is included, and cancellation terms.

scopeChecklist.why: A quote for 12 sessions at 45 minutes is a different product than 12 at 60 minutes, so state both.

scopeChecklist.item: Training location and any facility fees
scopeChecklist.why: Gym access, studio rental, or travel to a client's home can change your cost, and the client should know who pays for it.
Spell out assessments, written programs, between-session messaging, meal guidance, and progress check-ins so clients know what the price covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, schedule, and package expiration
