scopeChecklist.why: A clear time window avoids disputes when clients stretch a package over many months.
Stating the notice period and the charge for late cancels up front makes the policy enforceable.
Many trainers require a health questionnaire (such as the PAR-Q) and a signed waiver, and the quote should say they are needed before training starts.
Spell out whether payment is due in full upfront or monthly so there is no confusion at the first session.

pricingTips.title: Quote a package price with the per-session math shown
pricingTips.body: List the total and the effective per-session rate, such as 20 sessions at $65 each for $1,300. Clients can see the discount versus your single-session price.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: For example, two sessions per week, three sessions per week, and a hybrid of one in-person plus online coaching. Tiers give clients a choice other than yes or no, and many pick the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Price for your real hourly take-home
pricingTips.body: Count setup, travel, programming time, messaging, and cancellations, not just the hour on the floor. If program writing takes an hour per client per month, include it in the price.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 14 to 30 days keeps pricing current when your schedule or rates change and encourages decisions.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the initial consultation or assessment?
faqs.answer: Either approach is common. Many trainers offer a free 15 to 30 minute consult to discuss goals, then charge for a full fitness assessment. If you charge for it, say so in the quote and consider crediting the fee toward a package.

faqs.question: How do I quote for a small group or corporate client?
faqs.answer: Quote per person per session for small groups, with a minimum group fee. For corporate work, quote a flat rate per class or per month, and list headcount limits, location, equipment provided, and who handles scheduling.

faqs.question: Can I change my quoted price after a client signs?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. You can raise rates for new packages or after a package ends, with advance notice. If the client adds sessions or services, send a revised quote for the added work.

pest-control.intro: Pest control operators, from solo technicians to small multi-truck companies, bill homeowners, landlords, property managers, and small businesses for inspections, one-time treatments, recurring service plans, and specialty work like termite and wildlife exclusion. Invoices cover labor, products applied, and often a warranty or retreatment period.
pest-control.pricingModel: Most residential general pest work is priced as a flat fee per visit or as a recurring plan (monthly, bimonthly, or quarterly) with an initial setup visit that costs more than follow-ups. Price usually scales with home square footage, lot size, and pest pressure. Specialty jobs are quoted individually: termite treatments by linear foot of foundation, bed bug heat or chemical treatments by room or by home size, rodent exclusion by hour plus materials, and wildlife removal by trap visit plus repairs. Commercial accounts like restaurants and property managers are usually billed on a monthly contract with extra charges for call-backs. Many operators also charge separately for materials such as bait stations, exclusion mesh, and monitoring devices, and offer a discount for prepaying an annual plan.

rates.service: Initial general pest treatment (interior and exterior)
Ant, roach, or spider one-time treatment

items.description: Initial general pest treatment, interior and exterior perimeter, 2,200 sq ft home
Rodent exclusion: seal entry points with steel wool and copper mesh (technician labor)
Exclusion materials (mesh, sealant, door sweeps)
Snap trap placement and set-up, attic and garage (6 traps)
Wasp nest removal, eave of rear porch

sampleInvoice.notes: Service performed 3/12. Products applied are listed on the attached service report. 30-day retreatment guarantee on general pest treatment, provided the property is not disturbed in treated areas. Payment due within 14 days. Please pay by check, card, or bank transfer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service date, arrival time, and technician name
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives a record of exactly when treatment happened, which matters for warranty periods and any later dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Applicator license or certification number
invoiceChecklist.why: Pesticide application is regulated, and in many states the license number must appear on service records and sometimes on customer paperwork. Check your state agriculture department rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Products applied, EPA registration numbers, and amounts used
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require application records be kept and given to the customer on request. Attaching or referencing the service report covers this.

invoiceChecklist.item: Areas treated and pests targeted
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies scope so the customer knows what was and wasn't covered if a different pest appears later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty or retreatment terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States how long the guarantee lasts, what triggers a free return visit, and what voids it, such as clutter or missed prep steps.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Exclusion supplies, bait stations, and monitors are often billed apart, and itemizing prevents questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring plan details and next scheduled visit
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the plan frequency, price per visit, and cancellation terms so customers on contract know when the next charge and service are coming.

pest-control.paymentTerms: One-time residential jobs are commonly paid at the time of service by card or check, or invoiced as due on receipt or net 14. Recurring plans are often charged automatically per visit or billed monthly or annually, with a prepay discount. Large jobs such as termite barrier treatments, bed bug heat treatments, or wildlife exclusion typically take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials and scheduling, with the balance due on completion. Commercial accounts are usually net 15 to net 30. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing on the agreement or invoice. Accept cards, ACH, and checks, since many property managers pay by check or ACH.

tips.title: Charge more for the first visit
tips.body: The initial service takes longer, uses more product, and includes inspection and sealing recommendations. Price it separately from the follow-up visits and say so on the quote and invoice.

tips.title: Put warranty terms in writing on every invoice
tips.body: Most disputes are about whether a pest returning after 20 days is covered. State the guarantee period and conditions so there is no argument.

tips.title: Bill for call-backs outside the guarantee
tips.body: Set a clear policy for return visits after the warranty ends or when the customer has not done prep like laundering bedding or clearing storage. Add a trip charge line item so the cost is not absorbed.

tips.title: Get recurring plans on automatic payment
tips.body: Quarterly customers are easy to forget to invoice and easy to forget to pay. A card or bank draft on file with signed authorization reduces chasing and missed revenue.

tips.title: Track chemical and materials cost per job
tips.body: Termite and rodent jobs can use a lot of product and exclusion material. Knowing the cost per job helps you set flat fees that still leave margin.

faqs.question: Do I need to list the pesticides I used on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary by state, but most states require licensed applicators to keep application records, and many require that customers receive them. The simplest approach is to attach or reference a service report that lists products, EPA registration numbers, amounts, and target pests, and keep a copy for the period your state requires.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on pest control services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax pest control as a service, some tax only materials, and some do not tax it at all. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant and show tax as its own line when it applies.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a recurring service plan?
faqs.answer: Agree on frequency, price per visit, and term in a signed service agreement. Then either bill per visit after each service, bill monthly or annually in advance, or charge a card on file automatically. Each invoice should show the service date and the next scheduled visit.

faqs.question: Can I charge a trip fee if no one is home or access is blocked?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement or quote states it ahead of time. Put the fee amount and the conditions in writing, and itemize it on the invoice when you charge it.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a termite or bed bug job?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common for larger jobs, since you buy product and block out time on your schedule. Put the deposit and balance due date on the quote and show the deposit as a credit on the final invoice.

estimate.intro: Pest control operators send estimates for one-time specialty jobs and before enrolling a customer in a recurring plan. Termite treatments, bed bug removal, rodent exclusion, and wildlife work are almost always quoted after an inspection. Customers usually compare the total price, the method used, how long the guarantee lasts, and whether follow-up visits are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Target pest and findings from the inspection
scopeChecklist.why: Naming the pest and the evidence you found, such as droppings, mud tubes, or live bugs, shows the quote is based on the actual problem and not a guess.
Heat versus chemical, bait versus liquid barrier, interior versus perimeter. Customers compare methods, and the scope sets what is and is not included.
Bed bug and roach jobs often need two or three visits. Stating how many are in the price prevents surprise charges for follow-ups.
Laundering, clearing closets, moving furniture, or leaving pets out of the home can determine whether treatment works. Say the guarantee depends on completing prep.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions and conditions you may find on site
scopeChecklist.why: Hidden damage, inaccessible crawl spaces, or structural repairs needed for exclusion work may change the price. List what is not covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Guarantee period and what voids it
scopeChecklist.why: Sets the retreatment window and the conditions, which is the most common source of customer disputes after the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Price, deposit, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a clear total, when payment is due, and how long the price is valid, since product costs and your schedule change.

pricingTips.title: Price by the method, not just the pest
pricingTips.body: A heat treatment, a chemical treatment, and a bait system for the same pest have very different labor, equipment, and product costs. Quote each option separately if the customer has a choice.

pricingTips.title: Use per-foot or per-room pricing where it fits
pricingTips.body: Termite barrier work is commonly priced per linear foot and bed bug work per room. Showing the unit and quantity makes the total easy to understand and easy to adjust if scope changes.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: For example, a one-time treatment, a treatment with a 90-day guarantee, and an annual plan with quarterly visits. Many customers choose the middle or highest option when they can see the difference.

pricingTips.title: Quote materials and labor separately on exclusion work
pricingTips.body: Rodent exclusion can vary widely depending on how many entry points you find. Listing hourly labor and a materials allowance lets you adjust if the job grows.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an inspection before giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Many companies do inspections for free on general pest and termite work and charge for detailed ones such as bed bug or wildlife inspections, often $75 to $200. If you charge, say so when booking and consider crediting the fee toward the job if the customer accepts the quote.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: For general pest control on a typical home, a phone or online quote based on square footage is common. For termites, bed bugs, rodents, or wildlife, quote only after an inspection because the scope can change a lot once you see the property.

faqs.question: How long should a pest control quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. For active infestations like bed bugs or termites, a shorter window such as 14 days is reasonable since conditions and your schedule can change.

faqs.question: What if I find more problems after the customer accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Write into the quote that hidden conditions, such as additional entry points or a second infestation area, may change the price. If it happens, send a written change order with the added cost before doing the extra work.

pet-boarding.intro: Pet boarding businesses include home-based boarders, kennel operators, and small facilities that house dogs, cats, and sometimes small animals while owners travel or are away. Invoices usually cover nightly boarding, add-on services like medication or bathing, and extras such as holiday surcharges or late pickup fees. Most operators are solo or run a small team, and they bill after the stay ends or collect payment at drop-off or pickup.
pet-boarding.pricingModel: Most boarders charge a flat nightly rate per pet, with a lower rate for each additional pet from the same household sharing a space. Rates vary by species, size, and whether the pet stays in a kennel run, a suite, or inside your home. Add-ons are usually priced per item or per day: medication administration, extra walks, playgroups, grooming or baths, and special diets. Many businesses charge a holiday surcharge, often $5-20 per night, on peak dates like Thanksgiving, Christmas, and the Fourth of July. Some bill by the calendar day (any part of a day counts as a night), while others bill by the night and charge a half-day or day-care fee for late pickup. Long-stay discounts for 7 or 14+ nights are common. Deposits or full prepayment during peak season help protect against cancellations and no-shows.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pet names, species, and breed
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear which animal each line item applies to, which matters when a household has several pets with different services.

invoiceChecklist.item: Exact check-in and check-out dates and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Nights are the main billing unit, and disputes often come down to when the pet arrived or left, especially with late pickups.

invoiceChecklist.item: Nightly rate and number of nights per pet
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the total was calculated, including any multi-pet or long-stay discount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and medications
invoiceChecklist.why: Medication, extra walks, baths, and special diets are billed separately and should be easy to match against the care instructions the owner gave you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Holiday or peak-date surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the dates it applies to avoids surprises, and should match what was in your booking policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit paid and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners want to see their deposit credited, and it gives you a clear record of what was already collected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license or permit number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many cities and counties require a kennel or animal boarding license. Check your local rules on whether it should appear on customer documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vet expenses or emergency costs, with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: If you took a pet to a vet under your authorization form, list the cost as a pass-through so the owner can see exactly what was spent.

pet-boarding.paymentTerms: Boarders commonly require a deposit of 25-50% at booking, or full prepayment for holiday and peak-season stays, with the balance due at pickup. Deposits are often non-refundable or refundable only with 48-72 hours of notice, so state your cancellation policy in writing. Many businesses ask for a card on file to cover add-ons, emergency vet costs, and unpaid balances. Late pickup fees, often a half or full night charge, should be spelled out in your boarding agreement. Common payment methods are credit and debit cards, Venmo, Zelle, and cash. If a balance is still unpaid after a set period, such as 7-14 days, some businesses add a late fee or hold future bookings until it is resolved.

tips.title: Define what counts as a night
tips.body: Decide whether you bill by the calendar night or by 24-hour periods, and state a check-out cutoff time such as 11:00 AM or noon. Put it on your booking confirmation and on every invoice so late pickups are billed consistently.

tips.title: Get vet authorization in writing
tips.body: Have owners sign a form that authorizes emergency care, names their vet, and sets a spending limit. When you invoice for vet costs, attach the receipt and bill the exact amount so there is no question about markup.

tips.title: Bill holidays and peak dates differently
tips.body: Set a clear list of holiday dates, require minimum stays around them, and collect full prepayment. Peak weekends fill quickly, and last-minute cancellations are expensive to replace.

tips.title: Charge for the care a pet actually needs
tips.body: Pets with medication schedules, special diets, or separation anxiety take more time. Price those add-ons per day or per dose instead of absorbing the work into the nightly rate.

tips.title: Keep vaccination records on file
tips.body: Most boarders require current rabies, DHPP or distemper, and often Bordetella for dogs. If records are missing, you can decline the booking or charge a fee for handling the paperwork, but say so in your policy before the stay.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit for pet boarding?
faqs.answer: Yes, most boarders do. A deposit of 25-50% at booking is typical, and many require full prepayment for holidays. It reduces no-shows and covers the income you lose when a reserved spot goes unfilled.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a pet that is picked up early?
faqs.answer: That depends on your policy. Many businesses bill the full reserved stay because the space was held, while others refund unused nights beyond a notice window. Whatever you choose, put it in your boarding agreement and apply it the same way each time.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on pet boarding?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax pet boarding or animal care services, and others do not. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant before adding or omitting sales tax.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for a second pet in the same household?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most boarders charge a discounted rate for a second pet sharing the same space, often $20-40 less per night than the first pet. Pets housed separately are usually billed at the full rate.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client won't pay after pickup?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder with the invoice, the signed boarding agreement, and your late fee terms. If you have a card on file with authorization for unpaid balances, you can charge it per your agreement. For larger balances, small claims court is an option, and a signed agreement makes your case stronger.

estimate.intro: Pet boarders send quotes when a client is booking a longer stay, boarding multiple pets, or has special needs like medication or a senior dog with mobility issues. Clients usually compare nightly rates, what is included, and extras such as playtime and exit baths between a few facilities or home boarders.

scopeChecklist.item: Dates and times of the stay
scopeChecklist.why: Check-in and check-out times affect the number of nights billed, and a stay that spans a holiday may include a surcharge.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of pets, species, and size
scopeChecklist.why: Rates often vary by size and species, and multi-pet discounts depend on pets sharing a space.
A standard run, private suite, and in-home stay carry different rates, and owners should know exactly which one they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the nightly rate
scopeChecklist.why: List meals, walks, playtime, bedding, and updates so clients can compare accurately and know which services cost extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Add-on services and how they are priced
scopeChecklist.why: Medication, special diets, baths, and extra walks are billed separately, and clients should see the per-unit price before they agree.
Stating required vaccines and any temperament evaluation up front avoids last-minute cancellations or refused check-ins.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation, and late pickup terms
scopeChecklist.why: Putting these in the quote means the client has agreed to them before booking and you can enforce them later.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total, not only a nightly rate
pricingTips.body: Add up nights, additional pets, expected add-ons, and any holiday surcharge into one estimated total. Clients compare totals, and a clear number avoids confusion at pickup.

pricingTips.title: Offer a long-stay discount openly
pricingTips.body: A modest discount of 5-10% for stays of 7 or more nights keeps longer bookings steady. List it as a line item so the client sees the savings.

pricingTips.title: Price special care by the task
pricingTips.body: For pets with insulin, multiple daily medications, or mobility needs, charge per dose or per day. This covers the extra time and stays fair if the pet's needs change.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration on the quote
pricingTips.body: Quotes for peak dates should expire in a few days to a week, since spots fill fast. Say clearly that dates are not held until the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: Should I give a free meet-and-greet before quoting?
faqs.answer: Many boarders do, especially for dogs. It lets you assess temperament and needs before committing to a price. Some charge a small evaluation fee or credit it toward the first stay.

faqs.question: Is a boarding estimate binding?
faqs.answer: A quote is generally an estimate of the expected total. State that the final bill may change if the stay is extended, if the pet needs extra care, or if emergency costs come up. Stay inside the quote when the circumstances are the same.

faqs.question: How do I quote a stay when the owner's return date is uncertain?
faqs.answer: Quote the nightly rate with a minimum number of nights and state that additional nights are billed at the same rate, or the holiday rate if applicable. Ask for a card on file to cover extended stays.

faqs.question: Do I need to give separate quotes for each pet?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. One quote can list each pet with its own rate and add-ons, then show a combined total. This keeps the paperwork simple and makes multi-pet discounts easy to see.

pet-daycare.intro: Pet daycare owners care for dogs (and sometimes cats) during the day while owners work or travel. Invoices usually cover full-day and half-day attendance, multi-day packages, overnight boarding add-ons, and extras like baths, training sessions, or medication handling. Most operators bill families on a recurring basis, so clear invoices help avoid disputes over attendance and package balances.
pet-daycare.pricingModel: Most daycares charge a flat rate per dog per day, with a lower rate for half days (usually under 4 to 5 hours). Multi-day packages (5, 10, or 20 days) are sold at a discount and paid upfront, with the balance tracked as days are used. Monthly unlimited or set-schedule memberships are common for regular clients. Boarding is priced per night, often with a daycare discount for existing clients. Add-ons such as baths, nail trims, feeding, medication, one-on-one play, or training are billed as separate line items. Many facilities charge extra for late pickup, multi-dog households get a small discount on the second dog, and some charge a one-time evaluation or temperament assessment fee for new dogs. Holiday surcharges are typical for peak dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dog's name and owner's name
invoiceChecklist.why: Households often have several dogs or more than one person paying, so each charge needs to be tied to the right animal and account.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates attended, with full-day or half-day marked
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute attendance more than rates. A dated list lets them match charges to their own calendar.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance (days purchased, used, remaining)
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages are a liability on your books and a common question from clients. Showing the balance prevents confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Boarding check-in and check-out dates and number of nights
invoiceChecklist.why: Nights are counted differently across facilities. Spell out the count and any daycare charge on departure day.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and extras (baths, medication, training, late pickup)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show what was optional and make surcharges easier to justify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Multi-dog or loyalty discounts applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the discount as its own line makes the pricing visible and avoids questions about why a rate differs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late pickup times and your posted closing time
invoiceChecklist.why: A fee with the actual arrival time next to it is far easier to collect than a bare surcharge.

pet-daycare.paymentTerms: Many daycares collect payment upfront for packages and monthly memberships, and bill drop-in days at the end of the week or month. Boarding often requires a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking, with holiday dates sometimes requiring full prepayment. Due dates are typically due on receipt to net 7 for attendance invoices. A late fee or account hold after 14 days is common, as long as it is stated in your service agreement. Card on file with auto-pay is the most common method because it handles recurring billing and last-minute add-ons, with ACH, checks, and cash also accepted. State your cancellation and no-show policy in writing, especially for boarding and holidays.

tips.title: Put your closing time and late fee in the service agreement
tips.body: Late pickups are one of the most common disputes. Have clients sign a policy that states closing time, the grace period, and the fee, then reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Track packages by days used, not dollars
tips.body: Show purchased, used, and remaining days on each invoice. Decide up front whether packages expire, whether they can be shared among a household's dogs, and whether they are refundable, and write it down.

tips.title: Charge for evaluations
tips.body: A temperament evaluation takes staff time and often a half day of supervision. A small fee, or a fee credited toward the first package, covers the cost and filters out casual inquiries.

tips.title: Bill add-ons the same day
tips.body: Baths, medication, and extra play sessions are easy to forget if you wait until month end. Log them daily so they land on the next invoice.

tips.title: Use a card on file for recurring clients
tips.body: Weekly or monthly auto-pay reduces chasing payments and lets you collect holiday and peak-season charges without separate requests.

faqs.question: Should I charge for days a dog is scheduled but doesn't show?
faqs.answer: Many daycares do, particularly for recurring schedules and holidays, because the spot was held. If you do, state a cancellation window (often 12 to 24 hours) in your agreement and charge full or reduced rate for late cancellations and no-shows.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a daycare package?
faqs.answer: Invoice the package as a single line item when it is purchased, such as 10-day daycare package at a set price. On later invoices or account statements, show days used and days remaining rather than charging again.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on pet daycare?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax pet boarding or grooming services and others do not, and rules can differ for daycare versus boarding. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant before setting up tax on invoices.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee for overdue invoices?
faqs.answer: In most places yes, if you disclosed it in advance in a signed agreement or on your invoice terms. Keep the amount reasonable, state when it applies, and check any local limits on late fees.

faqs.question: How should I bill a second dog from the same household?
faqs.answer: A common approach is a discount of 10 to 15 percent on the second dog, shown as a separate discount line or as a lower rate for that dog. Make sure each dog is listed by name so attendance is clear.

estimate.intro: Pet daycares send estimates mostly for boarding stays, holiday bookings, multi-dog households, and recurring schedule or membership pricing. Clients comparing facilities look at the daily rate, what is included, and extra charges such as late pickup, add-ons, and cancellation fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Dates and type of care (daycare days, half days, boarding nights)
scopeChecklist.why: Dates determine rates, especially around holidays, and confirm the spot is reserved for those days.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of dogs and their names
scopeChecklist.why: Multi-dog pricing and capacity depend on how many animals are coming, and it avoids a surprise when a second dog shows up.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the daily rate
scopeChecklist.why: Make clear whether meals, treats, play groups, webcam access, and basic enrichment are included or extra.
Dogs usually need a passed temperament evaluation and current rabies, DHPP, and often bordetella vaccines. A dog turned away without these should not become a billing dispute.
Baths, medication, training, and one-on-one time are optional extras. Listing prices up front prevents surprise charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Cancellation, no-show, and late pickup policies
scopeChecklist.why: These are the most common sources of disagreement, and clients should see the fees before they commit.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount and when full payment is due
scopeChecklist.why: A clear deposit and payment schedule protects you from last-minute cancellations, especially in peak periods.

pricingTips.title: Quote peak dates separately
pricingTips.body: Holidays and school breaks fill quickly. List a holiday surcharge or minimum stay as its own line so clients see why the rate differs from normal weeks.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package comparison
pricingTips.body: For regular clients, show the pay-per-day price next to a 10 or 20-day package price and a monthly option. Clients usually choose the one that fits their schedule when they can see the savings.

pricingTips.title: Set realistic capacity rates
pricingTips.body: Price based on your staff-to-dog ratio and the space you have, not just competitors. A rate that works only when you are at full capacity leaves no room for slow weeks.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Rates and availability change. A quote valid for 14 to 30 days, or until the dates are booked, keeps you from honoring old prices.

faqs.question: Do I need to give a written estimate for daycare?
faqs.answer: For standard daycare, a posted price list is often enough. A written estimate is useful for boarding stays, holiday bookings, multiple dogs, and anything with add-ons, since the total is higher and more variable.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit when I send a boarding estimate?
faqs.answer: Many facilities do, often 25 to 50 percent, and full prepayment for holidays. Include the deposit amount and the refund terms on the estimate so it is agreed before the booking is confirmed.

faqs.question: What if a dog fails the temperament evaluation?
faqs.answer: State in your estimate and agreement what happens. Many facilities keep the evaluation fee and refund any deposits or package payments. Whatever your policy is, put it in writing before the evaluation.

pet-groomer.intro: Pet groomers run salons, mobile vans, or home-based studios and bill dog and cat owners for baths, haircuts, nail care, and add-on treatments. Most invoices are for a single appointment, though some groomers also bill for prepaid packages, recurring schedules, and boarding or daycare clients who add grooming to a stay.
pet-groomer.pricingModel: Most groomers price per appointment, with a base price set by breed or weight class and then adjusted with add-ons. Common add-ons include de-shedding, teeth brushing, blueberry facials, flea and tick treatments, and medicated shampoos. Surcharges are normal for matted coats, extra-large or double-coated breeds, aggressive or anxious animals that need extra handling, and senior pets that need frequent breaks. Matting is usually billed as a dematting fee per 15 minutes or as a flat fee, and severe cases may require a shave-down at a higher price. Mobile groomers typically charge 20 to 40 percent more than salons to cover the van, fuel, and travel time, and may add a trip fee outside a set radius. Many groomers offer discounted multi-pet pricing or prepaid packages of four to six visits, and some charge a hourly rate for specialty work like creative grooming or show trims.
