sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due at pickup. Cash, card, and Venmo accepted. Next appointment recommended in 6 weeks. Matting fees are charged when coat condition requires extra time. Rabies vaccination records on file expire 09/2025.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pet name, breed, and weight
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing is tied to breed and size, so listing them backs up the base price if a client questions the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Appointment date and service performed
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners with recurring appointments need a clear record, and it helps you track grooming history for each pet.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and surcharges
invoiceChecklist.why: Dematting, de-shedding, and handling fees are the charges clients dispute most, so list each one separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Matting or coat condition note
invoiceChecklist.why: A short note such as 'severe matting on hindquarters' explains the extra charge and may justify a shorter trim than the owner requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: Multi-pet discounts or package credits
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how a discount or prepaid session was applied and how many visits remain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tip line or suggested gratuity
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients tip, and having a line for it keeps your income records accurate for tax time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vaccination status or record expiry
invoiceChecklist.why: Many groomers require current rabies vaccination, and noting it protects you if a health or bite issue comes up later.

pet-groomer.paymentTerms: Most groomers collect payment at pickup, so the invoice acts as a receipt and due-on-receipt is standard. Mobile groomers often charge the card on file after the appointment. For new clients, large dogs, or long sessions, a deposit of $15 to $30 or 25 to 50 percent of the service is common, particularly during holidays. Many shops charge a no-show or late-cancellation fee of 50 to 100 percent of the service if less than 24 hours' notice is given. Late pickup fees, often $1 to $2 per minute after a set grace period, are common in salons. Accepted methods usually include cards, cash, and mobile payment apps. For prepaid packages, state the expiry date and the refund policy up front.

tips.title: Charge for time, not only breed
tips.body: Two dogs of the same breed can take very different amounts of time. Set a base price for a well-kept coat and bill dematting or extra handling separately so a neglected coat does not cost you the margin.

tips.title: Get approval before big extras
tips.body: If you find heavy matting or a skin issue mid-groom, call or text the owner before proceeding with a shave-down or added treatment. Record the approval so the invoice matches what they agreed to.

tips.title: Keep a written cancellation policy
tips.body: Send your no-show and late-cancellation fees when the client first books. Charging a fee is easier when the policy was agreed in writing and printed on the invoice.

tips.title: Track repeat clients by schedule
tips.body: Recurring clients on 4, 6, or 8 week cycles are your steadiest income. Use consistent line items so their invoices are easy to compare and you can raise prices at a predictable time.

tips.title: Raise prices on a set schedule
tips.body: Product, insurance, and rent rise every year. Review prices once or twice a year and give existing clients 30 days' notice of the change.

faqs.question: Should I charge by breed or by weight?
faqs.answer: Either works. Many groomers use weight classes for simplicity and add breed-specific pricing for high-maintenance coats such as poodles, doodles, and double-coated breeds. Whatever you pick, list it on your price sheet and put the pet's breed and weight on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for matted dogs?
faqs.answer: Charge a separate dematting line, either per 15 minutes or as a flat fee, and explain it to the owner before starting. If the coat is too matted to brush out without hurting the dog, a shave-down is usually safer, and you should get the owner's agreement first.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on grooming?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax pet grooming services, some do not, and retail items like shampoo or treats are often taxable. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant and list tax as a separate line if it applies.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for aggressive or difficult dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes, many groomers add a handling surcharge for dogs that need extra time, a second person, or muzzling. Tell the owner about the fee when you book or before starting, and list it separately on the invoice.

faqs.question: How should I handle tips on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Include an optional tip line or let clients add a tip when paying by card. Tips are generally taxable income, so record them. If you have employees, check the rules on reporting and distributing tips.

estimate.intro: Groomers give quotes when a new client calls or messages with a photo, when a dog has a heavily matted or overgrown coat, or when the job is outside the normal menu, such as a mobile visit to a multi-dog household. Owners often compare your price to other local groomers, so the quote should say what is included and what could change the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Pet breed, weight, and coat condition
scopeChecklist.why: These drive the price, and coat condition is the main reason final bills differ from quotes.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included in the base price
scopeChecklist.why: State whether bath, blow dry, haircut, nail trim, ear cleaning, and anal gland expression are included so owners know what the base price covers.
Explain that matting is charged extra and that severe matting may require a shave-down, so the owner is not surprised.
A breed-standard cut and a detailed scissor style take different amounts of time, and a written style prevents arguments about the result.
Listing de-shedding, teeth brushing, and special shampoos with prices makes it easy for owners to say yes before the groom starts.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated time and drop-off or pickup window
scopeChecklist.why: Owners need to know how long the dog will be with you, and it sets expectations for late pickup fees.
Requiring current rabies proof and disclosing behavior surcharges and cancellation fees in the quote avoids problems later.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for unknown coats
pricingTips.body: If you have not seen the dog, give a price range with a clear final price after the coat is assessed at drop-off. Photos help, but they miss mats close to the skin.

pricingTips.title: Price by time for tough jobs
pricingTips.body: For senior, nervous, or heavily matted dogs, estimate the hours and set a price that covers breaks and slower work. Do not discount these jobs to match a standard groom.

pricingTips.title: Offer a first-visit price that reflects reality
pricingTips.body: New clients often have dogs who have not been groomed in months. Book a longer slot, quote higher, and show that regular visits cost less by listing the maintenance price.

pricingTips.title: Show package savings
pricingTips.body: Offer a quote for a single groom alongside a four or six visit package with a modest discount. Owners with regular schedules often choose the package, which gives you prepaid income.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the quote says the price depends on coat condition and behavior. Contact the owner before adding charges and note their approval. Without that language and approval, expect pushback.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an evaluation or consultation?
faqs.answer: Most groomers do not charge for a quick phone or photo estimate. For on-site visits, such as a mobile groomer assessing a multi-pet household or a specialty groom, a small consultation fee applied to the first service is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. A dog's coat can change quickly, so a quote given months earlier may not match the current condition, and you should reassess at drop-off.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a quote to be accepted?
faqs.answer: Not for most regular grooms, but a deposit is reasonable for large dogs, long specialty sessions, or holiday slots. State the amount and whether it is refundable in the quote.

pet-sitter.intro: Pet sitters care for animals while owners are away or at work. They bill for drop-in visits, dog walks, overnight stays in the client's home, boarding in the sitter's home, and extras like medication, pickup of mail, or care for additional pets. Most are solo operators or run small teams, and invoices often go out weekly, per trip, or after each booking.
pet-sitter.pricingModel: Pet sitters usually charge per visit or per night rather than by the hour. A drop-in visit is priced by length (typically 20, 30, or 60 minutes), and overnight stays are priced per night with a set number of visits or hours included. Add-ons are common: a fee for each additional pet, medication fees (higher for injections), puppy or senior-care surcharges, and holiday rates. Many sitters add a flat holiday surcharge or charge 1.5x on major holidays. Travel fees apply when a client lives outside your normal service area. Some sitters sell prepaid packages of walks at a small discount, and many require a deposit or full prepayment for longer bookings. Meet-and-greets are either free or charged as a small fee that is credited toward the first booking. Cancellation and short-notice fees are usually part of the service agreement.

rates.unit: per pet, per visit or night

items.description: Overnight pet sitting in client's home, Mar 14-18 (Biscuit, 2 dogs)
Additional dog, overnight stays
Midday potty-break visit (30 min), Mar 15-17
Oral medication, Biscuit (twice daily)
Holiday surcharge, Mar 17

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of the last day of service. Accepted: card, bank transfer, or check payable to Jordan's Pet Care. Late balances are subject to a $10 fee after 14 days. Thank you for trusting us with Biscuit and Daisy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service and number of visits or nights
invoiceChecklist.why: Pet care is billed by the visit or night, and owners compare your invoice with their travel dates. Listing each date prevents questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pet names and number of animals
invoiceChecklist.why: Additional-pet fees depend on how many animals you cared for, and names make it clear which pets each line covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Visit length and type
invoiceChecklist.why: A 30-minute drop-in and a 60-minute visit are priced differently, as are walks and potty breaks.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed on separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Medication, extra pets, holiday surcharges, and travel fees are easier to approve when they are itemized rather than rolled into a total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or prepayment already received
invoiceChecklist.why: Show the credit and the remaining balance so the client does not pay twice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: If you bought food, litter, waste bags, or paid a vet co-pay on the client's behalf, list it as a separate expense and attach receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, contact details, and any license or insurance info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities have business license rules, and clients often want proof of bonding and insurance on file. Check your local requirements.

pet-sitter.paymentTerms: Many pet sitters collect a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking for overnight stays, boarding, and holiday dates, with the balance due at the end of service or within 7 days. Regular walk and drop-in clients are often billed weekly or monthly, or pay from a prepaid package. Due-on-receipt works well for one-off bookings. Payment is commonly accepted by card, bank transfer, or check, and cash is less common. Late fees, usually a flat amount or a small percentage, should be stated in your service agreement before the first booking. Cancellation terms, such as losing the deposit within 48 hours of the start date, should be in writing as well.

tips.title: Bill the booked time, not the time you guessed
tips.body: Define what each visit includes (feeding, fresh water, a walk, play, litter, photo update) and its length. If a client regularly runs long, such as a dog that needs a longer walk, move them to the next visit tier.

tips.title: Charge more for holidays and peak travel
tips.body: Christmas, Thanksgiving, July 4th, and spring break fill up fast. Set a surcharge and list the holiday dates in your policy so it is never a surprise on the invoice.

tips.title: Get paid before you leave on a long booking
tips.body: For stays of a week or more, take a deposit up front and ask for the balance by the day the client returns. It is easier to collect before the pet goes home than after.

tips.title: Keep records of expenses you front
tips.body: If you buy supplies or pay for an emergency vet visit, document it and bill it as a pass-through with receipts. Have written authorization from the owner for vet spending limits.

tips.title: Use recurring invoices for regular walkers
tips.body: A weekly or monthly invoice for standing walks keeps cash flow steady and reduces the work of billing the same clients each week. Note any skipped or added days.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a meet-and-greet?
faqs.answer: It is a personal choice. Many sitters offer the first meet-and-greet free, while others charge $20 to $30 and credit it to the first booking. A fee helps filter out people who are only shopping around, especially if you travel to the home.

faqs.question: Do I charge extra for cats, dogs, and other animals in the same home?
faqs.answer: Most sitters include one or two pets in the base price and add a fee for each additional animal, usually $5 to $15. Exotic pets, livestock, or aquariums that require extra care can be priced separately.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client cancels at the last minute?
faqs.answer: Put a cancellation policy in your service agreement, for example a deposit that is non-refundable within 48 hours or a fee for the first night or visit. Then invoice according to that policy and reference it on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and locality. Some states tax pet care or pet grooming services and others do not. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for every booking?
faqs.answer: Not for every booking, but it is a good idea for overnights, boarding, holidays, and new clients. Regular drop-in clients with a good payment history can often be billed after service.

estimate.intro: Pet sitters send quotes before a first booking, usually after a meet-and-greet or a message with dates and pet details. Clients compare your price per visit or night, what is included, and your policies on holidays, cancellations, and emergencies. A clear quote also works as a record of what the owner agreed to.

scopeChecklist.item: Dates, times, and number of visits or nights
scopeChecklist.why: The total depends on the schedule. Listing exact dates also shows whether any fall on a holiday with a surcharge.

scopeChecklist.item: Pets covered, with species, ages, and special needs
scopeChecklist.why: Puppies, seniors, and animals with medical needs take more time and may carry extra fees, so the quote should match what you saw at the meet-and-greet.
Feeding, walking, litter, play, plant watering, mail pickup, and photo updates should be listed so the client knows what the base price covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Add-on fees and when they apply
scopeChecklist.why: Medication, extra pets, travel outside your service area, and holiday rates should be disclosed up front to avoid disputes.
State what is due at booking, what is due at the end, and which payment methods you accept.
Clients who come home early or cancel late still affect your schedule. Say whether visits are refunded or billed.
Note who covers vet costs, the spending limit the owner approves, and which vet you will use. This avoids delays and billing disputes.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total and show the breakdown
pricingTips.body: Clients like to see a single number, but a line-by-line breakdown of nights, extra pets, and surcharges explains how you got there and helps you defend your rates.

pricingTips.title: Price by the animal's needs, not just the visit
pricingTips.body: A calm cat needs less than a young dog that needs exercise and training reinforcement. Use visit length tiers and add-on fees to reflect the work involved.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Holiday and peak dates fill quickly. State that your quote and availability are held for a set number of days, such as 5 to 7, so you do not hold dates indefinitely.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package for repeat services
pricingTips.body: If a client needs daily walks for a month, a prepaid package at a small discount can lock in revenue and simplify billing.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before or after the meet-and-greet?
faqs.answer: After. Meeting the pet and seeing the home tells you about size, behavior, medication needs, and travel time, which all affect the price. You can give a rough range beforehand.

faqs.question: How long should I hold a quote?
faqs.answer: Five to seven days is common for standard dates. For major holidays, a shorter window or a deposit to confirm the booking protects you from losing other clients.

faqs.question: What if the client's plans change after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Send a revised quote with the new dates or services and ask them to approve it in writing. Do not rely on a verbal change, since the total and any holiday fees may be different.

faqs.question: Can a quote become the service agreement?
faqs.answer: It can if it includes your policies and the client accepts it in writing, but many sitters use a separate service agreement for liability, vet authorization, and home access, and refer to the quote for pricing.

photo-booth-rental.intro: Photo booth rental businesses supply and staff booths for weddings, corporate events, school dances, birthday parties, and fundraisers. Most are solo operators or small teams with a handful of booths, an attendant or two, and a van. Invoices usually cover the booth package, extra hours, custom print or backdrop design, travel, and add-ons like props or guest books.
photo-booth-rental.pricingModel: Most photo booth companies sell packages built around event hours, usually two to four hours, with a base price that includes an attendant, setup and teardown, unlimited prints or digital sharing, and a standard backdrop and props. Extra hours are billed at a lower hourly rate than the first block. Booth type matters: enclosed and open-air booths sit at the low to mid range, while 360 booths, mirror booths, and glam booths cost more. Add-ons such as custom print templates, premium backdrops, guest books, green screen, GIF or boomerang, and branded overlays are priced as separate line items. Travel is usually free within a set radius and charged per mile or as a flat fee beyond it. Most companies collect a non-refundable retainer to hold the date and bill the balance before the event. Corporate clients often pay more for the same package and may need custom branding, a PO number, and a certificate of insurance.

rates.service: Standard open-air or enclosed booth package (2-3 hours)
Mirror or glam booth package (3 hours)
Custom print template or overlay design
Premium or custom backdrop (sequin, floral wall, printed)
Setup outside normal window or stairs/no elevator

items.description: Open-air photo booth package, 3 hours, attendant, unlimited prints, props
Additional hour of service
Custom print template design (wedding monogram)
Sequin backdrop upgrade
Guest book with prints and supplies
Travel, 22 miles beyond 30-mile radius

sampleInvoice.notes: Event date: Saturday, June 14, 2025, venue Riverside Lodge. Retainer of $200 received on booking and applied to this total. Balance due 7 days before the event. Accepted: card, ACH, Zvenmo-style transfers. Overtime beyond booked hours billed at $125 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, venue name, and address
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific booking and avoids confusion with clients who rebook for later events.

invoiceChecklist.item: Booked hours and start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what the base package covers and supports any overtime charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Booth type and package name
invoiceChecklist.why: Open-air, enclosed, 360, and mirror booths are priced differently, so name the one delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons and design work
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom templates, backdrops, and guest books are the most common line items clients question later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the deposit applied so the client sees the remaining amount and the date it is due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel charge with mileage or flat fee basis
invoiceChecklist.why: Explains the extra cost for venues outside your service radius.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number and billing contact for corporate events
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable departments often reject invoices without a PO or the right contact.

photo-booth-rental.paymentTerms: A non-refundable retainer of 25 to 50 percent is standard at booking, since it holds a date you could have sold to someone else. The balance is typically due 7 to 14 days before the event, or on the day of the event for smaller parties. Corporate clients often ask for net 15 or net 30 terms after the event, and some require a W-9 and certificate of insurance first. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common on post-event invoices, and overtime is usually billed on the spot or added to a follow-up invoice. Most operators accept cards, ACH, and digital wallet payments, and some add a card processing fee for large balances.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the event
tips.body: Chasing wedding clients after the event is awkward and slow. Set the due date a week before and state it in the contract and on the invoice.

tips.title: Put overtime in writing
tips.body: Clients often ask to extend on the night. Agree on the hourly rate in the contract so you can add it without a debate, and have the host approve it with a text or signature.

tips.title: Bill add-ons as separate lines
tips.body: Listing templates, backdrops, and guest books individually makes it easy to remove one and keeps the base package price consistent.

tips.title: Charge for difficult load-ins
tips.body: Stairs, long walks from parking, or tight setup windows add labor. Set a flat fee for them and note it in the quote so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

tips.title: Track mileage and attendant hours per event
tips.body: Knowing your true cost per event helps you set travel fees and decide which small bookings are worth taking.

faqs.question: Should my photo booth retainer be refundable?
faqs.answer: Most operators make it non-refundable because the date is blocked and turned-away bookings are lost revenue. State this clearly in your contract and on the invoice, and consider allowing a one-time date change at no cost.

faqs.question: How do I bill for overtime on the night of the event?
faqs.answer: Agree on the hourly overtime rate in advance. On the night, get the host's approval by text or signature, then add the extra hours to a final invoice or collect payment on the spot.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on photo booth rentals?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes the city. Some treat rentals, photo prints, or event services as taxable and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant and show tax as its own line if it applies.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client cancels close to the event?
faqs.answer: Follow your cancellation policy, which usually keeps the retainer and may require a percentage of the balance inside 14 to 30 days. Send a cancellation invoice that references the signed agreement.

faqs.question: Can I invoice a corporate client after the event?
faqs.answer: Yes, and many expect to. Get a PO number and billing contact beforehand, send the invoice within a day or two, and use net 15 or net 30 terms that you confirmed in the agreement.

estimate.intro: Photo booth estimates are sent after an inquiry that gives an event date, venue, guest count, and hours wanted. Clients usually compare several companies on package price, hours included, booth style, and what is covered like prints, props, and the attendant. A clear quote shows what is in the base price and what costs extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, venue, and start and end times
scopeChecklist.why: Confirms availability and locks in the hours the price is based on.

scopeChecklist.item: Booth type and what is included
scopeChecklist.why: State whether it is open-air, enclosed, 360, or mirror, and whether prints, digital gallery, props, and attendant are included.
Unlimited prints, number of strips, text or email sharing, and online gallery duration are common sources of disagreement.
Say whether a custom print template or backdrop is included, how many revisions you allow, and the deadline for final artwork.
Power access, space dimensions, load-in time, and stairs affect labor and can change the price if the venue does not meet them.
Clients should see the service radius, any mileage fee, and the hourly rate for extra time before they book.
Prevents disputes about refunds and when the rest is due.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium package with different hours and add-ons helps clients choose without asking for discounts on a single price.

pricingTips.title: Price the first hours higher than extra hours
pricingTips.body: Setup, travel, and teardown are fixed costs, so the first block should carry most of them. Extra hours can be cheaper and are an easy upsell.

pricingTips.title: Price weekends and peak season accordingly
pricingTips.body: Saturdays in spring and fall, plus holiday party season, fill early. Higher prices or minimum hours for those dates protect your calendar.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Holding a date indefinitely costs you bookings. A quote valid for 7 to 14 days encourages a decision.

faqs.question: How quickly should I send a photo booth quote?
faqs.answer: Within a day if you can. Couples and planners often inquire with several companies, and the first clear quote often gets the booking or sets the comparison.

faqs.question: Should I include the price of every add-on in the quote?
faqs.answer: List your main add-ons with prices, such as custom templates, backdrops, and guest books, but only include the ones the client asked about in the total. This keeps the quote simple while showing what is available.

faqs.question: Can I quote a different price for corporate events?
faqs.answer: Yes. Corporate events often need custom branding, insurance certificates, longer hours, and invoicing terms, so higher pricing is common and reasonable.

faqs.question: Does a quote hold my date?
faqs.answer: No. Only a signed agreement and the retainer should hold a date. Say this in the quote so clients know they need to book to reserve it.

photographer.intro: Photographers bill for portrait sessions, weddings, events, headshots, product shoots, real estate listings, and commercial work. Most are solo or run a small studio, and invoices typically cover shooting time, editing, image delivery, and usage rights, plus any travel or second shooter costs.
photographer.pricingModel: Photographers usually price by package or flat session fee for consumer work like portraits, weddings, and newborn sessions, often with a non-refundable retainer to hold the date. Commercial and editorial work is more often priced by the hour, half-day, or day rate, with a separate licensing fee based on how, where, and how long the images will be used. Real estate and product photography are commonly priced per listing or per image. Extras such as additional edited images, prints, albums, rush delivery, second shooters, travel, and equipment rental are billed as separate line items. Retouching is often billed by the hour or per image beyond a set number included in the package.

rates.service: Portrait or family session (1 hour, edited digital gallery)

items.description: Wedding photography, 8 hours of coverage including edited digital gallery (retainer of $750 already paid, shown as a credit below)
Second shooter, 8 hours
Engagement session, 1 hour, 40 edited images
20-page 10x10 linen-cover album
Travel outside 50-mile radius
Retainer received on contract signing

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 14 days of the invoice date. Final gallery is delivered once payment is received. Images are licensed for personal use under the terms of the signed contract. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event or session date, time, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the specific job and helps if the client disputes what was booked or delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and what it includes
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out hours of coverage, number of edited images, and delivery format so extras are clearly separate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit already paid
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the credit applied so the client sees the correct balance and your records match the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license or rights granted
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients need to know how images can be used, for how long, and where. Personal clients benefit from a print release reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons and overage charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra hours, additional retouching, rush delivery, prints, and albums should each appear as their own line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, mileage, and expenses
invoiceChecklist.why: Mileage, parking, lodging, equipment rental, and assistants are real costs that are easy to forget if not itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate clients often require a purchase order number to process payment, and a contract reference confirms terms.

photographer.paymentTerms: Most photographers collect a non-refundable retainer of 25-50% at booking to reserve the date, with the balance due before the session, on the day of a wedding, or within 7-14 days of invoicing for commercial work. Many portrait photographers require full payment before delivering the final gallery. Commercial clients often pay on net 30 terms, so state the due date clearly and consider a deposit for large projects. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Card payments, bank transfers, and checks are all accepted, and processing fees may be built into pricing.

tips.title: Hold the date with a retainer
tips.body: Your calendar is your inventory. A non-refundable retainer in the contract protects you if a client cancels and you turned down other bookings for that date.

tips.title: Separate shooting from licensing
tips.body: For commercial jobs, list the creative fee and the usage license as separate lines. If the client later wants wider use, you have a clear basis to charge more.

tips.title: Deliver after payment
tips.body: Release full-resolution files or the final gallery once the balance clears. Previews or watermarked proofs let clients see progress without giving up leverage.

tips.title: Bill for editing time on large shoots
tips.body: Culling and editing often take longer than the shoot itself. Build it into the package price or bill it as a distinct line item for hourly commercial work.

tips.title: Track expenses per job
tips.body: Keep receipts for travel, props, assistants, and rentals. Passing them through at cost or with a modest markup keeps the job profitable and makes tax time easier.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the shoot?
faqs.answer: Send an invoice for the retainer at booking, and invoice the balance either before the shoot or right after, depending on your policy. Many photographers require full payment before delivering final images.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for usage rights?
faqs.answer: Add a separate line for the license that describes the use, such as web and social media for one year, along with the territory. Reference the licensing terms in your contract so the invoice and agreement match.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services or tangible goods like prints and albums, while others do not. Check with your state's department of revenue or a local tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I charge a cancellation or rescheduling fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is in your signed contract. Most photographers keep the retainer for cancellations and may charge a fee for late rescheduling. Reference the policy on the invoice if a fee applies.

faqs.question: What if a client wants more edited images than the package includes?
faqs.answer: Bill additional images at a per-image rate stated in your contract or price list. Put the extra count and rate on a separate invoice line so the original package price stays clear.

estimate.intro: Photographers send quotes when a client inquires about a wedding, event, brand shoot, or real estate listing, and before any date is held. Clients usually compare package contents, hours of coverage, number of edited images, and usage rights across several photographers, so clear scope matters as much as price.

scopeChecklist.item: Hours of coverage and shoot schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Defines when you start and stop, so overtime is billed at an agreed rate rather than argued about on the day.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of edited images and turnaround time
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for deliverables and avoids disputes about how many photos the client should receive and when.
Clarifies whether the client can print, post online, or use images in advertising, and for how long.
Location fees, park or venue permits, and mileage beyond your normal radius can add real cost.
Shows how and when you are paid and that the date is not held until the retainer is received.
Albums, prints, second shooters, rush delivery, and extra retouching should be listed as optional so they are not assumed.
Outdoor sessions and weddings are affected by weather and changing plans, so state what happens in each case.

pricingTips.title: Offer three package tiers
pricingTips.body: Presenting a small, mid, and full option helps clients choose by need rather than shopping on price alone, and the middle package often sells most.

pricingTips.title: Price from your real hours
pricingTips.body: Count consultation, travel, shooting, culling, editing, and delivery. Divide your target income by billable hours to see whether a package price works.

pricingTips.title: Quote commercial work by usage
pricingTips.body: A shoot used on a national campaign is worth more than one used on a small website. Build licensing into the quote rather than offering only an hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should state how long the price is valid, since your availability and costs change. Thirty days is common, or shorter for peak wedding season dates.

faqs.question: Should I give a price range or a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: A fixed price for a defined scope is clearer for most clients. For commercial projects with unknowns, give a range or a base fee with listed add-ons, and update the quote if the scope changes.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a consultation or a quote?
faqs.answer: Most photographers offer a free initial consultation for weddings and larger projects. For complex commercial work involving scouting or detailed planning, some charge a planning fee that is credited to the project if booked.

faqs.question: When does a quote become a booking?
faqs.answer: When the client signs the contract and pays the retainer. Until then, the date is not held, and you can say so in the quote.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants to negotiate the price?
faqs.answer: Adjust the scope rather than the rate where possible, such as fewer hours, fewer edited images, or no album. This keeps your hourly value intact and gives the client a version that fits their budget.

physical-therapist.intro: Physical therapists who run cash-based practices, mobile or in-home PT, or small clinics send invoices for evaluations, treatment sessions, and packages of visits. Many also bill patients directly for the portion insurance does not cover, or provide itemized statements (superbills) that patients submit to their insurer for out-of-network reimbursement.
physical-therapist.pricingModel: Cash-based and out-of-network PTs usually charge a flat fee per visit, with a higher fee for the initial evaluation and a lower or equal fee for follow-up sessions. Session length drives price, commonly 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Many practices sell prepaid packages of 4, 6, or 10 visits at a small discount. Mobile and home-visit PTs add a travel fee or charge a higher visit rate. Specialty services such as pelvic floor therapy, dry needling, vestibular rehab, or sports performance testing are priced separately. Add-ons like braces, resistance bands, taping supplies, and written reports or letters for employers and attorneys are billed as separate lines. Practices that bill insurance invoice patients for copays, deductibles, coinsurance, and non-covered services, and the amounts depend on the payer contract.

rates.service: Written report, letter, or records summary

items.description: Initial evaluation and treatment plan, right shoulder rotator cuff strain (60 min)
Follow-up treatment session: manual therapy and therapeutic exercise (45 min)
Dry needling add-on
Resistance band set and home exercise handout
Kinesiology taping supplies

sampleInvoice.notes: Dates of service: March 4, 11, 18, and 25. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A detailed superbill for out-of-network reimbursement is available on request. Cancellations with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50% of the visit fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Patient name, date of birth, and account or invoice number
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the correct patient and ties the invoice to the right record, which insurers also require on superbills.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of each service
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and patients need exact dates of service, and it prevents disputes about how many visits occurred.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes and ICD-10 diagnosis codes (if the patient will submit to insurance)
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-network claims are usually rejected without procedure and diagnosis codes, such as 97110 for therapeutic exercise or 97140 for manual therapy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers generally require rendering provider identification on reimbursement claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Practice name, address, and tax ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Required on superbills and needed for the patient's records and HSA or FSA reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for evaluation, treatment, add-ons, and products
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing makes it clear what is a treatment service and what is a product, which matters for reimbursement and sales tax where it applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments received, copays collected, and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what is still owed and avoids double billing when patients pay part at the visit.

physical-therapist.paymentTerms: Cash-based PTs commonly collect payment at the time of service by card, HSA or FSA card, or bank transfer. When invoicing after the fact, due on receipt or net 14 is typical, and net 30 is more common for attorney, employer, or contracted facility billing. Prepaid packages are paid in full upfront and usually carry an expiration date, such as 90 or 180 days. Many clinics keep a card on file and charge a late-cancel or no-show fee, often 50% to 100% of the visit fee, as stated in a signed policy. Late fees on unpaid balances, if used, are typically 1% to 1.5% per month, and you should confirm what your state allows and that the patient agreed to it in writing.

tips.title: Put cancellation terms in writing at intake
tips.body: Have patients sign a policy covering late cancellations and no-shows before the first visit. It is much easier to charge the fee when it is already agreed to.

tips.title: Offer a superbill with every paid visit
tips.body: Patients with out-of-network benefits often ask for one. Giving it automatically saves back-and-forth and makes your cash rate easier to accept.

tips.title: Be clear about what insurance will and will not cover
tips.body: If you are out-of-network, tell patients that reimbursement is between them and their insurer and is not guaranteed. This heads off disputes over unpaid balances.

tips.title: Sell packages with clear expiration and refund terms
tips.body: State how many visits are included, the expiration date, and what happens to unused visits. Unclear package terms are a common source of refund requests.

tips.title: Keep billing records secure
tips.body: Invoices contain health information. Send them through a secure channel and keep records for the period required by your state and any payer contracts.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and when do I need to provide one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement showing the dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis codes, fees charged, amounts paid, and your provider details. Patients submit it to their insurer for out-of-network reimbursement. Provide one whenever a patient asks, or by default for cash-pay patients with out-of-network benefits.

faqs.question: Can I charge a no-show or late cancellation fee?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, if the patient agreed to the policy in writing beforehand. Insurers generally do not reimburse these fees, so they are billed directly to the patient. Check your state rules and any payer contracts, which may restrict charging insured patients.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on PT services?
faqs.answer: Treatment services are generally not subject to sales tax, but products you sell such as braces, bands, or supplements may be taxable depending on your state. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Should I bill the initial evaluation differently from follow-up visits?
faqs.answer: Yes. The evaluation takes more time for history, testing, and documenting the plan of care, so it is usually priced higher and listed as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can patients pay with HSA or FSA cards?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, since physical therapy is generally an eligible medical expense. Provide an itemized receipt or superbill, as some plan administrators ask for documentation of the service and provider.

estimate.intro: Physical therapists give estimates when a patient is paying cash, is out-of-network, or wants to know the total cost of a course of care before committing. Patients often compare your per-visit rate and package pricing with in-network copays, other cash clinics, and the cost of going through their insurance. Because the number of visits depends on how the patient responds, estimates are ranges based on the expected plan of care.

scopeChecklist.item: Evaluation fee and what it includes
scopeChecklist.why: Patients should know whether the evaluation covers the first treatment, testing, and a written plan of care or whether those are billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated number and frequency of visits
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a realistic total, such as 8 to 12 visits over 6 weeks, while making clear the plan may change after reassessment.

scopeChecklist.item: Visit length and fee per visit
scopeChecklist.why: A 30-minute and 60-minute visit are priced differently, and patients need to know which they are getting.
Dry needling, taping, bracing, and equipment are often extra and can surprise patients if not listed.
States whether you are in-network or out-of-network and that any reimbursement is not guaranteed.
Prevents disputes over missed visits, expiration dates, and refunds of unused sessions.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate validity period and re-evaluation points
scopeChecklist.why: The estimate is based on the current condition, so state when it will be revisited and how long the pricing holds.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range tied to the plan of care
pricingTips.body: Give a low and high number of visits rather than one fixed total. Explain that progress, flare-ups, and goals can change the length of care.

pricingTips.title: Show package savings next to the per-visit price
pricingTips.body: Listing the single visit cost and the discounted package cost side by side lets patients see the saving and often increases prepayment.

pricingTips.title: Price against the patient's true insurance cost
pricingTips.body: Many patients compare your rate to their copay. Acknowledging high deductibles and showing the total cost of a course of care can make a cash rate easier to accept.

pricingTips.title: Quote home visits with travel built in
pricingTips.body: For mobile PT, either set a higher visit rate or add a travel fee by distance, and show it as its own line so the pricing is clear.

faqs.question: Can I give an exact price for a full course of treatment?
faqs.answer: Only for a defined package. Otherwise give an estimate based on the expected number of visits and note that it may change after reassessment, since recovery varies from patient to patient.

faqs.question: Do I need to give an estimate before the first visit?
faqs.answer: It is good practice, especially for cash-pay patients, and some states have price transparency or good faith estimate rules for certain situations. Check your state requirements and any payer contract terms.

faqs.question: What if the patient needs more visits than I quoted?
faqs.answer: Discuss it at the reassessment, explain why more care is recommended, and give an updated estimate before continuing. Getting agreement in writing avoids billing surprises.

piano-teacher.intro: Piano teachers are mostly independent instructors who teach children, teens, and adults in a home studio, at the student's house, or online. They bill for weekly lessons, monthly tuition, recital participation, method books and sheet music, and sometimes exam or competition fees. Many run a small studio with 10 to 40 students and send invoices monthly or per term.
piano-teacher.pricingModel: Most piano teachers charge per lesson by length (30, 45, or 60 minutes) and then convert that to monthly or term tuition so income stays steady even when a month has five weeks or a holiday. Monthly tuition is usually the lesson rate multiplied by the average number of lessons per month (often 4 regardless of the calendar), or tuition is set per semester of 12 to 18 lessons. Teachers commonly add a yearly registration or materials fee, a recital fee, and charge extra for travel to the student's home. Discounts for siblings or prepaid terms are common. Adult learners and advanced students preparing for auditions or exams often pay higher rates for longer lessons. Online lessons are typically priced the same as or slightly below in-person lessons.

items.description: Piano tuition, March 2025 (45-minute weekly lessons, 4 lessons)
Annual registration and materials fee, 2024-25
Spring recital participation fee
Alfred's Basic Piano Library, Level 3 Lesson Book
Makeup lesson, 30 minutes (teacher-cancelled February 20)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due by March 5. Accepted by check, Zelle, or cash. A $15 late fee applies after March 10. Lessons cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice are billed in full. Thank you for studying with us.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or payer name
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents often pay for a child, and adult students may be reimbursed by an employer or family member, so the invoice should name both.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and lesson dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the dates taught shows exactly what the tuition covers and settles questions about missed or makeup lessons.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson length and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: A 30-minute and a 45-minute lesson are priced differently, and families with multiple students need each one itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and makeup policy reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Charges for late cancellations or no-shows are easier to collect when the policy is restated on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized fees for books, music, and recitals
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating materials and event fees from tuition keeps tuition consistent and shows where the extra costs come from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or mileage for in-home lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: A separate line for travel makes clear that the cost is for the commute, not the teaching time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment methods and due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Families pay by check, Zelle, Venmo, or card, so stating the options and deadline reduces late and confused payments.

piano-teacher.paymentTerms: Most piano teachers bill monthly in advance, due on or before the first lesson of the month, or bill by semester with payment due before the term starts. A registration fee collected at enrollment holds the student's lesson slot. Late fees of $10 to $25 after a grace period of about five days are common and should be in a written studio policy. Teachers typically accept checks, Zelle, Venmo, cash, and card payments, and some offer a small discount for paying a full term upfront. Tuition for missed student lessons is generally not refunded, though many teachers offer a limited number of makeups for advance notice.

tips.title: Bill tuition as a flat monthly amount
tips.body: Charging the same monthly figure, based on about 36 lessons a year divided by 12, avoids recalculating for five-week months and holidays and gives you steady income.

tips.title: Put your studio policy in writing at enrollment
tips.body: State cancellation notice, makeup rules, vacation weeks, and late fees in a policy that parents sign. Then the invoice only has to refer to it.

tips.title: Bill in advance, not after the lesson
tips.body: Collecting tuition at the start of the month means a student who quits mid-month has already paid, and you are not chasing payment for lessons you have taught.

tips.title: Itemize books and music separately
tips.body: Sheet music and method books are reimbursable costs. Listing them separately avoids students assuming they are included in tuition.

tips.title: Review rates once a year
tips.body: Raise rates in small steps, often 3 to 8 percent each fall, and give families at least 30 days' notice in writing before the new rate starts.

faqs.question: Should I charge per lesson or monthly tuition?
faqs.answer: Either works, but monthly tuition is more common because it gives predictable income and fewer small payments to track. Per-lesson billing suits adult students or irregular schedules.

faqs.question: Do I charge for lessons a student misses?
faqs.answer: Most teachers do, since the time slot was reserved for that student. Many offer a makeup if given 24 hours' notice, and always refund or reschedule lessons that the teacher cancels.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, private music instruction is not taxed, but a few tax certain educational services, and sales of books may be taxable. Check with your state department of revenue.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on tuition?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, as long as the fee was stated in advance in your studio policy and is reasonable. Include it on the invoice as a separate line only when it applies.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a family with multiple students?
faqs.answer: Send one invoice to the parent with each child's lessons listed separately. Apply any sibling discount as its own line so the amount is transparent.

estimate.intro: Piano teachers send a written quote or fee schedule when a new family inquires, when offering a package such as exam preparation, or when quoting a one-off event like a wedding performance or accompanying job. Clients usually compare per-lesson rate, lesson length, location, and what extras like recital fees or books are added to the base price.

scopeChecklist.why: A weekly 30-minute lesson costs far less than a 60-minute one, and the quote should show which one the price covers.
State whether lessons are at your studio, the student's home, or online, and what travel fee applies if you go to them.
A quote for a 16-week semester differs from open-ended monthly tuition, and a clear start date locks in the lesson slot.
Clarify whether registration, books, sheet music, recitals, and exam fees are in the price or billed separately.
Students need a piano or full-size weighted keyboard at home for practice. Saying so up front avoids problems after enrollment.
Families want to know how much notice is needed and whether unused prepaid lessons are refunded if they quit.
Rates change each year, so a quote that expires in 30 days avoids honoring an old price for a long time.

pricingTips.title: Quote monthly tuition and the per-lesson rate
pricingTips.body: Showing both lets parents see how a month is calculated and compare you to teachers who list only per-lesson rates.

pricingTips.title: Offer a trial lesson at a set price
pricingTips.body: A single paid trial lesson, usually your regular rate or a small discount, lets you assess fit before the family commits to a term.

pricingTips.title: Price event work by the hour plus prep
pricingTips.body: For weddings, church services, or accompanying, quote performance time, rehearsal, travel, and any music you need to learn, since prep time is often longer than the performance.

pricingTips.title: Offer a prepay discount rather than lowering your rate
pricingTips.body: A 5 percent discount for paying a semester upfront keeps your published rate intact while improving cash flow.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before the first lesson?
faqs.answer: Yes. Send a short fee schedule with lesson lengths, rates, fees, and policies so families know the full cost before booking a trial.

faqs.question: How do I quote for exam or competition preparation?
faqs.answer: Estimate the number of additional or longer lessons needed, add any accompanist or exam entry costs as pass-through items, and state which fees the family pays directly to the exam board.

faqs.question: Can I change my rate after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: You can raise rates for future terms with written notice, but a quote you gave should be honored for its stated validity period and for the term it covered.

pilates-instructor.intro: Pilates instructors bill private clients, small groups, and sometimes studios or corporate clients for mat and equipment instruction. Invoices usually cover single sessions, session packages, group classes, and extras like workshops, teacher training hours, or travel to a client's home. Many instructors work solo or rent space at a studio, so billing is often handled directly with each client.
pilates-instructor.pricingModel: Most instructors price by the session, with the rate depending on format. Private reformer or apparatus sessions cost the most, duets and small groups (3-4 people) are priced per person at a lower rate, and mat classes are the least expensive per head. Packages of 5, 10, or 20 sessions are common and usually carry a small discount in exchange for payment upfront, often with an expiration window of 2 to 6 months. Monthly memberships or unlimited-class plans are used by studio owners. Mobile instructors add a travel fee or a higher in-home rate. Corporate classes, events, and retreats are usually a flat fee per class or per day. Instructors who rent studio space or equipment may also factor in rent, either as a flat fee or a percentage split, which affects what they charge clients. Rates rise with certifications (comprehensive vs. mat-only), years of experience, and specialties such as pre/postnatal or rehabilitation work.

items.description: Private reformer sessions, 10-session package (Mar 3 - Apr 28)
Additional private mat session (Apr 30)
Duet session with client's partner (Apr 14)
In-home session travel fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Package sessions expire 90 days from purchase date. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice are forfeited. Payment due within 7 days by card, Zelle, or check payable to the instructor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session or package dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client see which sessions were used and supports package expiration terms if there is a question.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session type and length
invoiceChecklist.why: Private, duet, group, mat, and reformer have different rates, and 45 versus 55 minutes can change the price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package size and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget how many sessions they have left; showing used and remaining sessions prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expiration date for packages
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents the terms so unused sessions are handled consistently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late-cancel and no-show charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing them with the date shows the charge is tied to your stated policy rather than arbitrary.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel or equipment fees
invoiceChecklist.why: In-home or mobile sessions involve drive time and sometimes portable equipment, which should appear as separate lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications and business details
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing your certification (such as comprehensive or mat) and business name or tax ID where needed helps with insurance reimbursement requests, corporate clients, and bookkeeping.

pilates-instructor.paymentTerms: Many instructors collect payment upfront for packages and memberships, and bill single sessions at or right after the lesson. For invoiced clients such as corporate accounts or studios, net 7 to net 15 is typical, and net 30 is common for larger organizations. Some instructors charge a late fee or pause scheduling once an invoice is past due, which should be stated in a written policy before the first session. Common payment methods include credit cards, ACH or bank transfer, Zelle, Venmo, and checks. Late-cancel and no-show fees, often the full session price when notice is under 24 hours, should be written into the client agreement and referenced on the invoice. Some clients ask for a receipt to submit to an HSA or FSA, so keep your invoice detailed.

tips.title: Sell packages with clear expiration terms
tips.body: Packages bring in cash upfront and encourage consistency, but only if the expiration and transfer rules are written down. State whether unused sessions expire, can be extended for illness, or can be shared, and repeat it on each invoice.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every invoice
tips.body: A short line such as 24 hours' notice required, otherwise the session is charged makes it easier to bill a no-show without an awkward conversation.

tips.title: Separate studio rent from client pricing
tips.body: If you rent a studio or pay per-client fees to a gym, track those costs and make sure your session rate covers them after rent, insurance, and cancellations.

tips.title: Charge differently for specialty work
tips.body: Pre/postnatal, rehabilitation, and injury-related sessions need extra training and intake time. Price them at the upper end of your range and bill intake or assessment sessions separately.

tips.title: Keep records for HSA/FSA requests
tips.body: Some clients ask for itemized receipts with dates, services, and your business name. Keeping consistent invoices saves time and helps them with reimbursement questions, which vary by plan.

faqs.question: Should I invoice each session or sell packages?
faqs.answer: Both work. Packages give you upfront payment and fewer billing tasks, and clients tend to attend more regularly. Per-session billing suits drop-in or new clients. Many instructors offer a single-session rate and a discounted package rate.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a late cancellation or no-show?
faqs.answer: Add a line item for the missed session on the date it occurred, and reference your written policy. Charging the full or a partial session rate is common. If you deduct the session from a package instead, show the updated remaining balance.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on Pilates sessions?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes the city. Some places tax fitness or recreation services and others do not, and rules can differ for memberships, classes, and retail items like grip socks. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How should I bill a client who is also paying a studio for class access?
faqs.answer: Keep your private instruction separate from the studio's charges. If you are an independent contractor at the studio, invoice the client for your sessions or follow the studio's split arrangement, and clearly name who is being paid for what.

faqs.question: What should I do about unused sessions on an expired package?
faqs.answer: Follow the policy you stated at the time of purchase. If you decide to make an exception, note it on the invoice or account record so the exception is clear and does not become an expectation for other clients.

estimate.intro: Pilates instructors send estimates or quotes for work that is not a simple per-session booking, such as corporate classes, events, retreats, in-home programs, teacher training, and studio rentals. Clients compare per-session cost, package discounts, travel, and equipment requirements across instructors, so a clear quote helps them see what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and format of sessions
scopeChecklist.why: Private, duet, group, mat, and equipment sessions have different costs, and clients should know exactly what they are getting.
Quote whether you bring mats, small props, or a portable reformer, or whether the client or venue supplies them, since this affects price and setup time.
Mobile and corporate work involves drive time, loading equipment, and sometimes parking fees that should not come out of your pay.
A flat fee for a class assumes a maximum headcount. State it so a class of 8 does not become 20 at the same price.
Say that participants must complete intake forms or liability waivers and note any medical clearance requirements for injuries or pregnancy.
Corporate and event bookings can be cancelled at short notice, so state deposits, notice periods, and what is refundable.
Note how long the price is valid and when package sessions expire if the quote includes a series.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from your session rate
pricingTips.body: Start with your standard private or group rate, add travel and setup time, and then adjust for volume. A series of 10 classes at an office might be priced lower per class than a one-off event.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: Presenting a single-session, 5-pack, and 10-pack option, or a 6-week and 12-week series, lets the client choose without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Charge for equipment and setup time
pricingTips.body: If you transport reformers or set up a space, include a setup fee or build it into the rate. This time is often unpaid if it is left out of the quote.

pricingTips.title: Ask for a deposit on larger bookings
pricingTips.body: For retreats, workshops, and corporate series, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent holds the date and reduces last-minute cancellations.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an estimate for a regular private client?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Your published session and package rates and a signed client agreement are enough. Estimates are most useful for custom work like events, corporate programs, or multi-week series.

faqs.question: How do I quote a corporate wellness class?
faqs.answer: Quote a flat fee per class or per month based on class length, headcount, and travel. Include whether you provide mats and props, and confirm the space is suitable. Many instructors also set a minimum number of classes.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as more participants, longer sessions, or a different location. State in the quote that changes to scope may change the price, and send a revised quote in writing.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is common. For events, tie the validity to the date you can hold, since your schedule may fill, and note that the price is confirmed once a deposit is received.

plumber.intro: Plumbers send invoices for service calls, repairs, fixture installations, water heater replacements, drain clearing, repipes, and new construction rough-in and finish work. Most are solo operators or small shops with one to five trucks, billing homeowners, landlords, property managers, and general contractors. A good invoice separates labor, parts, and trip charges so the customer can see what they paid for.
plumber.pricingModel: Plumbers price in two main ways. Service and repair work is usually billed either by the hour with a trip or service call fee, or by flat-rate pricing, where each task (replace a toilet fill valve, clear a kitchen drain) has a set price that includes typical labor and parts. Larger jobs such as water heater replacements, sewer line repairs, bathroom rough-ins, and repipes are normally quoted as a flat fee for the whole job, often with progress payments. Parts and materials are typically marked up 15-50% over cost to cover sourcing, warranty, and trips to the supply house. Emergency, after-hours, weekend, and holiday calls often carry a higher hourly rate or a fixed surcharge. New construction work for builders is often bid per fixture or per phase (underground, rough-in, trim-out).

rates.service: Tank water heater replacement (40-50 gal, installed)

items.description: Service call and diagnosis, no hot water
Remove and dispose of old 40-gal gas water heater
40-gal gas water heater (6-year warranty), supplied and installed
Install labor, vent connection, gas line, and testing
Flex connectors, dielectric nipples, T&P valve, and fittings
Expansion tank, installed

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on completion. Check, card, or ACH accepted. Water heater carries a 6-year manufacturer tank warranty; installation labor is warranted for 1 year. Permit pulled under license #PL-12345. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances over 30 days past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Plumbing license number and contractor registration
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require the license number on invoices, estimates, and ads, and it tells the customer you are legitimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and work order or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Landlords, property managers, and insurers often need to match the invoice to a specific unit or claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor listed separately from parts, with hours or flat-rate task names
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers dispute lump sums more often than itemized charges, and itemizing supports your markup and hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts and fixtures with brand, model, and size where it matters
invoiceChecklist.why: Warranty claims and future repairs depend on knowing exactly what was installed, such as the water heater model or faucet cartridge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and inspection date
invoiceChecklist.why: Water heaters, repipes, and sewer work often need permits. A record helps with home sales and insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge, after-hours surcharge, and disposal fees as their own lines
invoiceChecklist.why: These are the charges customers question most, so showing them clearly prevents pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for labor and parts
invoiceChecklist.why: It sets expectations and limits disputes about leaks or failures that appear later.

plumber.paymentTerms: Residential service work is usually due on completion, often collected by card on site or by a payment link sent right after. Larger jobs commonly take a deposit of 25-50% to cover materials and permits, with a progress payment at rough-in and the balance after final inspection. Commercial and contractor accounts are typically net 15 to net 30, and builders may pay on a draw schedule. Late fees of 1-2% per month are common, but check your state's rules and put the fee in writing on the estimate or invoice. Many plumbers accept cards, checks, and ACH, and add a small card-fee policy only where local law allows.

tips.title: Collect payment before leaving the job
tips.body: Residential service calls are easiest to collect on the spot while the customer sees the finished work. Send the invoice from your phone before you pull out of the driveway.

tips.title: Take deposits on special-order parts
tips.body: Tubs, specialty faucets, tankless units, and custom fixtures can be hard to return. Collect a deposit or the full part cost before ordering.

tips.title: Charge for the diagnosis even if the customer declines the repair
tips.body: Your trip charge covers your time and truck. Tell the customer up front that it applies whether or not they approve the work, and put it on the invoice.

tips.title: Track change orders in writing
tips.body: Hidden rotted pipes, galvanized lines, or code upgrades behind a wall often change the scope. Get a signed or texted approval and add the extra work as a separate line item.

tips.title: Keep supply house receipts tied to each job
tips.body: Attach or note material costs per job so your markup is consistent and you can justify charges if challenged. It also makes tax time simpler.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat rate?
faqs.answer: Both work. Flat-rate pricing is common for repeatable tasks like toilet installs and drain clearing because customers know the cost before you start. Hourly with a trip fee suits unpredictable troubleshooting. Whatever you choose, tell the customer before work begins.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up parts?
faqs.answer: Many plumbers mark up parts 15-50%, with higher percentages on small items like fittings and lower percentages on expensive items like water heaters. The markup covers sourcing, handling, warranty risk, and the time spent getting the part.

faqs.question: Do I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Most plumbers cover travel with a trip charge or service call fee, sometimes with extra mileage for jobs outside the normal service area. List it as its own line so it is clear.

faqs.question: What if a customer won't pay after the work is done?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder referencing the invoice and agreed terms, then follow up by phone. Depending on your state, you may be able to file a mechanic's lien on real property, but deadlines and notice rules vary, so check local requirements or ask an attorney.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on plumbing work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials only, some tax labor and materials, and some treat repair and new construction differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Plumbers give estimates before larger jobs such as water heater replacements, repipes, sewer line repairs, remodel rough-ins, and fixture upgrades. Customers often compare two or three quotes, so they look at the total, the brand and quality of the fixtures, what is included, and the warranty. Small repairs are usually quoted verbally or by flat-rate price at the door.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact fixtures and equipment, with brand, model, and size
scopeChecklist.why: A 40-gallon builder-grade heater and a 50-gallon high-efficiency model are very different prices. Naming them prevents disputes about what was promised.
Customers often buy their own faucets or toilets. State whether you warrant customer-supplied parts and what happens if they arrive wrong or defective.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, inspections, and code upgrades included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Permit fees and required upgrades like expansion tanks, seismic straps, or pressure-reducing valves can add cost. Say whether they are in the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Access, wall, floor, and drywall repair responsibility
scopeChecklist.why: Cutting into walls or digging for a sewer line leaves damage. State whether patching, concrete, landscaping, or tile repair is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Hidden conditions and how extra work will be priced
scopeChecklist.why: Corroded pipe, failing shutoffs, or non-code work found after opening walls is common. A stated hourly rate for unforeseen work avoids arguments.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, water shutoff time, and work hours
scopeChecklist.why: Customers need to know when the water will be off and how long the job takes, especially in occupied homes and businesses.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate expiration date and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change, so a 15 to 30 day expiration is reasonable. List the deposit and progress payments so there are no surprises.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options on replacements
pricingTips.body: For water heaters and fixtures, present two or three options at different price points with different warranties. Customers feel in control and you are less likely to be undercut on a single price.

pricingTips.title: Price from a walkthrough, not a phone call
pricingTips.body: Phone quotes for anything beyond simple swaps lead to underbidding. Look at access, pipe material, shutoff condition, venting, and distance to the main before committing to a number.

pricingTips.title: Include a cushion for the unknown
pricingTips.body: Older homes hide problems. Build in time for seized valves and difficult access, or clearly exclude them and state your hourly rate for extras.

pricingTips.title: Charge for estimates on complex work when appropriate
pricingTips.body: Camera inspections, repipe surveys, and detailed remodel plans take real time. Many plumbers charge a fee and credit it toward the job if the customer accepts.

faqs.question: Should I give free estimates?
faqs.answer: Many plumbers do for installations and replacements, but charge a diagnostic fee for troubleshooting a problem. Charging for time-intensive work like sewer camera inspections is common and reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Shorter windows make sense when copper, PVC, or equipment prices are moving quickly.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the customer accepts?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. You can add charges for conditions you could not see or for work the customer requests, but get written approval first and show the change as a separate line.

faqs.question: Is an estimate a binding quote?
faqs.answer: It depends on the wording. A fixed-price quote commits you to the amount for the stated scope, while an estimate may allow variation. Label the document clearly and state what could change the price.

plumbing-and-heating.intro: Plumbing and heating contractors are solo plumbers, small shops, and hydronic or HVAC-adjacent tradespeople who repair and install water supply, drain, gas piping, water heaters, boilers, and heating systems. Invoices usually cover a service call or diagnostic fee, labor, parts and materials, permits, and sometimes equipment such as a boiler or water heater. Customers include homeowners, landlords, property managers, and general contractors.
plumbing-and-heating.pricingModel: Service and repair work is usually billed either hourly with a minimum service call fee, or by flat-rate pricing from a book of set prices per task (for example, replace a toilet fill valve or flush a boiler). Many shops charge a trip or diagnostic fee that covers the first half hour to hour and then bill labor in increments after that. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 20 to 50 percent depending on the part and whether you carry it in stock. Installations such as water heaters, boilers, radiant floor systems, and repipes are normally quoted as a flat price that includes equipment, labor, permit, and disposal of the old unit. New construction and remodel rough-in work is often priced per fixture or per bathroom, or billed in progress draws. After-hours, weekend, and emergency calls typically carry a premium of 1.5 to 2 times the normal rate. Many contractors also offer annual maintenance agreements for boiler or furnace tune-ups at a fixed yearly price.

rates.service: Boiler annual tune-up and combustion check
Drain cleaning (main line, cable or snake)
