Remove and dispose of old 50-gal gas water heater
New 50-gal gas water heater, 6-year warranty
Install labor, including venting, gas connection, and expansion tank
Fittings, flex connectors, gas fittings, and dielectric unions
Plumbing permit and inspection fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due on completion. We accept check, card, and ACH. Tank carries a manufacturer 6-year parts warranty; our labor is warranted for 1 year. A $35 fee applies to returned checks. Past-due balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and business name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require the plumbing license number on invoices and contracts, and customers and insurers often want it for records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Landlords and property managers often manage multiple properties and need to know which address a charge belongs to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts and materials with brand, model, and size
invoiceChecklist.why: Equipment such as water heaters and boilers carry warranties, so the model and serial number are needed for claims. Itemized parts also reduce disputes over markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours and rate, plus any trip or diagnostic fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Clear labor lines show what the customer paid for when the repair was quick but the diagnosis took time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and inspection status
invoiceChecklist.why: Water heater, boiler, gas line, and repipe jobs often need a permit. Listing it shows the work was done to code and helps when the home is sold.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often call back about leaks or failed parts. Stating the warranty period in writing sets expectations for what is covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders or approved extras
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden problems like corroded shutoffs or code upgrades are common once walls are open. Referencing the approval prevents disputes over price differences from the estimate.

plumbing-and-heating.paymentTerms: Residential repair work is usually due at completion, with payment by card, check, or ACH. Larger installations typically require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to order equipment, with the balance due on completion or after final inspection. Commercial and property management accounts commonly use net 15 or net 30 terms and may require a PO number. Many contractors state a late fee, often 1.5 percent per month, and a returned check fee on the invoice; check your state's rules on interest limits. Some jurisdictions require specific written notices or contract language for home improvement work, so confirm what applies where you work.

tips.title: Charge a service call fee every time
tips.body: Driving to the job, parking, and diagnosing a problem takes time even when no repair is made. A posted minimum service call fee keeps small jobs from losing money and makes it clear before arrival.

tips.title: Take deposits on equipment
tips.body: Water heaters, boilers, and specialty fixtures are special-order items or tie up cash. A deposit covers the supplier cost and protects you if the customer cancels.

tips.title: Record serial numbers and model numbers
tips.body: Putting the equipment model and serial on the invoice helps with warranty claims and shows the customer exactly what was installed. It also protects you if a manufacturer defect is disputed.

tips.title: Mark up materials consistently
tips.body: Apply a set markup structure so small parts, fittings, and consumables are not forgotten. Many plumbers lose money by absorbing solder, flux, PTFE tape, and fasteners instead of billing a shop supplies line.

tips.title: Invoice the same day
tips.body: Sending the invoice before you leave or the same afternoon gets payment faster. Waiting a week increases the chance the customer questions charges they no longer remember.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or use flat-rate pricing?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Hourly billing is simple for small repairs and unclear scopes. Flat-rate pricing works well when you can predict the task, because customers see a fixed price up front and you are rewarded for working efficiently. Many shops use flat rate for common jobs and hourly for troubleshooting.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on plumbing work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax materials only, some tax labor on certain repairs, and others treat installation as a nontaxable contract. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant before deciding how to show tax on invoices.

faqs.question: How should I bill for a job that takes multiple days?
faqs.answer: Use progress billing. A common pattern is a deposit up front, a draw after rough-in or inspection, and a final payment on completion. Tie each draw to a clear milestone so the customer knows what they are paying for.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses to pay after a repair?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder with the invoice, work order, and any signed approvals. If that fails, many states allow you to file a mechanic's lien on the property for unpaid work, but deadlines and notice rules vary, so check your state's requirements promptly.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for emergency calls?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as you disclose the premium before starting. Put the after-hours rate on the work authorization or tell the customer in writing so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Plumbing and heating contractors give estimates before replacing a water heater or boiler, repiping a house, adding a bathroom, or doing any work that is more than a simple repair. Customers often get two or three quotes and compare the total price, the brand and size of equipment, the warranty, and what is included. A clear estimate helps you win the job without underbidding.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact equipment make, model, size, and efficiency rating
scopeChecklist.why: A 40-gallon standard tank and a 50-gallon high-efficiency unit are very different prices. Naming the equipment keeps quotes comparable and avoids substitutions arguments.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the install
scopeChecklist.why: Venting, gas line changes, expansion tanks, shutoff valves, drain pans, and electrical work can be added costs. Listing what is in or out prevents surprise extras.
Some customers assume the price includes permits, while others expect to pull them. State who pulls the permit and whether the fee is included.
Old homes often reveal corroded pipe, missing shutoffs, or non-code venting. State that required code corrections found during work will be quoted separately.
Opening walls or ceilings to reach pipes is common. Clarify whether patching, painting, and tile repair are included, because most plumbers exclude them.
Customers need to know when work can start and how much is due up front. This also shows lead time on special-order equipment.
Material costs for copper, PEX, and equipment change. Setting a validity window of 14 to 30 days protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting three tiers, such as a standard tank, a higher-efficiency tank, and a tankless unit, lets customers choose by budget and gives you a chance to sell higher-margin equipment without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Price from supplier costs and real labor time
pricingTips.body: Get current supplier pricing for the equipment, add a materials markup, then multiply realistic labor hours by your rate. Include time for permits, haul-away, and a possible second trip.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for older homes
pricingTips.body: Houses with galvanized pipe, old gas lines, or past DIY work often have surprises. Either add a modest contingency to your price or write a clear allowance for unforeseen conditions.

pricingTips.title: Separate the diagnostic from the repair quote
pricingTips.body: For hard-to-diagnose issues like a failing heating loop or hidden leak, charge for the diagnostic visit, then give a repair quote based on what you find. This avoids guessing and unpaid troubleshooting.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many plumbers give free estimates on installs and replacements, but charge for diagnostic visits on repair problems. If a job requires extensive design time, such as a radiant heat layout, a paid estimate that is credited toward the work is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. Shorten it if you are quoting during times when material prices change quickly or equipment is hard to source.

faqs.question: Is an estimate the same as a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: No. An estimate is an approximate price that may change, while a quote or proposal is a fixed price for a defined scope. Label your document clearly and state how changes will be handled.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over the estimate?
faqs.answer: Do not exceed the agreed price without written approval. If you find extra work needed, stop, explain the issue, give a price for the change, and get the customer's approval before continuing.

podcast-producer.intro: Podcast producers handle the work between a host's recording and a published episode. That can include recording and remote guest sessions, editing, mixing, show notes, artwork, distribution, and sometimes booking guests or managing a release schedule. Invoices usually go to independent hosts, businesses with branded shows, agencies, or networks, and bill either per episode or as a monthly package.
podcast-producer.pricingModel: Most podcast producers price per finished episode or on a monthly retainer tied to a set number of episodes. Per-episode pricing is usually scaled by raw recording length and editing complexity, since a tightly scripted solo show takes far less time than a 90-minute unstructured interview with crosstalk. Hourly rates are common for one-off work such as consulting, cleanup of old audio, or strategy, and for overages. Setup work like show naming, cover art, intro music licensing, hosting account configuration, and launch trailers is often billed as a separate flat fee. Many producers offer tiered packages (editing only, full production, full production plus promotion) and charge extra for rush turnaround, additional revisions, video clips, transcripts, and guest booking. Licensed music, stock audio, and paid software or hosting fees are either passed through at cost or built into the package, and either way should be stated clearly.

rates.service: Full episode production (edit, mix, show notes, publishing)
Podcast launch setup (artwork, hosting, feed, trailer)
Studio or remote recording session with engineer
Consulting, audio cleanup, or ad hoc work

items.description: Full production, Episode 24 (edit, noise reduction, level mixing, intro/outro, mastering)
Full production, Episode 25 (same scope, 72 min raw audio)
Show notes with timestamps and episode descriptions
Short video clips with captions for social media
Additional revision round beyond 2 included (Episode 24)

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers episodes delivered March 1-31. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Two revision rounds per episode are included; extra revisions are billed hourly. Raw files and project sessions are archived for 90 days after delivery. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Episode numbers and titles, with delivery dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often run several episodes in a billing period, and listing each one makes it easy to match the charge to the work and prevents disputes about what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Raw audio length or editing tier per episode
invoiceChecklist.why: If your price depends on recording length or complexity, showing the length (e.g. 72 minutes raw) justifies the rate and explains why one episode costs more than another.

invoiceChecklist.item: Included revision rounds and any extra revisions billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Revisions are the most common source of unpaid hours. Noting what was included and what was extra shows the charge follows the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on services itemized separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Show notes, video clips, transcripts, rush fees, and guest booking are easy to forget or argue about when they are bundled into one total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as music licensing, stock audio, or hosting fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Third-party costs should appear as their own lines, at cost or with a stated markup, so the client sees what was a production fee and what was an expense.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer period and episode count for monthly packages
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the month covered and how many episodes were included clarifies what happens to unused or extra episodes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or contact for accounts payable, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Businesses and agencies often cannot pay without a PO or a specific billing contact, and missing details delay payment.

podcast-producer.paymentTerms: Podcast producers commonly require a deposit of 25-50% for launch packages and new clients, with the balance due on delivery or approval of the first episodes. Retainer clients are typically billed at the start of the month, or on the first day of the production cycle, so that work does not begin unpaid. Per-episode clients are usually billed on delivery or monthly in arrears with net 7 to net 15 terms, and net 30 is common when working with agencies or companies with accounts payable departments. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is typical if stated in the agreement. Payment is accepted by ACH transfer, card, or online payment link, and some producers pause the publishing schedule or hold final files until an overdue balance is cleared.

tips.title: Price by raw recording length, not just finished length
tips.body: A 30-minute episode cut from 2 hours of raw tape takes far longer than a clean 30-minute recording. Set tiers or overage rates based on raw minutes so unpredictable hosts do not eat your margin.

tips.title: Cap revisions in writing
tips.body: Include one or two revision rounds per episode and bill additional rounds hourly. Define a revision as changes to a delivered edit, not a different creative direction after the fact.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Charging at the start of the month protects you if a client stops sending recordings or goes quiet. Spell out whether unused episodes roll over or expire.

tips.title: Charge separately for rush and cleanup work
tips.body: Same-day turnaround, poor-quality remote audio, and heavy noise repair all take extra time. A rush surcharge of 25-50% and a hourly cleanup rate keep these from becoming free favors.

tips.title: Keep file delivery tied to payment
tips.body: Deliver final masters and project files after payment on new or slow-paying clients. For established clients, publish on schedule and hold project files or raw archive access if invoices go unpaid.

faqs.question: Should I charge per episode or per hour?
faqs.answer: Most producers charge per episode with a defined scope and length cap, because clients want predictable costs. Hourly makes sense for consulting, audio repair, and work with unclear scope. If you charge per episode, track your actual hours for the first few episodes to confirm the price works.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a podcast launch?
faqs.answer: Bill launch work as a flat fee covering defined deliverables such as artwork, hosting setup, feed submission to Apple Podcasts and Spotify, a trailer, and the first episodes. Collect a deposit up front and invoice the balance at launch or on delivery of the final assets.

faqs.question: Can I mark up music licenses and hosting fees?
faqs.answer: Yes, as long as it is agreed to in advance. Many producers pass licenses and subscriptions through at cost and list them as separate lines. If you mark them up for the time spent sourcing or managing them, say so in your contract or estimate.

faqs.question: What if a client keeps sending late audio but expects the same publish date?
faqs.answer: Put submission deadlines in your agreement, such as raw audio due 5 business days before publish date. Charge a rush fee or move the episode to the next open slot when files arrive late.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: In the US, businesses that pay you $600 or more in a year (threshold may change) often request a W-9 and may send a 1099-NEC. Having a W-9 ready speeds up onboarding with business clients. Check current IRS rules or ask a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Podcast producers send estimates before a launch, when a host asks for a monthly package, or when a company wants to compare producers for a branded show. Clients usually compare per-episode price, what is included in editing, turnaround time, and whether extras like show notes and clips are bundled or separate.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of episodes and expected raw length per episode
scopeChecklist.why: Price depends on recording length. If a host sends 3 hours for a 'one-hour' show, a stated cap gives you a basis for charging more.

scopeChecklist.item: Editing level included (cleanup only, filler word removal, content editing, full mix)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume editing means everything. Defining the level prevents arguments when they expect heavy cutting and you scoped light cleanup.
Poor remote audio or noisy rooms can double the work. State that the price assumes reasonably clean recordings and that repair is billed hourly.
Without limits, one episode can be revised endlessly. Say how many rounds are included and how long the client has to approve.
List final audio files, show notes, clips, transcripts, artwork, and the number of days from receiving files to delivery.

scopeChecklist.item: Costs not included, such as music licensing, hosting, software, or guest booking
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a quote covers all expenses to run a show. Naming exclusions avoids surprise charges later.

scopeChecklist.item: Rights, file ownership, and raw file retention
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify that the client owns the finished episodes and how long you keep raw files and sessions, since clients sometimes ask for old projects months later.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as editing only, full production, and full production with promotion. Clients tend to pick the middle tier, and it makes comparison with other producers easier.

pricingTips.title: Quote launch and ongoing work separately
pricingTips.body: A launch is a one-time cost with different tasks from ongoing episode production. Separate lines show the client what the recurring cost will be after launch.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for the first month
pricingTips.body: New clients often send longer, messier audio than they describe. Ask for a sample episode before quoting, or put a review clause that lets you adjust pricing after the first two episodes.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Software costs, your schedule, and your rates change. A 14 to 30 day validity period prevents clients from coming back months later expecting the original price.

faqs.question: Should I ask for a sample recording before quoting?
faqs.answer: Yes, whenever possible. A 10-minute sample shows audio quality, how much the host rambles, and how many guests are involved. It is the most reliable way to avoid underquoting.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding if the scope changes?
faqs.answer: A quote is a price for a defined scope. State that significant changes in episode length, number of episodes, or deliverables will be re-quoted or billed at your hourly rate, and get the client to accept the quote in writing.

faqs.question: How do I quote a show with no set schedule?
faqs.answer: Quote a per-episode rate with a minimum monthly commitment or a block of prepaid episodes that expire after a set period. That keeps your income predictable without forcing a rigid release schedule.

pool-cleaning.intro: Pool cleaning businesses, from solo route operators to small crews, invoice homeowners, HOAs, apartment complexes, and vacation rental owners. Most billing is for recurring weekly service, with add-on charges for chemicals, equipment repairs, and one-time cleanups like green-to-clean pool recoveries or spring openings.
pool-cleaning.pricingModel: Most residential pool companies charge a flat monthly fee for weekly service, usually billed at the start of the month or on a card on file. The fee covers skimming, brushing, vacuuming, emptying baskets, and testing and balancing water. Some companies sell two tiers: chemicals included or chemicals billed separately. Chemicals-included plans are simpler to bill but risk losing money in hot months when chlorine use spikes. One-time jobs such as green pool cleanups, opening and closing, filter cleans, and acid washes are priced as flat fees or hourly, and large cleanups often add a chemical charge. Repairs and parts (pump motors, salt cells, o-rings, filter cartridges) are billed at cost plus markup plus labor, often at a set hourly or per-visit rate. Commercial accounts are typically priced per visit or monthly, with required service frequency and chemical logs.

items.description: Weekly pool service, June (4 visits: skim, brush, vacuum, baskets, water testing)
Liquid chlorine, 12.5% (used above standard allowance)
Cartridge filter deep clean
Replace pump lid o-ring
Repair labor

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Recurring service is billed on the 1st of each month. Water test results for each visit are available on request. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and pool type (chlorine, salt, or other)
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients have rental properties or multiple homes, and the pool type shows what service and chemicals were used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service dates or number of visits in the billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute monthly charges when weeks were skipped for rain, vacation, or access issues, and dates settle it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Chemicals itemized by product and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate chemical charges, such as chlorine, acid, stabilizer, or salt, show the client what drove costs above the base fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts and equipment with brand or model where relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Pump motors, salt cells, and heater parts have warranties, and the client or manufacturer may need the details later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours and rate for repairs or one-time work
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating repair labor from routine service prevents confusion about what is covered in the flat monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number, if your state requires one
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require a license for pool service or repair work, and it is often required on invoices and contracts. Check local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on parts and, where applicable, services
invoiceChecklist.why: Tax treatment of pool service and chemicals varies by state, so collect and show it as your state requires.

pool-cleaning.paymentTerms: Recurring residential customers are usually billed monthly, often in advance, with automatic card or ACH payments to reduce chasing. Net 15 is common for repairs and one-time work. Large jobs like acid washes, equipment replacement, or pool recoveries often need a deposit of 25-50% or payment of parts up front. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if disclosed in your service agreement. Most solo operators accept cards, ACH, and checks, and many require a card on file. For commercial accounts, net 30 is typical, and property managers may require a W-9 and proof of insurance before first payment.

tips.title: Decide whether chemicals are included, and say so in writing
tips.body: Chemical costs swing with heat, rain, bather load, and algae. If chemicals are included in a flat fee, set the price with summer in mind and define what happens with heavy use or a neglected pool. If chemicals are separate, list them on every invoice.

tips.title: Add a rule for skipped visits
tips.body: Decide whether visits canceled because of storms, locked gates, or customer travel are billed, credited, or rescheduled. Put it in the agreement so the monthly fee is not argued every time.

tips.title: Bill repairs when they are done, not at the next monthly cycle
tips.body: Waiting to roll a parts purchase into a later invoice makes it easier to forget and harder for the client to remember why it was needed. Send a separate invoice or clearly marked line items soon after the work.

tips.title: Use a card on file for recurring accounts
tips.body: Pool service is a small recurring charge, and chasing 20 or 50 monthly payments takes time. Autopay for recurring accounts and manual invoices for repairs keeps cash flow steady.

tips.title: Keep service logs and photos
tips.body: A water test record and before and after photos of a green pool cleanup protect you if a client claims the work was not done or blames you for an equipment failure.

faqs.question: Should I bill pool service monthly or per visit?
faqs.answer: Monthly is more common for recurring residential service because it is predictable for both sides and reduces invoicing work. Per-visit billing is better for one-time cleanings, seasonal customers, and some commercial accounts that need each visit documented.

faqs.question: How do I bill for chemicals if they are not included in my monthly fee?
faqs.answer: List each chemical as a line item with the quantity and a unit price that includes your markup. Many operators mark up chemicals 20-50% over cost to cover transport, storage, handling, and testing. Show the total clearly so clients can see what changed from one month to the next.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for a green pool?
faqs.answer: Yes. A green or neglected pool takes extra labor, chemicals, filter cleaning, and repeat visits. Most companies charge a separate flat fee or hourly rate for recovery before starting regular weekly service. Quote it up front and take a deposit or bill when finished.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client does not pay for pool service?
faqs.answer: Follow your written terms: send a reminder, apply the late fee if disclosed, and pause service after a stated period. Water can turn green within days, so many operators stop service and make a clear date for restart once the account is current. Do not touch or alter the client's equipment in a way that could create damage or liability.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on pool cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax pool service, some tax only parts and chemicals sold, and some tax neither. Check your state revenue department or ask an accountant, and show tax on the invoice if it applies.

estimate.intro: Pool cleaning companies send estimates for new recurring service, green pool cleanups, openings and closings, equipment replacement, and larger repairs. Clients often compare two or three quotes, and they usually look at monthly price, whether chemicals are included, visit frequency, and what is excluded.

scopeChecklist.item: Pool size, type, and condition at the time of quote
scopeChecklist.why: Volume, surface type, salt versus chlorine, and current water condition affect labor and chemical costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Visit frequency and what each visit includes
scopeChecklist.why: Clients assume different things by weekly service, so spell out skimming, brushing, vacuuming, basket emptying, and water testing.
This is the most common cause of billing disputes, and it is the largest difference between competing quotes.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as repairs, filter cleans, and storm cleanup
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume heavy debris after storms or equipment maintenance is part of regular service.

scopeChecklist.item: Initial cleanup or recovery fee for a neglected pool
scopeChecklist.why: A new account with a green or dirty pool needs more work than routine maintenance and should be priced separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts markup and labor rate for repairs
scopeChecklist.why: If the client approves service now, they know how future repairs will be billed and are less likely to object.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and contract terms
scopeChecklist.why: Chemical and equipment prices change, so state how long the price holds and how either side can cancel.

pricingTips.title: Price from pool size and condition, not a flat neighborhood rate
pricingTips.body: A 10,000-gallon pool under no trees costs less to service than a 25,000-gallon pool surrounded by oak trees and heavy debris. Adjust monthly pricing for size, debris, and equipment such as robotic cleaners or heaters.

pricingTips.title: Offer two tiers
pricingTips.body: Present a basic plan with chemicals billed separately and a full plan with chemicals included. Clients can choose, and it makes your price comparison more obvious against competitors who bundle differently.

pricingTips.title: Quote cleanups after you see the pool
pricingTips.body: Photos can help, but green pools vary in difficulty. For a firm quote, inspect first or give a range with a stated process, such as price per visit until the pool is clear.

pricingTips.title: Include equipment checks in your estimate for new accounts
pricingTips.body: A quick check of the pump, filter pressure, and salt cell can reveal needed repairs before the first month. Note them separately so repair costs are not mistaken for service fees.

faqs.question: Should I give a firm price or a range for a green pool cleanup?
faqs.answer: A range, or a firm price after an in-person inspection, is safer. Water clarity, algae type, filter condition, and debris all change the work. Put a cap or approval step in writing for added chemicals or extra visits.

faqs.question: How long should a pool service quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Chemical prices and your route schedule change, so a short validity period keeps you from holding a rate for a pool that starts months later.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement for recurring service?
faqs.answer: It is strongly recommended. A signed agreement covering visit schedule, chemicals, payment method, late fees, and cancellation notice prevents most disputes. A written estimate that the client accepts can serve as a simple version.

portrait-photographer.intro: Portrait photographers photograph individuals, families, couples, graduating seniors, newborns, and professionals for headshots and personal branding. Invoices usually cover a session fee, the time spent shooting and editing, and the images or prints the client receives. Many work solo from a studio, a rented space, or on location, and bill both private clients and small businesses.
portrait-photographer.pricingModel: Most portrait photographers charge a session fee that covers the shoot, a set amount of editing time, and a consultation, then sell digital images or prints separately. Others bundle everything into packages, such as a one-hour session with 25 edited digital files. Headshots are often priced per person or per hour for team days, with a per-image retouching fee for extra edits. Location sessions can add a travel fee past a set mileage. Newborn and family sessions often have longer booking windows and a retainer. Prints, albums, and framed wall art are usually priced as products with a markup over lab cost. Usage licensing is rarely a separate line for private clients but matters for commercial headshots and brand work.

rates.service: Standard portrait session (individual or couple, 30-60 min)
Family or group session (up to 5-6 people)

items.description: Family portrait session at Riverside Park, 90 minutes, up to 6 people
Edited digital images delivered via online gallery (30 images included)
Additional edited digital images
11x14 fine art print, lab-printed
Travel beyond 20-mile service area

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $150 received at booking and applied to this invoice. Balance due within 14 days of gallery delivery. Digital files are licensed for personal use and printing. Commercial use requires written permission.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date, location, and length
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms what was booked and delivered, and helps if the client disputes time or location later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of edited images included
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the package limit so extra image charges are clear and not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-on images, prints, and products
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often order after viewing the gallery, and separate lines show what was ordered and at what price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit or retainer received
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the amount already paid and the remaining balance, which prevents double payment confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license or print release terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States whether the client can print and share files, and whether commercial use needs a separate license.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee with mileage or location
invoiceChecklist.why: Explains the extra charge for locations outside your usual service area.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax on prints and products
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, physical prints and sometimes digital files are taxable, so list tax separately and check your state's rules.

portrait-photographer.paymentTerms: A non-refundable retainer or booking fee of 25 to 50 percent is common, often due at booking to hold the date. The balance is usually due on the day of the session or before the final gallery is delivered, which keeps you from chasing payment after files are released. For print orders, many photographers require full payment before ordering from the lab. Commercial and corporate clients often pay net 15 to net 30 and may need a PO number. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated up front. Cards, bank transfer, and digital payment apps are the usual methods.

tips.title: Deliver files after payment
tips.body: Hold the full gallery or high-resolution downloads until the balance is paid. Once clients have the images, the urgency to pay often drops.

tips.title: Make the retainer non-refundable and say so
tips.body: Your time is blocked off once a date is booked. Put the retainer terms and rescheduling policy on the contract and the first invoice.

tips.title: Separate session fee from products
tips.body: Billing the session fee and print or file sales as separate lines makes pricing clearer and lets clients add products later without renegotiating the session.

tips.title: Charge for extra editing and rush work
tips.body: Heavy retouching, background removal, and rush turnaround take real hours. List them as add-ons with a per-image or per-hour rate.

tips.title: Invoice corporate clients with their details
tips.body: Include the company name, PO number, and billing contact for headshot days. It speeds up approval in accounts payable.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the session?
faqs.answer: Many portrait photographers invoice the retainer at booking and send a final invoice for the balance before or right after the session. For print orders, invoice when the client places the order and collect before ordering from the lab.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on portrait photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax photography services, some tax only physical prints and products, and some tax digital files. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill when a client wants more images than the package includes?
faqs.answer: Add a line item for additional edited images at your per-image rate or offer a discounted full-gallery upgrade. State the price in your contract so the add-on is not a new negotiation.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels or reschedules the session?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say whether the retainer is non-refundable and whether it can be applied to a new date. A common approach is to allow one reschedule with notice, usually 48 hours or more, and charge a new retainer after that.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on a portrait invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the fee and rate are written in your contract or invoice terms before the work starts. Check your state's rules on maximum interest for late payments.

estimate.intro: Portrait photographers send a quote when a client asks about pricing for a session, a headshot day, or a package that includes prints or an album. Clients typically compare session fees, what is included in the price, and how many edited images they receive. A clear quote avoids confusion over extras that other photographers may bundle.

scopeChecklist.item: Session length, location, and number of people
scopeChecklist.why: These affect time and price, and a larger group or extra location can change the fee.
Clients often assume they get every shot. State the exact count and what extra images cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Outfit changes and backdrops or setups
scopeChecklist.why: Each change adds time, so list how many are included.
Basic color and exposure correction differs from skin retouching or background replacement, and clients should know which they are getting.
Sets expectations for when the gallery arrives, such as two weeks for standard or five days for rush.
Clarifies what the client can do with the images, especially for business headshots and social media.
For outdoor sessions, state what happens if rain or poor light forces a reschedule.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three packages
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and premium option based on session length and image count helps clients choose without asking you to build a custom price each time.

pricingTips.title: Price for the full time, not just the shoot
pricingTips.body: A one-hour session often takes four to six hours with prep, travel, culling, editing, and delivery. Set fees based on total hours and your costs.

pricingTips.title: Quote travel and parking separately
pricingTips.body: If the location is far or requires a permit, show those costs as separate lines so clients see what they are paying for.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Prices and availability change, so a 14 to 30 day quote window keeps you from honoring old rates on a busy date.

faqs.question: Should I give a price range or a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: Fixed packages work best for standard sessions. Use a range only when scope is uncertain, such as a team headshot day where the number of people is not confirmed, and set the final price once headcount is known.

faqs.question: Do I charge for a consultation before the quote?
faqs.answer: Most portrait photographers offer a short free call or email exchange. For complex projects like multi-location family sessions or large corporate shoots, some charge a planning fee that is credited to the booking.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope rather than the rate. Offer a shorter session, fewer edited images, or a smaller print package at a lower total.

faqs.question: Does the quote turn into the contract?
faqs.answer: Many photographers pair a quote with a contract and retainer. The quote shows what is included and the price, and the signed contract and retainer confirm the booking.

post-construction-cleaning.intro: Post construction cleaning companies clean new builds, remodels, and tenant improvements after the trades are done and before the owner, buyer, or tenant moves in. Invoices usually go to general contractors, builders, property managers, and homeowners. Most jobs are billed per square foot, by cleaning stage, or as a flat fee for the project, with add-ons for specialty work like window scraping or pressure washing.
post-construction-cleaning.pricingModel: Most post construction cleaners price by square foot of finished interior space, then adjust for condition, number of stages, ceiling height, glass count, and access. Many jobs run in three stages: a rough clean after framing and drywall, a final clean after finishes and fixtures, and a touch-up clean right before handover. Contractors often want a flat bid per stage or per unit, especially on multi-unit or commercial work. Hourly rates are used for small remodels, change orders, and extra visits, usually with a minimum crew charge. Add-ons such as window cleaning, floor scrubbing or buffing, dumpster-area debris removal, and pressure washing are listed as separate line items. Heavy dust from drywall sanding, paint overspray, adhesive, and stickers on glass can push a job into a higher price tier, so document condition before you start. Commercial work is often billed against a purchase order or a schedule of values with progress billing.

rates.service: Crew labor for small remodels or extra visits
Pressure washing of patios, walks, and garage floors

items.description: Rough clean, 2,400 sq ft new residential build (dust removal, debris pickup, vacuum all surfaces)
Final clean, 2,400 sq ft (cabinets, fixtures, bathrooms, floors, trim, appliances)
Window cleaning, interior and exterior, with paint and sticker scraping
Garage floor degreasing and pressure wash
Additional touch-up visit requested by builder (2 cleaners)

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: 142 Alder Ct, PO #4471. Rough clean completed 3/4, final clean 3/18, touch-up 3/21. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Re-clean requests for work disturbed by other trades after sign-off are billed at the hourly rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address, lot or unit numbers, and square footage cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Per square foot pricing only holds up if the client can see which areas and how much space you billed for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cleaning stage and date for each visit (rough, final, touch-up)
invoiceChecklist.why: Builders often pay per stage and need dates to match against their construction schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number, job number, or GC reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial and contractor accounts commonly will not process payment without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed separately (windows, floors, pressure washing, debris haul)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show what was extra and make it easier to approve or dispute individual items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders or extra visits with who requested them
invoiceChecklist.why: Re-cleans after other trades return are the most common source of disputes. A name and date back up the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business license number and insurance reference, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many GCs and property managers require proof of licensing and liability insurance, and some local jurisdictions require a business license.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lien or retainage notes if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: On larger commercial projects, retainage and lien waiver paperwork can affect when and how much you get paid.

post-construction-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential builders and homeowners often pay within 7 to 15 days of final walkthrough. Commercial general contractors commonly pay net 30, and some pay only after the owner pays them, so confirm terms before you start. For large jobs, ask for a 25 to 50 percent deposit or bill by stage, and consider progress billing for multi-week projects. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is common if it is stated in your estimate or contract in advance. Checks, ACH transfers, and card payments are all common, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client where allowed.

tips.title: Walk the site before quoting
tips.body: Take photos of dust levels, paint overspray, stickers on glass, and debris. A site visit lets you price the real condition, and the photos protect you if someone later claims the space was already dirty.

tips.title: Bill by stage, not only at the end
tips.body: Invoice the rough clean when it is done instead of waiting for final handover. Construction schedules slip, and unbilled work can sit for months.

tips.title: Charge for return visits
tips.body: Other trades often come back after you finish and leave new dust or debris. Put a re-clean rate in your estimate and invoice those visits separately.

tips.title: Track dumpster and hauling costs
tips.body: If you remove construction debris, extra trash, or hazardous-looking materials, price disposal separately. Do not absorb it into the per square foot rate.

tips.title: Get sign-off at handover
tips.body: Have the contractor or owner sign off on the final walkthrough. A signed acceptance makes it harder to delay payment over small punch-list complaints.

faqs.question: Should I charge per square foot or per hour for post construction cleaning?
faqs.answer: Per square foot works best for new builds and larger remodels because clients can compare bids easily. Hourly rates fit small jobs, change orders, and return visits. Many cleaners use both on the same project.

faqs.question: How do I bill a general contractor who pays late?
faqs.answer: State payment terms in your estimate and on every invoice, including any late fee. Send invoices right after each stage, follow up on a set schedule, and consider stopping work on later stages if earlier ones are unpaid.

faqs.question: Can I invoice for window cleaning and pressure washing separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is a good idea. Listing them as separate line items keeps the base clean price clear and lets the client approve add-ons individually.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on post construction cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax cleaning services or janitorial services and others do not, and rules can differ for new construction. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client says the space was not clean enough after final clean?
faqs.answer: Refer to your scope of work and the signed walkthrough. Offer a limited touch-up for items that fall within the original scope, and bill separately for new dust or damage caused by other trades after your visit.

estimate.intro: Post construction cleaners send estimates before the build is finished, often when a contractor is collecting bids for the closeout phase or a homeowner needs a cleaner before move-in. Clients compare price per square foot, the number of cleaning stages included, and whether windows, floors, and exterior areas are covered. A detailed quote helps you win the job and avoid arguments about what was included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of cleaning stages and what each includes
scopeChecklist.why: A rough clean, final clean, and touch-up involve different work. Clients assume different things unless the stages are written out.

scopeChecklist.item: Total square footage and how it was measured
scopeChecklist.why: Square footage drives the price. Specify whether garages, basements, and unfinished areas are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Windows, tracks, screens, and glass scraping
scopeChecklist.why: Window work is time-consuming and often assumed to be included. List the number of windows and whether exterior glass is covered.
Vacuuming, mopping, scrubbing, degreasing, and polishing are priced differently. State which floor types are covered.
Clarify whether you remove leftover construction debris or only clean surfaces. Hauling and dumpster use should be priced separately.
State that trades must be finished, utilities on, and the site accessible. Otherwise you can bill for delays or return visits.
Sets expectations for what happens if dust or damage appears after you finish.

pricingTips.title: Quote per stage with a total
pricingTips.body: Show a price for each stage and a combined total. Contractors can then drop or defer a stage without asking you to re-bid.

pricingTips.title: Build in a condition adjustment
pricingTips.body: Include language that final pricing may change if the site condition differs from what you saw, such as heavy overspray or concrete splatter. Many cleaners add a stated percentage or hourly overage.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum charge
pricingTips.body: Small remodels can take more time in setup, travel, and supplies than the square footage suggests. A minimum job fee protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Include an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Material costs and labor availability change, and construction schedules shift. A 30-day validity period keeps old quotes from being held against you.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or site visit?
faqs.answer: Most post construction cleaners do free estimates for typical jobs. For large or distant sites, some charge a visit fee that is credited back if they get the job.

faqs.question: Can I quote from blueprints instead of visiting the site?
faqs.answer: Many cleaners do for new builds and commercial projects, but add a clause that the price can change if the finished condition or square footage differs from the plans.

faqs.question: How firm should my estimate be?
faqs.answer: A flat bid works when the scope and square footage are clear. If the condition is uncertain, give a price range or a base price with stated add-on rates for extra work.

faqs.question: Should I ask for a deposit on an estimate?
faqs.answer: For larger jobs, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, especially with new clients. For repeat contractors, billing after each stage is usually enough.

pressure-washing.intro: Pressure washing businesses clean exterior surfaces for homeowners, property managers, and commercial clients. Typical invoices cover house washing, driveway and concrete cleaning, deck and fence cleaning, and roof or gutter work, often with add-ons like sealing or chemical treatments.
pressure-washing.pricingModel: Most residential pressure washing is priced per square foot for flat surfaces like driveways, patios, and sidewalks, and by flat fee for house washing based on home size or story count. Many operators set a minimum job charge of $150 to $250 to cover travel, setup, and equipment wear. Decks, fences, and roofs are priced per square foot or linear foot, with soft washing (low pressure with cleaning solutions) usually priced higher than standard pressure cleaning. Commercial work such as storefronts, parking lots, and dumpster pads is often quoted per visit or on a recurring contract. Sealing, rust removal, oil stain treatment, and efflorescence removal are billed as separate line items. Some owners also bill hourly at $60 to $120 for odd jobs, with a second worker adding to the rate. Water access, hot water needs, and travel distance can all justify surcharges.

items.description: Soft wash exterior of 2-story home (siding, trim, soffits)
Driveway pressure cleaning with surface cleaner
Front walkway and patio cleaning
Pre-treatment for oil stains on driveway
Wood fence cleaning (rear yard)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of service. Accepted: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on cards). Results on heavily stained or aged concrete may vary. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and areas cleaned
invoiceChecklist.why: Properties often have several surfaces. Listing each one shows what was done and prevents disputes over missed areas.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage or linear footage per surface
invoiceChecklist.why: Most pricing is per square foot, so clients can check the math against the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cleaning method used (pressure wash vs. soft wash)
invoiceChecklist.why: Soft washing and high-pressure cleaning are priced differently, and the method explains the rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Chemical or treatment line items
invoiceChecklist.why: Degreasers, rust removers, mildewcides, and sodium hypochlorite mixes cost money and should be itemized when they are charged separately.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surcharges such as travel, water supply, or hot water
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client had no outdoor spigot or the site was far away, a visible line item keeps the total from looking inflated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed estimate or quote number
invoiceChecklist.why: Connecting the invoice to the agreed scope prevents arguments over price changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license and insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial clients and property managers ask for proof of coverage, and some cities require a contractor or business license number on paperwork.

pressure-washing.paymentTerms: Residential jobs are often paid on completion, with payment by card, check, cash, or ACH collected the same day. Larger jobs such as full house washes with sealing may require a 25 to 50 percent deposit when scheduling. Commercial and property management clients usually pay net 15 or net 30, sometimes requiring a W-9 and certificate of insurance first. Recurring accounts are typically billed monthly. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing up front. Some operators add a card processing fee, though rules on surcharges vary by state and card network, so check before adding one.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: Small jobs like a single porch or short walkway cost nearly as much to travel to and set up as larger ones. A minimum of $150 or more protects your margin.

tips.title: Take before and after photos
tips.body: Photos tied to the job date and address help settle complaints about streaks, damage, or leftover staining. Keep them with your invoice records.

tips.title: Separate stain treatment from base cleaning
tips.body: Rust, oil, and tire marks take extra product and time. Billing them as their own lines makes the base price easier to compare and lets you decline to guarantee full removal.

tips.title: Note pre-existing conditions
tips.body: Cracked concrete, loose siding, peeling paint, or failing sealant can be damaged or worsened by washing. Write these down before starting and include a note on the invoice or work order.

tips.title: Offer recurring schedules
tips.body: Storefronts, HOAs, and apartment complexes often want quarterly or annual cleanings. Billing them on a set schedule at a slightly lower rate smooths out your income.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the square foot?
faqs.answer: Per square foot or by flat fee is more common for standard surfaces because it rewards efficient equipment and rewards you for speed. Hourly works for odd jobs, mixed tasks, or when scope is unclear.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for using the client's water and electricity?
faqs.answer: Usually you do not charge for client water since the usage is small. You can charge a surcharge if you must bring your own water tank or hot water unit, which adds real cost. State it in the quote.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on pressure washing?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax cleaning or property maintenance services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department, and list tax separately on invoices where it applies.

faqs.question: What if a client says the surface still looks dirty?
faqs.answer: Refer back to the signed quote and any notes about pre-existing stains or aged surfaces. Offering a limited touch-up on the problem area is often cheaper than losing a payment or a review.

faqs.question: How do I bill for sealing after cleaning?
faqs.answer: Bill it as a separate line item per square foot, including the sealer product and application labor. Note the cure time and any restrictions on foot or vehicle traffic.

estimate.intro: Pressure washing estimates are usually sent before the first visit, often after a site walk-through or based on photos and measurements the customer sends. Clients compare price per surface, the method used, and whether chemicals and sealing are included. Many ask for several quotes, so a clear itemized quote helps.

scopeChecklist.why: List driveway, house siding, deck, fence, and so on. Anything left out can turn into an argument on the day.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured square footage or linear footage
scopeChecklist.why: Square footage drives the price, and showing it proves the estimate is based on real measurements.
Soft wash with solution costs and works differently from high-pressure cleaning, and clients should know which they are getting.
Deep rust, old oil, paint stains, and etched concrete may not fully come out. Saying so up front sets expectations.
You need an outdoor spigot and clear access. Specify any surcharge if water must be brought in or if gates are locked.
State who moves items and who is responsible for protecting landscaping, which could be damaged by chemicals.
Rain, wind, or freezing temperatures can delay work. A 30-day quote window protects you from price changes in chemicals and fuel.

pricingTips.title: Measure before quoting
pricingTips.body: Use a measuring wheel or satellite measurement tools rather than guessing. Underestimating a large driveway can cost hundreds of dollars in lost labor.

pricingTips.title: Price by surface type
pricingTips.body: Textured, stained, or sloped concrete takes longer than smooth flatwork. Pricing at the higher end of your range for difficult surfaces keeps your hourly return steady.

pricingTips.title: Offer bundles
pricingTips.body: A house wash plus driveway and walkway package at a modest discount encourages bigger jobs and saves you extra trips.

pricingTips.title: Show optional add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: List sealing, gutter brightening, or rust treatment as optional lines. Clients can pick what they want and you avoid padding the base price.

faqs.question: Should I give quotes over the phone?
faqs.answer: A rough range is fine, but confirm with photos or a site visit before giving a firm price. Surface condition, size, and access often change the final number.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Chemical, fuel, and labor costs shift, and seasonal demand can change your schedule, so an expiration date keeps you covered.

faqs.question: Do I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential estimates are free. For large commercial properties that need extensive measurement and planning, some operators charge a fee that is credited back if the client books the job.

faqs.question: Can the final invoice be higher than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changed, such as extra surfaces or heavier staining than expected. Get the client's approval in writing before doing additional work and bill it as a separate line.

print-on-demand.intro: Print on demand sellers and service providers create custom products such as apparel, mugs, posters, and phone cases that are printed and shipped only after an order comes in. Invoices go to wholesale buyers, brands, event organizers, and businesses that want custom merchandise, as well as to clients who hire you for design and store setup. Typical billing covers product costs, design work, setup fees, shipping, and sample orders.
print-on-demand.pricingModel: Most print on demand work is priced per unit, with the base product cost, print cost, and your margin rolled into one price. Bulk orders get tiered pricing, so the per-unit price drops at 25, 50, or 100 pieces. Design and artwork prep is billed separately, either hourly or as a flat fee per design. Many sellers add a one-time setup fee for new designs, mockups, or store integration. Sample orders are usually billed at full price or credited against a later bulk order. Shipping is either passed through at cost, billed at a flat rate, or built into the unit price. Custom branded packaging, inserts, and neck labels are priced as add-ons. For store management clients, a monthly retainer is common, sometimes combined with a share of sales.

rates.service: Custom printed T-shirt (blank plus print, small order)

items.description: Custom printed cotton T-shirts, front chest logo, assorted sizes (event staff order)
Custom printed pullover hoodies, back print and sleeve logo
Artwork prep and print-ready file conversion
New design setup fee (two designs)
Shipping to single address, ground, 3 boxes

sampleInvoice.notes: Order placed from approved mockup dated May 6. 50% deposit received at order. Balance due within 14 days of delivery. Printed items are custom made and non-returnable, except for print defects reported within 7 days of delivery with photos.

invoiceChecklist.item: Product details for each line (item type, color, size breakdown, print locations)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often order mixed sizes and colors, and a clear breakdown prevents disputes about what was ordered and delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the approved mockup or proof, with date
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client later says the design looks wrong, the approved proof shows what they signed off on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Order number and any client PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Business and school buyers usually need a PO number to process payment, and it helps you match supplier orders to invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line items for design, setup, and shipping
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating these from product cost makes pricing transparent and shows what drives the total when a client asks about it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate details
invoiceChecklist.why: Sales tax rules for custom goods and shipping vary by state, and wholesale buyers may give you a resale certificate that you need to keep on file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Production and shipping timeline, with tracking numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Production time is separate from transit time, and recording both avoids arguments over late delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return and reprint policy for defects
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom items cannot be resold, so stating when you will reprint or refund keeps expectations clear.

print-on-demand.paymentTerms: For custom orders, a 50% deposit at order is common, with the balance due before shipping or within 14 to 30 days for repeat business clients. Small orders and first-time customers are often paid in full upfront, since the items are made specifically for them. Established wholesale clients may get net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Most sellers accept credit cards, ACH transfers, and online payment links. Checks still show up with schools and local organizations. Keep enough margin in deposits to cover your supplier costs, because you often pay the print partner before you get paid by the client.

tips.title: Collect a deposit that covers your supplier cost
tips.body: Print partners charge you when the order is placed. A deposit of at least 50% means you are not floating the cost of custom products if the client delays or disappears.

tips.title: Get written proof approval before production
tips.body: Send a mockup with colors, placement, and sizing, and get a reply approving it. Color shifts between screen and print are the most common source of complaints, so note that slight variation is normal.

tips.title: Bill shipping honestly and clearly
tips.body: Shipping costs vary with weight and destination. Either pass through actual cost with a small handling fee or set a flat rate, and state which you are using before the order is placed.

tips.title: Charge for revisions after the first rounds
tips.body: Include one or two design revisions in the quote and bill additional rounds hourly. Without this, clients can ask for endless changes to a design.

tips.title: Track supplier price changes
tips.body: Blank garment and print provider prices change often. Review your price list every few months so margins do not slip on repeat orders.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after printing?
faqs.answer: For custom orders, invoice before production, at least for a deposit. The items cannot be resold if the client backs out, so collect payment up front or a 50% deposit, with the balance due before shipping or on delivery.

faqs.question: How do I bill for samples?
faqs.answer: Bill samples at the full per-unit price plus shipping. Many sellers offer to credit the sample cost toward a larger order placed within 30 days, which you can show as a discount line on the later invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on print on demand orders?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and where the buyer is located. Many states tax tangible custom goods, and some tax shipping too. Resale buyers may be exempt with a valid certificate. Check your state's rules or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the print provider makes a mistake?
faqs.answer: Report the defect to your provider with photos right away, since most offer free reprints or refunds. Tell the client a replacement is coming and note it on the invoice or a credit memo rather than quietly changing the original amount.

faqs.question: Should design work be a separate charge?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Bill artwork creation and prep as its own line item at an hourly or flat rate, so it is clear that print costs cover only production and not design time.

estimate.intro: Quotes are common before a business, school, team, or event organizer places a custom merchandise order. Clients usually compare per-unit prices, minimum quantities, turnaround time, and whether design and shipping are included. A clear quote helps them judge your price against other suppliers and online vendors.

scopeChecklist.item: Product specs: garment brand or style, color, material, size range
scopeChecklist.why: Different blanks have very different costs and quality, so naming the style avoids a swap that changes the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Print method and number of print locations
scopeChecklist.why: Direct to garment, screen print, embroidery, and sublimation cost different amounts, and each extra print location adds cost.
Showing the price at several quantities helps clients choose an order size and sets the exact quantity the quote applies to.

scopeChecklist.item: Design work included and number of revisions
scopeChecklist.why: If the client has no print-ready art, you need to say what design time is included and what extra rounds cost.
Clients often have an event date, so state turnaround after proof approval and whether rush options exist and what they cost.
Extended sizes like 2XL and above usually cost more from the supplier, and you should say whether that is added per unit.
Blank and supplier prices change, so a 14 to 30 day expiry protects your margin.

pricingTips.title: Price from landed cost, not just the base product
pricingTips.body: Add the blank, print cost, shipping from your provider, payment processing fees, and packaging before adding margin. Many sellers target 30 to 50% gross margin on custom orders.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered quantity pricing
pricingTips.body: Show the per-unit price at 12, 24, 50, and 100 pieces. Clients often move up to the next tier, which raises your order total and spreads setup costs.

pricingTips.title: Include a sample option
pricingTips.body: Offering a paid sample before a large order lets the client check quality and color. State whether the sample cost is credited toward the order.

pricingTips.title: Keep setup fees visible
pricingTips.body: List design setup and mockup fees as separate lines. Clients are more accepting of them when they can see what each charge covers.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or mockup?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are free. For custom mockups that take real design time, many sellers charge a small fee, often $25 to $75, and credit it toward the order if the client goes ahead.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Supplier prices and shipping rates change, so a shorter window is safer if you work with items that fluctuate in price.

faqs.question: What happens if the final quantity differs from the quote?
faqs.answer: State that pricing applies to the quoted quantity and re-price if the order falls into a different tier. Allow a small tolerance, such as plus or minus 10%, only if your provider permits it.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. If the client changes the product, adds print locations, or sends new artwork, issue a revised quote. Written approval of the revision keeps the record clear.

printing-services.intro: Print shops, copy centers, and small commercial printers bill clients for business cards, flyers, brochures, banners, posters, booklets, and other printed materials. Customers range from local businesses and nonprofits to schools, event planners, and individuals. Invoices need to show exactly what was produced, in what quantity, on what stock, and with what finishing, since reprint disputes usually come down to specs.
printing-services.pricingModel: Most print work is priced per piece or per run, with the unit price dropping as quantity goes up. A quote usually combines setup or prepress fees, the cost of paper or substrate, ink and press time, finishing (cutting, folding, laminating, binding), and delivery. Large-format work such as banners, vinyl, and posters is typically priced per square foot. Digital short runs are priced per click or per sheet, while offset jobs have higher setup costs but lower per-piece costs at volume. Design and file-fix time is billed hourly or as a flat fee. Rush jobs carry a surcharge, often 25 to 50 percent. Many shops set a minimum order charge so tiny jobs still cover setup time. Repeat customers may get a standing discount or a price list by quantity tier.

rates.service: Vinyl banner (13 oz, hemmed with grommets)
Black and white copies / digital prints

sampleInvoice.notes: Quantities and specifications are as approved on proof dated the invoice date. Please inspect the order within 5 business days of delivery and report defects in writing. Payment due within 15 days. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job number and approved proof date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact artwork and specs the customer signed off on, which settles most reprint disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Quantity, size, and finished dimensions
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often question quantity or size after delivery, so state them for every line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Paper stock and weight, coating, and color mode
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock like 100 lb gloss versus 14 pt uncoated changes cost and appearance, and it justifies the price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finishing details
invoiceChecklist.why: Folding, cutting, lamination, binding, grommets, and drilling each add cost and should appear as line items or in the description.

invoiceChecklist.item: Prepress and design charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the customer that file fixes or layout time were work outside the print run itself.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number
invoiceChecklist.why: Printed goods are taxable in many states, but resale or exempt customers need their certificate on file. Check your state rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery or shipping charge and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when the goods left your shop and what the customer paid for freight.

printing-services.paymentTerms: Print shops commonly collect a deposit of 50 percent on custom jobs and larger orders, with the balance due at pickup or delivery. New customers and walk-in orders are often paid in full before printing starts. Established business accounts may be put on net 15 or net 30 terms. Late fees of 1 to 2 percent per month are common if stated on the quote and invoice. Most shops accept cards, checks, ACH, and cash, and some add a small surcharge for card payments where state law allows. Many shops hold finished jobs until the balance is paid, especially for custom items that cannot be resold.

tips.title: Get written proof approval before you run the job
tips.body: Have the customer sign or email approval of the proof, including spelling, colors, and quantity. Print errors that were approved by the customer are generally their cost, and this record protects you.

tips.title: Bill for custom work upfront
tips.body: Custom printed items such as business cards, branded banners, and event signs have no resale value if the customer walks away. Taking a deposit of half or more limits your risk on materials and press time.

tips.title: Charge for file problems
tips.body: Low-resolution images, missing bleeds, wrong color mode, and RGB files take time to fix. List prepress as its own line at your hourly rate and tell the customer before you start.

tips.title: State overrun and underrun policy
tips.body: Commercial printing often allows a variance of about 10 percent in quantity. Put your policy on the quote and invoice so a delivery of 1,060 pieces against 1,000 ordered does not cause an argument.

tips.title: Keep a minimum order charge
tips.body: Very small jobs still need file handling, machine setup, and cutting. A minimum of $25 to $50 per job keeps these from losing money.

faqs.question: Should I itemize paper, ink, and labor on a print invoice?
faqs.answer: Most shops quote and invoice per finished piece or per run rather than breaking out ink and paper. Itemize the things the customer chose or that were extra: stock upgrades, finishing, prepress, rush fees, and delivery.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on printing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax printed materials, some exempt certain items, and some treat them differently when they are resold or shipped out of state. Collect a resale or exemption certificate when a customer claims an exemption, and check with your state revenue department.

faqs.question: What if a customer says the colors do not match what they expected?
faqs.answer: Point to the approved proof and any color disclaimer on your quote. Screen colors and printed colors often differ, so many shops state that exact color matching is not guaranteed unless a hard-copy proof was approved. Decide in advance when you will reprint at your own cost, such as for a clear production defect.

faqs.question: Can I charge a rush fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is agreed before work starts. A rush surcharge of 25 to 50 percent is common for same-day or next-day turnaround. List it as a separate line so the customer sees it.

faqs.question: When should I require full payment before printing?
faqs.answer: Require it for new customers, small orders, highly customized goods, and large-format work. Offer terms only to customers with a payment history or a signed account agreement.

estimate.intro: Printing customers usually request quotes before ordering and often compare two or three shops on price and turnaround. Quotes are sent for custom or larger jobs, any run that needs special stock or finishing, and recurring work such as monthly newsletters or menus. Customers compare price per piece, paper quality, turnaround time, and whether proofs and delivery are included.

scopeChecklist.why: Price depends heavily on run length and trim size, and a change in either changes the quote.
A switch from 80 lb text to 100 lb gloss, or adding UV coating, changes cost and the final look.
Full color, spot color, and one-sided versus two-sided printing all have different costs.
Folding, scoring, die cutting, lamination, stapling, and drilling add labor and should be named.

scopeChecklist.item: Artwork requirements and who supplies files
scopeChecklist.why: State file format, resolution, and bleed needs, and say whether design or file fixes cost extra.
Specify digital or hard-copy proof and how many rounds are included, so changes do not become unpaid work.

scopeChecklist.item: Turnaround time and delivery or pickup
scopeChecklist.why: The production clock usually starts at proof approval, not at order time, and freight can be a significant cost.

pricingTips.title: Quote in quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Show prices at three quantities, such as 250, 500, and 1,000. Customers often choose the middle or higher option once they see the per-piece price drop, which raises order size.

pricingTips.title: Price off real material costs and press time
pricingTips.body: Check current paper and substrate prices before quoting. Paper costs can change, so set a quote expiration of 14 to 30 days.

pricingTips.title: Separate design and prepress from the print run
pricingTips.body: If a customer may take the quote to another printer, a separate design line lets them compare the print cost fairly and lets you get paid for layout work you did.

pricingTips.title: Include a clear rush option
pricingTips.body: Offer a standard turnaround price and a rush price on the same quote so the customer sees the cost of speed upfront.

faqs.question: How long should a print quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Paper and material prices change, so state an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a quote or sample?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are normally free. For complex jobs, custom samples, or mockups, many shops charge a fee and credit it toward the order if the customer proceeds.

faqs.question: What happens if the customer changes the quantity after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Re-quote at the new quantity, since unit price and setup costs shift. State on the quote that pricing applies only to the listed specs and quantity.

faqs.question: Should the quote include sales tax and shipping?
faqs.answer: Show shipping as its own line when known. Tax rules vary by state and customer, so list it separately or state that applicable tax will be added on the invoice.

private-chef.intro: Private chefs cook for individuals, families, and small groups in the client's home or a rented space. They bill for dinner parties, weekly meal prep, in-home tasting dinners, holiday meals, and sometimes full-time household cooking. Invoices usually combine a chef fee, grocery costs, and any staff or equipment charges.
private-chef.pricingModel: Most private chefs charge a service fee plus groceries at cost. The service fee is either a flat price per event (often calculated per guest), an hourly or daily rate, or a weekly or monthly package for ongoing meal prep. Groceries are billed separately with receipts, or built into a per-person price that covers food and labor. Many chefs add a shopping and planning fee, a travel charge for distant clients, and a rental or equipment fee when they bring specialty gear. Holiday dates, large parties, and short-notice bookings usually carry a premium. Hired servers, sous chefs, or bartenders are passed through at their cost plus a small coordination fee. Weekly meal prep clients often pay a flat weekly rate with a set number of meals, with groceries billed on top.
