rates.service: Weekly meal prep (4-5 dinners, family of 4, labor only)
Cooking class or hands-on lesson at client's home

items.description: Private dinner, 4-course tasting menu, 8 guests (chef fee)
Groceries and specialty ingredients at cost (receipts attached)
Menu planning and grocery shopping
Server for the evening (includes setup and cleanup)
Travel, 28 miles each way

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $300 received on booking is applied to this invoice. Balance due within 7 days of the event. Accepted: check, Zelect, Venmo, or card (3% fee on card payments). Please report any dietary or service concerns within 48 hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, location, and guest count
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-guest pricing depends on the final headcount, so the invoice should show what was cooked for and if it differs from the original booking.

invoiceChecklist.item: Menu or meal summary
invoiceChecklist.why: A short list of the courses or meals delivered reminds the client what they received, which cuts down on disputes about value.

invoiceChecklist.item: Groceries as a separate line with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who pay for groceries at cost expect proof. Attaching or itemizing receipts keeps the markup question out of the conversation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most chefs take a deposit to hold the date. Showing it as a credit prevents double payment confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Staff and rental charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Servers, bartenders, rented plates, or chafing dishes are pass-through costs that should be listed separately from your fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity line or note
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often tip privately chefs in cash or by app. Adding an optional line makes it easy to do so and clarifies whether any service charge is already included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, health permit or food handler card number if required locally
invoiceChecklist.why: Rules differ by state and county, and some clients, venues, or insurers ask to see proof of certification.

private-chef.paymentTerms: Most private chefs collect a nonrefundable deposit of 25-50% when the date is booked, with the balance due on the day of the event or within 7 days after. For large events, some require full payment a few days in advance because grocery costs are paid up front. Weekly meal prep clients are typically billed at the start of each week or month, with groceries reimbursed after each shopping trip. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common but rarely enforced on repeat clients, so state them in the booking agreement. Payment is usually taken by card, ACH, or a payment app, and many chefs pass along card processing fees or build them into the price.

tips.title: Bill groceries separately and keep receipts
tips.body: Photograph or save every receipt. Billing at cost with documentation protects you from accusations of padding, and you can add a small shopping fee for the time instead of marking up the food.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before you buy anything
tips.body: Never front a large grocery bill without money in hand. A deposit that covers expected groceries means a cancellation will not leave you out of pocket.

tips.title: Set a cancellation and headcount policy in writing
tips.body: State the date after which the guest count is locked and what happens if the client cancels within 72 hours. Perishable food is already purchased by then.

tips.title: Charge for the invisible hours
tips.body: Menu development, shopping, prep at home, and cleanup take far more time than the dinner itself. Build these into your flat fee or list them as lines so the price reflects real time.

tips.title: Quote a floor for small groups
tips.body: A dinner for two takes nearly as much planning and travel as a dinner for six. Set a minimum fee so smaller bookings are still worth taking.

faqs.question: Should I include groceries in my per-person price or bill them separately?
faqs.answer: Both work. Billing groceries at cost with receipts is more transparent and common for private events with variable menus. An all-inclusive per-person price is simpler for the client but puts the risk of cost swings on you, so it suits repeat menus you can price accurately.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on my services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax prepared food and catering services, and some tax only the food or only certain services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and if you collect tax, show it as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How should I handle tips?
faqs.answer: Decide whether gratuity is included. If not, a line for optional gratuity or a note on the invoice works. Report tips as income. If you pay hired servers, make sure they get their share and keep a record of it.

faqs.question: Do I need a license or insurance to work as a private chef?
faqs.answer: Requirements vary widely. Many places require a food handler card or food manager certification, and some regulate cooking for pay in a client's home differently from catering. General liability insurance is common practice and often requested by clients and venues. Check your local health department.

faqs.question: How do I bill a client who wants ongoing weekly service?
faqs.answer: Set a flat weekly or monthly rate that states the number of meals, servings, and visits included, and bill groceries separately or as a set weekly budget. Invoice at the start of the period and note how holidays, travel weeks, and skipped weeks are handled.

estimate.intro: Private chefs send a quote after the first conversation about the event or ongoing service, before any menu is final or groceries are bought. Clients often compare you against caterers, restaurant takeout, and other chefs, so the quote needs to show clearly what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, start time, location, and guest count
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on these. Stating them makes it clear what the quote covers if the count changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Menu format and number of courses
scopeChecklist.why: A three-course plated dinner and a family-style buffet involve very different labor. Define the format so expectations match.
Accommodating allergies or multiple diets can raise costs and prep time. Record what you have agreed to prepare.

scopeChecklist.item: Who buys groceries and how they are billed
scopeChecklist.why: State whether groceries are at cost, capped at a budget, or included, and whether there is a shopping fee.
Say whether you serve, whether servers are included, and whether you wash dishes and leave the kitchen clean.
If you bring your own gear or the client needs to rent tableware, note who supplies and pays for it. Also note whether you need to inspect the kitchen beforehand.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, cancellation, and final headcount deadline
scopeChecklist.why: These protect you from losses on perishable food and held dates.

pricingTips.title: Price from your total hours, not just the dinner
pricingTips.body: Add planning, shopping, prep, travel, cooking, service, and cleanup, then divide to see your effective hourly rate. A quote that only covers the time at the stove usually undercharges.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three menu tiers
pricingTips.body: Presenting a simple, standard, and premium option lets the client choose a budget without negotiating your rate. Proteins like beef tenderloin or lobster shift the grocery cost noticeably.

pricingTips.title: Give a grocery estimate with a cap or range
pricingTips.body: Clients dislike open-ended food costs. Provide an expected range and agree to check in if prices will exceed it.

pricingTips.title: Add premiums for peak dates
pricingTips.body: Holidays, New Year's Eve, Mother's Day, and short-notice requests are in demand. A 15-25% premium is common and should be shown on the quote, not added later.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a tasting or consultation before the event?
faqs.answer: Many chefs offer a short phone or video call for free, and charge for an in-person tasting. The tasting fee can be credited toward the event if the client books, which encourages commitment.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen days is common, but state an end date. Ingredient costs and your calendar change, and a deadline lets you release the date to another client if they do not respond.

faqs.question: What if the guest count changes after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Set a lock-in date, usually 5 to 7 days before the event. Increases are billed at the per-guest rate if you can accommodate them. Decreases after the lock date usually do not reduce the fee because the food is already purchased.

faqs.question: Can I charge more than the quote if the client adds requests?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the quote states that changes to the menu, guest count, or service hours are billed separately. Confirm the changes and new price in writing, such as by email or text, before you do the extra work.

private-investigator.intro: Private investigators bill attorneys, insurance carriers, businesses, and individuals for fact-finding work such as surveillance, background checks, locating people, and case research. Most solo and small-firm PIs invoice by the hour plus expenses like mileage, database fees, and travel. Invoices often go to law firms or claims departments that expect detailed time logs and itemized costs.
private-investigator.pricingModel: Most PIs charge an hourly rate for field and desk work, with a higher rate for surveillance and a lower rate for records research or report writing. Mileage is billed separately at a per-mile rate, often at or above the IRS standard rate, and many investigators add a flat fee or per-hour charge for vehicle and equipment use such as video gear or GPS-permitted tools. Database searches, court record pulls, and records requests are passed through at cost or with a modest markup. Larger clients typically pay a retainer against which hours are billed, and insurance work often has a negotiated rate and a cap on hours per assignment. Flat fees are common for defined products like a basic background check, an asset search, or process service. Minimum blocks, such as four hours for surveillance, protect you from short, unproductive days. Overnight travel, out-of-area work, and rush or weekend assignments are usually billed at higher rates or with added costs.

rates.service: Background check or records research (desk work)
Expert or court testimony and deposition prep

items.description: Surveillance, subject residence and workplace, 3/12 and 3/13 (video evidence obtained)
Review and edit video footage, 6 clips
Written investigative report with timeline and still images
Mileage, personal vehicle
Database search fees (address and vehicle records)

sampleInvoice.notes: Reference: Claim No. 24-118839, Smith v. Delta Freight. Retainer of $1,000 applied. Balance due within 30 days of invoice date. Footage and report delivered via secure link; originals retained for 3 years per our file policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and case or claim number
invoiceChecklist.why: Law firms and insurers route invoices by file number, and missing references delay payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your PI license number and agency license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Most states license investigators, and clients such as attorneys and carriers often require proof of licensure on file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dated time log with start and end times for each task
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients audit hours, and a day-by-day breakdown of surveillance, travel, and review supports each charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized mileage with total miles and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Mileage is a significant cost on surveillance, and clients often question it without a clear trip record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Database fees, records fees, and travel costs should be visible so the client sees what is labor and what is out-of-pocket.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer received and amount applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the balance due accurately and avoids confusion about what the client already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed engagement agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the billing rates and scope to the contract, which helps if a charge is disputed.

private-investigator.paymentTerms: Private investigators commonly require a retainer up front, often $500 to $2,500 for individual clients, and draw down against it as hours accrue. Law firms and insurance carriers are more often billed in arrears on net 30 terms, sometimes net 45 or 60 for larger carriers. Many PIs deliver the final report only after payment or after the retainer is replenished for individual clients. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the engagement agreement. Payment is usually accepted by check, ACH, or card, and many PIs add a card processing fee only if the agreement says so.

tips.title: Bill a minimum block for surveillance
tips.body: Set a minimum such as four hours per surveillance day in your agreement. Subjects cancel plans, and you still have to travel, set up, and stay available.

tips.title: Replenish the retainer before it runs out
tips.body: Set a trigger, such as notifying the client when the balance drops below 25 percent. Stopping work mid-case because funds ran out is awkward, and clients rarely like surprises.

tips.title: Keep contemporaneous notes
tips.body: Log times and activities daily. If an invoice is questioned by an attorney or carrier, your notes and report should match the hours billed.

tips.title: Get approval before exceeding the budget
tips.body: Insurance and law firm clients often cap hours. Ask in writing before going over the cap, and document the approval before billing the extra time.

tips.title: Separate delivery of work from payment
tips.body: For individual clients, hold the final report or footage until the invoice is paid, if your agreement says so. It is hard to collect after the client has what they wanted.

faqs.question: Should I charge a different rate for surveillance than for desk research?
faqs.answer: Many PIs do. Surveillance involves long hours, equipment, vehicle wear, and unpredictable conditions, so it usually has a higher hourly rate than records research or report writing. List each rate on your engagement agreement and show it on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I bill for travel time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many investigators bill travel time at a reduced rate or at the full rate, and bill mileage on top. Be specific about whether travel to and from the first location counts.

faqs.question: Do I need to itemize database search costs?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. Clients often want to see what was paid for and may be reimbursed by their own client or carrier. Show the cost of each search or a total with a short description, and state any markup in your agreement.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes my hours?
faqs.answer: Provide the dated time log and any supporting materials such as the report and video review notes. A clear agreement and detailed notes make most disputes easy to resolve. Keep confidentiality in mind when sharing details.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax investigative or security services, and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional about your services.

estimate.intro: Private investigators usually give an estimate or fee proposal before accepting an engagement, especially for surveillance, background investigations, and litigation support. Clients, often attorneys or insurance adjusters, compare hourly rates, estimated hours, and how expenses will be handled. Investigations are unpredictable, so a good estimate explains what is included and what could change the cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Objective and scope of the investigation
scopeChecklist.why: A written description of what you are and are not investigating keeps the work focused and limits disputes about what the client expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated hours and the cap or budget
scopeChecklist.why: Clients want a ballpark cost, and a stated budget gives a point at which you must check in before continuing.
Surveillance, research, interviews, and testimony are priced differently, and listing them avoids surprises.
Sets expectations that a short or canceled day is still billable because of travel and setup.

scopeChecklist.item: Expenses and how they are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Mileage, databases, records fees, lodging, and equipment charges should be listed with rates or stated as pass-through costs.
Spells out the amount due before work starts and when you will ask for more funds.

scopeChecklist.item: No guarantee of results and legal limits
scopeChecklist.why: Investigations may not produce evidence, and you will not break the law to get it. Stating this protects both sides.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range with assumptions
pricingTips.body: Give a range of hours, such as 20 to 30, and state the assumptions, such as number of surveillance days and a known subject address. If the facts change, you have a basis to revise.

pricingTips.title: Price for the unknowns
pricingTips.body: Surveillance often runs longer than planned because of traffic, waiting, and subjects who do not appear. Build in time for these and a second investigator if safety or coverage requires it.

pricingTips.title: Use flat fees for defined products
pricingTips.body: Background checks, locates, and asset searches have predictable steps. A flat fee is easy for clients to approve, but state what is included and what triggers additional charges.

pricingTips.title: Offer phased work
pricingTips.body: Propose an initial phase, such as two days of surveillance, and a check-in before continuing. It lowers the client's commitment and gives you a natural point to report results and ask for more funds.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price for a surveillance case?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Surveillance outcomes depend on what the subject does, so most PIs quote an hourly rate with an estimated number of hours and a cap that requires approval to exceed.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Rates, availability, and the facts of the case can change, so put an expiration date on the estimate.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before I start?
faqs.answer: Yes, in practice. Most states and many clients expect a written contract that covers scope, fees, and confidentiality. Many PIs treat a signed estimate and retainer payment as the start of the engagement, but check your local rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge for preparing the estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple estimates are usually free. For complex litigation support or large corporate projects that require significant planning, some PIs charge a consultation fee and credit it toward the work if hired.

process-server.intro: Process servers deliver summonses, complaints, subpoenas, petitions, and other legal documents to the people named in them, and then provide proof that service was made. Clients are mostly law firms, paralegals, and legal document services, along with some self-represented individuals and property managers. Invoices usually list each service attempt, any skip tracing, mileage, and the filing of the affidavit of service.
process-server.pricingModel: Most process servers charge a flat fee per service, with the price set by how quickly the papers must be served. Routine service typically takes several days, rush service takes 24 to 48 hours, and same-day service costs more. Extra attempts, long distances, and difficult targets are often billed separately, as are mileage, skip tracing, and stakeouts. Some servers bundle a set number of attempts (often three) into the base fee and charge for each attempt after that. Subpoena service may include witness fees or mileage checks that the client has to cover, and these are passed through at cost. Regular law firm clients often get volume discounts or a monthly invoice, while one-time clients usually pay up front. Some states and counties set maximum fees for certain kinds of service, such as sheriff-equivalent service, so check your local rules.

rates.service: Routine service of process (standard turnaround, up to 3 attempts)
Additional attempts beyond the included number
Mileage outside the standard service area
Stakeout or surveillance for evasive defendants
Document filing, court runs, or notarized affidavit of service

items.description: Service of summons and complaint on J. Rivera, 412 Oak St (rush, served on 2nd attempt)
Additional attempt, evening (attempt 3 on R. Chen, 88 Pine Ave)
Routine service of subpoena duces tecum on Metro Records Custodian
Skip trace for current address of R. Chen
Mileage beyond 25-mile service area
Notarized affidavit of service and e-filing

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Affidavits of service have been emailed to the file contact. Please include the invoice number with payment. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Case name, case number, and court
invoiceChecklist.why: Law firms track costs by matter, and a clear case reference lets their accounting team match your invoice to the right file without calling you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Person or entity served and the documents delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the recipient and document type (summons, subpoena, petition) confirms what you did and avoids confusion when one client sends several jobs at once.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date, time, and address of each attempt and of final service
invoiceChecklist.why: These details back up the affidavit of service and justify charges for extra attempts if the fee is ever questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service type and turnaround (routine, rush, same-day)
invoiceChecklist.why: The speed of service drives the fee, so stating it shows why the price differs between jobs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons: extra attempts, mileage, skip trace, stakeout time
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients are more willing to pay extras when each one is itemized with quantity and rate instead of rolled into a lump sum.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as witness fees or court fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Show these at cost and separately from your service fee so the client can see what you earned versus what you advanced.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your license or registration number, if your state or county requires one
invoiceChecklist.why: Some jurisdictions require registered or certified process servers, and including your number supports the validity of the service. Check your local rules.

process-server.paymentTerms: Many process servers invoice law firms on net 30 terms, with monthly statements for high-volume accounts. New clients, individuals, and out-of-area jobs are often paid up front or with a deposit, especially when the work includes rush fees or heavy travel. Pass-through costs like witness fees should be paid before service. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common, and it helps to state them on the invoice. Typical payment methods are check, ACH, and credit card. Some servers hold the affidavit of service until payment arrives on first-time or past-due accounts, though many release it right away to avoid hurting the client's case deadlines.

tips.title: Define what a base fee includes
tips.body: State how many attempts are covered, usually three, and what counts as an attempt. This prevents arguments when a hard-to-find defendant takes six trips.

tips.title: Bill for non-service and failed attempts
tips.body: If the person has moved or the address is bad, you still did the work. Bill a reduced fee or per-attempt rate for non-service, and put it in your terms ahead of time.

tips.title: Separate pass-through costs from your fee
tips.body: Witness fees, court filing charges, and records fees should be listed at cost. Mixing them with your service fee makes it hard for clients to reconcile and can muddy your income reporting.

tips.title: Invoice when the affidavit is done
tips.body: Send the invoice together with the completed affidavit of service. The client has just received something they need, which makes it the best time to get paid and cuts down on follow-up.

tips.title: Keep a mileage and attempt log
tips.body: Contemporaneous notes with times, addresses, and odometer readings support your charges to clients and also help at tax time if you deduct vehicle expenses.

faqs.question: How much should I charge for serving papers?
faqs.answer: Routine service in the US typically runs about $40 to $90 per service, with rush service at $75 to $150 and same-day at $125 or more. Rates vary a lot by region, distance, and local competition, so look at what other servers in your area charge.

faqs.question: Can I charge for failed service attempts?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Many servers include a set number of attempts in the base fee and charge for each additional one. Some also charge a reduced fee for non-service when the person cannot be found. Put this policy in writing so the client agrees before you start.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit?
faqs.answer: For new clients, individuals, and jobs with long travel, a deposit or full prepayment is common. Established law firms are usually fine on net 30. Any witness fees or court costs you must advance should be paid by the client up front.

faqs.question: Do I need to list my license number on an invoice?
faqs.answer: It depends on where you work. Some states and counties require process servers to be registered, licensed, or appointed, while others do not. If yours does, including your number on invoices and affidavits is a good habit. Check your local rules.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on service of process?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax certain services and others do not, and legal support services may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional before deciding whether to add tax.

estimate.intro: Process servers quote before work starts when a law firm is comparing vendors, when the job involves many defendants or distant addresses, or when the client needs a rush turnaround. Clients typically compare the per-service price, the speed, how many attempts are included, and whether you will bill extra for travel or difficult targets.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of documents and people to be served
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for one summons is very different from a quote for six subpoenas. Listing the count prevents scope creep after you have started.
Speed is the biggest driver of price. Spell out the deadline you are working to and what happens if it changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Attempts included and the fee for extras
scopeChecklist.why: This sets expectations for evasive or hard-to-find recipients and explains later charges.

scopeChecklist.item: Service addresses and whether they are verified
scopeChecklist.why: Bad or outdated addresses are the most common reason for extra cost. State whether skip tracing is included or billed separately.
Define the zone covered by the base fee and the per-mile rate beyond it so out-of-area jobs do not surprise the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Proof of service deliverable and timing
scopeChecklist.why: State that you will provide a signed or notarized affidavit of service, and how quickly, since clients have court deadlines.

scopeChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Witness fees, court fees, and records charges should be identified as client responsibility and payable in advance where needed.

pricingTips.title: Use a tiered price list
pricingTips.body: Publish routine, rush, and same-day rates in a simple table. Law firms like to see clear options and can choose the speed that fits their deadline.

pricingTips.title: Price for difficulty, not just distance
pricingTips.body: Gated communities, workplaces with security, and people known to avoid service take more time. Quote a higher rate or require a stakeout budget when the client warns you about this.

pricingTips.title: Offer volume pricing carefully
pricingTips.body: A discount for law firms that send many jobs a month can win steady work. Set a minimum monthly volume and keep rush and out-of-area work at full price.

pricingTips.title: Give a not-to-exceed figure for open-ended work
pricingTips.body: For skip tracing or stakeouts, quote an hourly rate with a cap that the client must approve before you go beyond. This protects both of you.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat fee or by the attempt?
faqs.answer: A flat fee covering a set number of attempts is the easiest for clients to compare. Then list the per-attempt charge for extras. For jobs likely to be difficult, quoting by the attempt or the hour may protect you better.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Addresses, fuel costs, and your schedule can change, and a short validity period lets you update the price if the client waits.

faqs.question: Can I quote before I know if the address is good?
faqs.answer: Yes, but say so in the quote. State that the price assumes the address provided is correct, and that skip tracing or additional travel will be billed if the person cannot be found there.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a price for service anywhere in the state?
faqs.answer: Quote the base fee for your own area and give a per-mile rate or a flat surcharge for distant counties. For remote locations, many servers subcontract to a local colleague and pass on that cost with a modest markup.

product-analyst.intro: Freelance and contract product analysts help software companies, startups, and e-commerce teams understand how people use their product. They bill for work like funnel and retention analysis, event tracking plans, dashboard builds, A/B test design and readouts, and ongoing metrics support. Clients are usually product managers, founders, or growth leads who need analysis but not a full-time hire.
product-analyst.pricingModel: Most independent product analysts bill hourly for open-ended or ongoing work and flat project fees for well-defined deliverables such as a tracking plan, a dashboard set, or a single experiment analysis. Monthly retainers are common for ongoing support, typically with a fixed number of hours or a defined list of recurring reports, such as a weekly metrics review. Day rates are used for embedded contract work and workshops. Price on the outcome and the scope, not just the hours, because a clean tracking plan can save a client months of bad data. Pass through tool costs (for example, a BI seat or a data warehouse query bill) at cost only if the contract says so. Rush work, data cleanup caused by messy instrumentation, and extra revision rounds are usually billed separately.

rates.service: Ad hoc product analysis (funnels, retention, cohorts)
Event tracking plan and analytics instrumentation spec
A/B test design and results analysis
SQL query writing and data modeling
Stakeholder workshop or metrics definition session

items.description: Onboarding funnel analysis: signup to first key action, segmented by acquisition channel
SQL data modeling: cleaned events table and weekly active user definitions
Retention dashboard build (6 charts, cohort view, filters)
A/B test analysis: new pricing page (power check, results, recommendation memo)
Findings presentation to product team (60 minutes plus prep)

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers work from March 3 to March 28 under the signed statement of work dated February 24. Payment due within 15 days. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to overdue balances. Dashboard and queries are handed over on receipt of payment for the final milestone.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the statement of work or contract and its date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each line to agreed scope, which helps when a client asks why a deliverable was billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable names and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often need to match the invoice to specific outputs such as a dashboard, tracking plan, or experiment readout.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged by task for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Analysis hours are invisible to clients, so a breakdown (querying, modeling, review) shows where time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often reject invoices that lack a PO, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and tool fees at cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Warehouse query charges, BI licenses, or survey tools should be listed separately so they are not mistaken for labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone status for fixed-fee projects
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing which milestone is complete, such as tracking plan delivered or dashboard live, supports staged billing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Data access and IP handover terms
invoiceChecklist.why: A line noting that queries, models, and dashboards transfer upon payment gives you leverage on unpaid balances.

product-analyst.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is standard for analytics contracts, and larger companies often run net 45 or 60 through accounts payable. For fixed-fee projects, many analysts take 25 to 50 percent upfront and the rest at delivery or in milestones. Retainers are usually billed at the start of the month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract, though enforceability varies by state. Payment is commonly accepted by ACH or bank transfer for larger amounts and by card for smaller ones, with the card fee sometimes passed to the client.

tips.title: Define metrics in writing before you start
tips.body: Disputes often come from two people defining active user or conversion differently. Put metric definitions in the scope so rework on changed definitions can be billed as a change order.

tips.title: Bill for data cleanup separately
tips.body: If the client's event data is incomplete or inconsistent, flag it early and estimate cleanup as its own line. Otherwise, hours can balloon under a flat fee.

tips.title: Tie fixed fees to deliverables, not time
tips.body: Use named deliverables and a set number of revision rounds. Extra rounds, new data sources, or added segments become billable add-ons.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones for longer projects
tips.body: Bill after the tracking plan, after the first dashboard version, and after the final readout. This keeps cash coming in and makes scope creep visible.

tips.title: Track time even on flat fees
tips.body: Keeping a log shows you whether your fixed prices are realistic and gives you proof of effort if a client disputes scope.

faqs.question: Should a product analyst charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for exploratory or ongoing work where scope is unclear. Use a flat fee when the deliverable is well defined, such as a dashboard set or a tracking plan. Many analysts mix both, with a fixed fee for the core deliverable and hourly billing for extra requests.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent waiting on data access?
faqs.answer: Only if your contract says so. A common approach is to state that the timeline depends on timely access to data and tools, and that delays caused by the client may be billed at a reduced rate or push out the delivery date.

faqs.question: Who owns the dashboards and queries I build?
faqs.answer: That depends on your contract. Many analysts retain ownership until final payment and then transfer the work, or license it to the client. Put it in writing and state the transfer terms on the invoice or in the SOW.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on analytics services?
faqs.answer: It varies. Many states do not tax professional services, but some tax data processing, software-related, or digital services. Check your state and your client's state, and ask an accountant if the work involves delivered software or reports.

faqs.question: How do I bill for an A/B test that is inconclusive?
faqs.answer: Bill for the work done, not the result. Define the deliverable as test design and analysis, not a winning variant. An inconclusive result is still a finding, and the scope should say that.

estimate.intro: Product analysts send an estimate or proposal when a client wants a defined project such as a tracking plan, a dashboard build, or a test analysis, or when a retainer is being considered. Clients usually compare your estimate against other freelancers, an agency, or the cost of hiring in-house, so clarity on deliverables and assumptions matters as much as price.

scopeChecklist.why: Say whether the client gets a slide deck, a dashboard, a SQL repo, or a memo, so nobody expects extras.
The work depends on access to the warehouse, product analytics tool, and CRM. Missing access is the biggest cause of delay.
Fixing definitions upfront prevents rework when stakeholders disagree later.
State that the estimate assumes reasonably complete event data, and that cleanup beyond a set number of hours is extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and review meetings
scopeChecklist.why: Caps unlimited changes and gives you a basis for pricing additions.
Tie delivery dates to when data access, stakeholder feedback, and approvals arrive.
Clarify who pays for BI seats, warehouse compute, and experiment platforms.

pricingTips.title: Estimate a range for exploratory work
pricingTips.body: If the data has not been seen, quote a range or a discovery phase first. A short paid audit of the data lets you give a firm price for the full project.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three scope options
pricingTips.body: For example, a basic dashboard, a dashboard with segmentation, and a full package with a tracking plan. Clients tend to choose a middle option and see exactly what each level covers.

pricingTips.title: Price in a buffer for stakeholder alignment
pricingTips.body: Meetings, definition debates, and feedback cycles take more time than the analysis itself. Include them in the estimate, not as a surprise.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 30 days is typical, because client data and priorities change and your availability does too.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed price when deliverables and data are well understood. If you have not seen the data, give an hourly estimate with a cap or do a paid discovery phase first.

faqs.question: How much should I ask for as a deposit?
faqs.answer: Many analysts ask for 25 to 50 percent upfront on fixed-fee projects, especially for new clients. Retainers are normally billed in advance for the month.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change scope after accepting?
faqs.answer: Use a change order. Describe the new request, the added cost, and the effect on the timeline, and get written approval before starting that work.

product-designer.intro: Freelance and small-studio product designers bill startups, agencies, and in-house product teams for designing digital products such as web apps, mobile apps, and SaaS dashboards. Invoices typically cover discovery and research, UX flows, wireframes, UI design, prototypes, design system work, and developer handoff.
product-designer.pricingModel: Most product designers price in one of three ways: hourly, a day rate, or a fixed fee per project phase. Hourly and day rates suit open-ended or embedded work with a product team, where scope shifts week to week. Fixed fees work for defined deliverables such as a design sprint, an MVP design, or a design system starter kit, and are usually split by phase (research, UX, UI, handoff). Longer engagements are often billed as a monthly retainer for a set number of days or hours per month. Charge separately for revisions beyond the agreed rounds, user testing participant incentives, stock assets, font licenses, and paid plugins or tools passed through to the client. Rates vary with experience, specialty (fintech, healthcare, and enterprise tend to pay more), and whether the client is a startup or an established company.

rates.service: Day rate for embedded team work
UX research and user interviews (planning, sessions, synthesis)
MVP app or web app design (flows, wireframes, UI, prototype)

items.description: UX flows and wireframes - onboarding and dashboard (Phase 2)
High-fidelity UI design - 24 screens, desktop and mobile
Clickable prototype for user testing (Figma)
Usability test sessions - moderation and summary report (5 participants)
Participant incentives (5 x $50 gift cards, at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Phase 2 of 3 per the agreement dated March 4. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month. Includes two rounds of revisions on UI; additional rounds billed at $110 per hour. Design files transfer to client upon final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and phase or milestone
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's finance team can match it to the contract or statement of work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed (screens, flows, prototype, design system components)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the client is paying for, since design work is less visible than physical goods.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours or days worked with dates, if billing time-based
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often ask for backup on hourly work, and a short log prevents back-and-forth.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and any out-of-scope requests
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when extra billing is justified and reminds the client of the limits in your agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (participant incentives, stock photos, icon sets, font licenses, plugins)
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets you recover expenses at cost or with an agreed markup, with receipts available if requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client contact for accounts payable
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often will not process an invoice without a PO or cost center reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: IP and file transfer terms or reference to the contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear when ownership of final files passes, which is commonly tied to payment in full.

product-designer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25-50% before work starts is common for fixed-fee projects, with the remainder tied to milestones such as end of research, approved wireframes, and final handoff. Hourly and retainer work is usually invoiced monthly or biweekly, with retainers billed in advance at the start of the month. Net 15 or net 30 is typical, though larger companies may insist on net 45 or net 60, so confirm before signing. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract. Clients usually pay by ACH, wire, or card; card payments may carry a processing fee you can pass on if your agreement allows it.

tips.title: Tie final files to final payment
tips.body: State in your contract that source files and full usage rights transfer once the invoice is paid. Share view-only prototypes until then so you keep leverage on the last milestone.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds
tips.body: Define the number of revision rounds per phase and bill extra rounds at your hourly rate. Without a cap, feedback cycles can double the real hours on a fixed-fee project.

tips.title: Bill at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: Invoice at the close of research, UX, UI, and handoff. A single invoice at the end of a three-month project leaves you carrying the risk if the client stalls.

tips.title: Charge for stakeholder time
tips.body: Workshops, review calls, and async feedback rounds take real hours. Either include them in your fixed fee with a stated limit or log them on time-based invoices.

tips.title: Track scope changes in writing
tips.body: When a client adds a flow or a platform, send a short change note with the added cost before starting. Then reference it on the next invoice.

faqs.question: Should a product designer bill hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use hourly or day rates when scope is unclear or you are embedded with a team. Use fixed fees when deliverables are well defined, such as an MVP design or design system. Many designers use fixed fees per phase with hourly billing for anything outside scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge for discovery and research separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is common to. Discovery often determines the scope of everything that follows, so many designers bill it as its own phase or paid workshop before quoting the rest of the project.

faqs.question: How do I bill for user testing participant incentives?
faqs.answer: List them as a separate line item at cost, with the number of participants and incentive amount. Keep receipts. Some designers add a small handling fee, which should be agreed in advance.

faqs.question: What if the client keeps asking for changes after sign-off?
faqs.answer: Refer to the revision limit in your agreement and send a change estimate for the extra work. Bill it as a separate line item on the next invoice, labeled as out-of-scope revisions.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax digital or professional services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax collected as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Product designers send an estimate or proposal before any design work begins, usually after an intro call and a look at the client's product, goals, and timeline. Clients often compare several designers or studios, so they look at the scope, number of screens or flows, timeline, and whether the price is fixed or open-ended.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables by phase (research, flows, wireframes, UI, prototype, handoff)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume 'design' includes everything from strategy to production assets. Naming each deliverable sets the boundary.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of screens, flows, or platforms covered
scopeChecklist.why: Adding an iOS app or a tablet layout can significantly change the hours. A stated count makes extra requests easy to price.
Prevents endless feedback loops and gives you a clear point to bill additional work.
Delays in feedback, content, or brand assets push timelines. State how quickly the client needs to respond and what happens if they do not.

scopeChecklist.item: Tools, file formats, and handoff method
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you deliver Figma files, exported assets, or developer specs, and whether the client needs their own licenses.

scopeChecklist.item: What is excluded (front-end development, copywriting, brand identity, illustration, ongoing support)
scopeChecklist.why: These are common assumptions that lead to disputes if they are not ruled out in writing.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline, start date, and estimate validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Locks in your availability and protects you if the client takes weeks to approve and your schedule fills up.

pricingTips.title: Quote by phase
pricingTips.body: Break the estimate into discovery, UX, UI, and handoff with a price for each. Clients can see where the money goes and can approve a first phase without committing to the whole project.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Product work often uncovers new requirements mid-project. Add a contingency of 10-20% to fixed fees, or offer a lower fixed fee with a clear change process.

pricingTips.title: Offer options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three tiers, such as core flows only, full app design, or full app plus design system. Clients tend to choose the middle option and it shifts the conversation from price to scope.

pricingTips.title: Price on value for larger projects
pricingTips.body: For work tied to revenue, such as a checkout redesign or onboarding overhaul, a fixed fee based on business impact can be higher than an hourly calculation. Be ready to explain the outcome you are working toward.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or proposal?
faqs.answer: A short estimate after a call is usually free. If the client needs a detailed scoping document, audit, or discovery workshop, charge for it and credit the fee against the project if they proceed.

faqs.question: How detailed should a design estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list the phases, deliverables, number of screens or flows, revision rounds, and timeline. Most estimates fit on one to three pages. More detail helps when the project is large or the client is unfamiliar with design work.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change scope after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Point to the scope section and send a written change estimate for the additional work. Get approval before starting, and add it as a separate line item on the next invoice.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. After that, your availability or rates may change, so state an expiration date and say the price may be revised if the client accepts later.

product-photographer.intro: Product photographers shoot items for e-commerce stores, Amazon and marketplace listings, catalogs, ads, and brand websites. Clients are usually small brands, retailers, agencies, and manufacturers. Invoices typically cover per-image or per-product fees, shoot time, styling and props, retouching, and usage licensing.
product-photographer.pricingModel: Most product photographers price per image or per product, since clients think in terms of a catalog of SKUs. White-background e-commerce shots are often sold per image with volume discounts, while lifestyle, styled, or campaign work is usually priced by the day or half day plus production costs. Retouching is either bundled into the image price or billed separately by the image or hour for complex work such as compositing, clipping paths, or ghost mannequin edits. Extras that show up as separate lines include props and set styling, a stylist or assistant, studio rental, rush turnaround, and usage licensing for advertising or long-term commercial use. Many photographers set a minimum project fee or a half-day minimum to cover setup, editing, and file delivery time.

rates.service: Amazon listing pack (main image plus 5-7 supporting images)
Advanced retouching (compositing, ghost mannequin, clipping paths)

items.description: White-background product photography, 30 SKUs, 3 angles each (90 images)
Lifestyle styled shots, hero images for homepage and ads
Standard retouching and color correction (included for all selects)
Prop sourcing and set styling
Studio assistant
Commercial web and social usage license, 2 years

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 50% deposit of $1,710 was received on booking and is deducted from the total shown due. Final images are licensed for the client's website, marketplace listings, and social channels for two years from delivery. Additional usage requires a separate license. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot date(s) and location (studio, client site, or rental)
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties charges to a specific job and helps when a client's accounting needs dates for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of products/SKUs and number of final images delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-image pricing only holds up if the count is clear, and it prevents disputes over how many were agreed on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage license terms (media, territory, duration)
invoiceChecklist.why: Product images are often licensed, not sold outright. Stating the terms on the invoice protects you if the client later uses them in paid ads or print.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retouching level and number of revision rounds included
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what was covered so extra rounds or complex edits can be billed without argument.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for props, styling, assistants, and studio rental
invoiceChecklist.why: Production costs are often reimbursable or marked up, and clients want to see them apart from your creative fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most shoots are booked with a deposit, and showing it avoids double-payment confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or SKU list reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Brands and agencies often require a PO or project code to approve payment.

product-photographer.paymentTerms: Product photographers commonly collect a 25-50% deposit to hold the shoot date, with the balance due on delivery of final files or net 15 to net 30 for established clients and agencies. Some photographers deliver watermarked or low-resolution previews first and release full-resolution files once payment clears. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract or estimate. Payment is usually accepted by ACH, card, or check, and agencies may pay on net 45 or net 60 cycles, so confirm their terms before the shoot.

tips.title: Hold final files until the balance clears
tips.body: Deliver proofs or watermarked previews for selection, then release full-resolution, retouched files after payment. This is standard in the field and keeps leverage in your hands without being adversarial.

tips.title: Bill usage separately from creative time
tips.body: List the license as its own line item. It makes your rate easier to compare, and it gives you a clear way to charge more if the client later expands into ads, packaging, or retail print.

tips.title: Charge for product handling and returns
tips.body: If you receive samples by mail, steam garments, clean items, or handle returns and shipping, add a line for it or set a minimum. This time is easy to forget and adds up on large catalogs.

tips.title: Set a revision limit
tips.body: Include one or two rounds of minor edits in the price and bill additional rounds by the image or hour. Clients often request color changes or background tweaks after delivery.

tips.title: Add a rush fee on the invoice, not after the fact
tips.body: If a client needs files in 24-48 hours, put the surcharge on the estimate and invoice as a separate line so it is clear it was agreed on.

faqs.question: Should I charge per image or per hour?
faqs.answer: Per image or per product is more common for e-commerce work because clients budget by catalog size. Hourly or day rates make more sense for lifestyle and campaign shoots where setup and styling take most of the time. Many photographers combine them: a day rate for the shoot plus a per-image fee for retouching.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on product photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax photography services or the delivery of digital files, and others do not. Check your state's department of revenue rules or ask an accountant, and note any tax charged as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for usage rights?
faqs.answer: Add a line item for the license that states the media (web, social, print, paid ads), territory, and duration. Keep the wording short on the invoice and put the full terms in your contract or estimate.

faqs.question: Can I bill for props and supplies I buy for a shoot?
faqs.answer: Yes. List them as reimbursable expenses at cost or with a modest markup, depending on what you agreed to. Keep receipts and attach them if the client asks, especially with agencies and larger brands.

faqs.question: What if a client cancels or reschedules a shoot?
faqs.answer: State a cancellation policy in your estimate, such as keeping the deposit if canceled within 48-72 hours of the shoot date. If you incurred costs for studio rental or an assistant, bill those on a final invoice.

estimate.intro: Product photographers send an estimate before any shoot is booked, usually after the client shares a product list, shot requirements, and reference images. Clients often compare quotes from several photographers on price per image, turnaround, and what is included, so a clear breakdown helps your quote stand up to comparison.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of products and shots per product
scopeChecklist.why: The total image count drives the price. Specifying angles, such as front, back, and detail, prevents later requests for extra views at no cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Background and style (white, colored, lifestyle, in-use)
scopeChecklist.why: Different setups take different amounts of time and may require props, models, or location work.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies the products, and when they must arrive
scopeChecklist.why: Late or damaged samples delay the shoot. State whether you charge for pickup, shipping, or reshoots caused by missing items.

scopeChecklist.item: Retouching level and number of revisions
scopeChecklist.why: Basic cleanup is much cheaper than compositing or ghost mannequin work. Define what counts as included.
Image size, format (JPEG, PNG, TIFF), and marketplace requirements such as Amazon's affect editing time and clients' expectations.
Clarifies how images can be used and whether additional licensing will cost extra.
Gives the client a delivery date and sets a rate if they need faster work.

pricingTips.title: Offer volume tiers
pricingTips.body: Price the first 10 images at a standard rate and drop the per-image cost on larger batches. Clients with big catalogs appreciate the discount, and it rewards you with bigger jobs without cutting your minimum.

pricingTips.title: Build in setup and editing time
pricingTips.body: Per-image prices should reflect the whole workflow, including setup, lighting changes, culling, retouching, and delivery. If a product is reflective, transparent, or very small, charge more per image.

pricingTips.title: Quote tiers for different budgets
pricingTips.body: Present a basic package (white background only) and a premium option (white background plus lifestyle shots). Clients often choose the middle option when they can compare.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the estimate
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you if costs, studio availability, or your schedule change before the client accepts.

faqs.question: How do I estimate a job when I haven't seen the products?
faqs.answer: Ask for a product list with dimensions, materials, and photos. Reflective, transparent, or complex items take longer, so note that the estimate may change if the actual products differ from what was described.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit with the estimate?
faqs.answer: Most photographers do. A 25-50% deposit at acceptance holds the date and covers early costs like studio booking and prop purchases. State it clearly on the estimate.

faqs.question: Is it okay to give a price range instead of a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: A range works when the product list or style is not final. Once the scope is confirmed, send a fixed quote so the client knows the final price before the shoot.

product-sales.intro: Product sellers are small businesses, independent reps, and makers who sell physical goods to retailers, businesses, or individual customers. They send invoices for wholesale orders, bulk purchases, custom or personalized runs, and direct sales that are not paid at checkout. A good invoice lists each SKU, quantity, unit price, shipping, and tax treatment so the buyer can match it to what arrived.
product-sales.pricingModel: Product sales are priced per unit, not per hour. Most sellers set a retail price (MSRP) and a wholesale price, often around 40 to 60 percent of retail, with volume tiers that drop the unit price at higher quantities such as case packs or pallets. Shipping and handling is usually billed separately, either at actual freight cost or as a flat or percentage charge. Custom or private-label work often adds one-time setup fees for artwork, molds, or labels, plus a minimum order quantity. Independent sales reps who sell for other brands may instead earn commission, typically 5 to 20 percent of the order value depending on the product and margins. Terms such as Net 30 are common with established business buyers, while new accounts often pay up front.

rates.service: Custom label, artwork, or personalization setup

items.description: 8 oz soy candle, assorted scents (SKU CN-08)
Reed diffuser, 4 oz (SKU RD-04)
Gift set, candle plus matches (SKU GS-02)
Custom shelf-tag printing, store logo
Shipping, 2 boxes via ground, 38 lbs total

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 30 from invoice date. Resale certificate on file, no sales tax charged on products. Report shortages or damage within 10 days of delivery. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Thank you for your order.

invoiceChecklist.item: SKU or item number, description, and quantity for every line
invoiceChecklist.why: Buyers match the invoice against the packing slip and their receiving count. Missing SKUs cause short-pay disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number and order date
invoiceChecklist.why: Many business buyers cannot process payment without a PO number on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ship date, carrier, and tracking number
invoiceChecklist.why: Proves delivery timing and helps resolve lost or delayed shipment claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line or resale/exemption certificate reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Wholesale sales to resellers are often tax exempt in many states, but you generally need the certificate on file. Retail buyers may owe tax, so check your state rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping, handling, and any setup or rush fees as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show what the product cost versus what logistics cost, and avoid arguments over unit price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Discounts applied, such as volume or early-pay discounts
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the discount as a line or note documents the agreed price and the terms to earn it, such as 2/10 Net 30.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return and damage claim policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the window and process on the invoice makes it easier to enforce restocking fees and defect claim deadlines.

product-sales.paymentTerms: New business customers commonly pay a deposit of 30 to 50 percent on custom orders and the full amount up front on first orders. Established accounts are often offered Net 30, sometimes Net 15 or Net 60 for larger buyers. An early-pay discount like 2 percent if paid in 10 days is common in wholesale. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in writing before the sale. Accepted methods usually include ACH, credit card, check, and wire for larger orders. Card payments carry processing fees, so some sellers add a small surcharge or encourage ACH, though surcharge rules vary by state and card network.

tips.title: Ship after payment on first orders
tips.body: Require prepayment or a deposit from new accounts until they have a payment history. Once an order ships, collecting is much harder than getting paid first.

tips.title: Set a minimum order amount
tips.body: Small wholesale orders can lose money after packing, shipping, and invoicing time. A minimum such as $250 or a case-pack quantity protects your margin.

tips.title: Keep resale certificates on file
tips.body: If you do not charge sales tax on a wholesale order, you generally need the buyer's certificate if audited. Collect it before the first invoice and note it on each one.

tips.title: Invoice on shipment, not on order
tips.body: For backorders or partial shipments, bill only what shipped and list what remains. This keeps your records accurate and avoids buyers paying for goods they have not received.

tips.title: Offer a clear early-pay incentive
tips.body: A small discount for fast payment often gets you paid sooner than a late fee gets you paid later. Spell the terms out on the invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on a product invoice?
faqs.answer: In most states you charge sales tax on retail sales to end customers and not on sales to resellers who give you a valid resale certificate. Rules vary on shipping charges, exemptions, and out-of-state sales, so check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Do I bill shipping separately or include it in the price?
faqs.answer: Most sellers list shipping as a separate line so the product price stays consistent across customers. Free-shipping thresholds are common for larger orders, in which case note the waived amount on the invoice.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice, at order or at shipment?
faqs.answer: For prepaid orders, send it at order confirmation. For credit terms, invoice when the goods ship so the Net 30 clock starts on a real delivery. Invoice partial shipments separately or clearly show the shipped portion.

faqs.question: How do I handle returns and credits?
faqs.answer: Issue a credit memo or a revised invoice that references the original invoice number, the returned SKUs, and any restocking fee. Do not simply edit the original, since the buyer's records need to match.

faqs.question: What if a customer short-pays because of damaged goods?
faqs.answer: Ask for photos and a count within the claim window stated on your invoice. If the claim is valid, issue a credit for the damaged units and request payment of the remaining balance by the original due date.

estimate.intro: Product sellers send quotes before a customer commits to a bulk, custom, or recurring order. The buyer is usually comparing unit price, minimums, lead time, and shipping cost across several suppliers. A quote that shows the full landed cost avoids surprises when the invoice arrives.

scopeChecklist.item: Items, SKUs, and quantities with unit price
scopeChecklist.why: Locks in exactly what is being priced so a change in quantity or variant is clearly a new quote.
Material and wholesale costs change. A 15 to 30 day expiration protects you from honoring old pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Minimum order quantity and tier breaks
scopeChecklist.why: Shows how price drops at higher volumes and prevents buyers from claiming a tier price on a smaller order.

scopeChecklist.item: Lead time and estimated ship date
scopeChecklist.why: Buyers plan around delivery. Stating production time and whether it starts at deposit or artwork approval prevents disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Shipping method, estimated cost, and who pays
scopeChecklist.why: Freight can be a large part of the total. Say whether it is estimated or actual, and who owns the risk in transit.

scopeChecklist.item: Custom setup, artwork approval, and sample terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies one-time fees, how many proof revisions are included, and that production begins only after written approval.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment terms, and cancellation policy
scopeChecklist.why: Custom or special-order goods cannot be resold easily, so state what is non-refundable once production starts.

pricingTips.title: Quote landed cost
pricingTips.body: Include product, setup, shipping, and tax treatment on one page. Buyers compare totals, and a low unit price with hidden freight loses trust.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Showing prices at 50, 100, and 250 units lets the buyer choose and often raises the order size. Make sure each tier still meets your margin.

pricingTips.title: Price from current replacement cost
pricingTips.body: Base the quote on what it costs to restock today, not what you paid for existing inventory. Include a note that pricing may change if supplier costs shift before the order.

pricingTips.title: Add a short expiration date
pricingTips.body: A clear end date creates a reason to decide and covers you if costs or availability change.

faqs.question: Should I charge for samples?
faqs.answer: Many sellers charge for samples and credit the cost against a first order. Free samples are usually reserved for serious buyers with a clear volume. Shipping on samples is often paid by the buyer.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the buyer accepts a quote?
faqs.answer: Generally not if the quote is still valid and the order matches. If quantities, specs, or ship dates change, issue a revised quote. Include language that pricing assumes the listed quantities.

faqs.question: How do I quote when supplier prices are unstable?
faqs.answer: Use a short validity window, state that the price is subject to supplier cost changes, and ask for a deposit to lock in materials once the order is accepted.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting a custom order?
faqs.answer: It is strongly advised. A written acceptance, even by email, along with the deposit and approved artwork, gives you documentation if the buyer later disputes specs or cancels.

professional-services.intro: Professional services providers are independent consultants, advisors, and small firms that sell expertise and time instead of a physical product. They invoice for things like discovery and analysis, deliverables such as reports and plans, workshops, monthly advisory retainers, and reimbursable project expenses. Typical clients are small and mid-sized businesses, nonprofits, and departments inside larger companies.
professional-services.pricingModel: Most professional services work is priced one of four ways: hourly, per project, per day, or on a monthly retainer. Hourly billing is common for open-ended or unclear work, and it needs time records the client can follow. Fixed project fees work better when the scope and deliverables are clear, and they reward you for working efficiently. Day rates are common for on-site work, workshops, and interim roles. Retainers cover a set number of hours or a defined ongoing service each month, usually billed in advance. Many providers combine these, for example a fixed fee for an assessment followed by an hourly or retainer arrangement for follow-up. Expenses such as travel, software licenses, and third-party fees are normally billed separately at cost, sometimes with a small handling markup that is agreed in writing beforehand.

items.description: Discovery: stakeholder interviews and document review (March 3-14)
Operations assessment report with prioritized recommendations (deliverable 1 of 2)
Leadership team workshop, half day, on site
Monthly advisory retainer, March (up to 6 hours)
Mileage to client site, 3 trips

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Please reference project 2025-014 when paying. Reimbursable expenses are billed at cost with receipts available on request. Balance of the report fee is due on delivery of deliverable 2. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month after the due date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project or engagement name and reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several vendors and projects. A reference lets accounts payable match your invoice to the right budget line.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Many mid-sized and large organizations will not process an invoice without a PO number, which delays payment if it is missing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work period and dates of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what time frame the charges cover, which matters for retainers and for clients who accrue expenses by month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours or milestone completed
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly work needs dates and hours per task. Fixed-fee work needs the milestone or deliverable that triggered the billing, so the invoice ties back to the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses listed separately with receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeping expenses apart from fees prevents disputes over markup and lets the client's finance team code them correctly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer hours used, remaining, or rolled over
invoiceChecklist.why: If the retainer includes a set number of hours, the client should see the balance so overages and unused time are not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, address, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients in the US usually need a W-9 from independent contractors to issue a 1099 at year end if they pay you above the reporting threshold.

professional-services.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is standard, and larger clients often insist on net 30 or net 45 because of their payables cycle. For new clients, it is common to take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent of a fixed project fee before starting, and to bill the rest at milestones or on delivery. Retainers are typically invoiced at the start of the month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common, but they should be stated in your agreement before work begins and check your state's rules on interest limits. Most clients pay by ACH or check, and credit cards are accepted by many providers who pass the processing fee along or absorb it.

tips.title: Put scope and change handling in writing
tips.body: Scope creep is the most common billing problem in this field. State what the engagement includes, and what happens when the client asks for more, such as additional work billed at your hourly rate with written approval.

tips.title: Bill milestones on a schedule, not at the end
tips.body: For projects longer than a month, split billing into a deposit, one or more milestone invoices, and a final invoice. This protects your cash flow and keeps the client engaged.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed-fee work
tips.body: Recording hours against a flat fee shows you whether the project was priced correctly. It also gives you data to back up your next quote and a record if a dispute arises.

tips.title: Learn the client's payables process
tips.body: Ask who receives invoices, whether a PO is required, whether they use a vendor portal, and when their payment runs happen. Submitting the invoice in the right format the first time can save weeks.

tips.title: Invoice promptly after delivery
tips.body: Send the invoice the same day a deliverable is accepted or a month closes. Delays in billing usually mean delays in getting paid.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or charge a flat project fee?
faqs.answer: Use hourly billing when the scope is unclear or likely to change. Use a flat fee when deliverables are well defined and you can estimate the effort with confidence. Many providers use a flat fee for a defined first phase and hourly or retainer billing for later work.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent on proposals and initial calls?
faqs.answer: Short intro calls and standard proposals are usually unbilled and treated as a cost of sales. Custom scoping work, such as a detailed audit before a quote, can be billed as a paid discovery phase if you agree to that up front.

faqs.question: How do I handle unused retainer hours?
faqs.answer: Decide this in the agreement. Common choices are that unused hours expire at month end, roll over for a limited period, or are credited toward a different service. Whatever you choose, show hours used and remaining on each invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on the type of service. Many states do not tax general consulting, but some tax certain professional or digital services. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional for your situation.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client does not pay?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder the day after the due date, then follow up by phone or email with the invoice attached. Refer to the payment terms in your agreement. If it continues, pause work, send a formal demand letter, and consider small claims court or a collection process, depending on the amount.

estimate.intro: Professional services providers send a proposal or quote before starting almost any engagement, since clients want to know the cost and what they will get. Clients typically compare total cost, scope, timeline, and how the fee is structured against other providers or an in-house option. A clear quote also becomes the reference point for later invoices.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming the specific outputs, such as a written report, a financial model, or a training session, defines what counts as finished.
Listing items outside the scope, such as implementation, ongoing support, or additional revisions, prevents the client from assuming those are included.
Dates for kickoff, interim reviews, and delivery make it clear what you are committing to and what you need from the client.
Delays often come from late access to data, people, or approvals. State what the client must provide and how delays affect the schedule and fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds or review cycles
scopeChecklist.why: Unlimited revisions can turn a fixed fee into a loss. A set number, with extra rounds billed hourly, keeps the work bounded.
Spell out whether the price is fixed, hourly with a cap, or a retainer, along with the deposit, milestone payments, and due dates.

scopeChecklist.item: Expenses and how they are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Specify whether travel, software, and third-party costs are included or billed at cost so the final total does not surprise the client.

pricingTips.title: Price on value and effort, not just hours
pricingTips.body: A fixed fee based only on hours undersells work that saves the client a lot of money. Estimate your hours, then consider the outcome to the client and your experience before settling on the number.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Add 10 to 20 percent to hour estimates for meetings, revisions, and waiting on client input. These costs appear in nearly every engagement and are easy to leave out of a quote.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three packages, such as a basic assessment, an assessment with an implementation plan, and an assessment with ongoing support, lets the client choose a budget level rather than decide whether to hire you at all.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Rates, availability, and scope can change. A validity period of 30 days is common and gives you a basis to reprice if the client waits.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an estimate and a fixed quote?
faqs.answer: An estimate is a good-faith projection that can change as the work unfolds, and a fixed quote is a committed price for a defined scope. If you give an estimate, say so clearly and say how you will notify the client if costs will exceed it.

faqs.question: Should I give a price range or a single number?
faqs.answer: A range is useful when the scope is uncertain, and it sets expectations early. Once discovery is complete, narrow it to a fixed fee or a not-to-exceed amount that the client can approve.

faqs.question: How do I handle requests that go beyond the quote?
