faqs.answer: Reference the scope in the signed proposal and provide a short written change request with the added cost and timeline. Begin the extra work after the client approves it in writing, even if by email.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement or is an accepted quote enough?
faqs.answer: An accepted quote can form a contract in many cases, but a signed agreement covering scope, payment terms, confidentiality, and ownership of work product is stronger. For larger or longer engagements, use a written agreement and consider having an attorney review your template.

project-manager.intro: Freelance and independent project managers run projects on behalf of small businesses, agencies, nonprofits, and larger companies that need delivery help without a full-time hire. They bill for planning, schedule and budget management, stakeholder coordination, vendor management, and status reporting. Invoices usually tie to hours worked, a monthly retainer, or milestone payments on a defined project.
project-manager.pricingModel: Most independent project managers bill hourly or on a monthly retainer. Hourly works for short or open-ended engagements, while a retainer with a stated hour allotment suits ongoing work such as a six-month website rebuild or a product launch. Fixed-fee pricing is common for defined deliverables like a project plan, a project audit, or a kickoff and planning package, and is often split into milestone payments. Some PMs charge a percentage of project budget (often 5-15%) on construction or event work, but this is less common for solo consultants. Certified PMs (PMP, PMI-ACP, CSM) and those with industry experience in IT, construction, or healthcare tend to charge at the upper end. Expenses such as software licenses, travel, and printing are usually billed separately at cost. Define what happens when hours exceed the retainer, and bill change requests separately.

rates.service: Senior or certified PM (PMP, IT, construction)
Day rate for on-site or embedded work

items.description: Project management retainer - website redesign (June, up to 30 hrs)
Additional hours beyond retainer (vendor coordination, approved in advance)
Stakeholder workshop facilitation (June 12)
Project management software seat (June, billed at cost)
Client site visit mileage (round trip, 2 trips)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Retainer hours do not roll over. Additional hours beyond the retainer require written approval and are billed at $105 per hour. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and engagement or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often run several projects at once, and accounts payable needs to match the invoice to the correct contract or budget line.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or cost center code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients often will not process payment without a purchase order number, which delays payment when missing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and itemized hours by task or phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the client paid for, such as planning, vendor management, or reporting, and heads off questions about time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer allotment and overage hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear how many hours were included and what was billed above that at the agreed rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestones completed with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: For milestone-based billing, tying the invoice to a signed-off deliverable supports your right to payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Software, travel, and printing costs billed at cost need backup, and many clients require receipts before reimbursing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders referenced by number
invoiceChecklist.why: Work added after the original scope should point to an approved change order so extra charges are not disputed.

project-manager.paymentTerms: Independent PMs commonly invoice monthly in arrears for retainer and hourly work, with net 15 or net 30 terms. Corporate clients often insist on net 30 or net 45, so confirm this in the contract and add a late fee (1-1.5% per month is typical where permitted) if it is allowed. For fixed-fee projects, a deposit of 25-50% at kickoff is common, with the remainder tied to milestones. Some PMs invoice retainers in advance at the start of each month to protect cash flow. ACH transfer and check are the most common payment methods for business clients, and card payments are accepted by some, though processing fees may apply.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoicing the retainer at the start of the month keeps you from financing the client's project. Hours worked beyond the allotment can be billed in arrears.

tips.title: Track time by task, not just total
tips.body: Logging time under planning, meetings, reporting, and vendor coordination makes your invoice easier to defend and helps you estimate future projects more accurately.

tips.title: Get change requests approved in writing
tips.body: Scope creep is the most common billing dispute in project work. Require an email or signed change order before you start extra work, and reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Tie final payment to a clear closeout
tips.body: Define what project closeout includes, such as a lessons-learned document and handover of files, so the final invoice is not held up by open-ended requests.

tips.title: Separate your fee from pass-through costs
tips.body: If you pay vendors or buy tools on the client's behalf, list them as separate lines at cost, or decide up front whether you add a handling markup, and say so in the contract.

faqs.question: Should a project manager bill hourly or on retainer?
faqs.answer: Hourly suits short or unpredictable work. A retainer works better for ongoing projects because it gives you steady income and gives the client a predictable cost. Many PMs use a retainer with a set hour cap and an overage rate.

faqs.question: Can I charge for meetings and status reports?
faqs.answer: Yes. Meetings, reporting, and stakeholder communication are core parts of project management. Make sure your agreement states that time spent on them is billable, and show it on the invoice as its own line or task category.

faqs.question: What if the project runs over its original timeline?
faqs.answer: If the delay is caused by the client, such as late approvals or changed requirements, your agreement should allow you to bill additional time or extend the retainer. Document the cause in writing and raise it before the extra time accumulates.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on project management services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional or consulting services, but some do tax certain services. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional for your location.

faqs.question: How do I bill when I manage a vendor's work on the client's behalf?
faqs.answer: Bill your own time as a fee, and list vendor costs as separate pass-through lines at cost, or have the vendor bill the client directly. Your contract should say which approach applies and whether you add any markup.

estimate.intro: Project managers send a proposal or quote before an engagement starts, usually after a discovery call about the project's goals, timeline, and team. Clients typically compare your rate, the number of hours or months you propose, and how clearly you define what you will and will not do. A good quote sets expectations about scope and authority as well as price.

scopeChecklist.item: Project scope and objectives being managed
scopeChecklist.why: Defines what project you are responsible for delivering, so the client does not assume you also own design, development, or other specialist work.
Listing items such as project plan, weekly status reports, risk log, and budget tracking prevents disagreement over what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated hours, duration, or retainer allotment
scopeChecklist.why: Gives the client a basis for budgeting and shows when the hours or time period will be exceeded.
Delays from late feedback or approvals are a leading cause of overruns, so state how fast the client needs to respond.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions about team size, tools, and meeting cadence
scopeChecklist.why: A quote built for a five-person team and weekly meetings will not hold if the project grows to fifteen people and daily standups.

scopeChecklist.item: Change request process and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: Sets the rule for how added work is approved and priced before it begins.

scopeChecklist.item: Expenses and who pays for software or travel
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids surprise charges and clarifies whether tools are covered by you or the client.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range with assumptions for open-ended projects
pricingTips.body: If the scope is unclear, give an estimated hour range and list what it depends on, such as number of vendors or stakeholders. Offer to revisit the estimate after a two-week planning phase.

pricingTips.title: Start with a paid discovery or planning phase
pricingTips.body: A fixed-fee planning package lets you define scope and timeline with real information, then price the delivery phase more accurately.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for coordination time
pricingTips.body: Meetings, follow-ups, and status reporting often take more time than expected. Build a 10-20% allowance into your estimate rather than discounting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer a retainer option alongside hourly
pricingTips.body: Presenting both lets the client choose between flexibility and a lower effective rate, and often moves them toward the retainer you prefer.

faqs.question: How many hours should I estimate for a project?
faqs.answer: A common rule is that project management takes about 10-20% of total project effort, depending on complexity and team size. Use that as a starting point, then adjust based on the number of stakeholders, vendors, and reporting requirements.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed price only when scope and deliverables are clearly defined, such as a planning package or audit. For ongoing delivery management, an hourly estimate or capped retainer protects you if the project changes.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Project timelines and your availability shift, so an expiration date keeps you from being held to old pricing and a start date you can no longer meet.

faqs.question: What should I do if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope or hours rather than your rate. For example, drop weekly reporting to biweekly or limit your involvement to a defined phase, and update the quote to reflect the change.

proofreading.intro: Proofreaders are freelancers and small business owners who check finished or near-finished text for spelling, grammar, punctuation, typos, and formatting errors. Clients include self-published authors, academic publishers, graduate students, marketing teams, law offices, and businesses with websites, manuals, or reports. Invoices usually bill by word, by page, or by hour, with add-ons for rush turnaround or style guide work.
proofreading.pricingModel: Most proofreaders price by word, by page, or by hour. Per-word pricing is common for book manuscripts and articles, and per-page pricing (based on 250 or 300 words per page) is common in academic and publishing work. Hourly rates suit messy files, formatted documents like InDesign proofs or PDFs with tracked comments, and projects where the scope is unclear. Many proofreaders set a per-project minimum so that small jobs are worth taking. Rush work, heavy-error files, specialized subject matter (legal, medical, technical), and style guide requirements (APA, Chicago, AP, house style) usually raise the rate. Some solo proofreaders offer a flat fee after seeing a sample of the text, and repeat clients such as agencies or publishers may be billed monthly or on a retainer. Light editing beyond proofreading, such as rewording sentences or fixing consistency problems, should be billed as copyediting at a higher rate.

rates.service: Style sheet creation or consistency check

items.description: Proofreading of novel manuscript, 82,000 words (Chicago style), per word
Rush surcharge, 7-day turnaround (25% of $2,050 base fee)
Style sheet for character names, place names, and spelling choices
Second-pass review of author's corrections

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. A 50% deposit of $1,300 was received on signing and has been credited to this invoice. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month. Accepted by check, ACH, or bank transfer. Proofread file and style sheet delivered by email as tracked-changes Word documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: Document title, file name, and word or page count
invoiceChecklist.why: The count is what most fees are based on, so the client can check the math and see what was covered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pricing basis (per word, per page, or hourly) and how words were counted
invoiceChecklist.why: Word counts differ between programs and between including or excluding footnotes, references, and headers, which can lead to disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Style guide followed (APA, MLA, Chicago, AP, or house style)
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents the standard you worked to if the client later questions a change.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date and turnaround time
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports any rush surcharge and shows you met the agreed deadline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for surcharges, add-ons, and extra rounds
invoiceChecklist.why: Rush fees, style sheets, and re-reading revised files are extra work that should be visible, not folded into the base fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Many proofreaders collect part of the fee upfront, and the invoice should show it was credited.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, contact details, and tax ID or W-9 status if requested
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients who pay you $600 or more in a year may need your information for 1099 reporting, depending on current rules.

proofreading.paymentTerms: Proofreaders commonly ask for payment in full before starting on small jobs and a deposit of 25-50% on larger manuscripts, with the balance due on delivery or within 7-30 days. Net 14 or Net 30 is typical for business and publisher clients, who may have their own payment cycles, so confirm those before you start. A late fee of 1-1.5% per month is common if stated in your agreement or on the invoice. Most freelancers accept bank transfer (ACH), checks, PayPal, or card payments. For new authors and individuals, holding the final file until the balance is paid is a common safeguard.

tips.title: Look at a sample before you quote
tips.body: Ask for 500 to 1,000 words from the middle of the document. A clean file and a heavily flawed one can take very different amounts of time, and a sample lets you adjust your rate or switch to hourly before you commit.

tips.title: Define the number of review rounds
tips.body: State whether your fee covers only one pass or also includes checking the author's accepted changes. Many proofreaders include a short follow-up check and bill additional rounds hourly.

tips.title: Separate proofreading from editing
tips.body: If a client sends a draft that needs rewording or restructuring, tell them before you start and quote copyediting rates. Otherwise you can end up doing editing at proofreading prices.

tips.title: Say how you count words
tips.body: Use the count from your word processor and state whether it includes footnotes, references, captions, and front matter. Put the figure on the estimate and the invoice.

tips.title: Charge for rush work
tips.body: Moving other clients around or working evenings and weekends has a cost. A flat 25-50% rush surcharge, stated before the work begins, is standard.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word or per hour for proofreading?
faqs.answer: Per word is easier for clients to compare and works well when the text is in reasonable shape. Hourly is safer for messy files, complex layouts, or unclear scope. Many proofreaders use per word for quotes and track their hours to see whether their rates are working.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a second round of proofreading?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you said so in your agreement. Many proofreaders include a quick check of the client's responses to queries, then bill further rounds or large rewrites at an hourly rate or per word on the new text.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client says they found errors I missed?
faqs.answer: Check the file against the scope you agreed on. No proofreader catches everything, and published standards are often around 95 to 99 percent accuracy. Many freelancers fix reported errors for free within a short window, such as 7 to 14 days, but won't re-proofread text the client has changed since.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on proofreading?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax certain professional or editorial services, while many do not. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional about your own situation.

faqs.question: Do I have to send a 1099 or get a W-9?
faqs.answer: As a freelancer, you generally do not send a 1099 to clients. You may be asked for a W-9 by a business that pays you above the IRS reporting threshold so they can file one for you. Keep your own records of all income whether or not you receive a form.

estimate.intro: Proofreaders usually send a quote after seeing the document or a sample, and before agreeing on a deadline. Clients often compare several proofreaders on per-word price, turnaround, experience with their type of writing, and what is included. A clear estimate that states the word count, rate, style guide, and number of rounds helps you stand out from a vague lower price.

scopeChecklist.item: Word count or page count, and how it was measured
scopeChecklist.why: Your fee is based on it, and the final file may be longer or shorter than the client's estimate.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of work included: proofreading only, or copyediting too
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents clients from expecting rewrites or fact-checking at proofreading rates.

scopeChecklist.item: Style guide and spelling standard (US or UK English)
scopeChecklist.why: Different style guides lead to different corrections, so both sides need to agree up front.

scopeChecklist.item: File format and method of marking changes
scopeChecklist.why: Tracked changes in Word, comments in PDF, or hard-copy marks each take different amounts of time and require different tools.

scopeChecklist.item: What is excluded: references, footnotes, tables, images, or text in graphics
scopeChecklist.why: These parts can add hours, so say whether they are covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery date and when the clock starts
scopeChecklist.why: Deadlines should run from receipt of the final file and deposit, not from the first email.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of review rounds and the fee for extra rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Authors often send revised versions, so set limits on how much follow-up is included.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a sample
pricingTips.body: Read a sample and note the error density. A page with five errors takes less time than one with fifty, and your quote can reflect that or include a clause allowing a price change if the full file is much worse than the sample.

pricingTips.title: Set a project minimum
pricingTips.body: A one-page document can take almost as long to set up and invoice as a longer one. A minimum fee of $30 to $75 keeps very small jobs worthwhile.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers when the client is unsure
pricingTips.body: Presenting proofreading and a lighter or heavier copyedit as separate options helps clients see the difference and choose without pushing you to cut your rate.

pricingTips.title: Add an expiry date
pricingTips.body: Your availability and the document may change. Stating that the quote is valid for 14 or 30 days keeps you from being held to old pricing and an old schedule.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an estimate range?
faqs.answer: A flat fee works when the word count is final and you have seen the text. If the document is still changing, give a per-word rate with an estimated total and say the final price depends on the final word count.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time it takes to review a sample?
faqs.answer: Most proofreaders offer a short free sample, usually under 1,000 words. For longer trial edits or large documents, charging a small fee that you credit against the project is reasonable.

faqs.question: What if the final document is longer than quoted?
faqs.answer: Put in your estimate that the price is based on the stated word count and will be adjusted at the quoted rate if the final file differs by more than a set amount, such as 5 or 10 percent.

prop-stylist.intro: Prop stylists source, select, and arrange objects, furniture, food props, surfaces, and florals for photo shoots, commercials, catalogs, editorial work, film sets, and social content. Clients are usually photographers, ad agencies, brands, production companies, or magazines, and the invoice covers creative time, prep and shopping days, and reimbursable purchases and rentals.
prop-stylist.pricingModel: Most prop stylists charge a day rate for shoot days and a lower or equal rate for prep, shopping, and wrap days, often with a half-day option for short shoots. Day rates are typically based on a 10-hour day, with overtime billed at 1.5x after that. Props are billed separately from the styling fee: purchases are billed at cost or with a handling markup of 10-20%, rentals at the rental house price, and returns or restocking fees passed through. Many stylists also charge a kit fee for personal inventory and supplies, and bill a flat fee for small jobs such as e-commerce batches or a single hero image. Assistants are billed at their own day rate. Travel time, mileage, parking, and van or truck rental are itemized. Commercial usage and union status can move rates up, and large agency or production budgets typically pay more than small brands or editorial work.

rates.service: Half-day shoot or short styling session
Kit fee for personal inventory and supplies
Van or personal vehicle use for prop transport

items.description: Prop styling, lifestyle kitchen campaign (shoot day, 10 hrs)
Prep, shopping, and sourcing
Prop assistant, shoot days
Personal inventory kit fee
Props purchased (receipts attached), $1,240 at cost plus 15% handling
Cargo van rental and mileage for prop transport

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 30. Purchased props remain property of the client unless returned in resalable condition; return credits will be issued on receipt of items. Overtime beyond 10 hours billed at 1.5x. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot name, job number, and PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and production companies route payment by PO or job number, and invoices without one often get stuck in accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for shoot days, prep days, and wrap or return days
invoiceChecklist.why: Each can be billed at a different rate, and clients want to see where the time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized prop purchases and rentals with receipts attached
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reimburse expenses against documentation, and it keeps the handling fee clearly separate from the cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Handling fee or markup percentage
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating it as its own line avoids questions about why prop totals differ from receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime and weekend or holiday terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Hours beyond the agreed day length need to match what was in the quote or booking confirmation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Kit fee and assistant charges
invoiceChecklist.why: These are easy to forget and are separate from your creative fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return and damage policy for purchased and rented props
invoiceChecklist.why: It clarifies who owns the items after the shoot and who pays for damage or restocking fees.

prop-stylist.paymentTerms: Freelance stylists working directly for brands or photographers often ask for a 25-50% deposit to cover prop purchases, especially on larger jobs, and bill the balance net 15 to net 30. Agencies and production companies commonly pay net 30 to net 60, so confirm terms in the booking agreement before the shoot. Large reimbursable expenses can be billed up front or paid by the client directly using a company card or rental account. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and some clients require a W-9 and vendor setup first.

tips.title: Get a prop budget advance
tips.body: Ask for a deposit or an expense float before shopping. Fronting thousands of dollars on your own card for a client that pays net 60 is a common cash-flow problem.

tips.title: Keep every receipt and tag it to the job
tips.body: Photograph receipts the day you buy and label them by job. Clients will ask for backup, and you need clean records for your own taxes.

tips.title: Bill prep and returns, not just the shoot
tips.body: Sourcing, pickups, steaming, cleaning, and returns can take as many hours as the shoot itself. Quote and invoice them as their own days or lines.

tips.title: State overtime and cancellation terms in writing
tips.body: Shoots run long and get postponed. A written overtime rate and a cancellation fee for short-notice changes protect your held dates.

tips.title: Decide what happens to leftover props
tips.body: Spell out whether purchased items go to the client, come back to your inventory at a credit, or get returned. Unclear ownership leads to disputes after the shoot.

faqs.question: Should I charge a markup on props I buy?
faqs.answer: Many stylists add a handling fee of 10-20% on purchased props to cover shopping time, fronting the money, and returns. Whatever you choose, state it in your quote and show it as a separate line from the cost of the items.

faqs.question: Do I charge for prep days at the same rate as shoot days?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some stylists charge the same day rate for all days, others charge 60-80% for prep and shopping. Either approach works if it is stated in your estimate and consistent across clients.

faqs.question: How do I bill for items I own and bring to the shoot?
faqs.answer: Use a kit fee for general supplies and a rental line for specific inventory pieces. Rental charges for personal items are usually a fraction of what a rental house would charge, and should be agreed in advance.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to keep the props I bought?
faqs.answer: Bill the full purchase cost plus any handling fee and note on the invoice that the items now belong to the client. If you are keeping them, issue a credit or agree on a reduced charge before you buy.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by state. Services are often not taxed, while props sold to a client may be taxable, and resale certificates can come into play. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant about how to handle props you buy and pass on.

estimate.intro: Prop stylists send estimates after a creative brief or treatment call, and before any shopping starts. Clients often compare several stylists on day rate, how many prep days are included, and how props are budgeted, so a clear breakdown makes the numbers easy to compare. Agencies commonly ask for a formal bid with a prop budget attached.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of shoot days, prep days, and wrap days
scopeChecklist.why: Prep and returns are where hours expand, so the estimate should show how many are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Prop budget and whether it is a cap or an estimate
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to know if the number is a limit you will stay under or a rough guide that may change.

scopeChecklist.item: Handling fee or markup on purchases
scopeChecklist.why: Disclosing it upfront prevents surprise at invoice time.
Says whether you will rent from prop houses, buy and return, or use your own inventory, which affects cost and timeline.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of looks, sets, or final images
scopeChecklist.why: Scope is easiest to dispute when the number of setups is not defined.

scopeChecklist.item: Assistant needs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: A multi-set day often requires help, and the cost should be in the quote or flagged as an add-on.
Shoots change, and you need agreed terms for extra hours or lost held dates.

pricingTips.title: Separate your fee from the prop budget
pricingTips.body: Show creative fees and prop costs in two sections. Clients can then adjust the prop budget without feeling like they are negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for props, a firm number for time
pricingTips.body: Props depend on availability and creative decisions, so offer a budget with an agreed ceiling. Your time can be quoted as fixed days at a set rate.

pricingTips.title: Build in a revision buffer
pricingTips.body: Last-minute swaps and re-shopping trips are common. Include a note on how additional sourcing is billed beyond a set number of rounds.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered option for small budgets
pricingTips.body: A lean version using owned inventory and fewer rentals alongside a full-scope version helps clients choose based on budget, and keeps your rate intact.

faqs.question: Should I charge for creating a mood board or treatment?
faqs.answer: For larger jobs, many stylists include a short mood board in the quote process and charge for detailed concept work or multiple rounds. Say upfront what is included so clients do not expect unlimited rework for free.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days. Prop prices, rental availability, and your calendar all change, so include an expiration date and note that held dates are only confirmed with a deposit or signed approval.

faqs.question: What if the final prop spend goes over the estimate?
faqs.answer: Ask for client approval before exceeding the budget. Include a line in your estimate stating that overages need written approval, and send a quick update by email when you see costs climbing.

propane-service.intro: Propane service businesses deliver fuel to homes, farms, and commercial customers, and install and maintain the tanks, regulators, lines, and appliances that use it. Invoices usually cover gallons delivered, tank rentals, delivery or hazmat fees, and labor and parts for installs, leak checks, and repairs. Many operators are solo or run a small fleet, so clear invoices matter when each delivery is tied to a fluctuating fuel price.
propane-service.pricingModel: Fuel is priced per gallon, and the price changes with wholesale markets, delivery volume, and whether the customer is on a will-call, automatic delivery, or fixed-price contract plan. Small deliveries often carry a minimum charge or a delivery fee, and some operators add a fuel surcharge or hazmat fee. Tank rental is typically billed annually or seasonally if the customer does not own the tank. Service work such as installs, leak tests, regulator swaps, appliance hookups, and gas line runs is billed hourly or flat rate per task, plus parts with a markup. Emergency and after-hours calls usually carry a higher rate or a trip charge. Commercial and agricultural accounts often get tiered per-gallon pricing based on annual volume.

rates.service: Leak check and system safety inspection

items.description: Residential propane delivery, 500 gal tank filled to 80%
Delivery fee
Hazmat/fuel surcharge
Annual tank rental, 500 gal above-ground tank
Leak check and system safety inspection
Technician labor, replace first-stage regulator

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Gallons are based on truck meter reading at time of delivery; price per gallon reflects your current account rate. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days. Call us at the number above if you smell gas or have a safety concern, and leave the house first.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gallons delivered and price per gallon
invoiceChecklist.why: Fuel price changes often, so customers need to see exactly what they were charged and how it was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date, tank size, and tank level before and after
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents the fill percentage and prevents disputes over how much fuel was actually needed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery fees, hazmat fees, and surcharges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing keeps the per-gallon price clean and shows customers where extra charges come from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tank ownership and rental charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often forget whether they own or lease the tank, and rental terms affect whether they can switch suppliers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and account or tank ID number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many customers have multiple tanks or properties, and tracking by tank prevents billing mix-ups.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts and labor for installs and repairs, with parts itemized
invoiceChecklist.why: Regulators, hoses, valves, and fittings are billed separately from labor, and itemizing supports your markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: License or registration number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states license propane dealers and gas fitters, and including your number shows the work is done by an authorized provider.

propane-service.paymentTerms: Delivery customers are commonly billed on net 10 to net 30 terms, with many residential accounts paying by check, card, or autopay. Will-call customers often pay on delivery or within a short window, while automatic delivery and budget plan customers may be billed monthly or in fixed installments. Installs and larger gas line jobs usually require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover materials, with the balance due at completion and inspection. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common, but check your state rules on allowable charges. Commercial and farm accounts may be on net 30 with a credit application, and some suppliers require prepay or a credit hold when balances run long.

tips.title: Show the per-gallon price on every delivery invoice
tips.body: Fuel price changes between fills, so printing the gallons, rate, and total prevents most billing complaints and makes it easier to explain price differences.

tips.title: Separate fuel from fees
tips.body: Break out delivery, hazmat, and tank rental charges instead of folding them into the gallon price. Customers compare per-gallon rates between suppliers, and clear fees look more honest than a vague higher rate.

tips.title: Bill tank rental and inspection on a set schedule
tips.body: Annual rental, leak checks, and tank inspections are easy to forget. Put them on a calendar and invoice them consistently so you do not leave recurring revenue uncollected.

tips.title: Take deposits on installs and new tank sets
tips.body: Tanks, regulators, and gas line materials are real out-of-pocket costs. A deposit before ordering protects you if the customer backs out or delays.

tips.title: Document safety work
tips.body: Note pressure tests, leak checks, and any red-tagged appliances on the invoice. It protects you if there is a later dispute and shows you followed proper procedure.

faqs.question: Should I charge a delivery fee in addition to the per-gallon price?
faqs.answer: Many propane companies do, especially for small fills. A flat delivery fee or minimum charge covers truck and driver time on low-volume stops. List it as its own line so customers can see it and compare suppliers fairly.

faqs.question: How do I bill customers on a budget or fixed-price plan?
faqs.answer: Invoice the agreed monthly amount, then reconcile at the end of the plan year. Show gallons delivered, the plan price, and any credit or balance carried forward so the customer can see the reconciliation.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on propane?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and use. Some states exempt residential heating fuel or agricultural use, and others tax it. Check with your state revenue department and keep exemption certificates for any tax-exempt customers.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for a tank I own that is sitting at a customer's property?
faqs.answer: Yes, many suppliers charge annual tank rental, especially for customers who buy little fuel. Put the terms in writing at setup and show the charge on the invoice. Some states regulate rental fees and switching rules, so check local requirements.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer disputes the gallons delivered?
faqs.answer: Pull the delivery ticket with the meter reading and tank gauge percentages, and share it with the customer. Keeping signed or time-stamped delivery records makes these disputes easy to resolve.

estimate.intro: Propane service businesses send estimates for tank installations, gas line runs, appliance hookups, conversions, and fixed-price fuel plans. Customers usually compare the equipment cost, install labor, tank ownership terms, and per-gallon price against other suppliers. A clear written quote helps customers see what is included before you set a tank or run a line.

scopeChecklist.why: Buy versus lease changes the total cost and the customer's ability to switch suppliers later, so state it plainly.
Above-ground or buried placement, distance from buildings, and site access affect labor and permitting, and can change the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Gas line length, pipe material, and route
scopeChecklist.why: Footage, trenching, and the type of line, such as black iron, CSST, or polyethylene underground, drive the cost.
Spell out which appliances you are hooking up, such as furnace, range, water heater, generator, or fireplace, and whether the customer supplies them.
Many jurisdictions require permits and inspections for new gas work. Say who pulls them and who pays.
Customers need to know whether the first fill is included, and what price they will pay going forward.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions, such as trenching, concrete pads, or tree removal
scopeChecklist.why: Site prep surprises are a common source of disputes, so list what is not covered.

pricingTips.title: Quote installs as a flat price with itemized parts
pricingTips.body: Customers prefer a firm number for a tank set or line run. Show equipment, materials, labor, and permits separately so the total makes sense and change orders are easy to explain.

pricingTips.title: Build in site risk
pricingTips.body: Rock, tight access, long runs, and frozen ground can double labor. Visit the site before quoting and add a contingency or state that unforeseen conditions are billed separately.

pricingTips.title: Be clear about fuel pricing in plan quotes
pricingTips.body: For fixed-price or capped plans, state the per-gallon rate, the term, any minimum purchase, and what happens if the customer leaves early.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Material and fuel costs move. A 15 to 30 day expiration keeps you from honoring an outdated price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most propane companies do free estimates for installs and conversions. For complex jobs that need engineering, load calculations, or multiple site visits, a fee that is credited toward the work if accepted is reasonable.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the tank is set?
faqs.answer: Only if the quote allowed for it. Include language about unforeseen conditions and require written change orders for extra trenching, longer runs, or added appliances.

faqs.question: How long should a propane quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Fuel prices and equipment costs can change, so put an expiration date on every quote.

property-maintenance.intro: Property maintenance providers keep rental properties, HOA communities, small commercial buildings, and vacation homes in working order. They send invoices to landlords, property managers, HOAs, and owners for recurring service plans, one-off repairs, turnover work, and seasonal tasks. Many are solo operators or small crews who handle a mix of light repair, grounds care, and make-ready work.
property-maintenance.pricingModel: Most property maintenance work is billed hourly for repairs and odd jobs, with a trip charge or minimum visit fee for short calls. Recurring work such as lawn care, snow removal, or monthly walk-throughs is usually a flat monthly or per-visit fee under a service agreement. Turnover and make-ready jobs for rental units are often quoted as a flat fee per unit based on size and condition. Materials are billed at cost plus a markup, commonly 10-25%, and larger vendors or subcontractors are passed through with a handling fee. Property managers often negotiate a lower hourly rate in exchange for steady volume, and may require a work order or PO number on every invoice. After-hours and emergency calls are typically billed at 1.5 to 2 times the normal rate.

rates.service: Apartment turnover (clean-out, patch, touch-up paint, minor repairs)
Lawn mowing and edging, residential lot
Monthly property walk-through and inspection (vacant or seasonal home)
Snow plowing and shoveling, residential driveway

Lawn mowing and edging, Maple St. property
Trip charge, second property visit same day

sampleInvoice.notes: Work order #1187 for Oak Ridge Rentals. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Materials receipts are available on request. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit number for every line
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and landlords track costs per unit for owner statements and tax records, so a vague invoice gets sent back.

invoiceChecklist.item: Work order or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many management companies will not process a bill without one, and it ties your invoice to the tenant request or approved scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and a short description of work done
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates help resolve disputes about repeat repairs and let owners match charges to tenant requests or inspections.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized materials with markup shown clearly
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners often want receipts for parts, and clear itemization avoids questions about the markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours and hourly rate, plus any trip or after-hours charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating labor from fees shows why a short call cost more than the hours alone.

invoiceChecklist.item: License and insurance information where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require a contractor or handyman license above certain job sizes, and commercial clients often ask for proof of liability insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subcontractor charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Passing through plumbers, electricians, or tree crews at cost plus a handling fee is easier to defend when it is its own line.

property-maintenance.paymentTerms: Recurring clients are usually billed monthly, with payment due in 15 to 30 days, while one-off repairs and tenant-paid work are better due on receipt or within 7 days. Property managers often pay net 30 and may batch payments, so confirm their process before the first job. For larger turnovers, renovations, or jobs with big material costs, ask for a deposit or have the client pay for materials upfront. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in writing before the work begins. Most providers accept checks, ACH transfers, and cards, and many add a small surcharge or build the fee into rates for card payments where state law allows.

tips.title: Set a minimum visit charge
tips.body: Driving to a property, getting parts, and writing up the job takes time even when the fix takes 20 minutes. A minimum of one hour or a flat trip charge keeps small calls from losing money.

tips.title: Put recurring work under a written agreement
tips.body: For mowing, snow removal, or monthly inspections, spell out visit frequency, what triggers a snow push, and the monthly fee. It prevents arguments when a mild winter or a skipped week changes the bill.

tips.title: Bill materials the day you buy them
tips.body: Keep receipts, photograph them, and add them to the invoice quickly. Waiting weeks to bill parts means they get forgotten or disputed.

tips.title: Take before and after photos
tips.body: Photos of turnover condition, completed repairs, and damage found on arrival protect you if an owner or tenant questions the work or the charge.

tips.title: Get approval before going over the quote
tips.body: If you find rot, a failing water heater, or other hidden problems, message the owner with a price and wait for a written yes before continuing. Unapproved extras are the most common reason invoices are disputed.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or flat rate for property maintenance?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for repairs where the scope is unknown, and flat rates for repeatable work like lawn visits, gutter cleaning, and standard unit turnovers. Flat rates work best once you know how long the job takes on average.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up materials?
faqs.answer: Most providers add 10-25% to cover the time spent buying parts, gas, and handling returns. Show it as a line item or build it into a materials subtotal, and be consistent across clients.

faqs.question: Can I charge tenants directly instead of the landlord?
faqs.answer: Only if the landlord has authorized it and agreed on who is responsible. Usually you invoice the owner or property manager, who then handles any tenant chargebacks. Make sure the invoice names the right billing party.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to do property maintenance work?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and city. Many places allow small handyman work under a dollar limit without a contractor license, but plumbing, electrical, and larger repairs often require one. Check local rules and keep insurance current.

faqs.question: What do I do when a property manager pays late every time?
faqs.answer: State your terms in writing, send invoices promptly after each job, and follow up a few days before the due date. If the pattern continues, shorten terms, require a deposit, or pause new work until the balance is cleared.

estimate.intro: Property maintenance providers send estimates for turnovers, repair projects, seasonal contracts, and bids to manage a portfolio of units. Owners and property managers often collect two or three quotes and compare price, availability, and how clearly the scope is written. A specific estimate helps you win the job and protects you from scope creep.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact property address, unit, and areas included
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you are covering only the interior, the whole building, or the exterior and grounds as well.

scopeChecklist.item: Itemized list of tasks with quantities
scopeChecklist.why: Lists such as 12 outlets replaced or 3 rooms painted make it clear what the price covers and what counts as extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies materials and what allowance is included
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids disputes over paint grade, fixture choices, and who pays when parts cost more than expected.
States that rot, mold, code issues, or pest damage found after work begins will be priced separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, access requirements, and tenant coordination
scopeChecklist.why: Turnover deadlines are tight, and delays from unreturned keys or tenant access should not fall on you.

scopeChecklist.item: Recurring service terms: visit frequency, snow trigger depth, seasonal start and end
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disagreements about what is included in a monthly or seasonal fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and payment terms
scopeChecklist.why: Material and labor costs change, and a validity period keeps you from being held to an old price.

pricingTips.title: Walk the property before quoting turnovers
pricingTips.body: Condition varies widely between units. A quick walk-through with photos lets you price patching, flooring touch-ups, and trash removal accurately instead of guessing from square footage.

pricingTips.title: Build in time for travel and material runs
pricingTips.body: Include drive time and supply trips in your labor estimate. Many small jobs lose money because only hands-on time was counted.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered or itemized quote for multi-unit work
pricingTips.body: Show a per-unit price and a bundled discount for several units. Property managers like clear unit pricing and may commit to more work.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency line for older buildings
pricingTips.body: Older properties tend to turn up surprises. Note an allowance or state that unexpected repairs will be quoted separately before proceeding.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many providers quote small jobs for free but charge a fee for detailed multi-unit bids or inspections that take significant time. If you charge, say so upfront and consider crediting the fee toward the job if hired.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is common. Shorten it if material prices are volatile or your schedule fills up quickly.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over the estimate?
faqs.answer: For fixed-price jobs, you absorb normal variance but can bill extras for approved changes or hidden conditions. For time-and-materials jobs, give a not-to-exceed figure and get approval before passing it.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: For anything beyond a small repair, get written acceptance, even by email or e-signature. It records the scope and price and makes it easier to collect if there is a dispute.

property-management.intro: Property managers, from solo agents with a handful of doors to small management firms, invoice owners for monthly management fees, tenant placement, maintenance coordination, and other services. They also bill owners for expenses paid on their behalf, such as repairs, advertising, and inspections. Invoices are sent mainly to property owners, though some firms also bill tenants for fees such as late charges or lease violations.
property-management.pricingModel: Most residential managers charge a monthly fee that is a percentage of collected rent, commonly 8-12% for single-family and small multifamily, with a minimum monthly fee per unit. Larger portfolios often get lower percentages. On top of that, managers bill separate fees for leasing (often 50-100% of one month's rent), lease renewals, move-in or move-out inspections, eviction handling, and project oversight on larger repairs (often 5-15% of project cost). Vendor costs are usually passed through at cost or with a disclosed markup. Some managers use flat per-unit fees, especially for commercial or HOA work, and bill hourly for consulting, owner reporting, or one-off tasks. Your management agreement should list every fee, and invoices should match it exactly.

rates.service: Move-in or move-out inspection with photo report
Eviction coordination (not including legal or court fees)
Consulting or administrative work outside the agreement

Tenant placement fee, 456 Oak Ave Unit B (75% of $1,800 monthly rent)
Move-in inspection with photo report, 456 Oak Ave Unit B
Water heater replacement oversight, 123 Maple St (10% of $1,650 vendor invoice)
Online listing and advertising costs, 456 Oak Ave Unit B (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days or deducted from owner proceeds per the management agreement dated 1/10/2025. Vendor invoices and listing receipts are attached. A late fee of 1.5% per month applies to balances not covered by owner proceeds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit number for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners with several properties need to see which fees belong to which door for their own books and tax filings.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and rent collected
invoiceChecklist.why: Percentage fees are based on collected rent, so showing the figure lets the owner verify your math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the management agreement and fee schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying each charge to the signed agreement prevents disputes over fees the owner forgot about.

invoiceChecklist.item: Attached vendor invoices and receipts for pass-through expenses
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners expect proof of repair and advertising costs, and it separates your fee from reimbursed expenses.

invoiceChecklist.item: Any markup on vendor work, shown as a separate line
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden markups cause trust problems and may violate disclosure rules in some states.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your real estate broker or property management license number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license to manage property for others, and some require it to appear on documents.

invoiceChecklist.item: How payment will be collected (deducted from owner proceeds or paid separately)
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners need to know whether the amount comes out of rent or must be paid on top of it.

property-management.paymentTerms: Most managers collect their fees by deducting them from rent before sending owner disbursements, which makes late payment rare. When you bill separately, such as for leasing fees or project oversight, net 10 to net 15 is common. Many managers require an owner reserve or advance deposit, often $300-1,000 per property, to cover repairs without waiting on reimbursement. Accept ACH transfers, checks, and card payments, and state any card fee in the agreement. Late fees of 1-2% per month are common, but check your state rules and make sure the fee is in the agreement. Keep owner funds and tenant security deposits in separate trust or escrow accounts as your state requires, and never pay your own invoices from the wrong account.

tips.title: Keep your fees and owner money separate
tips.body: Bill your fees as their own line items and never mix them with rent or reserve funds. Clean separation makes your reporting clear and helps if the owner or a state regulator reviews your records.

tips.title: Invoice pass-through costs promptly
tips.body: Bill repairs, advertising, and supplies in the same month you pay them. Costs that sit for several months turn into surprises and get questioned.

tips.title: Spell out what triggers a fee
tips.body: Define in the agreement when a leasing fee, renewal fee, or inspection fee is earned, such as when the lease is signed or when the tenant moves in. Fee disputes usually come from unclear triggers.

tips.title: Send a statement with every invoice
tips.body: Pair the invoice with an owner statement showing rent collected, expenses paid, and net disbursement. Owners pay more willingly when they can see the whole picture.

tips.title: Watch for vacancy months
tips.body: Percentage fees disappear when a unit sits empty. If you want a minimum monthly fee during vacancy, put it in the agreement and bill it clearly.

faqs.question: Should I invoice owners or just deduct my fee from rent?
faqs.answer: Deducting from rent is common and allowed when your agreement says so. Even then, send an itemized statement or invoice so the owner can see exactly what you took and why.

faqs.question: Can I charge a markup on repairs?
faqs.answer: In many places yes, if it is disclosed in the management agreement. Some states or license rules require disclosure of markups or referral fees. Show the markup as a separate line and check your local rules.

faqs.question: Do I bill the tenant or the owner for lease violation fees?
faqs.answer: Late fees and violation charges are billed to the tenant according to the lease and local law. Management fees and repair costs not caused by tenant damage go to the owner. Keep these separate on your records.

faqs.question: What if the owner doesn't have enough rent to cover my fees?
faqs.answer: Your agreement should say whether the owner must fund the account or pay you directly. Invoice the shortfall, and consider requiring a reserve so fees and repairs are not delayed by cash flow.

faqs.question: When is a leasing fee actually earned?
faqs.answer: That depends on your agreement. Most managers bill when the lease is signed or when the tenant moves in. State the trigger in writing so there is no argument if the tenant leaves early.

estimate.intro: Property managers send proposals or fee quotes when an owner is deciding whether to hire them, and again before larger projects like renovations, turnovers, or lease-up work. Owners usually compare your percentage against other managers and want to know what is included and what costs extra.

scopeChecklist.why: Say whether the percentage applies to rent collected or rent billed, and whether a minimum monthly fee applies during vacancies.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included in the monthly fee
scopeChecklist.why: List rent collection, accounting, owner statements, tenant communication, and routine maintenance coordination so the owner knows what is covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Separate fees for leasing, renewals, inspections, and evictions
scopeChecklist.why: Owners compare total cost, not just the percentage, so extras must be visible up front.
State the dollar amount you can spend without owner approval, such as $300 or $500, to avoid arguments about unauthorized repairs.
Disclose any markup, in-house maintenance rates, or vendor relationships before work starts.
Spell out the length of the agreement, any early termination fee, and notice required to end it.
Owners should know how much they must keep on account for repairs before you take on the property.

pricingTips.title: Quote the full cost, not just the percentage
pricingTips.body: A 7% fee with large leasing, renewal, and inspection fees can cost more than a flat 10%. Show a sample annual total for the owner's property so they can compare apples to apples.

pricingTips.title: Price by property type and condition
pricingTips.body: Older homes, scattered rentals, and units with frequent turnover take more time. Raise your percentage or add a minimum fee for properties that demand extra work.

pricingTips.title: Offer a portfolio discount carefully
pricingTips.body: A lower rate for five or more doors is common, but tie it to a minimum fee per unit so a few vacancies don't wipe out your margin.

pricingTips.title: Use written bids for projects
pricingTips.body: For turnovers or renovations you oversee, get two or three vendor bids and show them with your oversight fee separate. Owners trust the process more when they see the options.

faqs.question: Is a management proposal the same as a management agreement?
faqs.answer: No. A proposal outlines fees and services to help the owner decide. The management agreement is the signed contract that governs the relationship, and its fees should match your proposal.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: For management fees, 30 days is typical. For repair and renovation bids, vendor prices may change faster, so 14 to 30 days is common, especially when materials costs shift.

faqs.question: What if repair costs go over the estimate?
faqs.answer: Set an approval threshold in the agreement and contact the owner before exceeding it, except for emergencies like a burst pipe or no heat. Document the approval in writing.

faqs.question: Should I charge to prepare a rental analysis or proposal?
faqs.answer: A basic rent estimate is usually free as part of winning business. For detailed market studies, portfolio reviews, or consulting, an hourly or flat fee is reasonable.

property-manager.intro: Property managers run rental properties on behalf of owners, handling tenant placement, rent collection, maintenance coordination, and reporting. Solo managers and small firms bill owners for monthly management, leasing, renewals, inspections, and coordination of repairs. Invoices usually go to the property owner, not the tenant.
property-manager.pricingModel: Most residential property managers charge a monthly fee set as a percentage of collected rent, commonly 8% to 12% for single-family and small multifamily, often with a minimum monthly fee per unit. Leasing is billed separately as a tenant placement fee, typically half to a full month's rent. Other charges include lease renewal fees, setup or onboarding fees, routine and move-out inspections, maintenance coordination fees (often a percentage markup on vendor invoices, such as 5% to 10%), eviction filing and court appearance fees, and hourly rates for project work like renovation oversight. Commercial and larger multifamily management may use a lower percentage with a flat monthly minimum. Many managers deduct their fees from rent collected and send the owner a statement, so the invoice or statement needs to show exactly what was deducted.

rates.service: Move-in or move-out inspection with photos

Tenant placement fee - 123 Maple St (advertising, showings, screening, lease signing)
Maintenance coordination - water heater replacement, 8% of $1,450 vendor invoice
Move-in inspection with photo report

sampleInvoice.notes: Fees for this period were deducted from March rent proceeds per the management agreement. Owner statement with rent collected, expenses paid, and net disbursement is attached. Questions about any charge, please reply within 10 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and unit number for each charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners with several properties need to match fees to the right rental for their own books and tax filings.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and rent collected
invoiceChecklist.why: Percentage fees only make sense when the owner can see the rent amount they were calculated from.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the management agreement and fee schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to a signed term and heads off disputes over what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vendor invoice copies and amounts for coordinated repairs
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners expect to see the actual repair cost separately from your markup or coordination fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tenant placement details (lease start date, monthly rent, lease term)
invoiceChecklist.why: Leasing fees are based on rent and are earned at lease signing, so the dates support the charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of inspections and property visits
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the service was performed and supports hourly or per-visit fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your real estate license or broker information where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require property management to be done under a licensed broker, and some require the license number on documents. Check your state's rules.

property-manager.paymentTerms: Most managers do not wait for owners to pay: fees are deducted from rent collected before the monthly owner disbursement, which the management agreement should authorize in writing. For fees not taken from rent, such as leasing fees on a vacant unit or project oversight, set payment due on receipt or net 15. Owners often pay by ACH or check, and some managers hold a reserve of $250 to $500 per unit for repairs. Late fees on owner invoices, commonly 1.5% per month, should be stated in the agreement. Keep owner funds and tenant security deposits in the trust or escrow accounts your state requires, and never pay your fees from the wrong account.

tips.title: Deduct fees from rent, but show your math
tips.body: Taking your fee from collected rent gets you paid reliably. Send an itemized statement every month so the owner sees rent in, fees out, expenses paid, and the net sent to them.

tips.title: Bill leasing fees at lease signing
tips.body: Do not wait until the end of the month. Leasing work is front-loaded, and a fee tied to a signed lease keeps the billing clear and prompt.

tips.title: Separate your markup from the repair cost
tips.body: List the vendor's charge and your coordination fee as separate lines. Owners accept a disclosed fee far more readily than a padded repair price.

tips.title: Spell out what is and is not included
tips.body: Many disputes come from owners assuming the monthly fee covers inspections, renewals, or evictions. List extras in the agreement and itemize them when billed.

tips.title: Keep trust account records clean
tips.body: Track each owner's funds and deposits separately. Clean ledgers make invoices easy to defend and protect you in a licensing audit.

faqs.question: Should I charge a percentage or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Percentage fees scale with rent and are the norm for residential. A flat fee can work for low-rent units or large portfolios. Many managers use a percentage with a minimum monthly fee so a low-rent or vacant unit still covers the work.

faqs.question: Can I charge a management fee when a unit is vacant?
faqs.answer: If your fee is a percentage of collected rent, a vacant unit produces no fee. Some managers add a minimum monthly fee or a vacancy fee to cover ongoing work like inspections and marketing. It must be written in the agreement.

faqs.question: Do I invoice the owner or the tenant?
faqs.answer: The owner is your client, so management and leasing fees go to the owner. Tenants may be charged application fees, late fees, or lease violation charges allowed by the lease and local law. Check your state rules on what can be charged.

faqs.question: Can I mark up repair bills from vendors?
faqs.answer: Many managers charge a disclosed coordination fee or percentage on vendor work. It should be stated in the management agreement. Some states or licensing boards require disclosure of any compensation from vendors, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: When do I get paid for tenant placement?
faqs.answer: Usually when the lease is signed or when the first month's rent and deposit are collected. State this in your agreement, including whether any portion is refundable if the tenant leaves early.

estimate.intro: Property managers give quotes when an owner is deciding whether to hire them, or when a project goes beyond normal management, such as a renovation, turnover, or lease-up of several units. Owners usually compare monthly percentage, leasing fee, and what is included, so the quote has to show the whole fee structure, not just the headline percentage.

scopeChecklist.why: State the percentage, what rent it applies to, and any minimum so the owner can calculate real cost for a low-rent or vacant month.
These are the largest one-time costs and the most common surprise if not listed up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included in the monthly fee
scopeChecklist.why: Rent collection, statements, vendor coordination, and routine inspections should be named so extras are clear.
List evictions, court appearances, major project oversight, tax or insurance claim handling, and after-hours calls with their prices.
Set a dollar amount, such as $300 or $500, above which you need owner approval before spending money.
Owners compare exit terms. State the length, notice period, and any termination or lease-in-place fee.
Say whether you require an operating reserve and where security deposits and owner funds are held.

pricingTips.title: Quote the full cost on a sample month
pricingTips.body: Show what an owner would pay on a $2,000 rental in a normal month and in the month a tenant is placed. Real numbers beat a list of percentages.

pricingTips.title: Price by property type
pricingTips.body: Single-family homes spread across a city take more drive time than units in one building. Charge a higher percentage or a minimum fee for scattered or older properties.

pricingTips.title: Do not undercut on the monthly fee and recover it in extras
pricingTips.body: Owners notice when a low percentage is padded with many fees. A clear, slightly higher fee with fewer add-ons wins more trust and fewer disputes.

pricingTips.title: Offer project quotes at fixed fees
pricingTips.body: For turnovers or renovation oversight, quote a flat fee or a percentage of project cost with a cap so the owner knows the maximum.

faqs.question: Should I give a free quote to a prospective owner?
faqs.answer: Yes. A fee proposal is normal and expected. Many managers run the numbers after looking at the property, its rent estimate, and its condition, and the proposal is usually free.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for a management proposal. Rent estimates and market conditions change, and you may need to revise the fee if the property or its condition changes.

faqs.question: What if repairs cost more than I estimated?
faqs.answer: Set an approval limit in the agreement and contact the owner before exceeding it, except in emergencies involving safety or property damage. Get approval in writing, even by email.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time spent preparing a proposal?
faqs.answer: For a standard management proposal, most do not. For a detailed renovation scope, rent analysis, or portfolio assessment, a flat fee that is credited if the owner signs is reasonable.

property-photographer.intro: Property photographers shoot homes, condos, rentals, commercial spaces, and land for real estate agents, brokers, property managers, builders, and short-term rental hosts. Invoices usually cover a shoot by size or package, plus add-ons like drone, twilight, video, floor plans, and rush delivery. Many clients are repeat agents who book several listings a month, so clear and consistent billing matters.
property-photographer.pricingModel: Most property photographers price by package tied to the home's square footage, with tiers such as up to 1,500 sq ft, 1,501-3,000, 3,001-4,500, and custom quotes above that. Each package includes a set number of edited photos (for example 25, 35, or 50) and a standard turnaround, usually 24-48 hours. Add-ons are priced as flat fees: aerial drone photos, twilight shoots, virtual staging, 3D tours, floor plans, video walkthroughs, and same-day rush delivery. Travel fees apply beyond a set radius, often 20-30 miles, either as a flat fee or per mile. Commercial and architectural work is more often priced by half day or full day, or by project, with usage licensing discussed up front. Frequent agent clients may get a bundle rate or a monthly invoice covering all shoots in that period. Reschedule and cancellation fees are common when the home is not ready or access fails.

rates.service: Standard listing photo package (up to 2,000 sq ft, 25-35 photos)
Large home package (3,000+ sq ft, 40-60 photos)
