Aerial drone photos (10 images), lot and neighborhood
Twilight exterior set (5 images)
Floor plan with measurements
Travel beyond 25-mile radius (12 extra miles)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of delivery. Photos are licensed to the listing agent and brokerage for marketing this property. A $50 fee applies to reschedules with less than 24 hours notice. Accepted payment: card, ACH, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and shoot date
invoiceChecklist.why: Agents manage many listings at once and need to match each charge to a property, especially for brokerage reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name, square footage tier, and photo count
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the price was set and what was delivered, which heads off disputes about the number of images.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (drone, twilight, video, floor plan, rush)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often add services after booking, and listing each line shows what was requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: Name of the billed party and who ordered the shoot
invoiceChecklist.why: Sometimes the agent orders and the seller or brokerage pays. A clear bill-to avoids delays and misdirected invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Licensing and usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States who may use the images and for what, such as MLS, brochures, and social media, and whether other parties like stagers or builders need separate permission.

invoiceChecklist.item: Drone pilot certification number where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: In the US, paid drone work generally requires an FAA Part 107 certificate. Listing it reassures commercial and brokerage clients.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel, rush, and reschedule fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows these charges were agreed in advance and keeps them from looking like surprises.

property-photographer.paymentTerms: Many property photographers invoice when the gallery is delivered and ask for payment within 7-14 days, while some require payment before releasing full-resolution files. Agents often prefer payment at closing, so decide whether you will allow that, and many photographers do not. New clients may be asked for a deposit or card on file, and new builder or commercial clients may pay 25-50% up front. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated on the invoice or agreement. Payment is usually by card, ACH, or check. For repeat agents, a single monthly invoice listing every shoot can cut down on admin.

tips.title: Hold full-resolution files until paid for new clients
tips.body: Deliver a watermarked or low-resolution gallery first for new clients, or require card on file. Agents are often slow to pay if the photos already went live on the listing.

tips.title: Do not tie payment to closing
tips.body: Some agents ask to pay when the house sells. That can take months or never happen. Set a due date based on delivery and put it in writing.

tips.title: Set a clear cancellation and reschedule policy
tips.body: Unprepared homes, bad weather, and no-shows eat into your day. A reschedule fee, usually $25-75, or a charge for arriving to a home that is not ready, protects your time.

tips.title: Offer bundles for regular agents
tips.body: A monthly invoice with a set rate per shoot, or a discount on three or more shoots, saves you chasing separate payments and keeps agents booking with you.

tips.title: Track square footage disputes
tips.body: Pull the square footage from the listing or county record when booking and note it on the invoice. If the home is larger than stated, you can adjust the tier without argument.

faqs.question: Should I invoice the agent or the homeowner?
faqs.answer: Invoice whoever agreed to pay when booking, which is usually the listing agent. If a seller, builder, or brokerage pays instead, confirm that before the shoot and put their name on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for rush delivery?
faqs.answer: Yes. Same-day or next-morning delivery is commonly an add-on of $50-150 or a percentage of the package. List it as its own line so it is clear it was requested.

faqs.question: Do I need a drone license to bill for aerial photos?
faqs.answer: In the US, flying a drone for paid work generally requires an FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate. Some airspace needs extra authorization. Check current FAA rules and local restrictions.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax photography services or digital products, and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if a client pays late or refuses to pay after using the photos?
faqs.answer: Send reminders, then a written demand that cites your licensing terms. If the images are in use without payment, you can state that the license is not active until the invoice is paid. For larger balances, consider small claims court.

estimate.intro: Property photographers send quotes when an agent, builder, or property manager asks for pricing on a new listing, a large or unusual property, or a recurring arrangement. Clients usually compare per-shoot price, photo count, turnaround time, and add-ons like drone and twilight across a few local photographers.

scopeChecklist.item: Property address, square footage, and property type
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing tiers depend on size, and a condo, multi-unit, or acreage lot changes time on site.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of edited photos and delivery format
scopeChecklist.why: Defines what the client gets, such as MLS-sized and full-resolution files, so there is no argument over image counts.
Drone, twilight, video, floor plans, and virtual staging are priced separately. Spelling them out prevents scope creep.
Standard delivery is 24-48 hours. A rush request changes your schedule and should be quoted separately.
Homes should be cleaned, staged, and lit before arrival. State your fee for delays, re-shoots, or lockbox problems.
Exterior, drone, and twilight shoots depend on weather. Say how rescheduling works and whether fees apply.
Clarify who may use the images and where, especially if a builder, stager, or brokerage will also use them.

pricingTips.title: Publish a clear package menu
pricingTips.body: A simple tier chart by square footage lets agents quote themselves and cuts back-and-forth. Keep a custom quote for large or unusual properties.

pricingTips.title: Price commercial and architectural work by time and usage
pricingTips.body: For builders, hotels, and commercial clients, estimate a half or full day plus editing time, and charge more if the images will appear in advertising or on signage.

pricingTips.title: Add your travel rule to every quote
pricingTips.body: State your service radius and the fee beyond it. Remote properties and rural acreage can add hours of driving.

pricingTips.title: Offer an optional upgrade, not a discount
pricingTips.body: Presenting a base package with a drone or twilight upgrade lets clients choose a higher price without you cutting your rate.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Flat package pricing is standard for residential listings because clients want to know the exact cost. Use hourly or day rates for commercial, architectural, or large multi-property jobs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Many photographers keep quotes valid for 14-30 days. Rates and availability can change, and listings often move fast, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before the shoot?
faqs.answer: Not for established agents on regular accounts, but new clients, large commercial jobs, and remote travel shoots often justify a deposit of 25-50%.

faqs.question: What if the property is bigger than the client said?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that pricing is based on the stated square footage and may be adjusted if the actual size or room count differs. This gives you grounds to change the tier.

property-stager.intro: Property stagers prepare vacant or occupied homes for sale or rent by arranging furniture, art, and accessories so listings photograph well and show well in person. Clients are usually listing agents, home sellers, builders, and landlords. Invoices typically cover an initial consultation, the staging installation, a monthly rental period for furniture and decor, and removal at the end of the contract.
property-stager.pricingModel: Most stagers bill in two parts: a one-time design fee and installation fee, then a monthly rental fee for the furniture and accessories that stays in place until the home sells or the contract term ends. Consultations for occupied homes are often a flat fee or hourly, and many stagers credit the consultation fee toward a full staging if the client books. Installation pricing is usually based on the rooms staged or the size of the home, with a minimum project fee because moving trucks, labor, and inventory handling cost the same on small jobs. Rental terms commonly run 30 to 90 days, with a minimum of one to three months, and an extension rate for each additional month, often the same as or slightly lower than the original monthly rate. Many stagers also charge separately for de-staging and removal, delivery outside a set radius, and damaged or lost items. Some stagers sell the same work as tiered packages, such as a key rooms package (living room, primary bedroom, kitchen, entry) versus a full-home package.

Occupied home staging using client's furniture plus accessories
Rental extension beyond the initial term

Additional accessory styling for kitchen and secondary bedroom

De-staging and removal of all rental items

sampleInvoice.notes: Installation fee and first month's rental were due before delivery. Second month's rental is due on the 1st of the month following installation. Rental continues at $1,200 per month after the initial 60 days until items are removed. Items remain the property of the stager. The client is responsible for loss or damage beyond normal wear. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and listing agent name
invoiceChecklist.why: Stagers often work on several properties for the same agent or seller, and the address ties each charge to the right job and contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation date and rental start date
invoiceChecklist.why: Monthly rental billing begins on a specific date, and clients dispute charges when it is unclear when the clock started.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rental term and renewal rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the initial term (for example 60 days) and the monthly extension rate prevents surprises when a listing stays on the market longer than expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized breakdown of design, installation, rental, and removal
invoiceChecklist.why: Agents and sellers often pay different pieces at different times, and an itemized invoice shows which are one-time and which recur.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery and mileage charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Long-distance or multi-trip jobs cost more, and listing the surcharge separately explains the added cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Who is responsible for payment (seller, agent, or builder)
invoiceChecklist.why: Payer confusion is common in real estate, and the invoice should name the bill-to party matching your signed agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage, loss, and early termination terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Referencing the agreement's terms for damaged items or early removal gives you a clear basis for any added charges.

property-stager.paymentTerms: Most stagers collect a deposit or the full installation fee before delivery, since inventory, labor, and truck time are committed up front. The first month's rental is commonly due at the same time, and later months are billed in advance on a set date. Some stagers ask for payment at closing for agent-paid jobs, but that carries risk if the sale falls through or the listing sits, so a signed agreement is important. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common where allowed, and many contracts add a per-month extension charge after the initial term. Payment methods usually include check, ACH transfer, and credit card, with card fees sometimes passed on to the client. Check your state's rules on late fees and surcharges.

tips.title: Bill rental in advance
tips.body: Charge each monthly rental period at the start, not the end. Your inventory is tied up the whole time, and collecting in advance reduces chasing payment after the house has sold.

tips.title: Set a minimum term and a clear extension rate
tips.body: Put the minimum rental period and the monthly rate after that term in writing. Listings often take longer than planned, and a stated extension rate keeps those months from becoming a negotiation.

tips.title: Separate one-time fees from recurring fees
tips.body: List design, installation, and removal as one-time items and rental as monthly. Sellers understand the invoice better, and it is easier to see what continues if the home stays on the market.

tips.title: Document the condition of items at delivery and pickup
tips.body: Take dated photos of the staged home and of high-value pieces when you install and when you remove them. If you need to bill for damage or loss, the photos support the charge.

tips.title: Confirm who pays before you order or deliver
tips.body: Agents sometimes cover staging for a seller and expect payment at closing, while others expect the seller to pay directly. Settle this in the contract so the invoice goes to the right person.

faqs.question: Should I invoice the agent or the home seller?
faqs.answer: Invoice whoever signed the staging agreement and agreed to pay. Some agents pay for staging as a marketing cost, while in other cases the seller is responsible. If the agent said they would pay at closing, put that in writing and include what happens if the sale falls through.

faqs.question: Can I charge for staging if the home doesn't sell?
faqs.answer: Yes. Your fees cover design, labor, delivery, and rental of inventory, not the sale outcome. The agreement should say that fees are due regardless of whether the home sells, and that rental continues until items are removed.

faqs.question: How do I bill for rental after the initial term ends?
faqs.answer: Bill at the extension rate stated in your agreement, usually monthly in advance, until the items are picked up. Some stagers prorate partial months, others charge a full month. Whichever you use, state it in the contract and on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on staging?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax rental of tangible personal property, which can include furniture rental, and some tax design services differently or not at all. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional about how to treat the design fee, rental, and delivery.

faqs.question: Should I charge a consultation fee separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, for occupied-home consultations that include a walk-through and written recommendations. Many stagers apply it as a credit toward a full staging if the client books within a set number of days, and the invoice should show that credit as a line item.

estimate.intro: Property stagers send estimates after a walk-through of the property, often when a seller is interviewing several stagers before listing. Clients compare the total installation cost, the monthly rental fee, the minimum term, and what is included in delivery and removal. A clear written proposal helps you win the job and sets the terms for the rental that follows.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming each room prevents disputes over whether the kitchen, bathrooms, patio, or secondary bedrooms were included.

scopeChecklist.item: Occupied or vacant property and whose furniture is used
scopeChecklist.why: Vacant staging uses your inventory, while occupied staging may mean rearranging the client's items, and the labor and pricing differ.
Tying the quote to a target install date and minimum term clarifies when billing starts and when it renews.

scopeChecklist.item: Monthly rental rate and extension rate
scopeChecklist.why: Listings often outlast the initial term, and stating the post-term rate up front avoids price disagreements later.
Stairs, elevators, long carries, HOA move-in rules, and distance from your warehouse all affect labor and may carry added fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Damage, loss, and early removal terms
scopeChecklist.why: Spelling out responsibility for pets, smoking, staining, and damaged items protects your inventory.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and deposit required
scopeChecklist.why: Inventory availability changes, and a set expiration date and deposit hold the booking.

pricingTips.title: Price from a walk-through, not photos alone
pricingTips.body: Ceiling heights, floor plans, stairs, and the number of rooms affect how much furniture and labor you need. Walk the property or review a detailed floor plan before giving a number.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present a key rooms option and a full-home option side by side. Many sellers choose the middle option when they can see what each level includes.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum project fee
pricingTips.body: Delivery, setup, and removal take roughly the same time and truck cost on a small condo as on a larger home. A minimum keeps small jobs from costing you money.

pricingTips.title: Show the total cost over the expected listing period
pricingTips.body: Include the installation fee plus two or three months of rental in your quote so the client sees the real cost, not just the first payment.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: For vacant homes, most stagers provide a free walk-through and quote. For occupied homes, a paid consultation with written recommendations is common, since you are giving design advice the client can use without hiring you.

faqs.question: How long should a staging quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Inventory and your install schedule can change quickly, especially in busy listing seasons, so an expiration date protects you from holding items for free.

faqs.question: What if the home stays on the market longer than the quoted term?
faqs.answer: Include the monthly extension rate in the estimate and agreement. If the client accepts the quote, they have agreed to those terms, and you can bill extra months without renegotiating.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed contract in addition to the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. An estimate is a price, while a staging agreement covers ownership of items, damage responsibility, access, rental term, and payment. Many stagers combine both into one document the client signs and returns with a deposit.

proposal-writer.intro: Proposal writers help small businesses, nonprofits, consultancies, and contractors win work by writing bids, RFP responses, sales proposals, and grant applications. Most are freelancers or run small shops, and they bill for writing, research, editing, compliance review, and project management around a bid deadline. Invoices often tie to milestones such as outline approval, first draft, and final submission.
proposal-writer.pricingModel: Proposal writers price in a few ways. Hourly billing is common for editing, rewrites, and open-ended support, usually with a tracked time log. Flat fees per proposal are standard when the scope is clear, such as a 20-page RFP response, and are often scaled by page count, complexity, and turnaround time. Retainers suit companies that bid regularly and need a set number of hours or proposals each month. Some writers add a rush fee for deadlines under a week, and charge separately for templates, content libraries, and graphic or layout work. Success-based fees exist, especially in grant writing, but many professional associations discourage percentage-of-award pay for grants, and some funders prohibit it, so most writers charge a fixed or hourly fee and keep contingency arrangements rare and carefully documented.

rates.service: Proposal template or boilerplate library setup
Monthly retainer for ongoing bid support

items.description: RFP kickoff call, requirements review, and compliance matrix
Narrative draft: technical approach and management plan (sections 3-4)
Executive summary and past performance write-up
Revision round incorporating client and SME feedback
Final proofread, formatting check, and submission support
Rush fee for deadline under 7 days

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice covers work on the County Facilities Maintenance RFP submitted on the 14th. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Final deliverables remain with the writer until the invoice is paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Name of the bid, RFP number, or solicitation ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often work on several bids at once, and their accounting team needs to code the cost to the right opportunity.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables and milestones completed
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing outline, first draft, revision round, and final submission shows what the payment covers and ties to the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged by task, if billing hourly
invoiceChecklist.why: A breakdown of research, drafting, and editing time answers questions about the total before they turn into disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds used
invoiceChecklist.why: Most flat fees include a set number of rounds. Showing how many were used supports any extra charge for added rounds.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush or deadline surcharge, shown as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating it makes clear it was agreed to up front and not an arbitrary add-on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs such as stock graphics, design, or research databases
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through expenses should be itemized with receipts available so the client sees what is writing and what is not.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order number and client contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often will not pay without a PO or a named approver.

proposal-writer.paymentTerms: Many proposal writers take 30 to 50 percent upfront as a deposit, since the work is deadline-driven and the client's bid may be lost if the writer stops midway. A common split is half at kickoff and half at delivery of the final draft, or thirds at kickoff, first draft, and final. Net 15 is typical for small clients, and net 30 for companies with accounts payable departments. Retainers are usually billed at the start of the month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common where permitted, so check your state's rules. Most writers accept ACH, card, and checks. Because bid deadlines are fixed, it helps to state that final files are released after the deposit and any milestone payments are received.

tips.title: Require the deposit before you start
tips.body: Bid deadlines leave no room for chasing payment later. A kickoff deposit confirms the client is serious and covers your time if they cancel or decide not to bid.

tips.title: Define what counts as a revision round
tips.body: Say whether a round means one consolidated set of comments or any number of edits sent piecemeal. Without that, late-stage comment threads from several reviewers can double your hours.

tips.title: Bill the win-or-lose work the same way
tips.body: Your fee should not depend on whether the client wins. Make that clear in the agreement, and if you do take a bonus for a win, record it as a separate, documented line.

tips.title: Track time even on flat-fee jobs
tips.body: A private log tells you whether your flat fees match your real hourly rate, and it gives you evidence if the scope grows and you need to ask for a change order.

tips.title: Invoice right after submission
tips.body: Send the final invoice the day the proposal is submitted, while the client is relieved and the effort is fresh. Waiting for the award decision often means waiting months.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for proposals?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when the RFP is in hand and the scope is clear, since clients like knowing the total. Use hourly for open-ended work such as editing someone else's draft, or when the requirements may change. Many writers quote a flat fee with a defined number of revision rounds and bill extra hourly beyond that.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of the contract if the client wins?
faqs.answer: You can in some private-sector situations, but it carries risk because the payment depends on a decision you do not control. For grants, professional associations discourage percentage-based pay and some funders prohibit it. A fixed or hourly fee is safer, and any bonus should be written into the agreement.

faqs.question: When should I send the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it when you deliver the final submission-ready proposal, or on submission day. Do not tie your payment to the award announcement unless you have agreed to that in writing, since decisions can take months.

faqs.question: How do I bill for research time?
faqs.answer: Either include research in the flat fee or list it as its own line, such as competitor analysis or reviewing past proposals. If you bill hourly, log research under its own task so the client can see what it covered.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on proposal writing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain professional or digital services and many do not tax writing services. Check your state department of revenue or ask an accountant, and show any tax you collect as a separate line.

estimate.intro: Proposal writers send a quote after reading the RFP or talking through the opportunity, and usually before the client commits to the bid. Clients compare your price against other freelancers and against the cost of having staff do it, so the quote needs to show what is included and how much of the bid you are taking on.

scopeChecklist.item: The specific solicitation and its due date
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on the length, complexity, and deadline of the actual document, and a named deadline sets the schedule you are committing to.

scopeChecklist.item: Sections and page count you will write
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume you write everything. State which sections you draft and which they supply, such as pricing tables, résumés, or past performance data.

scopeChecklist.item: Inputs the client must provide and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Late subject matter input is the most common cause of missed deadlines and overruns. Put dates on their deliverables.
Limits the back-and-forth and sets a basis for charging more if feedback keeps coming.
Clarifies whether you deliver a text document, a formatted file, or work with their designer, and who pays for design.

scopeChecklist.item: Rush fee and what triggers it
scopeChecklist.why: If the schedule compresses or the client sends materials late, an agreed surcharge avoids an awkward conversation.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule and what happens if the bid is canceled
scopeChecklist.why: States that the deposit is non-refundable and that work done to date is billable if the client withdraws.

pricingTips.title: Read the full RFP before quoting
pricingTips.body: Evaluation criteria, mandatory forms, page limits, and required attachments drive the real workload. A quote based on a summary often turns out too low.

pricingTips.title: Price by complexity, not only page count
pricingTips.body: A 15-page federal response with a compliance matrix and several certifications takes more effort than a 30-page private-sector sales proposal. Tier your pricing by type of bid.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option such as drafting only, a standard option that adds editing and compliance review, and a full option that includes project management and submission support. Clients tend to choose the middle.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for reviewer feedback
pricingTips.body: Multiple stakeholders make comments late. A modest contingency or a stated limit on review rounds protects your margin.

faqs.question: How long should a proposal quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Because you are scheduling around a deadline, state that availability and pricing are held only until a set date and that the schedule depends on receiving the deposit.

faqs.question: Should I quote before or after seeing the RFP?
faqs.answer: After. Quoting without the full document is a guess. If you must give a ballpark first, label it as an estimate range and say the firm quote follows your review of the solicitation.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a quote or scoping call?
faqs.answer: A short call is usually free. If you are asked to do an in-depth bid/no-bid analysis or a detailed review of a large RFP, charge a modest flat fee, often credited to the project if the client hires you.

faqs.question: What if the scope grows after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Send a written change order describing the added work, cost, and any schedule impact before you do it. Examples include an added volume, a new required section, or an extension request from the agency.

real-estate-agent.intro: Real estate agents and small brokerages usually get paid at closing, so their "invoice" is often a commission invoice or demand sent to a title company, escrow officer, or closing attorney. Agents also bill for referral fees to other brokers, rental and leasing placements, transaction coordination, and flat-fee consulting, and they sometimes seek reimbursement for marketing costs they fronted.
real-estate-agent.pricingModel: Most agent income is a percentage of the sale price, set in the listing or buyer representation agreement and paid out of closing proceeds. Since the 2024 NAR settlement, buyer-agent compensation has to be agreed in writing up front and is more openly negotiated. Some agents instead charge a flat fee or a tiered fee. Rentals are usually priced as a share of the first month's rent (or a flat placement fee), and property management as a monthly percentage of collected rent. Referral fees between brokers are typically a percentage of the commission. Hourly or flat-fee pricing shows up in consulting, pre-listing advice, relocation help, and expert opinion work. Most agents are independent contractors who are paid through their brokerage, so the brokerage's split, desk fees, and transaction fees affect what you actually keep.

rates.service: Residential lease placement (tenant or landlord side)
Referral fee paid to another licensed agent
Buyer consultation, pre-listing advice, or relocation consulting
Broker price opinion or comparative market analysis for a non-client

items.description: Listing agent commission, 2.5% of $425,000 sale price, 1480 Maple Ridge Dr, per listing agreement dated 3/2
Transaction and compliance fee
Professional photography and 3D tour (advanced, per listing agreement)

sampleInvoice.notes: Please disburse at closing from seller proceeds to the brokerage's trust or operating account per the attached commission instructions. File no. and closing date are shown above. If closing is delayed, this invoice remains due at the actual closing date. Questions: contact the listing agent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Brokerage name, your license number, and the broker of record
invoiceChecklist.why: Commissions are almost always paid to the brokerage, and title companies need the licensed entity and its tax details to disburse.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address, parcel or file number, and escrow or closing file number
invoiceChecklist.why: Title and escrow offices handle many closings at once and match payments to the file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parties and your role (listing agent, buyer agent, dual agent, or referral)
invoiceChecklist.why: It determines which side's compensation you are claiming and who authorizes payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sale price, commission percentage or flat amount, and the date of the agreement that sets it
invoiceChecklist.why: It shows how the number was calculated and ties it to a signed listing or buyer representation agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expected closing date and wire or payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Payment is contingent on closing, and clear instructions prevent delays. Confirm wire details by phone to avoid wire fraud.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts (photography, staging, signage, inspections you advanced)
invoiceChecklist.why: Out-of-pocket costs are only recoverable if they were agreed in writing and itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Referral fee details: the other agent's name, brokerage, license number, and referral agreement date
invoiceChecklist.why: Broker-to-broker fees require a written agreement and the other brokerage's information to be paid properly.

real-estate-agent.paymentTerms: Sales commissions are due at closing and are normally paid from proceeds by the title or escrow company, so there is no net-30 term. Lease placement fees are usually due at lease signing or move-in. Flat consulting fees and transaction coordination are commonly collected up front or at the time of service. Referral fees are typically paid within a few days after the referring brokerage receives the commission. Late fees are rare on commissions, but a signed agreement can include interest or collection language for unpaid fees outside of closing. Payment is by wire or check through escrow, or ACH and card for consulting and administrative fees. Check your state's rules, since many states require commissions to be paid through a licensed broker rather than directly to an agent.

tips.title: Send the commission invoice before the closing date
tips.body: Submit your commission instructions to the title company at least a week before closing so the figure appears on the settlement statement. Chasing money after closing is much harder than getting it into the disbursement.

tips.title: Keep the signed agreement behind every number
tips.body: Attach or reference the listing or buyer representation agreement that sets your compensation. Under the current rules, a written agreement is the core protection if a dispute comes up.

tips.title: Know what the brokerage takes out
tips.body: Track your split, desk or franchise fees, transaction fees, and E&O charges so you can estimate net income. Set aside money for self-employment tax if you are an independent contractor.

tips.title: Separate fee-for-service work from commission work
tips.body: If you bill consulting, staging coordination, or rental placements, put them on their own invoice. Some states limit how licensees may be paid, so confirm with your broker.

tips.title: Document referral fees in writing before the deal closes
tips.body: A short referral agreement signed by both brokerages prevents arguments over percentage, timing, and what happens if the deal changes or falls through.

faqs.question: Do real estate agents actually send invoices?
faqs.answer: Yes, though it often takes the form of a commission invoice, commission instructions, or demand letter sent to the title or escrow company. Agents also invoice for referral fees, lease placements, consulting, and reimbursable expenses.

faqs.question: Who is the invoice made out to?
faqs.answer: For a sale, it is usually the closing agent (title company, escrow officer, or attorney), since they pay commissions from proceeds. For a referral fee, it goes to the other brokerage. For consulting or rental placement, it goes to the client.

faqs.question: Can I be paid directly by the client instead of through my brokerage?
faqs.answer: In most states, a licensed agent must receive real estate compensation through their supervising broker. Check your state's licensing rules and your brokerage agreement before accepting direct payment.

faqs.question: What if the deal falls through and I did a lot of work?
faqs.answer: Unless your agreement includes a cancellation fee, a consulting fee, or a protection period clause, you generally cannot bill for a failed transaction. Put those terms in writing before you start.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on commissions?
faqs.answer: Real estate commissions are generally not subject to sales tax, but a few services you provide (such as some consulting or property management in some states) might be. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Agents quote before work starts in the form of a listing presentation, a buyer representation agreement, a lease placement proposal, or a consulting scope. Sellers and buyers compare commission percentage, what services are included, and who pays marketing costs, and they often interview two or three agents.

scopeChecklist.item: Commission rate or flat fee, and who pays it
scopeChecklist.why: Compensation must be clear and in writing, and buyers and sellers should know exactly what they are agreeing to before signing.

scopeChecklist.item: Length of the agreement and how to cancel
scopeChecklist.why: Listing and buyer agreements run for a set term. Spelling out the term and cancellation conditions avoids conflicts if the relationship breaks down.

scopeChecklist.item: Marketing services included (photography, video, 3D tour, staging help, open houses, MLS and portal syndication)
scopeChecklist.why: Sellers compare marketing plans, and a written list shows what you provide at your cost and what the client pays for separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Costs the client pays out of pocket (staging, repairs, inspections, cleaning)
scopeChecklist.why: It prevents surprises when third-party bills arrive.

scopeChecklist.item: Protection or tail period for clients you introduced
scopeChecklist.why: It explains how long you are owed compensation if the client later buys or sells with someone you introduced.
Flat fees added on top of the commission are a common source of complaints if they appear for the first time at closing.

scopeChecklist.item: Price opinion disclaimer and estimated net proceeds
scopeChecklist.why: A suggested list price is an opinion, not a guarantee. Stating this and showing a net sheet sets realistic expectations.

pricingTips.title: Lead with the value, not just the percentage
pricingTips.body: Show recent comparable sales, your average days on market, and your marketing plan so the commission is compared against results and not against a discount agent.

pricingTips.title: Offer clear tiers if you vary services
pricingTips.body: A full-service option and a reduced-service or flat-fee option, each with a written list of inclusions, lets the client pick without you cutting your rate across the board.

pricingTips.title: Use a net sheet
pricingTips.body: Show the estimated costs of selling, including commission, title, taxes, and concessions, so the seller sees the commission as one line among known costs.

pricingTips.title: Be ready to explain buyer-side compensation
pricingTips.body: Buyers now often ask directly what they will owe. Explain whether you expect it from the seller's offer or from them, and put your fee in the representation agreement.

faqs.question: Is a listing presentation the same as an estimate?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. The presentation shows your pricing opinion and marketing plan, while the listing agreement is the binding document that states your commission. Give both so the client sees the proposal and the commitment.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a pre-listing consultation or CMA?
faqs.answer: Many agents give a CMA free to prospective clients. If the work is for someone who does not intend to hire you, such as a divorce, estate, or tax appeal, a flat fee is reasonable and should be agreed in writing first.

faqs.question: Should my quote include a guaranteed sale price?
faqs.answer: No. Give a recommended list price range based on comparables and market conditions, and state that the final price depends on buyers and market conditions.

faqs.question: How long should a commission quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Listing proposals are usually good for 30 days since market conditions change. A lease placement or consulting quote can state a shorter window, such as 14 days.

real-estate-appraiser.intro: Real estate appraisers are licensed or certified professionals who give an opinion of value on residential, commercial, or land properties. Most bill lenders, appraisal management companies (AMCs), attorneys, estates, or homeowners for a completed report, plus add-ons like rush fees, extra comparable research, or mileage. Many work solo or in small firms, so clear billing and quick collection matter.
real-estate-appraiser.pricingModel: Appraisers mostly charge a flat fee per assignment, set by property type, complexity, and report form. A standard single-family appraisal on a conventional loan is a fixed fee, while complex properties, large acreage, multi-unit buildings, and commercial assets are quoted by scope or sometimes hourly. Add-ons are common: rush turnaround, extra distance beyond a set radius, additional units or outbuildings, and revisions beyond a basic reconsideration of value. AMC work usually follows the AMC's fee schedule, which can be lower than direct-client fees, and rules around customary and reasonable fees for federally related loans apply, so check current requirements. Private clients such as attorneys, estates, and divorce matters often pay hourly for consulting, testimony, and review work, with a retainer up front. Appraisers who bill by the hour for litigation support typically charge more for deposition and court time than for report writing.

items.description: Residential appraisal, single-family, 1234 Maple Ave (URAR, FHA purchase), inspection 3/12, report delivered 3/16
Rush turnaround (delivered within 3 business days)
Complex property add-on: detached guest house and 6 acres
Extra mileage beyond 30-mile radius

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon delivery of report, net 10 for AMC and lender clients. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month after 30 days. Report release may be withheld until fees are paid for private-pay clients, subject to applicable rules. Please reference file number 2025-0312 with payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address, parcel number, and file or order number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact assignment and lets AMCs and lenders match payments to their orders.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name, lender or AMC name, and loan or reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many AMCs and lenders will not process payment without their own reference number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Type of report and intended use (e.g., URAR for FHA purchase, date-of-death valuation)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was delivered and supports the fee, since pricing differs by form and scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Inspection date, effective date of value, and report delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents the timeline and supports due dates, rush fees, and any later disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized fees and add-ons (rush, complexity, mileage, extra units)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients are less likely to dispute a fee when every adjustment from the base fee is listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: State license or certification number and expiration
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients and AMCs require it on billing documents, and it shows you are authorized to perform the work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment instructions, deposit credited, and due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Avoids delays caused by unclear remittance details or retainers that were not subtracted.

real-estate-appraiser.paymentTerms: For lender and AMC work, payment is commonly due at delivery or within 7 to 30 days, and many AMCs pay on their own schedule, so confirm their terms before accepting the order. For homebuyer-paid appraisals, the fee is often collected up front by card or ACH before the inspection, which removes collection risk. Private clients such as attorneys and estates are usually billed with a retainer for hourly work, and final balances are due on delivery of the report. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common but should be stated in your engagement letter. Accepted payment methods usually include ACH, card, and check.

tips.title: Collect payment before the inspection on private-pay jobs
tips.body: For buyers, refinancing owners, and estates, take payment or a deposit when you accept the order. Appraisers have little leverage after the report is delivered, and rules in many states limit withholding reports for reasons other than nonpayment of the appraisal fee.

tips.title: Keep a written fee schedule for add-ons
tips.body: List your charges for rush orders, complex properties, extra distance, and additional units. Quoting from a schedule keeps pricing consistent and makes it easier to defend an add-on.

tips.title: Track AMC payment terms and fee splits
tips.body: Some AMCs pay in 30 to 60 days and may deduct fees or ask for re-bills. Keep a log of order dates, delivery dates, and payment status per AMC so you can follow up on overdue items.

tips.title: Bill for revisions and extra work carefully
tips.body: A reasonable reconsideration of value or a correction of your own error is generally part of the job. Extra work caused by changed assignment details, such as a new intended use or added comparable research requested by the client, can be billed separately if your engagement letter says so.

tips.title: Separate hourly consulting from report fees
tips.body: When you do testimony, depositions, or review work, bill by the hour with travel and waiting time listed. Mixing these with the report fee makes the invoice harder to read and harder to collect on.

faqs.question: Can I charge a rush fee on an appraisal?
faqs.answer: Yes, for private-pay and many direct-lender orders, if you agree to it in advance. For AMC orders, check whether their fee schedule allows rush charges, since some set the total fee and may not pass through add-ons.

faqs.question: Do I have to bill the borrower or the lender?
faqs.answer: It depends on how the order was placed. The client who engages you is generally who you bill, which could be a lender, AMC, or the borrower directly. Fee disclosure and payment collection for loans often run through the lender or AMC, so follow the order instructions.

faqs.question: Can I hold the report until I get paid?
faqs.answer: For private-pay assignments, many appraisers do, if the engagement letter says so. For lender-ordered appraisals on federally related transactions, rules in many states limit withholding of a report from the lender or borrower for nonpayment of fees beyond the appraisal fee itself. Check your state board and the applicable regulations.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on appraisal fees?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Many states do not tax professional services like appraisals, but a few tax some services. Check with your state department of revenue or a local tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a cancelled order?
faqs.answer: Bill for work already done, such as the inspection, travel, and any research completed. State a cancellation policy in your engagement letter, for example a partial fee after the inspection, and itemize what was done on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Appraisers send a fee quote when a client calls before ordering, when an attorney or estate needs a valuation, or when the property is unusual. Lenders and AMCs often assign fees by schedule, but private clients compare quotes on price, turnaround, and experience with the property type. A clear quote with scope and timeline helps you win the job and reduces disputes later.

scopeChecklist.why: Fee depends on size, number of units, land, and outbuildings, so confirm what is being appraised before quoting.

scopeChecklist.item: Intended use and intended users of the report
scopeChecklist.why: Appraisal standards require these to be defined, and they affect the report form, scope of work, and who may rely on it.

scopeChecklist.item: Type of value and effective date
scopeChecklist.why: Market value today, retrospective value at a date of death, or as-complete value for new construction are different assignments with different work and pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Scope of work and report format
scopeChecklist.why: State the inspection type (interior, exterior only, desktop) and the form or narrative level so the client knows what they are getting.
Turnaround is a major factor in client choice, and it sets expectations for when your fee is due.

scopeChecklist.item: Access requirements and documents needed from the client
scopeChecklist.why: Delays often come from locked properties, missing plans, or lease information, and you can state that these may change the timeline or fee.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee, deposit, and what triggers additional charges
scopeChecklist.why: Lists the base fee and the conditions for add-ons, such as changed scope, extra units, or additional comparable research.

pricingTips.title: Price by complexity, not just square footage
pricingTips.body: Rural, unique, high-value, and older homes take more time for comparable research and adjustments. Build in a higher base fee or a complexity add-on rather than losing money on difficult files.

pricingTips.title: Use a fee range only when scope is uncertain
pricingTips.body: For commercial, litigation, or unusual properties, give a fixed fee for a defined scope or a not-to-exceed amount. If scope may expand, state the hourly rate for extra work.

pricingTips.title: Require a deposit for private clients
pricingTips.body: Ask for 50 percent or the full fee for residential private-pay work and a retainer for larger commercial or litigation assignments. It confirms commitment and covers your time if the job is cancelled.

pricingTips.title: Put the quote in an engagement letter
pricingTips.body: Combine the fee, scope, intended use, and cancellation terms in one document the client signs. It protects you if the client later tries to change the purpose or complains about the result.

faqs.question: Can I quote a fee before seeing the property?
faqs.answer: Yes, but base it on the information given and state that the fee may change if the property turns out to be larger or more complex than described. Many appraisers ask for the address, size, and property type, then check public records before quoting.

faqs.question: Should I tell a client what value I expect to reach?
faqs.answer: No. Never agree to a predetermined value or tie your fee to the value or the outcome of a loan. That is prohibited under appraisal standards and many state rules. Quote the fee for the work only.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for private clients, though local market conditions and your workload may call for a shorter window. State an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the client wants me to match another appraiser's price?
faqs.answer: You can decline or offer a reduced scope, such as an exterior-only or desktop assignment where acceptable, but avoid cutting the fee so low that you cannot do the work properly. Quality and compliance matter more than winning a price-driven job.

real-estate-consultant.intro: Real estate consultants advise investors, developers, landlords, businesses, and homeowners on property decisions without acting as the listing or buyer's agent. Typical invoices cover market and feasibility analysis, investment underwriting, site selection, portfolio reviews, and expert advice billed by the hour or by project milestone.
real-estate-consultant.pricingModel: Most real estate consultants bill hourly for open-ended advisory work and a flat project fee for defined deliverables such as a market study, a feasibility report, or an acquisition underwriting package. Retainers are common for ongoing clients like small landlords, investor groups, and developers, usually a fixed monthly fee covering a set number of hours. Larger engagements are split into milestones, for example 30 percent at signing, 40 percent at draft delivery, and 30 percent at final report. Some consultants add a success fee tied to a closed acquisition or lease, but check your state's licensing rules first, because being paid a transaction-based fee can require a real estate broker license in many states. Third-party costs such as data subscriptions, appraisal or environmental reports, travel, and printing are normally passed through at cost or with a small markup, and listed on separate lines.

rates.service: Investment property underwriting and pro forma
Commercial site selection for a tenant or business

items.description: Submarket analysis: multifamily rent and vacancy trends, 3 comparable corridors (Milestone 2 of 3)
Underwriting and 10-year pro forma, 24-unit apartment acquisition at 410 Alder St
Advisory calls with investor group and lender (strategy, financing structure)
Site visit and comparable property tours, including drive time
Mileage to site visits (reimbursable)
Third-party rent comp data export (at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Remaining balance of $2,800 will be invoiced on delivery of the final report. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Reports are for the client's internal use and are not an appraisal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Engagement or project name and agreement date
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the signed scope so the client's accounting team can match it to an approved contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address or market area covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Consultants often work on several properties or submarkets for one client; each charge should be traceable to a specific asset.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable or milestone being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Fixed-fee work is paid at stages, and naming the report or milestone (draft, final, presentation) shows the trigger was met.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours, dates, and short task descriptions for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Investors and corporate clients often audit hourly entries, and detail prevents pushback on calls, research, and site visits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses listed separately with receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Data fees, travel, and mileage are easier to approve when they are clearly separated from professional fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: License number and state, if you hold a broker or appraiser license
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require license information on documents tied to licensed activity, and it adds credibility with institutional clients.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO or reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate and fund clients frequently will not process payment without one.

real-estate-consultant.paymentTerms: Most consultants take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at signing for flat-fee projects and bill the rest at milestones or delivery. Hourly clients are usually invoiced monthly or biweekly with net 15 or net 30 terms; retainers are billed at the start of each month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the agreement. ACH and wire are standard for larger invoices, with checks and cards accepted for smaller ones, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client. Consider holding the final report until the last payment clears, since the report is the product.

tips.title: Separate advice from brokerage
tips.body: If you also hold a real estate license, state in your agreement whether you are acting as a consultant or an agent on each deal, and invoice accordingly. Mixing a fee-for-service engagement with commission income can create licensing and disclosure problems that vary by state.

tips.title: Bill by deliverable, not just time
tips.body: A market study that takes you 20 hours because you have the data ready is worth more than 20 hours of generic time. Price fixed-fee work on the value of the decision it supports, and keep hourly rates for open-ended calls and revisions.

tips.title: Define revision rounds
tips.body: Clients often keep asking for new scenarios in an underwriting model. Include one or two rounds of revisions in the fee and bill additional scenarios hourly or as a change order.

tips.title: Pass through data costs
tips.body: Subscriptions to CoStar, county records, or demographic data can be costly. Either build the cost into your fee or bill project-specific pulls at cost, and say which in your agreement.

tips.title: Invoice at the milestone, not later
tips.body: Send the invoice the day you deliver the draft or final report. Waiting until the deal closes or the client decides what to do tends to push payment back by weeks.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee as a real estate consultant?
faqs.answer: Use hourly for exploratory or open-ended advice where scope will change, and a flat fee when the deliverable is clear, such as a market study or acquisition underwriting. Many consultants combine the two: a flat fee for the report plus hourly billing for meetings and revisions outside scope.

faqs.question: Can I take a percentage of the deal as my fee?
faqs.answer: In many states, being paid a fee contingent on a property transaction can require a real estate broker license, even if you call yourself a consultant. Check your state real estate commission's rules or ask an attorney before agreeing to success fees.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: Most states do not tax professional consulting services, but a few tax certain services, and rules vary on reports or digital deliverables. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for travel and site visits?
faqs.answer: Decide up front whether you bill travel time at your full rate, a reduced rate, or not at all, and put it in your agreement. Bill mileage at a stated per-mile rate, such as the current IRS rate or your own, and list parking, tolls, and flights as separate reimbursable lines.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes the value of my report after delivery?
faqs.answer: Reduce this risk with a written scope, defined deliverables, and a statement that you provide analysis and opinion, not guarantees of investment performance. Milestone payments mean you are rarely owed the full amount when a dispute arises.

estimate.intro: Real estate consultants send a proposal or quote when a prospective client asks what a market study, feasibility analysis, or advisory engagement will cost. Clients typically compare your fee against other consultants, appraisers, or a brokerage's free market opinion, so the quote needs to show clearly what they receive that a free opinion does not.

scopeChecklist.why: State whether the client gets a written report, spreadsheet model, presentation, or verbal recommendation, and the approximate length, so expectations are set before work starts.
A study of one address is very different from a three-county submarket analysis, and unclear boundaries lead to unpaid extra work.
Naming the sources and who supplies client data, such as rent rolls and operating statements, protects you if inputs turn out to be wrong or late.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of meetings, site visits, and revision rounds
scopeChecklist.why: These are the main drivers of overruns, so set limits and an hourly rate for extras.
Delivery dates should depend on the client providing documents and access, so delays on their side do not count against you.

scopeChecklist.item: Third-party costs and who pays them
scopeChecklist.why: Environmental reports, appraisals, surveys, and data purchases may be outside your fee and should be stated as client expenses.
State that your work is advisory, is not an appraisal or legal advice unless licensed and engaged for that, and is for the client's use only.

pricingTips.title: Price the decision, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: A client deciding whether to buy a $4 million building will accept a higher fee for underwriting than one asking for general neighborhood information. Estimate your hours, then adjust based on the size of the transaction and the risk the client is managing.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered scopes
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option, such as a desktop market analysis, and a full option that adds site visits, interviews, and a presentation. Clients often choose the middle or upper tier when they can see what each adds.

pricingTips.title: Break out milestones in the quote
pricingTips.body: Show the fee split by stage with payment due at each. It makes a large number easier to approve and gives you a built-in payment schedule.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Market conditions and your availability change, so make the quote valid for 15 to 30 days.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or initial consultation?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is usually free. For anything that needs real analysis before you can quote, such as a preliminary feasibility look, charge a scoping fee and credit it toward the full engagement if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How detailed should a consulting quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list deliverables, timeline, assumptions, exclusions, and fees by milestone, typically one to three pages. Too little detail invites scope disputes, and too much can lead clients to cherry-pick pieces.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: Yes, when scope depends on information you have not seen, such as the condition of a portfolio or the quality of financial records. Give a range with the assumptions behind it and commit to a firm number once you have reviewed the materials.

faqs.question: What happens if the client wants more work than the quote covered?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order that describes the added work, the cost, and the effect on the schedule, and get approval before proceeding. Include this process in the original quote so it is expected.

real-estate-photographer.intro: Real estate photographers shoot listing photos for agents, brokers, homeowners, builders, and property managers. Invoices usually cover a photo package priced by property size, plus add-ons like drone shots, video, floor plans, twilight shoots, and rush delivery. Most clients are agents who book repeat work, so clear and consistent billing matters.
real-estate-photographer.pricingModel: Most real estate photographers price by package, tied to the home's square footage or the number of photos delivered. A typical tier structure might be under 1,500 sq ft, 1,500-2,500, 2,500-3,500, and so on, with larger or luxury properties quoted individually. Add-ons are billed as flat fees: aerial photos, walkthrough video, 3D tours, floor plans, virtual staging, twilight sessions, and twilight or rush editing. Travel fees often apply beyond a set radius, commonly 20 to 30 miles, and are billed per mile or as a flat fee. Many photographers offer volume discounts or monthly billing for agents and brokerages who book several shoots, and charge extra for reschedules, return trips, or properties that aren't ready on arrival. Usage and licensing are usually included for the listing agent, but separate fees may apply for use by other parties or for commercial advertising.

rates.service: Standard listing photo package (up to 1,500 sq ft, 20-25 photos)
Standard listing photo package (2,500-3,500 sq ft, 35-40 photos)
Walkthrough video or cinematic video tour

items.description: Listing photo package, 2,400 sq ft home, 35 edited photos (shoot date 6/12)
Drone aerial photos, 8 edited images
Floor plan with measurements
Virtual staging, living room and primary bedroom
Travel fee, 18 miles beyond 25-mile service area
Next-day rush delivery

sampleInvoice.notes: Property: 123 Maple Street, Springfield. Photos licensed to the listing agent and brokerage for marketing this property. Payment due within 7 days of delivery. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Rescheduling with less than 24 hours' notice is subject to a $50 fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and shoot date
invoiceChecklist.why: Agents book many shoots, and the address ties each invoice to a specific listing for their records and reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and square footage tier
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the price was set and prevents disputes if the home turned out bigger or smaller than expected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of edited photos delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms the client received what the package promised and gives a basis for charging extra photos.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each add-on as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Drone, video, floor plans, twilight, and staging are priced separately, and itemizing makes it clear what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee, mileage, and rush charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra costs look arbitrary if they are folded into the package price and are easier to defend when listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Licensing and usage terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States who may use the images and for what, which protects your copyright if the photos are reused elsewhere.

invoiceChecklist.item: Drone operator certification or business license number, if relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: In the US, commercial drone work generally requires FAA Part 107 certification, and some brokerages ask for proof and insurance details.

real-estate-photographer.paymentTerms: Practice varies widely. Many photographers bill agents on delivery with payment due in 3 to 7 days, or allow net 15 or net 30 for repeat clients who get one monthly invoice. New clients or large projects like luxury homes, new construction, and commercial properties often pay a deposit of 25 to 50 percent. Some photographers require payment before releasing the final gallery for first-time clients. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Cards, ACH transfers, and online payment links are the usual methods, and some agents pay at closing, which is a risk you should decide whether to accept.

tips.title: Hold the gallery until payment for new clients
tips.body: Deliver a watermarked preview or low-resolution proofs until the invoice is paid. Release full-resolution files once you have been paid, and relax this rule for agents with a good payment record.

tips.title: Be clear about who pays
tips.body: Agents sometimes want the seller, a brokerage, or a transaction coordinator billed. Decide at booking who is responsible and put that name on the invoice. Avoid arrangements that depend on the home selling.

tips.title: Charge for the conditions you encounter
tips.body: Cluttered homes, extra rooms, unmade beds, or long waits at the door add time. State a wait-time or return-trip fee in your booking terms and bill it as a separate line.

tips.title: Offer monthly billing for frequent clients
tips.body: Agents who book several shoots a month often prefer one statement. List each property address and date so they can match charges to their listings.

tips.title: Track mileage and equipment costs
tips.body: Mileage, drone batteries, software subscriptions, and insurance are deductible business expenses in many cases. Keeping records of travel per shoot also helps you set fair travel fees.

faqs.question: Should I charge by square footage or by number of photos?
faqs.answer: Square footage is the most common method because it reflects the time on site and editing workload. Many photographers also state a photo count in each tier so clients know what they receive. Both approaches work if the invoice states them clearly.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on real estate photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital products or photography services, while others do not. Check with your state's department of revenue or an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How long should I give agents to pay?
faqs.answer: Due on delivery or within 7 days is common for individual shoots. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for brokerages and monthly accounts. Shorter terms reduce the number of unpaid invoices, since agents are often paid only at closing.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra if the agent wants the photos reused for other purposes?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many photographers include licensing for the listing agent and brokerage to market that property, and charge more for use by builders, vendors, or national advertising. Put the licensing terms on the invoice or in your booking agreement.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client cancels the same day?
faqs.answer: Have a cancellation policy in your booking terms, such as a fee for cancellations under 24 hours or for arriving to a property that isn't ready. Bill the fee as its own line item and reference the policy.

estimate.intro: Real estate photographers send quotes when a client asks for pricing on a specific property, a new builder or brokerage account, or a large or unusual job such as a luxury home, multi-unit building, or new development. Clients usually compare package price, number of photos, turnaround time, and extras like drone, video, and floor plans. A clear written quote is also useful for agents who need approval from sellers or brokers.

scopeChecklist.why: The package price depends on size, so confirm it up front and state that the price may change if the actual size is different.
List photo count, video length, drone images, floor plan, and virtual staging so the client knows exactly what is covered.
Next-day, 24-hour, and 48-hour delivery are priced differently, and agents often need photos by a specific listing date.
Staging, cleaning, lights on, and cars removed affect the shoot. State that return trips or extra time may be billed if the home is not ready.
Exterior and twilight shots can need rescheduling. Explain whether rescheduling for weather is free and how far in advance it can be arranged.
Clarify who can use the images and for what purpose to avoid disagreements over resale or reuse.
Distance can change your cost, so state your included radius and what you charge beyond it.

pricingTips.title: Use a clear tier table
pricingTips.body: Offer three or four packages with set photo counts and add-ons. Clients can pick one quickly, and your pricing stays consistent across agents.

pricingTips.title: Quote large properties individually
pricingTips.body: Homes over about 4,000 sq ft, estates, and multi-building properties can take hours longer to shoot and edit. Base the quote on estimated shoot time plus editing time, rather than extending a standard tier.

pricingTips.title: Bundle popular add-ons
pricingTips.body: A package that combines photos, drone, and a floor plan at a modest discount is often easier to sell than separate add-ons and keeps the order simple.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Prices and your availability change. A 14 to 30 day validity period protects you if a client returns months later.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or a range?
faqs.answer: For standard homes, a flat quote based on the package is best. For large, unusual, or unclear properties, a range or a quote based on a confirmed square footage is safer.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a real estate photo shoot?
faqs.answer: Not usually for a single agent shoot. Deposits are more common for large properties, commercial or builder projects, and new clients, often 25 to 50 percent of the total.

faqs.question: What if the actual square footage is different from the quote?
faqs.answer: State in your quote that the final price is based on the actual property size on the shoot date. If the home is in a larger tier, adjust the price and tell the client before you start or deliver.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants extra edits after delivery?
faqs.answer: Define the number of revisions included in the quote and the fee for additional ones. Minor corrections like color or window adjustments are often free, while re-editing or new compositions can be billed.

recruiting-agency.intro: Recruiting agencies and solo recruiters bill employers for finding and placing candidates. Invoices usually cover placement fees on permanent hires, hourly markups on temp or contract workers, retainers for executive searches, and sometimes add-ons like background checks or job board postings.
recruiting-agency.pricingModel: Most permanent placements are priced as a percentage of the candidate's first-year base salary, commonly 15 to 25 percent for contingency searches and 25 to 33 percent for retained or executive searches. Retained searches are usually billed in installments, often a third at signing, a third at a shortlist milestone, and a third at placement. Contract and temp staffing is billed as an hourly bill rate that marks up the worker's pay rate, typically 25 to 60 percent depending on role and who handles payroll taxes and insurance. Contract-to-hire arrangements add a conversion fee, often a sliding scale that drops the longer the worker has been placed. Some agencies also offer flat-fee placements for lower-level roles, hourly consulting for RPO (recruitment process outsourcing) work, and monthly retainers for ongoing hiring support. Guarantee periods, usually 30 to 90 days, affect when a fee is considered earned and should be spelled out in the agreement.

rates.service: Candidate background or reference check pass-through

items.description: Placement fee: Senior Accountant, Jane Doe, start date 3/3. Base salary $90,000 at 20%
Retained search installment 2 of 3: Controller search (shortlist delivered)
Contract staffing: Data Entry Clerk, week ending 3/14 (40 hrs at $26 bill rate)
Premium job board posting, 30 days
Background checks (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due net 30 from invoice date. Placement fee is covered by a 90-day replacement guarantee per the signed fee agreement dated 1/15. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. ACH or check accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Candidate name, job title, and start date
invoiceChecklist.why: Most placement fees become due on the start date, so the invoice should show exactly which hire triggered the fee and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Salary basis and fee percentage
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the base salary and percentage lets the client verify the math and avoids disputes over what counts as compensation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed fee agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the terms on fee rate, guarantee period, and ownership of the candidate relationship.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guarantee or replacement period
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often hold payment until they understand the guarantee, and it protects you if a dispute comes up about a candidate who leaves early.

invoiceChecklist.item: Timesheet details and bill rate for temp workers
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly staffing invoices need weekly hours, approver name, and bill rate so the client's accounts payable team can match them to approved timesheets.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO or requisition number
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger employers often will not process an invoice without a PO or job requisition number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Background checks, job board postings, and candidate travel should be itemized so the client sees what is fee and what is reimbursement.

recruiting-agency.paymentTerms: Permanent placement fees are typically invoiced on or shortly after the candidate's start date, with net 15 or net 30 terms. Retained searches are billed in installments tied to milestones, and the first installment is often due before work begins. Staffing invoices for temps and contractors are usually weekly or biweekly, with net 15 to net 30 terms, and agencies that carry payroll often need faster payment from clients to cover wages. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if they are written into the agreement. ACH and wire transfer are standard for large amounts, and checks are still common. Credit cards are less common because of the size of fees.

tips.title: Get the fee agreement signed before sending any resumes
tips.body: Without a signed agreement, a client can hire a candidate you submitted and dispute the fee. Include fee percentage, guarantee, payment terms, and how long you own a candidate introduction, often 6 to 12 months.

tips.title: Invoice on the start date, not after
tips.body: Send the invoice the day the candidate starts, or the next business day. Waiting for a convenient time lets payment slip and gives the client time to forget the terms.

tips.title: Define compensation in the agreement
tips.body: State whether the fee includes signing bonuses, guaranteed commissions, or only base salary. Vague language leads to disputes when the offer includes a large bonus.

tips.title: Put a refund or replacement policy in writing
tips.body: Spell out what happens if the hire leaves or is terminated within the guarantee period, such as a free replacement or a prorated credit. Clients are more comfortable paying promptly when they know the rules.

tips.title: Watch cash flow on staffing work
tips.body: If you pay temps weekly while clients pay on net 30, you carry the gap. Ask for shorter terms, deposits, or consider financing arrangements before taking on large contract accounts.

faqs.question: When should I invoice a placement fee?
faqs.answer: Most agencies invoice on the candidate's first day of work, since that is the common trigger in fee agreements. Some invoice on offer acceptance for retained searches or when a deposit is required. Follow whatever your signed agreement says.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on recruiting fees?
faqs.answer: In most states, recruiting and placement services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax certain staffing or business services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the candidate quits during the guarantee period?
faqs.answer: Follow the guarantee in your agreement. Common remedies are a free replacement search or a prorated refund or credit. Document the departure date and keep the original invoice and payment record, then issue a credit memo if a refund applies.

faqs.question: Can I bill for a search that did not result in a hire?
faqs.answer: Only if the agreement allows it. Retained searches typically bill milestone installments whether or not a hire is made. Contingency searches usually bill only on a successful placement, though some agencies charge for expenses or a cancellation fee.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for temp workers on my payroll?
faqs.answer: Bill the hours worked at the agreed bill rate, usually weekly, and attach or reference the approved timesheet. Your bill rate covers the worker's wages, payroll taxes, workers' compensation, and your margin, so those costs are not listed as separate lines unless the contract is cost-plus.
