estimate.intro: Recruiting agencies send a proposal or fee quote before a client agrees to a search, often while several agencies compete for the same role. Clients compare fee percentage, guarantee length, exclusivity, and how quickly you can present qualified candidates.

scopeChecklist.why: The fee depends on salary, so stating the expected range and what counts toward it prevents surprises when the offer is made.
Make clear whether the fee is contingency, retained, or flat, and how it is calculated and when it is due.
Exclusive searches often justify a lower percentage or retainer. State how long the exclusivity lasts and what happens if the client hires outside your pool.
Clients weigh the guarantee heavily. Define the length, what triggers it, and what remedy applies.
This sets how long the client owes you a fee if they hire someone you introduced, even if the hire happens later.
List what you will provide, such as screened shortlists, interviews scheduled, reference checks, and expected time to first submission.
Job board ads, assessments, background checks, and candidate travel should be listed as billed or included so there are no surprise charges.

pricingTips.title: Trade percentage for exclusivity
pricingTips.body: Offer a lower percentage or flat fee in return for exclusivity or a retained deposit. It reduces your risk of spending weeks on a search that the client also gives to three other agencies.

pricingTips.title: Quote hard-to-fill roles higher
pricingTips.body: Specialized roles in engineering, healthcare, or finance with small talent pools justify fees at the top of the range. Easier volume roles can be priced lower or as flat fees.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for repeat clients
pricingTips.body: Volume discounts, such as a lower percentage after the third hire in a year, help win long-term accounts without cutting your standard rate on a first search.

pricingTips.title: Show a staffing quote as a bill rate
pricingTips.body: For temps, give the hourly bill rate and conversion terms, not your pay rate and markup. Clients compare total cost per hour and want to know what the conversion fee will be.

faqs.question: Should I negotiate my fee percentage?
faqs.answer: It is common to be asked, especially by larger employers. Trade concessions for something concrete, such as exclusivity, a shorter payment term, or a commitment to multiple roles, rather than lowering the rate alone.

faqs.question: How long should a fee proposal stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Market conditions and candidate availability shift, so set an expiration date and note that the signed agreement is required before you submit candidates.

faqs.question: Can I quote a range instead of a fixed fee?
faqs.answer: For percentage-based fees, the final amount depends on the actual starting salary, so quote the percentage and an estimated dollar figure based on the expected salary range. For retained searches, quote fixed installment amounts.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a contract-to-hire option?
faqs.answer: Quote the hourly bill rate along with a conversion fee that decreases over time, such as 20 percent in the first 90 days and lower after that, or waived after a set number of hours worked.

renovation.intro: Renovation contractors, remodelers, and small renovation firms send invoices for kitchen, bathroom, basement, and whole-room remodels, as well as additions and repairs to existing homes. Most bills combine labor, materials, subcontractor work, permits, and debris removal, often split into several payments over the life of the job.
renovation.pricingModel: Renovation work is priced several ways. Fixed-price (lump sum) contracts are common for defined scopes like a bathroom remodel, and are usually billed in milestone draws tied to stages such as demolition, rough-in, drywall, and finish. Cost-plus contracts bill actual materials, labor, and subcontractor costs plus a markup, typically 10-25 percent, or a management fee. Time and materials is used for repairs, small jobs, and unknowns found behind walls, with hourly labor rates plus materials at cost with markup. Some contractors quote per square foot for rough budgeting, but the invoice should still list actual work. Change orders are billed separately and need written approval. Subcontractors such as electricians, plumbers, and tile setters are either passed through with markup or bundled into the contract price.

items.description: Demolition of existing bathroom: fixtures, tile, vanity, and flooring removed
Drywall and cement board install and finish (60 sq ft shower and wall areas)
Floor and shower tile installation, labor only
Carpentry and finish labor (trim, vanity install, door)
Materials: tile, thinset, grout, backer board, vanity, fixtures (receipts attached)
Dumpster rental and disposal

sampleInvoice.notes: Milestone 3 of 4: tile and finish work complete. Balance of 10% due on final walkthrough and punch list completion. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Checks payable to the business name above. Any additional work requires a signed change order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and business name
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a contractor license number on contracts and sometimes on invoices, and clients use it to verify you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project address and contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the specific job and signed contract, which matters when you have several jobs for the same client.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or draw description with percent complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why this payment is due and keeps the draw schedule consistent with the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized materials with receipts or supplier names
invoiceChecklist.why: Cost-plus and time-and-materials clients expect proof of cost, and it reduces disputes about markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Approved change orders listed separately with number and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps extras distinct from the base contract price and shows written client approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Subcontractor charges and permit fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the client see pass-through costs, and permit fees are often reimbursable at cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Running contract total, paid to date, and balance remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Avoids confusion over how much has been paid and what is still owed across multiple draws.

renovation.paymentTerms: Renovation contractors commonly take a deposit at signing, often 10-30 percent, though some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts, so check your local rules. The rest is billed in progress payments tied to milestones, with due dates of 3-10 days. Final payment is usually held until the punch list is done and a walkthrough is complete. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is typically accepted by check, ACH, or card, and card fees are often passed on or avoided on large invoices. Keep lien rights in mind: in many states you must send preliminary notices and file lien waivers, so confirm the deadlines where you work.

tips.title: Tie draws to finished work, not dates
tips.body: Billing at completed stages like demo, rough-in passed inspection, and drywall done keeps you from being ahead of the money while staying fair to the client.

tips.title: Bill change orders immediately
tips.body: Hidden rot, outdated wiring, and client upgrades are the main source of unpaid extras. Get a signed change order before doing the work and invoice it with the next draw.

tips.title: Collect lien waivers as you pay
tips.body: Provide conditional and unconditional waivers where your state uses them, and get them from subs and suppliers so the client and lender stay comfortable.

tips.title: Pass through materials with receipts
tips.body: For large purchases like cabinets, windows, or tile, invoice them at order or delivery so you are not financing the client's materials.

tips.title: Keep final payment tied to a written punch list
tips.body: Agree on the list before the final walkthrough so the last payment is not held up by new requests.

faqs.question: How much deposit can I ask for on a renovation?
faqs.answer: Many contractors ask for 10-30 percent, but some states limit home improvement deposits to a set percentage or a fixed dollar amount. Check your state's contractor licensing rules before setting the deposit.

faqs.question: Should I bill renovation work weekly or by milestone?
faqs.answer: Fixed-price jobs usually use milestone draws written into the contract. Time-and-materials and cost-plus jobs are often billed weekly or biweekly because costs change as the work goes on.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for extra work found during demolition?
faqs.answer: Write up a change order describing the problem, the added cost, and any schedule impact, and have the client sign before you proceed. Then list it as its own line on the next invoice with the change order number.

faqs.question: Can I charge a markup on materials and subs?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is stated in your contract. Cost-plus contracts typically list the markup percentage, often 10-25 percent, and should say whether it applies to materials, subs, or both.

faqs.question: What if a client withholds the final payment?
faqs.answer: Refer to the contract and the punch list first. If the work is complete, send a written demand, and consider your lien rights, which in many states have strict deadlines. A local attorney can advise on your options.

estimate.intro: Renovation contractors send an estimate or bid after a site walkthrough and before signing a contract. Homeowners usually collect two or three bids and compare total price, scope, timeline, and how allowances for materials are handled, so the quote needs to be clear about what is and is not included.

scopeChecklist.item: Detailed scope of work by phase
scopeChecklist.why: Spelling out demo, rough-in, drywall, tile, trim, and paint prevents assumptions about what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Material allowances and who selects them
scopeChecklist.why: If the price assumes a $4 per sq ft tile allowance and the client picks $15 tile, the overage should be clearly the client's cost.
Mold, rot, asbestos, lead paint, old wiring, and structural surprises are common; stating how they are handled avoids disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, inspections, and who pulls them
scopeChecklist.why: Permit costs and responsibility vary, and delays in inspection affect the timeline.
Clients need to know whether electrical, plumbing, and HVAC are covered or priced separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, duration, and payment schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations for timing and shows when draws are due.

scopeChecklist.item: Change order process and quote validity period
scopeChecklist.why: Material and labor prices move, so state how long the price is good and how changes are approved.

pricingTips.title: Price from a takeoff, not a square foot rule
pricingTips.body: Measure the work, list materials, estimate labor hours by trade, and add subs, permits, disposal, and overhead. Square foot figures are only a sanity check.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency
pricingTips.body: Many renovators add 10-15 percent for older homes, either in the price or as a separate line the client approves, because hidden conditions are likely.

pricingTips.title: Include overhead and profit explicitly in your math
pricingTips.body: Insurance, vehicle costs, tools, and unpaid estimating time need to be covered. Many small contractors aim for 10-20 percent profit on top of overhead.

pricingTips.title: Offer options for big-ticket choices
pricingTips.body: Showing a base scope with priced alternatives, such as stock versus semi-custom cabinets, helps clients compare you to other bids on equal terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors give free estimates for straightforward jobs, but charge a design or planning fee for complex remodels, often credited toward the contract if the client signs. State this up front.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 15-30 days. Material prices and your schedule change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on the wording and local law. A fixed bid usually becomes binding once signed, while an estimate may allow for adjustments. Label it clearly as a fixed price or a non-binding estimate.

faqs.question: How detailed should my quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that the client could compare it line by line with another bid. List phases, allowances, inclusions, and exclusions, but you do not always need to show your markup on every line.

research-consultant.intro: Research consultants are independent professionals who run studies, gather and analyze data, and deliver findings that clients use to make decisions. Clients include nonprofits, startups, universities, government agencies, healthcare organizations, and corporate teams. Invoices typically cover project phases such as study design, fieldwork, analysis, and reporting, plus pass-through costs like participant incentives and survey platform fees.
research-consultant.pricingModel: Most research consultants price by project phase with a fixed fee, or by the hour for open-ended or advisory work. Fixed-fee proposals are common for defined deliverables like a literature review, a survey study, or a set of interviews, and are usually split into milestones tied to deliverables. Hourly billing suits ongoing support, data cleaning with unclear scope, or expert advice. Retainers work for clients who need a set number of hours each month. Some work is priced per unit, such as per interview conducted, per transcript coded, or per survey programmed. Pass-through expenses (participant incentives, recruitment panel fees, transcription, software licenses, travel) are billed at cost or with a modest markup of roughly 10-15 percent, and should be listed separately from professional fees. Government and grant-funded work often requires set labor categories and rates, so keep time records.

rates.service: Final report and presentation of findings

items.description: Phase 1: Research design and discussion guide (customer retention study)
Moderated customer interviews (45 min each, incl. scheduling and notes)
Thematic coding and analysis of interview transcripts
Findings report and 60-minute stakeholder presentation
Participant incentives (gift cards, $75 each), billed at cost
Transcription service, billed at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 30. Phase 1 deposit of $4,000 was paid on 3/1 and is credited on the next invoice. Expenses are billed at cost; receipts available on request. A late fee of 1.5% per month applies to balances past due. Interview recordings and coded data remain confidential under the signed agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, contract or PO number, and phase or milestone
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, especially universities and agencies, match invoices to specific budget lines and will delay payment without a reference number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables completed in this billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying charges to deliverables like a finished instrument or coded dataset shows the work was done and supports milestone payments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by task and date for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Analysis and advisory hours are easy to question. A short log with tasks and dates prevents disputes and satisfies grant auditors.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately with receipts available
invoiceChecklist.why: Incentives, panel fees, and transcription are reimbursable costs. Separating them from fees keeps your fee clear and makes any markup transparent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and prior payments credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Research projects often run over months with multiple payments, so a running balance avoids double-billing confusion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Data and confidentiality terms reference
invoiceChecklist.why: A line pointing to the signed agreement or NDA reminds the client of ownership and confidentiality terms, which matter when data includes participant information.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your tax ID or W-9 status and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Many organizations will not pay an independent contractor without a W-9 on file, and in the US they may issue a 1099 if payments exceed the IRS threshold.

research-consultant.paymentTerms: Typical terms are a 25-50 percent deposit at project kickoff, with the balance due at milestones or on delivery of the final report. For smaller projects, 50 percent upfront and 50 percent on delivery is common. Standard terms are net 15 to net 30, though universities, government agencies, and large companies may take 45 to 60 days through their vendor systems, so confirm this before you start. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card. Ask for incentive and panel costs to be paid upfront or by the client directly, so you are not financing participant payments.

tips.title: Bill by milestone, not at the end
tips.body: Tie payments to design approval, completion of fieldwork, draft report, and final delivery. Long projects that bill only on completion leave you carrying months of unpaid work.

tips.title: Get incentive and panel costs upfront
tips.body: Participant incentives and recruitment fees can run into thousands of dollars. Collect an expense deposit or have the client fund them in advance so you are not floating costs.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in the contract
tips.body: Reports often go through many rounds of stakeholder comments. Include one or two revision rounds in the fee and bill additional rounds hourly.

tips.title: Charge for scope changes in writing
tips.body: If a client adds interviews, a new survey wave, or extra subgroup analysis, send a short change order with the added cost before you do the work.

tips.title: Keep time records even on fixed fees
tips.body: Tracking hours shows you which project types are profitable, helps you set future quotes, and supports your invoice if a client questions the fee.

faqs.question: Should a research consultant bill hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed project fee when deliverables and scope are clear, such as a defined survey or set of interviews. Use hourly billing when scope is uncertain, for ongoing advice, or for messy data work. Many consultants use a fixed fee for design and reporting and hourly billing for extras.

faqs.question: Can I mark up participant incentives and other expenses?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Many consultants bill at cost, while others add 10-15 percent for handling and administration. Whatever you choose, list expenses on separate lines from professional fees and keep receipts.

faqs.question: What if the client's data is delayed and the project stalls?
faqs.answer: Include a clause stating that delays caused by the client, such as late data access or slow participant approvals, extend the timeline and may trigger billing for work done to date. Invoice completed phases rather than waiting for a restart.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on research services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional services, but some tax certain consulting or data services. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line when it applies.

faqs.question: How do I handle work for universities or government agencies?
faqs.answer: Expect vendor registration, a W-9, specific invoice formats, and slower payment cycles. Include the PO or contract number and follow their invoice instructions exactly. Grant-funded work may also require time records and may cap your hourly rate.

estimate.intro: Research consultants usually send a proposal or quote after an initial scoping call, and often when a client is comparing several consultants. Clients compare total cost, methodology, timeline, deliverables, and what is and is not included. A clear quote sets expectations for sample size, data ownership, and revisions before any money is spent.

scopeChecklist.why: Stating what the study will answer keeps the work focused and gives you a reference point if the client's goals shift later.
The number of interviews, survey respondents, or documents reviewed drives cost, so write it out. More participants means a change order.
Specify whether you or the client recruits participants. Hard-to-reach groups can take far more time than clients expect.
List whether the output is a slide deck, written report, dataset, or dashboard, and the expected length, so there is no confusion at delivery.
Tie dates to events like approval of the instrument or access to data, so client delays do not become your cost.
Incentives, panel fees, transcription, software, and travel should be listed as estimates, noting whether they are billed at cost.
State how many rounds of feedback are included and who owns raw data, instruments, and the final report, including any confidentiality or IRB requirements.

pricingTips.title: Price by phase
pricingTips.body: Break the quote into design, fieldwork, analysis, and reporting. Clients can see where the money goes, and you can bill each phase as it completes.

pricingTips.title: Offer scope tiers
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as 8, 12, or 20 interviews, with different prices. This lets clients choose within their budget rather than negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Pad for recruitment and analysis
pricingTips.body: Scheduling, no-shows, transcript cleanup, and coding usually take longer than planned. Build in a buffer of 15-20 percent or state the assumptions behind your hours.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Panel prices and your availability change, so valid for 30 days is a reasonable limit on a quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for writing a proposal?
faqs.answer: Short proposals are usually free as a cost of business. For large or complex projects, such as a full study design for an RFP, some consultants charge a scoping fee that is credited toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How do I quote when I don't know how many participants I can recruit?
faqs.answer: Quote based on a stated target sample and describe what happens if recruitment falls short or runs long. You can offer a per-interview rate for additional sessions or a fee for extended recruitment.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: A quote usually becomes binding once the client signs it or a contract references it. Include an expiration date and state that scope changes will be priced separately.

resume-writer.intro: Resume writers are freelancers and small business owners who write and edit resumes, cover letters, LinkedIn profiles, and related career documents for job seekers. Invoices usually cover a document package, an intake interview, a set number of revision rounds, and any add-ons such as a cover letter or LinkedIn rewrite. Clients range from recent graduates to senior executives, and the pricing reflects that range.
resume-writer.pricingModel: Most resume writers charge flat fees per document or per package, not by the hour, because clients want to know the total cost before they start. Pricing usually scales with career level: entry-level, mid-career, and executive or federal resumes sit in separate tiers. Packages often bundle a resume, cover letter, and LinkedIn profile at a discount. Add-ons such as thank-you letters, additional cover letters, or extra revision rounds are billed separately. Some writers charge hourly (typically $50-125) for consulting, interview coaching, or heavy edits to a client's existing draft. Federal resumes and academic CVs take longer and cost more. Rush turnaround under 48 hours usually carries a 25-50% surcharge. Most writers collect payment in full or a 50% deposit before starting, since the deliverable is a digital file that is hard to take back once sent.

rates.service: Career consultation or resume review call

items.description: Mid-career resume (marketing manager), includes 30-minute intake call and two revision rounds
Tailored cover letter
LinkedIn profile rewrite (headline, About, experience sections)
Additional revision round beyond package limit
Rush delivery (48 hours)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Final files in Word and PDF format are released upon payment. Package includes two revision rounds within 30 days of first draft delivery. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized list of each document delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often buy a bundle and need to see what each piece cost, especially if they ask for a partial refund or a later add-on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Career level or document type (entry, mid-career, executive, federal, CV)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows why the price was set where it was and avoids confusion if a client compares your fee to a different tier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds included and any extras billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Revision disputes are the most common billing issue in this work. Listing the limit and any overage keeps it clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush or turnaround surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: A separate line for rush work shows the client what they paid for speed and keeps your standard rates visible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date and file formats provided
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents the date work was completed and which files the client received, which helps if they later claim they did not get something.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit paid and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Many writers collect a deposit up front. Showing the credit prevents double payment questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision window expiry date
invoiceChecklist.why: States how long the client has to request edits included in the package, so open-ended revision requests do not drag on for months.

resume-writer.paymentTerms: Most resume writers collect payment before or at the start of the project, either in full or as a 50% deposit with the balance due when the first draft is delivered. Because clients are often job seekers on a tight budget, some writers offer a split payment plan on executive packages. Invoices for small projects are commonly due on receipt or within 7 days. Late fees are less common than in other fields, since most writers hold the final files until payment clears. Accepted methods are typically credit card, ACH, PayPal-style transfers, and Zelle. Be clear about your refund policy in writing, since the work is custom and cannot be resold. Many writers offer a limited revision window instead of refunds.

tips.title: Collect payment before delivering final files
tips.body: Send watermarked or PDF-preview drafts for review and release the editable Word file only after the balance is paid. This is the simplest protection against non-payment in a digital-delivery business.

tips.title: Cap revisions in the package
tips.body: Include a set number of revision rounds, usually two, and a time limit such as 30 days. Bill additional rounds at a flat rate or hourly. Without a cap, some clients will keep asking for tweaks indefinitely.

tips.title: Price by career level, not by page count
tips.body: Page count does not reflect the work. An executive resume may be two pages but take eight hours of interviewing, research, and drafting. Tiered pricing by seniority matches your time more closely.

tips.title: Bill add-ons separately
tips.body: Cover letters, LinkedIn work, thank-you notes, and follow-up consultations are easy to give away informally. Put each on its own line so the client sees the value and you get paid for it.

tips.title: State your no-guarantee policy
tips.body: You cannot promise interviews or job offers. Say so in your agreement and on invoices where appropriate, so a refund request tied to job search results has a clear answer.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly?
faqs.answer: Flat fees by document or package are the norm because clients want a known price. Hourly works for consulting, interview prep, or editing a client's heavily written draft, where scope is hard to predict.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on resume writing?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain written or digital services, and many do not. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional. If you do collect tax, show it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How should I handle refund requests?
faqs.answer: State your policy in your agreement before work begins. Many writers offer unlimited or capped revisions within a set window but no refunds once a draft is delivered, since the work is custom. Some offer a partial refund if the client cancels before drafting starts.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it when the client books, before you start work, for either the full amount or a deposit. Send a final invoice for the balance when the first draft is ready, and release the final files after it is paid.

faqs.question: How do I bill a client who wants more edits after the revision window closes?
faqs.answer: Quote a flat fee or hourly rate for the extra work and send a new invoice. Many writers charge $40-75 per additional round or $50-100 per hour for edits after the package window.

estimate.intro: Resume writers usually send a quote after a short discovery call or after reviewing the client's current resume and target roles. Clients often compare a few writers, so the quote needs to show what is included at each price point. A clear quote also sets limits on revisions and turnaround before any work starts.

scopeChecklist.item: Documents included (resume, cover letter, LinkedIn, CV)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume extras are included. Naming each deliverable prevents a later argument about what was covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Career level and any special format (federal, academic, executive)
scopeChecklist.why: Federal resumes and CVs take much longer than standard resumes. The quote should show why the price differs.
Setting expectations for how much client input is needed protects your time and tells clients what they must provide.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and revision window
scopeChecklist.why: This is the biggest source of scope creep. A stated limit with a time frame gives you a clear basis to bill extra rounds.

scopeChecklist.item: Turnaround time and what you need from the client
scopeChecklist.why: Delivery dates usually depend on the client returning the questionnaire or feedback. State that the clock starts when you have what you need.

scopeChecklist.item: File formats and ownership of final documents
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know they receive Word and PDF versions and can use them freely after payment.
Makes clear that you are writing documents, not promising interviews or job offers.

pricingTips.title: Offer three tiers or packages
pricingTips.body: A resume only, a resume plus cover letter, and a full package with LinkedIn gives clients a choice and tends to move buyers toward the middle option. Show the bundle discount clearly.

pricingTips.title: Look at the existing resume before quoting
pricingTips.body: Ask for the current resume and target job titles. A cluttered ten-year history or a career change takes more work than a clean, linear record, and the quote should reflect that.

pricingTips.title: Quote federal and executive work higher
pricingTips.body: These projects involve longer interviews, more research, and stricter formatting. Do not use your standard mid-career price for them.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Hold the quoted price for 7 to 14 days. This prevents clients from returning months later expecting the same rate after you have raised prices.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before a discovery call?
faqs.answer: Give a price range on your website, but confirm the exact quote after a short call or after seeing the current resume. Without that information you may underprice a complex case.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the discovery call or the quote?
faqs.answer: Most writers offer a free 15 to 20 minute call. Longer strategy sessions or resume critiques are often paid, either hourly or as a separate low-cost service.

faqs.question: What if the client's needs change after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Send a revised quote or an add-on invoice. For example, if a client later asks for a cover letter and LinkedIn rewrite, price those as separate line items instead of absorbing them.

retail.intro: Most retail sales are paid at the register, but shop owners still send invoices for the sales that don't close at the counter. These include wholesale and bulk orders, corporate gift orders, special orders with deposits, custom or personalized items, and deliveries or installations. The people sending them run boutiques, gift shops, furniture stores, hardware stores, and similar small businesses.
retail.pricingModel: Retail pricing starts with the product. Most shops set the shelf price as a markup over cost, often around 2x for keystone pricing, though margins vary a lot by category. Invoices for non-walk-in sales layer on a few other things. Bulk and business customers usually get a volume discount off the shelf price, commonly 10 to 30 percent depending on quantity and your margin. Special and custom orders are normally priced at item cost plus markup, with a deposit collected up front. Services around the sale, such as delivery, assembly, gift wrapping, engraving, and shipping, are charged as separate line items so the product margin stays clear. Sales tax is added on top unless the buyer is exempt, for example a reseller with a valid certificate.

rates.service: Gift wrapping or gift basket packing
Restocking fee on returned non-defective items

items.description: Cedar candle and tea gift set, SKU GS-204 (client holiday gifts)
Logo engraving on tin lid
Gift wrapping with ribbon and card
Local delivery to client office
Bulk order discount (10% on gift sets)

sampleInvoice.notes: PO #4471. 50% deposit of $866.50 received on order, balance due net 15 from delivery date. Sales tax calculated on merchandise, engraving, and wrapping at the local rate. Custom engraved items are not returnable. Please report any damage within 5 days of delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Item names with SKU or model numbers and quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the buyer match the invoice to what arrived and makes returns, reorders, and inventory reconciliation simple.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Business buyers often cannot pay an invoice without a PO reference, and it speeds up their accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax line, or the buyer's resale or exemption certificate number
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, wholesale buyers who hold a valid certificate don't pay sales tax, and you need the certificate on file to justify not charging it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for delivery, assembly, wrapping, and personalization
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the buyer what each service costs, and in some states the tax treatment of delivery or labor differs from merchandise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Special orders and custom items usually require a deposit, and the invoice should show it was applied so nobody pays twice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Bill-to and ship-to addresses
invoiceChecklist.why: Orders for gifts, job sites, or multiple locations often ship somewhere other than where the bill goes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return, exchange, and custom-item policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Putting it in writing reduces disputes, especially for special orders, personalized goods, and restocking fees.

retail.paymentTerms: Walk-in sales are paid in full at the time of sale, but invoiced orders follow different norms. Special orders and custom items typically require a 50 percent deposit, sometimes 100 percent for low-margin or non-returnable goods, with the balance due at pickup or delivery. Wholesale and business accounts are often net 15 or net 30, and some shops offer a small early-payment discount such as 2 percent if paid in 10 days. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common where state law allows, and they should be stated on the invoice or account agreement. Card, ACH, and check are all common, and card fees are often built into pricing for larger orders.

tips.title: Collect deposits on anything you can't resell
tips.body: Custom, personalized, and special-order items are hard to sell to anyone else if the customer walks away. Take a deposit before you place the order with the supplier, and state whether it is refundable.

tips.title: Keep resale certificates on file
tips.body: If you sell tax-free to resellers or exempt organizations, keep a copy of each certificate. Without one, you may owe the tax yourself if you're audited.

tips.title: Set account terms before the first order
tips.body: Agree on net terms, credit limits, and late fees up front with business customers. It is much harder to enforce terms after an invoice is already overdue.

tips.title: Bill freight and handling as actual costs
tips.body: Supplier freight on bulky or heavy goods can wipe out your margin if it is folded into the product price. List it separately or build it into a clearly stated shipping charge.

tips.title: Invoice partial shipments as they go out
tips.body: If part of an order is backordered, invoice what shipped and track the remainder. This keeps cash coming in and avoids confusion about what the customer has been billed for.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on an invoice?
faqs.answer: In most states, retail sales of tangible goods are taxable, and you add tax to the invoice unless the buyer gives you a valid resale or exemption certificate. Rules on whether delivery, labor, and personalization are taxable vary by state, so check with your state revenue department.

faqs.question: How much of a deposit should I ask for on a special order?
faqs.answer: Fifty percent is the usual starting point. For fully custom or non-returnable items, many shops ask for the full amount up front. Put the deposit policy in writing at the time of the order.

faqs.question: Can I charge a restocking fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you disclose it before the sale and in your return policy. Typical fees are 10 to 25 percent on non-defective returns of special-order or bulky items. Some states have rules on posted return policies, so check locally.

faqs.question: What payment terms should I give wholesale customers?
faqs.answer: Net 15 or net 30 is typical for established business customers. New accounts are often asked to pay a deposit or pay in full on the first few orders until they have a payment history with you.

faqs.question: Should I offer a discount for large orders?
faqs.answer: It is common, but only offer what your margin supports. A tiered discount based on quantity, such as 10 percent at 25 units and 20 percent at 100 units, is easy to explain and protects your profit on smaller orders.

estimate.intro: Retailers send quotes for bulk orders, corporate gifting, special or custom orders, and large purchases like furniture or appliances with delivery. Buyers usually compare your price against online sellers and other local shops, so the quote needs to show what is included beyond the product itself.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact products, SKUs, colors, sizes, and quantities
scopeChecklist.why: Small differences in model or finish change the price and cause returns if the customer expected something else.
Supplier costs change, and a quote that never expires can leave you selling below cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Lead time and expected delivery date
scopeChecklist.why: Special orders can take weeks, and customers need a realistic date, along with what happens if the supplier is delayed.
Sets expectations before the order is placed and protects you if the customer cancels.
These are easy to forget in a product quote and add real cost and labor to the sale.
Shows whether tax is included, added at invoicing, or waived because of an exemption certificate.

scopeChecklist.item: Return and cancellation policy for this order
scopeChecklist.why: Custom and special-order items often can't be returned, and the customer should agree to that before you order.

pricingTips.title: Quote from current supplier cost
pricingTips.body: Confirm the wholesale price and freight with your supplier before quoting a big order. Pricing from last season's cost is one of the most common ways shops lose margin.

pricingTips.title: Show the discount as a line item
pricingTips.body: Listing the full shelf price and then a volume discount line shows the customer the value, and it makes a repeat order easier to price consistently.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Giving prices at 25, 50, and 100 units lets corporate buyers choose and often nudges them to a larger order.

pricingTips.title: Include a price-match boundary
pricingTips.body: If customers compare your quote to online prices, say what is in your price that theirs lacks, such as local delivery, setup, or easy returns, rather than just cutting the number.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote on a large order?
faqs.answer: Usually not for standard product quotes. For custom designs that require samples or mockups, it is reasonable to charge a sample fee and credit it toward the order if they proceed.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 30 days is typical. Use the shorter end for items with volatile supplier pricing and the longer end for stable, in-stock goods.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if my supplier raises costs after I quote?
faqs.answer: Only if your quote says so. Put a validity date on every quote and a line stating that pricing is guaranteed only until then, or after the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: What if the customer wants substitutions after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Issue a revised quote with the new items and price, and get it approved before ordering. Changes made informally by phone or in the store are the usual source of invoice disputes.

retaining-wall-contractor.intro: Retaining wall contractors build and repair walls that hold back soil on residential and commercial sites. Typical work includes segmental block walls, poured concrete, natural stone, timber, and boulder walls, along with excavation, drainage, and backfill. Invoices usually combine labor, materials, equipment, and hauling, often billed in stages on larger jobs.
retaining-wall-contractor.pricingModel: Most retaining wall work is priced per square foot of wall face, with the rate depending on material, height, and site access. Walls over about 4 feet usually need engineering and permits, which are billed separately or passed through at cost. Contractors commonly price from a bid that rolls labor, materials, and equipment into one number, then invoice in stages: deposit, materials delivery, and completion. Extras such as geogrid reinforcement, rock removal, extra drainage, steps, caps, and lighting are added as separate line items. Change orders are common because soil conditions and hidden obstacles show up once excavation starts. Materials are usually marked up 10 to 25 percent to cover ordering, handling, and waste. Small repair or hourly work is billed by the hour with a minimum.

rates.service: Segmental concrete block wall (installed, under 4 ft)
Poured concrete wall (installed, with forms and rebar)
Excavation and base prep, gravel and drain pipe
Skid steer or mini excavator with operator

items.description: Excavation and compacted 6" gravel base, 40 ft wall, includes haul-off of spoils
Segmental block wall, 3 ft average height (120 sq ft face), installed with drainage stone and perforated drain pipe
Geogrid reinforcement, two layers
Wall cap blocks, adhesive, and corner units
Mini excavator with operator, extra boulder removal (change order #1)
Less deposit received

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due within 10 days of completion. Drainage and base work were inspected before backfill. Wall carries a 2-year workmanship warranty, excluding damage from changes to grade or water flow after completion. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and permit numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license on contracts and invoices, and permit numbers tie the work to the inspections it passed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wall specs: type, length, average and maximum height, and material brand
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly what was built and makes warranty claims or later repairs easier to sort out.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials listed separately from labor and equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: Block, gravel, geogrid, and drain pipe are large costs, and clients and their lenders often want to see them broken out.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders with date and client approval
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock, buried utilities, and wet soil often add cost after the bid. Referencing signed change orders prevents disputes over the final total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Engineering and inspection fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Engineered walls require stamped drawings and sometimes special inspections. List them as pass-through costs if they are not in your bid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: A running credit line makes the balance clear and matches your payment schedule in the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Site address, project name, and PO or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients, property managers, and general contractors often require a PO or job number to process payment.

retaining-wall-contractor.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, often enough to cover the first materials order, since block and stone are expensive and sometimes special order. Larger jobs are billed in stages, such as deposit, materials delivered, wall built, and final after cleanup and inspection. Final balances are typically due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Many contractors add a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month, stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, and card payments are all accepted; card fees are sometimes passed on for large balances. Some states restrict deposit size or require specific contract language, and mechanics lien deadlines vary by state, so check your local rules.

tips.title: Bill materials on delivery
tips.body: Block, stone, and gravel are costly to carry for weeks. Build a materials-delivered payment into your schedule so you are not funding the job out of pocket.

tips.title: Document hidden conditions with photos
tips.body: Photograph rock, old footings, buried debris, or groundwater when you find them. Attach the photos to the change order so the extra charge is easy to justify.

tips.title: Hold final payment until drainage is inspected and backfilled
tips.body: Drainage is the most common failure point. Having the inspection signed off before final billing protects both you and the client.

tips.title: Track lien deadlines
tips.body: In many states you must file preliminary notices or liens within a set window after your last work. Keep dates of delivery and completion on every invoice.

tips.title: Charge a minimum for small jobs
tips.body: Mobilizing equipment for a short wall costs nearly as much as a long one. Set a minimum job charge so small repairs are still worth the trip.

faqs.question: Should I invoice per square foot or as a lump sum?
faqs.answer: Either works. Quote per square foot of face so the client can see how changes affect price, and invoice in stages against the total. Itemizing on the invoice helps when change orders come up.

faqs.question: How do I bill for extra rock or unexpected soil problems?
faqs.answer: Use a written change order before doing the work, with the extra hours, equipment, or materials priced out. On the invoice, list each change order as its own line with its number and date.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on retaining walls?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials you buy and treat the job as non-taxable, while others tax the whole contract or only certain materials. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Can I bill for engineering and permits?
faqs.answer: Yes. Either include them in your price or list them as pass-through costs, with or without a small handling fee. Be clear in the contract about who pays if the permit or design changes.

faqs.question: When should I send the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it as soon as the wall is finished, backfilled, graded, and cleaned up, and any required inspection has passed. Attach your warranty terms so the client has them with the balance due.

estimate.intro: Retaining wall estimates are usually sent after a site visit, where you measure the wall length and height, check access, and look at the soil and drainage. Homeowners often compare two or three bids, so clear scope and material details matter as much as price. Written quotes also protect you when site conditions change.

scopeChecklist.item: Wall length, average and maximum height, and material
scopeChecklist.why: These drive cost and determine whether engineering or a permit is needed. Listing the block or stone type avoids substitutions being questioned later.

scopeChecklist.item: Excavation, base, drainage, and backfill details
scopeChecklist.why: Gravel depth, drain pipe, fabric, and backfill type are where cheaper bids cut corners. Spelling them out shows what the client is paying for.
State clearly who is responsible and whether fees are included, so these costs do not surprise the client.

scopeChecklist.item: Demolition and haul-off of existing wall or spoils
scopeChecklist.why: Removing old timber or failed block and trucking away soil can be a large cost and is often assumed to be included.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as rock, utilities, and water
scopeChecklist.why: State how unexpected rock, buried lines, or groundwater will be handled and priced, ideally with a per-hour or per-yard rate.
Limited access may require hand carrying or smaller equipment. Say whether lawn, irrigation, and landscaping repair are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule, start window, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices shift and weather delays work. A set expiration and schedule keep the price and timeline realistic.

pricingTips.title: Price by wall face, then adjust for height and access
pricingTips.body: Start with a per-square-foot rate for the material, then add for walls over 3 to 4 feet, tight access, steep slopes, or curves. Taller walls need more base, grid, and labor per foot.

pricingTips.title: Build in waste and delivery costs
pricingTips.body: Block and stone typically need 5 to 10 percent extra for cuts and breakage, and delivery fees can be significant. Price these in rather than absorbing them.

pricingTips.title: Offer material options
pricingTips.body: Showing a basic block, an upgraded block, and natural stone side by side helps clients choose by budget and reduces haggling over price.

pricingTips.title: Lock in prices with an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from changes in material and fuel costs, and nudge clients to book a start date.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many contractors give free estimates for standard residential walls. For large or engineered projects that need survey, soil testing, or design work, charge a fee and credit it to the job if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How do I handle a bid when the wall needs engineering?
faqs.answer: Give a price for the construction based on a stated design assumption, and note that the final price may change once the stamped plans are done. Or quote the engineering as a separate first phase.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price than my quote?
faqs.answer: Offer scope changes instead of a discount, such as a shorter wall, a different block, or the client handling cleanup. That keeps your margin and gives them a lower number.

faqs.question: Does the estimate become the contract?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Once the client accepts, have both parties sign a contract or a signed copy of the quote with payment terms and change order language. Check your state for required contract wording.

rideshare-driver.intro: Most rideshare drivers are paid by the app, but many also bill clients directly for scheduled airport runs, corporate accounts, medical appointment rides, event shuttles, and hourly driver service. These invoices cover trip fares, wait time, tolls, parking, and any cancellation or after-hours charges that were agreed in advance.
rideshare-driver.pricingModel: Direct-booked rides are usually priced as a flat fare for a set route (airport transfers, regular commutes), by the hour for as-directed service where the client sets the stops, or by the mile plus a base fee for longer trips. Wait time is often included for a short grace period (10 to 15 minutes at pickup) and billed per minute or per 15 minutes after that. Tolls, parking, and airport fees are normally passed through at cost. Many drivers add a late-night or holiday surcharge and a cancellation fee for short-notice cancellations. Regular business clients are often set up on a weekly or monthly invoice with a standing rate sheet. Set rates high enough to cover fuel, maintenance, commercial insurance, and your own time driving to the pickup, not just the miles with the passenger in the car.

items.description: Airport transfer, office to terminal (Mar 4 and Mar 11)
As-directed service, client meetings, Mar 7 (2:00-5:00 pm)
Wait time beyond 15-minute grace period, Mar 11 pickup
Tolls, reimbursed at cost (receipt attached)
Airport parking fee, reimbursed at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Accepted by ACH, card, or check. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Cancellations with less than 3 hours notice are billed at 50% of the flat fare.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip date, pickup time, and pickup and drop-off locations
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, especially businesses, need to match each charge to a specific ride before approving payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Passenger or booking name and any PO or reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate accounts often route invoices by department or cost code and will not pay without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or trip duration used for the fare
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how per-mile or hourly charges were calculated and heads off questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wait time start and end, and the grace period applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Wait time is the most common disputed charge, so list actual minutes and the rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, parking, and airport fees listed separately with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should appear at cost and apart from your fare so they are clearly reimbursements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surcharges and cancellation fees with the date they were agreed
invoiceChecklist.why: Late-night, holiday, and no-show fees are easier to collect when they match what the client accepted when booking.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, vehicle or license plate, and any local permit or license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Some cities and corporate clients require proof that you operate under a valid license and insurance. Check your local rules.

rideshare-driver.paymentTerms: For one-off private bookings, many drivers take payment at or before the ride by card, or collect a deposit for long trips or event work. Business and recurring clients are usually invoiced weekly or monthly on net 15 or net 30 terms. A late fee of 1% to 1.5% per month is common when it is stated in writing before the first trip. Payment methods typically include card, ACH transfer, and check; cash is easy for private riders but harder to track at tax time. For long-distance or multi-hour jobs, asking for 25% to 50% upfront reduces the risk of no-shows.

tips.title: Confirm that direct bookings are allowed
tips.body: Rideshare app terms, commercial insurance policies, and local transportation rules can limit or restrict taking paid rides outside the app. Check your platform agreement, your insurer, and your city or state rules before billing clients directly.

tips.title: Put wait time and cancellation rules in writing
tips.body: Text or email the grace period, per-minute wait rate, and cancellation fee when you confirm the booking. A written confirmation is your best support if a client disputes the charge.

tips.title: Keep receipts and a mileage log
tips.body: Tolls and parking need receipts to bill at cost. A simple mileage log also supports your own tax deductions. Ask your tax professional whether to use the standard mileage rate or actual expenses.

tips.title: Quote deadhead for long one-way trips
tips.body: If you drive 60 miles out and return empty, the return trip is unpaid time and fuel. Build it into a flat fare or add a return-trip fee so a long ride does not lose money.

tips.title: Invoice the same day for business clients
tips.body: Send the invoice right after the ride or at the end of the week while the trip details are fresh. Waiting a month makes it harder for clients to verify rides and delays your payment.

faqs.question: Can I invoice clients for rides I take outside the rideshare app?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but check first. Some platform terms, insurance policies, and local licensing rules limit private paid rides or require a different type of commercial coverage or permit. Confirm with your insurer and local transportation authority before taking direct bookings.

faqs.question: Should I charge tolls and parking separately?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. List tolls, parking, and airport fees as separate lines at actual cost with receipts. It keeps your fare clean and shows the client they are reimbursing real expenses rather than paying a markup.

faqs.question: How do I bill wait time fairly?
faqs.answer: Offer a short grace period, typically 10 to 15 minutes, then charge per minute or in 15-minute blocks. Record the arrival and departure times and state the rate in your booking confirmation so it is not a surprise on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on rides?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes the city. Passenger transportation is taxed in some places and exempt in others, and special taxes or fees may apply to for-hire rides. Check with your state revenue department or a local tax professional.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice a corporate client?
faqs.answer: Match what the client prefers, but weekly or monthly is typical for regular rides. Send one itemized invoice per period with each trip listed by date, route, and reference number, rather than a separate invoice for every ride.

estimate.intro: Drivers send quotes for airport transfers, long-distance trips, event shuttles, multi-stop days, and recurring corporate runs. Clients usually compare your fare to the app price, a taxi, or a black-car service, so a clear and fixed number matters.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact pickup and drop-off addresses and all stops
scopeChecklist.why: Added stops change distance and time. A quote tied to a named route makes it clear what is covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, pickup time, and expected trip duration
scopeChecklist.why: Time of day affects traffic, surcharges, and whether you can take other rides, so confirm it up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of passengers, luggage, and any special needs
scopeChecklist.why: Extra riders, large bags, child seats, or wheelchair access may need a different vehicle or add time and cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Wait time included and the rate after that
scopeChecklist.why: Flight delays and long meetings are the main reason trips run over, so state the grace period and overage rate.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: tolls, parking, fuel, airport fees
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume the quote is all-in, so say whether these costs are included or billed at cost.
A written policy protects the time you blocked off and the rides you declined.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration and deposit required to hold the date
scopeChecklist.why: Fares and your availability change, so a deadline and deposit lock in the booking.

pricingTips.title: Price the full trip, not just the loaded miles
pricingTips.body: Include the drive to the pickup, return miles if you go home empty, and time spent waiting. Many drivers undercharge on long one-way trips by counting only the miles the passenger rides.

pricingTips.title: Offer flat fares for routes people repeat
pricingTips.body: Airport runs and commutes are easier to sell with a set number than a meter. Use a rate sheet by zone or distance so quotes are fast and consistent.

pricingTips.title: Show the hourly alternative
pricingTips.body: For multi-stop days, give a flat total and an hourly option with a minimum, such as 3 hours. Clients can choose, and you are covered if the day runs long.

pricingTips.title: Add surcharges you can defend
pricingTips.body: Late-night, holiday, and peak-event pricing is normal if disclosed in the quote. Show it as a separate line so clients see where the higher price comes from.

faqs.question: Should I quote a flat fare or an hourly rate?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fare when the route and timing are fixed, such as an airport transfer. Use an hourly rate with a minimum when stops, waiting, or schedule are uncertain.

faqs.question: How do I compete with app prices?
faqs.answer: Compete on reliability, not just price: fixed fares, guaranteed pickup times, flight tracking, and a consistent driver. Do not drop below your costs for fuel, insurance, and vehicle wear.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a ride quote?
faqs.answer: For short local rides, usually not. For long-distance trips, event days, or dates when you turn down other work, asking for 25% to 50% upfront is common and reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is typical, or until a set date shorter than that if your calendar is tight. State the date on the quote so the price is not held indefinitely.

roofing.intro: Roofing contractors, from solo installers to small crews, invoice homeowners, landlords, property managers, and general contractors for tear-offs, re-roofs, repairs, and leak work. Bills usually combine labor, shingles or other roofing materials, underlayment, flashing, disposal, and sometimes permit fees. Insurance-related jobs add extra paperwork, such as claim numbers and supplements.
roofing.pricingModel: Most roofing is priced per square (100 square feet of roof surface), with the price covering tear-off, materials, labor, and cleanup. Full re-roofs are usually quoted as a flat fee for the whole job, built up from the number of squares, pitch, layers, and the roofing material. Repairs are often billed as a flat fee per repair or by time and materials, with a minimum service charge to cover the trip and setup. Extras such as rotted decking replacement, additional layers of tear-off, chimney flashing, skylights, and ventilation are priced separately, usually per sheet of plywood, per linear foot, or per item. Steep pitch, multiple stories, and hard access raise the labor rate. Large jobs commonly use a deposit, a draw at material delivery, and a final payment at completion.

rates.service: Asphalt shingle re-roof (tear-off and install, 3-tab or architectural)
Metal roof installation (standing seam or screw-down panels)
Roof repair (leak, flashing, a few shingles)
Ridge vent or roof vent installation
Flat roof (TPO, EPDM, or modified bitumen)

items.description: Tear-off of one layer of existing asphalt shingles, 28 squares, with dumpster and haul-away
Install architectural shingles with synthetic underlayment, ice and water shield at eaves and valleys, new drip edge
Replace rotted roof decking (1/2 in. OSB)
Replace chimney step and counter flashing
Install ridge vent
Pipe boot replacement (plumbing vents)

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $5,000 received on contract signing. Balance due on completion of work. Workmanship warranty of 5 years; manufacturer shingle warranty registered with the homeowner. Decking replaced beyond the estimate is billed at the per-sheet rate shown. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month after 15 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and property owner name
invoiceChecklist.why: Roofing liens and warranty claims are tied to the property, so the address must match the owner on record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a license number on contracts and invoices, and clients and insurers often ask for proof of coverage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized squares, material brand, and shingle or panel line and color
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents exactly what was installed, which matters for manufacturer warranties and later repairs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extra decking, flashing, or tear-off layers
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden damage found after tear-off is the most common billing dispute. Tie each extra to a signed or written approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number and fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Many municipalities require roofing permits, and listing the fee and number shows it was pulled and paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance claim number and deductible handling
invoiceChecklist.why: For storm or claim work, the invoice should match the adjuster's scope, show the supplement amounts, and make clear the homeowner owes the deductible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for workmanship and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients tend to ask about warranties when a leak appears. Putting the length and what it covers on the invoice avoids confusion.

roofing.paymentTerms: Re-roofs commonly require a deposit of 10 to 50 percent at signing, sometimes tied to ordering materials, with the balance due on completion and final walk-through. Larger jobs may use a draw schedule, such as a third at start, a third at material delivery or dry-in, and a third at completion. Repairs and small jobs are typically due on completion or within 7 to 15 days. Late fees of around 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Checks, ACH, card, and financing are all used, and card payments may carry a fee that some roofers pass through. In insurance jobs, the homeowner usually pays the deductible up front and the insurer pays the rest in one or two checks. Check your state's rules on deposit limits and lien notices.

tips.title: Get a signed change order for every surprise
tips.body: Rotted decking, extra layers, and damaged fascia often show up only after tear-off. Photograph each problem, get written or text approval of the price before fixing it, and put it on the invoice as a separate line.

tips.title: Bill materials delivery as a milestone
tips.body: Shingles, underlayment, and metal panels are a large up-front cost. A draw when materials are delivered protects your cash flow and keeps you from financing the client's roof.

tips.title: Photograph the before, during, and after
tips.body: Dated photos of the old roof, the decking, flashing details, and the finished work back up your invoice if a client or insurer disputes the charges or the quality.

tips.title: Know your lien deadlines
tips.body: Many states let roofers file a mechanic's lien on unpaid work, but notice and filing deadlines are strict and vary. Send any required preliminary notices early and keep your invoice dates accurate.

tips.title: Set a minimum service charge
tips.body: Small repairs eat up time on travel, ladders, and tarps. A minimum charge, such as $250, keeps a 30-minute fix from costing you money.

faqs.question: Should I invoice per square or as a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Quote and contract as a flat total for the whole job, but show the squares and unit prices on the invoice so the client can see how it was built. Itemizing also makes it easier to price extras consistently.

faqs.question: How much deposit should a roofer ask for?
faqs.answer: Deposits of 10 to 50 percent are common for full roofs, often enough to cover materials. Some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts, so check your local rules.

faqs.question: How do I bill for hidden damage found after tear-off?
faqs.answer: Stop, document it with photos, and send the client a change order with the price per sheet of decking or per linear foot of fascia or trim. Bill it as a separate line item on the invoice that references the approved change.

faqs.question: What goes on an invoice for an insurance claim job?
faqs.answer: Include the claim number, the carrier name, the approved scope, any supplements, and the deductible the homeowner owes. Keep the invoice consistent with the adjuster's estimate and note that the homeowner is responsible for any work outside the approved scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for paying by credit card?
faqs.answer: Some states restrict or regulate card surcharges, and card networks have rules about disclosure. If you add a fee, state it in the contract before the work and check your local rules.

estimate.intro: Roofers send a written estimate after an inspection, usually on the roof itself or with drone or ladder measurements. Homeowners often collect two or three bids and compare price, shingle brand, warranty, and what is included for decking and cleanup. Insurance work adds a second estimate, the adjuster's, which the roofer's scope is often measured against.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured squares, pitch, and number of existing layers
scopeChecklist.why: These drive material and labor cost. Stating them prevents arguments if the actual area or layer count differs.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact materials: shingle brand, line, color, underlayment, drip edge, and vents
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare bids on materials. Naming them avoids substitutions of lower grade products.

scopeChecklist.item: Decking replacement allowance and per-sheet price
scopeChecklist.why: Rot is unknown until tear-off. A stated price per sheet sets the rule for extras before they happen.

scopeChecklist.item: Flashing, chimney, skylight, and pipe boot work included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Flashing is a common leak source and an easy place for scope disagreements.

scopeChecklist.item: Tear-off, dumpster, haul-away, and magnet sweep of the yard
scopeChecklist.why: Cleanup is part of the expected result. Listing it shows what the price covers.
Clarifies who pulls the permit and whether the cost is in the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, weather delays, and estimate expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change and weather moves schedules, so say how long the price holds and what happens in rain.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from squares plus waste
pricingTips.body: Add 10 to 15 percent waste for shingles, more for complex roofs with hips, valleys, and dormers. Price tear-off, underlayment, shingles, and labor, then add overhead and profit rather than guessing a number per square.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting 3-tab, architectural, and premium shingles, or an upgraded underlayment, lets the client choose a price point and often raises the average job size.

pricingTips.title: Keep the price valid for a short window
pricingTips.body: Shingle and metal prices can change quickly. A 15 to 30 day expiration protects your margin if the client waits.

pricingTips.title: Include photos in the estimate
pricingTips.body: Pictures of damage, worn flashing, and soft spots help the client understand why the work is needed and why your price may be higher than a bid that ignored them.

faqs.question: Should I charge for roof estimates?
faqs.answer: Most roofers give free estimates for full replacements. Charging a flat inspection fee for leak diagnosis, report writing, or insurance documentation is common, and some roofers credit it toward the job.

faqs.question: How do I price decking replacement in an estimate?
faqs.answer: Give a per-sheet price and an allowance, for example up to 4 sheets included, with extra sheets billed at your stated rate. This keeps the base price competitive and sets the rule for hidden damage.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: Usually not until the client signs a contract or accepts it in writing, and the terms depend on your state. State the expiration date and note that the price assumes the conditions seen at inspection.

rv-repair.intro: RV repair technicians and shop owners fix the living systems and the chassis of motorhomes, travel trailers, fifth wheels, and campers. Invoices usually cover diagnostic time, labor on appliances, plumbing, electrical, roofs, slide-outs, and awnings, plus parts and shop supplies. Many techs work solo from a mobile service truck, while others run a small shop with a few bays.
rv-repair.pricingModel: Most RV repair is billed hourly at a shop or mobile labor rate, with parts added at a markup. Many shops charge a diagnostic fee, often one hour, that is either separate or credited toward the repair if the customer approves it. Mobile service adds a trip charge or mileage on top of labor. Some jobs are priced flat or by book time, such as roof resealing, awning replacement, or winterization, where the scope is predictable. Larger work like water damage repair, fiberglass or roof replacement, or slide-out rebuilds is quoted as a project with a deposit. Warranty and insurance work is billed to the third party at their allowed labor rate and book times, which are often lower than retail. Parts are marked up to cover sourcing, shipping, and warranty on the part, and shop supplies are usually a small percentage or flat line.

rates.service: Roof reseal (EPDM/TPO, lap sealant and inspection)

items.description: Mobile service call, travel to campground (28 miles)
Diagnostic: no 12V power to water pump and furnace
Labor: replace 30A converter/charger and repair corroded battery cable ends
Parts: 55A converter/charger
Parts: 2 AWG battery cable and terminal ends
Shop supplies (connectors, fuses, sealant)

sampleInvoice.notes: 2019 Forest River Georgetown, VIN ending 4821, 41,200 miles. Converter tested at 13.6V under load. Parts carry a 12-month manufacturer warranty; labor warranted for 90 days. Payment due on completion. Card payments incur a 3% fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Unit year, make, model, VIN, and mileage or hours
invoiceChecklist.why: RV parts vary widely by model year and chassis, and the record ties the work to the correct unit if a warranty or insurance claim comes up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Customer complaint and the cause you found
invoiceChecklist.why: Writing the original complaint and your diagnosis shows why the work was needed, and it supports warranty and insurance reimbursement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor broken out by task with hours and rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers dispute lump-sum labor more than itemized labor, and third-party payers often require line-by-line book time or actual hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Parts listed with part numbers, quantity, and price
invoiceChecklist.why: Part numbers help with future repairs, returns, and manufacturer warranty claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge or mileage for mobile calls
invoiceChecklist.why: Drive time is a real cost, and showing it as its own line prevents arguments about the hourly total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shop supplies, hazmat, or disposal fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Propane fittings, sealants, coolant, and old batteries cost money. Listing them separately keeps them from looking like padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Authorization reference, such as approved estimate number, change order, or warranty claim number
invoiceChecklist.why: It documents the customer approved the work and any additions, which protects you if the final bill is higher than the first quote.

rv-repair.paymentTerms: Payment is usually due on completion, especially for mobile work where the customer may leave the area soon after. Many shops require a deposit for parts orders, commonly 50 percent or the full cost of special-order parts, and a deposit on larger projects. Shops that hold a unit can charge storage after a stated number of days past completion, which should be in writing. Warranty and extended-service-contract work is paid by the administrator, typically net 30 or longer, with the customer paying any deductible at pickup. Accept cards, ACH, and checks, and consider a fee or discount to cover card costs where your state allows it. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common, but check your state rules, and note that some states have mechanic's lien rules that let you hold a unit until you are paid.

tips.title: Get approval before extra work
tips.body: RV problems often uncover more: water damage behind a leak, a failed slide seal, rotted subfloor. Stop, document with photos, and get written or texted approval before you continue, then add it as a change order.

tips.title: Separate diagnostic from repair
tips.body: Charge diagnostic time as its own line. Customers who decline the repair still owe for your time, and those who approve may have it credited, which you can state on the estimate.

tips.title: Keep your parts markup consistent
tips.body: Set a markup policy, such as a percentage that scales down on expensive items, and apply it every time. Include freight and sales tax where it applies in your state.

tips.title: Bill warranty work to the book
tips.body: For manufacturer or extended-warranty jobs, record the claim number, the authorized labor hours, and the failure code. Missing details are the most common reason claims are rejected or delayed.

tips.title: Address storage before it happens
tips.body: Put a storage policy on the intake form and invoice. Units that sit waiting for parts or payment take up bay or lot space you could use for paying work.

faqs.question: Should I charge for diagnostic time if the customer declines the repair?
faqs.answer: Yes. Diagnostic time is labor. Tell the customer the fee up front and put it in the estimate. Many techs credit the fee toward the repair if the customer approves the work.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on RV repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, parts are taxable and labor is not, while others tax both or neither. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax on its own line.

faqs.question: Can I hold an RV until the customer pays?
