faqs.answer: In many states a repair shop can keep possession of a vehicle until the bill for authorized work is paid, under a mechanic's or possessory lien. Rules about notice, storage fees, and sale of the unit vary, so check your state law and get signed work authorizations.

faqs.question: How do I bill for mobile calls out to a campground?
faqs.answer: Most mobile techs charge either a flat trip fee or a per-mile rate, often with a minimum of one hour of labor. List the charge as a separate line so the customer sees what it covers.

faqs.question: How should I bill insurance or warranty jobs?
faqs.answer: Invoice the administrator for authorized labor and parts, include the claim number and failure description, and bill the customer only for the deductible or any non-covered items. Keep photos and the authorization on file.

estimate.intro: RV owners usually ask for an estimate when the repair is large, when they are comparing shops with long wait times, or when an insurance company needs a written quote for water damage, collision, or roof work. Customers compare labor rate, parts cost, how soon you can start, and whether the number is firm or a rough range.

scopeChecklist.item: Unit details and the reported problem
scopeChecklist.why: Recording the year, model, VIN, and the symptoms shows what the quote is based on and what is not covered.
Many RV issues cannot be priced without opening walls, pulling the roof membrane, or testing systems. Say what is included and whether the fee is credited.

scopeChecklist.item: Labor hours and rate by task
scopeChecklist.why: A task-level breakdown lets the customer approve some items and defer others, and it makes later changes easy to explain.

scopeChecklist.item: Parts, with new, OEM, aftermarket, or used noted
scopeChecklist.why: Prices and warranties differ, and the customer should know what is going into the unit.

scopeChecklist.item: Hidden damage exclusion and change order process
scopeChecklist.why: Water intrusion, rotted framing, and seized components often appear after work starts. State that extra work needs approval before you proceed.
Customers often assume repairs take a day. Spell out ordering delays, scheduling, and what happens if backordered parts extend the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimate expiration, deposit, and storage terms
scopeChecklist.why: Parts prices change, and units left on your lot cost you space. Put the validity period, required deposit, and storage fee in writing.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for unknowns
pricingTips.body: When damage may be hidden, give a not-to-exceed figure or a low-to-high range and explain what drives it. A single low number that grows later damages trust.

pricingTips.title: Price parts at current cost
pricingTips.body: Check supplier pricing the day you write the quote, including freight. Slide-out gear, converters, and appliances can change price quickly or take weeks to arrive.

pricingTips.title: Use flat prices for repeatable jobs
pricingTips.body: Roof reseals, winterization, awning swaps, and inspections are predictable. Flat prices are easier for customers to compare and reward you for working efficiently.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best where it fits
pricingTips.body: For items like a failed water heater or AC unit, show a basic repair, a replacement with a standard unit, and a higher-end option so the customer can choose on cost.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Quick phone or photo estimates are usually free. A teardown, inspection, or on-site diagnostic is billable labor, so charge for it and consider crediting it toward the work if hired.

faqs.question: How long should an RV repair estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Parts prices and your schedule change, so set an expiration date and say that prices may be adjusted afterward.

faqs.question: How much over the estimate can I bill without asking?
faqs.answer: Many states have rules requiring customer authorization before charges exceed an estimate by a set percentage. Check your local rules, and get approval from the customer for any added work regardless.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit before ordering parts?
faqs.answer: It is common and reasonable to ask for a deposit, often for special-order or expensive parts. Say in the estimate that special-order parts are non-refundable or subject to a restocking fee.

sales.intro: Independent sales professionals include freelance sales reps, commission-only closers, outsourced appointment setters, manufacturers' reps, and fractional sales consultants. They invoice for retainers, hours, qualified meetings booked, and commissions on deals their clients close. Each invoice has to show how the amount was calculated, because the client is often paying a percentage of revenue they can check.
sales.pricingModel: Pay in sales usually mixes fixed and variable parts. Consultants and fractional sales leaders charge a monthly retainer or an hourly rate. Outsourced prospecting is billed per hour, per qualified meeting, or as a monthly package with a minimum number of dials or sequences. Reps and closers earn commission, usually a percentage of the contract value or of collected revenue, and often pair it with a smaller base or draw. Sales training and playbook work is normally a flat project fee or a day rate. Many solo sellers use a hybrid, for example a lower retainer plus a commission on closed deals. This protects them during long sales cycles and gives the client a reason to pay for results. Write down what counts as a qualified meeting, when a commission is earned, and whether it is paid on signed or collected revenue, before any invoice goes out.

rates.service: Fractional sales leader or head of sales
Outsourced appointment setting or SDR work
Sales process, playbook, or script development

items.description: Fractional sales lead retainer, June (pipeline management, weekly forecast, rep coaching)
Qualified meetings booked with decision-makers (per agreed criteria, list attached)
Call coaching sessions with two account executives
Commission on Harper Logistics annual contract ($24,000 signed 6/18, 8% rate)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Commission is calculated on the signed contract value per the services agreement dated March 3. A late fee of 1.5% per month applies to balances past due. Accepted by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and the work covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers, meetings, and commissions often land in different periods, so the client needs to see which month each charge belongs to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Commission basis: deal name, contract value, percentage, and signing date
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute commissions more than any other line. Showing the math and the deal it came from prevents questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the agreement or commission schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the invoice to the agreed terms on earned versus collected revenue, clawbacks, and tail periods.

invoiceChecklist.item: Qualified meeting list with dates and contact names
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-meeting billing only works if the client agrees each meeting met the definition. Attach or reference the log.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and activity detail for hourly or coaching work
invoiceChecklist.why: Consulting and coaching hours need dates and short descriptions so the client can approve them quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Expenses and pass-through costs (data lists, CRM seats, travel, trade show fees)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate reimbursables from fees so the client can see what was your cost and what was your pay.

invoiceChecklist.item: Prior draws, advances, or credits applied
invoiceChecklist.why: If you take a monthly draw against commission, show the balance so both sides agree on what is still owed.

sales.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually billed at the start of the month and due in 7 to 15 days. Project work such as playbooks or training often takes 30 to 50 percent upfront. Commission invoices should go out as soon as the deal is signed or the client collects, depending on your agreement, and many sales contractors ask for payment within 15 to 30 days. Common late fees run 1 to 1.5 percent per month where allowed. ACH and check are the norm for larger commission payments, with card payments for smaller items. If you are paid on collected revenue, say so in writing so you are not waiting on a client's customer who pays late.

tips.title: Define what counts before you bill
tips.body: Write a one-paragraph definition of a qualified meeting or a closed deal into your agreement. State whether commission is due on signature, first payment, or full collection. Most sales billing fights start with an unwritten definition.

tips.title: Bill commissions promptly and in detail
tips.body: Send the commission invoice as soon as the trigger event happens, with the deal name, amount, and rate. Waiting weeks lets clients forget what was agreed or argue that the deal was not yours.

tips.title: Get a tail period in writing
tips.body: If a deal you sourced closes after your contract ends, you may still be owed commission. Specify a tail of 3 to 12 months on named accounts, and list those accounts when the engagement ends.

tips.title: Use a retainer to cover long cycles
tips.body: If your deals take 3 to 9 months to close, commission alone leaves you unpaid for a long time. A modest monthly retainer or draw keeps income steady and signals the client is committed.

tips.title: Keep your own records of deals
tips.body: Keep copies of emails, intros, and CRM activity showing your involvement. If the client's records and yours differ, you can back up your invoice.

faqs.question: Should I invoice commission when the deal is signed or when the client is paid?
faqs.answer: Whatever your agreement says. Signed-contract commission is better for you, but many clients push for commission on collected revenue. If you agree to collected revenue, ask for a payment date within a set window after you invoice, so a slow-paying customer does not hold you up indefinitely.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent on calls that did not turn into meetings?
faqs.answer: Only if you are on an hourly or activity-based arrangement. If you are paid per qualified meeting, unsuccessful calls are your cost of doing business. Some contractors charge a lower hourly floor or a monthly minimum to cover prospecting effort.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client disputes a commission?
faqs.answer: Point to the written agreement and the deal records first. Send the contract date, deal value, your involvement, and the commission calculation. If the dispute continues, propose a short call to settle it before sending reminders or involving a lawyer.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on my services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the service. Many states do not tax professional sales consulting or commissions, but some tax certain training, data, or software-related services. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Am I a contractor or an employee when paid on commission?
faqs.answer: Being paid on commission does not decide it. Classification depends on how much control the client has over your work, your tools, and your schedule, and the rules vary by state. If you work as a contractor, you typically invoice, pay your own taxes, and may receive a 1099-NEC from clients who pay you $600 or more in a year.

estimate.intro: Sales professionals send estimates or proposals before a retainer, outsourced prospecting program, or training engagement starts. Clients usually compare a fixed monthly cost against a variable cost, such as commission or per-meeting fees, and against hiring a full-time rep. Your quote needs to make that comparison easy to understand.

scopeChecklist.item: Target market, territory, and account list
scopeChecklist.why: Defines who you are allowed to sell to, so there is no argument over house accounts or which leads earn commission.

scopeChecklist.item: Definition of a qualified meeting or closed deal
scopeChecklist.why: The payment trigger needs to be clear to both sides before work starts.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee structure: retainer, per-meeting fee, commission rate, or a mix
scopeChecklist.why: Shows the client what is fixed and what depends on results, which helps them budget.
State the number of calls, sequences, or meetings you expect to deliver, and whether a monthly minimum applies.

scopeChecklist.item: Tools, data, and lead sources and who pays for them
scopeChecklist.why: CRM seats, contact databases, and dialers add real cost. Say whether they are included or billed at cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Commission terms: earned date, clawbacks, and tail period
scopeChecklist.why: Covers what happens with refunds, cancellations, and deals closing after the contract ends.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract length, notice period, and what happens on termination
scopeChecklist.why: Sales needs time to ramp. A minimum term such as 3 months protects both sides.

pricingTips.title: Offer a fixed-plus-variable option
pricingTips.body: A lower retainer plus commission often wins over a pure retainer because the client shares the risk. Make sure the fixed part covers your time during ramp-up.

pricingTips.title: Price against a full-time hire
pricingTips.body: A mid-level salaried rep with benefits and tools often costs a client $80,000 to $150,000 a year or more. Showing your cost against that figure makes a retainer easier to justify.

pricingTips.title: Set a ramp-up period in the quote
pricingTips.body: Early months produce fewer results while you learn the product and build lists. Say so in the estimate, and consider a reduced rate or clear expectations for the first 30 to 60 days.

pricingTips.title: Avoid promising revenue numbers
pricingTips.body: Quote activity and process commitments you control, such as calls, meetings, and follow-ups, rather than guaranteed closed sales. Results depend on the product, pricing, and the client's team.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote for commission-only work?
faqs.answer: You can, but be careful. Commission-only means unpaid work until a deal closes. If you take it, ask for exclusivity on your territory or accounts, a high enough rate, and a defined tail period.

faqs.question: How long is a sales estimate good for?
faqs.answer: Usually 14 to 30 days. Put an expiration date on it, because pricing and territory availability can change once the client's priorities shift.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a retainer?
faqs.answer: Most solo sales contractors bill the first month in advance before starting. For training or playbook projects, 30 to 50 percent upfront is common.

faqs.question: Can I change the quote if the scope grows?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the quote includes a change clause. Add new territories, extra products, or more reps by written change order with revised fees, rather than absorbing the extra work.

salesforce-consultant.intro: Salesforce consultants are independent admins, architects, developers, and implementation specialists who configure, customize, and support Salesforce for small and mid-size businesses, nonprofits, and sometimes as subcontractors for larger partners. Invoices typically cover hourly project work, fixed-scope implementations, ongoing admin retainers, data migrations, integrations, and training sessions.
salesforce-consultant.pricingModel: Most solo Salesforce consultants bill hourly for open-ended work and support, and use fixed fees for well-defined projects such as a Sales Cloud setup, a CPQ rollout, or a data migration. Rates depend on certification level and specialty: general admin work sits at the low end, while architects, Apex and Lightning Web Component developers, and niche clouds (CPQ, Marketing Cloud, Experience Cloud, Nonprofit Cloud) command more. Many consultants offer a monthly retainer for a block of admin hours, often 10 to 40 hours, at a slight discount in exchange for a commitment. Discovery and requirements work is often billed separately from build work so the client can walk away with a scoped plan. Third-party app licenses, sandbox costs, and tools are normally the client's responsibility and are either purchased by the client directly or passed through at cost. Subcontracting through an agency usually means a lower hourly rate with steadier work and net 30 to 60 payment terms.

rates.service: Salesforce admin / configuration (flows, reports, page layouts)
Sales Cloud or Service Cloud implementation (small team)

items.description: Sales Cloud configuration: custom objects, validation rules, page layouts, and record types
Flow automation: lead assignment and opportunity stage approvals
Data migration: import of 12,400 accounts and contacts from spreadsheets, with deduplication
Report and dashboard build (6 reports, 2 dashboards)
Admin and end-user training session (2 hours, recorded)

sampleInvoice.notes: Work performed in the client's Salesforce sandbox and deployed to production on the 14th via change set. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Hours beyond the agreed 40-hour estimate require written approval. Salesforce licenses and third-party app fees are billed to the client directly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement of work or project name and reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's finance team can match it to an approved budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours by task or workstream with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often review time against what was built; clear entries reduce questions about admin versus development time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or deliverable name for fixed-fee items
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows which phase is being billed, such as discovery complete or UAT signed off, and supports milestone payment schedules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Environment worked in (sandbox, production) and deployment date
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents when changes went live, which helps if a problem is reported later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately (apps, sandbox refreshes, tools)
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps your labor distinct from third-party costs and makes clear whether any markup applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size and nonprofit clients often cannot process payment without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Remaining hours or budget balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeps clients informed about burn rate on capped or block-hour engagements and avoids surprise overages.

salesforce-consultant.paymentTerms: Fixed-fee implementations commonly require 25 to 50 percent upfront, with the remainder tied to milestones such as design approval, UAT, and go-live. Hourly work is usually invoiced monthly or biweekly, and retainers are billed at the start of each month. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for direct clients, while agencies and larger companies may pay on net 45 or net 60. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if written into the contract. ACH and wire transfers are most common for business clients, with cards used for smaller amounts. Consider pausing work on accounts more than 30 days past due, and put that right in your agreement.

tips.title: Separate discovery from build
tips.body: Bill discovery as its own fixed fee or hourly phase. It produces a scoped plan the client can use, and it prevents you from underquoting a build when requirements are still vague.

tips.title: Define what counts as a change request
tips.body: Salesforce projects grow quickly, with new fields, new flows, and new record types. State in your contract that work outside the approved scope is billed hourly, and send a short change order before starting it.

tips.title: Track time by workstream
tips.body: Logging hours as data migration, automation, reporting, and training makes invoices easier to read and helps you quote similar projects more accurately next time.

tips.title: Keep licenses in the client's name
tips.body: Have the client buy Salesforce licenses, sandboxes, and AppExchange apps directly. This keeps you out of reselling and avoids chasing reimbursement for large recurring charges.

tips.title: Bill support retainers for unused capacity clearly
tips.body: Decide in advance whether unused retainer hours roll over or expire, and note the balance on each invoice so there are no disputes at renewal.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or fixed price for a Salesforce project?
faqs.answer: Use hourly or a capped estimate when requirements are unclear or likely to change. Use a fixed fee when scope is well documented, such as after a paid discovery phase. Many consultants combine the two: fixed fee for the defined build and hourly for changes and support.

faqs.question: How do I bill when I work as a subcontractor for a Salesforce partner?
faqs.answer: Invoice the agency, not the end client, using the rate and terms in your subcontract. Include the agency's project code and the period worked. Expect longer payment terms, often net 30 to 60, and confirm whether the agency pays only after the client pays them.

faqs.question: Can I mark up Salesforce licenses or AppExchange apps?
faqs.answer: It is cleaner to have the client purchase these directly. If you do resell or pass through costs, list them as separate line items, state any markup in your agreement, and check whether you need to collect sales tax on them in your state.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on Salesforce consulting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain software, IT, or data processing services, while many do not tax professional consulting. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, especially for work that includes configured software or training.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes hours after I deploy?
faqs.answer: Detailed time entries, deployment notes, and written approvals of scope are your best defense. Invoice promptly after each phase while the details are fresh, and include a short summary of what was delivered.

estimate.intro: Salesforce consultants send estimates before implementation, integration, migration, and cleanup projects, usually after an intro call or a discovery phase. Clients typically compare estimates from several consultants and agencies, looking at total cost, timeline, who does the work, and what is excluded.

scopeChecklist.item: Clouds, editions, and licenses in scope
scopeChecklist.why: Features differ by edition, so state which Salesforce products you are building on and that the client is responsible for the licenses.
A list with counts, such as 8 custom objects or 5 dashboards, gives you a clear point at which the work is done.

scopeChecklist.item: Data migration details: record counts, source systems, and cleanup level
scopeChecklist.why: Messy source data is a leading cause of overruns, so state who cleans it and what format you need.
Connecting to billing, marketing, or ERP systems adds unknowns. Name each system and who provides API access and documentation.
Delays in feedback, user testing, or access can extend timelines. State what you need and by when.
Clarify how many rounds of revisions are included and how many days of post-launch support are covered.
Listing what is not included, such as custom Apex, training, or ongoing support, prevents scope disputes.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for uncertain scope
pricingTips.body: If requirements are not final, give a low and high figure with assumptions listed. Narrow it to a fixed price after discovery.

pricingTips.title: Break the estimate into phases
pricingTips.body: Splitting discovery, build, migration, training, and support lets clients choose what to start with and makes milestone billing straightforward.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for data and integrations
pricingTips.body: These areas are the hardest to predict. Many consultants add 15 to 25 percent contingency or limit estimates to defined record counts and systems.

pricingTips.title: Offer a support option
pricingTips.body: Include an optional monthly retainer after go-live. It sets expectations for post-launch changes and gives you recurring work.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: A short call and a rough range are usually free. A detailed scoping effort, such as reviewing an existing org or mapping processes, is better as a paid discovery phase that can be credited toward the build if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is common. Salesforce releases, your availability, and the client's data can change, so state an expiration date and note that pricing may change after it.

faqs.question: What happens if the project goes over the estimate?
faqs.answer: For hourly estimates, notify the client when you reach about 80 percent of the budget and get written approval before continuing. For fixed fees, overruns from your own mistakes are yours, but client-driven changes should go through a change order.

sat-tutor.intro: SAT tutors help high school students prepare for the SAT through one-on-one sessions, small groups, diagnostic testing, and practice exam review. Most are independent contractors, current or former teachers, or small test prep businesses billing parents directly. Invoices usually cover tutoring hours, package purchases, diagnostic tests, and custom materials.
sat-tutor.pricingModel: Most independent SAT tutors charge per hour or per session, with rates rising with experience, score history, and local demand. Many sell packages of 8, 10, or 20 sessions at a modest discount, billed upfront, which improves cash flow and commitment. Small group classes are priced per student, often as a flat fee for a multi-week course. Diagnostic tests, full-length practice exams with score reports, and college application add-ons are usually billed as separate flat fees. Online sessions are typically priced the same as or slightly below in-person, and travel to a student's home may add a fee or a higher hourly rate. Some tutors offer score-improvement guarantees, but these should be spelled out in writing, since they create billing and refund questions.

rates.service: Diagnostic SAT with score report and review
Essay or college application support add-on

items.description: Diagnostic SAT with scored report and 45-minute parent/student review (Sept 8)
One-on-one SAT tutoring, 10-session package, 60 minutes each (Sept 12 - Nov 14)
Additional tutoring session beyond package (Nov 21)
Proctored full-length practice exam with review (Oct 19)
Printed practice workbook and vocabulary materials

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Unused package sessions expire 6 months after purchase and are non-refundable after the first session. Sessions canceled with less than 24 hours notice are billed in full. Accepted: bank transfer, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and parent or guardian billing name
invoiceChecklist.why: The student is usually a minor and a parent pays, so the invoice should name who is responsible and who the service was for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates and lengths
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents often ask for proof of what they paid for, and dated sessions settle disputes about missed or shortened lessons.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and sessions remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: Prepaid packages create a running balance, so showing sessions used and left avoids confusion at renewal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Test date targeted
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting the SAT date the student is preparing for helps justify scheduling and documents the scope of the engagement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for diagnostics, practice exams, and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: These are billed differently from tutoring hours, and itemizing them keeps the hourly rate clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and late-session charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Billing for no-shows is easier to enforce when the policy is printed on the invoice and was agreed to earlier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Online or in-person location and any travel fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel surcharges look arbitrary without a label, and noting the format prevents rate questions.

sat-tutor.paymentTerms: Many SAT tutors collect payment upfront for packages and invoice monthly or per session for pay-as-you-go students. Due dates of 7 days or due on receipt are common, since tutoring runs on a short timeline before test dates. Late fees, if used, are often a flat $15-25 or 1.5% per month, and should be stated in the initial agreement. Late-cancellation fees of full or half the session rate with 24 hours notice are standard. Parents commonly pay by card, Zelle or bank transfer, or check. If you sell a score guarantee or refund policy, put the conditions in writing before the first session.

tips.title: Sell packages and bill them upfront
tips.body: Prepaying 8 or 10 sessions reduces chasing payments and gives families a reason to keep a regular schedule. Offer a small discount, and state an expiration window so sessions do not pile up unused.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: A 24-hour notice policy is typical, but it only works if the parent has seen it before the first session. Put it in your agreement and repeat it on every invoice.

tips.title: Time billing around test dates
tips.body: Demand peaks before fall, winter, and spring test dates. Invoice early in the prep cycle, and consider a premium or waitlist policy for last-minute cramming requests.

tips.title: Separate tutoring from materials and testing
tips.body: Charge diagnostics, practice exams, and printed materials as their own lines. It keeps your hourly rate clean and lets you adjust those fees without changing your base price.

tips.title: Keep records for tax time
tips.body: Track income by client and note any expenses like books, software, and mileage. Independent tutors in the US generally report self-employment income, so check with a tax professional about quarterly estimates.

faqs.question: Should I bill per session or per package?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Per-session billing is simple for new clients, while packages give you upfront payment and committed students. Many tutors start new families with a package and offer single sessions only for returning students.

faqs.question: Who do I address the invoice to, the student or the parent?
faqs.answer: Address it to the parent or guardian who is paying, and list the student's name as the service recipient. If the student is 18 or older and pays on their own, bill them directly.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a no-show or late cancellation?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy says so and the client agreed to it in advance. Many tutors charge the full session fee for cancellations with less than 24 hours notice, and some allow one courtesy exception.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax tutoring services, but some tax certain educational services or materials. Check your state's department of revenue or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a student does not improve their score?
faqs.answer: Unless you offered a written guarantee, you generally bill for the time delivered. If you do offer a guarantee, state exactly what counts, such as completing all sessions and practice tests, and what remedy applies, like extra sessions rather than a cash refund.

estimate.intro: SAT tutors send estimates when a family is comparing tutors or wants to know the total cost of a prep plan before committing. Clients usually compare hourly rate, package size, and what is included, like diagnostics and practice tests. A clear quote helps parents see the full cost and timeline.

scopeChecklist.why: Parents need to know whether the quote covers 8 or 20 sessions and whether each is 60 or 90 minutes.

scopeChecklist.item: Target test date and prep timeline
scopeChecklist.why: The plan and session pacing depend on how many weeks remain, and it sets expectations for when sessions end.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: diagnostic, practice exams, materials
scopeChecklist.why: Families often assume these are free, so listing what is included or extra avoids surprise charges.
Online, in-home, or at a library or office affects price, travel fees, and scheduling.
Setting these terms in the quote prevents arguments over lost sessions and unused packages.

scopeChecklist.item: Score goals and any guarantee terms
scopeChecklist.why: If you discuss target scores, state clearly whether they are goals or guarantees and what happens if they are not met.
A stated due date and a quote expiration, such as 14 days, protect your calendar and your rate.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total plan, not just an hourly rate
pricingTips.body: Parents think in terms of total cost to reach a score. Present a package with sessions, diagnostic, and practice exams, with the hourly equivalent shown underneath.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three package tiers
pricingTips.body: A smaller starter option, a standard 10-session plan, and an intensive plan let families choose by budget and timeline without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Start with a diagnostic
pricingTips.body: Pricing a diagnostic first lets you recommend an accurate number of sessions based on actual score gaps, which produces a more defensible quote.

pricingTips.title: Add a premium for short timelines
pricingTips.body: If a student wants intensive prep within a few weeks of the test, charge a higher rate or require a larger package, since it displaces other clients.

faqs.question: Should I offer a free consultation or trial session?
faqs.answer: Many tutors offer a free 15 to 30 minute consultation to discuss goals and fit. Fully free tutoring sessions are less common, though some offer a discounted first session.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical. Your availability and test dates change quickly, so an expiration date helps you hold a spot without keeping it open indefinitely.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Not for the agreed scope. If the family later asks for extra sessions, essay help, or a different test date, send an updated quote for the additional work.

faqs.question: Should I include the SAT registration fee in my quote?
faqs.answer: No. Registration is paid by the family directly to the testing organization. You can mention it as a separate expected cost so the family is not surprised.

satellite-installer.intro: Satellite installers set up and service dish systems for homes, businesses, RVs, boats, and multi-dwelling buildings. They bill for TV dish installs, satellite internet setups, dish alignment and repositioning, cable runs, and troubleshooting calls. Many work as independent contractors for providers, while others run their own shop and invoice customers directly.
satellite-installer.pricingModel: Most satellite installers price by the job rather than by the hour. A standard single-dish residential install is a flat fee, with add-ons for extra receivers, long cable runs, roof mounts, wall fishing, and additional TV connections. Service calls and realignments are usually a flat trip charge plus a time component after the first hour. Parts such as cable, splitters, LNBs, grounding blocks, and mounts are billed at cost plus a markup, often 20 to 50 percent. Commercial and multi-dwelling work is often quoted per drop or per dish, or by the day for large crews. Installers who subcontract for providers are often paid a fixed rate per work order, so direct customer invoices should be itemized separately and clearly.

rates.service: Standard residential dish install (single dish, 1-2 TVs)
Satellite internet install (dish, modem, Wi-Fi setup)
Roof mount or pole mount install
Cable run through walls or attic (beyond standard)

items.description: Satellite TV dish install, roof mount, 18-inch dish with Ka/Ku LNB
Additional TV connection, living room and bedroom (cable run and receiver setup)
RG6 coax cable, outdoor-rated, beyond included 50 ft
Grounding block and ground wire kit
Existing dish removal and haul away

sampleInvoice.notes: Install completed 3/14. Signal strength tested at 85+ on all transponders. Payment due within 14 days. Workmanship is warranted for 90 days; equipment warranty is through the provider or manufacturer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Install address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Satellite jobs are tied to a specific site and line of sight, and the address supports warranty claims and repeat visits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment installed with make, model, and serial numbers
invoiceChecklist.why: Serial numbers prove what was installed and help the customer with provider activation, returns, or warranty claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mount type and location (roof, pole, wall, fascia, ground)
invoiceChecklist.why: Mount location affects price and liability if the customer later has roof leaks or needs the dish moved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cable footage and parts listed separately from labor
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers dispute lump sums more often than itemized lines, and itemizing keeps your materials markup transparent.

invoiceChecklist.item: Signal readings or test results after install
invoiceChecklist.why: Recording signal strength shows the system worked when you left and helps if reception problems come up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or registration number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and localities require a license or registration for low-voltage or satellite work, and showing it on the invoice avoids questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for labor and any penetrations
invoiceChecklist.why: A stated workmanship warranty, such as 90 days or one year, sets expectations for callbacks on alignment or leaks.

satellite-installer.paymentTerms: Residential installers commonly collect payment on completion, by card, check, or digital payment, and send an invoice the same day for anyone who cannot pay on site. Net 14 is typical for invoiced residential work, while commercial and property management accounts often run net 30. Large multi-dwelling or commercial jobs usually take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover equipment, with progress payments tied to phases like cabling and head-end work. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing before the work begins. If you subcontract for a provider, expect their own payment schedule, often weekly or biweekly, and keep those work orders separate from direct customer billing.

tips.title: Sell the add-ons before you climb the roof
tips.body: Extra TV drops, longer cable runs, and wall fishing are where most margin is. Confirm the number of rooms and the routing before starting, and write the add-ons on the invoice as separate lines.

tips.title: Charge a trip fee for repeat service calls
tips.body: Realignments after storms, tree growth, or customer-moved dishes burn time and fuel. A flat trip charge of $50 to $75 plus time after the first hour keeps small calls worth taking.

tips.title: Document roof work with photos
tips.body: Take photos of the mount, sealed penetrations, and the finished alignment. Attach or reference them if a customer later blames you for a leak or a shifted dish.

tips.title: Separate provider pay from customer charges
tips.body: If you also do work for a provider, never mix those work orders with direct invoices. Track the per-job rate, any chargebacks, and what you billed the customer for extras the provider did not cover.

tips.title: Bill for mileage on rural jobs
tips.body: Satellite customers are often far from town. Add a mileage or travel line past a set radius, such as 25 miles, so the drive time does not come out of your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat fee for a dish install?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best for standard installs because customers can compare them easily. Use hourly rates for troubleshooting, long cable runs, or anything where the time is hard to predict, and state the rate on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I mark up equipment and cable on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you are supplying the parts. A markup of 20 to 50 percent over cost is common to cover sourcing, warranty risk, and carrying inventory. Show parts as separate lines so the markup is not hidden in labor.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to install satellite dishes?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and locality. Some require a low-voltage, electrical, or specialty contractor license for this work, while others do not. Check with your state licensing board and local building department, and list your license number on invoices if you have one.

faqs.question: How do I invoice when I install for a provider and also charge the customer for extras?
faqs.answer: Keep two records. The provider pays you for the work order under your agreement with them, and you bill the customer directly only for items outside that scope, such as extra drops or custom mounting. Label the customer invoice with the extras only, and note the work order number for reference.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer refuses to pay after the install?
faqs.answer: Send a written reminder with the invoice, install date, and signed work order or photos. If it stays unpaid, follow your stated late fee terms and consider small claims court, which is commonly used for amounts within local limits.

estimate.intro: Satellite installers usually quote before the visit for new installs, relocations, multi-room setups, and any job with a roof mount or long cable run. Customers often compare your total price against a provider's promotional install, so the quote needs to show what is included and what costs extra. Many quotes can be given by phone or text after a few questions, then confirmed on site.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of TVs, receivers, and rooms to be connected
scopeChecklist.why: Each connection adds labor and cable, and an unclear count is the most common source of price disagreements.

scopeChecklist.item: Dish size, mount type, and planned location
scopeChecklist.why: Roof, pole, and wall installs differ in time and risk, and the best signal location may not be where the customer expects.

scopeChecklist.item: Cable length included and the per-foot price beyond it
scopeChecklist.why: A clear included footage, such as 50 or 100 feet, prevents surprise charges on longer runs.

scopeChecklist.item: Line-of-sight assumptions and tree or obstruction limits
scopeChecklist.why: If trees or buildings block the signal, you may need a taller mount or a different location, and the customer should know that could change the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Equipment supplied by you versus the customer or provider
scopeChecklist.why: Customers often assume the dish and receivers are included, so state who supplies what and who handles activation.

scopeChecklist.item: Wall penetrations, attic work, and sealing method
scopeChecklist.why: Drilling through exterior walls or roofing adds liability and time, and the sealing method matters if leaks are a concern.

scopeChecklist.item: Access requirements, permits, or HOA approval
scopeChecklist.why: Some HOAs, landlords, and localities have rules on dish placement, and you should note who is responsible for approvals.

pricingTips.title: Give a base price and list add-ons separately
pricingTips.body: Quote a flat base for the standard install and list extra drops, mounts, and cable runs with set prices. The customer sees a low starting number and understands how the total can change.

pricingTips.title: Build in the drive for rural jobs
pricingTips.body: Add a travel charge or higher base for jobs far from your service area. Quote it as a visible line instead of folding it silently into labor.

pricingTips.title: Offer options that fit the customer's budget
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option, such as one TV on a pole mount, and a fuller option with multiple rooms and a roof mount. Customers pick more often when they can choose between clear packages.

pricingTips.title: Put an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Equipment costs and your schedule change. A 14 to 30 day validity period protects you from being held to an old price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an on-site estimate?
faqs.answer: Many installers do not charge for a standard residential estimate, but you can charge a site survey fee of $50 to $100 for complex jobs such as commercial buildings or difficult line-of-sight sites. Credit the fee toward the job if the customer books.

faqs.question: How firm should my quote be when I have not seen the roof?
faqs.answer: Give a range or a base price with clear conditions. State that the final price depends on mount location, cable routing, and signal at the site, and confirm the final number before starting.

faqs.question: What if the signal cannot be achieved at the planned location?
faqs.answer: Include a line in your quote that covers relocation or a taller mount at an additional cost, and charge a minimum fee for the site visit if no workable location exists. Tell the customer this before you start.

screen-printing.intro: Screen printers run small shops or home studios that print designs on apparel, tote bags, posters, and promotional items for businesses, schools, teams, bands, and events. Invoices usually cover printed garments by the piece, setup charges for screens and art, ink color counts, and extras like folding, bagging, or rush turnaround.
screen-printing.pricingModel: Most screen printers price per printed piece, with the price dropping as quantity goes up and rising with each additional ink color and each print location. Setup fees cover screen burning, film output, and press setup, and are charged per color or per screen. Art or vectorization time is billed as a flat fee or hourly. Blank garments are either included in the per-piece price or itemized separately, often with a markup of 20 to 50 percent over wholesale cost. Many shops set a minimum order (commonly 12 to 24 pieces) and add surcharges for specialty inks (water-based, discharge, metallic, puff), oversized prints, dark garments needing an underbase, extended sizes (2XL and up), and rush jobs. Reorders with the same art often waive setup fees if screens are still on file or the reorder happens within a set window.

rates.service: Standard 1-color front print on tee (24-48 pcs, print only)
Additional ink color or print location
rates.unit: per piece, per color or location

rates.service: Blank garments (basic cotton tee, supplied by shop)

items.description: Short sleeve tees, heather navy, sizes S-XL (blank garments)
Front chest print, 2 colors, white and orange
Back print, 1 color, white (large format)
Screen setup, 3 screens
Art cleanup and vectorization of logo
Individual folding and polybagging

sampleInvoice.notes: 50% deposit paid at approval. Balance due on pickup or within 14 days of delivery. Proof approved by client on 03/04. Reorders with the same art within 12 months will not be charged screen setup. Claims for printing defects must be made within 7 days of receipt.

invoiceChecklist.item: Garment brand, style, and color
invoiceChecklist.why: Blanks vary in price and quality, and clients often forget which style they chose when reordering or disputing cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Size breakdown and quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Extended sizes cost more and a size count prevents arguments about shortages or wrong sizes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Print locations, ink colors, and ink type
invoiceChecklist.why: Each location and color changes the price, and listing them documents exactly what was approved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Setup and art charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume setup is included, and itemizing shows what they avoid on a reorder.

invoiceChecklist.item: Approved proof date and reference
invoiceChecklist.why: A record of the signed proof protects you if the client later disputes colors, placement, or spelling.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how much has been paid and prevents confusion on custom goods that cannot be resold.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax or resale certificate number
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states apparel for resale is exempt with a valid certificate, while end-use sales are taxable. Check your local rules.

screen-printing.paymentTerms: Custom printed goods cannot be resold, so most shops require a deposit of 50 percent before ordering blanks or burning screens, and sometimes full payment up front for small or first-time orders. The balance is typically due at pickup or net 14 to net 30 for repeat business customers, schools, and corporate accounts. Many shops charge a late fee of 1.5 percent per month or a flat fee on overdue balances, stated on the quote. Payment is commonly accepted by card, ACH, check, or cash, and some shops pass on card processing fees where allowed. Large or recurring accounts may issue purchase orders, so include the PO number on the invoice.

tips.title: Take a deposit before ordering blanks
tips.body: Once garments are ordered and printed, you cannot return them. A 50 percent deposit covers blank costs and protects you if a client disappears or changes their mind.

tips.title: Get written proof approval
tips.body: Send a mockup showing size, placement, colors, and spelling, and get a written approval before burning screens. Keep it with the invoice so reprint disputes are easy to resolve.

tips.title: Set an overage and shortage policy
tips.body: Industry practice commonly allows a 2 to 5 percent variance in quantity because of spoilage. State that you may bill for the actual number of acceptable pieces delivered.

tips.title: Charge for color matching and reorders on file
tips.body: Pantone matching, ink mixing, and storing screens take time and space. Bill a mix fee or screen storage fee, and say how long screens are kept.

tips.title: Itemize rush and customer-supplied garments
tips.body: If a client brings their own blanks, bill a handling fee and add a spoilage allowance, since you will not replace garments you did not source.

faqs.question: Should I include garment cost in my per-piece print price?
faqs.answer: Either works, but listing blanks and printing as separate lines is clearer. It makes it easy to adjust if the client changes garment style and lets customers who supply their own blanks see the print-only price.

faqs.question: How do I bill for setup fees on reorders?
faqs.answer: Many shops waive setup when the same art and ink colors are reordered within a set window, such as 6 to 12 months. State your policy on the quote and invoice, and charge again if screens were reclaimed or the art changed.

faqs.question: Can I charge for misprints or defects?
faqs.answer: Reprint your own mistakes at no charge and do not bill for unacceptable pieces. If the error came from client art, wrong spelling in approved proofs, or client-supplied garments, you can charge for the reprint and replacement blanks.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on screen printed shirts?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the buyer. Many states tax sales to end users and exempt sales to resellers who give you a valid resale certificate. Some states also treat printing as a taxable service. Check with your state revenue department.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client does not pick up an order?
faqs.answer: Put a pickup window and storage policy on the quote, such as 30 days before a storage fee applies. Send a final invoice and written notice, and keep the deposit terms and proof approval on file.

estimate.intro: Screen printers send a quote before ordering any blanks or burning screens, usually after the client shares artwork, quantity, garment preferences, and a deadline. Clients often compare several shops, so they look at price per piece, setup fees, minimums, and turnaround.

scopeChecklist.why: Per-piece pricing depends on tier breaks and extended sizes cost more, so the quote should state what quantity it assumes.
Substituting a different blank changes cost and feel, and out-of-stock items can force changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of print locations and ink colors
scopeChecklist.why: Each color and location adds screens and press time, and extra colors added later change the price.
State what file formats are accepted, what counts as print-ready art, and what cleanup or vector redraw will cost.
Water-based, discharge, puff, and metallic inks cost more and behave differently on certain fabrics.
Clarify when production starts, usually after deposit and proof approval, and what a deadline-driven rush adds.
Setting expectations on a 2 to 5 percent quantity variance and what counts as a reprint avoids later arguments.

pricingTips.title: Quote by quantity tiers
pricingTips.body: Show pricing at breaks such as 24, 48, 72, and 144 pieces. Clients see what a larger order saves, and you can nudge them toward quantities that run efficiently on press.

pricingTips.title: Separate one-time and per-piece costs
pricingTips.body: List setup, art, and screen fees apart from the per-piece price. Clients compare shops more fairly and understand why a small run costs more per shirt.

pricingTips.title: Build in extras at the start
pricingTips.body: Include or list optional charges for folding, bagging, hang tags, names and numbers, and shipping. Missing extras are a common reason for margin loss on small jobs.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Blank garment prices change and stock runs out. Mark quotes valid for 14 to 30 days and note that pricing is based on current wholesale costs.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote or mockup?
faqs.answer: Quotes are usually free. Basic mockups are often free too, but many shops charge for multiple revisions or full custom design work, or credit the fee toward the order.

faqs.question: How long is a screen printing quote good for?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Garment prices and availability shift, so state an expiration date and that the final price may change if quantity, colors, or art change.

faqs.question: Can the final invoice differ from the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the client changes quantity, sizes, colors, garments, or art, or if actual delivered counts vary within your stated tolerance. Put those conditions in writing on the quote so changes are expected.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. Have the client approve the quote and the art proof in writing and pay the deposit before you order blanks or burn screens, since custom items usually cannot be resold.

security-consultant.intro: Security consultants assess risk and advise businesses, schools, houses of worship, and property owners on how to protect people, facilities, and information. Depending on the specialty, they bill for physical security assessments, security system design, policy and plan writing, training, expert witness work, and ongoing advisory retainers. Most work solo or in small firms, and many have a background in law enforcement, military, or corporate security.
security-consultant.pricingModel: Most security consultants bill hourly for open-ended advisory work and by flat fee for defined deliverables such as a site security assessment or an emergency action plan. Hourly rates rise with credentials (CPP, PSP, PCI, or similar), niche expertise, and liability exposure. Flat project fees are usually built from estimated hours plus travel, with a written scope so report revisions and extra site visits do not become free work. Ongoing clients are often put on a monthly retainer that covers a set number of hours, with overage billed hourly. Expert witness and litigation work is billed hourly with a retainer paid upfront, and often has separate rates for review, deposition, and trial testimony. Travel time, mileage, lodging, and report printing are typically billed separately. Security system design projects may be priced as a percentage of the project value or as a flat design fee, and consultants who stay independent of equipment sales usually avoid reseller markups to preserve objectivity.

rates.service: Physical security site assessment (small to mid-size facility)
Security system design and specification (CCTV, access control)
Emergency action plan or security policy development
Security awareness or active threat training session

items.description: On-site physical security assessment, 2 buildings and parking areas (Oct 14)
Review of existing access control logs, incident reports, and camera coverage
Written assessment report with prioritized recommendations (draft and final)
Findings presentation to leadership team (Oct 28)
Round-trip mileage to client site
Travel time

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Invoice covers the scope in the signed proposal dated Sept 30. One round of report revisions is included; additional revisions are billed hourly. This report is confidential and prepared solely for the client's use.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project or engagement name and reference to the signed agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and confidentiality terms, which helps if a client questions a charge months later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of site visits, interviews, and meetings
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows when work was performed on site and supports hourly billing, especially for litigation or compliance-related engagements.

invoiceChecklist.item: Breakdown of hours by task (fieldwork, analysis, report writing, presentation)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often need to justify security spending internally and want to see where time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel time, mileage, lodging, and other reimbursable expenses
invoiceChecklist.why: These are easy to forget and should be itemized separately, with receipts available for lodging and airfare.

invoiceChecklist.item: License number and credentials where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states require a private investigator or security consultant license, and clients may need it on file. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or matter number
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate and government clients often will not process payment without one, and law firms use matter numbers to allocate costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer applied and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Expert witness and retainer clients need to see how funds were drawn down and whether replenishment is due.

security-consultant.paymentTerms: Security consultants commonly collect a deposit of 25-50% on flat-fee projects before fieldwork begins, with the balance due when the final report is delivered. Hourly and retainer clients are typically billed monthly on net 15 or net 30 terms, while litigation work usually requires an upfront retainer that is replenished as it is used. Government and large corporate clients may require net 45 or net 60 and vendor registration. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually accepted by ACH, check, or wire, with cards used for smaller engagements.

tips.title: Hold the final report until the balance is paid
tips.body: Your report is the deliverable, and it is also the leverage. Deliver the final version after payment, or release a draft marked as such with the final to follow once the invoice clears. State this in your agreement.

tips.title: Define the number of site visits and report revisions
tips.body: Assessments tend to grow with follow-up questions, added buildings, and requests to rewrite recommendations. Put limits in the scope and bill additional work hourly.

tips.title: Bill travel and expenses separately
tips.body: Folding travel into a flat fee works for local jobs, but out-of-town work can erase your margin. List mileage, lodging, and travel time as their own lines.

tips.title: Keep consulting separate from product sales
tips.body: If you earn referral fees or resell equipment, disclose it. Clients paying for independent advice expect to know, and a clean fee structure protects your credibility.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on longer engagements
tips.body: For projects over a month, bill at the end of fieldwork, at draft delivery, and at final delivery. This keeps cash flowing and avoids a large unpaid balance at the end.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or charge a flat fee for a security assessment?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work well when the scope is clear, such as a defined number of buildings and one report. Hourly billing suits ambiguous or ongoing work. Many consultants quote a flat fee based on estimated hours and add hourly billing for anything outside the scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge for report writing time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Report writing is often the largest part of the work, and it is a legitimate billable activity. Either include it in the flat fee or list it as its own line on an hourly invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice expert witness work?
faqs.answer: Most expert witnesses require a retainer, then bill hourly for file review, analysis, report preparation, deposition, and trial testimony, often at different rates. Invoices usually go to the retaining attorney, and your agreement should say that payment is not contingent on the case outcome.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on consulting services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional consulting services, but some tax certain services, and tangible goods like printed reports or equipment may be taxable. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client disputes a bill after receiving the report?
faqs.answer: Point to the signed scope and the itemized hours or milestones. Offer to walk through the invoice, and address any real scope gaps in writing. Having clear deliverables and dated visit records makes these conversations short.

estimate.intro: Security consultants send a proposal or quote after an initial call or walkthrough and before any assessment, design, or training work begins. Clients are comparing scope, deliverables, credentials, and timeline as much as price, and often get quotes from several firms. A clear written scope is what separates a competitive quote from one that is just cheaper.

scopeChecklist.why: Number of buildings, square footage, parking areas, and remote sites determine the hours and keep the client from adding locations for free.
Naming the approach, such as a CPTED review, ASIS standards, or a state school safety framework, tells the client what they are buying and what you will not cover.
Specify whether you provide a written report, a slide deck, floor plan markups, or a cost estimate for recommended upgrades.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of site visits, interviews, and revisions
scopeChecklist.why: These are the most common sources of scope creep and should have defined limits.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as penetration testing, cybersecurity, or installation
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may assume a security assessment includes areas outside your expertise or licensing.
Your findings describe vulnerabilities. Clarify who can see the report and that you do not guarantee that incidents will be prevented.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline, client responsibilities, and access requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Delays in site access or document delivery should push the schedule, not cost you money.

pricingTips.title: Quote from hours, then round to a fixed fee
pricingTips.body: Estimate fieldwork, analysis, report writing, and presentation time separately at your hourly rate, then add a buffer of 10-20% for revisions and questions. Present the total as a flat fee.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: A basic assessment, an assessment with a prioritized budget, and an assessment with follow-up support give the client a choice and often lead them past the cheapest option.

pricingTips.title: Price travel explicitly
pricingTips.body: State whether travel is included or billed at cost, and include mileage and lodging estimates for jobs that require overnight stays.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire in 30 days or so. Staffing, travel costs, and your schedule change, and an open-ended quote can be accepted long after it makes sense.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or initial site walkthrough?
faqs.answer: A short intro call is usually free. A full on-site walkthrough for a large facility is often a paid half-day, and many consultants credit the fee toward the full engagement if the client signs.

faqs.question: How detailed should a security consulting quote be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that a reader can tell exactly what is included and excluded, typically two to four pages. Include scope, deliverables, fee, schedule, and terms, without revealing your full methodology.

faqs.question: What if the scope changes after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Issue a written change order with the added work, hours, and cost before proceeding. A short email approval is better than none, and the amended amount should show on the final invoice.

faqs.question: Can I give a rough number over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a range, but label it as preliminary and follow with a written quote. Early verbal numbers tend to become the price in the client's mind.

security-guard.intro: Security guards who bill clients directly are usually independent contractors, owners of small guard companies, or off-duty officers who take private jobs. They invoice property managers, retailers, construction sites, event organizers, churches, and homeowners associations for staffed hours, patrols, and special assignments. Most invoices are built around hours worked per post, with add-ons for holidays, overtime, vehicles, and equipment.
security-guard.pricingModel: Most guard work is billed hourly per guard, with the bill rate set well above the guard's pay rate to cover payroll taxes, workers' compensation, general liability insurance, licensing, uniforms, and supervision. Unarmed, armed, and specialty posts (executive protection, fire watch, event crowd control) each have their own rate. Overtime, holidays, and short-notice requests usually bill at 1.5x. Many jobs carry a minimum shift of 3 to 4 hours. Mobile patrol is often priced per visit or per patrol check, or as a monthly flat fee for a set number of drive-bys. Long-term contracts may use a monthly rate based on weekly hours. Vehicles, body cameras, and radios are sometimes billed as separate line items, and travel or mileage may apply for remote sites.

items.description: Armed guard, front lobby post, 6:00 PM to 6:00 AM, Mar 3-9 (1 guard, 12-hr shifts, 4 nights)
Overtime hours beyond 40 per guard per week (Mar 8-9 shifts)
Mobile patrol, parking lot and perimeter check with written report, Mar 3-9
Patrol vehicle use, overnight shifts
Short-notice request, additional guard for Mar 8 (under 24 hours notice), 4-hr minimum

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Daily activity reports and incident logs are available on request. Overtime and holiday hours are billed at 1.5x the standard rate per contract. A 1.5% monthly fee applies to balances past due. Please reference contract #2025-014 on payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Post location and site address
invoiceChecklist.why: Guards often cover multiple sites. Naming the exact post prevents the client from disputing which location a charge belongs to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates, shift start and end times, and guard count
invoiceChecklist.why: Hours are the core of the bill. Clear shift records settle disagreements about late arrivals, early releases, and overlapping coverage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guard type (armed, unarmed, supervisor)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different posts have different rates, and armed work carries higher insurance and licensing costs the client should see reflected.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime, holiday, and short-notice charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show the premium rate was agreed in the contract and keep the base hours easy to verify.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and corporate clients often cannot process payment without a reference number to match in accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Company license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states license security companies and require the license number on contracts and sometimes on billing. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to attached logs or reports
invoiceChecklist.why: Attaching or offering daily activity reports and patrol logs proves the work was done and answers questions about specific shifts.

security-guard.paymentTerms: Contract clients commonly pay net 15 or net 30, and weekly or biweekly invoicing is typical because guard payroll cannot wait on slow payers. For new clients, small companies often ask for a deposit or first week prepaid, and one-time event work is usually paid in full before or on the day of the event. Cancellations with short notice often trigger a minimum charge for the scheduled hours. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and recurring clients often set up automatic ACH payment.

tips.title: Set a minimum shift length
tips.body: Guards will not take a one-hour job that costs them two hours of travel and prep. A 3 or 4 hour minimum protects your payroll and should be written into the contract and shown on the invoice.

tips.title: Spell out overtime and holiday premiums in the contract
tips.body: Clients rarely object to 1.5x pay on holidays when it was agreed up front. Surprises on the invoice are what cause disputes.

tips.title: Bill weekly if payroll is weekly
tips.body: If you pay guards every week, waiting 30 days to bill creates a cash gap. Weekly or biweekly invoicing keeps cash flow close to payroll.

tips.title: Keep time records that match the invoice
tips.body: Use sign-in sheets, patrol check-ins, or a timekeeping app. If a client questions hours, matching records settle it quickly.

tips.title: Charge for no-shows by the client
tips.body: If a client cancels an event after you have scheduled guards, bill at least the minimum shift for each. State this in the agreement.

faqs.question: Should I bill per guard or per post?
faqs.answer: Most small operators bill per guard per hour. If a post needs two guards for 8 hours, that is 16 billable hours. Per-post pricing works for long contracts with a steady schedule, where you quote a weekly or monthly total.

faqs.question: Can I add a fuel or mileage charge for mobile patrol?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is agreed in advance. Many companies fold it into a per-visit rate. For distant sites, a separate mileage or travel line is common. Put it in the contract so it is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How do I handle sales tax on security services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax security or protective services and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional before deciding whether to add tax to invoices.

faqs.question: What if the client asks me to stay past the scheduled end time?
faqs.answer: Record the extra time and bill it at your overtime or extended-hours rate. Ask for written confirmation by text or email from the client contact, and note it on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need insurance information on the invoice?
faqs.answer: It is not required on the invoice itself, but clients often ask for a certificate of insurance before the job starts. Keep general liability and workers' compensation coverage current, since many contracts require them.

estimate.intro: Security companies send quotes before taking on a new site, event, or contract. Clients often compare several bids, looking at hourly bill rate, guard qualifications, insurance coverage, and what is included such as supervision, reports, and vehicles. A clear quote shows exactly what coverage the client is getting.

scopeChecklist.item: Post locations, hours of coverage, and number of guards
scopeChecklist.why: Coverage gaps and extra guards are the most common source of billing disagreements. Write down exactly which hours and posts are included.
State whether guards are armed or unarmed, licensed, and whether they have any special training such as CPR or crowd management.
Listing tasks such as patrols, access control, visitor check-in, or alarm response sets clear expectations about what guards will and will not do.
Putting premium rates in the quote avoids pushback when they appear on the first invoice.
Clients need to know that cancelling late still costs something, because you have already scheduled and committed staff.
If radios, patrol vehicles, cameras, or tour wands are billed separately, say so and list the rate.
Clients want proof of liability coverage and licensing, and need to know the term, renewal, and notice required to end the contract.

pricingTips.title: Build the rate from your costs
pricingTips.body: Start with guard pay, then add payroll taxes, workers' compensation, liability insurance, uniforms, supervision, and overhead, then add profit. Many small operators bill at about 1.3 to 1.6 times the guard's hourly wage, depending on region and post type.

pricingTips.title: Quote a weekly or monthly total for long contracts
pricingTips.body: Clients with ongoing needs often prefer a predictable figure. Show the hourly rate and the total side by side so the math is clear.

pricingTips.title: Price event work with a buffer
pricingTips.body: Events run long and often need extra guards. Include a setup and teardown window and a clear rate for hours beyond the agreed end time.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers when it fits
pricingTips.body: For example, quote unarmed guard plus mobile patrol as one option and armed guard as another. Clients can see what the extra cost buys without you rewriting the quote.

faqs.question: How long should a security quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. Labor costs and guard availability change, so set an expiration date and state that rates are subject to change after it.

faqs.question: Should I do a site visit before quoting?
faqs.answer: Yes, when possible. A walk-through shows the size of the property, lighting, entry points, and risks, which affect how many guards and what type are needed. Many companies do it for free for contract bids.

faqs.question: Can I charge for writing a security assessment?
faqs.answer: Many companies include a basic site walk-through in the quote. A detailed written risk assessment with recommendations is often billed separately, either as a flat fee or hourly, and credited toward the contract if the client signs.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement after the client accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes. A signed contract or accepted quote with scope, rates, term, and cancellation terms protects both sides. Some states also have rules about what security contracts must include, so check your local requirements.

security-service.intro: Security service businesses provide unarmed and armed guards, patrol and alarm response, event security, and sometimes alarm monitoring or camera installation. Owners and small firms bill commercial property managers, construction sites, retailers, HOAs, venues, and private clients. Most invoices are built from guard hours, with extras like patrol checks, response calls, and equipment.
security-service.pricingModel: Most security work is billed hourly per guard, with a bill rate set well above the guard's pay rate to cover payroll taxes, workers' compensation, general liability, insurance, supervision, uniforms, and overhead. Armed guards, supervisors, and specialized posts cost more than standard unarmed officers. Overtime, holiday, and night rates are often higher, commonly 1.5x on holidays or when the guard goes into overtime. Mobile patrols are usually priced per patrol visit or per month for a set number of checks. Event security is typically billed with a minimum shift length, often 4 hours. Alarm response and monitoring are often monthly flat fees with per-call charges for extra responses. Longer contracts are often billed weekly or monthly in arrears, with the rate fixed in a written service agreement.

items.description: Unarmed security guard, overnight post at Riverside Apartments construction site, 10pm-6am, 5 nights (week of 3/10)
Overtime hours (over 40 hours/week) for relief coverage on Saturday
Mobile patrol checks of adjacent staging lot, 3 per night
Alarm response and police coordination, 3/13 at 1:40am
Daily activity reports and incident report (gate left open)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date per service agreement dated 1/15. Rates reflect the agreed contract schedule. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Daily activity reports are available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Post location and shift dates and times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients check hours against their own gate logs and schedules, and clear dates head off disputes about who was on site and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by guard classification (unarmed, armed, supervisor)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different roles carry different bill rates, so listing them separately shows how the total was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime, holiday, and night differentials
invoiceChecklist.why: These premium rates should be broken out and tied to the terms in your contract so they are not seen as surprise charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service agreement or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and corporate clients often require a contract or PO reference before accounts payable will process payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your state security license or company license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require licensed security companies, and showing your license on paperwork supports your legitimacy to clients and their insurers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Incident and response charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Alarm response, police coordination, or extra patrols outside the base contract should be itemized with date and time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Weekly or monthly billing is common, and a defined period prevents overlap or missed shifts.

security-service.paymentTerms: Contract security is usually billed weekly or biweekly for small clients and monthly for larger accounts, with terms of net 15 or net 30. Because payroll must be met regardless of when the client pays, many firms ask for a deposit or the first week in advance for new accounts, and event work is often prepaid or billed 50% up front.
