Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is typically by ACH, check, or card, and ACH is the usual choice for recurring contracts. Many firms reserve the right to suspend service after a set number of days past due, which should be written in the agreement.

tips.title: Set your bill rate from your true labor cost
tips.body: Start with guard wages, then add payroll taxes, workers' compensation, liability insurance, training, uniforms, supervision, and admin time. Add a profit margin on top. Many new owners underprice by only adding a small markup to wages and then struggle with overtime weeks.

tips.title: Write minimum shift lengths into the contract
tips.body: A 4-hour minimum for events and short posts protects you from paying a guard for a full shift while billing only an hour or two. State the minimum on the quote and repeat it on the invoice.

tips.title: Attach daily activity reports to the invoice
tips.body: Clients who can see patrol logs and incident reports are less likely to question hours. Keep copies on file in case of a dispute or liability claim.

tips.title: Bill for call-outs and cancellations
tips.body: Set a policy for last-minute cancellations, such as charging the minimum shift if cancelled with less than 24 hours notice, because guards are already scheduled and unavailable for other work.

tips.title: Track overtime before you invoice
tips.body: Check weekly hours per guard before billing so you can apply overtime rates correctly and avoid either absorbing the cost or sending a corrected invoice later.

faqs.question: Should I bill by the hour or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Staffed posts are almost always billed hourly per guard because costs scale with hours. Flat monthly fees fit mobile patrols, alarm response, and monitoring, where the scope is a set number of visits or services.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for holidays and nights?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you state it in your contract or quote beforehand. Holiday premiums of 1.5x are common, and some firms add a smaller differential for overnight shifts. Check that the rates are listed in the agreement so the client expects them.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on security services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax security or protective services and others do not, and rules can differ for alarm monitoring or equipment sales. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle a guard who works past the scheduled end time?
faqs.answer: Bill the actual hours if the client requested or approved the extra time, and note it on the invoice. If the extension was due to a relief guard failing to show up, document it so the client understands the charge.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client pays late repeatedly?
faqs.answer: Follow the late fee and suspension terms in your contract. Send a reminder at the due date, a notice at 10 days past, and give written notice before pausing service. Giving notice and following the contract protects you from claims later.

estimate.intro: Security companies send quotes when a client asks for coverage at a site, such as a new construction project, retail location, event, or building needing after-hours patrol. Clients usually compare hourly bill rates, how many guards are required, insurance coverage, and what is included. A clear quote shows how you arrived at the number so it is not compared on rate alone.

scopeChecklist.item: Post details: address, days, hours, and number of guards
scopeChecklist.why: Cost depends mainly on coverage hours, so the post schedule must be exact. Changes after signing should be priced as additions.

scopeChecklist.item: Guard type and qualifications (unarmed, armed, licensed, CPR or first aid)
scopeChecklist.why: Armed or specialized staff cost more, and clients should know what they are paying for.
Whether guards patrol, check IDs, log visitors, or only observe affects staffing and liability. Anything outside the listed duties should be charged separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Overtime, holiday, and minimum shift rates
scopeChecklist.why: Putting premium rates in the quote prevents billing disputes when extra hours occur.
Clients often require proof of general liability, workers' compensation, and a state license before signing.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract length, notice to cancel, and rate changes
scopeChecklist.why: Cancellation terms protect your payroll commitments, and rate review language lets you adjust for wage increases.
Radios, vehicles, patrol tracking, and report delivery should be listed as included or as extra line items.

pricingTips.title: Quote a blended rate only after pricing each role
pricingTips.body: Build the price by role, with guard, supervisor, and patrol vehicle costs separate, then you can combine them if the client wants one rate. This makes it easier to adjust if the scope changes.

pricingTips.title: Account for the full schedule, not just the shift
pricingTips.body: A 24/7 post needs more than three 8-hour guards because of days off, sick time, and training. Include relief coverage so your margin holds on weeks with call-outs.

pricingTips.title: Visit the site before quoting
pricingTips.body: A walk-through shows the number of entry points, lighting, parking, and hazards, which affect staffing and patrol time. Note findings on the quote to justify your recommendations.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a single guard, a guard plus mobile patrol, or patrol only. Clients can compare real tradeoffs instead of only the lowest hourly rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site assessment?
faqs.answer: Many firms provide a basic walk-through free for contracts they expect to win. For detailed risk assessments or written security plans, a flat fee of a few hundred dollars or more is common, and some firms credit it toward the contract.

faqs.question: How long should a security quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is typical. Wages and insurance costs change, and guard availability can shift, so an expiration date keeps you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower rate than my quote?
faqs.answer: Reduce the scope before the rate, for example fewer hours, fewer patrols, or a longer contract term in exchange for a modest discount. Dropping the rate below your labor cost and overhead usually leads to losing money on the contract.

faqs.question: Should the quote be a contract?
faqs.answer: A quote can be accepted by signature, but most security companies also use a separate service agreement with liability, insurance, and termination terms. Have an attorney review your contract template, since requirements vary by state.

seo-agency.intro: SEO agencies and freelance SEO consultants help businesses rank higher in search results through technical fixes, content, and link building. Most invoices cover a monthly retainer, a one-time audit, or a project such as a site migration, plus any pass-through costs like software or content writers.
seo-agency.pricingModel: Most SEO work is sold as a monthly retainer, typically with a minimum commitment of three to six months because results take time. One-time projects such as technical audits, keyword research, and site migrations are usually flat fees. Hourly billing is common for consulting, training, and ad hoc fixes. Content and link building are often priced per piece or per placement, either bundled into the retainer or billed separately. Third-party costs such as paid tool seats, freelance writers, or digital PR placements are either built into the fee or passed through at cost or with a markup, and should be stated in the contract. Avoid pricing on a guaranteed ranking, since no one controls search engine results.

rates.service: Standard SEO retainer (small to mid-size business)
SEO blog post or landing page copy
Link building or digital PR placement

items.description: Monthly SEO retainer, March 2025 (technical fixes, on-page optimization, monthly report)
SEO blog posts, 1,500 words each, researched and optimized
Digital PR link placements (industry publications)
Schema markup implementation for product pages
Rank tracking software seat (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Retainer covers work for the stated month and is billed in advance. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. The monthly performance report will be sent by the 5th of next month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers bill for a month of work, so naming the exact period prevents confusion about what the charge covers and when the next one starts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing audits, posts, links, and fixes shows the client what they received when rankings have not yet moved.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement or statement of work
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the charge to the agreed scope, minimum term, and cancellation notice period if there is a dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Tools, freelance writers, and paid placements should be clear line items so the client can see what is your fee and what is third-party cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for any hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Ad hoc fixes outside the retainer need a date, task, and hours so they are easy to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Mid-size companies often route invoices through accounts payable that will not pay without a PO or the right contact name.

invoiceChecklist.item: Link to or mention of the monthly report
invoiceChecklist.why: Pointing to the report reinforces the value delivered, which helps retainer renewals.

seo-agency.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually billed in advance on the first of the month, due on receipt or within 15 days. Projects like audits and migrations commonly require 50% upfront and 50% on delivery, or milestone billing for larger jobs. Net 30 is typical for corporate clients, though it is reasonable to ask for shorter terms or auto-pay on retainers. Many agencies charge a late fee of 1-1.5% per month and pause work if an invoice is more than 15 to 30 days overdue. Payment is usually by ACH, credit card, or check. Card fees are sometimes passed on to the client, so check your local rules and your contract before adding a surcharge.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Search work starts costing you time and tool fees on day one. Billing at the start of the month keeps cash flow predictable and removes the temptation for a client to delay payment until they see results.

tips.title: Set a minimum term and notice period
tips.body: Put a three to six month minimum and a 30-day cancellation notice in the contract. SEO takes months to show results, and clients who quit after 60 days often blame the agency.

tips.title: Define what is out of scope
tips.body: State how many content pieces, links, and hours of development support the retainer includes. Anything beyond that is billed separately at your hourly rate, which stops scope creep from eating your margin.

tips.title: Separate fees from ad spend and tool costs
tips.body: If you buy tools, content, or placements on a client's behalf, list them as their own lines. This makes your fee easier to defend and makes markups transparent.

tips.title: Do not tie payment to rankings
tips.body: Rankings depend on search engines, competitors, and the client's site. Invoice for work done and deliverables, and use reports to show progress, rather than promising positions.

faqs.question: Should I bill SEO monthly or per project?
faqs.answer: Ongoing optimization, content, and link building fit a monthly retainer. One-time work like an audit, migration, or keyword research is better as a flat project fee with a deposit. Many agencies do both, starting with an audit and then moving the client to a retainer.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for tools like Ahrefs or Semrush?
faqs.answer: Either include tool costs in your retainer price or list them as a separate pass-through line at cost or with a small markup. Say which approach you use in your contract so the client is not surprised.

faqs.question: What if a client wants to pause the retainer because rankings have not improved?
faqs.answer: Point to the minimum term and cancellation notice in your agreement, and share the report of work completed and leading indicators like indexing, traffic, and impressions. If you agree to a pause, put the restart date and any rate changes in writing.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee?
faqs.answer: Yes, if it is in your contract or stated on the invoice terms. Rates of 1 to 1.5% per month are common, but maximum allowed late fees vary by state, so check local rules.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on SEO services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital or marketing services and many do not. Check with your state's revenue department or a tax professional, and list any tax as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: SEO agencies send a proposal or quote before starting any engagement, often after a discovery call and a quick review of the client's site. Clients typically compare your price against other agencies, an in-house hire, and what they have paid in the past, so the scope and deliverables matter as much as the number.

scopeChecklist.why: Say how many posts, links, page optimizations, and reports are included so the client knows what the retainer buys and you are not judged on vague effort.

scopeChecklist.item: Goals and the metrics you will report on
scopeChecklist.why: List measures such as organic traffic, impressions, keyword rankings, and leads, and avoid guarantees, so expectations are set around things you can influence.
SEO needs months to show results. A stated commitment period protects you from clients leaving early.
You need access to the CMS, Search Console, analytics, and developer time. Delays on the client side should not count against you.
Clarify whether software, writers, and paid link placements are included or billed at cost, so the budget does not change later.

scopeChecklist.item: Approval process for content and site changes
scopeChecklist.why: State who signs off on content and how many revision rounds are included, so delays and extra edits do not become disputes.
Web development, paid ads, design, and PR are often assumed to be included. List what is not covered and how extra work is priced.

pricingTips.title: Start with a paid audit
pricingTips.body: Charging for a technical audit and keyword research before quoting a retainer gives you real data to price from and filters out clients who only want free advice. Many agencies credit part of the audit fee to the first month of a retainer.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting three levels, for example a local plan, a growth plan, and an aggressive plan with more content and links, lets the client pick by budget and avoids a simple yes or no on one price.

pricingTips.title: Price on effort and competition
pricingTips.body: The number of pages, the size of the site, how competitive the keywords are, and how much content is needed drive your hours. Use these to build the price rather than copying a competitor's rate card.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire in 14 to 30 days. Competitive landscapes, your capacity, and tool costs change, and a date prompts a decision.

faqs.question: Should I give a free SEO audit with my quote?
faqs.answer: A short review of obvious issues is fine to show you know the site. A full audit takes real hours, so most agencies charge for it, or credit the fee toward the first months of a retainer.

faqs.question: Can I give a fixed price for a retainer when I do not know how much work the site needs?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you define the monthly deliverables and hours. Start with an audit or a short discovery period so your scope is based on what the site actually needs.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who gets a cheaper quote elsewhere?
faqs.answer: Compare deliverables, not price. Lower quotes often include fewer pieces of content, no technical work, or low-quality links. Show clearly what is included in yours, and be willing to offer a reduced scope instead of a lower rate for the same work.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: An estimate is a good faith projection and a quote or accepted proposal is a firm price for a defined scope. Label your document clearly, and use a signed agreement for anything you expect the client to be held to.

seo-consultant.intro: SEO consultants help businesses rank higher in search results through technical audits, keyword research, content strategy, on-page optimization, and link building. Most work solo or in small agencies and bill for monthly retainers, one-time audits, and hourly strategy work. Invoices need to show clearly what was delivered, since results in search take months and clients often ask what they are paying for.
seo-consultant.pricingModel: SEO is priced mostly by monthly retainer for ongoing work, flat fee for one-time projects such as site audits or migrations, and hourly for consulting, training, and ad hoc requests. Retainers typically scale with site size, competition, and hours of work included, and many consultants state the hours or deliverables covered each month. Audits are usually quoted as flat fees based on the number of pages and the depth of review (technical only versus technical, content, and backlinks). Link building and content writing are often billed as pass-through or per-piece costs, sometimes with a markup. Tool costs for rank trackers and crawlers are normally folded into the retainer rather than itemized. Consultants rarely guarantee rankings, so pricing is tied to work performed, not outcomes. Performance-based pricing exists but is uncommon and carries risk for both sides.

rates.service: Technical SEO audit (small to mid-size site)
Monthly SEO retainer (ecommerce or competitive niche)
Site migration or redesign SEO support
Local SEO setup (Google Business Profile, citations)

items.description: Monthly SEO retainer, June: on-page optimization, technical fixes, monthly reporting (up to 15 hours)
Keyword research and content brief for service pages (4 pages)
Guest post placements secured (DR 40+ sites)
Additional consulting beyond retainer hours (schema markup implementation)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Retainer covers work performed June 1-30. Hours beyond the included 15 are billed at $125 per hour with prior approval. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Rankings and traffic are not guaranteed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service period covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainers need clear start and end dates so the client knows which month of work they are paying for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables or hours used
invoiceChecklist.why: SEO results are slow, so showing the audit, briefs, fixes, or reports delivered backs up the charge when traffic has not moved yet.

invoiceChecklist.item: Included hours versus overage hours
invoiceChecklist.why: If the retainer includes a set number of hours, separating extra time prevents disputes about scope creep.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs and pass-throughs
invoiceChecklist.why: Link placements, content writers, or paid tool licenses billed at cost or with markup should be listed separately from your labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Domain or website being worked on
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several sites or brands need to know which property the invoice relates to for their own bookkeeping.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often require one to approve payment through accounts payable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement or proposal
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying the invoice to the agreed scope and rates helps if the client questions a charge.

seo-consultant.paymentTerms: Retainers are usually invoiced at the start of the month, in advance, and due on receipt or within 7 to 15 days. One-time audits and projects commonly take 50 percent upfront and 50 percent on delivery, or full payment upfront for small jobs. Hourly work is billed monthly in arrears, net 15 or net 30 for corporate clients. Many consultants add a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month and pause work when an invoice is more than 15 to 30 days overdue. Payment is typically by ACH, credit card, or bank transfer, and card fees are sometimes passed on or built into the rate. Put cancellation terms, such as 30 days written notice for retainers, in the contract.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: SEO work starts costing you time on day one, and results lag behind. Invoicing at the start of the month keeps cash flow predictable and avoids chasing payment after the work is done.

tips.title: Send a monthly report with every invoice
tips.body: A short summary of work completed, rankings, traffic, and next steps makes the invoice easier to approve. Clients who see activity are less likely to cancel during the slow early months.

tips.title: Define what happens to unused hours
tips.body: Decide whether unused retainer hours roll over or expire, and write it into your agreement. Without a rule, clients often assume they roll over and expect extra work later.

tips.title: Separate strategy from implementation
tips.body: If you also edit the site, write content, or build links, list those as separate lines. It makes it easier to adjust scope later and shows where the money is going.

tips.title: Do not tie fees to rankings
tips.body: Search results depend on factors you cannot control, such as algorithm updates and competitor activity. Bill for work performed and write that rankings are not guaranteed.

faqs.question: Should I bill SEO hourly or by retainer?
faqs.answer: Retainers suit ongoing work because they give you steady income and give clients a fixed cost. Hourly billing works better for short engagements, training, or one-off questions. Many consultants use a retainer with a stated hour cap and bill extra hours hourly.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for link building costs?
faqs.answer: List them as separate line items, either at your cost or with a disclosed markup, and include the number of links or placements. Some consultants fold these into a flat monthly fee. Either way, say in your agreement how outside costs are handled.

faqs.question: What if the client says SEO is not working and refuses to pay?
faqs.answer: Point to the scope in your signed agreement and the deliverables on the invoice. Since you are paid for work performed and not for rankings, a clear record of tasks and monthly reports is your best support. A written no-guarantee clause helps avoid this dispute.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on SEO services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain digital or marketing services, while many do not tax consulting. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show any tax collected as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for tools like Ahrefs or Semrush separately?
faqs.answer: You can, but most consultants include tool costs in their retainer or hourly rate because the tools are shared across clients. If a client needs a dedicated subscription, bill it at cost and say so in your agreement.

estimate.intro: SEO consultants send proposals or quotes after a discovery call or a quick look at the prospect's site, usually for audits, projects, or a first retainer. Clients often compare several consultants or agencies, so the quote has to show what is included and how long the work will take. A vague estimate leads to scope disputes once the client expects results.

scopeChecklist.why: Name what the client gets, such as a technical audit report, 10 optimized pages, or two blog posts a month, so there is no guessing later.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of pages or site size covered
scopeChecklist.why: Audit and optimization costs depend on how many URLs you review or edit, and a growing site can change the effort.
For retainers, stating included hours and the rate for extra work prevents unpaid scope creep.
Clarify whether you make changes in the CMS yourself or only provide recommendations for the client's developer or team.
List what you need, such as Google Search Console, Analytics, CMS login, and hosting access, since delays on the client side affect your timeline.
Give delivery dates for audits and set the frequency of reports so the client knows when to expect results and updates.
State that rankings and traffic are not guaranteed and list what is not included, such as paid ads, web development, or content beyond what is quoted.

pricingTips.title: Quote audits as a flat fee
pricingTips.body: Look at the site size and platform before pricing, and set the fee by pages and depth of review. A flat fee is easier for clients to approve than open hourly billing.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered retainer options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three packages with different hour levels or deliverables. Clients tend to pick the middle option, and tiers let you start smaller without discounting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Price in the first three months of ramp-up
pricingTips.body: Early months often involve audits, fixes, and setup work. Either charge a one-time onboarding fee or set the retainer high enough to cover the heavier initial workload.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Competition, site changes, and your own availability shift over time. A 14 to 30 day validity period protects you from clients accepting an outdated price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or initial audit?
faqs.answer: A quick review and call are usually free. A detailed audit that takes hours should be paid, and many consultants credit the audit fee toward a retainer if the client signs on.

faqs.question: How do I estimate hours for an SEO project?
faqs.answer: Break the work into tasks such as crawl and analysis, keyword research, page edits, and reporting, then estimate time per task based on site size. Add a buffer of 10 to 20 percent for revisions and client communication.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes. Include a clause that new requests, extra pages, or a site redesign require a revised quote or change order, and get approval in writing before doing the extra work.

septic-service.intro: Septic service businesses pump, inspect, repair, and install onsite wastewater systems for homeowners, landlords, real estate buyers, and small commercial properties. Most invoices cover tank pumping, inspections, filter cleaning, and repairs, and larger jobs include parts, excavation, and disposal fees.
septic-service.pricingModel: Routine pumping is usually a flat fee based on tank size (typically 1,000 to 1,500 gallons), with extra charges for gallons beyond the base amount, long hose runs, or hard-to-find and buried lids. Inspections, camera work, and locating are priced as flat fees or by the hour. Repairs are billed by the hour or by the job plus parts, often with a markup of 15 to 30 percent on materials. Installs and drain field work are quoted as a fixed price after a site evaluation, and often depend on permits, soil tests, and excavation. Many shops add a trip or after-hours fee for emergency calls, and some sell multi-year maintenance plans. Disposal or dump fees at the treatment facility are either built into the pumping price or passed through as a separate line.

items.description: Pump out 1,000-gallon septic tank, 2 compartments
Additional gallons pumped over 1,000 base
Locate and excavate buried tank lid (hand dig)
Install 24-inch polyethylene riser with lid
Clean effluent filter
Written inspection report with photos

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon completion. Total gallons pumped recorded on manifest and disposed at licensed facility. Next pumping recommended in 3 years. Late balances charged 1.5% per month after 30 days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and tank location
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often own several properties, and the record needs to show which system was serviced and where the tank and lids were found.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tank size, type, and number of compartments
invoiceChecklist.why: Justifies the base price and gives the next technician a record of what is in the ground.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gallons pumped and disposal details
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports any per-gallon charge and shows the waste went to a licensed facility. Many states require a manifest or pumping record.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your septic hauler or contractor license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and counties require licensed haulers or installers, and health departments or lenders may ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Condition findings and recommendations
invoiceChecklist.why: Notes on cracked baffles, standing water, or a failing filter protect you if the system fails later and give the customer a reason to approve repairs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts and materials
invoiceChecklist.why: Risers, lids, filters, pipe, and pumps should be listed separately so the markup is clear and warranty claims are easy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit numbers for repairs or installs
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties your work to the local health department record and may be needed for final approval or a home sale.

septic-service.paymentTerms: Routine pumping and inspections are typically due at the time of service, by card, check, or electronic payment, since the truck is already at the property and collecting later is harder. For repairs, many shops take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to cover parts, and installs commonly use a deposit, a progress payment after excavation or tank set, and a final payment after the inspection passes. Net 15 or Net 30 is common for property managers, realtors, and commercial accounts. If you charge late fees, state them on the estimate and the invoice, and check your state's rules on interest limits.

tips.title: Collect payment before the truck leaves
tips.body: Pumping is a one-visit job and the customer is usually home. Sending a payment link or taking a card on site avoids chasing small balances that cost more to collect than they are worth.

tips.title: Charge separately for digging and lid work
tips.body: Buried lids are the most common source of lost time. Bill locating and excavation by the hour or as a set fee, and tell the customer before you start digging.

tips.title: Put the next service date on the invoice
tips.body: A line such as pump again in 3 years gets repeat work and doubles as a service record. Many customers keep invoices for the home sale.

tips.title: Separate inspection fees from repair work
tips.body: Real estate inspections are often paid by the buyer or agent, not the owner. Invoice the right party and keep the report with the bill so there is no dispute about who ordered what.

tips.title: Pass through disposal costs when they rise
tips.body: Treatment plant tipping fees change. Either review your flat pumping price each year or list disposal as its own line so increases do not come out of your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or by the gallon for pumping?
faqs.answer: Most residential shops charge a flat fee for a standard tank size and add a per-gallon charge only if the tank is larger or you pump more than the base amount. Commercial and grease trap work is more often priced per gallon.

faqs.question: Do I need to put disposal information on the invoice?
faqs.answer: In many states, haulers must keep pumping records or manifests showing where waste went. Listing gallons pumped and the disposal site on the invoice is a simple way to keep that record, but check your state and county rules.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the tank is full of something unexpected, like grease or debris?
faqs.answer: Tell the customer before continuing, then bill the extra time or a heavy-waste surcharge. Note the condition on the invoice. If it was not agreed beforehand, expect pushback.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on septic service?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax services, some tax only parts and materials, and others tax neither. Check with your state revenue department and show any tax as its own line.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer does not pay after a repair?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice and your terms, then a formal demand letter. Depending on your state, you may be able to file a mechanic's lien on larger repair or install jobs, so keep signed estimates and photos of the work.

estimate.intro: Septic companies send estimates for repairs, replacements, new installs, and drain field work, where the cost depends on what is found in the ground. Routine pumping is usually quoted by phone. Customers comparing quotes are looking at scope, permit handling, and whether excavation and restoration are included.

scopeChecklist.why: A conventional gravity system, a pump-assisted system, and an aerobic system have very different costs, so name what you are quoting.
State whether you are replacing a baffle, a pump, a distribution box, lateral lines, or the whole tank, so the customer does not assume a full fix when you quoted a partial one.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, soil tests, and design fees
scopeChecklist.why: These can add hundreds or thousands of dollars and take weeks. Say who pulls the permit and who pays for it.
Disputes often start over grass, landscaping, driveways, or trees. State what you will restore and what you will leave rough graded.
Rock, high water table, or a collapsed line may be found only once digging starts. Explain how extra work will be priced and approved.
State that final payment is due after the health department inspection passes or after completion, whichever you have agreed to.
Material and fuel costs move, and permit timing affects start dates. Give an expiration date and a rough timeline.

pricingTips.title: Price repairs by the job after you have seen the system
pricingTips.body: Do not quote repairs over the phone. A quick look, a probe, or a camera run lets you give a firm number and avoids eating the cost of surprises.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options when it makes sense
pricingTips.body: A failing system might be fixed with a pump and filter now, or by replacing the drain field. Presenting options with costs lets the customer choose and shows why the bigger job is needed.

pricingTips.title: Show materials and labor separately
pricingTips.body: Customers accept line items for tanks, pumps, stone, and pipe more readily than one large number, and it makes change orders easier to explain.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for excavation work
pricingTips.body: Add a reasonable allowance for weather, rock, or a longer pipe run, or state a per-hour or per-yard rate for extras so you are not absorbing the overrun.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most shops do not charge for pumping or simple repair quotes. For installs or system designs that need a site visit, soil work, or drawings, many charge an evaluation fee and credit it toward the job if accepted.

faqs.question: How long should a septic quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for repairs. For installs tied to permits and material pricing, 14 to 30 days is typical. State the date on the quote.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after starting a job?
faqs.answer: Only if the quote says how unknown conditions are handled and the customer agrees to the change in writing. Without that, you are generally held to the quoted price.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: For anything beyond routine pumping, get a signature or written approval. Many states require written contracts for home improvement or installs over a set dollar amount, so check your local rules.

session-musician.intro: Session musicians are hired guns who record or perform on other artists' projects: guitarists, bassists, drummers, keyboardists, string players, horn players, vocalists, and others. They invoice artists, producers, studios, labels, and sometimes ad agencies or game and film composers for tracking time, remote recording, charts, and travel.
session-musician.pricingModel: Most session work is billed per hour, per session (typically a 3-hour block), or per song or track. Local rates for a standard session often run by the hour with a 2 or 3 hour minimum. Remote musicians who record from a home studio usually charge per track, which includes their own engineering, and may add fees for extra revisions or stems. Union (AFM) work follows published scale wages with set session lengths, overtime, and pension and welfare contributions, so union and non-union rates differ. Many players add separate line items for doubling (playing a second instrument), cartage for large gear like drum kits or amps, rush turnarounds, arranging or chart writing, and travel. Rates move up with experience, credits, and the budget behind the project. A flat buyout fee is standard for non-union work, which means you are paid once and typically do not receive royalties unless you negotiate them in writing.

rates.service: Remote track recorded from home studio (guitar, bass, keys)
Remote drum tracks (live kit, mixed or stems)
Strings, horns, or other specialty instruments
Cartage for large gear (drum kit, amps, keyboard rig)

items.description: Studio session: electric and acoustic guitar tracking for 'Harbor Lights' EP (4 songs), 3-hour call
Overtime past scheduled 3-hour call (billed in 30-minute increments)
Doubling: mandolin on 2 songs
Cartage: amp and pedalboard
Remote overdub: additional guitar track for 'Slow Tide', includes one revision round

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. This is a work-for-hire performance fee with no royalty participation unless otherwise agreed in writing. Additional revisions beyond one round are billed at $60 per hour. Session date: March 12. Accepted payment: ACH, Zelle, check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date, studio or location, and call time
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to a specific booking and makes overtime easy to verify against the actual schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Song or project titles and number of tracks delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-song billing requires clear counts, and it prevents disputes over what was included in the fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Instruments played, including doubles
invoiceChecklist.why: Doubling and specialty instruments are often billed separately, so each one should be itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Overtime hours and how they were calculated
invoiceChecklist.why: Sessions run long. Showing the scheduled block and actual end time supports the extra charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cartage, parking, mileage, or travel costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Hauling gear and traveling to a studio are real expenses that clients often forget unless they are listed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and credit terms (work-for-hire, buyout, or royalty split)
invoiceChecklist.why: Putting the payment basis in writing avoids later arguments over royalties, credits, or reuse of your performance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Union scale details if applicable, including contractor and pension and welfare contributions
invoiceChecklist.why: AFM-covered sessions require specific wage and contribution breakdowns, and the engaging party may need them for filings.

session-musician.paymentTerms: Session musicians commonly invoice right after the session, with payment due in 7 to 14 days, though labels and agencies may run net 30 or longer. Some players ask for payment on the day of the session for local studio work, and many ask for 50 percent upfront on remote or multi-song projects. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common to state on the invoice, though enforcement varies. Most musicians accept ACH, Zelle, Venmo, PayPal, or check. Cancellation terms are worth stating, such as full payment for the booked block if cancelled within 24 to 48 hours. If you are working as an independent contractor, you will typically be paid without withholding, so set aside money for taxes. Check your local rules on that.

tips.title: Set a minimum call
tips.body: Charge for a 2 or 3 hour minimum even if the studio finishes early. Travel, setup, and blocked time make short bookings unprofitable otherwise.

tips.title: Agree on revisions before you record
tips.body: Say how many rounds of changes are included, such as one re-take of a part. Charge hourly or per track for revisions beyond that.

tips.title: Bill doubles, rush, and gear separately
tips.body: Line items for a second instrument, same-day turnaround, or cartage make your total defensible and show clients where the money goes.

tips.title: Keep a rights record
tips.body: Note in writing whether you are being paid a flat buyout or have any claim to royalties. A short line on the invoice or the booking email is often enough for small projects.

tips.title: Send the invoice with the files
tips.body: For remote work, deliver the final files and the invoice together, or hold final stems until payment arrives for new clients.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the song?
faqs.answer: In-studio sessions are usually hourly with a minimum. Remote work is usually per song, since you are recording on your own time and equipment. Pick one basis per job and state it up front.

faqs.question: Do session musicians get royalties?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Most non-union session work is a flat fee with no royalties. Union sessions can involve contributions to the AFM and SAG-AFTRA funds under their agreements. If you want a royalty or credit, negotiate it before the session and write it down.

faqs.question: How do I bill for overtime?
faqs.answer: Define the scheduled session length in your booking, such as 3 hours, then bill extra time in 30-minute or hourly increments at your standard rate or a set overtime rate. List the actual start and end times on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a W-9 to the client?
faqs.answer: Many US companies, labels, and studios ask for a W-9 before paying an independent contractor, and may issue a 1099-NEC if payments pass the IRS reporting threshold in a year. Have a W-9 ready, and check current IRS rules.

faqs.question: Can I charge for rehearsal or prep time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if learning parts or writing charts takes real time. Either include it in your rate and state that, or list prep or chart writing as a separate line item.

estimate.intro: Session musicians send quotes when an artist, producer, or composer asks about availability and price for a project, often before hearing the full songs. Clients compare per-song rates, hourly minimums, turnaround times, and what is included, such as revisions, stems, or a home-studio recording chain.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of songs and approximate length or complexity
scopeChecklist.why: A 3-minute folk song and a 7-minute multi-part arrangement take different amounts of time, so the price should reflect scope.
Clarifies which instruments are included in the base price and which will cost extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Where and how you will record
scopeChecklist.why: In-studio and remote work have different costs, such as studio fees, travel, and your own engineering time.
Sets the limit on free changes so a producer's repeated requests do not turn into unpaid work.
Stems, dry and processed tracks, sample rate, and bit depth can all affect your time and the client's expectations.
Gives both sides a delivery date and a basis for charging more when asked to deliver faster.
States whether you are paid a flat fee, whether you receive credit, and whether any royalty applies.

pricingTips.title: Quote from the finished song, not the pitch
pricingTips.body: If possible, ask for a demo or reference track and the chart before quoting. Complex parts, tricky time signatures, or large track counts justify a higher rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer a per-song rate with a cap on revisions
pricingTips.body: Clients like knowing the total price up front. A flat per-song fee with one included revision keeps your income predictable and limits scope creep.

pricingTips.title: Price a tiered rush option
pricingTips.body: Give a standard turnaround and a faster option at a surcharge, such as 25 to 50 percent. Many clients accept it when deadlines are tight.

pricingTips.title: Ask for a deposit on larger projects
pricingTips.body: For an album or multi-song booking, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent secures your dates and covers the risk of cancellations.

faqs.question: Should I quote before hearing the music?
faqs.answer: It is better to hear at least a rough demo first. If you must quote without it, give a range or an hourly estimate with a stated minimum, and note that final pricing depends on the material.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is common. Your calendar and gear availability can change, so state an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the client adds songs after I send a quote?
faqs.answer: Treat additional songs as a new scope. Send an updated quote or add them at the same per-song rate if your original terms allow it.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement for a quote?
faqs.answer: Not always, but an email acceptance of the quote with the scope, price, and rights terms is useful. For bigger projects or unfamiliar clients, a short written agreement is safer.

set-designer.intro: Set designers create the physical environments for theater productions, film and TV shoots, commercials, photo shoots, trade shows, and live events. They bill production companies, theaters, ad agencies, photographers, and event planners for design work, drawings, sourcing, and sometimes the build and materials. Invoices often mix creative fees with reimbursable expenses, so clear itemization matters.
set-designer.pricingModel: Pricing depends on the sector. Theater and regional stage designers usually work for a flat design fee per production, often paid in installments (signing, design approval, opening). Film, TV, and commercial work is commonly a day rate or weekly rate, with prep days billed alongside shoot days. Photo shoot and event set designers often charge a flat project fee or a day rate plus a build budget. Materials, props, rentals, and subcontracted fabrication are usually passed through at cost, with a markup of 10-20% or a separate coordination fee when you manage purchasing. Revisions beyond an agreed number, rush turnarounds, and travel are billed separately. Union designers (such as those under United Scenic Artists) follow contract minimums, so the figures below reflect non-union and small-business work.

rates.service: Theater set design (small to mid-size production)
Commercial or photo shoot set design
Film/TV art department prep and shoot (independent productions)
Event or trade show environment design
Prop and décor sourcing or shopping
Build management and on-site installation supervision

items.description: Set design, regional theater production (concept, model, and design approval installment 2 of 3)
Technical drawings and build package (ground plan, elevations, paint elevations)
Prop and furniture sourcing, 3 shopping days
Build supervision at shop and load-in
Reimbursable materials: lumber, hardware, paint, fabric (receipts attached)
Mileage to lumber yard and rental houses

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Reimbursable expenses are billed at cost with receipts attached. Remaining installment of $1,500 is due on opening night. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Design drawings remain the property of the designer; usage is licensed for this production only.

invoiceChecklist.item: Production title, client name, and PO or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Production companies and theaters route invoices through accounting by job code, and a missing number delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Phase or installment labeled (concept, design approval, build, strike)
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing where the payment falls in the agreed schedule avoids confusion over what has already been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot, load-in, or performance dates covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Day-rate work needs dates so the client can match your charges to their call sheets and schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Prep days listed separately from shoot or install days
invoiceChecklist.why: Prep is often billed at a different rate or count, and separating it heads off disputes over how much time was worked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized reimbursables with receipts or rental invoices
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients reimburse materials from a production budget and usually require backup for each purchase.

invoiceChecklist.item: Markup or coordination fee shown as its own line
invoiceChecklist.why: Hiding markup inside materials costs invites questions; stating it openly keeps the invoice trustworthy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision, rush, and overtime charges tied to the original agreement
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra work outside the agreed scope is easier to collect on when it references the quote or contract terms.

set-designer.paymentTerms: Theater and independent film clients commonly pay in installments: roughly a third at signing, a third at design approval, and a third at load-in or opening. Commercial and agency work is often net 30 and sometimes net 45 or 60, so ask for a deposit of 25-50% on any job with a significant build budget. For large material purchases, request that the client fund the budget up front or pay vendors directly so you are not floating thousands on your own card. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Accepted methods are typically check, ACH, wire, and card, and some production companies pay only through their payroll or accounts payable system.

tips.title: Keep design fees separate from the build budget
tips.body: Invoice your creative fee on its own line from materials and fabrication. Clients often have separate budget lines for each, and it keeps your fee from being squeezed when build costs run over.

tips.title: Get a materials advance before buying
tips.body: Lumber, fabric, and rentals add up fast. Ask for an advance or a client-held credit account so you are not financing the set. Reconcile with receipts on the final invoice.

tips.title: Bill prep and travel, not just shoot days
tips.body: Research, drawing, shopping, and walk-throughs take real time. Set a prep-day rate in your agreement and track hours as you go, so those days show up on the invoice.

tips.title: Define a revision limit
tips.body: Allow a set number of design revisions per phase, such as two rounds of changes after concept. Bill additional rounds hourly and note them on the invoice with dates.

tips.title: Document strike and storage
tips.body: Teardown, hauling, and storing reusable pieces are easy to forget. Add strike days and any storage fees as line items so they are not absorbed into your fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or a day rate for set design?
faqs.answer: Flat fees fit theater and defined projects where scope is clear, such as a single-set photo shoot or a stage production. Day rates fit film, TV, and commercial work where schedules shift. If you quote a flat fee, state what it covers and how changes are billed.

faqs.question: Can I mark up materials and props?
faqs.answer: Yes, many designers add 10-20% to purchased materials or charge a separate coordination fee for sourcing and managing vendors. State the markup in your quote or contract so it is not a surprise on the invoice. Some clients require pass-through at cost, in which case bill your time for purchasing instead.

faqs.question: How do I bill for rentals and props that get damaged?
faqs.answer: Include damage and loss terms in your agreement. Production clients are typically responsible for rented or purchased items during their use. Bill damage fees at the vendor's charge with the vendor's invoice attached.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on my invoices?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and what you sell. Design services are often not taxed, but tangible items you build or sell to the client can be, and resale certificates may apply to materials. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: Who owns the designs after the job is done?
faqs.answer: Unless your contract says otherwise, you generally keep copyright in your drawings and designs, and the client gets a license for the production. If a client wants to reuse or own the design, charge a separate licensing or buyout fee and write it into the agreement.

estimate.intro: Set designers send estimates after a script read, a concept meeting, or a creative brief, and before any drawings or purchasing begin. Clients usually compare your design fee, the total build and materials budget, and how much of the work you manage yourself against other designers or in-house art departments. A clear quote also sets the design budget the director or producer will be working to.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables: sketches, renderings, models, drawings, paint elevations
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume different levels of documentation, and each deliverable takes a different amount of time.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sets, locations, or scenes covered
scopeChecklist.why: Adding a scene or a second location mid-project changes the workload, and the quote should show the baseline.

scopeChecklist.item: Build budget and who controls it
scopeChecklist.why: Stating whether materials, fabrication, and rentals are inside your fee, in a separate client-held budget, or billed as reimbursables prevents surprises.

scopeChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and the rate for extra rounds
scopeChecklist.why: Directors and clients often change their minds, so set a limit before the first concept meeting.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule: concept due, design approval, build dates, load-in, strike
scopeChecklist.why: Compressed timelines and late approvals are the main reason jobs go over, and a schedule gives you grounds for rush fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Services excluded: scenic painting, fabrication, installation, strike, storage
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may assume you handle the build; listing what you do not do avoids unpaid work.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage rights and ownership of drawings
scopeChecklist.why: Defining whether the client is licensed for one production or may reuse the design avoids later disputes.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from days and hours, then cross-check
pricingTips.body: Estimate the hours for concept, drawings, sourcing, and on-site days, then compare the total to the typical flat fee for that kind of production. If the two numbers are far apart, adjust your scope or your price.

pricingTips.title: Quote the design fee and the build estimate separately
pricingTips.body: Give the client one figure for your creative work and another estimate for materials and fabrication. This lets them cut build costs without cutting your fee, and shows where the money goes.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency line
pricingTips.body: Include 10-15% for unforeseen changes in materials pricing, last-minute script revisions, or venue constraints. Say that unused contingency is not billed.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for tight budgets
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option (drawings only), a standard option (drawings plus sourcing), and a full option (design plus build supervision). Clients with limited budgets can choose what to keep.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate or pitch?
faqs.answer: A brief conversation and a rough quote are normally free. If a client wants concept sketches, a mood board, or a rendering to pitch to their own client, charge a pitch or concept fee, and credit it toward the full fee if you get the job.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Lumber, fabric, and rental pricing change, and production calendars fill up, so state an expiration date and note that dates are held only after a deposit.

faqs.question: What happens if the script or scope changes after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Include a change clause stating that significant changes, such as added sets, a new venue, or major revisions after design approval, will be re-quoted or billed hourly. Send a short written change order before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the budget is not set yet?
faqs.answer: Ask for a range or a target build budget before you quote, since set design scales with it. If the client cannot say, give your design fee as a fixed number and the build as a rough estimate with a note that it will be updated after design approval.

shopify-developer.intro: Shopify developers build and maintain online stores for merchants, working as freelancers, small agencies, or contractors for larger agencies. Invoices usually cover theme customization, custom Liquid development, app integrations, store migrations, and ongoing support hours. Many also bill for custom app development, checkout customization, and performance or SEO fixes.
shopify-developer.pricingModel: Most Shopify developers price in one of three ways. Hourly billing is common for small fixes, support, and work with unclear scope, and is often tracked in 15-minute or 30-minute increments. Fixed-fee project pricing is typical for store builds, theme customizations, and migrations, usually split into milestones such as 50% upfront, a middle payment at design or staging approval, and the balance at launch. Monthly retainers cover a set number of support hours, theme updates, and small improvements, with unused hours either expiring or rolling over for a limited time. Work that needs paid third-party apps, premium themes, or stock assets should list those as separate pass-through lines, ideally paid by the client directly through their own Shopify account. Rates tend to rise for Shopify Plus, custom apps using the Admin or Storefront APIs, and rush work. Rate cards are usually split between junior and senior or between design-adjacent and engineering tasks.

rates.service: General Shopify development (theme edits, Liquid, small fixes)
Custom app or API integration development
Shopify Plus checkout and Functions work
Theme setup and customization for a small store
Custom theme build from design files
Store migration (WooCommerce, Magento, BigCommerce to Shopify)
Speed and performance audit with fixes

items.description: Theme customization: homepage sections, product page layout, mobile fixes (milestone 2 of 2)
Product and customer data migration from WooCommerce (CSV import, 600 products, redirects)
Custom Liquid development: size guide modal and metafield-driven product badges
Klaviyo and Shopify Flow setup: abandoned cart and back-in-stock triggers
QA testing across devices and checkout test orders

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. This is the final milestone; the 50% deposit was paid on project start. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Premium theme and app subscriptions are billed to the client's Shopify account and not included here. Thirty days of bug-fix support after launch is included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Store name and myshopify.com URL
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often manage several stores or domains, and this ties the invoice to the right project for their bookkeeper.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or phase name with percentage complete
invoiceChecklist.why: Fixed-fee projects are billed in stages, and naming the milestone shows why this payment is due now.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by task, with dates or a date range
invoiceChecklist.why: For hourly work, task-level detail prevents disputes about what the time covered, such as development versus QA versus meetings.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party app, theme, or license costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs are not your labor revenue, and clients need to see them split out for budgeting and tax records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Link or reference to the signed scope of work or estimate
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the charge to the agreed deliverables and makes it easy to flag out-of-scope change requests.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change request lines with the request date and approval
invoiceChecklist.why: Work added mid-project is the most disputed item, so a written approval reference protects you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger merchants often cannot pay without a PO or reference code on the invoice.

shopify-developer.paymentTerms: Most Shopify developers take a 30% to 50% deposit before starting a fixed-fee project, with the rest tied to milestones such as design approval, staging review, and launch. Hourly and retainer work is usually invoiced monthly or every two weeks, with retainers billed in advance on the first of the month. Net 14 is common for small merchants and net 30 for agencies and larger companies, and many freelancers add a late fee of 1% to 2% per month. Payment is typically by ACH, credit card, or wire; card payments often carry a processing fee that some developers pass on. Final theme or code handoff and removal from staging is commonly held until the last invoice is paid.

tips.title: Tie launch to the final payment
tips.body: Do not push a theme live or hand over admin credentials and repository access until the final milestone is paid. If the client holds the store, you can still keep control of unpublished theme code, custom app deployments, or private app credentials until payment clears.

tips.title: Have the client own their accounts
tips.body: Ask the client to add you as a staff or collaborator account and to pay for apps, themes, and domains directly. This keeps pass-through costs off your invoices, avoids you fronting money, and avoids any ownership confusion.

tips.title: Define what counts as a bug versus a change
tips.body: State a post-launch warranty period, often 14 to 30 days, covering defects in your work only. New features, edits to content, and issues caused by new apps or Shopify platform changes are billed at your hourly rate.

tips.title: Set a minimum for small tasks
tips.body: Quick fixes still cost you context switching. Use a minimum of 30 or 60 minutes per request, or bundle small items into a prepaid block of hours.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed-fee jobs
tips.body: Logging hours against a flat fee shows you where projects run over, helps you price the next one, and gives you evidence when scope creep needs a change order.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a Shopify build?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when scope is clear, such as a defined theme customization with a page list and feature list. Use hourly when requirements are fuzzy, the client keeps changing direction, or the work is troubleshooting. Many developers do a fixed fee for the core build and hourly for anything outside the written scope.

faqs.question: How do I bill for paid apps and themes?
faqs.answer: The cleanest approach is for the client to buy them under their own Shopify account. If you must purchase on their behalf, list the exact cost as a separate line and keep the receipt. Marking up app costs is possible but should be disclosed in your agreement.

faqs.question: Can I bill for discovery, audits, and meetings?
faqs.answer: Yes. Discovery, requirements gathering, store audits, and project calls are real work and are often billed as a separate paid phase before the build. Include them as their own line items rather than hiding them in the build price.

faqs.question: What if the client wants unlimited revisions?
faqs.answer: Set a fixed number of revision rounds in your scope, commonly two for design review and one for staging QA. Additional rounds are billed hourly. Put this in writing before you start.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on development services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax custom software or digital services, and others do not tax professional services at all. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax charged on a separate line.

estimate.intro: Shopify developers send estimates when a merchant asks for a build, migration, or custom feature and compares proposals from several freelancers or agencies. Clients usually compare total price, timeline, what is and is not included, and whether you have built similar stores. A clear quote with defined deliverables is often what separates you from a cheaper but vaguer bid.

scopeChecklist.item: Theme approach: existing theme customization versus custom build
scopeChecklist.why: Starting from a free or premium theme and building from scratch differ hugely in cost, and clients often assume the cheaper one when they see a custom design.
Naming the homepage, collection, product, cart, blog, and any landing page templates sets a limit on what is included.
List each feature, such as a subscription app, product bundler, ERP sync, or custom metafields, so nothing is assumed to be included.
State the number of products, customers, orders, and redirects, and whether you will clean up the source data, since messy data can double the effort.
Clarify who supplies copy, images, logos, and design files, and what happens to the timeline if assets arrive late.
Setting a number of rounds and listing the browsers and devices you will test avoids endless feedback cycles.
Defines how long you fix defects for free and what is billed separately, such as Shopify updates or new third-party app conflicts.

pricingTips.title: Break the quote into phases
pricingTips.body: Show discovery, design or theme setup, build, migration, QA, and launch as separate lines. Clients can see where the money goes, and it makes it easier to remove or defer a piece instead of negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Quote app and theme costs separately
pricingTips.body: List expected monthly app fees and theme licenses as client-paid costs so they can see the full cost of running the store, not just your development fee.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for ambiguous projects
pricingTips.body: A basic, standard, and extended version, for example theme setup only, setup plus custom sections, and full custom build, helps clients choose a budget and reduces back-and-forth.

pricingTips.title: Add contingency for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Migrations from older platforms and projects involving third-party APIs hide surprises. Add a buffer of 10% to 20% or state that API or data problems found later will be quoted as a change order.

faqs.question: How long should a Shopify estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Shopify platform changes, your availability, and app pricing can all shift, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For large or complex projects such as custom apps or Plus builds, many developers charge for a paid discovery or scoping phase, sometimes credited toward the build if the client moves forward.

faqs.question: What if the final cost goes over my estimate?
faqs.answer: With a fixed fee, you absorb overruns caused by your own errors, but additional work requested by the client should go through a written change order. With an hourly estimate, give a range and notify the client when you reach about 80% of the upper figure.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the estimate?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. The estimate gives the price and scope, while a contract covers IP ownership, payment schedule, revisions, and termination. Many developers combine both into one proposal the client signs before work starts.

shopify-store.intro: Online store owners usually collect payment at checkout, but invoices come up whenever an order falls outside the normal cart: wholesale and bulk orders, corporate gifting, custom or made-to-order products, pre-orders, and repeat B2B accounts on net terms. These invoices are sent by solo makers, resellers, and small brands who bill other businesses or organizations for products, customization, and shipping.
shopify-store.pricingModel: Most stores price from a retail price list and then adjust for the order type. Wholesale is commonly set at roughly 40-55% off retail, often with a minimum order quantity or minimum dollar amount. Volume tiers lower the unit price at set quantities such as 25, 50, or 100 units. Custom work adds a one-time setup fee plus a per-unit personalization charge. Shipping is either passed through at actual cost, billed as a flat handling rate, or built into the unit price. Rush production, special packaging, and gift wrapping are separate line items. Large or custom orders usually require a deposit before production or purchasing starts, with the balance due at shipment or on net terms for established accounts.

rates.service: Wholesale unit price (as a share of retail)
Custom order setup (artwork, label, or engraving prep)
Personalization such as monogram, engraving, or custom print
Custom or branded packaging and gift wrapping
Handling and packing for multi-box shipments
Freight or pallet shipping (passed through at cost)
Restocking fee on returned non-custom wholesale goods

items.description: Soy candle, 8 oz, assorted scents (wholesale)
Gift set, 3-candle box (wholesale)
Custom label setup, boutique logo
Custom label application
Shipping, 3 boxes via ground (actual cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Order #W-1042. 50% deposit received before production; balance due net 30 from ship date. Sales tax not charged; resale certificate on file. Custom-labeled items are non-returnable. Report damaged goods within 7 days of delivery with photos.

invoiceChecklist.item: Order number, PO number, and order date
invoiceChecklist.why: Wholesale buyers match invoices to their own purchase orders, and many will not pay without a PO reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: SKU, product name, variant, and quantity for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents disputes over sizes, colors, or scents and lets the buyer check the shipment against the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wholesale or tiered unit price and any discount applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the price was reached so the buyer does not ask why it differs from the website.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax status and resale certificate reference
invoiceChecklist.why: In many states, sales to a reseller with a valid certificate are tax-exempt, and you need the certificate on file to justify not charging tax. Check your state's rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shipping method, carrier, tracking numbers, and cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Separates shipping from product cost and gives the buyer proof of when goods left your hands.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear what has been paid and what remains, especially on custom or pre-order work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Return, damage, and custom-item policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Sets the terms for claims and states that personalized goods cannot be returned, before an argument starts.

shopify-store.paymentTerms: Online stores selling to consumers get paid at checkout, but B2B invoices follow different norms. New wholesale accounts are often asked to prepay or pay by card on the first order, then move to net 15 or net 30 after a few clean orders. Custom and made-to-order work commonly requires a 30-50% deposit before purchasing materials or starting production, with the balance due before shipping. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated on the invoice or in your wholesale terms in advance. Accepted methods typically include ACH bank transfer, card, and check; card payments on large orders carry processing fees, so some stores add a surcharge or offer an ACH discount where local rules allow it.

tips.title: Hold shipment until the deposit or balance clears
tips.body: For custom goods you cannot resell if the buyer walks away. Do not release the order until the agreed payment has cleared, and say so on the invoice.

tips.title: Keep resale certificates on file
tips.body: Collect a certificate from each tax-exempt wholesale customer before the first invoice, and note its expiration. Without it you may owe the tax yourself if audited.

tips.title: Bill shipping as its own line
tips.body: Combining shipping into product prices hides cost swings. A separate line lets you pass through actual carrier charges and adjust for freight on heavy orders.

tips.title: Set a minimum order
tips.body: A $150-300 minimum, or a minimum quantity per SKU, keeps small wholesale orders from costing more to pack and invoice than they earn.

tips.title: Invoice at shipment, not at order
tips.body: Net terms start from the invoice date. Sending it the day the order ships starts the clock at the right time and avoids invoicing for backordered items.

faqs.question: Do I need to send an invoice if the customer already paid at checkout?
faqs.answer: Usually not; the order confirmation works as a receipt. Send an invoice for orders you build manually, for wholesale accounts, for deposits and balances, and whenever a buyer needs a document for their accounting.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a wholesale customer who is tax-exempt?
faqs.answer: Get a valid resale or exemption certificate from the buyer, keep it on file, and show the tax as zero with a note referencing the certificate. Rules differ by state, so check your state's department of revenue.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit on custom orders?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. A deposit of 30-50% covers materials and setup and protects you if the buyer cancels after you have made personalized items. State the deposit amount and refund terms on the quote and invoice.

faqs.question: How do I handle partial shipments or backorders?
faqs.answer: Invoice only for what shipped, and list backordered items as pending with an expected date. Send a new invoice when the rest ships, or issue one invoice with the shipped and remaining amounts clearly separated.

faqs.question: What do I do if a buyer short-pays because of damaged goods?
faqs.answer: Ask for photos and the order number, then issue a credit memo or replacement for the verified amount. Keep the original invoice intact and reference the credit so your records match the buyer's.

estimate.intro: Store owners send quotes before bulk, wholesale, corporate gifting, and custom orders, where the price depends on quantity, customization, and shipping. Buyers usually compare unit price, minimum order, production lead time, and total landed cost against other suppliers.

scopeChecklist.why: Price tiers depend on quantity, so changes in count or mix after approval change the total.
Spell out logo, text, colors, and placement, and require written approval of a proof so errors in supplied artwork do not become your cost.
Buyers plan around events and restocks; state lead time from deposit and proof approval, not from the quote date.

scopeChecklist.item: Shipping method, destination, and who pays
scopeChecklist.why: Freight can be a large share of the total and varies by address, so say whether it is estimated, flat, or billed at actual cost.
State whether tax is included, excluded, or exempt with a resale certificate so the final invoice matches the quote.
Supplier costs and stock change, so limit how long the prices hold.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment terms, and cancellation or return rules
scopeChecklist.why: Sets expectations on when money is due and that custom items cannot be returned.

pricingTips.title: Build in tiered pricing
pricingTips.body: Show unit prices at two or three quantity breaks, such as 25, 50, and 100. Buyers often move up a tier once they see the per-unit savings.

pricingTips.title: Quote the landed cost
pricingTips.body: Include product, customization, packaging, and estimated shipping in one total so the buyer can compare it with competitors fairly, while keeping each line visible.

pricingTips.title: Price in your setup costs
pricingTips.body: Artwork prep, sample production, and packing time are real costs on small custom runs. Charge a flat setup fee rather than hiding it in the unit price.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer on stock-dependent items
pricingTips.body: If a quote depends on materials or inventory you do not yet hold, note that prices are subject to supplier changes after the expiration date.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. Use a shorter window if your supplier prices or stock levels change often.

faqs.question: Should I charge for samples before a bulk order?
faqs.answer: Many stores charge for the sample and shipping, then credit that amount toward the bulk order if it is placed within a set period. This filters out buyers who are not serious.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the buyer accepts the quote?
faqs.answer: Only for changes in scope, such as quantity, customization, or shipping address, or if the quote has expired. Otherwise honor the quoted price, and say this in your terms.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote for custom orders?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A signed or emailed written acceptance, together with proof approval, gives you documentation if the buyer later disputes quantities, designs, or price.

short-term-rental-cleaning.intro: Short term rental cleaners handle turnovers for Airbnb, VRBO, and vacation rental properties between guest stays. They invoice property owners, hosts, and property management companies for turnover cleans, linen service, restocking, deep cleans, and extras such as laundry or damage reporting. Most work is recurring, so invoices often cover a batch of turnovers across a week or month.
short-term-rental-cleaning.pricingModel: Most short term rental cleaners charge a flat fee per turnover, set by the number of bedrooms and bathrooms, with a higher price for larger or more detailed properties. Some charge hourly, usually when the property condition varies a lot or the owner wants a time-based arrangement. Extras are billed separately: laundry by the load or pound, linen rental or supply, restocking of consumables (billed at cost plus a modest markup), deep cleans, hot tub or outdoor area cleaning, and same-day or last-minute fees. Many cleaners also add a fee for travel to remote properties, and charge a reduced or full fee for late cancellations or when guests extend a stay and the clean cannot happen. Property managers with many units often negotiate a volume rate, while individual hosts typically pay standard per-turnover pricing.
