Some cleaners pass the guest-facing cleaning fee through, so it helps to agree up front whether pricing is per turnover or a share of what the guest pays.

rates.service: Deep clean or reset between long stays

items.description: Turnover clean - 2BR/2BA, Lakeview Cabin (Oct 3, 7, 12, 18)
Off-site laundry - sheets and towels, king and queen sets
Restock supplies (toiletries, coffee pods, paper towels) at cost plus 15%
Same-day turnover surcharge (Oct 12)
Hot tub wipe-down and cover cleaning

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Damage or maintenance issues were reported by text with photos on the dates above. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property name or address for each turnover
invoiceChecklist.why: Owners and managers with multiple units need to match each charge to a specific property for their own bookkeeping.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of each clean listed individually
invoiceChecklist.why: Lets the host reconcile against their booking calendar and catch any missed or duplicate turnovers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property size tier (bedrooms and bathrooms)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the per-turnover rate was set and prevents disputes if a listing is later changed to sleep more guests.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for laundry, linens, and restocking
invoiceChecklist.why: Supplies and laundry are often reimbursed or passed to guests differently from labor, so owners want them itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Receipts or cost basis for supplies purchased
invoiceChecklist.why: Hosts frequently deduct these as business expenses and may ask for backup, especially with a markup applied.

invoiceChecklist.item: Notes on damage, missing items, or maintenance reported
invoiceChecklist.why: Creates a dated record the host can use for guest damage claims or repair scheduling.

invoiceChecklist.item: Surcharges for same-day, late checkout, or extended stays
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes extra charges visible and tied to a specific event rather than looking like a rate increase.

short-term-rental-cleaning.paymentTerms: Recurring clients are commonly invoiced weekly, biweekly, or monthly, with payment due in 7 to 14 days. Some cleaners charge per turnover with payment due within a day or two for new or small hosts. New clients often pay a deposit or pay the first clean up front, and deep cleans or large properties may require half upfront. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common but should be written into your agreement. Payment is usually by bank transfer, card, or a payment app, and many cleaners set up automatic card billing on file for recurring hosts to avoid chasing payments. Keep a clear cancellation policy, since last-minute booking changes are routine in this business.

tips.title: Price by property size, not by guest count
tips.body: Bedrooms, bathrooms, and square footage drive your time. Set clear tiers and re-quote if a host adds a sofa bed, hot tub, or extra bathroom to the listing.

tips.title: Bill supplies and laundry as their own lines
tips.body: Folding consumables into the clean price hides your costs. Separate lines protect your margin and make it easy to adjust if supply prices rise.

tips.title: Include photo reports in your process
tips.body: Send before and after photos or a damage report on the day of the clean, and note it on the invoice. It speeds up approval and supports you if a guest disputes anything.

tips.title: Set a policy for cancelled and shortened stays
tips.body: When a booking is cancelled the day of, you may still have held the time slot. A reduced cancellation fee written in your agreement keeps this from becoming an argument.

tips.title: Review rates for holiday and peak weeks
tips.body: Many cleaners add a modest surcharge for holidays, peak-season same-day turnovers, or properties that need constant coverage. State it in advance rather than adding it afterward.

faqs.question: Should I charge per turnover or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Flat per-turnover pricing is most common because hosts can predict costs and it matches how they set their guest cleaning fee. Hourly works better when properties vary in condition, but it can lead to pushback if a clean takes longer than expected.

faqs.question: Can I charge more when a property is left very dirty?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Many cleaners include a clause for excessive mess, with extra time billed at an hourly rate. Take photos and note it on the invoice so the host understands the charge.

faqs.question: Who pays for supplies like toilet paper and soap?
faqs.answer: It depends on your agreement. Some hosts provide supplies, others expect you to buy and bill them back. If you purchase them, list the cost on the invoice, usually with a small markup for the time spent shopping and carrying inventory.

faqs.question: How often should I invoice a host with many bookings?
faqs.answer: Weekly or biweekly works well for busy properties because balances stay small and cash flow stays steady. Monthly invoicing is fine for lower-volume hosts, but the total can feel large if turnovers pile up.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It varies by state and sometimes by city. Some places tax cleaning services or the goods you resell, and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional before adding or leaving out tax.

estimate.intro: Short term rental cleaners send estimates when a host or property manager is choosing a cleaner, adding a new property, or asking about one-time services like a deep clean or a post-renovation reset. Clients usually compare per-turnover price, how reliably you meet check-in deadlines, and what is included in the price.

scopeChecklist.why: Bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, and number of floors determine time and price, and they stop disputes if the property differs from what was described.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact tasks included in a standard turnover
scopeChecklist.why: Spell out whether it covers linens, dishes, trash, restocking, and wiping appliances so the host knows what the price buys.
State whether you wash on-site, take linens off-site, or use a commercial linen service, since this affects time and cost.
Cleaning products, consumables, and equipment can be a major cost; clarify who buys what and how supplies are billed.
Note the expected check-out to check-in window and how you handle same-day or back-to-back bookings.
Hot tubs, patios, inside the oven, windows, and heavy-duty cleaning are often add-ons that should be priced separately.
Spell out fees for last-minute cancellations, access problems, or guests who have not left on time.

pricingTips.title: Quote a flat rate with defined add-ons
pricingTips.body: Hosts like a single per-turnover price with a short add-on list, such as laundry, extra beds, or hot tub care. It keeps comparisons simple and shields you from unlimited scope creep.

pricingTips.title: Walk through the property before quoting
pricingTips.body: A quick visit or video tour reveals things that change time, like many beds, tight bathrooms, or heavy furniture. Quoting from the listing alone often underestimates the work.

pricingTips.title: Offer volume pricing for multiple units
pricingTips.body: Property managers expect some discount for several properties or frequent turnovers. Build in a small reduction based on guaranteed volume rather than cutting your standard rate across the board.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on your quote
pricingTips.body: Labor and supply costs shift over time, so quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from honoring old rates after a long delay.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate visit?
faqs.answer: Most cleaners offer free estimates or video walk-throughs for recurring work. For large properties or one-time deep cleans that need a long on-site visit, some charge a fee and credit it to the first job.

faqs.question: What if the property turns out to be bigger or messier than quoted?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying the quote is based on the stated size and condition, and that you may adjust the price if the property differs. Tell the host before work begins and document it with photos.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of one price?
faqs.answer: For one-time deep cleans or properties in rough shape, a range is reasonable until you see the space. For routine turnovers, a single flat price is clearer and more competitive.

faqs.question: How do I handle price changes after the first quote?
faqs.answer: Review rates once or twice a year and give recurring clients written notice, usually 30 days. Explain the change in plain terms, such as higher supply costs or added property features.

shuttle-service.intro: Shuttle services move groups of people on set routes or charter schedules: airport transfers, hotel and resort loops, wedding guest transport, corporate event shuttles, campus and hospital runs, and brewery or winery tours. Owners and small fleet operators invoice hotels, event planners, businesses, schools, and private groups for trips, hours of vehicle time, and related charges.
shuttle-service.pricingModel: Shuttle work is priced in a few ways depending on the job. Charter and event work is usually billed per hour per vehicle with a minimum of 3 to 5 hours, because the vehicle and driver are committed for the whole block. Airport and point-to-point transfers are often a flat rate per trip or per person, with distance zones. Recurring contracts for hotels, employers, or campuses are commonly a monthly fee or a fixed rate per run or per route-hour. Most operators add separate lines for driver gratuity (or an auto-gratuity of 15 to 20 percent), tolls, parking, fuel surcharges on long trips, wait time past a grace period, deadhead or garage-to-garage mileage for remote pickups, and after-hours or holiday premiums. Vehicle size drives the base rate: a 14-passenger van costs less than a 30-passenger minibus or a 56-passenger coach.

rates.unit: per vehicle, per hour (3-5 hr minimum)

rates.service: Extra wait time past grace period

items.description: Wedding guest shuttle, 28-passenger minibus, Saturday 3:00 PM-11:00 PM (hotel to venue loop), 6 hr minimum applied
Second minibus, same schedule
Saturday premium surcharge, per vehicle
Extra wait time past 15-minute grace, venue departure
Tolls and venue parking fee
Driver gratuity (18% of transport charges)

sampleInvoice.notes: Booking confirmation #2291, deposit of $500 received 3/2 and applied. Balance due within 7 days of event date. Payment by ACH, check, or card (3% card fee). Overtime beyond the contracted end time is billed at $140 per hour per vehicle.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip date, pickup and drop-off locations, and scheduled times
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have to reconcile the invoice against the itinerary, and this settles disputes about when the clock started and stopped.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle type, capacity, and number of vehicles
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates change by vehicle size, so the client should see exactly what was provided and billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billable hours with start and end times, including minimums and garage-to-garage time
invoiceChecklist.why: Most charters bill from dispatch to return, and a minimum may apply. Showing the calculation prevents pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wait time, extra stops, and overtime as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Changes made on the day are the most common source of disputes, so itemize them against the original booking.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, parking, fuel surcharge, and airport fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should be shown separately so the client sees they are not part of the base rate. Keep receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Gratuity or auto-gratuity line
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients and event planners need to know whether tip is included, and drivers need a clear record of what was charged.

invoiceChecklist.item: Operating authority details, such as USDOT or state permit number, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate and school clients often require proof of authority and insurance for vendor records. Check what applies to your operation and state.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or booking reference and deposits already paid
invoiceChecklist.why: Businesses and schools often won't pay without a PO, and showing deposits avoids double billing.

shuttle-service.paymentTerms: Most shuttle operators take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the vehicle and driver for charters and events, with the balance due before the trip or within 7 to 15 days afterward. Corporate, hotel, and school accounts are often net 15 to net 30, sometimes net 45 for larger organizations. Cancellation terms matter: many operators keep the deposit if the client cancels within 7 to 14 days of the date. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is typically by ACH, check, or card, and some operators pass on a card processing fee. For one-time private clients, collecting the balance before the trip reduces the risk of chasing payment later.

tips.title: Put minimums and the billing clock in writing
tips.body: State the hourly minimum and that time runs garage to garage or from first pickup to last drop-off. Repeat it on the invoice so the client sees the same terms they agreed to.

tips.title: Log actual times on every trip
tips.body: Driver trip sheets with timestamps for arrival, loading, departure, and return are your proof if a client disputes wait time or overtime. Attach or reference them when billing extras.

tips.title: Bill changes the same day you approve them
tips.body: If an event planner adds a stop or extends the run by an hour, get it confirmed by text or email and add it to the final invoice right away. Waiting a week makes it harder to collect.

tips.title: Use auto-gratuity for groups
tips.body: Charter groups often assume tip is included. Adding a stated gratuity percentage to the quote and invoice keeps driver pay consistent and avoids awkward conversations on the day.

tips.title: Invoice recurring contracts on a fixed schedule
tips.body: For hotel, employer, or campus routes, invoice on the same day each month and list extra runs or special events as separate lines on top of the base fee.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat rate?
faqs.answer: Charters, weddings, and events are usually hourly with a minimum. Airport transfers and fixed-route runs are better as flat per-trip or per-person rates. Contracts can be monthly. Pick the model that matches how your costs behave: if the vehicle is tied up for hours, bill time.

faqs.question: Can I charge for deadhead miles and return trips?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so in the quote. Many operators bill garage to garage or add a mileage charge for pickups outside their service area. If the client hasn't agreed to it beforehand, it is hard to add afterward.

faqs.question: How do I handle sales tax on shuttle service?
faqs.answer: It varies by state and by type of service. Some states tax charter or ground transportation, some exempt it, and some tax only certain fees. Check with your state department of revenue or an accountant, and show any tax as its own line.

faqs.question: What do I do when a client's group runs over the booked time?
faqs.answer: Bill overtime at the rate in your contract, usually your hourly rate or a higher overtime rate, in set increments such as 15 or 30 minutes. Reference your trip log on the invoice.

faqs.question: Is a deposit refundable if the event is canceled?
faqs.answer: That depends on your terms. Many operators make deposits nonrefundable inside a set window, since the vehicle and driver were reserved and other bookings may have been turned away. State the policy in the quote, contract, and invoice.

estimate.intro: Shuttle operators send quotes before nearly every charter, event, or contract job, since the client needs to confirm availability and compare prices across several companies. Clients usually compare the hourly rate, minimum hours, vehicle size, and which extras are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Date, pickup and drop-off addresses, and the full schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Time and distance drive the price. An itinerary with specific times prevents disagreements about what was booked.
Capacity determines which vehicle you assign and the rate. Note what happens if the headcount changes.

scopeChecklist.item: Hourly minimum and how billable time is calculated
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether time runs garage to garage or from first pickup, and whether a minimum applies.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included and what is extra
scopeChecklist.why: List tolls, parking, fuel surcharge, gratuity, wait time, and extra stops so the client knows which costs can be added later.
Events run late. Setting the grace period and overtime rate up front keeps late-night charges from becoming arguments.
Spells out how the date is held and what the client forfeits if they cancel.
Venues and corporate clients may need a certificate of insurance. Say you can provide one and name any needed details.

pricingTips.title: Price from total vehicle time, not the event length
pricingTips.body: Include travel to the first pickup, loading time, and return to the garage. A four-hour wedding may be six hours of vehicle time, so quote that.

pricingTips.title: Offer vehicle options
pricingTips.body: Show a quote for a van and a minibus, or one large vehicle versus two smaller ones, so the client can choose by budget and passenger flow.

pricingTips.title: Add peak-date premiums
pricingTips.body: Prom season, New Year's Eve, holiday weekends, and major local events fill up quickly. Add a clear premium rather than discounting when demand is high.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fuel costs, driver availability, and vehicle schedules change. State that the price is held for 7 to 14 days, or until a deposit is received.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat quote or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: For events with a fixed schedule, a flat quote with stated hours and overtime terms is easy for clients to compare. If the schedule is uncertain, quote hourly with a minimum and an estimated total.

faqs.question: How far ahead can I hold a price?
faqs.answer: Many operators hold a quote for 7 to 14 days and only lock the date and rate once a deposit is paid. For events more than a few months out, note that fuel or tax changes may affect the final price.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price than my quote?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope instead of the rate: a smaller vehicle, fewer hours, a shorter route, or an off-peak time. Cutting the rate while keeping the same work leaves less margin for fuel, driver pay, and maintenance.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement for a quote?
faqs.answer: For most charters, yes. A quote with accepted terms, signed or confirmed by email, along with a deposit, protects both sides if the date changes or the client cancels.

siding-installer.intro: Siding installers are solo contractors and small crews who hang vinyl, fiber cement, wood, engineered wood, and metal siding on homes and light commercial buildings. Invoices cover the installed siding by the square, tear-off and disposal, house wrap and flashing, trim and soffit work, and any rot repair found once the old siding comes off.
siding-installer.pricingModel: Most siding work is priced by the square (100 square feet of wall area) or by the square foot, installed, with the price changing by material. Vinyl is the cheapest, and fiber cement, cedar, and metal cost more because they take more labor and are harder to handle. Tear-off and disposal, house wrap, trim, soffit and fascia, and window and door wrapping are usually separate line items. Rot repair is billed as extra work, either by the hour plus materials or at a unit price set in the contract, such as per sheet of sheathing or per linear foot of replaced trim. Many contractors take a deposit to order materials, then bill the balance on completion. Larger jobs may add a progress payment when the material is delivered or when the first elevations are done. Materials are either included in a per-square price or itemized with a markup of about 10 to 25 percent, and the invoice should make clear which method applies.

rates.service: Siding repair (small patch or replace damaged panels)

items.description: Tear off and dispose of existing vinyl siding, 2-story colonial
Install house wrap and seam tape on all elevations
Install James Hardie 7.25 in. lap siding, primed and painted ColorPlus finish
Replace rotted sheathing and corner trim found at rear wall (2 hours x 2 crew)
Install PVC trim at windows, doors, and corners
Caulk, flash, and seal all penetrations

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $8,000 received on signing. Balance due within 7 days of completion and final walkthrough. Rot repair was not in the original quote and is billed per approved change order dated 5/14. Accepted payment: check, ACH, or card (3% fee on card). Manufacturer warranty registration provided at payment. Workmanship warranty is 5 years.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job address and scope by elevation or area
invoiceChecklist.why: Tells the client exactly which walls were done, which matters on partial jobs or when they've got multiple buildings, such as a house and a garage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Total squares installed and how they were measured
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-square pricing is the core of the bill, and clients often question the number. Showing the quantity avoids disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Siding product, brand, profile, and color
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents arguments over what was ordered and provides a record for warranty claims or future repairs and matching.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders for rot, extra trim, or added walls
invoiceChecklist.why: Hidden damage is common once old siding is off. A signed or dated change order line protects you when the final bill exceeds the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tear-off, disposal, and dumpster costs
invoiceChecklist.why: These costs are easy to forget and are often a significant part of the total. Separate lines show where the money went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license and insurance info, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a contractor license number on contracts and invoices. Check your local rules. Proof of insurance also helps clients and insurers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear running total keeps the final payment simple and avoids confusion over what has already been paid.

siding-installer.paymentTerms: Siding contractors commonly collect a deposit of 10 to 50 percent at signing, depending on material cost and local rules, since some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts. On larger jobs, a second payment at material delivery or at the halfway point is common, and the final balance is due on completion, often net 7 or due on the day of the final walkthrough. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment methods include check, ACH, and card, and some contractors add a processing fee for card payments. If the job is paid by an insurance claim after storm damage, expect the check to pass through the homeowner and sometimes a mortgage company, which can slow things down, so state your terms clearly.

tips.title: Measure and record squares before you quote
tips.body: Take wall measurements, subtract large openings per your usual method, and add a waste factor of about 10 percent. Save the numbers so you can defend the quantity on the invoice if questioned.

tips.title: Put a rot and hidden damage clause in the contract
tips.body: State a unit price for replacing sheathing, trim, or framing, such as per sheet or per hour, so extra work doesn't have to be negotiated with half the siding already removed.

tips.title: Bill material deposits to cover your supplier order
tips.body: Custom-colored or special-order siding is hard to return. A deposit that covers the material keeps you from carrying the cost until the job is finished.

tips.title: Get sign-off at the final walkthrough
tips.body: Walk the house with the client, note any touch-ups, and have them acknowledge completion. Invoice the balance the same day to reduce the chance of delayed payment.

tips.title: Handle insurance jobs carefully
tips.body: On storm claims, don't promise to waive the deductible, which is illegal in many states. Bill the homeowner clearly for what the insurer covers and what they owe.

faqs.question: How do I bill siding: by the square or by the square foot?
faqs.answer: Either is fine, but a square is 100 square feet, so make sure the invoice shows which one you used. Most contractors quote by the square because material and labor rates are normally given that way.

faqs.question: Should I include materials in the per-square price?
faqs.answer: You can, and many do for a simple all-in price. If you itemize, list siding, wrap, trim, and fasteners separately with your markup built in. Pick one method and keep it consistent with what your quote said.

faqs.question: How do I charge for extra work I find after tear-off?
faqs.answer: Write up a change order with a description, price, and the client's approval before doing the work, then list it as a separate line on the final invoice. Even a signed text or email is better than a verbal agreement.

faqs.question: When should I send the final invoice?
faqs.answer: Send it the day the job is complete and the walkthrough is done. Include the deposit already paid and the balance due, plus the payment methods you accept.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on siding jobs?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. In many states a contractor pays tax on materials and doesn't charge it to the client on a lump-sum job, while others require tax on the total or on materials separately. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

estimate.intro: Siding installers give written estimates before any work starts, usually after a site visit to measure walls and inspect the existing siding and sheathing. Homeowners often compare two or three bids, looking at the product, the price per square, whether tear-off and trim are included, and the warranty.

scopeChecklist.item: Total squares and the walls included
scopeChecklist.why: Shows how the price was built and prevents arguments if the client thought a garage, gable, or dormer was part of the job.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact siding product, brand, profile, and color
scopeChecklist.why: Prices vary widely between a builder-grade vinyl and a premium fiber cement, so naming the product makes bids comparable.
Some bids leave out removing the old siding or hauling it away. State whether it is included and how many layers you're allowing for.

scopeChecklist.item: Underlayment, wrap, flashing, and trim details
scopeChecklist.why: Housewrap, window flashing, and trim material affect both performance and cost. Spelling them out keeps your bid from looking more expensive than a bid that omitted them.
State that sheathing and framing repairs are extra and give a unit price so surprises don't become disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Start window, duration, and weather delays
scopeChecklist.why: Siding is weather dependent. Giving an estimated schedule and noting that rain or wind can shift it avoids complaints.
State your workmanship warranty, who pulls any needed permit, and how long the price is good, since material prices change.

pricingTips.title: Price from squares plus add-ons
pricingTips.body: Start with total squares at your per-square rate, then add tear-off, wrap, trim, soffit, and repair allowances as separate lines. Clients can then see why one bid is higher than another.

pricingTips.title: Build in waste and material price changes
pricingTips.body: Include about 10 percent waste for lap siding, more for diagonal or intricate layouts. For quotes valid 30 days or less, you protect yourself from supplier price increases.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting vinyl, fiber cement, and an upgraded trim package side by side helps clients choose by budget rather than just picking the lowest number.

pricingTips.title: Explain the price of insulation or wrap upgrades
pricingTips.body: If you recommend continuous foam or a better weather barrier, show it as an optional line. Clients are more willing to pay when they see what it does.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most siding contractors give free estimates for full-house jobs. For complicated work, such as storm damage documentation or repairs requiring a lot of investigation, a fee that is credited back if the client hires you is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a siding quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Material prices can change, and fiber cement and trim products have had frequent increases, so a short expiration date protects your margin.

faqs.question: Can I give a flat price if I haven't seen behind the old siding?
faqs.answer: You can, but state that the price assumes sound sheathing and framing. Include a unit price for repairs so any extra work is already agreed upon in principle.

faqs.question: What if the client wants me to match my bid to a competitor's?
faqs.answer: Compare the scope first. Differences in product, tear-off, flashing, or warranty often explain the gap. If you do lower the price, adjust the scope in writing rather than cutting corners on installation.

sign-maker.intro: Sign makers design, fabricate, and install signage for businesses, property owners, and events. Typical invoices cover storefront and channel letter signs, vinyl lettering and vehicle graphics, banners, monument and pylon signs, and the permits, installation labor, and equipment needed to put them up.
sign-maker.pricingModel: Most sign work is priced per job as a flat fee built from several parts: design time, materials, fabrication labor, and installation. Flat items such as banners, yard signs, and decals are often priced per square foot or per piece, with quantity discounts on repeat orders. Vinyl lettering and vehicle wraps are commonly priced per square foot of printed or cut material plus an hourly or flat install charge. Custom fabricated signs (channel letters, routed or dimensional signs, illuminated cabinets) are quoted per project, with materials marked up 30-100% over cost depending on the shop. Installation is billed hourly or per trip, with extra for bucket truck or lift rental, travel, and engineered drawings. Permits are typically passed through at cost plus a handling fee. Many shops charge a minimum order or setup fee for small jobs and ask for 50% down on custom work.

rates.service: Aluminum or coroplast panel sign, printed

rates.unit: per letter / per inch of height
rates.range: $40-150 per letter for typical storefront sizes

rates.service: Bucket truck or lift and travel

items.description: Design and layout, storefront sign (2 proof revisions)
Aluminum composite sign panel, 24 x 96 in, digitally printed with laminate
Cut vinyl window lettering, hours and logo
Mounting hardware and standoffs
On-site installation, two technicians
Lift rental and travel

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $500 received on approval of proof. Balance due within 15 days of installation. Artwork was approved in writing on the proof dated as shown; changes after approval are billed at the design hourly rate. Warranty: 1 year on workmanship, 3 years on printed graphics against fading when installed as specified.

invoiceChecklist.item: Proof approval date and proof or job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the exact artwork the client signed off on, which settles disputes over spelling, colors, and sizing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized dimensions and quantity for each sign
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing by square foot or per piece only makes sense if the client can see the sizes and counts they paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Material and finish specifications
invoiceChecklist.why: Substrate, vinyl brand or grade, laminate, and LED type affect cost and lifespan and support any warranty claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit fees and who obtained them
invoiceChecklist.why: Permits are usually passed through at cost, so show the fee separately and note the permit number if issued.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation date, location, and equipment used
invoiceChecklist.why: Justifies labor and lift charges and records when the work was completed for warranty start dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Custom work is almost always paid in part up front, and the invoice should show what was already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and sales tax details
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states or cities require a sign or electrical contractor license, and tax treatment of signs and installation varies, so state what is taxed and what is exempt, including any resale certificate.

sign-maker.paymentTerms: Custom fabricated signs usually require 50% down at proof approval, since materials are bought and cut to order and cannot be resold. Small orders such as banners and decals are often paid in full before production. Remaining balances are commonly due on completion or within 15-30 days, with commercial accounts sometimes on net 30. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in writing on the quote and invoice. Accepted methods typically include checks, ACH, and credit cards, sometimes with a card surcharge where local law allows. For large jobs, some shops bill a third at order, a third at fabrication complete, and the rest at installation.

tips.title: Get written proof approval before production
tips.body: Have the client sign or email approval of the exact artwork, size, colors, and text. Misspelled words and wrong phone numbers are the most common cause of reprint disputes, and a signed proof protects you.

tips.title: Bill custom work in stages
tips.body: Take 50% before ordering materials and the balance at installation or pickup. Do not install a custom sign for a client who has not paid the deposit, since it cannot easily be resold.

tips.title: Pass through permits and outside costs with a handling fee
tips.body: Permit applications, engineering stamps, electrician subcontractors, and lift rentals take time to arrange. Bill them at cost plus a reasonable markup or admin fee, and list them as separate lines.

tips.title: Set a minimum order
tips.body: Small jobs eat up setup time for files, material loading, and weeding vinyl. A minimum of $50-100 per order keeps one-off requests from costing you money.

tips.title: State what is not covered by the warranty
tips.body: Note that vinyl lifespan depends on surface condition and exposure, and that damage from weather, vandalism, or third-party mounting is excluded. Put it on the invoice so it is on record.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the square foot or by the job?
faqs.answer: Use per-square-foot pricing for standard products like banners, panels, and cut vinyl. Use a flat project price for fabricated and illuminated signs, but build it from materials, labor, and install so you know your margin. Show the client a single total on the quote and itemized lines on the invoice if they want detail.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on signs and installation?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, tangible signs are taxable and installation labor may or may not be, and some states treat installed signs as real property improvements. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax on the invoice as its own line.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client refuses to pay for a custom sign?
faqs.answer: Refer to the signed proof and quote, and send a written reminder with the invoice and terms. For unpaid installed signs, some states allow a mechanic's lien, though rules vary and you may need to file within a short window. Taking a deposit and billing in stages reduces this risk.

faqs.question: Can I charge for design revisions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many shops include one or two rounds of revisions in the quote and bill additional rounds at the hourly design rate. State the revision limit on the quote so the charge on the invoice is not a surprise.

faqs.question: How should I bill for rush jobs?
faqs.answer: Add a rush fee, commonly 25-50% of the job price, for work needed in less than your normal turnaround. List it as a separate line so the client can see the cost of the faster schedule.

estimate.intro: Sign makers send a quote before almost every custom job, usually after a site visit or review of photos and measurements. Clients often get two or three quotes and compare price, materials, lead time, and whether permits and installation are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Sign dimensions, quantity, and mounting method
scopeChecklist.why: Size and how the sign is attached (flush, post, standoff, roof, wall) drive material and labor costs, and mistakes here are expensive.
Aluminum, acrylic, PVC, vinyl grade, LED type, and laminate affect cost and durability, and clients may compare quotes that use cheaper materials.

scopeChecklist.item: Design scope and number of revisions
scopeChecklist.why: Limits unpaid artwork changes and sets the rate for additional rounds.
Say who applies for the permit, who pays, and that timelines depend on the city or property manager.
State whether install, lift, electrical hookup, and removal of old signs are included, and note that hidden wall damage, wiring problems, or access issues may change the price.
Production time and permit delays set client expectations and give you cover if approvals run late.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment schedule, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Material prices change, so set a validity period, usually 30 days, and the deposit required to start.

pricingTips.title: Price from a full cost build-up
pricingTips.body: Add design time, materials with waste, fabrication hours, install hours, equipment, travel, permits, and overhead before applying margin. Quoting by feel on custom signs often leaves out lift rental or electrician time.

pricingTips.title: Measure on site before quoting installs
pricingTips.body: Check mounting surface, height, power access, and landlord rules. A quote based on a photo alone can miss stucco, brick, or electrical work that changes labor.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Give a basic option such as a printed panel and an upgraded one such as routed dimensional letters or LED illumination. Clients can compare within your quote rather than against a competitor.

pricingTips.title: Separate pass-through costs
pricingTips.body: List permits, engineering, and subcontractor work as their own lines so clients can see what is outside your labor and materials.

faqs.question: Should I charge for quotes or site visits?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are usually free. For complex jobs such as illuminated or monument signs, some shops charge a design or survey fee, often $100-300, and credit it to the project if the client goes ahead.

faqs.question: How long should a sign quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Aluminum, acrylic, vinyl, and LED costs change, so state an expiration date on the quote and reprice if the client accepts after it.

faqs.question: What if the final cost is higher than the quote?
faqs.answer: Only when the scope changes, such as a size increase, extra design work, or unexpected site problems. Put those conditions in the quote and send a written change order before doing additional work.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before ordering materials?
faqs.answer: Yes for custom work. Get a signed quote or written acceptance and the deposit before ordering, since custom-cut materials and printed graphics usually cannot be reused or returned.

smart-home-installer.intro: Smart home installers set up and configure connected devices in homes and small offices, including smart lighting, thermostats, locks, cameras, video doorbells, whole-home audio, networking, and control hubs. Most work solo or in small crews and bill for labor, hardware, programming time, and sometimes ongoing support. Invoices usually combine equipment resale with hourly or flat-fee installation and setup.
smart-home-installer.pricingModel: Most installers mix flat fees for standard installs with hourly billing for custom programming, troubleshooting, and network work. Common flat-fee items are a thermostat install, a video doorbell, or a smart lock, since the time is predictable. Larger projects such as whole-home lighting control or multi-room audio are often quoted per device or per room, or as a project fee with a deposit and progress payments. Hardware is typically resold with a markup of roughly 10 to 30 percent, or billed at cost plus a procurement or handling fee, and some installers instead charge a higher labor rate and pass hardware through at cost. Trip charges, after-hours rates, and wall-fishing or attic/crawlspace work are often priced separately. Ongoing monitoring, remote support, and system check-ups are sold as monthly or annual service plans, or as prepaid blocks of support hours.

rates.service: Video doorbell or smart lock install
Security camera install (wired or PoE, including cable run)
Hub setup and voice assistant integration

items.description: Smart thermostat install and app setup (client-supplied unit)
Smart dimmer switch install, living room and kitchen
Smart lock install and code programming, front door
Smart lock (keypad deadbolt), supplied by installer
Hub setup, scene programming, and voice assistant integration
Client walkthrough and app training

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Hardware is covered by manufacturer warranty; installation labor is warranted for 90 days. Client-owned accounts and admin credentials were transferred at handoff. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hardware with brand, model, and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need this for warranty claims, and you need it to show what you supplied versus what they already owned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for labor, programming, and equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: Programming time is easy to undervalue; listing it separately shows the work behind a system that looks simple once it runs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation address and areas or rooms covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Helps clarify which devices went where, especially on multi-room or multi-property jobs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Account ownership and credential handoff note
invoiceChecklist.why: Records that the client owns their cloud accounts, hub, and admin logins, which prevents disputes later about access.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for labor and manufacturer warranty reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what you will fix for free and what goes back to the manufacturer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip charge, mileage, or after-hours fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents surprise questions when travel or off-hours work is billed separately from the main install.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or registration number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Low-voltage and electrical work often requires a license in many states, and some clients and insurers ask to see it.

smart-home-installer.paymentTerms: For small installs, payment is usually due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. For larger projects, a deposit of 30 to 50 percent is common to cover hardware purchases, with the balance due at completion and sometimes a progress payment at rough-in. Many installers require full payment up front for special-order equipment. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in advance. Cards, ACH, and checks are common; card payments let clients pay on the spot after a walkthrough, and ACH is often preferred for larger projects to avoid processing fees.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before ordering equipment
tips.body: Hardware can be a large share of the total, and returns are often subject to restocking fees or are impossible on special-order items. A deposit that covers equipment protects you if the client changes their mind.

tips.title: Bill programming and troubleshooting time honestly
tips.body: Getting devices from different brands to work together often takes longer than the physical install. Track that time and bill it at a programming rate rather than folding it into a low flat fee.

tips.title: Charge for return visits outside warranty
tips.body: Clients often call back about Wi-Fi drops, app updates, or a device they added themselves. Define what your labor warranty covers and bill other visits at your normal rate or through a support plan.

tips.title: Offer a service plan for recurring revenue
tips.body: Monthly or annual plans covering remote support, firmware updates, and a yearly check-up give clients predictable costs and give you steadier income than one-off installs.

tips.title: Document the final state of the system
tips.body: Take photos of wiring and panel changes and list device names and locations. It saves time on later visits and supports your invoice if the client questions the scope.

faqs.question: Should I mark up hardware on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Many installers do, typically 10 to 30 percent, because they handle sourcing, shipping, returns, and warranty issues. Others bill hardware at cost and charge more for labor. Either works if you state your approach in the quote and show equipment as its own line item.

faqs.question: How do I bill when the client buys their own devices?
faqs.answer: Bill labor and setup only, and note on the invoice that equipment was client-supplied. Many installers charge a slightly higher rate or exclude warranty on labor if the client's device is defective or incompatible, so state that in writing before starting.

faqs.question: Do I charge for time spent troubleshooting a device that does not work?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, at your hourly rate, unless the problem comes from your own error. If a faulty unit is the cause, log the time and bill it, and tell the client early so they understand why the job is taking longer.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to install smart home systems?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the work. Low-voltage wiring, security systems, and anything that involves line-voltage wiring, such as replacing switches, often require a license or must be done under one in many places. Check your state and local rules and your insurance requirements.

faqs.question: How should I handle monthly support fees on invoices?
faqs.answer: Set up a recurring invoice with a clear description of what is included, such as remote support hours, monitoring, and updates. List the billing period and any overage rate for extra time so it is clear when additional charges apply.

estimate.intro: Smart home installers usually send a quote after a site visit or a call that covers the home layout, network, and which devices the client wants. Clients often compare quotes on total price, but also on which brands are included, how much programming is covered, and whether the system will keep working when the internet goes down.

scopeChecklist.item: Device list with brand, model, and quantity
scopeChecklist.why: Clients comparing quotes need to see exactly which products you are proposing, since a cheaper quote may use lower-end hardware.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in wiring and mounting
scopeChecklist.why: Fishing cable through walls, drilling, patching drywall, and attic or crawlspace access can add hours; say what is and is not covered.
Many devices need a strong Wi-Fi network or a specific router. State whether network upgrades are in scope or the client's responsibility.
Define how many scenes, schedules, and voice commands are included so that later requests are treated as changes, not omissions.
Specify which ecosystem you are building on, such as Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, or a dedicated controller, and note limits on mixing brands.
Clarify whether a walkthrough and app setup for household members are included, and how long they will take.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions, change orders, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Hardware prices change frequently, so state how long the quote is valid and how extra requests or electrical issues found on site will be billed.

pricingTips.title: Price from a site walkthrough
pricingTips.body: Wall construction, existing wiring, panel space, and Wi-Fi coverage change the time significantly. A short visit before quoting helps avoid underbidding, and some installers credit a paid consultation fee toward the project.

pricingTips.title: Quote by room or zone for larger jobs
pricingTips.body: Breaking a whole-home project into zones, such as entry, living areas, and exterior, lets clients choose phases or drop items to meet a budget without redoing the whole quote.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Older homes may have no neutral wire at switches, poor panel access, or weak signal. Include a line or a clause stating how hidden conditions will be handled and priced.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, and best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three tiers of hardware and features, such as basic lighting control versus full-home automation, helps clients choose based on their budget and your recommendation.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple installs are often quoted free. For whole-home designs that need a detailed site survey and system layout, many installers charge a design or consultation fee, commonly $100 to $500, and credit it if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Often 14 to 30 days. Because equipment prices and availability shift, a shorter window is reasonable for quotes with a lot of hardware cost. State the expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is a quote a fixed price or can it change?
faqs.answer: It is fixed for the scope described. If the client adds devices or you find conditions that were not visible, such as unsafe wiring or no access, you can issue a written change order with the added cost before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before ordering equipment?
faqs.answer: It is a good practice. A signed quote with a deposit confirms the scope and prices and protects you from being stuck with special-order hardware if the client backs out.

snow-removal.intro: Snow removal contractors plow, shovel, and de-ice driveways, parking lots, sidewalks, and roofs for homeowners, property managers, HOAs, and small businesses. Invoices usually cover individual storm events, monthly or seasonal contracts, and add-ons like salting, hauling, or roof clearing.
snow-removal.pricingModel: Snow removal is priced several ways. Residential driveways are usually billed per push (per visit) with a price tied to snowfall depth, or as a seasonal flat contract paid in installments. Commercial lots are often billed per push, per hour with a minimum, or on a seasonal contract, sometimes with a per-inch trigger such as 2 inches. Salting and de-icing are billed per application, per bag, or per ton of material. Snow hauling and stacking are billed per hour of equipment and operator time or per truckload. Many contractors set a minimum charge per stop to cover travel, and charge extra for heavy, wet, or drifted snow, or for storms deeper than a set depth like 6 or 12 inches.

rates.service: Commercial parking lot plowing (truck with blade)
Skid steer or loader with operator

items.description: Parking lot plowing, 8-inch storm, Jan 14 (2 trucks, 2.5 hrs each)
Sidewalk and entrance shoveling, Jan 14
Rock salt application, Jan 14
Skid steer stacking and pile relocation, Jan 15
Fuel surcharge, 2 storm events

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Storm dates, snowfall totals, and on-site times are logged and available on request. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances over 30 days. Please keep vehicles off the lot during plowing hours.

invoiceChecklist.item: Storm date and service date and time
invoiceChecklist.why: Snow jobs happen overnight and across multiple days. Dated entries let clients match charges to specific storms and prevent disputes about whether you came.

invoiceChecklist.item: Snowfall depth or trigger used
invoiceChecklist.why: Many contracts and per-push rates depend on accumulation. Recording the depth shows why the charge applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location or lot name
invoiceChecklist.why: If you plow several properties for one client, each site needs its own line so they can allocate costs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment and labor hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly jobs need hours broken out by truck, skid steer, and shovel crew so the billed rate matches the equipment used.

invoiceChecklist.item: De-icing material type and quantity
invoiceChecklist.why: Salt, calcium chloride, and sand have different costs. Listing bags or tons backs up the material charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract reference and installment number
invoiceChecklist.why: For seasonal contracts, referencing the agreement and which installment is being billed avoids confusion over what has been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance and license info, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and commercial clients often need proof of liability coverage and your business license or registration number for their records.

snow-removal.paymentTerms: Residential clients on seasonal contracts commonly pay half up front in the fall and the rest by midwinter, or in equal monthly installments. Per-push customers are often billed monthly, with payment due in 15 to 30 days. Commercial accounts may request net 30 terms and a certificate of insurance before the first push. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract. Accepted methods usually include checks, ACH, and cards, and many contractors offer autopay for recurring customers so they are not chasing payment in spring.

tips.title: Put the trigger depth in writing
tips.body: State the snowfall depth that starts service, such as 2 inches, and what happens with storms that continue or drift after you leave. This single line prevents most complaints about whether you should have come.

tips.title: Bill monthly instead of per storm
tips.body: A single monthly invoice listing each push is easier for clients to pay than a bill after every storm. It also smooths your cash flow in a heavy winter.

tips.title: Keep proof of service
tips.body: Take timestamped photos or use GPS logs showing arrival and departure times. This protects you against slip-and-fall claims and against clients who say service was skipped.

tips.title: Charge separately for salt and hauling
tips.body: Do not bury de-icing or hauling in the plow rate. Separate lines make it clear these are extra, and let you adjust when material prices change.

tips.title: Collect before spring
tips.body: Clients lose urgency once the snow melts. Use installment schedules that finish by March and send reminders while the season is still fresh.

faqs.question: Should I charge per push or a flat seasonal rate?
faqs.answer: Per-push pricing protects you in heavy winters, and seasonal pricing gives you predictable income. Many contractors offer both, with seasonal contracts that cap or limit the number of pushes. If you use a flat rate, define what is included and set a reasonable limit on total events or snowfall.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for heavy or wet snow?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract or quote says so. Common approaches are tiered pricing by snowfall depth, a surcharge for storms over a set amount, or hourly billing for unusually heavy accumulation. Without this in writing, clients may expect the base rate.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on snow removal?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain property services and others do not, and materials like salt may be treated differently. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay after the season ends?
faqs.answer: Send a final notice referencing your contract and late fee terms, then consider small claims court. Your service logs, photos, and signed agreement are the key evidence. Collecting installments during the season reduces this risk.

faqs.question: How should I bill a property manager with several sites?
faqs.answer: Use one invoice per billing period with separate line items for each site and date, or a separate invoice per property if they need to allocate costs. Ask for any purchase order number they require and include it.

estimate.intro: Snow removal quotes are usually sent in late summer or fall, before the first storm, so clients can lock in a contractor. Homeowners and property managers compare price, response time, trigger depth, and whether the quote is per push or seasonal.

scopeChecklist.why: Specify the driveway, walkways, steps, loading docks, and lot sections. Clients often assume more is included than you planned to clear.
State the snowfall that starts service and when you will arrive, such as within 4 hours after snow stops. This sets expectations on timing.
Stacking locations affect lot space and spring melt. Agreeing in advance prevents complaints and blocked parking.
Salt and ice melt are a common source of surprise charges. List whether they are included, priced per application, or not offered.

scopeChecklist.item: Contract term and number of visits
scopeChecklist.why: Seasonal quotes should say start and end dates and whether pushes are unlimited, capped, or billed beyond a limit.
Note that you are not responsible for unmarked hazards like landscaping edges, sprinkler heads, or loose pavers, and ask clients to mark them.
Commercial clients will ask for proof of liability insurance. Including coverage details up front shortens the approval process.

pricingTips.title: Price by site time and distance
pricingTips.body: Estimate the minutes needed to clear the site plus travel between stops. Set a minimum per stop so small driveways far from your route are still worth serving.

pricingTips.title: Offer per-push and seasonal options
pricingTips.body: Presenting both lets the client choose based on their risk tolerance, and often leads to a seasonal sale. Make sure the seasonal price covers an average winter in your area, not a mild one.

pricingTips.title: Build in a heavy-storm clause
pricingTips.body: Add a line for storms above a certain depth or for hauling, priced hourly. This protects you from a single major storm wiping out your margin.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration
pricingTips.body: Prices for salt, fuel, and labor shift quickly. Valid-through dates, such as October 31, keep you from honoring old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I give quotes without seeing the site?
faqs.answer: For simple driveways, a satellite view and a short call can be enough. For commercial lots, visit the site to check size, obstacles, and snow storage so you can price accurately.

faqs.question: Is a snow removal quote binding?
faqs.answer: A quote becomes a contract once the client accepts it, ideally in writing with a signature or written approval. State the price, scope, and expiration date so both sides know the terms.

faqs.question: How early should I send seasonal quotes?
faqs.answer: Late summer through early fall is typical. Many clients decide before the first snow, and early signups help you plan routes and equipment.

soccer-coach.intro: Soccer coaches who bill clients include private trainers who work one-on-one or with small groups, camp and clinic operators, club and team coaches paid by a league or parents' association, and goalkeeper or fitness specialists. Invoices usually cover private sessions, group training blocks, camps, team seasons, and sometimes extras like video analysis or field rental.
soccer-coach.pricingModel: Most private coaches charge per session, with a lower per-player rate for small groups of two to six. Many sell packages of 5 or 10 sessions at a small discount, paid upfront, which cuts down on cancellations and chasing payments. Group clinics and camps are priced per player per day or per week. Club, school, and rec-league coaches are usually paid a flat seasonal stipend or a per-practice or per-game rate, billed to the organization. Coaches who rent a field or buy equipment either build the cost into the rate or list it as a separate line. Experience, licensing level (such as USSF or NSCAA/United Soccer Coaches credentials), playing background, and local demand all move rates, with metro areas at the high end.

rates.service: Assistant or per-practice coaching for a team
Video analysis or player evaluation report

items.description: Private training sessions, ball mastery and finishing (Oct 2, 9, 16, 23)
Small group session, 1 of 3 players (Oct 12 and Oct 26)
Match video review and written feedback (Oct 20 game)
Field rental, Riverside Park turf (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 10 days of invoice date. Sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50 percent. Weather cancellations will be rescheduled at no charge. Accepted: check, Venmo, Zelle, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Player name and, for minors, parent or guardian name
invoiceChecklist.why: The person paying is often not the player, and parents of multiple kids need to know which child each charge covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, times, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents compare invoices to their calendars. Listing each date prevents disputes about missed or extra sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session type and group size
invoiceChecklist.why: Private, small group, and goalkeeper sessions have different rates, so labeling each one explains the pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and sessions remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client bought 10 sessions, show how many are used and left so the balance is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Field, facility, or equipment fees as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs like turf rental or camp jerseys should be itemized so they are not mistaken for a rate increase.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and weather policy
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellations and rain-outs are the most common billing disagreements in this work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Coaching license or certification and background check status, where relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Schools, clubs, and some parents ask for proof of credentials, especially for organizations paying the invoice.

soccer-coach.paymentTerms: Private coaches commonly collect payment at the session, monthly in arrears, or upfront for a package. Packages and camps are usually paid in full before the first day, often with a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold a camp spot. Organizations such as clubs, schools, and leagues typically pay on net 15 to net 30 terms, sometimes by check through an accounts payable office. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are used by some coaches but are less common with parents, who respond better to a clear due date and a short reminder. Popular payment methods include Zelle, Venmo, cash, check, and card; confirm any fees the payment method charges before passing them along.

tips.title: Sell packages instead of single sessions
tips.body: A prepaid block of 8 or 10 sessions gives you predictable income and fewer chasing conversations. Set an expiration, such as 90 days, so unused sessions do not pile up.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: A 24-hour notice rule with a 50 to 100 percent charge for late cancels works for most coaches. Include it on every invoice so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Bill by family when siblings train together
tips.body: One invoice per family with each child listed saves parents confusion and gives you one payment to track instead of several.

tips.title: Invoice organizations promptly after each month or season stage
tips.body: Clubs and schools often pay slowly and need a reference such as a PO number or contract date. Send invoices on a set schedule, not when you remember.

tips.title: Track mileage and field costs
tips.body: If you drive between sites or pay for fields and equipment, keep records. These are common deductible expenses for self-employed coaches, though you should check with a tax professional.

faqs.question: Should I charge parents per session or monthly?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per session suits irregular schedules, while a monthly invoice or prepaid package suits weekly training. Monthly or prepaid billing reduces the number of small payments you have to track.

faqs.question: Do I charge for rained-out sessions?
faqs.answer: Most coaches reschedule weather cancellations at no charge when the coach cancels. If the client cancels late for a session that was still on, the late cancellation fee applies. State this in your policy.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a club or school instead of parents?
faqs.answer: Bill the organization using its legal name, include the dates or season covered, the number of practices and games, and any contract or PO reference. Ask whether you need to submit a W-9 first, which is common for independent contractors.

faqs.question: Can I charge sales tax on coaching?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax personal instruction services, but some tax certain recreation or equipment sales. Check with your state revenue department, particularly if you sell gear or run camps.

faqs.question: What if a parent pays late or disputes a session?
faqs.answer: Send a friendly reminder with the invoice attached and the dates in question. Having session dates itemized and a written policy makes disputes easy to resolve. Pause further sessions if a balance stays unpaid.

estimate.intro: Soccer coaches send estimates when a club, school, or parent group is hiring for a season, camp, or ongoing training program, and when a family wants to know the cost of a multi-week plan. Clients compare per-session cost, total season cost, coach credentials, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions or practices and their length
scopeChecklist.why: A season price means little without knowing whether it covers 20 practices of 60 minutes or 30 of 90.
Pricing and planning change with a group of 4 under-10 players versus 14 high schoolers.

scopeChecklist.item: Location and who pays for the field
scopeChecklist.why: Field rental can be a large cost. State whether it is included, billed at cost, or the client's responsibility.
Clarify whether league games, weekend tournaments, and travel are included or billed separately.
Cones, balls, bibs, and jerseys should be listed as included, extra, or provided by the client.
It sets expectations before work starts and avoids arguments over rain-outs and no-shows.
If you bring staff or carry liability insurance, say so. Organizations often require proof of coverage.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total and show the per-session cost
pricingTips.body: Clients like a single seasonal number but want to see it breaks down fairly. Show both, for example $2,400 for 24 practices, which is $100 per practice.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered option
pricingTips.body: Present two or three levels, such as practices only, practices plus games, and a full package with evaluations. This lets the client choose without negotiating your rate.

pricingTips.title: Price in your travel and prep time
pricingTips.body: Driving between fields, planning sessions, and parent communication take unpaid hours. Build these into the rate rather than billing them as surprises later.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Field availability and your schedule change. A 14 to 30 day validity window keeps you from honoring an old price after a season fills up.

faqs.question: Should I give a free trial session?
faqs.answer: Many private coaches offer one free or discounted evaluation session. Put it in the estimate as a separate line so the client sees the value and the normal rate.

faqs.question: How do I quote a summer camp?
faqs.answer: Price per player per day or week, then calculate your break-even enrollment using staff, field, insurance, and equipment costs. Include a minimum enrollment clause so you can cancel or adjust if too few sign up.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a season or camp quote?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent at acceptance is common, with the balance due before the start or in installments. State whether the deposit is refundable and until when.

faqs.question: Can I change the price if the season runs longer?
faqs.answer: Only if the estimate says so. Include language that extra games, playoffs, or added practices beyond the stated schedule are billed at a set per-practice or per-game rate.

social-media-manager.intro: Social media managers plan, create, schedule, and monitor content for businesses, creators, and organizations across platforms like Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok, and YouTube. Most work solo or in a small agency and bill monthly for ongoing management, plus separate charges for one-time projects like audits, strategy documents, and content batches. Invoices usually cover a set number of posts or hours, community management, reporting, and sometimes paid ad management.
social-media-manager.pricingModel: Most social media managers bill a monthly retainer tied to a defined scope: number of platforms, posts per week, stories or short videos, community management, and a monthly report. Hourly billing is common for newer freelancers, for consulting, and for work that is hard to scope, such as crisis response or one-off training. Project fees apply to audits, strategy documents, content calendars, and account setups. Paid ad management is often charged as a flat fee or a percentage of ad spend, commonly 10-20 percent, and the ad budget itself is usually paid by the client directly to the platform or billed separately as a pass-through. Content creation such as photography, video editing, and graphic design is either bundled into tiered packages or priced as add-ons. Many managers set package tiers (for example 3, 5, or daily posts per week) and cap revisions, approvals, and response times to keep scope under control.

rates.service: Hourly social media management or consulting
Monthly retainer, one platform, 3 posts per week with light engagement
Monthly retainer, 2-3 platforms, 4-5 posts per week plus community management and reporting
Social media audit and strategy document
Paid social ad management (Meta, TikTok, LinkedIn)
rates.unit: per month or % of ad spend

items.description: Monthly social media management, Instagram and Facebook (12 posts, 8 stories, community management), March
Short-form video editing, Reels (client-supplied footage)
Meta ad campaign management, spring promotion
Monthly performance report and 30-minute review call
Stock photo licenses for March content

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Retainer covers the scope listed in the signed agreement dated January 8. Ad spend of $600 was charged directly to the client's ad account and is not included here. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and platforms covered
invoiceChecklist.why: A retainer invoice should say which month and which accounts the work applied to so there is no confusion about what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable counts
invoiceChecklist.why: List posts, stories, videos, or graphics delivered. Clients often ask what they paid for, and counts back up the retainer.

invoiceChecklist.item: Ad spend handling
invoiceChecklist.why: State whether ad budget was paid directly to the platform or is a pass-through on the invoice. Keep management fees and ad spend on separate lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs and licenses
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock images, music licenses, design tool seats, and scheduling software that you bill to the client should be itemized, ideally with receipts available.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the agreement or scope
invoiceChecklist.why: Pointing to the signed scope helps resolve disputes about extra revisions, added platforms, or out-of-scope requests.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope or add-on work
invoiceChecklist.why: Bill extras like additional video edits, event coverage, or rush turnaround on their own lines with hours or quantities so they are visible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment terms and late fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainer clients can drift on payment. Due date, accepted payment methods, and any late fee should be on every invoice, not just the contract.

social-media-manager.paymentTerms: Retainers are typically invoiced at the start of the month, or on the first day of the service period, with payment due in 7 to 15 days. Billing in advance is the norm because the work begins immediately and clients can otherwise accumulate unpaid months. Project work such as audits or strategy documents often requires 50 percent upfront and the balance on delivery. Hourly clients are usually billed monthly or biweekly. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common where permitted, though rules on late fees vary by state. Payment methods usually include ACH bank transfer, credit card, and sometimes checks. Many managers pause posting if an invoice is more than 10 to 14 days overdue, and state this in the agreement.

tips.title: Bill the retainer in advance
tips.body: Invoice at the start of the service month. Content calendars, scheduling, and creative work happen before the month's posts go live, so billing after the fact means you are financing your client.

tips.title: Define what a post is
tips.body: A single image, a carousel, a Reel, and a story are different amounts of work. Spell out what counts toward your monthly volume and price video separately from static posts.

tips.title: Keep ad spend off your revenue
tips.body: Have clients put their own card on the ad account where possible. If you front the ad spend, invoice it as a pass-through with documentation and consider requiring it upfront to avoid carrying that risk.

tips.title: Cap revisions and approval time
tips.body: Limit revision rounds per post and set a deadline for client approvals. Late approvals shouldn't lead to unlimited extra work or a claim that you missed the schedule.

tips.title: Review pricing every 6 to 12 months
tips.body: Scope grows quietly as clients add platforms, ask for more replies, and want more reporting. Compare your actual hours to the retainer and raise the price or trim scope at renewal.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a monthly retainer?
faqs.answer: Most social media managers move to retainers once they have a repeatable scope, because clients prefer predictable costs and you are paid for results and availability rather than minutes. Hourly makes sense for consulting, training, and projects where the scope is unclear. Even on a retainer, track your time for a few months to confirm the price is sustainable.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for ad spend?
faqs.answer: The cleanest approach is for the client to pay the platform directly, so ad spend never appears on your invoice. If you pay for ads on your own card, list the spend as a separate pass-through line, keep platform receipts, and ideally collect the funds in advance. Your management fee should be its own line.

faqs.question: Can I charge for content the client does not approve or use?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Work performed according to scope is billable whether or not the client publishes it. Include a revision limit and an approval window in your contract so unused content does not turn into a billing dispute.

faqs.question: What happens if a client wants to cancel mid-month?
faqs.answer: Your agreement should state a notice period, commonly 30 days, and whether the current month is refundable. Without that language, you may have difficulty collecting for work already scheduled. Many managers do not refund prepaid retainers once the month has started.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on social media services?
faqs.answer: It depends on where you and your client are located. Some states tax certain digital or advertising-related services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and add tax to the invoice only where it applies.

estimate.intro: Social media managers send quotes when a prospect asks for pricing after a discovery call, before a retainer begins, or when a client wants a one-time project like an audit or campaign. Clients typically compare your quote against other freelancers and agencies, so it should show exactly which platforms, how many posts, and what reporting is included.

scopeChecklist.why: Name each platform included and confirm the client owns the accounts and gives you admin access, not a shared password.
State posts per week, stories, Reels or short videos, and carousels. This is the main source of scope creep if left vague.
Clarify whether you shoot or design content, edit client footage, or work only with assets the client supplies, and how late asset delivery is handled.
Say whether you reply to comments and DMs, how often, and during what hours, so the client does not expect round-the-clock monitoring.
Define how many revision rounds are included and how long the client has to approve content before it is posted or rescheduled.
List the report frequency, metrics covered, and any monthly calls so clients know what accountability to expect.
Separate your management fee from ad spend, stock licenses, and software that the client pays for or reimburses.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three tiers
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic, standard, and expanded package lets clients choose a scope instead of negotiating your rate. Keep the middle tier as the one you actually want to sell.

pricingTips.title: Price to your hours, not the posts alone
pricingTips.body: Add up strategy, content creation, scheduling, engagement, reporting, and client communication for a typical month. A retainer that looks fine per post may be too low once all the unseen work is counted.

pricingTips.title: Charge a setup fee for new clients
pricingTips.body: Onboarding includes brand research, account audits, competitor review, and a first content calendar. A one-time setup fee covers this upfront work and filters out clients who are not committed.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date and minimum term
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 14 to 30 days is typical, and a three-month minimum is common for retainers because social media results take time to build.

faqs.question: Should I give a free audit with my quote?
