faqs.answer: A short review of the client's current accounts is a reasonable way to win work, but a full audit with recommendations is a paid deliverable. Keep free reviews brief and offer the detailed audit as a separate priced service that can be credited toward a retainer.

faqs.question: Is a quote a binding contract?
faqs.answer: Not by itself in most cases. A quote states your proposed price and scope, but you should pair it with a signed agreement covering term, payment, ownership of content, and cancellation. Many managers combine the quote and agreement into one document the client signs.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Reduce scope instead of the rate. Cut a platform, lower the number of posts, or remove video and reporting. Discounting the same work trains clients to expect more for less and makes it harder to raise prices later.

faqs.question: What if the client's needs change after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Issue a revised quote for the new scope before starting any extra work. Adding a platform, increasing post frequency, or launching a paid campaign should each update the monthly fee, with the change confirmed in writing.

sod-installation.intro: Sod installers lay new turf for homeowners, builders, landscapers, and property managers. Invoices typically cover sod material by the square foot or pallet, ground preparation, grading, delivery, installation labor, and removal of old turf or debris.
sod-installation.pricingModel: Most sod jobs are priced per square foot, with a rate that bundles material, delivery, and labor, or with sod and labor listed on separate lines. Sod is usually sold by the pallet (commonly about 400 to 500 sq ft, depending on the grower and grass type), so many installers pass through the pallet cost with a markup and add labor per square foot. Site prep such as sod removal, tilling, grading, topsoil, and soil amendments is billed separately, either per square foot, per cubic yard, or by the hour. Small jobs often carry a minimum charge to cover truck time, fuel, and delivery. Irrigation repairs, starter fertilizer, and first-watering visits are common add-ons. Large commercial or builder jobs may be bid as a flat price per square foot or per project with progress billing.

rates.service: Sod installation, material and labor (common warm- or cool-season grass)
Sod installation labor only (customer-supplied or separately billed sod)
Existing lawn or sod removal and disposal
Grading and soil preparation (tilling, raking, leveling)
Crew labor for repairs, patching, or odd-shaped areas
Minimum job charge or delivery fee

items.description: Remove and dispose of existing dead lawn, front yard
Grade and level, till top 3 inches, remove debris
Screened topsoil, delivered and spread
Tall fescue sod, 6 pallets (approx. 2,500 sq ft)
Sod installation labor, including trimming around beds and walkways
Starter fertilizer application and initial watering

sampleInvoice.notes: Water sod daily for the first 2 weeks, as directed on the care sheet provided. No foot traffic or mowing for 10 to 14 days. Sod is guaranteed for 30 days if watering instructions are followed. Balance due within 14 days of completion. Late balances are charged 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Total square footage installed and how it was measured
invoiceChecklist.why: Sod is billed by area, so clients and builders want to see the number behind the total, especially if the final measurement differs from the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Grass variety and sod source (e.g., Bermuda, Zoysia, tall fescue, Kentucky bluegrass)
invoiceChecklist.why: Varieties differ widely in price and performance, and this documents exactly what the client received if there is a later dispute.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pallet count and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Pallets are the unit you purchase, so listing them supports your material line and shows when the sod was fresh at installation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Site prep work listed separately (removal, grading, tilling, topsoil, amendments)
invoiceChecklist.why: Prep is often the largest labor cost, and separate lines show clients that the price covers more than rolling out turf.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extra work such as irrigation fixes or additional grading
invoiceChecklist.why: Surprises like buried debris, poor drainage, or broken sprinkler heads add cost, and written line items prevent arguments.

invoiceChecklist.item: Watering and care instructions or warranty terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Sod failure is usually a watering issue, so tying your guarantee to the care sheet protects you on callbacks.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or registration number, where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and municipalities require landscape contractor licensing, and builders or property managers may need it for their records.

sod-installation.paymentTerms: Residential sod jobs are often billed with a deposit of 25% to 50% to cover the sod order, since sod is perishable and cannot be returned once cut. The balance is typically due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Builders, HOAs, and property managers may pay net 30 and expect a purchase order or job number on the invoice. Accepted payment methods usually include checks, card payments, and bank transfers. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in writing up front. For large jobs, progress billing after prep and again after installation helps cover material and crew costs.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before ordering sod
tips.body: Sod is cut to order and cannot be restocked. If a client cancels after you place the order, you absorb the cost. A deposit that covers the material protects you.

tips.title: Verify square footage before final billing
tips.body: Measure the installed area after cutting around beds, trees, and curves. If the actual footage differs from the quote, show both numbers on the invoice and explain the adjustment.

tips.title: Bill prep as its own line
tips.body: Removal, grading, and soil work take time and equipment. Combining them into one low per-square-foot price makes it easy for clients to compare you unfairly to installers who skip prep.

tips.title: Include a minimum and a delivery charge
tips.body: Small patches and narrow strips cost nearly as much in truck time and fuel as bigger jobs. A stated minimum keeps small jobs profitable.

tips.title: Invoice on installation day
tips.body: Clients are happiest when the lawn is freshly laid. Sending the invoice the same day, with the care sheet attached, gets payment moving before questions about early browning arise.

faqs.question: Should I charge for sod by the square foot or by the pallet?
faqs.answer: Buy by the pallet, but quote clients by the square foot. Clients think in lawn size, and you should include extra sod for waste, usually 5% to 10%, in your calculation. Listing pallets on the invoice is fine if you want to show material costs separately.

faqs.question: How do I bill for waste and cutoffs?
faqs.answer: Build waste into your per-square-foot rate or round up the pallet count and show that on the invoice. Irregular lawns with many curves can waste more than 10%, so quote them with a higher allowance.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for sod installation on slopes or tight access?
faqs.answer: Yes. Slopes need pegging, and hand-carrying sod through gates or backyards takes more labor. Add a labor surcharge or higher rate and note it on the quote and invoice so the client sees the reason.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client pays late or disputes the sod condition?
faqs.answer: Refer to the written warranty terms and care instructions on the invoice. Photos taken at install help. For late payment, send a reminder, then apply the late fee stated on the invoice. If the amount is large, check your state's lien rights for landscaping work.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on sod installation?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax sod as a material sale, some tax only the material in a contract, and some exempt landscaping services. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Sod installers quote before work starts because clients want a firm number before ordering turf. Most clients compare two or three quotes, usually looking at the total price, grass type, how much prep is included, and the warranty.

scopeChecklist.item: Measured square footage and a site sketch or photos
scopeChecklist.why: The area drives material and labor, and a written measurement gives you a basis for adjusting the price if the area is larger than expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Grass variety, sod grade, and source
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume all sod is the same. Naming the variety prevents later claims that you installed a cheaper type.

scopeChecklist.item: Existing turf removal and disposal included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Removing old lawn is a major labor item. State whether you haul it away and where it goes.
Prep quality determines whether the sod roots well. Spell out depth, amount of topsoil, and any drainage work.
Make clear that you are not responsible for unmarked sprinkler lines, and note whether you will adjust heads or call for utility marking.
Most failures come from poor watering. State that the client waters per your instructions and what the guarantee covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, weather delays, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Sod is perishable and prices change. A date limit and weather clause protect you from locked-in prices and rain delays.

pricingTips.title: Price from measured area plus waste
pricingTips.body: Calculate the area, add 5% to 10% for cutoffs, and round up to full pallets. Then add prep and labor. This keeps you from running short mid-job.

pricingTips.title: Offer options at different prep levels
pricingTips.body: Present a basic option (light grading, sod only) and a full option (soil amendment, topsoil, starter fertilizer). Clients often choose the middle or upper option when they see what each includes.

pricingTips.title: Account for sod price changes
pricingTips.body: Grower prices shift with season and fuel costs. Keep quotes valid for 14 to 30 days and state that pricing depends on availability from the supplier.

pricingTips.title: Separate unknowns from the base price
pricingTips.body: Buried rocks, poor soil, and broken irrigation are common surprises. Put an hourly rate or per-unit price for extra work in the quote so you can bill it without a dispute.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many sod installers give free estimates for standard residential lawns. For large or complex sites that need grading plans or multiple visits, a fee that is credited toward the job if accepted is reasonable.

faqs.question: How firm should my quote be?
faqs.answer: Make it a fixed price for the measured area and listed scope, with extra work billed separately. If the site conditions are unclear, say the price is an estimate subject to confirmation once the old lawn is removed.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Sod and fuel prices change, and installation windows depend on season and weather, so an expiration date keeps pricing current.

faqs.question: What should I do if the client wants the lowest price?
faqs.answer: Show what the lower price removes, such as skipped grading, fewer pallets, or no warranty. If you do reduce scope, document the changes and note that poor prep can affect how well the sod roots.

software-developer.intro: Freelance and small-agency software developers bill clients for building, maintaining, and fixing web apps, mobile apps, APIs, integrations, and internal tools. Invoices usually cover hours worked, fixed-price milestones, monthly retainers for ongoing maintenance, and pass-through costs such as hosting or third-party licenses.
software-developer.pricingModel: Most independent developers charge hourly for open-ended work, bug fixes, and consulting, and use fixed-price or milestone billing for projects with a clear scope. Retainers are common for maintenance and support, typically a set number of hours per month at a slightly discounted rate. Rates rise with specialization (cloud architecture, security, mobile, data engineering) and with urgency. Day rates are used for on-site or full-time contract engagements. Third-party costs like cloud hosting, app store fees, API subscriptions, and paid libraries are either billed at cost, marked up modestly, or put on the client's own accounts. Many developers add a separate rate for after-hours emergency work, often 1.5x to 2x the normal rate.

rates.service: Web or backend development (general contract work)
Senior or specialized work (cloud, security, ML, mobile architecture)
Monthly maintenance retainer (updates, monitoring, small fixes)
Marketing site or small business web app
Code review, technical audit, or consulting

items.description: Milestone 2: Customer portal - authentication, dashboard, and account settings
Stripe subscription billing integration (webhooks, failed-payment handling)
Production bug fixes: report export timeout, email template rendering
Code review and deployment pipeline setup (CI, staging environment)
Cloud hosting, staging and production (billed at cost, March)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours are logged in the attached time report. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Accepted by ACH or card. Source code transfers to client on payment of final milestone per the signed agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and statement of work or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's accounts payable team knows which budget it belongs to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized hours with dates and task descriptions (or attached time report)
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly clients often ask what the time went toward. Specific entries like 'fixed checkout timeout' prevent disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone name and completion or acceptance date
invoiceChecklist.why: Fixed-price billing depends on a milestone being delivered. Referencing it shows you are billing per the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs listed separately (hosting, licenses, domains, app store fees)
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs should be visible and distinct from labor, and you may need to show receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often will not pay an invoice without a PO number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope or change-request work labeled as such, with the approval reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows that extra work was requested and approved, and avoids arguments about what was included in the original price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, tax ID or W-9 status, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients in the US usually need a W-9 on file and may issue a 1099 at year end if you are paid over the IRS threshold.

software-developer.paymentTerms: Hourly and retainer work is commonly invoiced every two weeks or monthly, with net 15 or net 30 terms. Fixed-price projects usually take a deposit of 25-50% before work starts, with the remainder tied to milestones or delivery. Retainers are often billed at the start of the month. Many developers include a late fee of 1-1.5% per month and reserve the right to pause work or withhold deployment of code on unpaid invoices if the contract says so. ACH and bank transfer are common for larger amounts because they avoid card fees; card payments work for smaller invoices, and some developers pass the processing fee on to the client.

tips.title: Track time as you go
tips.body: Reconstructing hours at the end of the month leads to undercounting. Log time per task with a short description, and attach the report to the invoice for hourly clients.

tips.title: Put change requests in writing before you build them
tips.body: Scope creep is the most common source of unpaid hours. When a client asks for something outside the statement of work, send a short written estimate and get a reply before you start.

tips.title: Tie payments to deliverables you control
tips.body: Structure milestones around things you can complete, such as a deployed staging build, rather than around client feedback or third-party approvals that can drag on. Add a clause that the milestone is billable after a set number of days without feedback.

tips.title: Have clients own the accounts
tips.body: Where possible, set up hosting, domains, and API accounts under the client's name and billing. This avoids fronting costs, chasing reimbursement, and awkward handover later.

tips.title: Hold final code or deployment until the last invoice is paid
tips.body: If your contract allows it, keep the final handoff of source code, admin credentials, or production deployment conditional on payment of the final milestone.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or fixed price?
faqs.answer: Bill hourly when scope is unclear, the work is exploratory, or the client changes direction often. Use fixed price or milestones when requirements are written down and you can estimate with confidence. Many developers use a fixed price with a defined number of revision rounds and bill extra work hourly.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent in meetings and emails?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so in your agreement. Many developers bill meetings, code review, and project communication at the normal rate. Some include a small amount of communication in fixed-price work, but long calls and frequent check-ins should be billable.

faqs.question: How do I bill for ongoing maintenance?
faqs.answer: A monthly retainer is the usual approach. Define what it covers (for example, dependency updates, uptime monitoring, and up to five hours of fixes), what happens to unused hours, and the rate for work beyond the included amount.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on software development?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on what you deliver. Some states tax custom software, prewritten software, or SaaS access, while others do not tax services. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, especially if you sell to clients in several states.

faqs.question: What if a client does not pay after delivery?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice and contract terms, then a firm written notice. If your agreement ties code ownership or license to payment, you can cite that. For larger amounts, a demand letter or small claims court may be options, depending on your state's limits.

estimate.intro: Developers send an estimate or proposal before a project starts, usually after a discovery call or after reading a written brief. Clients compare total cost, timeline, what is included, and how risk is handled if the work takes longer than expected.

scopeChecklist.item: Features and deliverables listed in plain language
scopeChecklist.why: A vague description like 'build an app' leaves room for disagreement. List screens, user roles, integrations, and reports that are included.

scopeChecklist.item: What is explicitly out of scope
scopeChecklist.why: Naming things like native mobile apps, data migration, content entry, or SEO prevents clients from assuming they are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions about third-party services and client responsibilities
scopeChecklist.why: Delays often come from missing API keys, design files, or content. State what the client must provide and by when.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline with milestones and review periods
scopeChecklist.why: Shows when work is delivered and how long the client has to give feedback before the schedule slips.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and how extra changes are billed
scopeChecklist.why: Sets a limit on rework and gives a clear hourly rate for anything beyond it.
Clients are often surprised by monthly cloud, email, or API fees. Say who pays and whether you bill them at cost.
Clarify when the client receives the code, whether a warranty period covers bugs, and what ongoing support costs.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in hours, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the project into tasks, estimate each, and add 15-30% for unknowns, testing, and communication. Quoting only the best-case hours is the most common reason projects lose money.

pricingTips.title: Charge for discovery separately
pricingTips.body: For larger projects, offer a paid discovery or scoping phase of a few days to a couple of weeks that produces a spec and a firmer quote. It protects you from pricing a project you do not yet understand.

pricingTips.title: Offer options instead of one number
pricingTips.body: Presenting a core version and an expanded version helps clients choose by budget and makes it easier to cut scope without cutting your rate.

pricingTips.title: Use a range for early estimates
pricingTips.body: If requirements are still loose, give a range and state that a fixed price will follow once the scope is confirmed. Make clear whether the number is an estimate or a binding quote.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Short quotes for small jobs are usually free. For larger or complex projects, many developers charge for a discovery phase, and may credit the fee toward the project if the client continues.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Your availability and the client's requirements can change, and tool or API costs may shift, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if the project takes longer than I estimated?
faqs.answer: On a fixed-price quote you absorb the overrun unless the client changed the scope. Protect yourself with a clear scope, a change-request process, and a buffer in the price. On hourly work with an estimate, tell the client early when you expect to exceed it.

faqs.question: Can I ask for a deposit when the client accepts the estimate?
faqs.answer: Yes. A deposit of 25-50% is common for fixed-price projects. Put the amount and due date in the quote so that the start date is tied to receiving payment.

software-development.intro: Freelance developers, small dev shops, and contract engineers send these invoices. They typically bill for hours spent building features, fixing bugs, integrating third-party APIs, and maintaining existing applications, along with fixed-price project milestones and monthly retainers for ongoing support.
software-development.pricingModel: Software work is priced in a few common ways. Hourly billing is the default for contract work, maintenance, and projects with unclear scope, usually tracked in 15 or 30 minute increments. Fixed-price quotes suit well-defined projects such as a marketing site, a mobile app MVP, or a specific integration, and are often split into milestone payments (for example 30% at start, 40% at midpoint, 30% at delivery). Monthly retainers cover a set number of hours or an on-call arrangement for bug fixes, updates, and hosting oversight. Some developers use day rates for embedded contract roles, usually 6 to 8 billable hours per day. Third-party costs such as hosting, domains, paid API usage, app store fees, and software licenses are typically passed through at cost or with a small handling markup, and listed separately from labor. Rates rise with specialization (security, machine learning, embedded systems) and with rush or after-hours work.

rates.service: Senior or specialized engineering (cloud, security, data)

items.description: Milestone 2: Customer dashboard and authentication (React front end, Node API)
Stripe subscription billing integration, including webhook handling and test mode QA
Additional work outside scope: CSV export of reports (Change Request #3)
Production deployment and environment setup (AWS)
AWS hosting, March (billed at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Hours reflect work logged March 1-28. Source code and deployment credentials transfer upon payment in full per the services agreement dated January 12.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and reference to the contract or statement of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's accounts payable team can match it to an approved engagement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or deliverable name, or a date range for hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the payment covers and prevents disputes about whether a milestone was actually reached.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by task, with rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often ask what the hours went to. Task-level lines such as 'API integration' and 'bug fixes' answer that before they ask.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change request numbers for out-of-scope work
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that the client approved extra work and keeps it separate from the fixed-price portion.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party and hosting costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through expenses like cloud hosting, licenses, and app store fees should be visible and at cost, not buried in labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or cost center, if provided
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies often reject invoices without a PO number, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: IP transfer or license terms reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Many contracts hand over code only after full payment. Stating this on the invoice reminds the client of the condition.

software-development.paymentTerms: Developers commonly require a deposit of 25% to 50% on fixed-price projects before any work begins, then bill by milestone. Hourly and retainer work is usually invoiced monthly, or every two weeks for larger engagements, with retainers billed in advance at the start of the month. Net 15 and net 30 are typical, and some freelancers use due on receipt for smaller clients. Late fees of 1% to 2% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment methods are usually ACH, wire transfer, or card, and many developers add a processing fee for cards or encourage bank transfer on larger invoices. Some developers pause deployments or withhold credentials when invoices go unpaid, which should be written into the contract in advance.

tips.title: Bill milestones tied to working software
tips.body: Define milestones as deliverables the client can see and test, such as 'login and user accounts working on staging'. Avoid milestones tied to dates alone, since clients may argue the work wasn't finished.

tips.title: Track change requests in writing
tips.body: Scope creep is the biggest billing problem in software. When a client asks for something new, send a short written change request with an hour estimate and get approval before starting, then invoice it as its own line.

tips.title: Keep time logs you can share
tips.body: Use a time tracker that exports task-level entries. If a client questions a 40-hour invoice, a log showing commits, tickets, and meetings resolves it quickly.

tips.title: Bill for non-coding time
tips.body: Meetings, code reviews, project management, deployment, and debugging in unfamiliar legacy code are real work. Set this expectation in your contract and include these on invoices, even if at the same hourly rate.

tips.title: Hold code and credentials until paid
tips.body: Retain ownership of the final code, or the production access, until the last invoice is paid. State this in the contract so it isn't a surprise.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or fixed price for software projects?
faqs.answer: Hourly works best when scope is unclear or likely to change. Fixed price works when requirements are written down and unlikely to shift. Many developers use fixed price for a defined first phase and hourly for later changes and maintenance.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent debugging my own bugs?
faqs.answer: That depends on your contract. Many developers include a warranty period, such as 30 days after delivery, where bugs in the delivered work are fixed free. After that, fixes are billed at the normal rate.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for hosting and software licenses?
faqs.answer: List them as separate lines from labor. Either bill them at cost with the vendor receipt available, or add a small handling markup if your contract allows it. If the client owns the accounts, have them pay the vendors directly instead.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: In the US, a business client that pays you $600 or more in a year (the threshold may change) will usually ask for a W-9 and send a 1099-NEC if you are an independent contractor. Send your W-9 early to avoid delays, and check current IRS rules or ask an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a client refuses to pay after I delivered the code?
faqs.answer: Start with a written reminder citing the contract and invoice date, then a formal demand letter. If you haven't transferred ownership or credentials, you may still have leverage. For larger amounts, small claims court or a collections attorney is an option, depending on your state's limits.

estimate.intro: Developers send estimates before a project starts, usually after a discovery call or after reviewing a written spec. Clients often compare quotes from multiple freelancers or agencies, so they look at total cost, timeline, what is included, and who owns the code at the end.

scopeChecklist.why: A list of specific features, screens, or endpoints sets the boundary of the quote. 'User accounts' can mean a login form or a full role-based permissions system, so be explicit.
Supporting older browsers, iOS and Android, or tablets changes the work considerably. State exactly what will be tested.

scopeChecklist.item: Third-party services and who pays for them
scopeChecklist.why: Hosting, payment processors, email services, maps APIs, and app store accounts have recurring costs. Say whether the client or you pays and whether they are in the quote.
Clarify whether the client supplies designs, copy, images, and data, and what happens to the timeline if they are late.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of revision rounds and review period
scopeChecklist.why: Without limits, feedback can continue forever. Specify how many rounds are included and how long the client has to give feedback.
State whether QA, production setup, documentation, and training are included, and whether you provide a warranty period for bugs.
Clients may assume they own everything. State when ownership transfers and whether you retain rights to reusable components.

pricingTips.title: Estimate in ranges, then commit to a number
pricingTips.body: Break the work into tasks, estimate hours for each, and add 20% to 30% for unknowns, testing, and communication. Present a fixed price or a not-to-exceed cap rather than a vague range.

pricingTips.title: Paid discovery before large quotes
pricingTips.body: For complex projects, charge for a short paid discovery or scoping phase that produces a spec and a firm estimate. This protects you from quoting blind on unclear requirements.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic version, a standard version, and a full version with different features. Clients can pick what fits their budget instead of negotiating your rate down.

pricingTips.title: State what triggers a change order
pricingTips.body: Say in the quote that anything not listed is out of scope and will be estimated separately, so the client knows how extra requests will be handled.

faqs.question: How long should a software estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Most developers set 14 to 30 days. Rates, availability, and third-party pricing can change, and a long-open quote can lock you into a price while the project's requirements drift.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Quick estimates for small jobs are usually free. For larger projects requiring architecture planning or technical research, many developers charge for a discovery phase and credit that fee toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the project takes longer than I estimated?
faqs.answer: On a fixed-price quote, you absorb overruns caused by your own estimating errors, but you can bill for client-driven changes through change orders. On hourly work, give the client a warning when you reach about 75% of the estimated hours.

faqs.question: Can an accepted estimate serve as a contract?
faqs.answer: A signed estimate can be binding in many places, but it is usually too thin for software work. Pair it with a services agreement covering IP, payment terms, termination, and liability, or reference the estimate in the contract as the statement of work.

solar-installer.intro: Solar installers design and install photovoltaic systems on homes and small commercial buildings, and many also add battery storage, EV charger circuits, and system repairs. Invoices usually cover equipment, labor, permitting, and interconnection work, often split into milestone payments because jobs run for weeks. Solo installers and small crews also bill for service calls, panel removal and reinstall for roof work, and monitoring or troubleshooting.
solar-installer.pricingModel: Most residential solar is priced per watt of installed system capacity (price per watt DC), which bundles panels, inverters, racking, labor, and overhead into one number. Small installers often show this as a flat contract price with line items behind it, then bill in milestones: a deposit at signing, a payment when equipment is delivered or installation starts, and a final payment after installation or after the utility grants permission to operate. Add-ons such as batteries, main panel upgrades, trenching, roof reinforcement, and critters guards are priced separately as flat fees or per unit. Service work such as inverter swaps, panel cleaning, and troubleshooting is billed hourly or per visit, usually with a minimum trip charge, and parts are billed at cost plus markup. Permit and interconnection fees are either built into the price or passed through at cost, and the invoice should say which.

rates.service: Battery storage installation (labor and equipment, single unit)
Solar panel removal and reinstall for roof work

items.description: Milestone 2 of 3: Equipment delivered and install started, 7.6 kW rooftop system (19 x 400 W panels, string inverter, rail racking)
Main service panel upgrade, 100A to 200A
Permit and utility interconnection application handling
Roof penetration sealing upgrade (additional flashing on 2 rafter sections, change order #1)
Conduit trenching, 40 ft to detached garage meter location

sampleInvoice.notes: Milestone 1 deposit of $6,000 received at signing. Milestone 3 is due upon utility Permission to Operate. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Change order #1 approved by homeowner on the install date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Equipment warranties and workmanship warranty details are in the signed contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: System size in kW DC and equipment list (panel and inverter make, model, quantity)
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the contract and permit, and gives the customer a record for warranty claims and incentive paperwork.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract reference and milestone number (for example, milestone 2 of 3)
invoiceChecklist.why: Progress billing is common, and the customer needs to see what has been paid and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and electrical license number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a contractor license number on contracts and invoices, and lenders and utilities often ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit number, utility interconnection application number, and inspection dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that the work was permitted and inspected, and helps resolve delays on Permission to Operate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders itemized separately with approval date
invoiceChecklist.why: Roof repairs, panel upgrades, and trenching surprises are the most common sources of billing disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (permit fees, engineering stamps) shown separately from labor and equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes clear what is a real fee versus your markup, and helps if the customer is claiming costs for incentives or financing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment source details when financing or incentives are involved (lender name, loan or dealer fee, rebate assignment)
invoiceChecklist.why: Lender-funded jobs often release payment on milestones, and the invoice must match the lender's draw requirements.

solar-installer.paymentTerms: Residential solar contracts commonly take a deposit of 10 to 30 percent at signing, with a further payment at equipment delivery or install start, and the balance at final inspection or Permission to Operate. Some states limit deposit size on home improvement contracts, so check your local rules. Net 7 to net 14 is typical for milestone invoices, and final payments are often due on completion. Customers pay by check, ACH, or card, and card fees on a five-figure invoice can be significant, so many installers pass them on or prefer ACH. If a customer is using a loan, expect payment from the lender after you submit completion documents, which can take several days. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract.

tips.title: Bill at milestones tied to events you control
tips.body: Tie payments to signing, equipment delivery, install completion, and inspection sign-off. Avoid making your final payment depend only on utility Permission to Operate unless the contract says so, because utility delays can hold your cash for weeks.

tips.title: Put change orders in writing before the work
tips.body: Rafters that need sistering, a panel that cannot take the backfeed, or extra trenching all change the price. Get a signed or emailed approval, then show it as its own line on the invoice.

tips.title: Show the price per watt on the invoice
tips.body: Customers compare quotes by price per watt. Listing system size and the effective rate makes your price easy to check and cuts down on questions.

tips.title: Keep equipment orders from running ahead of deposits
tips.body: Panels, inverters, and batteries are expensive to order. Collect the equipment milestone before you place the order, especially on custom or backordered items.

tips.title: Send completion paperwork with the final invoice
tips.body: Include the inspection sign-off, as-built details, warranty documents, and monitoring setup instructions. A customer who has everything in hand is more likely to pay promptly.

faqs.question: Should I bill solar by the watt or itemize everything?
faqs.answer: Most installers quote a total price and show the price per watt, then list add-ons separately. Itemizing every component can invite line-by-line haggling, but you should itemize anything outside the base scope, such as panel upgrades, trenching, and batteries.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a job that is financed through a loan?
faqs.answer: Match the invoice to the lender's milestone schedule and use the borrower's name and the loan reference if the lender requires it. Lenders often release funds after specific documents such as a signed completion certificate or permit sign-off, so confirm those requirements before you invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on solar installations?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states exempt residential solar equipment or installations, others tax materials, and some treat it differently for commercial customers. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and show any tax or exemption on the invoice.

faqs.question: Who is responsible for the federal tax credit paperwork?
faqs.answer: The customer claims any federal or state tax credit on their own return, and you generally cannot guarantee eligibility. It helps to provide an itemized invoice with system size, cost, and date placed in service so they have what their tax preparer needs.

faqs.question: What if the utility delays Permission to Operate and the customer will not pay the final balance?
faqs.answer: This is why contracts should define the final payment trigger clearly. If the contract ties final payment to completed installation and passed inspection, you can invoice then. If it is tied to Permission to Operate, document your submissions and follow up with the utility on the customer's behalf.

estimate.intro: Solar installers send a written proposal before any equipment is ordered, usually after a site visit or remote design review and a look at the customer's electric bills. Customers typically compare several quotes on price per watt, panel and inverter brands, warranties, and expected production. A clear proposal also sets expectations about roof condition, electrical upgrades, and utility timelines.

scopeChecklist.item: System size, panel and inverter models, and quantities
scopeChecklist.why: Equipment substitutions are common because of supply issues, and the customer should know what they are buying and when a substitution is allowed.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated annual production and the assumptions behind it
scopeChecklist.why: Shading, roof orientation, and tilt drive output. Stating assumptions and that estimates are not guarantees limits disputes about performance.

scopeChecklist.item: Roof and structural conditions included or excluded
scopeChecklist.why: Rotten decking, undersized rafters, and old roofing can force extra work. Say how these will be priced if found.

scopeChecklist.item: Electrical scope: panel upgrades, meter work, trenching, and conduit runs
scopeChecklist.why: The main panel and wiring distances are the biggest sources of cost changes after signing.

scopeChecklist.item: Permits, engineering, HOA approval, and utility interconnection responsibilities
scopeChecklist.why: Customers assume this is included. Spell out who submits applications and who pays the fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline and what could delay it
scopeChecklist.why: Permitting, inspections, and utility approval are outside your control. Give realistic ranges rather than fixed dates.

scopeChecklist.item: Warranty terms for equipment, workmanship, and roof penetrations
scopeChecklist.why: Warranty length is a main comparison point and should be written down, with who handles claims.

pricingTips.title: Quote a price per watt and a total
pricingTips.body: Customers compare per watt, so show it, but also give the final total after any known add-ons. Avoid surprise extras by including the main panel and trenching if the site visit shows they are needed.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting a base system, a larger system, and a system with battery storage helps the customer choose and often raises the average job size. Keep each option clearly priced.

pricingTips.title: Build a contingency path for roof and electrical surprises
pricingTips.body: State unit prices for common extras, such as sistering a rafter or adding a subpanel, so a change order is just a quantity times a known price.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Equipment costs, tariffs, and incentives can change. A 15 to 30 day validity period protects your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site assessment or proposal?
faqs.answer: Most residential installers provide this free as part of sales. For complex commercial work, engineering studies, or battery design with multiple site visits, a paid assessment that is credited toward the job if the customer signs is common.

faqs.question: How long should a solar quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Shorter windows make sense when equipment prices are volatile or an incentive deadline is near.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the customer signs?
faqs.answer: Only for items clearly outside the original scope, and only with the customer's written approval. Put the conditions that could change the price, such as hidden roof damage or a panel upgrade, in the original quote.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for on a quote?
faqs.answer: Ten to thirty percent at signing is common, though some states cap deposits on home improvement contracts. Check your local rules and state the deposit amount and schedule in the quote.

solar-panel-cleaning.intro: Solar panel cleaners are solo operators and small crews who wash residential rooftop arrays, ground-mount systems, and commercial installations. They invoice homeowners, property managers, HOAs, and solar installers or O&M companies for one-time washes, recurring maintenance plans, and add-ons like bird-proofing or inspections.
solar-panel-cleaning.pricingModel: Residential jobs are most often priced per panel or as a flat fee based on system size, with a minimum service charge to cover travel and setup. A typical home with 15 to 30 panels runs a flat visit price, and many cleaners quote a per-panel rate that drops slightly on larger arrays. Roof pitch, number of stories, and access difficulty add surcharges. Commercial and ground-mount work is usually priced per kilowatt or per square foot, or as a bid per site, and often sold as an annual contract with 1 to 4 visits per year. Recurring plans are typically discounted 10 to 20 percent compared to one-time visits. Add-ons such as bird-deterrent mesh installation, gutter or roof debris removal, and inspection reports are billed separately by the panel, by the hour, or as flat fees. Water costs are usually built into the rate, though some companies add a fee for hauling purified water in remote locations.

rates.service: Annual or semi-annual residential maintenance plan
Steep roof or three-story access surcharge

items.description: Pure-water wash of 24 rooftop panels (two-story home, standard pitch)
Roof access surcharge (second story, medium pitch)
Removal of leaf and pine needle debris under panel edges
Visual inspection with photo report (cracks, loose wiring, bird nests)
Bird-proofing mesh on south array edge

sampleInvoice.notes: Service completed on March 12 using deionized water, no detergents. Panels were photographed before and after. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Cash, check, or card accepted. Recommended next cleaning: September.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and system size (number of panels or kW)
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers with several properties and commercial clients need to match the invoice to the exact array, and it supports your per-panel or per-kW pricing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and cleaning method used
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting pure water, soft brush, or no-chemical washing documents that you followed manufacturer cleaning guidelines, which matters if a warranty question comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized surcharges (roof pitch, height, difficult access)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines show the customer why the price is above the base rate and reduce pushback.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on work listed separately (mesh, debris removal, inspection)
invoiceChecklist.why: Add-ons often happen on site and were not in the original quote, so a distinct line item records what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Findings from inspection, such as cracked panels or loose wiring
invoiceChecklist.why: Creates a written record that you reported the issue, protecting you if a problem is blamed on your visit later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license number and insurance reference where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many commercial clients, HOAs, and property managers ask for proof of license and liability coverage before they pay. Requirements vary by state and city.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or work order number for commercial clients
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and solar O&M companies often cannot process payment without one.

solar-panel-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential cleanings are commonly paid at completion by card, check, or digital payment, or invoiced with net 7 to net 14 terms. Recurring plan customers are often billed per visit or charged on a card on file. Commercial and HOA clients usually pay on net 30 terms, and larger contracts may require a deposit or quarterly billing. Deposits are uncommon for single residential washes but reasonable for large commercial jobs or bird-proofing projects that need materials. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated on the quote and invoice, though check your local rules on maximum rates.

tips.title: Set a firm minimum charge
tips.body: Small arrays of 8 to 10 panels take almost as long to reach, set up, and pack down as larger ones. A minimum service fee keeps these jobs profitable.

tips.title: Take before and after photos and attach them
tips.body: Photos show the customer the result and back up any inspection findings. They also help when a customer disputes a charge or claims damage.

tips.title: Price recurring plans so renewal is easy
tips.body: Offer a discounted rate for scheduled visits and bill them on a set calendar. Customers in dusty or pollen-heavy areas often need cleaning two to four times a year, and a plan gives you predictable revenue.

tips.title: Bill add-ons and extra time right away
tips.body: If you spend extra time on bird droppings, sap, or hard water buildup, write it on the invoice the same day. Adding it later invites questions.

tips.title: Account for water and travel costs
tips.body: Pure water systems, resin replacement, fuel, and drive time all cut into margin on remote jobs. Use a travel fee or a higher minimum for far-away addresses.

faqs.question: Should I charge per panel or a flat rate for a home?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Per-panel pricing is easy to explain and scales with the system. A flat rate works well when you offer tiers by system size, such as up to 20 panels or 21 to 30. Either way, set a minimum so small jobs still cover your costs.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for a steep or high roof?
faqs.answer: Yes. Roof pitch, height, and the need for fall protection or extra equipment justify a surcharge. List it as its own line on the quote and invoice so the customer sees it was agreed to.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on solar panel cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning or maintenance services and others tax only goods, so check with your state revenue department or an accountant. If you sell materials like bird mesh, those may be taxable even when labor is not.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a recurring maintenance plan?
faqs.answer: Most cleaners either invoice after each visit or bill the full season or year upfront at a discount. Put the visit schedule, the price per visit, and the cancellation terms on the plan agreement, and reference it on each invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do if I find damaged panels during a cleaning?
faqs.answer: Photograph the damage, note it on the invoice or a separate report, and tell the customer before you leave if possible. Recommend they contact their installer or a licensed solar technician for repairs, unless you are licensed and insured to do that work.

estimate.intro: Solar panel cleaners send estimates before first-time residential cleanings, for recurring maintenance plans, and for commercial bids. Customers usually compare price per panel, what water and method you use, and whether you are insured. Many also compare a one-time visit price against a discounted annual plan.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of panels or system size and array locations
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing depends on the count and layout, and a stated number prevents disputes if the actual system is larger than the customer described.

scopeChecklist.item: Roof type, pitch, and access method
scopeChecklist.why: Steep, tile, or multi-story roofs take longer and may require extra safety equipment, so access should be confirmed up front.
Stating deionized or pure water with soft brushes and no harsh chemicals reassures customers and aligns with typical manufacturer guidance.

scopeChecklist.item: What is and is not included
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether gutters, skylights, windows, debris under panels, or bird droppings are covered, so extra work is not a surprise.
If you need an outdoor spigot or power source, say so. Otherwise note that you bring your own water, which may affect pricing.

scopeChecklist.item: Scheduling, weather policy, and rescheduling terms
scopeChecklist.why: Rain, wind, high heat, or ice can delay work, and a stated policy sets expectations.
HOAs, property managers, and many homeowners want proof of liability coverage before approving work.

pricingTips.title: Offer a one-time price and a plan price
pricingTips.body: Showing both on the estimate makes the discount clear and gives customers an easy way to choose recurring service. A 10 to 20 percent reduction is typical.

pricingTips.title: Verify the panel count before quoting
pricingTips.body: Ask for the installer's system summary, a photo of the roof, or satellite imagery. A quote based on a guess can leave you underpaid or force a revision on site.

pricingTips.title: Build in a minimum and surcharges
pricingTips.body: List a base rate, a minimum visit fee, and any access surcharges separately. This keeps small and difficult jobs profitable without inflating the per-panel number.

pricingTips.title: For commercial bids, price per kW and show visit frequency
pricingTips.body: Facility managers compare vendors on annual cost and visits per year. Break out the price per cleaning and the annual total so they can evaluate easily.

faqs.question: Should I give quotes over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range if the customer knows their panel count, but confirm the details in writing before you book. Satellite imagery or photos help you verify roof access and array size.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for residential quotes. For commercial bids, 30 to 60 days is typical, especially if you are quoting annual contracts and fuel or labor costs may change.

faqs.question: Do I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential estimates are free, especially when done remotely. Charging for a site visit is more common for large commercial or ground-mount sites, and the fee is often credited toward the job if the customer signs.

faqs.question: What if the actual job is bigger than the estimate?
faqs.answer: State in the estimate that the price is based on the stated panel count and conditions, and that extra panels or heavy buildup will be billed at your listed rates. Tell the customer before doing the additional work and note it on the invoice.

sound-designer.intro: Sound designers create and edit audio for games, film, video, theater, apps, podcasts, and advertising. They bill for original sound effects, Foley, field recording, sound libraries, ambience, UI sounds, mixing, and implementation into game engines or edit timelines. Most work as freelancers or run small studios, and clients range from indie developers to ad agencies and production companies.
sound-designer.pricingModel: Sound designers price by the project, by the asset, by the hour, or by the finished minute of picture. Games often use per-asset pricing (for example per sound effect or per sound set) or a flat package for a defined list of assets, sometimes with a monthly retainer during production. Film, video, and ad work is commonly quoted as a flat fee for a sound design pass or as a day rate for studio or on-set work. Hourly rates are used for revisions, small fixes, and out-of-scope requests. Mixing, mastering, and audio middleware implementation (Wwise, FMOD, Unity, Unreal) are often priced separately from asset creation. Licensing matters: most clients want a buyout or work-for-hire, and exclusive rights or use of the work in a sound library can raise the price. Rush work, extra revision rounds, and delivery in multiple formats (stems, 5.1, various sample rates) are typically add-ons.

rates.service: Sound design for a game or app (custom SFX)
Sound design pass for short film or video
Studio or on-set sound day rate
Sound mixing for video or podcast

items.description: Custom SFX for indie game: UI, weapons, footsteps, and ambience (milestone 2 of 3)
Wwise implementation and event setup
Foley session recording and editing (cloth, props, doors)
Additional revision round beyond contract (weapon set)
Delivery of stems and source session files

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Rights to delivered assets transfer to client upon payment in full, per the signed agreement. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Accepted: bank transfer, ACH, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone or delivery batch
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the specific phase or asset list, which matters when work is billed in stages across a long production.

invoiceChecklist.item: Asset list or cue sheet reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to see which sounds, scenes, or events are covered so there is no confusion over what was delivered and paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and any extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how many rounds were included in the quote and documents out-of-scope changes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rights and licensing terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States whether the client gets work-for-hire, a buyout, or a limited license, and that transfer happens on full payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery format and specs
invoiceChecklist.why: Sample rate, bit depth, file format, stems, and channel layout can drive cost and avoid disputes over re-exports.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party libraries or licensed content costs
invoiceChecklist.why: If you pass through sample library fees, talent fees, or studio rental, list them separately so they are clear and not treated as your rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and studios often need it for their accounts payable to process payment.

sound-designer.paymentTerms: A deposit of 25-50% before work starts is common, especially for new clients, with the balance due on delivery or split across milestones. For game work, milestone-based billing tied to asset batches or builds is typical. Net 15 or net 30 are standard terms for studios and agencies, while smaller clients are often asked to pay sooner. Many sound designers add a late fee in the range of 1-2% per month, clearly stated in the contract. Payment is usually by bank transfer, ACH, check, or card, and international clients may use wire transfer. Larger companies may require a W-9 and may pay on 30-60 day cycles, so confirm their process before starting.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid
tips.body: Deliver watermarked previews or low-quality reference mixes for review, and release full-resolution files, stems, and session files only after the final payment clears.

tips.title: Limit revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Include two or three rounds in the quote and bill extra rounds hourly. Sound feedback tends to be subjective and can go on indefinitely without a defined limit.

tips.title: Bill implementation separately from creation
tips.body: Time spent integrating assets in Wwise, FMOD, or an engine is a different skill and workload from making the sounds. Listing it as its own line keeps scope and cost clear.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones on long projects
tips.body: Games and films can run for months. Bill when asset batches, a locked picture pass, or a mix is delivered so you are not carrying the cost until launch.

tips.title: Track licensed material and expenses
tips.body: Record costs for sample libraries, rented gear, studio time, and voice or Foley artists so they can be passed through or documented for tax purposes.

faqs.question: Should I charge per asset or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Per-asset pricing works well when the list is clear, such as a defined set of UI sounds or weapon effects. Hourly billing suits open-ended work, such as implementation, fixes, or exploratory sound design. Many sound designers combine them: per-asset for creation and hourly for revisions and integration.

faqs.question: How do I handle rights and ownership on the invoice?
faqs.answer: State what the client receives, such as full buyout, work-for-hire, or a limited license, and that it applies upon full payment. The details should be in your contract, and the invoice can reference it. If you reserve the right to reuse sounds in a library or portfolio, put that in writing.

faqs.question: Do I charge for source files and stems?
faqs.answer: Many do, either as a flat delivery fee or as part of a higher package. Final mixed files are the baseline, while project sessions, stems, and layered source files give the client more control and are often priced as an add-on.

faqs.question: What if a client keeps requesting changes?
faqs.answer: Point to the number of included revision rounds in your agreement and bill additional rounds at your hourly rate. Document each round's requests in writing so the invoice reflects what was actually asked for.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and what you deliver. Some states tax digital goods or certain creative services, while others do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and list any tax charged as a separate line.

estimate.intro: Sound designers send a quote before work starts on most projects, especially for games, films, ads, and custom libraries. Clients often compare quotes by price per asset, total fee, number of revisions, and what rights are included. A clear quote helps them understand the difference between a cheap set of sounds and a full package with implementation and delivery.

scopeChecklist.item: List of assets or scenes covered
scopeChecklist.why: Defines exactly which sound effects, ambiences, UI sounds, or picture reels are included so extra requests can be priced separately.
Sets a limit on subjective feedback and gives you a basis to bill additional rounds.
Clarifies whether sounds are newly recorded, synthesized, or built from licensed libraries, which affects uniqueness and cost.
Sample rate, bit depth, file type, stems, and surround formats can change the workload and avoid re-delivery disputes.
States whether you will integrate assets in Wwise, FMOD, or a game engine, or just deliver files for the client's team to implement.
Confirms whether the client receives a buyout, work-for-hire, or limited license, and whether you can use the work in your portfolio.
Ties your schedule to when the client provides builds, locked picture, or approvals, and covers rush fees if they delay and then need a fast turnaround.

pricingTips.title: Quote per asset with a bundle price
pricingTips.body: Show a per-asset rate and a total for the full list. Clients can see how much each addition costs, and you have a clear rate for later changes.

pricingTips.title: Add a rush fee for tight deadlines
pricingTips.body: Rush work often means other projects get pushed. A surcharge of 25-50% for short turnaround is common.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A basic package of core effects, a standard one with ambience and Foley, and a premium one with implementation and stems helps clients choose a budget while keeping scope defined.

pricingTips.title: Price for the complexity, not just the count
pricingTips.body: A layered creature vocalization or a long ambient loop takes much more time than a button click. Use higher per-asset rates or a separate category for complex sounds.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat fee or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: A flat fee suits clearly defined projects, such as a set number of effects or a single short film. An hourly estimate with a cap is better for projects where the scope may change, such as early game development.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Production schedules and your availability can change, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I take a deposit when the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Yes, most sound designers ask for 25-50% upfront. It confirms the client's commitment and covers early costs, such as recording sessions or library purchases.

faqs.question: Can I charge for creating a test sound or demo?
faqs.answer: Many sound designers do paid tests, especially for large projects, and credit the fee toward the final price. Unpaid tests are common for small jobs but can lead to extended unpaid work, so limit them to one or two sounds.

speech-therapist.intro: Speech therapists, also called speech-language pathologists (SLPs), who work privately bill families, adults, schools, and facilities for evaluations, therapy sessions, and related services. Private-pay clients, and insurance clients who need a receipt to submit for reimbursement, are the people who most often receive a standalone invoice. Typical charges include assessments, individual or group sessions, report writing, and consultations with teachers or other providers.
speech-therapist.pricingModel: Most private practice SLPs charge per session, with a set length of 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Evaluations are priced separately and higher than treatment, often as a flat fee that includes testing, scoring, and a written report. Some clinicians sell packages of sessions at a small discount, or bill monthly for a fixed number of weekly visits. Time outside the session, such as school meetings, IEP attendance, phone consults, and extended report writing, is usually billed hourly. Travel or mobile visits to homes and schools may add a trip fee or a higher session rate. Contract SLPs working for schools, clinics, or staffing agencies are often paid hourly and invoice the agency instead of the family. Clinicians who accept insurance bill through claims, while private-pay and out-of-network clients receive a superbill or invoice with the codes needed for reimbursement.

rates.service: Initial speech or language evaluation with written report
Group therapy or social skills group
Home, school, or telehealth visit surcharge or mobile rate
IEP meeting, teacher consult, or care coordination
Contract SLP work for school or agency
Progress report or letter for insurance or school

items.description: Individual speech therapy session, articulation (45 min) - dates: 3/4, 3/11, 3/18, 3/25
Teacher consultation by phone (30 min)
Written progress report for school
Late cancellation fee (less than 24 hours notice) - 3/13

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days. Accepted by card, check, or HSA/FSA card. A superbill with CPT and diagnosis codes is attached for out-of-network reimbursement. Cancellations need 24 hours notice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client and patient names, and date of birth
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents are often the payer while the child is the patient. Insurers and HSA/FSA administrators need to match the claim to the right person.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of each session and its length
invoiceChecklist.why: Families and reimbursement plans need each date of service, and listing them prevents disputes about how many sessions were billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes and diagnosis (ICD-10) codes
invoiceChecklist.why: Common codes such as 92507 for treatment or 92523 for evaluation let clients submit for out-of-network reimbursement. Only include codes you are qualified and permitted to use.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your name, credentials, license number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and many flexible spending accounts require the provider's credentials (such as CCC-SLP) and identifiers on documentation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location or telehealth indicator
invoiceChecklist.why: Place of service can affect reimbursement, and telehealth visits may be coded differently from in-person ones.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized fees for non-session work
invoiceChecklist.why: Reports, consults, and meetings should be listed with time and rate so they are not mistaken for therapy sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show policy and any fees applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Charging a late-cancel fee is easier to enforce when it references a policy the client agreed to in writing.

speech-therapist.paymentTerms: Many private practice SLPs collect payment at the time of service by card on file, and send invoices monthly or after a block of sessions for clients who prefer to pay later. Net 7 to net 14 is common for private-pay families, and net 30 is more typical for schools, agencies, and facilities. Evaluations are often paid in full at booking or on the day of testing. Late fees are usually small and should be stated in your intake paperwork. Accepted methods commonly include credit and debit cards, HSA/FSA cards, checks, and bank transfer. Contract SLPs invoicing districts or staffing companies should follow the payer's schedule and may wait 30 to 60 days.

tips.title: Put the cancellation policy in the intake paperwork
tips.body: Children get sick often, so late cancellations are common. Ask for 24 hours notice, state the fee, and have the parent sign the policy before the first session so a fee on an invoice is not a surprise.

tips.title: Keep billing records separate from clinical notes
tips.body: Your invoice should show dates, services, and codes without clinical detail. Share only what the payer needs, and follow HIPAA rules if you are a covered entity.

tips.title: Offer a superbill to out-of-network clients
tips.body: Many families submit your documents to their insurer for partial reimbursement. A clear itemized superbill with codes, your NPI, and proof of payment saves you repeated requests.

tips.title: Bill report writing and meetings
tips.body: Evaluation reports, progress summaries, and IEP meetings take real time. Include them in the evaluation fee or list them as separate line items so unpaid hours do not pile up.

tips.title: Invoice schools and agencies by the contract terms
tips.body: If you contract with a district or agency, match your invoice to their required format, including service logs, student IDs if permitted, and purchase order numbers.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for missed or late-canceled sessions?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if the policy is written and the client agreed to it before services began. Note the date and the fee on the invoice. Insurance plans often do not cover missed-session fees, so these are usually billed directly to the family.

faqs.question: What is a superbill, and should I include one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with your credentials, NPI, dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis codes, and the amount paid. Out-of-network clients send it to their insurer for reimbursement. If you do not bill insurance, offering one is a common courtesy.

faqs.question: Should I bill per session or per hour?
faqs.answer: Per session is the most common approach because it is simple for families. Use hourly billing for work outside sessions, such as consultations, meetings, and long report writing, where time varies.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on therapy?
faqs.answer: Healthcare services are generally not subject to sales tax in most states, but rules vary. Products like therapy materials you sell separately may be taxable. Check with your state department of revenue or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I handle invoices for school districts?
faqs.answer: Ask for the district's invoicing requirements before starting. They often need a contract or PO number, service dates, hours, and sometimes signed service logs. Payment is typically on net 30 or longer terms.

estimate.intro: Speech therapists send estimates when a family asks what an evaluation and a course of therapy will cost, when a school or agency requests a contract bid, or when a client wants to know out-of-pocket costs before starting. Families often compare cost per session, how many sessions are likely, and whether you provide paperwork for insurance reimbursement.

scopeChecklist.item: Evaluation fee and what it includes
scopeChecklist.why: State whether the fee covers testing, scoring, the written report, and a feedback meeting, so families know what is paid for up front.

scopeChecklist.item: Session length, frequency, and expected duration
scopeChecklist.why: A quote of weekly 45-minute sessions for about three months is clear. Make it explicit that actual need depends on progress.
Clinic, home, school, and telehealth visits can have different rates or travel fees. Spell out which one the quote assumes.
Reports, IEP meetings, teacher consults, and phone time beyond a set limit should be listed so they are not seen as hidden fees.
Say whether you are in network, out of network, or private-pay only, and whether you provide a superbill. Families should know you cannot guarantee reimbursement.
Including the policy at the quote stage sets expectations before the first appointment.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity and rate change policy
scopeChecklist.why: State how long the quote holds and when your rates may be reviewed, such as at the start of the year.

pricingTips.title: Quote the evaluation as a flat fee
pricingTips.body: Testing, scoring, and report writing take several hours. A flat fee is easier for families to compare and ensures your unbilled time is covered.

pricingTips.title: Give a range of sessions, not a promise
pricingTips.body: Outcomes vary, so estimate a likely number of sessions and say the plan will be reviewed regularly. This avoids implying a guaranteed result or length of care.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package only if it helps you
pricingTips.body: A prepaid block of sessions at a modest discount can improve cash flow, but state what happens to unused sessions and refunds.

pricingTips.title: Price contract bids on all-in hourly cost
pricingTips.body: For districts and agencies, include travel, documentation, and meeting time in your hourly rate, since many contracts pay only for direct service hours.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Many SLPs offer a short free phone call to discuss fit and fees, but charge for any in-depth consultation or evaluation. State clearly which one is free before the call.

faqs.question: Can I give a firm total price for therapy?
faqs.answer: Usually not, because the number of sessions depends on progress. Give a per-session rate and a likely range of sessions, and make clear the family can stop or adjust at any time.

faqs.question: How do I quote for a school or agency contract?
faqs.answer: Ask about caseload, hours per week, travel, documentation, and meeting expectations. Quote an hourly rate that covers non-direct time, and confirm the payment schedule and cancellation terms in the contract.

faqs.question: What if a family wants to know what insurance will pay?
faqs.answer: You can explain your fees and provide a superbill, but reimbursement depends on the plan. Suggest they call their insurer to ask about out-of-network speech therapy benefits, deductibles, and visit limits.

spray-tan-artist.intro: Spray tan artists apply sunless tanning solution by hand-held airbrush, booth, or automated systems. They work from salons, studios, home setups, or travel to clients. Invoices usually cover single sessions, multi-session packages, add-ons, travel fees, and group or event bookings such as weddings, proms, and photo shoots.
spray-tan-artist.pricingModel: Most spray tan artists charge a flat price per session, usually between $30 and $65 for a standard full-body application. Premium or organic solutions, rapid-develop formulas, and custom color blends often add $5 to $20. Mobile artists add a travel or convenience fee, or charge a higher base rate for in-home visits. Packages of three to five sessions are common and typically carry a 10 to 20 percent discount, paid upfront. Events and group bookings are often priced per person with a minimum, plus a travel fee and sometimes a setup fee for a pop-up tent. Retail items like tan extender lotion, mitts, and barrier cream are sold at a markup of about 40 to 100 percent over wholesale.

rates.service: Custom blend or organic solution upgrade
Group or event booking (wedding party, prom, photo shoot)
Tan extender lotion or aftercare product

items.description: Bridal party mobile spray tans (bride plus 4 bridesmaids), rapid solution
Custom blend upgrade for bride (trial and day-of)
Bridal trial spray tan, completed 2 weeks before event
Travel fee, venue 25 miles from studio
Tan extender lotion

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $100 received at booking and applied to this total. Balance due on the day of service by card, Venmo, or cash. Please arrive with clean, exfoliated, unmoisturized skin and wear loose dark clothing. Rescheduling requires 48 hours notice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Appointment date, time, and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and event work happens off-site, and a clear record of where and when you worked prevents disputes about missed or partial sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Solution type and any upgrades
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients pay different prices for standard, rapid, organic, or custom blends, so itemizing these shows exactly what they received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Number of people serviced
invoiceChecklist.why: Group bookings are billed per person, and the headcount on the invoice should match the final count, not the original estimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel fee or mileage
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating travel from the service price makes the cost transparent and justifies higher totals for distant venues.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Most artists collect a deposit to hold the date, so the invoice should show what was already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retail products sold
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing aftercare products separately keeps your service revenue and product sales clear for bookkeeping and sales tax.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation and reschedule terms
invoiceChecklist.why: A short policy line, such as a late-cancel fee, gives you a reference if a client no-shows or cancels the same day.

spray-tan-artist.paymentTerms: Single sessions are typically paid at the time of service by card, cash, or a payment app. Events and weddings usually require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to hold the date, with the balance due on the day of service or a few days before. Packages are normally paid in full upfront and often expire after a set period, such as 90 days. Many artists charge a late-cancel or no-show fee of 25 to 50 percent of the service price, and a small fee or lost deposit for changes with less than 24 to 48 hours notice. If you invoice ahead of time, net 7 days is common for private clients, and corporate or production clients may ask for net 15 or net 30.

tips.title: Require a deposit for events
