tips.body: Group bookings take a whole day and are hard to refill if someone cancels. Take a non-refundable deposit at booking and state it on the quote and invoice.

tips.title: Charge for cancellations and no-shows
tips.body: Solution is mixed and the time slot is held for the client. A written late-cancel policy, shown at booking and on the invoice, lets you charge consistently without awkward conversations.

tips.title: Set expiry dates on packages
tips.body: Unused sessions can sit on your books for a year. A 60 to 90 day expiry on the package invoice keeps your schedule and revenue predictable.

tips.title: Price travel separately
tips.body: Drive time and setup are real costs. A line item for travel, or a tiered fee by distance, keeps the base session price consistent and avoids discounting your own time.

tips.title: Track product costs
tips.body: Solution, disposable supplies, booth filters, and tent setup cost money per session. Review these every few months and adjust your rates if costs have risen.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on spray tans?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax tanning services, some tax only retail products, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant, and if you do collect tax, show it as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice a bridal party where people pay separately?
faqs.answer: Create one invoice per person or one per booking with each guest listed as a line item. If guests pay individually, send separate invoices or collect payment at the appointment, and keep the bride's deposit clearly applied to her own total.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee if a client shows up with lotion, makeup, or unprepared skin?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your policy says so in advance. Many artists include a preparation requirement in their booking terms and charge a prep or rebook fee if skin needs extra exfoliation or the client cannot be serviced properly.

faqs.question: What should I do about a client who is unhappy with their color?
faqs.answer: Set expectations in your policy: color varies by skin type and aftercare. Many artists offer a free or discounted adjustment within a short window, such as 48 hours, for a documented issue. Note any adjustment or credit on the original invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice if the client pays at the appointment?
faqs.answer: Yes, give a receipt or paid invoice for every payment. It protects you in a dispute, supports your tax records, and lets clients with business or event budgets get reimbursed.

estimate.intro: Spray tan artists send estimates mostly for events: weddings, proms, pageants, photo shoots, and corporate parties. Clients compare per-person price, travel fees, how many people you can handle in a set time, and whether solutions or touch-ups are included. A clear quote helps them plan their budget and your schedule.

scopeChecklist.item: Headcount and maximum number of people
scopeChecklist.why: Your time and solution depend on the number of guests. State what the quote covers and the price for additional people.

scopeChecklist.item: Event date, start time, and window available
scopeChecklist.why: Spray tans take about 15 to 30 minutes per person including dry time, so a time window determines how many people you can service.
You need a private space, a bathroom or changing area, power, and sometimes a tent. Note any extra setup or tent fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Solution type and color options included
scopeChecklist.why: Rapid, organic, or custom blends cost more. List what is included in the base price so upgrades do not cause disputes.
Brides often want a trial to test color. State whether the trial is separate and how much it costs.

scopeChecklist.item: Travel fee and parking or tolls
scopeChecklist.why: Distance and parking affect cost. Put these in the quote so they do not appear as a surprise on the final invoice.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amount, cancellation policy, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Dates book up around prom and wedding season, so the quote should say how long it holds and what is required to confirm.

pricingTips.title: Quote per person with a minimum
pricingTips.body: A per-person rate with a minimum total, such as five people or $250, covers your travel and setup time for small groups while staying simple for larger ones.

pricingTips.title: Add tiered prices for solution upgrades
pricingTips.body: Offer standard, rapid, and organic options with clear prices. Clients tend to choose a middle tier when they can see the choices side by side.

pricingTips.title: Build in time for no-shows and delays
pricingTips.body: Group events run late. Include a note that late guests may lose their slot or be charged, and price your minimum with a buffer in mind.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package incentive
pricingTips.body: For regulars or brides, bundle a trial, event-day tan, and one touch-up at a slightly lower combined price. It increases the total booking and gives the client a reason to commit.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a trial session?
faqs.answer: Most artists do, since the time and solution cost the same as a regular session. Some credit the trial fee toward the event booking if the client confirms.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is common for events, shorter in busy seasons. State an expiry date on the quote and make clear the date is not held until the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: What if the headcount changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the quote that the price is based on the stated headcount and that additions or removals are billed per person. Ask for the final count a few days before the event.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge a different price for rush bookings?
faqs.answer: Many artists add a rush or same-day fee of $10 to $25 for bookings with less than 24 hours notice, especially if you have to rearrange your schedule or travel on short notice.

sprinkler-repair.intro: Sprinkler repair technicians and small irrigation companies fix broken heads, leaking valves, damaged lines, faulty controllers, and zones that will not run for homeowners, HOAs, and small commercial properties. Invoices usually combine a service call or diagnostic charge, labor time, and parts, and seasonal work such as spring start-ups and fall blowouts is billed as flat-rate visits.
sprinkler-repair.pricingModel: Most sprinkler repair is priced as a service call fee plus time and materials. The service call covers travel and diagnosis and is often credited toward the repair or charged separately. Labor is billed hourly, often with a one-hour minimum, and parts are listed individually with a markup of roughly 20 to 50 percent over cost. Common small jobs like head replacement, valve replacement, and controller swaps are often flat-rated so customers know the price up front. Seasonal services (spring start-up, winterization or blowout) are flat fees, usually priced per zone or by a base fee plus a per-zone add-on. Larger work such as trenching to replace a broken mainline or adding zones is quoted as a flat price after a site visit. Maintenance plans and HOA or commercial contracts are billed monthly or per visit.

rates.service: Sprinkler head replacement (rotor or spray, parts included)

items.description: Service call and system diagnosis, 6-zone system
Replace 4 pop-up spray heads (heads, nozzles, swing joints)
Replace failed zone 3 valve (1" valve, solenoid, wire connectors)
Repair broken 1" PVC lateral line under driveway edge (fittings, glue, backfill)
Additional labor: test all zones, adjust coverage and rain sensor

sampleInvoice.notes: Work completed and all 6 zones tested and running. Parts carry a 90-day warranty and labor carries a 30-day warranty. Payment due within 14 days. Accepted: check, card, or ACH. Future winterization can be scheduled in October.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and zone or area worked on
invoiceChecklist.why: Many customers own several properties or have multiple systems, and zone numbers show exactly what was repaired if the same problem returns.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized parts with sizes and types
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing a 1" valve versus a 3/4" valve, or a rotor versus a spray head, justifies the price and helps the next technician.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate service call fee and labor hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often question a trip charge, and showing it separately from time on site prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor or irrigation license number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and municipalities require a license for irrigation work, and displaying it builds trust. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Backflow preventer work and test results
invoiceChecklist.why: If you repaired or tested a backflow device, many water utilities require a record, and the invoice can serve as documentation.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms on parts and labor
invoiceChecklist.why: A stated warranty period prevents confusion when a customer calls about a failure weeks later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of service and technician name
invoiceChecklist.why: This creates a clear history for seasonal visits and recurring problems, and helps with HOA or property manager records.

sprinkler-repair.paymentTerms: Residential repairs are commonly due on completion, with payment by card, check, or ACH at the end of the visit or from an emailed invoice. Small jobs rarely need a deposit, but larger installs or mainline replacements often require 25 to 50 percent up front, mainly to cover parts. Commercial, HOA, and property manager accounts are usually net 15 or net 30. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated on the invoice or agreement in advance, though rules on late fees vary by state. Seasonal customers on a maintenance plan are often billed monthly or per visit, sometimes with a card kept on file.

tips.title: Charge a service call fee and say so up front
tips.body: Diagnosis takes time and fuel even when the fix is a $4 nozzle. Quote the service call fee when booking and state whether it is credited toward repairs so there are no surprises at payment.

tips.title: Mark up parts consistently
tips.body: Valves, solenoids, heads, and fittings add up, and you carry the cost of stocking them and the warranty risk. Use a consistent markup, such as 25 to 40 percent, and list parts by line item.

tips.title: Offer flat rates for common repairs
tips.body: Head replacement, valve replacement, and controller swaps are predictable. A flat price list makes quoting on the phone easier and cuts disputes about how long a job took.

tips.title: Bill for what you find, and document it
tips.body: If you discover a leaking backflow preventer, a cracked mainline, or a controller wired incorrectly, note it on the invoice and send a separate estimate. Photos attached to the invoice help when customers question extra work.

tips.title: Build seasonal billing into your calendar
tips.body: Spring start-ups and fall blowouts are your steadiest revenue. Send reminders and invoice at the time of service so winterization does not go unpaid after the season ends.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a service call if the customer declines the repair?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. The visit covers your travel and diagnosis time. State the fee when scheduling and put it on the invoice even if no repair is done.

faqs.question: How do I bill for repairs that take longer than expected?
faqs.answer: If you quoted a flat price, honor it unless the scope changes, such as finding a second broken line. If you bill hourly, list the actual hours and explain any added work on the invoice. Contact the customer before starting extra work when possible.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on sprinkler repairs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax parts, some tax labor, some tax both, and some tax neither for repairs. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant.

faqs.question: Can I bill for winterization per zone or as a flat fee?
faqs.answer: Either works. Many companies charge a base fee that includes a set number of zones, such as up to 6, then add a per-zone fee for larger systems. Whatever you choose, state it on the invoice.

faqs.question: What should I do when a customer does not pay for completed repairs?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice attached, follow up by phone, and apply any late fee you disclosed in advance. In many states, licensed contractors may have lien rights on larger jobs, but rules vary, so check locally before relying on that.

estimate.intro: Sprinkler repair technicians usually give a phone range for simple fixes and a written estimate after a site visit for larger work such as mainline replacement, adding zones, or a controller upgrade. Customers typically compare the total price, the parts brand and quality, and whether the quote includes restoring the lawn or landscaping.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing zones and components prevents the customer from assuming you will also fix issues you did not diagnose.
Rain Bird, Hunter, and Toro products vary in price, and naming them avoids disputes about quality.
State whether you will replace sod, mulch, or concrete patches, or only backfill the trench, since lawn repair is a common source of complaints.
Digging often requires a utility locate call, and some jurisdictions require permits for backflow or new zones. Say who handles this and whether it affects price.
Testing, replacement, or a pressure regulator can add cost, so note it as included or excluded.

scopeChecklist.item: What happens if hidden damage is found
scopeChecklist.why: Cracked lines or buried valves often turn up mid-job, so state that extra work will be quoted before it proceeds.
Part prices change, and a validity window such as 30 days protects you while warranty terms set expectations.

pricingTips.title: Quote in tiers when the fix is open-ended
pricingTips.body: For an aging system, offer a basic repair, a repair plus replacing worn components, and a controller upgrade. Customers often choose the middle option when they see the choice laid out.

pricingTips.title: Estimate time for digging, not just parts
pricingTips.body: Finding a leak under turf can take longer than the repair. Build in locate and trench time, especially in clay or rocky soil, and in properties with irrigation lines under hardscape.

pricingTips.title: Separate the diagnostic from the repair quote
pricingTips.body: If the problem is unknown, charge the service call to diagnose, then give a fixed price for the repair. This avoids underquoting a mystery fault.

pricingTips.title: Include a line for contingencies on mainline work
pricingTips.body: Mainline repairs sit under pressure and may reveal multiple breaks. A stated allowance or unit price for additional fittings and pipe lets you adjust without a dispute.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Simple repair estimates are usually free, but a diagnostic or service call fee is common when you must troubleshoot. For design work or adding zones, some contractors charge a fee and credit it if the customer hires them.

faqs.question: Can I give a price over the phone?
faqs.answer: You can give a range for standard fixes like replacing a head or a timer. Say it is an estimate and that hidden problems found on site may change the price.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Parts costs change and seasonal demand shifts, so put an expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before starting?
faqs.answer: For larger jobs, get a signature or written approval by email or text. It documents the agreed scope and price and helps if a disagreement comes up later.

squarespace-designer.intro: Squarespace designers build and customize websites on the Squarespace platform for small businesses, creatives, restaurants, and service providers. Most work as freelancers or in small studios. They bill for site design and build, template customization, e-commerce setup, content migration, and ongoing maintenance.
squarespace-designer.pricingModel: Most Squarespace designers price new builds as flat project fees based on page count, complexity, and whether the client supplies content. A typical project is split into milestone payments, such as a deposit, a midpoint payment, and a final payment before launch. Hourly rates are common for small fixes, custom CSS or code injection, training sessions, and work outside the original scope. Add-ons such as online store setup, member areas, scheduling integrations, blog migration, and basic SEO setup are often priced separately or bundled into tiered packages. Ongoing work is usually sold as a monthly retainer for updates and support, or as a block of prepaid hours. Platform costs, such as the client's Squarespace plan, domain renewal, paid extensions, and stock photos, are normally paid by the client directly. If you buy them on the client's behalf, list them as separate line items and consider a small handling fee.

rates.service: Small business site (3-5 pages) built on a template
Site redesign or migration from another platform

Custom CSS for header styling and mobile layout adjustments
Blog migration from WordPress, 24 posts with images
Basic on-page SEO setup (page titles, descriptions, image alt text, sitemap submission)
Admin training session via video call

sampleInvoice.notes: Total reflects the final milestone payment for the project. Payment is due within 14 days of the invoice date. Site launch and DNS connection are scheduled once payment is received. Squarespace plan and domain renewals are billed to the client directly. Two weeks of post-launch bug fixes are included at no charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone being billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Builds are billed in stages, and the client should see which stage (deposit, design approval, launch) this invoice covers and what was already paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: List of pages and features delivered
invoiceChecklist.why: Naming the pages, store setup, forms, and integrations ties the charge to specific deliverables and heads off arguments about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for hourly and out-of-scope work
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra revisions, added pages, and custom code beyond the agreement should show hours and rate so the client understands why the total changed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs passed through
invoiceChecklist.why: Paid extensions, stock photos, fonts, or a domain you bought for the client should be itemized with receipts available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Account ownership and access note
invoiceChecklist.why: A line stating the client owns the Squarespace account and your contributor access ends at handoff avoids confusion about who holds the site.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used
invoiceChecklist.why: If your contract includes a set number of revision rounds, noting how many were used supports any overage charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment due date and late fee terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Clear terms matter because many designers hold the launch or domain connection until the final payment clears.

squarespace-designer.paymentTerms: Most Squarespace designers collect a 30-50% deposit before starting, since design time is committed upfront. Larger projects are often split into three payments: deposit, a mid-project payment at design approval, and the balance before launch. Net 7 to net 14 is common for milestone invoices, and many designers require the final payment before the site is published or the domain is connected. Late fees of 1.5% per month are typical if stated in the contract. Retainers are usually billed monthly in advance. Bank transfer, credit card, and ACH are common payment methods, and some designers add a small processing fee for cards.

tips.title: Tie the final payment to launch
tips.body: Keep your design access or hold the domain connection until the last invoice is paid. State this in your contract and on the invoice so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds
tips.body: Include two or three rounds of revisions in the flat fee and bill additional rounds hourly. Track rounds as they happen so the overage line is easy to justify.

tips.title: Bill content delays
tips.body: Late text, photos, and product data are the most common cause of stalled builds. Set a content deadline, and add a pause or restart fee in your agreement if materials arrive weeks late.

tips.title: Separate platform fees from your fees
tips.body: Have clients buy their own Squarespace plan and domain under their account. This keeps your invoice clean and avoids you being responsible for renewals.

tips.title: Sell maintenance after launch
tips.body: Offer a monthly update plan or prepaid hours at handoff. Small edits are frequent, and a set arrangement beats billing 20 minutes at a time.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a Squarespace site?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best for defined builds because clients want a known price and you are rewarded for working efficiently. Use hourly rates for small fixes, custom code, training, and anything outside the written scope.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 30-50% is typical. Many designers use 50% for small sites and split larger projects into three payments so the balance owed never gets too large.

faqs.question: Can I bill for Squarespace subscription costs?
faqs.answer: It is cleaner for the client to pay Squarespace directly under their own account. If you pay on their behalf, list the charge as a separate pass-through line with a receipt.

faqs.question: What if the client stops responding before launch?
faqs.answer: Include a clause in your contract that lets you close the project after a set period of inactivity, such as 30 days, and invoice for work completed. Send the invoice with a clear summary of what was done.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on web design?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital or web design services and others do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Squarespace designers send a quote after a discovery call or intake form, before any design work begins. Clients usually compare your price against other freelancers, agencies, and doing it themselves, so the quote needs to show clearly what they get for the money. A written proposal also locks in scope before content and revision requests start piling up.

scopeChecklist.why: Naming each page, such as Home, About, Services, and Contact, sets a clear boundary and makes added pages an obvious change.
State whether the client provides copy, photos, and logos, or whether you are writing or sourcing them. This is the biggest cause of delays and budget overruns.
List forms, newsletter signup, scheduling, online store, member areas, and third-party embeds so none are assumed to be free.
Specify how many rounds are included and who gives final approval, so feedback does not come from five people over three months.
Give a start date, review windows, and launch target, and note that the schedule depends on timely content and feedback.
Explain that the client buys the Squarespace plan, domain, and any paid extensions, and note which plan level the design requires.
Copywriting, photography, logo design, ongoing SEO, and post-launch support are often assumed to be included. Say plainly if they are not.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as a starter site, a standard build, and a full build with store and SEO. Clients tend to pick the middle option, and it gives them a way to adjust price without haggling.

pricingTips.title: Price content risk into the quote
pricingTips.body: If the client has not written their copy or gathered images, build in time for chasing and formatting content, or quote that work separately at an hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Show the milestone payment schedule
pricingTips.body: Put the deposit and payment stages in the quote itself so the client accepts the structure when they accept the price.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date
pricingTips.body: Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from price changes and scheduling shifts if the client takes weeks to decide.

faqs.question: Should I give a free estimate?
faqs.answer: Most designers give a free quote after a short discovery call or form. For complex projects like large stores or migrations, some charge a paid discovery or planning fee that is credited toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a price before I know the scope?
faqs.answer: Give a range based on typical project types and explain what moves the price up or down. Then issue a fixed quote once you have the page list, features, and content details.

faqs.question: How do I handle scope creep after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Refer back to the written scope and offer a change estimate for anything new, priced hourly or as a flat add-on. Get approval in writing before starting the extra work.

faqs.question: Is a quote legally binding?
faqs.answer: It depends on the wording and your state. A quote signed by the client, or accepted in writing and paired with a contract, is much stronger. State how long the price is valid and what could change it.

staffing-agency.intro: Staffing agencies place temporary, contract, and direct-hire workers with client businesses and bill those clients for the labor. Invoices usually go out weekly or biweekly, based on approved timesheets, and cover hours worked by each placed employee plus any overtime, premium, or placement fees.
staffing-agency.pricingModel: Most staffing agencies bill temporary and contract labor at an hourly bill rate, which is the worker's pay rate multiplied by a markup. Markups commonly run 25% to 60% for light industrial and clerical roles and higher for skilled, technical, or specialized roles, because the markup covers payroll taxes, workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, liability coverage, and agency overhead plus profit. Overtime is billed at 1.5 times the regular bill rate (or at the pay rate times 1.5 times the markup, depending on the contract), and double time or holiday hours are billed at their own multiples. Direct-hire (permanent placement) is a one-time fee, typically 15% to 25% of the first-year salary, often with a replacement guarantee of 30 to 90 days. Temp-to-hire arrangements add a conversion fee, or waive it after a set number of hours worked. Some agencies also offer payroll-only services or managed service programs billed as a flat fee or per-head fee.

rates.service: Light industrial temp (warehouse, packaging, general labor)
Skilled trades or technical temp (forklift, welder, CNC, IT help desk)

rates.unit: flat fee or percent of salary

items.description: Warehouse associates, regular hours, week ending 5/17 (4 workers, 160 hours total)
Warehouse associates, overtime hours, week ending 5/17 (1.5x bill rate)
Forklift operator, regular hours, week ending 5/17
Forklift operator, overtime hours, week ending 5/17 (1.5x bill rate)
Drug screen and background check, new assignment (per candidate)

sampleInvoice.notes: PO #44182. Hours are based on timesheets approved by J. Ramirez on 5/19. Payment due Net 15 from invoice date. Invoices past due are subject to a 1.5% monthly finance charge. Remit by ACH or check payable to the agency.

invoiceChecklist.item: Worker name and assignment dates for each line
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need to match charges to the people who actually worked, and it helps resolve disputes about who was on site.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay period or week-ending date
invoiceChecklist.why: Staffing invoices are tied to specific timesheet periods, and a clear period prevents double billing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Regular, overtime, and premium hours billed separately with their rates
invoiceChecklist.why: Overtime and holiday hours have different bill rates, and splitting them makes the math easy to check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number, cost center, or job code
invoiceChecklist.why: Many clients' accounts payable departments will not process an invoice without a PO or department code.

invoiceChecklist.item: Name of the client supervisor who approved the timesheets
invoiceChecklist.why: Approved timesheets are your proof of hours, and naming the approver heads off later challenges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Placement or conversion fee details, including candidate name, start date, and salary basis
invoiceChecklist.why: Direct-hire and conversion fees are calculated from salary and hire date, so the client needs to see how the fee was reached and whether the guarantee period applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through charges such as background checks, drug screens, or required equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: These are often billed separately from labor, and itemizing them avoids confusion over the bill rate.

staffing-agency.paymentTerms: Staffing agencies carry payroll costs every week, so they generally bill weekly or biweekly and ask for Net 15 or Net 30, with Net 7 or due on receipt for new or higher-risk clients. Because the agency pays workers before the client pays the agency, many agencies run credit checks on new accounts, ask for deposits or prepayment from startups, or use invoice factoring to cover payroll. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if stated in the service agreement. Direct-hire fees are usually due within 30 days of the candidate's start date. ACH and wire transfers are the most common payment methods, with checks still used by larger clients.

tips.title: Put the markup and overtime rules in the service agreement
tips.body: Spell out the bill rate for each role, how overtime and holiday hours are calculated, and what counts as a billable hour. Clients tend to question invoices when these terms were only discussed verbally.

tips.title: Bill from approved timesheets only
tips.body: Get a signed or electronically approved timesheet from the client supervisor before invoicing. It is your best evidence if the client later disputes hours.

tips.title: Tighten terms for new clients
tips.body: Since you fund payroll before you get paid, use shorter terms, deposits, or credit limits for clients without a payment history. Extending Net 45 or Net 60 to a client can strain your cash flow quickly.

tips.title: Track conversion and guarantee windows
tips.body: Note the date a temp can convert to permanent without a fee, and the replacement guarantee period on direct hires. Missing these windows means either lost fees or credits you did not plan to give.

tips.title: Invoice on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Send invoices the same day each week right after timesheets close. Predictable timing makes it easier for client payables teams to pay on time and for you to forecast payroll funding.

faqs.question: How do I calculate a bill rate for a temp worker?
faqs.answer: Start with the worker's hourly pay rate and add your burden costs, which include employer payroll taxes, workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, and any benefits, then add overhead and profit. In practice most agencies apply a markup multiplier, such as 1.40 on a $18 pay rate for a $25.20 bill rate. Your actual costs, especially workers' comp rates for the role, determine what markup works.

faqs.question: Do I charge overtime at 1.5 times the bill rate?
faqs.answer: Often yes, but it depends on the contract. Some agencies charge 1.5 times the regular bill rate, while others apply the markup only to the overtime pay rate, which produces a lower number. Decide which method you use, put it in writing, and apply it the same way on every invoice.

faqs.question: When is a direct-hire placement fee due?
faqs.answer: Most agreements make the fee due after the candidate starts, commonly within 30 days of the start date, and sometimes a portion is due at offer acceptance. If your agreement has a replacement guarantee, the fee is still typically invoiced at the start and a credit or replacement is given if the hire leaves within the guarantee window.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee if the client hires my temp directly?
faqs.answer: If your agreement includes a conversion or buyout clause, yes. It usually sets a fee that decreases as the worker logs more hours, or waives it after a set number of hours, such as 520 or 720. Without that clause in a signed agreement, it is hard to collect, so include it up front.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on staffing services?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Many states do not tax staffing or labor services, but some tax certain types of services or temporary help. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional about what applies to your services and to any pass-through items.

estimate.intro: Staffing agencies send a quote or rate proposal when a client is deciding on a vendor, needs workers for a new project or season, or wants to compare agencies. Clients typically compare bill rates, markup, overtime treatment, conversion terms, and how fast you can fill positions.

scopeChecklist.item: Job titles, number of workers, and duration of the assignment
scopeChecklist.why: Bill rates depend on role and volume, and a defined start and end date prevents arguments about open-ended commitments.

scopeChecklist.item: Bill rate for each role, including overtime, double time, and holiday rates
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often compare rates line by line, and unstated overtime rules are the most common source of billing disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Shift schedule, minimum hours, and cancellation or no-show terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you bill for short shifts, reporting pay when work is canceled, or workers who are sent home early.

scopeChecklist.item: Screening included, such as background check, drug screen, and skills testing
scopeChecklist.why: Screening costs are either built into the rate or billed separately, and the client needs to know which.

scopeChecklist.item: Conversion and direct-hire terms, including fee, hours threshold, and guarantee period
scopeChecklist.why: The client may want to hire the worker permanently, and setting the terms up front avoids a dispute at the moment they try.

scopeChecklist.item: Invoicing frequency, payment terms, and late fee policy
scopeChecklist.why: Tying the quote to your payment terms lets you hold the client to them and lets you spot credit risk early.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies equipment, PPE, training, and supervision
scopeChecklist.why: These responsibilities affect safety, liability, and workers' comp classification, and the client should be clear on what they handle.

pricingTips.title: Price from fully loaded cost, not pay rate alone
pricingTips.body: Work out pay rate plus payroll taxes, workers' comp, insurance, and any benefits before applying markup. Workers' comp rates differ widely by job class, so a warehouse role and an office role should not carry the same markup.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered markups for volume
pricingTips.body: Larger or longer commitments can justify a lower markup, such as a few points off at 25 or more workers. Showing the tiers in the quote gives the client a reason to commit to volume without you cutting rates piecemeal.

pricingTips.title: Show the bill rate clearly rather than only the markup
pricingTips.body: Many clients want a single hourly number per role. Give the bill rate for each position, and be ready to explain what it covers if asked about the markup.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Wage rates, workers' comp premiums, and minimum wage laws change. A 30-day expiration protects you if you quote a rate and the client takes weeks to decide.

faqs.question: Should I give clients my markup percentage or just the bill rate?
faqs.answer: Most agencies quote the bill rate per role, because it is simpler and keeps your cost structure private. Some larger clients, especially those using a vendor management system, require a markup percentage, in which case you quote that against an agreed pay rate.

faqs.question: How long should a staffing quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. If the quote depends on a specific pay rate or workers' comp class that could change, shorter validity or a clause allowing rate adjustments for wage or tax changes protects you.

faqs.question: Can I change the bill rate in the middle of an assignment?
faqs.answer: Only if your agreement allows it. Include a clause that permits adjustments for minimum wage increases, statutory cost changes, or a change in job duties, with written notice. Otherwise you are held to the quoted rate for the whole assignment.

faqs.question: Do I quote a flat fee or a percentage for direct-hire?
faqs.answer: Percentage of first-year base salary is standard, often 15% to 25%. Flat fees are used for lower-wage or high-volume hiring, where a percentage would be too small to cover recruiting effort. State what counts as salary, such as base only or including guaranteed bonuses.

staging-rental.intro: Staging rental businesses supply furniture, rugs, art, lighting, and accessories to real estate agents, homeowners, builders, and investors so listings photograph and show better. Invoices usually cover a design consultation, delivery and installation, a monthly rental term, and removal at the end. Clients are often agents who pay out of pocket or at closing, so clear terms matter.
staging-rental.pricingModel: Most staging rental companies charge an upfront install fee plus a monthly rental fee for as long as the furniture stays in the home. The install fee covers design time, truck and labor, delivery, setup, and usually the pickup at the end. It is often set by home size or number of rooms staged. The monthly fee is based on the value and volume of inventory in the home. Most companies require a minimum term of 1 to 3 months, commonly 60 or 90 days, and bill extra months at a lower or equal rate. Some companies bill per room, others per home package based on square footage. Add-ons such as outdoor sets, extra art, rush scheduling, stairs or walk-up fees, and storage are priced separately. Many states tax furniture rentals, so check how your state treats rental income and whether tax applies to delivery and labor.

Client is responsible for loss or damage beyond normal wear. Pickup requires 48 hours notice. Sales tax applied where required. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Property address and listing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows exactly where the inventory is located, which matters for pickup, damage claims, and billing when the agent and homeowner are different people.

invoiceChecklist.item: Install date and rental start date
invoiceChecklist.why: The rental term starts on delivery. A written start date prevents disputes about when monthly billing began.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimum term and renewal rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Spells out the 60 or 90 day minimum and what extra months cost so extensions do not cause surprises.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rooms staged and inventory summary
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists the rooms and major pieces. This supports the price and gives you a record if items go missing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery, stairs, elevator, and access fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Walk-ups, long carries, and building elevator reservations add labor time and should be billed as listed line items.

invoiceChecklist.item: Removal date and de-staging charge
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms who owes the pickup and when. It also covers weekend or short-notice pickups.

invoiceChecklist.item: Damage, loss, and cleaning terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States the client's responsibility for stains, pet damage, or missing items and how replacement value is calculated.

staging-rental.paymentTerms: Most staging companies collect the install fee and first month, or the full minimum term, before delivery. This is sometimes via a signed rental agreement with a card on file. Remaining months are invoiced monthly in advance, due on receipt or net 7. Agents who stage many listings may have a net 15 account, but new clients should pay upfront. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common, and some companies charge a daily holdover rate if furniture stays in place past the term without a signed extension. Accepted methods are typically card, ACH, and check. Some agents ask to pay from closing proceeds, so get that in writing and set a fallback due date in case the sale does not close.

tips.title: Bill the minimum term upfront
tips.body: Collect the install fee and the entire minimum term before delivery. Trucks, labor, and inventory are committed once you load the van, and chasing payment from a vacant seller is difficult.

tips.title: Decide who the client is
tips.body: Agents, sellers, and builders can all request staging. Put the paying party's name on the invoice, and get the seller's signature if the agent says they will pay at closing.

tips.title: Track the rental clock
tips.body: Keep a calendar of each home's start date, term end, and extension dates. Missed renewals are the biggest source of unbilled revenue in staging rental.

tips.title: Charge for extensions automatically
tips.body: Write in your agreement that rental continues at the monthly rate until pickup is complete. Send the next invoice before the term ends so the client can decide to extend or schedule removal.

tips.title: Photograph the home at install and pickup
tips.body: Dated photos of the staged rooms and the condition of pieces support a damage charge and prevent arguments over scuffs, stains, and missing accessories.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the room or for the whole home?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-room pricing is easier to explain to agents, while whole-home packages are simpler for vacant listings. Whichever you use, show the rooms staged on the invoice and make sure larger or higher-end rooms are priced to match inventory cost.

faqs.question: Do I have to charge sales tax on staging rentals?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states tax rentals of tangible personal property such as furniture, and some also tax delivery and setup when bundled. Check with your state's department of revenue or a tax professional, then list tax as a separate line.

faqs.question: What if the home sells before the minimum term ends?
faqs.answer: The minimum term should apply regardless. The furniture is reserved for that period, and you still pay for storage, depreciation, and the install. If you offer a credit or early-pickup discount, put the terms in writing before the rental starts.

faqs.question: Can I bill for damaged or missing items on the same invoice?
faqs.answer: Yes, but list them as a separate line with the item name and replacement or repair cost. Attach photos and the original inventory list so the client can see what changed.

faqs.question: How do I handle agents who pay at closing?
faqs.answer: Only accept this if the seller or agent signs an agreement that sets the amount owed and a backup due date. Many stagers still collect the install fee upfront and defer only the monthly rental.

estimate.intro: Staging rental quotes are usually sent after a walkthrough or after the agent sends the listing address, square footage, and photos. Agents and homeowners often compare two or three companies, so they look at the install fee, monthly cost, minimum term, and what is included in the inventory. A quote that is clear about rooms and term is easier to accept quickly.

scopeChecklist.item: Rooms to be staged and the level of staging
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies whether you are furnishing just the living room and primary bedroom or every room, and avoids requests to add rooms at no cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Install date and listing photo deadline
scopeChecklist.why: Ties your schedule to the photographer's date so the client knows how soon they must commit.

scopeChecklist.item: Minimum rental term and monthly rate after it
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes when a home takes longer to sell than expected.
States whether it includes design, delivery, setup, accessories, and pickup, or whether pickup is a separate charge.
Stairs, elevators, long carries, gated communities, and parking limits affect labor time and should be noted before you quote a flat fee.
Sets expectations on pets, smoking, showings, and wear before the furniture is in the house.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration and deposit to hold the date
scopeChecklist.why: Inventory and truck schedules fill up, so the quote should say how long it holds and how to reserve the install.

pricingTips.title: Price from inventory cost and move time
pricingTips.body: Estimate the labor hours for loading, driving, and setup, then add the monthly cost of the furniture based on purchase price, storage, and how many rentals it will do per year. A good rule is to recover each piece's cost within a year or two of rentals.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present a basic package (living, dining, primary), a standard one that adds bedrooms, and a full package including outdoor. Agents can quickly choose based on listing price and the buyer expected.

pricingTips.title: Use square footage and price tier as a check
pricingTips.body: A 1,200 sq ft condo and a 4,000 sq ft luxury home do not take the same inventory or labor. Adjust the install fee and monthly rate for both, rather than charging the same for every vacant home.

pricingTips.title: Add a rush and short-notice fee
pricingTips.body: If a client needs delivery in under three days, show the surcharge as a separate line on the quote so they know it reflects the disruption to your schedule.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a staging estimate or walkthrough?
faqs.answer: Many companies offer a free quote for vacant homes based on photos and a floor plan. For occupied-home consultations that include a room-by-room written plan, a fee of $150 to $500 is common, and it can be credited toward the install if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a staging quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to 14 days is typical. After that, inventory availability and truck schedules may change, so it's reasonable to requote.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit to hold an install date?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is common to require a deposit or the full install fee to hold a slot, especially during spring and early summer. Make it non-refundable or partly refundable depending on notice, and put that in the quote.

stone-restoration.intro: Stone restoration specialists clean, repair, grind, hone, polish, seal, and maintain natural stone such as marble, travertine, granite, limestone, slate, and terrazzo. Most work is for homeowners, property managers, hotels, restaurants, and commercial buildings. Invoices usually cover floor or countertop restoration by the square foot, plus repairs, sealing, and add-ons like grout work or travel.
stone-restoration.pricingModel: Most restoration work is priced per square foot because the labor and materials scale with the area. Typical services are priced separately: diamond grinding to remove lippage or deep damage, honing to remove etching and scratches, polishing to restore shine, and sealing. Many contractors bundle these into one per-square-foot price for a standard 'restore and seal' job. Repairs such as chip fills, crack repair, and epoxy work are billed per repair or per hour. Stain removal with poultices, grout cleaning and recoloring, and edge or seam work are usually line items. Most shops set a minimum charge per job to cover setup, equipment transport, and slurry cleanup. Travel, parking, after-hours work for commercial sites, and moving furniture are charged on top. Recurring maintenance for commercial sites like lobbies is often a monthly or quarterly flat fee. Always note the stone type and condition, because soft stones like marble and limestone behave differently than granite and take different time and materials.

rates.service: Marble or travertine floor honing and polishing
Diamond grinding to remove lippage or heavy damage
Grout cleaning and sealing or recoloring
Chip, crack, or seam repair with color-matched epoxy

items.description: Hone and polish marble foyer and hallway floor (diamond abrasives, 4 stages)
Grout cleaning and sealing, same area
Penetrating sealer, two coats
Epoxy fill of chips and cracks, color matched
Etch and stain removal at kitchen threshold
Furniture moving and floor protection

sampleInvoice.notes: Marble floor restored and sealed. Keep traffic off the floor for 24 hours and allow sealer to cure fully for 48 hours before wet cleaning. Use pH-neutral stone cleaner only. Balance due within 14 days of completion. Reapply sealer in 2 to 3 years.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stone type and location of each area (e.g. Carrara marble, entry hall)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different stones need different processes and materials, and this documents what you worked on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage worked and how it was measured
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-square-foot pricing is the most common source of disputes, so the number needs to match the estimate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized process steps (grinding, honing, polishing, sealing, grout work)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often assume a single price covers everything, and listing each step shows what was performed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Repairs and add-ons listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Chip fills, crack repair, stain removal, and furniture moving are usually extras beyond the base quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sealer and product used, with care instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports warranty claims and tells the client how to avoid damage that voids your guarantee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address, service dates, and any change order references
invoiceChecklist.why: Property managers and commercial clients need these for their records, and change orders explain any difference from the quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or insurance info where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and commercial clients require a contractor license number or proof of insurance, so check your local rules.

stone-restoration.paymentTerms: Residential jobs commonly take a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to book the date, especially for larger floors, with the balance due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Small jobs and countertop work are often paid in full on the day. Commercial and property management accounts usually pay net 30 and may require a purchase order number and certificate of insurance. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the estimate and on the invoice. Most contractors accept checks, cards, and bank transfer, and card fees are sometimes built into the price. For multi-day jobs, progress billing at the end of each phase keeps cash flow steady.

tips.title: Document condition before you start
tips.body: Take dated photos of etching, lippage, cracks, stains, and previous repairs. Stone often has damage the client does not notice until after polishing, and photos protect you from claims that you caused it.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: Setup, hauling grinders and wet vacs, protecting walls, and slurry cleanup take the same time on a 60 square foot bathroom as on a larger floor. A minimum charge keeps small jobs worthwhile.

tips.title: Be clear about what restoration cannot fix
tips.body: Deep etching, cracks, color loss, and old sealer failure may not be fully correctable. Put realistic expectations in writing and describe the result as improvement, not perfection.

tips.title: Bill for the process, not just the area
tips.body: A floor that needs grinding to remove lippage takes far longer than one that needs polishing. Price by condition and list each step on the invoice so the client sees why the cost differs.

tips.title: Charge for access and conditions
tips.body: Stairs, upper floors without elevators, occupied homes, and after-hours commercial work all add time. Put these on the estimate and invoice as line items instead of absorbing them.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the square foot or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Use square foot pricing for floors and countertops because clients can compare it easily. Use hourly rates for stain removal, small repairs, and jobs where the scope is uncertain. Many contractors combine both, with a per-square-foot base price and hourly add-ons.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit for a stone restoration job?
faqs.answer: Yes, deposits of 25 to 50 percent are common, especially for larger jobs or when you order materials. State the amount and due date in your estimate, and show it as a credit on the final invoice.

faqs.question: How do I handle damage that was already there?
faqs.answer: Note existing damage on the estimate and take photos before starting. If you discover more damage during the work, document it and send a written change order before continuing, then list the extra charge as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on stone restoration?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and whether the work is treated as a service, a repair, or real property improvement. Some states tax products and certain services, and others do not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What should I do if a client does not pay after the work is done?
faqs.answer: Send a reminder with the invoice and the terms agreed on the estimate. If it stays unpaid, follow up in writing, apply any late fee you stated, and consider small claims court. In many states, contractors may also have lien rights on property for unpaid work, so check your local rules.

estimate.intro: Stone restoration estimates are usually sent after an on-site inspection or detailed photos, because the condition of the stone drives the price. Clients often compare your quote against other restoration companies and against flooring replacement. Your estimate needs to show the process and expected result so they understand what they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: Stone type, condition, and areas included
scopeChecklist.why: Marble, travertine, granite, and limestone need different processes, and the condition determines how much work is needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact process and number of steps (grinding, honing, polishing, sealing)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients may assume polishing only, while the real need may include grinding and repairs.

scopeChecklist.item: Square footage and how it was measured
scopeChecklist.why: Per-square-foot quotes depend on this number, and agreeing on it up front prevents disputes later.

scopeChecklist.item: What is excluded, such as deep etching, cracks, replacing tiles, or baseboard work
scopeChecklist.why: Clearly stated exclusions prevent surprise charges and unrealistic expectations.
Stone cannot always be returned to like-new, so state what improvement is realistic.

scopeChecklist.item: Site requirements: water, power, furniture moving, access, and cure or downtime
scopeChecklist.why: Wet work, slurry, and cure times affect how the client uses the space and may add cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, deposit, payment terms, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Material and labor costs change, and you need a clear start date and payment plan.

pricingTips.title: Inspect before you quote
pricingTips.body: Test a small hidden area when possible to see how the stone responds. Hardness, existing sealers, and coatings can change the time needed, and a test patch also shows the client the likely result.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers where it makes sense
pricingTips.body: A cleaning and sealing option, a hone and seal option, and a full grind, polish, and seal option let clients choose based on budget and condition, and help you avoid underpricing a bigger job.

pricingTips.title: Include a condition-based allowance
pricingTips.body: If you suspect hidden damage, such as cracked tiles or uneven lippage, state a price per repair or per hour for extra work found during the job instead of guessing a lump sum.

pricingTips.title: Factor in consumables and disposal
pricingTips.body: Diamond pads, polishing powders, sealers, and slurry disposal can be a large cost on bigger jobs. Build them into your per-square-foot price rather than leaving them out.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Many residential contractors offer free estimates for local jobs, but some charge an inspection fee for far travel, complex commercial sites, or insurance claims. If you charge, say so when booking and credit it toward the job if the client hires you.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for residential work. Shorten it if material costs or your schedule change quickly, and put the expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: What if I find more damage once I start?
faqs.answer: Stop and document it with photos, then give the client a written change order with the extra cost before continuing. Your original estimate should say that hidden damage may change the price.

faqs.question: Can I quote from photos only?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range from photos, but a firm price is risky. Photos hide lippage, hollow tiles, old coatings, and the actual stone type, so confirm the price after an on-site inspection.

structural-engineer.intro: Structural engineers are licensed professionals who design and evaluate the load-bearing parts of buildings and other structures. Solo practitioners and small firms bill homeowners, contractors, architects, and developers for things like beam and header calculations, foundation design, site inspections, and stamped drawings. Invoices usually combine fixed-fee design work with hourly site visits and reimbursable expenses.
structural-engineer.pricingModel: Most structural engineers use a mix of pricing methods. Small residential work, such as a single beam calculation, a wall removal letter, or a deck design, is typically a flat fee. Condition assessments and forensic investigations are often billed hourly, with a minimum or a site visit fee. New construction and larger renovations are commonly priced as a flat fee for each phase (schematic design, construction documents, construction administration), or as a percentage of construction cost on bigger projects. Hourly rates differ by title, with principal and PE time billed higher than EIT or drafter time. Reimbursable expenses such as permit fees, printing, travel mileage, and third-party testing are billed at cost or with a small markup, as stated in the agreement. Many engineers require a retainer before starting and bill progress invoices at the end of each phase or each month. Revisions after client approval or changes in architectural layout are usually billed as additional services.

rates.service: Single beam or header calculation with stamped letter
Foundation or retaining wall design with stamped drawings
Residential addition or remodel structural design

items.description: Initial site visit and measurements, 14 Alder Lane (load-bearing wall removal)
Structural calculations for LVL beam and post/footing at kitchen opening
Stamped structural drawings, 2 sheets (framing plan and details)
Revision to beam location per revised architectural plan
Round-trip mileage to site

sampleInvoice.notes: Invoice 2 of 2 for Project 2024-031. Retainer of $1,000 received 3/4 has been applied. Balance due within 15 days. Stamped drawings are issued upon receipt of payment in full. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, address, and your project number
invoiceChecklist.why: Firms often run several jobs for the same client, and permit offices and accountants need to match the invoice to a specific structure.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or proposal reference and scope phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying each line to the signed scope makes it clear which work is included and which is an additional service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours by person and title with billing rate
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly billing at different rates for PE, EIT, and drafter time needs to be visible so clients can see why the total is what it is.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date of each site visit or inspection
invoiceChecklist.why: Dates support the charge and create a record that matters if a defect or dispute comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts for permit fees, testing, and printing
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients typically expect pass-through costs itemized at cost, or with the markup percentage stated in the contract.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer applied and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the retainer credit avoids confusion about what has already been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: PE license number and state, where required on documents
invoiceChecklist.why: Many jurisdictions require the license number on stamped deliverables, and including it on the invoice keeps your records consistent.

structural-engineer.paymentTerms: Structural engineers commonly collect a retainer or a deposit of 25-50 percent on small fixed-fee jobs, and a retainer of $1,000-5,000 on larger projects. Progress invoices are usually sent at the end of each phase or monthly, with terms of net 15 or net 30. Many engineers withhold stamped drawings or letters until payment is received, and say so in the agreement. Late fees of 1-1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Payment is typically accepted by check, ACH transfer, or card, and some clients such as developers and municipalities may pay on longer cycles or require a purchase order number.

tips.title: Withhold the stamp until paid
tips.body: Your seal is the product. State in the agreement that stamped documents are released on payment, so you are not left chasing a client who already submitted your drawings for a permit.

tips.title: Define what a revision is
tips.body: Architectural changes mid-design are the most common source of unbilled time. List a number of included review rounds in the proposal and bill additional changes hourly, with the date and reason on the invoice.

tips.title: Bill site visits with a minimum
tips.body: A two-hour inspection usually involves drive time, preparation, and a written follow-up. Use a minimum fee or include travel and report time so short visits are not underpriced.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: For design projects, bill when schematic, construction documents, and permit submittal are complete. Waiting until the building is finished can leave you carrying months of unpaid work.

tips.title: Keep construction administration separate
tips.body: Field visits, shop drawing review, and answering contractor questions are hard to predict. Bill them hourly or as a separate phase so a slow build does not erase your margin on the design fee.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or flat fee?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when the scope is clear, such as a single beam letter or a standard deck design. Use hourly billing when the scope is uncertain, such as an investigation of cracking or settlement, or when the client controls how many revisions happen. Many engineers combine them, with a flat fee for design and hourly billing for site visits and changes.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent talking with the building department or contractor?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the agreement says so. Plan review comments and contractor questions can take significant time. Either include a set number of hours in the fee or list them as hourly additional services.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on engineering services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax professional services, but some tax certain services or printed deliverables. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes a bill after a defect appears?
faqs.answer: Keep detailed records of site visits, calculations, and communications. A clear invoice with dates and scope helps, but disputes over professional liability are separate from billing and should be reviewed with your insurer or attorney. Your agreement should address limits of liability and the scope of your review.

faqs.question: Can I add a markup to reimbursable expenses?
faqs.answer: Many firms add 10-15 percent to cover handling, as long as the contract says so. If the contract is silent, bill at actual cost and attach receipts.

estimate.intro: Structural engineers send proposals before any design or inspection begins, often after a brief call or a first look at the plans or site. Clients, especially homeowners and contractors, usually compare two or three quotes and look at price, turnaround time, and what is included. A clear scope in the proposal is also how you protect yourself from open-ended work.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact deliverables, such as number of stamped sheets and calculation packages
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume a stamped letter includes full drawings, or the reverse. Naming each deliverable avoids that mismatch.
Travel and field time are real costs. State how many visits are in the fee and the hourly rate for extra ones.
Listing the applicable building code edition and the permitting authority shows what standard you are designing to.
Architectural plans, survey, soils report, and existing drawings drive your schedule. Delays on the client's side should not become free work for you.
Plans change as owners and architects make decisions. A fixed number of rounds keeps the fee tied to the scope.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as geotechnical testing, MEP design, and construction administration
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often expect structural engineers to cover related items. Naming exclusions makes it clear what is not included.
Material and labor costs for the client may change, and your workload will too. A proposal expiration date and a stated retainer set expectations.

pricingTips.title: Price by risk, not just hours
pricingTips.body: Wood-frame additions are routine, but work on older masonry, unknown framing, or damaged structures involves more risk and more field time. Add to the fee when conditions are unknown, or bill existing-condition investigation hourly.

pricingTips.title: Split the proposal into phases
pricingTips.body: Separate schematic design, construction documents, and construction administration into distinct line items. Clients can see what they are paying for and you can bill as each phase completes.

pricingTips.title: Offer a not-to-exceed for hourly work
pricingTips.body: For investigations, an estimate of hours with a cap that requires client approval to exceed gives the client confidence without committing you to a fixed fee on uncertain scope.

pricingTips.title: Include a first-look screening step
pricingTips.body: For uncertain projects, offer a paid site visit and short findings letter before quoting full design. It filters out clients who are only price shopping and gives you the information needed to price accurately.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple proposals for standard residential work are usually free. For a complex or uncertain job, such as a damaged structure, many engineers charge for an initial site visit, and credit that fee toward the full project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the existing structure is unknown?
faqs.answer: Quote the investigation as an hourly or fixed-fee first phase, then quote design once you have verified conditions. State in the proposal that hidden conditions may change the scope and fee.

faqs.question: Is a proposal a binding contract?
faqs.answer: Only if the client signs or accepts it, and the terms are clear. Many engineers use a proposal with terms and conditions that the client signs, covering scope, fee, payment terms, and limits of liability. Have an attorney review your standard terms.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Include an expiration date so you are not held to old pricing if the client comes back months later or the project scope changes.

stump-removal.intro: Stump removal businesses grind or dig out tree stumps for homeowners, property managers, landscapers, tree service companies, and municipalities. Invoices typically cover stump grinding by diameter, extra grinding depth, root flare or surface root work, debris cleanup or haul-away, and a minimum service charge for small jobs or long drives.
stump-removal.pricingModel: Most stump grinders price per stump based on diameter, measured in inches at the widest point about 6 inches above the ground, or per inch of diameter with a minimum job charge. Many operators set a minimum of $100 to $200 per visit so a single small stump is still worth the trip, and then discount the per-stump price when a customer has several on the same property. Add-ons are billed separately: grinding deeper than the standard 6 to 12 inches, following large surface roots, hauling away wood chips, backfilling and topsoil, or difficult access such as fenced yards where a smaller grinder or hand labor is needed. Some businesses charge hourly for large, multi-stump or land-clearing jobs, and a few charge extra for stumps with rocks, metal, or heavy root systems. Mileage or a trip fee is common for jobs outside a set service radius.

rates.service: Large stump (30 inches or more) or heavy surface roots
Extra depth or surface root grinding
Hourly rate for multi-stump or clearing work (operator and machine)
Trip or travel fee outside service area

items.description: Stump grinding, 18 inch oak, front yard (ground to 8 inches below grade)
Stump grinding, 12 inch maple, backyard (ground to 8 inches below grade)
Stump grinding, 26 inch pine with exposed surface roots
Surface root grinding, additional labor
Wood chip haul-away and disposal
Backfill with topsoil and rake smooth

sampleInvoice.notes: Stumps were ground to approximately 8 inches below grade. Wood chips left in the holes unless haul-away is listed above. Customer marked sprinkler lines before service. Payment due within 14 days. We are not responsible for unmarked utilities or irrigation lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stump location and description for each stump
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing species, diameter, and location (front yard, near fence) ties each charge to a specific stump and prevents disputes about what was ground.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diameter measurements and pricing method
invoiceChecklist.why: If you bill per inch, showing the measurement lets the customer verify the math and understand why a larger stump costs more.

invoiceChecklist.item: Grinding depth
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers expect stumps ground below grade. Stating the depth (for example, 8 inches) records what was delivered and protects you if they later want to plant a tree or lay sod.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons billed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Root grinding, extra depth, haul-away, and backfill are extra labor and disposal costs. Itemizing them shows they were outside the base price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimum charge or trip fee
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the minimum or travel fee explains why a small stump costs more than the per-inch math suggests.

invoiceChecklist.item: Utility locate and underground line notes
invoiceChecklist.why: Record whether the customer or a utility locate service marked lines, such as a 811 call, and that you worked around marked lines. It documents your diligence if damage is claimed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Debris handling
invoiceChecklist.why: State whether chips were left, spread, or hauled away, so there is no argument about leftover mulch piles.

stump-removal.paymentTerms: Most stump removal businesses are paid on completion, often by card, check, or digital payment before leaving the property for residential work. For larger jobs, multi-stump properties, or commercial and property management clients, invoice on net 14 or net 30 terms. Deposits are uncommon on single-stump jobs but reasonable on land clearing or jobs requiring equipment transport, often 25 to 50 percent. A late fee of 1.5 percent per month is common if stated in writing up front. Many operators ask for payment the same day for first-time residential customers and keep net terms for repeat commercial accounts.

tips.title: Set and enforce a minimum charge
tips.body: Hauling a grinder, fueling, and driving time cost the same whether you grind one stump or five. A minimum of $100 to $200 keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Measure and record diameters before starting
tips.body: Photograph or note each stump and its diameter at the start. Per-inch billing is easier to defend when the numbers were written down before grinding.

tips.title: Bill multiple stumps with a clear discount structure
tips.body: Offer a lower per-inch rate after the first stump or for jobs above a certain total inches. Show the discount as a line on the invoice so the customer sees the savings and you keep the job.

tips.title: Document underground hazards
tips.body: Record that you or the customer called 811 and noted marked lines. Unmarked sprinkler lines, invisible dog fences, and buried cables are the most common source of damage claims after grinding.

tips.title: Charge for conditions that slow you down
tips.body: Rocks, metal in the stump, wire fences, and narrow gates add time and wear on teeth. Add a line item or adjust the price and note why, rather than absorbing the extra cost.

faqs.question: Should I bill stump grinding per inch or per stump?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per inch is the most common because it scales with stump size and is easy to explain. Per stump flat pricing is simpler for the customer and works well for stumps in a narrow size range. Whichever you use, set a minimum charge.

faqs.question: Do I charge extra for wood chip removal?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases. Leaving chips in the hole or piled nearby is usually included, but hauling them away takes labor, truck space, and sometimes dump fees. Bill it as a separate line item per load or per stump.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for stumps with big roots?
faqs.answer: Add a line for surface root grinding, billed either per hour or per root. Large roots extend the work beyond the stump itself, so note on the invoice that the work was beyond standard stump grinding.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on stump removal?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax landscaping or property services and others do not, and rules can differ between labor and materials like topsoil. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the customer says I did not grind deep enough?
faqs.answer: Your invoice and estimate should state the grinding depth. If the agreed depth was met, point to the written scope. If the customer wants more, offer additional grinding as a billable add-on.

estimate.intro: Stump removal estimates are usually given before the visit from photos or on site, and customers often get two or three quotes to compare. They look at the total price, whether cleanup is included, and how deep the stump will be ground. Because many homeowners want a price quickly, a clear per-stump or per-inch quote with included and excluded items wins work and prevents later arguments.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of stumps and diameter of each
scopeChecklist.why: Price depends on size. Listing each stump and its measurement fixes the scope and lets you adjust if the customer adds another stump on the day.
State how many inches below grade you will grind. Customers planting grass, a tree, or building over the area may need a different depth.
Surface roots can double the work on a large tree. Say whether you are grinding only the stump or also the main roots, and the extra rate for roots.
Specify whether chips stay in the hole, get spread, are piled, or get hauled away. This is the most common source of cleanup complaints.
Say whether you will backfill, add topsoil, or seed. If not, state that the customer is responsible for finishing the area.
Gates under a certain width, steep slopes, or soft ground can require smaller equipment or extra time. Note any assumptions about access and what happens if conditions differ.
State that the customer should mark sprinklers and private lines, that 811 will mark public utilities, and that you are not liable for unmarked lines or hidden objects like rocks and metal.

pricingTips.title: Quote from photos, confirm on site
pricingTips.body: A photo with a tape measure or a reference object gives a workable estimate. Make the quote conditional on the stump matching what you saw, and confirm measurements when you arrive.

pricingTips.title: Offer a multi-stump price
pricingTips.body: When a property has several stumps, give a total price for all of them rather than separate quotes. It makes the job easier to say yes to and lets you schedule one trip.

pricingTips.title: Price access and difficulty up front
pricingTips.body: Stumps in backyards behind narrow gates, on slopes, or surrounded by fencing and landscaping take longer. Build that into the quote rather than adding charges afterward.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Fuel, labor, and demand change. Quotes valid for 14 to 30 days protect you from being held to an old price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most stump removal businesses give free estimates for residential jobs, often by photo or phone. For large clearing projects or remote sites, some charge a trip fee that is credited if the customer books the job.

faqs.question: How long should a stump removal quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is common. State the expiration date on the quote so a price from months ago does not come back to you.

faqs.question: What if the stump turns out larger or harder than quoted?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the quote that the price is based on the measurements and conditions described, and that changes like extra roots, rocks, or additional stumps will be billed at the stated rates. Tell the customer before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed quote before starting?
faqs.answer: A written acceptance, even by email or text reply, is a good idea. It confirms the scope, price, and grinding depth, and gives you something to point to if there is a disagreement.

subcontractor.intro: Subcontractors are specialty trade contractors hired by a general contractor or prime contractor to do part of a project, such as framing, electrical, drywall, concrete, roofing, or HVAC. They bill the GC rather than the property owner, usually against a signed subcontract and often on a progress basis tied to the schedule of values.
