subcontractor.pricingModel: Most subcontractors price by the job, using a lump sum bid built from labor, materials, equipment, overhead, and profit. Many trades also quote unit prices, such as per square foot for drywall finishing, per linear foot for fencing or trenching, or per square for roofing. Time-and-material rates apply to change orders, small repairs, and work with unclear scope. Larger projects are billed in progress payments, often monthly, based on percent complete, with the GC holding retainage (commonly 5 to 10 percent) until closeout. Materials are usually passed through with a markup of 10 to 25 percent, and extras need a written change order before the work is done.

items.description: Interior drywall hang and finish, Level 4, per schedule of values line 5 (Pay App #2, 60% complete of $24,000)
Change Order #1: add soffit framing and board in kitchen, per approved CO dated 3/12
T&M: patch water-damaged ceiling, journeyman labor
T&M: materials (board, compound, fasteners) with 15% markup
Scissor lift rental, 2 days (CO #1)

sampleInvoice.notes: Pay App #2 for period ending 3/31, Subcontract #2024-117. Retainage of 10% will be withheld per contract. Net 30 from GC receipt of invoice. Lien waiver (conditional progress) and current certificate of insurance attached. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, address, and subcontract or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: GC accounting departments match invoices to the specific job and contract number, and missing numbers delay approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pay application number and billing period
invoiceChecklist.why: Progress billing is tracked by period, and it prevents double billing or missed periods.

invoiceChecklist.item: Schedule of values with percent complete and previous billings
invoiceChecklist.why: The GC checks work completed against the contract amount, so show contract sum, billed to date, this period, and balance to finish.

invoiceChecklist.item: Approved change orders with CO numbers and amounts
invoiceChecklist.why: Extras are rarely paid without a signed change order reference, so list each one separately from base contract work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainage withheld and retainage balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the held amount keeps both sides' books aligned and sets up the final retainage release request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lien waiver and certificate of insurance
invoiceChecklist.why: Many GCs will not release payment without a lien waiver, and requirements for conditional versus unconditional forms vary by state.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and tax ID (W-9 on file)
invoiceChecklist.why: The GC needs it for compliance and for year-end 1099 reporting, and some states require the license number on all billing documents.

subcontractor.paymentTerms: Subcontractors are typically paid on the GC's terms, often net 30 after the GC receives the invoice, and sometimes pay-when-paid or pay-if-paid, meaning you are paid after the owner pays the GC. Check your subcontract and your state's prompt payment rules, which in many states set maximum payment windows and interest on late amounts. Deposits are uncommon on large jobs but mobilization payments or material deposits are reasonable on specialty or long-lead items. Retainage is commonly 5 to 10 percent and released at substantial completion or final closeout. Payment arrives mostly by check or ACH, and many GCs pay on a set weekly or monthly check run with a submission cutoff.

tips.title: Submit pay apps on the GC's cutoff date
tips.body: Many GCs run payments once or twice a month and a late submission can push your money back a full cycle. Find out the cutoff and send the pay app a day or two early.

tips.title: Never do extra work without a signed change order
tips.body: Verbal approval from a superintendent is hard to collect on. Get a written change order or at least an emailed approval with scope and price before starting, then reference it on the invoice.

tips.title: Track retainage and request release promptly
tips.body: Retainage balances are easy to forget and can add up to thousands of dollars. Calendar the release trigger in your contract and send a final invoice with a release request as soon as you finish.

tips.title: Know your lien and notice deadlines
tips.body: Many states require a preliminary notice within a set number of days of starting work and have strict deadlines to file a mechanics lien. Check your state's rules at the start of each job, not when you are unpaid.

tips.title: Keep daily logs and photos
tips.body: If a payment dispute or backcharge comes up, dated photos, signed time tickets, and delivery slips back up your billing.

faqs.question: What is a pay application and do I need one?
faqs.answer: A pay application is a progress billing form that shows your contract amount, work completed to date, previous payments, retainage, and amount due now. Most commercial and many residential GCs require one, often on a standard format such as the AIA G702/G703, rather than a plain invoice.

faqs.question: What is retainage and when do I get it back?
faqs.answer: Retainage is a percentage of each payment, commonly 5 to 10 percent, that the GC holds until the work is complete. It is usually released after substantial completion, final inspection, or project closeout, depending on your contract and state law.

faqs.question: Can I bill for materials I have bought but not installed?
faqs.answer: Often yes, if your contract allows stored materials billing. You may need to show invoices from suppliers, proof of storage, and insurance coverage. If the contract is silent, ask the GC in writing before including it.

faqs.question: What if the GC says they have not been paid by the owner?
faqs.answer: That depends on your contract. A pay-when-paid clause often only delays payment for a reasonable time, while pay-if-paid can put the risk on you, and courts treat these clauses differently by state. Review your contract and consider speaking with a construction attorney.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on a subcontract invoice?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and the trade. In many states, construction services are not taxed but materials may be, and some jobs for exempt owners need a resale or exemption certificate. Check with your state's department of revenue or a local accountant.

estimate.intro: Subcontractors send bids or quotes to GCs, often competing against other subs on the same plans and scope. The GC compares the total price, but also what is included, what is excluded, schedule availability, and insurance and license status.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact scope by plan sheets, spec sections, and addenda
scopeChecklist.why: Referencing the documents you priced prevents arguments about whether something was included.
Listing what is not included, such as permits, patching, painting, or demolition, protects you from being assigned work you did not price.
Specific products and allowance amounts keep you from absorbing cost overruns if the owner picks pricier finishes.
Pricing assumes a certain number of trips and a start window, and extra mobilizations should be billable.
Note assumptions such as power, water, hoisting, clear access, and a clean substrate that the GC will provide.
Material prices, especially lumber, copper, and steel, shift quickly, so state how long the price holds.
Stating your expected terms and what coverage you carry sets expectations before the subcontract is drafted.

pricingTips.title: Price from a takeoff, not a gut feel
pricingTips.body: Measure quantities from the plans, apply labor production rates and current material quotes, then add overhead and profit. Subs commonly add 10 to 20 percent for overhead and profit, depending on the trade and market.

pricingTips.title: Use unit prices for uncertain quantities
pricingTips.body: When quantities may change, such as extra footings or additional drywall area, include unit prices for add or deduct work so changes are priced upfront.

pricingTips.title: Get supplier quotes in writing
pricingTips.body: Lock material pricing with supplier quotes and note their expiration dates. If a supplier quote expires before the job starts, your bid price should say so.

pricingTips.title: Separate alternates and options
pricingTips.body: Show base bid, alternates, and optional upgrades as separate lines so the GC can pick and total them without asking you to rebid.

faqs.question: Should I give the GC a lump sum or a line-item breakdown?
faqs.answer: Lump sum is common for bids, but a breakdown helps later because it can become your schedule of values for progress billing. Provide a breakdown if asked and make sure it adds up to the bid total.

faqs.question: How long should a bid stay valid?
faqs.answer: Many subs use 30 days, shorter for volatile materials. Put the expiration date on the bid, and state that pricing may change if award or start is delayed.

faqs.question: What if the GC wants me to lower my price after the bid?
faqs.answer: That is common, and you can negotiate by reducing scope, adjusting schedule, or changing materials rather than just cutting profit. Whatever you agree to, get the revised scope and price in writing.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time spent estimating?
faqs.answer: Most subs absorb bid costs on competitive GC work. For complicated design-assist or repeated revisions on a private job, a flat estimating fee that is credited to the job if you win is reasonable.

swim-instructor.intro: Swim instructors teach children and adults to swim, either independently, through a swim school, or as contractors at a club or community pool. They bill for private lessons, semi-private and group sessions, stroke clinics, water safety courses, and sometimes lifeguard or coaching work. Solo instructors often invoice families monthly or per session block, while those working at private pools also bill for travel and pool access.
swim-instructor.pricingModel: Most independent swim instructors charge per lesson, usually for a 30-minute private session, with discounts when families prepay a package of four, eight, or ten lessons. Semi-private lessons (two to three swimmers) are priced per swimmer at a lower rate than private lessons, and group classes are priced per child for a multi-week session. Rates tend to be higher for infants and toddlers, adult beginners with water anxiety, competitive stroke correction, and lessons at a client's home pool where you travel. If you rent lane or pool time, many instructors build that cost into the lesson price or add a separate pool fee line. Travel fees, cancellation fees, and registration fees are common add-ons. Swim meet coaching and clinics are often billed per hour or as a flat day rate.

items.description: Private swim lesson, 30 min (beginner, age 6) - May 5, 12, 19, 26
Make-up lesson, 30 min - May 31
Travel to home pool (Maple Ridge HOA pool)
Seasonal registration fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Lessons cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at the full rate unless rescheduled within the same month. Please pay by card, Venmo, or check payable to the instructor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Swimmer's name and lesson dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents often book for multiple children, and a dated list lets them match the charges to their calendar and resolve any attendance questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson length and format (private, semi-private, group)
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by format and duration, so the invoice should show what was actually delivered for each session.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pool location or facility name
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who use more than one pool, or a facility that bills separately, need to know where each lesson took place.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pool rental or facility fee, if passed through
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing it as its own line shows it is a real cost and keeps your lesson rate comparable to others.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellations, no-shows, and make-up lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing which sessions were charged for late cancellation or credited as make-ups heads off disputes about your policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance or remaining lessons
invoiceChecklist.why: If a family prepaid for a block, showing how many lessons were used and how many remain prevents confusion on the next invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certifications and insurance reference, if relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Some facilities and organizations require proof of credentials like Red Cross water safety instructor or CPR, and listing them supports your rates and any contract work.

swim-instructor.paymentTerms: Many swim instructors collect payment in advance, either for the full package or at the start of each month, since lessons are scheduled around pool availability and no-shows leave an unfillable slot. Due dates of upon receipt to 7 days are typical for per-lesson billing, and net 15 or net 30 is more common for schools, camps, and HOAs. Registration fees are usually non-refundable and due at sign-up. A written cancellation policy, often requiring 24 hours notice, is standard, and some instructors charge a late fee or pause scheduling on overdue accounts. Common payment methods are cards, Venmo, Zelle, cash, and checks.

tips.title: Sell prepaid packages
tips.body: Offering a four, eight, or ten lesson package at a small discount gives you cash up front and makes families more likely to show up consistently. State an expiration window, such as 90 days, so unused lessons do not linger forever.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy on every invoice
tips.body: Weather, illness, and pool closures cause frequent reschedules. A clear 24-hour policy and a rule for pool closures (usually you reschedule or credit, not charge) avoids awkward conversations.

tips.title: Separate lesson fees from facility costs
tips.body: If you rent lane time or pay a per-swimmer pool fee, show it as its own line or build it clearly into your rate. This protects your margins if the facility raises its fees mid-season.

tips.title: Bill siblings and families on one invoice
tips.body: Combining children onto one monthly invoice with each child's name and lessons listed is easier for parents to pay and reduces your admin work.

tips.title: Track seasonal income
tips.body: Demand peaks in late spring and summer and drops in winter unless you work an indoor pool. Invoicing consistently, and setting aside money for taxes if you are self-employed, helps you manage uneven months.

faqs.question: How much should I charge for private swim lessons?
faqs.answer: Many independent instructors charge about $40 to $80 for a 30-minute private lesson, with higher rates in large metro areas, for specialized instruction, or when you travel to a client's pool. Adult and competitive stroke lessons often run longer and cost more.

faqs.question: Should I charge for missed lessons?
faqs.answer: Most instructors do charge for no-shows and late cancellations, since the time slot and pool access are lost. Set a clear notice window, commonly 24 hours, and include it in your sign-up agreement and on invoices. Many offer one make-up per month for illness or weather.

faqs.question: Do I bill per lesson or per month?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Per-lesson billing is simple for occasional clients, while monthly billing or prepaid packages suit weekly students and cut down on payment follow-ups. Group classes are typically billed per session block, such as 8 weeks.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on swim lessons?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and local rules. Many places do not tax instruction services, but some do tax certain recreational or athletic services. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant before you assume either way.

faqs.question: What if I teach at a facility that pays me directly?
faqs.answer: If a swim school or club pays you, you may be treated as an employee or a contractor depending on the arrangement. Contractors typically send invoices with hours or lessons taught and the agreed rate. Clarify how you are classified and how often you will be paid.

estimate.intro: Swim instructors send estimates when a family asks about a series of lessons, a group or party booking, or a longer program such as a summer session or swim team prep. Clients usually compare per-lesson price, lesson length, class size, and whether pool fees are included. A written quote also helps when working with schools, camps, and HOAs who need to approve a budget.

scopeChecklist.item: Number, length, and frequency of lessons
scopeChecklist.why: A quote for eight 30-minute lessons over eight weeks is very different from eight lessons over two weeks, and families need to know the schedule you are pricing.
Private, semi-private, and group pricing differ, and class size affects both the price and the quality of instruction.

scopeChecklist.item: Pool location and who pays for access
scopeChecklist.why: State whether the pool fee, lane rental, or guest pass is included, or whether the client is responsible for access to a pool.
Beginner water comfort, learning to swim freestyle, and stroke refinement take different amounts of time, so describe the target and make clear that progress varies by swimmer.
If you charge extra to go to a home pool or to travel beyond a certain distance, say so in the quote.
Clients should agree to your cancellation window and how rain, thunderstorms, or pool closures are handled before the first lesson.
State the deposit or prepayment, when balances are due, and how long the quote holds, since summer schedules fill quickly.

pricingTips.title: Quote a package, not just a single rate
pricingTips.body: Give a clear total for a set number of lessons, with the per-lesson price shown, and a small discount over paying lesson by lesson. Families can compare easily and you secure the booking.

pricingTips.title: Price for your real hours, not just pool time
pricingTips.body: Include travel, setup, deck time between students, and progress notes in your thinking. A 30-minute lesson often takes closer to an hour of your day once you add everything else.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers by format
pricingTips.body: Presenting private, semi-private, and group options side by side lets clients choose by budget, and moves some families toward higher-margin or fuller-schedule options.

pricingTips.title: Be careful promising outcomes
pricingTips.body: Quote lessons and instructor time rather than guaranteeing a child will swim a certain distance by a certain date. Learning pace varies, and a vague promise can lead to disputes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an initial assessment?
faqs.answer: Many instructors include a short evaluation in the first lesson. If you do a separate assessment for advanced swimmers or adults with specific concerns, a lower flat fee of $20 to $40 is reasonable, and you can credit it toward a package.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical, or until the start of the next session. Pool schedules and your availability change quickly, especially in spring and early summer.

faqs.question: What if the pool fee changes after I send a quote?
faqs.answer: Say in the quote whether pool fees are included or passed through at cost. If they are passed through, note that changes by the facility will be reflected on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I quote a group party or camp visit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Quote by the hour or per swimmer with a minimum, state the maximum swimmers per instructor, and note that you or the venue should have a lifeguard on duty as required by local rules.

sysadmin.intro: Independent sysadmins and small managed service shops bill small businesses, nonprofits, and offices for keeping servers, networks, user accounts, backups, and cloud environments running. Invoices usually cover monthly support retainers, hourly project work, after-hours emergency calls, and pass-through costs like licenses, hardware, and hosting.
sysadmin.pricingModel: Most solo sysadmins mix three models. Ad hoc work is billed hourly, often with a one-hour or half-hour minimum and a higher rate for after-hours or emergency calls. Ongoing support is sold as a monthly retainer, either a block of prepaid hours or a flat fee per user or per device that covers monitoring, patching, and help desk. Defined projects such as a server migration, Microsoft 365 tenant setup, or firewall replacement are quoted as a flat fee with a clear scope. Hardware, software licenses, and subscriptions are resold at cost plus a markup (commonly 10-25%) or passed through at cost with a separate management fee. Travel time and mileage are billed separately for onsite visits outside a local radius.

rates.service: Managed support retainer (monitoring, patching, help desk)
Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace tenant setup
Firewall and network install or replacement (labor)

items.description: Monthly managed support: 14 users, monitoring, patching, help desk
Project: replace firewall, configure VLANs and site VPN (labor)
After-hours emergency: mail server outage, Saturday 9pm-11:30pm
Firewall appliance with 3-year security subscription (cost plus 15%)
Onsite travel, round trip

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Hardware remains billable even if the project is paused. Emergency work is billed at 1.4x the standard rate with a one-hour minimum. Please pay by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized ticket or work log with dates and technician
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often need to match charges to specific incidents, and a log settles questions about how long something took.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate tier for each line (standard, after-hours, onsite, remote)
invoiceChecklist.why: Different rates apply to different work, and showing which one applied prevents disputes over emergency premiums.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hardware and license details with model, quantity, term, and serial numbers where relevant
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients need this for warranty claims, asset tracking, and renewal dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring subscription renewals and pass-through costs shown separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Domain, SSL, backup storage, and SaaS fees are easy to confuse with your labor and affect how clients budget.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or prepaid block balance (hours used and remaining)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see what the block covered and when it needs to be replenished.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel time and mileage for onsite work
invoiceChecklist.why: These are separate costs under most agreements and should be documented to avoid being treated as hidden fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement, estimate, or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger clients and accounts payable departments often require a PO number to process payment.

sysadmin.paymentTerms: Net 15 or net 30 is common, with monthly retainers billed in advance on the first of the month. Projects over a few thousand dollars usually take a 30-50% deposit, and hardware is often paid up front or at order time so you are not financing equipment. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are typical if stated in your service agreement. Most clients pay by ACH or card, and some sysadmins add a card processing fee or offer a small ACH discount. Many sysadmins also reserve the right to pause non-emergency support on accounts more than 30 days past due, which should be written into the agreement.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Monitoring, patching, and backup oversight happen whether or not the client opens a ticket. Billing at the start of the month keeps cash flow steady and makes the arrangement clear.

tips.title: Set minimums for small tasks
tips.body: A password reset that takes five minutes still costs you context switching and travel. A 30-minute or one-hour minimum keeps tiny requests from eating your day.

tips.title: Charge a higher rate for emergencies and say so up front
tips.body: Put the after-hours multiplier in your agreement and repeat it on the invoice. Clients rarely object when they have already agreed to it.

tips.title: Keep licenses in the client's name when possible
tips.body: Buying software or cloud services under the client's own account avoids disputes if you part ways and keeps you from carrying their recurring costs on your own card.

tips.title: Bill documentation and discovery time
tips.body: Network diagrams, password vault setup, and runbooks take real hours. List them as their own line so the client sees the value, not just the fixes.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat monthly fee?
faqs.answer: Hourly works for new clients and unpredictable work. Once you know a client's environment, a flat monthly fee per user or per device gives you steadier income and gives them a predictable cost. Many sysadmins offer a retainer for routine support and bill projects separately.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up hardware and licenses?
faqs.answer: A markup of 10-25% over your cost is typical for resold hardware and licenses, with lower percentages on expensive items. Some sysadmins instead pass items through at cost and charge a procurement or setup fee. Whichever you choose, state it in your agreement.

faqs.question: Do I charge for travel time?
faqs.answer: Most do for onsite visits beyond a local radius, either at a reduced hourly rate or as mileage plus a trip fee. Put the policy in writing and list travel on its own line.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes the hours on an invoice?
faqs.answer: Send the time log or ticket history showing dates, tasks, and durations. Keeping notes as you work makes these conversations short. If the agreement defines minimums and rounding, point to that language.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on my services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax IT services or software-related services, and many tax hardware sales. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant about what applies to your labor, hardware, and managed services.

estimate.intro: Sysadmins send quotes before projects such as migrations, office moves, new network builds, and compliance cleanups, and when a prospect is comparing managed support proposals. Clients usually compare total cost, what is included in monthly support, response times, and who owns the hardware and licenses.

scopeChecklist.item: Systems and users in scope (number of users, servers, devices, sites)
scopeChecklist.why: Pricing scales with environment size, so an agreed count prevents scope creep when new devices or staff appear.

scopeChecklist.item: Services included and excluded (help desk, patching, backups, security tools, vendor management)
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume everything IT-related is covered. Naming exclusions avoids surprise bills.
Whether you respond in one hour or next business day, and whether evenings are covered, directly affects price.

scopeChecklist.item: Hardware, licenses, and subscriptions with pricing and who owns them
scopeChecklist.why: Quotes can swing widely on equipment, and clients should know whether renewals are their cost or yours.

scopeChecklist.item: Client responsibilities such as admin credentials, vendor access, and downtime windows
scopeChecklist.why: Delays from missing access or a vendor who does not respond can stall a project and should not become your unpaid time.

scopeChecklist.item: Assumptions about current environment and what happens if they are wrong
scopeChecklist.why: Undocumented servers, expired licenses, or failing disks are common surprises. Define how discovered issues are handled and billed.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline, cutover plan, and acceptance criteria
scopeChecklist.why: A clear definition of done, such as all mailboxes migrated and a successful restore test, helps you close the project and trigger final payment.

pricingTips.title: Do a short paid or free discovery before quoting projects
pricingTips.body: Inventory servers, check backups, review licensing, and test the network before committing to a flat price. A quick audit prevents underquoting migrations that turn out to involve legacy systems.

pricingTips.title: Build in a contingency for legacy environments
pricingTips.body: Add 15-25% to project labor when the environment is undocumented or old, or write the quote as a range with a cap. Clients accept this more readily than an overrun later.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for managed support
pricingTips.body: A basic tier with monitoring and patching, a standard tier with help desk, and a premium tier with after-hours coverage lets clients choose and makes your price easier to defend.

pricingTips.title: Separate labor from equipment and recurring fees
pricingTips.body: Show one-time labor, one-time hardware, and monthly recurring costs in three groups. This makes comparisons with other bids clearer and keeps your labor from looking inflated by pass-through costs.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for labor. Hardware and license prices can change quickly, so many sysadmins set a shorter validity of 7-14 days on equipment or note that pricing is subject to vendor changes.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an estimate for a migration?
faqs.answer: A fixed price works when scope is well understood after discovery. If the environment has unknowns, give a range or a time-and-materials estimate with a not-to-exceed figure, and describe how changes will be handled.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before starting?
faqs.answer: It is strongly advisable. A signed quote or service agreement covering scope, payment terms, data access, and liability limits protects both sides, especially when you have administrative access to their systems.

faqs.question: Can I charge for the time spent preparing a quote?
faqs.answer: For simple quotes, most do not. For larger assessments that require a site visit, network scan, or security review, many sysadmins charge a flat assessment fee and credit it toward the project if the client moves forward.

tattoo-artist.intro: Tattoo artists bill clients for custom and flash tattoos, cover-ups, touch-ups, and design time. Most work in a shop as a booth renter or commission artist, or run their own private studio, so the invoice often has to separate the artist's fee from deposits, shop fees, and tips.
tattoo-artist.pricingModel: Tattoo pricing is usually either hourly or per piece. Most artists set a shop minimum (often $80-150) that covers setup, needles, ink, and sanitation supplies even for a tiny tattoo. Small flash designs are typically a flat price. Larger custom work is billed by the hour, or quoted as a flat fee for the whole piece, and big projects like sleeves and back pieces are often charged per session or by the day (a half-day or full-day rate). Custom design and drawing time may be built into the price or billed separately. A non-refundable deposit is nearly universal and is applied to the final total. Cover-ups and heavily detailed work such as realism or fine line often cost more per hour because they take more skill and time. Touch-ups are commonly free for a set window (such as 3-6 months) and billed after that. Tips are customary in the US and are usually handled separately from the invoice total.

items.description: Custom forearm tattoo, black and grey botanical piece, session 2 of 2
Custom design and drawing time
Studio supply fee (needles, ink, barrier film, aftercare)
Deposit received at booking (credited)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due at end of session. Deposit was applied to the total. Free touch-up within 4 months of completion if needed. Cash, card, and Venmo accepted. Tips are appreciated and not included in this total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date and session number
invoiceChecklist.why: Large pieces take multiple sittings, so the client and you both need a clear record of which session each charge covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Description of the tattoo, placement, and size
invoiceChecklist.why: Confirms what was done and where on the body, which protects against disputes and helps with future touch-ups or cover-ups.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours worked and hourly rate, or the agreed flat price
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how the total was reached and matches the quote the client agreed to before you started.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and the amount credited
invoiceChecklist.why: Deposits are standard, and the invoice should show the credit so the client sees the correct balance due.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate line for design or drawing time
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge for custom artwork, listing it separately avoids confusion and makes clear that design time is distinct from needle time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shop or studio fees and supply charges
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge a setup or supply fee, or the shop takes a booth or commission fee, itemize any client-facing portion so it is not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Touch-up policy and aftercare note
invoiceChecklist.why: States the free touch-up window and the client's responsibility to follow aftercare, which limits disputes over healing issues.

tattoo-artist.paymentTerms: Tattoo work is nearly always paid at the end of each session, with a non-refundable deposit taken at booking, commonly $50-200 or a percentage of the estimate for larger pieces. Deposits are applied to the final session or the total. Multi-session projects are usually billed session by session, with payment due the day of service rather than on net-30 terms. Cash, debit and credit cards, and mobile payment apps are all common. Many artists charge a rescheduling or no-show fee, or forfeit the deposit if the client cancels without notice (often 48-72 hours). State your policy in writing when booking. If you send a later invoice for design work or a completed piece, due on receipt is typical.

tips.title: Collect a deposit before drawing anything
tips.body: A deposit holds the date and protects your drawing time. Say clearly that it is non-refundable and that it is credited to the final price. Get the client to confirm the policy in writing before you take payment.

tips.title: Decide how design time is billed
tips.body: Either build it into the tattoo price or list it as its own line. If you draw a large custom piece and the client walks away, a design fee or a deposit that covers drawing time keeps that work from being free.

tips.title: Keep a set price for sessions on large projects
tips.body: For sleeves and back pieces, a day rate or per-session price is easier for clients to budget than an open-ended hourly total. Note on each invoice how many sessions you expect remain.

tips.title: Record tips separately
tips.body: Tips are income and, in the US, are generally reportable. Keep them separate from your fee in your records so your books and any split with the shop stay accurate.

tips.title: Track your touch-up window
tips.body: Write the length of your free touch-up period on each invoice. It sets expectations and gives you a clear reason to charge when a client returns after the window or for changes that are not touch-ups.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the piece?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Flat prices work well for flash and small to medium designs where the time is predictable. Hourly or day-rate pricing works better for large, detailed, or cover-up work where the time is hard to predict. Whichever you use, tell the client before you start.

faqs.question: Is a tattoo deposit refundable?
faqs.answer: Most artists treat deposits as non-refundable and credit them toward the final price. Rules about this vary by state and shop policy, so state your terms in writing at booking and have the client agree before paying.

faqs.question: Do I need to include sales tax on a tattoo invoice?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state and locality. Some states tax tattoo services and others do not. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant, and if tax applies, show it as a separate line.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for a multi-session piece?
faqs.answer: Bill each session on its own invoice with the date, hours or session rate, and any deposit credit. Add a note on the number of sessions completed and what remains, so the running total is clear.

faqs.question: How should I handle tips on the invoice?
faqs.answer: Keep tips off the service total and record them separately. Clients often tip in cash or through an app after the session. Keep a record for your own bookkeeping, since tips are generally taxable income.

estimate.intro: Tattoo artists give a quote before booking, usually after a consultation by message, email, or in person. Clients compare hourly rates, the total price, and the deposit, but they also weigh portfolio and style, so the estimate should be clear about what is included and how the price could change.

scopeChecklist.why: Size and body placement drive time and difficulty. Written details keep the final tattoo matched to the quote.
Fine line, realism, color packing, and heavy blackwork all take different amounts of time. Naming the style sets expectations on cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Pricing method and estimated hours or sessions
scopeChecklist.why: States whether the price is flat, hourly, or by the day, and how many sessions you expect so the client knows the overall commitment.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the price
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether design time, revisions, stencil, supplies, and aftercare products are included or billed separately.
Makes clear what the client pays up front, how it is applied, and what happens if they cancel or reschedule.
Unlimited changes to a design can take hours. Setting a limit (for example, one or two rounds) protects your time.

scopeChecklist.item: Touch-up policy and how long the estimate is valid
scopeChecklist.why: Tells the client when free touch-ups end and how long the quote holds before your rates or availability change.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for custom work, not a single number
pricingTips.body: Time is hard to predict on detailed pieces. Give a range or an estimated hours figure, and say you will confirm the price once the design is final.

pricingTips.title: Price the hardest part of the piece
pricingTips.body: Cover-ups, scar tissue, difficult body areas, and dense color work take longer and are more demanding. Price for the actual difficulty, not the size alone.

pricingTips.title: Offer a minimum and stick to it
pricingTips.body: A shop minimum covers setup and supplies for small tattoos. Show it in your quote so clients understand why a tiny design is not a few dollars.

pricingTips.title: Tie the quote to a design approval
pricingTips.body: Say the estimate applies to the design the client approves. If they ask for a larger or more complex version, the price is updated before you start.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many artists offer free consultations, while others charge a fee, often credited toward the tattoo if the client books. Decide based on how many consultations you do and how much time each takes.

faqs.question: How firm should a tattoo quote be?
faqs.answer: For flash and small pieces, a flat quote is usually firm. For large custom work, treat the quote as an estimate based on size and detail, and note that the final price can change if the design is enlarged or the scope grows.

faqs.question: What if the tattoo takes longer than I estimated?
faqs.answer: If you quoted hourly, bill the actual time and update the client as you go. If you quoted a flat price, honor it unless the client changed the design or asked for additional work, and keep that rule in your written terms.

faqs.question: How long should a tattoo quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty to ninety days is common. Include an expiry date because your rates, schedule, and the design itself may change, and a deposit usually locks in the price for the booked date.

tax-consultant.intro: Tax consultants help individuals, self-employed people, and small businesses with return preparation, tax planning, IRS and state notice response, and entity or filing-status questions. Many are solo practitioners, enrolled agents, CPAs, or former preparers who now advise year-round. Invoices usually cover a mix of flat-fee return work and hourly advisory or representation time.
tax-consultant.pricingModel: Most tax consultants use a hybrid. Return preparation is typically a flat fee based on forms and schedules (a 1040 with Schedule C costs more than a W-2-only return, and each state return, rental property, or K-1 adds to the price). Planning, research, and amendment work is usually billed hourly, often in tenths or quarter hours. IRS and state notice response and audit representation are billed hourly or as a flat fee after a scoping call. Some consultants offer annual retainers or monthly packages that bundle estimated-tax reviews, a mid-year planning meeting, and the return. Many require a minimum fee and charge more for late-season, rush, or messy-bookkeeping work. Fees should be tied to complexity and time, not to the size of the refund.

rates.service: Individual return (Form 1040, standard deductions, W-2 income)

items.description: 2024 federal return, Form 1040 with Schedule C and Schedule SE (self-employed graphic designer)
State income tax return (California)
Home office deduction (Form 8829) and vehicle expense worksheet
Tax planning session: estimated payments, SEP-IRA contribution review
Preparation of 2025 quarterly estimated tax vouchers

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of the invoice date. Returns will be e-filed once payment is received and Form 8879 is signed. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly charge. Fees cover the services listed only; IRS or state correspondence is billed separately at $175 per hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax year and return type for each service
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often use you for several years or several entities at once, and your records, theirs, and their bookkeeper's need to match up.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized forms and schedules prepared
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing Schedule C, Schedule E, state returns, and similar items explains why this year's fee differs from last year's.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly work with dates and time in tenths or quarters of an hour
invoiceChecklist.why: Advisory, research, and notice work is challenged most often when time is not itemized.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your preparer credentials and PTIN or the firm's identifying details
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, lenders, and some businesses want to see who prepared the work, and it documents that a credentialed preparer handled it. Check the rules for your credential.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client name and entity name with EIN or last four digits of the SSN, where appropriate
invoiceChecklist.why: Prevents mix-ups between a person and their business, but avoid printing full tax ID numbers on invoices.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer or deposit already received and the remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who paid at the organizer stage need to see the deposit credited so the balance is clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-pocket costs such as e-file fees, transcript fees, or postage
invoiceChecklist.why: Passing through these costs at actual price, listed separately, keeps your service fees clean and avoids disputes.

tax-consultant.paymentTerms: Many tax consultants collect a deposit or retainer at engagement, often $100-500 or 25-50% of the quoted fee for business and complex returns, and bill the remainder at delivery. Simple individual returns are often paid in full before e-filing or at the appointment. Advisory and notice work is usually billed monthly or at milestones, due in 14 to 30 days. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the engagement letter. Cards, ACH, and checks are the usual methods. Some preparers hold the e-file until payment clears, though the rules on withholding a client's records and returns vary, so check your state and professional body's guidance before refusing to release work product.

tips.title: Put fees in an engagement letter
tips.body: Spell out which years, returns, and services are included, what is billed hourly, and what is excluded, such as notices received after filing. This is the document you point to in a fee dispute.

tips.title: Price by complexity, not by refund
tips.body: Charging a percentage of a refund is prohibited for many preparers on ordinary returns, and it creates conflicts. Use forms, schedules, and time as the basis for the fee.

tips.title: Bill for messy records
tips.body: If a client delivers shoshoeboxes of receipts or unreconciled books, add a cleanup line at an hourly rate or send them to a bookkeeper. Do not absorb it into a flat fee quoted for organized records.

tips.title: Set a peak-season policy
tips.body: From February through April, many consultants add a rush fee or charge for documents received after a cutoff date. Put the cutoff and the surcharge in writing in January.

tips.title: Invoice notice work as it happens
tips.body: IRS responses can drag on for months. Bill monthly or at each response so you are not carrying unpaid work while waiting for the agency.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for tax returns?
faqs.answer: Most consultants charge a flat fee for return preparation, based on the forms involved, and bill hourly for planning, research, and notice response. Flat fees are easier for clients to compare, while hourly billing protects you when scope is uncertain.

faqs.question: Can I charge more for a late or disorganized client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your engagement letter or quote says so. Common approaches are a rush surcharge for documents received after your deadline and an hourly line item for organizing records or reconstructing income and expenses.

faqs.question: Can I withhold a completed return until the client pays?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state, your credential, and the type of document. Some rules limit withholding client-provided records, and some e-file rules restrict holding a return for fees. Check your state board and professional association guidance before doing it.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on tax preparation services?
faqs.answer: In most states, tax preparation and consulting services are not subject to sales tax, but a few states tax some professional services. Check your state department of revenue.

faqs.question: How should I bill for IRS audit representation?
faqs.answer: Most consultants bill hourly, with an up-front retainer applied against time. Some quote a flat fee for a defined stage, such as responding to a single notice, and switch to hourly if the matter escalates. Make clear that fees are owed regardless of the outcome.

estimate.intro: Tax consultants send quotes before taking on a new client, a new entity, a multi-year catch-up, or any engagement involving IRS or state correspondence. Clients usually compare your fee against national chains, other local preparers, and last year's invoice. A clear written quote helps explain why a self-employed or multi-state return costs more than a basic one.

scopeChecklist.why: A client asking for one year's return may assume prior-year cleanup or amendments are included. List each year and form.

scopeChecklist.item: Forms and schedules assumed in the price
scopeChecklist.why: The quote is based on the information given. State what you assumed, such as one Schedule C, no rental properties, and one state, so additions are priced fairly.

scopeChecklist.item: What the client must supply and by when
scopeChecklist.why: Late or incomplete documents are the main cause of delays and overruns. Set a deadline for the organizer, 1099s, K-1s, and books.
A quote assuming reconciled books will be wrong if you receive raw bank statements. Say what happens if cleanup is needed.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as audit support, notices, and amended returns
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume the fee covers anything that happens after filing. Say that representation is separate and how it will be billed.
Some quotes include a planning call, while others do not. State the number of hours or meetings so expectations are clear.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and filing deadlines
scopeChecklist.why: Fees change in peak season, and extension requests or late documents may affect your capacity. A set expiry date avoids disputes.

pricingTips.title: Quote from last year's return when you can
pricingTips.body: Asking for the prior-year return and a list of changes is the quickest way to get a reliable price. It shows the forms involved and likely issues such as carryovers and depreciation schedules.

pricingTips.title: Offer a flat fee with a stated hourly overage
pricingTips.body: Clients prefer a fixed number. Add that work beyond the described scope, such as extra Forms 1099 or unexpected state filings, will be billed at your hourly rate with prior notice.

pricingTips.title: Show a retainer option for ongoing clients
pricingTips.body: A package of quarterly estimates, a mid-year planning meeting, and the return gives clients a predictable monthly cost and gives you steady revenue outside filing season.

pricingTips.title: Quote catch-up work in phases
pricingTips.body: For multiple unfiled years, price each year separately and start with the most recent. The client sees progress, and you limit exposure if documents are missing.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before seeing the client's documents?
faqs.answer: Give a range, not a firm price. State that the final fee depends on the forms and records received, and confirm the number once you have reviewed the prior return or the organizer.

faqs.question: Can I charge for an initial consultation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many consultants charge for a first meeting, especially for planning or notice problems, and credit the fee toward the engagement if the client signs. Others offer a short free call to scope the work.

faqs.question: What if a quote is exceeded because of new information?
faqs.answer: Send a revised quote or change notice before doing the extra work. Referencing the assumptions in the original quote makes it easier for the client to see what changed.

tax-preparer.intro: Tax preparers prepare and file federal and state income tax returns for individuals, self-employed people, and small businesses. They may be solo practitioners, enrolled agents, CPAs, or seasonal preparers working under their own firm. Invoices typically cover return preparation by form or schedule, bookkeeping cleanup, amended returns, IRS notice responses, and year-round planning.
tax-preparer.pricingModel: Most preparers charge a flat fee per return, built from a base price for the main form (Form 1040 or a business return) plus add-ons for each extra schedule or form, such as Schedule C, Schedule E, Schedule D, or state returns. Business returns (1120-S, 1065, 1120) are usually priced as flat fees based on complexity and bookkeeping quality. Work outside return preparation, such as IRS representation, amended returns, back-year filings, and tax planning, is typically billed hourly or as a fixed project fee. Some firms offer monthly or annual packages that bundle bookkeeping, estimated tax calculations, and preparation. Many charge a rush or disorganized-records surcharge. Avoid pricing based on a percentage of the refund, which is widely considered improper and is prohibited for preparers in many contexts.

rates.service: Individual return (Form 1040, standard deduction, W-2 income)
IRS or state notice response, tax planning, consulting

items.description: Federal Form 1040 preparation, tax year 2024 (standard base)
Schedule C – freelance design business, with expense categorization
Schedule E – one rental property
State income tax return (additional state: nonresident)
Bookkeeping cleanup – organizing and categorizing bank exports
2025 estimated tax calculation and payment vouchers

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Returns are e-filed after payment or signed Form 8879 and payment of balance. Fee is not contingent on refund amount. Thank you for your business.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax year and return type
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have multiple years or entities with you, and the invoice needs to match the right return (for example, 2024 Form 1040 versus 2024 Form 1120-S).

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized forms and schedules prepared
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each schedule and state return explains the total and prevents pushback when the price is above the base fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly work with dates and hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Bookkeeping cleanup, notice responses, and planning calls are billed by time, so show the hours and what was done.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your PTIN and firm information
invoiceChecklist.why: Paid preparers must have a PTIN, and including your firm name, address, and credential (CPA, EA, or other) keeps records clear for the client.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed engagement letter
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying the invoice to the agreed scope shows what was authorized and supports you if a fee is questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Statement that the fee is not based on the refund
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear the fee is flat or hourly and not a percentage of the refund, which is restricted in many situations.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payment instructions and filing condition
invoiceChecklist.why: If you hold the filing until payment is received, say so on the invoice so there are no surprises near the deadline.

tax-preparer.paymentTerms: Many preparers collect a deposit or retainer for business returns, bookkeeping cleanup, and new clients, often 25-50 percent upfront. For individual returns, common practice is to invoice when the return is finished and require payment before e-filing or releasing the copy, though check your state rules and the IRS rules on withholding client records, since preparers generally must return client records on request even when a fee is outstanding. Net 7 to Net 14 is typical during busy season. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if written into the engagement letter. Accepted methods usually include card, ACH, check, and sometimes deducting the fee from a refund through a bank product, which has its own disclosure rules.

tips.title: Put the fee structure in an engagement letter
tips.body: Define the tax years, forms, what records the client must provide, and how extra work is billed. Without it, requests for amendments or extra state returns turn into arguments.

tips.title: Charge for disorganized records
tips.body: Use a clear add-on or hourly rate when clients drop off a shoebox of receipts or unlabeled bank exports. State the policy before starting so it does not feel like a surprise.

tips.title: Bill extensions as a separate line
tips.body: Filing Form 4868 or 7004 takes time. Many preparers charge a small fee or include it in the final return price, but either way show it so clients know what they paid for.

tips.title: Separate preparation from representation
tips.body: Responding to an IRS notice or audit is a different service from preparing the return. Bill it hourly or as its own project, and note whether you are authorized through Form 2848.

tips.title: Bill before the deadline crunch
tips.body: Send the invoice when you deliver the completed return, not weeks later. Collecting before April and October extension deadlines keeps your cash flow steady.

faqs.question: Can I charge a percentage of the client's refund?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Basing a fee on a percentage of the refund or the amount of tax savings is restricted or prohibited for return preparation under IRS rules, and many states also limit it. Use a flat fee, per-form pricing, or hourly rates.

faqs.question: Can I refuse to e-file until I'm paid?
faqs.answer: In most cases yes, you can hold filing until payment is made if that is stated in your engagement letter. However, you generally cannot hold the client's original records, and you should check your state rules on releasing completed returns.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the return is filed?
faqs.answer: Most preparers invoice when the return is complete and ready for client review, and collect before filing. For complex business returns or new clients, collect a deposit when work begins.

faqs.question: How do I bill for work after the tax deadline, like an IRS notice?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a separate engagement. Bill hourly or at a fixed fee, get a signed Form 2848 if you will represent the client, and invoice monthly or on completion with dates and hours listed.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on my services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Most states do not tax tax preparation services, but a few tax some professional or accounting services. Check with your state department of revenue.

estimate.intro: Tax preparers usually send a fee quote when a new client asks what it will cost, often after seeing last year's return or a list of income documents. Clients compare per-return pricing, what is included, and whether bookkeeping or planning is extra. A clear quote helps prevent surprises when forms are added later.

scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume prior years or a second entity is included. Naming the years and entities avoids disputes.
The quote should state the base form plus each schedule or state return priced, so any new forms added later are clearly billable.
Listing W-2s, 1099s, K-1s, mortgage statements, and organized expense totals sets a standard and supports a surcharge if records are incomplete.
For self-employed clients, specify whether you are using their books as provided or categorizing transactions, since that is where hours expand.
Clarify whether corrections caused by late-arriving documents or changed information are included or billed separately.

scopeChecklist.item: Extension, estimated tax, and planning services
scopeChecklist.why: Clients often assume these come with preparation. Say whether they are included or priced separately.
Set a date by which documents must arrive to meet the filing deadline, and state any rush fee after that date.

pricingTips.title: Price from last year's return
pricingTips.body: If a prospect provides last year's return, count schedules, states, and entities, and base your quote on that. Note that the final price may change if their situation does.

pricingTips.title: Use a base fee plus itemized add-ons
pricingTips.body: Show the base price and each schedule separately. Clients accept add-ons more easily when they see what each covers, and it protects you if new forms appear.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for uncertain situations
pricingTips.body: For first-time clients with cryptocurrency, rental properties, or messy business books, give a range and a cap, then confirm the final price once you have seen the documents.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package for ongoing clients
pricingTips.body: Self-employed clients may prefer a yearly price that covers return preparation, quarterly estimate calculations, and a planning call. It gives you predictable revenue and gives them a fixed cost.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before seeing the client's documents?
faqs.answer: You can give a starting price or range based on the forms they expect to file, but state that the final fee depends on the actual documents. A firm quote for complex returns is risky without reviewing them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Most preparers honor a quote through the filing season or for 30 days, as long as the client's situation stays the same. Tax-year-specific quotes should state the year.

faqs.question: Is a quote the same as an engagement letter?
faqs.answer: No. A quote gives the price and scope. An engagement letter is the signed agreement that covers responsibilities, record requirements, and terms. Many preparers combine them in one document the client signs.

faqs.question: What if the client's situation turns out more complex than quoted?
faqs.answer: Contact the client before doing the extra work, explain what changed, and send an updated quote or written change. Billing for unapproved additions is the most common source of fee disputes.

taxi-service.intro: Taxi services are owner-operators and small fleets that carry passengers for a fare. Most street-hail and dispatch rides are paid on the spot by meter, but invoices come into play for corporate accounts, medical and senior transport contracts, school districts, hotels, airport pre-bookings, and long-distance or hourly charters. These invoices usually bill for metered trips, flat-rate zone fares, wait time, and add-ons like tolls and airport fees.
taxi-service.pricingModel: Metered fares are set by city or county ordinance in many places, so the base rate is often fixed and you have little room to change it. A typical meter has a flag-drop (initial) charge, a per-mile rate, and a per-minute wait or slow-traffic rate. Where regulations allow, taxi companies set flat fares for airport runs and zone-to-zone trips, and quote hourly rates for charters or standby work. Corporate and contract clients are often billed monthly on account, with a discount off meter rates or a negotiated flat rate per route. Common extras include tolls, airport access fees, extra passenger or luggage fees, after-hours surcharges, and cleaning fees. Non-emergency medical transport usually has per-trip rates plus a mileage charge and a fee for wheelchair or assisted service. Always check your local taxi ordinance for what you can legally charge.

items.description: Corporate account rides, March (metered fares, 14 trips, per attached trip log)
Airport pre-booked transfer, flat rate (3/12, pickup 5:15 AM)
Wait time at client site, 3/18 (over 10-minute grace period)
Airport access fees and tolls (pass-through, receipts on file)
Wheelchair-accessible vehicle surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Net 30. Account discount of 10% off meter already applied to trip rates. Late balances over 30 days are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Pay by check, ACH, or card. Please reference the invoice number and include the PO number on any remittance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Trip log with date, pickup time, pickup and drop-off addresses, and passenger or employee name or ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Corporate accounts need to match each ride to a department or employee, and a log settles most disputes quickly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Fare basis for each trip (meter, flat rate, or hourly)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on contracts want to see which rate applied so they can check it against the agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tolls, airport fees, and parking itemized separately with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: These are pass-through costs, not your fare, and clients often reimburse or code them differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wait time with start and end times
invoiceChecklist.why: Wait charges are the most common thing clients question, so show the minutes and any grace period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle or cab number and driver name or badge number
invoiceChecklist.why: It lets the client trace a specific trip and matches your records if there is a complaint.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO or account number and contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable at companies, hospitals, and schools often will not process an invoice without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, taxi permit or medallion number, and tax ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Government and institutional clients often need these for vendor files, and it shows you are a licensed operator.

taxi-service.paymentTerms: Street and dispatch rides are paid at drop-off by cash or card, and you should keep a receipt record. For account clients, monthly billing on net 15 or net 30 terms is common, with the invoice sent right after month-end. Hotels and medical contracts may pay through a purchasing system that takes 30 to 60 days, so confirm terms before the first ride. For large charters or long-distance bookings, ask for a deposit or card on file when booking, often 25 to 50 percent, with the balance due at the end of the trip. A late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is typical if it is written into your agreement. Accept ACH, checks, and cards, and consider suspending account service if balances run well past due.

tips.title: Bill account clients on a fixed schedule
tips.body: Send invoices on the same day each month, such as the first business day. Clients who know when to expect the bill are more likely to pay on time, and your own bookkeeping stays tidy.

tips.title: Keep trip records that match the meter
tips.body: Save dispatch records, meter printouts, or trip app logs for every account ride. If a client questions a charge six weeks later, you can show the exact pickup time, route, and fare.

tips.title: Put wait time and cancellation rules in writing
tips.body: State the free wait period (often 5 to 15 minutes) and what you charge after that. For pre-booked airport and charter trips, add a no-show or late-cancellation fee so a wasted early-morning run is not a loss.

tips.title: Separate fares from pass-through costs
tips.body: List tolls, airport fees, and parking as their own lines with receipts. This keeps your fare revenue clear for taxes and avoids a client disputing the whole invoice over a $6 fee.

tips.title: Verify rates against your local ordinance
tips.body: Many cities cap or set taxi fares, and discounts may need to be formal. Check what you are allowed to charge before offering flat rates or surcharges to contract clients.

faqs.question: Can I charge more than the meter rate?
faqs.answer: In many cities the metered rate is set by ordinance and you cannot charge above it for regular street or dispatch trips. Some areas allow flat rates for pre-booked trips or airport runs if they are agreed in advance. Check with your local taxi or transportation regulator.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on taxi fares?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and city. Some places exempt passenger transportation from sales tax, while others apply a tax or a per-trip fee. Check with your state revenue department or local regulator and show any required tax or surcharge as its own line.

faqs.question: How do I bill a company that uses my cabs regularly?
faqs.answer: Set up a corporate account with agreed rates, a billing cycle, and payment terms. Send one monthly invoice with a trip log attached, including date, route, passenger or employee ID, and fare for each ride. Ask for a PO or cost center code up front.

faqs.question: Should I charge for tolls and airport fees?
faqs.answer: Yes, as pass-through costs, as long as local rules allow it. List them separately and keep receipts. For flat-rate trips, state in your quote whether tolls and fees are included.

faqs.question: What if a client disputes a wait-time charge?
faqs.answer: Point to your written terms and the pickup and departure times in your dispatch log. Having the grace period and per-minute rate in your account agreement or booking confirmation makes this a quick conversation instead of an argument.

estimate.intro: Taxi services give quotes for pre-booked and non-metered work such as airport transfers, long-distance trips, hourly charters, event shuttles, and recurring contract routes. Clients usually compare your flat price against rideshare, limo, and other taxi companies, so clear totals and inclusions matter. A quote is also how you set wait time, tolls, and cancellation terms before the trip.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off addresses, date, and time
scopeChecklist.why: Price depends on distance and time of day, and a change in route or timing changes the cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of passengers, luggage, and any special equipment
scopeChecklist.why: Larger groups may need a van or second vehicle, and extra luggage or child seats can affect price.

scopeChecklist.item: Fare basis: flat rate, metered estimate, or hourly
scopeChecklist.why: The client needs to know if the price is fixed or if the meter can go higher with traffic or detours.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included: tolls, airport fees, parking, and gratuity
scopeChecklist.why: These extras are the main reason final bills differ from quotes.

scopeChecklist.item: Wait time allowance and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: Flights get delayed and meetings run long, so say how many minutes are free and what happens after.
Early-morning and airport bookings take a vehicle off the road, so state when fees apply.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit, payment method, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Holding a vehicle for a future date requires commitment, and rates may change with fuel or schedule.

pricingTips.title: Quote flat rates for predictable routes
pricingTips.body: Airport and regular route trips are easiest to sell at a fixed price. Base it on the average meter fare plus a small cushion for traffic, and confirm your local rules allow flat fares.

pricingTips.title: Use hourly pricing for open-ended work
pricingTips.body: If the client cannot give you a firm itinerary, quote an hourly rate with a minimum, such as two or three hours. It protects you from long idle periods.

pricingTips.title: Add an after-hours or peak surcharge
pricingTips.body: Late-night, early-morning, and holiday trips cost more to staff. Show this as a line item so the client sees why the quote is higher than a daytime fare.

pricingTips.title: Offer two options when it helps
pricingTips.body: For events or groups, quote a standard sedan and a van or accessible vehicle side by side. Clients can choose without asking for a new quote.

faqs.question: Can I give a firm quote on a metered trip?
faqs.answer: You can give an estimate based on distance and typical traffic, but the final fare is usually whatever the meter shows. If the client needs certainty, offer a flat rate where local rules allow it.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Seven to fourteen days is common for future bookings, and shorter for busy dates like holidays or major events. State the expiration date on the quote.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit for a quote?
faqs.answer: For long-distance trips, multi-vehicle bookings, and charters, yes. A deposit of 25 to 50 percent secures the booking and covers you if the client cancels late.

faqs.question: What if the trip changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Say in your terms that changes in route, time, passenger count, or wait time can change the price. Send a revised quote or confirm the change in writing before the trip.

technical-writer.intro: Technical writers create documentation such as API references, user guides, knowledge base articles, SOPs, release notes, and training materials. Most freelance and small-business writers invoice software companies, medical device firms, engineering teams, and agencies, usually for a defined project or a block of hours each month.
technical-writer.pricingModel: Technical writers bill hourly, per project, per page, or on a monthly retainer. Hourly is most common for contract work embedded with a team, especially when scope shifts as engineers change the product. Fixed project fees work for well-defined deliverables like a 40-page user guide or an API reference for a set number of endpoints, and they should be based on an hours estimate with a buffer for review cycles. Per-page or per-word pricing is less common and tends to undervalue research and interviews, so many writers use it only as a sanity check. Retainers suit ongoing release notes, knowledge base upkeep, and docs-as-code work. Add separate line items for subject matter expert interviews, diagramming and screenshots, localization prep, and rush work. Software or tool costs (for example, a client-required authoring license) are usually either absorbed in the rate or billed at cost with approval.

rates.service: Diagrams, screenshots, and short video walkthroughs

items.description: Discovery: SME interviews and product walkthrough (3 sessions)
REST API reference: 24 endpoints, request and response examples
Getting Started guide (draft and final)
Diagrams and annotated screenshots
Review rounds 1 and 2: consolidating comments and revisions

sampleInvoice.notes: Project: Developer Documentation v2, PO #4471. Work delivered via the client's docs repository, merged 6/14. Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Additional revision rounds beyond the two included are billed hourly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and PO or contract number
invoiceChecklist.why: Accounts payable teams at larger companies often reject invoices without a PO number, which delays payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables with version or document names
invoiceChecklist.why: Naming the guide, article set, or API version makes it clear what was delivered and ties billing to the statement of work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours broken out by task and date range
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients on hourly contracts want to see research, writing, review, and revision time separately, particularly when engineers questioned the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or percentage complete for fixed-fee work
invoiceChecklist.why: Tying each invoice to an approved milestone, such as outline or first draft, prevents disputes about whether payment is owed yet.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Documentation work often grows through review cycles, so showing how many rounds were included protects you when extra rounds are billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs and approvals
invoiceChecklist.why: Stock images, translation vendors, or a client-required tool license should be itemized at cost with a reference to the approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax ID and W-9 status, or your business name and EIN
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients paying a contractor over the annual reporting threshold generally need a W-9 on file to issue a 1099.

technical-writer.paymentTerms: Technical writers commonly ask for 25-50% upfront on fixed-fee projects, with the balance tied to milestones or delivery. Hourly contractors usually invoice every two weeks or monthly, and corporate clients often pay on net 30 or net 45 terms. Net 15 is reasonable for small businesses and startups. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract in advance. Payment is typically by ACH or check, with credit cards less common because of processing fees. For first-time clients, consider requiring the deposit before starting and keeping final source files until the last payment clears.

tips.title: Define what counts as a revision
tips.body: Write into your agreement how many review rounds are included and what a round means, such as one consolidated set of comments per round. Without this, documentation projects can drift for weeks while product changes trigger rewrites.

tips.title: Bill SME time you spend chasing
tips.body: Waiting on engineers for answers and access to builds is real project time. Include interview scheduling and follow-up in your estimate, or set a rule that delays caused by the client extend the timeline and may be billed.

tips.title: Separate writing from production
tips.body: Diagramming, screenshot capture, video, and publishing to a help center or docs site take significant time. Itemize them so clients see why a 20-page guide costs more than 20 pages of text.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not only at the end
tips.body: Outline approved, first draft delivered, and final published are natural billing points. This keeps cash flow steady and gives you leverage if a client goes quiet.

tips.title: Raise rates on retainers annually
tips.body: Ongoing docs work often stays at the original rate for years. Include an annual adjustment clause or revisit the rate each renewal.

faqs.question: Should a technical writer charge hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Hourly is safer when scope is unclear or the product is still changing. Project pricing works when deliverables are well defined, and you can estimate hours confidently. Many writers quote a fixed price based on estimated hours plus a buffer of 15-25% for review and rework.

faqs.question: Can I bill for time spent learning the product?
faqs.answer: Yes. Research, product walkthroughs, and testing the software are part of the job and are normally billable. List discovery as its own line item so the client sees it as a planned phase rather than padding.

faqs.question: What do I do if a client keeps requesting revisions after delivery?
faqs.answer: Refer to the revision limit in your agreement and bill additional rounds at your hourly rate. If you did not set a limit, send a change order that states the new work and cost before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a W-9 to my clients?
faqs.answer: In the US, clients who pay you over the IRS reporting threshold during the year generally ask for a W-9 so they can issue a 1099-NEC. Sending it at the start of the engagement avoids payment delays later. Check current IRS rules or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: Should I charge for documentation that clients cancel mid-project?
faqs.answer: Yes, for work completed. Your contract should say that you are paid for hours worked or milestones reached through the cancellation date, and that any deposit is non-refundable up to that point.

estimate.intro: Technical writers send estimates when a client asks for a defined documentation project, such as a user manual, API docs, or a knowledge base build. Clients usually compare your total price, timeline, and how much of the work you handle versus what their team supplies. Because the product is often unfinished, a good estimate is as much about assumptions as it is about price.

scopeChecklist.why: State whether you are producing a PDF manual, help center articles, or Markdown in a repo, and roughly how many pages, topics, or endpoints, so both sides agree on the size of the job.
List what the client must provide, such as a test environment, existing docs, style guide, and engineer availability. Late access is the most common cause of schedule slips.
Specify how many interviews or hours of expert time you need, since limited access affects quality and your hours.
Say how many consolidated review cycles are included and who gives final approval, to prevent endless rework.
Clarify which authoring tools, version control, or content management system you will use and whether you are responsible for publishing.
Name items such as translation, video production, UI text rewrites, or ongoing maintenance, so they are quoted separately if requested.
Tie delivery dates to milestones and client inputs, and note that dates move if the product changes or feedback is late.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours by task, then add a buffer
