pricingTips.body: Break the project into discovery, outline, drafting, graphics, review, and publishing. Add 15-25% for product changes and feedback cycles, then present a fixed price or a not-to-exceed cap.

pricingTips.title: Offer phased pricing
pricingTips.body: Quote a paid discovery or documentation audit first, then price the main build once you understand the product. This reduces risk for both sides when the scope is vague.

pricingTips.title: Show assumptions next to the number
pricingTips.body: Write assumptions such as number of endpoints, existing content reuse, and review rounds directly under the price. If the assumptions change, you have a clear basis for a revised quote.

pricingTips.title: Offer a tiered option
pricingTips.body: Providing a core package and an expanded one that adds diagrams, a quick-start guide, or release-note maintenance lets clients choose without negotiating your rate.

faqs.question: How long should a technical writing estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is typical. Product plans and your availability change, so state an expiration date and note that pricing may change after it.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed price when the deliverables and inputs are clear. Use an hourly estimate with a cap when the product is still changing or access to experts is uncertain.

faqs.question: Do I charge for writing the estimate?
faqs.answer: A short quote is usually free. For large documentation projects that need an audit of existing content or a sample, charge a paid discovery fee and apply it toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What happens if the scope grows after the client accepts?
faqs.answer: Send a written change order describing the added work, hours, and cost before you proceed. Reference the assumptions in the original estimate to show what changed.

tennis-coach.intro: Tennis coaches bill for private lessons, semi-private and group clinics, junior programs, camps, and sometimes stringing, ball machine time, or tournament travel. Clients are usually parents paying for a child, adult recreational players, or clubs and schools that contract a coach. Invoices work best when they list lesson dates, the format (private or group), and any court fees passed through.
tennis-coach.pricingModel: Most tennis coaches charge per hour for private lessons, with a lower per-person rate for semi-private (2 players) and group lessons (3 or more). Rates depend on region, your certification (USPTA or PTR), your playing and coaching background, and whether you teach at a club, a public park, or a private court. Many coaches sell prepaid packages of 5 or 10 lessons at a small discount, which improves cash flow and reduces cancellations. Juniors programs and camps are often priced per session, per week, or per season. If you work at a club, you may pay court fees or a percentage to the club, so decide whether to build that into your rate or bill it separately. Extras such as stringing, video analysis, tournament coaching, and travel are billed as separate line items.

rates.service: Ball machine or hitting partner session
Tournament coaching or match play support

items.description: Private lessons, March 4, 11, 18, 25 (60 min each, Riverside Park courts)
Semi-private lesson, March 20 (second player: sibling)
Court rental, Riverside Park (passed through at cost)
Racquet restring, synthetic gut, 54 lbs
Video analysis of serve and forehand with written notes

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Lessons cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed in full. Unused lessons in a prepaid package expire 90 days from purchase. Venmo, Zelle, check, or card accepted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson dates, times, and duration
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents and adult clients want to match the bill to what actually happened, and dates settle most disputes about missed or extra sessions.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lesson format (private, semi-private, group) and number of players
invoiceChecklist.why: Rates differ by format, so the invoice should show which rate applied to each session.

invoiceChecklist.item: Court location and any court fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Court rental or club guest fees are often passed through at cost, and listing them separately shows they are not part of your coaching rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package details and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: If a client prepaid for 10 lessons, show how many were used and how many remain so there is no confusion later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Late cancellations cost you court time you cannot resell, and itemizing them with the date references your stated policy.

invoiceChecklist.item: Stringing, equipment, and balls charged
invoiceChecklist.why: Retail items and labor are separate from instruction, and in many states sold goods may be subject to sales tax, so keep them on their own lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification and business details (USPTA or PTR number, business name, contact)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clubs, schools, and some parents want proof of credentials, and a clear business name helps with reimbursement and tax records.

tennis-coach.paymentTerms: Private lesson clients often pay at the end of each session or monthly, while prepaid packages are paid up front. Junior camps and seasonal programs usually require full payment or a deposit at registration to hold a spot. For monthly invoicing, due dates of 7 to 14 days are common, and some coaches add a late fee of $10 to $25 or a percentage after the due date. Clubs and schools that contract you directly may pay net 30. Common payment methods are card, Venmo, Zelle, check, and cash. Put your cancellation window, usually 24 hours, in writing before the first lesson.

tips.title: Sell packages instead of single lessons
tips.body: A 10-lesson package paid in advance cuts down on chasing payments and no-shows. Offer a modest discount, state an expiration date, and track used lessons on each invoice.

tips.title: Put your cancellation policy in writing
tips.body: Weather, school events, and illness cause frequent cancellations. Decide in advance what is a rainout you reschedule at no charge and what is a late cancel you bill, and state both on the invoice notes.

tips.title: Separate court fees from coaching
tips.body: If you pay for court time, list it as its own line. Clients see what they pay for, and you can adjust the court cost without changing your hourly rate.

tips.title: Bill families, not just players
tips.body: When siblings or friends share a lesson, decide who is billed. Many coaches send one invoice to one parent and list each player under it, which avoids split payments.

tips.title: Track mileage and travel time
tips.body: If you travel to private courts or tournaments, charge a travel fee or mileage for distances beyond your normal area, and keep records for your own tax deductions.

faqs.question: Should I invoice after every lesson or monthly?
faqs.answer: Monthly invoicing is easier for recurring weekly students, and prepaid packages work well for newer clients. Single lessons for one-time clients are often paid on the spot. Pick one method per client and stick with it.

faqs.question: Can I charge for lessons cancelled because of rain?
faqs.answer: Most coaches do not charge for rainouts or unplayable courts and reschedule instead. Charge for late cancellations by the client when the weather is fine, as long as your policy says so beforehand.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on lessons?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Many states do not tax instruction, but some tax certain recreational services, and sales of strings or equipment are often taxable. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle a club that takes a cut of my lesson fees?
faqs.answer: Decide whether your quoted rate includes the club's share. If you invoice clients yourself, list the club fee separately or build it into the rate. If the club bills clients and pays you, invoice the club for your share.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice if I'm paid by the club or school?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you are an independent contractor. Send an invoice with dates, hours, and rates for each program. This gives you a record for taxes, and you may need to give the club a W-9.

estimate.intro: Tennis coaches send quotes for camps, junior programs, school or club contracts, tournament travel, and long-term coaching plans. Parents and organizations usually compare your price to other coaches, the club's pro shop, and local rec programs. A clear quote showing what is included helps you compete on value rather than only on hourly rate.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of sessions, length, and schedule
scopeChecklist.why: Clients compare total cost, so specify how many weeks, how many sessions per week, and the duration of each.
A clinic with 4 players is a different product than one with 10, and a cap protects both quality and your rate per player.

scopeChecklist.item: Court location and who pays court fees
scopeChecklist.why: Court rental or club fees can add significantly to the total, so state whether they are included or billed separately.
Say who provides balls, hoppers, ball machines, and any loaner racquets so there are no surprises on the first day.
Outdoor programs lose sessions to weather, and the quote should explain whether missed sessions are made up, credited, or refunded.
If you coach at away events, spell out how your travel time, mileage, and meals are covered and who books the hotel.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment schedule and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: A deposit and a date by which the quote must be accepted lets you hold court time and staff without risk.

pricingTips.title: Price per player and show the total
pricingTips.body: For clinics and camps, show the per-player price and the full program total. Parents like seeing the per-session cost, and organizations need the total for budgeting.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers or package options
pricingTips.body: Give two or three options, such as 5, 10, or 20 lessons, with a lower per-lesson rate as the count rises. This lets the client choose without negotiating your hourly fee.

pricingTips.title: Include your cost of court time
pricingTips.body: If you rent courts or pay a club a percentage, calculate your net per hour before quoting. A group clinic can look profitable but lose money after court fees.

pricingTips.title: Quote travel separately
pricingTips.body: Charge a flat travel fee or per-mile rate for anything outside your normal area, so a long drive does not reduce your effective hourly pay.

faqs.question: Should I give free trial lessons?
faqs.answer: Some coaches offer a discounted first lesson or a short evaluation instead of a free one. It screens out people who are not serious and still gives the client a chance to see your style.

faqs.question: How do I quote a school or club contract?
faqs.answer: Estimate your hours, including setup and planning, then add any court or equipment costs. Quote a per-session or per-season price, and clarify whether you are an independent contractor billing the organization.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a camp or season?
faqs.answer: A deposit of 25 to 50 percent, or full payment at registration, is common. It holds the player's spot and covers your costs if they withdraw.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical for programs, because court availability and schedules change. Shorter windows make sense when a start date is close or a spot is limited.

tent-rental.intro: Tent rental businesses supply and install frame tents, pole tents, and clearspan structures for weddings, graduations, corporate events, festivals, and backyard parties. Invoices usually cover the tent itself, installation and takedown labor, add-ons like sidewalls, flooring, lighting, and heating, plus delivery and any permit or site fees.
tent-rental.pricingModel: Most tent companies price by tent size and type, with a base rental price that includes delivery, setup, and takedown within a set radius. Pricing is typically a flat fee per tent for a standard weekend rental, with add-ons priced per item or per linear or square foot (sidewalls, flooring, liners). Large or complex jobs are quoted individually. Other charges include extra delivery miles, weekday or after-hours labor, stake versus ballast installation, site surveys, generator or utility locating, and cleaning or damage fees. Many companies take a deposit to hold the date, then collect the balance before or on the event day. Rental periods are usually one day or one weekend, with extra days billed at a fraction of the base rate.

rates.service: 20x30 or 20x40 pole or frame tent, installed
40x60 or larger clearspan or pole tent, installed

items.description: 20x40 frame tent, installation and takedown (Saturday event)
Clear sidewalls, 80 linear ft
Interlocking tent flooring, 800 sq ft
String lighting package
Propane heater
Delivery beyond 25-mile radius

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of 50% received to reserve date. Balance due 7 days before the event. Tent to remain set until Sunday 6 PM takedown. Customer is responsible for damage beyond normal wear and for contacting utility locators before staking. Weather-related cancellations within 48 hours are subject to a 25% restocking charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, setup window, and takedown time
invoiceChecklist.why: Rental periods are time-sensitive and this settles disputes if a client wants the tent to stay longer or setup was delayed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tent size, type, and color or top style
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often compare tents between vendors, and listing exact dimensions avoids disagreements about what was ordered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Event site address and setup surface
invoiceChecklist.why: Grass, asphalt, and patio installs are priced differently (stakes versus ballast), and the surface affects liability for any damage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons with quantities
invoiceChecklist.why: Sidewalls, flooring, lighting, heaters, and tables each carry their own price and are the most common line items clients question.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery and mileage charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows how any distance fees were calculated beyond your included service radius.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what has been paid, what remains, and when, particularly when a deposit held the date months earlier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit, utility locate, or site fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Local permits or fire marshal inspections are often required for larger tents, and listing them separately shows these are pass-through costs.

tent-rental.paymentTerms: Tent rental companies typically take a deposit of 25-50% at booking to hold the date, with the balance due 7 to 14 days before the event or on delivery. For smaller backyard rentals, payment in full at booking is common. Many businesses accept credit cards, ACH, and checks, and some add a card processing fee. Cancellation and weather policies are usually spelled out on the contract and invoice, such as keeping the deposit if the client cancels inside a certain window. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common on commercial accounts billed net 15 or net 30. Damage or cleaning charges are billed after takedown with photos if needed.

tips.title: Collect the balance before the event
tips.body: Once a tent is up, you have little leverage to get paid. Require the balance before delivery or on setup day, and put it in writing at booking.

tips.title: Separate deposits from the final balance
tips.body: Show the deposit as a credit line on the final invoice so the client sees the full total, the amount already paid, and the amount owed.

tips.title: Bill add-ons the moment they are requested
tips.body: Clients often add sidewalls, heaters, or extra flooring in the final week. Update the invoice immediately so there are no surprises on event day.

tips.title: Document damage and extra labor
tips.body: Take photos at delivery and takedown. If you charge for rips, stains, or extra cleanup, attach them so the charge is hard to dispute.

tips.title: Keep weather and cancellation terms on the invoice
tips.body: Wind, rain, and storms can change or cancel events. Stating your policy on the invoice as well as the contract reduces arguments about deposit refunds.

faqs.question: Should I charge a deposit for a tent rental?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most tent companies take 25-50% to hold the date since tents and crews can't be rebooked easily. Many make the deposit non-refundable or partly refundable depending on how close the cancellation is to the event.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on tent rentals?
faqs.answer: In many states, rentals of tangible property are taxable, and installation labor may or may not be. Rules vary, so check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a tent that stays up for multiple days?
faqs.answer: Include one day or one weekend in the base price and bill extra days at a set percentage of the base rate, often 25-50% per additional day. List the dates on the invoice so the extra days are clear.

faqs.question: Can I charge for cancellations due to weather?
faqs.answer: You can if your contract says so. Many companies keep the deposit or charge a restocking or labor fee if crews have already been scheduled or the tent is delivered. Put the policy in your agreement and on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for permits and inspections?
faqs.answer: List permit fees, fire marshal inspections, or utility locate costs as separate line items at cost, with a small handling fee if you do the legwork. This keeps your tent pricing clean and shows what is a pass-through charge.

estimate.intro: Tent rental companies usually send a quote after a phone call or site visit, once they know the guest count, date, and location. Clients often get several quotes and compare tent size, included services, and add-ons, so a clear itemized estimate helps you stand out and avoids misunderstandings later.

scopeChecklist.why: A 20x40 frame tent seats fewer guests than clients expect. Stating size and approximate seating for rounds or rows sets realistic expectations.
Clients compare totals, so spell out what the base price covers and what costs extra.
Stakes require utility locates and may not be allowed on some surfaces, so ballast pricing and limits should be clear.
Specifies when the tent goes up and comes down, and what happens if the site is not ready or the client wants it to stay longer.
Sidewalls, flooring, lighting, heating, cooling, and furniture should be listed so clients can pick options without surprises.
Clearing the site, marking sprinklers, getting permits, and providing power are common sources of disputes if not stated.
Explains when you may refuse to install or require takedown for safety, and how that affects fees.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic tent, a package with sidewalls and lighting, and a full setup with flooring and climate control. Clients tend to choose a middle option when they can see the difference.

pricingTips.title: Charge for site surveys on complex jobs
pricingTips.body: For large tents or tricky sites, charge a site visit fee and credit it toward the rental if the client books.

pricingTips.title: Price peak dates higher
pricingTips.body: Saturdays in May, June, September, and October often book first. Many companies add a peak season premium or require larger deposits for those dates.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on quotes
pricingTips.body: Inventory is limited and a quote that sits open for weeks can cost you a booking. A 14 to 30 day validity window is common.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a site visit before quoting?
faqs.answer: For standard backyard tents, a visit is usually free. For large or commercial installs, many companies charge a fee and credit it back if the customer books.

faqs.question: How long should a tent rental quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Typically 14 to 30 days, or until another customer books the same date. Put an expiration date on the quote and state that the date is only held once a deposit is received.

faqs.question: What if the final guest count or tent size changes?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that changes to size, layout, or add-ons will be repriced. Update the estimate in writing and have the client approve it before you adjust inventory.

faqs.question: Do I need to include permits in my estimate?
faqs.answer: If your area requires permits or fire inspections for tents above a certain size, note who is responsible. Either quote the fee as a separate line or state clearly that the client must obtain it.

test-prep-tutor.intro: Test prep tutors help students prepare for exams such as the SAT, ACT, PSAT, GRE, GMAT, LSAT, MCAT, AP exams, SSAT/ISEE, and state or professional licensing tests. Most work solo or run a small tutoring business, and they bill families, adult learners, schools, or sometimes companies for one-on-one sessions, small groups, diagnostic tests, and custom materials.
test-prep-tutor.pricingModel: Most test prep tutors charge per hour for one-on-one sessions, with higher rates for harder or higher-stakes exams like the LSAT, MCAT, and GMAT. Many also sell prepaid packages (for example 10 or 20 sessions) at a small discount, which gives the tutor predictable income and gives the family a clear commitment through test day. Diagnostic tests and score reports are often billed as a flat fee or bundled into the first package. Small group classes are priced per student per session or per course. Some tutors charge a flat fee for a full program that covers a set number of sessions, practice tests, and a study plan. Materials such as printed practice tests, workbooks, and online question banks are billed at cost or folded into the rate. Rates differ by region, experience, and track record with score improvements, and tutors with 5 or more years or a high personal score on the exam often charge at the top of the range.

items.description: Full-length ACT diagnostic test and 45-minute score review
ACT one-on-one tutoring (Math and Science sections), 60-minute sessions, 3/4 - 4/22
ACT English and Reading strategy sessions, 60 minutes, 4/24 - 5/8
Printed practice tests and workbook

sampleInvoice.notes: Student: Jordan M. Target test date: June 14. Payment due within 7 days of invoice date. Sessions canceled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at the full rate. Unused prepaid sessions can be used until 60 days after the test date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Student name and the name of the person paying
invoiceChecklist.why: The student is often a minor and a parent pays, so the invoice should name both for clear records and for any reimbursement or employer benefit claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Exam and section covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing the SAT, ACT, GRE, or LSAT and the sections worked on (for example Reading or Logic Games) shows what the client paid for and helps if they ask about progress.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session dates, length, and format
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to match charges to sessions on their calendar, and it should be clear whether sessions were in person or online and whether they were 45, 60, or 90 minutes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package balance or sessions remaining
invoiceChecklist.why: For prepaid packages, showing sessions used and remaining prevents disputes over leftover time, especially after the test date passes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Late cancellation or no-show charges
invoiceChecklist.why: If your policy bills missed sessions, listing them as separate line items with the date shows they followed your stated terms.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials and testing fees you purchased
invoiceChecklist.why: Practice test printing, question bank access, or registration fees you paid on the client's behalf should be itemized so they are not mistaken for tutoring charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, contact info, and tax ID if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some families, schools, and employers need a W-9 or business details to reimburse or issue payment, and a clear sender identity helps your own bookkeeping.

test-prep-tutor.paymentTerms: Many test prep tutors bill monthly in arrears for hourly work or collect payment up front for packages, with the full package or the first month due before sessions begin. Net 7 or net 14 is common for invoices sent after sessions, and some tutors require payment before each session or by the first of the month. Late fees, if used, are usually a flat amount or 1 to 1.5 percent per month and should be stated in writing before work starts. Typical payment methods include bank transfer, card, check, and peer-to-peer payment apps. When working with a school, tutoring company, or employer, expect longer terms such as net 30 and possibly a purchase order number.

tips.title: Sell packages timed to the test date
tips.body: Build packages around the exam calendar, such as an 8-week plan ending the week before the test. Bill the package up front so a student who drops off mid-prep still covers your reserved time.

tips.title: Write a clear cancellation policy
tips.body: Test prep schedules get crowded near test dates and students often cancel last minute. A 24-hour notice rule with full billing for late cancels, stated on the first invoice, saves awkward conversations later.

tips.title: Decide what happens to unused sessions
tips.body: Set an expiration, such as 60 days after the test date, and put it in writing. Without one, families may ask for refunds or credits months later, after you have filled that time with other students.

tips.title: Bill diagnostics and planning separately
tips.body: Scoring a diagnostic, analyzing errors, and building a study plan takes unpaid-feeling hours. Charge a flat fee for it, or state clearly that it is included in a package price.

tips.title: Send invoices before the next block starts
tips.body: For ongoing weekly tutoring, invoice at the start or end of each month on a consistent date. Parents tend to pay faster when the invoice arrives at a predictable time and lists each session.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the package?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Hourly billing is simple for students who need flexible help, while packages guarantee income and encourage commitment through test day. Many tutors offer an hourly rate and a modest discount, often 5 to 10 percent, for a prepaid package.

faqs.question: Can I charge for lesson planning and prep time?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you say so up front. Some tutors fold prep into a higher hourly rate, while others bill a separate fee for diagnostics, custom materials, or score analysis. Whichever you choose, put it on the invoice as a clear line item or note that it is included.

faqs.question: What if a student reschedules because of school conflicts or illness?
faqs.answer: Set a policy before the first session. A common approach is to allow free rescheduling with 24 hours notice and bill the full session for later cancellations, with an exception for real emergencies at your discretion. Write it on the invoice or in your agreement.

faqs.question: Do I need to collect sales tax on tutoring?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states do not tax tutoring services, but some tax certain educational services or materials. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and keep materials charges separate on the invoice in case they are taxed differently.

faqs.question: Should I offer refunds if a student does not hit a target score?
faqs.answer: Most tutors do not guarantee scores because results depend on the student's effort and the test day. Some offer a limited guarantee, such as extra sessions at no charge. If you offer anything like this, spell out the conditions in writing before you start.

estimate.intro: Test prep tutors send an estimate or proposal when a family or adult learner asks what a full prep program will cost, usually weeks or months before a test date. Clients often compare you against test prep companies, online courses, and other private tutors, so the quote should show total cost, session count, and what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Exam, test date, and target score
scopeChecklist.why: Tying the quote to a specific exam and goal sets expectations and shows the number of sessions you recommend is based on the starting point and timeline.
State how many sessions per week, how long each is, and over how many weeks, so the total hours are not open to interpretation.
If the first step is a diagnostic and a custom plan, say whether it is included or charged separately so the client is not surprised by an extra line.
Clarify whether books, printed tests, and question banks are included or billed at cost, since families often assume they are covered.
Say if sessions are online or in person, where they take place, and whether travel to the student's home adds a fee.
Tutoring only works if the student practices, so note expected weekly practice and that results depend on it. This also protects you if progress stalls.
Include your late-cancel rule, how long sessions remain valid, and what happens if the student stops early, so these terms are agreed before payment.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total, not just an hourly rate
pricingTips.body: Families budget for a full program. Show the hourly rate and the package total, for example 12 sessions at $90 for $1,080, so they can compare it to a course or company program.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three options
pricingTips.body: A basic package, a standard package with a diagnostic and extra practice tests, and an intensive package before the exam give clients a choice without needing to negotiate your rate.

pricingTips.title: Base the session count on the score gap
pricingTips.body: A student looking to raise a score by a few points needs fewer sessions than one aiming for a large jump. Explaining this in the quote shows your recommendation is reasoned, not padded.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Test dates are fixed and your schedule fills up near them. A quote valid for 14 days encourages a decision and protects your availability.

faqs.question: Should I give a free consultation before quoting?
faqs.answer: Many tutors offer a short free call, around 15 to 30 minutes, to learn the student's goals and timeline. A free full session is less common. If you want to offer a trial, consider a discounted first session instead.

faqs.question: How do I quote when I do not know the student's starting level?
faqs.answer: Quote the diagnostic first as a flat fee, then provide a program quote after reviewing results. Alternatively, give a range of sessions and say the final recommendation follows the diagnostic.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the quote?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short written agreement or accepted quote that includes the session count, price, payment schedule, and cancellation terms gives both sides a clear record, especially for large prepaid packages.

faqs.question: Can I change the price after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Only if the scope changes, such as the student asking for extra sessions or a second exam. Keep the original quote as written and send a new quote or add-on for the additional work.

therapist.intro: Therapists in private practice, including licensed counselors, clinical social workers, marriage and family therapists, and psychologists, bill clients for sessions, assessments, and related services. Many are solo practitioners who take self-pay clients, provide superbills for out-of-network reimbursement, or bill insurance through a separate system. This page covers self-pay invoicing and superbills.
therapist.pricingModel: Most therapists charge a flat fee per session, usually for a 45 to 55 minute hour, with a higher fee for intake sessions and longer sessions of 75 to 90 minutes. Couples and family sessions typically cost more than individual sessions. Many practices offer a sliding scale for clients with limited income and set aside a limited number of reduced-fee slots. Other billable items include psychological testing and report writing (often hourly or a flat package), letters and forms, court-related work such as record preparation or testimony (hourly, often at a much higher rate), and late cancellation or no-show fees. Some therapists bill by the month for weekly sessions, which simplifies payment but still requires dated session records. Rates vary widely by license type, specialty, region, and whether you accept insurance.

rates.service: Couples or family therapy session (60-90 min)

items.description: Individual psychotherapy, 53 min (CPT 90837), dates of service: 3/4, 3/11, 3/18, 3/25
Late cancellation fee, session of 3/20 (less than 24 hours notice)
Letter of treatment participation for employer

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Cards, HSA/FSA cards, and ACH are accepted. A superbill with diagnosis and CPT codes is available on request for out-of-network reimbursement. Please contact the office with billing questions rather than through session time.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates of service for every session
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients submitting to insurance, HSA, or FSA plans need exact dates, and it ties each charge to your clinical records.

invoiceChecklist.item: CPT codes and session length
invoiceChecklist.why: Codes such as 90791, 90834, 90837, and 90847 are needed on superbills for out-of-network reimbursement and show what service was provided.

invoiceChecklist.item: Diagnosis code only when needed (superbill)
invoiceChecklist.why: Include an ICD-10 code only on a superbill the client requests for reimbursement, since clients may not want a diagnosis on a general invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Provider name, license type and number, and NPI
invoiceChecklist.why: Insurers and flexible spending plans typically require credentials to process a claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: Tax ID or SSN and practice address
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed on superbills so the client's plan can identify the provider; consider using an EIN to avoid sharing your SSN.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payments received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows copays or prepayments already collected so the client is not billed twice.

invoiceChecklist.item: Cancellation or no-show fee labeled clearly
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifying the missed appointment date and referencing the policy the client agreed to reduces disputes.

therapist.paymentTerms: Many therapists collect payment at the time of service by card on file, which avoids chasing balances. Others send a monthly invoice or superbill with payment due in 7 to 30 days. Prepayment is common for psychological testing, often half up front, and for court-related work, often through a retainer. Late fees are less common in therapy than in other trades and should be stated in your written policies and signed informed consent paperwork before they are applied. Typical payment methods are credit and debit cards, HSA and FSA cards, ACH, and checks. Keep billing communications separate from clinical conversations and send invoices through a secure channel because they can reveal that someone is in treatment.

tips.title: Put your fee and cancellation policy in writing before the first session
tips.body: Have clients sign your fee schedule and late cancellation policy with the intake paperwork. A fee you can point to in a signed document is much easier to enforce, and clients are more comfortable when charges are not a surprise.

tips.title: Keep an on-file card for no-shows and balances
tips.body: Storing a card with written consent lets you charge the session or a missed appointment fee without an awkward conversation. Make sure the authorization states exactly what you may charge.

tips.title: Protect privacy on every billing document
tips.body: Use a neutral business name on statements and payment descriptors if possible, and send invoices over secure email or a client portal. Limit diagnosis details to what a superbill requires.

tips.title: Be consistent with sliding scale and fee changes
tips.body: Decide in advance who qualifies for reduced fees and how often you review them. Give clients written notice, often 30 days, before raising rates so the change does not strain the relationship.

tips.title: Separate clinical time from administrative time
tips.body: Decide which paperwork you will charge for, such as forms, letters, and phone calls over 10 minutes, and list those rates up front. Unpaid admin work adds up quickly for solo practitioners.

faqs.question: What is a superbill and when do I need to give one?
faqs.answer: A superbill is an itemized statement with your credentials, dates of service, CPT codes, diagnosis code, and fees paid. Out-of-network clients submit it to their insurance for possible reimbursement. Provide one when a client asks, and note that reimbursement is not guaranteed.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a missed session?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, if your policy is in writing and the client agreed to it ahead of time. Many therapists require 24 to 48 hours notice. Insurance usually does not pay for missed sessions, so the fee is typically the client's responsibility. Check your licensing board's rules and any insurance contract terms.

faqs.question: Should I include a diagnosis on my invoice?
faqs.answer: Usually not on a standard invoice. Include an ICD-10 code only on a superbill the client requests, since the document may be shared with an insurer, employer, or HSA administrator.

faqs.question: Can I bill for phone calls, emails, and letters?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you disclose it in your informed consent or fee policy. Many therapists allow short check-ins for free and charge a prorated hourly rate for calls longer than 10 to 15 minutes, forms, and letters.

faqs.question: Are therapy fees taxable income for my practice?
faqs.answer: In general, yes. Self-pay fees are business income, and sole proprietors usually owe self-employment tax in addition to income tax. Session fees are usually not subject to sales tax, but rules vary by state, so confirm with a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Therapy sessions are usually priced from a posted fee schedule, so formal estimates are less common. They come up for psychological testing, court-related work, group programs, intensive therapy, and when a client asks what treatment might cost over several months. Clients typically compare your per-session fee, whether you take their insurance, and how long treatment may last.

scopeChecklist.why: State the per-session rate, the length it covers (for example 53 minutes), and the expected frequency so the client can estimate monthly costs.
Therapy duration depends on clinical progress, so give a range or say it is open-ended instead of promising a number of sessions.

scopeChecklist.item: What a testing or evaluation package includes
scopeChecklist.why: List the interview, test administration, scoring, report writing, and feedback session so the client knows what is covered and what is extra.

scopeChecklist.item: Billing for reports, letters, and court work
scopeChecklist.why: Spell out hourly rates and retainer requirements for records preparation, depositions, and testimony, which can be much more than regular session fees.
Putting the notice window and fee in the quote prevents surprises later.
Tell clients you do not bill insurance directly, that they may seek reimbursement themselves, and that coverage is not guaranteed.

scopeChecklist.item: Fee review and rate change policy
scopeChecklist.why: Explain when fees are reviewed and how much notice clients will get for increases.

pricingTips.title: Base fees on your market and your costs
pricingTips.body: Work backward from your target income, office or telehealth costs, insurance and licensing fees, and the number of sessions you can see in a week without burning out. Then compare with local therapists with similar credentials and specialties.

pricingTips.title: Price testing as a package
pricingTips.body: Psychological and neuropsychological evaluations take many hours of scoring and report writing. Quote a flat fee based on the total hours, and collect a deposit or half up front.

pricingTips.title: Be open about sliding scale availability
pricingTips.body: If you offer reduced fees, state the number of slots and how you decide, so clients understand the full fee is not the only option and you do not have to negotiate case by case.

pricingTips.title: Quote court and legal work separately
pricingTips.body: Forensic work is time-consuming and unpredictable. Use a higher hourly rate, require a retainer, and charge for preparation, travel, and cancellations of scheduled testimony.

faqs.question: Do therapists give estimates for treatment?
faqs.answer: Usually they share the session fee and expected frequency rather than a total. Because length of treatment depends on the client's needs, a total cost is an estimate at best. Testing and forensic work are more likely to receive formal written quotes.

faqs.question: How long should a quote for testing stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty to 60 days is common. Testing slots and report time are limited, so a deadline helps you plan your schedule and protects you if your fees change.

faqs.question: Should I require a deposit for evaluations?
faqs.answer: Many practices do, often 50 percent for testing and a retainer for court-related work. The deposit commits the client to a time slot and covers early hours of scoring and report preparation.

faqs.question: What should I say when a client asks about insurance?
faqs.answer: Be clear about whether you are in-network, out-of-network, or self-pay only. If out-of-network, offer a superbill, explain that reimbursement depends on their plan, and suggest they check their out-of-network benefits before starting.

tile-installer.intro: Tile installers set ceramic, porcelain, natural stone, glass, and mosaic tile on floors, walls, showers, backsplashes, and fireplaces. Most work solo or with a helper, billing homeowners, general contractors, and remodelers. Invoices usually cover labor by the square foot, surface prep, waterproofing, materials, and any extras like demolition or custom cuts.
tile-installer.pricingModel: Most tile installers price labor per square foot, with the rate depending on tile size, layout pattern, and surface. Large-format tile, small mosaics, herringbone patterns, and natural stone cost more per square foot than a straight lay of 12x12 tile. Prep work such as demolition, leveling, and underlayment is billed separately, either per square foot or hourly. Showers and tub surrounds are often a flat fee because of waterproofing, niches, benches, and the number of cuts. Small jobs like backsplashes are commonly flat-priced, and many installers set a minimum job charge to cover travel and setup. Materials such as thinset, grout, backer board, membrane, and trim are either billed at cost plus a markup (commonly 10-25%) or bundled into the price. Tile itself is usually bought by the homeowner or billed at cost with a markup if the installer sources it. Larger jobs often take a deposit and progress payments.

rates.service: Floor tile installation (standard sizes, straight lay)
Large-format tile (24x24 or larger) or diagonal/herringbone layout
Shower or tub surround (walls, waterproofing, standard tile)
Demolition and removal of old tile
Hourly labor for small repairs and odd jobs

items.description: Demolish and haul away existing vinyl flooring, master bathroom
Install cement backer board and seal seams
Install 12x24 porcelain floor tile, brick-offset pattern
Thinset, grout, caulk, and edge trim (materials)
Install wall tile at tub surround (3 walls), including waterproofing membrane
Schluter edge trim and niche installation

sampleInvoice.notes: Tile purchased by homeowner and not included. 50% deposit of $1,722.50 received on 3/4. Balance due on completion. Grout needs 72 hours to cure before heavy cleaning; sealer applied to grout lines. Workmanship warranted for 1 year.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job site address and rooms or areas tiled
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies which work the invoice covers, especially on multi-room jobs or for contractors billing several units.

invoiceChecklist.item: Square footage by area with tile size and pattern
invoiceChecklist.why: Labor rates change with tile size and layout, so listing them shows how the price was calculated.

invoiceChecklist.item: Prep work listed as separate line items
invoiceChecklist.why: Demolition, leveling, backer board, and waterproofing take real time and materials and are the first things clients question.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials itemized, with notes on who supplied the tile
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was billed versus what the client bought, and prevents disputes over missing or extra tile.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and added work with dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Subfloor repairs, out-of-square walls, and added niches are common mid-job and need a paper trail.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance details where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices for work above a set dollar amount. Check your local rules.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received, balance due, and cure or care instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the payment history clearly and records that you gave guidance on grout curing and sealing, which helps if a complaint comes up later.

tile-installer.paymentTerms: Tile installers typically ask for a deposit of 30-50% to cover materials and schedule the job, with the balance due on completion or within 7 days. Larger remodels may use progress payments tied to milestones such as demo and prep complete, tile set, and grouting done. General contractors often pay net 15 to net 30, so confirm terms before starting. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract in advance, though some states limit them. Payment is usually accepted by check, bank transfer, or card, and some installers add a processing fee for cards if allowed locally.

tips.title: Bill prep work as its own line
tips.body: Subfloor flattening, patching, and demolition often take as long as setting tile. Listing them separately makes the total easier to justify and protects your margin when conditions are worse than expected.

tips.title: Add a waste factor to quantities
tips.body: Tile is normally ordered with 10-15% extra for cuts, and more for diagonal or herringbone patterns. Bill labor on actual installed area, but note the overage in your materials line so the client understands the order.

tips.title: Set a minimum charge
tips.body: A 15 sq ft backsplash still requires loading the truck, setup, mixing, and cleanup. A minimum job fee of $300-600 keeps small jobs worth taking.

tips.title: Document site conditions with photos
tips.body: Photos of cracked subfloors, uneven walls, and existing water damage before you start support your change orders and protect you if the client later blames you for pre-existing problems.

tips.title: Invoice the final balance the day you finish
tips.body: Clients are most satisfied right after a clean finished job. Waiting weeks to bill usually means slower payment.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the square foot or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Square foot pricing is standard for floors, walls, and backsplashes because clients can compare bids. Hourly works better for repairs, regrouting small areas, and unpredictable jobs. Showers are often flat-priced because the work involves more than the tiled area alone.

faqs.question: Do I charge for tile I did not supply?
faqs.answer: No, you only bill for materials you bought. If the client supplies tile, bill labor and your own materials such as thinset, grout, and trim. Note on the invoice that tile was client-supplied.

faqs.question: How should I bill for extra work found after demolition?
faqs.answer: Stop, document it with photos, and give the client a written change order with the added cost before continuing. Then list the added work as a separate line item on the final invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge a markup on materials?
faqs.answer: Yes, most installers mark up materials 10-25% to cover pickup time, waste, and carrying costs. State the markup in your contract or estimate so it is not a surprise at invoicing.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on tile jobs?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some tax materials you sell to the client, some tax only the materials you buy as the contractor, and many do not tax labor on repairs or improvements. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Tile installers send estimates after a site visit, since price depends on the surface, layout, and condition of the substrate. Clients usually compare per-square-foot labor, what prep is included, and who supplies materials. A clear written quote helps you win the job and stops arguments over extras later.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact areas, square footage, and measurements
scopeChecklist.why: Sets the quantity the price is based on and gives a basis for adjusting if the real area differs.
Large-format, mosaic, stone, and herringbone layouts change labor time and the difficulty of cuts.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies tile and how much overage is included
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids disputes over running short or leftover boxes, and clarifies whether the tile cost is in your price.
Demolition, floor leveling, backer board, and waterproofing should be listed. Say that hidden subfloor damage will be quoted separately.
Membrane systems, niches, benches, curbs, and edge trim add cost and should be specified in showers.
Epoxy grout costs more and takes longer than cement grout, and clients often assume sealing is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, payment terms, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Locks in your pricing against material cost changes and sets expectations on start date and deposit.

pricingTips.title: Measure the site yourself
pricingTips.body: Do not rely on client measurements or plans. Measure each surface, check for flatness with a straightedge, and note out-of-square walls before quoting.

pricingTips.title: Price complexity, not just area
pricingTips.body: Many cuts, niches, inside corners, and small rooms take more time per square foot. Raise your rate for bathrooms with tub surrounds, borders, and pattern layouts.

pricingTips.title: Include an allowance for hidden problems
pricingTips.body: Either add a contingency line or state a unit price for subfloor repair, for example $X per sheet of replaced plywood. The client then knows the cost before it happens.

pricingTips.title: Offer options when it helps
pricingTips.body: Present alternatives such as standard versus epoxy grout or a basic versus upgraded waterproofing system. Clients can choose and see what they are paying for.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Free estimates are common for standard residential jobs. For large or complex projects, some installers charge a fee of $50-200 and credit it toward the job if the client hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a tile quote be valid?
faqs.answer: 30 days is typical. Tile and setting material prices change, so a shorter window is reasonable for natural stone or imported tile.

faqs.question: What if the final area differs from the estimate?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that labor is based on the measured square footage and will be adjusted at the quoted unit rate if the installed area changes. For flat-fee jobs, say what changes would trigger a revised price.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include the tile cost?
faqs.answer: Only if you are buying it. Many clients pick tile themselves, so separate labor from materials. If you supply it, list the tile cost, overage, and your markup clearly.

towing-service.intro: Towing services are run by owner-operators and small fleets that move disabled, wrecked, illegally parked, or repossessed vehicles. Invoices go to private customers, motor clubs, insurance companies, body shops, property managers, and sometimes police departments for rotation calls. Typical charges include the hookup, loaded mileage, winching, storage, and after-hours fees.
towing-service.pricingModel: Most towing work is priced as a base hookup fee plus a per-mile charge for loaded miles, meaning the miles the vehicle is on the truck. Private-pay jobs are often quoted as a flat price for a short local tow. Extras are billed on top: winching or recovery by the hour, dolly or flatbed use, labor for tire changes, jump starts, and lockouts, plus after-hours, holiday, and weather surcharges. Storage is charged per day after a free period, and gate or release fees apply when a vehicle is picked up from your lot. Heavy-duty tows and accident recovery are billed hourly per truck and per worker, often with a minimum. Motor club and police rotation work usually follows set rate sheets or local ordinances that cap what you can charge, so check what applies to you. Many cities and states regulate nonconsensual tows, such as private property impounds, with maximum rates.

rates.service: Jump start, lockout, or tire change

items.description: Flatbed tow hookup, 2019 Honda Accord, disabled on I-85 (includes first 5 miles)
Additional loaded miles to Ridgeway Auto Repair (total 23 miles)
Winching vehicle from roadside ditch
After-hours surcharge (call received 11:40 PM)
Storage at yard, 1 day after free 24-hour period

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon vehicle release or within 14 days for billed accounts. Vehicle pickup/drop-off: Unit 7, call received 11:40 PM, arrived 12:15 AM. Storage accrues daily after 24 hours. We accept cash, card, and check. Late balances over 30 days incur a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, color, VIN, and plate
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies exactly which vehicle you towed and protects you in damage or ownership disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off addresses with odometer or loaded mileage
invoiceChecklist.why: Supports the per-mile charge and settles any argument about distance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Call, arrival, hookup, and drop-off times
invoiceChecklist.why: Justifies hourly winching, wait time, and after-hours surcharges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Truck or driver ID and your USDOT or state towing license number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require operator identification, and insurers and fleets often ask for it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons: winching, dolly, labor, fuel, gate fee, storage dates
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing keeps customers and insurers from disputing a lump sum.

invoiceChecklist.item: Authorization source and name (owner, police, motor club, property manager) with PO or claim number
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows who agreed to the tow and lets insurers and motor clubs match the invoice to their file.

invoiceChecklist.item: Storage start date, daily rate, and release terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Storage balances grow over time and are commonly challenged, so dates and rates must be clear.

towing-service.paymentTerms: Private-pay customers are normally expected to pay at the time of service or at vehicle release, and many operators will not release a stored vehicle until the balance is paid. Roadside customers often pay by card on a mobile reader. Motor clubs, fleets, body shops, and insurers are billed on net 15 to net 30 terms, and motor clubs may pay through their own dispatch systems on a set schedule. Written late fees, often 1.5% per month, should be listed on the invoice. Cash discounts are common but should be applied consistently. Check local rules on lien sales, notice requirements, and storage fee limits before holding a vehicle for nonpayment.

tips.title: Quote the total before you hook up
tips.body: Give private customers the hookup, mileage, and any known add-ons before you start. Stranded drivers remember surprises, and chargebacks often follow. Get a signature or recorded verbal approval.

tips.title: Photograph the vehicle at pickup and drop-off
tips.body: Timestamped photos of damage, condition, and location protect you against claims and support winching or recovery charges when an insurer reviews the bill.

tips.title: Keep separate rate sheets for each account type
tips.body: Private pay, motor club, police rotation, and commercial accounts often have different rates and caps. Applying the wrong sheet is a common source of underbilling and rejected claims.

tips.title: Send storage notices on time
tips.body: Many states require you to notify the owner and lienholder within a set period before charging full storage or selling a vehicle. Track the days and keep copies of notices so storage charges hold up.

tips.title: Bill insurance jobs right away
tips.body: Insurers often pay only what they approve. Include the claim number, adjuster name, photos, and tow ticket so the claim does not stall for lack of documents.

faqs.question: What should a towing invoice include?
faqs.answer: Include your business name and license information, the customer, vehicle details with VIN and plate, pickup and drop-off locations, mileage, time stamps, an itemized list of charges, authorization details, and payment terms. Add storage dates and rates if the vehicle was held.

faqs.question: Can I charge for storage if the customer is slow to pick up the car?
faqs.answer: In most places yes, but states and cities often set maximum daily rates, free periods, and notice rules. Put your daily rate and free period on the invoice and on any signage at your lot, and check your local rules.

faqs.question: Do I charge for mileage from my garage or only loaded miles?
faqs.answer: Most private tows charge only loaded miles, plus a hookup fee that covers getting to the scene. Some operators charge deadhead miles for long-distance calls or remote areas. Whichever you use, state it up front.

faqs.question: How do I handle a customer who disputes the bill after the tow?
faqs.answer: Send the itemized invoice with time stamps, photos, and the authorization record. A clear tow ticket usually resolves it. For unpaid balances, follow your state's lien rules rather than withholding or selling a vehicle without proper notice.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on towing?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax towing services, some do not, and parts or materials may be taxed separately. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Towing quotes are usually given by phone or text at the time of the call, often within minutes, though pre-arranged work such as relocating several vehicles, equipment transport, or recovery from a difficult spot may get a written quote. Customers compare the total price, estimated arrival time, and whether you take cards or insurance.

scopeChecklist.item: Pickup and drop-off locations with estimated loaded miles
scopeChecklist.why: Mileage drives the price, and a quote based on a vague destination is easy to dispute.

scopeChecklist.item: Vehicle type, weight class, and drivetrain
scopeChecklist.why: AWD, lowered, or oversized vehicles may need a flatbed or dollies, and heavy-duty trucks cost more.
A car in a ditch, parking garage, or locked in with no keys may need winching or extra labor.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included in the base price and what is extra
scopeChecklist.why: Tolls, winching, waiting time, and after-hours fees should be listed so the final bill matches the quote.
Customers choose between providers on arrival time, and delays can lead to canceled calls.
Covers your cost if the truck is dispatched and the customer cancels or the vehicle is already gone.

scopeChecklist.item: Payment method and when payment is due
scopeChecklist.why: Setting this before the tow avoids standoffs at the drop-off location.

pricingTips.title: Use a flat price for short local tows
pricingTips.body: Customers want a single number. Quote a flat fee covering the hookup and a set number of miles, then add per-mile pricing beyond that.

pricingTips.title: List add-ons at hourly or per-item rates
pricingTips.body: If recovery or winching may be needed, quote the hourly rate and a minimum rather than guessing the total. Confirm the extra charge before starting.

pricingTips.title: Adjust for time of day and conditions
pricingTips.body: Nights, holidays, snow, and long wait times raise your costs. Explain the surcharge when you quote so it does not look like an add-on later.

pricingTips.title: Put big-job quotes in writing
pricingTips.body: For multi-vehicle moves, heavy-duty recovery, or long-distance tows, send a written quote with an expiration date and a deposit request.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote over the phone?
faqs.answer: Yes for standard tows. Ask for the pickup, destination, and vehicle type, then give a price that covers the hookup and miles. Follow with a text or email if possible, so the customer has it in writing.

faqs.question: Can the final bill be higher than the quote?
faqs.answer: Only if the job changed, such as a difficult recovery, extra miles, or longer wait times, and the customer agreed to it. If you quote a flat price, honor it unless conditions differ materially.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed authorization before towing?
faqs.answer: For private-pay and consent tows, getting a signature or recorded approval is a smart practice. Non-consent tows, such as private property impounds, are regulated in many areas and may have specific signage, notice, and rate requirements.

faqs.question: Should I charge a fee if the customer cancels after I'm dispatched?
faqs.answer: Many operators charge a partial or dry-run fee because the truck, driver, and fuel are committed. Mention it when quoting and keep it modest and consistent.

translation-service.intro: Translation services are run by freelance translators, interpreters, and small agencies who convert written or spoken content between languages for businesses, law firms, medical providers, schools, and individuals. Typical invoices cover document translation priced per word, certified translations for immigration or court use, proofreading and editing, and interpreting by the hour or half day.
translation-service.pricingModel: Written translation is usually priced per source word, with rates set by language pair, subject matter, and turnaround. Common pairs like Spanish to English cost less than rarer ones like Japanese or Finnish, and technical fields such as legal, medical, and patent work cost more than general content. Many translators set a minimum fee per project so small jobs are worth taking. Certified translations for USCIS, courts, or schools are often charged per page for standard documents like birth certificates and diplomas, with a flat fee that includes the certification statement. Editing and proofreading are billed per word at a lower rate or per hour. Interpreting is billed per hour with a two-hour minimum, or as a half-day or full-day rate, plus travel time. Rush work commonly carries a surcharge of 25 to 100 percent. Desktop publishing, subtitling, and formatting are billed separately per page, per hour, or per minute of media. Agencies and direct clients may offer a discount for repetitions found with translation memory software, so some translators bill repeated segments at a reduced percentage.

rates.service: Certified translation of a standard document (birth certificate, diploma)

items.description: Spanish to English translation of commercial lease agreement (source word count 4,200)
Second-linguist proofreading of translated lease
Rush turnaround surcharge (delivery in 3 business days), 25% of translation fee
Certified translation statement with signature and notarization
Reformatting to match original layout (tables and signature blocks)

sampleInvoice.notes: Word count based on source file received March 3. Payment due within 15 days of delivery. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Final files are released as signed PDF; the certification covers the translation only and does not verify the authenticity of the original document.

invoiceChecklist.item: Language pair and direction
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing Spanish to English versus English to Spanish makes the job clear and supports the rate, since each direction can be priced differently.

invoiceChecklist.item: Source word count and how it was counted
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-word billing is the most common dispute. State whether you counted the source or target text and which tool or file version you used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Document names or project reference and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and law firms handle many files at once. Matching the invoice to a file name or PO number gets it paid faster.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or job ID
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and corporate accounts often will not process an invoice without one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification or notarization line items
invoiceChecklist.why: These are separate services with their own cost. Itemizing them avoids confusion when a client needs only some of the documents certified.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush, formatting, and minimum-fee charges listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing surcharges as their own lines explains the total and keeps the base rate consistent across projects.

invoiceChecklist.item: Interpreting date, start and end times, location, and travel time
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly minimums, overtime, and travel billing all depend on exact times, and clients often ask for proof.

translation-service.paymentTerms: Individual and small business clients are often asked for a deposit of 25 to 50 percent on large projects, with the balance due on delivery. Many freelancers require full payment up front for certified translations for individuals, since the work is small and the client may disappear after delivery. Agencies typically pay on net 30 to net 60 terms, sometimes counted from the end of the month, so confirm terms before accepting the job. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in writing beforehand. Payment is accepted by bank transfer, ACH, card, check, or online payment platforms. Translators working with overseas clients should state the currency and who pays transfer fees.

tips.title: Set a minimum fee and state it
tips.body: A 50-word document still requires setup, research, and a certification statement. A stated minimum protects you from small jobs that cost more time than they pay.

tips.title: Agree on the word count method before starting
tips.body: Say whether you charge on source or target words and how you handle numbers, headers, and text in images. Sending the count with the quote prevents later disagreement.

tips.title: Charge for rush work and weekend delivery
tips.body: Standard turnaround is roughly 1,500 to 2,500 words per day for one translator. Anything faster should carry a surcharge that is written into the quote.

tips.title: Bill revisions according to who caused them
tips.body: Correcting your own errors is free. Changes caused by an updated source file or a client's preferred terminology should be billed as a new word count or hourly editing.

tips.title: Keep the signed certification and invoice together
tips.body: Clients often need a receipt for immigration or school applications. Keep records so you can reissue a copy of the certification and invoice later.

faqs.question: Should I charge per source word or per target word?
faqs.answer: Most US translators charge per source word because it is known before work starts and does not change with the language. Some charge per target word, particularly in certain markets. Whichever you use, put it in the quote and on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on translation services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax certain professional or information services, and many do not tax translation. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional before adding or leaving out tax.

faqs.question: How do I invoice an agency that pays on net 60?
faqs.answer: Invoice as soon as the work is delivered, include the agency's PO number, and note the agreed terms on the invoice. Track the due date and follow up a few days before. If you cannot wait 60 days, negotiate shorter terms before accepting work.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a certified translation if the client only needs a signed statement?
faqs.answer: Yes. A certification statement is a distinct service and many translators charge a flat fee for it, either included in the per-page price or listed separately. Notarization, if requested, is usually an added charge.

faqs.question: How should I bill for interpreting that runs over the scheduled time?
faqs.answer: Spell out your overtime policy in the agreement. Many interpreters bill in 15 or 30 minute increments after the booked block, and charge a cancellation fee if the client cancels with less than 24 to 48 hours notice.

estimate.intro: Translation clients usually ask for a quote after sending a file or describing the project, and they compare per-word rates, turnaround, and whether certification is included. A written quote sets the word count, deadline, and deliverables before you begin, which matters most for large or technical documents.

scopeChecklist.item: Language pair, direction, and regional variant
scopeChecklist.why: Spanish for Mexico differs from Spanish for Spain, and Portuguese varies similarly. Naming the variant sets expectations for vocabulary and style.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated word count and pricing basis
scopeChecklist.why: Clients can see how the total was calculated. Note that the final price will be adjusted if the final file differs from the sample.

scopeChecklist.item: File format of the source and the deliverable
scopeChecklist.why: Scanned PDFs, images, and layouts with tables take extra time. State whether you will return an editable file or a PDF and whether formatting is included.
A clear delivery date, and the extra cost for earlier delivery, prevents last-minute pressure.
Clients often assume these are included. State what you provide and what the client must arrange with a notary or state office.
If the client has a preferred glossary or style guide, say that you will follow it and that conflicts with it may cost extra time.
Define how many rounds of client feedback are included and how long the quoted price is valid.

pricingTips.title: Quote from the actual file
pricingTips.body: Ask for the document, not a description. Run a word count and check for scanned pages, tables, or specialist terms before giving a number.

pricingTips.title: Show the rate and the total
pricingTips.body: List the per-word rate, estimated words, and any fees as separate lines. Clients comparing several translators can see where your price comes from.

pricingTips.title: Offer a lower rate for repeated text
pricingTips.body: If a file contains many repeated sentences, a reduced rate for repetitions is common and can make your quote more competitive without cutting your base rate.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for research-heavy material
pricingTips.body: Patents, clinical trials, and legal contracts need extra research. Price those at the higher end of your range rather than at your general rate.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote before seeing the document?
faqs.answer: You can give a range, but a firm price needs the file. Without it, quote a per-word rate and a minimum, and confirm the total once you have the word count.

faqs.question: What if the final word count differs from the estimate?
faqs.answer: Include a line saying the final invoice is based on the actual word count of the delivered source file. Most clients accept this when it is stated up front, and you can note a threshold such as 5 percent before a revised quote is sent.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a quote on a large project?
faqs.answer: Most translators quote for free on typical documents. For very large or complex projects that need a sample translation or detailed analysis, some charge a small fee that is credited to the project if it goes ahead.

faqs.question: How long should a translation quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common. Since your availability changes, a quote expiration date lets you reprice or decline if the client waits too long to confirm.

translator.intro: Translators convert written content from one language into another for businesses, law firms, medical providers, publishers, agencies, and private individuals. Invoices typically cover document translation billed by word, certified translations for immigration or court use, proofreading and editing of existing translations, and rush or formatting work. Many translators work solo, and some also take on agency work where the agency sets the rate and payment terms.
translator.pricingModel: Most translation is priced per source word, with rates varying by language pair, subject matter, and turnaround. Common languages like Spanish to English sit at the lower end, while rarer pairs and technical fields such as legal, medical, patent, and financial text cost more. Short, personal documents like birth certificates, marriage certificates, and diplomas are often billed as a flat fee per page or per document, which usually includes a signed certification statement. Minimum charges are standard, since even a 100-word job takes time to set up, research, and deliver. Editing and proofreading are billed per word at a lower rate, or per hour. Rush work (under 24 to 48 hours) commonly adds 25 to 100 percent. Extras such as desktop publishing, working with PDFs or scanned images, translation memory discounts for repeated text, notarization, and shipping of hard copies are listed as separate lines. Agencies often pay lower rates but supply steady volume, and many pay on net 30 to net 60 terms.

rates.service: General document translation (e.g. Spanish to English)
Certified translation of a short civil document (birth certificate, diploma)
Proofreading or editing of an existing translation

items.description: Translation of commercial lease agreement, Spanish to English (source word count 4,200)
Certified translation of two birth certificates with signed certification statement
Rush turnaround surcharge on lease translation (delivered in 48 hours, 25%)
Proofreading of client-supplied English glossary
Notary acknowledgment and priority mail of hard copies

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Word count is based on the source document as received on the project start date. Revisions requested within 14 days for errors in translation are free of charge; changes to the source text are billed at the standard word rate. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Language pair and direction
invoiceChecklist.why: Spanish to English and English to Spanish can be priced differently, and it removes any doubt about what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Source word count and how it was counted
invoiceChecklist.why: Most disputes are about word count. State whether you counted the source or target text and which tool or method you used.

invoiceChecklist.item: Document names, page counts, and project or PO number
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and corporate clients often need a PO or job number to match your invoice to their records and release payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery date and any rush surcharge
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the agreed deadline was met and justifies any premium over the standard rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Certification or notarization line items
invoiceChecklist.why: Immigration, court, and school submissions often require a signed certificate of accuracy, and the extra cost should be visible and separate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Repetitions, fuzzy matches, or discounts applied
invoiceChecklist.why: If you give a discount for repeated text from a translation memory, showing it explains why the total differs from the raw word count.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, tax ID or W-9 status, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients paying over a set threshold need your taxpayer information to issue a 1099, and clear payment details speed things up.

translator.paymentTerms: Individual clients and small jobs, especially certified translations for immigration, are usually paid in full upfront or on delivery, since the translator holds the finished files. For larger projects, a 30 to 50 percent deposit is common, with the balance due on delivery. Direct business clients typically get net 15 or net 30, while agencies often pay net 30 to net 60, so check their terms before accepting. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Accepted methods usually include bank transfer, ACH, card, and online payment platforms; international clients may need wire transfer or a currency-conversion option, so state the invoice currency clearly.

tips.title: Agree on word count method in writing
tips.body: Say up front whether you charge by source or target word and whether headers, footers, numbers, and text in images are included. This single line prevents most invoice disputes.

tips.title: Set a minimum fee
tips.body: A 50-word email still takes time for setup, research, and delivery. A minimum charge keeps small jobs from costing you more than they earn.

tips.title: Hold final files until deposit or payment for new clients
tips.body: With a new individual client, deliver a watermarked or locked preview, or release the signed certified copy only after payment. This protects you without needing to chase.

tips.title: Charge separately for formatting and scanned documents
tips.body: Retyping a scanned PDF, rebuilding tables, or matching a complex layout takes real time. Bill it as hourly or per-page desktop publishing rather than absorbing it in the word rate.

tips.title: Track agency payment terms and work volume
tips.body: Agencies may pay 45 or 60 days after invoice. Note this on your calendar, follow up politely at 30 days past due, and consider whether the rate and terms justify the work.

faqs.question: Should I charge by source word or target word?
faqs.answer: Source word count is more common in the US because it is known before you start and does not depend on how the translation turns out. Some translators charge by target word, particularly when the language pair expands or shrinks a lot. Whichever you pick, state it in the quote and on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a certified translation separately?
