estimate.intro: Tutors usually send a quote when a parent or student asks about a multi-week plan, a test-prep program, or a flat-fee service like essay coaching. Clients typically compare your rate and total cost against other tutors, learning centers, and online platforms. A clear written estimate shows how many sessions you recommend and what the total will be.

scopeChecklist.why: Defining the target, such as raising a math grade or reaching a 1400 SAT, sets expectations and shows what you are committing to.
Clients need to know how many weeks the plan covers and how long each session lasts to compare cost accurately.
Online, at your home, or at the student's home affects price and logistics, including any travel fees.

scopeChecklist.item: What is included and not included
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify whether practice tests, grading, parent updates, and between-session email help are covered.
List books, printed tests, or software costs and who pays for them so there are no surprises.
Setting this up front prevents arguments after the first missed session.
Rates change and your schedule fills up, so state how long the quote holds and when the first session can begin.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range of session counts
pricingTips.body: Offer a plan of 8, 12, or 16 sessions with the total price for each. Parents often pick the middle option, and it avoids committing you to an open-ended arrangement.

pricingTips.title: Be honest about what results you can promise
pricingTips.body: Do not guarantee a specific grade or score. Describe the plan and expected effort instead, which protects you from refund disputes.

pricingTips.title: Offer a short trial session
pricingTips.body: A single paid or discounted first session helps you assess the student's needs before quoting a longer plan, and makes the estimate more accurate.

pricingTips.title: Price by value for specialized work
pricingTips.body: AP sciences, MCAT prep, and college essays take more skill and preparation. Charge at the higher end of local ranges if you have credentials or a track record.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before the first session?
faqs.answer: For a single hourly rate, a message with your rate and policies is enough. For a multi-week plan or flat-fee service, send a written quote so the parent can approve the scope and total.

faqs.question: Can I change my rate after giving a quote?
faqs.answer: Honor the quote for the stated period and number of sessions. If the student needs more sessions than planned, send an updated estimate and get agreement before continuing.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit for a tutoring package?
faqs.answer: Many tutors collect full payment for a package up front, or at least the first month. It secures the time slot and reduces unpaid sessions.

faqs.question: How detailed should a test-prep quote be?
faqs.answer: List the number of sessions, practice tests included, materials cost, and total price. Parents comparing you with a prep course want to see exactly what they get for the money.

tv-mounting.intro: TV mounting businesses are usually solo installers or small crews who hang televisions on drywall, brick, stone, and tile, and run cables and power for a clean finish. Invoices typically cover the mounting labor, the wall mount hardware, and add-ons like in-wall wire concealment, soundbar installation, and device setup.
tv-mounting.pricingModel: Most TV mounting work is priced as a flat fee per TV, because the job is predictable and customers like to know the total up front. The base price usually depends on TV size and mount type, with add-ons priced separately: in-wall cable concealment, outlet installation, masonry or brick surfaces, fireplace installs, soundbar mounting, and hiding components in a cabinet. Wall mounts are either supplied by the customer or sold by the installer with a markup, often 20 to 50 percent over cost. Some installers set a minimum service call fee to cover travel and small jobs, and charge hourly for custom work like multi-TV setups, commercial installs, or home theater wiring. Large TVs (75 inches and up) often carry a surcharge because they need two people.

rates.service: Standard TV mounting, up to 55 inches (customer supplies mount)
Large TV mounting, 56 to 75 inches (two-person install)
Extra-large TV mounting, 76 inches and up
In-wall cable concealment with power and cable pass-through kit
Mounting over brick, stone, or concrete
Wall mount hardware (tilt, full-motion, or fixed)
Custom or multi-device work (home theater wiring, outdoor TVs)

items.description: Mount 65-inch TV on drywall, full-motion mount, stud-mounted and leveled
Full-motion wall mount, heavy-duty (installer supplied)
In-wall cable concealment kit with power and HDMI pass-through
Soundbar mounting below TV
Device connection and input setup (cable box, streaming device, soundbar)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due upon completion of installation. Accepted: card, cash, check, or Zelle. Installation is warrantied for 1 year against mount failure when installed per manufacturer specifications. TV and equipment are the customer's responsibility; please test all connections before the installer leaves.

invoiceChecklist.item: TV size and mount type for each installation
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing depends on screen size and mount style, and listing them shows exactly what was installed if the mount is ever questioned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wall surface type (drywall, brick, plaster, tile)
invoiceChecklist.why: Masonry and tile take more time and specialized bits, so the surcharge needs an explanation on the bill.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mount hardware as a separate line item with brand and model
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows materials versus labor, supports your markup, and helps with warranty claims on the mount itself.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on services itemized individually
invoiceChecklist.why: Cable concealment, outlets, soundbars, and device setup are each priced separately and customers often forget they approved them.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installation address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives a record of where the mount was installed and starts the warranty period.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or insurance number where required
invoiceChecklist.why: Some states and cities require a license for electrical work such as installing an in-wall outlet, and clients or property managers often ask for proof of insurance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and load or weight limit disclaimer
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies that you are responsible for the installation but not for the TV, and sets expectations if the customer later changes the TV.

tv-mounting.paymentTerms: Most TV mounting jobs are paid on the day of installation, once the customer has seen the TV mounted and working, since the job is quick and the invoice is small. Card, cash, and peer-to-peer apps are the most common methods, and many installers send the invoice by text or email right as they finish. For larger jobs such as multi-room installs, home theaters, or commercial work, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent is common, along with payment of the balance on completion. Property managers, builders, and businesses may pay on net 15 or net 30 terms, in which case a late fee of 1 to 1.5 percent per month is typical if stated in writing beforehand. Charge a cancellation or trip fee if the installer shows up and the job cannot proceed.

tips.title: Quote a flat price by TV size
tips.body: Customers want one number. Publish base prices by TV size range and list add-ons separately so the total is easy to calculate before you arrive.

tips.title: Check the wall before quoting
tips.body: Ask for the wall material, whether it is a fireplace, and where outlets are. A photo of the wall saves a trip and prevents surprises like metal studs, brick, or plaster that change the price.

tips.title: Mark up the hardware
tips.body: If you supply the mount, add a reasonable markup. You are paying for the trip to buy or stock it, the quality control, and the liability if it fails.

tips.title: Be clear about electrical work
tips.body: Moving or adding an outlet may require a licensed electrician where you work. Know your local rules, and list in-wall power kits as a code-compliant option, or refer that work out.

tips.title: Charge for return trips caused by the customer
tips.body: If the customer ordered the wrong mount, the TV is not on site, or the wall is not as described, a trip fee or reschedule fee should be on the invoice and stated in advance.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or per TV?
faqs.answer: Most installers charge per TV with add-ons, because it is easier for customers to compare and the job time is predictable. Use hourly rates for custom work, troubleshooting, or jobs where the scope is unclear.

faqs.question: How much should I mark up wall mounts?
faqs.answer: A markup of 20 to 50 percent over your cost is common. Itemize the mount separately from labor so the customer can see both the hardware and the service.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on TV mounting?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax labor, some tax only the materials you sell, and some tax neither. Check with your state revenue department or a local accountant, and show tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for a trip if the customer cancels at the door?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you have told them in advance. Put a minimum service or trip fee in your quote or booking confirmation, and then invoice it if the job cannot go ahead.

faqs.question: What should I do if a customer wants a discount for mounting multiple TVs?
faqs.answer: Many installers give a modest reduction for the second and later TVs at the same address since there is only one trip and setup. Show the discount as a line item so it is clear and does not reduce the rate for future work.

estimate.intro: TV mounting estimates are usually sent after a phone call, text, or photos of the wall and TV, and often before the first visit. Customers compare the flat price for the install, whether the mount is included, and what add-ons like cable concealment cost. Many accept on the spot, so the quote should be clear and easy to approve.

scopeChecklist.item: TV size, brand, and weight for each TV
scopeChecklist.why: Determines the mount rating required and whether two installers are needed, which affects price.

scopeChecklist.item: Wall type and condition (drywall, brick, plaster, tile, fireplace)
scopeChecklist.why: Different surfaces need different anchors and tools, and some may be unsuitable for mounting at all.

scopeChecklist.item: Who supplies the mount and the model
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents disputes when a customer-supplied mount is wrong for the TV or wall, or when your supplied mount is a different price than they expected.
Surface raceways, in-wall pass-through kits, and fully concealed wiring are very different jobs and prices.
State whether device setup, soundbar installation, outlet work, patching, and painting are included so there are no surprises.

scopeChecklist.item: Mounting height and location agreed in advance
scopeChecklist.why: Avoids rework if the customer expected a different position, and lets you spot stud or wiring problems before drilling.

scopeChecklist.item: Trip fee, cancellation terms, and quote expiry date
scopeChecklist.why: Protects your time if the job cannot proceed and keeps pricing from being held indefinitely.

pricingTips.title: Use tiered base pricing
pricingTips.body: Price by TV size range, such as up to 55, 56 to 75, and 76 and up. It is easy for customers to understand and for you to quote quickly by text.

pricingTips.title: List add-ons as options
pricingTips.body: Show in-wall concealment, soundbar mounting, and device setup as optional lines. Customers can select what they want, and the upsell is visible without pressure.

pricingTips.title: Allow for the unexpected
pricingTips.body: Include a line stating that hidden obstacles such as metal studs, fire blocking, or insulation may raise the price. Tell the customer you will confirm any change before proceeding.

pricingTips.title: Offer a good, better, best mount choice
pricingTips.body: Give a fixed, tilt, and full-motion option with prices. Customers tend to choose the middle option, and you avoid the back-and-forth over hardware.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most installers give free quotes based on photos or a phone call. If an on-site visit is required for a complex job such as a multi-room installation, a fee that is credited to the job if accepted is reasonable.

faqs.question: How firm should my quote be?
faqs.answer: A flat quote should hold if the job matches the description. State what could change it, such as a different wall type, a larger TV, or extra devices, and require written or text approval of changes.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for small jobs, but hardware prices and your schedule can change, so many installers use 14 days. Put the expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: Do I need a deposit on an estimate?
faqs.answer: Not usually for a single TV. For larger projects, or when you must buy special mounts or materials, ask for a deposit of 25 to 50 percent to secure the date and cover your costs.

ui-design.intro: UI designers are freelancers and small studio owners who design the visual interface of websites, mobile apps, and software products. They invoice startups, agencies, and small businesses for work such as screen design, design systems, prototypes, and developer handoff files.
ui-design.pricingModel: Most UI designers price in one of three ways: hourly, per project, or on a monthly retainer. Hourly billing works for open-ended or uncertain work and for small fixes after launch. Fixed project fees are common for defined deliverables, such as a 10-screen mobile app design or a marketing site redesign, and are usually split into milestones (for example 50% upfront, 25% at first-round designs, 25% at handoff). Retainers suit ongoing product teams that need a set number of hours or a steady flow of design tickets each month. Design systems and component libraries are often quoted separately from screen design because they take longer than clients expect. Extra revision rounds, new screens added mid-project, and stock asset or font licenses are usually billed as add-ons. Rates scale with experience, portfolio, and whether the client is a startup or an established company.

rates.service: Mobile app UI design (up to 10 screens)
Website or landing page UI design

items.description: Mobile app UI design, milestone 2 of 3: high-fidelity screens (12 screens, iOS)
Component library and style guide (colors, type, buttons, form elements)
Clickable prototype for user testing
Additional revision round requested after approval (onboarding flow)
Icon pack license (extended commercial use), billed at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Remaining balance of $2,400 is due at final handoff. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Final Figma files are transferred upon payment of the full balance. Accepted payment: ACH, credit card, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope and payment schedule, so the client's accounting team can match it to the contract or proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed (screens, flows, components)
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing counts such as '12 screens' or 'onboarding flow' shows exactly what the payment covers and heads off disputes about what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used and extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget how many rounds were included. Showing used versus included justifies any added charges.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for hourly or out-of-scope work
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing time by task, such as prototyping or handoff fixes, makes hourly charges easy to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs (fonts, icon sets, stock photos, plugins)
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through licenses should be listed separately at cost so they are not mistaken for design fees.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and file transfer terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States when the client owns the final files. Many designers retain rights until the invoice is paid in full.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often will not process an invoice without one.

ui-design.paymentTerms: UI designers commonly collect a deposit of 25-50% before starting, especially on fixed-fee projects and with new clients. The rest is tied to milestones, such as approval of wireframes, high-fidelity screens, and final handoff. Net 15 and Net 30 are the usual terms, with agencies and larger companies often asking for Net 30 or Net 45. Many designers add a late fee of around 1-1.5% per month, written into the contract or proposal. Retainers are generally invoiced at the start of the month. Payment methods include ACH transfer, credit card, and check; international clients may use wire transfer or other platforms that support multiple currencies.

tips.title: Tie final files to final payment
tips.body: Hold the editable source files, such as the Figma or Sketch file, until the last invoice is paid. Share view-only links or exported images during the project. This protects you without needing to chase unpaid balances.

tips.title: Define a revision limit in the proposal
tips.body: Two or three rounds of revisions per milestone is common. Name the number on the proposal and on invoices so extra rounds are billed as expected work, not as a surprise.

tips.title: Bill scope changes as they happen
tips.body: When a client adds screens or a new feature mid-project, send a short change order and invoice it at the next milestone. Waiting until the end makes the charge harder to defend.

tips.title: Separate design system work from screen work
tips.body: Components, variants, and documentation take real time. Give them their own line item so clients see the value and so you are paid for it even if the project ends early.

tips.title: Invoice retainers in advance
tips.body: Bill the retainer at the start of the month, not the end. State what happens to unused hours, whether they roll over for one month or expire.

faqs.question: Should a UI designer charge hourly or per project?
faqs.answer: Either works. Per-project pricing suits defined deliverables and rewards efficiency, while hourly suits unclear scope, ongoing maintenance, and small fixes. Many designers quote a fixed fee for the main project and bill hourly for anything outside it.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Between 25% and 50% is typical for new clients. For larger projects, a milestone schedule (such as 40% upfront, 30% at mid-point, 30% at handoff) keeps cash flowing and limits your exposure.

faqs.question: Do I charge for stock assets, fonts, or icons?
faqs.answer: If you buy a license specifically for the client's project, bill it at cost as a separate line item. If the client already has licenses or will buy their own, note that in the proposal so it is clear who is responsible.

faqs.question: When does the client own the design files?
faqs.answer: This depends on your contract. Many designers transfer ownership and usage rights once the final invoice is paid. Put this in writing in your proposal and mention it on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for work if the client cancels midway?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Deposits are often non-refundable, and you can invoice for completed milestones or hours worked to date. Without a written agreement it is harder to collect, so include a kill fee or cancellation clause in your proposal.

estimate.intro: UI designers send an estimate or proposal before a project begins, usually after a discovery call or after reviewing a brief. Clients often compare several designers by price, but also by number of screens, revision rounds, and what is included at handoff, so the details of scope matter as much as the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and type of screens or pages
scopeChecklist.why: Screen count is the biggest driver of price. Stating '10 mobile screens' or '5 web pages' sets a clear boundary for what is covered.
Designing for iOS, Android, and responsive web is separate work. List which breakpoints and platforms are included.
Wireframes, high-fidelity mockups, clickable prototypes, and a design system are different deliverables with different costs. Name each one.
Setting a number, such as two rounds per milestone, prevents endless feedback cycles and gives you a basis for charging more.
Delays in content, branding assets, or feedback stall projects. State what you need and when, and note that delays may shift the schedule.
Specify whether you provide Figma files, exported assets, specs, or a walkthrough call, and how much developer Q&A is included after handoff.
Fonts, icons, stock imagery, and plugins may be extra. State who pays and who holds the license.

pricingTips.title: Estimate by screens and flows, then add buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the project into flows such as onboarding, checkout, and settings. Estimate hours per flow, add 15-20% for feedback and revisions, and convert to a fixed fee if the scope is clear.

pricingTips.title: Price the design system separately
pricingTips.body: Clients often assume a design system comes with the screens. List it as its own line or as an optional add-on so you are paid for the extra component and documentation work.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: A basic package with core screens, a standard package with a prototype, and a full package with a design system give clients a choice and often lead them to the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Rates and availability change. A 30-day validity window keeps you from being held to old pricing, especially if the client delays a start.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates or proposals?
faqs.answer: Short quotes based on a brief are normally free. If a client wants detailed research, a discovery workshop, or a full scoping document, many designers charge a paid discovery phase, which can be credited toward the project if they proceed.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who wants a fixed price with unclear requirements?
faqs.answer: Propose a paid discovery or wireframing phase first, then quote the rest once scope is clearer. Alternatively, quote a fixed fee for a defined set of screens and bill hourly for anything beyond that.

faqs.question: What happens if the project grows beyond the estimate?
faqs.answer: Your estimate should state that changes to scope are billed separately. When something new comes up, send a written change order with the added cost and timeline before starting that work.

faqs.question: Should the estimate include development?
faqs.answer: Only if you actually do development. Otherwise, state clearly that the quote covers design and handoff only, and that coding and implementation are outside the scope.

ui-ux-auditor.intro: UI/UX auditors review websites, apps, and software products and report on usability problems, accessibility gaps, and design inconsistencies. Clients are usually product teams, startups, agencies, and ecommerce owners who want a prioritized list of fixes before a redesign, launch, or conversion push. Invoices typically cover the audit itself, any stakeholder presentation, and follow-up work such as retesting or design guidance.
ui-ux-auditor.pricingModel: Most auditors price audits as a flat fee based on scope: number of screens or flows, platforms (web, iOS, Android), and depth of method (heuristic review only versus review plus analytics and user testing). Hourly rates are common for ad hoc consulting, workshops, and retainers, and are also used internally to build the flat fee. Accessibility audits against WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 are often priced separately per page template or per flow, since manual testing with screen readers takes extra time. Usability testing adds pass-through costs such as participant recruiting and incentives, which are usually billed at cost or with a small markup. Follow-up support, like a fix-review pass or a retainer for ongoing design critique, is billed hourly or as a monthly block of hours.

rates.service: Heuristic UX review (small site or app, up to 10 screens)
Full UX audit with analytics review and prioritized roadmap
WCAG accessibility audit (manual plus automated testing)
Ad hoc UX consulting and design critique

items.description: UX audit: checkout and account flows (web, 14 screens), heuristic review with prioritized findings report
Analytics and session recording review (funnel drop-off analysis)
WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility testing, page templates (home, product, cart, checkout)
Findings presentation to product and engineering team (90 min, includes prep)
Participant incentives for 5 usability sessions (passed through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Deposit of 50% ($3,737.50) was received on contract signing; balance due shown on the invoice total. Report delivered as PDF with annotated screenshots. One round of clarification questions is included for 30 days after delivery; additional retesting billed at $125/hour.

invoiceChecklist.item: Audit scope with screens, flows, and platforms covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often ask later why a page was not reviewed. Listing what was in scope ties the fee to the work delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Method and standards used (heuristic framework, WCAG version and level)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what the fee covered and helps clients who need documentation for compliance or procurement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables and delivery date
invoiceChecklist.why: Names the report, annotated files, or recorded sessions that were handed over, which supports the payment milestone.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours or milestone breakdown for non-flat work
invoiceChecklist.why: Workshops, analytics review, and retests are often billed separately and need a clear basis.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as participant incentives, recruiting fees, and testing software
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want these itemized at cost so they are not confused with your professional fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and remaining balance
invoiceChecklist.why: Audits usually start with a deposit, and the invoice should reconcile it to avoid double payment questions.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number, project code, or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often cannot process payment without it.

ui-ux-auditor.paymentTerms: Many auditors take a 30% to 50% deposit before starting, with the balance due on delivery of the report. Net 14 or net 30 is typical, and larger companies may insist on net 30 to net 60 through their accounts payable. Retainers are billed monthly in advance. A late fee of 1% to 1.5% per month is common if stated in the contract before work begins. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check, and pass-through expenses like participant incentives are sometimes paid upfront because they have to be fronted to recruits.

tips.title: Define the scope in screens and flows
tips.body: Vague audits expand quickly. State the exact flows, device types, and number of screens, and price extra pages or platforms as add-ons.

tips.title: Bill the presentation separately
tips.body: Walking a team through findings takes prep and live time. Listing it as its own line item prevents it from being assumed free.

tips.title: Pass through recruiting and incentives at cost
tips.body: Recruiting platforms and participant payments can add up fast. Collect these upfront or invoice them clearly so they do not eat into your margin.

tips.title: Set a limit on follow-up questions
tips.body: Clients often come back with weeks of questions after the report. Include a defined clarification window and bill retests and extra calls hourly.

tips.title: Tie the final payment to delivery, not to implementation
tips.body: Your work ends when findings are delivered. If payment depends on the client fixing issues, it can be delayed for months.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for a UX audit?
faqs.answer: Flat fees are more common for defined audits because clients want a fixed cost and you can price on value and scope. Use hourly for open-ended consulting, workshops, and retests where the scope is not fixed.

faqs.question: Can I invoice for participant incentives?
faqs.answer: Yes. List them as a separate pass-through line item at cost, with the number of participants and amount per person. Keep receipts or payout records in case the client asks.

faqs.question: When should I send the invoice for an audit?
faqs.answer: Send the deposit invoice when the contract is signed and the final invoice when the report is delivered. For longer audits, you can split into milestones such as research complete and report delivered.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on an audit?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax digital or consulting services and many do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as a separate line when it applies.

faqs.question: How do I bill for an accessibility audit that finds more issues than expected?
faqs.answer: Price per template or flow rather than per issue, so the fee does not depend on how many problems exist. If the client adds pages after you start, bill them under a change order.

estimate.intro: UI/UX auditors send a quote after an initial call or a quick look at the product, before any testing starts. Clients often compare several auditors or agencies, so they look at scope, deliverables, timeline, and whether the price is a fixed fee. A clear estimate also sets expectations about what the audit will and will not cover.

scopeChecklist.why: The size of the audit drives the price. Naming exact flows and devices prevents arguments over what counts as in scope.
Heuristic review, analytics analysis, accessibility testing, and usability sessions take very different amounts of time. State which are included.
If the audit is against WCAG 2.2 AA or a specific heuristic set, say so, since clients sometimes assume legal compliance is guaranteed.

scopeChecklist.item: Access and materials needed from the client
scopeChecklist.why: Delays often come from missing logins, analytics access, or staging environments. List what you need and when.
Specify whether the output is a PDF report, a spreadsheet of issues, annotated Figma files, or a recorded walkthrough, and how many revision rounds are included.
Give start date, delivery date, and how client delays affect the schedule.
State that redesign work, development fixes, and legal compliance advice are not included unless quoted separately.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: A quick heuristic review, a full audit, and an audit with usability testing give clients a way to choose by budget. Most pick the middle option when the options are clearly laid out.

pricingTips.title: Price from your hours, then add margin for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for each method and add a buffer for revisions and client communication. Present it as a flat fee so the buffer does not look like padding.

pricingTips.title: Quote research costs separately
pricingTips.body: Recruiting and incentives vary by audience. B2B participants can cost much more than general consumers, so list those costs as an estimate based on participant count.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date on the quote
pricingTips.body: Audit pricing depends on your availability. A 14 to 30 day validity window avoids being held to an old price.

faqs.question: Should I do a free mini-audit before quoting?
faqs.answer: A short walkthrough or a few observations during the sales call is fine. A full free review gives away the work, so keep it brief and use it to explain what the paid audit would cover in depth.

faqs.question: How do I handle scope changes after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Include a line in the quote saying added screens, platforms, or methods will be quoted as a change order. Get written approval before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: How detailed should the estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list the flows, methods, deliverables, and timeline, but you do not need an hour-by-hour breakdown for a flat-fee audit. Itemize research costs and optional add-ons.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement along with the estimate?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A short agreement that includes the accepted quote, payment schedule, ownership of the report, and confidentiality terms protects both sides, especially when you receive access to client analytics.

ux-ui-designer.intro: UX/UI designers are freelancers and small studio owners who design websites, mobile apps, and software products for startups, agencies, and established businesses. Invoices typically cover research, wireframes, visual design, prototyping, design systems, and developer handoff, billed by project phase, hourly, or on a monthly retainer.
ux-ui-designer.pricingModel: Most UX/UI designers price in one of three ways: hourly for open-ended or small work, fixed fees per project phase for defined deliverables, or a monthly retainer for ongoing product design. Fixed-fee projects are usually split into phases such as discovery and research, wireframes, UI design, prototype, and handoff, with a set number of revision rounds included. Day rates are common for embedded contract work with a product team. Deliverables like design systems or usability test rounds are often priced as separate line items. Stock fonts, icon sets, stock photography, user testing platform fees, and participant incentives are usually passed through at cost or with a small markup. Work beyond the agreed scope is billed hourly as a change order.

rates.service: UX research and user interviews (5-8 participants, including synthesis)
Wireframes for a marketing website (5-10 pages)
UI design for a mobile app (10-20 screens)

items.description: Discovery and stakeholder workshop (2 sessions) with competitive review
User interviews: recruiting, 6 sessions, and findings report
Wireframes for onboarding and dashboard flows (14 screens)
High-fidelity UI design, mobile app, including 2 revision rounds
Additional revision round beyond agreed scope
Participant incentives (6 x $50 gift cards), passed through at cost

sampleInvoice.notes: Phase 2 of 3 per proposal dated March 4. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Final design files and source files transfer upon payment of the final invoice. Accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and phase billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Design projects run in stages, and the client needs to match each invoice to a milestone in the proposal or statement of work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables completed with file or link references
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing items such as wireframes, a prototype link, or a design file shows what was delivered and reduces disputes about what was paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds used versus included
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often lose track of how many rounds they have used. Showing it justifies any out-of-scope hours billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours and dates for any hourly or change-order work
invoiceChecklist.why: Time-based charges are the most questioned, so dates and brief task descriptions help approval.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as fonts, stock assets, plugins, and participant incentives
invoiceChecklist.why: Itemizing out-of-pocket expenses at cost keeps them separate from your fee and lets the client reimburse you cleanly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Purchase order or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger companies and agencies often cannot pay without a PO number or internal reference on the invoice.

invoiceChecklist.item: License and ownership terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating when rights to final files transfer, usually on full payment, protects you if a client delays payment but starts using the work.

ux-ui-designer.paymentTerms: Freelance designers commonly collect a 30 to 50 percent deposit before starting, then bill the remainder at milestones such as approval of wireframes, UI design, and handoff. Net 14 or net 15 is common for small clients, while larger companies may insist on net 30 or net 45. Retainers are usually billed at the start of each month. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are typical if stated in the contract. Many designers hold final source files until the last invoice is paid. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check, and international clients often use wire transfer.

tips.title: Tie payments to approvals, not dates
tips.body: Billing at milestones such as wireframe sign-off keeps cash flowing and prevents a project from stalling with most of the work done and little paid.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Define how many rounds are included at each phase and the hourly rate for extras. Scope creep in design usually shows up as endless small tweaks.

tips.title: Charge for research and strategy separately
tips.body: Clients often see only the pretty screens as the work. Listing discovery, research, and testing as their own line items shows where the value comes from.

tips.title: Bill pass-through costs promptly
tips.body: Participant incentives, font licenses, and plugin fees can add up. Include receipts or list them on the next invoice so they do not get forgotten.

tips.title: Hold source files until paid
tips.body: Handing over editable files and handoff specs is your leverage. Make the final payment condition clear in your agreement.

faqs.question: Should I invoice hourly or by project?
faqs.answer: Use a fixed fee when scope and deliverables are clear, since clients like predictability and you are rewarded for working efficiently. Use hourly or a day rate when the scope is unclear, requirements are likely to change, or you are embedded with a product team.

faqs.question: How do I bill for revisions beyond what was agreed?
faqs.answer: Refer to the revision limit in your proposal and add a separate line for the extra work at your hourly rate, with dates and hours. Telling the client before you cross the limit prevents surprises.

faqs.question: Can I charge a deposit for a design project?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is standard. Many designers ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront, which covers the discovery work and confirms the client is committed.

faqs.question: Should I include design handoff in the project fee?
faqs.answer: Include a defined handoff, such as annotated files and one developer walkthrough, in the fee. Ongoing developer support during build is better billed hourly or under a retainer.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on design services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital or professional services and many do not. Check with your state revenue department or a tax professional, and if tax applies, show it as a separate line.

estimate.intro: Designers send a proposal or estimate after an intro call or brief and before any work begins. Clients often compare several quotes, so they look at the number of phases, included revision rounds, who owns the files, and whether research and handoff are covered.

scopeChecklist.why: Listing research summary, wireframes, UI screens, prototype, and handoff specs separately makes clear what the fee includes.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of screens or pages and platforms
scopeChecklist.why: A 10-screen app and a 40-screen app are very different jobs, and platforms such as iOS, Android, and web multiply the work.
Without a limit, feedback can continue indefinitely. State how many rounds are included and the rate for more.
Delays in content, access, or feedback stall projects. Setting expected turnaround times protects your schedule and lets you adjust deadlines.
Clients should know whether they get Figma files, exported assets, or only a prototype link.
State when rights transfer, usually on final payment, and whether you can show the work in your portfolio.
Items like branding, illustration, copywriting, front-end development, and post-launch support should be listed as excluded or quoted separately.

pricingTips.title: Price the outcome, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate your hours to set a floor, then price based on scope and business impact. A checkout redesign for an e-commerce business is worth more than the same hours spent on a brochure site.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic, standard, and expanded package, for example with or without user testing. Clients tend to choose a middle tier and see exactly what each extra adds.

pricingTips.title: Add buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Stakeholder feedback, scope clarification, and meetings take longer than expected. Add 15 to 25 percent contingency or fix the number of meetings included.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity period
pricingTips.body: Quotes should expire in 14 to 30 days, since your availability and rates change.

faqs.question: Should I do a free discovery call before quoting?
faqs.answer: A short call of 30 to 45 minutes is normal. For deep research, audits, or workshops, offer a paid discovery phase and apply the fee to the project if they continue.

faqs.question: How detailed should a design estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough that someone could tell what is and is not included. A phase-by-phase breakdown with deliverables, timeline, and fee is usually enough.

faqs.question: What if the client's scope grows after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: Refer back to the written scope, then send a change order with the added work, cost, and timeline impact. Get approval before continuing.

faqs.question: Is an estimate binding?
faqs.answer: A fixed-fee quote that the client accepts in writing generally becomes the agreed price. An estimate of hours is usually non-binding. Label which one you are sending and spell out how overages are handled.

venue-rental.intro: Venue rental businesses include event halls, barns, banquet rooms, lofts, studios, community spaces, and outdoor sites that rent to wedding couples, corporate teams, nonprofits, and private hosts. Invoices usually cover the room rental itself, plus add-ons such as tables and chairs, cleaning, staffing, security, and damage deposits.
venue-rental.pricingModel: Most venues price by the event or by the block of time. Weddings and large events are often a flat package for a set number of hours, with extra hours billed hourly. Weekday, off-season, and Friday or Sunday dates are usually discounted compared with Saturday evenings in peak season. Smaller rooms and studios often charge hourly with a minimum of 2 to 4 hours. Many venues add separate line items for setup and teardown time, cleaning, tables and linens, A/V equipment, on-site coordinator or attendant, security, and parking staff. A refundable security deposit is collected separately from the rental fee, and a non-refundable booking deposit holds the date. Some venues set a food and beverage minimum instead of, or on top of, a rental fee if they provide catering. Overtime is billed per hour past the contracted end time.

rates.service: Event hall or banquet room, Saturday peak
Event attendant or venue manager on site

items.description: Venue rental, Saturday 4:00 PM to 11:00 PM (main hall and patio)
Setup and teardown access, Friday 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM
Tables and chairs for 120 guests
On-site venue attendant
Post-event cleaning
Overtime, 11:00 PM to 11:30 PM

sampleInvoice.notes: Booking deposit of $1,500 received on March 3 has been applied. Balance is due 14 days before the event date. The $1,000 refundable security deposit is held separately and will be returned within 10 days after the event, less any documented damage or extra cleaning. Accepted payment: ACH, check, or card (3% fee on cards).

invoiceChecklist.item: Event date, start and end times, and any setup or teardown windows
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often forget that load-in time or the Friday rehearsal was part of the contract, and exact times support any overtime charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Spaces and areas included (ballroom, patio, bridal suite, kitchen)
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out the rooms covered avoids disputes when a client assumes extra areas were part of the price.

invoiceChecklist.item: Guest count or capacity cap
invoiceChecklist.why: Pricing, furniture, and fire code limits often depend on headcount, and the invoice should match what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (rentals, staff, cleaning, A/V, security)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separate lines let clients see what they chose and help you track costs for each service.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits received and how they were applied
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients want to see the booking deposit credited, and it prevents double billing on the balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Security deposit amount, hold terms, and return date
invoiceChecklist.why: Keeping this separate from the rental fee makes it clear what is refundable and when.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract or booking reference number and balance due date
invoiceChecklist.why: It ties the invoice to the signed rental agreement, which controls cancellations, overtime, and damage terms.

venue-rental.paymentTerms: Most venues collect a non-refundable booking deposit of 25 to 50 percent when the contract is signed, then the remaining balance 14 to 30 days before the event. A separate refundable security deposit, often $500 to $2,500, is commonly collected with the final payment. Smaller hourly rentals are often paid in full at booking or at least 48 hours ahead. Overtime, damage, and extra cleaning charges that come up after the event are billed afterward, or deducted from the security deposit according to the contract. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common on unpaid balances, but they should be written in the contract. Venues usually take ACH, checks, and credit cards, and some pass card fees on to the client. State the cancellation and refund schedule clearly, since this is the most frequent source of disputes.

tips.title: Collect the final balance before the event
tips.body: Once guests have arrived and the event has happened, you have far less leverage. Require full payment 2 to 4 weeks in advance, and bill only extras, overtime, and damage afterward.

tips.title: Keep the security deposit separate
tips.body: List it as its own line or document so it is not mixed up with revenue. Take dated photos before and after the event to support any deduction, and send an itemized list if you keep any part of it.

tips.title: Document overtime in real time
tips.body: Have the on-site attendant note when guests actually left and when the last vendor loaded out. A time log makes overtime charges easy to defend.

tips.title: Charge for the setup day separately
tips.body: If clients want the space the day before for decorating or rehearsal, bill it as its own block rather than folding it into a vague package. Many venues offer it at a lower hourly rate than the event itself.

tips.title: Check tax rules for rentals
tips.body: In some states, short-term rental of event space or related services is taxable, and in others it is not. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any sales tax as its own line if it applies.

faqs.question: Should the booking deposit be refundable?
faqs.answer: Most venues make it non-refundable because the date is held and other bookings are turned away. Say so plainly in the contract and on the invoice, and consider offering to apply it to a new date if you can rebook the original one.

faqs.question: How do I bill for damage after the event?
faqs.answer: Compare the space against your before photos, then deduct documented repair or cleaning costs from the security deposit and send an itemized statement. If damage exceeds the deposit, send a separate invoice with photos and repair quotes or receipts.

faqs.question: Can I charge a fee for paying by credit card?
faqs.answer: Many businesses add a card surcharge or offer a discount for ACH or check, but card surcharge rules vary by state and card network. Check your local rules and your processor's terms, and disclose the fee in the contract and on the invoice.

faqs.question: How should I invoice for a multi-day or recurring rental?
faqs.answer: For multi-day events, list each day and its time block as its own line. For recurring rentals such as weekly classes or monthly meetings, invoice monthly with each date listed, or bill in advance at a set rate per session.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice a nonprofit or community group differently?
faqs.answer: The format is the same, but you may offer a reduced rate. Show the standard rate and the discount as separate lines so the value is clear, and ask whether they need a tax-exempt certificate on file for any taxable items.

estimate.intro: Venue operators send quotes when a couple, planner, or company is touring spaces and comparing dates, capacity, and what is included. Clients usually compare the base rental fee, the hours covered, what furniture and staffing are included, and the cost of extras such as cleaning or security. A clear quote often decides which venue gets the booking.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact date, start and end times, and load-in and load-out windows
scopeChecklist.why: Time is the main thing you sell, and unclear windows lead to overtime arguments.
List rooms, outdoor spaces, kitchen access, parking, and restrooms so clients know what they are getting.

scopeChecklist.item: Guest count limit and furniture included
scopeChecklist.why: Capacity affects fire code compliance, layout, and the number of tables and chairs you must provide.
Outside vendors, insurance requirements, and open flame or confetti rules change costs and should be known before booking.
These are often mandatory and clients are frustrated when they appear only on the final invoice.

scopeChecklist.item: Deposit amounts, payment schedule, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should see when money is due and what is refundable before they sign.
Dates book up and pricing changes with season, so a held date should have a deadline.

pricingTips.title: Price by date demand
pricingTips.body: Set tiers for peak Saturdays, shoulder-season dates, and weekdays. A lower weekday rate fills slow days without discounting your best dates.

pricingTips.title: Show a base package and optional add-ons
pricingTips.body: Present the rental fee first, then list optional services with prices. Clients can compare options easily, and you avoid hiding mandatory fees.

pricingTips.title: Include all mandatory fees in the quote
pricingTips.body: If cleaning, staffing, insurance, or a security deposit is required, list it up front. Surprise charges lose bookings and cause disputes later.

pricingTips.title: Set a short hold period
pricingTips.body: Hold a date for 3 to 7 days with the quote, then release it if no deposit arrives. This keeps prime dates from being tied up by undecided clients.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a venue tour or site visit?
faqs.answer: Most venues offer tours free. Some charge a small fee for peak-season Saturday tours or for private tours with a coordinator, and credit it toward the booking deposit if the client signs.

faqs.question: Is a quote binding?
faqs.answer: Only if you say so. State an expiration date and that the date is not held until the contract is signed and the deposit is received. Pricing is typically guaranteed only through the expiration date.

faqs.question: How do I quote for events with an uncertain guest count?
faqs.answer: Set pricing around a maximum capacity or tiered guest count ranges, such as up to 75, up to 125, and up to 200. State that furniture, staffing, and fees may change if the final count moves into a different tier.

faqs.question: Can I raise the price after sending a quote?
faqs.answer: Not after the client accepts it. Before acceptance, you can update the quote if the scope changes, such as added hours or a different date. Keep the original in writing so changes are clearly documented.

video-editing.intro: Freelance and small-studio video editors invoice for turning raw footage into finished videos: YouTube episodes, corporate promos, wedding films, social clips, ads, documentaries, and training content. Clients are usually creators, marketing teams, agencies, production companies, and event videographers. Bills typically cover editing time, motion graphics, color and audio work, revisions, and delivery formats.
video-editing.pricingModel: Video editors price in several ways. Hourly billing is common for ongoing or unclear work, while per-project flat fees suit defined deliverables like a 3-minute brand video. Per-finished-minute pricing is common for YouTube and corporate content, and it rises with complexity (talking head versus heavily cut documentary style). Short-form social editors often sell per-clip packages or monthly retainers, such as 12 Reels or Shorts per month. Day rates apply when you edit on-site or in a client's suite. Add-ons such as motion graphics, subtitles, color grading, sound design, music licensing, stock footage, and rush turnaround are usually itemized separately. Most editors include a set number of revision rounds (often two) and bill extra rounds hourly. Source footage volume, such as hours of raw material to review, strongly affects the real time involved, so many editors price on raw footage hours as well as finished length.

items.description: Edit of 8-minute brand story video (assembly, rough cut, fine cut) from 90 minutes of raw footage
Motion graphics: animated lower thirds and logo sting
Color correction and grade
Audio cleanup, mixing, and licensed music placement
Burned-in captions (English)
Additional revision round beyond the two included

sampleInvoice.notes: Final files delivered via download link in H.264 MP4 (1080p) and ProRes master. Music license receipt attached. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Project files are archived for 60 days after final delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and deliverable description
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the bill to a specific video, length, and version so the client's accounts team can match it to the project.

invoiceChecklist.item: Finished runtime and raw footage volume
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the scope behind the price, especially when you quote per finished minute but spent hours reviewing long footage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for editing, motion graphics, color, audio, and captions
invoiceChecklist.why: Different skills carry different rates, and itemizing makes add-ons easy for the client to understand and approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents what was agreed and justifies charges when feedback goes beyond the original scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs such as stock footage, music licenses, plugins, or fonts
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real expenses that should be listed with receipts or license details, and they show the client what usage rights they received.

invoiceChecklist.item: Delivery formats and specs
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists codecs, resolutions, aspect ratios, and platforms (for example 16:9 for YouTube and 9:16 for Reels) so there is no dispute over what was delivered.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and file retention terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies who owns the final video and project files, and how long you keep archives before deleting them.

video-editing.paymentTerms: Many editors take a 30 to 50 percent deposit before starting, especially for new clients or projects over a few hundred dollars, with the balance due on delivery or within 7 to 30 days. Large corporate and agency clients often pay net 30 or net 45 and may require a PO number and a W-9. Recurring work is often billed monthly in advance on a retainer. Holding the final high-resolution export or unwatermarked files until payment clears is a common protection, and sending a watermarked preview for review is standard practice. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in advance. Payment is typically by ACH, card, or check.

tips.title: Deliver watermarked previews first
tips.body: Send review links with a watermark or low resolution and release the final master only after payment. This keeps leverage on your side without being confrontational.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: State how many rounds are included and what counts as a round, such as one consolidated set of notes. Bill extra rounds hourly so endless tweaks do not cost you unpaid time.

tips.title: Charge for footage review and organization
tips.body: Messy, unlabeled, or hours-long footage takes real time to sort and sync. Add a prep line or price based on raw hours so disorganized projects do not eat your margin.

tips.title: Bill milestones on long projects
tips.body: For documentaries and multi-video series, invoice at rough cut, fine cut, and final delivery. You get paid as work progresses and the client stays engaged in the schedule.

tips.title: Add rush fees for tight turnarounds
tips.body: Work that must be done in 24 to 48 hours displaces other jobs. A rush surcharge of 25 to 50 percent is common and should be agreed before you start.

faqs.question: Should I bill hourly or per project?
faqs.answer: Per project works well when scope and deliverables are clear because the client knows the cost up front and you are rewarded for working efficiently. Hourly is safer when footage volume, feedback, or scope is unclear. Many editors quote a flat fee based on estimated hours and bill extras hourly.

faqs.question: How do I charge for revisions?
faqs.answer: Include a set number of rounds, commonly two, in your price and bill additional rounds at your hourly rate. Put this in your quote and on the invoice so extra charges are not a surprise.

faqs.question: Can I withhold the final files until I am paid?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is common practice and usually stated in your terms. Share watermarked or low-resolution review copies during the project and deliver the final export once payment is received or the final installment clears.

faqs.question: Do I charge for music or stock footage?
faqs.answer: If you purchase licenses for the client, bill them as pass-through costs, with or without a small markup, and include the license details. If the client supplies their own assets, note that on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9?
faqs.answer: Freelancers in the US often provide a W-9 to business clients who need to report payments, and clients may send you a 1099-NEC if they pay you $600 or more in a year (thresholds can change). You are responsible for reporting all income either way. Check current IRS guidance or ask a tax professional.

estimate.intro: Video editors send a quote before work starts, usually after the client shares a brief, sample footage, or reference videos. Clients compare price, turnaround time, number of revisions, and what is included, such as music, captions, and motion graphics. A clear quote also protects you from scope creep once the footage arrives.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables with runtime, aspect ratio, and count
scopeChecklist.why: A 60-second 16:9 ad and three 9:16 cutdowns are very different jobs, so listing each prevents disagreement about what is included.
Hours of footage, camera types, and log or RAW formats affect review and rendering time. State the assumed amount and charge extra if it goes above that.
Setting a limit, such as two rounds of consolidated notes, prevents unlimited feedback cycles.
Pointing to example videos clarifies expected polish, such as simple cuts versus heavy motion graphics and effects.

scopeChecklist.item: Assets supplied by the client versus you
scopeChecklist.why: Specify who provides music, logos, fonts, voiceover, b-roll, and stock footage, and who pays for licenses.
Tie your delivery date to when footage and feedback arrive so client delays do not become your penalty.

scopeChecklist.item: Ownership, usage rights, and file retention
scopeChecklist.why: State what the client receives (final exports only or project files too) and how long you will store source material.

pricingTips.title: Estimate by editing hours, then check against market per-minute rates
pricingTips.body: Estimate time for review, assembly, fine cut, graphics, color, audio, and revisions, then multiply by your rate. Compare the result to typical per-finished-minute pricing to make sure you are not far off.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present basic, standard, and premium options, for example cuts only, cuts with graphics and color, and a full package with captions and social cutdowns. Clients can choose a level and it anchors the conversation on value.

pricingTips.title: Build in a buffer for unknowns
pricingTips.body: Add 10 to 20 percent for slow file transfers, unexpected footage problems, and communication overhead, especially with new clients.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes should be valid for 14 to 30 days. Software costs, your availability, and project timelines change, and an expiry keeps you from being held to old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I give a free estimate without seeing the footage?
faqs.answer: You can give a rough range from a brief, but a firm quote should wait until you see sample footage or know the total volume. State in the quote that the price depends on the assumptions listed and may change if the footage differs.

faqs.question: How detailed should a video editing quote be?
faqs.answer: List each deliverable, the included services, revision rounds, delivery date, and price. One page is usually enough. More detail is helpful for corporate clients who need to compare bids.

faqs.question: Do I ask for a deposit on the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, most editors include a deposit of 30 to 50 percent due on acceptance, with the balance on delivery or on milestones. This secures the client's commitment and your schedule slot.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to add more videos after accepting?
faqs.answer: Issue a change order or an updated quote for the extra work rather than absorbing it. Note the added deliverables, price, and any effect on the delivery date, and get written approval before continuing.

video-producer.intro: Video producers plan, shoot, and deliver video for businesses, agencies, nonprofits, and individuals. Typical projects include corporate promos, interviews and testimonials, event coverage, social media content, product videos, and short documentary pieces. Invoices usually cover pre-production, shoot days, crew and equipment, post-production, and revisions.
video-producer.pricingModel: Most video producers price by project with a flat fee built from line items: pre-production, shoot days, crew, gear, editing, and deliverables. Day rates are common for shooting and are usually quoted as a half day (up to 4-5 hours) or full day (up to 10 hours), with overtime billed after that. Editing is billed either hourly or per finished minute, depending on complexity. Equipment such as cameras, lighting, audio, drones, and teleprompters is often a separate kit fee. Crew members hired for a job (shooter, sound, gaffer, editor, motion designer) are billed at their rates, often with a markup of 10-20% for coordinating them. Licensed music, stock footage, location fees, travel, and talent are pass-through costs. Retainers are common for ongoing social or monthly content. Revisions are usually limited to a set number of rounds, with extra rounds billed hourly.

rates.service: Corporate promo or brand video (1-2 minutes)
Social media video package (4 short edits)

items.description: Pre-production: scripting, shot list, location scouting, scheduling
Shoot day: producer and lead videographer, interviews and b-roll (up to 10 hours)
Camera, lighting, and audio kit
Sound recordist
Post-production: edit, color correction, audio mix, lower thirds
Licensed music track (commercial use, single project)

sampleInvoice.notes: Price includes two rounds of revisions. Additional revisions billed at $85 per hour. Final files delivered in 4K and 1080p H.264 plus a social cut. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies after that. Footage license transfers to client on payment in full.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and phase billed (deposit, shoot, delivery)
invoiceChecklist.why: Video jobs are often billed in stages, and a clear phase label stops confusion about what each invoice covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot dates, locations, and hours worked
invoiceChecklist.why: Backs up day-rate charges and any overtime if the shoot ran past the agreed day length.

invoiceChecklist.item: Crew names or roles and their rates
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what they are paying for when a coordinator markup or subcontractor costs appear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment and rental charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating kit fees, drone, and specialty gear from labor makes the invoice easier to approve and shows rented gear passed through at cost.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs with receipts or a reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Music licenses, stock footage, location permits, talent fees, and travel are often reimbursed and clients may ask for proof.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and any extra rounds billed
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents that overages were outside the original scope and ties them to the revision limit in your quote.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable specs and usage rights
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing formats, resolution, and license terms (duration, territory, media) avoids disputes about what was delivered and how it can be used.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or client project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often will not process payment without one.

video-producer.paymentTerms: Most video producers take a deposit of 30-50% before booking the shoot, since crew and gear are committed and dates are held. A common split is 50% upfront and 50% on delivery, or thirds: booking, after the shoot, and on final delivery. Final files are often held until the last payment clears, or a watermarked review version is shared until then. Net 15 or Net 30 is typical for businesses, and agencies sometimes push for Net 45 or Net 60, so confirm before you start. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually by ACH, check, or card, and card payments on large invoices may carry a processing fee that you can pass on if you disclose it.

tips.title: Tie final delivery to final payment
tips.body: Send a watermarked or low-resolution review link for approvals and release the full-resolution files and project files only after the balance is paid. State this in your quote and contract so it is not a surprise.

tips.title: Bill cancellation and reschedule fees
tips.body: Shoots involve crew, locations, and talent booked for a specific day. Charge a fee, often 50% of the shoot day, for cancellations with short notice, and bill it as its own line.

tips.title: Track overtime and extra shoot time
tips.body: Log call and wrap times on each shoot day. If the day passes your agreed length, bill overtime at a stated rate, commonly 1.5 times the hourly equivalent of the day rate.

tips.title: Invoice pass-through costs promptly
tips.body: Music licenses, travel, and location fees can pile up and eat into profit if you wait until the end. Bill them with the stage they relate to, with a markup if your contract allows.

tips.title: Separate licensing from production
tips.body: If a client wants broad usage such as paid ads, broadcast, or unlimited duration, list the license as its own line. Fees for usage rights are separate from the cost of making the video.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or a flat project fee?
faqs.answer: Most clients prefer a flat project fee because it is easier to budget, and it lets you price based on value and deliverables. Build the fee from hours and day rates internally, set a revision limit, and bill extra work hourly. Hourly billing works better for open-ended edits, ongoing support, or when scope is unclear.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: 30-50% of the project total is typical, and for a project with large crew or rental costs, many producers ask for 50%. On large projects, you can also have the client pay rental or talent costs directly or in advance.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on video production?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax video production services or the delivered media as tangible or digital goods, and others do not tax services at all. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show any tax you collect as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Who owns the footage and project files?
faqs.answer: Unless your contract says otherwise, the creator generally holds the copyright, and the client gets a license to use the finished video. Many producers transfer rights to the final video on full payment and keep raw footage and project files, or sell them separately. Put this in writing in your contract and refer to it on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a client keeps asking for more revisions?
faqs.answer: Define the number of revision rounds in your quote, and say what counts as a round, such as one consolidated set of notes. When the limit is reached, send a short change order or invoice extra rounds at your hourly editing rate. Stating this early keeps the conversation simple later.

estimate.intro: Video producers send a quote after a discovery call, before booking crew, gear, or dates. Clients often get several bids and compare total price, number of shoot days, crew size, and what deliverables are included. A clear quote that breaks the work into phases helps you stand out from vague bids.

scopeChecklist.item: Video length, format, and number of deliverables
scopeChecklist.why: A 90-second hero video and four social cutdowns are very different workloads. Listing each deliverable prevents requests for extra edits at no cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Shoot days, locations, and crew size
scopeChecklist.why: Defines how many days and people you have budgeted. If the client adds a location or a second day, it is clearly a change from the quote.
State whether scripting, storyboards, location scouting, casting, and meetings are in the price and how many hours are covered.
Specify how many rounds are included, who gives consolidated feedback, and what happens after the limit. This is where most budget overruns happen.
Logos, scripts, product samples, location access, permits, and on-camera talent affect your schedule and cost if they arrive late or not at all.
Say where, how long, and in what media the video can be used. Broader usage like paid ads or broadcast may cost more.
Clarify whether music, stock footage, travel, permits, talent, insurance certificates, and catering are included, estimated, or billed at cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Timeline, delivery date, and quote expiration
scopeChecklist.why: Gear and crew availability change, so give the quote a valid-through date and note that delivery depends on timely feedback and footage access.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from phases
pricingTips.body: List pre-production, production, and post-production separately with a subtotal for each. Clients see where the money goes, and you can adjust a phase to meet a lower budget without cutting quality across the board.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Present a basic version, a standard version, and a fuller version with extra shoot time, motion graphics, or more cutdowns. Clients often choose the middle option and it opens a budget conversation.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency for uncertain scope
pricingTips.body: If you do not know interview count, location, or script status, say so and include a contingency or range, such as an estimate of $6,000-7,500 until script approval. Convert to a fixed price when the details are set.

pricingTips.title: Price post-production by realistic hours
pricingTips.body: Editing usually takes longer than clients expect: reviewing footage, assembling, color, audio, graphics, and revisions. As a rough guide, a polished minute of interview-based video often takes several hours of editing, and more with motion graphics.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or a range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed quote when the script, locations, and deliverables are defined. If major details are open, give a range and say what will fix the price, such as approval of the script or number of interview subjects. A range with clear conditions is better than a low number you cannot hold.

faqs.question: Should I charge for creating the quote or treatment?
faqs.answer: A simple quote is usually free. If the client asks for a detailed creative treatment, storyboards, or sample edits, many producers charge a development fee, often credited toward the project if the client books.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is typical. Crew availability, equipment rental prices, and your own schedule change, so put an expiration date on the quote and say that the shoot date is held only after the deposit is paid.

faqs.question: What if the client's budget is lower than my quote?
faqs.answer: Offer to reduce scope instead of reducing your rates. Options include fewer shoot days, a smaller crew, shorter running time, fewer cutdowns, stock footage in place of original shots, or fewer revision rounds.

videographer.intro: Videographers shoot and often edit video for businesses, events, agencies, and individuals. Typical invoices cover corporate videos, event coverage, wedding films, promo and social content, and interview shoots. Many are solo operators who bill for their time, their gear, and post-production separately.
videographer.pricingModel: Most videographers price in one of three ways: a day rate or half-day rate for shooting, an hourly rate for editing and smaller jobs, or a flat project fee for a defined deliverable such as a 60-second brand video. Day rates usually cover the operator plus a base camera kit, with extras like second shooters, drones, lighting packages, wireless mics, and teleprompters billed as add-ons. Editing is billed hourly or folded into a package, and the number of revision rounds is usually capped. Wedding and event work is often sold in packages by coverage hours. Pass-through costs such as music licensing, stock footage, travel, permits, and location fees are billed at cost or with a small markup. Usage rights matter for commercial work, and some videographers charge more when a client wants broadcast use, paid ads, or full ownership of raw footage.

rates.service: Corporate or commercial shoot (one operator, base kit)
Wedding film package (6-8 hrs coverage, highlight film)
Short promo or social video (30-90 seconds, shot and edited)

items.description: Brand video shoot day at client office and showroom (1 operator, camera, lighting, wireless mics)
Second shooter / B-roll camera
Post-production: edit of 90-second brand video with color grade and audio mix (includes 2 revision rounds)
Additional revision round (round 3)
Licensed music track (commercial use, web and social)
Mileage to and from shoot location

sampleInvoice.notes: Shoot date: May 14. Final video delivered as 4K MP4 plus 1080p social cuts via download link. Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. A 50% deposit of $1,650 was received on April 30 and is credited on this invoice. Late balances accrue 1.5% interest per month. Raw footage is not included unless agreed in writing.

invoiceChecklist.item: Shoot date(s) and location
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties each charge to a specific day on set and settles questions about how long you worked.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized crew and equipment
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what the day rate includes and justifies add-ons like a second shooter, drone, or lighting kit.

invoiceChecklist.item: Editing hours and revision rounds
invoiceChecklist.why: Documents how many rounds were included and which were extra, so charges for added revisions are not disputed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverables and file formats
invoiceChecklist.why: Lists the final length, resolution, and versions delivered (for example 4K master and vertical cuts) so the client confirms they received what was agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and license terms
invoiceChecklist.why: States where and for how long the video can be used, and whether raw footage is included. This prevents later disputes about ownership or reuse.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (music, stock footage, permits, travel)
invoiceChecklist.why: These are real out-of-pocket expenses. Listing them separately keeps your rate clean and makes reimbursement clear.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the booking deposit as a credit so the client sees the remaining amount and the due date.

videographer.paymentTerms: Most videographers take a deposit of 25-50% to hold the date, since a booked shoot day turns away other work. For larger projects, a common split is a deposit at booking, a second payment at the shoot or rough cut, and the balance before final files are released. Net 15 or net 30 is typical for businesses, while wedding and individual clients usually pay in full before or shortly after delivery. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in your contract. Many videographers hold final high-resolution files until the balance is paid, and send a watermarked or low-resolution preview in the meantime. Payment is usually accepted by bank transfer, ACH, check, or card, and agencies may require a W-9 and a PO number before they pay.

tips.title: Charge for prep, travel, and download time
tips.body: Scouting, gear prep, travel, and offloading and backing up footage take real hours. Build them into your day rate or list them as line items, since billing only for time on camera undercuts you.

tips.title: Cap revisions in writing
tips.body: State the number of included revision rounds on the quote and invoice, and the hourly rate for extras. Open-ended editing is the most common way a fixed fee turns into unpaid work.

tips.title: Hold final files until paid
tips.body: Deliver a watermarked or low-resolution review copy first and release the full-quality files once the balance clears. This is standard and keeps leverage on your side.
