tips.title: Separate shoot days from edit time
tips.body: Day rates and hourly editing rates reflect different work. Showing them separately makes your pricing easier to understand and helps when scope changes.

tips.title: Bill cancellations and reschedules
tips.body: Spell out a fee for late cancellations or weather reschedules of outdoor shoots. A day blocked off for a client is income you cannot recover if you do not charge for it.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the day?
faqs.answer: For shooting, most videographers use a half-day or full-day rate, because setup, travel, and breakdown make short hourly bookings unprofitable. Hourly works better for editing, small add-on tasks, and event coverage where the hours are clear. Many set a minimum booking, such as 3 or 4 hours.

faqs.question: Do I charge extra if the client wants the raw footage?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Raw footage lets the client or someone else re-edit your work, and it removes a future editing sale. Some videographers charge 25-100% more for raw files, or only release them under a separate agreement. State whether raw footage is included on the quote and invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to put usage rights on an invoice?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea, especially for commercial work. A short line stating the permitted use, such as web and social media for 2 years, protects you and sets expectations. The full terms should be in your contract, and the invoice can reference them.

faqs.question: How do I bill for music and stock footage?
faqs.answer: List licensed music, stock clips, and similar costs as separate line items at your cost, or with a modest markup if you handle the licensing. Make sure the license you buy covers the client's intended use, such as paid ads or broadcast, which often costs more than a personal or web license.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on video services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital products or certain production services and others do not. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant, and if you do collect sales tax, show it as a separate line on the invoice.

estimate.intro: Videographers usually send a quote after a discovery call or brief, before any shoot dates are held. Clients often compare several quotes, so they look at the number of shoot days, the deliverables, the editing scope, and what is and is not included. A clear quote helps you stand apart from a lower price that leaves out key items.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables with length, format, and quantity
scopeChecklist.why: Say exactly what the client gets, for example one 2-minute video, three 30-second cuts, and vertical versions. Vague deliverables lead to requests for extra edits at no charge.
Defines the time you are booked and prevents a 4-hour shoot from stretching to 8 without extra pay.
Lists operators, second shooters, lighting, audio, drone, and any rentals so the client understands what is covered and what is optional.
Sets the limit on included edits and the rate for extra rounds, which keeps editing time from growing unchecked.
Covers script or talking points, location access, talent releases, permits, and feedback deadlines. Late client input is a main cause of schedule slips.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage rights, music licensing, and raw footage
scopeChecklist.why: States how the video may be used, who owns the final files, and whether licensed assets and raw footage are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Delivery timeline, deposit, and cancellation terms
scopeChecklist.why: Gives a turnaround date after final approval, the deposit needed to hold the date, and what happens if the shoot is postponed.

pricingTips.title: Quote in tiers
pricingTips.body: Offer two or three options, such as a single-camera shoot with one edit, a two-camera shoot with extra cuts, and a premium package with drone and social versions. Clients tend to pick a middle option and it shows where your extras add cost.

pricingTips.title: Price from your day rate and edit hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate shoot days, then edit hours at roughly 3-8 hours of editing per finished minute depending on complexity, and add pass-through costs. This keeps flat fees tied to real time and not guesswork.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for uncertainty
pricingTips.body: If the client has not finalized a script or location, include a contingency or state that scope changes will be billed at your hourly rate. This protects you when the brief shifts.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiration date
pricingTips.body: Gear rentals, crew availability, and your calendar all change. A validity window of 14 to 30 days encourages decisions and prevents old prices from being used months later.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat price or an hourly estimate?
faqs.answer: For defined projects with clear deliverables, a flat fee is easier for clients to approve and rewards your efficiency. For projects where the scope is uncertain, such as ongoing event work or open-ended editing, an hourly estimate with a cap or range is safer.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the time spent creating a quote?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are normally free. For large productions that need scouting, treatments, storyboards, or detailed budgets, many videographers charge a planning or pre-production fee, which can be credited toward the project if the client books.

faqs.question: What happens if the scope changes after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Include a line that changes to scope, such as additional shoot hours, locations, or deliverables, will be quoted separately or billed at your standard rates. When a change comes up, send a short written change order before doing the extra work.

faqs.question: Should the quote include a deposit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most videographers require a deposit of 25-50% to confirm the date and cover prep costs. Put the amount and the due date on the quote, and state that the date is not held until the deposit and signed agreement are received.

vinyl-wrap-installer.intro: Vinyl wrap installers apply color-change wraps, commercial fleet graphics, paint protection film, and window tint to cars, trucks, vans, boats, and storefronts. Most are solo installers or small shops who invoice retail customers for personal vehicle wraps and businesses for fleet lettering and branded graphics. A typical invoice covers film, labor, design or print time, and surface prep or removal of old graphics.
vinyl-wrap-installer.pricingModel: Most wrap work is priced as a flat project fee based on vehicle size and complexity, because customers want a single number up front. Behind that number, installers usually calculate material cost (by the linear foot or roll), plus labor at a shop rate of roughly $60-120 per hour, plus a markup on film. Full color-change wraps are priced by vehicle class (coupe, sedan, SUV, truck, van). Commercial wraps add design and printing charges, and partial wraps, spot graphics, and lettering are often priced per panel or per square foot. Prep and removal are billed separately, since peeling old vinyl or fixing paint defects can take as long as the install. Premium films such as chrome, textured, or color-shift cost more in material and take longer to install, so they carry higher prices. Many shops take a deposit to order film and book the bay.

rates.service: Full color-change wrap, sedan or coupe
Full color-change wrap, SUV or pickup
Partial wrap or spot graphics (hood, roof, mirrors)

items.description: Full color-change wrap, satin black, mid-size SUV (film, install, door jambs excluded)
Chrome delete: window trim and grille wrapped in gloss black
Removal of existing roof decal and adhesive cleanup
Door handle and mirror removal/reinstall during wrap
Deposit received on 03/04

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due at vehicle pickup. Do not wash vehicle for 7 days and avoid automatic car washes with brushes. Wrap installation is warrantied for 1 year against lifting and bubbling under normal use; film manufacturer warranty is separate. Pre-existing paint damage noted on intake form. Late balances after 7 days of completion may incur a storage fee of $25 per day.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, and VIN or plate
invoiceChecklist.why: Identifies the exact vehicle, and the size and body style behind the price, if a dispute or warranty claim comes up later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Film brand, series, color name, and finish
invoiceChecklist.why: A 3M 2080 gloss and a cheaper cast film differ in cost and durability. Listing them supports your price and any manufacturer warranty claim.

invoiceChecklist.item: Areas covered and areas excluded
invoiceChecklist.why: Door jambs, under the hood edges, and bumpers inside are common sources of arguments. State what was wrapped and what was not.

invoiceChecklist.item: Prep, removal, and repair charges as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers often assume the wrap price includes stripping old vinyl or fixing paint. Separate lines show where the time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pre-existing condition note
invoiceChecklist.why: Rock chips, clear coat failure, and aftermarket paint can cause paint to lift on removal. Documenting condition protects you.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit and balance due
invoiceChecklist.why: Film is ordered for the job and often cannot be returned, so show the deposit credited and the remaining amount.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms and care instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out your workmanship warranty, what voids it, and cure time before washing reduces callbacks.

vinyl-wrap-installer.paymentTerms: Most wrap shops take a deposit of 30-50% to order film and reserve a bay, with the balance due when the customer picks up the vehicle. Commercial and fleet clients often pay net 15 or net 30 after completion, with a deposit up front on larger jobs. Accepted methods usually include card, ACH, and check, and some shops add a card fee on large invoices. Many shops charge a daily storage fee if a finished vehicle sits more than a few days after the pickup notice. Late fees on net terms are commonly 1.5% per month, if your local rules allow it and the terms were agreed in writing.

tips.title: Charge a deposit that covers the film
tips.body: Cast film is cut to order and large rolls are rarely returnable. Set the deposit at least equal to your material cost so a canceled job does not leave you holding vinyl.

tips.title: Bill removal and prep as their own line items
tips.body: Removing old wraps, cleaning adhesive, sanding or fixing paint, and disassembling bumpers or lights can add hours that were not in the base quote. Itemize them so customers see what the wrap price covers.

tips.title: Keep photos with the invoice
tips.body: Take intake photos of the vehicle before work and after completion. Attach or reference them to document paint condition and deliver proof of finished work.

tips.title: Add a waste and reprint charge policy
tips.body: If a customer changes the color or design after film is cut or printed, the material is gone. State in writing that changes after approval are billed as additional work.

tips.title: Separate design from install for commercial clients
tips.body: Fleet and business clients revise artwork several times. Bill design hours and print setup separately from install so revisions do not eat your margin.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or hourly for a vehicle wrap?
faqs.answer: Flat fee is the norm for full and partial wraps, since customers want a firm price. Work out the flat fee from film cost plus estimated hours, and bill hourly for add-ons like removal, repairs, or extra disassembly that were not in the original scope.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for film I ordered if the customer cancels?
faqs.answer: State in your agreement that the deposit is non-refundable once film is ordered or printed. On cancellation, invoice for materials purchased, design time spent, and any restocking fees, and apply the deposit against that amount.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on a vehicle wrap?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states tax the sale of tangible goods and some tax installation or labor on vehicles, while others treat custom graphics differently. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant before setting up your invoice tax lines.

faqs.question: Can I charge a storage fee for vehicles left after the job is done?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you put it in your written terms before the work begins and tell the customer when the vehicle is ready. A common approach is a short grace period of a few days followed by a per-day fee.

faqs.question: How should I bill a fleet of identical vans?
faqs.answer: Quote a per-vehicle price and list each vehicle on the invoice by unit number or plate. Give a volume discount only in writing, and bill design and print setup once instead of per vehicle.

estimate.intro: Customers usually ask for a quote before choosing a shop, and many get two or three to compare. They look at the total price, the film brand, how long the vehicle will be in the shop, and what warranty comes with it. A written estimate that lists film, coverage, and prep helps your price stand up against a cheaper quote that leaves things out.

scopeChecklist.item: Film brand, series, color, and finish
scopeChecklist.why: Customers compare price without realizing different films vary widely in quality and lifespan. Naming the product keeps quotes comparable.
Specify whether door jambs, inside edges, roof, mirrors, bumpers, and trim are included. Unwritten assumptions lead to disputes at pickup.

scopeChecklist.item: Surface prep and paint condition requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Wrap adhesion depends on sound paint. State that peeling clear coat, rust, or poor repaint work may need repair at extra cost.

scopeChecklist.item: Removal of existing wrap or graphics
scopeChecklist.why: Removing old vinyl can take many hours and may damage paint. Quote it separately or state it is excluded.
A full wrap often takes 3-5 days. Setting expectations avoids pressure and frequent calls during the install.
For printed wraps, state how many proof revisions are included and that production starts only after written approval of the artwork.
Customers want to know what is covered and for how long, and what actions such as pressure washing or skipping cure time void the warranty.

pricingTips.title: Build the price from film plus hours
pricingTips.body: Measure the vehicle, add 10-20% for waste and complex curves, price the film at cost plus markup, then add estimated labor hours at your shop rate. This keeps small cars and large trucks priced properly and avoids underquoting.

pricingTips.title: Quote by vehicle class and list add-ons
pricingTips.body: Give a base price for the vehicle and list options such as door jambs, chrome delete, or premium finishes as separate lines. Customers can choose what fits their budget and you avoid discounting the base.

pricingTips.title: Charge for the unseen work
pricingTips.body: Disassembly of bumpers, lights, and handles, plus cleaning and claying paint, takes time customers do not see. Include it in the estimate so it does not look like padding later.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Film prices change and your schedule fills up. Mark quotes valid for 14-30 days and note that the price may change if the film is discontinued or costs rise.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most shops quote vehicle wraps for free, since customers shop around. For complex jobs involving custom design mockups or fleet audits, some shops charge a design fee that is credited toward the job if the customer goes ahead.

faqs.question: Can I give a quote without seeing the vehicle?
faqs.answer: You can give a ballpark by vehicle make, model, and year, but a firm quote should follow an in-person look or detailed photos. Paint condition, existing graphics, and body damage can change the price.

faqs.question: What if the final job costs more than the estimate?
faqs.answer: Note in the estimate that hidden paint problems or customer-requested changes can raise the price. If something comes up mid-job, stop and get the customer's approval in writing, by text or email, before billing the extra.

faqs.question: How long should I keep a quote open?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is typical. Film pricing and shop availability change, so an expiration date protects you from a customer returning months later expecting the old price.

virtual-assistant.intro: Virtual assistants provide remote administrative, operational, and sometimes specialized support to business owners, executives, and small teams. They typically invoice for hours worked on tasks like inbox and calendar management, data entry, customer support, bookkeeping support, travel booking, social media scheduling, and project coordination, or for monthly retainers that reserve a set number of hours.
virtual-assistant.pricingModel: Most virtual assistants charge hourly, either pay-as-you-go or through a monthly retainer that reserves a block of hours (for example 10, 20, or 40 hours) at a slightly discounted rate. Retainers are popular because they give the VA predictable income and give the client priority access. Specialized tasks such as podcast production, bookkeeping entry, CRM setup, or website updates often carry higher hourly rates than general admin work. Some VAs sell fixed-price projects (an inbox cleanup, a database build, a travel itinerary) or per-task packages. Rates generally rise with experience, niche skills, and the level of responsibility. Time is usually tracked in 15- or 30-minute increments, with a minimum billable block for urgent or after-hours requests. Software subscriptions or third-party costs that the VA buys on the client's behalf are normally passed through at cost, listed separately from labor.

rates.service: General administrative support (email, calendar, data entry)
Social media scheduling and community management
Podcast or video editing and show notes

items.description: Monthly retainer: inbox and calendar management (20 hours included)
Additional hours beyond retainer: travel booking for conference (itinerary, hotel, ground transport)
Social media scheduling: 12 posts across two platforms
CRM contact cleanup and tagging (480 contacts)
Software pass-through: email scheduling tool subscription (client-approved)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 15 days of invoice date. Hours are logged in 15-minute increments; the attached time report lists tasks by date. Unused retainer hours do not roll over. Late balances incur a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by ACH or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and invoice number
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainer clients get invoiced on a cycle, and a clear period prevents confusion about which month's hours are being billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized task log or attached time report
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients cannot see your work, so dated entries with hours per task are the best defense against questions about where the time went.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer hours included versus overage hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating included hours from extra hours at their own rate shows exactly what was covered and what was additional.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hourly rate and time increment
invoiceChecklist.why: Stating the rate and whether you bill in 15- or 30-minute blocks avoids disputes over rounding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through expenses listed separately at cost
invoiceChecklist.why: Software subscriptions, stock images, postage, or purchases made for the client should be visible and backed by receipts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rush or after-hours surcharge, if applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: If you charge extra for same-day or weekend requests, noting it on the line item ties it back to your agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business name, contact info, and tax ID or W-9 on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients who pay you $600 or more in a year (US) may need your W-9 for 1099 reporting, so keep your details consistent.

virtual-assistant.paymentTerms: Retainer clients are commonly billed at the start of the month, in advance, since the hours are reserved for them, while hourly clients are billed at the end of the month or every two weeks. Net 7 to Net 15 is common for solo VAs, and many require payment before the next period of work begins. New clients are often asked for a deposit or a first-month retainer up front. Late fees of 1.5% per month are typical if stated in your agreement. ACH transfer, credit card, and online payment links are the most common methods, and some VAs pause work on accounts that are more than a week overdue.

tips.title: Bill retainers in advance
tips.body: Invoice the retainer at the start of the period so the money covers the work rather than chasing it afterward. State clearly that unused hours expire or roll over for a limited time, whichever you choose.

tips.title: Keep a running time log
tips.body: Track time as you go, with the task and date, and attach the log to every invoice. Reconstructing a month from memory leads to under-billing and arguments.

tips.title: Set a minimum for small requests
tips.body: Five-minute tasks add up in interruptions. A 15-minute minimum per request protects your day and keeps billing simple.

tips.title: Charge more for specialized skills
tips.body: Bookkeeping entry, CRM configuration, or video editing are not general admin. Bill them at a higher rate on separate lines so the client sees the distinction.

tips.title: Get approval before buying anything
tips.body: If you pay for software, subscriptions, or services on the client's behalf, get written approval first and pass the cost through with a receipt, or have the client use their own account.

faqs.question: Should a virtual assistant charge hourly or by retainer?
faqs.answer: Both work. Hourly suits new or occasional clients. A retainer suits ongoing work because it gives you steady income and gives the client reserved capacity. Many VAs start clients hourly and move them to a retainer after a few months.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect a W-9 from clients?
faqs.answer: As an independent contractor in the US, you generally do not send a 1099 to clients. Clients who pay you above the IRS threshold (currently $600 for many payments, though rules change) may ask you for a W-9 so they can report it. Check current IRS guidance or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I bill for tasks that take less than an hour?
faqs.answer: Bill in 15- or 30-minute increments and put the increment in your agreement. Some VAs also set a minimum charge per request so that very short tasks are still worth doing.

faqs.question: What happens to unused retainer hours?
faqs.answer: That is up to your agreement. Many VAs let unused hours expire at the end of the month because the time was reserved. Others allow rollover for one month. Whatever you choose, write it down before the first invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for time spent in meetings and on messages with the client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your agreement says so. Calls, check-ins, and time spent reading and replying to messages are work, and many VAs bill them at the same rate as task time. Be upfront about it so it is not a surprise.

estimate.intro: Virtual assistants send estimates when a prospective client wants to know what ongoing support or a defined project will cost. Clients usually compare hourly rates, retainer sizes, and what is included, so it helps to show expected hours and the types of tasks they cover.

scopeChecklist.item: List of tasks and responsibilities covered
scopeChecklist.why: Admin work is open-ended, and naming the tasks (inbox, calendar, travel, data entry) keeps scope clear.

scopeChecklist.item: Estimated hours per week or month
scopeChecklist.why: Clients need to budget, and you need to know whether the work fits your capacity.

scopeChecklist.item: Hourly rate or retainer price, and overage rate
scopeChecklist.why: Stating what happens when the client goes past the included hours avoids surprise charges.
Expectations about same-day replies, time zones, and availability are a common source of friction.
Clients often need to provide email, calendar, password manager, or software access, and any subscriptions you will need to be covered must be named.
Tasks like design, bookkeeping, or ad management may be separate services at a different rate.

scopeChecklist.item: Start date, minimum term, and notice period
scopeChecklist.why: Retainer work needs a clear start date and how much notice either side must give to end it.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three retainer sizes
pricingTips.body: Presenting 10, 20, and 40 hour options with a small discount at higher tiers helps clients choose without negotiating your hourly rate.

pricingTips.title: Start with a trial period
pricingTips.body: A 30-day trial at a defined number of hours lets both sides test the fit and gives you real data on how long tasks take before you commit to a long-term price.

pricingTips.title: Price projects with a buffer
pricingTips.body: For fixed-price work like a database cleanup, estimate your hours, then add 15 to 25 percent for revisions and unclear instructions, and state how many revision rounds are included.

pricingTips.title: Do not price to the lowest bidder
pricingTips.body: Clients who compare you to offshore or entry-level rates often want a different service. Show the specific skills, reliability, and time zone coverage you offer rather than cutting your rate.

faqs.question: How do I estimate hours when a client is not sure what they need?
faqs.answer: Ask for a list of recurring tasks and how often they happen, then estimate each. If it is still unclear, propose a short trial retainer and adjust after the first month based on logged time.

faqs.question: Should an estimate be binding?
faqs.answer: For hourly or retainer work, an estimate is a projection, and you should say that the final bill depends on actual hours. For fixed-price projects, state that the price holds for the defined scope and that changes will be quoted separately.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the discovery call before an estimate?
faqs.answer: Short intro calls are normally free. If the client wants a detailed process audit or workflow plan before hiring you, many VAs charge for that as a paid first project.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Your availability can change quickly as you take on other clients, so a validity date helps you avoid holding a slot for free.

voice-actor.intro: Voice actors record narration, commercials, character voices, e-learning, audiobooks, telephone prompts, and video game dialogue for ad agencies, production companies, game studios, publishers, and small businesses. Most work from a home studio and invoice per project, per finished hour, or per word, with separate line items for usage rights, revisions, and extras like editing or live-directed sessions.
voice-actor.pricingModel: Voice work is priced by project, not by the hour of your time. Common units include per finished hour (audiobooks and long-form narration), per word or per 100 words (e-learning, explainers, IVR), a flat fee per spot (commercials), and a per-line or per-session rate (games and animation). Commercial work adds a usage fee based on where the spot runs, for how long, and in which market, such as regional radio for 13 weeks or national online for one year. Union work (SAG-AFTRA) follows published scale rates, session fees, and holding or reuse payments, with payroll handled by the signatory company rather than by your invoice. Many non-union actors set a minimum session fee, typically for a short script, to cover setup and editing time. Add-ons are billed separately: rush turnaround, pickups and revisions beyond the included rounds, self-directed versus directed sessions, editing and mastering, multiple tags or alternate reads, and buyouts for extended or perpetual usage.

rates.unit: per finished minute or per 100 words

rates.service: Local or regional radio/TV commercial (non-union, 13 weeks)
Video game or animation character voice

items.description: Corporate e-learning narration, 12 modules, approx. 4,800 words, WAV files delivered
Usage license: internal training use, unlimited duration, US only
Script revisions and pickups (client-requested wording changes, beyond 1 included round)
Custom file naming and per-module splitting/editing
Rush delivery (48-hour turnaround)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 30 days of invoice date. Recording is licensed for internal employee training only, in the US, in perpetuity. Any external, broadcast, or paid-media use requires a separate license. Raw takes are not included. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Payment accepted by ACH, check, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, script version, and word count or finished length
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the fee to the exact script recorded, so later script changes can be billed as new work instead of disputed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights: media, territory, term, and exclusivity
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial rates depend on where and how long the spot runs. Stating it on the invoice limits unauthorized reuse and sets the price for any extension.

invoiceChecklist.item: Revision and pickup rounds included, plus charges for extra rounds
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often send script changes after delivery. Listing included rounds shows what is billable.

invoiceChecklist.item: Session date, length, and type (self-directed or live-directed)
invoiceChecklist.why: Directed sessions take more of your time and often carry a separate hourly or minimum session fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deliverable format and extras (WAV/MP3, edited, mastered, alternate takes, tags)
invoiceChecklist.why: Editing, mastering, and alternate reads are real labor. Itemizing them keeps the base rate clean and protects you if the client expected raw files.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or agency job number
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and corporate accounts payable departments often cannot process an invoice without one.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your legal name or business name, tax ID or W-9 on request, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: US clients paying $600 or more in a year generally need your W-9 to issue a 1099, and clear payment details speed up payment.

voice-actor.paymentTerms: Many voice actors take full payment upfront for small projects under a few hundred dollars, often by card or online payment before sending final files. Larger jobs, such as audiobooks or multi-session game work, commonly use a 25-50% deposit with the balance due on delivery or net 15-30. Ad agencies and corporate clients often pay net 30 to net 60, so confirm terms before booking and ask for a PO. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in advance. Payment methods usually include ACH, check, wire, PayPal, and card. Final licensed files are often released only after payment clears. For union work, payment and payroll are handled by the signatory producer, with deadlines set by the applicable SAG-AFTRA agreement.

tips.title: Separate the session fee from the usage fee
tips.body: Quote the recording as one line and the license as another. When a client wants to extend a spot from 13 weeks to a year, you invoice only the usage and do not renegotiate everything.

tips.title: Set a minimum for short scripts
tips.body: A 30-word phone greeting still takes setup, recording, editing, and file delivery. A minimum of $100-250 stops tiny jobs from costing more time than they earn.

tips.title: Define revisions by cause
tips.body: Fix your own errors, mispronunciations, and sound quality problems for free. Charge for client script changes and new direction after approval. Put this distinction in your quote and on the invoice.

tips.title: Hold final files until payment
tips.body: For new clients, send watermarked or low-quality auditions and release clean WAV files after payment. This works well for non-agency clients you have not worked with before.

tips.title: Track the clock on audiobooks
tips.body: Pay-for-production audiobook rates depend on finished hours, not recording hours. Track your actual time, including editing and proofing, so you know your real hourly return and can adjust your PFH rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge per word or per finished hour?
faqs.answer: Per word or per 100 words is common for short scripts like e-learning, explainers, and IVR, since the length is fixed. Per finished hour is the norm for audiobooks and long-form narration. Whichever you choose, state the unit and the minimum on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for usage rights on a commercial?
faqs.answer: Add a separate line or state the license terms: media (radio, TV, web, social), territory (local, regional, national), and term (13 weeks, 1 year, perpetual). Longer or broader usage costs more. If the client wants to extend later, invoice a renewal fee.

faqs.question: Do I need to send a 1099 or collect one?
faqs.answer: Clients who pay you as an independent contractor generally issue you a 1099 if they pay $600 or more in a year, and may ask for a W-9. You do not issue 1099s to clients. Thresholds and rules can change, so check current IRS guidance or ask a tax professional.

faqs.question: What if the client asks for unlimited revisions?
faqs.answer: Offer one or two rounds included in the fee, and bill additional rounds at a per-round or hourly rate. For ongoing work, a per-project cap or a monthly retainer can cover a defined number of changes.

faqs.question: How is union voice work invoiced differently?
faqs.answer: On SAG-AFTRA jobs, the signatory producer or their payroll company pays you through payroll under the union contract, with session fees, usage, and reuse payments set by scale. You typically submit a time or session record rather than a freelance invoice. Check the specific agreement and your union's guidance.

estimate.intro: Voice actors usually quote before booking, often after receiving a script, audition request, or a rate inquiry from a client or casting platform. Clients compare per-project fees, what usage is included, turnaround time, and how many revisions are covered.

scopeChecklist.item: Final script or word count, and what happens if it changes
scopeChecklist.why: A quote based on 500 words is not valid for 900. State that fees are based on the supplied script.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage: media, territory, term, and exclusivity
scopeChecklist.why: The same read costs very different amounts for an internal training video and a national TV campaign.
Specify WAV or MP3, edited or raw, one file or split files, and whether alternate takes or tags are included.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of included revision rounds and pickup policy
scopeChecklist.why: Clarifies that client-driven script changes after approval are billable, while your own errors are fixed free.
Self-directed, live-directed, or unattended sessions require different time commitments and sometimes different fees.
Standard delivery is usually 24-72 hours. Same-day or overnight work carries a surcharge.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote validity period and payment terms
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents a client from accepting an old quote months later at a rate you have since raised.

pricingTips.title: Quote usage separately from the recording
pricingTips.body: Show the session fee and the license fee as two lines. Clients can see what they are buying, and you can offer cheaper or broader license options without reworking the whole quote.

pricingTips.title: Ask what the project is before naming a number
pricingTips.body: A script labeled a simple online video can turn out to be a paid ad running nationally. Ask where it will run, for how long, and who the end client is, then price accordingly.

pricingTips.title: Offer a package for repeat or multi-part work
pricingTips.body: For series like training modules or a set of phone prompts, a bundled rate with a lower per-unit price encourages commitment and makes scheduling and invoicing simple.

pricingTips.title: Keep a minimum fee in every quote
pricingTips.body: State a minimum session fee clearly so short scripts are priced fairly. Clients accept it more easily when it is part of a standard rate sheet.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the client will not share usage details?
faqs.answer: Quote the narrowest reasonable license, such as internal use or a single online channel for one year, and state that wider usage requires an additional fee. This protects you without losing the job.

faqs.question: Should I give a free sample or custom audition?
faqs.answer: Short auditions of a few lines are standard and unpaid for most casting calls. For a long script, offer to record a short section or a paid test. Do not record the full script for free.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before recording?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. A written acceptance, even an email reply approving the quote, confirms the word count, usage, and fee. For larger jobs, use a short agreement and take a deposit.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Fourteen to thirty days is typical. Mention the expiry date on the quote, since rates, availability, and script details can change.

warehouse-services.intro: Warehouse services providers store, handle, and move goods for other businesses. That includes third-party logistics (3PL) operators, public warehouses, fulfillment shops, cross-dock and transload operators, and small outfits that offer pallet storage and pick-and-pack. Invoices usually bundle recurring storage charges with per-transaction handling fees and one-off accessorial charges.
warehouse-services.pricingModel: Warehouse work is billed by unit of activity rather than by the hour. Storage is charged per pallet position, per bin, or per square foot, usually monthly, and often with a minimum. Some warehouses use an initial storage charge on receipt plus a renewal charge each month or on each anniversary date. Handling is billed per pallet in and out, per case, per carton, or per piece, and fulfillment is billed per order plus per additional item picked. Value-added work such as labeling, kitting, repacking, and returns processing is billed per piece or per labor hour. Accessorial charges cover things like detention, after-hours receiving, special equipment, shrink wrap, pallets, and re-palletizing. Many contracts include a monthly minimum, an onboarding or setup fee, and an annual rate review or fuel-related adjustment on any freight you arrange. Larger accounts often negotiate a rate sheet, so the invoice should map line by line to that sheet.

items.description: Pallet storage, March (average 40 positions, 48x40)
Inbound receiving and put-away (PO 4471, 12 pallets)
E-commerce orders picked and packed (first item)
Additional items picked
Relabeling of cartons (FNSKU labels)
Stretch wrap and pallet materials

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due net 30 from invoice date. Storage billed monthly on average daily pallet count. A 1.5% monthly late fee applies to balances past due. Inventory report for the billing period is attached. Questions about charges must be sent within 15 days of invoice date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Billing period and inventory report reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Storage and handling charges are tied to a date range. Clients will check the numbers against their own inventory counts.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pallet or bin count and how it was calculated
invoiceChecklist.why: Average daily, end-of-month, or peak counts give different totals. State the method so the storage line is not disputed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Receiving and shipping references (PO, ASN, BOL, or order numbers)
invoiceChecklist.why: Matching each handling charge to a document lets the client tie your invoice to their purchase and sales records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Separate lines for accessorial charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Detention, after-hours work, shrink wrap, and re-palletizing should appear on their own lines with quantities, so they do not look like padding.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours with task description
invoiceChecklist.why: For value-added work, list the task, hours, and date. Clients often want to verify the hours against what was requested.

invoiceChecklist.item: Rate sheet or contract reference
invoiceChecklist.why: Pointing to the agreed rates shows the charges match the agreement and reduces back-and-forth.

invoiceChecklist.item: Minimums and setup fees
invoiceChecklist.why: If a monthly minimum applies, show the calculation so a slow month does not look like a billing error.

warehouse-services.paymentTerms: Most warehouse providers invoice storage monthly and handling either weekly or monthly, with net 15 or net 30 terms. Smaller or new accounts are often asked for a deposit or a prepaid balance, and some shops hold inventory release if an account is far past due, which is often permitted under the warehouse agreement and in many states by a warehouse lien, so check your contract and local rules. Late fees of 1% to 1.5% per month are common if written into the agreement. ACH and wire are standard for business clients, with checks and cards used for smaller accounts, and card payments are sometimes subject to a surcharge to cover fees.

tips.title: Put the billing method in the contract
tips.body: Decide whether you bill storage on average daily count, month-end count, or per pallet received with monthly renewals, and write it down. Most storage disputes come from clients assuming a different method.

tips.title: Bill accessorials as they happen
tips.body: Record detention, special requests, and extra labor on the day they occur and attach the note or email approving it. Adding them months later makes them hard to collect.

tips.title: Set a monthly minimum
tips.body: Minimums cover your fixed cost of space, racking, and systems when a client's volume drops. Show the minimum on the invoice when it applies.

tips.title: Reconcile inventory before invoicing
tips.body: Count discrepancies, damaged goods, and unreceived freight cause credits and re-bills. Resolve them before the invoice goes out, not after.

tips.title: Review rates yearly
tips.body: Labor, rent, and equipment costs change. Include a clause allowing an annual rate adjustment with 30 to 60 days notice.

faqs.question: How should I bill storage for pallets that come and go during the month?
faqs.answer: Pick one method and put it in the agreement. Common choices are average daily pallet count, peak count, or a per-pallet initial charge with a renewal each month on the anniversary date. Average daily count is the fairest for clients with fluctuating inventory.

faqs.question: Can I charge for inventory I am holding if the client has not paid?
faqs.answer: Often you can keep charging storage, and in many states a warehouse has a statutory lien on stored goods for unpaid charges if a proper warehouse receipt or agreement exists. Rules differ, so check your state law and have a written agreement before relying on it.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on warehouse services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax storage or certain services, others do not, and resale or exemption certificates may apply. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: How do I bill for damaged or lost goods?
faqs.answer: Handle claims separately from invoices. Your agreement should state liability limits, often a per-pound or declared-value cap. Issue a credit memo against the invoice if you owe a credit, rather than editing past invoices.

faqs.question: What is a reasonable late fee?
faqs.answer: 1% to 1.5% per month on the overdue balance is common in B2B work. It must be stated in your contract or on earlier invoices, and some states cap the rate, so check local rules.

estimate.intro: Warehouse providers send quotes when a prospective client is comparing 3PLs or public warehouses, or when an existing client adds a new product line, seasonal volume, or a one-time project. Clients compare per-pallet and per-order rates, minimums, setup fees, and what is or is not included in handling.

scopeChecklist.why: State the assumed pallets stored, orders per month, and SKU count. Rates are based on these figures and should change if volume differs.
Dimensions, weight, stackability, temperature or hazmat needs, and pallet type affect storage and handling cost.
List what the per-order or per-pallet rate covers, such as receiving, put-away, and standard packaging, and what is billed separately.
Monthly minimums, onboarding fees, and integration or system setup should be stated up front so they are not a surprise.
Say how pallets are counted and when charges start, so the first invoice matches expectations.
Order cutoff times, ship-by windows, and receiving appointments determine whether you can meet the client's expectations.
Contract length, termination notice, and when rates can change protect you from long-term cost increases.

pricingTips.title: Quote from a rate sheet
pricingTips.body: Build a standard rate sheet for storage, receiving, shipping, pick and pack, and labor. Quoting from it keeps pricing consistent and makes comparison with other warehouses easy.

pricingTips.title: Base rates on your real cost per square foot
pricingTips.body: Work out rent, racking, labor, insurance, and utilities per pallet position, then add margin. Cheap storage rates with high handling fees, or the reverse, should still add up to a profit at the client's volume.

pricingTips.title: Price the unknowns separately
pricingTips.body: For irregular items, rework, or unknown receiving condition, quote an hourly rate or a not-to-exceed amount rather than a fixed price.

pricingTips.title: Set a validity period
pricingTips.body: Rent and labor costs move. Say the quote is good for 30 days and that rates assume the stated volumes.

faqs.question: Should I give a flat monthly price or itemized rates?
faqs.answer: Itemized rates are standard because volume changes each month. A flat monthly fee only works for fixed space, such as a dedicated cage or a set number of pallet positions.

faqs.question: How do I quote when the client does not know their volume?
faqs.answer: Ask for a range, quote tiered rates for different volume levels, and add a minimum. You can also offer a short trial period at an agreed rate before locking in a longer contract.

faqs.question: Do I charge for providing a quote?
faqs.answer: Usually not for standard storage and fulfillment. For complex projects that need site visits, process design, or system integration work, a paid scoping fee that is credited against the first invoice is reasonable.

faqs.question: What happens if actual volume is different from the quote?
faqs.answer: State in the quote that rates are based on the stated volumes and may be adjusted if volume varies materially. A monthly minimum protects you if volume comes in lower.

water-damage-restoration.intro: Water damage restoration companies respond to burst pipes, appliance leaks, sewage backups, roof leaks, and storm flooding. They extract water, set drying equipment, remove materials that can't be saved, and document the drying process. Most invoices go to a homeowner and an insurance carrier at the same time, so the paperwork has to satisfy both.
water-damage-restoration.pricingModel: Most mitigation work is billed by line item rather than one flat price. Common units are square feet affected for extraction, demolition, and antimicrobial treatment, per unit per day for drying equipment (air movers, dehumidifiers, air scrubbers), and per hour for technician labor. Many companies add an emergency response or minimum service fee. Insurance-paid jobs are often priced against a carrier-accepted price list, and some carriers push back on rates above it, so know what your local adjusters accept. Contents pack-out is billed by the hour, the box, or the item count. Reconstruction (new drywall, flooring, paint) is usually quoted as a separate project. Disposal and dumpster fees, and any subcontractor work, are normally billed at cost plus markup.

rates.service: Demolition (drywall flood cut, baseboard, wet pad and carpet removal)

items.description: Emergency response, after-hours arrival, moisture mapping and initial assessment
Water extraction, kitchen and hallway (Category 1, Class 2)
Air movers, set for 3 days (8 units)
LGR dehumidifiers, set for 3 days (2 units)
Flood cut drywall 2 ft high and remove baseboard, wet carpet pad removal
Antimicrobial application to affected surfaces and cavities

sampleInvoice.notes: Loss date: supply line failure, kitchen. Insurance claim # and adjuster listed on work authorization. Drying logs and photos attached. Customer deductible is due on completion; the balance is billed to the carrier under the signed direct-pay authorization. Any amount the carrier does not pay is the customer's responsibility. Balance due within 30 days of invoice date.

invoiceChecklist.item: Date and time of loss, date and time of first call, and arrival time
invoiceChecklist.why: Carriers use these to judge response and confirm the loss date. Disputes about when the water started are common.

invoiceChecklist.item: Water category and damage class (per IICRC S500 guidelines)
invoiceChecklist.why: Category 1, 2, or 3 and Class 1 to 4 justify the equipment count, the demolition, and the antimicrobial treatment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment list with type, quantity, set date, and pickup date
invoiceChecklist.why: Equipment is billed per unit per day, so adjusters check the day count against your drying logs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Moisture readings and drying log reference, with photos
invoiceChecklist.why: Daily readings show why equipment stayed on site and when materials reached dry standard. Without them, carriers often cut equipment days.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance carrier, claim number, adjuster name, and policy holder
invoiceChecklist.why: This routes the invoice to the right person and avoids delays in payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Signed work authorization and direct-pay authorization reference
invoiceChecklist.why: It proves the customer approved the work and your right to be paid by the carrier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Disposal, dumpster, and subcontractor charges as separate lines with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through costs are scrutinized. Clear receipts make them easier to approve.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and IICRC firm certification, where applicable
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require a contractor license for this work or for rebuilding, and carriers often prefer certified firms. Check your local rules.

water-damage-restoration.paymentTerms: For insurance jobs, many companies collect the deductible at the start of work or on completion, and bill the carrier for the rest under a signed direct-pay authorization. Carriers commonly pay in two to six weeks, so state net 30 terms. Some companies ask for a deposit or full payment up front on cash jobs with no claim, or progress billing on large losses. Late fees such as 1.5% per month are common if you state them on the work authorization and invoice, though state rules on interest vary. Accept checks, ACH, and credit cards, and consider a card on file for the deductible.

tips.title: Keep drying logs for every job
tips.body: Daily moisture readings and photos are your best defense when a carrier challenges equipment days or demolition. Record them as you go and attach them to the invoice.

tips.title: Get the work authorization signed before you start
tips.body: Even on an emergency call, get a signature on the authorization, direct-pay agreement, and a statement that the customer is responsible for any unpaid balance. This protects you if the carrier denies part of the claim.

tips.title: Bill equipment by actual days set
tips.body: Count from the day you set it to the day you remove it. Pulling equipment promptly once readings meet the dry goal keeps you credible with adjusters.

tips.title: Submit supplements promptly
tips.body: If you find hidden wet insulation or a wider affected area after the first estimate, tell the adjuster right away with photos and an updated scope instead of adding it to the final invoice.

tips.title: Collect the deductible early
tips.body: The deductible is the customer's debt to you, and it is much harder to collect after the house is dry. Ask for it on completion at the latest.

faqs.question: Should I bill the homeowner or the insurance company?
faqs.answer: The homeowner is your customer and is responsible for the bill. If they sign a direct-pay authorization, you can send the invoice to the carrier and collect the deductible from the homeowner. Put both parties and the claim number on the invoice.

faqs.question: Can I charge for equipment on days when I only visit to check readings?
faqs.answer: You bill each equipment unit for every day it is on site and running. Monitoring visits may be billed as labor or included in your equipment rate. Be consistent, and check what your local carriers accept.

faqs.question: What if the insurance company pays less than I invoiced?
faqs.answer: Provide your drying logs, photos, and authorization, and ask for a written explanation of what was cut. Your authorization should state that the customer owes any balance the carrier doesn't pay. Check your state's rules before pursuing it.

faqs.question: Do I need a license to do water damage restoration?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some states license mitigation or require a general contractor license for demolition and rebuilding, while others do not. IICRC certification is a industry standard, not a legal requirement in most places. Check with your state licensing board.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for mold found during the job?
faqs.answer: Stop and document it. Mold remediation is usually a separate scope, estimate, and authorization, and some states require a separate license or testing. Do not add it to the mitigation invoice without customer and carrier approval.

estimate.intro: Emergency water jobs often start before a full quote exists, so many companies send a written estimate after the first assessment and update it as the scope becomes clear. Reconstruction after mitigation is quoted separately. Customers and adjusters compare line items, equipment counts, and how clearly you explain what could change the total.

scopeChecklist.item: Rooms and square footage affected, with a moisture map
scopeChecklist.why: This sets the base for extraction, demolition, and antimicrobial pricing and shows where the water went.
A Category 3 sewage loss needs different materials, protection, and disposal than a clean supply line leak, and the price reflects that.
State the number of air movers and dehumidifiers and note that the actual days depend on daily readings.

scopeChecklist.item: Materials to be removed and disposed
scopeChecklist.why: List drywall, baseboard, carpet pad, insulation, and flooring so the customer knows what is coming out and why.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions, including reconstruction, mold remediation, and contents
scopeChecklist.why: This prevents the assumption that mitigation includes rebuilding or mold work.
Older homes may contain asbestos or lead paint, and testing may be required before demolition. Note that wet cavities may reveal additional damage.
Include the signature line, deductible due date, direct-pay language, and your policy on unpaid balances.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for drying days
pricingTips.body: Show an estimated equipment duration, usually three to five days, and state that billing follows actual days on site as shown in the drying logs.

pricingTips.title: Know your carrier-accepted pricing
pricingTips.body: On insurance jobs, rates far outside a carrier's accepted price list lead to reductions and delays. Learn the pricing in your market before you quote.

pricingTips.title: Separate mitigation from rebuild
pricingTips.body: Give the mitigation estimate immediately and a distinct reconstruction quote after the structure is dry. It's easier for customers and carriers to approve each one.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency line for unknowns
pricingTips.body: If you can't see inside walls or under flooring, say so, and list unit prices for extra demolition or extra equipment so changes can be approved quickly.

faqs.question: Can I start work before the customer signs a full estimate?
faqs.answer: Many companies do for emergency mitigation, because delays let damage spread. Get a signed work authorization first, even if the estimate is only a preliminary scope, and follow up with the written estimate as soon as you can.

faqs.question: How long should an estimate be valid?
faqs.answer: For mitigation, the price is typically good only for the emergency window since conditions change daily. For reconstruction, 30 days is common, and you can note that material prices may change.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the estimate itself?
faqs.answer: Most companies do not charge for a mitigation assessment, as it is part of the emergency response. If the visit is for a large reconstruction quote with no mitigation, some charge a fee and credit it to the job.

faqs.question: What if the final cost exceeds the estimate?
faqs.answer: State in the estimate that the scope may change after demolition or as readings come in. Get written approval, or the adjuster's approval, before adding significant work, and show the changes as supplement line items.

water-well-service.intro: Water well service businesses drill, repair, and maintain private wells for homes, farms, and small commercial sites. Invoices usually cover new well drilling, pump and pressure tank replacement, well pump repair, water testing, and hydrofracturing or cleaning of existing wells. Most work is done by a small crew with a drill rig, a pump hoist truck, or both.
water-well-service.pricingModel: Drilling is priced per foot, with a separate charge for casing, and often a different rate for rock versus overburden. Pump and tank work is priced as equipment plus labor, with a markup on parts, and service calls carry a trip charge or a minimum. Troubleshooting and repair are billed hourly with a truck or hoist fee. Many contractors quote drilling as a price per foot with an estimated depth, and bill actual footage drilled, so the final total can differ from the estimate. Pump installs are commonly a flat price for a package that includes the pump, pipe, wire, and fittings. Add-ons such as water testing, disinfection, hydrofracturing, and permit fees are listed separately.

rates.service: Steel or PVC well casing, installed
Pump hoist truck / pulling a pump

items.description: Drill 6-inch residential water well, rock and overburden (actual depth 285 ft)
6-inch steel casing, installed (60 ft)
1 HP submersible pump, 285 ft drop pipe and wire, pitless adapter, installed
Pressure tank, 86-gallon, with gauge and pressure switch
Well disinfection and water sample drawn for lab
State well permit fee (pass-through)

sampleInvoice.notes: Static water level 42 ft, yield 12 GPM at completion. Well log filed with the state as required. Deposit of $5,000 received. Balance due on receipt. Lab results are sent directly from the testing lab.

invoiceChecklist.item: Well location and property address
invoiceChecklist.why: Many properties have more than one well, and the record needs to show which one you worked on.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license or registration number
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states require well drillers and pump installers to be licensed and to show the number on contracts and records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Drilled depth, casing length, and diameter
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-foot billing needs actual footage that matches the well log, and the customer will want it for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Yield (GPM), static water level, and pump setting depth
invoiceChecklist.why: These show what the customer got for the money and help in any later dispute about water supply.

invoiceChecklist.item: Equipment model numbers and sizes
invoiceChecklist.why: Pump HP, tank size, and brand matter for warranty claims and future repairs.

invoiceChecklist.item: Permit numbers and state or county fees
invoiceChecklist.why: Pass-through fees should be itemized so the customer sees they were not markup.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposit received and change orders
invoiceChecklist.why: Hitting rock early or drilling deeper than estimated changes the total, and the invoice should show what was agreed.

water-well-service.paymentTerms: Drilling jobs usually require a deposit of 25 to 50 percent before mobilizing the rig, often with a progress payment when drilling is complete and the balance due when the pump is running or at completion. Pump and tank replacements are often due on completion, sometimes with a deposit for special-order equipment. Service calls are typically due on the spot. Late fees of 1 to 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Checks, card, and ACH are common, and larger drilling jobs sometimes involve a bank draw or a payment from a lender. Check your local rules on lien rights and notice requirements.

tips.title: Bill actual footage and say so up front
tips.body: Put in the quote that the price is per foot and that final cost depends on depth reached. State how you handle a dry hole or low yield so there are no surprises when you invoice.

tips.title: Separate drilling from equipment
tips.body: Itemize drilling, casing, pump, tank, and testing as different lines. If the customer disputes one item, the rest of the invoice stays clear.

tips.title: Get change orders in writing
tips.body: Extra casing, a deeper well, or a larger pump should be agreed in writing or a text before you do it, then added as its own line.

tips.title: Charge for mobilization and trip time
tips.body: Rigs are expensive to move. Add a mobilization or trip charge for remote sites so a short job does not lose money.

tips.title: Keep records of the well log
tips.body: Attach or reference the well log number on the invoice. It protects you if the well performance is questioned later.

faqs.question: Do I get paid if the well comes in dry or low yield?
faqs.answer: Most drillers charge for work performed, since drilling time and materials are spent regardless of the result. Put this in your contract and explain it before starting, and say whether you will drill a second hole at a reduced rate.

faqs.question: Should I invoice per foot or flat rate for drilling?
faqs.answer: Per foot is standard because depth is unknown. A flat rate works for pump and tank replacements, where the scope is more predictable. Some contractors quote a fixed price for a set depth and bill per foot beyond that.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on well work?
faqs.answer: It varies by state. Some states tax materials, parts, or the whole job, and others treat drilling as a nontaxable service. Check with your state department of revenue or a tax professional.

faqs.question: How do I handle permit and lab fees?
faqs.answer: List them as separate pass-through lines at cost, or include them in the price and say so in the quote. Keep the receipts.

faqs.question: Can I put a lien on the property for an unpaid well?
faqs.answer: Many states allow mechanics liens for well drilling and pump work, but deadlines and notice rules vary. Check your state rules early, because filing windows can be short.

estimate.intro: Water well service businesses send a quote before drilling, replacing a pump, or doing a rehab on an existing well. Homeowners often get two or three quotes and compare the per-foot rate, what casing is included, and what happens if the well is deeper than expected. A clear quote helps you win the job and avoid arguments later.

scopeChecklist.item: Per-foot rate, estimated depth, and a depth range
scopeChecklist.why: Final depth is unknown, so the customer needs to see how the total changes if the well is deeper or shallower.

scopeChecklist.item: Casing type, diameter, and included footage
scopeChecklist.why: Casing beyond the included amount is a common source of extra charges and disputes.

scopeChecklist.item: Pump, pipe, wire, and tank specifications
scopeChecklist.why: Brand, HP, and tank size should be listed so the customer can compare quotes accurately.

scopeChecklist.item: Dry hole, low yield, and second well terms
scopeChecklist.why: State clearly whether you charge for a hole that does not produce enough water and what the options are.
Say who pulls the permit, who pays fees, and whether a lab test or disinfection is included.
A rig leaves ruts and spoils. State who handles cleanup, grading, and trenching to the house.
List whether you handle the wiring to the pump and the line to the house, or if a licensed electrician or plumber is needed.

pricingTips.title: Quote a range for depth
pricingTips.body: Use nearby well logs to estimate depth, then show a low and high total. Customers accept a range better than a surprise at the end.

pricingTips.title: Include mobilization
pricingTips.body: Rig move-in, setup, and travel to remote sites should be in the quote as a line item or built into the per-foot rate.

pricingTips.title: Offer pump options
pricingTips.body: Present a standard and an upgraded pump or tank option. Customers often pick the middle choice when they can see the differences.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Steel, pumps, and fuel costs change. Make quotes good for 30 days so you are not stuck with old pricing.

faqs.question: Should I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Quotes for new drilling are usually free. For troubleshooting an existing well, charge a service call fee, which you can credit to the repair if the customer hires you.

faqs.question: How accurate can a drilling estimate be?
faqs.answer: Only as accurate as local knowledge allows. Use nearby well logs and explain that actual depth and rock conditions can change the final cost.

faqs.question: What happens when the job goes beyond the estimate?
faqs.answer: Stop and get written approval before drilling past the estimated depth range or adding equipment. Add the approved change as a separate line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before starting?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many states require a written contract for well work, and a signed quote with a deposit protects both sides. Check your state licensing rules for required contract terms.

web-design.intro: Web designers are freelancers and small studios who plan, design, and often build websites for small businesses, nonprofits, and startups. Invoices usually cover project milestones such as discovery, design mockups, development, and launch, plus ongoing maintenance or hosting. Many also bill for add-ons like copywriting, stock photos, plugins, and extra revision rounds.
web-design.pricingModel: Most web designers price by project with a flat fee split into milestones, commonly 50% upfront and 50% at launch, or thirds for larger jobs (deposit, design approval, launch). Hourly billing is common for small fixes, change requests, and work with unclear scope. Some designers use tiered packages, such as a 5-page brochure site, a 10-page site, or an e-commerce build, with a stated number of revision rounds. Recurring work is billed as a monthly retainer for maintenance, updates, and support, or as a yearly fee for hosting and domain renewals. Third-party costs such as premium themes, plugins, stock images, fonts, and paid hosting are either built into the price or passed through at cost or with a small markup, and should be listed clearly either way.

rates.service: Custom website design and build (10-15 pages)

items.description: Website design and build, 8 pages (Home, About, Services, Contact, etc.) - Milestone 2 of 2: launch
Contact form and Google Analytics setup
Premium theme license (1 year)
Additional revision round (beyond 2 included)
Training session on editing the site

sampleInvoice.notes: Milestone 1 deposit of $2,750 was paid on the project start date. Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Final site files and admin credentials are transferred once this invoice is paid. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. Accepted: ACH, check, credit card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often get several invoices for one project. Naming the milestone (deposit, design approval, launch) shows what this payment covers and what has already been paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed proposal or contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Linking to the agreed scope and date makes it easier to settle disputes about what was included.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized third-party costs
invoiceChecklist.why: Themes, plugins, stock photos, fonts, and domain purchases should be listed separately so the client can see what they own and what renews yearly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change requests and extra revisions
invoiceChecklist.why: Work outside the original scope should appear as its own line with hours and rate, tied to the written request or email that approved it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Domain, hosting, and renewal details
invoiceChecklist.why: State who owns the accounts, what is included, and when renewals are due so no one is surprised when the site goes offline.

invoiceChecklist.item: Handoff and ownership terms
invoiceChecklist.why: Noting that final files, logins, and licenses transfer on full payment protects you from giving away the work before you are paid.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or billing contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Larger organizations often require a purchase order or accounts payable contact to process payment.

web-design.paymentTerms: A 40-50% deposit before work starts is standard and often non-refundable, since it reserves your calendar time. The balance is typically due at launch, and many designers hold the final files or switch the site live only after payment. Net 7 to Net 14 is common for milestone invoices, while retainers and hosting are billed monthly or annually in advance. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract. Most designers accept ACH, credit card, and checks; card fees run around 3%, and some add that to the invoice or build it into pricing.

tips.title: Tie payments to milestones, not dates
tips.body: Bill when the client approves design or content is delivered, not on a calendar schedule. Projects stall when clients are slow with feedback, and you should not be left waiting on money while the clock runs.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: State how many rounds are included, such as two on design and one on development, and bill extras hourly. Without a limit, scope creep eats the margin on fixed-price projects.

tips.title: Pause the project when invoices go unpaid
tips.body: Include a clause that work stops and the staging site stays offline if a milestone invoice is overdue. Do not launch until the final payment clears.

tips.title: Bill recurring services separately
tips.body: Keep maintenance, hosting, and domain renewals on their own recurring invoice so they continue after the build is done and clients do not assume they are included in the project fee.

tips.title: Charge for content delays
tips.body: If the client does not supply copy and images by the agreed date, add a clause that moves the schedule and allows a restart fee. Late content is the most common cause of unpaid final balances.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a website?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work best when the scope is clear, since clients like knowing the total and you benefit from working efficiently. Use hourly rates for maintenance, small changes, and projects where requirements are unclear or likely to shift.

faqs.question: How much deposit should I ask for?
faqs.answer: Most web designers ask for 40-50% before starting. For larger projects, splitting into thirds (start, design approval, launch) keeps cash flowing and limits your exposure if the client goes quiet.

faqs.question: Can I keep the website files until I'm paid?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says ownership and final files transfer on full payment. Many designers build on a staging site and only move it to the client's domain or hand over logins after the final invoice is paid.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on web design?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax digital services or custom software, others do not tax web design at all. Check your state department of revenue or ask an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for hosting and domains I purchase for the client?
faqs.answer: Either put the accounts in the client's name and have them pay directly, or buy on their behalf and list the cost as a separate line item, with a small markup if your contract allows it. For recurring renewals, bill annually in advance.

estimate.intro: Web designers send a proposal or quote after a discovery call or intake form, before any design work starts. Clients usually compare a few quotes on price, number of pages, timeline, and what is included, such as copywriting, SEO setup, and training. A clear scope helps your quote stand out from cheaper ones that leave things out.

scopeChecklist.why: List each page or page template. Clients often assume a blog, shop, or extra landing pages are included unless the quote says otherwise.
Name the platform (WordPress, Webflow, Shopify, custom code) and any required plugins or paid apps, since this affects ownership, cost, and how the client can edit the site later.
State how many rounds of changes are included on design and development and the hourly rate for extras, so feedback does not stretch indefinitely.
Specify who writes copy, supplies photos, and provides logos, and by what date. Late or missing content is the top cause of delays and budget overruns.
Spell out forms, booking tools, payment gateways, email signups, analytics, and migrations. Each can add hours that clients do not expect.
Give estimated start, review, and launch dates tied to client approvals, and note that delays on their side move the schedule.
List what is not included, such as SEO strategy, photography, hosting, and maintenance, and show expected recurring costs like hosting and domain renewals.

pricingTips.title: Price from hours, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Estimate hours for discovery, design, build, content entry, testing, and project management, multiply by your rate, and add 15-20% for feedback rounds and surprises. Many designers underprice by counting only design and build time.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three tiers, such as a basic 5-page site, a standard site with blog and SEO setup, and a full custom build, gives clients a choice and anchors the middle option.

pricingTips.title: Separate one-time and recurring costs
pricingTips.body: Show the build fee, then monthly maintenance and annual hosting as distinct lines. This makes the project price look clear and sets up recurring revenue from the start.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quotes typically stay valid for 14 to 30 days. Software costs and your availability change, and a deadline encourages a decision.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a proposal or quote?
faqs.answer: Short quotes are usually free. For complex projects that need a detailed discovery phase, such as a site audit, sitemap, or technical planning, many designers charge a paid discovery fee of a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars, often credited toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to change the scope after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Write a short change order listing the new work, added cost, and any schedule impact, and get written approval before starting. Your quote should say that out-of-scope requests are billed separately.

faqs.question: Is a quote a binding contract?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. A quote becomes enforceable when the client accepts it, ideally with a signature or written approval, and it works best when paired with a contract covering ownership, payment, and cancellation terms. Check local rules or have a lawyer review your template.

faqs.question: How do I handle a client who says another designer quoted much less?
faqs.answer: Compare scope rather than price. Cheaper quotes often leave out custom design, revisions, SEO setup, or training. Offer to trim features to meet their budget instead of cutting your rate for the same work.

web-developer.intro: Web developers build and maintain websites, web applications, and e-commerce stores for small businesses, agencies, and startups. Most solo developers bill for design and build work, ongoing maintenance, hosting or plugin resale, and one-off fixes. Invoices usually tie to project milestones, hours logged, or a monthly retainer.
web-developer.pricingModel: Web developers price in four main ways. Hourly billing is common for fixes, consulting, and projects with unclear scope. Fixed-price project fees are typical for brochure sites, Shopify or WordPress builds, and landing pages, and are usually split into a deposit, a mid-project milestone, and a final payment at launch. Monthly retainers cover maintenance, updates, backups, security monitoring, and a set number of support hours. Some developers also resell hosting, domains, premium plugins, or third-party licenses, usually at cost plus a markup or as a flat annual fee. Rates depend on stack, experience, and client type. Custom application work and specialized skills such as React, API integrations, or performance work command more than template-based site builds. Define what counts as a revision round and bill extra work as change orders, since scope creep is the most common reason web projects go unpaid or underpaid.

rates.service: Senior or specialized development (custom apps, API work)
Brochure or small business website (5-10 pages)
Bug fix or small change request

items.description: Small business website, milestone 2 of 3: page templates built and content loaded (8 pages)
Contact form with spam protection and email routing
Additional revision round beyond 2 included (header and navigation changes)
Premium theme license, annual (billed at cost)
Managed hosting setup and first month

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Milestone 3 (launch) invoice will be sent when the site goes live. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Accepted by ACH, check, or card. Source files and admin credentials transfer after final payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone number
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often have several open projects. Naming the milestone, such as 2 of 3, ties the invoice to the signed proposal and shows where the project stands.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the contract or proposal date
