invoiceChecklist.why: If a client questions a charge, you can point to the agreed scope, deposit schedule, and revision limits.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged with dates and short task descriptions (for hourly work)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients dispute vague lines like 'development work'. Specific entries such as 'fixed checkout bug on mobile Safari' hold up under review.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs listed separately at cost or with markup
invoiceChecklist.why: Domains, premium plugins, themes, stock images, and hosting should be visible line items so clients see what is a recurring or pass-through charge.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders billed as separate lines
invoiceChecklist.why: Work outside the original scope should show the approved change order or email date so the extra charge is not a surprise.

invoiceChecklist.item: Renewal dates for domains, licenses, and hosting
invoiceChecklist.why: Annual charges are easy to forget. Listing the renewal period prevents lapses and disputes over who owns the renewal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client's PO number or billing contact, if required
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger companies often reject invoices without a PO number or the right accounts payable contact, which delays payment.

web-developer.paymentTerms: Most web developers collect a deposit of 30-50% before starting, then bill the balance at milestones or at launch. For small projects under about $1,500, many ask for full payment up front or 50% up front and 50% at delivery. Net 14 is common for solo developers, and net 30 is typical when working with agencies or corporate clients. Late fees of 1-2% per month are common if stated in the contract. Retainers are usually billed monthly in advance. Payment methods include ACH, card, check, and wire transfer. Card fees run around 3%, and some developers pass that on or offer a small discount for ACH. Holding final files, admin access, or the launch itself until the last payment clears is a common and reasonable practice if the contract says so.

tips.title: Tie the launch to final payment
tips.body: State in your contract that the site goes live or credentials transfer once the final invoice is paid. Staging links and a locked-down admin give you leverage without any dispute over work already delivered.

tips.title: Cap revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Include two or three rounds of revisions in the fixed fee and bill extra rounds hourly. List each extra round on the invoice with the date so clients see the pattern.

tips.title: Separate build fees from recurring fees
tips.body: Bill hosting, maintenance, and licenses as their own recurring lines rather than burying them in the project price. It makes renewals predictable and keeps cash flow steady after launch.

tips.title: Invoice at milestones, not at the end
tips.body: Splitting a project into deposit, design approval, build complete, and launch keeps you paid as you work and limits how much you are owed if a client goes quiet.

tips.title: Track time even on fixed-price jobs
tips.body: Logging hours shows you whether your flat fees are profitable and gives you data to back up change orders when scope grows.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a website?
faqs.answer: Use a flat fee when scope is clear, such as a set number of pages and features, since clients prefer knowing the total. Use hourly when requirements are vague, when you are fixing or extending an existing site, or when the client keeps adding requests. Many developers quote a flat fee with hourly billing for anything outside the written scope.

faqs.question: Can I charge for hosting and plugins I buy for the client?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Either pass costs through at cost or add a markup for managing the account. List each item separately on the invoice. If the client owns the account directly, it is often cleaner to have them pay the vendor and avoid reselling.

faqs.question: What happens if a client stops responding mid-project?
faqs.answer: Your contract should say that the project is paused after a set period of inactivity, such as 30 days, and that milestones completed to that point are due. Send an invoice for work completed and any unpaid milestone, and note the pause policy on it.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on web development?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax custom software or website services, some tax only prewritten or digital products, and many do not tax services at all. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax as its own line on the invoice.

faqs.question: Who owns the code and design after the project?
faqs.answer: That is set by your contract, not the invoice. Many developers transfer ownership of the custom work upon full payment while keeping rights to their own reusable code and tools. Put a short note on the invoice that rights transfer on payment in full, and make sure the contract says the same.

estimate.intro: Web developers send estimates or proposals before any code is written, usually after a discovery call about goals, pages, features, and timeline. Clients commonly compare quotes from freelancers, agencies, and template platforms, so the estimate has to show exactly what is included and what is not.

scopeChecklist.item: List of pages, templates, and features
scopeChecklist.why: Say how many pages, which custom features, and which integrations are included, such as contact forms, booking, payments, or CRM connections. Anything not listed becomes a change order.
Naming WordPress, Shopify, or a custom stack sets expectations about hosting, plugin costs, and how the client can edit the site later.
State who provides copy, images, logos, and product data and by what date. Late content is the most common cause of delays and cost overruns.
Define how many rounds of feedback are included and how extra rounds are billed, so feedback does not turn into unlimited work.
Give estimated dates for design, build, and launch and note that they depend on timely feedback. This protects you if the client stalls.
Domains, hosting, premium plugins, stock photos, and email services are usually separate from your fee. Listing them avoids a surprise later.
Clarify whether training, a warranty period for bugs, and ongoing maintenance are included, and what they cost afterward.

pricingTips.title: Price the project, not just the hours
pricingTips.body: Estimate your hours, add a buffer of 15-25% for revisions and unknowns, and quote a fixed fee. Clients see a single number and you are protected from small overruns.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered options
pricingTips.body: Present two or three packages, such as basic, standard with e-commerce or booking, and a version with a maintenance retainer. Clients tend to pick the middle option and it opens the maintenance conversation.

pricingTips.title: Break the quote into phases
pricingTips.body: Show design, development, content loading, and launch as separate lines with their own prices. It makes the total easier to justify and sets up your milestone invoices.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiration date
pricingTips.body: Quote validity of 15-30 days is typical. Plugin prices, your availability, and your rates change, so an open-ended quote can commit you to old terms.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates or discovery?
faqs.answer: A short call to understand the project is usually free. For larger projects that need a detailed technical spec, wireframes, or a requirements document, many developers charge a paid discovery phase, often $500-3,000, that is credited toward the build if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: How accurate does a web development quote need to be?
faqs.answer: A fixed quote should be accurate for the defined scope, with a clear process for changes. If scope is uncertain, give a range or an estimate with an hourly cap and state that final cost depends on the confirmed requirements.

faqs.question: Can the client change the scope after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Yes, but changes should be written up as a change order with price and timeline impact before you do the work. Say this in the quote so the client expects it.

faqs.question: Should the quote become the contract?
faqs.answer: Often the accepted proposal works as the agreement if it includes scope, payment schedule, ownership terms, and signature or written acceptance. For larger projects, a separate contract reviewed by a lawyer is a safer choice.

webflow-developer.intro: Webflow developers build and maintain marketing sites, CMS-driven blogs, and landing pages for startups, agencies, and small businesses. Invoices usually cover design-to-Webflow builds, CMS setup, custom interactions and code, migrations from other platforms, and ongoing site support. Many work solo or as subcontractors to design agencies, so invoices often need to line up with a scope document or milestone schedule.
webflow-developer.pricingModel: Most Webflow developers price new builds as a flat project fee, often split into milestones (deposit, design approval, build complete, launch). Fixed pricing is usually based on page count, number of CMS collections, and complexity of interactions. Hourly billing is common for small changes, audits, and work with unclear scope, and agencies subcontracting developers often pay hourly or per-page. Ongoing work is commonly sold as a monthly retainer with a set number of hours, or as a care plan covering edits, backups checks, and minor updates. Extras such as custom code, third-party integrations, copywriting entry, and migrations are normally itemized separately. Client-side costs like Webflow site plans, workspace seats, and paid apps are usually either billed directly to the client's account or passed through at cost, so say which one on every invoice.

rates.service: Marketing website build (5-10 pages, from approved design)
Site migration from WordPress or other platform

items.description: Webflow build of 8-page marketing site from approved Figma design (milestone 2 of 3, 40%)
CMS setup: Blog and Case Studies collections with templates and filtering
Custom scroll interactions on home page
Custom code: HubSpot form embed and tracking scripts
Webflow Business site plan, 12 months (pass-through at cost)

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Remaining 30% is due at launch. Revisions beyond two rounds per page are billed at $95/hour. Site plan cost is passed through at cost with no markup; billing transfers to the client's Webflow account after launch.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name, site URL, and milestone or phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to the agreed scope so the client's accounts team can match it to the contract or proposal.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized deliverables (pages, CMS collections, integrations)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows what was built and prevents disputes over whether something was included in the flat fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged for out-of-scope or hourly work
invoiceChecklist.why: Change requests and extra revisions need dates and hour counts to be defensible.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pass-through costs (site plans, paid apps, fonts, stock assets)
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing these at cost separately keeps them distinct from your labor and shows you aren't marking them up unless agreed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed proposal or statement of work
invoiceChecklist.why: Helps when a client or agency asks which approved scope the invoice falls under.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number or agency project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger clients often will not process payment without it.

invoiceChecklist.item: Handoff and ownership notes (workspace transfer, client billing)
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies who owns the project, who pays Webflow hosting, and when final payment releases the transfer.

webflow-developer.paymentTerms: A 30-50% deposit before work starts is standard for fixed-price builds, with the balance split across milestones or due at launch. Many developers hold the workspace transfer, DNS changes, or publishing to the live domain until the final invoice is paid. Net 14 is common for direct clients, while agencies often pay net 30 or net 45, so confirm before you start. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated in the contract in advance. Payments usually come by ACH, card, or wire; card payments often carry processing fees, which some developers pass on. Retainers are normally billed at the start of the month.

tips.title: Tie milestones to approvals, not dates
tips.body: Invoice on design handoff, staging review, and launch rather than calendar dates. Client feedback delays then do not stall your cash flow.

tips.title: Define revision rounds in writing
tips.body: Limit rounds per page or per milestone, and bill extra rounds hourly. Most Webflow scope creep is small copy and layout tweaks that add up.

tips.title: Keep Webflow plan billing in the client's account
tips.body: Have clients create their own workspace or add a card for site plans. It avoids fronting costs and removes confusion about renewals after launch.

tips.title: Log hours even on flat-fee jobs
tips.body: Tracking time shows when a project is running over and gives you evidence when pricing the next change request or retainer.

tips.title: Bill post-launch support separately
tips.body: Offer a short free bug-fix window, such as 14-30 days, then move edits to hourly or a retainer. State the window on the final invoice.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a Webflow site?
faqs.answer: Flat fees work well when the design is finished and the page and CMS counts are known. Hourly suits unclear scope, ongoing edits, and cleanup of someone else's build. Many developers use a flat fee for the build and hourly for changes after approval.

faqs.question: Do I bill the client for the Webflow hosting plan?
faqs.answer: Either approach works if it is written down. The cleanest option is for the client to pay Webflow directly from their own account. If you pay first, list the plan as a pass-through at cost and note the renewal date.

faqs.question: How do I bill for work done on a designer's or agency's behalf?
faqs.answer: Invoice the party who signed your agreement, which is often the agency. Include their project code or PO, and use the rate or per-page price you agreed on. Agencies often want hours broken out by task.

faqs.question: Can I withhold the site transfer until I'm paid?
faqs.answer: Many developers do, as long as the contract says final payment is due before transfer or launch. Put that term in the proposal up front rather than raising it at the end.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on web development?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax digital services or custom software, and others do not. Check your state's rules or ask an accountant, and show any tax collected as a separate line.

estimate.intro: Webflow developers send estimates after a discovery call, a review of designs or an existing site, and a look at required integrations. Clients often compare several quotes, so the estimate needs to show clearly what is included and how many pages, collections, and revisions the price covers.

scopeChecklist.why: Static pages and CMS templates take different amounts of time, and listing them prevents arguments over whether a new page is extra.
Collection structure drives build time. Naming the collections and rough item counts sets the boundary for migration and data entry.
State whether you are building from approved Figma files, a template, or designing as well. Unfinished designs are the largest source of overruns.
Complex scroll effects and scripts can double build time, so list which ones are included.
Forms, CRMs, analytics, e-commerce, memberships, and payment tools each add setup and testing time.
Clarify who writes copy, supplies images, and enters CMS content, and how many items you will migrate.

scopeChecklist.item: Revision rounds, timeline, and launch support
scopeChecklist.why: Set the number of feedback rounds, review turnaround times, and what post-launch support is included.

pricingTips.title: Price by components, not a guess at total hours
pricingTips.body: Build the quote from pages, collections, integrations, and interactions, then check the total against your hourly rate. This makes it easy to adjust if the client trims scope.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiers for the same project
pricingTips.body: Presenting a basic build, a standard build with CMS, and a full build with integrations helps clients pick a budget without pushing you to discount.

pricingTips.title: Add a buffer for feedback and QA
pricingTips.body: Responsive checks, cross-browser testing, and client feedback cycles take more time than the build itself on some projects. Include 15-25% for them.

pricingTips.title: Set an expiry date
pricingTips.body: Webflow plan prices and your availability change. A 14-30 day validity period keeps old quotes from coming back at outdated prices.

faqs.question: How detailed should a Webflow estimate be?
faqs.answer: Detailed enough to list pages, CMS collections, integrations, and revision rounds, with a price per phase. One or two pages is usually enough. A single total with no breakdown invites scope disputes.

faqs.question: Should I charge for the estimate or discovery?
faqs.answer: A short call is typically free. For large builds or migrations that need a site audit or technical review, many developers charge a paid discovery phase, often $500-2,000, and credit it toward the project.

faqs.question: What happens if the client changes the design after I quote?
faqs.answer: Say in the estimate that the price assumes the approved design. Design changes after build starts are billed as change orders at your hourly rate or a new fixed price, agreed before work continues.

faqs.question: Can I give a range instead of a fixed price?
faqs.answer: Yes, when scope is uncertain, such as with a migration or a site you have not seen. Give a range with a stated cap, and say what would move the price to the top or bottom of it.

wedding-photographer.intro: Wedding photographers are usually solo operators or small studios that shoot weddings, engagement sessions, and related events, then deliver edited galleries and sometimes albums or prints. Invoices typically cover a booking retainer, a package or hourly coverage fee, add-ons like second shooters or albums, and a final balance due before the wedding day.
wedding-photographer.pricingModel: Most wedding photographers sell packages rather than billing purely by the hour. A package usually bundles a set number of coverage hours (commonly 6 to 10), an edited digital gallery, a print release, and sometimes an engagement session. Add-ons such as a second shooter, extra hours, albums, parent albums, prints, and rush editing are priced separately. Some photographers quote hourly rates for short elopements or micro-weddings, typically with a minimum of 2 to 4 hours. Travel is often billed separately: mileage or a flat fee for local trips, and airfare, lodging, and a day rate for destination weddings. Payment is structured in stages, with a non-refundable retainer to hold the date, followed by one or more installments, and the balance due before the wedding. Pricing is tied to demand, so Saturdays in peak season (May to October in much of the US) often cost more than Fridays, Sundays, or off-season dates.

rates.service: Wedding coverage package (6-8 hours, one photographer)
Full-day wedding coverage (8-10 hours, with second shooter)

items.description: Wedding photography package: 8 hours of coverage, one photographer, edited online gallery, print release
Second shooter, 8 hours
Engagement session (60 minutes, 1 location, 40+ edited images)
Additional coverage past contracted end time (reception extended)
Travel to venue (62 miles each way, 124 miles total)
Retainer received on contract signing (non-refundable)

sampleInvoice.notes: Balance due 30 days before the wedding date for the package, with any additional hours due within 7 days of the event. Late balances are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee. The gallery is delivered once the final balance is paid. Payment accepted by card, ACH, or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wedding date, venue name, and city
invoiceChecklist.why: Photographers book many couples a year, and the date and venue tie the invoice to the correct contract and event.

invoiceChecklist.item: Package name and contracted coverage hours
invoiceChecklist.why: Spelling out the hours and start and end times makes it clear what is included and what counts as overtime.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer paid and date received
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing the retainer as a credit proves what has already been paid and avoids confusion about the remaining balance.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons (second shooter, extra hours, albums, prints)
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating add-ons from the base package makes changes after booking traceable to a client request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Travel charges with mileage or lodging detail
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients are more likely to accept travel costs when they see the distance, rate, or hotel nights behind the number.

invoiceChecklist.item: Installment schedule and final due date
invoiceChecklist.why: Putting due dates on the invoice, ahead of the wedding, protects you from chasing payment while editing or after delivery.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed contract
invoiceChecklist.why: Linking to the contract date or number supports your cancellation, retainer, and late-fee terms if a dispute comes up.

wedding-photographer.paymentTerms: The standard structure is a non-refundable retainer of 25 to 50 percent at signing to reserve the date, with the remainder due in one or two installments and the final balance due 2 to 6 weeks before the wedding. Collecting in full before the event is common because you cannot reasonably chase a newlywed couple afterward and the date is already blocked. Add-ons ordered after the wedding, such as albums and prints, are typically paid in full before ordering. Late fees of 1 to 2 percent per month are common, as are written terms allowing you to withhold the gallery until the balance is paid. Most photographers accept cards, ACH transfers, and checks, and some pass along card processing fees or offer payment plans with automatic monthly charges.

tips.title: Collect the full balance before the wedding
tips.body: Setting the final due date 2 to 4 weeks before the event removes the risk of post-wedding nonpayment and keeps your cash flow steady through the busy season.

tips.title: Define overtime in the contract and on the invoice
tips.body: Receptions often run late. State your hourly overtime rate and bill it as its own line item so the extra charge is clear and not seen as a surprise.

tips.title: Keep retainers non-refundable and say why
tips.body: You turn away other couples for that date, so the retainer pays for that lost opportunity. A short explanation on the invoice and contract reduces pushback if plans change.

tips.title: Bill albums and prints separately after delivery
tips.body: Keep post-wedding product orders on their own invoices. This keeps your wedding package paperwork clean and lets you collect product costs up front before ordering from the lab.

tips.title: Track mileage and travel costs as you go
tips.body: Keep records of drive distances, flights, and hotel receipts. They support what you bill the client and your own business expense deductions at tax time.

faqs.question: Should I invoice the full package amount at booking?
faqs.answer: Most photographers invoice a retainer at booking, commonly 25 to 50 percent, and schedule the remainder in one or more installments with the final payment due before the wedding. Full prepayment at booking is allowed, but it is more common for lower-priced packages or elopements.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on wedding photography?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Some states tax photography services or the tangible products you deliver, such as prints and albums, while others do not tax services at all. Check with your state's department of revenue or a local accountant for how it applies to digital galleries, prints, and albums.

faqs.question: Can I hold the gallery until the balance is paid?
faqs.answer: Yes, if your contract says so. Many photographers deliver the gallery only after the final balance is paid, which is easiest when the full balance is due before the wedding. State this in the contract and on the invoice.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a second shooter?
faqs.answer: Either include the second shooter in a named package or list it as a separate line item with the hours covered. If you pay an associate or contractor, the billed amount should cover their pay, your editing time, and your overhead.

faqs.question: What if the couple cancels or reschedules?
faqs.answer: Your contract should set the terms. Typically the retainer is non-refundable, and later cancellations may owe a larger share of the balance. Rescheduling is often allowed once, subject to availability, and may keep the retainer as a credit. Have your contract reviewed locally, since enforceability varies.

estimate.intro: Wedding photographers send a quote or proposal after an initial inquiry or consultation, usually before the couple has decided on a photographer. Couples compare package contents, hours of coverage, editing style, delivery timeline, and the total cost including travel and extras.

scopeChecklist.item: Hours of coverage and start and end times
scopeChecklist.why: Couples often assume coverage continues until the last dance. Stating exact hours avoids disputes about overtime.
The difference between one photographer and two affects coverage of simultaneous moments and the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Deliverables: number of images, gallery format, and print release
scopeChecklist.why: Clients should know whether they receive a full gallery or a curated set, and how they can print or share the images.
Editing turnaround, typically 4 to 12 weeks for weddings, sets expectations. Rush delivery can be priced as an add-on.
Spell out whether the engagement session, bridal portraits, or a rehearsal dinner are part of the price or optional.
Out-of-town weddings add cost. Say whether travel is included, flat, or billed at actual cost, and who covers lodging and venue access fees.

scopeChecklist.item: Retainer, payment schedule, and quote expiration date
scopeChecklist.why: Dates in high demand are booked quickly, so a clear expiration date and retainer terms encourage a decision and secure the date.

pricingTips.title: Offer two or three clear packages
pricingTips.body: Tiered packages by coverage hours make it easy for couples to compare, and most pick a middle option. Keep the differences visible: hours, second shooter, engagement session, and album.

pricingTips.title: Price Saturdays in peak season higher
pricingTips.body: Saturdays between May and October are in highest demand. Many photographers add a premium or set higher minimums for those dates and discount Fridays, Sundays, and off-season weddings.

pricingTips.title: Build in unpaid time
pricingTips.body: A wedding takes more than the coverage hours: consultations, planning calls, travel, culling, editing, and delivery. Divide your target income by the realistic total hours when setting package prices.

pricingTips.title: Quote add-ons as menu items
pricingTips.body: List extra hours, albums, and second shooters with set prices so couples can add them later without renegotiating, and so your final invoice matches the original quote.

faqs.question: Should I post my prices publicly or send them on request?
faqs.answer: Either approach works. Publishing a starting price filters out mismatched inquiries and saves time, while sending full pricing after a conversation lets you tailor packages. Whichever you choose, the quote itself should be written and specific.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Two to four weeks is common. Because a wedding date can only be sold once, set an expiration date and make it clear that the date is not held until the contract and retainer are received.

faqs.question: Is a quote the same as a contract?
faqs.answer: No. A quote is an offer of price and scope, while a contract is the signed agreement covering terms like cancellation, copyright, liability, and delivery. Many photographers combine them into one proposal, but the signed contract is what binds both sides.

faqs.question: What if the couple wants to change the package after accepting the quote?
faqs.answer: Changes before the contract is signed can be re-quoted. After signing, handle changes in a written amendment or updated invoice, such as adding hours or a second shooter, so the final price reflects what was agreed.

wedding-planner.intro: Wedding planners coordinate the planning and execution of weddings, from full-service planning over many months to partial planning and day-of coordination. They invoice couples, and sometimes parents or a corporate sponsor, for planning fees, coordination packages, design work, and occasionally vendor costs paid on the client's behalf.
wedding-planner.pricingModel: Most wedding planners sell packages at a flat fee rather than billing hourly. Common packages are full planning, partial planning, month-of or day-of coordination, and design-only or destination planning. Full planning is often priced as a flat fee or as a percentage of the total wedding budget, typically 10 to 20 percent, often with a minimum fee. Day-of coordination is priced flat and usually includes a set number of planning meetings, a venue walkthrough, and the rehearsal. Add-ons such as extra assistants, additional site visits, travel, rehearsal dinner planning, or welcome-party coordination are billed separately. Hourly rates are used for consulting, one-off vendor sourcing, or work outside the package scope. Fees are usually paid in installments tied to milestones, with a non-refundable retainer to book the date.

rates.service: Extra venue visit or vendor meeting outside package
Destination wedding travel and planning surcharge
Rehearsal dinner or welcome event coordination

items.description: Partial wedding planning package (vendor referrals, budget and timeline management, design guidance, 6 planning meetings)
Wedding day coordination, up to 10 hours, including rehearsal
Additional day-of assistant
Extra vendor tasting and venue visit beyond package
Welcome event coordination

sampleInvoice.notes: Wedding date: October 11, 2025. Retainer of $1,000 received on signing is credited to this invoice. Remaining balance is due 30 days before the wedding date. Vendor payments are made directly by the client to each vendor. Late payments are subject to a 1.5% monthly fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Wedding date, venue, and package name
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties the invoice to a specific event and contract so the couple and any third-party payer know exactly what is being billed.

invoiceChecklist.item: Milestone or installment schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: Most planners are paid in stages (retainer, midpoint, final), so each invoice should show what was paid, what is due now, and what remains.

invoiceChecklist.item: Retainer credit and non-refundable status
invoiceChecklist.why: Clarifies that the booking deposit was applied and prevents disputes if the date changes or the couple cancels.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-on services itemized separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Extra meetings, assistants, rehearsal dinner coordination, and travel fall outside the base package and are easy to dispute if lumped together.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts
invoiceChecklist.why: Mileage, parking, printed materials, décor supplies, or items you purchased for the client should be listed individually with receipts available on request.

invoiceChecklist.item: Payer name if different from the couple
invoiceChecklist.why: Parents or a company often pay, and the invoice and receipt need to name the right person for their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contract date and reference number
invoiceChecklist.why: Links the invoice to the signed agreement that defines scope, cancellation terms, and payment deadlines.

wedding-planner.paymentTerms: Planners typically collect a non-refundable retainer of 25 to 50 percent at signing to hold the date, with the balance split into one or two installments and the final payment due two to four weeks before the wedding. Some planners require full payment before the event so they are not chasing money after the couple leaves for the honeymoon. Late fees of 1.5 percent per month are common if stated in the contract. Payment is usually accepted by check, ACH transfer, or card, and card fees are sometimes passed on to the client or built into the fee. Add-ons and expenses are often billed as they occur, with payment due in 7 to 14 days.

tips.title: Keep vendor money out of your invoice when you can
tips.body: Have clients pay caterers, florists, and venues directly. If you do pay vendors and bill the client, list those costs separately from your fee, keep receipts, and be clear in the contract about who is responsible if a vendor cancels.

tips.title: Tie each payment to a date, not a feeling
tips.body: Write fixed due dates into the contract and invoice, such as 90 days and 30 days before the wedding. Couples are busy and emotional in the final weeks, and a clear schedule keeps you from having to ask for money at the worst time.

tips.title: Define what day-of coordination includes
tips.body: Spell out the hours covered, the number of meetings, and whether the rehearsal is included. Weddings that run late are common, so state an overtime rate and bill it on the final invoice.

tips.title: Bill scope changes as they happen
tips.body: When a couple adds a welcome party, moves the venue, or doubles the guest count, send an updated invoice or change order right away instead of waiting until the end.

tips.title: Collect the final payment before the event
tips.body: Once the wedding is over, the leverage to collect is gone and the client is focused on other things. Make the last installment due before the wedding day.

faqs.question: Should I charge a flat fee or a percentage of the wedding budget?
faqs.answer: Both are common. Flat fees are simpler and easier for couples to understand. A percentage, usually 10 to 20 percent, scales with the work on larger weddings but can create friction if the budget changes. Many planners use a percentage to set a flat fee with a minimum.

faqs.question: Is the retainer refundable?
faqs.answer: Most planners make it non-refundable because it takes your date off the market. State that clearly in the contract and on the invoice, and check your state's rules on deposits and cancellation terms.

faqs.question: How do I bill for vendor purchases I make on the client's behalf?
faqs.answer: List them as separate reimbursable lines, not as part of your fee, and attach receipts. If you add a markup, disclose it in your contract. Many planners avoid this by having clients pay vendors directly.

faqs.question: When should the final invoice be due?
faqs.answer: Usually 2 to 4 weeks before the wedding. Collecting before the event avoids chasing payment after the couple returns from the honeymoon.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on my planning services?
faqs.answer: It depends on your state. Many states do not tax services, but some tax certain event services or goods you resell. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

estimate.intro: Wedding planners send a proposal or quote after an initial consultation, once they know the date, guest count, venue, and level of help the couple wants. Couples usually compare several planners, so they look at package contents, how many meetings are included, and whether the fee covers the wedding day or only planning.

scopeChecklist.item: Package type and what is included
scopeChecklist.why: Full, partial, and day-of services are very different. List the number of meetings, vendor sourcing, design help, and timeline creation so the couple knows what they are buying.

scopeChecklist.item: Wedding date, venue, and estimated guest count
scopeChecklist.why: Fees and workload depend on these. If the guest count or venue changes materially, you have a basis to revise the quote.

scopeChecklist.item: Hours of wedding day coverage and overtime rate
scopeChecklist.why: Receptions often run late. Defining the covered window and an hourly overtime rate prevents disputes on the night.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of assistants and staff provided
scopeChecklist.why: Larger weddings need a lead plus assistants. Stating who will be there avoids confusion about who is actually working the event.

scopeChecklist.item: Exclusions such as vendor costs, rentals, and travel
scopeChecklist.why: Couples often assume the planner's fee covers everything. Clearly state that vendor payments, rentals, and travel are separate.
Showing installment dates and the retainer up front sets expectations and reduces back-and-forth at signing.
Weddings are postponed and canceled. Specify what is refundable and what happens if the date moves.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as day-of, partial, and full planning, so the couple can choose a level of help. This keeps the conversation on scope rather than on negotiating a single price.

pricingTips.title: Set a minimum fee on percentage pricing
pricingTips.body: If you price at a percentage of budget, set a floor so a small budget does not leave you underpaid for a similar amount of work.

pricingTips.title: Price your time realistically
pricingTips.body: Full planning often takes 100 to 250 hours over a year. Divide your fee by estimated hours to check that the effective hourly rate makes sense after expenses and taxes.

pricingTips.title: Quote travel separately
pricingTips.body: For destination weddings, itemize flights, lodging, and per diem or add a flat travel fee so the couple can see what drives the total.

faqs.question: How long should a wedding planning quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Often 14 to 30 days. Wedding dates are limited, so state that the date is not held until the contract is signed and the retainer is paid.

faqs.question: Should I give a quote before meeting the couple?
faqs.answer: Share a price range or package menu, but give a firm quote after a consultation. You need the date, venue, guest count, and what they want help with.

faqs.question: What if the couple's budget changes after I send the quote?
faqs.answer: If you quoted a flat fee, it stays the same unless the scope changes. If you used a percentage, specify in the proposal whether the fee adjusts when the budget changes.

faqs.question: Can I include vendor costs in my estimate?
faqs.answer: You can list expected vendor costs as a separate section for budgeting, but make clear they are estimates paid to the vendors and not part of your fee.

welder.intro: Welders who work for themselves or run small shops bill for fabrication, structural and repair work, mobile welding calls, and custom projects like gates, railings, trailers, and equipment repair. Clients include homeowners, farms, contractors, property managers, and manufacturers. An invoice needs to cover labor, materials, consumables, travel, and any certifications or inspections tied to the job.
welder.pricingModel: Most independent welders charge hourly for repair and mobile work, often with a trip charge or a one-hour minimum. Shop fabrication is commonly quoted as a flat price per project based on estimated labor plus materials, with a markup on steel, aluminum, or stainless of roughly 10-30 percent. Gas, wire, rod, grinding discs, and other consumables are billed either as a flat percentage of labor or as a line item. Certified or code welding (structural, pipe, pressure vessel) earns higher rates than general repair, and TIG on aluminum or stainless costs more than MIG or stick on mild steel. Mobile rigs carry a premium for the truck, machine, and fuel. Large jobs may be billed in stages, with a deposit to cover material purchases.

rates.service: Trip or travel charge for mobile calls

rates.unit: percent of labor or flat fee

items.description: Mobile welding labor: repair cracked frame on skid steer bucket
Trip charge, 25 miles one way
1/2 in. A36 plate and flat bar for reinforcement
Hardfacing rod and 7018 electrodes
Shielding gas, grinding and cutting discs

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Welds on this repair were visually inspected; no code certification was requested. Work warrantied for 30 days against workmanship defects, excluding misuse or overload. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Job location and equipment or item repaired
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile and repair jobs often involve several sites or machines, and a clear description ties the charge to specific work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Base metal, filler, and process used (MIG, TIG, stick, flux-core)
invoiceChecklist.why: Shows the client what they paid for and supports different rates for aluminum, stainless, or certified work.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor hours separated from travel time
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients often question drive time, so listing it separately, with the trip charge or mileage, heads off disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: Materials and consumables as line items
invoiceChecklist.why: Steel prices change, and itemizing materials, gas, and wire shows where the money went and lets you apply a markup openly.

invoiceChecklist.item: Welder certifications, procedure numbers, or code standard (AWS D1.1, ASME)
invoiceChecklist.why: Contractors and inspectors may require proof the work met a specified code, and it supports a higher rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: PO number, job number, or work order
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial and industrial customers usually cannot pay without a reference number matching their records.

invoiceChecklist.item: Sales tax treatment and resale or exemption certificate on file
invoiceChecklist.why: Tax rules for materials and fabrication labor vary by state, so show how tax was handled and keep exemption paperwork if applicable.

welder.paymentTerms: Small repair jobs for homeowners and farms are often paid on completion by card, check, or cash app, sometimes before the truck leaves. Custom fabrication usually requires a deposit of 30-50 percent to buy material, with the balance due on delivery or pickup. Commercial accounts commonly run net 15 or net 30, and many shops add a late fee of 1-2 percent per month, stated in writing before the work starts. Larger projects can be billed in progress payments tied to milestones such as material delivery, fit-up, and final install. Some welders hold finished items until payment clears, which should be stated in the quote.

tips.title: Charge for the whole clock, not just arc time
tips.body: Fit-up, layout, cutting, grinding, setup, cleanup, and drive time are real labor. Bill an hourly rate that covers the whole job, or quote a flat price that does.

tips.title: Take a deposit on any job that needs material
tips.body: Steel, stainless, and aluminum are paid for up front by you. A deposit of 30-50 percent protects you if the customer backs out of a custom piece that no one else can use.

tips.title: Set a minimum call-out charge
tips.body: Short repairs still cost you the drive, the setup, and fuel for the rig. A one-hour minimum plus a trip charge keeps small jobs from losing money.

tips.title: Document change orders in writing
tips.body: Customers often add a bracket, a second gate, or extra reinforcement mid-job. Send a short message or revised line item before doing the extra work and include it on the final invoice.

tips.title: Track material receipts by job
tips.body: Keep supplier receipts matched to each job number. It makes markup defensible, speeds up commercial billing, and simplifies your taxes.

faqs.question: Should I charge by the hour or by the job?
faqs.answer: Hourly works best for repairs and unknowns, like a cracked frame where the extent of damage is unclear. Flat pricing suits fabrication with a clear drawing and known material list. If you quote flat, build in time for fit-up, finishing, and a margin for surprises.

faqs.question: Can I mark up steel and materials?
faqs.answer: Yes, most shops do. A markup of 10-30 percent is common to cover sourcing, cutting waste, delivery, and price changes. Show materials as a line item and be consistent so clients are not surprised.

faqs.question: How do I bill for consumables like gas, wire, and grinding discs?
faqs.answer: Either add a flat percentage of labor, often 5-15 percent, or list gas, wire, and discs as separate items. A flat consumables line is simpler on small jobs, and itemizing is better on long jobs with heavy wire or gas use.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on welding work?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and on whether the job is a repair, new fabrication, or a construction contract. Many states tax materials, and some tax fabrication or repair labor. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and keep any customer exemption certificates.

faqs.question: What if a customer refuses to pay for a finished repair?
faqs.answer: Start with a written reminder that cites the invoice, the agreed price, and the due date. In many states, you can also file a mechanic's lien on certain types of construction work, or hold fabricated items until paid if your quote said so. For larger balances, consider small claims court or a demand letter.

estimate.intro: Welders send estimates for custom fabrication, structural work, installs, and larger repairs where the customer wants a price before approving the job. Customers usually compare total price, material grade, finish, lead time, and whether the welder carries insurance and certifications. A clear written quote also protects you when steel prices change or the scope grows.

scopeChecklist.item: Drawings, dimensions, or a clear description of the finished piece
scopeChecklist.why: Gates, railings, and brackets are easy to misunderstand. A sketch or dimensions with sign-off prevents arguments about size and design.
A36 steel, galvanized, stainless 304, and 6061 aluminum differ widely in cost and workability, so the quote must state what is included.

scopeChecklist.item: Welding process and any code or inspection requirements
scopeChecklist.why: Certified or inspected welds take more time and documentation, and the cost should be agreed to before work starts.

scopeChecklist.item: Surface prep and finish (grind, paint, powder coat, galvanize)
scopeChecklist.why: Finishing is often outsourced or time-consuming. State what is included and who pays for third-party coating.
On-site install requires travel, lifting, anchoring, and sometimes permits, which may not be included in a shop price.

scopeChecklist.item: Price validity period and material price escalation
scopeChecklist.why: Metal prices move, so state how long the quote holds and what happens if material costs rise before the order is placed.
Sets expectations on when you buy material, start work, and expect payment, and shows lead time clearly.

pricingTips.title: Build the quote from labor hours plus materials
pricingTips.body: Estimate cutting, fit-up, welding, grinding, and finishing hours separately, then add materials, consumables, and outside services. Quoting from a total feeling instead of this breakdown is how fabrication jobs lose money.

pricingTips.title: Add a contingency for repair work
pricingTips.body: Hidden damage, rust, or contaminated metal can double the work. For repairs, quote an estimated range or hourly with a cap, and state that you will contact the customer before exceeding it.

pricingTips.title: Offer material options
pricingTips.body: Give a choice such as painted mild steel versus galvanized or stainless. Customers can pick based on budget, and the choice documents what they approved.

pricingTips.title: Charge for estimating on complex jobs
pricingTips.body: For jobs needing drawings, engineering review, or multiple site visits, charge a design or estimate fee that is credited toward the work if the customer accepts.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Quick quotes for simple jobs are normally free. For complex projects that need site visits, drawings, or takeoffs, many welders charge a fee and credit it to the final bill if the customer hires them.

faqs.question: How long should a quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to thirty days is common for fabrication because metal prices change. If the job relies on a large steel purchase, shorten it or add a clause that lets you adjust for material cost changes.

faqs.question: What if the job takes longer than the estimate?
faqs.answer: A flat quote means you absorb overruns unless the customer changes the scope. For hourly or repair work, give a range and agree to check in before going past it. Put any scope additions in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed estimate before ordering material?
faqs.answer: For custom work, yes. Get a signed quote and a deposit before buying material so you are not stuck with cut-to-size steel if the customer cancels.

window-cleaning.intro: Window cleaners, from solo operators with a squeegee and a ladder to small crews running residential and storefront routes, send invoices after completing interior and exterior glass cleaning. Typical line items include per-pane or per-window cleaning, screen and track cleaning, hard water stain removal, post-construction cleanup, and high-access work such as ladder, pole, or lift jobs.
window-cleaning.pricingModel: Residential window cleaning is most often priced per pane or per window, with add-ons for screens, tracks, and sills. Many cleaners also set a job minimum (often $125-200) to cover travel and setup. Commercial and storefront work is usually priced as a flat fee per visit on a recurring schedule (weekly, monthly, quarterly), or per square foot of glass for large buildings. Jobs with difficult access, such as third-story windows, steep roofs, or French panes with many small lites, are priced higher per pane or billed hourly. Stain removal, paint and sticker scraping, and construction debris cleanup are usually billed separately by the hour or per window because they take far longer than routine cleaning. Many businesses offer discounts for exterior-only work or recurring service plans.

rates.service: Standard residential windows, interior and exterior

rates.range: $2-6 per small lite, or $15-35 per window

rates.service: Second-story or high-access work (ladder, pole, lift)

items.description: Exterior and interior window cleaning, 2-story home (standard panes)
Screen and track cleaning
Hard water stain removal, west-facing windows
Sliding glass door, interior and exterior
Second-story ladder access surcharge

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of service. Please report any streaks or missed spots within 48 hours and we will return to correct them at no charge. Hard water stains may not be fully removable on etched glass. Accepted: check, ACH, or card.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service address and date of service
invoiceChecklist.why: Many customers have multiple properties, and recurring clients need a record of which visit the invoice covers.

invoiceChecklist.item: Pane or window count by type
invoiceChecklist.why: A count (for example 32 standard panes, 2 sliding doors) lets customers see how the total was reached and avoids disputes over what was cleaned.

invoiceChecklist.item: Scope: interior, exterior, or both
invoiceChecklist.why: Exterior-only and in/out cleaning are priced differently, so the invoice should match what was quoted.

invoiceChecklist.item: Add-ons listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Screens, tracks, sills, stain removal, and scraping take extra time and should be visible as their own lines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Access surcharges or equipment used
invoiceChecklist.why: Ladder, water-fed pole, or lift work carries extra cost and risk, and noting it supports the higher rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Business license and insurance details
invoiceChecklist.why: Commercial clients and property managers often require proof of general liability coverage, and some jurisdictions require a local business license (check your local rules).

invoiceChecklist.item: Recurring service schedule
invoiceChecklist.why: For routes such as monthly or quarterly storefront cleaning, noting the schedule and next visit date prevents confusion about billing cycles.

window-cleaning.paymentTerms: Residential customers commonly pay at completion by card, check, or digital payment, often right at the door. For larger jobs such as post-construction cleanup or multi-story buildings, a deposit of 25-50% is common, with the balance due on completion. Commercial and property management accounts typically run net 15 or net 30, and many require a purchase order number or vendor paperwork. Recurring accounts are often billed monthly in one invoice covering all visits. Late fees of 1.5% per month are common if stated in advance, but many window cleaners offer a small discount for prepaying a season of service instead.

tips.title: Set and enforce a job minimum
tips.body: A 10-window job can take as long to drive to and set up as a 30-window job. A minimum of $125-200 keeps small jobs from costing you money.

tips.title: Price difficult windows separately
tips.body: Divided-lite windows, hard-to-reach panes, and heavily soiled glass take much longer. Add a per-window surcharge or switch to hourly so slow jobs do not eat your margin.

tips.title: Photograph stains and damage before you start
tips.body: Etched glass, failed seals, scratches, and mineral deposits can look like your fault afterward. Dated photos protect you if a customer disputes the result.

tips.title: Move residential customers to recurring plans
tips.body: Offer semi-annual or quarterly service at a modest discount. Recurring jobs are faster to clean, need less quoting, and give you predictable income.

tips.title: Bill add-ons before you leave
tips.body: If you scrape paint or clean screens that were not in the original quote, tell the customer on site and note it on the invoice so the final total is not a surprise.

faqs.question: Should I charge per pane or per window?
faqs.answer: Per pane is more accurate for homes with varied window styles, since a large picture window and a small divided window are not equal work. Per window is simpler and works for uniform homes. Either way, state the unit clearly on the invoice.

faqs.question: Do I need to charge sales tax on window cleaning?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Some states tax cleaning or building maintenance services and others do not, and rules can differ for residential and commercial work. Check with your state department of revenue or a local accountant.

faqs.question: How do I invoice recurring storefront customers?
faqs.answer: Most window cleaners send a monthly invoice listing each visit date and the flat fee per visit. Include the schedule, any extra cleanings, and the payment terms so the client knows what to expect.

faqs.question: Can I charge extra for hard water stains?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stain removal takes special products and much more time, and results are not guaranteed on etched glass. Quote it as a separate line item, ideally before starting, and note the limitations on the invoice.

faqs.question: What if a customer says the windows look streaky after I leave?
faqs.answer: Most professionals offer a short callback window, often 24-72 hours, to fix issues at no charge. Put that policy in the invoice notes so expectations are clear, and photograph the work before leaving.

estimate.intro: Window cleaners usually send an estimate before the first visit for a home, a post-construction job, or a recurring commercial account. Customers often compare several quotes, so they look at price per pane, whether interior and exterior are included, and whether screens and tracks are part of the price.

scopeChecklist.item: Window and pane count with types
scopeChecklist.why: Counting standard panes, French or divided-lite windows, sliders, and skylights sets the price and avoids disputes on the day.
Customers often assume both are included. Spell out which sides are being cleaned.
These are commonly add-ons. List whether they are in or out of the quote.
Second- and third-story windows, steep terrain, and lift requirements can change both price and safety planning.
Hard water, paint overspray, stickers, and construction residue take extra time. State what is included and what is billed extra if found on site.
Etched glass, failed seals, and scratches cannot be cleaned away. Say so to avoid being blamed for pre-existing damage.

scopeChecklist.item: Schedule, weather policy, and quote validity
scopeChecklist.why: Rain, freezing temperatures, and high wind delay work. Give an expiration date and rescheduling terms.

pricingTips.title: Count before you quote
pricingTips.body: Walk the property or use photos to count panes yourself rather than trusting the customer's estimate. An off-by-ten count on a large home can cost you a half day.

pricingTips.title: Give good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Offer exterior only, interior and exterior, and a full package with screens and tracks. Customers often choose the middle or top tier when the options are clear.

pricingTips.title: Include a minimum and a re-quote clause
pricingTips.body: State your job minimum and note that the price may be adjusted if conditions differ from what was described, such as heavy stains or additional windows found on site.

pricingTips.title: Quote commercial work on a per-visit basis
pricingTips.body: For storefronts and offices, give a flat price per visit with a set frequency. Include a discount for committing to a longer agreement instead of cutting your hourly rate.

faqs.question: Should I charge for estimates?
faqs.answer: Most residential quotes are free, and many can be done by phone or photos. For large commercial buildings or work needing a site visit and safety plan, some companies charge a fee that is credited to the job if accepted.

faqs.question: How long should a window cleaning quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for residential work. Commercial quotes may be valid longer, but material and labor costs change, so set an expiry date.

faqs.question: What if the customer's window count is wrong?
faqs.answer: Include a line stating that the price is based on the listed count and will be adjusted if the actual number differs. Confirm any change with the customer before starting.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed agreement before starting?
faqs.answer: For one-time residential jobs, an accepted written quote is often enough. For recurring commercial service, a signed agreement covering frequency, price, insurance, and cancellation terms is a good idea.

window-installer.intro: Window installers replace and install windows in homes and light commercial buildings, either as independent contractors, small crews, or subcontractors for remodelers and window dealers. Invoices typically cover labor per window, the windows themselves if you supply them, trim and flashing materials, and disposal of old units.
window-installer.pricingModel: Most window installers price per window opening, with the price changing by window size, type, and story height. Labor-only installs are common when the homeowner or a dealer supplies the windows, while full-service jobs add the cost of the windows plus a markup, often 15 to 35 percent. Retrofit (insert) installs into an existing frame cost less than full-frame replacements that involve removing trim, flashing, and sometimes repairing rot or framing. Extras are billed separately: interior and exterior trim, custom wraps, second-story or hard-to-reach access, lead-safe work in pre-1978 homes, stucco or brick cutting, and haul-away. Large jobs are often quoted as a flat total with a deposit and progress payments, while small repairs and add-ons are billed hourly. Subcontractors working for a general contractor usually bill per opening or on a schedule of values.

rates.service: Large picture window or slider install (labor only)
Interior casing and exterior trim wrap

items.description: Full-frame replacement, double-hung vinyl windows (labor, includes flashing tape and foam insulation)
Large sliding window install, 72" x 48" (labor)
Vinyl windows supplied per order #4471 (8 double-hung, 1 slider)
Interior casing and paint-ready trim
Sill rot repair, rear bedroom
Old window removal and disposal

sampleInvoice.notes: Deposit of $3,500 received on 03/04 and applied. Balance due within 10 days of completion. Windows carry manufacturer warranty per attached documentation; installation is warranted for 2 years against leaks caused by workmanship. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month.

invoiceChecklist.item: Window count, locations, and sizes
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing each opening (for example, "Master bedroom, 36x60 double-hung") prevents disputes about what was installed and helps with warranty claims later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Manufacturer, model, and order number
invoiceChecklist.why: If the client or you purchased the windows, the brand and order details tie the invoice to the product warranty and make reorders or defect claims easier.

invoiceChecklist.item: Labor vs. materials breakdown
invoiceChecklist.why: Separating installation labor from supplied windows and materials helps with sales tax treatment, which varies by state, and shows clients what they are paying for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Contractor license number and insurance info
invoiceChecklist.why: Many states and cities require a license number on contracts and invoices, and clients and insurers often ask for proof of coverage.

invoiceChecklist.item: Change orders and extras
invoiceChecklist.why: Rot repair, unexpected framing issues, and trim upgrades found mid-job should appear as separate lines referencing the signed change order.

invoiceChecklist.item: Lead-safe or permit notes
invoiceChecklist.why: For pre-1978 homes, note any lead-safe work practices used, and include permit numbers where your area requires them for window replacement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Deposits and progress payments received
invoiceChecklist.why: Showing amounts already paid and the remaining balance avoids confusion on large jobs billed in stages.

invoiceChecklist.item: Warranty terms for workmanship
invoiceChecklist.why: A clear statement of how long your install is covered, and what is excluded, sets expectations before a leak call comes in.

window-installer.paymentTerms: Window jobs often require a deposit of 30 to 50 percent at signing, mainly to cover the cost of ordering custom windows, which are usually non-refundable once in production. On larger projects, a second payment may be due when windows are delivered, with the balance due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Small labor-only jobs are commonly paid on the day of completion. Common payment methods include checks, ACH transfer, and credit cards, sometimes with a card processing fee passed on where allowed. State your late fee and any final-payment-before-warranty policy in the contract. Check your state's rules on deposit limits for home improvement contracts, as some states cap them.

tips.title: Collect the deposit before ordering windows
tips.body: Custom-sized windows cannot be returned, so never order until the deposit clears. Put the non-refundable nature of custom orders in writing.

tips.title: Bill materials at cost plus markup
tips.body: Mark up supplied windows, trim stock, and sealants to cover ordering time, delivery, handling, and the risk of damaged or mis-sized units. Itemize the window cost so clients see the product price.

tips.title: Document conditions before you start
tips.body: Take photos of rot, water damage, and existing interior finishes. This supports extra charges for repairs and protects you if clients later claim you caused damage.

tips.title: Invoice change orders as you go
tips.body: Get written approval for hidden damage repairs or upgrades before doing the work, then list them as separate invoice lines so the final bill matches what was agreed.

tips.title: Hold final payment until walkthrough is complete
tips.body: Do a walkthrough on completion day, fix punch-list items, and collect the balance at sign-off so small touch-ups do not turn into weeks of delayed payment.

faqs.question: Should I charge per window or by the hour?
faqs.answer: Per window is standard for installs because it is easy for clients to compare and rewards efficiency. Use hourly rates for repairs, rot, and anything where the scope is unknown until the wall is open.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on windows and labor?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In many states, materials you sell are taxable, while installation labor on real property may not be, and some states treat contractors as the final consumer of materials. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant.

faqs.question: What if the client supplies their own windows?
faqs.answer: Bill labor only and state on the invoice that the client supplied the windows. Add a line in your contract that you are not responsible for defects, wrong sizes, or manufacturer warranty on client-supplied product.

faqs.question: Can I charge a restocking or reorder fee if a window is the wrong size?
faqs.answer: If the error comes from the client's measurements or a change in order, yes, and your contract should say so. If you measured and ordered incorrectly, expect to absorb the cost, which is why many installers have clients sign off on measurements.

faqs.question: When is the final invoice due on a big window job?
faqs.answer: Most installers make it due on completion or within 7 to 14 days. Collecting at the final walkthrough works best because the client has just seen the finished work.

estimate.intro: Window installers usually give a written quote after an in-home measure and inspection, often for free on full-house jobs. Homeowners typically gather two to four quotes and compare window brand and grade, what is included in the labor, and the warranty offered.

scopeChecklist.why: List brand, series, size, style, glass package, color, and grid options for each opening so the quote can be compared accurately and the order matches.
State whether it is an insert replacement or full-frame, because the difference affects labor, trim, and how much of the wall is disturbed.
Spell out whether interior casing, exterior capping, caulking, and painting are in or out, since clients often assume they are included.
State that unforeseen rot or framing damage is billed separately and give an hourly or per-repair rate so surprises do not become disputes.
Note who pulls permits, whether lead-safe practices apply to older homes, and any HOA approval the client must obtain.
Custom windows often take 4 to 10 weeks, so give an expected delivery window and note that the install date depends on it.
State that old units are removed and disposed of, and describe both the manufacturer warranty and your labor warranty.

pricingTips.title: Price from measured openings
pricingTips.body: Quote only after measuring each window and checking wall condition. Phone or photo quotes lead to underestimates when you find stucco, brick molding, or out-of-square frames.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best options
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three window grades, such as basic vinyl, mid-grade vinyl, and fiberglass or wood-clad, lets clients choose by budget and often raises the average job size.

pricingTips.title: Build in material and supplier price changes
pricingTips.body: Window pricing can change between quote and order. Put a validity period of 15 to 30 days on the quote and note that pricing may be adjusted after that.

pricingTips.title: Show labor and product separately
pricingTips.body: A quote with the product price and install price on separate lines makes your labor look reasonable and helps clients who want to compare with a dealer-only price.

faqs.question: Should I charge for window estimates?
faqs.answer: Many installers measure and quote for free on full-job estimates. For small jobs, long drives, or consultations on complex repairs, a trip fee that is credited back if the client hires you is reasonable.

faqs.question: How long should a window quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Fifteen to 30 days is common, since manufacturer pricing and material costs change. State the expiry date on the quote.

faqs.question: Is a quote a fixed price?
faqs.answer: It can be, but include conditions: the price assumes normal wall conditions and the specified windows. Hidden rot, structural damage, or a change in product should trigger a written change order.

faqs.question: What deposit should I ask for in a quote?
faqs.answer: Many installers ask for 30 to 50 percent to cover ordering custom windows. Check your state's home improvement rules, since some states limit the deposit amount on residential contracts.

windshield-repair.intro: Windshield repair technicians fix chips, cracks, and damaged glass for individual drivers, fleets, dealerships, and insurance-referred customers. Many work solo from a mobile van, while others run a small shop with a few techs. Invoices typically cover resin chip repairs, crack repairs, full windshield replacement, mobile service fees, and add-ons such as ADAS recalibration or rain sensor transfer.
windshield-repair.pricingModel: Chip and crack repairs are usually a flat fee per repair, with a lower price for each additional chip on the same windshield. Full replacements are priced as a flat job total that combines the glass, moldings and clips, urethane adhesive, and labor, and the glass part is often marked up from your supplier cost. Mobile service is either built into the price or billed as a trip fee, with extra for long distances. ADAS camera recalibration is billed as a separate line, either static in-shop or dynamic on the road. Fleet and commercial accounts often get a negotiated per-repair rate or a volume discount. Insurance work is billed to the carrier or a third-party administrator at agreed schedules, with the customer paying any deductible or safety-related items directly.

rates.service: Windshield replacement (with rain sensor, heated or acoustic glass)

items.description: Windshield replacement, 2019 Honda CR-V, OEM-equivalent glass with rain sensor bracket, new molding and urethane
Forward camera static ADAS recalibration
Mobile service, on-site at customer's home
Chip repair on passenger side rear window tint area (not applicable) - wiper blade replacement
Glass disposal fee

sampleInvoice.notes: Do not drive the vehicle for at least 1 hour after installation. Leave retention tape on for 24 hours and avoid car washes for 48 hours. Workmanship warranty covers leaks and wind noise for as long as you own the vehicle. Payment due upon completion. Card, cash, and check accepted. Balance unpaid after 15 days is subject to a 1.5% monthly late fee.

invoiceChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, and VIN
invoiceChecklist.why: Windshields are specific to trim and options, so the VIN shows exactly which glass was installed and supports warranty or insurance claims.

invoiceChecklist.item: Glass part number and manufacturer (OEM, OEE, or aftermarket)
invoiceChecklist.why: Customers and insurers want to know the type and brand of glass, and it protects you if a dispute comes up about quality.

invoiceChecklist.item: Adhesive brand and safe drive-away time
invoiceChecklist.why: Documenting the urethane used and when the car is safe to drive shows you followed the adhesive manufacturer's guidelines.

invoiceChecklist.item: Itemized add-ons: moldings, clips, rain sensor gel pad, camera bracket
invoiceChecklist.why: These small parts are easy to forget and add real cost, so listing them prevents questions about the total.

invoiceChecklist.item: ADAS recalibration type and results
invoiceChecklist.why: Static or dynamic calibration is a separate service, and noting it with the date shows the safety system was handled.

invoiceChecklist.item: Service location and date
invoiceChecklist.why: Mobile work happens at homes and workplaces, and the address and date support trip fees and warranty start dates.

invoiceChecklist.item: Insurance claim number, deductible, and policy holder name
invoiceChecklist.why: Carriers and third-party administrators reject invoices without a claim reference, and the customer needs to see what they owe.

windshield-repair.paymentTerms: Most retail customers pay at completion by card, cash, or check, and mobile techs often take payment on site with a card reader. For special-order glass, some shops ask for a deposit of 25-50% when the part is ordered, especially for expensive or hard-to-source glass. Insurance jobs are usually billed to the carrier or administrator, which can take 30-60 days to pay, while the customer pays their deductible at the time of service. Fleet and commercial accounts are commonly net 15 or net 30. Late fees of 1-1.5% per month are common if stated on the invoice or agreement ahead of time.

tips.title: Collect the deductible on site
tips.body: When an insurance claim covers the job, collect the customer's deductible before you leave. Chasing a small balance weeks later costs more in time than it is worth.

tips.title: Bill ADAS recalibration as its own line
tips.body: Calibration takes equipment, space, and time. If you fold it into the glass price, you lose track of its cost and customers may push back on the total. A separate line makes the work visible.

tips.title: Photograph the damage before you start
tips.body: Take photos of existing chips, cracks, and dash or paint damage before work. Attach the notes to the job record so you can answer disputes quickly.

tips.title: Charge a cancellation or no-show fee for mobile jobs
tips.body: Driving to an empty driveway costs fuel and a slot in your day. State a trip fee for no-shows in your quote and on the invoice terms.

tips.title: Set a repair-to-replace credit policy
tips.body: If a chip repair fails and the customer upgrades to a replacement, many shops credit the repair fee toward the replacement. Write your policy down and show the credit as a line item.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on windshield repair?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. Many states tax parts but not labor, and some tax both. Replacement glass is usually taxable as a part, while repair labor may not be. Check with your state revenue department or an accountant, and show tax as its own line.

faqs.question: How do I invoice an insurance company for a glass claim?
faqs.answer: Include the claim number, policy holder name, vehicle VIN, date of loss, and an itemized list of parts and labor at the agreed rates. Many carriers route glass claims through a third-party administrator with its own portal or submission process, so follow their format.

faqs.question: Can I bill for chip repair if the chip cracks during the repair?
faqs.answer: Most techs state in their quote that repairs aim to stop spreading and improve appearance but do not guarantee the chip will not crack. If a crack occurs during repair, many shops still bill the repair fee and offer a replacement credit, but your written terms should say which applies.

faqs.question: What do I do if a customer disputes a leak after replacement?
faqs.answer: Refer to your workmanship warranty on the invoice, inspect the vehicle, and fix the leak at no charge if it is a workmanship problem. Keep photos and the invoice record showing the adhesive used and the installation date.

faqs.question: Do I need to put the warranty on the invoice?
faqs.answer: It is a good idea. Print the warranty terms or a short summary on the invoice so the customer has proof of coverage, and so you have a record of what you promised.

estimate.intro: Windshield technicians usually quote before work when a customer calls or texts for a price, when a fleet manager is comparing vendors, or when a replacement requires special-order glass. Customers compare the total price, the type of glass, whether the work is mobile, how soon it can be done, and what the warranty covers.

scopeChecklist.item: Vehicle year, make, model, trim, and VIN
scopeChecklist.why: Glass fit depends on options such as heads-up display, rain sensor, acoustic layer, and heating, so the quote must match the exact vehicle.

scopeChecklist.item: Glass type: OEM, OEE, or aftermarket
scopeChecklist.why: Prices and quality differ, and customers should know which grade they are paying for.

scopeChecklist.item: Repair or replace recommendation, with damage size and location
scopeChecklist.why: Chips in the driver's line of sight or cracks over a certain length may not be repairable, and writing the reason avoids disputes.
Many newer vehicles require camera recalibration after replacement, and it can add hundreds of dollars if not stated upfront.

scopeChecklist.item: Mobile service location and trip fee
scopeChecklist.why: Weather, parking, and a safe work area affect mobile jobs, and the fee should be clear before you travel.

scopeChecklist.item: Safe drive-away time and care instructions
scopeChecklist.why: Customers need to know how long the car is out of use and what to avoid, such as washing the car right away.

scopeChecklist.item: Quote expiration date and price assumptions
scopeChecklist.why: Glass costs change, and the price should be tied to a date and to the vehicle details given.

pricingTips.title: Quote a total, not just the glass
pricingTips.body: Customers compare totals. Include glass, moldings, adhesive, labor, calibration, and any mobile fee in one clear number so a competitor's lower glass-only price does not look like a better deal.

pricingTips.title: Offer good, better, best glass options
pricingTips.body: Give a price for aftermarket, OEE, and OEM glass when available. Letting the customer choose lowers the chance they walk away over price.

pricingTips.title: Verify options before locking the price
pricingTips.body: Ask for the VIN or a photo of the lower corner of the glass and the area behind the mirror. Wrong assumptions about sensors or cameras are a common reason quotes turn out too low.

pricingTips.title: Offer a repair price that leads to a sale
pricingTips.body: Chip repairs are often priced low to be affordable and to build trust. Mention that repairing early is cheaper than replacement, and note your credit policy if a repair does not hold.

faqs.question: Should I give windshield quotes over the phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, but make them conditional on the vehicle details. Ask for the VIN or year, make, model, trim, and options, and state that the final price may change if the glass features differ from what was described.

faqs.question: How long should a windshield quote be valid?
