faqs.answer: Seven to thirty days is common for retail quotes. Glass prices can shift, so put an expiration date on the quote, and shorten it for special-order or hard-to-find parts.

faqs.question: Do I charge for an estimate?
faqs.answer: Most windshield techs quote for free, since the damage is easy to assess from photos or a quick look. Some charge a fee for inspections that require travel, such as fleet assessments across multiple vehicles, and credit it if the customer books the work.

faqs.question: What if the final job costs more than the quote?
faqs.answer: Tell the customer before doing extra work and get their approval in writing or by text. Common surprises are rust under the molding, broken clips, or a sensor that needs replacing, so list these as possible extras in the quote.

wordpress-developer.intro: WordPress developers build and maintain sites on the WordPress platform. Most work solo or in small studios, and they bill for custom theme and plugin development, site builds, WooCommerce setups, speed and security work, migrations, and ongoing maintenance. Clients range from small businesses to agencies that subcontract overflow work.
wordpress-developer.pricingModel: Pricing varies by the type of work. Custom development and troubleshooting are often billed hourly, typically with a minimum block such as one hour or 15 minutes. Full site builds are usually a flat project fee, split into milestone payments, with a defined number of revision rounds. Ongoing care plans are sold as monthly retainers that cover updates, backups, uptime monitoring, and a set number of support hours. Many developers also pass through third-party costs such as premium plugin licenses, themes, hosting, and stock assets, either at cost or with a modest markup. Work outside the agreed scope, such as new features or extra page templates, is billed separately at the hourly rate. Agency subcontract work is often billed at a lower hourly rate in exchange for steady volume.

rates.service: Brochure site build (5-10 pages, existing theme)

items.description: Custom theme development: homepage, services, and contact templates (milestone 2 of 3)
Contact form integration and spam protection setup
Premium plugin license: SEO plugin, annual (billed at cost)
Out-of-scope work: add event calendar custom post type
Staging site setup and content migration

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Premium plugin license is registered to the client account and renews annually. Final milestone is due before launch to the live domain.

invoiceChecklist.item: Project name and milestone or phase
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with multi-payment projects need to see which stage this invoice covers, and it ties the charge back to the signed agreement.

invoiceChecklist.item: Site URL or staging URL
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients with several sites, and agencies with many client sites, need to know which one the work applies to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Hours logged with dates and task descriptions
invoiceChecklist.why: Hourly work gets questioned more than flat fees. Entries like 'debugged checkout redirect loop' hold up better than 'development'.

invoiceChecklist.item: Third-party costs listed separately
invoiceChecklist.why: Plugin licenses, themes, hosting, and domains should appear as their own lines so the client sees what is a pass-through cost and what is your labor.

invoiceChecklist.item: Out-of-scope work flagged as change requests
invoiceChecklist.why: Marking additions against the original scope shows why the total differs from the quote and prevents disputes.

invoiceChecklist.item: License ownership and renewal details
invoiceChecklist.why: If you purchase a plugin license, the client should know whose account it is under and when it renews, so they are not surprised later.

invoiceChecklist.item: Maintenance period covered
invoiceChecklist.why: Retainer invoices should state the month, what is included, and any hours used or rolled over.

invoiceChecklist.item: Client PO number or agency project code
invoiceChecklist.why: Agencies and larger organizations often cannot process an invoice without one.

wordpress-developer.paymentTerms: Most WordPress developers take a deposit of 30-50% before starting a site build, then bill the rest at milestones such as design approval, staging delivery, and launch. Many hold final files, admin credentials, or the go-live switch until the last payment clears. Hourly and one-off fixes are commonly invoiced on completion with net 7 to net 15 terms, while agencies may require net 30 or longer. Maintenance retainers are best billed monthly or annually in advance by card or ACH on a recurring basis. A late fee of 1-2% per month is common if stated in your contract. Payment is usually by ACH, card, or check.

tips.title: Hold launch until the final payment
tips.body: State in your contract that the site goes live, or that you hand over admin access and full backups, after the last milestone is paid. This gives you leverage without having to take a site down later.

tips.title: Bill plugin and hosting costs in the client's name when possible
tips.body: Having clients buy their own licenses and hosting avoids fronting money, avoids renewal confusion, and keeps you out of the role of reseller. If you do buy on their behalf, invoice at cost promptly.

tips.title: Set a revision limit
tips.body: Include a set number of revision rounds in each flat-fee project. After that, bill at your hourly rate. Without a limit, design tweaks and content changes can quietly double the time spent.

tips.title: Put maintenance limits in writing
tips.body: A care plan should say what is covered, such as core, theme, and plugin updates, backups, and uptime checks, and how many support hours are included. Anything beyond is billed hourly, and fixes caused by a client installing their own plugins are not covered.

tips.title: Log time as you work
tips.body: Track hours by task, even on flat-fee jobs. The data shows you whether your quotes are accurate and gives you proof if scope disputes arise.

faqs.question: Should I charge hourly or a flat fee for a WordPress site?
faqs.answer: Use flat fees when the scope is clear, such as a defined number of pages from an existing theme. Use hourly billing for open-ended work like debugging, custom feature development with unknown requirements, or ongoing support. Many developers combine them, with a flat fee for the build and hourly for changes after approval.

faqs.question: How do I bill for plugin licenses and hosting?
faqs.answer: List each as a separate line item at cost, with the product name and license period. Some developers add a small markup for the time spent purchasing and configuring, which should be disclosed in your agreement. When possible, have the client buy directly so the license is in their name.

faqs.question: Can I withhold site access if a client has not paid?
faqs.answer: Many developers include a clause that ownership of custom code and admin access transfers on full payment. This should be in your signed contract. Whether and how you can restrict access varies by situation, so check your agreement and local rules before locking a client out of a live site.

faqs.question: How should I invoice a monthly maintenance plan?
faqs.answer: Bill on the same date each month or annually in advance, and list the plan name, the period covered, and the services included. If hours are included, show how many were used. Recurring card or ACH payment reduces late payments.

faqs.question: What do I do about work the client says was part of the original project?
faqs.answer: Refer back to your signed scope or estimate. If the work was not listed, note it on the invoice as a change request with the date it was requested. A written scope with explicit exclusions, such as content entry, copywriting, and image sourcing, prevents most of these disagreements.

estimate.intro: WordPress developers send an estimate before any site build, redesign, WooCommerce setup, or custom plugin work, and often for larger migrations or fixes. Clients usually compare your quote against other freelancers, agencies, and page-builder or DIY alternatives, so the quote needs to make clear exactly what they are getting.

scopeChecklist.item: Number and type of pages or templates
scopeChecklist.why: 'A 10-page site' is vague. Naming the templates, such as home, about, services, blog, and contact, sets a clear limit on what is included.
Whether you use a custom theme, a starter theme, or a page builder affects cost, future maintenance, and which licenses the client must pay for.
State who writes copy, supplies images, and enters content. Late or missing content is one of the most common causes of project delays and extra charges.
List features such as forms, memberships, booking, payment gateways, or integrations. Anything not listed is a change request.
Naming a set number of rounds for design and development changes keeps flat-fee projects from growing.
Hosting, domains, premium plugins, themes, and stock photos should be listed as client expenses, with estimated amounts and who pays.
Dates depend on prompt feedback, content, and access to hosting and DNS. Say so, and say what happens if the client causes delays.
Clarify whether a bug-fix warranty period is included, such as 30 days, and what ongoing support costs afterward.

pricingTips.title: Estimate hours, then add a buffer
pricingTips.body: Break the project into tasks such as setup, design, development, content entry, QA, and launch. Add 15-25% for communication, revisions, and surprises, then convert the total to a flat fee if the scope is firm.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Presenting two or three options, such as a basic site, a site with blog and SEO setup, and a site with e-commerce, helps clients choose based on budget rather than just comparing your price to a cheaper competitor.

pricingTips.title: Price discovery separately for unclear projects
pricingTips.body: For complex builds or work on an existing messy site, charge a paid audit or discovery phase first. The quote for the main project is more accurate once you have seen the code and hosting.

pricingTips.title: Break the payment schedule into milestones
pricingTips.body: Show the total and when each portion is due, such as 40% to start, 30% at staging, and 30% at launch. Clients see the structure up front, and your cash flow is protected.

faqs.question: Should I give a fixed quote or an estimate range?
faqs.answer: Give a fixed quote when the scope is defined and a range when requirements are still unclear. If you give a range, state what would push the cost to the higher end, such as additional integrations or extra revisions.

faqs.question: How long should my quote be valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common. Plugin prices, your availability, and project scope can change, so an expiry date lets you requote if the client waits.

faqs.question: Do I charge for the time spent preparing an estimate?
faqs.answer: Simple quotes are normally free. For large or complex projects, such as a custom web application or a rescue of a broken site, many developers charge for a paid discovery or audit, which can be credited toward the project if the client proceeds.

faqs.question: What if the client wants to use an existing page builder or theme they already bought?
faqs.answer: Write it into the estimate, including the theme name and version. Note that you are not responsible for limitations of that product, and that extra work needed to work around them will be billed hourly.

yoga-instructor.intro: Yoga instructors teach group classes, private sessions, workshops, teacher trainings, and corporate wellness classes. Many work as independent contractors for several studios, gyms, and companies at once, while others run their own classes or online programs. Invoices usually go to studios, employers, event hosts, or private clients who pay per session or per package.
yoga-instructor.pricingModel: Pricing depends on the setting. Studios and gyms often pay a flat rate per class, sometimes with a base amount plus a per-student bonus above a minimum attendance. Private sessions are billed per session, with discounts for packages of 5 or 10. Corporate classes, retreats, and private group events are usually a flat fee for the session or a half-day or full-day rate. Workshops are either a flat teaching fee or a revenue split on ticket sales. Online classes may be sold as memberships, drop-in fees, or a flat fee per live session. Travel time, props, and mat rentals are sometimes billed separately, especially for off-site work.

rates.service: Studio or gym group class (contractor pay)
Private group or event class (parties, small groups)

items.description: Weekly corporate vinyasa class, Acme Insurance office (March 4, 11, 18, 25)
Mat and prop rental (10 mats, blocks, straps)
Chair yoga workshop for staff, 90 minutes (March 20)
Travel, round trip beyond 15 miles

sampleInvoice.notes: Payment due within 14 days of invoice date. Classes cancelled with less than 24 hours notice are billed at 50 percent. Payment accepted by check, ACH, or card. Please make checks payable to the name above.

invoiceChecklist.item: Dates and times of each class or session
invoiceChecklist.why: Clients, especially studios and companies, reconcile invoices against their schedules, and a dated list prevents disputes over what was taught.

invoiceChecklist.item: Class type and length
invoiceChecklist.why: A 60-minute vinyasa class, a 90-minute workshop, and a 30-minute chair session are priced differently, and the description shows which rate applies.

invoiceChecklist.item: Attendance numbers if pay depends on them
invoiceChecklist.why: Per-student bonuses or revenue splits need headcounts so the studio can verify the math.

invoiceChecklist.item: Substitute or cancelled class notes
invoiceChecklist.why: If you covered for someone or a class was cancelled late, noting it explains why the count or amount differs from the usual schedule.

invoiceChecklist.item: Props, mat rental, or equipment charges
invoiceChecklist.why: Listing these separately keeps your teaching rate clean and shows the client what they are paying for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Mileage or travel time for off-site work
invoiceChecklist.why: Travel to offices, homes, or event venues is a real cost and is easier to get paid when it is itemized with miles and rate.

invoiceChecklist.item: Your business name, tax ID or W-9 status, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Studios and companies that pay contractors need this on file for year-end 1099 reporting, and clear instructions speed up payment.

yoga-instructor.paymentTerms: Private clients commonly pay at the time of the session or prepay for a package, often by card, Venmo, Zelle, or similar. Studios usually pay contractors on a set schedule such as biweekly or monthly, so ask early what that schedule is. Corporate clients typically pay net 15 to net 30 and may need an invoice or PO number. For workshops, retreats, and private events, a deposit of 25 to 50 percent at booking is common, with the balance due before or on the day. Many instructors state a 24-hour cancellation policy and a late fee, often 1.5 percent per month or a flat amount, on invoices that run past due. Package sessions often expire after a set period such as 3 to 6 months, which should be stated in writing.

tips.title: Confirm how studios calculate pay
tips.body: Get the formula in writing: flat rate, per-head pay, minimum guarantee, or a split. Then keep your own attendance record so you can check a studio's payment against it.

tips.title: Sell packages with an expiration date
tips.body: Prepaid packages improve cash flow and retention, but unused sessions create confusion. State the expiry and whether sessions are transferable or refundable on the invoice or receipt.

tips.title: Separate teaching time from travel and prep
tips.body: Corporate and in-home clients often accept travel charges if they are stated up front. Add a travel fee or a per-mile rate to the quote and then itemize it on the invoice.

tips.title: Track income by source
tips.body: If you teach at several studios and privately, you may receive 1099s from some clients and nothing from others. Tracking each invoice helps you report all income and set aside money for self-employment tax.

tips.title: Invoice workshops and events promptly
tips.body: For one-off events, send the invoice or balance request right after the date while the details are fresh. Waiting weeks makes follow-up harder.

faqs.question: Do I need to invoice a studio that pays me every month?
faqs.answer: Often the studio generates its own pay statement, but sending your own invoice with dates, classes, and attendance gives you a record and lets you catch mistakes. Ask the studio what it prefers.

faqs.question: Should I charge sales tax on yoga classes?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state and sometimes on the type of service. Some states tax fitness or recreation services and others do not. Check with your state's tax agency or an accountant before you decide.

faqs.question: How do I bill for a cancelled private session?
faqs.answer: State your cancellation policy when the client books, such as 24 hours notice. If the client cancels late, bill the agreed percentage as a separate line item that references the cancelled date.

faqs.question: Can I charge a late fee on an unpaid invoice?
faqs.answer: Generally yes if the fee is stated in advance on the quote, contract, or invoice. Check your local rules for any limits on late fees, and apply them consistently.

faqs.question: How do I invoice for substitute teaching?
faqs.answer: Invoice the studio at the rate agreed for covering classes, listing each date and class name. Confirm in writing whether you are paid the sub rate or the original teacher's rate.

estimate.intro: Yoga instructors send quotes for corporate programs, private group classes, workshops, retreats, teacher trainings, and recurring private clients. The client is usually comparing your fee to other instructors, to studio drop-in prices, and to what a wellness vendor would charge for the same time slot.

scopeChecklist.why: A gentle 45-minute chair class and a 75-minute power vinyasa class require different preparation and set different expectations.

scopeChecklist.item: Number of participants and maximum group size
scopeChecklist.why: Price and teaching approach change with group size, and a cap prevents the class from growing without a fee adjustment.

scopeChecklist.item: Location, space requirements, and setup time
scopeChecklist.why: Clarify who provides the room, floor space, and music, and whether you need arrival time to set up, which affects total time billed.
State whether you bring mats, blocks, and straps for a fee or whether participants or the client supply them.
For a recurring series, list dates, frequency, and what happens to holidays or missed sessions.
Events get moved or cancelled often, so state the notice required and what is owed if the client cancels late.
Corporate and venue clients may require proof of insurance, and participants may need to sign a waiver before attending.

pricingTips.title: Quote by time block, not just class length
pricingTips.body: Include prep, travel, and setup in the total. A 60-minute office class that needs 90 minutes of travel and setup should not be priced like a 60-minute studio class.

pricingTips.title: Offer a series discount
pricingTips.body: A 4-week or 8-week series at a slightly lower per-class rate gives the client a reason to commit and gives you predictable income.

pricingTips.title: Present two or three options
pricingTips.body: For corporate clients, offer a single class, a monthly series, and a longer program. Clients tend to choose a middle option, and it makes comparison easier.

pricingTips.title: Ask for a deposit on events
pricingTips.body: For workshops, retreats, and private parties, require 25 to 50 percent to hold the date. It protects you if the client cancels and signals a firm booking.

faqs.question: How long should a quote stay valid?
faqs.answer: Thirty days is common for ongoing work, but for events with fixed dates, a shorter window such as 7 to 14 days makes sense so you do not hold the date indefinitely.

faqs.question: Should I charge for a trial class or consultation?
faqs.answer: Many instructors offer a short free call to discuss goals and then charge normal rates for a trial session. For corporate clients, a discounted demo class can be reasonable if it leads to a series.

faqs.question: What if the client wants a lower price?
faqs.answer: Adjust the scope rather than the rate where possible, for example a shorter class, a larger minimum group size, or the client supplying mats. This keeps your hourly value intact.

faqs.question: Do I need a written contract with a quote?
faqs.answer: For events, corporate series, and retreats, yes. An accepted quote with scope, price, cancellation terms, and payment schedule works as a simple agreement, and a short contract adds more protection.

youtuber.intro: YouTubers who bill clients are usually creators with an established channel who get paid by brands for sponsored videos, integrations, and dedicated reviews. Some also invoice for licensing clips, producing videos for other businesses, consulting, or appearing in a partner's content. Platform ad revenue is paid by YouTube directly, so invoices cover the work you do for outside parties.
youtuber.pricingModel: Sponsorship pricing is usually a flat fee per deliverable, set by your typical views, audience fit, and usage rights. Many creators start from a rate tied to average views (a CPM-style figure, often $20-50 per 1,000 average views for dedicated or integrated placements, higher in finance, software, and B2B niches) and adjust from there. Dedicated videos cost more than 60 to 90 second integrations. Add-ons are priced separately: exclusivity windows, whitelisting or Spark-style ad usage, raw footage, extra revisions, Shorts cutdowns, and link placement in pinned comments or descriptions. Channel-owned work is different from contract production. When you produce video for a client's channel, you bill per finished video, per day, or on a monthly retainer, and the client owns the result. Agency deals often include a deposit and net 30 to 60 payment, so build that into your price.

rates.service: Usage rights / whitelisting (paid ads on your handle)
Video production for a client's channel

items.description: Dedicated sponsored video: product review, approx. 10 min, published on channel
Two Shorts cutdowns from sponsored video
30-day paid usage rights (whitelisting) on brand-run ads
30-day category exclusivity (competing project management tools)
Additional revision round beyond two included

sampleInvoice.notes: Campaign: Spring Launch, PO #4471. Video published May 14, 2025 at the agreed link. Payment due net 30 from invoice date. Late balances accrue 1.5% per month. Usage rights run May 14 to June 13, 2025; extensions billed separately. Pay by ACH or check.

invoiceChecklist.item: Campaign name, PO number, and agency or brand contact
invoiceChecklist.why: Brands and agencies often route invoices through accounts payable that rejects anything without a PO or campaign reference.

invoiceChecklist.item: Video title, publish date, and live URL
invoiceChecklist.why: Gives the payer proof the deliverable ran as agreed and ties the charge to a specific piece of content.

invoiceChecklist.item: Each deliverable listed as its own line (integration, Shorts, community post)
invoiceChecklist.why: Makes it clear what was delivered and lets the client approve each line without disputes over scope.

invoiceChecklist.item: Usage rights and exclusivity terms with start and end dates
invoiceChecklist.why: These are billable add-ons, and dates prevent a client from running your content in ads beyond what they paid for.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reference to the signed agreement or insertion order
invoiceChecklist.why: Ties your payment terms and rates back to a document both sides agreed to.

invoiceChecklist.item: Legal name or business name, address, and payment instructions
invoiceChecklist.why: Needed for the payer to set you up as a vendor. US payers usually need a W-9 on file before first payment.

invoiceChecklist.item: Reimbursable expenses with receipts (props, travel, product shipping, freelance editor)
invoiceChecklist.why: Only billable if agreed in advance, and receipts keep reimbursements from being questioned.

youtuber.paymentTerms: Many sponsorship deals pay 30 to 60 days after the video goes live or after invoice receipt, and some agencies pay only after the brand pays them. Ask for 30 to 50 percent upfront on larger deals or when working with a new brand, with the balance due on publish. State net terms and a late fee, such as 1.5% per month where allowed. ACH and wire are the most common payment methods, with PayPal and checks also used. International brands may pay in another currency, so state the currency on the invoice. Send a W-9 early so payment is not delayed by vendor setup.

tips.title: Invoice on publish, not on approval
tips.body: Set the invoice trigger in your contract as the publish date. If you wait for a final sign-off, payment clocks start late and brands can stall.

tips.title: Price usage rights separately
tips.body: If a brand wants to run your video as an ad or whitelist your handle, that is a different product from an organic placement. Bill it by the 30-day period and charge more for longer terms.

tips.title: Cap revisions in the quote and bill extras
tips.body: Include one or two revision rounds. Anything beyond that goes on the invoice as its own line so scope creep does not eat your margin.

tips.title: Keep agency payment terms in mind
tips.body: Agencies commonly pay net 45 or net 60 and may pay only when the brand pays. Raise your rate or require a deposit if the terms are slow.

tips.title: Track income for taxes
tips.body: Brand payments are usually self-employment income, and brands that pay you $600 or more in a year in the US may send a 1099-NEC. Set money aside for estimated taxes and check with an accountant.

faqs.question: Should I invoice before or after the video goes live?
faqs.answer: Take a deposit before production on larger deals, and send the final invoice on the publish date. Invoicing at publish gives you a clear trigger for net terms and confirms the deliverable was completed.

faqs.question: Do I charge sales tax on sponsored videos?
faqs.answer: Usually not, since most states do not tax advertising or influencer services, but rules vary. Check with your state tax agency or an accountant, especially if you sell physical products or produce video for clients in states that tax digital services.

faqs.question: What if a brand asks for a W-9 or vendor form?
faqs.answer: This is normal. Fill out a W-9 with your legal name or business name and tax ID, and return it before you invoice. Brands use it to issue a 1099 if you are paid above the IRS threshold.

faqs.question: Can I charge more if the brand wants to reuse my video in ads?
faqs.answer: Yes. Usage rights and whitelisting are separate from the organic placement. Specify the platforms, ad duration, and start and end dates, and bill for them as their own line.

faqs.question: How do I handle a brand that wants to pay after the campaign performs?
faqs.answer: Performance-only deals shift risk onto you. If you accept, put the metric and the payout in writing, and ask for a flat base fee plus a bonus rather than all payment tied to results.

estimate.intro: YouTubers send quotes when a brand or agency asks for a rate card, a proposal, or a price on a specific campaign. Clients compare your price against other creators with similar audiences, so the quote needs to show what they get for the number: deliverables, timing, usage, and exclusivity.

scopeChecklist.item: Exact deliverables and format (dedicated video, 60-sec integration, Short, community post)
scopeChecklist.why: Brands often assume more than you planned to deliver, so spelling it out sets the baseline.

scopeChecklist.item: Video length, placement, and number of brand mentions or calls to action
scopeChecklist.why: A pre-roll mention is not the same work or value as a 90-second mid-roll with a demo.

scopeChecklist.item: Publish date window and approval timeline
scopeChecklist.why: Delayed brand feedback or product shipping can push your schedule, so tie deadlines to when you receive the product and brief.

scopeChecklist.item: Revision rounds included and turnaround for each
scopeChecklist.why: Prevents endless script and edit changes without extra pay.

scopeChecklist.item: Usage rights, whitelisting, and exclusivity terms and duration
scopeChecklist.why: These carry separate value, and unclear terms are a common source of disputes.
You are required to disclose paid promotions in the US, so state how the sponsorship will be labeled and where links will go.
Clarifies who supplies product and who covers shipping, travel, or props.

pricingTips.title: Start from average views, not subscribers
pricingTips.body: Brands care about views per video and audience fit. Base your quote on your recent median views, then adjust for niche, production effort, and content type.

pricingTips.title: Offer tiered packages
pricingTips.body: Present two or three options, such as an integration only, an integration plus Shorts, and a dedicated video with usage rights. Clients tend to pick the middle tier.

pricingTips.title: Quote add-ons as separate lines
pricingTips.body: List exclusivity, usage rights, raw footage, and rush turnaround as optional items so the base price stays competitive and extras are billed when needed.

pricingTips.title: Set a quote expiry date
pricingTips.body: Audience size, upload schedule, and your calendar change. A 14 to 30 day validity window keeps you from honoring an old rate months later.

faqs.question: Should I share my rate card publicly?
faqs.answer: It is optional. Many creators send a rate card on request and tailor quotes to the campaign. A public card can anchor expectations, but it may underprice larger or longer deals.

faqs.question: What if a brand's budget is below my rate?
faqs.answer: Offer a reduced scope, such as a shorter integration or fewer add-ons, instead of cutting the price for the same deliverables. Remove usage rights or exclusivity first.

faqs.question: Do I need a signed contract after the quote is accepted?
faqs.answer: Yes. Get the quote and terms in a signed agreement or insertion order before filming, including payment schedule, approval process, and usage rights.
